entries.tittle: Plátano FHIA-21, un plátano para mercados nacionales
entries.summary: El híbrido FHIA-21 es un plátano tipo francés, que fue desarrollado en 1987. En la actualidad, se encuentra en producción comercial en Cuba, Honduras, Nicaragua, Guatemala, Venezuela, Ecuador, Perú, Colombia, entre otros países. Se consume en estado verde hervido o frito, o maduro.
entries.description:
Descripción

1. Características

1.1 Morfología

  • La planta mide entre 3,5 y 4 m; tiene hojas decumbentes y un tallo brillante.
  • El racimo es ligeramente inclinado y asimétrico.
  • Los frutos, de color verde claro, son rectos hacia la punta, la cual presenta una forma ligeramente puntiaguda.
  • En comparación al plátano Falso Cuerno, la cáscara es más fácil de remover, pero también es un poco más susceptible a golpes.
Figura 1. Fotografía de los frutos del plátano FHIA-21

©FHIA

1.2 Fenología

  • El tiempo de la siembra hasta la floración es entre 240 a 280 días; el primer ciclo productivo, o sea, de parición a cosecha es de 85 a 100 días.
  • La segunda floración se presenta a los 540 a 570 días después de la siembra.

1.3 Producción

  • El peso neto del racimo, que es el peso sin raquis, está entre 22 y 27 kilos, con un número de dedos por racimo de 120 a 150.
  • Sin embargo, se recomienda el desmane a 5 manos, para asegurar el desarrollo adecuado de éstos.
  • En este caso, el número de dedos es de 70 a 80.
  • El peso de los dedos individuales oscila entre 250 y 350 gramos.
  • En comparación al plátano ‘Cuerno’, el rendimiento total es aproximadamente el doble, sin realizar control de Sigatoka negra.
Figura 2. Diferencias de producción entre el plátano FHIA-21 y el Falso Cuerno

©FHIA

1.4 Características de resistencia

  • El híbrido es resistente a la Sigatoka negra y al Mal de Panamá, pero susceptible a los dos nematodos de mayor importancia: Radopholus similis y Pratylenchus coffeae.

2. Aspectos agronómicos

2.1 Requerimientos agroecológicos

  • Las plantas toleran condiciones no óptimas de cultivo, pero conviene seleccionar suelos no inundables bien drenados y que sean accesibles durante todo el año.
    • Altura: FHIA-21 crece bien a alturas de 0 a 1 200 metros sobre el nivel del mar.
    • Suelos: requiere suelos francos.
    • Precipitación pluvial: debe ser aproximadamente 2000 mm por año.
    • Temperatura: la temperatura óptima es de 28 °C.

2.2 Manejo agronómico

  • Se recomienda densidades de siembra de 1 600 plantas/ha en siembras permanentes.
  • La fertilización se realiza de acuerdo a los resultados del análisis del suelo.
  • Para las condiciones del Valle de Sula (Honduras), se recomienda aplicar 300 kg de nitrógeno (N) y 450 kg de potasio (K2O) por hectárea por año.
  • Se ha observado que bajo condiciones de riego la planta manifiesta un mayor potencial de producción, con rendimientos más altos que los obtenidos en áreas sin riego.
  • Se debe realizar un deshoje de saneamiento cada dos semanas, eliminando hojas dobladas y las afectadas por Sigatoka negra.
  • Cada ocho semanas se realiza un deshije.
  • El deshermane se efectúa a los cuatro meses después de la siembra, con el fin de seleccionar la mejor planta madre y su retoño.
  • Se recomienda el desbellote y el desmane de la falsa más dos manos, para lograr el desarrollo apropiado de los dedos.

2.3 Poscosecha

  • FHIA-21 madura más rápido que el plátano Cuerno, por lo tanto, es importante determinar el tiempo óptimo para la cosecha.
  • Al igual que en el banano de exportación, en FHIA-21 la cosecha deberá realizarse utilizando un sistema de control de edad de los racimos, y debe empacarse en bolsas al vacío (Banavac) para extender la vida verde de fruta para exportación.

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Plátano FHIA-20 un plátano resistente a la Sigatoka negra: ID 5937.
  • Producción de cormos de plátano y banano para siembra directa en campo: ID 8149.
  • Manejo de Sigatoka negra (Mycosphaerella fijiensis Morelet) en plantaciones de plátano y banano: ID 8306.
  • Material de siembra de alta calidad en la en renovación de plantaciones de plátano y banano: ID 8336.
  • Renovación de plantaciones de plátano cambiando la época y sistema de siembra: ID 8339.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

El plátano FHIA-21 da una descripción general de cómo producir plátanos de manera eficiente para el mercado nacional.

5.2 Atiende a las necesidades de la mujer

La tecnología no requiere mucha mano de obra y se puede realizar con cualquier trabajo manual.

5.3 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta práctica permite a los agricultores producir plátanos adecuados para la venta, aumentando así sus ingresos.

entries.tittle: Fodder management: hay and silage making
entries.summary: Hay-making is the most important method of preserving forage in many countries, including tropical ones. Silage-making is highly developed in temperate countries, especially in Europe, and goes with intensification. In tropical countries, plant growth coincides with the rainy season, which sometimes makes hay-making difficult. The objective of this technology is to preserve forage resources for the dry season (hot countries) or for winter (temperate countries) in order to ensure continuous regular feed for livestock. This is to sustain growth, fattening or milk production, or to continue production in difficult periods when market prices are highest.
entries.description:
Description

The preparation of green forage (containing between 65 and 80 percent water) for storage relies on three different techniques.

1. Green forage preparation techniques

1.1 Haymaking

  • Hay is obtained after dry-storage or desiccation of the grass that contains less than 15 percent water.
  • During tedding, green forage is cut and dried as quickly as possible.
  • Drying can be done naturally or artificially by the active circulation of air.
  • Natural drying is exposure to the sun on the ground aerating the forage regularly by turning it over.
    • Sun-drying requires two or three days without rain.
    • The hay must then be kept in appropriate conditions (covered area).
    • If, when harvesting, the grass has matured and has already dried standing, then it is not hay but straw.
  • Hay produced on grazing land (Sahel) has the nutritive value of straw, because it is harvested when the plants reach maturity.
  • The product obtained only meets basic maintenance needs and, in rare cases, the marginal production of milk and meat.

1.2 Silage making

  • In contrast to hay, silage is the product obtained from wet storage.
  • This method of storage uses the acidifying power of lactic bacteria, which reduces the pH to around four, below which all chemical reactions and fermentation cease.
    • This fermentation process preserves forage in its wet state away from air.
    • This ensures that minimum dry matter and nutritional value is lost and to avoid creating products that are toxic to the animal.
  • To obtain good silage, it is necessary to use airtight silos (total anaerobiosis).
    • Several types of silo are used around the world.
    • These are tunnel silo, trench silo, corridor silo, tower silo, etc.
  • Clean forage is collected without soil from the earth.
    • It is then chopped and piled.
  • If necessary apply additional techniques such as pre-tedding for forage with high water content, or use preservatives (sugar products, formic acid, anti-moulds, etc.) to improve preservation.
  • It is essential to harvest forage at the optimal time, from the viewpoint of nutritional quality, quantity available and climatic conditions, and then to store it properly to reduce losses.

1.3 Round bale silage

  • Round bale silage is a relatively new method of preserving forage.
  • It is a combination of hay and silage making and has certain advantages and disadvantages over other forage preservation systems.
  • Round bale silage is simply forage of a relatively high moisture content that is baled with a round baler and then stored in a sealed container, usually a plastic bag.
  • Both grasses and legumes can be preserved as round bale silage if proper techniques are followed.
  • It is much easier to make good hay crop silage in silos than in large round bales.
  • Although the silage obtained can be kept for approximately a year, baled silage is more likely to spoil, compared to silage in traditional silos.
    • Fermentation is less complete.
    • The damage to the plastic covering results in the harmful introduction of oxygen.
      • Some people think that baled silage is best adapted for use late in the growing season, with bales fed as early as possible
      • Late in the season may often be a difficult time to dry hay in the field, increasing the value of round bale silage.

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm. 

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Improving fodder by incorporating legumes in the cropping system: ID 4370.
  • Growing fodder for livestock: Calliandra and Elephant grass: ID 6989.
  • Improved cattle breeds zero grazing with drought tolerant fodder: ID 8926.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology introduces the options to optimize the preservation of fodder for the dry season, to ensure a continuous supply of feed to livestock especially during times of high market prices. 

4.2 Pro-poor technology

This technology provides the farmer with options for silage and fodder making instead of purchasing fodder. This reduces the cost of the forage of fodder and controls its quality.

entries.tittle: Cassava processing: cassava wet flour
entries.summary:
Cassava (Manihot Esculenta Crantz) is the third most important source of calories in the tropics, after rice and maize. Millions of people depend on cassava in Africa, Asia and Latin America. It is grown by poor farmers, many of them women, often on marginal land. For those people and their families, cassava is vital for both food security and income generation. Cassava is a raw material base for an array of processed products that could effectively increase demand for cassava and contribute to agricultural transformation and economic growth in developing countries. The following technology describes how to obtain cassava flour from cassava tubers.

This technology is also available in: Portuguese (ID2826)
entries.description:
Description

The raw material for baked products is the flour scooped up from sedimentation tanks or tables after the supernatant, or excess water, has been drained and the "yellow" flour scraped off. Clearly the use of moist starch, an intermediate stage in the processing of the Dour, is economically advantageous. Only very white first-quality flour can be used in the manufacture, Figure 1.

To obtain this, sulfurous acid is often added in the first sedimentation. This chemical should, however, be washed out as completely as possible by second sedimentation in clean water. Any traces of the acid left in the flour tend to spoil the quality of the end product. It is strongly advised not to use active chlorine preparations in this case, as they influence the agglomeration of the starch into pearls and other forms in an unfavourable way.

The cake of moist flour, containing about 45 percent water, is broken up by a small mill, spades or pressing it through frames strung with steel wire spaced about 10 cm to 20 cm apart, after which the lumps are rubbed through a screen of about 20 mesh per inch to produce a coarse-grained moist flour. At this stage, the flour is ready only for gelatinization and the production of flakes.

To prepare pearls and seeds, the small aggregates of moist starch should be subjected to a process of building up and consolidation, which gives them the size and cohesive strength desired for further treatment. The operation is known by the Indonesian name as the gangsor method.

A portion of the moist starch is put into a long cylindrical bag of twill cloth which is held at each end by one person. Together with rhythmical strong jerking movement, they throw the mass of starch lumps from one end of the bag to the other. After a few minutes of this treatment, the irregular lumps have grown into beads of varying sizes and have gained firmness. Another portion of the moist flour is added and the gangsoring is continued.

The operation is repeated until the beads have grown more or less to their desired size. Depending on the skill of the worker, the size of the starch balls is fairly uniform. Curiously enough, the knack of gangsoring is achieved only by a fraction of all workers, so the operation should be classified as skilled labour.

In Malaysia the flour is fed into open, cylindrical rotating pans about 0.9 m in diameter and 1.2 m deep. During rotation the starch grains are forced to adhere together in the form of small particles or beads. The resulting product depends on the speed and the length of time of rotation. After gangsoring, beads of the right size are sorted out by screening between plates with circular holes corresponding to the required dimensions.

Figure 1. Cassava flour

©FAO/TECA

1. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

2. Related/associated technologies

  • Make bitter cassava safe for consumption: ID 4372.
  • Storage and preservation of wet cassava: ID 4520.
  • Production of high-quality cassava flour: ID 4574.
  • Sustainable livelihoods: new market opportunities for cassava: ID 4575.

Since cassava is an important calorie source in the tropics, this practice allows for it to be transformed and stored in a more long term manner.

3.3 Pro-poor technology

The practice, through the transformation of cassava into flour, provides food security and income generation for poor households.

entries.tittle: Bamboo toothpick manufacturing unit, China
entries.summary: Bamboo wood is relatively soft, not particularly dense, and is ideal for the production of toothpicks. INBAR’s priority is giving people at all levels the knowledge and skills they need for long-term development involving bamboo. The following technology describes how to establish a toothpick manufacturing unit.
entries.description:
Description

Bamboo is a very important tree species, as it grows more rapidly than other trees and begins yielding three to four years after planting. The establishment of the plantation does not require high capital investments and builds upon the inherent plant cultivation skills of local farmers and foresters. In addition, bamboo can be harvested every year and non-destructively. 

Bamboo is also excellent for rejuvenating degraded lands and protecting against soil erosions, especially when intercropped with other shallow-rooted crops. The other parts of the bamboo plant can be used in rural livelihoods such as the shoots for food, the leaves for fodder, and the branches for brooms and for firewood. 

1. Why bamboo toothpicks?

  • Bamboo wood is relatively soft, not particularly dense, and is ideal for the production of toothpicks.
  • Bamboo is a renewable resource that can be harvested annually and if cultivated well, produces a known yield per unit area.
  • This makes it ideal for supplying the relatively low, but regular inputs of raw materials required by the toothpick unit.

2. How are they produced?

  • Toothpicks are produced by splitting bamboo culms into thin splits that are then split further into circular rods 2 mm in diameter.
  • These are then cut to length, polished and the ends are sharpened.
Figure 1. Bamboos are split into thin splits

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Splits are further split into 2 mm diameter rods

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Rods are dried in the sun

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Rods are cut to length 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. The ends are sharpened

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Toothpicks are packaged for sale

©FAO/TECA

3. What is the market for bamboo toothpicks?

  • The market for bamboo toothpicks is very large, although figures are not available.
  • Toothpicks are very widely used throughout Asia and in other regions of the world.
  • In order to develop the market still further, the environmentally friendly nature of using bamboos to produce toothpicks could be stressed.

4. What are the requirements for success?

  • Sustained supply of bamboos suitable for toothpick production.
    • The species with long internodes are preferred.
  • Technically trained personnel to manage and maintain the unit
  • Capital for investment.
  • Access to markets and a creativity and packaging and marketing. 

5. What is the role of a bamboo toothpick-manufacturing unit in rural development?

  • A bamboo toothpick-manufacturing unit can provide employment opportunities for a range of people.
  • The unit itself will employ a minimum of 20 people;
    • More employment will be generated in its forward and backward linkages, such as cultivation and harvesting of bamboo, marketing and retailing.
  • The need for substantial quantities of raw bamboo will encourage the sustainable management of bamboo plantations, which can easily be intercropped with food crops and thus increase the food security of the rural poor that grow them.

6. How do I establish a bamboo toothpick unit?

  • The establishment of a toothpick unit requires a regular supply of bamboos, electricity, labour, and access to markets.
  • The equipment required can be purchased for as little as USD 13 000 and with other start-up costs, which amount to USD 12 000- USD 17 000.
    • This totals to about USD 25 000 to USD 30 000.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Commercial scale community bamboo harvesting: ID 7948.
  • Production of bamboo mat board: ID 3860.
  • Bamboo match sticks production: ID 3862.
  • Bamboo splitting and the slivering unit: ID 3865.
  • Community bamboo nursery: ID 3868.
  • Improved cultivation technique for high yielding bamboo stands: ID 3874.
  • Village bamboo preservation unit: ID 3892.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

9.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology provides rural communities with knowledge and skills they need for long-term development involving bamboo, particularly on how to establish a toothpick manufacturing unit.

9.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology provides rural communities to sell a new good, using local materials (bamboo). This allows for an added source of income.

entries.tittle: Preservation of strawberries
entries.summary: Strawberries have to be harvested when 75 percent of the fruit surface turns red and the berry is still firm. The strawberry fruit perishes easily and deteriorates within two to three days of harvesting at natural environmental conditions. The temperature is very important for the duration of berry life. Strawberries soften very quickly and become moldy as temperatures rise. So, to keep them longer, fruits must be picked at sunrise, transported to the processing place as soon as possible, and maintained in the shade in a cool place until processing.
entries.description:
Description

1. Steps for simple preservation technique for strawberries

1.1 Step one

  • First, you must wash your hands. Hand-washing would be "number one" on everyone's list of things to do. Use soap and water to wash your hands front and back and between the fingers.
  • Fresh strawberries are thoroughly rinsed with tap water to eliminate dirt, Figure 1 and 2, soil and residues of pesticides, insecticides and fertilizer. Then, the strawberries are hand decapped. Don't forget to remove the injured part of the fruits or to separate the deteriorated ones. And do not prepare fruits that are moldy.
Figure 1. Put strawberries into a plastic tank

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Rinse strawberries using a nail brush

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two

  • The strawberries are washed again, drained with a sieve or colander and put into a clean bucket or container.
  • The fruit that was separated for preservation by each technique must be quickly weighed, Figure 3. If a scale is not available, use a measuring jug, such as the one used for measuring quantities in cooking.
Figure 3. Strawberries weight

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Step three

  • The strawberries have to be heated in a steam bath for a few minutes. This treatment is called "blanching" and it deactivates compounds that alter the colour and the firmness of the fruit. It also destroys germs. To blanch the fruit in steam, you need a heater, a stainless steel saucepan or other recipient with a lid, and a stainless steel tray, perforated or made with a screen to support the fruit, Figure 4.
Figure 4. Strawberries monolayer on a tray

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Step four

  • A small quantity of strawberries is placed in a single layer on the tray. Remove the lid quickly from the heating pot, put the tray in and again, as soon as possible, put the lid on. Keep the strawberries in the vapour for two minutes.
  • After two minutes, the strawberries are taken out of the steam and plunged quickly into cold water for a few minutes, Figure 5.
Figure 5. Strawberries cooling

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Step five

The strawberries are removed from the cooling water and drained using a sieve or a colander, Figure 6.

Figure 6. Strawberries removed from the cold water

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Step six

  • Then, the blanched and cooled fruits are placed in a plastic bucket or a tank. This container must be clean, figure 7.
Figure 7. Strawberries placed in clean containers

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Strawberries

©FAO/TECA

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable strawberry puree: ID 3943.
  • Preservation of fruits: intermediate moisture whole​: ID 3944.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable whole strawberries of high moisture: ID 3942.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Women-friendly

The technology does not require using a lot of energy and so it can be done by women​.

4.2 Resource use efficiency

Preservation of strawberries reduces post-harvest losses​.

entries.tittle: Preservation of fruits: Intermediate moisture whole strawberries
entries.summary: Fruits and vegetables are nutritious, valuable foods full of flavour. Therefore, fruits and vegetables represent an important and in many cases an under-appreciated resource that could benefit from better utilisation and exploitation in rural communities. However, in low-income countries, poor care and handling of these crops frequently result in loss of quality, especially when not consumed immediately. The intermediate moisture whole strawberries is a technique that keeps the strawberries for a year if stored in a cool and dark place.
entries.description:
Description

1. Steps for obtaining intermediate moisture whole strawberries

This technique for obtaining the intermediate moisture of whole strawberries is in five steps.

1.1 Step one

The first steps are the same as those followed for preparing shelf-stable whole strawberries (see the technique for shelf-stable whole strawberries) except that the amounts of sugar and additives are different.

For one kilogram of fruit, you must add:

  • 291 g sucrose or glucose (you can measure the sugar with a measuring jug);
  • 1.3 g potassium sorbate (one level teaspoon);
  • 17 g citric acid (two level tablespoons);
  • 0.32 g sodium bisulphite (a quarter level coffee-spoon); and
  • 0.32 g ascorbic acid (a third level coffee-spoon).

The fruit product is not packaged but the fruit and the juice are separated with a colander or a sieve, Figure 1.

Figure 1. Fruit and juice seperated with a colander

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two

The drained strawberries are spread evenly on trays of stainless steel screen to be partially dried (that is, some water will be removed from the strawberries), Figure 2.

Figure 2. Drained strawberries spread evenly on trays

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Step three

The juice is collected and packaged into bottles, demijohns or other containers, Figure 3. Be careful to put only a single layer of strawberries on the trays, so that they dry more quickly.

Figure 3. Juice packed in a bottle

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Step four

The trays are placed in the dryer, Figure 4. When the moisture of the fruit is in the range 20 to 24 percent (that is 20 g to 24 g water per 100 g partially dried fruit), the trays are removed from the dryer.

Figure 4. Trays placed in the dryer

©FAO/TECA

The time of drying depends on many variables, such as the size and shape of the fruit; the temperature, humidity, flow and direction of the air; and the way in which the fruit is supported during drying. In this dryer, for an air velocity equal to 2 m per sec and a temperature of 50˚C, the drying time was approximately six hours. For obtaining intermediate moisture strawberries of good quality, it is convenient to use air temperatures in the range 50˚C to 65˚C.

1.5 Step five

The partially dried strawberries (also called intermediate moisture strawberries) are cooled at room temperature and then packaged in polyethylene or polypropylene bags or in glass or high density polyethylene jars, Figure 5. The products are labelled indicating the name and form of the fruit product ("intermediate moisture strawberry" or "strawberry juice"), the ingredients, the date of manufacture, the "use by" date and the name and place of the manufacturer.

Figure 5. Strawberries stored at a cool temperature

©FAO/TECA

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Preservation of strawberries: ID 3941.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable whole strawberries of high moisture: ID 3942.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable strawberry puree: ID 3943.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

Preservation of the strawberries reduces post-harvest losses​.

entries.tittle: Preservation of fruits: Shelf-stable strawberry puree.
entries.summary: Fruits and vegetables are nutritious, valuable foods full of flavour. Therefore, fruits and vegetables represent an important and in many cases an under-appreciated resource that could benefit from better utilisation and exploitation in the rural communities. However, in low-income countries, poor care and handling of these crops frequently result in loss of quality, especially when not consumed immediately. The shelf-stable strawberry puree is a preservation technique. The strawberries can be consumed as is or used to prepare jams, jellies, fruit drinks and dairy products.
entries.description:
Description

1. Techniques for the shelf-stable strawberry puree

The technique for the shelf-stable strawberry puree is made in five steps and it is advised to see the technology for the preservation of strawberries first.

1.5 Step one

The blanched and cooled strawberries reserved for pulp are quickly processed. The puree is poured into a clean bucket or tank or other recipients with a lid, Figure 1.

Figure 1. Pour puree into a clean bucket or tank

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two

Afterward, a mixture of sugar and additives is rapidly mixed to the strawberry pulp, Figure 2. For each kilogram of pulp, you need:

  • 440 g sucrose or glucose (you can measure the sugar with a measuring jug);
  • 1.5 g potassium sorbate (a level teaspoon);
  • 17 g citric acid (two-level tablespoon);
  • 0.22 g sodium bisulphite (one fifth level coffee-spoon); and
  • 0.36 g ascorbic acid (one third level coffee-spoon).
Figure 2. Mixture of sugar and additives

©FAO/TECA

You can also add vanillin as a preservative instead of potassium sorbate and sodium bisulphite. For each kilogram of pulp, replace 1.5 g potassium sorbate and 0.22 g sodium bisulphite by 4.3 g vanillin (four and a half level coffee-spoons). Vanillin is a natural antimicrobial, it is produced from a plant and tastes good!

1.3 Step three

The sugar, the additives and the pulp are mixed well with a wooden or plastic stick or spoon, figure 3. Next, the bucket is closed with the lid and let stand for two days. Stir the pulp with the additives at least twice a day to blend the mixture.

Figure 3. Additives and pulp mixed with a wooden spoon

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Step four

After two days, the shelf-stable strawberry purée is ready for packaging. The strawberry purée can be packaged into a glass or high-density polyethylene jars or into flexible pouches, Figures 4 and 5. Or it can be stored in bulk in tanks or in the same bucket where it was prepared.

Figure 4. Strawberry puree packaged into a glass or high-density polyethylene jars

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Strawberry puree packaged into glass or high density polyethylene jars

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Step five

  • The product is labelled with the name and form of the fruit product ("strawberry puree"), the ingredients (strawberry pulp, sugar, potassium sorbate, citric acid, sodium bisulphite), the manufacture day, the "use by" date and the name and place of the manufacturer.
  • The shelf-stable strawberry puree can be consumed for three or four months, according to the storage temperature. When the temperature is lower than 20˚C and glass jars are used for packaging, the colour is better preserved.

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Preservation of strawberries: ID 3941.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable whole strawberries of high moisture: ID 3942.
  • Preservation of fruits: intermediate moisture whole: ID 3944.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

Preservation of fruits reduces post-harvest losses​.

entries.tittle: Preservation of fruits: Shelf-stable high moisture pineapple - Dry infusion
entries.summary:
The following provides specific steps for shelf-stable high moisture content pineapple production. The steps include methods of blanching, steaming, cooling methods, draining, ingredient to add to the fruit, blending techniques, extraction, as well as packaging, storing and labelling processes.
​​​
entries.description:
Description

1. Steps for producing shelf-stable high moisture content pineapple

The technique for producing shelf-stable high moisture content pineapple has eight steps. However, it is advisable to read about the technique for preserving pineapple.

1.1 Step one

The pineapple triangles are blanched by heating in steam for 1.5 minutes, Figure 1.

Figure 1. Pineapple triangles blanched by heating in stem

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two

Then, the fruit is immediately cooled in water for a few minutes, Figure 2.

Figure 2. Pineapple is cooled in water

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Step three

The fruit is drained and put in a clean bucket.

1.4 Step four

Afterward, a mixture of sugar and additives is added to the pineapple triangles, Figure 3. For each kilogram of pineapple triangles, you need:

  • 291 g sucrose or glucose (you can measure the sugar with a measuring jug);
  • 1.3 g potassium sorbate (1 level teaspoon);
  • 9 g citric acid (1 level tablespoon); and
  • 0.20 g sodium bisulphite (1/5 level coffee-spoon).

Be careful to blend the sugar and the additives well before adding the mixture to the fruit.

Figure 3. Mixture of sugar and additive

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Step five

You must gently stir the fruit, sugar and additives with a wooden or a plastic stick or spoon until all the pineapples triangles are well coated with the solids, Figure 4. Put the lid on the bucket and leave the fruit to stand for six days in a cool place, Figure 5. During this period, some juice is extracted from the fruit. Take care to gently mix the fruit, the juice and the solids twice a day to blend the mixture and to avoid letting the solids settle to the bottom of the bucket.

Figure 4. Stir the fruit sugar and additives with a wooden spoon

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Put the lid on the bucket and leave the fruit to stand

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Step six

Six days later the fruit in its own juice can be packaged, Figure 6.

Figure 6. Fruit in its own juice labelled and packaged

©FAO/TECA

1.7 Step seven

  • The fruit and the juice can be stored in the same bucket where they were prepared (don't forget to put the lid on!). Or they can be taken out of the bucket and packaged in glass or high-density polyethylene jars. The jars must be immediately closed to avoid contamination, Figure 7.
  • Each package must be labelled indicating the name and the type of fruit product ("pineapple pieces"), the net weight, the ingredients (pineapple, sugar, citric acid, potassium sorbate, sodium bisulphite), the manufacture date, the "use by" date, and the name and address of the manufacturer.
Figure 7. Fruit and juice stored

©FAO/TECA.

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Preservation of pineapple: ID 3945.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable pineapple of high moisture: ID 3946.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable pineapple puree: ID 3948.
  • Preservation of fruits: intermediate moisture pineapples​​​: ID 3949.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology provides a more efficient way on how to collect and preserve pineapple fruit and its juice. This leads to improved product quality, food source and additional income.

entries.tittle: Preservation of fruits: Shelf-stable pineapple puree
entries.summary: The following provides specific steps on how to use the technique of obtaining shelf-stable pineapple puree. The steps include methods of processing, pouring, ingredients to add to the pulp, blending techniques, as well as the storing, packaging and labelling process.
entries.description:
Description

1. Steps for obtaining shelf-stable pineapple puree

The technique for obtaining shelf-stable pineapple puree has five steps. (See first how to preserve pineapple).

1.1 Step one

The blanched and cooled pineapples reserved for pulp is quickly processed, Figure 1. The purée is poured into a clean bucket or tank or other recipients with a lid.

Figure 1. Processing pineapples reserved for pulp

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two

Quickly add a mixture of sugar and additives to the pineapple pulp, Figure 2. For each kilogram of pulp, you will need:

  • 291 g sucrose or glucose (you can measure the sugar with a measuring jug)
  • 1.3 g potassium sorbate (one level teaspoon)
  • 9 g citric acid (one level tablespoon)
  • 0.32 g sodium bisulphite (a quarter level coffee spoon)

You can also add vanillin as a preservative instead of potassium sorbate. For each kilogram of pulp, replace 1.3 g potassium sorbate by 3.9 g vanillin (four level coffee-spoons). Vanillin is a natural preservative since it is produced from a plant.

Figure 2. Mixture of sugar and additives to the pineapple pulp

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Step three

The sugar, the additives and the pulp are blended well with a wooden or plastic stick or spoon, Figure 3. Next, the lid is put on the bucket it and the mixture left to stand for two days. You must stir the pulp with the additives at least twice a day to homogenize the mixture.

Figure 3. Sugar, additives and pulp blended well

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Step four

After two days, the shelf-stable pineapple puree is ready for packaging, Figure 4. The pineapple purée can be packaged into glass or high-density polyethylene jars or into flexible pouches. Or it can be stored in bulk in a tank or in the bucket it was prepared. Be careful to keep any recipient closed to avoid contamination from outside.

Figure 4. Shelf-pineapple puree ready for packaging

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Step five

The product is labelled with the name and form of the fruit product ("pineapple purée"), the ingredients (pineapple pulp, citric acid, potassium sorbate, sodium bisulphite), the net weight, the manufacture day, the "use by" date and the name and place of manufacture.

Figure 5. Pineapple puree labelled

©FAO/TECA

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

entries.tittle: Preservation of fruits: Shelf- stable pineapple of high moisture.
entries.summary: The following provides specific steps for shelf-stable high moisture pineapple production. The steps include methods of tray usage, heat management, fruit placement, vapour bath usage, and cooling techniques.​​​
entries.description:
Description

1. Steps for obtaining shelf-stable pineapple of high moisture

1.1 Step one

A few rings are placed as a monolayer on the tray, Figure 1. The same can be done for whole pineapples fruit as in Figure 2.

Figure 1. Pineapple rings placed on monolayer tray

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Pineapple placed on monolayer tray and heated

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two

Remove quickly the lid of the recipient, put the tray in and again, as soon as possible, put the lid on.

1.3 Step three

  • Let stand the rings for two minutes.
  • Be careful that the bottom of the tray does not touch the boiling water.
  • The tray must be hanging from the walls of the recipient.

1.4 Step four

  • Two minutes later, the pineapple rings are removed from the vapour bath and plunged as soon as possible into cold water for a few minutes, Figures 3 and 4.
  • Cooling in cold water minimizes the damage produced in the fruits by heat.
Figure 3. Pour the rings into a bucket of water with a wooden spoon

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Pineapple placed in boiling water

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Step five

Remove the rings from the water using a colander, Figure 5.

Figure 5. Pineapple of high moisture

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Additives

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Step six

Remove pineapple ring from the vapour bath, Figure 7.

Figure 7. Pineapple ring removed of the vapour bath

©FAO/TECA

1.7 Step seven

Cool the rings in water, Figure 8.

Figure 8. Rings are cooled in water

©FAO/TECA

1.8 Step eight

Store pineapple rings in bottle and jars at a cool temperature, Figure 9.

Figure 9. Pineapple rings storing

entries.tittle: Preservation of fruits: Intermediate moisture pineapples
entries.summary: The following provides steps on how to obtain intermediate pineapple moisture, which resemble the steps for high moisture shelf-stable pineapples. The steps provide information on separation techniques, draining, layering, juice collection, dehydration techniques, cooling procedures and labelling.
entries.description:
Description

1. Steps for obtaining intermediate moisture pineapple

The technique for obtaining the intermediate moisture pineapple has seven steps, but first it is important to see the technique for preparing high moisture, shelf-stable pineapple. The process to be followed before the steps below is the same.

1.1 Step one

The fruit product is not packaged but the fruit and the juice are separated with a colander or a sieve, Figure 1.

Figure 1. Fruit and juice separated by colander

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two

The drained pineapple triangles are then partially dried in hot air, Figure 2. They are spread evenly on a tray of stainless steel screen. Be careful to put only one layer of triangles on the tray, so they dry more quickly.

Figure 2. Drained pineapple triangles partially dried

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Step three

The juice is collected and packaged in bottles, demijohns or other containers, Figure 3.

Figure 3. Juice collected and packaged in bottles

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Step four

The tray with the pineapple triangles is placed in the dryer, Figure 4. The pineapple pieces are dehydrated by the passage of hot air across and through the bed of fruit pieces.

Figure 4. Tray with pineapple triangle placed in a dryer

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Step five

When the moisture content of the fruit is 15 to 20 percent (that is 15 g to 20 g water per 100 g partially dried fruit), the tray is removed from the dryer. The time of drying depends on the size and shape of the fruit, the temperature, humidity, flow and direction of the air, and the way in which the fruit pieces are supported during drying. For instance, with the dryer used for this explanation, the air velocity was 2 m per sec at a temperature of 60 ˚C. Drying took about five hours.

1.6 Step six

  • The partially dried pineapple (also called intermediate moisture pineapple) is cooled at room temperature and then packaged in polyethylene or polypropylene bags or into a glass or high-density polyethylene jars, Figure 5.
  • The products are labelled indicating the name and type of fruit product ("intermediate moisture pineapple" or "pineapple juice"), the net weight, the ingredients, the manufacture day, the "use by" date and the name and place of the manufacturer.
Figure 5. Products labelled and packaged

©FAO/TECA

entries.tittle: Preservation of fruits: Shelf-stable whole strawberries of high moisture.
entries.summary: Fruits and vegetables are nutritious, valuable foods full of flavour. Therefore, fruits and vegetables represent an important and, in many cases, an under-appreciated resource that could benefit from better utilisation and exploitation in rural communities. However, in low-income countries, poor care and handling of these crops frequently result in loss of quality, especially when not consumed immediately. Shelf-stable whole strawberries with high moisture is a technique to preserve strawberries that can be used in confectionery, bakery goods and dairy products.
entries.description:
Description

1. This six-step technique creates shelf-stable whole strawberries

1.1 Step one

A mixture of sugar and additives is prepared. The amount of these substances must be determined according to the weight of strawberries registered during the preservation process. If you do not have a scale, use measuring jugs or spoons. The following are the quantities of sugar and additives needed to process 1 kg of strawberries:

  • 440 g sucrose or glucose (you can measure the sugar with a measuring jug)
  • 1.5 g potassium sorbate (one level teaspoon)
  • 17 g citric acid (two-level tablespoons)
  • 0.22 g sodium bisulphite (one fifth level coffee-spoon)
  • 0.36 g ascorbic acid (a third level coffee-spoon)
  • 1.4 g calcium lactate (optional) (one and a half level coffee-spoon).

1.2 Step two

The different additives and the sugar are put together in a bowl or other recipient and blended by gently mixing.

1.3 Step three

The mixture of sugar and additives is added to the bucket of blanched and cooled fruit. You must gently stir the fruits, the sugar and the additives with a wooden or a plastic stick or spoon until all the fruit is well coated with the solids. Put the lid of the bucket on and let the fruit stand for six days.

1.4 Step four

During this period, you will observe that some juice is extracted from the fruit. Mix the fruit gently along with the juice, the sugar and the additives twice a day.

1.5 Step five

Six days later, the strawberries and their own juice are ready to be packaged! The fruit and the juice can be stored in the same bucket where they were prepared. The shelf-stable whole strawberries must be stored in a dark, cool place and can be consumed for three or four months, depending on the temperature of the room and the type of jar. The strawberries packaged in glass jars maintain good colour, however, when packaged in plastic jars, the colour changes during storage. The product packed in plastic is safe for three or four months, but the colour may change.

1.6 Step six

Each package must be labelled indicating the name and the form of the fruit product (whole strawberries), the net weight, the ingredients (strawberries, sugar, citric acid, potassium sorbate, ascorbic acid, sodium bisulphite, calcium lactate), the manufacture date, the "use by" date, and the name and address of the manufacturer. These preserved strawberries look good, are firm and have good flavour.

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Preservation of strawberries: ID 3941.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable strawberry puree: ID 3943.
  • Preservation of fruits: intermediate moisture whole strawberries: ID 3944.
  • Preservation of pineapple: ID 3945.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable pineapple of high moisture: ID 3946.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable high moisture pineapple- dry infusion: ID 3947.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable pineapple puree: ID 3948.
  • Preservation of fruits: intermediate moisture pineapples: ID 3949.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable high moisture peach halves: ID 3951.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable peach puree: ID 3952.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable peach halves (dry infusion): ID 3953.
  • Preservation of fruits: intermediate moisture peaches: ID 3954.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Women friendly

This technique is not labour-intensive and can be done by any hand labour individual.

4.2 Resources use efficiency

Preservation of strawberries reduces post-harvest losses.

4.3 Pro-poor technology 

Strawberries can be preserved using a simple technique, this offers a new marketing opportunity for farmers.

entries.tittle: Preservation of fruits: Shelf-stable peach halves (dry infusion)
entries.summary:
Fruits and vegetables are nutritious, valuable foods full of flavour. Therefore, fruits and vegetables represent an important and in many cases an under-appreciated resource that could benefit from better utilisation and exploitation in rural communities. However, in low-income countries, poor care and handling of these crops frequently result in loss of quality, especially when not consumed immediately. 

The preservation method used for shelf-stable peach halves dry infusion is simple and permits the consumption of the product for three or four months depending on the storage temperature. These peaches can be consumed as is, or used for preparing jams and jellies.
entries.description:
Description

1. Steps for preparing shelf-stable peach halves

The shelf-stable peach halves will be prepared, using a method called "dry infusion".

1.1 Step one

Instead of preparing a syrup with water, the (previously well mixed) sugar and the additives are directly added to the blanched and cooled peach halves.

Mix per kilogram of peach halves:

  • 440 g sucrose or glucose;
  • 1.5 g potassium sorbate (one level teaspoon);
  • 0.22 g sodium bisulphite (one fifth level coffee-spoon); and
  • 17 g citric acid (two level tablespoons).
Figure 1. Additives directly added to cooled peach halves

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two

Stir the mixture gently with a wooden or plastic stick or spoon until all the fruit is well coated with the sugar and the additives, Figure 2. Put the lid on the bucket then let stand for seven days. During this period, you will note that some juice is extracted from the fruit. Mix the juice, the fruit, the sugar and the additives gently twice a day. Be careful that the solids do not settle in the bottom of the bucket.

Figure 2. Mixture of juice, sugar and additives

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Step three

Seven days later, the peach halves and their juice are ready to be packaged.

1.4 Step four

The shelf-stable peach halves are packaged in glass or high density polyethylene jars or they can be stored in bulk in tanks or in the same bucket they were prepared, Figure 3. After packaging, remember to close the different containers to avoid contamination.

Figure 4. Shelf-stable peach packaged in glass and high-density polythene jars

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Step five

  • The product is labelled with the name and type of fruit product ("peach halves"), the ingredients (peach halves, citric acid, potassium sorbate, sodium bisulphite), the day of manufacture, the "use by" date and the name and place of the manufacturer.
  • The shelf-stable peach halves can be consumed for up to three or four months, depending on the temperature of storage. When the temperature is lower than 25˚C and a glass jar is used for packaging, the colour is better preserved.
  • These peaches can be consumed as such, or for preparing jams, jellies, fruit drinks, fruit cakes, etc. or as an ingredient in yogurt, ice-creams and other dairy products.

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

4.1 Women friendly

This technology is not labour intensive and can be done by any manual hand labour.

4.2 Resource use efficiency

4.3 Pro-poor technology

entries.tittle: Preservation of Pineapple
entries.summary: Pineapple fruit is hand harvested. The fruit is firmly attached to the plant and requires considerable physical force to remove it at harvest. Each plant bears a single fruit. Fruit must be harvested ripe, at half-yellow or quarter-yellow shell colour stage. The full ripe fruits are unsuitable for transporting large distances or for processing. However, if the fruits are immature, they may not develop good flavour and colour. This practice describes how to preserve pineapple.
entries.description:
Description

1. Steps for preserving pineapple

Figures 1 and 2 show pineapples fields and harvested pineapples, respectively.

Figure 1. Pineapples

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Harvested pineapples

©FAO/TECA

1.1 Step one

Wash your hands and wash pineapple using nail brush, Figure 3.

Figure 3. Wash pineapple using a nail brush

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two

Select the fruit for processing by separating the defective fruit from those that are free of defects and disease. The fruit must be of a uniform colour and maturity, Figure 4.

Figure 4. Pineapple selection

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Step three

  • Remove the crown and the shell of the pineapple using a sharp knife.
  • Remove any brown and/or dark areas of the flesh, Figure 5.
Figure 5. Slice the pineapples

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Step four

Wash the peeled pineapples with tap water and drain them immediately, Figure 6.

Figure 6. Wash the pineapples

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Step five

Cut the peeled and washed fruits into uniform 2 cm thick disks, remove the core of the disks. This is for preparing shelf-stable pineapple slices of high moisture by moist infusion. For other preservation techniques, cut the whole disks into four triangles. You can also preserve the whole peeled pineapple (without cutting) using moisture infusion.

1.6 Step six

The fruit to be preserved by each technique is separated and quickly weighed. If you do not have a scale, you can use a measuring jug, such as the one utilized for measuring liquids, sugar and flour in cooking. In this case, you can consider that a 2 litre jug full of pineapple triangles contains approximately 1 kg of fruit and eight rings (2 cm thick and 9 cm diameter) weigh approximately 1 kg, Figure 7.

Figure 7. Weighing the pineapple

©FAO/TECA

1.7 Step seven

Heat the pineapple slices using vapour for a few minutes. This treatment is called "blanching" and is done to deactivate some compounds that alter the colour and the firmness of the fruit and also to destroy germs, Figure 8.

To blanch the fruits in vapour, you will need:

  • a heater;
  • a stainless steel saucepan or another recipient with a lid; and
  • a stainless steel tray, perforated or made with a screen, to support the fruit. 

Pour a little water in the recipient, put the lid on, heat and let the water boil vigorously to eliminate the air and generate enough vapour before introducing the fruit.

entries.tittle: Camel milk products: producing butter
entries.summary: Camel milk can certainly play a far more important role in the prevention of malnutrition than it does today. Growing and raising foodstuffs for the rapidly increasing human population is especially precarious in the hot and arid zones of the world. These are the very areas where the camel is one of the few animals not only to survive, but to also benefit man. Camels can produce an adequate amount of milk in drought areas where other domestic animals have very low production. The following technology is part of FAO's publication on camels and camel milk
entries.description:
Description

1. Producing butter and butter milk

  • The methods of making butter and butter milk products can be summarized under key points.
    • Fresh milk is poured into a goat skin and allowed to ferment for 12 to 24 hours at 25°C to 30°C.
    • Fermented milk is churned for 15 to 20 minutes at 12°C to 18°C.
      • Butter and butter-milk are obtained.
    • Butter is mixed with clarifying agent and heated at 100 to 120°C for 30 minutes so as to obtain preserved butter fat.
    • Butter-milk is used to make dried cheese, to prepare soup, or after sauce or water has been added, it can be consumed immediately.
  • The fermented milk is sometimes churned with a little water and is called "Mattha".
  • When more water is added and the butter is removed it is called 'Lagsi".
  • These make pleasant and nutritious drinks in the heat of summer.
  • The lactose is converted into lactic acid by bacteria and into alcohol by the yeasts.
  • There is normally no alcohol in yoghurt because of the rapid development of the lactic acid forming bacteria, which depress the growth of the yeasts.
  • In the Sahara, butter is made by placing camel milk into a thin, hairless, goat-skin for 12 hours.
    • This skin is never washed with water.
    • Inside, the temperature rises to 28°C.
    • In winter, the goat-skin is often placed into the ground near a warm fire to obtain the optimum temperature before making butter.
    • This aids in the fermentation.
  • Churning is done when the container is half filled with sour milk.
    • Air is blown into the container and the top is tied off.
    • It is hung on a tent pole and rapidly swung to and from.
    • This is done in the early morning and the amount of butter obtained is determined by the skill of the man doing the churning.
    • No churning is done during the day as solar heat apparently impedes proper separation.
    • Some cold water is added into the goat-skin before the end of churning.
    • This aids in solidifying the butter.
    • It is then placed in a wooden bowl or kettle.
  • Fresh butter is not eaten, but is often used as a base for medicines.
    • The fresh butter is difficult to preserve.
    • It is not limpid and becomes rancid rapidly.
  • Most of the butter is thus melted down to make Shmen or Semma.
    • The butter is melted at 100°C to 120°C for 30 minutes.
    • A clarifying agent is added to hot butter, and it is stirred with a wooden spoon.
    • This agent can be crushed dates or a grated, roasted piece of ram horn, or leaves of certain plants or seeds.
    • Heating destroys the bacteria and the clarification agent collects the dirt and floats to the top, where it can be skimmed off.
    • If dates are used as clarifying agent it is then given to children.
    • If not, it is thrown away.
    • The leaves give the specific colouring and aroma to the butter.
  • The Bedouin in the Sinai Peninsula place the camel milk that is left over in a big clay jar, where it is allowed to partially ferment.
    • Then they place the milk into a leather container and shake it for about four hours and subsequently extract butter.
    • Milk from quite a few camels is normally required to obtain enough butter for the requirements of the herder families.
    • Camel butter has a harder consistency than the butter of sheep milk.
    • The butter has a greasy appearance and taste, so only little is eaten and it is used mainly for cooking.

2. Fermented milk production

  • Under warm conditions, raw milk does not keep for long and actually its fermentation appears to be a means to preserve it not only for a limited period of time.
  • Fermented products have various names in various parts of the world.
  • The method of preparation of fermented milk, even if referred to different countries, goes through specific steps.
    • Heat the milk to the boiling point so as to kill bacteria.
    • Cool to body temperature.
    • After adding a small quantity of previously fermented milk to work as a starter, the milk itself is well stirred and kept overnight at ambient temperature.
      • By next morning it has curdled.
      • At that stage it has acquired a sour taste and the typical flavour of fermented milk has developed.
    • Boil to kill pathogenic bacteria and develop conditions which will make it difficult for them to develop, assuring that a re-infection took place at a later stage.
      • Therefore, fermented milk products are edible for some time.

3. Other camel milk products

  • "Khoa" is made by evaporating small amounts of milk over a hot, steady fire.
    • The milk is continuously stirred to prevent scorching.
    • At first the mass left over has a buttery consistency.
    • After cooling, it turns into a semi-solid dough with a sweet taste.
    • Khoa can be kept for about 200 days.
    • If sugar is added, it keeps for longer periods.
  • "Rabbri" is also made by heating milk in a shallow iron pan over a hot fire.
    • The difference with Khoa is that the solids are removed successively from the thin layer of coagulated milk on the surface.
    • Then the product is allowed to cool.
    • When the milk reaches a fifth to an eighth of the original volume, it is removed from the fire.
    • The mass is now gently mixed, without damaging the flakes that have formed.
    • Sugar is added, and it is then allowed to cool.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Methods of processing camel milk into cheese: ID 7149.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Women-friendly

Women are usually responsible for processing milk into cheese and butter. This practice can be easily implemented by all. 

6.2 Resource use efficiency

This practice offers a possibility to process milk into butter and thus having a product that lasts for a longer period. 

6.3 Pro-poor technology

Poor farmers can proccess milk into butter, which can be seen as an additional source of income.

entries.tittle: Beekeeping in Asia: Keeping Apis Cerana in box hives
entries.summary: Maintaining colonies of oriental honeybees in box hives is an improved and often less expensive version of loghive beekeeping. In view of current wood prices in many parts of Asia, the cost of building hives from good solid logs can be prohibitive. In some coastal areas of tropical Asia, coconut bark is frequently available for log-hive construction. Where such bark is not readily available and good lumber is expensive, box hives can be built of discarded wooden crates and boxes, or even from scrap lumber. FAO's publication Beekeeping in Asia provides some useful information and general guidelines on A. cerana beekeeping.
entries.description:
Description

1. Keeping Apis cerana in box hives

  • Maintaining colonies of oriental honeybees in box hives is an improved and often less expensive version of log-hive beekeeping.
    • In view of current wood prices in many parts of Asia, the cost of building hives from good solid logs can be prohibitive.
    • In some coastal areas of tropical Asia, coconut bark is frequently available for log-hive construction.
    • But where such bark is not readily available and good lumber is expensive, box hives can be built of discarded wooden crates and boxes, or even from scrap lumber.
  • One advantage of box hives is that their design makes it possible for the beekeeper to open them to inspect the colony.
    • Some progressive beekeepers build their hives in such a way that they can be used with frames or top bars, so that the bees can be managed in a manner similar to beekeeping with standard movable-frame hives.
  • Unfortunately, there has been no standardization in the size and design of wooden box hives for the entire continent of Asia.
    • One major difficulty being the wide differences in colony populations among the various geographical races of Apis cerana.
  • In general, the Apis cerana box hives, most common in tropical Asia, are smaller than the full depth Langstroth hive, which has a volume of about 40 litres (465 mm x 365 mm x 238 to 240 mm inner dimensions).
    • An internal volume of about 20 to 25 litres is considered adequate for most tropical colonies of Apis cerana.
    • Colonies in larger hives have difficulty in defending their nests against the bees' natural enemies and in controlling the hives' microclimate.
  • In temperate Asia, where the population size of Apis cerana colonies is normally larger than in the tropics, traditional beekeepers use larger box hives, which may reach the dimensions of hives used for temperate A. mellifera, e.g. 35 to 45 litres.
  • Box-hive beekeepers may find the following suggestions useful.
    • In order to better protect the colonies against pests, all cracks in the hive walls should be sealed, and the size of the hive entrance should not exceed 5 cm2.
    • In order to ensure that the hive is properly insulated, its walls should not be less than 2 cm thick.
    • A box hive should, whenever possible, be placed in the shade, preferably on a stand suitably protected against ants.
    • Movable-frame hives
      • Keeping Apis Cerana colonies in movable-frame hives is the most advanced form of beekeeping with native honeybees employed in Asia.
      • The method allows for virtually any manipulation of the colony: brood-nest adjustments, inspection for diseases and pests, verifying food-store levels, queen rearing, supering during the honey-flow season, etc.
    • Whereas the full-depth Langstroth hive can be used for temperate and sub-tropical races of Apis cerana, smaller hives are required for the tropical races, often from half to two-thirds of the size of the Langstroth.
      • Some beekeepers prefer hives with 8-frame supers and 10-frame brood boxes.
  • Keeping oriental honeybees in movable-frame hives appears to meet with varying degrees of success, most of the difficulty lying not so much in questions of hive design and size as in the bees' biological characteristics.
    • Beekeepers in temperate, sub-tropical and tropical Asia agree in finding that absconding by colonies is their main problem, even more prevalent in the tropics than in the other regions.
    • In this particular case, absconding is not caused primarily by colony mismanagement.
      • It is a form of the bees' genetic behaviour, which enables them to evade attacking enemies and to migrate to other foraging areas during dearth periods.
      • Although this trait is biologically favourable to the bees, it constantly threatens beekeepers with the loss of their colonies.
      • Thus, the economic success of beekeeping with Apis cerana depends essentially on minimizing the rate the honeybees abscond.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • temperate, cool.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Good beekeeping practices: ID 8409.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: honey flow: ID 4011.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: choosing the equipment: ID 4007.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: queen rearing (Apis Mellifera): ID 4012.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: examining a bee colony: ID 4009.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: obtaining colonies with Apis Cerana: ID 4004.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology is not costly. Good honey production thanks to improved hive construction allows for additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Beekeeping in Asia: Examining a bee colony
entries.summary: A very important part of the skill of beekeeping is to learn to handle bees with confidence and manage them well. FAO’s publication Beekeeping in Asia discussed Pongthep Akratanakul’s experiences with European honeybees (Apis mellifera) introduced in northern Thailand; It also discussed the principal features of beekeeping activities in the other zonal and socio-cultural contexts in Asia at different stages of development. The following technology provides good practices to examine a bee colony.
entries.description:
Description

1. Examining the colony

  • The best time to examine a colony is when most of the foragers of the colony are out of the hive.
    • The older field bees being most apt to sting, the beekeeper has less chance of being stung when they are away.
    • Working with colonies on cloudy or rainy days is to be avoided, because at such times most of the older workers are within the hive.
  • On entering the apiary, the beekeeper should be fully prepared.
    • A veil should be worn to protect the face, trouser-legs should be well attached around the ankles, a hive tool should be carried in one hand and a well-lit smoker in the other.
    • Always work at the side of the hive, not in front of it.
    • This avoids blocking the hive entrance and reduces the chance of being stung by returning or departing foragers.
  • All movements, when working with or near a colony, must be slow and deliberate.
    • In handling the hive, a small puff of smoke should be directed into the hive entrance.
    • Wait for 30 to 60 seconds, lift the hive cover slightly, puff a little smoke within, and only then gently remove the cover of the hive, placing it on the ground in front of the hive.
    • Again puff a little smoke, while using the hive tool to prize free the inner lid, which is then placed upside down in front of the hive.
    • With the hive tool prize all the frames apart.
    • It may find be necessary at this stage, and throughout further manipulations, to administer a little smoke occasionally to calm the bees.
    • The first frame removed is the second one on the beekeeper's side.
    • After inspecting both sides of it carefully, gently lean it against the front corner of the hive.
    • The remaining frames are removed one at a time, inspected, and replaced.
    • When all the frames have been inspected, replace the frame that was set aside and restore the inner lid and cover to their original position.
  • In inspecting the frames, the beekeeper pays particular attention to:
    • the presence and number of brood cells, honey-storage cells, pollen cells and egg cells;
    • the pattern of the brood comb; the presence or absence of queen cups and cells;
    • the appearance of the adult workers; and
    • especially signs of disease and other abnormalities.
  • In a relatively large colony, it is not essential for the queen to be seen at every inspection.
    • The mere presence of eggs laid uniformly in a relatively large worker-comb area indicates the presence of a good-laying queen.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • temperate, cool.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Beekeeping in Asia: queen rearing (Apis Mellifera): ID 4012.
  • Good beekeeping practices: ID 8409.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: honey flow: ID 4011.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: choosing the equipment: ID 4007.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: keeping Apis Cerana in box hives: ID 4003.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: obtaining colonies with Apis Cerana: ID 4004.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology provides specific steps on how to examine a bee colony, thereby assuring its health and providing better quality products like honey and beeswax. These can provide for additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Treating straw for animal feeding: the Beckmann method
entries.summary:
The objective of straw treatment is to increase the digestibility of straw and/or the amount of it voluntarily consumed so that digestible energy intake by animals from straw is increased. Methods of treating straw may be classified broadly into physical, chemical and biological categories. Among physical methods of significance are grinding and pressure cooking. Very fine grinding in ball mills and irradiation, while effective in improving digestibility, are so expensive that they are unlikely ever to become commercially significant. 

Chemical methods currently being developed all employ alkalis. Other chemicals like chlorine can also be used to improve digestibility but are more expensive and more difficult to handle than the alkalis and no technology involving their use has yet been developed. The alkali treatment methods may be classified as follows. One of the method of treating straw to increase the digestibility is the Beckmann method which belongs to the chemical treatment - wet methods.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • The scale of operation and the degree of mechanisation of the Beckmann treatment process vary widely, but in all installations, two tanks are employed.
  • The straw is immersed in a 1.5 per cent solution of NaOH for 18 to 20 hours.
  • The volume of the solution is 8 to 10 litre per kg of dry straw, which is enough to cover the straw, and provides 12 kg to 15 kg NaOH per 100 kg straw.
  • After 18 to 20 hours, the treatment solution is pumped to the other tank and freshwater is pumped in.
  • The wash water overflows into a drain when the tank is full.
    • This washing continues for 18 to 20 hours after which the tank is drained.
    • The straw is then ready to be fed.
  • Straw is treated in a loose or baled form and chaffing is unnecessary for treatment or for subsequent feeding.
  • On the other hand, long baled straw is easier to handle during treatment than chaffed straw.
  • The used NaOH treatment solution, after being transferred to the second tank, is made up to volume (by adding about 300 litre water per 100 kg straw) and NaOH strength (by adding approximately 8 kg NaOH per 100 kg straw).
  • In most plants, the volume of the treatment solution is made up of the first wash water from the first tank to economize on alkali.
    • In this way, net consumption of alkali is about 6 kg per 100 kg straw.
    • he next day, the treatment solution is pumped back to the first tank again and thus one batch of treated and washed straw is produced every day.

2. The Beckmann method

  • In the Norwegian installations, both on the cooperative and farm-scale, the straw is lifted into and out of the tanks with travelling with electric chain hosts.
  • The Beckmann treatment may also be done manually on small farms, as was recommended before the mechanized versions came into use in the 1950’s.
  • The treatment solution remains in the same tank and the straw is transferred to the second tank which is used for washing only.
  • Treated straw contains about 20 percent dry matter and is limp.
  • The nodes should be soft.
    • The softness of the nodes should be tested by a simple hand test applied to straw to determine the effectiveness of treatment.
  • Well-washed straw should not feel slippery or soapy.
  • The sodium content is 0.5 to 0.6 percent on a dry-matter basis (0.07 to 0.16 percent in original straw); the legal limit is 0.3 percent.
  • Dry-matter losses are 20 kg to 25 kg per 100 kg original dry-matter.
  • The effectiveness of the treatment depends upon time, temperature, pressure and amount of alkali.
  • Twelve kg NaOH per 100 kg straw may be near the amount needed to achieve a maximum increase in digestibility.
  • In the spray-treatment process maximum increase in digestibility in vitro is achieved with about 10 kg NaOH per 100 kg straw.
    • Fernandez Carmona and Greenhalgh (1972) found that the digestibility in vitro of treated straw increased linearly up to a level of 14 kg per 100 kg straw (2 percent solution) and levelled off thereafter.
    • In many of the cooperative plants in Norway 20 kg or more of NaOH per 100 kg straw is routinely used (15 to 18 volumes of a 1.5 percent solution), the managers feeling that these quantities of NaOH are needed to give the soft texture they aim at in treated straw.
    • The exact amount of alkali needed in any situation will depend upon the length of time the straw is soaked, the environmental temperature and the nature of the starting material.
  • The influence of time and temperature are discussed in the following paragraphs.
  • No experimental data is available on the relative alkali needs of different types of straws for maximum increases in digestibility, but cooperative treatment plant managers in Norway use a greater amount of alkali to treat wheat straw than to treat other types to get comparable texture in the finished products.
  • Fortunately, the use of a sizeable excess of alkali is feasible since all but about 6 kg NaOH per 100 kg straw is recovered in each treatment cycle whatever the amount present in the treatment solution.
  • The digestibility can be obtained if the treatment solution is heated up to the boiling point.
  • Boiling was a feature of various pre-Beckmann methods, a feature that was dropped because it added unduly to the treatment cost.
Table 1. The effect of amount of NaOH used on the digestibility of Beckmann-treated straw

Source: Fingerling et al, 1923

3. Objectives fulfilled by the project

3.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology improves straw quality and digestibility by reducing dry-matter loss. It also reduces environmental pollution.

3.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for better livestock feed. Healthier livestock provide households with additional sources of income and food.

entries.tittle: Camarones: Metodo de Cultivo
entries.summary:
La cría de camarones y langostinos en ambientes naturales o seminaturales tiene tres fases principales:

  • Engorde desde postlarva a tamaño comercial.
  • Desove y cría desde huevo a postlarva, maduración y reproducción.
entries.description:
Descripción

1. Engorde de postlarvas y/o juveniles obtenidos en la naturaleza

Consiste en capturar pequeños ejemplares que llegan a zonas costeras como lagunas o esteros, llevándolos a estanques o brazos de agua, de hasta 100 hectáreas de superficie para su engorde.

Una forma rudimentaria que todavía se utiliza en Asia, consiste en dejar entrar con las mareas las postlarvas o juveniles a estanques previamente fertilizados con abonos orgánicos o inorgánicos, para luego cerrar las compuertas. Esta forma de trabajar tiene la desventaja que junto con los camarones entran otras especies que son predadores o competidores del organismo en cultivo. Los países donde se realiza este tipo de operación son: India, Filipinas, Bangladesh, Tailandia, Indonesia, etc; cultivando especies como Penaeus monodon, P. indicus, P. semisulcatus, Metapenaeus monoceros, etc, con rendimientos que anual van de 70 a 1 000 kg/ha.

En Ecuador, en cambio, se capturan las larvas de Penaeus stylirostris y P. vannamei a mano o con redes, para evitar los predadores, obteniéndose hasta 427 kg cola por ha en el caso de P.vannamei.

2. Cría de postlarvas a partir de huevos y su posterior engorde

Para realizarla es necesario obtener hembras maduras e impregnadas de la naturaleza, las cuales desovan entre 18 y 48 horas después de su captura. Los huevos así obtenidos se colocan en tanques de diversas formas. Las larvas se alimentan primero con fitoplancton (principalmente diatomeas) y posteriormente en zooplancton (preferentemente estadios naupliares de Artemia salina). Los estadios de postlarva avanzados pueden ser alimentados con algún alimento preparado y molido.

Una vez alcanzado el estado de postlarva, están trasladadas a pequeños estanques denominados precriaderos o versarios, colocándolas en densidades de hasta 150 animales por m2. Cuando pesan entre 1 y 3 g, los camarones están transferidos a tanques de engorde, de mayores dimensiones (entre 3 y 16 ha), donde quedan hasta alcanzar la talla comercial (entre 18 y 25 g).

Tanto en los precriaderos como en los estanques de engorde se realizan:

  • fertilización con distintos tipos de abono;
  • se alimenta con comidas preparadas;
  • se realizan cambios de agua mediante bombas;
  • y se lleva control de todas las variables ambientales (temperatura, salinidad, oxígeno disuelto, etc).

Este tipo de cría, que podríamos llamar semi-intensivo o intensivo, de acuerdo con el grado de producción y sofisticación en la metodología de trabajo, produce altos rendimientos en los paises que lo crian.

3. Ciclo completo en cautividad

Para este método, es necesario obtener machos y hembras maduros en cautividad para que haya copulación y desoves viables. El ciclo completo en cautividad se llevó a cabo en distintas especies, por lo menos al nivel experimental, utilizando por lo general ablación unilateral y comidas especiales.

Esta metodología presenta la ventaja independizarse de la naturaleza para el camaronicultor, independizarse de la naturaleza en cuanto a la obtención de hembras grávidas o postlarvas. Sin embargo, se estima que en el estado actual de los conocimientos, el segundo método es lo más adecuado porque presenta menos problemas y màs resultados que los otros. Los métodos de cría de larvas se encuentran generalizados en todo el mundo, no presentan grandes problemas al reproducirles cuando se cuente con personas calificadas.

El método de cría de larvas puede resultar costoso para inversores pequeños o medianos. Iniciar una granja camaronera comprando las postlarvas y juveniles a los laboratorios ya instalarlos para realizar el engorde tiene un costo alto.

4. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

5. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Potential yield of South Asian small reservoir fisheries: ID 4474.
  • Adaptive co-management: improved management of fisheries resources: ID 4481.
  • Management of fish in the pond: ID 7235.

6. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

6.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Debido al uso eficiente de los recursos, esta tecnología conduce a altos rendimientos en los países en los que se usa.
