entries.tittle: Beekeeping in Asia: Honey flow
entries.summary: Although all the colonies of Apis Mellifera in Asia belong to the same racial group, no unified colony-management scheme exists which is suitable for the entire continent. How a beekeeper handles his colonies at a given time of year depends on the bees, their environment and how they react to changes in it. The following paragraph from FAO’s publication Beekeeping in Asia gives guidelines on how to manage the colony during honey flow.
entries.description:
Description

1. Preparing colonies for the honey flow

  • The honey-flow season is the busiest time of the beekeeper's year.
    • Before it arrives, therefore, he should take a number of measures in order to be prepared for it.
    • He must have all his necessary equipment, appliances and supplies ready.
    • His colonies must have:
      • enough space for brood-rearing,
      • enough space for honey storage,
      • empty drawn combs,
      • frames fitted with comb foundation, and
      • supers must be readily available to be given to the trees as and when they are needed.
  • The honey-flow season is the time when the beekeeper must bring his colonies to a state of readiness.
    • While colonies in temperate regions can be built up gradually in early spring, before the arrival of the major honey flow, in areas of tropical Asia where the honey-flow season is short, the beekeeper must manage his colonies in such a way that their strength reaches its peak at the start of the flow, and not later in the season.
    • In order to do this, he will have to envisage any necessary requeening and combining of colonies, supplemental feeding to increase brood-rearing, and controlling tree pests and diseases.
  • For migratory beekeeping, all prospective apiary sites should be visited and surveyed before the colonies are moved to them.
    • This enables the beekeeper to collect a great deal of needed information.
    • The general outlook for forage availability in the sector, the estimated time of blossoming of the honey plants, when to move the colonies, the extent of the risk of bee poisoning by insecticides, other risk factors, etc.

2. Determining the honey flow

  • The best means the beekeeper has to determine the arrival and end of the honey flow is to monitor changes in the weight of his hives.
    • When there is no food in the area, the hives lose weight because food stores are being consumed.
    • A gradual increase in hive weight indicates that the flow period has arrived.
    • It is not uncommon for a strong colony to gain as much as 3 kg or more in a day in good nectar areas, such as the longan orchards of northern Thailand.
    • When the weight gain ceases (when the food consumed is equal in amount to the food collected), this indicates that the honey-flow season is ending.
  • During the honey flow, inclement weather may prevent the bees from flying for a few days, and this may cause a sudden drop in the rate of the colonies' weight gain.
    • The beekeeper must judge the situation properly and not misinterpret this decrease as a sign of the end of the honey flow.

3. Colony management during the honey flow

  • If all has been well-prepared before the arrival of the honey-flow season, colony management during the season itself usually involves routine apiary inspection, management of brood areas, supering and adding frames, and swarm prevention and control.
  • Every hive must be inspected frequently to ensure that all is going well.
    • The colony must be provided with enough comb space for food-hoarding and brood-rearing.
    • If the apiary is located near farmland, the beekeeper must be certain that his bees are safe from pesticide poisoning, and he must ward off other potential bee enemies and intruders.
  • The management of colony's brood area is critical during this season.
      • Brood combs and honey combs must be separated carefully.
      • A queen excluder is often used for this purpose.
      • Another method is based on the fact that the queen starts laying eggs at the bottom of the hive and gradually works upward.
      • When bees are kept in multi-storey hives, with at least two brood chambers, the beekeeper can reverse the position of these boxes and so confine the egg-laying activity of the queen to the lower part of the hive, while the supers are spared for honey storage.
  • Research has demonstrated that the amount of food collected and stored by a colony depends on the amount of empty comb space available to it.
    • The beekeeper will therefore find it profitable to provide his colonies with more empty frames than they actually need.
    • This practice also ensures that the colony will not lack storage space when the season is exceptionally good.
  • With strong colonies, super containing empty frames with drawn combs or comb foundation can be simply placed over the brood chamber, while for a less populous colony, a few frames may be given at a time.
    • The beekeeper should however have enough drawn combs in stock to be able to use them as the situation requires.
  • For the honey supers, placing nine frames in a 10-frame standard body is generally a good practice.
    • Not only can the combs be harvested more easily, but the expansion of the top of the combs, resulting from the fact that more bee space is available, simplifies not only the harvesting but also the uncapping process.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • temperate, cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Good beekeeping practices: ID 8409.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: queen rearing (Apis Mellifera): ID 4012.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: choosing the equipment: ID 4007.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: keeping Apis Cerana in box hives: ID 4003.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: examining a bee colony: ID 4009.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: obtaining colonies with Apis Cerana: ID 4004.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

6.1  Pro-poor technology

The technology provides detailed guidance on how to manage a bee colony during honeyflow. This improves colony health and product quantity and quality in terms of honey, beeswax etc. These provide additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Simple Techniques for Production of Dried Meat
entries.summary: Drying meat under natural temperatures, humidity and circulation of the air, including the direct influence of sun rays, is the oldest method of meat preservation. It consists of gradual dehydration of pieces of meat cut to a specific uniform shape that permits the equal and simultaneous drying of whole batches of meat. The warm, dry air of low humidity of about 30 per cent and relatively small temperature differences between day and night are optimal conditions for meat drying. This technology is part of FAO's publication: Manual on simple methods of meat preservation, which is mainly intended to disseminate information on traditional methods of meat preservation and addresses aspects of hygienic slaughtering under rural conditions in Africa.
entries.description:
Description

There is relatively high evaporation of water out of the meat during the first day of drying, after which it decreases continuously. After drying the meat for three or four days, weight losses of up to 60 to 70 per cent can be observed, equivalent to the amount of water evaporated. Consequently, moisture losses can be monitored by controlling the weight of a batch during drying.

Continuous evaporation and weight losses during drying cause changes in the shape of the meat through shrinkage of the muscle and connective tissue. The meat pieces become smaller, thinner and to some degree wrinkled. The consistency also changes from soft to firm to hard. In addition to these physical changes, there are also certain specific biochemical reactions with a strong impact on the organoleptic characteristics of the product. Meat used for drying in developing countries is usually derived from un‑chilled carcasses, and rapid ripening processes occur during the first stage of drying as the meat temperature remains relatively high. For that reason, the specific flavour of dried meat is completely different from the characteristic flavour of fresh meat. Slight oxidation of the meat fats contributes to the typical flavour of dried meat.

1. Selection of meat for drying

As a general rule, only lean meat is suitable for drying. Visible fatty tissues adhering to muscle tissue have a detrimental effect on the quality of the final product. Under processing and storage conditions for dry meat, rancidity quickly develops, resulting in flavour deterioration. Dry meat is generally manufactured from bovine meat although meat from camels, sheep, goats and venison (antelopes, deer) is also used. The meat best suited for drying is the meat of a medium‑aged animal, in good condition, but not fat. Carcasses have to be properly cut to obtain meat suitable for drying.

1.1 Carcass cutting

The carcass is firstly split into two sides along the spinal column and then cut into quarters. Fore and hindquarters are separated after the last rib, thus leaving no ribs in the hindquarter. For suspension, the hindquarter is hooked by the Achilles tendon and the forequarter by the last two ribs (Figure 1).

Figure 1. The dehydration process of a piece of meat

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Trimming

After the quarters are suspended so that they do not touch the floor or anything around them, they are trimmed. Careful trimming is very important for the quality and shelf‑life of the final product. The first step is to remove (with a knife) all visible contamination and dirty spots. Washing these areas will spread bacterial contamination to other parts of the meat surface without cleaning the meat. After completing the necessary cleaning of the meat surfaces, knives and hands of personnel must be washed thoroughly. Using a sharpened knife, the covering fat from the external and internal sides of the carcass and the visible connective tissue, such as the big tendons and superficial fasciae, are carefully trimmed off ( Figure 2).

Figure 2. Trimming

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Deboning

It is recommended that this operation should start with the hindquarters and follow with the forequarters. The aim is to remove the bones with the least possible damage to the muscles. Incisions into the muscles are inevitable but only at spots where the bones adhere and have to be cut off. Deboning of the suspended hind quarter should start from the leg and proceed to the rump and muscles along the vertebral column. Deboning of the forequarter must start with cutting and deboning the shoulder separately, followed by cutting off the rib set, together with the intercostal muscles. Deboning of the forequarter is completed by removing the meat from the neck and the breast region of the spinal column.

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Technique of cutting meat pieces for drying: ID 4070.
  • Simple techniques for dried meat production: methods of suspending meat: ID 4071.
  • Simple methods of meat preservation: meat dryers: ID 4072.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology improves livestock management and land use.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

Improved dried meat techniques allow for improved food conservation and food security. It also provides a potential additional source of revenue since the product can be stored long‑term.

entries.tittle: Simple Techniques for Dried Meat Production: Methods of Suspending Meat
entries.summary: The traditional way of suspending meat for drying by hanging strips over tree branches, wire or rope is not recommended; This is because meat pieces remain in contact with these supporting devices or may touch each other, and thus not dry properly in these contact areas. The following description is part of FAO's publication manual on simple methods of meat preservation.
entries.description:
Description

The suspending meat strips method should be to suspend the meat strips individually from one end, thus ensuring, through appropriate arrangement on the drying facility, free air circulation along the whole length of the pieces and fast and uniform drying. The contact of meat pieces with each other during drying must absolutely be avoided, since these areas will remain wet and humid for a prolonged period, thus making them a favourable environment for spoilage, bacteria and flies.

1. Suspension using metal hooks

  • This is a very simple but efficient way of suspending the meat strips.
  • The meat strips are hooked at one end, always the thicker end for stability, and suspended on a horizontal wooden stick, tightrope or wire.
  • The metal hooks can easily be made, preferably from galvanized (non-corrosive) wire.
  • A wire of 1 mm to 1.5 mm in diameter is cut into pieces 15 cm long, with a slanting cut so that the ends are sharp to allow piercing of the meat.
  • In order to obtain an S-shaped hook, both ends of each piece are simply twisted around a circular stick (see Figure 1).
Figure 1. Suspension of meat strips on hooks

©FAO/TECA

2. Suspension using loops

  • For this purpose, a thin string or a somewhat stronger thread is best suited.
  • The string is divided into pieces about 30 cm long with the ends knotted.
  • The string is fixed to the stronger end of the meat strip by a double loop and pulled tight in order to prevent the meat from slipping out of the loop (see Figure 2).
Figure 2. Preparing loops from string

©FAO/TECA

3. Suspension using metal clips

  • Clips of 4 to 7 cm wide are best suited.
  • They are easily placed on the stronger end of the meat strips.
  • Whereas metal hooks and rope loops can only be used for the suspension of rectangular or similar shaped strips, the metal clips are very practical for the suspension of flat, leaf-shaped pieces.
  • The special advantage of hanging leaf-shaped pieces by means of a clip, is that the edges of the meat do not fold in during drying (see Figure 3).
Figure 3. Suspension of meat strips on hooks

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Simple methods of meat preservation: meat dryers: ID 4072.
  • Dried meat techniques: examples from different regions: ID 4075.
  • Simple techniques for production of dried meat: ID 4069.
  • Improved method of preserving hides and skins: ID 4368.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for a more efficient means of preserving meat.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

Processing and preserving meat allows farmers to benefit from their livestock production over a longer period of time.

entries.tittle: Beekeeping in Asia: Queen rearing (Apis Mellifera).
entries.summary:
Good laying queens are important to productive beekeeping. Although queens may be able to live for several years, it is to the beekeepers' advantage that their colonies possess good young queens. To ensure that they will have an ample supply of queens, many of them rear their own. The following paragraph from FAO’s publication Beekeeping in Asia gives guidelines on rearing queens.

The practice of queen rearing is in Asia and it’s usually done between mid-spring and mid-summer in the temperate regions and between June and October in tropical zones. The technology helps increase the number of queen bees and therefore be able to increase the number of hives a farmer has.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • The best time of year to rear queens is when pollen and nectar are abundant and there are enough drones present to ensure successful mating.
    • In temperate Asia, this is the period between mid-spring and mid-summer, while in tropical zones the best season is often between June and late October or early November.
  • Basic queen-rearing supplies and equipment include a grafting tool, wax or plastic queen cups, a queen excluder, queen cages, and mating nuclei.
  • The grafting tool can be anything small enough to be conveniently used in the safe transfer of young larvae from worker cells to queen cups.
    • Metal tools are commercially available, but many Asian beekeepers prefer to make their own from a bamboo sliver not much larger than a toothpick, sandpapering its tip finely to shape it into a tiny flat spoon or an angled spatula.
  • Wax and plastic bee cups can also be obtained from bee-supply firms, but wax cups can easily be made by dipping a wooden mould, soaked in soapy water, into melted wax.

2. Grafting

  • The first step in grafting is to fasten not more than 20 queen cups to each cell bar of a wooden frame, and to prime each cup with a drop of fresh royal jelly removed from queen cells.
  • Using a grafting tool, the beekeeper gently transfers worker larvae about 24 hours old from the cells of the selected colony into the queen cups taking extreme care that the delicate larvae are not injured and that they do not roll over.
  • The frame, bearing 20 to 40 grafted queen cups, is then placed in a nursing colony, prepared in advance.
  • This is a healthy colony, intentionally crowded with the greatest possible number of young adult workers that have emerged from brood combs given to the colony shortly before, and copiously fed with pollen and sugar syrup.
  • The colony may be queenright or queenless; in the former case, a queen excluder is used to prevent the queen from destroying the developing queen cells.
  • If the grafting has been well executed and the larvae are uninjured, the nurse bees will accept them and feed them lavishly with royal jelly.
    • As the larvae develop, the adult bees will add wax to the queen cups and expand them into queen cells, which will be sealed when the larvae are being transformed into pupae.
    • To ensure that the larvae are lavishly fed with royal jelly, many beekeepers use two nursery hives instead of one.
    • The developing queen larvae are first placed in a ""starter colony"" for 24 to 48 hours and then transferred to a ""finishing colony"".
    • 80th colonies, often made queenless, are crowded with heavily-fed young adult bees.
    • Workers in the starter colony are not allowed to fly, while those in the finishing colony have free flight.
  • On the ninth or tenth day after grafting, part of the wax on the tips of the queen cells will have been eaten away by the workers.
    • At this stage, the cells are gently removed from the colony and transferred to a ""mating nucleus"", which is a small hive unit usually consisting of one frame of honey, one of pollen, and one or two of empty combs.
    • Each mating nucleus accommodates one capped queen cell, which is attached to the side of an empty comb placed in the middle of the hive.
    • A few thousand workers are shaken into the hive.
    • Within a day or two, the new queen will emerge from her cell and be fed by the workers.
    • After several days she will have gained enough strength to make orientation flights, and soon thereafter she will mate with drones in her nuptial flights.
  • Within a period of 7 to 14 days, the queens in the mating nuclei should be mated and begin to lay eggs.
    • They are now ready for sale or to be used for requeening or to increase the number of colonies.
    • The entire process of queen-rearing and mating takes from 21 to 30 days, given good weather and a sufficient number of drones for mating.
    • When laying queens are removed from the mating nuclei, it is best to put them in wooden cages called ""queen cages"", together with some worker bees from the nucleus hive.
    • The entrance of the cage is plugged with queen candy, care being taken that the candy is not too moist, lest it run into the cage. More queens must be reared than the number the beekeeper actually needs.
  • In the process of grafting, some larvae may be injured, and these will not be accepted by the nurse bees.
    • A rate of success in grafting of 70 percent is normally considered good, although it is not uncommon for experienced queen-breeders to attain rates above 90 percent.
    • A 75 to 85 percent rate of success in mating is accepted as good.
  • An apiary consisting of many mating nuclei is called a ""mating yard"".
    • It must be situated in or near a place where drones are abundant.
      • Commercial queen-breeders often intentionally prepare colonies to rear large numbers of drones, by simply crowding the colonies and providing them with empty drone combs.
    • The site should also be protected against such predators as Insectivorous birds and insects.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • temperate, cool.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Good beekeeping practices: ID 8409.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: honey flow: ID 4011.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: choosing the equipment: ID 4007.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: keeping Apis Cerana in box hives: ID 4003.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: examining a bee colony: ID 4009.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: obtaining colonies with Apis Cerana: ID 4004.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Pro-poor technology

By providing guidance in how to rear queens, the technology assures improved colony healthy and increases quality and quantity of products such as honey and beeswax. These provide for additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Simple Methods of Meat Preservation: Meat Dryers
entries.summary: The meat dryers are constructions of wood, metal and/or concrete, stationary or mobile, without or with a roof. For strips suspended by hooks or with a loop attached or fixed by clips, removable horizontal bars, either made of wood or metal or horizontal wire strings are needed. The following description is part from FAO ́s publication Manual on simple methods of meat preservation.
entries.description:
Description

1. Sun meat dryer made of wood or metal

  • This dryer consists of four wooden forks planted into the ground which are connected with two longitudinal, wooden traverses of about 4 m.
  • Wooden or metal sticks for hanging the meat strips are placed on the traverses at a distance of 15 cm from each other (see Figure 1).
  • If there are no sticks available, strong metal wire or plastic rope can be spanned between the two longitudinal traverses and two additional transversal traverses should be fitted for reinforcement (see Figure 2).
  • Similar constructions, but with iron parts and traverses instead of the wooden ones are suited for the more industrial type of meat drying (see Figure 3).
  • These constructions can also easily support a roof and meat drying can be done on two or more levels.
  • However, care has to be taken that the traverses at the lowest level are not less than 1 m from the ground.
Figure 1. Metal construction for meat drying

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Meat dryer with an insect screen

©FAO/TECA

2. Mobile meat dryer

  • This type of dryer, which can be easily assembled or dismantled, can be moved to places where the animals are slaughtered.
  • Although wooden constructions can be used for this purpose, for easy assembly and for a firm base metal constructions, using 40 mm tubular iron bars are more convenient (see Figure 4).
  • This type of dryer consists of two rectangular frames (2 m x 2 m) placed 4 m apart from each other.
  • They are connected with four longitudinal and eight transversal metal traverses in two levels from the ground (approx. 1 m and 2 m), thus permitting meat drying on the two levels (see Figure 5).
Figure 3. Roofed meat dryer

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Sticks to suspend meat

©FAO/TECA

3. Meat dryer with protection against external influences

  • In regions with strong and frequent winds, meat placed on the dryer must be protected from contamination by dirt, dust, sand, etc.
  • In these cases, it is recommended that the side walls of a roofed dryer (e.g. roof of corrugated aluminium as in Figure 6) be covered with plastic foil up to a height of 0.80 m to 1.20 m from the floor.
  • It is important to ensure that the upper parts of the dryer remain open for air circulation.
  • Protection against insects is provided by covering the sides of the dryer with insect screen (see Figure 7 and 8).
Figures 5 and 6. Simple wooden construction for meat drying using sticks

©FAO/TECA

Figures 7 and 8. Suspending meat strips on wooden sticks by metal hooks

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Improved method of preserving hides and skins: ID 4368.
  • Simple techniques for dried meat production: methods of suspending meat: ID 4071.
  • Dried meat techniques: examples from different regions: ID 4075.
  • Simple techniques for production of dried meat: ID 4069.

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for more efficient means of preserving meat.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

Processing and preserving meat allows farmers to benefit from their livestock production over a longer period of time.

entries.tittle: Rapid composting methods: use of effective micro-organisms (EM)
entries.summary: The potential of composting to turn on-farm waste materials into a farm resource makes it an attractive proposition. Composting offers several benefits such as enhanced soil fertility and soil health, thereby increased agricultural productivity, improved soil biodiversity, reduced ecological risks and creating a better environment. While traditional composting procedures take as long as four to eight months to produce finished compost, rapid composting methods offer possibilities for reducing the processing period up to three weeks.
entries.description:
Description

1. Use of Effective Micro-organisms (EM): EM based quick compost production process

  • Since 1999, seven small-scale organic fertilizer plants, using the EM based quick production process have been in operation in Myanmar.
  • They are owned and operated by Women's Income Generation Groups (WIGG).
  • A unit plant consists of nine pits of 6 ft (l) x 4 ft (w) x 3 ft (d), enclosed by low walls and covered with roof.

2. Raw materials for organic fertilizer production

  • Cow dung: two portions.
  • Rice husk: one portion.
  • Rice husk: charcoal, one portion.
  • Rice bran: milled, one portion.
  • Accelerator 33 litres of EM solution or Trichoderma solution per pit.

3. Preparation of EM solution (accelerator)

  • First, one litre of "instant solution" is made by mixing 10 ml EM, 40 ml molasses and 950 ml water and leaving it for five to seven days, depending on temperature.
  • Then the solution is added to one litre of molasses and 98 litres of water to obtain 100 litres of ready-to-use EM solution.
  • This amount is enough for three pits.
  • The EM solution functioning as accelerator reduces the composting period from one to three months.

4. Procedure

  • Firstly, mix all the ingredients, except accelerator.
  • Then make 0.5 ft layer of mixture in the pit and sprinkle accelerator over.
  • Repeat the same procedure until the pit is full.
  • Cover with plastic sheet.
  • Two or three weeks later, mix the whole pit to boost aerobic decomposition.
  • The fertilizer is ready to use a couple of weeks later.
  • A pit turns out 900 kg of final product per batch, which are usually packed in 30 kg plastic bags.
  • Assuming that it takes 30 days on average to produce a batch and only eight pits may be used for technical reasons, the annual potential production capacity works out to 86.4 tonne (0.9 tonne x 8 pits x 12 months).

5. Agroecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • On-farm composting methods: traditional methods (anaerobic decomposition): ID 4293.
  • On-farm composting methods: large scale passive aeration: ID 4295.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of cellulolytic cultures: ID 4298.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of forced aeration: ID 4299.
  • Rapid composting methods: vermicomposting: ID 4301.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently enhances soil fertility, soil health, and soil biodiversity, leading to reduced ecological risks and an improved environment.

7.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology increases agricultural productivity, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: On-farm composting methods: traditional methods (anaerobic decomposition)
entries.summary: Growing concerns relating to land degradation, threat to eco-systems from over and inappropriate use of inorganic fertilizers, atmospheric pollution, soil health, soil biodiversity, and sanitation have rekindled the global interest in organic recycling practices, like composting. The potential of composting to turn on-farm waste materials into a farm resource makes it an attractive proposition. Composting offers several benefits such as enhanced soil fertility and soil health. It also leads to increased agricultural productivity, improved soil biodiversity, reduced ecological risks, and a better environment. The following technology is part from FAO's publication on-farm composting methods and summarizes the traditional methods of composting (anaerobic decomposition).
entries.description:
Description

1. Traditional methods (anaerobic decomposition)

1.1 The Indian Bangalore method

  • This method of composting was developed at Bangalore in India by Acharya (1939).
  • The method is basically recommended when night soil and refuse are used for preparing the compost.
  • The method overcomes many of the disadvantages of the Indore method such as the problem of heap protection from adverse weather, nutrient losses due to high winds / strong sun rays, frequent turning requirements, fly nuisance etc.
  • However, the time involved in the production of finished compost is much longer.
  • The method is suitable for areas with scanty rainfall.

2. Preparation of the pit

  • Trenches or pits about one metre deep are dug; the breadth and length of the trenches can be made depending on the availability of land and the type of material to be composted.
  • The selection of site for the pits is made as in the Indore method.
  • The trenches should preferably have sloping walls and a floor of 90-cm slope to prevent water logging.

3. Filling the pit

  • Organic residues and night soil are put in alternate layers and, after filling, the pit is covered with a 15 cm to 20 cm thick layer of refuse.
  • The materials are allowed to remain in the pit without turning and watering for three months.
  • During this period, the material settles down due to reduction in the volume of the biomass and additional night soil and refuse are placed on top in alternate layers and plastered or covered with mud or earth to prevent loss of moisture and breeding of flies.
  • After the initial aerobic composting which is for about eight to ten days, the material undergoes anaerobic decomposition at a very slow rate and it takes about six to eight months to obtain the finished product.

4. Passive composting of manure piles

  • Passive composting involves simply stacking the materials in piles to decompose over a long time period with little agitation and management.
  • The process has been used for composting of animal wastes.
  • Needless to mention that simple placement of manure in a pile does not satisfy the requirements for continuous aerobic composting.
  • Without considerable bedding material, the moisture content of manure exceeds the level, which enables an open porous structure to exist in the pile.
  • Little, if any, air passes through it.
  • Under these circumstances, the anaerobic micro-organisms dominate the degradation.
  • All of the undesirable effects associated with anaerobic degradation occur including low temperatures, slow decomposition, and the release of hydrogen sulphide and other malodorous compounds.
  • When a livestock management system relies on bedding to add to livestock comfort and cleanliness, the bedding becomes mixed with the manure and creates a drier, of a more porous mixture.
  • This provides some structure and, depending on the amount of bedding, enables the mixture to be stacked in true piles.
  • The bedding also tends to raise the C:N ratio of the manure.
  • A mixture of manure and bedding requires a considerable proportion of bedding to provide the porosity necessary for composting.
  • At least equal volumes of bedding and manure are required.
  • If the amount of bedding is too low to provide a porous mix, then additional dry amendments must be provided by either increasing the bedding used in the barn or adding amendments when piles are formed.
  • Manure from horse stables or bedded manure packs can often compost in piles alone, whereas non-bedded manure from dairy, swine, and many poultry barns needs drying or additional amendments.
  • The pile must also be small enough to allow passive air movement, generally less than 6 feet high and 12 feet wide.
  • This passive method of composting is essentially windrow composting but with a much less frequent turning schedule.
  • It is a common method used for composting leaves.
  • It demands minimal labour and equipment.
  • Passive composting is slow because of its low aeration rate, and the potential for odour problems is greater.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • On-farm composting methods: large scale passive aeration: ID 4295.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of effective micro-organisms (EM): ID 4297.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of cellulolytic cultures: ID 4298.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of forced aeration: ID 4299.
  • Rapid composting methods: vermicomposting: ID 4301.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

7.1 Resource-use efficiency

The technology improves soil fertility, soil health and soil biodiversity, thereby reducing ecological risks and providing a better environment.

7.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology improves agriculural productivity, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Rapid composting methods: use of forced aeration
entries.summary: The potential of composting to turn on-farm waste materials into a farm resource makes it an attractive proposition. Composting offers several benefits such as enhanced soil fertility and soil health, thereby increased agricultural productivity, improved soil biodiversity, reduced ecological risks and creating a better environment. While traditional composting procedures take as long as four to eight months to produce finished compost, rapid composting methods offer possibilities for reducing the processing period up to three weeks.
entries.description:
Description

1. Use of forced aeration: aerated static pile

  • The aerated static pile method takes the piped aeration system a step further, using a blower to supply air to the composting materials.
    • The blower provides direct control of the process and allows larger piles.
  • No turning or agitation of the materials occurs once the pile is formed.
  • When the pile has been properly formed and if the air supply is sufficient and the distribution is uniform, the active composting period will be completed in approximately three to five weeks.
  • With the aerated static pile technique, the raw material mixture is piled over a base of wood chips, chopped straw, or other very porous material.
    • The porous base material contains a perforated aeration pipe.
    • The pipe is connected to a blower, which either pulls or pushes air through the pile.
  • The initial height of piles should be 5 to 8 feet high, depending on the material porosity, weather conditions, and the reach of the equipment used to build the pile.
    • Extra height is advantageous in the wintertime to retain heat.
  • It may be necessary to top off the pile with 6 inches of finished compost or bulking agent.
  • The layer of finished compost protects the surface of the pile from drying, insulates it from heat loss, discourages flies, and filters ammonia and potential odours generated within the pile.
  • Two forms of aerated static piles are common: individual piles and extended piles.
    • Individual piles are long triangular piles with a width (10 to 16 feet, not including the cover) equal to about twice the pile height.
    • The aeration pipe runs lengthwise beneath the ridge of the pile.
    • Individual piles hold a single large batch of material or a few batches of roughly the same recipe and age (within three days, for example).
    • Individual piles are practical when raw materials are available for composting at intervals rather than continuously.
  • Since the pile does not receive additional turnings, the selection and initial mixing ofraw materials are critical.
  • Otherwise, poor air distribution and uneven composting occur.
  • The pile must have good structure as well as to maintain porosity through the entire composting period.
  • This generally requires a fairly stiff bulking agent such as straw or wood chips.
    • Wood chips are commonly used for composting sewage sludge by this method.
    • Because of their large size, wood chips pass through the process only partially composted.
    • They are usually screened from the finished compost and reused as bulking agents for an additional two or three cycles.
    • Since straw decomposes over the composting period, a pile with straw as an amendment can gradually lose structure.
    • This is partially compensated by the drying which takes place as composting proceeds.
  • Other possible bulking agents and amendments for static pile composting include recycled compost, peat moss, corn cobs, crop residues, bark, leaves, shellfish shells, waste paper, and shredded tires.
  • Uncomposted material like shredded tires and mollusc shells must eventually be screened from the compost and reused.
  • To obtain good air distribution, manure or sludge must be thoroughly blended with the bulking agent before the pile is established.
  • The required airflow rates and the choice of blowers and aeration pipe depend on how aeration is managed.
    • As in, how the blower is controlled.
  • The blower can be controlled in several modes.
    • It can be run continuously or intermittently.
    • In the latter case, the control mechanism can be either a programmed time clock or a temperature sensor.
  • The airflow rates are based on the dry weight of the primary raw material, such as sludge or manure.
  • They should take into account the presence of typical amendments like wood chips, straw, and compost.
  • In practice, it may be necessary to adjust the timer cycle, pile size, or blower, to suit the specific conditions and materials.
  • For static pile composting, the air can be supplied in two ways: a suction system with the air drawn through the pile or a pressure system with the blower pushing the air into the pile.
    • Suction draws air into the pile from the outer surface and collects it in the aeration pipe.
    • Since the exhaust air is contained in the discharge pipe, it can be easily filtered if odours are occurring during the composting process.
  • With positive pressure aeration, the exhaust air leaves the compost pile over the entire pile surface.
    • Therefore, it is difficult to collect the air for odour treatment.
    • If better odour control is desired, a thicker outer layer of compost can be used.
    • Pressure aeration provides better airflow than suction aeration, largely because of the lack of an odour filter.
    • The lower pressure loss results in greater airflow at the same blower power.
    • Therefore, pressure systems can be more effective at cooling the pile and are preferred when temperature control is the overriding concern.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • On-farm composting methods: traditional methods (anaerobic decomposition): ID 4293.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of Effective Micro-organisms (EM): ID 4297.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of cellulolytic cultures: ID 4298.
  • On-farm composting methods: large scale passive aeration: ID 4295.
  • Rapid composting methods: vermicomposting: ID 4301.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently enhances soil fertility, soil health and soil biodiversity, thereby reducing ecological risks and improving the environment.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology is time-saving and increases agricultural production, leading to additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Management of cotton bollworns using predators ants in Uganda
entries.summary: Insect pests are the most important production constraints in Uganda. American bollworms, spiny boll worms and pink boll worms are among the ten insect pests, which are feeding and damaging flower buds, flowers, and young and maturating bolls. This is causing plant abortions, amounting to up to 87 percent resulting to yield reduction and income for the farmer. The following technology from The National Agricultural Research Organisation (NARO) describes how to use predator ants as a biological means to suppress bollworms.
entries.description:
Description

To eliminate bollworms, farmers usually spray chemicals, which have an impact on their surroundings. To avoid the side effects of chemical usage, research has introduced the use of black ants, a safer alternative for the control of cotton bollworms. This technology is largely used in Eastern, Western, Central, and Northern Uganda.

1. Advantages and challenges of using predatory ants

1.1 Advantages of using ants

  • The reduction of environmental risk hazards resulted from pesticide usage. 
  • Food contamination elimination. 
  • Farm products become pesticide free.
  • The sale of farm produce is at premium prices.
  • The predatory ants are easy to bait and mass rear in homes by farmers. 
  • This is an easy to learn the practice.
  • It saves money as farmers do not need to purchase chemicals and therefore, it saves on labour and time.
  • Farmers get maximum net profits from the premium prices.

1.2 Challenges

For a successful implementation, the following requirements are recommended.

  • A community-based organization needs to agree on good environmental management practices.
  • Keep sugar, honey, fish and meat meals in closed containers to avoid ants feeding on them.

2. Methods of using the predatory ants

  • Attracting crops like either beans, groundnuts and cowpeas that are host plants to aphids can be inter-cropped with cotton, attract predatory ants. 
  • Introduction of ants from a place where they are existent to a new place.
    • The ants should include males, females and workers.
  • Maintenance of surroundings to create favourable environmental conditions like breeding sites and hiding places for ants to allow good establishment, colonization and subsequent spread.
  • Mass trapping of ants for subsequent release in cotton fields heavily infested by bollworms for immediate population suppression.

For successful management of cotton bollworms, farmers should avoid:

  • the use of chemicals near or where these ants are present; and 
  • areas with vegetation destruction by either burning or cutting down trees in order not to destroy breeding sites and hiding places.

3. Conclusion

  • The use of predatory ants to biologically eliminate cotton apple caterpillar populations boosts farmers' profits.
  • It is environmentally friendly and risk-free to humans and other non-target organisms.
  • The successful use of predatory ants depends on the full collaboration of the community concerned.

4. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • Predatory black ants.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Cotton culture: ID 6901.
  • Beneficial insects and the cotton pests they control: ID 8677.
  • Promoting drought and water logging tolerant cotton varieties: ID 7394.

This technology is available in Portuguese: ID 2337.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

There is no need to apply chemicals which is a labour-based activity.

7.2 Women-friendly

Women can apply this in their fields as it does not include any hazards.

7.3 Pro-poor technology

The use of ants does not require any investment or purchasing of equipment, and at the same time saves the cotton field. It, therefore, prevents the loss of capital.

entries.tittle: Grow Epuripur Sorghum, Uganda
entries.summary:
Sorghum is the third most important staple cereal food crop in Uganda after maize and millet occupying 285 000 ha of arable land. It is mainly used for food and brewing. In an attempt to improve food security and incomes among the rural poor households, The Serere Agricultural and Animal Research Institute (SAARI) has generated a number of technologies, among which are Sekedo and Epuripur improved sorghum varieties released in 1995.

This technology is also available in: Portuguese (ID2334)
entries.description:
Description

Epuripur is an early maturing sorghum variety. It has three and a half month maturity periods and it can be grown twice a year.

It is an improved variety, with yield ranges from 2 500 to 3 000 kg per ha under good management. However, at farmer level the yield ranges from 500 to 800 kg per acres.

1. How to obtain high yields for epuripur sorghum

1.1 Seedbed preparation

  • Select well-drained and fertile site.
  • Open the land four to six weeks before planting to allow proper decomposition of plant residue.
  • Ploughing can be done twice to attain a fine seedbed.

1.2 Planting time

  • Plant at the onset of rains, e.g. March to April or August to September.
  • Late planting leads to high disease attack.

1.3 Planting method

Most farmers broadcast, however row cropping is recommended as it has advantages.

  • Field operations are made easy e.g. weeding, spraying.
  • Use of Ox-drawn equipment is practical.
  • There are high yields and therefore high income.

1.4 Spacing

  • Plant at a spacing of 60 cm between rows and 20 cm between plants.
  • Plant five to ten seeds per hole and then to two plants per hole when the plants are about 6 inches tall.

1.5 Seed rate

  • 4 kg per acre or 10 kg per ha is sufficient.

1.6 Weeding

  • Two weedings are sufficient for a good crop establishment.

1.7 Maturity

  • It takes about 110 days or three and a half months for epuripur to mature.

2. How do you know it is ready for harvesting?

  • The crop is ready for harvesting when the black scar appears underneath the seed.

2.1 Drying

  • Dry on the drying floor for three to five days.
  • Keep the harvest crop away from the rain or most conditions as this encourages grain moulding.

2.2 Threshing

  • Separate foreign seed or matter to obtain high quality produce that will fetch a good price.

2.3 Storage

  • Threshed produce should be stored in a cool dry place.

3. Common pests

  • Sorghum Fly (Contarinia sorghicola (Coquillett))
  • Striga (also known as sorcerer grass, little sorcerer or witch's weed).
Figure 1. Sorghum midge

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Striga

©FAO/TECA

4. Common diseases

4.1 Covered Kernel Smut

  • Use recommended pesticides and fungicides currently available on the market.
  • Follow the manufacturer’s instructions when applying them.
Figure 3. Covered kernel smut

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Winnowing for quality produce

©FAO/TECA

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies 

  • Transplanting sorghum and pearl millet in semi-arid regions: ID 4456.
  • Seed priming to improve stand establishment and yield in sorghum: ID 4452.

entries.tittle: Controlo das lagartas da maçã do algodoeiro (cotton bollworms) com a utilização de formigas predadoras, Uganda
entries.summary: O insetos são o principal constrangimento da produção agrícola no Uganda. A Helicoverpa armigera (a lagarta americana), Earias vittella (lagarta da maçã) e Pectinophora gossypiella (lagarta rosada) estão entre os dez insetos mais comuns que se alimentam e danificam os botões florais, flores, e maçãs jovens e maduras do algodoeiro, Estes ataques provocam o aborto de até 87 por cento dos frutos da cultura, com a consequente redução da produtividade e perda rendimento pelo agricultor. Este guia prático da ONIA (Organização Nacional de Investigação Agrícola - Uganda) descreve o uso de formigas predadoras como meio de controlo biológico das lagartas da maçã do algodoeiro.
entries.description:
Descrição

Antes da descoberta das formigas, os agricultores costumavam pulverizar as culturas com produtos químicos para eliminar as lagartas da maçã do algodoeiro. No entanto, estes químicos também afetam o que está na vizinhança. A fim de evitar esse impacto a investigação propôs o uso das formigas negras, como uma alternativa mais segura e ecológica para controlar as lagartas da maçã do algodoeiro. Esta prática é amplamente utilizada no Este, Oeste, Centro e Norte do Uganda.

1. Vantagens

As formigas predadoras têm as seguintes vantagens sobre os produtos químicos de uso agrícola:

  • redução do risco ambiental;
  • eliminação das fontes de contaminação dos alimentos;
  • venda e / ou consumo de produtos agrícolas livres de pesticidas;
  • venda de produtos agrícolas a melhores preços (preços premium); 
  • as formigas predadoras são fáceis de atrair e de manter em cativeiro pelos agricultores;
  • grupos de agricultores podem ser convenientemente capacitados para o uso destas novas tecnologias à medida que são desenvolvidas;
  • os agricultores não gastam dinheiro na compra aplicadores químicos e, portanto, economizam no tempo e mão-de-obra; e
  • os agricultores maximizam os seus rendimentos, com a obtenção de preços premium.

1.2 Desafios

Os requisitos recomendados para uma implementação bem-sucedida da técnica são:

  • uma organização baseada na comunidade de acordo com as boas práticas de gestão ambiental; e
  • manter as refeições com açúcar, mel, peixe e carne em recipientes fechados, para evitar que as formigas se alimentem delas.

2. Método de utilização de formigas predadoras

  • Culturas, como o feijão, amendoim e o feijão-fradinho, são plantas hospedeiras de afídios (pulgões), que podem ser consociadas ao algodão, atraindo rapidamente as formigas predadoras.
  • Transferência das formigas do local, onde existem, para outro, onde são necessárias. A colónia de formigas deve incluir machos, fêmeas e operárias.
  • Manutenção do espaço envolvente, por forma a serem criadas condições ambientais favoráveis, como locais de reprodução e esconderijos, para um bom estabelecimento, colonização e subsequente dispersão das colónicas.
  • Captura de um grande número de formigas para posterior libertação em plantações de algodão fortemente infestadas com a lagarta, para uma rápida eliminação da infestação.

Para uma gestão bem-sucedida das lagartas da maçã, os agricultores devem evitar:

  • o uso de produtos químicos perto ou onde as formigas estão presentes; e
  • a destruição de toda a vegetação da área e envolvente, queimando ou cortando as árvores para não destruir os locais de reprodução e esconderijos das formigas.

3. Conclusões

O uso de formigas predadoras para eliminar biologicamente as populações de lagartas da maçã do algodoeiro, permite aumentar os rendimentos dos agricultores. 

Esta prática é ambientalmente amigável e isenta de riscos para saúde dos humanos e outros organismos não-alvo.

A utilização com sucesso de formigas predadoras depende da total colaboração da comunidade local.

4. Requisitos mínimos para a implementação bem-sucedida da prática

Formigas pretas predadoras.

5. Zona agroecológica

  • Tropical, quentes.

6. Tecnologias relacionadas/associadas

  • Cotton culture (Cultura do algodoeiro): ID 6901.
  • Beneficial insects and the cotton pests they control (Insectos benéficos e o control das pestes do algodão): ID 8677.
  • Promoting drought and water logging tolerant cotton varieties (Promoção de variedades de algodão tolerantes à seca ou ao alagamento): ID 7394.

Esta tecnologia está também disponível em Inglês: ID 4337.

7. Objectivos atingidos pelo projecto

7.1 Tecnologia de economia de mão-de-obra (LST)

A economia da mão-de-obre resulta da ausência de necessidade de aplicar produtos químicos que requerem trabalho braçal.

7.2 Adequado às necessidades específicas das mulheres

As mulheres podem aplicar esta prática nos seus campos, pois não inclui nenhum perigo.

7.3 Tecnologia em prol de populações desfavorecidas

O uso de formigas não requer nenhum investimento ou compra de equipamentos. A aplicação da técnica permite salvar a produção de algodão, o que evita a perda de capital.

entries.tittle: How to produce Mirrow Carp fry (Cyprinus carpio), Uganda
entries.summary: The commonly farmed fish in Uganda, the Nile tilapia, grows very slowly in the cooler regions like Kabale, Kapchorwa and parts of Mbale and Kabarole. In 1957, the mirror carp (simply called Carp), was introduced into Uganda from Asia. Carp, unlike tilapia, takes eight months to attain an average weight of 500 g. In similar regions, the tilapia reaches an average weight of 100 g in a year. Therefore, carp is recommended for these regions. However, carp does not produce fry easily in ponds. This technology explains the process and steps to be followed to produce carp fry in ponds.
entries.description:
Description

As carp does not produce fry easily in ponds, special treatments are required. 

1. Steps to produce carp fry

1.1 Pond requirement

  • A minimum of four ponds is required for producing carp fry.
  • One pond holds the stock of fish from which the brood stocks are selected.
  • The second and third ponds are brood stock ponds; one holding only males and the other only females.
  • The fourth pond is the fry production pond.

1.2 Preparation of brood stock

  1. Separate mature males, and females from each other.
  2. Stock them at one fish per five square metres and feed intensively.
  3. Ensure there are no signs of bad health, bruise or deformity (Figure 1).
    • The Figure shows the differences between females and males.
  4. The mature females ooze eggs while mature males ooze white liquid out of its anal vent when the belly is pressed.
    • The ripe brood stocks ooze out the eggs and white liquid more easily (Figure 2).
  5. Feed brood stock intensively with food rich in protein at a rate of half a "tumpeco" (one tumpeco is equivalent to one-half litre-cup) per kg of its weight per day at mid-morning and early afternoon.
    • To make 50 kg of the feed, mix 35 "tumpecos" of maize of rice bran, 60 'tumpecos" of sunflower cake.
    • Mingle the mixture in hot water to make the dough.
  6. Feeding continues until the fish is ripe (Figure 3: Ripe female oozing eggs).
Figure 1. Female with well-rounded belly

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Ripe male oozing white liquid

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Ripe female oozing eggs

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Preparation of fry production pond

  • While the brood stock is getting conditioned, drain, dry and remove the mud from the fry production pond.
  • Disinfect the pond by spreading a layer of white builders lime thinly over the bottom.
  • Screen the inlet and outlet pipes using netting materials with fine meshes similar to mosquito nets.
    • Screening prevents the entry of wild fish or escape of eggs and fry.
  • Fill the pond with fresh stream water.
  • Plant mature papyrus heads such that they are just submerged underwater when the pond has filled the maximum.
    • The papyrus heads are for egg attachment.
    • Small branches of a pine tree or water cabbage can also be used.
  • Maintain strong water current through the pond.

1.4 Fry production

  • Select the ripest female and male brooders and bring them together, at a ratio of one female to two males into the fry production pond.
    • A ripe brood stock is very delicate and should be handled with great care otherwise it fails to spawn.
    • Avoid handling fish during very hot hours, and use wet towels or blankets to handle the ripe brood stocks during transfer.
  • Eggs are laid at night.
    • Mirror carp eggs become sticky on fertilization.
    • Simply lift and examine the strands of the papyrus heads to check for the eggs.
  • Reduce water current to a minimum to avoid washing away the fry.
  • Fertilize the pond with animal manure.
  • The eggs hatch within two to three days, depending on the warmth on the water.
  • Remove papyrus heads from the pond after five days from egg-laying.
  • Remove the brood stocks after one week and transfer them back to the brood stock holding pond to recover (Figure 4).
  • Fry starts feeding on the natural food in the water.
    • Importantly, start feeding the fry after one week with the same feed given to the brood stock.
    • Break the feed into small crumbs and broadcast into the pond in small quantities four to five times daily.
    • Two "tumpecos" of the feed per day is adequate for fry produced by one set of one female and two male brood stocks.
    • The fingerlings are ready for distribution at 2 g to 5 g measuring about 5 cm to 6 cm after two months.
Figure 4. Roots and branches with eggs attached

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Carp fry

©FAO/TECA

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Assessing post-harvest fish losses: informal fish loss assessment method (IFLAM): ID 4436.
  • Post-harvest fish loss model: ID 4463.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The practice allows for efficient and environmentally-friendly management of pond preparation as well as brood stock and fry production.

entries.tittle: The Control of Common Predators of Pond Fish in Uganda
entries.summary: The Cajuns Aquaculture Research and Development Centre (KARDC) is the government research centre that is carrying out research on solving problems associated with fish growing in ponds. The KARDC has prepared this technology to address the concerns of four common predators of fish growing on ponds. The production of this technology will teach fish farmers how to identify and control four very common predators of fish in ponds.
entries.description:
Description

1. Controlling predators around a pond

1.1 Birds

  • Maintain a 1.5-feet (0.5 m) depth of water in the pond especially in the dry season when the water levels usually drop.
    • When the water level is at least 1.5 feet (0.5 m), the birds can easily drown in the water if they try to enter the pond.
  • Fertilize the pond and make the water green using cow dung and chicken, goat and duck dropping.
    • Put in 2 kg of cow dung per 100 m2 of pond area weekly.
    • When the colour of the water is green, the birds cannot easily see the fish in the water and this keeps the fish safe.
  • Cut shrubs and small trees around the pond area.
    • Clear at least 15 m and beyond the edge of your pond so that the birds do not find a resting place where they can watch the fish and fly to the pond and eat them.
  • Patrol the ponds once in a while so that any birds that may have flown near the pond side are scared away.
    • Small children would enjoy chasing away these birds in their free time, so ask them to.
  • The Marabou storks hunt in groups and each of them eats many small, medium and big sized fish.
    • Because they move in a group they are very destructive in a short time (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Marabou storks

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Marabou storks eating fish in a draining pond

©FAO/TECA

  • The hammerkop and the egrets both eat many of the small fish called fry (of between 1 cm to 3 cm long) and fingerlings (of between 3 cm to 7 cm long) (Figure 3).
Figure 3. Hammerkop

©FAO/TECA

  • The egrets wait by the pond side for water levels to drop before eating the fish (Figure 4).
Figure 4. Egrets waiting by the pond side for water levels to drop before eating the fish

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Reptile Animals

  • The grass around the pond should be cut short so that there is no place for animals to hide and eventually come out to eat the fish.
  • Many animals come out at night to eat the fish.
    • You can set traps like poisoned fish for them to eat.
  • Some scarecrows of dead animals keep other animals away because they will come to know that there is danger near the pond when they see one of them dead.

1.2.1 Snakes

  • A python mainly eats the adults in a pond.
    • You can discourage it from coming near your pond by planting tobacco, which smells like fire.
    • Snakes do not like this smell, so they will keep away (Figure 5).
Figure 5. Python

©FAO/TECA

  • Fish farmers should know how to identify the different predators in their ponds.
  • They should also know how to prevent and discourage such predators from entering the ponds.
  • In this way, they shall harvest fish that are not injured, hence, of good market value.

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Post-harvest handling and processing of fish: ID 4351.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for increased amounts of fish production leading to hiring yields, accounting for an additional source of food and income.

entries.tittle: Post-harvest Handling and Processing of Fish in Uganda
entries.summary: Fish is the cheapest source of protein and provides between 50 to 100 percent of animal protein in developing countries and 12 percent worldwide. Fish is the second highest source of income in Uganda and main revenue to the country’s fisherfolk. However, it is a perishable commodity. Its quality deteriorates quickly if it is not properly handled and processed immediately.
entries.description:
Description

Proper methods of fish handling and fish processing described in this guide, contribute towards achieving the following beneficial objectives:

  • extend fish shelf life;
  • improve smoked fish quality; and
  • promote fish distribution.

1. Fish handling

  • Implement good hygiene practice when handling fish to avoid contamination.
  • Use raised racks for scaling, gutting and selling fish.
  • Do not expose fish to high temperatures before preserving (i.e. sun heat) which promotes spoilage.
  • Avoid damaging fish by mishandling, dropping or cutting it them when removing them from the nets.
    • Physical damage is a gateway to bacteria spoilage.
Figure 1. Fish handling

©FAO/TECA

2. Fish processing/smoking

  • Prepare the fish (scaling, gutting, washing, brining and dripping) before processing.
  • Process the fish immediately after catching them in order to avoid spoilage.
  • Use an improved method of smoking, (i.e. chorkor kiln).
  • Store the fish in a cool dry place.
Figure 2. Fish processing

©FAO/TECA

2.1 Fish smoking methods

There are two smoking methods.

2.1.1 Traditional methods (dug out pit and open fire)

Traditional methods have the following setbacks:

  • an uncontrolled fire results in poor products;
  • this method produces low output at any given time;
  • an uncontrolled fire leads to firewood wastage; and
  • this method is short-lived - due to the nature of the material.

2.1.2 Improved methods (chorkor kiln)

Improved methods have the following advantages:

  • controlled fire and proper construction materials result in high quality products;
  • there is no firewood wastage due to controlled wind;
  • many racks can be used simultaneously for smoking, providing a high output each time; and
  • chorkor kiln is durable because if properly maintained and constructed with unbaked and uncemented bricks, it can last for at least three years.
Figure 3. Chorkor kiln

©FAO/TECA

3. Recommendations

It is recommended that fisherfolk process fish using improved methods, focusing on the advantages of the chorkor kiln method over traditional smoking methods in order to obtain better quality products.

If the above recommendations are adhered to, they will improve fish shelf life and quality. As a result, fisherfolk will earn more for each household.

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Fish and their byproducts: ID 8717.
  • Post-harvest fish loss model: ID 4463.
  • Construction of raised drying racks for fish - the experience from Burundi: ID 8215.
  • The control of common predators of pond fish: ID 4353.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The preservation of fish improves product quality and reduces fish spoilage and wastage.

6.2 Pro-poor technology 

Fish can be preserved using more advanced techniques, this offers a new marketing opportunity for fisherfolk.

entries.tittle: Improved Method of Preserving Hides and Skins
entries.summary: Hides and skins are of very little economic and commercial value if they are not well preserved. Particularly in Uganda, Lango Farming System, most hides and skins which are produced, go to waste due to poor preservation practices. Improved methods and advice on how to preserve hides and skins of livestock are described below.
entries.description:
Description

The current method of preserving hides and skins is open air-drying, which includes:

  • frame drying for hides; and
  • triple wire drying for skins.

Some livestock farmers, butchers and hides and skins buyers still practice other rudimentary and unrecompensed methods, namely:

  • ground-drying
  • pole-drying
  • roof-drying
  • wall-drying.

However, these methods do not result in properly seasoned stocks acceptable to international markets. This is one of the reasons why the current earnings from hides and skins are very low.

1. Salting

This method uses salt to preserve hides and skins. In Uganda two modalities are used:

  • wet salting; and
  • dry salting.

1.1 Preliminary activities

Whether wet or dry salting, the following preliminary activities are important:

  • preparation;
  • defatting (removal of fat);
  • defleshing (removal of excess/ loose meat from stocks ) (see Figure 3);
  • washing using scrubbing brush to remove dirt and any other contamination elements from stocks (see Figure 5); and
  • weighing the hide (not skin).

2. Salting process

Based on the hide weight:

  • evenly sprinkle one-third of Magadi salt over the flesh-surface;
  • for skin only, evenly sprinkle three or more handful of Magadi salt on the flesh side. On average five handfuls of salt are needed;
  • dry salting requires only 10 percent of salt to hide weight, or four tupelo mug falls.

2.1 Bundling hides and skins after salting

  • bundle the stock with flesh side inwards;
  • fold the side edges first (see Figure 1); and
  • fold just once along the back bone line, with the flesh side outwards.

Salt reduces moisture content to a safe level of 20 to 30 percent.

The hides and skins will be protected for up to two months from bacterial infection and are ready for:

  • sale or
  • storage.
Figure 1. Bundling hide after wet-salting

©FAO/TECA

1.1 Advantages of salting

  • higher quality leather is produced for tanning;
  • market oriented, especially for European Union markets;
  • small amount of water used in soaking during tanning;
  • salt is often free of charge by exporters; and
  • livestock farmers and buyers get better incentives upon sale of hides and skins.
Figure 2. Higher quality leather

©FAO/TECA

3. Potential benefits

With the above explanation that clearly states the ease of preserving hides and skins using salt as well as the assured markets from the European Union, the hides and skins dealers will definitely benefit. A good hide or skin starts from the farm. It is therefore essential that farmers keep theirs livestock healthy. Similarly, the hides and skins buyers would earn more money from the improved method of preservation using the salting method.

Figure 3. Defatting/Defleshing

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Hides and skin covers

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Washing the hide

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Simple methods of meat preservation: meat dryers: ID 4072.
  • Simple techniques for dried meat production: methods of suspending meat: ID 4071.
  • Dried meat techniques: examples from different regions: ID 4075.
  • Simple techniques for production of dried meat: ID 4069.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Women-friendly

The technologies related, in particular, to smaller skin drying processing are easy to implement and accessible to all, due to their handling size.

6.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for preserving skin and hides, reducing water consumption.

6.3 Pro-poor technology

Skins and hides can be preserved using more advanced techniques, offering a new marketing opportunity and reducing production losses.

entries.tittle: Raising Citrus Rootstock in Uganda
entries.summary: Improved citrus varieties are not resistant to soil borne pests and diseases. However, they can be successfully grown if grafted on resistant rootstocks like rough lemon. Rough lemon is quick-growing, drought-resistant, shortens maturity period and is resistant to pests and diseases.
entries.description:
Description

1. Advantages of using rough lemon

  • Rough lemon is quick growing drought resistant, shortens maturity period and is resistant to pests and diseases.

1.1 Seed selection

  • Choose ripe rough lemon fruits free from pests and diseases.
  • Extract seeds from the fruits.
  • Select well-formed seeds and dry them under shed for two to three days.

1.2 Planting

  • Plant seeds in a box filled with mixture of soil, manure and sand.
  • Provide moisture, warmth and free air movement.
  • Sow the seeds thinly in rows in the soil mixture.
  • The seeds normally take two weeks to germinate.
Figure 1. A box containing rough lemon seedlings

©FAO/TECA

2. Transplanting in poly pots

  • One month after germination, transplant strong and healthy looking seedlings into ploypots.
  • Fill polypots with sand, followed by rotten saw dust and topsoil mixed with compost.
  • The polypot should have holes at the bottom and to the sides to improve drainage.
Figure 2. Ploy pot

©FAO/TECA

2.1 Grafting

  • During grafting, budding occurs.
    • Whereby the lemon and orange plants are joined together and tied.
  • The lemon bud is cut to create space for fixing the young orange stems of the improved variety.
  • The grafting can be done using the Valencia and Washington navel onto the lemon and tangerine rootstock.

2.2 Budding

  • Budding is done by cutting off a lemon bud.
  • The young orange stem is then inserted into the lemon cut bud and tied.

3. Field preparation

  • Prepare the field, remove all perennial weeds and allow trash to rot.
  • Dig holes spaced 6 m x 6 m, 60 cm deep and 1 m wide.
  • Fill the holes with manure mixed with topsoil.
  • Transplant potted grafted seedlings at the beginning of the rains, that is between March and June, for first rains and between August and September for second rains.
  • Water the plants in the morning and evening depending on availability of rain until they are established.
Figure 3. Field preparation

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Integrating lemon trees in vegetable farms for slope protection: ID 7703.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for more improved citrus varieties that are more resistant. This increases yields, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Improving Fodder by Incorporating Legumes in the Cropping System in Uganda
entries.summary: This practice gives examples of different legumes that can be incorporated as livestock fodder to improve livestock productivity. Detail is given on the importance and use of legumes in terms of their nutritional content and their positive impact on soil quality. Information is provided on how to plant them and which sources to use to get good quality seeds. Finally the advantages of legume use are also highlighted.
entries.description:
Description

1. Importance and use of legumes

  • Legumes are plants with high protein content and can fix nitrogen in the soil.
    • In addition, at the peak of the growth stage (flowering stage), they contribute to better forage for livestock and increase crop productivity.
  • Plant protein is the cheapest source of protein.
    • It constitutes 20 to 30 percent crude protein.
    • An animal’s protein requirement is one-third of the total daily feed requirement.
  • Research has shown that there are a number of legumes in various areas of Uganda with a variety of uses.
  • There are legumes like beans and soya beans, Centrosema species, Stylosanthes species (Stylo), desmodium, sirato, Lablab purpureus, Cajanas Cajana (pigeon pea), and acacia which have many uses.
    • When establishing a paddock, legumes such as sirato, stylo, or cetrositema can be inter-cropped with grasses such as chloris gayana or bracheria to provide cheap and balanced forage for animals as well as for conserving soil.
    • Legumes like mucuna are planted after the weeding of crops so that it is incorporated in the soil when ploughing.
      • This can also restore and improve soil fertility.
    • Maize or elephant grass inter-cropped with legumes like sirato and centrosema increase the herbage in quantity and quality.
    • Hay made from legume is of good quality.
    • It has a higher protein content compared to that made from grass.
      • For example, Lablab hay fed to milking cows shows an increase in milk production 0.5 to 2 litres per day depending on breed.
      • Multi purpose trees, such as Calliandra, Sesbania, Leuceana, are leguminous plants that serve the same purpose as other legumes.
      • They can be fed to animals fresh with the grass or as hay mixed with dairy meal at a ratio of 1:3 leaf hay: dairy meal.

2. How to plant legumes

  • Sirato or Cetrosema seeds are planted between rows of either maize or elephant grass at a spacing of 1 m apart.
  • Multi purpose trees are planted along edges of gardens at a spacing of 1 m apart. 

3. Source of seed

  • Farmers can buy seeds from Uganda Seed Project, Kawanda and the Forestry Research Institute Nakawa.
  • For multi purpose trees, these can be bought from Agricultural Research Development Centres in your area.
  • Legumes seeds are a very good source of income. At the time of writing one kilogram of seed ranged from UGX 5 000 (equivalent to approx. USD 2.73) to UGX 30 000 (equivalent to approx. USD 6.4) depending on the type.

3.1 Advantages of incorporating legumes as livestock fodder

  • A grass-legume yield will provide sufficient animal nutrients for body maintenance and production.
  • A local cow will produce up to 5 litres of milk daily while the cross can give about 8 litres on average.
  • This will also increase farmers’ incomes.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: woodlots, agro-forestry and improved fallow: ID 7320.
  • Evergreen agriculture: the use of fertilizer trees in maize production in Malawi: ID 7847.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

Inserting legumes into livestock fodder can increase their productivity.

entries.tittle: LOG-IT: A tool for capturing and organising data on factory production and quality
entries.summary: The ability to capture, log and organise information is essential to the efficient management and control of food production factories. It is of particular importance in demonstrating control of food safety systems. Although initially developed for use in export fish processing factories in Uganda, the technology can be used by anyone with an interest in producing and maintaining daily records of factory production information.
entries.description:
Description

1. The Log-IT

  • The Log-IT is designed to capture different types of useful factory information on a daily basis, providing a diary of production details, such as quality and quantity.
  • It can be used to log the quantities of resources used by a factory for sanitation on a daily basis.
  • The costs of resources are also entered, and the cost of sanitation is then calculated.
  • Other information relating to quality and yield can also be logged in the program, including time/temperature and assessments of the product through the chain.
  • Daily record sheets can be generated by the program and used for data collection, or in-house data collection systems can be used.
  • Log-IT is currently being used by several Ugandan factories.
  • Full details of the technology and the software tool itself can be accessed via the software tools for costing and monitoring control points pack? Which is on a separate CD Rom entitled Log-IT, Cleanse-IT, Ice-IT: software tools for costing and monitoring control points.
  • For an overview, check Figures 1 and 2 below. 
Figure 1. Examples of information captured and generated by the system

©DFIF/Dillon et al.,(2000)

Figure 2. Example of the LOGIT interface

©DFIF/Dillon et al.,(2000)
