entries.tittle: Participatory approaches: client-oriented breeding of rice for rainfed, medium and low lands of Easter India
entries.summary: Poor farmers in marginal areas have benefited little from high yielding, "green revolution" varieties that have transformed the productivity of more favourable areas. In the states of northeastern India, farmers who cultivate upland rice on low-fertility, sloping soils continue to grow low yielding landraces that are susceptible to diseases and pests. More efficient plant breeding that is highly client oriented provided a rapid, cost effective solution to these problems by developing new upland rice varieties superior to the landraces.
entries.description:
Description

  • Farmers of rainfed rice require early varieties that escape end of season drought but still give a good yield of grain and fodder.
  • Indian farmers were given a choice of varieties to test for themselves in their own fields.
    • This process is called participatory varietal selection (PVS) and farmers identified Kalinga III as the best of the modern varieties; it had early maturity, high grain and fodder yield and good cooking quality.
  • Farmers did not adopt it in large numbers or areas because of its poor inherent resistance to drought, and so Kalinga III was crossed with another rice variety, IR64, in a breeding programme targeted at improving the traits that farmers wanted.
  • This client-oriented breeding programme produced some outstanding rice varieties (Ashoka 165 and 900F, among others), officially recommended for the rainfed farming systems in Jharkhand.

1. Outcomes

  • Farmer preference for the new varieties was high.
    • In 2002, about 97 percent of farmers indicated that they would grow them next year, and 90 percent or more of farmers perceived them to be higher yielding.
    • Most farmers also perceived the new varieties to be earlier maturing, higher yielding, and more resistant to drought and lodging.
  • In a 2004 survey, farmers reported that in 2002 and 2003 their grain fetched a higher price in the market, with an average premium of 12 percent.
    • The new varieties significantly improved household income, with most farming households reporting that the effect on income was large.
    • Over 60 percent of farmers reported increases in on-farm income of at least 20 percent.
    • Farmers adopted the varieties on a high proportion of their land.
    • In villages that had only recent access to seed, overall adoption was around 26% of the rice area.
  • Seed multiplication was undertaken by non-governmental and governmental organizations to meet the high demand.
    • A seed multiplication and dissemination programme is also underway in western India where the varieties have also proven to be highly accepted by farmers.
  • The work is described in non-specialist publications (CAZS undated); (CAZS 2005), and (Stirling and Witcombe 2004); (Witcome et al 2002), which provide other examples of farmers and plant breeders working in partnership to improve productivity and reduce poverty.
  • Impacts of the work are discussed in the Further reading section.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • ​Participatory varietal selection: improved varieties of chickpea for rainfed conditions in Western India (ICCV 88202 and ICCV 2): ID 4442.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2440.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Women-friendly

The practice is easy to use and can be undertaken by all forms of hand-labour. 

4.2 Pro-poor technology

Developing new upland rice varieties superior to the landraces is a more efficient method of plant breeding that is highly client oriented and provides rapid, cost-effective solutions.

entries.tittle: Participatory varietal selection: rice in eastern India (Judi 578, Sugandha-1, Barkhe 3010)
entries.summary: Using participatory plant breeding, poor and marginal farmers in Eastern India, who previously grew old and low yielding land races, produced several new varieties of upland rice. Self-help groups produced truthful seed of these rice varieties, with production rising from 39 in 2002-2003 to 81 t in 2003-2004. It was expected to be nearly 300 tonne of certified seed between 2005 and 2006. Foundation and breeder seeds were also produced in 2005. Demand for the seed of upland rice varieties was very great, at about 690 tonne. Farmers adopted the new varieties on 8 to 63 percent of the upland areas, improving the food security of households from an average of seven months to ten months. The average rice selling ability of a household improved from 34 kg to 80 kg per year. Nearly 80 percent households reported more than 10 percent improvement in their income after growing the new varieties.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • The project targeted poor and marginal farmers in Eastern India (Jharkhand, West Bengal and Orissa), who grew old and low yielding landraces because of lack of suitable modern varieties.
  • About 33 percent of the rice area in West Bengal, 38 percent in Jharkhand and 41 percent in Orissa, was upland in the project areas.

2. Outcomes

  • Two varieties of upland rice (Komal 6 and Richa 5) were identified by Birsa Agricultural University for release.
    • In addition, several varieties of transplanted rice (including Sugandha-1, Barkhe 3010 and Judi 578) were identified as farmer-preferred and are in the advanced stages of testing, using plant participatory breeding (PPB) methods.
  • Sixteen self-help groups in Orissa and Jharkhand produced seed of these rice varieties.
  • Farmers produced truthful seed.
    • Seed production in 2002 - 2003 was 39 tonnes, which rose to 81 tonnes in 2003 - 2004 and was expected to be nearly 300 tonnes of certified seed between 2005 and 2006.
    • Foundation and breeder seeds were also produced in 2005.
    • Demand for the seed of upland rice varieties was very great at about 690 tonnes.
  • The seed produced by communities was widely dissemination through government, NGOs and private companies all over India.
    • For example, seed given to Catholic Relief Services was distributed to 5 000 farmers in 2004 and 2005.
  • Determining whether Participatory Plant Breeding (PPB) varieties were genetically more variable was addressed.
    • This was done by comparing the intra-varietal variation of varieties developed, by bulk breeding and linebreeding from the same cross.
    • Intra-varietal variation for quantitative traits was low and 43 SSR markers showed more variation in the bulk-selected varieties than the line bred varieties.
    • However, all varieties met the criteria of distinctness, uniformity and stability required for seed production.
    • Comparisons between pedigree, bulk and single seed descent methods were also made.
  • Seed flow among farmers was documented and farmers adopted the new varieties on 8 to 63 percent of the upland areas.
  • Farmers replaced their landraces for new varieties because they did not have to trade-off for many good traits in the new varieties.
  • Farmers liked them for higher yield, good grain quality, better drought tolerance, and earlier maturity.
  • The adoption of new varieties improved the food security of households from an average of seven months to ten months.
  • The average rice selling ability of a household improved from 34 kg to 80 kg per year.
  • Nearly 80 percent households reported more than 10 percent improvement in their income after growing the new varieties.
  • A financial analysis with conservative assumptions revealed a net benefit of about £300 million by 2014 which is much higher than the total expenditure incurred on PSP.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Rice seedbed preparation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 6973.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7210.
  • Intensive rice cultivation: ID 7666.
  • Participatory varietal selection: improved rice varieties: ID 4459.
  • Use of Early-Maturing Rice Variety (EMRV) to reduce typhoon impacts: ID 7719.
  • Applying flexible cropping schedules for rice (t. aman) production: ID 6853.
  • Aerobic rice: ID 7941.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology allowed for higher yield, good grain quality, better drought tolerance, and earlier maturity in seeds. This led to increased in selling quantity and revenue.

entries.tittle: Seed Priming to Improve Stand Establishment and Yield in Finger Millet, India
entries.summary: Crop establishment is often poor in the semi-arid tropics. However, good crop stand establishment is essential for the efficient use of water and light, and a uniform stand is a pre-requisite for cropping success. Seeds that germinate quickly produce viable seedlings that are not dependent on rapidly declining moisture in the soil that may occur in rain fed systems. Soaking seeds in water before sowing gives the germinating seeds a head start and speeds up seed establishment with a corresponding increase in survival rates and yields.
entries.description:
Description

Seed priming of finger millet was developed and tested using a combination of in vitro, on-station and on-farm participatory trials. Work was done in India, in marginal areas where seed soaking was a known practice but was not pursued except on a conditional basis, for example when sowing was late or otherwise forced to take place under sub-optimal conditions. Seeds were soaked in water, usually overnight, surface dried and then planted.

1. Objective

  • Initially, the objective was to improve crop establishment under marginal conditions, on the grounds that optimal, uniform stands would be able to utilize light, water and nutrients most effectively.
    • This objective was achieved early in the project, but it became clear that rapid, vigorous establishment conferred benefits in addition to good stands.
    • Primed crops emerged earlier, flowered sooner, required fewer cultivations and less weeding, produced grain and pods faster and became mature earlier than the same crop sown at the same time using dry seeds.
    • Farmers reported better drought tolerance and higher yields using primed seed, with yield increases of 10 to 30 percent.
  • Secondly, system-level effects were also reported.
    • There was the need for less seed per unit area.
    • Reduced labour demand for weeding.
    • Greater incentive to apply fertilizer to good stands.
    • Earlier harvest of kharif crops allowed rabi crops to be sown sooner, thus avoiding the yield penalties of late sowing.
    • Earlier harvest of rabi crops allowed earlier migration in search of paid work.
    • Farmers' choice of cropping sequence was increased, allowing two short duration rabi crops to take advantage of high seasonal prices.
  • Priming characteristics of wheat were determined in response to farmers who wished to take advantage of extra water made available as a result of other soil and water conservation activities.

2. Impact

  • The impact of on-farm seed priming has not been confined to marginal areas.
  • Trials with wheat by farmers in a high potential area in India over two years also improved establishment.
  • Over 90 percent of the farmers reported a one to two day acceleration in emergence and average yields were increased by 5 percent.
  • Feedback from farmers in both countries and in vitro work identified other areas in which seed priming could be useful and additional collaborative work was undertaken in a number of countries.
  • A large body of research was completed in collaboration with ICRISAT on the effect of priming on the establishment of pearl millet, particularly in relation to performance in crusting soils, where priming was found to be worthwhile.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Seed priming to improve stand establishment and yield in maize: ID 4450.
  • Seed priming to improve stand establishment and yield in sorghum: ID 4452.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for the efficient use of water and light, leading to cropping success.

entries.tittle: Seed priming to improve stand establishment and yield in sorghum
entries.summary: Crop establishment is often poor in the semi-arid tropics. However, good crop stand establishment is essential for the efficient use of water and light, and a uniform stand is a pre-requisite for cropping success. Seeds that germinate quickly produce viable seedlings that are not dependent on rapidly declining moisture in the soil that may occur in rain fed systems. Soaking seeds in water before sowing gives the germinating seeds a head start and speeds up seed establishment with a corresponding increase in survival rates and yields.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Seed priming of sorghum was developed and tested using a combination of in vitro, on-station and on-farm participatory trials.
  • Work was done in Zimbabwe and Pakistan, in marginal areas where seed soaking was a known practice but was not pursued except on a conditional basis, for example when sowing was late or otherwise forced to take place under sub-optimal conditions
  • Seeds were soaked in water, usually overnight, surface dried and then planted.

2. Objective

  • Initially, the objective was to improve crop establishment under marginal conditions, on the grounds that optimal, uniform stands would be able to utilize light, water and nutrients most effectively.
    • This objective was achieved early in the project, but it became clear that rapid, vigorous establishment conferred benefits in addition to good stands.
    • Primed crops emerged earlier, flowered sooner, required fewer cultivations and less weeding, produced grain and pods faster and became mature earlier than the same crop sown at the same time using dry seeds.
    • Farmers reported better drought tolerance and higher yields using primed seeds, with yield increases of 10 to 30 percent.
  • Secondly, system-level effects were also reported.
    • There was the need for less seed per unit area.
    • Reduced labour demand for weeding.
    • Greater incentive to apply fertilizer to good stands.
    • Earlier harvest of kharif crops allowed rabi crops to be sown sooner, thus avoiding the yield penalties of late sowing.
    • Earlier harvest of rabi crops allowed earlier migration in search of paid work.
    • Farmers' choice of cropping sequence was increased, allowing two short duration rabi crops, to take advantage of high seasonal prices.
  • Surveys in Musikavanhu communal area in Zimbabwe established a link between crop establishment and varietal diversity.
    • On-station trials over four seasons in Zimbabwe confirmed that a major constraint to good establishment and seedling vigour in sorghum was the weather following sowing.
    • Rate of emergence was positively correlated with seedling vigour.
    • Seed priming, by increasing the rate of emergence, improved seedling vigour.
    • Farmer trials in Zimbabwe during the 1997/98 and 1998/99 seasons confirmed that priming was effective in maize and sorghum and was popular with farmers.
  • The sense of ownership engendered by farmer trials and community/group evaluation ensured that adoption and uptake of on-farm seed priming technology was swift.
  • Summaries of the work on seed priming funded by DFID.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Grow epuripur sorghum: ID 4334.
  • Transplanting sorghum and pearl millet in semi-arid regions: ID 4456.
  • Traditional feeding of cattle with intercropped forage Sorghum: ID 8764.
  • Use of sorghum stover as dry season fodder for ruminants: ID 4492.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology, through the efficient use of water and light, allows for crop success, leading to additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Participatory approaches: Client-oriented breeding of rice for the Terai and low hills of Nepal
entries.summary: High potential rice production systems have diverse biophysical and socio-economic environments, but there is a lack of rice varieties matching this diversity. A number of advanced breeding lines have recently been developed to match these production systems. Therefore, suitable varieties for diverse rice-producing environments were developed in high potential production systems through participatory plant breeding. This technology from DFID describes how to implement this method.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • In the chaite season (early rice) in Nepal, CH-45 is the most widely grown variety.
    • It is about 40 years old, prone to diseases such as rice blast caused by Pyricularia grisea, and prone to damage by the white-backed planthopper.
    • Similarly, in the main season, Masuli is the dominant variety in Chitwan and Nawalparasi districts, although it is highly susceptible to leaf and neck blast, and to damage by the brown planthopper.
    • In the lowlands, Masuli is also prone to lodging.
  • A few, widely adapted rice varieties are promoted by the formal system throughout the country, but without due consideration of the diverse environmental and socioeconomic conditions.
    • Farmers’ participation in the selection of suitable plant types is uncommon in conventional breeding systems.
    • There is also a lack of participation by farmers in the assessment of post-harvest qualities and market acceptability of rice varieties.
  • In conventional breeding systems, testing of advanced breeding materials is conducted within the confines of the research station.
    • Farmers are involved as part of the variety release requirements, rather than to assist in variety development or to help make final decisions on acceptance or rejection of breeding lines.
  • Generally, the National Rice Research Programme (NRRP) develops and recommends varieties mainly for use in the larger (districts/regions), such as Eastern Terai, Central Terai, Western Terai, Mid Hills and High Hills.
    • Although there are considerable differences within all these environments.
    • Variety release by the formal sector is slow, and farmers receive finished products late in the process.
    • Previous baseline surveys in Chitwan indicated a lack of varietal choice.
    • It has also been demonstrated that for a marginal agricultural environment for high altitude rice, farmers’ involvement in selection in the early stages successfully produced their preferred varieties.
    • Hence, it was possible that Participatory Plant Breeding (PPB) could also be effective in high potential production systems.
  • The initial and important steps for involving farmers and other stakeholders in a PPB scheme are setting the breeding objectives and priorities.
    • PPB allows the involvement of farmers in the initial stages of generation segregation so that they can select preferred breeding lines.
    • Farmers’ preferences and needs, market acceptability, variety testing and verification are all addressed simultaneously so that the cost of variety development is reduced.
    • PPB thus minimizes the risk of varieties being rejected by farmers late in the breeding process, which is a common problem in the conventional system.

2. Outcomes

  • The application of PPB to more favourable environments involved the development of productive strains and genotypes and promoting them in the target environments.
    • The programme was initiated with F3 lines of two crosses obtained from GVT East in India.
    • A few carefully chosen crosses were subsequently made, involving a large population size targeted for different rice production systems in chaite and main seasons.
  • The project activities included:
    • the selection of genotypes in the target environments;
    • the involvement of participating farmers in pre- and post-harvest evaluation;
    • testing advanced lines widely;
    • scaling-up PPB processes and products; and
    • dissemination.
  • By the end of the 2001 main season, 72 advanced breeding lines from seven crosses had been selected.

3. Further details

  • For further details of these processes mentioned above, refer to Gyawali (2002), Witcombe et al. (2004) and “A brief introduction to participatory varietal selection and participatory plant breeding” (Annex 1 in WITCOMBE et al., 2004).
  • Simple breeding methods were used to extract these lines, which allowed increased farmer participation in the programme.
  • Farmers selected during pre- and post-harvest evaluations of genotypes.
  • Organoleptic taste assessment and micromilling were important selection criteria.
  • The seed of superior lines were increased and tested in a wider area through another DFID project, R8071 (see Devokta et al. 2006).
  • In an effort to integrate the products of PPB into the national system, chaite and barkhe lines were included in national disease-screening nurseries of the NRRP.
    • It was found that PPB products were resistant to, or tolerant of, blast (leaf and neck blast) and bacterial leaf blight. 
  • Partnerships with CBOs, NARC and DOA were established to share new knowledge, as well as disseminate PPB outputs to the stakeholders.
    • The definition of rice production systems in PPB/HPPS has helped to identify the right domain of particular breeding lines, and has improved the management of these lines more efficiently in terms of testing in the target environments (Gyawali,2002). 
  • Adoption, spread and impact of the PVS/PPB approach can be found in Witcombe et al., (2002), Joshi et al., (2003, 2005), Devokta et al., (2005, 2006), whereas Witcombe et al., (2002) provide further examples of farmer and plant breeders working in partnership to improve productivity and reduce poverty. 

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cool; and
  • subtropics, warm/mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Marker Assisted Selection (MAS) and Participatory Plant Breeding (PPB) in rice: ID 4572.
  • Participatory approaches: client-oriented breeding of rice for rainfed, medium and low lands of Easter India: ID 4440.
  • Participatory varietal selection - rice: ID 4445.
  • Participatory varietal selection - improved rice varieties: ID 4459.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficient allows for the development of more resistant rice varieties and the increased involvement of farmer communities.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology, through improved rice breeding, provides for additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Management of self-recruiting species in aquaculture
entries.summary: In farmer-managed aquatic systems, poor people do not always have the resources to stock ponds with different fish species. Furthermore, in the dry season, water bodies dry out and access to food sources becomes limited. Self-recruiting species (SRS) are animals that do not require repeated stocking in farmer-managed systems and include both indigenous and exotic species. Management strategies for the maintenance and enhancement of SRS include: keeping of breeding stock, re-stocking of collected juveniles, and screening of pond entrances. These strategies help increase the yield of SRS, without extra financial inputs. This makes them particularly important for poor communities, especially during the dry season when access to other waterbodies is limited.
entries.description:
Description

Aquatic animals that can be harvested sustainably from a farmer-managed system without regular stocking are referred to as Self Recruiting Species (SRS). A range of indigenous and introduced fish species, as well as molluscs, crustacea and amphibians are inevitably present in many rural aquaculture systems even where deliberately eradicated. Exotic species may also be considered as self-recruiting species.

1. SRS resources

  • SRS resource systems operate at the interface of capture fisheries and aquaculture, involving both active management and private ownership of animals during all or part of their life cycle, but remaining closely linked to the wider, natural aquatic ecosystem.
  • As aquatic habitats are increasingly modified, active management of wild aquatic animals on farms serves not only to increase their availability for harvest but to conserve the natural aquatic biodiversity of rice-based farming landscapes.
  • Existing information indicates that self-recruiting aquatic animals in farmer-managed systems, such as ponds and rice fields, may contribute substantially to rural livelihoods in the rice-growing regions of Asia.
  • SRS management strategies that maintain and enhance the production of SRS in farmer-managed aquatic systems include the keeping of broodstock, re-stocking of collected juveniles, and the screening (or not) of pond entrances.
  • Lists of species that are popular with poor producers and consumers can inform future work on the development of species of poverty-focused aquaculture.
  • SRS are most important in upland areas, where other water bodies are limited.
    • Fish, frogs, snails, crabs and shrimps are all valued SRSs.
  • Including SRS in a system was found not to negatively affect the production of stocked fish.
  • Value-addition, such as drying and fermenting, is an important activity resulting from increased seasonal availability of non-stocked aquatic species from farmer-managed systems in rural, peri-urban and urban situations.
  • Local resource group management of SRS in tracts of farmland can be effective in increasing benefits to individual farmers from their SRS-based aquatic systems.
  • Due to the strong linkages between large water bodies and farmer-managed systems, location-specific group management shows promise in the maintenance and enhancement of SRS in poor communities.

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Management strategies to optimize production of and access to Self-Recruiting Species (SRS): ID 4511.
  • Integration of aquaculture into the farming systems in India: ID 4590.
  • Beje aquaculture and inland fishery in tropical peatland of Indonesia: ID 8619.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

Since aquatic habitats are increasingly modified, this practice allows for the active management of wild aquatic animals on farms to increase their availability for harvest and conserves the natural aquatic biodiversity of rice-based farming landscapes.​

entries.tittle: Soil conservation: Contour ploughing, Grenada
entries.summary: Contour ploughing mitigates the impacts of floods, storms, and landslides on the crops by reducing soil erosion up to 50 percent, controlling runoff water, increasing moisture infiltration and retention and thus enhancing soil quality and composition. This practice describes contour ploughing and contour beds which can be constructed manually using on farm equipment.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Contour ploughing is a soil conservation technology that is practised throughout Grenada to mitigate the negative consequences of natural disasters on soil quality and composition.
  • It is performed by following the natural contours when tilling the soil, planting and cultivating.
  • It is best practised on slopes between 15 and 20 degrees, it is a very cost-effective and is a sustainable practice when properly planned and applied.

2. Objectives

  • Contour ploughing mitigates the impacts of floods, storms and landslides on the crops.
  • It does this by reducing soil erosion up to 50 percent, controlling runoff water, increasing moisture infiltration and retention and thus enhancing soil quality and composition.

3. Implementation of the technology

  • Mark out contour lines along the plot of land to be cultivated using a Frame, Abney Level cut contour drains using contour lines as a guide.
    • Using a trained machine operator, plough at right angles to the natural slope of the land to create a series of stepped ridges/beds above each contour drain (see Figures 1 and 2).
    • Contour beds can also be constructed manually using tools such as hoe, fork and spade.
    • Ensure that the edge of each contour bed is made with a slight slope about 5 degree to prevent unnecessary soil erosion.
  • The edges of contour beds can be further strengthened by using one or more of the following methods.
    • Plant grass barriers along alternating beds of at least 30 to 40 feet (915 to 1 220 cm) between beds.
    • Construct a stone/bamboo embankment on the front edge of each bed using large stones at the bottom with smaller stones at the top (bamboo should be replaced ideally every five years).
  • The principles of strip cropping can be integrated into any contour farming practice to promote additional soil conservation benefits.
  • The system of contour ploughing and strip cropping can be augmented by integrating hedgerows or boundary planting to reduce the velocity of ground and upper altitude wind depending upon farmers’ needs.
  • This practice can increase erosion if rainfall amount exceeds the ability of the contours to remove the runoff.
  • Therefore, the practice is usually planned in conjunction with other practices needed for support in the event that runoff exceeds the carrying capacity of the contours.
  • It is most effective when used as part of a planned conservation system that integrates crop rotation, minimum tillage etc.
Figure 1. Contour ploughing in (Ludhur) Grenada

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Contour ploughing in (Ludhur) Grenada

©FAO/TECA

  • The measures to preserve soil structure and nutrients and avoid erosion will have a positive impact on the agro-system.
  • Soil will maintain its potential yield or increase it in the case of adding other conservation agriculture practices.
  • This makes it more resilient against weather hazards, in this case against flash floods.
  • Farmers´ livelihood will benefit from the preservation of soil conditions and the positive effects of achieving higher yields.

3.1 Inputs

  • Mechanized equipment
  • A hoe
  • A fork
  • A spade.

3.2 Costs

  • Machine (EC$ 90.00 per hour).

3.3 Maintenance

  • Maintain ridges and remove extra soil and weeds in furrows.
  • Technical support from the Extension Division of the Ministry of Agriculture is required.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Soil and water conservation: ID 7861.
  • Strategies for improved soil and water conservation practices in hillside production systems: ID 5571.
  • Mechanical soil conservation strategies to reduce soil erosion: ID 8208.
  • Soil and water conservation practices to reduce soil erosion and enhance water conservation: ID 7861.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

6.1 Pro-poor technology

This practice benefits the farmers by achieving higher yields as a result of soil conservation.

entries.tittle: Diversified cropping system: Strip cropping, Grenada
entries.summary: Soil conservation is crucial to sustainable agriculture. This technology involves growing row crops, forages, small grains, or fallow in a systematic arrangement of equal width strips across a field. This arrangement of strips reduces water and wind-induced soil erosion. It also reduces the transport of sediment and other water-borne contaminants so the water quality can be maintained, thus increasing soil moisture.
entries.description:
Description

Strip cropping has been advocated and adopted by conservationists and agricultural technicians in Grenada since the late 1950s as a soil conservation practice in response to the detrimental effects of Hurricane Janet in 1955. Implemented on various farms, particularly in areas where farming is done on slopes greater than 10 degrees, the practice has proved to be very effective regarding soil and water conservation. Specifically, monitoring and evaluation of the practice has shown to reduce runoff velocities; to reduce the transport water-borne contaminants; to increase and prolong infiltration rates; to protect water quality in adjacent water bodies; and to protect growing crops from wind-borne soil particles. The technology involves growing row crops, forages, small grains or fallow in a systematic arrangement of equal width strips across a field. Strip cropping is presently practised in hillside areas including the Madigras and Points fields, and the flood prone area of Lasagesse, which is part of the Eastern Agricultural District. Signs of traditional implementation of the technology are currently visible in old agricultural estates.

Figure 1. Strip cropping

©FAO/TECA

1. Implementation of the technology

  • For the implementation of the technology, mark out contour lines along the plot of land to be cultivated using a Frame Abney Level.
  • Establish strips of equal distances along the contour or across the general slope if sheet or rill erosion is a concern, or perpendicular to the prevailing wind to limit wind erosion.
  • The effectiveness of this practice is maximized when the strips are as close as possible to the contour.
  • Strips susceptible to erosion should be alternated down the slope with strips of erosion-resistant cover.
  • Arrange crops so that strips requiring intense cultivation with less protective cover are alternated with more permanent crops offering greater protective cover during times when erosion is expected to occur.
  • Erosion susceptible strips are generally defined as row crops or fallow with less than 10 percent surface residue cover and minimal surface roughness when erosion potential is greatest.
  • An erosion-resistant strip generally consists of dense grasses and/or legumes; hay crops nearing the end of the first year; or row crops with surface cover greater than 75 percent during heightened periods of soil erosion.
  • A variety of vegetables, fruit trees, tree crops, and tubers/cover crops can be grown depending on farmers' needs.
    • For example, the following three options can be cultivated as part of a strip cropping system.

1.1 First option

  • Strip 1
    • Use corn as a protective cover.
  • Strip 2
    • Vegetables (e.g. hot peppers) and beans can also be integrated into this system by allowing to run on mature corn stalks.

1.2 Second option

  • Strip 1
    • Use fruit trees as a protective cover.
  • Strip 2
    • Use vegetables.
  • Strip 3
    • Use cinnamon (Cinnamomum zeylanicum) and vegetables or other more suitable crops.

The soil is prepared based on crop needs, and crops are cultivated simultaneously.

To ensure effective planning, the following must be considered. 

    • Spatial arrangements of plants
    • Planting rates
    • Maturity dates.
  • In the case of cinnamon, a staggered harvesting strategy is recommended to limit soil and water loss.
    • For instance, each row of cinnamon can be harvested at intervals of three months or alternating plants in each row.
  • This practice maintains consistent vegetative cover, minimizing soil erosion and associated externalities.
  • This practice can be augmented by integrating grass barriers or field borders, such as hedgerows of angelica fence, fruit trees or tree crops to further reduce the velocity of ground and upper altitude wind.
  • It is important to note that strip cropping is most effective when used as part of a resource management system, integrating a variety of conservation practices, such as crop rotation, minimum tillage, etc.
  • Strip cropping is one of the least costly conservation practices implementing.
  • This investment usually includes the cost of labour and/or fuel, and in some cases may involve a change in planned cropping sequences.
  • The primary installation cost could include the cost of establishing grasses and legumes in a long-term crop rotation.
  • Technical support from the extension division of the Ministry of Agriculture is required.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Soil and water conservation: ID 7861.
  • Strip intercropping to reduce climate hazard impacts: ID 7705.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: manually operated strippers and shellers: ID 7318.
  • Soil and water conservation practices: ID 5571.
  • Mechanical soil conservation strategies to reduce soil erosion: ID 8208.
  • Multi-storied agroforestry cropping systems for micro-climatic modification and erosion control: ID 7711.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Pro-poor technology

This practice benefits the farmers by achieving higher yields as a result of soil conservation.

entries.tittle: Routine tree management practices: Pruning and Cutting tree tops, Grenada
entries.summary: The routine tree management practices, such as pruning and cutting tree tops have been identified as among the most cost effective, easy to replicate and highly sustainable agricultural risk reduction technologies currently implemented. These practices comprise of cutting tree tops and shrubs strengthens trees so that they better withstand hurricanes and strong winds. Additionally, this prevents branches from falling on and damaging underlying crops. This practice also allows sun light to penetrate through the tree branches, thus benefiting crops. In addition, the cut vegetation, if left on the ground, may contribute to soil fertilization.
entries.description:
Description

The devastations caused by the extremely severe hurricane seasons in Grenada in the past few years highlighted the great vulnerability of its agricultural sector. The application of this technology helps in reducing damages of trees from hurricanes and strong winds during hazardous events.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • Pruning should be undertaken once a year before the blossoming period (October to November).
  • Pruning can be achieved by applying the following steps. 

1.1 Pruning steps

  • Identify the terminal shoot in the targeted tree.
  • Use a saw or other appropriate tools to cut the terminal shoot at the desired height and work from the top centre of the plant.
    • Maintain the height of the tree at about 15 ft. to 25 ft. (4.5 m to 7.5 m) by routinely topping the terminal shoot to allow auxiliary branches to expand.
    • This increases the amount of sunlight filtering through the tree, which is beneficial to crops.
  • Identify unwanted branches (e.g. dry) and suckers and balance the tree by carefully removing unwanted branches on both sides.
    • This is critical for improving the resilience of the tree to hurricanes and strong winds.
    • Branches must be cut as close to the trunk as possible.
      • This encourages quick healing of wounds and helps to prevent the entry of insects (e.g. termites) and pathogenic organisms.
  • Apply a small amount of tar on the cut surface and cover with plastic or other water-resistant containers to prevent rotting and entry of pests and pathogenic organisms

1.2 Tools

The tools needed are a pruning knife, a saw, tar, a container and plastic sheets.

Figure 1. Before tree pruning

©FAO/TECA

  • For the tree pruning, it is recommended to request technical support from the Extension Division of the Ministry of Agriculture.
  • The Ministry of Agriculture working in collaboration with a number of strategic partners, including The Caribbean Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI) is training farmers on the best pruning practices for decades.
    • The adoption of the practice is fairly widespread at this time.
Figure 2. After tree pruning

©FAO/TECA

2. Validation of the practice

  • This practice was applied by farmers in Grenada.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Coconut leaf pruning in Bicol region: ID 7699.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology helps in reducing damages of trees during hazardous events, improving the livelihoods of poor communities.

entries.tittle: Raised bed lotus cultivation, Viet Nam
entries.summary: Cultivating lotus in raised beds is a local adaptation practice in flood prone areas of the Quang Tri province of north central Viet Nam. Communities traditionally collected lotus seeds from plants grown in common water bodies and sold them in markets. However, there was no initiative to further develop, promote and disseminate this practice. The practice of raised beds has been recognized as suitable for broader replication in flood prone areas only recently, and communities have started to engage in cultivating lotus in low lying flood prone areas.
entries.description:
Description

Lotus cultivation on raised beds can be implemented during the rainy season from September to December in the low-lying areas of the country, on land that farmers would otherwise leave fallow due to excessive water stagnation. The objective of this practice is, to ensure production at a time when cultivation would ordinarily be impossible, providing employment opportunities and household income during floods.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • The cultivation of lotus in raised beds requires drainage of excess water through small channels in order to create favourable soil conditions for the cultivation and to counteract the impact of heavy rainfall and strong cyclonic storms that regularly affect north-central Viet Nam.
  • This practice is most successful in freshwater ecosystems with heavy textured soils.
    • The raised beds should be 30 cm to 50 cm high and 100 cm wide, in order to create favourable soil conditions.
    • Drainage channels should be wide (100 cm).
    • Lotus seeds are sown on the raised beds.

1.2 Costs

  • The initial cost of land preparation is substantial.
    • However, family labourers can be engaged in preparing the raised beds.
    • Lotus seeds for cultivation are usually available locally.
  • Primary beneficiaries are small farmers and small local businessmen.
  • Lotus cultivation provides employment opportunities during flood season and increases household income.
  • This practice does not imply any maintenance costs, but the raised beds need a slight readjustment every year before the beginning of the rainy season.
  • Institutional support is required to disseminate this practice into other ecologically similar regions.
  • Local market facilities to procure lotus seeds have to be established and should be connected with export institutions.
  • Institutional interventions are necessary in order to curtail exploitation by middlemen.
  • Local community‑based organizations and financial institutions need to be strengthened to promote the replication of the practice.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Cultivating lotus on raised beds in flood prone areas: ID 7578.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The practice allows for crop production to take place during a time when cultivation would ordinarily be impossible during rain/ flood seasons.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

This practice requires very little investment and provides employment opportunities. It generates income during the rainy season.
entries.further_reading:
5. Further reading

  • Sayre, Kenneth D. 2006. Raised Bed Cultivation, in Encyclopedia of Soil Science, Taylor & Frances.

entries.tittle: Construction of hurricane - resistant poultry pen, Grenada
entries.summary: The construction of low-cost and hazard‑resistant poultry units is a disaster mitigation measure as it ensures immediate post-disaster food availability and protects income sources. The construction of hurricane-resistant farm structures was recommended during a national workshop in Grenada as one of the most easily reproducible, effective, affordable, and sustainable disaster risk reduction strategies for the Caribbean region. This practice describes the steps needed to build a poultry unit.
entries.description:
Description

Protecting poultry during hazardous events is crucial because poultry is an important livelihood asset for farmers. Post hazard selling of eggs or poultry increases farmers’ flexibility and ability to quickly recover after a hurricane has occurred.

1. Implementation of the technology

To implement the technology farmers should follow these steps:

  • Build concrete walls at least 2 feet underground and 8 inches (20.3 cm) above the floor area, with posts cast 1 foot into a concrete wall and studded with galvanized nails.
  • Posts should be 8 feet (2.44 m) tall on the long sides and 10 feet (about 3 m) or more on the gable or short side and planted 5 feet (about 1.52 m) apart.
    • The higher the gable, the more effective ventilation will be.
  • A gable roof is ideal for houses, as opposed to a flat or shed shaped roof, facilitating better heat control.
  • Rafters should be placed 3 feet (92 cm) apart and bolted down to the post or the laths with hurricane straps.
  • Galvanized sheets should be screwed down to laths, if drive screws are used, each protruding nail must be bent underneath.
  • The floor area should preferably be of concrete slab, (2.5 inches to 3 inches; 6.4 cm to 7.6 cm) thick, allowing easy cleaning and disinfecting.
  • A floor depth of 8 inches to 10 inches (20.3 cm to 25.4 cm) is recommended for good litter airflow.
  • Sixteen gauge 0.5 inch x 1 inch (1.3 cm x 2.5 cm) or half-inch square are the recommended wire mesh for poultry houses.
    • It should be attached from the side of the floor up to the galvanized sheet, to keep out wild birds and rodents.
  • Where necessary, curtains should always be attached from the base of the pen to the optimal height to facilitate better control of natural elements (sun, wind, rain).
    • Attaching the curtain from the base gives the farmer greater control in managing the temperature inside the pen since the curtain can be rolled up to the point where protection is needed and not necessarily cover the entire side of the pen.

1.1 Implementation and maintenance requirements

  1. Inputs: Building materials
  2. Costs: EC$ 2.50 per square foot
  3. Maintenance: Routine inspection
  • The floor area of the poultry pen should preferably be of concrete slab 2 inches to 3 inches (6.4 cm to 7.6 cm) thick to allow for easy cleaning and disinfecting.
    • A floor depth of 8 inches to 10 inches (20.3 cm to 25.4 cm) is recommended for good litter airflow. 
Figure 1. The floor area of the poultry pen

©FAO/TECA

  • Curtains should always be attached from the bottom of the pen to facilitate better control of natural elements such as sun, wind and rain. 
Figure 2. Curtains attached to the poultry pen

©FAO/TECA

2. Validation of the practice

  • The technology was tested in mixed coastal plantation farming systems (in the agro-ecological zone of warm subhumid tropics).

3. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Construction of a concrete floor and foot bath within an existing poultry pen to reduce the risk of infection and disease in poultry: ID 7741.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

Poultry units can be built at low costs, and farmers benefit from building them by maintaining their income.
entries.further_reading:
6. Further reading

  • Roberts, Dianne A., Shears, Randolph. 2007. Assistance to Improve Local Agricultural Emergency Preparedness in Caribbean Countries Highly Prone to Hydro-Meteorological Disasters – Grenada Case Study (TCP/RLA/3101), Interim Findings and Recommendations, January 2007.
  • Grenada Ministry of Agriculture. 2004. Assessment of damages resulting from hurricane Ivan.

For more information, please contact: Stephan Baas at Stephan.Baas@fao.org

entries.tittle: Sylvi-pastoral and hedgerow systems in integrated farming systems, India
entries.summary: Low income farmers in semi-arid tropics, such as in the low rainfall areas of southern India traditionally combine different activities to diversify livelihoods so as to reduce the impact of natural hazards like drought. The Acacia Leucophoea and Cenchrus Ciliaris sylvi-pastoral system is an integrated sylvi-pastoral farming system that provides adequate fodder for goats and sheep, along with firewood to meet household requirements. Annual crops like maize and sorghum can be grown between the tree rows, which helps to protect the soil, reduce soil erosion and diversify livelihoods. Forage grasses are planted between the tree rows to increase total fodder supply to animals. Trees also act as windbreaks. The objective of the practice is to reduce the risk of complete production loss in the case of droughts and helps to diversify the livelihoods of low-income farmers.
entries.description:
Description

Combining different activities to diversify livelihoods and income dependencies is an age-old practice among the low-income small farmers in semi-arid India. However, recent research and development work has identified an optimized mix of household strategies for drought risk management in semi-arid tropics. The technology was implemented in the low rainfall uplands in peninsular India.

1. Implementation of the practice

  • This technology was tested in mixed rainfed farming systems in India (agro-ecological zone of warm semi-arid tropics).
  • One of the solutions suitable for low rainfall areas is the Acacia leucophoea and Cenchrus ciliaris based silvopastoral system, which is an integrated farming system that provides adequate fodder for goats and sheep, along with firewood to meet household requirements.
  • Annual crops like maize and sorghum can be grown between tree rows to maximize the benefits under silvo-agriculture systems.
  • This practice is suitable for protecting the soil and reducing soil erosion.
  • Similarly, Leucaena leucocephala (Lam.) may be planted as single or multiple hedgerows, depending on the rainfall pattern and the type of alley cropping component.
  • In the case of multiple hedgerows, the rows may be closely spaced (75 cm to 100 cm) to achieve maximum yield per hectare for cutting-and-carry feeding or more widely spaced (3 m to 10 m) for alley cropping or grazing.
  • Forage grasses may be planted in widely spaced rows for grazing.
  • Grasses may be planted between Leucaena rows to increase total fodder supply to animals.
    • Panicum maximum, Digitaria decumbens and Cenchrus ciliaris were found to be successful companion grasses for Leucaena.
  • The hedgerows system is useful as windbreaks and it is suitable for a wide range of rainfall environments, from 650 mm to 3 000 mm.

1.1 Suitability

  • The Acacia leucophoea and Cenchrus ciliaris silvopastoral systems are most suitable in low rainfall zones with less than 700 mm of rainfall.
  • It is also effective to protect the soil from excess erosion on steep slopes.
  • The Leucaena based alley system performs well in a wide range of rainfall environments from 650 mm to 3000 mm.
  • However, extreme dry conditions and water stagnation in impeded drainage soils are not suitable for this system.

2. Cost estimate

  • The costs for setting up silvopastoral systems are relatively low.
  • The initial costs include the preparation of pits for planting tree species and grass cuttings.
  • The grass cuttings can be collected from existing pastures. Minimum maintenance costs are necessary for pruning and maintaining small basins surrounding the trees to facilitate water harvesting.

2.1 Institutional support

  • Adequate awareness regarding the use of silvopastoral systems is required.
  • Technical support for the cultivation aspects of growing tree species and grass is necessary.
  • The provision of quality tree seedlings is important.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Silvopastoral systems for cattle raising: ID 8954.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2666.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Pro-poor technology

Small farmers benefit most from the silvopastoral system. In addition, landless people with livestock may benefit, if collaborative arrangements with farmers can be established.

entries.tittle: Risk diversification through taro (Colocasia esculenta) cultivation in areas prone to floods and water logging, Bangladesh
entries.summary: The objective of latiraj kachu cultivation is to enable small farmers to grow crops even during flooding season on seasonally flooded land, and to enhance diet diversification and food security of households during a period of the year characterized by food scarcity. This practice describes the conditions under which latiraj kachu can be cultivated.
entries.description:
Description

Seasonal floods leave parts of Bangladesh, especially the northern/central districts, inundated for a number of months. During the flood period, farmers have few choices of what crops to grow, and often lack access to adequate food and nutrition. However, certain crops, like aroids, have good potential for production in the wet season, since most of them (such as latiraj kachu (pani kachu), an improved variety of mukhi kachu (Colocasia esculenta) known as taro), can be grown in the seasonally flooded land and can survive a certain period under water. Latiraj is a good source of carbohydrate and other nutrients, supplementing a diet that tends to be deficient during this particular period. The leaves and tubers are edible when cooked. This excellent tropical Taro can grow up to 1.5 m. Colocasia esculenta can be easily propagated by dividing the rhizomes.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • For latiraj cultivation, farmers must have access to supplementary irrigation facilities.
    • Silty loam and clay loam soils are suitable for latiraj.
    • Before sowing the land needs to be tilled three to four times to reduce soil to small particles.
    • The optimum time of sowing for an early crop is October, and seeds must be sown in line at a rate of 38 000 per hectare.
    • The distance between lines should be 36 cm, and between plants within the line it should be 5 cm.
  • The crop requires adequate fertilizer application at the rate of 25 kg urea per bigha (1 330 m2) urea, 18 kg per bigha triple super-phosphate (TSP) and 25 kg per bigha of muriate of potash (MoP).
    • Organic manures, preferably cow dung at the rate of 2 500 kg per bigha should be applied at the time of sowing.
    • Basal application of entire TSP and MoP is recommended, while urea should be applied in three splits before 20 to 25 days of planting.
  • The plants can also be grown indoors all year round, in a pot if preferred.
    • In that case, they require plenty of water in the growing season and need to be kept very dry from October to March to prevent rot.
Figure 1. Mukhi kachu

©FAO/TECA

2. Validation of the practice

The taro cultivation was tested in mixed rainfed farming systems in north-western Bangladesh, in the agro-ecological zone of warm humid tropics. 

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for the diversification of crop production and use during different seasons.

entries.tittle: Banano FHIA-03
entries.summary: El híbrido FHIA-03 es un banano de cocción enano tipo “Bluggoe”, que fue desarrollado en 1987. Tiene un alto potencial para varios países de África del Oeste y Este, donde existen muchas veces áreas marginales que no permiten un buen desarrollo del banano Cavendish. En la actualidad, se encuentra en producción comercial en Cuba, donde ya existen más de 3 500 hectáreas sembradas con este híbrido. También se encuentra distribuido en Burundi, Camerún y Nigeria, entre otros.
entries.description:
Descripción

1. Características

  • El híbrido FHIA-03 es un banano de cocción enano tipo “Bluggoe”, que fue desarrollado en 1987.
  • Tiene un alto potencial para varios países de África del Oeste y Este, donde existen muchas veces áreas marginales que no permiten un buen desarrollo del banano Cavendish.
  • En la actualidad, se encuentra en producción comercial en Cuba, donde ya existen más de 3 500 hectáreas sembradas con este híbrido.
  • También se encuentra distribuido en Burundi, Camerún y Nigeria, entre otros.

1.1 Morfología

  • La planta mide entre 2,5 y 3,7 m; tiene hojas decumbentes y un tallo opaco.
  • El racimo es cilíndrico y cuelga verticalmente a la planta.
  • Los frutos, de color verde, son rectas en la parte distal; el ápice de las frutas es puntiagudo.
  • FHIA-03 es un tetraploide que no produce semillas.
  • Por ser una planta de porte bajo y muy resistente, puede sostener racimos de hasta 50 kg sin soporte.
Figura 1. Racimo de FHIA-03

©FHIA/TECA

1.2 Fenología

  • El tiempo de la siembra hasta la floración es entre 271 y 307 días; el primer ciclo productivo, o sea, de parición a cosecha es de 100 a 110 días.
  • La segunda floración se presenta a los 430 a 530 días después de la siembra.

1.3 Producción

  • El peso neto del racimo, que es el peso sin raquis, está entre 30 kg y 40 kg, con un número de dedos por racimo de 198 a 226.
  • El peso de los dedos individuales oscila entre 155 y 179 g.
Figura 2. Racimos de FHIA-03 (izquierda), la variedad Bluggoe (centro) y una variedad proveniente de África Oriental (derecha)

©FHIA

1.4 Características de resistencia

  • El híbrido es resistente al Mal de Panamá, la Sigatoka negra y la Marchitez bacteriana (Moko).
  • Además, presenta resistencia parcial al nematodo Radopholus similis. Es susceptible al nematodo Pratylenchus coffeae.

2. Aspectos agronómicos

2.1 Requerimientos agroecológicos

  • El cultivo es capaz de prosperar en una amplia gama de condiciones agroecológicas en las cuales otras variedades similares muestran limitaciones.
  • Es tolerante a períodos prolongados de sequía y produce aún en suelos pobres. También es adaptado a alturas más elevadas.
    • Altura: FHIA-03 crece bien a alturas de 0 a 1 500 metros sobre el nivel del mar.
    • Suelos: produce aún en suelos marginales.
    • Precipitación pluvial: debe ser aproximadamente 2000 mm pro año, bien espaciada.
    • Temperatura: la temperatura óptima es de 28 °C.

2.2 Manejo agronómico

  • Se recomiendan densidades de siembra altas, empleando doble hileras a una distancia de 1 m entre sí y 5 m entre surcos.
  • De esta manera, y si se siembra a una distancia de 2 m entre plantas, se obtendrá una densidad de 2000 plantas por ha.
  • Con un distanciamiento de 1 metro entre plantas, la densidad será de 4 000 plantas a ha.
  • Este sistema requiere resiembra después de 1 a 2 ciclos de producción, pero es mucho más rentable que el sistema convencional de siembra a bajas densidades (1 600 a 1 700 plantas por ha).
  • La fertilización se realiza en base a los resultados del análisis de suelo realizado.
  • Para las condiciones del Valle de Sula (Honduras), se recomienda aplicar 300 kg de nitrógeno y 250 kg de potasio por hectárea por año.
  • Se debe realizar un deshoje cada cuatro semanas, eliminando hojas dobladas y realizando despunte.
  • Cada ocho semanas se realiza un deshije.
  • El deshermane se efectúa a los cuatro meses después de la siembra.

2.3 Poscosecha

  • FHIA-03 presenta un excelente sabor cuando es cocido verde.
  • Cuando está maduro, tiene sabor a “manzana”.
  • El tiempo de cocción es la mitad del requerido por la variedad “Bluggoe”.
  • Hay que tener en cuenta, sin embargo, que su vida verde es corta una vez cosechado el racimo.
  • Se sugiere su utilización solamente para consumo en los hogares y no para su venta.
  • También es recomendable cosechar mano por mano.

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Producción de cormos de plátano y banano para siembra directa en campo: ID 8149
  • Manejo de Sigatoka negra (Mycosphaerella fijiensis Morelet) en plantaciones de plátano y banano: ID 8306
  • Prácticas de protección de plantas de banano (Musa AAA) en su fase productiva: ID 8335
  • Material de siembra de alta calidad en la en renovación de plantaciones de plátano y banano: ID 8336
  • Banano FHIA 18, ideal para procesamiento: ID 3751

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

El banano FHIA-03 da una descripción general de cómo producir bananos de manera eficiente para el mercado nacional.

5.2 Atiende a las necesidades de la mujer

La tecnología no requiere mucha mano de obra y se puede realizar con cualquier trabajo manual.

5.3 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta práctica permite a los agricultores producir bananas adecuadas para la venta, aumentando así sus ingresos.
entries.further_reading:
6. El contacto

De esta manera, la FHIA continúa apoyando la modernización de la agricultura de Honduras y de otros países, generando innovaciones tecnológicas y proporcionando servicios de asistencia técnica de calidad.

Persona de contacto: 

  • Adolfo Martínez
  • Email de contacto: fhia@fhia-hn.org
  • Web: http://www.fhia-hn.org/
  • País: Honduras

entries.tittle: Producción Caprina y pase de Cadena, Guatemala
entries.summary: Las personas beneficiadas por la aplicación de esta tecnología han recibido capacitaciones en el manejo de la especie caprina, construyen cabrerizas y luego reciben una cabra hembra en etapa reproductiva, sin coste, pero con el compromiso escrito de entregar una cría hembra de más de 6 meses para favorecer a otro nuevo usuario la misma oportunidad.
entries.description:
Descripción

  • El proyecto se inició en 1987 apoyado por Heifer International Project en la aldea El Pinalito (Guatemala).
  • En 1996 se llegaron a beneficiar 546 familias y en 2004 poseen cabras alrededor de 300 familias.

1. Área y causas de difusión actual

  • Nueve comunidades de la parte alta de Chiquimula (Guatemala): Pinalito, El Conacaste, Guayabo, Palmar, Guayabillas, El Mojón, El Limón, El Durazno y El Limar.
  • Se considera un área potencial la región oriental.

2. Pasos del proceso concreto de implementación de esta práctica

  • Las personas beneficiadas han recibido capacitaciones para el manejo de la especie, construyen cabrerizas (ver archivo adjunto) y luego reciben una cabra hembra en etapa reproductiva, sin coste, pero con el compromiso escrito de entregar una cría hembra de más de seis meses para favorecer a otro nuevo usuario la misma oportunidad que han tenido ellos.
  • A este procedimiento se le llama pase de cadena.
    • Se recomienda el manejo estabulado de la cabra y su alimentación se basa principalmente en pastos y hojas de árboles forrajeros que son cortados y llevados a las cabras.
    • La producción de leche por cabra es de 1,25 litros por día de media.

3. Costos de referencia

  • El costo aproximado de la cabreriza es de 300 Q (unos 27,5 EUR) y el de la cabra de 450 Q (41 EUR aproximadamente).
  • La cabra produce dos partos por año, de dos crías cada uno.
  • En algunos casos se obtienen ingresos por venta de excedentes de leche, en aquellos productores que poseen más de una cabra.

4. Instituciones u organizaciones que apoyan la implementación de la práctica

  • Actualmente ACODAPCHI (Asociación de Comités de Desarrollo Agropecuario de Chiquimula) con sede y área de acción en las comunidades mencionadas en el primer apartado contribuye, con bastantes limitaciones, en el mantenimiento y seguimiento de este proyecto.

5. Justificación de la aplicación y difusión actual y/o potencial de la práctica

  • El proyecto caprino de la parte alta de Chiquimula (Guatemala) se considera que es el que ha mostrado la mayor sostenibilidad entre todos los proyectos caprinos del oriente de Guatemala.
  • Se han alcanzado interesantes logros en aspectos genéticos y de producción, lo que ha propiciado que diferentes proyectos de desarrollo a nivel nacional busquen a las cabras de esta zona para fortalecer sus actividades caprinas.

6. Observaciones y ampliaciones

  • Para proyectos de seguridad alimentaria esta tecnología presenta la ventaja de que la leche, por ser un producto perecedero, no puede almacenarse, lo que limita su almacenamiento para comercialización y el producto se consume por la familia y generalmente más por los niños.
  • Existen otros proyectos caprinos de reciente introducción que trabajan con metodologías similares a la de la parte alta de Chiquimula (Guatemala).
  • En San José La Arada, MOVIMUNDO (ver referencia adjunta), ha introducido cabras en 5 comunidades. PRODERT (ver referencia adjunta) ha introducido cerca de 20 cabras en comunidades de Ipala (Chiquimula) y Asunción Mita (Jutiapa), el Proyecto FAO-CUNORI ha iniciado la introducción de cabras en algunas escuelas de Jocotán (Guatemala).

7. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

8. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Rearing dairy goats: ID 6925.
  • Stall fed systemrearing goats: ID 8770.
  • Farmers dairy goat production handbook: ID 6939.
  • Improvement of livestock production: community based goat production: ID 4495.
  • Goat raising in controlled areas and vaccination: ID 8937.
  • Intensive stall-fed system for rearing goats: ID 8770.

9. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

9.1 Eficiencia en el uso de los recursos

La cría de cabras permite a los agricultores una producción caprina de manera asequible y sostenible y todos se benefician eficientemente del intercambio regular de cabras.

9.2 Atiende a las necesidades de la mujer

La tecnología no es un trabajo pesado y puede emprenderse con cualquier trabajo manual.

9.3 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

La práctica facilita el acceso a capacitaciones para el manejo de la especie y al intercambio de conocimientos sobre prácticas mejoradas de crianza y cría. Esto proporciona fuentes de ingresos mayores y contribuye a la seguridad alimentaria.

entries.tittle: Módulos Pecuarios Escolares, Guatemala
entries.summary: Los diagnósticos participativos llevados a cabo en las comunidades Kaqchiqueles y en las que trabaja el PESA (Xibalbay, Oratorio y Chaquiyá, municipio de Sololá) indicaron un déficit en acceso y consumo de proteína animal, por lo que se decidió trabajar con Módulo Pecuario (MP) de pollos de engorde. Las aves sirven como fuente de ingresos (al venderlas vivas o como carne), y como fuente de proteínas (al ser consumidas por los beneficiarios). Esta actividad es promovida por un grupo de 20 a 30 mujeres de promedio.
entries.description:
Descripción

1. ¿En qué consiste un módulo pecuario?

  • El MP estándar consiste en una jaula de 2 m3 con potencial para albergar un máximo de 25 pollos.
    • Esta jaula está hecha de malla al frente y en los laterales (para poder recibir luz solar directa).
    • La parte de atrás está cerrada con tablas o caña de carrizo.
    • El piso de la jaula es de tablas o madera rústica, sobre la que se coloca el colchón de aserrín o viruta.
    • El techo es de lámina de zinc.
    • El MP se cubre con cortinas de costal para protegerlo del frío nocturno.
    • En el interior de la jaula están colocados los comederos, hechos de tablas o de bambú, y los bebederos, hechos de envases de gaseosas.
      • Algunas familias utilizan guacales de plástico.
    • La altura al suelo de la jaula es de 0,30 a 0,50 m.
      • Esta es una recomendación fundamental debido a la humedad del suelo.
    • En algunos casos las familias han construido la jaula de manera que se pueda mover de un lado a otro.
    • Otras familias han construido una jaula rústica, con materiales sencillos, fácilmente disponibles en la comunidad (adobe y madera).
      • En este tipo de módulo entra menos luz (porque la madera sustituye a la malla de acero) pero es mucho más barato.

2. Organización de un módulo pecuario

  • La metodología de diseminación de esta buena práctica ha sido especialmente cuidada y elaborada por el PESA.
  • Una vez detectada la necesidad, y tras haber discutido con la comunidad beneficiaria la idoneidad del MP, se procede a organizar una primera reunión en la que se les explican los pasos del proceso. La organización del proceso de implantación incluye:
    • el compartir los gastos del paquete entre las beneficiarias;
    • la formación de un comité para dirigir, gestionar, organizar y administrar las actividades del grupo;
    • la capacitación sobre el manejo de los pollos;
    • la formalización de la entrega del módulo mediante un convenio donde la socia se compromete a devolver el 50 por ciento de la inversión inicial que hace el PESA (para ir formando un fondo revolvente o capital semilla).
  • El siguiente paso, después de aceptados los requisitos, es la formación del comité mediante una elección democrática entre las socias.
  • Con la participación del comité, se establece un reglamento interno para regular las actividades del grupo.
    • Este reglamento incluye las obligaciones y derechos de las socias, las funciones del comité y el uso del fondo del grupo.
  • El PESA le brinda asesoría al comité en relación a las funciones de la junta directiva, la elaboración de los convenios y la importancia del trabajo solidario y en equipo, poniendo especial énfasis en la participación en la toma de decisiones del grupo.
  • Estas capacitaciones para el fortalecimiento de la organización de mujeres se realizan durante todo el periodo de ejecución de la actividad.
  • Otra de las actividades importantes del grupo es la capacitación sobre el manejo de las aves.
  • Además de la diseminación de estas técnicas, el PESA asesora al comité en la compra de los pollos y los insumos.
    • Este proceso se da sólo en el primer ciclo.
    • En los sucesivos, todas las acciones son realizadas exclusivamente por el grupo a través del comité.
  • Al finalizar el convenio entre el PESA y el comité (con una duración máxima de dos meses), el grupo se reúne para hacer liquidar los aspectos financieros pendientes en dicho convenio y planificar el siguiente ciclo.
    • En el convenio (primer ciclo) cada socia debe reintegrar al grupo el 60 por ciento de la inversión inicial del PESA.
    • En el segundo ciclo cada socia debe reintegrar el 100 por ciento de la inversión, más el 2 por ciento en concepto de interés.
    • Esto último tiene por objeto incrementar el capital del grupo y poder así beneficiar a más familias de la comunidad.
  • Actualmente (marzo 2003) el PESA Guatemala apoya a tres grupos de mujeres en el municipio de Sololá con esta buena práctica.
    • Estos grupos se encuentran en diferentes ciclos de producción.
    • En total contabilizan 60 beneficiarias-socias.

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Huertos escolares: ID 7219.
  • Huerto familiar integrado: ID 7221.
  • Guía para el funcionamiento de huertos escolares: ID 7220.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta práctica contribuye a una mejora en acceso y consumo de proteína animal, creando una dieta sostenible y saludable, entre otros.

5.2 Atiende a las necesidades de la mujer

Las mujeres juegan un papel importante en esta práctica, porque particpan en ella y muchas otras familias también se benefician de ella.

5.3 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Los módulos pecuarios escolares conducen a largo plazo al incremento del capital y la seguridad y soberanía alimentaria.
entries.further_reading:
6. Lecturas complementarias

  • FAO. 2017. Guia para la Formulación de los Proyectos de Inversión del sector agropecuario. Bajo el enfoque planificación estratégica y gestión por resultados.

entries.tittle: Silos para el Almacenamiento de Granos Básicos, Guatemala
entries.summary: El uso de los silos para el almacenamiento de granos básicos en Guatemala ha sido fomentado durante varios años por organizaciones como Digesa, Postcosecha, Prozachi, Caritas. El enfoque principal es evitar los daños producidos por insectos y roedores en los granos básicos asegurando el alimento para la familia.
entries.description:
Descripción

1. Áreas y causas de difusión actual

  • Es una práctica sencilla difundida en el municipio de Chiquimula y alrededores que evita los daños producidos por insectos y roedores en los granos básicos asegurando el alimento para la familia.

2. Pasos del proceso

  • El proceso concreto de aplicación de esta tecnología se puede resumir en los siguientes puntos:
    1. cosecha;
    2. desgrane, trilla;
    3. secado;
    4. acondicionamiento y tratamiento (silos y trojas mejoradas);
    5. aireación;
    6. sellado de silos;
    7. revisiones periódicas;
    8. comercialización.

2.1 Costos de referencia (2004)

  • La inversión que será necesaria realizar para la instalación de la tecnología será aproximadamente: costo del silo de 810 kg: 280 Q.

3. Instituciones u organizaciones que apoyan la implementación de la práctica

  • Los apoyos más importantes para la instalación de los silos para almacenamiento de granos básicos por parte del agricultor son realizados por instituciones como: Postcosecha, Caritas, FAO-PESA y Prozachi.

4. Justificación de la aplicación y difusión actual y/o potencial de la práctica

  • La principal razón para la instalación de estos silos es la utilización de éstos como medio para asegurar la alimentación de la población y reducir las pérdidas postcosecha.

5. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

6. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Silo metálico plano para granos básicos: ID 6486.
  • Cultivo de granos básicos con manejo integrado de la fertilidad con bioabonos: ID 5994.
  • Elaboración y utilización de silos de montón: ID 6472.
  • Silos (trojas) de grano: limitar pérdidas por humedad: ID 6485.
  • Silos (trojas) de grano: descripción y características básicas: ID 6484.

7. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

7.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología conlleva muchos efectos positivos, como una mejor calidad del grano y la garantía de la seguridad alimentaria, lo que conduce a una dieta sana y rica en nutrientes para los seres humanos.

7.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta práctica contribuye a evitar pérdidas de granos básicos en el almacenamiento, reduciendo así las pérdidas postcosecha.

entries.tittle: Producción de Aceite de Zapote o Zapuyul (Diospyros Digyna), Guatemala
entries.summary: Esta tecnología tiene su fundamento en el aprovechamiento de recursos naturales. Describe brevemente el proceso de elaboración del aceite de zapuyul (Diospyros digyna), desde la compra de semilla hasta su comercialización. Esta tecnología se practica desde hace 50 años en el municipio de San Agustín Acasaguastlán en el departamento de El Progreso (Guatemala).
entries.description:
Descripción

Esta tecnología es una práctica que utiliza la semilla del zapote (Diospyros digyna) como materia prima (Figuras 1 y 2). El zapote es cultivado en diferentes comunidades del departamento del Progreso (Guatemala) y otras zonas de Latinoamérica. Esta práctica se realiza desde la época colonial debido a que al aceite de zapote o zapuyul se le atribuyen propiedades medicinales.

Figura 1. Fruto del zapote en las ramas del árbol

©FAO/TECA

Figura 2. Fruto del zapote abierto y su semilla al centro

©FAO/TECA

1. Áreas y causas de difusión actual

Tres familias de la comunidad han replicado esta práctica debido a la demanda del aceite de zapuyul. Área potencial de difusión: Oriente de Guatemala.

1.1 Pasos del proceso

Los pasos de esta práctica son los siguientes:

  • compra de semilla seca sin cáscara;
  • picado de la semilla;
  • molido de la semilla;
  • cocimiento de la masa;
  • extracción del aceite;
  • envasado del aceite;
  • comercialización del aceite.

1.2 Costos de referencia

Compra de un quintal de semilla: Q 200.

  • Picado de un quintal de semilla: Q 20.
  • Molido de un quintal: Q 30.
  • Cocimiento: 1 jornal Q 20.
  • Envases: Q 2 c/u.
  • Comercialización: 1 jornal Q 20.
  • Precio de venta por botella: Q 28.

Nota: Los precios pueden no estar actualizados. Sería necesario recalcular los costes previamente a su aplicación.

2. Instituciones u organizaciones que apoyan la implementación de la práctica

Actualmente no existe ninguna institución que está apoyando este proceso. Se ha convertido en una microempresa familiar.

3. Justificación de la aplicación y difusión actual y/o potencial de la práctica

Se trata de una fuente de empleo y de ingresos a nivel familiar siempre y cuando exista disponibilidad local de materia prima.

4. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

5. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Procesamiento de semilla de marañon (anacardo): ID 6021.
  • Integrated Pest Management (IPM) in the quality control for the production of extra virgin olive oil: ID 8607.
  • Method to extract coconut oil: ram press: ID 4588.
  • Coconut oil extraction: intermediate moisture content method: ID 4589.

6. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

6.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

La producción conduce a una elaboración más eficaz del aceite debido a la disponibilidad local de la materia prima.

6.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta práctica representa una fuente estable de ingresos para los productores, ya que el aceite se produce de recursos naturales.
entries.further_reading:
7. Lecturas complementarias

  • Próximamente aparecerá una publicación impresa con estas y otras tecnologías sistematizadas por el programa PESA en Guatemala.
