entries.tittle: Mini Ponds for Resource Poor Households to Provide Supplementary Irrigation during Drought Spells in Rainfed Areas of NW-Bangladesh
entries.summary:
The drought-prone areas of western Bangladesh are characterized by high rainfall variability, with different types of seasonal droughts (initial, mid and terminal) posing regular threats to rice production. During monsoon season in wide areas of NW Bangladesh T. aman rice is cropped on rainfed basis. Risk management options need to include rainwater harvesting, recycling and conservation, essential to counteract seasonal drought spells, which are common also during monsoon season through supplemental irrigation. But huge amounts of the water available during high intensity rainfalls run-off unused, due to non-availability of proper water storage structures. The excavation and/or re-excavation of mini ponds is a simple but most feasible adaptation option, which can be realized with low investment, in particular in clayey soil. Adequate awareness of the utility of these structures must be raised at community level. Obstacles to the practice which is not yet widely spread in northwestern Bangladesh are most commonly the lack of investment capital and of organization among poor farmers.

This practice aims to reduce the impacts of drought spells frequently faced by small and marginal farmers in low rainfall regions of north-western Bangladesh. In addition, farmers can allot larger pieces of land to growing other crops in the post monsoon period, if irrigation is available through the water stored in mini ponds during the monsoon period.
entries.description:
Description

Traditional ponds are good sources for supplementary irrigation for T. aman (transplanted aman) rice production in case of severe drought during monsoon (kharif-II) season in NW Bangladesh. However, they are usually owned or controlled by big farmers in villages and often used as well for fish culture during monsoon season. As fish culture requires considerable water, the use of water from these ponds for the purpose of supplementary irrigation to t.aman rice fields is problematic; poor and marginalized farmers usually do not get access to this water source. Thus, the establishment of mini ponds on their own or on sharecropped fields is a good option for small and marginal farmers with no or limited access to other ponds to harvest rainwater and provide supplementary (emergency) irrigation to their rice fields, in case urgently needed. By doing this the losses from drought spells during monsoon season can be reduced. The technology was successfully tested and frequently replicated by farmers on clay soils, in mixed rainfed farming systems in north-western Bangladesh, agro-ecological zone of warm humid tropics.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • In farmlands with no irrigation source, rainwater harvesting through mini ponds can provide supplemental irrigation.
  • Excavation or re-excavation of mini ponds to store excess rain water is recommended preferably in (at least slightly) sloping terrains.
  • Mini ponds of 5 m x 5 m x 2 m (length x breadth x depth) are preferred in small farms, but larger ponds of 10 m x 10 m x 2 m may be excavated as per requirement and rainwater availability.

1.1 Advantages of implementing the technology

  • The practice is suitable to small and medium landowners.
  • Limited family labour is required for the excavation of the mini pond, which farmers prefer to locate on a corner of the field.
  • The practice is highly suitable and an inexpensive option in low rainfall zones with less than 1 000 mm rainfall and where soils are clay.
  • Ponds can be constructed without cement in heavy clayey soils.
  • This practice is also effective on steep slopes to harvest excess rain water, however exposure to steep topography may require wall enforcements.

1.2 Costs

  • Excavation of mini ponds has minimum costs where soil conditions are suitable.
  • Wherever family labour is available, setting up the structure does usually require only low investment.
  • Excavated soil may be used for the construction of low cost houses with mud walls, or to increase the height of homestead areas, chalas, in seasonally flood prone areas.
    • The cost of excavation of a mini pond in north-western Bangladesh has been estimated at USD 40.
    • If the soil conditions are sandy and cement is needed, costs will be significantly higher.
  • Timely access to small pumps is crucial to ensure supplementary irrigation when and once needed.
    • Access to pumps must be negotiated in advance with pump owners in case poor farmers do not own pumps themselves.
  • Minimum maintenance expenditure for de-silting is required once a year.

1.3 Tips for successful implementation of the technology

  • Technical support for the design and excavation of mini-ponds should be available to farmers.
  • Improved access to micro credit which qualifies for this purpose could facilitate broader replication.
  • The practice may be replicated in other similar areas through local institutional support.
  • Design aspects need to be considered, based on the soil type, rainfall patterns and requirement of water for supplemental irrigation.

1.4 How to improve the implementation of the technology

  • An additional benefit of the pond can be obtained by growing short duration vegetables along the pond.
  • Where needed, to protect the vegetables and/or water from free ranging livestock, light fencing of the ponds and vegetables, is recommended.
Figure 1. Construction of a mini pond

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Mini ponds for resource poor households to provide supplementary irrigation during drought spells in rainfed areas of NW - Bangladesh

©FAO/TECA

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Water conservation ponds: ID 7378.
  • Water management in organic agriculture: ID 8366.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

Limited labour is required for the excavation of the mini pond.

4.2 Resource use efficiency 

Water can be stored in mini ponds during the monsoon period.

4.2 Pro-poor technology 

Excavation of mini ponds has minimum costs.

entries.tittle: Soil conservation through multi - purpose wind breaks/shelter belts in Vietnam
entries.summary:
Properly spaced trees help provide many of the same benefits of a complete perennial cover. Fine soil particles contain most of the humus and nutrients in the soil, and if lost, soil fertility is reduced, while windbreaks help protect cropland by reducing wind velocities for a distance approximately 15 times the height of the tallest trees, thus providing significant reductions in the rate of soil loss over large areas.

Establishing windbreaks is a practice that is highly suitable for degraded soils in the coastal regions of Viet Nam prone to water erosion and to the winds accompanying typhoons during the rainy season. Eucalyptus and cashew, the tree species that have been identified to break the cycle of land degradation, are also suitable for moderately saline soils.
entries.description:
Description

Traditional tree species may be used to protect soils along coasts which are prone to severe soil erosion due to strong winds. Recent interventions of local institutions and community-based organizations in Viet Nam promoted the planting of multi-purpose tree species suitable for moderately saline soils that hold promise for soil conservation and for other benefits. Through this practice, local communities are able to protect their natural resources.

The landless labourers, wage earners and handcraft makers who are the beneficiaries of the practice can also exploit it for livelihood diversification.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • Coastal areas in Viet Nam are prone to soil erosion due to dry winds during the summer season and to the winds that accompany typhoons during the rainy season.
  • Severe soil erosion, the accumulation of sand dunes and salt encrustation on surface soil have reduced the productivity of lands.
  • In addition, the fertility status of soils has been further significantly reduced due to the removal of the topsoil.
    • To break the cycle of further degradation, a number of tree species were identified and their seedlings were raised in community nurseries.
  • The most important tree species identified by local institutions together with the community are eucalyptus and cashew.
    • Cashew trees are usually established on degraded soils in the central coastal provinces.
      • The current spacing adopted is 10 m x 5 m (200 plants per ha).
      • Before 1990, farmers resorted to a density of planting of up to 400 trees per ha.
      • The selected tree species were found to be resistant and effective in reducing soil erosion and wind speed.
  • The practice requires minimum costs for the establishment of plantations.
  • Participation of community members and local disaster management committees can reduce establishment costs.
  • The practice may be implemented in coastal areas through community-based organizations.
    • The provision of spacing, row arrangement and row direction need to be decided on the basis of the tree species and of the rainfall pattern.
  • The maintenance costs for re‑planting and for water control structures along the streams such as check dams to reduce the overland flow of water are minimal.
  • Adequate awareness is required on the use of tree species for windbreaks, the spacing between trees to minimize the mutual shade effect and to protect the soil.
  • Local institutions can supply the tree saplings through community nurseries.

2. Validation of the practice

This practice was applied in Viet Nam.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Mechanical soil conservation strategies to reduce soil erosion: ID 8208.
  • Soil conservation: contour ploughing: ID 4641.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

Planting of multi-purpose tree species improves soil quality and allows local communities to protect their natural resources.

entries.tittle: Construction of traditional granary locally called "Colombier" in Haiti
entries.summary: Traditional agricultural adaptation practices in Haiti address the consequences of natural disasters, preventing and mitigating them. One such practice, intended to reduce the impact of droughts, floods and tropical cyclones and storms, is the construction of a granary called “Colombier”. It is a structure built on high posts where grains and beans may be stored for extended periods of time. This secures them from being washed away or otherwise damaged by catastrophic events. This technology explains how to use and construct a “Colombier”.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

Haiti’s agricultural sector, sustaining 70 per cent of the population is particularly exposed to the impact of hydro-meteorological hazards periodically hitting the island, and poor farming households are compelled to put marginal land under intense cultivation, thus increasing their vulnerability.

The practice of constructing a granary called “Colombier” presented in this document is traditional and common to the Artibonite and Central part of Haiti, where it dates back centuries (Figure 1). It is used to store grains like sorghum and/or common beans for extended periods of time (six months or longer). The natural disasters this technique addresses are drought, flood, rain, and windstorm. In the rest of the country, alternative dominant ways to store the harvested grains include silo storing, installation on a tree branch in the case of unpicked-off corn, and storing on the ìgallatasî, that is, the room between the ceiling and the roof of the farm house.

Figure 1. Traditional granary, “Colombier” in French (up) to store and conserve the won crops, particularly harvested grains placed in bulk (down left and right) when not yet picked off, or initially placed in a pre-processed calabash (down center) for better and longer protection

©FAO/TECA

  • Calabashes (Figure 2), small capacity containers for long time storing, “are most commonly used for storing seed and pulse grains, such as cowpeas.
    • Having a small opening, they can be made hermetic, by sealing the walls inside and out with liquid clay and closing the mouth with stiff clay, cow dung, or a wooden bung reinforced with cloth.
    • If the grain is dry (less than 12 percent moisture content) there is usually no problem with this kind of storage.
Figure 2. Calabash

©FAO/TECA

2. Objectives

  • The objectives of a “Colombier” are to secure storing of harvests and grains (sometimes initially placed in pre-processed calabashes), and to function as a farm household kitchen, constituted by the granary ground-floor, as well as a general purpose warehouse.

3. Implementation of the technology

  • The technology has been used by people in the agro-ecological zone of warm semi-arid tropics and mixed coastal plantation farming systems in Haiti.
  • The implementation of this technology and the kind of structure, obviously built before disasters, can be afforded by farmers of a medium to high socio-economic level.
  • In the study site at Bassin Magnan (south of Haiti), the structure has changed in that the supporting posts are now also made of iron while the past posts were exclusively wooden.
    • Architecturally, the farm granaries in Marmelade (Artibonite department, Haiti) are built on four supporting poles instead of the six as they do it in Bassin Magnan.
    • Materials include posts, timber, poles, straw and/or corrugated iron, iron, ropes, nails.
    • The structure is built on a pile made of four or six wooden or metallic posts, about two meters high, which in turn support a 1.5 m high floor, the actual roof of the system (Figure 3).
    • The space between the upper part of the pile and the roof constitutes the storing section.
    • The roof is A-framed, with a window placed at either of the two smaller sides of the roof.
    • The upper three quarters of each of the posts are covered with a metallic upside-down funnel to prevent rodents to access the stored harvests and damage them.
Figure 3. Scheme of the structure of a “Colombier”

©FAO/TECA

4. Costs

  • Unit installation fees in 2008 were about 2 000.00 HTG for a 3 m x 2 m structure at the ground level with a thatched roof.
  • Associated maintenance fees are 300.00 HTG every two to three years (that is, roughly 100.00 to 150.00 HTG yearly) to repair/fill in breaches in the roof.

5. General improvements

  • Modernize harvest storing facilities infrastructures through the promotion of galvanized iron individual or community silo. 
    • The traditional way of storing grains can provide an accessible solution for storing grains for poor households.
    • However, galvanized iron silos could be more resistant to extreme weather conditions, and protect grains better from pests.
    • This technology (Silo metálico: plano para granos básicos in Spanish) gives a short overview about the management of metallic silos.
  • Provide post-harvest technology and organic/natural insecticide based training. 
    • The following technology gives an overview about some types of plants with pesticidal properties which can be used to control insects during on-farm grain storage.
  • Promote other seed conservation techniques.
    • The following technology describes how to use eucalyptus leaves to preserve maize and bean seeds.

6. Validation

  • The technology has been used by people in the agro-ecological zone of warm semi-arid tropics and mixed coastal plantation farming systems in Haiti.

7. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Grain stores construction: ID 4499.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: improved storage facilities: ID 7308.
  • Diatomaceous earth to protect farm-stored grain: sorghum, maize and cow-peas: ID 4498.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: manual and motorised cleaning of grains and pulses: ID 7310.
  • Silo metálico plano para granos básicos: ID 6486.

This technology is also available in Spanish: ID 8853.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology protects grains and beans from harsh climatic impacts. In doing so, it provides for an additional source of income and more secure source of food.
entries.further_reading:
10. Further reading

  • FAO. 2007. TCP/RLA/3101 Assistance to Improve Local Agricultural Emergency Preparedness in Caribbean Countries Highly Prone to Hydro-Meteorological Disasters – Completion of phase I in Haiti: draft report March 2007. (p. 60f). 
  • FAO. 1994. Grain storage techniques, evolutions and trends in developing countries, by D.L. Proctor (ed).
  • FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin No. 109. Rome. 
  • Smucker, G., et al 2007. Environmental vulnerability in Haiti. Washington DC, USAID Report.

entries.tittle: Double transplanting of (t. aman) rice to reduce impacts of drought spells during monsoon (Kharif II) season in Bangladesh
entries.summary:
In Bangladesh, rice, and variations in its yield, is the key staple crop. It is critical to the livelihoods of that part of the population depending on agriculture. Transplanted aman (t. aman) is the second rice crop grown in the wet kharif II season, between July and November. However it may be strongly affected by drought spells. 

On the other hand, with early and heavy rainfall in the rainy season, fields are flooded and seedlings cannot be easily transplanted. In the case of continuous rain for 10 to 15 days, seedlings go down to the water and transfer from the seedling bed becomes urgent. If seedlings are ready to be transplanted but the main field is not ready for transplantation due to excessive flooding, it is essential to transfer the seedlings to another interim seedling bed on higher land with drainage facilities. This needs to be done before the final transplantation into the main field, when the situation allows, can be done.
entries.description:
Description

The objective of this agricultural adjustment practice is to manage the risk of seedling damage and crop losses of transplanted t. aman crops induced by floods and heavy rainfall. This is achieved by transplanting seedlings to a safe area until the main field is free of rainwater and ready for transplantation.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • Recommended varieties for this technique are BR-11, BR-41, aromatic rice or any other variety suitable to the area. T. aman seedlings should be temporarily transplanted in flood-free, medium high land near the main field if the main fields are flooded at the stage when the seedlings are 30 days old and normally need to be transferred.
  • Drainage facilities should be put in place in seedling beds during early heavy rainfall.
  • Organic matter and other nutrients should be ensured before sowing the seeds.
  • The first ten days of July are the appropriate period for sowing.
    • The main land should be well-prepared by plowing and harrowing three to four times.
    • Fertilizer should be applied when the land is prepared in the doses shown in the table below.
    • For sandy loam to silty loam soils, two to three cross plowing with subsequent three to four laddering are required, for the soil to have good tilth.
    • For a clay type of soil, soil preparation requires more tillage operation with appropriate soil moisture status.
  • The seed rate will be 4 kg to 5 kg per bigha (3 300 m²), and in case of line sowing, the line to line spacing should be 15 cm x 20 cm.
Table 1. Fertilizer dose for one bigha t. aman production demonstration
Name of fertilizer Quantity per bag ha (3 330 m2)
Urea 24 kg
Triple Super Phosphate 14 kg
Muriate of Potash 10 kg
Gypsum 8 kg
Zinc Sulphate 1 kg
Cowdung 800 kg

Source: FAO 2012

Figure 1. Farmers engaged in fertilizer application before land preparation in the main field

©FAO/TECA

2. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Community seedbed for rice in drought-prone areas: ID 6857.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

Resource efficiency is improved by this technology through the transplanting of seedlings to a safe area until the main crop field is rainwater free. This prevents crop loss and seedling damage during floods and heavy rainfall.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

​​The prevention of crop loss thanks to this practice allows for higher yields, more stable livelihood and more robust food security. ​

entries.tittle: Cotton culture, Uganda
entries.summary: The National Agricultural Research Organisation (NARO) aims to enhance the contribution of agricultural research to sustainable agricultural productivity, economic growth, food security and poverty eradication. It aims to do this through the generation and dissemination of appropriate technologies, knowledge and information. The following technology promotes good practices for cotton culture in Uganda.
entries.description:
Description

There are several cotton varieties that are optimal for Uganda and countries with similar agroecological zones. BPA 2000 and BPA 2002 are two varieties that will be discussed in this technology. 

1. Varieties

Table 1. Cotton varieties 
Variety Yield (kg/ha) Ginning out (GOT) (%) Staple length (mm) Fibre strength (g/tex) Farming System
BPA 2000 3000 39 33 30 Eastern, Northern, Western, Central regions
BPA 2002 3500 40 33 30

Source: NARO 2010

2. Management

2.1 Planting schedule

  • Between May and July
    • Plant between May and July in a good seedbed, three to six weeks after first ploughing.
    • Use land which has been fallowed for at least three years.
    • Plant when there is enough moisture in the soil, at a seed rate of 25 kg per ha for undelinted seed and 18 kg per ha for delinted seed, at a spacing of 75 cm x 30 cm.
    • Plant seed dressed in Bronopol/Bronocot at 1 kg of chemical to 150 kg of seed.
  • Between August and September
    • Plant between August and September, in a good seedbed three to six weeks after first ploughing in the land, which has fallowed for at least three years.
    • Plant when there is enough moisture in the soil, at a seed rate of 20 kg per ha (8 kg per acre) for undelinted seed and 13 kg per ha (5 kg per acre) for delinted seed, at a spacing of 90 cm x 30 cm.
    • Plant seed dressed in Bronopol/Bronocot at 1 kg of chemical to 150 kg of seed.

2.2 Planting recommendations

  • For areas with low soil fertility, apply 125 to 250 kg per ha of SSP before planting and top dress in 125 to 250 kg per ha of NPK.
  • Gap fill when necessary but must be before two weeks after germination.
  • Thin to two plants per hole when the seedling is 5 cm high.
  • Weed 15 to 30 days after germination and weed three to four times.
  • For very fertile areas, control vegetative growth by topping cotton crop at 45 to 60 days from planting or spray with 1 liter of Pix at 45 to 60 days from planting.
  • Cotton can be intercropped with beans, soybeans or groundnuts.
  • Plant cotton at the spacing of 90 cm x 30 cm.
  • Plant at the same time or at a one to two-week interval.

2.3 Disease and pest control using IPM packages

  • Seed dressing with Bronopol/Bronocot at 1 kg of chemical to 150 kg of seed, or use varieties resistant to bacterial blight, wilts and nematodes.
  • Carry out weekly scouting for lygus bugs, ball worms and stainers from 60 days after planting.
    • Spray according to Economic Threshold Levels (ETL) of six bollworm larvae per 100 plants sampled, 15 lygus bugs per 50 sweeps of the sweep net or 22 aborted squares of flowers or bolls on plants.
  • If ETLs are exceeded use synthetic pyrethroids, e.g. Ambush Super, fenkill, Bulldock, Cypermethrin etc. at recommended rates.
    • Or use a combination of synthetic Pyrethroids with organophosphates, e.g. Sydon super etc.
  • For biological control, use predatory ants or intercrop cotton with crops which attract predatory ants , such as beans, groundnuts and cowpeas.

3. Post-harvest and storage

  • For the Eastern and Northern regions, pick cotton when dry and don’t mix with trash.
  • Dry cotton properly on clean surfaces.
  • Sort and store in clean, dry and rat proof place.

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropical, warm. 

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Promoting drought and waterlogging tolerant cotton varieties: ID 7396.
  • Beneficial insects and the cotton pests they control: ID 8677.
  • Cotton cultivation with laser levelling, ridge sowing, Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and compost application under drought conditions: ID 10016.
  • Management of cotton bollworms using predators ants: ID 4337.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology provides intricately detailed steps on the efficient planting of cotton varieties.

entries.tittle: Rainwater syringe: Low cost technology for rainwater harvesting in coastal areas
entries.summary:
Due to saline conditions, drinking and pure water is a major problem in coastal areas. Most of the open wells and tube wells in the coastal areas contain salty water. Rainwater harvesting is a viable option for solving the issue of drinking water. Construction of rainwater overhead tanks is a costly affair and marginal farmers cannot afford it. Moreover the tank has limited capacity for storing water. 

The method developed by Mr Antoji from Kerala, India is a cost effective method for harvesting rainwater in coastal areas. Rainwater is collected from the roof tops of houses and stored in a pressure tank in the ground and with the help of PVC pipes. The water is retained in the underground water column and this harvested water can be subsequently collected by a simple piston pump or motor before mixing with saline water. The water thus harvested is used both for drinking and for minor irrigation. He has installed more than 150 tanks in different parts of Kerala including in his home village of ‘chellanum’ in Ernamkulam district.
entries.description:
Description

This method is very cost-effective in coastal areas where the mean sea level is the same or below sea level. Despite the area receiving very heavy rainfall during the monsoon period (June to October), the coastal areas of Kerala face very acute shortages of drinking water. Water available in the tube wells is saline and the shortage of water aggregates in summer seasons.

1. Objective

Implement a low-cost technology/method that enables the harvesting of rainwater in coastal areas.

Rooftop rainwater is stored in a pressure tank and the pressure of water can be used to recharge water up to a depth of 16 to 24 feet. The harvested water can be collected using piston pumps or motors before it dilutes the saltwater.

2. Construction of pressure tank in the ground

  • Make a pit 8 feet deep and 6 feet wide on the surface or ground.
  • Remove the soil in the pit and fill with sand.
  • Construct border wall around the pit, 2 feet deep into the pit and 3 feet high above the ground level.
  • The portion that is seen over the ground can be used as a collection tank.

3. Rainwater harvesting

  • The pipe collecting the rainwater from the roof of the house or building is connected to this tank. Tank should be leakproof. 
  • Six to seven pipes of 16 feet length are erected deep into the ground from the tank. 
  • The water coming from the roof, with pressure, goes through the pipe deep into the soil. 
  • The harvested water can be collected using a piston pump erected in the vicinity of the tank by constructing a tube well. 
  • Every day 500 to 2 500 litres of water can be drawn from the well.

4. Impact and results

More than 150 tanks have been installed in different parts of coastal villages in Kerala, catering to the needs of several farmers in different villages.

5. Validation

Some rainwater harvesting tanks were installed in the state of Kerala. The quality of water has been tested scientifically and approved for drinking and other domestic purposes. The innovation has been awarded by the National Innovation Foundation, an autonomous body under the Government of India.

6. Editor’s comment

This low-cost technology has been developed by a mechanic Antoji, hailing from the remote coastal village of Chellnam, in Cochin, Kerala, India. The innovation of ‘rainwater syringe’ was totally accidental in the mid-’90s. His village is situated in the coastal area, where sea and land levels are the same. Getting good drinking water is a major problem in this area. Even in the bore well, villagers were not able to get good quality water.

One evening, he was watering the plants in his house with a hose using the water from the overhead tank. He had to attend a phone call, and he put the hose in the garden itself and went to the room to receive the call. He forgot to close the tap and came back to the field after five to ten minutes. Once he came back, he observed that the water was spreading over the soil and not going into the ground or soil. Then out of curiosity, he tried to pierce the ground with the hose, to see if it would easily go into the sand. Even then the water did not go too deep. The hose overflowed and spread over the soil. But when the hose reached about 7 to 8 meters deep inside the soil, water did not come back to surface. He initially thought there might be some blockage. He checked the overhead water tank. The water level in the tank went down. Then he realized that water got stored under the soil at a specific depth. An idea clicked in his mind. Why can we not store water under the ground? Drinking water is a major problem in coastal areas. The water is salty and is not good to drink. If we can store the rainwater under the soil and can use it when needed, that would be a great achievement. He continued his experiments. With the help of a piston pump, he tried to pump the water from this depth of 7 m. The quality of water was good without any salty taste.

Figure 1. Rainwater syringe: low-cost technology for rainwater harvesting in coastal areas

©FAO/TECA

7. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Water harvesting from concentrated runoff for irrigation purposes: ID 7512.
  • Cost benefit analysis of rain water harvesting systems: roof top rain water harvesting combined with gravity drip irrigation: ID 10011.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: roof water harvesting: ID 7304.
  • Improved rainwater harvesting for fodder shrub production and livestock grazing: the Vallerani micro-catchment system in the Badia of Jordan: ID 8758.
  • Rainwater harvesting systems for cabbage growing: ID 8932.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for efficient water collection and storage using underground pressure tanks. The water can either be used for drinking or minor irrigation.

9.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for increased access to drinking water and increased food source, should the water be used for crop growth.

entries.tittle: Making high-quality cassava flour
entries.summary: Cassava is not fully utilized in Eastern Africa compared to West Africa (Nigeria, Ghana). Cassava is drought tolerant, easy to grow and simple to harvest. All parts of the cassava plant are valuable. Cassava leaves can be used to make soup or as feed for livestock, the stems can be used for planting more cassava, for mushroom production or as firewood, the root can be cooked and eaten fresh or processed into flour. High-quality cassava flour is made within a day of harvesting the root. Below are steps in processing high quality cassava by small holder farmers.
entries.description:
Description

1. Importance and benefits of cassava

Cassava is not fully utilized in Eastern Africa compared to West Africa (Nigeria, Ghana). Cassava can earn you extra income, provide employment opportunities and serve as a reserve food in times of scarcity. Cassava is drought tolerant, easy to grow and simple to harvest. All parts of the cassava plant are valuable. Cassava leaves can be used to make soup or as feed for livestock, the stems can be used for planting more cassava, for mushroom production or as firewood, the root can be cooked and eaten fresh or processed into flour.

Cassava can also meet industrial needs such as the production of bio-fuel and starch for use in the paper- and drug-making industries. High-quality cassava flour is made within a day of harvesting the root. It is very white, has low fat content, is not sour like traditional, fermented cassava flour, does not give a bad smell or taste to food products and can mix very well with wheat flour for use in bread or cakes.

2. What you need to make high-quality cassava flour

To establish a small-scale enterprise to make high-quality cassava flour, you require:

  • space for processing the cassava;
  • a store;
  • a facility for safe disposal of waste materials;
  • cassava roots;
  • processing equipment (knife, bowl, drying platform, grater, press and milling machine); and
  • trained machine operators along with casual workers for peeling, washing, grating, pressing, drying, milling, sifting and packing.

You may be able to hire a press and grater locally. Local fabricators of processing equipment are also available in some areas – ask your local extension officer or agricultural research station. Accessible markets include bakeries, millers and paper industries, schools, hospitals, shops, kiosks, hotels, restaurants and local famine relief agencies.

3. How to make high-quality cassava flour

3.1 First step: selecting roots

Harvest or buy healthy, mature, firm and freshly harvested cassava roots. These should have no bruises. The flesh of the roots should be white with no cracking and few fibrous roots.

3.2 Second step: peeling

Peel the roots and remove the stalk, woody tips and any fibrous roots using a sharp knife. Failure to peel properly will result in off-colour in the final product. Cassava peel (after drying) can be used for animal feed or composting – so do not waste it!

3.3 Third step: washing

Wash peeled cassava roots with clean water to remove any dirt, including sand, soil, leaves or other impurities.

3.4 Fourth step: grating

Use a simple perforated iron sheet or mechanical grater to grate cassava roots into a fine mash.

3.5 Fifth step: pressing

Pack the grated cassava mash into a clean bag, such as a jute or sisal sack that will allow extra water to escape. Press the sack using a screw press or hydraulic jack to remove excess water until the cassava is crumbly.

3.6 Sixth step: drying

Spread the pressed cassava mash thinly on a clean black plastic sheet placed on a gentle slope in full sun. Ideally, this should be raised off the floor. Dry mash until it is very floury. Cover with netting to keep off flies and birds. Though solar, stove and hot-air dryers are more expensive, the drying process is more reliable and of higher quality.

3.7 Seventh step: milling

Mill the dried cassava mash to produce flour. Milling can be done using a hammer mill (village posho mill).

3.8 Eighth step: sifting

Using a simple home-made sieve, sift the milled flour to remove fibrous materials and any lumps. This is important to obtain high-quality free-flowing flour, free of fibre with good particle size.

3.9 Ninth step: packaging and storing

Pack sifted cassava flour in airtight moisture-proof black plastic bags. Seal the bag using a burning candle (or an electrical polysealer if electricity is available) and label it with the date of manufacture and expiry date (after six months). Pack bags in a carton to protect them from light. Store the cartons in a well-ventilated, cool, dry place. The packaged flour will keep for about six months.

Table 1. What can go wrong and how to deal with it
Potential problems Caused by How to prevent and/or solve it
Spoilt cassava roots Roots that are too old or damaged
  • Use 10- to 12-month old cassava roots
  • Harvest carefully to avoid damaging roots
Mould in stored flour Improper drying leaving flour too wet
  • Ensure complete drying of mash
  • Flour must be free-flowing after milling
Bad smell of flour (fermented odour)
  • Rusty equipment
  • Delay in pressing and drying the grated mash
  • Use stainless steel knives Wash and dry equipment after use
  • Process cassava within 24 hours of harvesting
Muddy environment Poor drainage system
  • Ensure proper flow of cassava wastewater into a soak pit and keep your processing area clean
Contaminated flour Dirt and insects in mash while drying
  • Use of porous or damaged packaging materials
Poor ventilation in the storage area Avoid dirt and insects by raising the platform and cover with netting while drying mash
  • Use clean, strong plastic bags
  • Avoid storing flour in warm or damp places
Sickness/poisoning from eating bitter roots Use of very bitter cassava roots
  • Improper processing methods
  • Use proper processing methods and low -cyanide (less bitter) varieties

Source: CTA 2010

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies 

  • Making sweet potato chips and flour: ID 6904.
  • Improved cassava fufu processing methods, West Africa: ID 4522.
  • Cassava processing: cassava wet flour: ID 3826.
  • Make bitter cassava safe for consumption: ID 4372.
  • Participatory breeding of superior, mosaic disease-resistant cassava for Africa: ID 4513.
  • Storage and preservation of wet cassava: ID 4520.
  • Participatory breeding of superior, mosaic disease resistant cassava: ID 4536.
  • Sustainable livelihoods: new market opportunities for cassava: ID 4575.
  • Production of high­-quality cassava flour: ID 4574.
  • Introduction of early maturing cassava varieties in Bolivia, a cost benefit analysis: ID 8952.
  • Cassava brown streak disease: control measures: ID 7004.
  • Production of glucose syrup from high-quality cassava flour: ID 4576.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

Cassava is drought tolerant, easy to grow, and simple to harvest.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

All parts of the cassava plant can be used for nutrition, livestock feed, and firewood. By using improved techniques to process high-quality cassava, households can also obtain additional sources of income.

entries.tittle: Cashing in with parboiled rice (demonstration video)
entries.summary:
Rice is highly nutritious, however a lot of its quality is lost during processing. This results in poor quality rice on the market. Therefore, consumers turn to imported rice. In this video you will learn about parboiling, a way to improve rice quality by treating paddy with warm water and steam. There are many good reasons for parboiling rice.
The market for quality rice is growing. Food vendors and restaurant owners use parboiled rice because it is already clean and easy to cook. Most importantly, parboiled rice is more nutritious than non-parboiled rice. This video presents the technique of parboiling.

entries.tittle: Small-scale freshwater fish farming
entries.summary: This practice provides basic information on how to set up a small-scale fish farm for subsistence purposes with regards to daily protein needs. Since fish farming practices are so diverse, this manual focuses on land-based freshwater fish farming. In the tropics, pond fish farming is the most common form of fish farming. Therefore, the information provided in this practice concerns pond construction and pond management.
entries.description:
Description

1. Planning an aquaculture enterprise

  • Land, water and climatic conditions are probably the most important natural factors which need to be assessed. One of the most important requirements is water availability in terms of quality and quantity.
  • The type of aquaculture and species of animals or plants which you will be able to culture will depend largely on the properties of the site.
  • Fish need protein in order to grow and reproduce.
  • This means they can become competitors for products, which could otherwise be used directly for human consumption.
  • Furthermore, the cost of production is fairly high and therefore pond grown fish are not always able to compete financially with fish caught in the wild.
  • Some very important factors a prospective fish farmer, which should be considered before embarking on a fish farming venture are:
    • finance;
    • soil;
    • fish stock; and
    • harvesting.

2. Planning the site and type of fish farm

2.1 Site selection

  • Proper selection of a site is probably the most important factor in the success of a fish farm.
  • Before this, you should decide which species to raise based on the available foods (e.g. agricultural by-products) and possible fertilizers (e.g. compost or animal manure). 
  • Site selection will depend on the kind of fish farm you plan to use.
  • For pond construction you need to consider the following factors:
    • soil type;
    • quality and quantity of the water available; and
    • the requirements for filling and drainage of the pond.

2.1.1 Soil

  • The quality of soil influences both productivity and water quality in a pond.
  • However, it must also be suitable for dike construction.
  • To determine soil suitability the two most important properties to examine are soil texture (particle size composition) and porosity or permeability (ability to let water pass through).
  • The pond bottom must be able to hold water (have a low porosity like clay).
    • The soil should also contribute to the fertility of the water by providing nutrients (soil texture consists of a lot of clay particles) so the best soil for pond construction contains a lot of clay.
  • The three ways one should follow to predict whether the soil will be suitable for pond construction are:
    1. Squeeze method
      • Wet a handful of soil with just enough water to make it moist as in Figure 1(a).
      • Squeeze the soil by closing your hand firmly as in Figure 1(b).
      • If it holds its shape after opening the palm of your hand, the soil will be good for pond construction as in Figure 1(c).
  •  
Figure 1. Squeeze method

©CTA/Chakroff, 1976

2. Groundwater test

      • This test should be performed during the dry period in order to get reliable results.
      • Dig a hole with a depth of one meter.
      • Cover it with leaves for one night to limit evaporation.
      • If the hole is filled with groundwater the next morning a pond could be built.
        • Take into account that you will probably need more time to drain the pond due to the high groundwater levels filling the pond again.
      • If the hole is still empty the next morning, no problems will occur as a result of high groundwater levels (Figure 2).
        • The site will perhaps be suitable for pond fish farming.
      • Now you should test the water permeability.
Figure 2. Groundwater test

©CTA/Viveen et al., 1985

3. Water permeability test (Figure 3)

      • Fill the hole with water to the top.
      • Cover the hole with leaves.
      • The next day the water level will be lower due to seepage.
        • The dikes of the hole have probably become saturated with water and might hold water better now.
      • Refill the hole with water to the top
      • Cover it once more with leaves.
        • Check the water level the next day.
      • If the water level is still high, the soil is impermeable enough and is suitable for pond construction.
      • If the water has disappeared again, the site is not suitable for fish farming, unless the bottom is first covered with plastic or heavy clays.
Figure 3. Water permeability test

©CTA/Viveen et al., 1985

  • The land contour, and especially the land slope, determine the way to build the pond.
  • The slope of the land can be used for the pond's drainage at harvest.
  • Totally flat land and hilly terrain with a slope of more than 2 to 4 percent are unsuitable for pond construction.
  • All slopes between 2 and 4 percent can be used for pond construction.
  • A 2 percent land slope means a 2 cm drop in elevation for every meter of horizontal distance.
  • If the slope is sufficient you can fill and drain by using gravity.
  • However, you should take care to prevent erosion of the pond dikes.

2.1.2 Water 

  • Constant water supply is needed, not only to fill the pond but also to make up for the losses caused by seepage and evaporation (Figure 4).
  • A water temperature between 20°C and 30°C is generally good for fish farming.
  • For salinity, some fish species can withstand a wider salinity range than others.
    • For example, tilapia and catfish can withstand a wide range from fresh to seawater while carp can only withstand freshwater.
Figure 4. Water supply and water loss in a fish pond. a: inlet; b: overflow; c: evaporation; d: seepage

©CTA/Viveen et al., 1985

3. Type of aquaculture farm

3.1 Pond culture

  • Ponds are usually located on land with a gentle slope.
  • They are rectangular or square-shaped, have well-finished dikes and bottom slopes and do not collect run-off water from the surrounding watershed.
  • It is important that sufficient water is available to fill all ponds within a reasonable period of time and to maintain the same pond water level.
  •  You should also be able to drain the pond completely when the fish are to be harvested.
  • Side slopes should be 2:1 or 3:1 (each meter of height needs 2 or 3 m of horizontal distance), which allow easy access, will not encourage vegetation to grow, and help to reduce erosion problems.
  • To prevent fish theft, bamboo poles or branches might be put in the pond which makes netting and rod-and-line fishing impossible.
  • Another method to keep thieves away from your fish pond is to have the pond as close to your home as possible.

3.1.1 Diversion ponds

  • Diversion ponds (Figure 5A)
    • These are made by bringing water from another source to the pond.
    • There are different types of diversion ponds (Figure 6).
  • Embankment ponds
    • The dikes of an embankment pond are built above ground level. A disadvantage of this type of pond is that you may need a pump to fill the pond (Figure 6A).
  • Excavated ponds
    • An excavated pond is dug out of the soil.
    • The disadvantage of this type is that you need a pump to drain the pond (Figure 6B).
  • Partially excavated ponds with low dikes
    • Soil from digging out the pond is used to build the low dikes of the pond.

3.1.2 Barrage ponds

  • Barrage ponds (figure 5B) are made by building a dike across a natural stream.
  • The ponds are therefore like small conservation dams. 
    • The advantage of a barrage pond is that it is easy to construct.
    • However, it is very difficult to control this system: it is difficult to keep wild fish out and a lot of food added to the pond will be lost because of the current. 
    • A properly built barrage pond (with overflow) overflows only under unusual circumstances.
Figure 5. Different pond types. A: diversion pond; B: barrage pond

©CTA/Bard et al., 1976

Figure 6. Different types of diversion ponds. A: embankment pond B: excavated pond; C: partially excavated pond

©CTA/Viveen et al., 1985

4. Selection of fish species

4.1 Monoculture

  • In monoculture, only one fish species is raised in the pond.
  • An advantage of the monoculture is that it is easier to give certain supplementary foods to the fish as there is only one fish species to consider with regard to food preference.
  • A disadvantage is a risk that a single disease may kill all fish in the pond as different fish species are usually susceptible to different diseases.

4.2 Polyculture

  • In polyculture, more than one fish species is raised in the fish pond.
  • In this way, the various natural food resources in the pond are better utilized.
  • Each fish species has a certain food preference which are related to the position of the fish in the pond (e.g. bottom-living or mid-water-living fish).
  • For example, mud carp live mostly on the bottom of the pond and feed on mud and dead material, which they find on the bottom.
  • Tilapia, on the other hand, live more in the deeper part or end of the pond.
    • Some species feed on plants and others on plankton.
  • By combining different species in the same pond, the total fish production can be raised to a higher level than would be possible with only one species or even with the different species separately.
  • An example of a Chinese polyculture fish farming system is the culture of silver carp, bighead carp and grass carp together in one pond (Figure 7).
Figure 7. Carp polyculture. A: silver carp: B: algae; C: bighead carp; D: zooplankton; E: grass carp; F: water plants

©CTA

  • Silver carp feeds mainly on algae, bighead carp mainly on tiny animals (called zooplankton) and grass carp mainly on water plants so there will hardly be any food competition.
  • Another much-used example is the polyculture of tilapia and common carp as tilapia feed mainly on algae and common carp on zooplankton and pond bottom material.
  • A special form is the concurrent culture of tilapia and catfish or snake-head (in general a predatory fish) to control the excessive breeding of tilapia.
  • But to obtain a production of fish that is as high as possible it is better to breed as few prey fish as possible in the pond.
  • The emphasis should be on fish species that can live on different kinds of feed.

4.3 Fish nutrition

4.3.1 Natural fish food

  • The natural fish food in the pond consists of a big part out of algae. 
  • Oxygen is a gas that is produced by all plants in the pond (therefore also by algae) with the help of sunlight.
    • The more sunlight falls on the pond and the larger the quantity of algae, the higher will be the oxygen-production in the fishpond.
  • The oxygen produced solves partly in the water and the rest escapes to the air.
    • The oxygen level of the water varies during the day because the production and absorption of oxygen by the plants changes with light and darkness (with or without sunlight in the fishpond).
  • The algae in the pond only produce oxygen when there is light.
    • At night they need oxygen like any other plant or animal in the pond, while no oxygen can be produced due to lack of sunlight.
  • Due to this, the quantity of solved oxygen in the water decreases after sunset.
  • Normally the oxygen level is at the highest at the end of the afternoon (oxygen has been produced throughout the day) and at the lowest in the early morning (oxygen has been used up throughout the night).
  • A shortage of oxygen is the main death cause of fish in fisheries, where the pond has been manured or fed too much.
  • An oxygen level that is sufficiently high is important for good fish production.

4.3.2 Supplemented fish food 

  • When supplementary food is given to the fish most of it is directly eaten by the fish.
  • The uneaten food will act as an additional fertilizer for the pond.
  • But even in ponds receiving a high amount of supplemented food, natural fish food still plays a very important role in the growth of fish. 
  • Typical examples of supplementary fish feeds are:
    • rice bran
    • broken rice
    • bread crumbs
    • cereals
    • cereal wastes
    • maize meal
    • Guinea grass
    • napier grass
    • fruits
    • vegetables
    • peanut cake
    • soybean cake
    • brewer's waste.

5. Health and disease

5.1 Preventing fish diseases

  • Good nutrition and proper water quality (with plenty of dissolved oxygen) are the most important factors for good fish health needed to cope with diseases. 
  • There are some basic rules which must be observed if outbreaks of disease are to be prevented or, if they occur, to be controlled.
    • Ponds must have separate water supplies.
      • It is not recommended to supply a pond with water from another pond, since this water may carry diseases and the level of dissolved oxygen may be lower.
      • It is therefore wiser not to design ponds in series. 
    • Fish must not be stressed.
      • If you handle the fish, except when you are taking them to the market, take great care so that you upset them as little as possible.
      • Extreme stress can be the direct cause of fish death. 
      • Damage to their skin, or rubbing off the scales and the protective slime layer, means disease-causing animals (pathogens) can enter the fish more easily. 
    • Fish must be kept in good condition at all times by using water with plenty of oxygen, with the correct pH and with a low ammonia content.
    • Great care must be taken when mixing fish from different ponds, or when introducing new fish into the farm, that no sick fish are introduced.
      • Fish new to the farm site should be kept in a separate pond until it is certain that they do not carry disease.
      • Only then can they be brought into contact with on-farm fish stocks.
  • Any change in normal behaviour may be a sign of disease.
    • Signs to look for include:
      • gasping at the surface for air;
      • rubbing the body or head against the sides of the pond;
      • ragged fins; and
      • sores on the body.
    • Something is wrong when the fish stop eating suddenly.
    • You must check the fish often, especially in very hot weather when dissolved oxygen shortages occur more often.
      • Less oxygen can be dissolved in warmer water.

5.2 Fish diseases

  • Diseases can be classified in infectious and nutritional ones.
    1. Infectious diseases can be carried from one pond to another by the introduction of new fish or by the farmer and his equipment.
    2. Nutritional diseases are caused by dietary shortages.
  • There are also diseases caused by pollutants and bad water quality and there is evidence that most fish deaths probably result from these types of problems. 
  • The fish farmer should focus on the prevention of diseases as the treatment of fish diseases is often difficult, time-consuming and expensive.

6. Harvesting the fish

  • As in any other type of farming the final phase in the fish farming cycle is the harvest and possible sale of the fish.
  • When most of the fish are big enough to be eaten or sold harvest can start (usually after five to six months) but harvest only what can be eaten or sold within one day.
  •  At harvest, start emptying the pond a few hours before dawn while it is still cool.
  • There are two ways to harvest fish.
    1. Take out all fish in the pond at the same time.
    2. Selectively cull fish from the pond throughout the whole year.
  • In the latter method, usually, the larger fish are taken out and the smaller fish are left in the pond to grow on.
  • It is, of course, possible to combine these two methods by taking out large fish as required and finally removing all the remaining fish at one time. 

7. Maintenance and monitoring

  • In order to achieve a high fish production in the pond, regular maintenance and monitoring are necessary.
  • Daily management
    • Check the water quality (temperature, pH, early morning dissolved oxygen levels).
    • Check the pond for possible water leaks.
    • Clean the screen of the water in- and outlet.
    • Watch the fish while feeding
      • Do they eat normally?
      • Are they active?
      • If not, check dissolved oxygen level (if near-zero stop feeding and fertilizing and flow water through the pond until fish behave normal again).
      • Look for symptoms that could indicate diseases.
    • Watch out for predators and take precautions if necessary.
    • Remove aquatic weeds growing in the pond.

7.1 Turbidity

  • Turbidity is the term for the amount of dissolved suspended dirt and other particles in the water, which give the water a brown colour.
  • High turbidity of water can decrease fish productivity as it will reduce light radiation into the water and thus oxygen production by the water plants, clog filters and injure fish gills.
  • A suitable method for reducing turbidity is a siltation tank.
    • This is a small reservoir at the inlet to the pond.
    • The water flows into this reservoir and is kept there until the mud settles on the bottom.
    • Then the clear water is let into the fish pond.
  • Another way to clear muddy water is to put hay and/or manure into the pond and leave it there to decompose (lime, gypsum or alum can also be used).
  • In the case of water turbidity caused mainly by other factors than algae abundance (water colour is not greenish), some much-used practices to decrease this turbidity are the following. 
  • Bring animal manure in the pond before stocking of the fish at a rate of 240 g/m2 three times with a time interval between the applications of three to four days.
  • Another method to decrease turbidity is by applying lime, gypsum but preferably alum at a rate of 1 gram per 100 litre of water.
  • This method should not be used during very hot weather because the hay will begin to rot very quickly.
  • However, the only real long-term solution to turbidity is to divert muddy water away from the pond and ultimately protect roads and dikes from erosion causing the high water turbidity.

7.2 Water acidity, alkalinity and hardness

  • Water suitable for aquaculture should have a certain degree of acidity indicated by the water pH-value, which should preferably be between 6.7 and 8.6.
    • Values above or below this range inhibit good fish growth and reproduction.
    • Algae require a pH of about 7 and a slightly lower (alkaline) pH of 6.5 favours good zooplankton (tiny animals in the pond water on which the fish feed) and fish growth.
  • Sometimes the pH of the pond water can change quickly.
    • For example, a heavy rain may carry acid substances coming from the soil dissolved in the run-off water into the pond.
    • In this way, the pond water gets more acid and thus the pH value decreases.
    • The best way to increase the pH-value of the water again to neutral (about 7) is to add lime to the pond.
  • Water hardness is the measure of total water-soluble salts.
    • Water that contains many salts is called "hard" and water that contains few salts is called "soft" water.
    • One method of measuring hardness is to look closely at the pond dikes where the water line is.
    • If there is a white line on the dike of the pond where the water was, there are salts present in the water which have dried on the pond dikes.
    • Water hardness is important for good fish growth.
    • If the water is too soft (i.e. the amount of water-soluble salts is low), the farmer can increase the hardness by adding lime to the water and thus increase water fertility so natural fish food production and ultimately fish production in the pond will increase.

7.3 Oxygen supply

  • If fish are gulping for oxygen at the water surface, you can solve this problem by flowing extra freshwater through the pond.
  • Stirring up the water in the pond also helps to increase the amount of dissolved oxygen in the water.
  • Do not feed and fertilize the pond at this moment because this is often one of the reasons for the oxygen shortage.
  • Another possible cause of oxygen shortage problems can be an over-stocking of fish in the pond.
  • This can causes oxygen stress for the fish which can result in disease outbreaks and mortality.

7.4 Toxic substances

  • Toxic substances in the water supply of the pond can decrease fish production seriously.
  • It is wise to investigate any existing or potential sources of water pollution in the vicinity of the pond.
  • Many chemicals used in animal husbandry and crop cultivation are poisonous to fish.
  • Chemicals should never be used in the area around the pond especially when sprayed on windy days.

8. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Make a living through fish farming: ID 7357.
  • Rice-fish Culture System (RFC): ID 8732.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology provides efficient guidelines on how to create and manage ponds in a more sustainable and environmentally-friendly way, using ecologically-friendly techniques and tools.

10.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology is cost-saving and improves fish health and quantity. The latter ultimately leads to increases in sources of food and income.

entries.summary:
African Rice Center: “The quality is very important for us to push back the dumping from outside, if we don’t do it; whether its from Africa, whether it’s from my mother’s kitchen, people are not going to buy it, so we have to become competitive, we have to develop competitive advantage and quality is the most important element in competitive advantage and, it’s within our reach, we can do it.”

The following video from Africa Rice Center (Africarice) describes how farmers in Benin use various techniques to obtain and maintain a good quality of their locally produced rice.

entries.tittle: Technique Culturale de la Patate Douce, Congo (RDC)
entries.summary:
La patate douce, en tant que plante à tubercule, sert non seulement comme source de nourriture, mais également protège le sol contre l’érosion grâce à son feuillage. Avec ses trois variétés, la cultivation de la patate douce est préférablement faite sur billons ou sur buttes. Cette récolte, qui peut durer jusqu’à quatre mois, se passe en fonction du cycle végétatif de la variété. En suite les boutures de la plante sont replanter après la récolte. Ces boutures ont une capacité de conservation à longue durée. Pour l’entretien et la conservation de cette plante, le remplacement des manquants, la refaite des buttes en cas de dégâts et le sarclage ainsi que le triage et le séchage des tubercules est recommandé.

Cette technologie est aussi disponible en : Portugais (ID2017)
entries.description:
La description

La patate douce est une plante à tubercule, cultivée pour l’alimentation de l’homme et des animaux. Elle couvre bien le sol avec son feuillage abondant et ses longues tiges; elle aide donc à protéger le sol contre l’érosion. Les feuilles de la patate douce sont de très bons légumes. Les variétés de patate douce à chair orange sont riches en vitamine A. Trois variétés de patate douce utilisées au Congo sont présentées dans le ficher joint. 

1. Itinéraire technique de la patate douce

1.1 Préparation du terrain

  • Un travail profond est envisageable si la plantation se fait à plat.
  • Pour avoir un bon rendement, la plantation sur billons ou sur buttes est favorable.
  • La longueur des billons varie mais les billons de 3 m à 6 m sont plus aisés et faciles à faire.

1.2 Préparation du matériel de plantation

  • Le matériel de plantation est constitué des boutures récoltées sur des plantes âgées d’au moins cinq mois.
  • Ce sont des boutures apicales jeunes de 30 cm à 40 cm de longueur (c’est donc différent du manioc où l’on prend les parties les plus âgées).
  • Les boutures sont plantées immédiatement après leur coupe.
  • Elles peuvent aussi être conservées si le terrain n’est pas encore prêt pour la plantation.
    • Dans ce cas, la conservation se fera dans un endroit sec et aéré.
    • Toutes les feuilles sont enlevées, sauf celles du bout.
    • La conservation dans ces conditions peut aller jusqu’à trois semaines.

1.3 Plantation

  • La plantation peut se faire à plat, sur buttes ou sur billons aux écartements de 100 cm x 30 cm, soit une densité de 33 000 plants par ha.
  • On plante trois boutures par butte ou on fait deux rangées de poquets en quinconce sur billon et on plante une bouture par poquet.
  • On doit planter les trois-quarts de la bouture dans la terre et ne laisser que le bout avec la feuille à la surface du sol.

1.4 Entretien

L’entretien de la patate douce consiste à:

  • remplacer les manquants;
  • refaire les buttes ou les billons détruits par les fortes pluies ou les passages des animaux; et
  • sarcler à chaque fois que poussent les mauvaises herbes.

1.5 Récolte

  • Le moment de la récolte arrive en fonction du cycle végétatif de la variété et varie de trois à cinq mois.
  • La récolte peut se faire au fur et à mesure des besoins à partir de trois à quatre mois.
  • Si la récolte est retardée au-delà de six mois, on peut avoir des tubercules qui commencent à pourrir.

1.6 Conservation

Conseils pour la conservation des patates douces.

  • Trier les tubercules avant la conservation.
  • Les tubercules se conservent mieux dans un en-droit sec et frais.
  • Les tubercules préalablement séchés au soleil peuvent se conserver pendant plusieurs semaines.

2. Zones agro-ecologiques

  • Tropicale, chaude.

3. Les technologies associées/relatives

  • Fabrication de cossettes et de farine de patate douce: ID 7657.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en portugais: ID 2017.

4. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

4.1 Favorable aux femmes

La pratique est facile à entamer et peut-être entreprise par toute forme de main-d'oeuvre. 

4.2 L’efficacité d’utilisation des ressources

La pratique permet l'utilisation efficace des boutures de la patate douce à travers la cultivation de ses trois variétés. Ceci protège le sol contre l'érosion et améliore l'entretien de cette plante. 

4.3 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvre

La pratique sert en tant que source de nourriture et de rendements.

entries.tittle: Processing mango and guava nectar
entries.summary: Raw materials are one of the most important aspects to consider in fruit and vegetable processing. The fruit and vegetables themselves are the raw materials, the reason for the development of preservation processes. This technology focuses on mango and guava nectar processing. It has been extracted from FAO's Technical Manual on Small-scale Processing of Fruits and Vegetables, and it briefly presents the necessary raw materials, equipment and stages of the processing to obtain mango and guava nectar.
entries.description:
Description

Raw materials are one of the most important aspects to consider in fruit and vegetable processing. The fruit and vegetables themselves are the raw materials, the reason for the development of preservation processes. This technology focuses on mango and guava nectar processing.

1. Raw materials

The raw materials are:

  • mature mangoes and guavas;
  • sugar;
  • lemon juice or citric acid; and
  • water.

2. Materials and equipment

Materials and equipment are:

  • an aluminium pot with lid; 
  • a pulper; 
  • a copper;
  • crown corks and glass bottles;
  • kitchen utensils: wooden spoons, knives, funnel, skimmer, chopping blocks, an assortment of plastic containers and kitchen cloths; and
  • a source of heat 18:18.

3. Processing

The following steps describe the processing procedure.

  • Wash the mangos and guavas in clean water.
  • Drain.
  • Peel the mangos and separate the pulp from the pit, Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Mangos peeled and separated from the pulp from the pit

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Peel the guava

©FAO/TECA

  • Cut the guavas in four sections and blanch them in boiling water for three to ten minutes, according to their degree of maturity.
  • Extract the mango and guava pulp by means of the pulper, Figure 3.
Figure 3. Extract the mango

©FAO/TECA

4. Mixing

The following steps describe the mixing of the ingredients.

  • Boiling water: 1 litre per kilo of pulp, Figure 4.
Figure 4. Boil the water with lemon and sugar

©FAO/TECA

  • Sugar: 200 g per kilo of pulp.
  • Lemon juice: two spoonfuls per kilo of pulp.
  • Boil the water with the lemon and sugar, and then add the pulp, so that the mixture has a 19 percent solids concentration, measured by means of a refractometer, and a pH value between 3.5 and 3.8.
  • Remove the foam with a skimmer, Figure 5.
Figure 5. Remove foam with skimmer

©FAO/TECA

  • Pack while it is still hot, cover with a lid and sterilize for 10 minutes in boiling water for 0.33 litre bottles; 15 minutes for 0.5 litre bottles, and 20 minutes for 0.75 litre bottles, Figure 6.
Figure 6. Pack in a bottle using a funnel

©FAO/TECA

  • Let the bottles cool, Figure 7.
Figure 7. Let bottles cool

©FAO/TECA

  • Label and store.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Increasing yield of mango with selective harvest: ID 8844.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Women-friendly

This practice is not labour-intensive and can be undertaken by any manual hand labour.

6.2 Resource use efficiency 

As key sources of income and food, this practice allows mango and guava nectar to be processed and stored more efficiently.

entries.tittle: Técnicas y metodologías de extensión – Guatemala
entries.summary: A continuación se comparten cuatro afiches con información sobre la extensión, metodologías de extensión, medios de extensión en el campo y técnicas de extensión y medios auxiliares pertenecientes todas ellas a la Colección Extensionista. El material ha sido elaborado por el Proyecto Altiplano de la FAO en Guatemala, “Apoyo a la Formación de Grupos y Organizaciones de Desarrollo Local en el Departamento de San Marcos y Municipios de Suroeste de Huehuetenango”. Dicho proyecto tenía como objetivo contribuir a la consolidación de la organización social, el manejo sostenible de los recursos naturales y las economías locales en comunidades rurales de los departamentos de San Marcos y Huehuetenango (municipios del suroeste). Inició en 2007 y finalizó en 2010.
entries.description:
Descripción

La tecnología sobre técnicas y metodologías de extensión en Guatemala está formada por los siguientes cuatro afiches trifoliares:

1. ¿Qué es extensión?

  • En este afiche se define que es la extensión agrícola y se determinan los componentes y los objetivos.
  • También se especifican cuáles tienen que ser las tareas de un promotor campesino y que cualidades debe poseer.

2. Metodologías de extensión

  • En el afiche de metodologías se define que es un método de extensión y qué importancia tiene su uso en el campo.
  • Así mismo, se explica en que consisten tres de los métodos más comunes:
    • E.R.C.A. (experiencia, reflexión, conceptualización, acción).
    • Diagnóstico participativo.
    • Mapa histórico.

3. Medios de extensión de campo

  • En este afiche se resumen los medios de extensión en campo más utilizados, como por ejemplo la reunión grupal, gira de intercambio, días de campo, etc.

4. Técnicas de extensión y medios auxiliares

  • En este caso se desarrollan técnicas de extensión, demostraciones, sociogramas o entrevistas, junto con diversos medios auxiliares de la extensión como la radio, carteles, transparencias.
  • Los cuatro afiches están elaborados por el Proyecto Altiplano de la FAO, “Apoyo a la Formación de Grupos y Organizaciones de Desarrollo Local en el Departamento de San Marcos y Municipios de Suroeste de Huehuetenango”.
  • Dicho proyecto ha estado apoyado por la FAO en coordinación con el Ministerio de Agricultura Ganadería y Alimentación (MAGA), con el apoyo financiero de la Agencia Catalana de Cooperación para el Desarrollo (ACCD) y en coejecución con Organizaciones Locales del Altiplano Marquense y del suroeste de Huehuetenango.

5. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

6. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Plan de Finca-Hogar: ID 7217.

7. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

7.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Las técnicas y metodologías de extensión contribuyen a efectos positivos, como una consolidación de la organización social, manejo sostenible de los recursos naturales y economías locales en comunidades rurales.

7.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta técnica le da al agricultor un plan de pasos para expandir la agricultura.

  • Blum, M.L., Cofini, F., Sulaiman, R.V. 2020. Agricultural extension in transition worldwide: Policies and strategies for reform. Rome, FAO.

entries.tittle: Rice seed drying (africa rice center video on rice advice)
entries.summary: Farmers face great difficulties with drying their seeds because seed absorbs moisture from the soil. As a result, seed quality deteriorates, and no-one can expect good yields by using poor quality seed. In this video you can see how farmers of the Maria village in Bangladesh solved this problem by themselves. Now they are no longer worried about drying seed, even during the rainy season. This video presents the technique of seed drying.

entries.tittle: Plan de Finca - Hogar
entries.summary: El PESA El Salvador aplica la metodología de transferencia conocida como familia demostradora, que consiste en enfocar la asistencia técnica a una pareja (hombre-mujer) que toman protagonismo en la comunidad para aprender, experimentar y adoptar tecnologías en la finca e implementar las buenas prácticas en el hogar las cuales las comparte con otras familias cercanas. Por lo anterior, contar con un plan de Finca-Hogar se hace necesario e indispensable para la planificación de actividades, tanto en la finca como en el hogar, en busca del mejoramiento integral de la vida de las familias participantes. Este material proviene de los documentos y publicaciones del Programa Especial para la Seguridad Alimentaria (PESA Centroamerica).
entries.description:
Descripción

1. El programa PESA

  • Esta tecnología y/o práctica proviene del Programa Especial para la Seguridad Alimentaria (PESA) en Centroamérica.
    • El PESA es una iniciativa promovida por la FAO para contribuir al cumplimiento de los acuerdos de las dos grandes Cumbres Mundiales sobre Alimentación (1996 y 2002), y los compromisos de la Declaración del Milenio de reducir el hambre en el mundo a la mitad para el 2015.
    • En Centroamérica el PESA se ejecuta con la colaboración de los Gobiernos de Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua y El Salvador.
  • El programa trabaja, entre otras actividades, atendiendo a pequeños productores agrarios, mostrándoles como incrementar su producción y sus ingresos mediante tecnologías novedosas y promoviendo la inversión en infraestructura rural, generación de ingresos no agrícolas, agricultura urbana y redes de protección.

2. Objetivos del plan de Finca-Hogar

  • El PESA aplica la metodología de transferencia conocida como familia demostrada, que consiste en enfocar la asistencia técnica a una pareja (hombre y mujer) que toman protagonismo en la comunidad para aprender, experimentar y adoptar tecnologías en la finca e implementar las buenas prácticas en el hogar las cuales las comparte con otras familias cercanas.
  • Por lo anterior, contar con un plan de Finca-Hogar se hace necesario e indispensable, para la planificación de actividades, en la finca como en el hogar, en busca del mejoramiento integral en la vida de las familias participantes.
  • Se espera que cada plan de Finca-Hogar se convierta en el plan de trabajo de cada una de las familias y que sea ejecutado en forma conjunta, con el apoyo de los equipos conjuntos conformados por los técnicos del CENTA, promotores de salud y consejeros voluntarios, brigadistas de saneamiento; con la finalidad de facilitar un hogar digno y una finca productiva, que contribuya con la seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de cada uno de los miembros de la familia participante en el programa.
  • El plan de Finca-Hogar a completar está disponible como archivo adjunto.

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Guía metodológica Patio-Hogar: ID 7223.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

A través de esta tecnología, la pareja aprende técnicas que funcionan, que también pueden compartir a otras familias cercanas. Esto también crea una unión social entre las familias.

5.2 Atiende a las necesidades de la mujer

Dado que la pareja (mujer-hombre) aprende las técnicas juntos, ambos participan igualmente en la implementación de las prácticas.

5.3 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Debido a esta tecnología toda la comunidad se beneficia de las técnicas aprendidas, ya que se intercambian conocimientos entre sí, que a largo plazo conduce a la seguridad y soberanía alimentaria.
entries.further_reading:
