entries.tittle: Labour saving technologies and practices: solar drying equipment
entries.summary: The following describes the preservation by solar drying of perishable fruits and vegetables. It highlights the features of solar drying as well as its advantages and disadvantages. These include labour saving, livelihood resilience strengthening, equipment, cost, skills, risk and infrastructure.
entries.description:
Description

Many perishable fruits and vegetables, such as raisins, prunes, and yams are preserved by solar drying. Speciality foods such as sun-dried tomatoes are also preserved this way. The crop is laid out in the sun at the start of the dry period on the ground. Sheets of material or simple racks are raised off the ground. When the crop is laid on bare ground, it can be damaged by pests and contaminated with soil, which later has to be removed. Grains and pulses need to be dried below 15 percent moisture content to minimize losses during storage and also to ensure their suitability for sale. Drying of the crop starts before harvest. It frequently continues after harvest and before shelling or threshing. For example, this is done by storing maize in drying cribs, and is continued after this process if necessary. The importance, difficulty and amount of labour involved with drying increases in humid countries, where there is a short period between the two rainy seasons.

1. Features of solar drying

  • Simple equipment is needed for solar drying, such as the use of black polyethylene covers and chimneys to draw the air over the grain.
    • This substantially increases the drying rate and protects the crop.
    • More sophisticated systems use shallow rectangular boxes or trays with perforated bottom plates.
  • The crop is placed on the plate and air is blown up through the crop from a lower chamber.
    • The air could be solar heated, by drawing it from under black painted corrugated iron or polyethylene sheets, and using the chimney effect to draw it through the crop.
  • Faster mechanized systems of the above batch drying system commonly have a power requirement of 1.5 kW for a 1 tonne capacity dryer.
  • The air may be heated by burning rice hulls, maize cobs, or a non-renewable fuel such as electricity, fuel oil or gas.
  • A diesel or electrically operated fan is commonly used.
  • Typical drying rates are of 1 percent of moisture removed per hour.
  • Access to moisture meters is important so that farmers can use them regularly to verify their own accuracy at determining moisture content.

2. Advantages

  • Labour-saving
    • Simple technologies improve the rate of drying over traditional methods.
    • Automatized processes or semi-automatic ones allow processing faster and bigger volumes of product.
  • Livelihood resilience strengthening
    • Drying to the correct moisture levels reduces losses during storage and increases the value of final output.
    • Selling crops at the correct moisture level increases their value.
    • The improved final product contributes to improve income and food security.
  • Equipment
    • Using the equipment is relatively simple.
  • Cost
    • Solar drying systems are generally cheap to install and have minimal maintenance costs.

3. Disadvantages

  • Equipment
    • Solar drying systems are slow unless the heat-gathering surface is large and the air draught is fan-assisted.  
  • Cost
    • Mechanized systems using non-renewable fuel sources are expensive to run.
  • Skills
    • Although the solar heaters are simple, the technology behind them needs to be carefully explained so that the solar heaters are constructed to operate efficiently
  • Risk
    • The technology may be operated ineffectively.
  • Infrastructure
    • Local manufacture or importation of mechanized equipment is required.
Figure 1. Solar drying equipment

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Well dried maize benefits all: the solar maize dryer: ID 8285.
  • Dryer construction for solar-dried fruit and vegetables production: ID 4502.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

6.1 Labour saving technology (LST)

The practice allows, through automatized processes or semi-automatic ones, to process faster and bigger volumes of product.

6.2 Women friendly

This technology is easy to implement and accessible to all.

6.3 Pro-poor technology

The practice helps poor farmers to improve their income by increasing the value of the dried products. Selling crops at the correct moisture level increases their value.

entries.tittle: Jab Planter User Manual
entries.summary: Hand-jab planters are popular amongst small-scale farmers. They are the primary means of sowing seeds under no-tillage for most farmers. The implement is also suitable for filling in gaps after crop germination. There are many different models of jab planters from different companies. The operational principles are however similar. The implement may have either separate hoppers for seed and fertilizer or one hopper for seed only. This practice includes a user manual for jab planter, describing how to operate and maintain a jab planter.
entries.description:
Description

Figure 1. A jab planter

©FAO/TECA

1. How to operate a jab planter

  • The action of pulling the handles apart triggers the seeds/fertilizer to be conveyed from the hopper to temporarily settle at the furrow opener (the beak). This action occurs simultaneously with piercing/punching the soil.
  • The second action which occurs immediately after the first one is pulling the handles together. This action triggers the opening of the furrow opener (beak) in order to deliver the seed/fertilizer in the created planting furrow. The action also triggers the closing of the seed/fertilizer metering devices.
  • These two actions are undertaken repeatedly, and they have to be synchronized with the operator’s footsteps in order to achieve the desired plant population.
  • The operator will need to carefully listen to the dropping sounds made at every action to ascertain that indeed the implement is planting and there is no blockage.
  • The operator will have to use his / her judgment of the weight to re-fill the seed/fertilizer hoppers accordingly when they are about to be emptied.
  • Seeding rates can be adjusted according to the number of holes in the seed plate that are exposed to the outlet.

2. How to maintain a jab planter

  • Prior to any operation, the implement must be calibrated for the specific seed to be planted. Several seed plate sizes are available and the operator will have to select the one with holes that fit the particular seed. Seeding rates can be adjusted accordingly. There is a provision to plant one, two or three seeds per hole. This is achieved by positioning the pin in any of the three holes.
  • The implement must be cleaned and dried properly after every operation and stored in a cool dry place.
  • Where possible, apply graphite on the seed plate. This acts as a lubricant for the moving parts to minimize tear and wear.
  • The implement is mostly suited to dry, light or soft mulch covered soils. It is unlikely to work well in muddy or surface crusted soils.

3. Why do we need a jab planter?

  • Part of the attraction of hand-jab planters is that they do not require access to animal or tractor power, are low cost, light and easy to operate, although some skill is required and for these reasons, they are often accessible to women.
  • Enormous labour is saved by the use of jab planter. The work done by three to four people under conventional tillage is done by one person. One person is able to planter 1 fedan in two to three hours, saving valuable time that enables farmers to plant in time under conservation agriculture.
  • With direct seeding by the jab planter, there is minimal (less than 5 percent) soil disturbance, so weed germination is minimized.
  • The small size of the devices makes them suitable for operation on hilly, stony and stumpy areas and for intercropping.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Animal traction and single-axle tractor drawn planters in conservation agriculture: ID 7416.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: Draught Animal Power (DAP) planters and weeders: ID 7305.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: row planting, hand seeders and planters: ID 7301.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

​​The technology does not require animal or tractor power, is easy to operate and is labour-saving. ​

5.2 Women-friendly

​​The technology is easy to use and accessible to all. ​

5.3 Resource use efficiency

​​The technology provides little soil disturbance and prevents weed germination. ​

5.4 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for an increase in crop yields which in turn provides an additional source of food and income.

entries.tittle: Bagar Farming (Baluwa kheti) in River Banks of Nepal
entries.summary: Farmers located along the river banks in the Kapilvastu district in Nepal face frequent floods and subsequent land degradation that deeply affects their livelihoods, as the sand that deposits in this area makes cultivation of crops unfeasible. The introduction of watermelon and sweet potato crops along the river banks, also known as bagar farming, protects the land from excessive degradation. In addition, this livelihood activity ensures additional income and benefits not only local farmers, but also some local businessmen of Taulihawa and the local haat bazar. Main advantages of these crops include that if paddy crops fail due to floods or droughts, these crops can be cultivated as late season crops, and they do not need irrigation facilities during winter or can be cultivated during summer with some irrigation water. This practice describes how introducing different crop cultivation along the Banganga river banks in Nepal helps protecting the land from excessive degradation.
entries.description:
Description

The banks of the Banganga river in the Kapilvastu district in Nepal were degraded due to frequent floods and subsequent land degradation. For several years, these lands were kept fallow without crop cultivation and as local farmers possess small size lands, they often depend on the daily wage labour for their livelihoods. Farmers report that the river has been changing its course for the past 15 to 20 years, posing a risk to monsoon season crops. In the recent past, more than 100 bigha (1 337 m²) of land has been affected by sedimentation along the river bank in the Dhankauli village.

In this context, farmers located along the river banks in the Terai region cultivate watermelon and sweet potato in the river banks during winter (January-February), also known as bagar farming (Baluwa kheti). The introduction of these crops along the river banks is particularly beneficial. Erosion is a major problem for smallholder agriculture and this practice protects the land from excessive degradation. In addition, this livelihood activity benefits local businessmen of Taulihawa and the local haat bazar.

The objective of this practice is to protect the land affected by river bank cutting and to promote alternative livelihood activities for the poor farmers.

1. Implementation of this technology

  • As part of the land preparation activities, 30 cm deep and 30 cm wide pits are excavated with a 1 m spacing in between, and then left to dry for about 10 to 15 days.
  • The pits are then filled with farmyard manure, Diammonium Phosphate (DAP) and urea.
    • Three or four seeds are sown per pit.
  • The pits are covered with mulching materials, preferably straw and tree branches to maintain soil temperature and moisture until the plants reach a four to five leaf stage.
    • The vines need to be watered daily until they reach from two to three leaf stage.
    • The crop is ready to harvest in May.
  • Farmers usually wait for the monsoon rain and sometimes extend this cultivation until late August before transplanting paddy.
    • If there is no sufficient rain after August for paddy, sweet potato is cultivated.
      • Cultivation is done through vegetative propagation with vine cuttings of matured crops or produced from tubers in rows with a 60 cm space between rows and 10 cm to 15 cm between plants.
      • Farmers leave some tubers and vines in the field while harvesting, for produces during the subsequent year harvest.
  • As sand normally deposits in the bank, cultivation of other crops is not feasible.
    • In these conditions, watermelon and sweet potato cultivation is the best option. With this initiative, the landless households and small farmers, who depend on daily wage labour, are benefited.
    • Given the advantages, farmers show an increasing interest, in particular the cost ratio, the short duration and the low cost of technology and investment.
    • There are not many other employment opportunities between February and June.
    • Despite these benefits however, some problems reduce the possibilities of up-scaling this crop, such as the poor availability of quality seeds and other inputs at reasonable prices, or the need of irrigation facilities at times of long dry spells.
  • The collective marketing system is still poor and small farmers are deceived by middlemen.
    • Institutional support is required to disseminate this practice in other similar areas at larger scale.
Figure 1. River bank

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Bagar farming

©FAO/TECA

2. Costs

  • The overall cost of cultivation of watermelon cultivation in 1 kattha (67 m2) of land is Rs 4 500 (USD 56.96) are explained below.
    • Rs 1 800 (USD 22.78) are for DAP and urea.
    • Rs 1 500 (USD 18.99) for improved seeds.
    • Rs 500 (USD 6.33) is for labour cost.
    • Rs 700 (USD 8.86) for harvesting and marketing purposes.
  • The normal production of watermelon is 3 quintals per kattha.
    • The total income from 1 kattha of land is 15 000 (USD 189.87), Rs 5 (USD 0.06) per kg for 3 000 kg.
  • The overall cost of sweet potato cultivation per unit in 1 kattha of land is Rs 1 700 (USD 21.52).
    • Rs 500 (USD 6.33) for seeds.
    • Rs 500 (USD 6.33) for labour.
    • Rs 700 (USD 8.86) for harvesting and marketing purposes.
  • As farmyard manure can be applied for better production, there is no need to add chemical fertilizers.
  • The total income is Rs 4 500 (USD 56.96).
  • Higher productivity can be ensured even with traditional variety and locally available tubers.
  • Poor small farmers also benefit, as it can be consumed at household level or sold at the local market.
  • Although farmers have proven knowledge about the cultivation of this crop, technical support, input supply and market facilities are required for wider replication.

3. Validation of the practice

  • Farmers of the Banganga river in the Kapilvastu district in Nepal applied this practice and cultivated watermelon and sweet potato.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Slope agriculture land technology (SALT) in the mid-hills of Nepal: ID 7717.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

No large investment is required to apply this practice. However, marketing activities may constitute obstacles for poor farmers as the collective marketing system is still poor. Also, many small farmers are deceived by middlemen.

entries.tittle: Water Conservation Ponds in Nepal
entries.summary: During the pre-monsoon season, between March-and May, some areas in Nepal experience water shortages. On the other hand, during the monsoon season, water excess causes regular floods and landslides. In this situation, activities such as agriculture or livestock, as well as the availability of drinking water and women’s workload are deeply affected. Guaranteeing water availability throughout the year is therefore essential to reduce the vulnerability of Nepalese farmers. Water conservation ponds prove strategic, storing water and replenishing groundwater reserves for the dry season and protecting hillsides from landslides during the rainy season. Conservation ponds are not a new practice in Nepal. Indigenous populations in the mid-hill region have used them in the past, but these practices were lost due to the introduction of piped water supply. Currently, water conservation ponds are being reintroduced as a local adaptation strategy.
entries.description:
Description

In Nepal, increasingly irregular rainfall patterns have been affecting the livelihoods of Nepalese farmers. Households face water shortages during the pre-monsoon season, between March and May, as well as during the post-monsoon season and winter, between October and February.

In this context, it is essential to guarantee water supply throughout the year in order to reduce vulnerability of farmers caused by erratic rainfall patterns. Water conservation ponds prove a strategic adaptation practice, collecting rain water and replenishing groundwater reserves during the monsoon, as well as preventing excessive erosion and surface runoff down landslides slopes. In addition, the availability of water during the dry season is key for traditional rural livelihoods, such as livestock and crop cultivation, as well as in the development of new activities, providing habitat for fish-raising. Additional advantages include the stabilization and re-vegetation of gullies; water availability for cultivation of small-scale fodder; vegetables and fruit trees along the boundaries of the pond; irrigation of kitchen gardens during dry periods; and manure from dredged silt.

Finally, conservation ponds ensure nearby water sources, considerably reducing the amount of time women dedicate to fetching water.

1. Implementation of the technology

1.1 Construction

  • Conservation ponds may be built in many ways and sizes to suit the need of farmers.
  • It is strongly encouraged to use local tools, materials and labour in order to facilitate maintenance and reduce costs.
  • A critical feature is the size of the pond, which depends on land availability, household needs and slope considerations, as small ponds are better suited for porous soil and over-topping concerns.
  • Location is another important feature, as the pond can hold a potentially troubling runoff in landslide-prone areas and increase soil moisture in strategic places.
  • The pond-bed lining determines the seepage rate and varies in terms of replacement frequency, examples include plastic, stones, clay, and manure.
  • On average, ponds tend to be about 1 m to 1.5 m deep.
  • All these factors are determinant in the length of water availability.
  • Ponds may be for individual or communal use.

1.2 Handling excess water

  • It is important that ponds contain a diversion waterway that shunts excess water into a safe area village trenches often serve to this purpose.

1.3 Maintenance

  • Annual maintenance work is recommended prior to monsoon season.
  • Tasks include dredging fine soils from pond bottom and maintaining diversion waterway.

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Pond construction

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. A finished pond

©FAO/TECA

  • In addition, institutional support is necessary to renew traditional ponds and raise awareness among rural communities in the mid-hill regions on the benefits, construction techniques and maintenance activities necessary.
  • Local community-based organizations need to be strengthened to promote replication of the practice.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cool.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Water management in organic agriculture: ID 8366.

4.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology helps poor farmers to conserve water for dry seasons.

entries.tittle: Bio-engineering Practices to Control Erosion of River Embankments in Nepal
entries.summary: Heavy rainfall and landslides in the up-streams of the Churia range cause sedimentation of river beds, leading to erosion of river embankments by fast flows of water. This heavily affects the livelihoods of farmers downstream, causing loss of infrastructure, crops and livestock. In addition, the continuous erosion of agricultural lands has led to floods and gradual deposition of sand, silt and boulders in agricultural land. Cultivation of fast-growing live barriers and building of gabion wires are some bio-engineering practices promoted in the Terai region of Nepal to control erosion of river embankments by fast flows of water. These activities to control erosion of productive land along the river bank increase agriculture productivity and sustainability, while providing additional income for farmers. These practices are technically sound, as well as economically feasible and socially accepted.
entries.description:
Description

The Churia range in Nepal is the youngest mountain system located in the outskirts of the Himalayas, and it is of ecological, hydrological and socio-economic importance for Nepal, in particular for the Terai region. Activities such as uncontrolled grazing and forest depletion upstream lead to heavy sedimentation of sand, silt and boulders in riverbeds, causing subsequent erosion of river embankments by fast flows of water downstream.

The objective is to strengthen the Kharare river embankments with live barriers to control soil erosion and to safeguard/reclaim productive lands (paddy).

1. How to prevent the erosion on the river banks

  • Local farmers located near the riverbanks organize into local committees in order to identify sites for intervention.
  • It is important that they contribute in kind/labour in order to familiarize with the interventions, guaranteeing sustainability of actions.
  • Saplings of different species are provided to be planted along the river and dykes embankments.
    • Species need to be soil binding and fast growing, in order to better control erosion.
    • Some examples include fodders or grasses, bamboo, simal, trees, etc.
  • Retaining walls made of containers fabricated of thick galvanized wire and filled with stone stacked on one another are built along the river banks to control erosion.

2. Activities for successful regulation implementation and maintenance of the river

  • It is important that farmers are facilitated and guided in the set-up of rules and regulations for implementation and maintenance of river control activities.
    • The establishment of bamboo spur check dams to protect embankments.
    • The removal of sand, silt and boulders from river beds to allow smooth flow of water.
    • The construction of gabion wires with boulders to stabilize points of erosion.
    • The construction of proper outlet channels for diverting runoff.
    • The selection of tall varieties of paddy suitable for inundation prone areas.
  • Training on social and community mobilization is required to improve the vegetation and promote afforestation.
Figure 1. Bioengineering

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Gabion wire

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Bioengineering

©FAO/TECA

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cool.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Multi-storied Agroforestry cropping systems for micro-climatic modification and erosion control: ID 7711.
  • Slope agriculture land technology (SALT) in the mid-hills of Nepal: ID 7717.
  • Bagar Farming (Baluwa kheti) in river banks: ID 7376.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology helps poor farmers to reduce the impact of uncontrolled grazing and forest depletion, which leads to the erosion of river embankments.

entries.tittle: Observation of bioindicators as early warning systems to mitigate the impacts of frosts and droughts in Bolivia
entries.summary: Weather in the Andean high plateau is characterized by extreme climate events with serious impacts on agriculture, increasing the vulnerability of farmers. The lack of forecast weather stations in the region leads to a lack of data, weakening timely decision-making. The implementation of modern agro meteorological services would imply high costs. However, local communities in the Omasuyo province in Bolivia traditionally rely on the observation of local bioindicators, which provide a kind of local agro meteorological service that has produced reliable guidance for mitigating the impacts of extreme climate events on crops.
entries.description:
Description

This practice aims to reduce the vulnerability to climate events in the high plateau through the observation of bioindicators.

1. Implementation of technology

1.1 Qariwa o waycha (Senecio clavicolus)

  • The waycha bush grows in the Bolivian high-plateau and is often located in river banks.
  • This small bush blooms three times a year.
    • The first flowering period occurs during June, the second in September and the third in November.
    • Its three yearly blossoms are considered as bioindicators.
    • Blossom periods are directly related to the three harvests, early harvests (nayra satas), middle harvests and late harvests (qhipa satas).
    • If frosts do not affect the bush or its flowers during these periods, harvest is expected to be successful. (Figure 1)
    • On the contrary, if the waycha is affected by a frost while blooming, the corresponding harvest will not be successful (Figure 2).
    • Furthermore, places where this bush grows indicate good spots where potatoes should be cultivated.
Figure 1. Flowering of quariwa

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Flowering of quariwa

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Ch’illiwa (Festuca dolichophylla)

  • This grass is widely present in the high-plateau, in particular in humid places nearby river banks.
  • As a bioindicator, the colour of the stem is observed.
    • If transparent and scaly, it is a sign of regular precipitations and a favourable production.
    • In addition, ripen and big seeds are a sign of good production of quinua. (Figure 6)
  • The validity of bioindicators is monitored by communities, by filling cards every day describing the local weather (Figures 7 and 8).
Figure 3. Flowering Sankayu

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Flowering Sankayu

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Sankayu fruits

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Ch'illiwa grass

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Weather monitoring card

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Weather monitoring card

©FAO/TECA

2. Validation of the practice

  • Local communities in the Omasuyo province in Bolivia traditionally rely on the observation of local bioindicators which provide a kind of local agro-meteorological service that has produced reliable guidance for mitigating the impacts of extreme climate events on crops. 

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, cool/ cold/ very cold.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Use of bocachi fertilizer to reduce the impacts of frosts: ID 7390.

This technology is also available in Spanish: ID 7391.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

By observing local flora, this technology efficiently allows for precise meteorological deductions. 

5.2 Pro-poor technology

Bioindicators inform farmers about climate forecasts. Farmers are therefore able to take preventative action in order to safeguard their crops, ensuring a more stable source of food and income.

entries.tittle: Pineapple as Alternate Cropping to Control Soil Erosion in Nepal
entries.summary: This practice shows that pineapple cultivation not only minimizes soil erosion but also promotes the rehabilitation of degraded sloppy lands for additional income. Technical details are provided for the implementation of this practice including pit preparation and seedling plantation. The economic advantages of this practice include local labour generation and additional income.
entries.description:
Description

Pineapple cultivation for household consumption is a traditional practice in the hills of Bengri in Nepal. However, the concept of cultivating pineapple in degraded land as a means of erosion control and alternative income source was itself a new practice adopted by local farmers.

Cultivation of pineapple is appropriate in sloppy land, prone to erosion and even degraded lands. Before adopting the practice, maize was cultivated for household consumption. However, land management practices such as tillage were not properly adopted for maize cultivation and thus resulted in severe soil erosion. Due to unpredictable rain and longer droughts even during the rainy season, maize cultivation is riskier. The objective of pineapple cultivation is to minimize soil erosion and promote the rehabilitation of degraded sloppy lands for additional income through pineapple cultivation.

1. Technical details of the implementation of the practice/technology

  • Pineapple plantation in sloppy land is implemented in small 4-inch depth pits unlike the traditional 2 feet depth to apply some composted manure in the pits.
  • Seedling plantation of pineapple sets should be carried out between February and March.
  • An advantage of pineapple is its resistance to pests/diseases compared to maize.
  • Pineapple cultivation has important economic advantages for small and marginal farmers in the mid-hills of Nepal.
    • The per-unit cost for pineapple cultivation in 1 kattha (around 67 m2) of land is estimated at Rs.1 200 (USD 15.19), of which Rs. 450 (USD 5.70) are for land preparation and labour cost; Rs. 150 (USD 1.90) for weeding; and Rs.600 (USD 7.59) for seeding.
    • The net income from pineapple cultivation in the same plot of land is between Rs. 3 500 and Rs. 4 000 (between USD 44.30 and USD 50.63).
    • The net income from maize in the same plot of land is Rs. 600 (USD 7.59), far less to that of pineapple.
  • Given the income advantage and its multiple benefits, farmers showed interest in large‑scale pineapple cultivation.
  • If this practice is carried out with commercial aims, it can generate local labour and additional income.
  • The practice’s capacity to generate additional income with low investment provides the farmers with the opportunity to put in practice this alternative crop to protect sloppy and degraded lands.
Figure 1. Pineapple cropping

©FAO/TECA

2. Validation of the practice

  • In the Bengri village in Udaypur district, 44 poor and medium categories of Tamang families with low landholding were selected to study and monitor the impact of pineapple cultivation in sloppy land.
  • A further 82 families in Bengri are currently adopting this practice.

3. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • Seedling plantation of pineapple sets should be carried out between February and March, and depth of implantation should be small as recommended for sloppy land.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cool; and
  • temperate, cold.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Diversified cropping system: strip cropping: ID 4643.
  • Diversifying cropping patterns in drought prone areas: ID 6855.
  • Soil and water conservation practices to reduce soil erosion and enhance water conservation: ID 7861.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

This practice does not require intensive labour.

6.2 Women-friendly

One of the benefits of this practice is that it is a women-friendly practice, easily implemented by all.

6.3 Resource use efficiency

Protects sloppy and degraded lands.

6.4 Pro-poor technology

This practice requires low investment and generates higher income.

entries.tittle: Crop Rotation in Conservation Agriculture
entries.summary:
Conservation Agriculture (CA) is an approach to managing agro-ecosystems for improved and sustained productivity, increased profits and food security while preserving and enhancing the resource base and the environment. The three fundamental principles of CA are:

  • direct planting of crop seeds;
  • permanent soil cover; and
  • crop diversity.

This practice encourages crop rotation for its positive impact on crop productivity.
entries.description:
Description

In Conservation Agriculture, crop rotation becomes even more important because residues of previous crops accumulate on the soil surface.

These residues can have a negative effect on crop productivity in the case of monoculture, principally by favouring an increase in pests and diseases (example: cotton), and from possible allelopathic effects from the preceding crop.

There are three fundamental and basic principles of crop rotation (Cook and Ellis, 1987).

  • Rotation is better than monoculture, even when plants of the same family are cultivated.
  • The most efficient rotations are those that include legumes.
  • Crop rotation as an isolated practice is generally not enough to maintain stable productivity for many years; the addition of some external nutrients is necessary.

1. Aspects to take into account in order to establish crop rotations

  • Always include green manure/cover crops (GMCCs), prioritizing the production of biomass to improve soil cover and organic matter content.
  • The same species should never be sown on the same field in the following season.
  • The GMCCs utilized should be adapted to the region’s microclimate, to the soil, and to the farmer’s production system, and should result in important benefits for cash crops.

In order to plan crop rotations, the effects of one crop on the following should be taken into account, considering:

  • compatibility with the following crop;
  • degree of resistance to attack by pests and diseases;
  • biomass production;
  • root system; and
  • nutritional requirements.

2. The advantages of crop rotations

  • Many crops may have positive effects on succeeding crops in the rotation, leading to greater overall production.
  • Rotation is used to reduce pests and diseases in the cropping system and to control weeds by including smothering crop species (e.g. cowpeas) or green manure cover crops.
  • Rotations may also give benefits in terms of improved soil quality (more or deeper roots; root exudates), better distribution of nutrients in the soil profile (deep-rooted crops bring up nutrients from below) and to increase biological activity.
  • Through rotations, peak labour times may be reduced and labour better distributed throughout the year if planting and harvest times are different.
  • Crop rotations may decrease the risk created by extreme weather events such as droughts or floods and their effects, as bad seasons or bad parts of a season may affect some crops more than others.
  • Crop rotations can balance the production of residues by alternating crops that produce few and/or short-lived residues with crops that produce a lot of durable residues.
  • Crop rotation enhances the resilience of farmer ́s livelihood by improving the soil properties and improving the potential of higher yields.

Crop rotation is the most efficient and economical way to break the biological cycles of pests and diseases, thereby making Conservation Agriculture feasible.

3. Validation of the practice

With the utilization of green manure/ cover crops (GMCCs) in crop rotation, great achievements have been obtained in the maintenance and increase of agricultural production in several Latin American countries, facilitating the diffusion and adoption of Conservation Agriculture on small, medium, and large farms.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • tropics, cool/cold/very cold.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Cover crop species, with a special focus on legumes: ID 7414.
  • Introduction to conservation agriculture: principles and benefits: ID 7413.
  • Cover crop and residue management in conservation agriculture in East Asia and Pacific Regions: ID 7419.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: conservation agriculture: ID 7294.
  • Green manure/cover crops and crop rotation in Conservation Agriculture on small farms: ID 7250.

This technology is also available in Spanish: ID 8159. 

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology highlights the importance of crop rotation in conservation agriculture which permits the planting and harvesting of multiple types of crops and plants. This provides the farmer with opportunities to harvest larger varieties of plants, and benefit from the increase in income.

entries.tittle: Guide to Harvesting and Post-Harvest Handling of Cashew Nuts
entries.summary:
Production of high-quality cashew nuts is dependent on the application of excellent and thorough harvest and post-harvest techniques and practices. This technology is used as part of the African Cashew Initiative’s extension material. It helps farmers to understand how to approach the period just before harvesting begins and what do after they have harvested their cashew farms. This is to ensure that their final products are of the utmost quality.
This technology gives guidelines on how to harvest and store cashew nuts.
entries.description:
Description

Cashew nuts may be cultivated for both the:

  • nut
  • apple.

The cashew tree comes into bearing three to five years after planting. In Ghana, mature cashew trees normally start flowering in late November to December. The fruit matures in 90 to 100 days after flowering. The ripe fruits normally start to drop in late January. The peak fruit collection period is between February and March, with a few late maturing trees dropping their fruits in April.

It is important to remember that the excellence and thoroughness of post-harvest handling affects the quality of the product, which in turn affects the country’s reputation for those products.

Product quality influences the demand for those products on the whole market, which in turn positively affects the price.

1. Before harvesting

  • It is important to clean the weeds under the trees, ahead of harvesting.

    • This will facilitate the picking of fruits (apples and nuts).

2. Nut harvesting

  • Allow fruits to drop to the ground before picking.
  • In the southern parts of Ghana, collect fruits at least every three days. In hotter areas (i.e. Northern parts) of the country, collect fruits daily.
  • Leaving the nuts uncollected on hotter days lowers the quality.

3. Handling of nuts

3.1 Detach

  • The quality of the nut is affected when the apple is not neatly detached from the nut, hence it is important to detach the apple completely from the nut, using a:
    • nylon thread; or
    • sharp knife.

3.2 Drying

  • Air-dry collected nuts, under shade for three to four days, on:
    • concrete floors;
    • drying mats; or
    • tarpaulins.
  • Turn nuts frequently during the drying period to ensure uniform drying.
  • To maintain the quality of the nuts to avoid drying:
    • indoors;
    • on metallic surfaces; or
    • directly in scorching sun.
  • Well-dried nuts produce a rattling sound when turned on the drying floor.

3.3 Discard

  • Remove and discard nuts that are:
    • immature
    • diseased
    • shrivelled
    • damaged.
  • Remove any foreign matter when drying.

4. Storage of nuts

  • Store well-dried nuts in jute sacks, (no plastic or fertilizer sacks containers like boxes, buckets, etc.).
  • Stitch jute sacks tightly to avoid spillage.
  • Place the jute sacks on wooden pallets in a dry, well-ventilated leak proof room.
  • Leave a clearance of at least 0.5 m between the packed jute sacks and the roof as well as between sacks and walls of the storage room to allow air to circulate freely.
  • Sell nuts within the same year of harvest to prevent loss in quantity.

5. Validation of the practice

  • This technology has been applied in Ghana.

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Good practices for the establishment of a new cashew farm: ID 7461.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2467.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Women-friendly

Women can participate in the post-harvesting process, as the above recommendations are easy to implement and accessible to all.

8.2 Resource use efficiency

The handling and proper storage of cashew nuts and apples contribute to resource use efficiency and reduce post-harvest losses.

8.3 Pro-poor technology 

Cashew nuts and apples can be stored using a simple technique, this offers a new marketing opportunity for farmers.

entries.tittle: How to Estimate the Quality of Cashew Nuts (RCN)
entries.summary: The quality of cashew produced from country to country and region to region determines the reputation as well as the competitiveness of the product on the international market. The price that farmers may expect is directly linked to the quality of their produce. It is important; therefore, to teach farmers who may not have any or limited knowledge about how to assess the quality of nuts about exactly what determines whether their product is of high quality, meeting the demands of what consumers want. This simple, well-illustrated technical manual is used as training material by the African Cashew initiative and functions as a tool via which farmers may be taught how to assess and recognize good quality nuts. Not only does it demonstrate how to do this, but it also displays which tools and mechanisms may be used to implement this, providing information on the physical criteria used worldwide, across the cashew producing industry.
entries.description:
Description

This technology/practice provides the reader with information on the physical criteria used by the market players worldwide to assess the quality of the raw cashew nut (RCN). The main criteria used are the Out-turn (Kernel Output Ratio), Moisture, Nut Count, and the Total Defective Nuts. This technology will facilitate the jobs of quality inspectors when inspecting the quality of the raw cashew nut. 

1. Which parts of the fruit of the cashew tree are usable?

  1. The kernel
    • It is mainly consumed roasted and salted. Crushed kernels are used in the food industry (chocolate factory, pastry factory, biscuit factory). The oil obtained from kernels is used in cosmetic products or in food preparations.
  2. The balm
    • It is also called Cashew Nut Shell Liquid (CNSL) and has several uses in the industry. Extracted from the shell, this liquid is mostly composed of anacardic acids. It is used, after purification, in chemical products manufacturing. This liquid is dangerous, as it cannot be handled with bare hands. Its handling requires the use of gloves.
  3. The apple
    • It is juicy, lightly flavoured, sour and contains vitamin C.
    • This apple is edible.
    • Juice can be extracted from the apple to produce alcohol, vinegar and syrup.
  4. The shell
    • It is used as a fuel to drive the nuts processing (cooking or drying).
  5. The peel or testa
    • It is sometimes used either like the shells or as a complement livestock food, it can also be used to produce dyeing.
Figure 1. Parts of the cashew fruit

©FAO/TECA

2. Who assesses the raw cashew nuts quality?

  • During the raw cashew nuts marketing, quality control occurs at several levels. 

2.1 Farmers

  • Farmers ensure the quality of the cashew nuts they sell in order to get a good price from the buyers.

2.2 Local buyers

  • They assess the quality of the cashew nuts they buy in order to avoid the return of bad batches from their clients (local processers, exporters).

2.3 Exporters

  • Most of the raw cashew nuts produced in Africa are, then, exported to Asian countries (India, Vietnam). In exportation harbours, the exporters always check the quality of the cashew nuts batches.

2.4 Local shelling factories

  • Quality control is carried out when the cashew nuts arrive at the selling factories. If the processing occurs after a long time, the cashew nuts quality can decrease. That is why it is important to check the cashew nuts' quality just before their processing.
  • Therefore, quality control occurs throughout the supply chain and throughout its marketing. 

3. Why is the quality control of the raw cashew nuts necessary?

  • During a commercial transaction between a farmer and a tracker, for instance, several criteria can be used to specify the cashew nuts quality such as colour, shape, brightness, exterior aspect.
  • But the most important criterion is the quality of the kernel inside the shell.
Figure 2. View of the cashew kernel from outside and inside

©FAO/TECA

4. Criteria used to assess the quality of the raw cashew nuts

  • As mentioned in the description, there are four main criteria used to assess the quality of the RCN: the Out-turn, the defective nut rate, the nut count, and moisture. 

4.1 The Out-turn also called KOR (Kernel Output Ratio)

  • In general, Out-turn means the number of usable kernels after de-shelling the nuts. It is expressed in lbs quality, which means the weight of useful kernels weighed in pounds in one 80 kg jute bag of RCN. 
  • An example: an Out-turn of 49 lbs/bag of 80 kg means that we can have 49 lbs (22.2 kg) of kernels usable by the manufacturer if we shell 80 kg nuts. (Kindly refer to Table 1). 
  • To package the cashew nuts, use gunny bags of 80 kg (same bag used to store cocoa). The assessment of the kernel quality takes place using this 80 kg-bags. 
  • Then the kernels are sold in pounds. This is why the Out-turn means: kernels weighed in 80-kg bags. 
  • The out-turn is an important parameter for the user to control the quality of the nuts. Its prices are determined based on the quality of the kernels; thus, the buyers will be able to avoid the underestimation of their products by shady buyers. 
  • The value of the Out-turn helps improve the technical route. 
  • The Out-turn allows farmers to correct some weaknesses in the technical route and is also very important for the nuts marketing.
  • Marketing is a very important step for all the players of the cashew value chain as this is where the quality is defined.
  • The nuts price is set according to the value of the Out-turn; thus, the player who knows the Out-turn is able to negotiate prices.
  • Buyers (often from Asia) are specialists in this area; therefore, farmers and buyers have to know the Out-turn to avoid the underestimation of their products. 
Table 1. Conversion lbs/kg between the metric and the English system
1lb=0.45359 kg (or also 11.33 kg=25 lbs)
1 kg=2.2 lbs

Source: GIZ 2012

4.2 The Defective Nut Ratio

The Defective Cashew Nut ratio provides the number of defective nuts in the samples, mainly the:

  • premature kernels (blue category)
  • spotted kernels (blue category) + stunted kernels (red category)
  • void nuts (red category)
  • moth-eaten kernels (red category)
  • mouldy kernels (red category)
  • brown kernels (red category). 

To determine this rate, we weight the kernels and the shells of these two categories (blue and red) and express it in terms of percentage. 

In general, a sample that has more than 24 percent of defective nuts is rejected. This method is easier and faster than the Out-turn to determine the defective rate; thus, it is used to have a first insight into the batch quality. 

4.3 The Nut Count

  • This is the number of nuts per kilogram. It is expressed in nuts/kg. 
  • In general, it fluctuates between 150 nuts/kg and 240 nuts/kg. 
  • The smaller is the number, the bigger are the nuts. 
  • Combined with the Out-turn, the Nut Count gives information about the kernel size that we might get after shelling. 
  • The bigger the nuts, the higher is the Out-turn, and the more likely we are to get big kernels. These are especially easily sold on the world market. 

4.4 The Moisture Rate

  • This is an important element concerning nuts storage. It is expressed in percentage and has to be under control from harvest to the shelling. 
  • It is better to keep the Moisture Rate below 10 percent after the drying. 
  • If the rate exceeds 10 percent, nuts can go mouldy; however, if the rate is too low (under 6 percent), kernels become dry and lose weight. There is a shortfall for the seller.
  • Moreover, kernels too dry are too flimsy during processing.
  • Therefore, it is best to keep the moisture content between 7 and 10 percent. 

5. How to measure and quantify the assessment criteria

A checklist will help understand the measurement and steps to the assessment and quality control process. 

Table 2. Checklist for the steps of quality control
Steps Status
The material used to calculate the Out-turn
Sampling-and taking the "mother sample"
Weighing of the sample
calculation of the Nut Count
Opening of then nuts, and classification into three categories
Weighing 
Calculations

Source: GIZ 2012

5.1 Materials needed to calculate the Out-turn

  • One electronic balance with a precision of 0.5 g
  • catheter bag
  • one pair of scissors specially designed for shelling raw cashew nuts
  • one scooper ( could be adapted from a screwdriver)
  • plastic bucket
  • four plastic bowls
  • latex gloves. 
Figure 3. Material needed to calculate the Out-turn

©FAO/TECA

5.2 Sampling: to take the mother sample

  • Nuts are taken from the stocks of different places either from the farmer's place, from local shops, cargos, or warehouses (Figure 4). Quality can be checked at any location. 
  • First, a sample has to be taken.
    • Sampling is very important to calculate the Out-turn and it has to be done carefully by following a specific process. 
Figure 4. Examples of nuts batches

©FAO/TECA

5.2.1 How to take a mother sample?

  • In this example shown in Figure 5, we see a truck unloaded at a harbour. During the unloading of the truck, nuts are taken from the bag with a catheter bag.
Figures 5 and 6. The sample is taken from the bag 

©FAO/TECA

This sampling is done in one every ten bags for big batches (30-40 tonnes), or in every five bags for small batches (15-20 tonnes). For the buyer, it is useful to take a sample in each bag for better accuracy and to prevent suppliers from hiding bad-quality bags in the middle of the batch. 

The quantity of nuts taken from the entire batch is scraped up on a flat area. This quantity is the "mother sample". Then the sample has to be taken for its analysis. The "quarter method" has to be followed to take the sample. 

This is a 3 steps method.

  1. First, a mixture of the mother sample is taken; 
  2. then the composition of the quarters is done; and
  3. lastly, the composition of the samples is analysed.

Here in Figure 8, the sampler mixes the "mother sample" which has to be done carefully in order to get a homogenous pile. 

Figures 7 and 8. "Mother sample" and its mixing

©FAO/TECA

5.2.2 How to compose quarters (Figure 11)

  • The mother sample is divided into four parts more or less equal. Each part is called a "quarter". We have four quarters: two to two opposite.
  • Therefore, the first quarter is opposite to the third quarter, and the second quarter is opposite to the fourth quarter.
  • Each sample has to come from two opposite quarters. For this, we take small amounts more or less equal of nuts from the opposite quarters and mix them in a bucket. 

Thus we get:

  • sample one form the first and the third quarter; and
  • sample two from the second and the fourth quarter. 
Figures 9 and 10. Composition of the quarters for later analysis

©FAO/TECA

Figure 11. Scheme to describe the composition of the quarters

©FAO/TECA

5.3 Weighing the sample

Each sample, composed like described before, is weighed to get about 1 kg of nuts.

  • Let W(1) be the weight of the sample. When conducting the weighing write down W(1) =...kg. 
  • It can fluctuate between 980 g and 1 002 g. 
  • It can also be useful to keep a witness-sample of about 1 kg to check, in case somebody contests the results. 
Figure 12. Weighing W(1)

©FAO/TECA

5.4 Calculation of the Nut Count (NC)

After weighing the sample, we calculate how many nuts are in the sample. 

During this step, we also check if foreign matters are in the batch such as leaves, stones, dry apples and branches. 

For each sample, the nuts are brought together in small piles of ten nuts to avoid the mistake during the counting (Figures 13 and 14). Thanks to the nut piles, it is easy to know how many nuts are in the sample by counting the number of ten-nuts piles and the extra nuts. 

Figures 13 and 14. Ten-nut piles

©FAO/TECA

  • For example: for 193 nuts, we will count 19 piles of 10 nuts + 3 nuts
  • Write the result. N= ...!

5.5 Opening of the nuts, control of the kernels and classifications in three categories

Each nut (shell and kernel) of each sample is cut through with the scissors; thus, we get two halves with or without flaws. The split nuts are classified according to their characteristics. 

Figure 15 and 16. Each nut (shell and kernel) of each sample is cut through with the scissors

©FAO/TECA

  • Make sure that the two halves of each nut are kept together and that the kernel stays with their shells. 
  • Notice the position of the nut in the scissors.
  • Cut slightly the nut lengthwise, and dry the scissors after each cutting. 
  • Use gloves, and make sure there is enough good light 

By observing the split nuts, we can observe the kernels and classify them into three categories. 

  • Wholesome kernels (100 percent accepted) -green colour (Figure 17).
  • 50 percent rejected kernels - blue colour (Figure 18).
  • 100 percent rejected kernels -red colour (Figure 19). 
Figure 17. Wholesome kernels (100 percent accepted)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 18. 50 percent rejected kernels (blue colour)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 19. 100 percent rejected kernels -red colour 

©FAO/TECA

These controlled kernels are put in bowls of  green, blue and red according to their respective colour category. 

5.6 Weighing

This stage has two steps.

  1. Weighing of the defective kernels. 
  2. Weighing of usable kernels (kernels that are 100 percent or 50 percent accepted).

Good kernels are removed from the shells with the help of the scooper preferably without removing the peel (or testa). We get on one side kernels (with peel), and on the other side shells. 

These good kernels are the "100 percent accepted kernels", and are weighed with their peel.

  • Let W(2) be the total weight of the good kernels, W(2)= ....kg. 

Weigh the kernels+shells of the categories (premature and spotted).

  • Let W(3) be the total weight of the nuts (kernels +shells) that are 50 percent accepted.
  • W(3)= weight of the "spotted kernels" +weight of the "premature kernels"(kernels+shells).

Then the kernels (premature and spotted) are removed from their shells. All these kernels are the "50 percent accepted or rejected kernels". They are put in the blue bowl. 

The kernels (premature and spotted ) are weighed.

  • Let W(4) be the total weight of the "50 percent rejected kernels".

In the same way, each other category of defective kernels (mouldy, brown, moth-eaten, empty and stunted) is weighed with the shells.

  • Let W(5) be the total weight of the "100 percent rejected kernels". 

5.7 Calculation

The below figures describe the calculations required for the Nut Count, the Total Defective rate, the Out-turn and the useful kernels. 

Figure 20. Calculation of the Nut Count

©FAO/TECA

Figure 21. Calculation of the Total Defective Rate

©FAO/TECA

Figure 22. Calculation of the Out-turn

©FAO/TECA

Figure 23. Calculation of useful kernels

©FAO/TECA

If the above technology/practice is followed and abided by, the farmers, sellers and buyers will ensure a good quality product to be sold at fair prices for all actors. 

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Good practices for the establishment of a new cashew farm: ID 7461.
  • Guide to harvesting and post-harvest handling of cashew nuts: ID 7467.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology supports the farmer, the seller and the buyer in ensuring a better quality product across the value chain. If kernels are of 100 percent good quality, the farmer can negotiate the prices for a higher value product. If the kernels are of lesser quality, the buyer can also benefit from the negotiation of the prices.

entries.tittle: No-till technology - A no-till system with crop residue management for medium scale wheat and barley farming
entries.summary: The following technology describes the development of a special no-till drill with the purpose of simultaneously planting seeds and fertilizing annual crops. Information is given on how to drill cuts, how to plant seeds, correctly apply herbicides and tillage replacement. The advantages of using such a technology, which include low cost, improved resource use and higher yields, are also given.
entries.description:
Description

1. A no-till system

The following describes a no-till system with crop residue management for medium scale wheat and barley farming. This no-till technology (NTT) system, with direct seeding and crop residue management, was designed by the National Institute of Agricultural Research (INRA) in Settat, Morocco.

  • A special no-till drill was developed to simultaneously seed and fertilize annual crops. The drill cuts through residue opens a 20 cm wide slot which, after seed and N/P-fertilizers are dropped into it, is closed firmly to encourage contact between seed and soil.
  • Seeding is earlier than in the case of conventional tillage which requires seedbed preparation.
  • Spacing between rows is adjusted according to crop type: 20 cm for wheat or barley, and 40 cm for lentils and chickpeas. Tillage depth is between 5 cm to 12 cm depending on soil workability and moisture content.
  • Crops, planted in rotation with a fallow period, are barley, wheat, legumes (lentils and chickpea), and also fodder species.
  • Application of special herbicides replaces tillage for weed control and enables the farmer to have an 18-month fallow period (a ‘chemical fallow’) after two crops have been taken over a six-month period.
  • Fallowing is essential for water conservation in this semi‑arid area. 

2. Benefits and attributes of the no-till system

  • NTT reduces passes with heavy machines to three times per year. Residue management involves maintaining the soil partially covered with stubble and straw.
  • Overall, yields are higher and costs are lower than under conventional tillage.
  • NTT reduces soil erosion and soil compaction while conserving water in the soil.
  • Optimum use of scarce and low rainfall to stabilise/increase crop yields is essential in this area.
  • The use of the special no-till drill ensures both the minimal working of the soils and the precise incorporation of phosphate fertilizer beneath seeds.
  • Depending on the specific site, residue management is adjusted from low residue maintenance (stubble/ controlled grazing) to medium surface cover (stubble/straw maintenance, forage crops and exclusion of grazing).
  • Erosion and evaporation suppression/ control are the main impacts of the system. Runoff and concentrated flow in watersheds are reduced.
  • Chemicals are applied for weed control, but this takes into account the environment and can be reduced over time.
  • Maintaining crop residues in the fields increases soil organic matter and thus, the amount of carbon sequestered, as well as nutrient levels. Hence, the application of inorganic fertilizers can be reduced.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool. 

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Zero/minimum tillage in the rice-wheat system: ID 7715.
  • Introduction to conservation agriculture: principles and benefits: ID 7413.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The technology requires minimal soil work through precise steps and techniques.

5.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology reduces soil erosion and compaction. It also increases water conservation, improves crop residue maintenance, increases soil organic matter and reduces carbon dioxide emissions.

5.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology provides higher yields and lower costs.
entries.further_reading:

  • WOCAT 2012. No-till technology [Morocco]

entries.tittle: Intensive agroforestry system
entries.summary: Intensive agroforestry system is a protective and productive high-input agroforestry system comprising multi-purpose ditches with bunds, live barriers of grass, contour ridging, annual crops and fruit trees. The main purpose is to increase and diversify production, and at the same time, to protect natural resources and regenerate degraded areas, avoiding traditional slash and burning practices.
entries.description:
Description

1. Intensive agroforestry system

The intensive agroforestry system (silvoagricultura) combines traditional and newly developed practices adapted to conditions in areas of Colombia. The system is implemented on degraded and often steep slopes in sub-humid areas where intensive rainfall and dry periods alternate.

The land is officially communally owned, an ‘Indigenous Reserve’, but land use rights are individual. The region has a high population density: people are of indigenous origin and live in very poor conditions.

The main purpose of intensive agroforestry system is to:

  • increase production;
  • diversify production;
  • protect natural resources; and
  • regenerate degraded land areas.

2. Agroforestry plot

Cropping is concentrated on a limited area, a plot of 0.4 ha per household, in a highly integrated, intensive and diversified continuous land use system, thereby:

  • integrating soil and water conservation; and
  • avoiding traditional slash and burn practices.

Each ‘agroforestry plot’ comprises:

  • Four to five 50 cm wide and 40 m long multi purpose ditches excavated along the contour, 6 m to 12 m apart, depending on the slope.

2.1 Ditches

The main functions of the ditches are to:

  • retain runoff water which infiltrates the soil, thus reducing erosion and improving soil moisture; and
  • act as compost ditches for all types of organic residues on the farm. Residues, enriched with manure from chickens and guinea pigs, are tipped into the ditches. Within 8 to 12 months this decomposes into a fertile medium for the cultivation of vegetables and other crops.

The grass is cut several times a year to feed guinea pigs, which in turn recycle this into manure.

2.2 Earth bunds

Grass strips are planted on the earth bund on the upper side of the ditch to:

  • stabilize the structure;
  • retain runoff; and
  • capture eroded sediment.

2.3 Intercrops

 The lower side of the contour ditches, are planted with:

  • Fruit trees and bananas.

Each agroforestry plot is surrounded by:

  • rows of multi purpose indigenous tree species, to function as:
    • windbreak; and
    • extra income, yielding fruit and timber.

Between the structures, sited along the contour, on hand-dug micro-terraces/ridges, other crops are also grown:

  • annual (and semi-perennial) crops; or
  • intercrop with legumes.

2.4 Supportive technologies

Supportive technologies are:

  • protection of wells;
  • afforestation (where possible); and
  • irrigation to enhance production.

Production is based on principles of organic farming. High initial inputs of external manure are subsidised by the project. The remainder of each farmer’s land is left to natural regeneration, reforested, or where needed, used for conventional cropping.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

4. Related/associated technologies 

  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: woodlots, agro-forestry and improved fallow: ID 7320.
  • Vegetative trees in agroforestry: ID 7794.
  • Multi-storied Agroforestry cropping systems for micro-climatic modification and erosion control: ID 7711.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Resource use efficiency 

The practice increases and diversifies production, protects natural resources and regenerates degraded areas.

5.2 Pro-poor technology 

An increase in yields leading to improved food security and additional income thanks to limited area cropping concentration, diversified land use and soil and water conservation integration.
entries.further_reading:
6. Further reading

  • WOCAT. 2012. Intensive agroforestry system [Colombia]

entries.tittle: Roof top rainwater harvesting - Concrete Tank
entries.summary: The rooftop rainwater harvesting system uses a concrete tank designed to improve household access to water during the hot and dry seasons. A 16 cubic metre concrete tank situated in the shadow of the house is constructed to retain rainwater collected by the roof guttering. The purpose of the tank is to retain water to be used during summer months, for drinking, sanitation and irrigation of kitchen garden plots and diverse crops improving the livelihoods of households.
entries.description:
Description

The construction of the rainwater harvesting system requires three main elements:

  • metal gutter on wooden supports around the roof perimeter;
  • concrete pool in the shadow of the house; and
  • drainpipe connecting the gutter to the pool.

1. Classification

1.1 Land use problems

At critical times of the year there is a lack of water. The household village has a mean 600 mm annual rainfall concentrated during two months of the year.

The surrounding land has become increasingly dry and thus more denuded and unsuitable for cultivation.

Figure 1. Overview of the land use problem

©WOCAT

2. Environment

In general, the technology is applied mostly on soils of shallow to medium depth (20 cm to 60 cm), and on slopes that are gentle to moderate (5 to 15 percent).

Figure 2. Overview of the natural environment

©WOCAT

2.1 Tolerant of climatic extremes

  • temperature increase;
  • seasonal rainfall increase;
  • seasonal rainfall decrease;
  • heavy rainfall events (intensities and amount); and
  • decreasing length of the growing period.

2.2 Sensitive to climatic extremes

  • Droughts/dry spells.

2.3 If sensitive

Possible modifications to overcome extreme climate conditions are:  

  • Tank size could be increased.

In times of:

  • heavy rainfall; and
  • prolonged summer drought.
Figure 3. Human environment

©WOCAT

3. Technical illustration

The illustration in Figure 4 shows the metal guttering, approximately 15 cm wide, around the roof perimeter. The guttering collects the rainwater runoff from the roof and, through a drainpipe made of old plastic bottles stitched together by thin wire, drains the water into a concrete tank.

Figure 4. Technical illustration

©WOCAT/Soisin Peter

4. Implementation activities, inputs and costs

4.1 Establishment activities

  • Activities to establish rooftop rainwater harvesting systems include the construction of:
    • concrete tank
    • guttering.

4.1.1 Establishment inputs and costs

Table 1. Costs
Inputs Costs (USD) % met by land user
Labour 100 100%
Equipments tool 15 100%
Construction material
- wood 30 100%
- cement, stone, sand 150 100%
- metal sheet for roof gutter 100 100%
- plastic pipe 2 100%
Total 397 100%

Source: WOCAT 2012

4.2 Maintenance/recurrent activities

  • Cleaning.

4.2.1 Maintenance/recurrent inputs and costs per year

Table 2. Labour costs
Inputs Costs (USD) % met by land user
Labour 5 100%
Total 5 100%

Source: WOCAT 2012

The land user can provide:

  • labour
  • tools
  • piping.

Stone for the foundation is locally available.

However, there is an initial outlay of USD 300 for:

  • cement
  • wood
  • metal guttering.

The costs were calculated per tank based on 2012 prices.

5. Assessment

Figure 5. Impacts of the technology

©WOCAT

6. Validation of the technology

Approximately 70 percent of the land user families have implemented the technology voluntarily. The urban rooftop rainwater harvesting has been replicated by many members of the community without external support. 

There is moderate trend towards (growing) spontaneous adoption of the technology. People observed and experienced the benefits, and decided that it was worth the initial investment.

7. Concluding statements

7.1 Strengths and how to sustain/improve

7.1.1 Specialists’ opinion

The implementation of the rooftop rainwater harvesting system has:

  • improved the provision of irrigated water for the hot dry summer periods;
    • sustain further dissemination to other households;
  • allowed for the improvement and expansion of kitchen gardens;
    • training on keeping a kitchen garden;
  • improved the access of water for sanitation and drinking water purposes;
    •  education on sanitation methods.

7.1.2 Land users’ opinion

The increased access to water has:

  • improved the standard of living; and
  • allowed the households to have more autonomy over what to grow and eat.

7.2 Weaknesses and how to overcome

7.2.1 Specialists’ opinion

  • The perception was that the water was not clean in the concrete pool.
    • The water was tested and proved safe to use providing reassurance to the household members. The water tank would benefit from remaining covered and cleaned periodically.
  • The initial outlay may be considered expensive for some families.
    • If a whole community aims to build the system all at the same time, the material costs would be reduced.
    • The technology could be tied in with micro-finance activities.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies 

  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: roof water harvesting: ID 7304.
  • Rainwater harvesting for schools: ID 7645.
  • Improved rainwater harvesting for fodder shrub production and livestock grazing: the Vallerani micro-catchment system in the Badia of Jordan: ID 8757.
  • Rainwater harvesting systems for cabbage growing: ID 8932.
  • Rainwater syringe: low cost technology for rainwater harvesting in coastal areas: ID 6919.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

10.1 Resource use efficiency 

The implementation of this technology helps to secure an additional supply of water during the dry months and prevents soil quality depletion.

10.2 Pro-poor technology 

The practice allows for cleaner hence healthier water. Irrigation and water storage increase yields creating additional income.

entries.tittle: Shade-grown coffee
entries.summary: Shade-grown coffee is an agroforestry system which combines coffee with shade trees, including fruit, timber and leguminous species, in a systematic fashion. Shade-grown coffee is a traditional and complex agroforestry system where coffee is associated with various other species in different storeys (or ‘levels’). This provides ecologically and economically sustainable use of natural resources. While based on a traditional system the shade-grown coffee technology has a specific layout, and a reduced number of intercropped species.
entries.description:
Description

Shade-grown coffee is a traditional and complex agroforestry system where coffee is associated with various other species in different storeys (or ‘levels’). This provides ecologically and economically sustainable use of natural resources. Café arbolado, the example promoted by PRODAF (Programme for Agroforestry Development, see related approach: ‘Agroforestry Extension’) since 1987 is one technical option for shade-grown coffee.

1. Shade-grown coffee

While based on a traditional system the shade-grown coffee technology has a specific layout, and a reduced number of intercropped species. 

  • Coffee (Coffea arabica) planted on the contour at approximately 5 000 plants per hectare.
  • Associated trees.
    • Fruits, most commonly oranges (120 trees per ha), cedar (Cedrela odorata) or caoba (Swietenia macrophylla) for timber (60 tree per ha) and also two legumes, poró (Erythrina poeppigiana) and chalum (Inga spp.), which act as shade trees and at the same time improve the soil by fixing nitrogen (60 trees per ha).
    • Farmers often include bananas in the system.
    • In some cases, orange trees have partly been substituted by avocado (Persea americana), soursop (Anona muricata), and/or jocotes (Spondias purpurea).
    • The latter two command good market prices and do not compete with labour needed for harvesting and other activities.
  • Supportive soil conservation measures on steep slopes to avoid soil erosion, predominantly strips of lemon grass (Cymbopogon citratus) on the contour, retention ditches and soil cover improvement.
  • Fertilizers
    • Both organic and inorganic combined.
    • Full establishment of a shaded coffee plot can be achieved in two years – after replanting trees which fail to establish.
    • Coffee yields a harvest after two years, but timber from associated trees can be expected after only 25 years.
    • The trees grown in association allow more efficient cycling of nutrients (because of deep rooting and nitrogen fixation) and provide a favourable microclimate for coffee.
  • This production system is well adapted to the local biophysical and socio-economic conditions, characterized by steep erosion-prone mountain slopes, humid climate and small to medium scale agriculture.
  • Based on café arbolado a new, and further developed system of ‘sustainable coffee’ has evolved.
  • This involves certification of the overall process and is attractive to the growing number of environmentally conscious consumers.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Integrated crop and pest management (ICPM) for smallholder coffee in South Africa: ID 4541.
  • Enhancing climate resilience in mountainous regions through coffee intercropping for forest enrichment: ID 7701.
  • Agroforestry coffee cultivation in combination with mulching, trenches and organic composting: ID 8928.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2511.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The practice provides an ecologically and economically sustainable use of natural resources. It combines coffee with shade trees, associating with various other species, and reduces the number of intercropped species.

entries.tittle: Furrow-enhanced runoff harvesting for olives in Syria
entries.summary: Runoff collection has been used to plant olive orchards in north-west Syria in areas, which are considered too dry for olives. In one trial, trees were planted 8 m apart, within and between rows. Around individual trees ‘fish-bone’ shaped furrows were dug to harvest runoff water. The furrows were constructed manually with a hoe and reinforced with stones. They divert rainwater runoff to the micro catchments, where it concentrates in basins around the trees. Each tree is served by a catchment area of 60 m2. The furrows are re-made every year.
entries.description:
Description

The Khanasser Valley in north-west Syria is a marginal agricultural area, with an annual rainfall of about 220 mm per year. Soils are shallow and poor in productivity. The foot slopes of degraded hills are traditionally used for extensive grazing or barley cultivation. However, to achieve self-sufficiency in olive oil production, several farmers have developed orchards in this area, which is generally considered too dry for olives. Trees are spaced at 8 m apart, within and between rows. Traditionally, farmers prefer to till their orchards by a tractor in order to keep them weed-free (weeds may attract sheep, lead to fires and compete for water with the olive trees). As this tillage operation is usually practised up and down the slope, the resulting furrows stimulate runoff and erosion. However, when this is combined with V-shaped and/or fish-bone shaped micro catchments around individual trees, the furrows created can be used to harvest runoff water for improved production.

The V-shape earthen bunds (reinforced with some stones) are constructed manually, by hoe, around each tree. The furrows then divert runoff systematically to the micro catchments where it concentrates in basins around the trees. Each tree is effectively served by a catchment area of 60 m2.

The catchment's cultivated area ratio is thus approximately 60:1 (assuming the area exploited by the tree roots to be, initially at least, one square metre).

1. Advantages of runoff harvesting

  • This technology saves irrigation water during the dry season, enhances soil moisture storage, and stimulates olive tree growth.
  • Furthermore, fine particles of eroded soil are captured in the micro catchments.
  • While these may be nutrient-rich, they also tend to seal the surface.
  • The catchment areas between the trees are sometimes planted with low water-demanding winter annuals (lentils, vetch, barley, etc) especially when the trees are young.
  • This helps to reduce surface erosion.
  • The adoption of this practice will improve the resilience of the agrosystem against soil losses from erosion and yield losses due to droughts.
  • The improvement of soil moisture conditions and the limitation of the erosion will help the crop to be more resistant against extreme climate events.
Figure 1. Furrow enhanced

©WOCAT/Francis Turkelboom

2. Handling and compatibility with other crops

  • The bunds need to be rebuilt every year. If the structures are damaged after a heavy storm, they need to be repaired.
  • Labour input for establishment and maintenance is low, the technology is easy and cheap to maintain, and there is enough local skill to sustain and expand the system.
  • Supporting technology is to mulch the area around each tree with locally available stones (limestone and/or basalt) to reduce soil temperature during the summer, decrease surface evaporation and improve infiltration.

3. Validation of the practice

  • Implementation of furrow-enhanced runoff water harvesting in olive orchards started in 2002, and adoption by farmers is growing gradually.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool; and
  • subtropics, cool. 

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Planting pits and stone lines: ID 7516.
  • Pepsee micro-irrigation system: ID 7517.
  • Small level bench terraces: ID 7519.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Labour saving technology

This technology provides the farmers with the opportunity to collect rainwater around the olive trees. Subsequently, minimizing the labour time required to irrigate the trees with water in times of drought. 

6.2 Resource use efficiency

This technology optimizes natural resources as it relies on rainwater harvesting and catchments instead of purchasing of additional water for irrigation.

  • WOCAT. 2013. Water Harvesting Guidelines to Good Practice.
