entries.tittle: Sunken streambed structure
entries.summary: This practice consists of rectangular excavations in streambeds, named dohs, to provide temporary storage of runoff to enhance groundwater recharge, increasing water yields from shallow wells for supplementary irrigation. They also collect and impound subsurface flow. The technology is used in conjunction with shallow wells (odees), which enable farmers to harvest the increased groundwater for supplementary irrigation of annual crops. In summary, dohs are low cost water recharge alternatives for poorer communities, and in this case study, the extra area brought under production has meant that all families can have access to some water for irrigation.
entries.description:
Description

1. Dohs

Dohs are rectangular excavations in seasonal streambeds, which are intended to capture and hold runoff to enhance groundwater recharge, thus increasing water for irrigation from nearby shallow wells. They also collect and impound subsurface flow. Dohs are built in semi-arid areas where rainfall is low and seasonal.

2. Dohs dimension

The dimensions of a typical doh is 1.0 m to 1.5 m deep with variable length (up to 40 m) and width (up to 10 m) depending on streambed section, with an average capacity of 400 m3.

3. Working principle

The excavated material is deposited along the stream banks as a barrier against siltation from surrounding areas.

The slopes of the excavation are gentle (an upstream slope of 1:6 or 17 percent and a downstream slope of 1:8 or 12 percent) so that water flows into it, and excess water comes out again, carrying silt rather than depositing it. For this reason dohs are generally built in sequence.

The sides however are steep, to increase capacity – and benefit from stone pitching to stabilize them.

A silt trap comprising a line of loose boulders is constructed upstream across the streambed.

Dohs may be as close as a few metres apart. Bends in the stream are avoided as these are susceptible to bank erosion.

The technology is used in conjunction with shallow wells (odees), which enable farmers to harvest the increased groundwater for supplementary irrigation of annual crops – including vegetables such as chilli peppers. Water is pumped out of the wells.

4. Case study

In the case study of the village Mohanpada, each doh supplies an underground source of extra water to one well.

Communities worked together with project staff to:

  • carry out site selection; and
  • define with project technical assistance the details of:
    • design
    • estimates
    • layout.

4.1 Supportive measures

  • The catchment area is treated with gully plugs (small stone checks in gullies).
  • Water harvesting tank (small reservoir or dam) may be excavated upstream in a sufficiently large catchment area or suitable site.

The capacity of the tank at Mohanpada is around 600 m3 and thus also has a positive impact on groundwater recharge.

4.2 Maintenance

Maintenance is agreed through meetings of user groups regarding:

  • manual desilting; and
  • repairs of gully plugs.

In summary, dohs are low cost water recharge alternatives for poorer communities, and in this case study, the extra area brought under production has meant that all families requiring water for irrigation can access it.

Figure 1. Sunken streambed structure 

©Mats Gurtner

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • subtropics, warm/ mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies 

  • Water harvesting from concentrated runoff for irrigation purposes: ID 7512.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: roof water harvesting: ID 7304.
  • Rainwater harvesting for schools: ID 7645.
  • Improved rainwater harvesting for fodder shrub production and livestock grazing: the Vallerani micro-catchment system in the Badia of Jordan: ID 8757.
  • Rainwater syringe: low cost technology for rainwater harvesting in coastal areas: ID 6919.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

6.1 Resource use efficiency 

The technology is a low cost water recharge alternative, and through the streambed excavations runoff storage efficiently increases water yields.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology provides poor communities with access to water for consumption and for irrigation.

entries.tittle: Pepsee micro-irrigation system
entries.summary: A grassroots innovation that offers most of the advantages of conventional micro-irrigation at a much lower establishment cost. Pepsee micro-irrigation systems slowly and regularly apply water directly to the root zone of plants through a network of economically designed plastic pipes and low-discharge emitters. Technically speaking pepsee systems use low-density polythene (65 to 130 microns) tubes which are locally assembled. Being a low-pressure system the water source can be an overhead tank or a manually operated water pump to lift water from a shallow water table. Such a system costs less than USD 40 per hectare for establishment. But the tubes have a short life span of one or two years. The critical factor is the low entry cost. Pepsee systems thus act as ‘stepping stones’ for poor farmers who are facing water stress but are short of capital and cannot afford to risk relatively large investment in a technology that is new to them, and whose returns are uncertain.
entries.description:
Description

The continued expansion of irrigation in India is causing increasing water shortages. This may be compounded by the potential effects of climate change. Drip irrigation, delivering small amounts of water directly to the plants through pipes, is a technology that could help farmers deal with water constraints. It is considerably more efficient in terms of water use than the usual open furrows or flood irrigation.

In West Nimar, Madhya Pradesh, droughts, diminishing groundwater, limited and erratic power supply coupled with poverty, compelled farmers to look for a technology that would enable them to irrigate their crops (mainly cotton) within these constraints. They tried out several cost-saving options such as using old bicycle tubes instead of the conventional drip irrigation pipes. But nothing caught on until about five years ago when a local farmer experimented with thin poly-tubing normally used for frozen fruit-flavoured ‘lollypops’ called pepsee. It spread to neighbouring cotton farmers, and its popularity has meant that today pepsee has become widespread in the region.

Pepsee micro-irrigation systems slowly and regularly apply water directly to the root zone of plants through a network of economically designed plastic pipes and low-discharge emitters. Technically speaking pepsee systems use low-density polythene (65 - 130 microns) tubes which are locally assembled. Being a low-pressure system, the water source can be an overhead tank or a manually operated water pump to lift water from a shallow water table. Such a system costs less than USD 40 per hectare for establishment. But the tubes have a short life span of one or two years. An equivalent standard buried strip drip irrigation system amounts to between five and ten times the initial cost. The latter would, however, last for five to ten years. The critical factor is the low entry cost. Pepsee systems thus act as ‘stepping stones’ for poor farmers who are facing water stress but are short of capital and cannot afford to risk relatively large investment in a technology that is new to them, and whose returns are uncertain. The technology is today available in two variants the original white pepsee and a recently introduced black pepsee which is of slightly better quality. Recently, a more durable and standardized version of pepsee, given the brand name ‘Easy Drip’, has been developed and promoted by a local NGO, IDEI (see corresponding approach). Easy Drip is one product within a set of affordable micro-irrigation technologies (AMIT) promoted by IDEI.

Figure 1. Pepsee micro-irrigation

©WOCAT/Shilp Verma

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm. 

3. Related/associated technology

  • Furrow enhanced runoff harvesting for olives: ID 7515.
  • Planting pits and stone lines: ID 7516.
  • Small level bench terraces: ID 7519.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology is low costing and efficiently improves water usage for areas where little sources of water are found.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology reduces water stress for poor populations.

entries.tittle: Planting pits and stone lines
entries.summary: Rehabilitation of degraded land can be achieved through manured planting pits, in combination with contour stone lines. Planting pits are used to prevent water runoff and thereby increase infiltration and reduce erosion. This method is suitable on soil with low permeability, such as silt and clay and applicable for semi-arid areas for annual and perennial crops (such as sorghum, maize, sweet potato, bananas, etc.). One main advantage is its simple implementation and maintenance.
entries.description:
Description

The combination of planting pits (tassa) with stone lines is used for the rehabilitation of degraded, crusted land. This technology is mainly applied in semi-arid areas on sandy/loamy plains, often covered with a hardpan, and with slopes below 5 percent. These denuded plains are brought into crop cultivation by the combination of tassa and stone lines.

1. Planting pits and stone lines

  • Planting pits are holes of 20 cm to 30 cm diameter and 20 cm to 25 cm depth, spaced about 1 m apart in each direction.
    • The excavated earth is formed into a small ridge downslope of the pit.
    • Manure is added to each pit, but its availability is sometimes a problem.
    • At the start of the rainy season, millet or sorghum is sown in these pits.
    • The overall aim of the system is to capture and hold rainfall and runoff, and thereby improve water infiltration while increasing nutrient availability.
  • Stone lines are small structures, at most three stones wide and sometimes only one stone high.
    • The distance between the lines is a function of the slope and availability of stone.
    • Typically they are sited 25 m to 50 m apart on 2 to 5 percent slopes.
    • Stones are usually collected from nearby sites though sometimes up to 5 km to 10 km away and brought to the fields by donkey carts or lorries (when a project is involved).
    • They are positioned manually, along the contour.
    • Stone lines are intended to slow down runoff.
    • They thereby increase the rate of infiltration, while simultaneously protecting the planting pits from sedimentation.
  • Often grass establishes between the stones, which helps increase infiltration further and accelerates the accumulation of fertile sediment.
    • Wind-blown particles may also build up along the stone lines due to a local reduction in wind velocity.
    • The accumulation of sediment along the stone lines, in turn, favours water infiltration on the upslope side.
    • This then improves plant growth, which further enhances the effect of the system.
    • Construction does not require heavy machinery (unless the stones need to be brought from afar by lorry).
  • The technique is therefore favourable to spontaneous adoption.
    • Stone lines may need to be repaired annually, especially if heavy rains have occurred.
    • Manure is placed every second (or third) year into the previously dug pits and sand is removed annually.
      • Normally the highest plant production is during the second year after manure application.
Figure 1. Planting pits

©Charles Bielders

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Furrow-enhanced runoff harvesting for olives: ID 7515.
  • Pepsee micro-irrigation system: ID 7517.
  • Small level bench terraces: ID 7519.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently improves water usage and reduces erosion, thereby allowing the planting of diverse crops in semi-arid areas. 

4.2 Pro-poor technology

Through its simple implementation and maintenance, the technology allows for increases of sources of food and income through crop diversification and improved land usage.
entries.further_reading:
5. Further reading

  • WOCAT. 2011. Planting pits and stone lines [Niger]

entries.tittle: Small level bench terraces
entries.summary: Bench terraces with narrow beds are built on hillsides cleared from forests and used for growing tea, coffee and horticultural crops. This technology describes how terraces can be used to improve crop cultivation on hillsides.
entries.description:
Description

In northern Thailand, bench terraces, hereby described, are found on hilly slopes with deep soils. The climate is humid and tropical, with 1 700 to 2 000 mm annual rainfall.

The technology was pioneered and continues to be practised, by refugee immigrants from China looking for new areas to start farming. These immigrants first came in the 1950s and cultivated simply through slash and burn techniques. During the 1970s, they visited relatives in Taiwan and brought back the concept of small terraces. Originally they settled illegally, but eventually, they were given official permission to stay. However, official title deeds to their land have not yet been allocated.

1. Why terraces

The main aim of the terraces is to facilitate cultivation of tea or coffee on sloping land: erosion control is secondary.

The government policy to eradicate opium poppies cultivation has created viable alternative crop opportunities, such as:

  • coffee
  • tea
  • flowers
  • vegetables.

 To create bench terraces natural and secondary forests are cleared by:

  • slashing; and
  • burning

Terraces are then:

  • aligned by eye; and
  • constructed by hoeing.

2. Terraces building

Depending on the slope inclination, as there are no specific technical guidelines, the width of the terrace beds are:

  • about 1.0 m to 1.5 m;
  • up to 25 m long.

The risers are steep and have a 100 percent slope grade, without a defined lip.

Every three to four terraces, there are lateral drainage channels along the rise foot, approximately 20 to 30 cm wide and 10 cm deep, with a slope grade of 0.5 percent or less.

Excess water is partly drained by the soil, the overflow spills from the terrace risers and is discharged through draining channels to natural waterways.

Natural grass, which grows on risers, is cut back by:

  • hand hoe
  • machete

or

  • completely often removed by burning.

After harvesting annual crops, the land is then left until the next rainy season. At this stage the terraces are covered by weeds and grasses. Land is then tilled by hoeing.

The weeds and grasses are removed and heaped in piles outside the cropped area. However those are not composted or used for mulching, disappointingly where soil fertility is poor, chemical fertilizers are used instead.

Maintenance includes:

  • building up of risers;
  • repairing of risers; and
  • levelling of terrace beds.
Figure 1. Small level bench terraces

©WOCAT/Samran Sombatpanit

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • subtropics, warm/ mod cool.

4. Related/associated technologies 

  • Vegetated earth-banked terraces: ID 7520.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Resource use efficiency 

This practice facilitates crop cultivation on sloping land and allows for efficient control of soil erosion restoring land degradation.

5.2 Pro-poor technology

This practice improves soil quality and increases production, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Water harvesting from concentrated runoff for irrigation purposes in Spain
entries.summary: Water shortage is one of the most limiting factors for sustainable agriculture in large parts of South East Spain. Part of the solution of this problem may come from the restoration of traditional water harvesting structures. This technology describes small earthen or stone-built bund that diverts flood water, during runoff events, from intermittent streams towards nearby cultivated fields. The diverted water will temporarily flood the fields and provide the crops with water. Depending on the slope gradient and the amount of water to be harvested, the fields are organised as single terraces, or as a staircase of terraces. Water is diverted from one terrace to the next through small spillways in the terrace. The goal of this technology is to increase crop yield. In addition, these structures help to reduce the intensity of floods and reduce the damage caused by them by reducing runoff volume in intermittent streams.
entries.description:
Description

Part of the solution to water shortage for sustainable agriculture  may come from the restoration of traditional water harvesting structures. Many of these structures were widely used in South East Spain already during Arab and Roman times, and are also widespread in North Africa and the Middle East. However, nowadays in Spain many of them are abandoned and forgotten.

1. Application and features

The technology is generally applied mostly on soils of shallow to medium depth (20 cm to 60 cm), and slopes are gentle to moderate (5 to 15 percent). The climate  in Spain is semi-arid with a mean 300 mm annual rainfall. Droughts, peaking in summer, commonly last for more than four to five months. Annual potential evapotranspiration rates higher than 1 000 mm are common.

A Small earthen or stone-built bund diverts flood water from intermittent streams towards cultivated crop fields, generally planted with almond orchards and/or cereals. The diverted water will temporarily flood the fields and provide the crops with water. The fields are organized as:

  • single terraces; or
  • a staircase of terraces.

The choice depends on:

  • the slope gradient; and
  • the amount of water to be harvested.

On fields with gradients above 3 percent, terraces are necessary to reduce the gradient and to retain the floodwater as long as possible.

Water is diverted from one terrace to the next through small spillways in the terrace. The spillways can best be fortified with stones to prevent bank gully formation. The extra input of surface water can double the crop yields.

1.1 Environmental conditions

The use of these water harvesting structures is only possible under certain environmental and topographic conditions:

  • the cultivated fields should be at a relatively short distance from an intermittent stream (<50 m); and
  • the stream should have a sufficiently large upstream contributing area to provide significant amounts of runoff water during rainfall events.

This requires assessment of expected water inflow based on:

  • simple field observation during rainfall events; and
  • local knowledge of land users.

It is, however, important to consider:

  • if there are activities upstream that possibly affect the water quality (e.g. farm animals); and
  • the implications the water harvesting might have downstream.

Permission is required from the water authorities to construct any type of water harvesting structure.

1.2 Construction of diversion structure

Water harvesting requires the identification of a suitable location for the construction of a diversion structure.

Such structures are built by creating a small bund (<1 m height):

  • in the centre; or
  • to the side of a stream.

Depending on the size, the bund can be built with a:

  • shovel
  • tractor.

Maintenance:

  • Water harvesting structure will require control and some maintenance after each important runoff event.
  • If strengthened with concrete, maintenance will be reduced to approximately once every five years.

With these systems, water can be harvested up to eight times per year, mostly in spring and autumn during high intensity rainfall events. A well-designed Boquera system may provide up to 550 mm of additional water, in areas with an average annual rainfall of 300 mm.

2. Objective

The goal of this technology is to:

  • increase crop yield;
  • help to reduce the intensity of floods; and
  • reduce flood damages by reducing runoff volume in intermittent streams.

The implementation of this technology helps to secure an additional supply of water during the dry months. This benefits the resilience of farmers’ livelihoods against drought impact, allowing them to obtain higher crop yields, subsequently, improving their nutritional status and opening opportunities to market access. The agro-system also will be more resilient, since erosion is controlled to some extent, and the effects of drought are minimized, with all the benefits that this provides.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies 

  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: roof water harvesting: ID 7304.
  • Rainwater harvesting for schools: ID 7645.
  • Improved rainwater harvesting for fodder shrub production and livestock grazing: the Vallerani micro-catchment system in the Badia of Jordan: ID 8757.
  • Rainwater syringe: low cost technology for rainwater harvesting in coastal areas: ID 6919.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Resource use efficiency 

The implementation of this technology helps to secure an additional supply of water during the dry months.

5.2 Pro-poor technology

This practice improves soil quality and growth facilitation increasing production, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Aloe Vera living barriers
entries.summary:
The following technology provides information on the use of aloe vera as a cross-slope barrier structure. This structure is particularly effective barrier to retain soil erosion by decreasing surface runoff and increasing soil infiltration. 
Aloe vera is a durable herbaceous plant, which is planted in the form of living barriers to recover degraded slopes on the Cape Verde Islands. The plants are placed to form an efficient barrier for retention of eroded sediments and superficial runoff. The living hedges of aloe vera stabilize the soil and improve groundwater drainage. On steeper slopes the living barriers are often combined with stone walls, making this combined technology one of the most efficient measures for soil erosion control on the Cape Verde Islands.
entries.description:
Description

1. Implementation of the technology

The plants are closely planted along the edge of stone risers to build an efficient barrier for retention of eroded sediments and superficial runoff.

The technology is applied:

  • in sub humid and semi-arid areas;
  • on steep slopes;
  • on shallow soils;
  • on soils with poor vegetation cover; and
  • on soils with high erosion rates.

These areas are generally used by poor subsistence farmers for rainfed agriculture with crops which are considered inappropriate for such slope angles, such as:

  • maize
  • beans.

On slopes steeper than 30 percent the living barriers are often combined with stone walls (width 40 cm to 50 cm; height 80 cm to 90 cm). The plants stabilize the stone risers, making this combined technology one of the most efficient measures for soil erosion control on the Cape Verde Islands.

The herbaceous plant is well adapted to the local biophysical conditions and to the land use system. It is also:

  • grown with any crop;
  • available for any farmer;
  • simple to establish and transport;
  • not palatable for livestock;
  • extremely resistant to water stress;
  • grown on any bioclimatic zone on the island.

Furthermore, aloe vera is known for its multiple uses in traditional medicine.

Figure 1. Living barriers

©WOCAT/Jacques Tavares

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • subtropics, warm/ mod cool.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Natural vegetative strips: ID 7522.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Resource use efficiency 

The practice allows for soil stabilization and soil humidity increase through effective infiltration and soil structure improvement.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

The practice improves soil quality and water availability and allows for additional sources of food and income. Furthermore, aloe vera has an additional positive use for medicinal purposes.
entries.further_reading:
5. Further reading

  • WOCAT. 2010. Aloe Vera Living Barriers [Cape Verde]

entries.tittle: Natural vegetative strips
entries.summary: Natural vegetative strips (NVS) are narrow live barriers comprising naturally occurring grasses and herbs. Wide strips are left unploughed to allow vegetation to grow and to slow surface runoff. Natural terraces form over time as a result of the eroded soil accumulation on the strips. The vegetation on the established NVS needs to be cut back to a height of 5 to 10 cm: once before planting a crop, and once or twice during the cropping period. The residual material can be reused in different applications such as incorporated during land preparation, applied to the cropping area as mulch, or used as fodder. NVS is a low-cost technique, no planting material is required, and only minimal labour is necessary for establishment and maintenance. Furthermore, some farmers plant fruit and timber trees, other cash perennials and bananas or pineapples on or above the NVS these, provide an additional source of income.
entries.description:
Description

1. Formation and features of natural vegetative strips: how to implement them

Strips of land on individual cropland plots are marked out on the contour and left unploughed in order to form permanent, cross-slope barriers of naturally established grasses and herbs.

Contour lines are established:

  • with an A-frame; or
  • by the ‘cow's back method’ (a cow is used to walk across the slope: it tends to follow the contour and this is confirmed when its back is seen to be level).

The contours are then pegged to serve as an initial guide to ploughing. The 0.3 m to 0.5 m wide strips are left unploughed to allow vegetation to establish.

Runoff flowing down the slope during intense rain is slowed and infiltrates when it reaches the vegetative strips.

Eroded soil collects on the strips and natural terraces form over time. This levelling is assisted by ploughing along the contour between the NVS through ‘tillage erosion’, which also moves soil downslope.

The vegetation on the established NVS needs to be cut back to a height of five centimetres to ten centimetres: once before planting a crop and once or twice during the cropping period.

The cut material can be:

  • incorporated during land preparation;
  • applied to the cropping area as mulch; or
  • used as fodder.

This depends on:

  • whether the farmer has livestock or not;
  • the farmer’s personal preference; and
  • the time of cutting.

If the grass is applied as mulch or incorporated, the technology is:

  • agronomic
  • vegetative.

During establishment of the NVS contour lines, or later, some farmers optionally plant:

  • fruit trees
  • timber trees
  • bananas
  • pineapples.

The trees and other cash perennials provide an additional source of income, at the cost of some shading of the adjacent annual crops.

2. Natural vegetative strips advantages

  • is a low-cost technique;
  • no planting material is required; and
  • only minimal labour is necessary for establishment and maintenance

Some farmers had already practised the technology for several years before the intervention of the ICRAF (The World Agroforestry Centre) in 1993. ICRAF came to realize that farmers here preferred NVS to the recommended ‘contour barrier hedgerows’ of multipurpose trees, which land users viewed as being too labour-intensive.

When farmers became organized into ‘Land care’ groups, NVS began to gain wide acceptance. Land users appreciate the technique because of it:

  • effectively controls soil erosion;
  • prevents loss (through surface runoff) of fertilizers applied to the crop;
  • constitutes a low-cost technique because:
    • Cash Perennial provide an additional source of income, at the cost of some shading of the adjacent annual crops.
Figure 1. Natural vegetative strips

©WOCAT/Philippine Overview of Conservation Approaches and Technologies

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm;
  • subtropics, warm/ mod cool.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Aloe Vera living barriers: ID 7521.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Women-friendly

The above recommendations are easy to implement and accessible to all.

4.2 Resource use efficiency

The practice allows for effective soil erosion control and loss prevention of applied fertilizers.

4.3 Pro-poor technology

This practice is not costly as no planting material is required, and only minimal labour is necessary for establishment and maintenance. Additional crops planted provide an additional source of income.
entries.further_reading:
5. Further reading

  • WOCAT. 2011. Natural Vegetative Strips (NVS) [Philippines]

entries.tittle: Improved trash lines
entries.summary: Trash lines of organic material, composed of weeds and crops, laid in bands across the slope of annual crop fields, constitute a traditional land husbandry practice in south-west Uganda. These trash lines incorporate organic matter into the soil after decomposition and help to maintain soil fertility and control runoff. The improved trash lines are more efficient than traditional method and are a low-cost option for soil and water conservation.
entries.description:
Description

Trash lines, both improved and traditional, are composed of cereal stover (straw) and weeds that are collected during primary cultivation (hand hoeing) and heaped in strips along the approximate contour. The improved trash line method has been designed through Participatory Technology Development (PTD).

1. Implementation of the technology

The trash lines are developed, along with annual crops, on the lower slopes of the hilly area in the south-western region of Uganda. This is a highly populated area (nearly 200 persons per square kilometre); the families are large (eight to ten per family). The climate is subhumid, with a bimodal rainfall regime and average annual rainfall of around 800 mm. In these areas, hilltops are used for grazing and the valleys are dedicated to bananas and other cash crops.

1.1 Trash line characteristics

The trash lines are composed of:

  • cereal stover (straw); and
  • weeds.

Creeping grasses should not be used in trash lines. Therefore, these grasses should be decomposed in bundles, and then be used as mulch in nearby banana plantations.

Both improved, and traditional trash lines use organic material, which is:

  • collected during primary cultivation (hand hoeing); and
  • heaped in strips along the approximate contour.

1.2 Formation of improved trash lines

Trash lines are implemented in hillside fields where annual crops are grown, including:

  • sorghum
  • finger millet
  • beans
  • peas.

The recommended spacing between the improved trash lines between 5 and 10 m, according to the slope, the steeper the closer.

The cross-section of each trash line, determined by the amount of material available, is approximately 0.5 m wide and 0.3 m high.

The length of time the improved trash lines are left in place, before they are dug into the soil four seasons (there are two seasons a year in Kabale).

1.3 Advantages

Advantages of improved trash lines:

  • smaller and closely spaced lines;
  • longer lifespan (four seasons);
  • new trash lines can be established between the sites of the former lines;
  • efficiency in maintaining soil fertility because:
    • much of the material used has, by this time, decomposed or been eaten by termites;
    • effectively act as ‘mobile compost strips’ (through the incorporation into the topsoil);
  • multipurpose in retarding dispersed surface runoff and maintaining soil fertility; and
  • low-cost option for soil and water conservation.

However, they need to be complemented by other measures on the steeper slopes.

1.4 Maintenance 

Maintenance comprises:

  • removal of sprouting weeds within the lines, before they set seed; and
  • adding more trash during each of the:
    • new cultivation; and
    • weeding cycles.
Figure 1. Improved trash lines

©WOCAT

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Weed management in conservation agriculture: ID 7418.
  • Weed management in organic agriculture: ID 8375.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Women-friendly

The above recommendations are easy to implement and accessible to all.

4.2 Resource use efficiency 

This practice allows for efficient control of runoff and soil fertility maintenance. 

4.3 Pro-poor technology

Through improved soil and water conservation, this practice increases crop growth, leading to higher yields. This provides additional sources of food and income.

  • WOCAT. 2011. Improved trash lines [Uganda]

entries.tittle: Better Quality Farmyard Manure Through Improved Decomposition
entries.summary: Farmyard manure is a varying mixture of animal manure, urine, bedding material, fodder residues, and other components. This form of manure is the most common form of organic manure applied in the midhills of Nepal. This practice describes how collecting and good storage of farmyard manure can help improve land productivity in Nepal.
entries.description:
Description

1. Farmyard manure and its characteristics

  • Farmyard manure is a varying mixture of animal manure, urine, bedding material, fodder residues, and other components.
  • It is the most common form of organic manure applied in the midhills of Nepal.
  • Farmyard manure has a high proportion of organic material which nurtures soil organisms and is essential in maintaining an active soil life.
  • Only about half of the nutrient content of farmyard manure becomes available for crop growth during the first year.
    • This is after it has been applied to the soil and the rest is channelled through soil biotic processes and the nutrients are released in the following years.
  • The high organic matter content and the active soil life:
    • improve or maintain friable soil structures,
    • increase the cation exchange capacity,
    • increase water holding capacity,
    • increase infiltration rate, and
    • reduce the risk of soil pests building up.
  • Indigenous methods of preparing and using farmyard manure vary widely depending on the ecological zone, access to bedding material from crop or forest land, access to crop residues and fodder, labour availability, and other factors.
Figure 1. Farmyard manure

©WOCAT/Richard Allen

2. Prerequisites for an optimal manure usage

  • A prerequisite for the manure having a positive impact on soil fertility is that it is properly decomposed.
  • The application of partially decomposed manure can increase the number of white grubs, red ants and other soil pests.
  • Decomposition is enhanced and the time it takes to happen is reduced if the manure is kept warm and moist (but not wet) at all times.
  • Heaping the manure up or storing it in a pit helps.
  • Whether it is best to heap up the manure or put it in a pit depends on the local climate.

3. Heaping vs the pit method

  • Heaping has the advantage of being less costly, while the pit method reduces runoff and the loss of nutrient rich fluids.
  • Adding nitrogen in the form of urine improves the carbon to nitrogen ratio.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/ mod cool; and
  • temperate, cool.

5. Related/associated technologies 

  • Farm yard manure and water hyacinth compost applications to enhance organic matter: ID 6836.
  • Soil fertility for sustainable vegetable production: green and animal manures in the humid forest belt: ID 4525.
  • Green manure for enhancing upland rice productivity on Striga-infested fields: ID 4550.
  • Green manure cover crops and crop rotation in conservation agriculture: ID 7250.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

6.1 Resource use efficiency 

Manure can be used to improve land productivity, changing its role from agricultural output to a value-adding input.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

Through improved soil quality, the practice allows for additional sources of food and income.
entries.further_reading:
7. Further reading

  • WOCAT. 2011. Better quality farmyard manure through improved decomposition [Nepal]

entries.tittle: Vegetated earth-banked terraces
entries.summary: In Spain earth-banked terraces are constructed on moderately gentle slopes by agricultural machines to reduce slope gradient and length and improve soil organic matter and structure. Terraces reduce the formation of gullies and retain water from upslope and often stones are used to reinforce the terrace ridge. The terrace ridges are optimal locations to plant olives, almonds or fruit trees, trees, shrubs and grasses adapted to semi-arid conditions. This technology reduces flooding and minimise soil erosion through decreased slope gradient, it also improves soil organic matter by encouraging vegetation growth along the terrace ridges.
entries.description:
Description

Earth-banked terraces are constructed by carefully removing a superficial soil layer (10 cm to 20 cm) from one part of a field, concentrating it on the lower end of that field in order to reduce slope gradient and length. Another terrace is created directly downslope to form a cascade of terraces.

Terrace risers must have a restricted height (50 cm to 150 cm) to prevent steep and unstable terraces.

After terrace construction, fields should form a sloping gradient of less than three percent in the direction of the main slope.

The distance between terraces, hence the bed width, must allow tractor movement during normal cultivation activities. The width depends also on the slope gradient, the steeper the slope, the shorter the distance between terraces.

Terraces reduce the formation of gullies and retain water from upslope. The terraces are made  using locally available machinery (tractor, small bulldozer).

The terrace ridges are optimal locations to plant:

  • olive trees
  • almond trees
  • fruit trees.

Moreover, to be most effective, the terrace ridges are vegetated with shrubs and grasses adapted to semi-arid conditions and with a good surface cover (greater than 30 percent) throughout the year.

Shrubs and grasses adapted to semi-arid conditions:

  • Stipa tenacissima
  • Rosmarinus officinalis
  • Thymus vulgaris
  • Ulex parviflorus
  • Rhamnus lycioides
  • Pistacia lentiscus.

Natural regeneration of vegetation is allowed without limitation on the terrace ridges, so no herbicide application or burning is carried out to remove weeds. Where possible, regeneration should be stimulated by:

  • Planting the same adapted species in at least 25 percent of the terrace ridge.
  • Optionally, in the remaining 75 percent of the terrace ridge, cereals or other leguminous species can be sown, but should not be harvested or used for grazing.

1. Application and features

The technology is generally applied on soils of shallow to medium depth (20 cm to 60 cm), and slopes are gentle to moderate (5 to 15 percent).

Terraces can best be located on thalwegs and on areas where gully formation is often observed.

This technology reduces:

  • floods;
  • damages to water reservoir infrastructures; and
  • siltation of water reservoirs.

It also maintains, and in some cases slightly increases, crop productivity. This is achieved by:

  • hydraulic connectivity through a decreased slope gradient and an increased vegetation cover, hence reducing:
    • runoff; and
    • soil erosion.

The terrace ridge functions as a sink for runoff on fields and reduces runoff velocity. The vegetation improves:

  • soil organic matter content below plants;
  • soil structure; and
  • higher infiltration capacity.

The use of stones from the fields to reinforce the terraces is optional, these increase:

  • field crop production;
  • ridge resistance to higher runoff velocities.

The technology requires an initial investment in the construction of the terraces.

Maintenance:

  • filling up possible bank gullies developed in the terraces after important rainfall; and
  • substituting decayed shrubs with new ones, where needed.

The climate in Spain is semi-arid with a mean 300 mm annual rainfall. Droughts, peaking in summer commonly last for more than four to five months. Annual potential evapotranspiration rates larger than 1 000 mm are common.

The production system is highly mechanized and market-oriented but depends strongly on agricultural subsidies.

All croplands are privately owned.

Figure 1. Vegetated banked terraces

©WOCAT/Joris de Vente

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Small level bench terraces: ID 7519.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Resource use efficiency 

This practice prevents runoff on fields and reduces runoff velocity. The quality of the soil, in terms of structure and infiltration capacity, is improved through additional vegetation growth.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

Through improved soil quality, the practice increases yield production, which in turn provides additional sources of food and income.
entries.further_reading:

entries.tittle: Comment faire un simple voile qui protège le corps des piqures d’abeilles
entries.summary:
Le vêtement de protection est un élément important de l’équipement d’un apiculteur parce qu’il protège le corps des piqûres d’abeilles et rend la récolte du miel plus simple. Il peut éviter l’usage du feu pour chasser les abeilles pendant la récolte du miel. Le vêtement de protection peut être un simple voile. Le voile ne protège que le visage et le cou. Il peut être fabriqué avec du matériel disponible localement, tel qu’un sac de mais. Il est important que les matériaux soient forts et que les abeilles ne puissent pas piquer à travers le matériel.
Un autre élément du vêtement de protection est les gants, qui protègent les mains des piqûres d’abeilles. Les gants en caoutchouc sont une bonne option car les abeilles ne peuvent pas piquer à travers le caoutchouc. Pour protéger les pieds des piqûres d’abeilles, portez des bottes en caoutchouc ou des sacs en plastique couvrant les chaussures et nouées aux chevilles (pour éviter que les abeilles entrent dans le sac). Attention, les sacs en plastique peuvent être glissants. Il faut donc faire attention lorsque vous grimpez dans les arbres pour installer les ruches.
entries.description:
La description

Voir le dépliant ci-joint pour une description détaillée et illustrée sur comment procéder. Le fichier contient une description de comment faire un simple voile. Le modèle expliqué dans le fichier n’est qu’un exemple de modèles de voile. Il existe plusieurs modèles.

Les instructions sur comment faire des vêtements de protection sont extraites du « Manuel d’Apiculture Elémentaire » de Pam Gregory et Gay Marris. 

1. Comment faire un simple voile

  • Il est facile de faire un simple voile pour protéger le visage et la tête des piqûres d’abeilles.
  • Les matériaux utilisés pour faire les sacs de farine de maïs sont résistants et peu cher.
Figure 1. Le sac de farine de maïs

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Coupez le sac en deux dans la longueur.
  • Ensuite, coupez chaque côté chaque moitié en trois morceaux.
  • Chaque pièce va faire le chapeau du voile.
Figure 2. Le sac coupé en deux

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Il est possible de faire six voiles dans un même sac de farine si le sac est découpé avec précaution.
Figure 3. Le sac coupé en six voiles

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Cette matière se déchire facilement.
  • C’est pour cette raison que les bords doivent être retournés en ourlet et cousus pour les protéger.
Figure 4. Les bords des sacs

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Cousez chaque pièce pour faire un coin (une capuche).
Figure 5. Comment faire un coin pour la capuche

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Ensuite, insérez un morceau de tissu à maille.
  • De la gaze à moustiquaire fait bien l’affaire.
Figure 6. Tissu à maille inserée 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Dans Figure 7, voici ce à quoi cela doit ressembler.
Figure 7. La capuchon après avoir ajouté le filet

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Ajoutez un carré de tissu pas cher et cousez-le sur le devant et sur l’arrière de la capuche pour protéger la poitrine et le dos.
  • Ajoutez quelques cordes ou ficelles pour nouer les côtés ensemble.
Figure 8. L'ajout du tissu supplémentaire au capuchon 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Lorsque vous vous préparez pour travailler avec les abeilles, le voile est la première chose que vous devez enfiler.
  • Vous devez bien l’attacher à l’intérieur du vêtement épais.
  • Si vous n’avez pas de varreuse, portez un manteau au dessus du voile pour compléter votre tenue.
Figure 9. Le résultat final

©FERA/Pam Gregory

2. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Beekeeping: how to make a simple veil to protect the head: ID 7242.

3. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

3.1 L'efficacité d'utilisation des ressources

La téchnologie permet à utiliser des matériaux locaux, réutilisables, et peu couteux pour créer des vêtements de protection.

3.2 Favorable aux populations pauvres

La technologie est peu coûteuse et permet à une amélioration plus protégée de la récolte de produits d'abeilles et de la gestion de rûches.

entries.tittle: Comment récolter et extraire du miel de bonne qualité
entries.summary:
Une bonne récolte de miel est importante puisque du miel de bonne qualité se garde bien et se vend au meilleur prix. Plusieurs récoltes de miel par an sont possibles, quoique la période de récolte puisse varier d’un endroit à un autre. Cette technologie explique comment récolter du miel d’une ruche à barres supérieures mobiles tout en garantissant sa qualité.

Faire de la fumée calme les abeilles et il est conseillé de récolter le miel dans la fraicheur du soir. Le rayon de miel doit être coupé de la barre et conservé dans un seau propre avec couvercle pour empêcher les abeilles de voler le miel récolté et pour garder le taux d’humidité du miel bas. Cette technologie décrit également comment extraire du miel de bonne qualité avec deux seaux, et un tissu filtrant propre. Il est également expliqué comment faire un pressoir à miel.
entries.description:
La description

1. Comment récolter du miel du qualité

1.1 Les outils nécessaires (Figure 1)

  • Les outils dont on a besoin sont:
    • un seau propre avec couvercle;
    • un enfumoir et un combustible;
    • un couteau;
    • un coutelas;
    • un lève-cadres;
    • des gants en caoutchouc et une combinaison de protection; et
    • une brosse est aussi nécessaire pour brosser les abeilles qui couvrent le rayon pour les repousser dans la ruche.
      • La brosse peut être faite en plumes de poules ou en brins d’herbe.
Figure 1. Les outils nécessaires

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Le processus de la récolte du miel

  • Faites de la fumée pour calmer les abeilles.
  • Le miel est généralement entreposé auusi loin que possible de l'éntrée de la ruche.
  • Ici, l'éntrée de la ruche est dans le pignon avant, ce qui fait que la plupart du miel sera entreposée à l'arrière de la ruche (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Fumer la ruche

©FAO/TECA

  • Vérifier ou se trouvent les abeilles et ouvrez la ruche doucement (Figure 3).
Figure 3. L'ouverture douce de la ruche

©FAO/TECA

  • Brossez doucement les abeille qui couvrent le rayon pour les repousser dans la ruche.
  • Vous pouvez utiliser une brosse faite en plumes de poules ou une brosse en brins d'herbe (Figure 4). 
Figure 4. Brossez doucement les abeilles a l'interieur de la ruche

©FAO/TECA

  • Pour la récolte, ne sélectionnez que les rayons avec du miel scellé( Figure 5).
  • Il est mieux de récolter le miel dans la fraicheur du soir, de cette facon les abeilles ont toute la nuit pour se calmer.
  • Si on récolte le miel pendant la nuit, il est difficile de voir si la qualité du miel est bonne.
  • Récolter aussitôt après la pluie peut augmenter le taux d’humidité du miel et en réduire la qualité.
Figure 5. Miel bien scellé

©FAO/TECA

  • Coupez le rayon de miel de la barre dans un seau propre.
  • Le couvercle du seau doit être remis en place aussitôt que le rayon est détaché de la barre afin d'empêcher les abeilles de revenir (Figure 6).
  • Pour empêcher les abeilles de s'approcher du miel, vous aurez besoin d'un seau propre.
  • Il vous aidera aussi à garder le taux d'humidite du miel bas (Figure 7). 
Figure 6. Coupez le rayon de miel de la barre dans un seau propre

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Les barres dans un seau propore

©FAO/TECA

  • Récoltez chaque rayon un à un jusqu'a ce que vous atteignez les rayons avec le couvain.
  • Laissez amorce de base pour que les abeilles construisent un nouveau rayon.
  • Il faut laisse du miel pour servir de nourriture aux abeilles ou il se peut que la colonie s'en aille ou meure (Figure 8).
  • Si vous souhaitez protéger la vie de la colonie, les rayons avec le couvain doivent pas être récoltes (Figure 9). 
Figure 8. La selection des rayons

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Rayon avec le couvain

©FAO/TECA

2. Comment extraire du miel de bonne qualite

2.1 Le processus d'extraction du miel de bonne qualité

  • Lorsque vous extrayez le miel du rayon, vous avez besoin de deux seaux, d'une epuratrice et d'un endroit à l'abris des abeilles (Figure 10). 
Figure 10. Les differents seaux

©FAO/TECA

  • Les mains doivent être gardées très propre (Figure 11).
Figure 11. Lavage des mains

©FAO/TECA

  • Le miel va être épuré en passant à travers un tissu filtrant propre et la cire va rester dans l'étoffe ( Figure 12). 
Figure 12. La filtration du miel et la collecte du cire

©FAO/TECA

  • Le rayon du miel est coupé en petits morceaux affin de libérer le miel (Figure 13). 
Figure 13. Petits morceaux de rayon du miel 

©FAO/TECA

  • Ensuite, il est filtré à travers un autre tissu filtrant propre dans un second seau (Figure 14).
  • Le seau est couvert et laissé à égoutter jusqu'à ce que la plupart du miel se soit ecoulée. 
Figure 14. Deuxiéme filtration

©FAO/TECA

  • Les dernières gouttes de miel peuvent être extraites du tissu en utilisant des mains propers.
  • Des arbres différents producent du miel de couleurs de goûts différents.
  • Il ne faut pas melanger du miel de differente qualité.
  • Les personnes avec de nombreuses ruches peuvent extraire le miel en utilisant un pressoir à miel. 
Figure 15. Le pressoir du miel

©FAO/TECA

  • Pour une alternative moins chère, vous pouvez utiliser la facon decrit en Figure 16.
  • Le seau en métal a bords droits est troué dans le fond.
  • Un seau est placee sous le pressoir pour recueillir le miel.
  • Il y a une presse centrale faite d'un cercle de bois.
  • Le rayon de miel a presser est placée dans un tissu filtrant ou un sac et est pressé en le plaçant sous la presse.
  • La manche est utilisé pour exercer de la pression sur le sac avec le rayon afin d'en extraire le miel. 
Figure 16. L'alternative moins chère

©FAO/TECA

3. Les zones agro-écologiques

  • Les tropiques, chaud.

4. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Comment récolter la cire d'abeille: ID 7580.
  • Comment établir un bon rucher: ID 7581.
  • Comment inspecter une ruche en toute sécurité: ID 7586.
  • Bonnes pratiques apicoles: ID 8674.
  • Apiculture: utilisation d’un enfumoir metallic a soufflet: ID 8727.

5. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

5.1 Favorable aux femmes

L'apiculture est une technologie accessible à tous. 

5.1 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvres

L'apiculture peut servire comme source de revenue supplémentaire sans investissements très élevés.

entries.tittle: Comment faire une ruche à barres supérieurs mobiles (modèle du Kenya)
entries.summary: Cette technologie décrit méthodiquement comment faire une ruche à barre supérieures (modèle du Kenya). Une ruche à barres supérieures, (ou une ruche à barres mobiles) est une caisse rectangulaire couverte avec des barres d’une largeur fixées. Les abeilles commenceront la construction de leurs rayons à partir du centre des barres supérieures. Pour attirer un essaim à la ruche et pour «guider» les abeilles à la construction des rayons le long de la barre, une bande de démarrage en cire doit être mise sur le centre de la barre supérieure. Les ruches mobiles permettent l’inspection de la ruche en soulevant les barres supérieures et de remplacer les rayons matures (le rayon sellé) avec une barre vide, pour que les abeilles continuent à collecter du nectar.
entries.description:
La description

Les instructions sur comment faire une ruche à barres supérieures mobiles sont extraites du manuel « Manuel d’Apiculture Élémentaire » de Pam Gregory et Gay Marris. Le manuel est disponible en anglais, français, shona, kinyarwanda, swahili et chichewa.

À noter que l’espace de l’abeille (la distance entres les rayons, et les rayons et la caisse) est toujours fixe pour les abeilles de la même race, mais diffère un peu entres les races différentes (A.m. scutellata, A.m. adasonnii, etc.) dû a la taille de l’abeille (voir le dépliant). C’est important de respecter l’espace de l’abeille et d’ajuster la distance centre-au-centre des barres supérieures selon l’espace de l’abeille.

1. Les dimensions d'une ruche

Figure 1. Les femmes du Projet Nessuit (Rift Valley au Kenya) tapissent une ruche de bouse de vache et de boue 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Le plan donne les dimensions d’une ruche.
  • Les dimensions standardisées permettent à l’apiculteur de bouger les rayons d’une ruche à l’autre, de gérer ses abeilles et de récolter le miel plus facilement.
Figure 2. Les dimensions d'une ruche

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Les barres supérieures sont en coin (parallélogramme).
  • Il est essentiel que les barres supérieures soient exactement de 3.2 cm de large. 
Figure 3. La barre supérieure

©FERA/Pam Gregory

2. Les différents methodes de construire une ruche

2.1 Faire une ruche a partir de planches

  • Coupez le bois choisi aux dimensions.
  • Voici les paneaux de côté. 
Figure 4. Les panceaux

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Il sera peut-être nécessaire de rabotter le bois pour assurer un assemblage précis.
Figure 5. La rabotage de bois

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Deux morceaux sont cloués ensemble pour faire les deux pignons (avant et arrière).
  • Coupez les bouts de deux clous (ou applatissez avec une pierre) afin d’afin d’avoir un clou avec deux bouts pointus.
  • Enfoncez les côtés pointus des clous dans les planches pour assembler les morceaux de bois.
Figure 6. Clouage des morceaux

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Les morceaux de bois assemblés forment sommairement les pignons (avant et arrière).
Figure 7. Les pignons d'avant et d'arrière

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Sciez les formes rudimentaires de pignon à la taille et forme correctes.
Figure 8. Ajuster la taille de pignon

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Utilisez un patron pour que les mesures soient plus faciles.
  • Celui-ci est fait en carton.
  • Si vous prenez les mesures à partir du centre, vous serez certains d’avoir des angles précis.
Figure 9. Un patron pour les pignons

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Faîtes une entaille ou un rang en forme de « V » ou percez des trous (pas plus gros que le diamètre d’un stylo Bic) dans l’un des pignons pour l’entrée.
  • Les entrées ne doivent pas être plus hautes de 8 mm afin d’éviter que les animaux nuisibles pénètrent la ruche.
Figure 10. La dimensions du l'entrée

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Une fois que les pièces ont été coupées, il est possible d’assembler la ruche.
  • Sur cette photo, les côtés ont été cloués aux pignons.
  • Ensuite, ajoutez le fond.
Figure 11. L'assemblage des pièces

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Construire le corps de la ruche.
Figure 12. Continuation du l'assemblage pour construire le corps de la ruche

©©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Certaines personnes fabriquent des ruches aves des pignons un peu plus hauts sur les côtés afin de recevoir les barres supérieures.
Figure 13. Ruches fabriquer avec des pignons plus hauts

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • D’autres personnes mettent un suspendeur afin que les barres soient parfaitement ajustées aux côtés.
Figure 14. L'ajoute d'un suspendeur pour un meilleur ajustment 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

2.2 Faire une ruche a partir de materiux locaux moins chers

  • Il est faux de dire que les ruches doivent être faites de bois cher.
  • On peut utiliser avec succès de nombreux matériaux plus disponibles et moins chers.
  • Voici du bois de palmier à raphia.
Figure 15. Une ruche faites de palmier à raphia

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Vous pouvez faire les pignons à partir de bois de récupération et les côtés et le fond à partir de matériaux locaux.
  • Cette ruche est faite de bâtons droits.
Figure 16. Ruche faite de bâtons droits

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Cette “Grande Ruche”, ruche à barres supérieures du Congo, est habilement faites sans utiliser une seule planche ou un seul clou.
  • Les matériaux souples ont été assemblés avec des épingles de bois pointu.
Figure 17. Grande ruche faites des épingles de bois pointu

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Les interstices de cette ruche en bambou doivent être bouchées avec précaution avec des matériaux adéquats afin d’empêcher les animaux nuisibles d’entrer dans la ruche.
Figure 18. Nécessaire de boucher avec des matériaux adéquats

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Cette ruche ougandaise est faite de tiges de plantes recouvertes de boue, de cendre de bois et de bouse de vache.
Figure 19. Une ruche ougandaise faite de tiges de plantes, de cendre de bois, et de bouse de vache

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Cette robuste ruche ougandaise est en roseaux tressés.
Figure 20. Ruche ougandaise en roseaux tressés

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Le fond et les côtés de cette ruche doivent être couverts de boue pour empêcher la lumière de pénétrer et les fourmis et autres animaux nuisibles d’entrer.
Figure 21. Les femmes du Projet Nessuit (Rift Valley au Kenya) tapissent une ruche de bouse de vache et de boue 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Le toît n’a pas besoin d’être fait avec des matériaux chers, à partir du moment où la ruche est à l’abris de la pluie.
  • Ce toît est recouvert avec du plastique.
Figure 22. Toît en plastique

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Ce toît est fait d’un cadre de bois et de deux pièces de tapis de bambou superposés.
  • Il y a une épaisseur de sac plastic poubelle entre les deux afin d’aider à l’imperméabilisation de la ruche.
  • Le dessus est également recouvert de plastique.
Figure 23. Toît fait de tapis de bambou superposés

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Ce toît est fait de chaumes, comme les maisons locales.
  • Il a des extrémités solides afin que les serpents et autres animaux nuisibles ne puissent entrer et des poignées afin d’aider à soulever le toît.
Figure 24. Toît fait de chaumes

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Le toît d’une ruche peut être fait de bambou fendu, comme le toît de ce bâtiment local au Kenya.
Figure 25. Toît fait de bambou fendu 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Le bambou est coupé en deux et ensuite assemblé ainsi, de la même façon que de la tôle ondulée.
  • Couvrez le bambou avec du polythène pour une protection supplémentaire.
Figure 26. Polythène au-dessus de bambou pour une protection supplémentaire

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Un toît très simple peut être fabriqué avec une bâche de polythène est de deux pieux insérés sur les côtés.
  • Leur poids est suffisant pour tirer la bâche vers le bas.
Figure 27. Les avantages de polythène

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • S’il n’est pas possible de créer un toît ajusté à la ruche, cet abris de chaumes peur aider à protéger les ruches du soleil et de la pluie.
Figure 28. Abris de chaumes sert a protéger les ruches 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Cette ruche en bâtons de bois terminée est placé dans un support fait en longs morceaux de bois assemblés auquel on a attaché des cables.
  • Cela permet de suspendre la ruche et ainsi de protéger les matériaux locaux les plus fragiles des dégâts.
  • On peut déplacer les ruches en les enlevant de leur support, ce qui rend le procédé de diviser la ruche plus facile.
Figure 29. La suspension du ruche protege les matériaux 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

2.3 Faire la barre superieure

  • Coupez les barres est la partie la plus difficile et la plus chère de la construction de la ruche.
  • Il est essentiel que les barres soient de 32 ou 33 mm (3.2 ou 3.3cm) de large.
  • La largeur des barres supérieures peut être mesurée en utilisant une capsule de bouteille en verre ou une pile de 9 volts usagée (seulement les piles rectangulaires).
Figure 30. La mesure du barre supérieur

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • La plupart des barres sont coupées en coin dans le sens de la coupe.
  • Cependant de nombreuses personnes ont du succès avec des barres beaucoup plus simples, faîtes en matériaux locaux, qui sont plus faciles à couper que le bois de meilleure qualité.
  • Cette barre est faîte en palmier de raphia.
Figure 31. Barre faîte en palmier de raphia

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Cette barre n’est pas coupée en coin.
  • Elle est plate.
Figure 32. Une barre plate

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Bâtons, bambou ou autres matériaux adéquats peuvent être soigneusement coupés à la bonne taille.
Figure 33. Rafinage du barre

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • La bande de démarrage de cire peut être faite avec une bougie de cire d’abeilles.
Figure 34. Une bougie de cire d'abeilles utilisée pour la bande de démarrage de cire

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Regardez cette photo.
  • Prenez le temps d’en discuter avec d’autres apiculteurs.
  • Ces barres ont été faites en bambou remplies de cire, ce qui est une bonne idée à essayer soi-même. Cependant l’apiculteur va avoir des difficultés à faire en sorte que les abeilles construisent un rayon sur une des barres parce qu’elles ne sont pas coupées proprement.
Figure 35. Barres faites en bambou remplies de cire

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Des barres mal coupées sont la cause de la majorité des problèmes qui peuvent se produire lorsque l’on utilise des ruches à barres supérieures.
  • Si les barres sont coupées correctement et bien cirées, les abeilles construiront un rayon sur une barre.
  • Cela permet à l’apiculteur de faire la récolte plus facilement et de bouger les rayons d’une ruche à l’autre, pour une gestion similaire à celle des ruches à cadres.
Figure 36. Des barres correctement coupées offrent un travail plus propre et meilleur

©FERA/Pam Gregory

3. Les zones agro-écologiques

  • Tropiques, chaud. 

4. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Comment établir un bon rucher: ID 7581.
  • Comment inspecter une ruche en toute sécurité: ID 7586.
  • Fabrication d’une ruche traditionnelle africaine à deux ouvertures: ID 8570.
  • Fabrication d'une ruche Kenyane trapézoidale à barettes: ID 8707.
  • Comment fabriquer une ruche a barrettes « la grande »: ID 8744.
  • Comment fabriquer une ruche a barrettes en Nkoko: ID 8745.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en anglais: ID 7274.

5. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

5.1 L'efficacité d'utilisation des ressources

La technologie utilise efficacement des matériaux locaux tout comme le bamboo, les cendres de bois et la boue. La technologie ne coûte pas cher à installer.

entries.tittle: Comment récolter la cire d'abeille
entries.summary: La cire d’abeille est une marchandise de valeur qui peut être utilisée pour faire toute sorte de produits comme par exemple des bougies, de la crème de corps, du cirage, etc. Cette technologie présente, méthodiquement, trois méthodes différentes pour récolter la cire d’abeille. La première méthode décrite utilise des matériaux locaux, tels qu’un sac de tissu, une casserole, et un t-shirt. La deuxième méthode utilise un extracteur de cire solaire qui peut être fabriqué aussi avec des matériaux locaux, tels qu’une feuille d’étain, un couvercle en verre et une langue de métal. La troisième méthode, l’extracteur de cire à vapeur, consiste à pendre un sac de cire au dessus d’un récipient qui flotte au dessus d’eau bouillante.
entries.description:
La description

Les instructions pour récolter la cire d’abeille sont extraites du manuel « Manuel d’Apiculture Élémentaire » de Pam Gregory et Gay Marris. Le manuel est disponible sur TECA en Anglais, Français, Shona, Kinyarwanda, Swahili et Chichewa.

Avec l’extracteur de cire solaire, il est importante de ne pas laisser que la cire se surchauffe, se noircisse ou se brûle. Avec l’extracteur de cire à vapeur, faire attention à ce que l’eau bouillante ne s’évapore pas totalement.

1. Les produits en cire d'abeilles

Figure 1. Cire d’abeille raffinée du Malawi 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

Figure 2. Produits en cire d’abeille ougandais, produits par Hives Save Lives Africa 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

2. Les étapes du récolte du cire d'abeille

  • La cire d’abeille est une marchandise de valeur qui peut être utilisée pour faire toute une sorte de produits.
  • On ne devrait pas la jeter.
Figure 3. Les differents produits en cire d'abeille du Cameroun

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Gardez la cire du rayon récolté pour le miel à l’écart des rayons vieux et sombres qui ont contenu le couvain (les jeunes larves d’abeilles avant qu’elles éclosent).
Figure 4. Rayon propre

©FERA/Pam Gregory

Figure 5. Rayon utilisé pour le couvain

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Le rayon propre du miel récolté fait la meilleure cire.
Figure 6. Cire récolté 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Lavez les rayons de miel écrasé dans de l’eau jusqu’à ce qu’ils se libèrent de la saleté et du miel.
  • Placez-les dans un sac de tissu convenable et nouez le sac avec de la ficelle.
  • Faites chauffer une bonne quantité d’eau dans une vieille casserole.
  • Placez-y le sac de rayons de miel et poussez-le sous l’eau.
Figure 7. La façon de pusser le sac

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Continuez à chauffer l’eau doucement.
  • Il ne faut pas qu’elle bouille.
  • Continuez à presser le sac jusqu’à ce que tout le rayon ait fondu.
  • La cire fondue va passer à travers les mailles et monter à la surface de l’eau. 
Figure 8. La cire s'écoule en l'eau

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Extrayez le restant de cire hors du sac en l’enroulant entre deux baguettes.
  • Faites attention, le sac est chaud.
  • La cire va se solidifier sur la surface de l’eau au fur et à mesure qu’elle se refroidit.
  • La cire solidifiée devrait être à nouveau traitée afin de retirer la saleté qui reste. 
Figure 9. Les débris sur la cire

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Cassez la cire sale en de petits morceaux.
Figure 10. Petits morceaux de cire

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Faites fondre la cire dans une casserole placée à l’intérieur d’une seconde casserole. 
Figure 11. Le cire en bain marie 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Faites chauffer jusqu’à ce que toute la cire soit fondue.
  • Sur cette photo, vous pouvez voir la saleté de la cire dans le find de la casserole.
Figure 12. Collection du debris

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Versez la cire fondue à travers un tissu filtrant pour retirer la saleté.
  • Le tissu d’un t-shirt propre est idéal.
Figure 13. La filtration du cire

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Un moûle en plastique fera une forme agréable ou utile.
  • Frottez le moûle avec du savon afin d’empêcher la cire de coller lorsqu’elle se refroidit.
Figure 14. L'application du savon a l'intérier du moûle 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • La cire se refroidit dans le moûle et peut être retiree quand elle est solidifiée.
  • La saleté est restée sur le tissu.
  • Le tissu peut être lavé et reutilisé.
Figure 15. La refroidissement du cire 

©FERA/Pam Gregory

Figure 16. Le tissu peut être réutilisé

©FERA/Pam Gregory

Figure 17. La solidification de la cire

.

©FERA/Pam Gregory

  • Nettoyez tout après usage.
Figure 18. Nettoyer les moules

©FERA/Pam Gregory

Figure 19. Le produit final de la cire

©FERA/Pam Gregory

2. Autres méthodes pour recolter la cire

2.1 Extracteur de cire solaire

  • La chaleur du soleil peut être utilisée pour faire fondre la cire.
  • La cire est mise dans un sac filtrant, placée sur un plateau en métal dans une boite isolée sous un couvercle de verre et mise au soleil.
  • Une ‘langue’ en métal conduit directement la cire dans un récipient.
  • Il faut faire attention de ne pas laisser la cire surchauffer et de noircir ou de brûler.
Figure 20. Extracteur du cire solaire

©FERA/Pam Gregory

2.2 Extracteur de cire à vapeur

  • La cire peut également être nettoyée en utilisant de la vapeur.
  • Un sac de capsules de cire ou de rayons est pendu au dessus d’un récipient qui flotte au dessus d’eau bouillante.
  • La cire qui fond tombe goutte à goutte du sac pour s’amasser dans le récipient.
  • Faites attention à ce que l’eau bouillante ne s’évapore pas totalement.
Figure 21. L'extraction à vapeur

©FERA/Pam Gregory

Figure 22. Les matériaux nécessaires

©FERA/Pam Gregory

3. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Comment établir un bon rucher: ID 7581. 
  • Comment inspecter une ruche en toute sécurité: ID 7586.
  • Comment faire une ruche à barres supérieurs mobiles (modèle du Kenya): ID 7561.

4. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

4.1 L'efficacité d'utilisation des ressources

La technologie propose l'utilisation efficace de trois méthodes pour récolter la cire d'abeilles qui serait autrement jetée.

4.2 Favorable aux populations pauvres

En récoltant de la cire d'abeilles, la technologie permet à la production d'autres produits, menant à de sources supplémentaires de revenu.
entries.further_reading:
5. Les lectures complémentaires

  • Manuel d’apiculture élémentaire de Pam Gregory and et Gay Marris.
  • Technologie sur comment produire a solar wax extractor.

entries.tittle: Cultivating lotus on raised beds in flood prone areas, Vietnam
entries.summary: This practice describes how cultivating lotus in raised beds can create employment and generate income in the rainy season. The example of the flood prone areas of the Quang Tri province of north central Vietnam is used to highlight its benefits. Steps on how to implement the technology are listed in terms of drainage, soil type selection, bed measurements, sowing methods and costs.
entries.description:
Description

Cultivating lotus in raised beds is a local adaptation practice in flood prone areas of the Quang Tri province of north central Viet Nam. Communities traditionally collected lotus seeds from plants grown in common water bodies and sold them in markets. However, there was no initiative to further develop, promote and disseminate this practice.

The practice of raised beds has been recognized as suitable for broader replication in flood prone areas only recently, and communities have thus started to engage in cultivating lotus also in low-lying flood prone areas. The objective of lotus cultivation on raised beds is to ensure production at a time when cultivation would normally be impossible, providing employment opportunities and household income also during flooding periods.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • Lotus cultivation on raised beds can be implemented during the rainy season from September to December in the low-lying areas of the country, on land that farmers would otherwise leave fallow due to excessive water stagnation.
    • The cultivation of lotus in raised beds requires drainage of excess water through small channels.
    • This is in order to create favourable soil conditions for the cultivation and to counteract the impact of heavy rainfall and strong cyclonic storms that regularly affect north central Vietnam.
    • Primary beneficiaries are small farmers and small local businessman.
  • The practice is most successful in freshwater ecosystems with heavy textured soils.
    • The raised beds should be 30 to 50 cm high and 100 cm wide, in order to create favourable soil conditions.
    • Drainage channels should be wide (100 cm).
    • Lotus seeds for cultivation are usually available locally.
    • The lotus seeds are sown on the raised beds.
  • The raised beds need a slight readjustment every year before the beginning of the rainy season.
    • The initial cost of land preparation is substantial.
    • However, family labourers can be engaged in preparing the raised beds.
    • This practice does not imply any maintenance costs.
    • Lotus cultivation provides employment opportunities during flood season and increases household income.
    • Institutional support is required to disseminate this practice into other ecologically similar regions.
    • Local market facilities to procure lotus seeds have to be established and should be connected with export institutions.
    • Institutional interventions are necessary in order to curtail exploitation by middle men.
    • Local community-based organizations and financial institutions need to be strengthened to promote replication of the practice.
Figure 1. Raised beds in flood prone areas

©FAO/TECA

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropical, warm. 

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Increasing flexibility in crop production through DAPOG nursery to reduce the impact of droughts and floods: ID 8216.
  • Drought-tolerant maize varieties: ID 8920.
  • Raised bed lotus cultivation: ID 4663.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently provides intricate steps in terms of soil drainage, selection, measurements, sowing and costs in order to effectively cultivate lotus flower crops in flood prone areas and during rainy seasons. 

4.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology leads to employment creation and income generation.
entries.further_reading:
5. Further reading

  • Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Asian Disaster Preparedness Centre. 2007. Sharing Lessons. Hazard Risk Preparedness in Agriculture: Good Practice Examples from South and South East Asia, Case Study, Project TCP/RLA/3101, Assistance to Improve Local Agricultural Emergency Preparedness in Caribbean countries highly prone to hurricane related disasters, by R. Selvaraju.
  • Sayre, Kenneth D., Raised Bed Cultivation, in Encyclopedia of Soil Science, Taylor & Frances, 27 March 2006

For more information, please contact Selvaraju Ramasamy at: Selvaraju.Ramasamy@fao.org

entries.tittle: Fuel-saving stoves for health, better nutrition and livelihoods
entries.summary: Fuel-saving stoves have many advantages. They save wood resources, time, money, and improve health conditions by reducing fumes in homes. Foods that are not adequately cooked can transmit food-borne diseases. Families that cannot purchase sufficient fuel might be even unable to consume their food. Farmers can increase household incomes by building and selling the fuel-saving stoves they build. Compared to traditional stoves the energy-saving stoves reduce deforestation, since they use a third of the fuel. Therefore they decrease smoke from cooking, thus diminish respiratory problems. Many African families cook on open fire, which uses lots of wood and creates unhealthy smoke, causing respiratory problems. Traditional open-air stoves are fuel consuming and slow in reaching appropriate cooking temperatures. The energy-saving stoves improve food processing and provide a good heat source in cool areas.
entries.description:
Description

1. The advantages of using this technology

  • Fuel-saving stoves have a closed structure that limits heat dispersion.
  • They reach adequate cooking temperatures more quickly, reducing the time necessary to process and the risk of food-borne diseases, and preserving nutritious value of foods.
    • Less fuel is required, meaning that workload and expense to procure fuel are reduced.
    • Moreover, the improved stoves are provided with a venting system that emits the smoke directly outside homes through a chimney, dramatically reducing respiratory problems.
  • You can build different improved cooking stoves according to different dietary habits and traditions (e.g. habit of cooking while sitting or standing, etc.).
  • The materials used are all inexpensive and readily available in the community.
    • These materials include oiled pipes, clay, cow dung, top soil, anthill soil, flat stones and water.
  • After combustion of timber, ashes can be used to fertilize and improve the water retention of soils in household vegetable gardens.
Figure 1. A stove

©FAO/TECA

2. The building process

  • The stove can be built 50 cm above the floor level, in-house or outside.
  • Stoves built in-house should always include a chimney to evacuate smoke outside.
    • Mix the cow dung, top soil, anthill soil and water.
      • Use the mixture to shape the stove around an oiled drainpipe.
      • Use bricks of flat stones to make the structure of the walls and floor, using the mud mixture as mortar and plaster.
    • Make two gaps a little smaller than the size of the pots.
    • Remove carefully the tube when the mud mixture is dry enough.
    • Make your chimney using an oiled pipe to shape the mud mixture and then carefully remove it when the mixture is dry enough.
    • Leave your stove to dry for a few weeks.
      • When you are ready to cook, push timber and sticks into the open-end light and push them inside the stove until they are under the pot-holes.
Figure 2. Fuel stove - mother and child

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Open air stoves

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Fuel saving stoves

©FAO/TECA

3. Useful recommendations for facilitators before starting

  • Community groups should be involved from the planning process through participatory approaches, and interagency collaboration.
  • A four-hour training session is usually sufficient for a “hands-on” demonstration on how to build a fuel-saving stove.
  • Posters and at scale models can be used to illustrate the technique to the participants.
    • Videos and slides can be used to show the construction of stoves and provide testimonials on the impact that these stoves have on their daily life.
  • However, although these materials are nice to have, success can be achieved by having the following basic requirements.
    • Availability of the necessary materials to build fuel-saving stoves, a good trainer and a hands-on learning method.
    • Beneficiaries should be encouraged to work in groups to build fuel-saving stoves and should be asked to complete reflective exercises with three or four questions to verify that they have memorized the main points and information.
    • Participants should designate someone as the knowledge keeper, to take records of the demonstration so that the community can build other fuel-saving stoves even in the absence of the training.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Farmer field schools on integrated plant nutrient systems: ID 7527.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

Building the stove in inexpensive. Additionally, farmers can increase household incomes by building and selling the fuel-saving stoves they build.
