entries.tittle: Tip-Taps for improved hygiene and water management
entries.summary: A Tip-tap is a simple water conserving hand-washing device, which helps to diminish the risks of infection contamination, improves hygiene, and reduces disease spreading. Tip-taps reduce water usage and can be operated by foot, avoiding the risk of picking up germs from tap handles. It is used to clean hands after using a latrine, working in a garden, or before cooking, eating or caring for young children, elderly or ill persons. Improved hygiene reduces the incidence of infectious disease and thereby contributes to better nutrition. In target communities, the incidence of infectious diseases, such as cholera and dysentery, has diminished since the use of Tip-taps has been introduced.
entries.description:
Description

1. The advantages of using this practice

  • Tip-taps can be made from non-costly material, easily available locally:
    • pegs,
    • wire,
    • string,
    • soap dishes made of old cans and used plastic water containers of medium size (mostly 5 litre),
    • oiled pipes,
    • clay,
    • cow dung,
    • topsoil,
    • anthill soil,
    • flat stones, and
    • water.
  • All are inexpensive and readily available in the community.
  • After combustion of timber, ashes can be used to fertilize and improve the water retention of soils in household vegetable gardens.

2. The building process

  • There are several ways to make a Tip-tap, as illustrated hereafter.
  • Independently of the type of Tip-tap, there are basics steps to take.
    • Build a frame with pegs, about 1 meter high and soundly planted in the ground.
    • Dig a hole between the pegs and fill it with rocks, for the drainage of used water, or with a container, to collect waste water to be used for the irrigation of vegetable ‘keyhole’ gardens.
    • Use string, wire or sticks to tie a used plastic container to the pegs’ frame.
      • If necessary, holes can be made in the container using a heated nail or metal wire.
    • Attach a peg, or any other object that can serve as pedal, to one end of a long string.
      • The other end of the string is to be tied to the container, next to the hole(s) from which the water is supposed to pour.
      • The length of the string must be such that the pedal touches the ground without laying completely on it.
        • Stepping on the pedal will put the string in tension, and tip the container, making water pour out from the opposite hole(s).
    • If soap is available, make a soap dish with a used can or other available material, to be tied to the pegs frame.
Figure 1. Presentation of Tip-tap

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Tip-taps next to a vegetable garden

©FAO/TECA

3. Useful recommendations for facilitators before starting

  • A three-hour training session is normally sufficient for a “hands-on” demonstration on how to build a Tip-tap device.
  • Posters and models at scales can be used to illustrate the technique to the participants.
    • Videos and slides can be used to show the construction of Tip-taps in other villages and show other beneficiaries’ reactions and testimony on the impact of Tip-taps on their daily life.
    • Participants should designate one of them as knowledge keeper, to take records of the demonstration so that the community can build other Tip-taps even in the absence of the trainer.
    • However, the only basic requirements for the training on Tip-tap construction and use are:
      • the availability of the necessary materials to build the Tip-tap; and
      • a good trainer and a hands-on learning method.
  • The actual promotion of and training on Tip-taps may be implemented simultaneously with interventions supporting food and nutrition security and safety, to have a relevant impact on the health status of population.
    • The promotion and set up of Tip-taps can be easily integrated as support side-activity in nutrition and health projects.
    • A participatory approach should always be adopted to actively involve beneficiaries in the construction and training activities, to develop sense of ownership and responsibility.
      • People will care more for things that they perceive as theirs.
  • The training sessions on construction and use of Tip-taps should be combined with basic health care and nutrition education sessions.
Figure 3. Tip-taps 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. A Tip-tap can be constructed in any location/place

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Farmer field schools on integrated plant nutrient systems: ID 7527.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

Improved hygiene reduces the incidence of infectious disease and thereby contributes to better nutrition.

entries.tittle: Small-Scale Conservation Tillage-Ripping of Soil Using Oxen-Drawn in Kenya
entries.summary: The form of conservation agriculture described in this technology involves the use of ox-drawn ploughs, modified to rip the soil. The aim of ripping is to increase water infiltration and reduce runoff. In contrast to conventional tillage, the soil is not inverted, minimising water loss and improving soil productivity, as well as yields.
entries.description:
Description

Ripping of soil using oxen-drawn implements, to improve root water storage capacity and cropland productivity on small-scale farms. Laikipia District in Kenya is characterised by a semi-arid climate, high altitude and rolling terrain. Most of the soil and water loss occurs during a few heavy storms at the beginning of each growing season. More than 90 percent of families have under two hectares of land, and few have alternative sources of income.

1. How to apply the ox-drawn

Ripping of soil is performed in one pass, to a depth of 10 cm, after harvest. Spacing between the rip lines is 30 cm in the case of wheat. Deep ripping, subsoiling, with the same implement, is done, when necessary, to break a plough pan and reaches depths of up to 30 cm.

A modification to the ordinary plough beam (the common mould board ‘Victory’ plough) allows the adjustment to different possible depths and turns it into a ripper for surface and deeper ripping.

2. Why use ox-drawn soil ripping

The aim of ripping the soil by ox-drawn implements is to:

  • increase water infiltration; and
  • reduce runoff.

In contrast to conventional tillage, the soil is not inverted, thus leaving a certain amount of crop residue on the surface, hence:

  • the soil is less exposed;
  • splash and sheet erosion is minimised; and
  • water loss through evaporation and runoff is also minimised.

In addition, there are savings in terms of energy used for cultivation. In well-ripped fields, rainfall from storms at the beginning of the growing season is stored within the rooting zone and is therefore available to the crop during subsequent drought spells.

Ripping the soil during the dry season combined with a mulch cover:

  • reduces germination of weeds. In case of stubborn weeds, pre-emergence herbicides are used for control; and
  • leaves fields ready for planting.

Yields from small-scale conservation tillage are higher than under conventional ploughing. An additional important benefit is:

  • crops mature sooner in conservation agriculture, as they can be planted earlier.

Earlier crop maturity means that yields can be sold to markets when prices are still high. Whereas with inversion tillage the farmer has to wait for the soil to become moist before ploughing.

3. Supportive technologies

There are various supportive technologies in use that can improve the effectiveness of the ripping. These include:

  • use of compost/manure to improve soil structure for better water storage;
  • use of a cover crop (Mucuna pruriens) planted at the end of the season to prevent erosion, control weeds and improve soil quality;
  • agroforestry: principally Grevillea robusta planted on the field boundaries (see also WOCAT, 2010, Grevillea agroforestry system).

3.1 Advantages

The joint effects of this type of tillage have various advantages, which are:

  • improvement of livelihood resilience of the farmers against natural hazards in the Lakipia District;
  • improvement of soil permeability and infiltration which helps resistance against intense rainfall and drought; and
  • improvement in crop yield positively affecting the nutritional status of the farmers;
  • improvement in crop yield allowing farmers to diversify and increase their income.

4. Land use problems

Loss of rainwater through runoff and direct evaporation from soil surface and runoff cause:

  • surface erosion;
  • fertility decline and nutrient mining.

5. Validation of the practice

Yields from small-scale conservation tillage can be more than 60 percent higher than conventional ploughing.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Having an oxen-drawn ploughs.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies 

  • Soil cultivation and tillage in organic agriculture: ID 8376.
  • Conservation tillage management for marginal small farm systems: ID 4465.
  • Zero/Minimum tillage in rice-wheat system: ID 7715.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST) 

The practice allows for time-saving and labour-saving as fields are left ready for planting.

9.2 Resource use efficiency 

​​This practice facilitates crop cultivation and allows for efficient control of runoff and soil fertility maintenance.

9.3 Pro-poor technology 

This practice helps poor farmers improve their land productivity, thereby providing additional sources of food and income. It also reduces the risk of soil and water loss.

entries.tittle: Producción de Miel a Nivel Rural, Guatemala
entries.summary: La producción de miel a nivel rural se realiza todo el año en las áreas rurales por ser una actividad rentable y poco exigente en cuanto a tiempo requerido y necesidades de mano de obra. La recolección de la miel se realiza de manera colectiva en las comunidades. Esta práctica ha sido probada en Ipala, Chiquimula (Guatemala), durante cuatro años.
entries.description:
Descripción

1. Áreas y causas de difusión actual

  • Ochenta y un (81) productores distribuidos en comunidades de Asunción y Santa Catarina (Jutiapa), Ipala, Esquipulas, Quezaltepeque y Anguiatú (Chiquimula a toda la región oriental de Guatemala).

2. Pasos del proceso concreto de implementación de esta práctica

  • ACODERJO y PRODERT realizaron capacitaciones en las comunidades de sus respectivas áreas, para presentar la actividad.
    • Las familias que asisten a todas las reuniones reciben una colmena compuesta por tres cajas, a crédito blando.
    • Cada caja contiene unos tres marcos enredados.
    • El pago de los créditos concedidos se inicia al cosechar la miel.
    • Parte o la totalidad de los créditos puede ser pagada con el producto obtenido (miel).
    • Un agricultor ya capacitado realiza la asistencia técnica referida al manejo de las abejas y la inseminación de cada nueva colmena.
    • Esto se realiza preferentemente en octubre o noviembre, al empezar la floración en campo.
    • Esta acción se realiza retirando un marco de una colmena ya en producción y trasladándolo a la nueva colmena.
    • Todas las actividades de manejo de las abejas se realizan con guantos protectores y con una gorra especial con retina (parte frontal) protectora para evitar picaduras.
  • Las colmenas son productivas alrededor de un mes después de la inseminación, y la producción es constante todo el año.
    • Cada colmena de 3 cajitas produce entre 15 y 20 botellas de 700 ml al mes, que se venden directamente a los comerciantes de la ciudad.
    • De momento no hay una cadena de comercialización, pero la cuestión está siendo sometida a estudio por parte de miembros de las asociaciones.
  • La mayoría de productores están agrupados en asociaciones formadas en cada municipio por PRODERT.
    • En Ipala, esta organización se denomina Asociación de Desarrollo Comunitario "Granero de Oriente" (ADEGO) que cuenta con 700 socios.
    • La miel que se cosecha se lleva a la asociación donde es envasada, empacada y comercializada.

3. Costos de referencia

  • El costo aproximado de una colmena con un alza es de 400.00 Q (valor no actualizado).
  • La producción de miel es de 15 a 30 botellas, que se venden en 28,00 Q cada botella (valor no actualizado).
  • El crédito es del 10,5 por ciento anual y puede ser pagado con producto (miel).

4. Instituciones u organizaciones que apoyan la implementación de la práctica

  • La asesoría técnica es cubierta por técnicos pecuarios contratados por PRODERT.
  • Las actividades de crédito y comercialización son ejecutadas por las organizaciones formadas en los distintos municipios del área de influencia de PRODERT.

5. Justificación de la aplicación y difusión actual y/o potencial de la práctica

  • La aplicación de esta práctica se justifica por la buena aceptación que ha tenido dentro de los productores, que la consideran una actividad que requiere de poca mano de obra (una visita de revisión quincenal o mensual y la actividad de castración en los últimos meses del año) y que deja buena rentabilidad.

6. Observaciones y ampliaciones

  • Otros proyectos apícolas que han tenido buen impacto en la zona incluyen a PROZACHI que en el 2002 instaló 62 colmenas mediante 13 productores de las zonas de Chiquimula.
  • También destaca el proyecto apícola de la Asociación de Productores de Miel de El Progreso con más de 30 productores activos.

7. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

8. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Cómo cosechar miel, polen y propóleos de las abejas sin aguijón: ID 8671.
  • Las buenas prácticas en apicultura: ID 8675.
  • Buenas prácticas apícolas: ID 8217.
  • Harvesting honey from giant honey bees: ID 8263.

9. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

9.1 Tecnología de ahorro de trabajo

Esta práctica requiere de poca mano de obra y así ahorra tiempo.

9.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

La producción de miel a nivel rural conduce a altos rendimientos en la comunidad y, por lo tanto, crea mayores ingresos para los apicultores.

entries.tittle: Improving Farmers' Resilience And Income Diversification in Flood and Typhoon Prone Areas Through Backyard Tilapia Farming, Philippines
entries.summary: Fisheries is of paramount importance in the Bicol region in the Philippines, with its 3 100 km of coast line of various fishing grounds. The region is, however, flood and typhoon-prone and, as in most areas in the Philippines, fishing in the Bicol region is characterized by declining fish catch. Backyard tilapia farming provides an option to improve farmers resilience and income. This is because Tilapia is a fast growing and disease resistant species; is prolific; and is able to breed in captivity. Due to these characteristics and by stocking bigger size fingerlings, the culture period can be shorted, which will reduce the impact of hazards such as floods and hurricanes. This farming practice is suitable for lowland and wetland areas that are frequently flooded for several months.
entries.description:
Description

This technology refers to the grow-out tilapias using modified farming practices in the farmer’s backyard as a means to increase the farmer’s income and food requirements. It should be noted that tilapia is a widely known and accepted food fish not only in land-locked areas, but also in coastal areas. Tilapia is specifically recommended as a candidate species because tilapias are a hardy, fast growing and disease resistant species. They are also prolific and able to breed in captivity. They also feed low in the food chain. Therefore, they are an appropriate farmed species in flood and typhoon-prone areas  such as in the Bicol region of the Philippines.

1. Implementation of the technology

1.1 Pond preparation

  • The first step is to drain the pond completely in order to eradicate predators and other unwanted species.
  • After draining, level the pond bottom sloping towards the outlet pipe/gate for easy draining whenever necessary.
  • If the pond cannot be totally drained and dried, apply 10 kg of seed powder to eliminate predators or unwanted species.

1.2 Fertilization

  • Prior to fertilization, if the pond is acidic, apply 350 to 650 kg per ha of agricultural lime.
  • Apply chicken manure applied at the rate of 2 000 to 3 000 kg per ha and inorganic fertilizer (16-20-0) at the rate of 100 to 200 kg per ha before filing the pond by broadcasting method.
  • After fertilization, fill the pond with water just to cover the pond bottom and gradually increase it when natural food organisms, such as lumut or plankton, is growing to a depth of 1.0 to 1.2 m.

1.3 Stocking

  • The pond will be stocked with two pieces of improved tilapia strain fingerlings per square meters.
  • Stocking will be done when the pond has enough natural food as indicated by greenish colour or abundance of green algae locally known as “lumut”.
  • The stock shall be acclimated prior to stocking preferably early in the morning or late in the afternoon.

1.4 Feeding

  • The stock will be fed with supplemental feeds (rice-bran-D1) when the natural food sources in the pond, such as “lumut”, has been exhausted.
  • Supplemental feeding should be at the rate 3 to 5 percent of the fish biomass.
    • This is computed as average fish weight x number of stock x 5 to 10 percent = daily feed ration per day.

1.5 Water management

  • To ensure good water quality, daily checking of water entering the pond should be done.
  • Water exchange will be done when the colour of water is blue-green (indicating heavy plankton bloom), when the water is emitting some kind of bad odour, or when the fish are gasping for air at sundown or late in the afternoon.

1.6 Harvesting

  • When tilapia reaches marketable size (for the Philippines market size preferred is 150 to 200 g each) of six to eight pieces per kg after three to four months, harvesting should be done by totally draining the pond or by selective harvesting using a seine net.
Figure 1. Backyard tilapia farmer

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Another backyard tilapia farmer

©FAO/TECA

2. Validation of the practice

  • The pilot testing results showed that although the majority of the fishermen want to continue and expand the tilapia farming, some farmers faced natural and economic challenges.
    • Continuous heavy rain in December 2011 triggered a flood that severely damaged pilot farms.
    • The damage resulted in totally wiped-out ponds, ponds completely covered with mud and debris, and ponds over flowed resulting in the escape of approximately 20 to 60 percent of the stock and entry of predators.
    • Some still managed to harvest 20 to 50 kg from the remaining stock, valued at 1,200 to 3,000 PhP at a selling price of 60.00 PHP per kg (in 2010).
    • On the other hand project-cooperators in another municipality, who established backyard tilapia farming adjacent to their rice field had successful experiences.
      • This is because they were spared of flooding despite experiencing the same rainfall pattern.
    • The pilot farms which were located adjacent to their rice field, used a mixed size of tilapia hybrid fingerlings.
    • Farmer-cooperators yielded between 21 and 125 kg and earned a net income ranging from of 981 to 5,826 PhP (2010) depending on the numbers of fingerlings (330 to 1 900) and pond area (100 to 600 m2).
  • Some farmer-cooperators used the concept of polyculture where two or more species are farmed together in the same area as long as these species does not feed in the same feeding niche.
    • The fish stocks attained approximately 80 to 100 g in three months rearing.
    • The positive outcomes were that the expected fish for harvest were enough as an incentive to expend and it can contribute to quality of life.
    • Farmers also learned to use azolla (Azolla spp.), duckweed (Lemna spp.) and golden apple snail (Pomacea canaliculata) as cheap sources of supplemental feed.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Integration of aquaculture into the farming systems: ID 4590.
  • Fish pond lay out and construction: ID 4384.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology improves the resilience and income of farmers thanks to the Tilapia's resistant and fast-growing nature. It provides for a more reliable and increased source of food and income.

entries.tittle: Community Action Planning (CAP) to Promote Adaptation to Drought and Flood Risks in Nepal
entries.summary: In Nepal, monsoon rains start around July and end between October and November. Livelihoods of rural populations heavily rely on monsoon rains. However, highly variable and erratic rainfall pattern often causes droughts and floods. To manage the risks of these climate extremes, community action planning is being developed to promote the development of hazard specific alternative plans for various crops. This can provide farmers with faster and more efficient tools to adapt to the impacts of adverse climate conditions. The action plan is developed mainly by the community members. It is location specific and considers environmental, climatic, social and economical factors.
entries.description:
Description

Community action planning (CAP) is a tool for faster and better planned adaptation in case of droughts and floods. The plan suggests suitable crops and/or agronomic management practices, such as the adoption of suitable crop varieties, proper spacing and application of plant nutrients based on the number of rainfall events.

1. Implementation of this practice

  • The community action plan (CAP) is led by a local task group formed through the community mobilization process.
  • The task group should get endorsement from the key community members to develop a plan on behalf of the community.
  • Usually, preparation of the CAP is facilitated by development practitioners or by extension officers.

1.1 The preparation of a plan has a sequence of steps

  • The local task groups organizes information sessions with the community on the advantages of such plans to manage the climate risks and identifies key risks and potential management practices.
  • The task group meets to discuss the priority risks, potential management practices, and the feasibility to adopt such practices.
  • The group meets the community members again to validate the key elements of the plan.
  • Preparation of the draft community action plan, incorporating all feedbacks and priorities are identified by the community members.
  • The task group presents the draft action plan to the community for endorsement.
Table 1. A community action plan (CAP) by crop, developed by a community in the Terai region (Kapilvastu district) of Nepal
Crops Measures
Rice

Dry seed-bed under drought conditions, direct seeding or dapog nursery if early or very late rain.

Transplanting if normal rain.

More number of seedlings (six to eight) for transplanting under rainfed condition.
Maize Maize-cowpea rotation between alleys of leucaena to reduce soil erosion.
Pulses

Long dry spell affecting crops especially pulses in winter season are protected through mechanical weeding and hoeing for moisture conservation.

Life saving irrigation protects black gram and green gram from drought impacts.
Potato Planted in raised bed (24 to 31 cm) with spacing of 90 to 100 cm.
Vegetables Drip irrigation during dry spells and water shortage.
Lucerne Lucerne crop rotation in sloppy lands reduces soil erosion.
Multi-purpose trees Amla-based agro-forestry system to reduce drought impacts and in-situ moisture conservation.
Many crops In-situ moisture conservation for maize, commercial crops and orchards and in-situ green manuring for cowpea, horse gram and sun hemp.

Source: FAO 2013

  • The community action plan must have clear objectives and expected outcomes.
    • For each objective key activities should be specified.
  • In order to ensure local ownership of the plan, the external facilitators and the local task team should mobilize and consolidate local engagement through the identification of the priorities, planning, evaluation and endorsement.
  • The Table below shows an example of a community action plan developed by a community in the Terai region (Kapilvastu district) of Nepal facilitated by the district agriculture extension office and field monitors of FAO project.
    • The plan considers both the indigenous practices as well as improved techniques introduced by the extension system.
Table 2. A community action plan (CAP) by event, developed by a community in the Terai region (Kapilvastu district) of Nepal
Event Measure
Rainfed conditions Avoid crops with high water requirement.
Drought condition Urea spray (2 percent) along with life saving irrigation given to crops under moisture stress.
Early season drought Mulching instead of inter-culture to conserve moisture in maize and vegetables.

Source: FAO 2013

2. Technical, economic, financial, social and environmental attributes of the technology

  • Increases efficiency of farm inputs use.
  • A combination of practices followed under drought conditions in different crops.
  • Stabilizes production under moisture stress.
Figure 1. Community meeting

©FAO/TECA

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool;
  • temperate, cool.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Community based landslide treatment: ID 7710.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

Community action planning is a tool for faster and better adaptation to the impacts of floods and droughts.
entries.further_reading: This technology was documented by Dr. A.K. Gautam, Environmental Unit, Nepal Agriculture Research Council, Khumaltar, Kathmandu, Nepal.

entries.tittle: Community Based Landslide Treatment in Nepal
entries.summary: Frequent landslides in mid-hill districts in Nepal have caused damage to productive land at the lower basin and affected human settlements and agriculture activities both upstream and downstream. Extensive areas of productive land were left fallow because of their vulnerability to landslides, and many settlements were displaced, mostly from the mid-hills to the Terai region. The communities in the mid-hills practice an integrated approach for landslide treatment, which includes a series of conservation practices strategically planned along the river.
entries.description:
Description

In Nepal, especially in the mid-hill areas, more than 80 percent of the territory is characterized by steep hills and mountains prone to landslides, especially during the rainy season. Landslides are aggravated by improper land use patterns and deforestation, leading to vegetation loss, exposure of soil surface to run-off water and eventual soil erosion. Slope failure is developed due to progressive external loads and the deterioration of slope geo-materials. Other factors include soil properties, the presence of water bodies and the unavailability of proper vegetation on the soil surface.

1. Implementation of the practice

1.1 The landslide treatment committee (LTC)

  • A Landslide Treatment Committee (LTC) is established, in charge of coordinating the overall development and implementation of the community-based landslide treatment, as well as the monitoring and maintenance of interventions.
  • Several rounds of consultations with the community are undertaken by the facilitators to identify the critical areas vulnerable to landslides and to explore the best possible alternatives before setting the comprehensive landslide treatment model.
  • The committee sets regulations for the enhancement of vegetative barriers and the construction of infrastructure to reduce the runoff speed in strategic locations across the streams and gullies.
    • In this case, regulations are set for grazing control, the planting of forage, grass, fodders and bamboo, as well as for the construction of check dams and brushwood dams.
    • The work is carried out by the community itself, guaranteeing ownership of interventions and the sustainability of actions.
  • Institutional support is essential to provide communities with technical advice and inputs that ensure adequate implementation of interventions.
    • In this case, The District Soil Conservation Office (DSCO) and the District Agriculture Development Office (DADO) provided saplings, grass seeds and jute sacks for the bio-engineering work.
    • In addition, the Department of Water Induced Disaster Prevention (DWIDP) provided gabion boxes for the construction of spur dykes.
      • These structures extend out of the bank of the stream to deviate the current away from the bank, protecting it against erosion.
    • Until recently, it was believed that spur dykes were sufficient for landslide treatments, but plantation of fast growing plants, grass and properly implemented conservation rules are equally needed to minimize the effect of landslides.
    • The plantation of non-timber forest products (NTFPs) is part of a set of community agreed rules and regulations for long-term conservation.

2. Technical, economic, financial, social and environmental attributes of the technology

  • Landslide protection during rainy season.
  • Reduces landslide frequency and impacts.
  • Reduces land fallowing.
  • Provides protection to slopes.
  • Increases soil productivity.
Figure 1. Community based landslide treatment in Nepal

©FAO/TECA

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/ mod cool; and
  • temperate, cool.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Community Action Planning (CPA) to promote adaptation to drought and flood risks: ID 7706.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

Community-based integrated methods for landslide treatment reduces the impacts of landslides on settlements and agricultural lands.

entries.tittle: Strengthening of Community Seed Production Groups (CSPG) in Nepal
entries.summary:
The seed replacement rate in Nepal is very low and this should be increased to at least 25 to 33 percent from the current level of 4.7 percent in the country. Farmers have been growing deteriorated seeds of crop varieties for many years, without replacement. Farmers prefer local varieties in rain-fed areas due to low input and low management requirements and low risks compared to improved varieties. So, for successful production of quality seeds, farmers need to be organized in Community Seed Production Groups (CSPG). The programme also provides production inputs, credit, training, and technical know-how on seed production, storage, and marketing.
The objective of strengthening the community seed production groups are: to produce quality seeds and store them for future use and to improve the capacity of the community seed bank with revolving funds and storage facilities.
entries.description:
Description

Farmers have been growing the same seeds of crop varieties for many years, without replacement. As a result, seed quality has deteriorated. For successful production of quality seeds, farmers need to be organized in Community Seed Production Groups (CSPG) under a Community Seed Bank (CSB) scheme. The programme aims to provide food grain exchange for seeds and credit to allow the community to store seeds for the next season. This practice will either provide space for participating farmers to store their seeds in big silos or mini seed houses, or to collect the seeds produced by farmers at reasonable prices and store them in a community seed storage facility. Since CSBs will bear the costs of cleaning, storage, and fumigation, they will charge some nominal fee that will be deposited in a revolving fund. Farmers are provided with inputs and soft production loans to allow them to produce quality seeds. Member farmers will also be provided with training and technical know-how on seed production, storage, and marketing. The CSBs sell the surplus seeds to other districts or to the neighbouring villages at better prices and thus member farmers  have a fair share of the benefits.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • CSPGs were formed in the Siraha district and organized into a CSB as part of the FAO supported TCP project.
  • The existing farmer groups were involved and promoted to organize themselves intoCSPGs.
  • The member farmers were provided with source seeds of the crop varieties.
    • These were locally adapted or found tolerant to stress conditions in order to include them in the seed production program.
  • The CSPGs were also provided with the latest technology and production inputs.
  • Assistance was provided to establish a CSB, with revolving funds and a non-conditioned mini seed house / store with cleaning facilities.
  • The facilities provided space to participating farmers to store their seeds in mini seed houses and locally available seed storage facilities.
  • The community members organized to collect the seeds produced by farmers at reasonable prices and store them in community seed storage facilities.
  • The CSPGs bear the costs of cleaning, storage and fumigations and charged nominal fee that was deposited in a revolving fund.
  • Members of the community seed production groups were trained on technical know-how on seed production, storage, and marketing.
Figure 1. Strengthening of Community Seed Production Groups (CSPG) in Nepal

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Seed storage facilities

©FAO/TECA

2. Technical, economic, financial, social and environmental attributes of the technology

  • Increases efficiency of community seed storage systems.
  • Maintains food security through seed security.
  • Improves quality of seed produced by farmers.
  • Maintains crop yields through quality seeds within acceptable limit of risk.

3. Factors underlying success

  • Mobilization of community groups.
  • Quality source seeds.
  • Community seed bank providing needed facilities to farmers.
  • Poor farmers provided food grain as exchange for seed and pledging money.
  • Provision and technical know-how on seed production and storage.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cool; and
  • subtropics, warm/mod cool. 

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Community Action Planning (CPA) to promote adaptation to drought and flood risks: ID 7706.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The technology allows farmers to access seeds of crop varieties which require low input and low management requirements as well as low risks.

6.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology provides means for farmers to organise themselves efficiently and have access to production inputs, credit, training, and technical know-how on seed production, storage, and marketing.

6.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for higher yields and a greater source of revenue and food for poor farmers.
entries.further_reading:
7. Further reading

  • Results of Community Seed Bank in Kachorwa of Bara district under a project “Strengthening the scientific basis of in-situ conservation of agricultural bio-diversity on-farm” supported by IPGRI since 1995 and programs on CSB under DOA, Nepal.

entries.tittle: Improved Pit Storage Method for Ginger Rhizomes in Nepal
entries.summary:
Farmers in the Mahintada village, in the Surkhet District cultivate ginger as a major income generating cash crop to be used as food or medicine. Ginger rhizomes selected for seed purposes are stored in pits to be used in the next season. It has been observed that around 25 to 30 percent of rhizomes rot in the pit itself and about 10 to 15 percent of rhizomes sprout in the pit and are rendered useless for sowing due to a build-up of pathogenic inoculums. Therefore, there is a need to improve storage conditions. The pit storage method, with some improvements, constitutes an eco-friendly and less expensive method with respect to tradition and local knowledge.

This practice shows how to improve and maintain the quality of ginger rhizomes selected for seeds through improved pit storage technology.
entries.description:
Description

In the predominantly rain-fed area of Surket, ginger is raised either as a sole crop, or as an intercrop. Seed rhizomes are usually planted from March to April. Most of rural families living in remote places follow traditional methods for cultivation and storage, which are usually eco-friendly; less expensive; and utilize local resources, knowledge and labour. The improved pit storage method provides cool conditions, ensuring freshness for prolonged storage. Ideal storage conditions should have a temperature of 12 to 14° C and a relative humidity of 65 to 75 percent. Under these conditions, ginger seed rhizomes can be easily stored for five to six months without damage and deterioration in quality as it will minimize shrinkage, rhizome rot and improve germination capacity. Approximately 350 kg of ginger rhizomes can be stored in one pit.

1. Implementation of this practice

To implement a proper ginger pit storage, farmers need specific materials.

  • Disease free and vigorous rhizome seeds are selected to be stored immediately after harvest.
    • For this purpose, healthy and disease-free clumps are marked in the field when the crop is six to eight months old and still green.
  • Rhizomes are disinfected with fungicides and pesticides.
  • A circular or rectangular pit of about 1 to 2 m depth is dug in a shady and well-drained area, e.g. under the shade of a tree, provided water does not enter the pits.
  • Pit walls may be coated with cow dung and disinfected with the same solution used in the second bullet point, for rhizomes.
    • If this is not possible, fire should be lit inside the pit to improve hygienic conditions within the pit.
  • Prior to storage of the rhizomes, the top of the pit (up to 6”) is covered with grass and soil and is raised slightly above ground level to prevent entry of rainwater into the pit.
  • A 3 to 4 cm layer of rice husk, saw dust, straw or dry grass should be placed in the bottom of the pit to serve as a cushion.
    • Ginger rhizomes are placed in layers with 1 to 2 cm of sand/straw layers in between.
  • The pit is covered with a wooden plank with holes and plastered with thatch, soil or cow dung in an oval shape.
  • A temporary thatched roof is made over the pit to lower the inside temperature and protect it from water entry.
    • Ventilation inside the pit can be maintained with the help of a pipe.
  • Pits are to be inspected every 20 days approximately to remove shrivelled and disease affected rhizomes, and dried every two months to protect them from insect pests and moulds.

2. Technical, economic, financial, social and environmental attributes of the practice

  • Improves efficiency of storage through improvements on traditional system.
  • Maintains quality of ginger rhizome selected for seed.

3. Factors underlying success

  • Temperature and relative humidity in the improved storage is well maintained.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Composting associated with planting pits: ID 7525.
  • Planting pits and stone lines: ID 7516.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology improves storage efficiency maintains the quality of ginger rhizome selected for seed.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology prevents seed damage and deterioration, and improves germination capacity. This allows for extended preservation and quality, leading to a more secure food source and increased income.

entries.tittle: Use of submergence rice variety NSIC Rc-194 to counteract impacts of flooding in the Bicol region, Philippines
entries.summary: The Philippines is particularly prone to natural disasters due to its geographical location and physical environment. The country experiences an average of 20 typhoons yearly, which trigger landslides, flash-floods, mudslides, widespread flooding, and cause destruction and damages to homes, community buildings, communications, infrastructure, and agriculture. Within the Philippines, Bicol is one of the most hazard prone regions and agriculture is regularly among the most effected sectors. About 42 percent of the region’s workforce depends on agricultural production. Because it is expected that the impacts of climate change will further exacerbate the regions’ exposure to climate–induced risks, farmers need to adapt their farming systems to the new conditions. Cultivation of flood-tolerant varieties is a potential adaptation option in flood affected rice areas. For flood-prone areas, the cultivation of NSIC Rc194, can be an appropriate submergence rice variety and a cost-effective coping mechanism. The practice has been recommended by the farmers and local experts and approved by the scientists as a suitable technology to be tested.
entries.description:
Description

Rice is the staple food of Filipinos. Farmers experienced high risk of crop losses (40 to 80 percent) during the typhoon month of October, November and December. In the Bicol region, San Buena, Buhi, and Camarines Sur, crop lands get/remain flooded during parts of the months September and October after the harvest. This challenging situation can be mitigated without the need for investing in additional the land preparation and other inputs.

The flood tolerant rice variety NSIC Rc-194 (IRRI) survives, grows, and develops even after ten days of complete submergence at the vegetative stage. The variety was tested in three pilot municipalities (San Buena, Buhi, and Camarines Sur) between June and October 2010 (wet season) in lowland irrigated farming systems in the Philippines. The use of NSIC Rc-194 has enabled farmer cooperators to produce acceptable rice yield under above stagnant water conditions, during the second and third crop seasons.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • The use of submerge tolerant variety is suitable for testing by farmers with about 1 000 m2 of land for cultivation exposed to normal / seasonal flooding (7 to 14 days).

1.1 Land preparation

  • The required land preparation is a farmer known practice.
  • Generally it is recommended to plough and to harrow the land three to four times.
  • For sandy loam to silty loam soil, two to three ploughing and cross ploughing with subsequent three to four laddering are recommended.
  • For a clay type of soil, soil preparation requires more tillage operation at appropriate soil moisture status.

1.2 Fertilizer dose

  • Apply fertilizer in appropriate dose at the final land preparation as illustrated in Table 1.

1.3 Seedling and spacing, weeding and harvesting

  • The variety used in the pilot site of NSIC Rc-194.
  • Farmers have to be advised that Rc194 is not suitable to grow in blast- and tungro-stricken areas.
  • A plant spacing of 20 cm x 20 cm is advised and as needed.
  • Rotary or hand weeding can be used.
  • An appropriate IPM methodology can be applied for rat control based on Regional Crop Protection Centre’s recommendation.
  • While 80 to 85 percent of the grains are ripe, the harvesting should be initiated.
Table 1. Fertilizer use
Name of fertilizer Quantity per 1 000 m2
Urea or equivalent vol. of manure 0.5 kg
Trichoderma Two packets

Source: PhilRice-DA-5

2. Results and findings

Ten farmers participated voluntarily in the initial technology dissemination - demo project. For three crop cycles, 50 demo sites were established. The costs for setting up the demonstration sites amounted to around 2 250 PHP (in 2010) including seeds, fertilizer, sign board, register and soil test. The use of NSIC Rc-194 has enabled farmer cooperators to produce acceptable rice yield under above normal rainfall conditions, during the second and third crop seasons in 2010 and 2011. NSIC Rc-194 variety was able to tolerate the La Niña effects (e.g. above normal precipitation) from December 2010 to March 2011. Statistically, the yield difference obtained was significant at 5 percent level, with a t-value = 2.88 and p-value = 0.045. Under submerged conditions the average yield amounted 2.5 tonne per hectare and the growing cycle included 125 days. Under normal conditions the variety even yields 3.50 tonne per hectare and matures within 112 days. The variety’s other characteristics in which farmers were interested besides the submergence tolerance, were high milling recovery (65 percent), good eating quality, and better yield adaptation under rainy-environment. Cost wise, farmer cooperators spent about PHP 1 800 (2010) for the cost of seeds, other farm inputs, and family labour in a 1 000 m2 plot. Thus, a farmer will spend PHP 18 000 in one hectare for this practice. In terms of economic benefits, an additional rice yield of 1 700 kilos in each season is possible. This implies that a farmer could earn, on the average, PHP 20 400 per hectare (in 2010), which is 38 percent higher than the earnings from the existing farming or control farmers.

One important need of farmers to ensure sustained seeds supply during climatic disturbances is hands-on training on seed production and storage of stress-tolerant variety like NSIC Rc-194. Additional support of Local Government Units (LGU) is highly desirable to establish functional seed systems, storage and distribution of stress tolerant varieties. These should be accessible to farmers and enables them to mitigate effects of natural hazards.

Figure 1. Yield results of submergence rice

©FAO/TECA

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool; and
  • temperate, cool.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Participatory varietal selection: improved rice varieties: ID 4459.
  • Rice transplanting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7214.
  • Rice seed sorting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7205.
  • Improving rice quality: video from Africa Rice Center: ID 6976.
  • Aerobic rice: ID 7941.
  • Intensive rice cultivation: ID 7666.
  • Use of Early-Maturing Rice Variety (EMRV) to reduce typhoon impacts: ID 7719.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

Rice tolerant varieties reduces crop losses due to intensive rainfall and stagnant water. They contribute to food and economic security in the region.

  • De La Torre, E.B. 2010. Detailed Implementation Guidelines, GPOs Lowland Irrigated Agro-Eco Zone for project TCP/PHI/3203 Philippines Rice Research Institute.
  • Philippine Rice Research Institute.

entries.tittle: Zero / Minimum Tillage in Rice-Wheat System in Nepal
entries.summary: The objective of this practice is to facilitate timely planting of the wheat crop while minimizing soil degradation and conserving residual soil moisture and energy with minimum or zero tillage in wet and marshy land, where land preparation is not possible.
entries.description:
Description

By tradition, in the Terai region, farmers believe that wheat planting needs well-prepared and pulverized soil for high yields, carrying out several ploughing, and harrowing. However, after rice cultivation, the land is marshy or wet and ploughing is not possible, delaying wheat planting. Zero or minimum tillage provides minimum disturbance of the soil by placing the seeds directly in furrows. Seeds are then covered with well-decomposed compost and rice stubbles left in the field. Some advantages of zero-tillage are the reduction of about 30 percent in the use of water, compared to conventional tillage, as well as an improvement in the physical properties of soil. In addition, by planting wheat on time, higher yields may be obtained.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • Land should be moist at the time of planting wheat under zero tillage so that the seed drill can be operated under unploughed land after the rice harvest.
  • Farmyard manure (FYM) should be spread in the field at 5 tonnes per ha with rice stubbles left in the field after the paddy harvest.
  • An improved seed cum fertilizer drill attached with a roller and tines is run by a power tiller to plant five to six rows of wheat at a time.
  • Seeds and fertilizers are kept in advance in separate boxes which will be dropped through separate holes fitted with plastic pipes.
  • The tines fitted in the seed cum fertilizer drill at a recommended row to row spacing. This will simply scrap the land making a 2 cm to 3 cm furrow, remove weeds, and drop the fertilizer and seeds simultaneously.
  • The holes for dropping fertilizer and seeds are calibrated in advance based on their recommended rates. This causes minimal disturbance to the soil and surface residues in the soil with a small furrow opening for seed and fertilizer placement.
  • Wheat planting is normally done in early November. Wheat seeds can be planted as a relay crop under this condition.
  • The recommended seed rate is 120 kg per ha, and the fertilizer dosage is 100: 50: 25 kg NPK per ha. Only Di‑ammonium Phosphate (DAP) is applied at the time of sowing seeds. Urea and potassium fertilizers are applied 10 to 20 days after sowing.
  • The no-tillage in wheat is economical and produces comparable yields with conventionally ploughed land and uses only three-quarters of the ploughing effort.
  • The zero-tillage method reduces production costs, reverses soil degradation in intensive cropping systems and increases agroecosystem productivity.
Figure 1. Zero/minimum tillage in the rice-wheat system in Nepal

©FAO/TECA

1.1 Impact of zero/minimum tillage

Zero tillage has a positive impact on the resilience of agrosystems and farmers' livelihoods. The improvement of soil conditions and structure and the protection offered by the cover crops makes it more resistant against water deficits from droughts and water saturation from heavy rainfall. The crop yield increases and the lower labour requirements benefit farmers, who can save money and time, improve their food security and explore market possibilities thanks to higher yields.

Figure 2. Zero/minimum tillage in the rice-wheat system in Nepal

©FAO/TECA

These tillage practices enhance the resilience of farmers´ livelihoods when they adopt them. For instance, soils increase their productivity and their resistance to natural hazards. Consequently, farmers can benefit from the yield improvement in their nutritional status and open business opportunities to increase their income.

2. Technical, economic, financial, social and environmental attributes of the technology

  • Increases efficiency of farm inputs use.
  • Increases the possibility of timely cultivation under marshy wetlands.
  • Improves the utilization of residual soil moisture after rice.
  • Increases farm production.
  • Reduces soil degradations.
  • Reduces the cost of cultivation.
  • Helps improve livelihood's resilience against climate-related risks.

3. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

There are some minimum requirements that are necessary for the successful implementation of the practice such as:

  • timely planting; 
  • low cost of production; and
  • resource conservation under the intensive system.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cool; and
  • temperate, cold.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Introduction to conservation agriculture: principles and benefits: ID 7413.
  • No-till technology: a no-till system with crop residue management for medium scale wheat and barley farming: ID 7507.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

This practice helps in reducing ploughing efforts.

entries.tittle: Warehouse Receipt Systems: Lessons from Niger
entries.summary: This documentation provides a summary experience of a microfinance system called the “warrantage system“, or inventory credit system. Farmers access small loans from banks and microfinance institutions to finance their household generating activity incomes. The practice recognises the role of micro credit to smallholder farmers’ success and provides an appropriate response. Farmers store their end of season production surplus in a secured storage facility owned by the farmers’ cooperative. The cooperative retains one key to the storage facility while the other is given to the bank or microfinance institution. The bank then issues farmers having production surplus in the storage facility, with loans to finance their household commercial activities.
entries.description:
Description

Since early 1990s the “warrantage system” has been adapted in Niger by local farmer organizations and microfinance institutions (MFIs), becoming a popular financial product.

The principal crops used for inventory credit are:

  • millet
  • rice and
  • peanuts.

However, any crop that can be stored without damage, can be used.

Producer organizations or cooperatives provide:

  • storage facilities; and
  • loan transactions.

The loans enable farmers to:

  • finance their household generating income activities during the storage period;
    • thereby allowing for smoother cash flows.

Revenues from financed short-term activities often enable farmers to:

  • pay back the loan without using revenues from the future sale of the stored production.

The access to the warrantage system phases are:

  • Farmers, after harvesting, meet the head of the cooperative to discuss the amount of each member’s surplus production.
  • The head of the cooperative negotiates a loan from a local bank or microfinance institution using the grain as collateral.
  • Once an agreement is reached, the grain is stored in a secure storage facility owned by the cooperative.
  • The cooperative retains one key while the other is given to the bank or microfinance institution who then issues the loan.
Figure 1. A typical warrantage storage facility

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Negotiating a loan with the bank

©FAO/TECA

1. The benefits

The benefits of the warrantage are:

  • To enable the farmers to sell their grain at a later stage when prices are higher (sometimes after six months).
  • To purchase, with the loan, good seeds for the next season.
  • To engage in other small businesses generating additional revenue helping farmers increase their incomes and wellbeing.
    • Income increase ranged from 19 to 113 percent for participating farmers.
    • Yields increase ranged from 34 and 120 percent, as farmers were able to buy better seeds and fertilizer.

The warrantage system also benefits other participants in the practice including the microfinance institutions. Tanadi, for example, earned 27 percent in interest in 2011. The stock is serving as collateral and the Tanadi loans at 80 percent of the value of the stock. After four to six months the farmers pay back the loan and get back their stored grain from the warehouse (or bank).

Warrantage is promoted by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations with funding from the European Union, Belgium, Luxembourg and Spain.

2. The challenges

However, the system has its challenges depending upon growth condition:

  • During bad harvest seasons, farmers have little or no surplus to put into storage.
  • During good harvest seasons, there is a lot to store but insufficient financing from the banks.

Several conditions need to be met for warehouse receipt financing to work. Some important ones include:

  • lender’s detailed knowledge of agricultural value chain dynamics;
  • stability of agribusiness opportunities faced by borrowers;
  • legal and financial regulatory framework;
  • existence of proper storage management; and
  • facilities and sound governance among producer organizations.

The experience in Niger highlights the relative importance of these conditions. The constant demand for cereal imports from neighbouring Nigeria has created stable business opportunities for farmers in Niger. This represents an effective incentive to build strong producer organizations.

Farmers, through their organizations, have worked steadily to benefit from these opportunities by building storage facilities and making joint loan requests backed by cereal stocks. Lenders understand the worth of these stocks and therefore accept them as collateral. Despite the court system in Niger makes credit contracts difficult to enforce, the combinations of:

  • stable agribusiness opportunities;
  • strong farmer organizations; and
  • lenders familiar with agricultural markets.

All of the above factors make warehouse receipt finance work in the country.

Video: Financing the future: smallholder inventory credit in Niger

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Women-friendly

The above technology is easy to implement and accessible to all.

4.2 Resource use efficiency

The above technology allows for safe crop storage facility and minimise crop losses.

4.3 Pro-poor technology

The above recommendations contribute to agri-food business development and marketing opportunities.

entries.tittle: Commercial scale community bamboo harvesting
entries.summary: Traditional vegetation based bamboo production of four villages of Meung districts in Lao PDR, are being shifted to industrial processing oriented bamboo production. This is being done with the technical and operational support from ForInfo, Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Finland. The project allowed for improved management practices, participatory decision making, beneficial opportunities for villagers, and the private sector, as well as reducing CO₂ emissions.
entries.description:
Description

Bamboo species play a key role in Northern Laos PDR (see map in Figure 1), but traditional production practices are not efficient. These practices entail poor management, low productivity, suppression of the regeneration of permanent tree species, accumulation of biomass creating enormous fuel load, low income for local populations, less information access, and high CO₂ emissions. With this situation, two private companies are being established with contractual agreements with local villagers supported by ForInfo. Local households provide a regular supply of bamboo year-round to the private company at a fair price. It is expected to become a significant contributor to household income either year round or on a seasonal basis.

Figure 1. Bamboo species play a key role in Northern Laos PDR

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Ready for transport: the ForInfo bamboo crawler is loaded with over 350 kg of fresh bamboo

©FAO/TECA

2. Approach

  • Besides private entrepreneurs, the ForInfo project will benefit government officials, community associations and other Non-Govermental Organizations (NGOs), by fostering wide stakeholder ownership and sharing the responsibilities in the role of activities.
    • Activities are:
      • the efficient exact methods to harvest bamboo,
      • the planting of improved species of bamboo,
      • an overall perennial cropping system,
      • the raising of local community awareness of environmental protection, 
      • a reduction CO₂ emission as much as possible, and
      • forest management improvement.
  • ForInfo supports innovative information, education, communication campaigns in partnership with government agencies, local NGOs, and other partners.
  • Ultimately, the project aims to lay the groundwork for a sustainable, efficient and competitive forest-based livelihoods system.
    • This is through the use of innovative approaches and closer collaboration between smallholders, forestry officials, sawmill owners, timber traders and credit associations.

3. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies 

  • Bamboo toothpick manufacturing unit: ID 3888.
  • Bamboo splitting and slivering unit: ID 3865.
  • Bamboo in sericulture: a case study from India: ID 3859.
  • Bamboo treadle pump: ID 3866.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allowed for management practice improvement, participatory decision-making, and a reduction in CO₂ emissions.​

5.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology provided beneficial opportunities for villagers and the private sector through increased income generation.

entries.tittle: Aerobic Rice
entries.summary: Aerobic rice is a production system in which rice is grown under non-flooded, non-puddled, and non-saturated soil conditions. Because aerobic rice needs less water at the field level than conventional lowland rice, the system is targeted at relatively water-short irrigated or rain-fed lowland environments. Irrigation can be applied through flash-flooding, furrow irrigation (or raised beds), or sprinklers. Site-specific nutrient management can be used to determine the optimal management of fertilizers. This growing system experiences more weed growth and more species of weeds, therefore there is a need to control weeds. Soil-borne pests and diseases such as nematodes, root aphids, and fungi are known to occur more in aerobic rice than in flooded rice, especially in the tropics. It is recommended to grow aerobic rice in rotation with upland crops suitable in the area. This practice explains where and how to manage ”aerobic rice”.
entries.description:
Description

1. What is Aerobic Rice?

Aerobic rice is a production system in which especially developed “aerobic rice” varieties are grown in well-drained, non-puddled (dryland preparation), and non-saturated soils. It is a system, in which the field is not flooded at all any more but just “wetted” like a farmer does with irrigated maize or wheat. With appropriate management, the system aims for yields of at least 4 to 6 tonnes per hectare. 

2. Target area

  • “Favourable uplands."
    • Areas where the land is flat, where rainfall with or without supplemental irrigation is sufficient to frequently bring the soil water content close to field capacity, and where farmers have access to external inputs such as fertilizers.
  • Fields on upper slopes or terraces in undulating, rain-fed lowlands.
    • Quite often, soils in these areas are relatively coarse-textured and well-drained, so that ponding of water occurs only briefly or not at all during the growing season.
  • Water-short irrigated lowlands.
    • Areas where farmers do not have access to sufficient water any more to keep rice fields flooded for a substantial period of time.

3. Management

  • The usual establishment method is dry direct seeding.
  • Aerobic rice also allows practices of conservation agriculture as used in upland crops, such as mulching and minimum tillage.
Figure 1. A dry seeded aerobic rice field

©FAO/TECA 

Figure 2. Dibbling aerobic rice seeds

©FAO/TECA 

  • Aerobic rice can be rain-fed or irrigated.
  • Irrigation can be applied through flash-flooding, furrow irrigation (or raised beds), or sprinklers.
  • Unlike flooded rice, irrigation, when applied, is not used to flood the soil but to just bring the soil water content in the root zone up to field capacity.
  • Site-specific nutrient management (SSNM) can be used to determine the optimal management of fertilizers.
  • In the absence of knowledge on SSNM, 70 to 90 kg N per ha could be a useful starting point to obtain a yield of 4 to 6 tonnes per ha.
  • The first split can best be given 10 to 12 days after emergence, the second at active tillering, and the third at panicle initiation.
  • The application of Phosphorus fertilizer can be more critical for aerobic rice than for flooded rice.
  • Rice fields that are not permanently flooded tend to experience more weed growth and more species of weeds.
  • Appropriate herbicide use, plus additional manual or mechanical weeding in the early phases of crop growth, is therefore needed to control weeds.
  • Soil-borne pests and diseases such as nematodes, root aphids, and fungi are known to occur more in aerobic rice than in flooded rice, especially in the tropics.
  • It is recommended to grow aerobic rice in rotation with upland crops suitable in the area.
Figure 3. A ripening aerobic rice field

©FAO/TECA 

Figure 4. Aerobic rice growing side by side with soya bean

©FAO/TECA 

4. Validation of the practice 

  • Aerobic rice was validated with farmers in Kaifeng, in north-central China along the Yellow River, demonstrated yields of up to 5.5 tonne per ha with as little as 230 mm of irrigation and 340 mm of rainfall in localities where flooded rice required 1 300 mm of water for yields of 6.5 to 9.0 ton per ha.
  • With good management, aerobic rice yield can be 75 to 80 percent of flooded rice yield while using only half as much water or even less.
  • Aerobic rice is now being tested by farmers in northern China on an estimated 200 000 ha and actively researched in the Philippines, India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, and many other countries.
  • In the Philippines, aerobic rice has been tested and adopted by farmers in about 10 provinces.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Rice seedbed preparation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 6973.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7210.
  • Intensive rice cultivation: ID 7666.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2941.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

The practice grows “aerobic rice” varieties through the efficient use of irrigation and maintenance of well-drained, non-puddled, and non-saturated soils.

entries.tittle: Contract farming handbook
entries.summary: This guide was published by the 'Competitive African Cotton Initiative' (COMPACI) in collaboration with other partners  as such as Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), AISP II. It is a powerful tool for linking farmers to buyers, in an increasingly concentrated agri-food sector, and buyers to supply sources in ever-more competitive agricultural markets. The purpose of this guide is to provide a practical and process-oriented approach for a sound planning and implementation of contract farming (CF) schemes. This guide has been developed as a hands-on and process-oriented approach to serve practitioners involved in starting up, managing or supporting the initiation and implementation of contract farming schemes. While giving orientation for a focused approach, the guide remains flexible leaving the selection of tools and sequencing of activities to the discretion of users according to the reality on the ground. The proposed approaches are applicable to any type of product and situation. This depends on whether users are capable of using it in a flexible way, as well as adapting the tools and recommendations to the specific local situation and the ever-faster changing production and market contexts in developing countries.
entries.description:
Description

This guide defines ‘Contract Farming’ (CF) as forward agreements specifying the obligations of farmers and buyers as partners in business. Lawfully, farming contracts entail the sellers’ (farmers’) obligation to supply the volumes and qualities of produce as specified and the buyers’ (processors’/ traders’) obligation to off-take the goods and make payments as agreed. This type of contract already exists in Asia and Latin America since the 19th century. It subsequently spread throughout the United States and Europe in the 20th century and was also introduced to North and Sub-Sahara Africa. Such contracts may be concluded with individual farmers or farmer groups and in a formal or informal manner. The guide states that CF has different business models such as informal, intermediary, multipartite, centralized and nucleus estate models. Aside from the normal agreement, the buyer also provides additional services to assist the farmer to produce better outputs.

1. Contract farming categories

Incentives are classified into two categories:

  • monetary incentives; and
  • non-monetary incentives.

The success and the sustainability of a contract farming scheme is situation-specific,purposely designed based on:

  • market opportunities;
  • product features;
  • suppliers’ and buyers’ capacities;
  • existing business development services; and
  • overall local, national, regional and international framework conditions for agricultural and agri-food business development and private investments.

In short, there is a vast range of conditions for success and failure that need to be taken into consideration when analysing the situation at local level and planning CF arrangements. No aforementioned model is considered to be the overall best option ever for all circumstances. However, six key conditions for successful CF and related success factors have been identified:

  • trust and scope of negotiations;
  • economic viability and incentives;
  • CF arrangements and risks;
  • technology transfer and innovation;
  • investment climate and third party support; and
  • sound analysis, planning and monitoring.

Alongside the successes, there are factors that play in favour of the failure of CF. In order to develop a successful CF, the steps below should be followed:

  • plan initiation;
  • implementation and learning phase of the plan; and
  • sustain and growth within the plan.

It is necessary to follow the steps of the plan, carry out the necessary activities and keep an eye on the projected milestones in order to be able to achieve CF  objectives. The technology is used globally. For example, since 2004, 75 percent of poultry is under CF in Brazil and 36 percent of agricultural productions are under CF in the United States.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Warehouse receipt systems: lessons from Niger: ID 7745.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology helps raising farmers' awareness regarding their obligations and rights as farmers and buyers and partners in business.

  • GIZ. Contract farming handbook.

entries.tittle: Cero Labranza en Chile
entries.summary: La práctica de cero labranza consiste en el establecimiento de un cultivo sin preparar el suelo, así las semillas se dejan en surcos que tengan el ancho y la profundidad suficiente sin remover el suelo. En el mismo proceso de trabajo se pueden aplicar fertilizantes y otras enmiendas para mejorar el suelo. En este ejemplo, en la comuna de San Ignacio, la cero labranza se utilizó para establecer praderas. Esta práctica funciona, principalmente, como defensa de la erosión hídrica aumentando la cobertura del suelo, especialmente durante los meses de invierno. La cero labranza está considerada como un sistema económico pero con el riesgo de generar compactación del suelo. La disponibilidad de maquinaria puede ser una limitante para implementar esta práctica.
entries.description:
Descripción

La comuna de San Ignacio, ubicada en la Región del Biobío (Chile), presenta suelos con una agricultura intensiva producto de un constante laboreo, lo que ha generado procesos de erosión, especialmente durante los meses de invierno. Con el fin de mitigar los problemas de erosión, algunos de los productores de la zona han modificado el uso del laboreo convencional hacia un sistema de cero labranza.

La cero labranza consiste en el establecimiento de un cultivo sin preparar el suelo con arado y volteo, así las semillas se dejan en surcos que tengan el ancho y la profundidad suficiente removiendo el suelo lo mínimo necesario. En la comuna de San Ignacio, las praderas naturales o praderas de alfalfa que han completado su ciclo productivo son sembradas en forma directa con una mezcla de forrajeras usando una sembradora de cero labranza de origen brasileño, que cuenta con una cajón fertilizador que aplica una mezcla de fertilizante en la misma hilera de siembra para apoyar el establecimiento de la pradera que se siembra. No existe aplicación previa de herbicidas como en otros sistema de cero labranza.

Para la implementación de esta tecnología, se debe verificar la presencia de estratos de suelos compactados, espinas o raíces de árboles y retirarlas, ya que dificultan el paso de la sembradora. Además, como parte de las actividades para la preparación del suelo, y si se requiere, se debe adicionar cal con el fin de aumentar el pH. A continuación, se procede a sembrar las semillas de alfalfa y/o forrajeras con la ayuda de la sembradora para cero labranza. Dentro de las actividades recurrentes se encuentran: la fertilización química del suelo, y la adición de cal, además de la resiembra de semilla cada dos años, aproximadamente.

Figura 1. Sembradora de chorro o flujo continuo, de siembra directa de origen brasileño Marca KUHN Modelo SDE 2217/19, que posee un sistema de doble disco desencontrado, que permite cortar la vegetación como una tijera y generar un surco en el suelo donde queda depositada en forma superficial la semilla con el abono

©FAO/TECA

Figura 2. Trabajo del tractor junto con la sembradora sobre una pradera a entrada de invierno

©FAO/TECA

1. Descripción del ambiente donde la estrategia fue aplicada

Las siguientes características describen el ambiente natural y social donde se implementó la práctica de cero labranza. Las condiciones ambientales no son determinantes o excluyentes para el éxito de la práctica, pero deben tenerse en cuenta para implementar o modificar la técnica que sean más apropiada a las condiciones naturales de la zona donde la práctica se quiera replicar.

1.1 Ambiente natural

  • Promedio de precipitación anual: 1 000 a 1 500 mm.
  • Altitud: 100 a 500 m.s.n.m.
  • Pendiente: Casi plana.
  • Profundidad del suelo: 80 a 120 cm.
  • Clima: Templado/mediterráneo.
  • Textura del suelo: Franco arcilloso.
  • Fertilidad del suelo: Media.
  • Contenido de la materia orgánica del suelo: Muy alto.
  • Drenaje del suelo/infiltración: Bueno.

1.2 Ambiente social

  • Tipo del usuario tierra: Individual/gran escala.
  • Tenencia de la tierra: Individual con título.
  • Mecanización: Sí.

El costo total para el establecimiento de la práctica por hectárea es de 1 020 USD e incluye arriendo de maquinaria, semillas, fertilizante y la aplicación de cal.

2. Impactos y resultados

Los beneficios de esta práctica en la zona han sido los siguientes:

2.1 Impactos ecológicos

  • Mejora de la cobertura del suelo.
  • Aumento de la biomasa sobre el suelo.
  • Mejora el ciclo y recarga de nutrientes.
  • Mejora de la resiliencia del sistema agroecológico ante la erosión y desastres naturales.

2.2 Impactos socioeconómicos

  • Incremento de la cantidad y calidad del forraje.
  • Mejora la productividad de los animales.
  • Incremento de la resiliencia del modo de vida de los agricultores ante fenómenos adversos.

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, húmedo/seco.
  • Templado, seco.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Zero or minimum tillage in rice-wheat system: ID 7715.
  • Mejora de la producción agrícola y optimización del uso del agua mediante la tecnificación del riego: ID 8032.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Tecnología de ahorro de trabajo

Debido a la práctica de cero labranza que consiste en el establecimiento de un cultivo sin preparar el suelo, se ahorra una labranza intensiva.

5.2 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta práctica de cero labranza contribuye no solo a la mejora ecológica sino también socioeconómica, así como una mayor productividad, resiliencia, fortalecimiento de la compactación del suelo y aumento de la cobertura del suelo.

entries.tittle: Mejora de la Producción Agrícola y Optimización del Uso del Agua Mediante la Tecnificación del Riego en Ecuador
entries.summary: Una forma de garantizar la producción de alimentos limpios y suficientes para las familias agrícolas es optimizar el uso del agua, en ese sentido, la modernización del riego es una opción atractiva. Para lograr un mejor uso del agua se debe optimizar su captación y conducción mejorando la infraestructura de almacenamiento y distribución. Estas medidas permiten hacer un uso más eficiente del recurso y reducir las pérdidas de suelo por erosión hídrica. Dado que esta medida tiene un fuerte componente técnico, se requiere una alta inversión y una adaptación a una nueva cultura del riego.
entries.description:
Descripción

El Proyecto de Modernización del Riego a Pequeña Escala, ejecutado por la FAO en convenio con el Gobierno Provincial del Carchi (Ecuador), propone el presente plan, cuyo objetivo es mejorar la producción agrícola y optimizar el uso del agua, con la tecnificación del riego en la comunidad de San Pablo de la Cangahua, para garantizar la producción de alimentos limpios y suficientes para las familias del sector.

Las medidas que se implementaron permitieron:

  • mejorar la captación y conducción del agua en un tramo de 16 km;
  • mejorar la infraestructura de almacenamiento de agua;
  • tecnificar el sistema de distribución del riego parcelario;
  • y mejorar la tecnología de cultivos.

Para lograr el objetivo se implementó un sistema de riego presurizado mediante la aplicación de riego por aspersión y riego por goteo, que permitió alcanzar una mayor eficiencia en el uso y aplicación del agua a los cultivos, asegurando su desarrollo y garantizando la producción, junto con otros beneficios antes mencionados.

Figura 1. Construcción de reservorio con capacidad de 800 m3

©FAO/TECA

1. Descripción del ambiente donde la estrategia fue aplicada

Las siguientes características describen el ambiente natural y social donde se implementó la práctica. Las condiciones ambientales no son determinantes o excluyentes para su éxito, pero deben tenerse en cuenta al implementarla o adaptarla a las condiciones naturales de la zona donde se quiera replicar.

1.1 Ambiente natural

  • Altitud: 500 a 1 000 m.s.na.m.
  • Pendiente: Poco inclinada.
  • Forma del terreno: Parte baja de la ladera.
  • Profundidad del suelo: 20 a 50 cm.
  • Clima: Subtropical.
  • Textura del suelo: Franco.
  • Fertilidad del suelo: Baja.
  • Drenaje del suelo/infiltración: Bajo.

1.2 Ambiente social

  • Tipo del usuario tierra: Familiar/pequeño escala.
  • Tenencia de la tierra: Individual con y sin título.
  • Mecanización: Sí.

El costo total estimado para el establecimiento del proyecto descrito es de 120 000 USD. Es un proyecto bastante grande e incluye costos por la preparación del terreno, implementación en la infraestructura de conducción principal, implementación en la infraestructura de riego por goteo e infraestructura de almacenamiento. El mantenimiento por año se estima en 1 100 USD aproximadamente.

2. Impactos y resultados

Los beneficios de esta práctica en la zona han sido los siguientes:

2.1 Impactos ecológicos

  • Aumentó la cantidad de agua disponible para cultivos.
  • Mejoró la recolección de agua.

2.2 Impactos socioeconómicos

  • Aumentó la diversificación de los productos agrícolas.
  • Se incrementó el área de producción (nuevas tierras útiles).
Figura 2. Evaluación de la producción de cebolla de bulbo bajo sistema de riego por goteo

©FAO/TECA

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Trópicos, cálido.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Construcción de lagunas, cisternas y pozos para el abastecimiento seguro de agua: ID 8349.
  • Prácticas de conservación del suelo y el agua para la reducción de la erosión del suelo y reforzar: ID 8689.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta práctica de mejorar la producción agrícola y optimizar el uso del agua contribuye no sólo a la mejora ecológica sino también socioeconómica a través del uso eficiente de los recursos, así como una mayor productividad, sostenibilidad y seguridad alimentaria.
