entries.tittle: Beekeeping in Asia: choosing the equipment
entries.summary:
A period of over a century of widespread movable-frame beekeeping with the common honeybee Apis mellifera in many parts of the world has resulted in the development and marketing of virtually all types and sizes of beekeeping equipment. Many innovations in design and the use of different materials enable beekeepers to select their equipment according to their own needs and preferences, but certain standard appliances and items of equipment are required in almost any type of beekeeping operation.

It is of great importance that the hive equipment used in any apiary be of standard size under the Anglo American or metric system. This is not only because standardization of equipment offers beekeepers operating convenience and high resale value, but also because most of the supplies and appliances available commercially are tailored to fit standard size designs.
entries.description:
Description

1. Hive bodies and supers

  • Properly speaking, the expression “hive body” refers to the box containing brood frames, whereas a “super” is a box placed above the hive body to accommodate frames containing combs of honey.
    • The standard hive body is 9.5 ft (238 mm to 240 mm) high.
    • Many beekeepers often use hive bodies as full-depth supers, but the height of supers can vary from full-depth (standard hive body) through “honey supers” (three-quarter depth = 7.5 ft or 185 mm) to “section supers” (half depth = 4.75 ft or 133 mm).
  • Since the dimensions of the Langstroth hive were originally established in the Anglo‑American system, whereas a number of countries in Asia currently use the metric system, the sizes of equipment discussed in this chapter are presented in both systems.
  • It should be borne in mind, however, that the metric-system figures are not derived directly from the Anglo-American, but refer to similar (but not identical) measurements in general use in countries where the metric system has been adopted.
    • The width and length of standard ten‑frame hive bodies and supers are 16.25 ft x 19.314 ft (405 mm x 505 mm) outer measurements; and
    • 14.75 ft x 18.5 ft (365 mm x 465 mm) inner measurements.
    • Running along the upper inner rim of the width of the box, a recess of 3/8” x 5/8” (10 mm x 13 mm), known as the “rabbet” or “rebate”, serves to hold the top-bars of the free‑hanging frames inside.
  • Wood is the material most generally preferred for hive construction, offering durability, flexibility and convenience, as well as improving the colony’s efficiency in regulating hive interior temperature and humidity.
  • Bodies and supers painted externally will last longer than those without paint.
    • White is the colour generally preferred for its action in radiating direct heat from the sun.
  • Wooden hive bodies and supers should be built to be as strong as possible.
    • The weakest points in the hive’s architecture are the corners of the boxes.
  • There are three basic ways of making corner joints (box corner, special box corner and dove-tail joints). See Figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1. Langstroth hive bodies, showing different corner constructions and details of the rabbet (Redrawn from Miller, 1976)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Major types of corner joints for the construction of hive bodies and supers Upper left: Box corner Upper right: Special box corner Below: Dove-tail loins

©FAO/TECA

2. Hive cover

  • The outer cover is essentially the roof of the hive.
    • It should be long-lasting and provide good insulation for the bees.
    • Most beekeepers prefer telescoping covers fitted with sheet metal or aluminium (see Figure 3).
  • In some areas, an inner lid or cover is used in addition to the outer cover.
  • In severe weather, it assists in insulating the interior of the hive.
  • Inner covers are commonly made of boards, plywood or masonite in a wooden frame.
Figure 3. Telescoping hive cover

©FAO/TECA

3. Bottom board

  • The bottom board that is the floor of the hive, is built to fit the hive body.
    • In order to provide a landing board for the bees, the length is extended past the front of the hive body for about 2 inches (50 mm), so that the total length of the bottom board is 22 inches (555 mm to 560 mm).
  • The board consists of a flat floor mounted on side-rails.
  • An entrance reducer is generally used at the front of the hive to permit alteration of the size of the hive entrance. See Figure 4.
Figure 4. Bottom board

©FAO/TECA

4. Frames

  • The concept of movable frames in box hives is the noblest innovation in beekeeping.
  • The basic function of such frames is to hold individual combs firmly in place so that the entire comb can be moved while remaining intact.

4.1 Details of frame construction

  • The left side contains the top-bar end and the right side the bottom-bar and frame end.
  • A frame consists basically of a top-bar, two end-bars and a bottom-bar, nailed together.
  • Since the frames must fit the supers, and these are of uniform length, the top‑bars of all frames must be:
    • 19 inches (482 mm) long; 
    • 0.75 inches (16 mm) thick; and
    • 1.06 inches (25 mm) wide.
  • The height of the end-bar reflects the depth of the super and should measure 9.125 inches (230 mm), by 7.25 inches (175 mm) by 4.5 inches (125 mm) for full-depth, three-quarter depth and half-depth respectively.
  • End‑bars are 1.375 inches (33 mm) wide and 0.375 inches (10 mm) thick.
  • The bottom-bar is 17.625 inches (450 mm) long, 0.75 inches (25 mm) wide and 0.375 inches (10 mm) thick.
  • When these elements are assembled, both ends of the top-bar protrude so that the frame can rest on the rabbet. See Figure 5.
Figure 5. Full-depth (9.125 inches = 230 mm) end-bars

©FAO/TECA

5. Comb foundation

  • The invention of a comb foundation for use with movable frames marks another milestone in the history of beekeeping.
    • A comb foundation is a thin sheet of beeswax stamped with a pattern of hexagons of a size equal to the base of natural brood cells.
    • Providing beeswax foundation accelerates comb construction, thus making better honey harvests possible. 
    • t also leads the bees to construct a comb whose cells are of a uniform size.
  • The overall dimensions of comb foundations available on the market are calculated to fit standard frame sizes:
    • full-depth
    • three-quarter depth; and
    • half-depth.
  • While foundation types vary, the medium-brood plain foundation offers reasonably good performance under normal conditions.
  • As a rule, the foundation is fixed to the frames by being mounted on four fine but strong wires, threaded through holes in the end‑bars and stretched tight.
    • A spur embedder or an electrical heating device is used to embed the wires into the comb foundation.
  • Making a comb foundation is a complicated task, requiring not only skill and experience but also a costly foundation mill, preferably of the type composed of two precision‑engraved rollers, used by manufacturers.
    • While a few large-scale beekeeping operators and cooperatives may be in a position to own such a mill, most beekeepers find it more convenient to buy their foundation ready-made.

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • temperate, cool.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Beekeeping in Asia: obtaining colonies with Apis Cerana: ID 4004.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: examining a bee colony: ID 4009.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: keeping Apis Cerana in box hives: ID 4003.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: honey flow: ID 4011.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: queen rearing (Apis Mellifera): ID 4012.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: site selection for beehives: ID 7327.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: traditional and modern beehives and beekeeping equipment: ID 7273.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

Measurement standardization of beekeeping equipment provides more operating convenience.

8.2 Pro-poor technology

This practice enables a higher resale value since most of the supplies and appliances available commercially are tailored to fit standard size designs. It also allows for improved function of equipment. Such improved management also improves bee colony health, providing beekeepers with additional income and a source of food through improved quality of products such as honey.

entries.tittle: Technique of Cutting Meat Pieces for Drying
entries.summary:
Meat drying is a complex process with many important steps. It involves animal slaughtering, carcass trimming, raw material selection, meat cutting, pieces pre-treatment, meat drying and proper arrangement of drying facilities. In addition, weather conditions must also be considered to avoid quality problems or production losses. 
The following technology describes proper meat cutting techniques for drying. This technology is part of FAO's publication: Manual on simple methods of meat preservation, 1990, Rome, which is mainly intended to disseminate information on traditional methods of meat preservation and addresses aspects of hygienic slaughtering under rural conditions in Africa.
entries.description:
Description

Different techniques can be followed to cut meat muscles. First the anatomical cuts are separated from the carcass and can be big individual muscles or smaller muscles group. Then the muscles are cut into thin strips. This operation is crucial for appearance and quality of the final product. All meat strips to be dried in the same batch must be cut to an identical shape and long enough (≥ 20 cm and ≤ 70 cm).

Figure 1. Cutting meat strips from a suspended muscle

©FAO/TECA

1. Cutting techniques

There are two ways of cutting muscles or smaller muscle groups into strips:

  • cutting the muscle in hanging position (see Figure 1);
  • cutting the meat after placing it on an appropriate clean chopping board (see Figure 2).

In both cases:

  • muscles must be split precisely along the muscle fibres;
  • strips must be cut as uniformly and as smoothly as possible; and
  • strip diameter must remain the same throughout the length.
Figure 2. Cutting meat strips from the muscle on a chopping board

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Draining the brine from the meat strips after soaking using a plastic sieve

©FAO/TECA

1.1 Meat strips length and thickness

  • The length of the strips may differ, though they should be:
    • longer than 20 cm, as shorter strips require considerably more time for hooking; and
    • shorter than 70 cm, as longer strips may break under their weight.
  • Beef muscles suitable for drying are usually no longer than 50 cm (except the sirloin strip attached to the spinal column).
  • However, strips longer than 50 cm can be produced by cutting the muscle along the fibre in one direction, without cutting through the end of the muscle (see Figure 4).
    • Long strips can be obtained by using this technique, but their length should not exceed 70 cm for stability reasons.
  • The thickness of the strips determines the duration of the drying process.
    • To avoid insufficient or over dried pieces it is essential to batch together all strips of the same thickness because thick strips take longer to dry than thin ones.
Figure 4. Special cutting technique to obtain long meat strips

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Suspended anatomical cut from the hindquarters (“silverside”) (A) and splitting into individual muscles (B) which result in (C)

©FAO/TECA

  • In a dry climate two basic shapes of meat pieces proved to be the most suitable for natural drying, those are:
    • rectangular strips with a cross-section of 1 cm x 1 cm; and
    • flat or leaf-shaped pieces with cross-sections of max. 0.5 cm x 3 cm, 4 cm or 5 cm (approx.).

2. Recommended treatment before drying

  • Because meat is always consumed slightly salted, the raw material may be pre-salted before drying either with dry salt or in a solution.
  • This procedure contributes to:
    • a tastier product; and
    • a more technological and hygienic approach.
  • The preferred pre-treatment method before drying for meat strips or flat pieces is by dipping the pieces in a 14 percent salt solution.

2.1 Salting

  • Materials
    • Pure common edible salt (dry or dissolved in water)
    • water.
  • Preparation of solution
    • Dissolve the necessary amount of salt in water and stir thoroughly.
    • The quantity of salt and volume of water (expressed in litres) to obtain the recommended 14 percent concentration of solution is indicated below.
  • The salting stages
    • Dipping meat strips into the salt solution, soaking for about five minutes and then draining.
    • Draining by placing the strips in a plastic sieve to allow the brine to drip in a bucket for collection and re-use (Figure 3).

2.2 Contamination

  • To avoid contamination and ensure a long shelf-life of dried product, the handling of meat strips before drying should be carried out in strictly:
    • clean conditions; and
    • hygienic conditions.
  • If accidental contamination occurs the following additional precautions and processes can reduce contamination:
    • rinsing the contaminated pieces in clean water; and
    • soaking the contaminated pieces of meat separately in salt solution in special buckets.
  • However, the original quality of contaminated pieces cannot be reinstated and must:
    • be dried separately;
    • stored only for a short period; and
    • be used as soon as possible in meal preparations.

2.2 Advantages of salting

  • Meat salting process (dipping the meat in salt solution) has several advantages.
    • Inhibit microbiological growth on meat surfaces.
      • Salting must be carried out within five hours after slaughter, otherwise substantial microbiological growth occurs which cannot be reduced by salt treatment.
    • Protect meat against insects.
      • The freshly cut meat surfaces attract various insects, in particular domestic flies, which feed on the moisture excreted from muscle fibres.
      • These insects cause considerable contamination of the meat and may also deposit their eggs in it.
      • The salt concentration on the meat surfaces keeps insects away and meat is no longer attractive to insects.
    • Preserve meat surfaces by keeping them dry.
      • The salt crystals formed on the surface of the meat during drying are hygroscopic and absorb part of the water excreted by the meat.
      • Dry meat surfaces inhibit the growth of bacteria and moulds which is one reason for the preservability of pre-salted and dried meat.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Simple methods of meat preservation: meat dryers: ID 4072.
  • Simple techniques for dried meat production: methods of suspending meat: ID 4071.
  • Preservation of fish and meat: ID 6961.
  • Dried meat techniques: examples from different regions: ID 4075.
  • Simple techniques for production of dried meat: ID 4069.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for preserving meat which is market popular and can be consumed over a longer period.

5.2 Pro-poor technology 

Meat can be preserved using more advanced techniques, this offers a new marketing opportunity and reduces production losses.

entries.tittle: Preservation of fruits: Shelf-stable high moisture peach halves
entries.summary: Fruits and vegetables are nutritious, valuable foods full of flavour. Therefore, fruits and vegetables represent an important and in many case an under-appreciated resource, which could benefit from better utilization and exploitation in the rural communities. However, in low-income countries, poor care and handling of these crops frequently result in loss of quality, especially when not consumed immediately. The technique for shelf-stable high moisture content peach halves permits the use of the product for up to four months after harvesting. It can be used as-is, or as bulk for off-season processing, in bakery goods, confectionery and dairy products.
entries.description:
Description

1. Steps for shelf-stable high moisture peach halves​

1.1 Step one

After weighing, place a small quantity, one layer of fruit halves on a tray made of a stainless steel screen, Figure 1. Next, the tray is placed in a steam bath for two minutes. This operation is called "blanching" and deactivates compounds that cause the browning of the fruit and kills bacteria.

To blanch the fruit in steam, you need:

  • a heat source (or fire);
  • a stainless steel saucepan or other recipients with a lid; and
  • a stainless steel tray, perforated or made with a screen, to support the fruit.

Pour a little water in the container, put the lid on, heat and let the water boil vigorously to eliminate the air and generate enough steam before introducing the tray with the fruit. Remove the lid quickly, put the tray into the container and quickly put the lid on. Let the fruit stand for two minutes. Take care that the bottom of the tray does not touch the boiling water.

Figure 1. Layer of peach halves on a tray stainless steel

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two

After two minutes, the peach halves are taken out of the steam bath and plunged quickly into cold water for a few minutes. It is very important to cool the halves. Heating produces a softening of the fruit and cooling in water lessens the damage.

Figure 2. Peach halves cooled in water

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Step three

The peach halves are removed from the cooling water and drained using a sieve or a colander. Then, they are put into a clean container, Figure 3.

Figure 3. Peach halves are put into a clean container

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Step four

Next, the syrup is prepared with water, sugar and some additives, Figure 4. The amount of water and additives must be determined according to the weight of fruit. The following are the quantities to prepare 1 kg of peach halves:

  • 0.85 litre tap water
  • 852 g sucrose or glucose (you can measure the water and the sugar with a measuring jug)
  • 2.7 g potassium sorbate (two level teaspoons)
  • 34 g citric acid (four-level tablespoons)
  • 0.41 g sodium bisulphite (a third level coffee-spoon).
Figure 4. Additives

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Step five

First, weigh and blend all the solid additives and the sugar. After, additives and sugar are gradually mixed into the water, Figure 5. Stir the liquid mixture with a wooden or plastic stick or spoon while adding the additives and until all the solids are dissolved and the liquid is transparent. For sugar, you can use sucrose or glucose, but remember, glucose gives the fruit a less sweet taste.

Figure 5. Additives mixing

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Step six

Pour the syrup onto the peach halves. Mix the fruit and syrup with a wooden or plastic stick or spoon.

1.7 Step seven

Remember to place the lid on the bucket to prevent contamination of the fruit by dust, or germs. The fruit halves must be immersed in the syrup for seven days. During this time, stir the tank of fruit and syrup gently at least twice a day and keep the container in a dark cool place. Seven days later, the peaches are ready to be packaged.

2. The process

2.1 Step one

The fruit pieces are drained and packed into a glass or high-density polyethylene plastic jars, fitting snugly against each other. Some syrup is then added to cover the peach halves.

2.2 Step two

The fruit can also be packed in bulk into plastic buckets or tanks with a lid.

2.3 Step three

Close the containers up and stored them in a cool place and in the dark to avoid colour changes; fruit pigments are very sensitive to the light.

2.4 Step four

You can store these peaches at room temperature; you don't need anything more to preserve them! That's why they are considered "shelf-stable". These shelf-stable peach halves are of good quality used for up to four months. The product may be safe after this date but may not be at peak quality.

2.5 Step five

A label must be stuck on each package indicating the name and the form of the fruit product (peach halves), the quantity by weight, the ingredients (peach halves, sugar, citric acid, potassium sorbate, sodium bisulphite), the manufacture date, the "use by" date and the name and address of the manufacturer. These peaches can be used as such, or as bulk for off-season processing, in bakery goods, confectionery, and dairy products, or for prepare jams and jellies. Fruit pieces can be utilized for fruit salads, barbecue sauces, pizza, fruit drink formulates, fruit cakes or other preparations.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies 

  • Preservation of strawberries: ID 3941.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable strawberry puree: ID 3943.
  • Preservation of fruits: intermediate moisture whole strawberries: ID 3944.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable high moisture strawberries: ID 3942.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable pineapple of high moisture: ID 3946.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable high moisture pineapple- dry infusion: ID 3947.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable pineapple puree: ID 3948.
  • Preservation of fruits: intermediate moisture pineapples: ID 3949.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable peach puree: ID 3952.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable peach halves (dry infusion): ID 3953.
  • Preservation of fruits: intermediate moisture peaches: ID 3954.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

5.2 Pro-poor technology

entries.tittle: Rapid composting methods: use of cellulolytic cultures
entries.summary: The potential of composting to turn on-farm waste materials into a farm resource makes it an attractive proposition. Composting offers several benefits such as enhanced soil fertility and soil health, thereby increased agricultural productivity, improved soil biodiversity, reduced ecological risks and creating a better environment. While traditional composting procedures take as long as four to eight months to produce finished compost, rapid composting methods offer possibilities for reducing the processing period up to three weeks.
entries.description:
Description

1. Use of cellulolytic cultures: IBS rapid composting technology

1.1 IBS rapid composting

  • IBS rapid composting technology involves inoculating the plant substrates used for composting with cultures of Trichoderma harzianum, a cellulose decomposer fungus.
  • The fungus, grown in a medium of sawdust mixed with the leaves of ipil ipil (Leucaena leucocephala), a leguminous tree, is termed as Compost Fungus Activator (CFA).
  • The technology is a development of the windrow type of composting.
  • The composting time, using this procedure, ranges from 21 to 45 days, depending on the plant substrates used.
  • The procedure consists of two parts: the production of the compost fungus activator, and the composting process.

1.1.1 Preparation of substrates

  • Substrates such as rice straw, weeds and grasses should be chopped.
  • Chopping helps speed up decomposition by increasing the surface area available for microbial action, and providing better aeration.
  • If large quantities of substrates are to be used (e.g. several tons), a forage cutter/chopper is needed.
  • Chopping can be dispensed with if the compost is not needed in the near future.

1.1.2 Adjustment of moisture content

  • Substrates should be moistened with water.
  • Plant substrates can be soaked overnight in a pond, which cuts down on the need for water.
  • If a large volume of substrates are to be composted, a sprinkler is more convenient.

1.1.3 The compost mixture

  • Carbonaceous substrates should be mixed with nitrogenous ones at a ratio of 4:1 or less, but never lower than 1:1 (on a dry weight basis).
  • Possible combinations.
    • Three parts rice straw - one part ipil-ipil.
    • Four parts rice straw - one part chicken manure.
    • Four parts grasses - one part legume materials and one part manure.
    • Four parts grasses - one part Chromolaena odorata or Mikania cordata and one part animal manure.

1.1.4 Composting procedure

  • The substrates should be piled loosely in a compost pen to provide better aeration within the heap.
  • The material should not be too compact and no heavy weights should be put on top.
  • Compost heaps should be located in shady areas such as under big trees.
  • The platform should be raised about 30 cm from the ground, to provide adequate aeration at the bottom.
  • Alternatively, aeration can be provided by placing perforated bamboo trunks horizontally and vertically at regular intervals, to carry air through the compost heap.
  • The compost activator, consisting of a cellulolytic fungus, is broadcast onto the substrates during piling.
    • The amount of activator used is usually 1 percent of the total weight of the substrates.
    • About 1 kg compost activator per 100 kg substrate.
  • Decomposition is faster if the activator is mixed thoroughly with the substrate.
  • A greater amount of activator can be used if faster decomposition is desired.
  • The heap should be covered over completely.
  • This maintains the heat of decomposition, and minimizes water evaporation and ammonia volatilization.
  • White plastic sheets, or plastic sacks with their seams opened and sewn together, can serve as a cover.
  • The compost heap usually heats up in 24 to 48 hours.
  • Heat should be maintained at 50°C or higher, and the heap should be turned over every five to seven days for the first two weeks, and thereafter once every two weeks.
    • After the first week, the volume of the pile should be reduced by one-third.
    • After two weeks, the volume of the pile should be reduced to one half the original.
  • The mature compost should be removed from the pen, and dried in the sun for two days.
  • It should then be put into sacks and stored in a shaded area.
  • Decomposition will continue until the substrate is finely fragmented, so that the finished product has a powdery texture.
  • Then, once decomposition is complete, the compost should be sundried again until the moisture content is at 10 to 20 percent.
  • If mature compost is needed at once, it should be sun-dried for one day, as soon as its temperature drops to 30°C.
  • Drying removes excess moisture, and makes the compost much easier to handle.
  • Although the compost still retain some fibres, it can be applied immediately as fertilizer.

1.2 IBS rapid commercial compost production

  • In the large-scale commercial production of compost, key operations need to be mechanized, other steps remaining the same.
    • Chopping of substrates.
    • Mixing/turning.
      • When there are several tons of substrate, a pay loader will make mixing of substrates or turning of heaps much easier.
    • A hammer mill should be used to break up big lumps of mature compost before drying.
    • During rainy months, it is more economical to dry compost mechanically than try to sun dry it.

1.3 IBS rapid rice straw composting

  • At harvest time, rice straw is heaped on to one side of the paddy field.
  • It saves labour to have one compost pile for each paddy field instead of one central pile.
  • Various steps need to be followed.
    • Rice straw is soaked overnight in water or in the rain until saturated.
    • A simple platform is made in the middle of the field.
    • A layer of saturated rice straw 10 to 15 cm thick is loosely piled on the platform.
    • On top of the layer, one or two handfuls of the activator is broadcast (25 kg per ha).
    • Straw is alternately layered with the activator until all the straw has been used.
    • Manure and nitrogenous plants are put on top of the straw layers.
      • The nitrogen substrate is 15 to 25 percent of total composition.
    • The compost is covered (with plastic, banana leaves, or coconut fronds) and heats up within 25 hours.
    • The compost must be moistened frequently to compensate for evaporation.
    • The compost is left unturned and matures within one month.
      • It is ready for use when the pile has cooled and is 30 percent of its original size.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • On-farm composting methods: traditional methods (anaerobic decomposition): ID 4293.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of Effective Micro-organisms (EM): ID 4297.
  • On-farm composting methods: large scale passive aeration: ID 4295.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of forced aeration: ID 4299.
  • Rapid composting methods: vermicomposting: ID 4301.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology enhances soil fertility, soil health, and soil biodiversity, thereby reducing ecological risks and creating a better environment.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology increases agricultural productivity, leading to additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: On-farm composting methods: large scale passive aeration
entries.summary: Growing concerns relating to land degradation, threats to eco-systems from over and inappropriate use of inorganic fertilizers, atmospheric pollution, soil health, soil biodiversity and sanitation have rekindled the global interest in organic recycling practices, like composting. The potential of composting to turn on-farm waste materials into a farm resource makes it an attractive proposition. Composting offers several benefits such as enhanced soil fertility and soil health, thereby increasing agricultural productivity, improving soil biodiversity, reducing ecological risks and providing a better environment. The following technology is part from FAO's publication on-farm composting.
entries.description:
Description

1. Large scale passive aeration

1.1 Windrow composting

1.1.1 Turned windrows

  • Windrow composting consists of placing the mixture of raw materials in long narrow piles or windrows, which are agitated or turned on a regular basis.
    • The turning operation mixes the composting materials and enhances passive aeration.
    • Typically the windrows are initially from 3 feet high for dense materials like manures to 12 feet high for fluffy materials like leaves.
    • The width varies from 10 to 20 feet.
    • The equipment used for turning determines the size, shape, and spacing of the windrows.
    • Bucket loaders with a long reach can build high windrows.
    • Turning machines produce low, wide windrows.
  • Windrows aerate primarily by natural or passive air movement (convection and gaseous diffusion).
    • The rate of air exchange depends on the porosity of the windrow.
    • Therefore, the size of a windrow that can be effectively aerated is determined by its porosity.
    • A light fluffy windrow of leaves can be much larger than a wet dense windrow containing manure.
    • If the windrow is too large, anaerobic zones occur near its centre, which release odours when the windrow is turned.
    • On the other hand, small windrows lose heat quickly and may not achieve temperatures high enough to evaporate moisture and kill pathogens and weed seeds.
  • For small to moderate scale operations, turning can be accomplished with a front-end loader or a bucket loader on a tractor.
    • The loader simply lifts the materials from the windrow and spills them down again, mixing the materials and reforming the mixture into a loose windrow.
    • The loader can exchange material from the bottom of the windrow with material on the top by forming a new windrow next to the old one.
    • This needs to be done without driving onto the windrow in order to minimize compaction.
    • Windrows turned with a bucket loader are often constructed in closely spaced pairs and then combined after the windrows shrink in size.
    • If additional mixing of the materials is desired, a loader can also be used in combination with a manure spreader.
  • A number of specialized machines have been developed for turning windrows.
    • These machines greatly reduce the time and labour involved, mix the materials thoroughly, and produce a more uniform compost.
    • Some of these machines are designed to attach to farm tractors or front-end loaders.
    • Others are self-propelled.
    • A few machines also have the capability of loading trucks or wagons from the windrow.
  • It is very important to maintain a schedule of turning.
    • The frequency of turning depends on the rate of decomposition, the moisture content and porosity of the materials, and the desired composting time.
    • Because the decomposition rate is greatest at the start of the process, the frequency of turning decreases as the windrow ages.
    • Easily degradable or high nitrogen mixes may require daily turnings at the start of the process.
    • As the process continues, the turning frequency can be reduced to a single turning per week.
  • By the end of the first week of composting, the windrow height diminishes appreciably and by the end of the second week it may be as low as 2 feet.
    • It may be prudent to combine two windrows at this stage and continue the turning schedule as before.
    • Consolidation of windrows is a good wintertime practice to retain the heat generated during composting.
    • This is one of the advantages of windrow composting.
    • It is a versatile system that can be adjusted to different conditions caused by seasonal changes.
  • With the windrow method, the active composting stage generally lasts three to nine weeks, depending upon the nature of the materials and the frequency of turning.
    • Eight weeks is a common period for manure composting operations.
    • If three weeks is the goal, the windrow requires turning once or twice per day during the first week and every three to five days thereafter.

1.1.2 Passively aerated windrows

  • The method of the passively aerated windrow system eliminates the need for turning by supplying air to the composting materials through perforated pipes embedded in each windrow.
    • The pipe ends are open. Air flows into the pipes and through the windrow because of the chimney effect created as the hot gases rise upward out of the windrow.
  • The windrows should be 3 to 4 feet high, built on top of a base of straw, peat moss, or finished compost to absorb moisture and insulate the windrow.
    • The covering layer of peat or compost also insulates the windrow; discourages flies; and helps to retain moisture, odour, and ammonia.
    • The plastic pipe is similar to that used for septic system leach fields with two rows of half-inch diameter holes drilled in the pipe.
    • In many aerated pile applications, the pipe holes are oriented downward to minimize plugging and allow condensation to drain.
    • However, some researchers recommend that the holes face upwards.
    • Windrows are generally formed by the procedures described for the aerated static pile method.
    • Because the raw materials are not turned after the windrows are formed, they must be thoroughly mixed before they are placed in the windrow.
    • Avoid compacting the mix of materials while constructing the windrow.
    • Aeration pipes are placed on top of the peat/compost base.
    • When the composting period is completed, the pipes are simply pulled out, and the base material is mixed with the compost.
  • This method of composting has been studied and used in Canada for composting seafood wastes with peat moss, manure slurries with peat moss, and solid manure with straw or wood shavings.
    • Manure from dairy, beef, swine, and sheep operations has been used.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • On-farm composting methods: traditional methods (anaerobic decomposition): ID 4293.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of effective micro-organisms (EM): ID 4297.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of cellulolytic cultures: ID 4298.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of forced aeration: ID 4299.
  • Rapid composting methods: vermicomposting: ID 4301.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently uses on-farm waste materials, transforming them into a farm resource. This has beneficial consequences for soil health, reduces ecological risks and provides a better environment. 

4.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology increases agricultural productivity, thereby providing additional revenue and sources of food.

entries.tittle: Rapid composting methods: vermicomposting
entries.summary: The potential of composting to turn on-farm waste materials into a farm resource makes it an attractive proposition. Composting offers several benefits such as enhanced soil fertility and soil health, thereby increasing agricultural productivity, improving soil biodiversity, reducing ecological risks and creating a better environment. While traditional composting procedures take as long as four to eight months to produce finished compost, rapid composting methods offer possibilities for reducing the processing period up to three weeks.
entries.description:
Description

1. Use of worms: vermicomposting

  • The term "vermicomposting" had recently been coined to mean the use of earthworms for composting organic residues.
  • Earthworms can consume practically all kinds of organic matter and they can eat their own body weight per day.
    • For example, one kilogram of worms can consume one kilogram of residues every day.
    • The excreta or castings of the worms are rich in nitrate, available forms of phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium.
  • The passage of soil through earthworms promotes bacterial and actinomycetes growth.
    • Actinomycetes thrive well in the presence of worms and their content in worm casts is over six times more than in the original soil.

2. Kinds of worms

  • A moist compost heap of 2.4 m by 1.2 m and 0.6 m high can support a population of more than 50 000 worms.
  • The introduction of worms into a compost heap has been found to mix the materials, aerate the heap and hasten decomposition.
  • Turning the heaps is not necessary if earthworms are present to do the mixing and aeration.
  • The ideal environment for the worms is a shallow pit and the right sort of worms are necessary.
  • Lumbricus rubellus (the red worm) and Eisenia foetida are thermo-tolerant and so particularly useful.
  • Field worms Allolobophora caliginosa and night crawlers (Lumbricus terrestris) will attack organic matter from below.
    • The latter do not thrive during active composting, being killed more easily than the others at high temperature.
  • European Night Crawlers (Dendrabaena veneta or Eisenia hortensis) are commercially produced as well and have been successfully used in most climates.
    • This night crawler grows to about 4 inches and up to about 8 inches.
  • The African Night crawler (Eudrilus eugeniae), is a large, tropical worm species.
    • It does tolerate heats a bit higher than does E. foetida, provided there is ample humidity, but has a narrow temperature tolerance range
    • . However, it cannot survive at temperatures below 45°F.

3. Vermicomposting in the Philippines

  • The worms used are Lumbricus rubellus and/or Perionyx excavator.
  • The worms are reared and multiplied from a commercially-obtained breeder stock in shallow wooden boxes stored in a shed.
    • The boxes are approximately 45 cm x 60 cm x 20 cm and have drainage holes.
    • They are stored on shelves in rows and tiers.
    • A bedding material is compounded from miscellaneous organic residues such as sawdust, cereal straw, rice husks, bagasse, cardboard and so on, and is moistened well with water.
    • The wet mixture is stored for about one month, being covered with a damp sack to minimize evaporation, and is thoroughly mixed several times.
    • When fermentation is complete, chicken manure and green matter such as ipil ipil leaves or water hyacinth is added.
  • The material is placed in the boxes and should be sufficiently loose for the worms to burrow and should be able to retain moisture.
  • The proportions of the different materials will vary according to the nature of the material but a final protein content of about 15 percent should be aimed at.
  • A pH value as near neutral as possible is necessary and the boxes should be kept at temperatures between 20°C and 27°C.
    • At higher temperatures, the worms will aestivate and, at lower temperatures, they hibernate.
  • In spite of their being able to eat the bedding material, the worms at this stage are fed regularly.
    • For every kilogram of worms a kilogram of feed is given every 24 hours.
  • For each 0.1 m2 of surface area, 100 g of breeder worms are added to the boxes.
  • The feedstuffs used are again various and include chicken manure, ipil ipil, vegetable wastes and so on.
    • At one farm, water hyacinth is grown specifically and used fresh (chopped up) as the sole source of feed.
  • Some form of protection against predators is necessary.
    • Predators can include birds, ants, leeches, rats, frogs and centipedes.

4. Composting procedure

  • A series of pits (the number depending on available space) are dug approximately 3 m x 4 m x 1 m deep, with sloping sides.
  • Bamboo poles are laid in a parallel row on the pit floor and covered with a lattice of wood strips.
    • This provides the necessary drainage as the worms cannot survive in a waterlogged environment.
  • The pit is then lined with a suitable material to keep the worms from escaping into the surrounding soil and yet permit drainage of excess water.
    • Although, with the abundant feed provided in the compost heap, this may not happen.
  • At the farm under consideration, old animal feedstuff sacks were used.
  • The pit can now be filled with rural organic residues such as straw and other crop residues, animal manure, green weeds, leaves and so on.
  • The filled pit is covered loosely with soil and kept moist for a week or so.
  • During this period, another pit can be filled as necessary.
  • One or two spots on the heap are then well watered and worms from the breeding boxes are place on top.
    • The worms immediately burrow down into the damp soil.
  • To harvest the worms from the boxes, two-thirds of the box is emptied into a new box lined with banana leaf or old newspaper.
    • The original box can now be provided with fresh bedding material and those worms remaining will again multiply.
    • The worms emptied from the box are picked out by hand for adding to the heap.
  • The compost pit is left for a period of two months.
    • Ideally it should be shaded from hot sunshine and it must be kept moist.
  • Within two months, about 10 kg of castings will have been produced per kilogramme of worms.
  • The pit is then excavated to anextent of about two-thirds to three-quarters and the bulk of the worms removed by hand or by sieving.
    • This leaves sufficient worms in the pit for further composting and the pit can be refilled with fresh organic residues.
  • The compost can be sun-dried and sieved to give a very good quality material.
  • A typical analysis is:
    • organic matter 9.3 percent,
    • nitrogen 8.3 percent,
    • phosphorus 4.5 percent,
    • potassium 1.0 percent (water-soluble),
    • calcium 0.4 percent, and
    • magnesium 0.1 percent.
  • The excess worms that have been harvested from the pit can be:
    • used in other pits,
    • sold to other farmers for the same purpose,
    • used or sold for use as animal feed supplement, used or sold for use as fish food, or
    • if there is no social taboo, used in certain human food preparations.

5. Vermicomposting in Cuba

  • In Cuba, different methods are used for worm propagation and vermicomposting.

5.1 Worm troughs in a row

  • The first and most common is cement troughs, two feet wide and six feet long, much like livestock watering troughs, used to raise worms and create worm compost.
  • Because of the climate, they are watered by hand every day.
  • In these beds, the only feedstock for the worms is manure, which is aged for about one week before being added to the trough.
  • First, a layer of three to four inches of manure is placed in the empty trough, then worms are added.
  • As the worms consume the manure, more manure is layered on top, roughly every ten days, until the worm compost reaches within a couple inches of the top of the trough, about two months.
  • Then the worms are separated from the compost and transferred to another trough.

5.2 Windrows

  • The second method of vermicomposting is windrows.
  • Cow manure is piled about three feet across and three feet wide.
  • Then it is seeded with worms.
  • As the worms work their way through it, fresh manure is added to the end of the row, and the worms move forward.
  • The rows are covered with fronds or palm leaves to keep them shaded and cool.
  • Some of these rows have a drip system.
    • A hose running alongside the row with holes in it.
  • But mostly, the rows are watered by hand.
  • Some of these rows are hundreds of feet long.
  • The compost is gathered from the opposite end when the worms have moved forward.
  • Then it is bagged and sold.
  • Fresh manure, seeded with worms, begins the row and the process again.
  • Some of the windrows have bricks running along their sides, but most are simply piles of manure without sides or protection.
  • Manure is static composted for 30 days, then transferred to rows for worms to be added.
  • After 90 days, the piles reach three feet high.
  • Worm populations, they say, can double in 60 to 90 days.
  • Windrows are also used to compost rice hulls and sugar cake (cake is what is left after sugar cane is processed), but this too is mixed with animal manure.
  • Sometimes food scraps are added to worm beds.

6. Vermiculture in India

6.1 Preparing vermicompost

  • Materials:
    • breeder worms,
    • a wooden bed, and
    • organic wastes.
  • The bed should be 2.5 ft. high x 4 ft. wide x any length desired.
    • Apply worms for every part of waste.
  • Sieving and shredding
    • Decomposition can be accelerated by shredding raw materials into small pieces.
  • Blending
    • Carbonaceous substances like sawdust, paper and straw can be mixed with nitrogen rich materials such as:
      • sewage sludge,
      • biogas slurry, and
      • fish scraps.
    • This is to obtain a near optimum C/N ratio of 30:1 / 40:1.
    • A varied mixture of substances produces good quality compost, rich in major and micro nutrients.
  • Half digestion
    • The raw materials should be kept in piles and the temperature allowed to reach 50 to 55°C.
    • The piles should remain at this temperature for seven to ten days.
  • Moisture, temperature and pH
    • The optimum moisture level for maintaining aerobic conditions is 40 to 45 percent.
    • Proper moisture and aeration can be maintained by mixing fibrous with nitrogen rich materials.
    • The temperature of the piles should be within 28°C to 30°C.
    • Higher or lower temperatures will reduce the activity of micro flora and earthworms.
      • The height of the bed can help control the rise in temperature.
      • The pH of the raw material should not exceed 6.5 to 7.
  • After about a month the compost is ready.
    • It will be black, granular, lightweight and humusrich.
    • To facilitate separating the worms from the compost, stop watering two to three days before emptying the beds.
    • This will force about 80 percent of the worms to the bottom of the bed.
    • The rest of the worms can be removed by hand.
    • The vermicompost is then ready for application.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • On-farm composting methods: traditional methods (anaerobic decomposition): ID 4293.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of Effective Micro-organisms (EM): ID 4297.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of cellulolytic cultures: ID 4298.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of forced aeration: ID 4299.
  • On-farm composting methods: large scale passive aeration: ID 4295.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology, by using organic materials such as worms, enhances soil fertility, soil health, and soil biodiversity thereby reducing ecological risks and creating a better environment. 

9.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology increases agricultural productivity, leading to additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Cocoa farming: Improving production and quality of cocoa through macropropagation
entries.summary: Theobroma cacao (cocoa) is an ecologically beneficial crop in tropical agroecosystems, and can serve as a cash crop for farmers in developing countries. The growing demand for cocoa products coupled with increasing disease pressures has led to the concept that enhanced germplasm with disease tolerance and high yields could dramatically impact the lives of cocoa farmers in a positive way. Utilization of such cocoa trees will increase cocoa-farming profitability, promoting expanded and sustainable production. Methods have been developed to enhance the development of cocoa germplasm and its deployment through the combined approaches of biotechnology, applied horticulture and technology transfer. The following describes the macro propagation method which is a very low-cost method with very high multiplication rate.
entries.description:
Description

1. Rooting of orthotropic stem cuttings under greenhouse conditions

1.1 Semi-hardwood stock plant production

  • Juvenile somatic embryo plants at the sapling stage (at or near jorquette height) should be used as stock plants for generation of orthotropic cutting material.
    • Hard prune the fan branches as this promotes release of dormant axillary orthotropic meristems leading to greater orthotropic shoot production.
    • With the pots remaining upright, arch the plant over so that the main trunk is at a horizontal position and secure the shoot with a metal hook or some rope.
    • Many orthotropic shoots should proliferate in one to two weeks along the top side of the trunk length.
  • Two to three months after bending several orthotropic shoots of 0.7 to 1.0 m height will have proliferated (first 4, then 8 to 12 or more in successive harvests) and be ready for harvest.
    • Harvest shoots at their base at the main stock plant trunk.
    • New shoots are generated at or near the cut, and these may be repeatedly harvested.
  • Harvest hardened and dark green orthotropic shoots from the stock plants early in the morning while leaf water potential is still high.
    • Well-hardened and even material showing beginnings of characteristic browning of the stem works well, so use it all.
  • Prune all leaves to 100 mm.
    • Make single leaf cuttings with stems at least 40 mm long.
    • Stems should be cut such that 5 to 10 mm remains above the leaf axil (so that the axillary bud will not die as the stem is rooting), and 20 to 30 mm of the stem remains below the node.
    • If there are shorter internodes on some portions of the stem, lower leaves may be removed where the petiole narrows (approx. 10 mm.).
  • Dip the stem in the rooting hormone mixture for five seconds.
    • The quick dip method as described by Evans, 1951 has been quite successful for the propagation of single-leaf cuttings under our conditions. Rooting solutions should be prepared beforehand.
    • A 1:1 mixture of Naphthalene acetic acid (NAA) and βIndole-3-butyric acid (IBA) at a total combined concentration of 4 g per litre in 50 percent ethanol should be stored in a dark refrigerator for no more than one month.
    • Rooting mixtures should be used for only one day in the greenhouse and the remainder discarded.
    • If three-leaf cuttings are desired, use a greater concentration of NAA + IBA, 8 to 10 g per litre combined.
  • After dipping, strike the cutting in the rooting media. Any well-draining media can be used for root development.
    • 100 percent silica or sharp sand or a 1:1 mix of sand and soil may be used.
  • Place under mist/fog.
    • Intermittent mist (10 seconds every 10 or 15 minutes) or fogging should be utilized for rooting of cuttings.
    • Relative humidity should be maintained at or near 100 percent, keeping the leaves wet without inundating the cuttings.
    • Light intensity should remain under 1 000 µgmol * m-2 * sec.-1 PAR, or 50 to 60 percent shade.
  • Prop the leaves at an angle with a string or tack on a stick to allow any water droplets to drain off the leaf.
    • Most of the cuttings whose leaves remain wet do none-the-less root.
  • Cuttings should be watered or fertigated every two to three days to keep the media moist and to ensure the stem does not dry out.
    • A complete liquid fertilizer (modified Hoaglund's) at 150 ppm nitrogen works well.
  • Roots will appear in as little as three weeks.
    • By four to five weeks all cuttings that will root will have done so.
    • Any cutting with two or more roots and a live axillary bud of even the smallest size may be transplanted to polythene bags.

1.2 Acclimating, pot establishment, and general cultural management

  • After transplanting, cuttings should remain under 50 percent shade, and RH above 80 percent.
    • Fertilizing will promote bud break.
    • Care should be taken when watering to not damage the many times tender shoots.
  • After the first flush has hardened, the cuttings may be treated as any other material.
    • Light may be increased and RH may be lowered.
  • Orthotropic cuttings have a tendency to jorquette prematurely.
    • To achieve a more standard height of jorquette, the jorquette bud may be removed as soon as it appears.
    • Following removal, an axillary orthotropic shoot from below the cut will release, and the plant will reach a more standard height (1 to 1.5 m) prior to the appearance of the next jorquette.

1.3 Softwood stock plant production

  • Newly acclimatized SE plants may be grown for two to three months and used as stock plants for rooted cuttings.
    • After two months of establishment, orthotropic shoots longer than 0.15 m should be harvested by strong head cuts leaving three to four nodes with leaves of 80 mm long.
  • Successive harvests are then comprised of orthotropic shoots from 0.20 to 0.40 m length and left only two nodes above the previous harvest cut.
    • Multiple orthotropic axillary meristems swell during the first week, and bud break occurs by seven to ten days.
  • Individual shoots are allowed to flush mostly two to three and up to four times prior to harvesting orthotropic shoots depending on shoot morphological characteristics.
    • Stem diameter less than approximately 5 mm was found to be inadequate for rooting.
    • Therefore, shoots are allowed to flush until stem diameter at 40 to 60 mm distance basipedal from apex is at least 5 mm.
  • Softwood cuttings of 40 to 60 mm in length and mostly two leaf nodes were made from the entire harvested orthotropic shoot.
    • Node number varies from one to seven and does not affect rooting success.
    • The bottom 20 mm of each cutting is trimmed of leaves at the petiole base.
    • A maximum of four leaves per cutting remain.
    • These leaf laminae are trimmed to 60 mm length.
  • Rooting of cuttings follows the same method described above.

2. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Producción de semilla mejorada de cacao (Theobroma cacao) ó híbridos comerciales (IMC-67 y UF-296): ID 6471.
  • Uso de sombra en el cultivo de cacao: ID 6475.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2317.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for more efficient use of the cacao crop, increasing yield and profitability. 

4.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for an additional source of income for farmers in developing countries.

entries.tittle: Raising Calliandra Tree Seedlings in Uganda
entries.summary: This practice describes how Calliandra tree can be planted and grown in Uganda. First starting by seed collection and pre-treatment, then construction of seeds bed, seed sowing, and finally filling of polyethene pots with soil.
entries.description:
Description

Calliandra has many advantages.

  • It grows fast and sprouts after cutting.
  • It reduces soil and water run-off.
  • It has excellent fodder for livestock.
  • It has good fuelwood.
  • It increases soil fertility.

Production of Calliandra seedling will require the following inputs:

  • seeds,
  • sand,
  • forest soil,
  • hoes,
  • spades,
  • pangas,
  • polythene tubing,
  • papyrus mats,
  • watering cans,
  • eucalyptus poles, and
  • nails.

1. Seeds

1.1 Seed collection

  • Collect seed mature Calliandra trees when the pods have started to turn brown in order to avoid shuttering of seed.
  • Dry the pods in the sun in a sack.
  • Thresh the pods and separate the seed from the residue.
  • Store the seeds in tightly closed tins.
  • The seeds can be sown immediately or stored for several months.

1.2 Seed pre-treatment

  • Calliandra seeds have a hard coat, so when sown untreated will germinate after two weeks.
  • For quick germination soak the seeds in cold water overnight.
  • Soaking is complete once most of the seeds have swollen.
  • Sow the seed immediately after pre-treatment.
  • Never boil the seed as this kills them.

2. Stage of seedbed construction

2.1 Seedbed construction

  • Seedbed construction requires the following materials:
    • eucalyptus poles (small size of 4 cm diameter),
    • papyrus mats, and
    • sand.

2.1.1 Stage one

  • Mark area (1 m wide and 8  to 10 m long) where the seedbed will be constructed (see Figure 1).
Figure 1. Stage one

©FAO/TECA

2.1.2 Stage two

  • Erect eucalyptus poles in the marked area (see Figure 2).
Figure 2. Stage two

©FAO/TECA

2.1.3 Stage three

  • Fill the market area with sandy soil up to a height of about 4 cm (see Figure 3).
Figure 3. Stage three

©FAO/TECA

2.1.4 Stage four

  • Erect a shade (1.2 m high at the front and 0.8 m high at the back) over the bed and cover the seedbed with papyrus mats, grass or banana leaves (see Figure 4).
Figure 4. Stage four

©FAO/TECA

3. Seed sowing

  • Sow the pre-treated seed on the seed bed.
  • Cover the sown seed with a thin layer soil but they should not be seen.
  • Water immediately after sowing, thereafter water twice a day (morning and evening).
  • Seed germinate after four to five days.
  • Remove seedling from the seedbed to polythene pots when they reach 3 cm to 4 cm tall (after one and half months).
  • The pots are filled with forest soil.

4. Filling of polythene pots with soil

  • Collect forest soil and leave it for two weeks to allow seeds to germinate from it.
  • Cut the polythene in lengths of 4 inches.
  • Fill the pots with forest soil.
  • Water the pots before transplanting the seedlings from the seedbed.
  • Keep the seedlings in the transplant bed for one and half months.
  • Plant seedling on the field immediately after heavy rain.

5. Advantages/benefits

  • Seedlings are readily available to the farmers.
  • Seedlings raised can be sold to generate money or to increase family income.
    • Each seedling can be sold at 100 UGX, while 1 kg of seed can be sold at 20 000 UGX.
  • When planted in the field and managed properly, they can increase crop yields.
  • Trees planted provide rapidly available fuelwood to the family.

6. Validation of the practice

  • ​​This practice was applied successfully in Uganda.​

7. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • Production of Calliandra seedling will require the following inputs:
    • seeds,
    • sand,
    • forest soil,
    • hoes,
    • spades,
    • pangas,
    • polythene tubing,
    • papyrus mats,
    • watering cans,
    • eucalyptus poles, and
    • nails. 

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Growing fodder for livestock: Calliandra and elephant grass: ID 6989.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

10.1 Women-friendly

​​This practice can be applied as well by women farmers, as it does not require heavy machinery and does not include risks.​

10.2 Pro-poor technology

Planting Calliandra can be a source of income for poor farmers since seedling can be sold at 100 UGX, while 1 kg of seed can be sold at 20 000 UGX.

entries.tittle: Supplementary Feeding for Farmed Fish, Uganda
entries.summary: Most fish farmers believe that a fish is a wild animal. They think that once put in pond water, it will survive naturally without adding any food supplement. This has resulted in pond fish taking a long period to reach a reasonable size. Most farmers add manure like cow dung and chicken droppings. This technology focuses on supplementary feeding and lists some recommended types of fish for farming in Uganda.
entries.description:
Description

The practices show how to overcome shortages in natural feeds such as small plants (algae) and small animals in ponds. Natural feeds need time to grow so they cannot be used to feed fish immediately. Therefore, there is a need to further extend the existing natural feeds with artificial ones which can be available for the immediate consumption of fish.

1. Supplementary feeding

  • Supplementary feeding involves adding feed from other sources than the natural feeds from the pond, because natural food may not be adequate for fish growth.
  • Farmers are therefore advised to use supplementary feed to enhance proper fish growth.
  • Supplementary food provides nutrients like proteins, oils and carbohydrates that are essential for fish growth.
  • The food supplements can be produced at home and include:
    • cassava flour;
    • mukene (omena or silver cyprinid); and
    • maize bran - sunflower cake (residue got after extracting oil from sunflower seeds using a ram press).

1.1 Mixing supplementary feeds

  • Four tumpecos (equivalent to 2 litres) of maize bran.
  • Three (equivalent to 1.5 litres) of cassava flour.
  • Two (equivalent to 1 litre) of mukene (pounded/ground).
  • One (equivalent to 0.5 litre) sunflower cake in order to get a good feed mixture.

2. Applying supplementary feeds

  • The application of supplementary feeds differs with different farmed fish species.

2.1 For tilapia (ngege)

  • In the first two months sprinkle one tumpeco (equivalent to 0.5 litre cup) of the above mixture (half in the morning and half in the evening) for 400 fish in the pond.
    • The quantities vary according to the number of fish in the pond as illustrated in Table 1.
  • When the fish is two months in the pond, mingle one tumpeco of the above mixture in hot water.
    • Put in the flat container that has small holes at the bottom and lower it in the water in the morning, add another half in the evening.
    • Increase the quantity of the feed as fish grows in the pond.
  • The fish is fed twice at 09.00 hours and 15.00 hours.
  • When the fish is between three and eight months of age, the farmers mingle feed mixture with hot water.
    • The mingled feed mixture is divided into smaller pieces and placed into flat containers and lowered gently into the pond.
    • These containers are distributed uniformly in the pond depending on how many fish are there.
    • The more fish there are, the more food should be distributed.
Table 1. Quantity feed of tilapia
No. of fish Total feed (Tumpecos) No. of Tumpecos (Morning) No. of Tumpecos (Evening)
400 1 1/2 1/2
800 2 1 1
1 200 3 1 1/2 1 1/2

Source: FAO 2007

2.2 For clarias (catfish, mmale or ekolet)

  • Mingle and apply 0.5 tumpeco (equivalent to 0.25 litre cup) of the mixture of maize bran, mukene and sunflower cake to the pond in the morning.
  • Add the same quantity in the evening.
    • This should start right from the time of stocking.
  • After two months increase the quantity as the fish demand for food increases.

3. Benefits of food supplements

  • The benefits are faster growth of fish, best yields, and improved incomes.
  • There is an increasing demand for fish in the country, especially in rural communities.
    • This is due to the growing export market and the rise of the population.
    • As an alternative, the demand can be catered for through fish farming.
    • However, farmers lack the knowledge of the type of fish to farm in their ponds.

4. Fish for farming

  • The following are the recommended types of fish for farming in Uganda.

4.1 Nile tilapia (ngege or kibaati)

  • It breeds easily in ponds.
  • It tastes good.
  • It grows fast to about 300 g in eight months in hot areas of the country e.g. North and some parts of eastern Uganda.
  • Its seed production is easily available and inexpensive.
  • It can withstand harsh conditions in the pond.
  • It grows well with mmale and common carp in the same pond.
  • It can be linked with other farming practices such as poultry, where poultry wastes are used to fertilise the fish pond.
Figure 1. Nile tilapia

©FAO/TECA

4.2 Common carp (mirror carp)

  • It grows well in highland areas like south-western Uganda, Bundibugyo, Kabale and eastern Uganda (Mbale and Kapchorwa).
  • it grows up to 500 g in eight months.
  • It can be grown together with ngege.
Figure 2. Common carp

©FAO/TECA

4.3 African catfish (mmale)

  • It withstands harsh conditions in the pond.
  • It tastes good.
  • It can grow up to 500 g in a period of seven to eight months.
  • It can grow in both hot and cold areas.
  • It is a good bait for Nile perch fishing.
  • It controls the overpopulation of ngege by eating its young.
  • It grows well with ngege.
Figure 3. African catfish

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Catfish

©FAO/TECA

4.3 Tilapia zilli (ngege kifudu)

  • It breeds very easily.
  • It eats locally available plant materials, potato vines, cabbages and yam leaves.
  • It can grow up to 200 g in seven to eight months.
  • It can grow together with catfish.
Figure 5. Tilapia Zilli

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Fingerling

©FAO/TECA

5. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Fish and their byproducts: ID 8717.
  • The control of common predators of pond fish: ID 4353.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Women-friendly

This practice can be applied by women.

7.2 Resource use efficiency

With this practice, farmers will have more resources to feed their fish.​

7.3 Pro-poor technology

​​This practice offers poor farmers the possibility to feed their fish and avoid losing them due to a lack of natural fish feeds.​

entries.tittle: Light attraction method to catch Mukene fish on Lake Victoria
entries.summary: Mukene, also called Dagaa or Omena, is found in Lakes Victoria, Kyoga and Nabugabo and in the Victoria Nile. It is among the three most important commercial fish species in Lakes Victoria and Kyoga. The mukene fish is fished by light attraction. Compared to gillnetting, light fishing is relatively new in Uganda. Therefore, the National Fisheries Resources Research Institute (NaFIRRI), as one of the established public agricultural research institutes, provides the following technology for a better understanding of the light attraction method.
entries.description:
Description

Fish are a cheap source of fish proteins for both humans and domestic animals. In the lakes, the species the most important as a food source is the Nile perch, the most important export fish in the country. The mukene fish (also called Dagaa or Omena), is fished by light attraction. Compared to gillnetting, light fishing is relatively new in Uganda. Kerosene pressure lamps are floated on water, attracting fishes to light. Mukene thus attracted, is fished out using scoop-nets and nets pulled from the shores (beach seines) and from canoes (lampara nets). Since mukene is a small fish (it grows to an average standard length of 48 mm), the nets used in fishing are meshes 3 mm, 5 mm and 10 mm stretched (see Figure 1).

1. Problems to the fishery

1.1 Fishing grounds

  • Owing to the specialized nature of mukene fishing (light fishing), favourable weather conditions are necessary.
  • Safe fishing grounds consisting of shallow sheltered bays and near-shore waters attract large numbers of fishing boats.
  • These shallow inshore waters and small bays are nursery grounds for immature mukene, Nile perch and Tilapia.
  • The high exploitation rates when added to predation by the Nile perch results in localized mukene over-fishing.
  • In such areas, the fish is harvested before maturity.

1.2 Fishing gears and methods

  • Initially, mukene was fished by beach seines constructed out of 10 mm mesh nets.
  • A more efficient lampara net was later introduced but the mesh size was reduced to 5 mm and in some cases to 3 mm.
  • Nets of small meshes capture mainly immature fishes.

1.3 By-catch

  • Fishing for mukene also captures immature Nile perch and Tilapia as by-catch.
  • The light used in the fishery attracts water insects.
  • Young Nile perch and Tilapia are in turn attracted to the plentiful supply of insect food around the lamps.
  • These fishes are therefore caught as by-catch during fishing for mukene.
  • The mesh size of nets used to fish mukene can catch immature Nile perch and Tilapia.
  • This will affect stocks of fish and will harm the fishery of these two important export fish species (see Figure 2).

1.4 Solutions and recommendations

  • For a regular supply of mukene from Lake Victoria, management measures should be aimed to avoid capture of immature mukene and other fish species that commonly appears as by-catch of the mukene fishing.
    • Control of fishing grounds
      • To avoid capture of immature mukene and by-catch species, fishing should be carried outside the small bays less than 3 km diameter and at least 1.4 km away from the shoreline.
      • This will also solve the conflict with Tilapia fishery that occurs within one-kilometre belt off the shoreline.
    • Control mesh size fishing gear and methods
      • The most popular mesh size of nets in use on Lake Victoria in 5 mm stretched.
      • When this net is operated away from the nursery grounds mentioned above, it captures mainly mature mukene.
      • Nets of meshes smaller than 5 mm capture mainly immature mukene and by-catch and should be discouraged.
      • Likewise fishing for mukene using beach seines (nets pulled from the shore) should be prohibited as these are operated in nursery grounds.
      • Boat (Lampara) seine nets can be operated away from the shoreline and thus are most appropriate for mukene fishing.
      • Mukene fishing depends on the fish being attracted to light; use 5 to10 mm
      • See Figure 3.
    • Fishing seasons
      • Mukene breeds throughout the year but shows two breeding peaks in August and December to January.
      • Mukene produced during these breeding peaks appear in commercial catches as immature fishes in November/December and April/May.
      • These periods could qualify as closed to mukene fishing.
      • However, fishing away from the shore avoids the capture of these immature fishes.

1.5 How to reduce/avoid polluting the water environmental measures

  • The sustainable management of fish in Lake Victoria needs corrective actions to stop water pollution.
  • This requires a combined effort by the water and fisheries managers and grass-root communities.
  • This will involve effective watershed management.
  • Educational programmes aimed at sensitizing the local people about impacts of intense subsistence crop farming and animal husbandry on the atmosphere and water environment and subsequently fish production should be carried out.
  • These practices include:
    • uncontrolled grass and bush burning;
    • tree cutting (deforestation);
    • wetland destruction;
    • shoreline destruction by farming very close to the lake/ river banks; and
    • excessive use of pesticides and herbicides.
  • Pollution control will lead to improved water health that will support high fish yields and sustain high production.
  • It also would contribute to and enhance excess nutrient releases into the water environment.

2. Benefits from the solution suggested above

  • Catching mature fish allows stocks to replenish themselves.
  • These fish will have bred and left offspring for the future.
  • Mukene caught in the open waters far away from the shore are larger than those inshore.
  • They are easier to dry and therefore fetch better prices to the fishers.
  • By avoiding by-catch, the Nile perch and Tilapia are allowed to grow and support the export market which depends on the Nile perch.
Figure 1. Mukene fish

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Mukene cover

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Mukene light fishing

©FAO/TECA

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Small-scale freshwater fish farming: ID 6958.
  • Fish harvesting and post-harvest handling: ID 7024.
  • Fry/seed quality and stocking: ID 7025.
  • Management of fish in the pond: ID 7235.
  • Supplementary feeding for farmed fish: ID 4363.
  • Sustainable fishery on Lake Victoria: exploitation, gears, fishing methods and management: ID 4359.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

This practice allows for the efficient and sustainable harvesting of fish. It also contributes to the prevention of overexploitation of fish in Lake Victoria.

5.2 Pro-poor technology

The practice provides additional sources of food and income.
