entries.tittle: Selection of site and water quality testing for fishpond, Uganda
entries.summary: The fishponds are not just a hole in the ground containing water. They are unnatural water environments that farmers must manage in order to produce profitable fish harvests. Ponds should provide a good environment for fish to live in, all requirements for fish to live a healthy life, grow well and reproduce well. The following technology gives advice on the selection of site and water quality.
entries.description:
Description

To raise healthy fish, the pond water must be free from diseases, toxic chemicals and other fish enemies. Pond fish should also be supplied with sufficient fresh air and food. Physical characteristics of fishponds affect water quality and influence their production potential. Fish ponds have to be sited where they can be managed well to achieve the highest production potential.

1. Factors to consider when selecting a site and water quality for fishpond

1.1 Land area

  • The area of land required must be large enough to allow for the construction of ponds.
    • The larger the pond, the bigger the area of land required.
    • Extra space is required for water channels, and for walking on or movement of vehicles (e.g. tractor, pickups) (Figure 1).
  • Generally, small ponds can only provide fish for household food and nothing more for sale.
    • The minimum commercial fishpond size starts at 20 m x 25 m (500 m2) can produce 120 kg of Tilapia a year, which can be sold at UGX. 180 000 (about USD 98).
    • This amount of money can be significant in rural areas.
    • Therefore, the pond size of 20 m x 25 m can be regarded as the minimum small-scale commercial size.
    • Larger ponds from 20 m x 50 m to more than 2 ha are recommended for commercial fish production.
    • The larger the pond the more commercial viable it becomes.
  • As far as possible, the land must be fully owned by the farmer who wants to build the fish pond.
    • Often disputes arise when there is no proper agreement on the use of communal land for fish ponds.
Figure 1. Water channels and dykes size

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Dyke size

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Location, wetlands and legal consideration

  • Not only is establishing ponds in wetlands destructive to the environment, but it also is not economical to grow fish in wetlands.
  • Therefore, avoid constructing ponds in the wetlands (Figure 3).
Figure 3. Beyond the wetlands

©FAO/TECA

  • The most suitable location of land for ponds is a land on a slope (Figure 4) next to a flowing stream or river, where a portion of the water is diverted into the pond without disrupting the other uses of the same water downstream.
    • It could be a stream beyond the wetland.
  • The National Environmental Management Authority (NEMA) of Uganda requires anybody who wishes to make a development in the wetland to first carry out an Environment Impact Assessment and seek approval of the plan before the development.
  • An area of open and flat land with a gentle slope that allows water to flow by gravity is ideal.
    • Any land surface that is not flat increases the cost of construction.
    • Constructing a pond on a steep slope involves the expense of removing a lot of earth to level the ground.
    • This is called bad slope and it requires a lot of labour to remove a great amount of the soil, the lower dyke is not firm and it allows only small ponds (Figure 4: Land slope A).
  • Constructing ponds in a very sharp V-valley involves extra costs of widening the valley (Figure 4: Land slope C) as a lot of soil must be removed.
    • To avoid the problem of hidden rocks and stones it is necessary to bore holes down to 1.5 m at various points of the site during the inspection of the site (Figure 5).
Figure 4. Land slope

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Boring holes down

©FAO/TECA

2. The soil type

  • For purposes of aquaculture, soils can broadly be classified as sandy, clay, murrum, humus and loam.
    • The characteristics of these types of soils are given in Table 1. 
  • In general, good soils are those that hold water; sticks and holds together.
    • A sticky soil is good for constructing ponds.
    • It makes firm dykes and walls, which do not collapse and maintains the pond shape.
  • To test this:
    • loosen the soil;
    • add water;
    • mix the soil with the water;
    • roll it in your hand to make a ball and dry the ball for one hour in the shade; and
    • drop the ball from a height of 2 feet (about 61 cm) to the ground.
  • If the ball does not break, the soil is firm and sticky enough to build a pond with strong walls.
  • Many of the negative characteristics of soils can be corrected during construction.
Table 1. Types of soils for ponds
Soil type Positive characteristics Negative characteristics Effect on ponds
Sandy  
  • Has loose grains.
  • Does not hold water well.
  • Has loose grains.
  • Difficult to shape the pond.
Murrum    
  • Difficult to dig.
  • Keeps water dirty brown (unproductive).
Clay
  • Firm and sticks together.
  • Holds water.
  • When pure, cracks in dry season.
  • Grains too fine and do not settle down easily.
  • Maintains shape of pond.
  • Loses water through cracks in dry season.
  • Retains water outside dry season.
  • Keeps pond cloudy (unproductive).
Humus
  • Rich in organic materials.
  • Composed of loose freshly decoying plant parts, hardly any soil.
  • Good source of nutrients for fish.
Loam
  • Firm
  • little loose.
  • Pond shape can be maintained - not for long.
  • Pond shape can be maintained - not for long.
  • Source of nutrients.
Clay/Loam
  • Firm
  • hold water
  • organic material
  • not slity
  • elastic.
  
  • Maintains shape of pond.
  • Retains water.
  • Rich in nutrients.
  • Keeps water not turbid.
  • Doesnot crack in dry season.

Source: NAADS-Uganda 2007

3. Water source, quantity and quality 

  • Leave some distance between the swamp to the pond to allow the grass to filter the water.
    • Water flowing from swamps or a lot of rotting vegetation and other materials tends to contain acid levels that are not suitable for fish.
  • White builder’s lime is used to reduce the acid levels of water.
    • A paper strip (litmus paper) is used to determine the level of acid in the water.
  • A pack of 100 strips costs UGX. 12 000 (about USD 6.54) from a laboratory supplies shop.
  • The use of the water upstream may pose water quality risks for the pond.

3.1 Examples of upstream use of water that can negatively affect the fish in the pond 

  • Garages may be disposing old engine oil into the stream that may find its way into the pond to kill fish.
  • Waragi distillers may be disposing of residues into the stream, which finds its way into the pond to kill fish (Figure 6).
  • Upstream communities may be washing or bathing in the water.
  • Untreated or insufficiently treated sewage may be deposited into the stream.
Figure 6. Discharging Waragi residue into the stream

©FAO/TEC

4. Security

  • Ponds should not be located far from home or from human habitation.
  • They should be near habitation for the security of the fish even though birds may eat the fish from the pond.
  • The pond may leak or flood, and there may be a reduction in fresh air that may not be noticed.
  • Access roads to the ponds should be easy to facilitate transportation of inputs and products.

5. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Fishpond layout and construction: ID 4384.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

Efficient land-use to construct a fishpond on it. The land can be transformed to generate commercial benefits from the fishpond.

entries.tittle: Improving the quality of parboiled rice in Ghana
entries.summary: Parboiled rice is rice that has been boiled in the husk. Parboiling makes rice easier to process by hand, improves the nutritional value of white rice, and changes its texture. Today, it is the preferred rice of many in the southern parts of the Indian subcontinent, and elsewhere. The quality of any manufactured product is only as good as the quality of the raw materials and the controls exercised during processing. The best market price is achieved by a product which has a good colour (white); no odour; few broken grains; is free from stones and black grains; has no husk; is well milled; and is properly dried. The process of parboiling is carried out mainly by women.
entries.description:
Description

Parboiled rice is rice that has been boiled in the husk. Parboiling makes rice easier to process by hand, improves the nutritional value of white rice, and changes its texture. Today, it is the preferred rice of many in the southern parts of the Indian subcontinent, and elsewhere. The quality of any manufactured product is only as good as the quality of the raw materials and the controls exercised during processing. The best market price is achieved by a product which has a good colour (white); no odour; few broken grains; is free from stones and black grains; has no husk; is well milled; and is properly dried.

1. Reasons for carrying out the parboiling process

The process of parboiling is carried out mainly by women. Parboiling is a hydro-thermal process (e.g. uses both water and heat), which is carried out for a number of reasons.

  • To improve the nutritional status of the product during parboiling the water-soluble vitamins and minerals present in the bran layer
    • These penetrate the grain thus making them available to the consumer, so that parboiled white rice is nutritionally similar to brown rice.
    • In raw rice, these vitamins are largely polished-off during milling.
  • To reduce breakage during milling, the parboiling process effectively seals cracks in the raw rice kernel, making the grain much harder and more resilient to the milling process.
    • This is particularly important in areas such as, northern Ghana, where the climatic conditions result in over-drying of the grain, which is likely to produce severely cracked grain.
  • To change the cooking characteristics it is commonly thought that parboiled rice is quicker to cook than raw rice, but this is in fact not true.
    • Parboiled rice takes longer because water absorption is slower through the hardened grain.
    • However, parboiled rice is firmer and less sticky than raw-milled rice.
  • To impart different eating characteristics parboiled rice has a firmer, nuttier texture than raw rice and the grains remain separate when cooked.
    • It also has a characteristic aroma during cooking, which is preferred by most parboiled rice consumers.

2. An improved parboiling process

  • In Ghana, parboiling is carried out using simple household items, such as cooking pots, wood fires, baskets, oil drums/large clay pots.
  • The resources available govern the amount of paddy parboiled.
  • Many women can only parboil about 30 kg in each batch.
  • The work is time-consuming and arduous.
  • In addressing this problem, a DFID Crop Post Harvest Programme (CPHP) funded project in Ghana and introduced a simple parboiling vessel that enables batches of up to 100 kg to be processed at a time and enables greater control over the process (see Figure 1).
  • Apart from making it possible to parboil more paddy at a time, the vessel also has other additional advantages.
    • Less firewood is used (about half the amount used in the traditional method).
    • Discolouration that results when truncated oil drums are used is avoided.
    • Drudgery is reduced with fewer unit operations and the presence of the drain-pipe eliminates draining with baskets.
    • The presence of the separating mesh ensures that no paddy is in direct contact with water during the steaming phase.
    • Less water is used in the parboiling process.
Figure 1. Parboiling vessel

©FAO/TECA

3. Parboil stages

The process includes the specific stages.

3.1 Paddy

  • Always use good quality raw material.
  • Women often have little choice in the paddy they buy, simply purchasing whatever is available locally.
  • Wherever possible you should try to buy a clean paddy with as few stones as possible and avoid paddy that has lodged (dirty paddy).
  • Wherever possible you should buy paddy of a single variety, and which has been correctly dried and stored.

3.2 Water

  • Similarly, good quality of water is important. In some areas clean pipe water or well-water is readily available.
  • In other areas, water is difficult to find and can be of very variable quality (see Figure 2).
Figure 2. Water

©FAO/TECA

3.3 Washing and cleaning

  • Paddy should be washed carefully to remove residual dirt and stones. (see Figure 3).
Figure 3. Washing and cleaning

©FAO/TECA

3.4 Removal of floating debris

  • Careful removal of floating immature grains will reduce the number of blackened grains in the final product (see Figure 4).
Figure 4. Removal of floating debris

©FAO/TECA

3.5 Soaking

  • Paddy should be covered in water and brought almost to the boiling point and then transferred to another vessel in the traditional method for overnight soaking.
  • Extra water must be added to the soaking vessel to ensure that all grains will still be covered in water the following morning.
  • If this is to be done, the added water must be hot (see Figure 5 and Figure 6).
Figure 5. Soaking

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Washing

©FAO/TECA

3.6 Steaming

  • If traditional pots are used, the amount of water needs to be carefully controlled.
    • Too little and the pot will boil dry, and too much and significant portions of the paddy grains will be billed and not steamed.
  • The new parboiling vessel overcomes this problem by separating the grains completely from the boiling water.
  • The surface of the paddy should be covered to ensure even steaming.
  • Steaming is complete when 25 percent of the surface paddy has just split open, many women over-steam the paddy resulting in damaged kernels (see Figure 7). 
Figure 7. Steaming

©FAO/TECA

3.7 Drying paddy

  • The surface of the drying floor is critical.
  • Ideally it should be a concrete pad with no cracks etc.
  • In reality the drying surface is either beaten clay of badly maintained concrete.
  • It must be as well maintained as possible and swept clean before each use.
  • The paddy should be spread in an even, thin layer as soon as it has been drained.
  • Leaving hot, steamed paddy in a heap for some time before spreading should not be allowed (see Figure 8 and Figure 9).
  • Constant turning to allow even drying of the paddy is important.
    • This is usually done by hand and this stage can be used to pick out any stones/debris.
  • Drying in the middle of the day should be discouraged as the heat intensity can lead to cracking.
    • Paddy should be heaped in a shady place and covered with sacks, then be re-spread for final drying later in the afternoon of the following morning (see Figure 10).
  • Children and animals should be discouraged from walking on drying paddy both for reasons of hygiene and to prevent the introduction of stones.
Figure 8. Drying

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Steamed paddy in heap for sometime before spreading

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10. Paddy heaped in a shady place and covered with sacks

©FAO/TECA

3.8 Milling

  • Milling produces refined whole grains with their indigestible parts removed.
  • It is a mechanical process that transforms paddy grains into an attractive marketable product.
  • This is achieved in two stages.
    1. Removal of the outer inedible outer husk.
    2. Removal of the bran layer.
  • The bran layer is an edible layer containing many nutrients, such as vitamins, fat and minerals.
  • However, some consumers prefer this layer to be removed as it alters the cooking and flavour characteristics of the grain.
  • There are two types of mill available for the small-scale processor.
    • Rubber roll mills and steel ('Engleberg') dehullers.
    • The latter is the most widely sued type of mill in Northern Ghana.
Figure 11. The process flow chart of parboiling

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Rice seedbed preparation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 6973.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7210.
  • Intensive rice cultivation: ID 7666.
  • Rice transplanting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7214.
  • Aerobic Rice: ID 7941.
  • Participatory varietal selection: improved rice varieties: ID 4459.
  • Participatory varietal selection: improved varieties of upland rice: ID 4568.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Women friendly

The technology is easy to implement and the process of parboiling is carried out mainly by women.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

Improving the quality of rice allows for optimum selling and thus improves farmers' incomes.

entries.tittle: Sustainable fishery on Lake Victoria: exploitation, gears, fishing methods and management
entries.summary: Fish is important for good nutrition and fishery activities generate income and employment. However, industrial and intensive fishing and also wrong fishing methods deplete fish stocks. In Uganda, the major fishing activities are on Lake Victoria, one of the African great lakes and the second largest in the world. These activities provide employment, income, and export earnings to the communities living around the lake. Lake Victoria fishing is a mainly commercial fishery and needs to be well managed in order to make it sustainable and preserve the commercial fish species. The National Fisheries Resources Research Institute (NaFIRRI), as one of the established Public Agricultural Research Institutes, generates knowledge base and develop fisheries technologies for increased but sustainable fish production, conservation of the fisheries genetic resources, water quality, and fish habitat. It ensures product dissemination and quality, develop and manage research and required linkages with stakeholders. Below is some advice they give for fisher communities and fishery managers for sustainable commercial fishery management on Lake Victoria.
entries.description:
Description

Recent activities in the exploitation of the fisheries, biodiversity and environment of water system in Uganda threaten to reduce fish catches and in some cases fish death.

1. Constraints to increased and sustainable fish production

  • Under capture fisheries, the Fisheries Resources Research Institute (FIRRI) focuses research efforts to generate scientific information on the key constraints.
    • Decline in fish stock and fish species diversity due to excessive fishing.
    • Use of destructive fishing gears and methods.
    • Capture of immature fish.
    • Pollution and degradation of the fish habitat including infestation by aquatic weeds especially water hyacinth.
    • High post-harvest fish losses.
    • Ineffective management of fisheries due to limited community participation.
    • Inadequate investment skills among fishers.

2. Addressing the constraints

  • In order to overcome the constraints mentioned above, FIRRI has developed this technology to empower fisherfolk communities with information to increase and sustain fish production and utilization to overcome poverty.

3. Measures to increase and sustain fish production

3.1 Use recommended fishing gears and methods

  • Some commonly used fishing gears and methods are destructive.
  • Such methods are highly non-selective, catch fish of all types and sizes, disrupt breeding and feeding patterns of the fish and deplete the fish stocks rapidly.
  • Examples of these methods include beach seines, seine nets, cast nets, basket traps and tycooning (beating water).
    • These methods should therefore be avoided.
  • The fisherfolk are encouraged to use recommended fishing gears and methods, like hook fishing and passive gillnetting (use of stationery gill nets).
    • These methods are selective.
    • Bigger nets catch bigger fish.

3.2 Avoid polluting and degrading the fish habitat

  • Communities living around the water system should avoid polluting it.
  • Pollution leads to fish deaths and hence a decline in fish stocks and fish species diversity.
  • If a pollution source is identified within a community, it should be immediately reported to the local or district authorities.
  • There causes of pollution.
    • Wetland degradation.
    • Poor agricultural practices such as exposure of soils and cutting of trees leading to soil erosion.
    • Improper use of farm chemical that may lead to fish poisoning.
    • Industrial pollution.

3.3 Increased community participation

  • Increased community participation leads to increased and sustainable fish production.
  • Communities around water systems should ensure that proper fishing methods are used.
  • They should report observations that may lead to unhealthy and unproductive water environment to Beach Management Units (BMUs) or the Landing Site Committees.
    • See the images: Fisherfolk and Fish production cover and poster.
  • Fish is important for good nutrition, income generation, provision of employment and foreign exchange earning.
  • Uganda earned over USD 80 million in 2001 through the export of Nile perch and other related products.
  • Fishing can also be a social activity.
  • In particular, this technology is to advise the fisher communities and fishery managers on appropriate commercial fish harvesting gears and methods on Lake Victoria, Uganda.
Figure 1. Water hyacinth

©FAO/TECA

4. Problem statement

  • The following are the main problems with fishing in the lake
    • Collapse or decline of important commercial fisheries on the lake.
    • Indiscriminate use of certain fishing gears.
    • Use of small mesh size of gill nets.
    • Uncontrolled fishing methods.
    • The decline of per unit catch (kg per boat yearly) and size of the three major commercial fish species (Nile perch- Mputa, Nile tilapia-Ngege, and Mukene).
      • See the image: Fish market.
Figure 2. Fish market

©FAO/TECA

5. Research statement

  • The size of fish that should be caught is set at first maturity.
  • This is the size at which 50 percent of the fish in a population are allowed to breed before they are caught.
  • The size at the first maturity for Nile perch is 50 cm total length (TL) for male fish and 90 to 100 cm TL for female.
  • For the Nile tilapia it is 23 cm TL for males and 25 cm TL for female.
  • All Nile tilapia are mature at 29 cm TL.
  • The size at the first maturity for mukene is 42 mm standard length.
  • By 45 mm all fish are mature.

6. Fishing gears

6.1 A recent fishing method operated in open waters. Use 6" to 10"

  • Mukene nets
    • Mukene fishing depends on the fish being attracted to light.
    • Use 5 to 10 mm.
    • See the image: Mukene light fishing.
Figure 3. Mukene light fishing

©FAO/TECA

6.2 Some of the destructive fishing gears and methods

  • Beach seine and trawl nets
    • See images: Beach seine net and Trawl nets.
  • Cast nets and tycoon fishing
    • See images: Cast nets, and Tycoon fishing, and Basket traps.

6.3 Some of the recommended fishing gears and fishing methods

  • Gill nets (passive) 5" to 10"
    • See the image: Gill nets.
  • Hooks size 10 to 6 mm
    • See the image: Hooks size.
  • Drift nets.
Figure 4. Tycoon fishing

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Trawl nets

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Basket traps

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Gill nets

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Hooks

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Beach seine net

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10. Cast nets

©FAO/TECA

7. Benefits of using recommended gears and fishing methods

  • It allows uninterrupted fish breeding and growth.
  • It allows enough female Nile perch to breed.
  • Some organisms that act as food for fish become available.
  • It increases fish catches, resulting in income and improved livelihood among fishing communities.
  • It increases foreign exchange earnings from the export of fish and other fish products.
  • It ensures better food security and increased fish protein availability to people.
Figure 11. Fish production

©FAO/TECA

Figure 12. Fisherfolk

©FAO/TECA

7. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Small-scale freshwater fish farming: ID 6958.
  • Fish harvesting and post-harvest handling: ID 7024.
  • Fry/seed quality and stocking: ID 7025.
  • Management of fish in the pond: ID 7235.
  • Supplementary feeding for farmed fish: ID 4363.
  • Light attraction method to catch Mukene fish on Lake Victoria: ID 4357.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Resource use efficiency

This practice allows for the efficient and sustainable harvesting of fish. It also contributes to the prevention of overexploitation of fish in Lake Victoria.

9.2 Pro-poor technology

The practice provides additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Assessing post-harvest fish losses: load tracking method
entries.summary: Load Tracking is one of a suite of loss assessment tools, including the Informal Fish Loss Assessment Method (IFLAM) and the Questionnaire Loss Assessment Method (QLAM). Prior to the research which informed their development, with the exception of work by FAO and NRI, little effort had been made to develop systematic and practical assessment methodologies for generating accurate information on post-harvest fish losses. Load Tracking is used by researchers to assess post-harvest fish losses with communities and people working in small-scale and industrialized fisheries. Losses can be quantified at most parts of the processing or distribution chain.
entries.description:
Description

1. Load Tracking

  • Load Tracking is one of a suite of loss assessment tools, including the Informal Fish Loss Assessment Method (IFLAM) and the Questionnaire Loss Assessment Method (QLAM).
    • Prior to the research which informed their development, with the exception of work by FAO and NRI, little effort had been made to develop systematic and practical assessment methodologies for generating accurate information on post-harvest fish losses.
    • Furthermore, existing historical data on post-harvest losses was derived from limited and unsystematic observations and studies.
  • In many cases, the way that data had been collected and interpreted was not clear and and neither was the type of loss being measured.
  • The absence of reliable data on fish losses presented a major constraint to the formulation of informed policy on the efficient utilization of fishery products.
  • The Load Tracking method can be used to obtain statistically valid and meaningful results for the assessment of loss between two stages in a distribution chain.
    • Load Tracking is used by researchers to assess post-harvest fish losses with communities and people working in small-scale and industrialised fisheries.
    • Losses can be quantified at most parts of the processing or distribution chain.
    • Typical examples are:
      • losses incurred between hauling time and landing;
      • handling and packaging losses; and
      • physical and quality loss during processing and transport.
    • Load Tracking focuses on obtaining data that can be used to:
      • assess how fish quality can change within a distribution chain;
      • identify why and where losses occur;
      • estimate the value of losses in monetary terms; and
      • measure the effect of interventions to reduce losses.
  • Appropriate experimental designs need to be applied as well as biometric support is important.
  • Load Tracking gives the most accurate results when the data take one of the following forms:
    • a physical loss, defined as actual weight loss of fish;
    • an increase in loss, measured by weight or count; and
    • any continuous measurement that quantifies loss.

2. Load Tracking assessment

  • If scores, grades or ranks are used to quantify loss, it is more difficult to get a meaningful loss assessment.
  • These discrete types of measurements are more appropriate for a simpler, empirical load tracking assessment.
  • Load Tracking can be used both to identify opportunities for loss reduction and to test the impact of any interventions.
  • The data generated by Load Tracking can be used in the Predictive Loss Model.
    • This is available on the CD Rom entitled "og-IT, Cleanse IT, Ice-IT: software tools for costing and monitoring control points".
  • This is a Fish Loss Assessment and Control (FLAC) tool designed to model the effects of loss reduction interventions.
  • Load Tracking can be used as a rapid way of troubleshooting for businesses that are having problems with poor quality raw material supplied externally or to analyse losses internally within a factory environment.

3. Key components of Load Tracking

  • Planning
    • Objectives, clear statement of the purpose of the experiment and experimental design.
  • Fieldwork
    • Identification and transport of appropriate equipment; establishment of trust and a productive working relationship with the fisherfolk involved in the experiment; and designing robust data-recording protocols and data-management systems.
  • Reporting
    • Data analysis, report writing, and appropriate dissemination.
  • A successful Load Tracking experiment should:
    • use an appropriate measure for loss,
    • obtain good estimates of loss,
    • quantify the accuracy of the estimates, and
    • give results that are valid for whole communities.

4. Load Tracking equipment

  • Before performing a Load Tracking experiment, the availability of resources should be considered.
  • The following equipment is required:
    • weighing scales;
    • a calibration weight;
    • 3 m x 3 m tarpaulin to place on ground when sorting fish;
    • marker pens;
    • pen and paper;
    • a watch;
    • tagging material;
    • a torch;
    • knife/scissors; and
    • a clipboard.
  • The implementation of a Load Tracking experiment requires at least two field-based staff with biometric support to undertake and co-ordinate the whole process.
  • These staff would be expected to have a basic scientific training.
  • Key skills
    • Good numeracy level.
    • Good communication skills.
    • Ability to co-operate with the relevant communities.
    • Basic knowledge of experimental design.
    • Ability to implement random sampling.
    • Ability to accurately read quantitative measurements, such as weights.
    • Data management skills.
  • In addition, the team could include members of the community/ies with which the loss assessment is to be conducted.
    • This gives a sense of ownership of the research to communities and encourages co-operation between the researchers and the community.
    • This will improve the quality and efficiency of the research.
  • The successful outcome of Load Tracking depends on an appropriate design and a satisfactory level of replication.
    • It is important to seek biometric assistance during the initial design stage of the experiment, rather than at the final analysis and reporting stages.
    • The sampling necessary for load tracking is non-destructive and has a minimal impact on the distribution chain under investigation.
  • Good co-operation between local communities and researchers will mean that researchers may be able to sell their fish at the end of a load tracking experiment to recuperate costs.
    • If the local communities are well informed and supportive of load tracking, it might not even be necessary for researchers to purchase the fish.

5. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • ​Assessing losses in the fish supply chain: questionnaire loss assessment method (QLAM): ID 4438.
  • ​Assessing post-harvest fish losses: load tracking method: ID 4437.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology uses data, which allows for improved fishery harvest management and prevents post-harvest losses.

7.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology prevents post-harvest fish losses, which amounts to increased yields, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Assessing post-harvest fish losses: informal fish loss assessment method (IFLAM)
entries.summary: Planning and policy-making for the development of the post-harvest fisheries sector have been hampered by the lack of practical tools to understand post-harvest fish losses. The Informal Fish Loss Assessment Method (IFLAM) is a practical, flexible way to quickly generate qualitative and indicative quantitative data on post-harvest fish losses. This method is based on the tools and principles associated with rapid and participatory rural appraisal (RRA and PRA).
entries.description:
Description

The Informal Fish Loss Assessment Method (IFLAM) is one of a suite of loss assessment tools, including Load Tracking and QLAM. Prior to the research which informed their development, with the exception of work by the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the Natural Resources Institute (NRI), little effort had been made to develop systematic and practical assessment methodologies for generating accurate information on post-harvest fish losses. Furthermore, existing historical data on post-harvest losses were derived from limited and unsystematic observations and studies. In many cases, the way that data had been collected and interpreted was not clear, and neither was the type of loss being measured. The absence of reliable data on fish losses presented a major constraint to the formulation of informed policy on the efficient utilisation of fishery products.

1. Informal Fish Loss Assessment Method (IFLAM)

  • This tool is a planned yet flexible way to quickly generate qualitative and indicative quantitative data on post-harvest fish losses.
    • The method is based on the tools and principles associated with rapid and participatory rural appraisal (RRA and PRA) research and development methods.
    • Application of IFLAM involves a team of researchers systematically using a variety of data collection tools and principles, including semi-structured interviews, direct observation and diagram tools, to engage with members of fishing communities.
    • The tools and principles facilitate dialogue and discussion, from which data and information on post-harvest losses are derived.
  • The key components of IFLAM 
    • Planning: objectives, sources of information, site selection, tools, team roles, when and how long, equipment, and checklist.
    • Fieldwork: tools and principles.
    • Reporting: report writing.

2. Use of Informal Fish Loss Assessment Method (IFLAM)

  • IFLAM is used by researchers to assess post-harvest fish losses with communities and people working in small-scale and industrialized fisheries.
  • It is used to produce data on:
    • indicative physical and quality loss levels;
    • estimates of monetary losses;
    • reasons for losses;
    • variables which affect losses such as fishing gear type, processing methods, species of fish, products;
    • seasonal variations in loss levels;
    • perceptions of fish losses by those who are affected;
    • importance of fish losses compared to other issues;
    • opportunities loss reduction intervention; and
    • historical levels of fish losses and trends over time.
  • Using IFLAM can help to identify opportunities for loss reduction.
    • The data generated by IFLAM can be used in a Predictive Loss Model, which models the effects of loss reduction interventions.
    • Businesses having problems with poor quality raw material supplied externally, or who need to analyse losses within their operation, can use IFLAM as a rapid way of troubleshooting.
  • IFLAM can be used to identify opportunities for more precise quantitative loss assessment using techniques such as Load Tracking.
    • It can also be used to identify opportunities for validating data on losses over a wider geographical area, or within a number of communities, using a tool such as the Questionnaire Loss Assessment Method (QLAM).
  • If you are contemplating using Load Tracking or a Questionnaire Loss Assessment, it is recommended that IFLAM is used first, in order to plan the use of these other methods.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • ​Assessing losses in the fish supply chain: questionnaire loss assessment method (QLAM): ID 4438.
  • ​Assessing post-harvest fish losses: load tracking method: ID 4437.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology uses data, which allows for improved fishery harvest management and prevents post-harvest losses.

5.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology prevents post-harvest fish losses which amount to increased yields, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Solarisation: reducing insect damage from cowpeas
entries.summary: Cowpea is important to rural households in Ghana for its nutritional value and to supplement income. Poorer producers typically have to sell grain legumes soon after harvest, either to meet debts or because they cannot prevent storage losses (weight losses and value reduction) associated with insect damage. Market sellers are also affected. This technology describes a solarization method for controlling cow pea infestations.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction and background

Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) plays an important role in the diet and economy of many small-scale farmers in northern Ghana. Cowpea is a traditional legume, cultivated widely by small-scale farmers in sub-Saharan Africa. Being a traditional crop, it is well adapted to semi-arid climates and therefore withstand relative droughts and requires less fertilization and as for all legumes, enriches the nitrogen content of the soil. Cowpea is high in protein content and is important nutritionally in areas where meat is not available in sufficient quantities. Traditionally the whole plant is used, young leaves are used as a vegetable, generally cooked like spinach, and the fodder is used for feeding livestock.

Figure 1. Cowpea Field in Northern Ghana

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Adult cowpea bruchids

©FAO/TECA

In semi-arid areas, food harvested during the rainy season need to be stored over the dry season, which can last six to eight months. During storage, heavy damage is caused by an insect pest, which can destroy the entire harvest.

Cowpea suffer substantial damage and loss of quality as a result of infestation by members of the Bruchidae family, Callosobruchus maculates. The damage that typically occurs during on-farm and market storage, and is caused by the bruchid larvae which hatch from the eggs attached by the adults to the seed, and also in the case of cowpea to the pod before or after harvesting.

Figure 3. Cowpea damaged by bruchids

©FAO/TECA

The bruchid life cycle takes about one month, adults mate and lay eggs within five days of emergence and each female can lay up to 100 eggs.

Figure 4. Bruchid life cycle

©FAO/TECA

The damage caused by the bruchid can be very high, and the entire stock could be destroyed in a few months. Farmers, therefore, are reluctant to store their cowpea, and sell it early after harvest, when the price is lowest.

A project funded by the DFID Crop Post Harvest Programme (R7442) tested the selected methods of controlling the infestation, traditional and modern alternatives, without using synthetic chemicals, to assess their efficiency. The methods tested were hermetic storage, solar disinfestation, ash, chilli, shea nut butter or residue, and plant extracts. The most effective control method as judged by the participating farmers was solarization repeated monthly. Its only drawbacks were perceived to be its cost and, for some, the time involved. The cost was discussed in terms of a cost-benefit analysis, which showed that the profit to be made in the lean season (and therefore the time when cowpea is most expensive) was at least 100 percent of the lowest price at harvest. It was found that an investment of 15 percent of the expected profit would secure the material necessary for solarization.

Figure 5. Cowpea sold in market

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Cowpea pounding

©FAO/TECA

2. Solarization technique

  • Select an open area with no shade. Sweep the area selected so that it is clean.
    • Roll out a straw mat on the clean area and make sure that it is flat. See Figure 7.
Figure 7. Roll out a straw mat on the clean area

©FAO/TECA

  • Bring several old but clean jute bags and shake the bags thoroughly to make sure that there are no pests hidden in the fabric.
    • Shake the bags well away from the area where the mats have been laid. See Figure 8.
Figure 8. Bring several old but clean jute bags

©FAO/TECA

  • Place the mats on the straw mat making sure that they are arranged so that they overlap at the edges (or cowpea will be lost at the next stage.) See Figure 9.
Figure 9. Place the mats on the straw mat making

©FAO/TECA

  • Pour the cowpea on the jute bags and spread it evenly the thickness of the cowpea layer should be the same throughout the mat. See Figure 10.
Figure 10. Pour the cowpea on the jute bags

©FAO/TECA

  • Check the thickness of the layer using your finger as a guide.
    • The depth of the cowpea layer should not be more than 2 to 3 cm throughout.
    • This is very important or the temperature will not rise high enough to kill all the beetles. See Figure 11.
Figure 11. Check the thickness of the layer using your finger

©FAO/TECA

  • Place a transparent plastic sheet on top of the cowpea layer and weigh it down at the edges with stones and pieces of wood, heavy enough to hold it from being disturbed by the wind.
    • Make sure that the sheet is well fixed and there is no space between the cowpea layer and the plastic sheet.
    • Keep animals away from the area. See Figures 12, 13 and 14.
Figure 12. Place a transparent plastic sheet on top of the cowpea layer

©FAO/TECA

Figure 13. Place a transparent plastic sheet on top of the cowpea layer

©FAO/TECA

Figure 14. Keep animals away from the area

©FAO/TECA

  • Keep the cowpea in the sun as long as it is hot, at least between 10 am and 3 pm for best results.
    • The heat of the sun generated under the plastic sheet kills the cowpea beetles on and inside the cowpea. See Figure 15.
  • The process should be repeated once a month, during the storage period.
Figure 15. Keep the cowpea in the sun

©FAO/TECA

3. Context and potential problems

  • This technique, which is both simple and effective, is generally limited to small quantities of grains.
    • It is of particular interest to individual farmers or small groups and is applicable mainly at an individual household level.
  • The main problem encountered may be the supply of suitable plastic film and the UV resistance of these materials.
    • UV makes most plastic films brittle.
    • This therefore does not last long and will need to be replaced regularly.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • ​​Using plants with pesticidal properties to control insects during on-farm grain storage: ID 4506.
  • ​Using eucalyptus leaves to preserve maize and bean seed: ID 7639.​

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2425.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for an improved cultivation of cow pea and improves soil by avoiding the use of chemicals. With improved yields, the whole plant can be used for food and fodder.

entries.tittle: Participatory varietal selection: improved maize for western India (ZM-421)
entries.summary: The centralised plant breeding techniques of the green revolution have yielded good results in more favourable agricultural environments. However, most low-resource farmers in marginal areas have not benefited from these varieties. As an alternative to centralised breeding, farmer participatory approaches using Paticipatory Varietal Selection (PVS) and Participatory Plant Breeding (PPB) can be used. In PPB, farmers are actively involved in the breeding process, from setting goals to selecting variable, early generation material. In PVS, farmers are given a wide range of new cultivars to test for themselves in their own fields.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • The centralized plant breeding techniques of the green revolution have yielded good results in the more favourable agricultural environments.
  • However, most low-resource farmers in marginal areas have not benefited from these varieties.
  • As an alternative to centralized breeding, farmer participatory approaches using Participatory Varietal Selection (PVS) and Participatory Plant Breeding (PPB) can be used.
  • PPB is an extension of PVS.
    • In PPB, farmers are actively involved in the breeding process, from setting goals to selecting variable, early generation material.
    • In PVS, farmers are given a wide range of new cultivars to test for themselves in their own fields.
    • In PPB programmes, the results of PVS were exploited by using identified cultivars as parents of crosses.

1.1 When can Participatory Plant Breeding be used?

  • When no existing cultivars are identified that are suitable for testing in a PVS programme.
  • When PVS has been tried but has failed to identify any varieties that farmers prefer.

1.2 What crosses to make?

  • PVS can be efficiently followed by PPB since farmers preferred cultivars are the ideal parents for PPB programmes.
  • Examples are PVS cultivar x high-yielding variety, local landrace x PVS cultivar and local landrace x high-yielding variety.

2. Key assumptions for Participatory Plant Breeding

  • Farmers are interested in taking part in plant breeding and farmers and scientists can successfully collaborate.
  • PPB is very unlikely to fail because the parents of crosses include locally adapted material, selection is in the local environment, and varieties are selected by farmers for the traits they consider important.

3. Types of participatory plant breeding

  • PPB can be consultative and collaborative.
  • The approach used will depend on the crop and the availability of resources.

3.1 Consultative

  • Farmers are consulted at every stage.
    • For example, in setting the breeding objectives, choosing the appropriate parent, and by making joint selections with breeders from material grown by breeders.
    • Hence, until there is a finished product from the breeding programme for farmers to test in PVS trials, farmers are not involved in growing material in their fields.

3.2 Collaborative

  • Farmers grow the variable PPB material in their own fields and select the best plants from it.
  • Scientists can then obtain seed from farmers to test their selections in research station and participatory trials.

4. Steps for participatory plant breeding

  • Set the breeding objectives
    • Crop-focused participatory rural appraisals.
    • Analyse results of participatory varietal selection.
  • Identify the parent material
    • From local landraces, from varieties tested by PVS, from high-yielding varieties with complementary characteristics.
  • Decide on the model (consultative/collaborative)
    • On the basis of available resources and on the crop.
    • Collaborative participation is simpler in an inbreeding crop.
  • Enter the best participatory plant breeding lines in PVS trials and facilitate their entry in formal on-station trials.
  • Prepare release proposal, if success is achieved.

5. Benefits of Participatory Plant Breeding

  • Production gains
    • Yield and stability increases, faster uptake, wider diffusion, and higher market value of products.
  • Biodiversity enhancement
    • Communities have wider access to germplasm, wider access to related knowledge, and increased inter- and intra-varietal diversity.
  • Cost-efficiencies and effectiveness
    • Fewer research dead-ends, more opportunities for cost sharing in research, and less expensive means of diffusing varieties.
  • Effective meeting of user needs
    • Higher degree of farmer satisfaction, broader range of users reached, including marginal farmers, and promotion of group learning through farm walks.
  • There is often a trade-off between yield and early maturity.
    • An early variety escapes common end of season droughts, and produces a harvest at the hungriest time of the year, before other crops mature.
    • It also reaches the market first, so its grain fetches a higher price.

6. A case study on PPB in maize

Maize is the most important rainy season cereal crop in the marginal, upland areas of the project. Farmers were given new maize varieties to try in a PVS programme. These included white- and yellow-grain types. The farmers did not markedly prefer any of the varieties to their local ones. However, some of the varieties had specific traits that the farmers wanted, so in a PPB programme six were crossed to produce a composite population. The initial selections were made from this population based on characteristics identified by farmers, and at later stages farmers selected for themselves from populations grown by the project. Three of the most promising white-grain varieties produced from the population were then assessed in formal and participatory trials.

7. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Maize production: ID 7018.
  • Drought-tolerant maize varieties: ID 8920.
  • Growing soybean and maize in rotation: ID 6911.
  • The role of standards in maize: ID 7020.
  • Participatory approaches: client-oriented breeding of maize for western India: ID 4448.
  • Seed priming to improve stand establishment and yield in maize: ID 4450.
  • Disease resistant upland maize varieties validated by and promoted to farmers: ID 4528.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for crop diversification and increased yield thanks to their increased participation in breeding processes, goal setting, material generation and new cultivar testing.

entries.tittle: Participatory varietal selection: Improved varieties of chickpea for rainfed conditions in Western India (ICCV 88202 and ICCV 2)
entries.summary: The centralised plant breeding techniques of the green revolution have yielded good results in the more favourable agricultural environments. However, most low-resource farmers in marginal areas have not benefited from these varieties. As an alternative to centralised breeding, farmer participatory approaches using Participatory Varietal Selection (PVS) and Participatory Plant Breeding (PPB) can be used. In PPB, farmers are actively involved in the breeding process, from setting goals to selecting variable, early generation material. In PVS, farmers are given a wide range of new cultivars to test for themselves in their own fields.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • The centralised plant breeding techniques of the green revolution have yielded good results in the more favourable agricultural environments.
  • However, most low-resource farmers in marginal areas have not benefited from these varieties.
  • As an alternative to centralised breeding, farmer participatory approaches using Participatory Varietal Selection (PVS) and Participatory Plant Breeding (PPB) can be used.
  • PPB is an extension of PVS.
    • In PPB, farmers are actively involved in the breeding process, from setting goals to selecting variable, early generation material.
    • In PVS, farmers are given a wide range of new cultivars to test for themselves in their own fields.
    • In PPB programmes the results of PVS were exploited by using identified cultivars as parents of crosses.

1.1 When can Participatory Plant Breeding be used?

  • When no existing cultivars are identified that are suitable for testing in a PVS programme.
  • When PVS has been tried but has failed to identify any varieties that farmers prefer.

1.2 What crosses to make?

  • PVS can be efficiently followed by PPB since farmer preferred cultivars are the ideal parents for PPB programmes.
  • Examples are PVS cultivar x high-yielding variety, local landrace x PVS cultivar and local landrace x high-yielding variety.

2. Key assumptions for Participatory Plant Breeding

  • Farmers are interested in taking part in plant breeding and farmers and scientists can successfully collaborate.
  • PPB is very unlikely to fail because the parents of crosses include locally adapted material, selection is in the local environment, and varieties are selected by farmers for the traits they consider important.

3. Types of participatory plant breeding

  • PPB can be consultative and collaborative.
  • The approach used will depend on the crop and the availability of resources.

3.1 Consultative

  • Farmers are consulted at every stage.
  • For example, in setting the breeding objectives, choosing the appropriate parent, and by making joint selections with breeders from material grown by breeders.
  • Hence, until there is a finished product from the breeding programme for farmers to test in PVS trials, farmers are not involved in growing material in their fields.

3.2 Collaborative

  • Farmers grow the variable PPB material in their own fields and select the best plants from it.
  • Scientists can then obtain seed from farmers to test their selections in research station and participatory trials.

4. Advantages of participatory over conventional breeding methods

  • At least one parent in any cross is well adapted to the local environment.
  • Genotype x environment interactions are used positively because breeding is done in the target environment.
    • The impact of genotype x year interaction is probably reduced because local parental materials have adapted to local year-to-year variations, and only a few crosses are made.
    • This is so that large F2 and F3 populations can be grown to increase the likelihood of selecting desirable segregants.

5. Steps for Participatory Plant Breeding

  • Set the breeding objectives
    • Crop-focused participatory rural appraisals.
    • Analyse results of participatory varietal selection.
  • Identify the parent material
    • From local landraces, from varieties tested by PVS, from high-yielding varieties with complementary characteristics.
  • Decide on the model (consultative/collaborative)
    • On the basis of available resources and on the crop
    • Collaborative participation is simpler in an inbreeding crop.
  • Enter the best participatory plant breeding lines in PVS trials and facilitate their entry in formal on-station trials.
  • Prepare release proposal, if success is achieved.

6. Benefits of Participatory Plant Breeding

  • Production gains
    • Yield and stability increases, faster uptake, wider diffusion and higher market value of products.
  • Biodiversity enhancement
    • Communities have wider access to germplasm, wider access to related knowledge and increased inter- and intra-varietal diversity.
  • Cost-efficiencies and effectiveness
    • Fewer research dead-ends, more opportunities for cost sharing in research and less expensive means of diffusing varieties.
  • Effective meeting of user needs
    • Higher degree of farmer satisfaction, broader range of users reached, including marginal farmers and promotion of group learning through farm walks.
  • There is often a trade-off between yield and early maturity.
    • An early variety escapes common end of season droughts, and produces a harvest at the hungriest time of the year, before other crops mature.
    • It also reaches the market first, so its grain fetches a higher price.

7. A case study on chickpea

Farmers wanted early (70 days) maturity with less water requirement, better insect resistance and high market price. They were asked to compare four new varieties of chickpea with their local variety for many traits, including degree of pest attack, crop maturity, seed size and colour, taste, and market value. From farm walks, all farmers were aware of the four chickpea varieties, so they could make judgements on their overall preferences. Farmers were asked whether they would purchase seed of a new variety. A marked preference was shown for the cultivars that had a good combination of earliness and yield. There was a 35-fold preference for ICCV 2, the most preferred cultivar, over ICCC 4, which was the recommended cultivar for the area. ICCV 2 and ICCV 88202 had the most preferred combination of yield and earliness, followed by ICCV 10, which was high yielding but late to mature. The cultivars ICCV 37 and ICCC 4 were markedly inferior to the local cultivar, Dahod yellow, because they flowered later but failed to yield more. Farmers prefer early cultivars because grain prices are higher early in the season and because they perceive that earlier-maturing cultivars will escape drought caused by receding soil moisture.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Participatory varietal selection: improved chickpea yield: ID 4458.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

10.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently combines many practices, allowing increased participation in breeding processes, goal setting, material generation and new cultivar testing.

entries.tittle: Assessing losses in the fish supply chain: questionnaire loss assessment method (QLAM)
entries.summary: Planning and policy-making for the development of the post-harvest fisheries sector has been hampered by the lack of practical tools to understand post-harvest fish losses. The Questionnaire Loss Assessment Method (QLAM) is based on a formal questionnaire survey approach to post-harvest loss assessment. Enumerators interview a population sample using a questionnaire focused on post-harvest losses. Data are analysed and presented using appropriate biometric principles. The method produces quantitative data on key aspects of loss such as the type of loss incurred, reasons for loss and the variables which affect loss (such as fishing gear or processing method). It is also used to validate the results of the associated tools Informal Fish Loss Assessment Method (IFLAM) and Load Tracking, over a wide geographical area or within a number of communities.
entries.description:
Description

The Questionnaire Loss Assessment Method (QLAM) is one of a suite of loss assessment tools, including Load Tracking and the Fish Loss Assessment Method (IFLAM). Prior to the research which informed their development, with the exception of work by FAO and NRI, little effort had been made to develop systematic and practical assessment methodologies for generating accurate information on post-harvest fish losses. Furthermore, existing historical data on post-harvest losses was derived from limited and unsystematic observations and studies. In many cases, the way data had been collected and interpreted was not clear; and neither was the type of loss being measured. The absence of reliable data on fish losses presented a major constraint to the formulation of informed policy on the efficient utilisation of fishery products.

1. The Questionnaire Loss Assessment (QLAM) and its uses

  • The Questionnaire Loss Assessment Method is based on a formal questionnaire survey approach.
    • Questionnaires are used by enumerators to interview a population sample in a community at a particular site.
    • Providing the survey has been planned according to a statistical protocol.
    • The data on fish losses should be representative of the community, communities, fishery or geographical area within which the survey was conducted.

1.1 Key elements of the QLAM 

  • Planning
    • Objectives defined, survey designed, and questionnaires developed.
  • Survey
    • Interview strategy (who and when to interview)and using questionnaires.
  • Data management and analysis
    • Inputting; checking; graphical techniques and tests; and archiving.
  • Reporting
    • Report writing and dissemination.
  • The QLAM is used by researchers to quantitatively assess key aspects of post-harvest fish losses.
  • It has been used most effectively to generate statistically valid data on many issues.
    • Type of loss
    • Reasons for losses
    • Frequency of loss
    • Variables which affect losses, such as type of fishing gear, processing method, species.
    • Livelihood activities and profiles of those affected by loss.
  • The QLAM can be used to build on and validate the findings of the associated loss assessment tools IFLAM and Load Tracking.
  • It can be used to validate data over a wide geographical area or within a number of communities.
  • The quantitative results produced will inform decision-making by planners and policy-makers.

2. Requirements for Questionnaire Loss Assessment

  • Specialist skills
  • Possible training/orientation of users
  • Equipment
  • Finance

2.1 Specialist skills

  • It is essential that a biometrician or statistician is involved in designing the QLA and advises on/ undertakes the data management and analysis.
  • Co-ordination and implementation of the QLAM is best done by a research centre, an appropriate consultancy company or a university department.
    • The co-ordinator should have experience of design and implementation of questionnaire surveys.
  • If the QLA is to cover a wide geographical area and to be conducted over several months or more, it may be practical to enlist the help of regional/ area supervisors.
  • Enumerators are required to conduct the questionnaire interviews.
    • They may be recruited and travel to the survey sites when required or they could already be working at or near a site.
    • Enumerators should be diligent, honest and have good interpersonal skills.
    • Their job is to ask the questions and try to ensure that the fishermen, processors or traders give an accurate answer.
    • People who are involved in revenue collection or law enforcement activities do not always make the best enumerators as interviewees may be reluctant to disclose accurate information to people who may be seen to have conflicting roles.
  • Whilst a biometrician should oversee survey design and data management and analysis, it may be practical for someone else to assist by:
    • developing a computer database for the survey data,
    • inputting data into the database, and
    • undertaking basic analysis.
  • However, researchers should also be involved in database design and basic analysis, as they will know what basic analysis should generate in the way of results and information on losses.
  • Data inputting may be best done by someone not involved in the research, as there would be less chance of data being changed without checking.

2.2 Training

  • Training of enumerators may be a requirement as part of a QLA.
  • The trainer should be someone with previous experience of survey work.
  • Training should include as much practical interviewing work as possible.
  • The practical sessions should be backed up with appraisals to identify strengths and weaknesses of the trainees.

2.3 Equipment

  • The key equipment for a QLA is a computer with database or spreadsheet software for storing and analysing data.
  • A biometrican should advise on the choice of software.
    • However, this will depend upon what software and skills are available locally.
  • As a rule of thumb, spreadsheets can be better for mathematical analysis of the data, but errors during data inputting are more common.
  • Database software, on the other hand, allows the design of data inputting screens which reduces the chance of errors during the inputting process.
  • A good printer will be invaluable for producing reports.
  • Enumerators will need work materials:
    • a clipboard,
    • a calculator,
    • pens,
    • a notebook,
    • a plastic folder,
    • a ruler, 
    • copies of questionnaires, and
    • possibly answer forms.

2.4 Finance

  • Typical expenditure associated with the use of the QLAM.
    • Staff fees
      • Co-ordinator; supervisors; enumerators; trainer training; planning; fieldwork; data management and analysis; and report writing.
    • Travel
      • Training, planning, and to and from fieldwork during survey.
    • Accommodation
      • Training, planning, and survey.
    • Stationery
      • Training, planning, survey, photocopying, postage, and other communication costs.
    • Equipment
      • See above.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • ​Assessing post-harvest fish losses: informal fish loss assessment method (IFLAM): ID 4436.
  • ​Assessing post-harvest fish losses: load tracking method: ID 4437.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology uses data, which allows for improved fishery harvest management and prevents post-harvest losses.

5.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology prevents post-harvest fish losses which amounts to increased yields, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Participatory varietal selection: improved varieties of blackgram for rainfed conditions in western India (IU8-6)
entries.summary: The centralised plant breeding techniques of the green revolution have yielded good results in the more favourable agricultural environments. In PPB, farmers are actively involved in the breeding process, from setting goals to selecting variable, early generation material. In PVS, farmers are given a wide range of new cultivars to test for themselves in their own fields. This technology describes a case study with blackgram.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • The centralized plant breeding techniques of the green revolution have yielded good results in the more favourable agricultural environments.
  • However, most low-resource farmers in marginal areas have not benefited from these varieties.
  • As an alternative to centralised breeding, farmer participatory approaches using Participatory Varietal Selection (PVS) and Participatory Plant Breeding (PPB) can be used.
  • PPB is an extension of PVS.
    • In PPB, farmers are actively involved in the breeding process, from setting goals to selecting variable, early generation material.
    • In PVS, farmers are given a wide range of new cultivars to test for themselves in their own fields.
    • In PPB programmes the results of PVS were exploited by using identified cultivars as parents of crosses.

1.1 When can Participatory Plant Breeding be used?

  • When no existing cultivars are identified that are suitable for testing in a PVS programme.
  • When PVS has been tried but has failed to identify any varieties that farmers prefer.

1.2 What crosses to make?

  • PVS can be efficiently followed by PPB since farmer preferred cultivars are the ideal parents for PPB programmes.
  • Examples are PVS cultivar x high-yielding variety, local landrace x PVS cultivar and local landrace x high-yielding variety.

2. Key assumptions for Participatory Plant Breeding

  • Farmers are interested in taking part in plant breeding and farmers and scientists can successfully collaborate.
  • PPB is very unlikely to fail because the parents of crosses include locally adapted material, selection is in the local environment, and varieties are selected by farmers for the traits they consider important.

3. Types of participatory plant breeding

  • PPB can be consultative and collaborative.
  • The approach used will depend on the crop and the availability of resources.

3.1 Consultative

  • Farmers are consulted at every stage
  • For example, in setting the breeding objectives, choosing the appropriate parent, and by making joint selections with breeders from material grown by breeders.
  • Hence, until there is a finished product from the breeding programme for farmers to test in PVS trials, farmers are not involved in growing material in their fields.

3.2 Collaborative

  • Farmers grow the variable PPB material in their own fields and select the best plants from it.
  • Scientists can then obtain seed from farmers to test their selections in research station and participatory trials.

4. Steps for Participatory Plant Breeding

  • Set the breeding objectives
    • Crop-focused participatory rural appraisals; analyse results of participatory varietal selection.
  • Identify the parent material
    • From local landraces, from varieties tested by PVS, from high-yielding varieties with complementary characteristics.
  • Decide on the model (consultative/collaborative)
    • On the basis of available resources and on the crop (collaborative participation is simpler in an inbreeding crop.
  • Enter the best participatory plant breeding lines in PVS trials and facilitate their entry in formal on-station trials.
  • Prepare release proposal, if success is achieved.

5. Building on the success

  • The Western India Rainfed Farming Project now has probably the largest ,certainly the most diverse PPB programme of any development project.
  • Collaborative arrangements for PPB programmes are in place with three universities in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Gujarat.
  • These programmes include six crops: maize, rice, horsegram, black gram, niger and sunn hemp.
    • A big advantage of this multi-crop approach is that large gains can be expected from breeding neglected crops, such as horsegram.
    • They can also be bred to fit better into local farming systems.
      • Current horsegram varieties mature too late to successfully intercrop with maize.
    • In time, short duration maize and horsegram varieties from the PPB will be grown together by farmers.
  • These collaborative PPB programmes follow the principles described here, and products from PPB in rice and maize are already in advanced trials.
  • Considering the impact that just one new variety can have on improving farmers' livelihoods, the potential impact of this collaborative programme is immense.

6. Benefits of Participatory Plant Breeding

  • Production gains
    • Yield and stability increases, faster uptake, wider diffusion and higher market value of products.
  • Biodiversity enhancement
    • Communities have wider access to germplasm, wider access to related knowledge and increased inter- and intra-varietal diversity.
  • Cost-efficiencies and effectiveness
    • Fewer research dead-ends, more opportunities for cost sharing in research and less expensive means of diffusing varieties.
  • Effective meeting of user needs
    • Higher degree of farmer satisfaction, broader range of users reached, including marginal farmers and promotion of group learning through farm walks.
  • There is often a trade-off between yield and early maturity.
    • An early variety escapes common end of season droughts, and produces a harvest at the hungriest time of the year, before other crops mature.
    • It also reaches the market first, so its grain fetches a higher price.

7. A case study on blackgram

Black gram was found to be the most important pulse crop in the cropping system of the project area. It is grown both as a mixed crop or an inter-crop with maize, and as a sole crop on many fields with poor soil fertility and stony, hilly areas. An exploratory PRA revealed that farmers grew two landraces, both of which were highly susceptible to powdery mildew and pod borer. Farmers had never seen or heard of any of the new disease-tolerant cultivars.

Following the PRA, a search for new back gram cultivars identified four promising possibilities. Trials of four new varieties were conducted in each of three villages – one each in Gujarat, MP and Rajasthan. Focus group discussions took place after farm walks in the villages. The two most preferred cultivars, TPU-4 and IU 8 - 6, were liked for their higher yield. This is because the pods were borne on bunches of four to five pods, whereas the local landrace had only one or two pods per bunch. All the farmers commented on the lower pest attack in all the test varieties. Overall, IU 8-6 was the most preferred cultivar as it had a better grain colour than T-9. Neither T-9 nor IU 8 - 6 were recommended by any of the extension services in the three states in which trials were done.

8. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Maize production: ID 7018.
  • Drought-tolerant maize varieties: ID 8920.
  • Growing soybean and maize in rotation: ID 6911.
  • The role of standards in maize: ID 7020.
  • Participatory approaches: client-oriented breeding of maize for western India: ID 4448.
  • Seed priming to improve stand establishment and yield in maize: ID 4450.
  • Disease resistant upland maize varieties validated by and promoted to farmers: ID 4528.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for crop diversification and increased yield thanks to their increased participation in breeding processes, goal setting, material generation and new cultivar testing.

entries.tittle: Preservation of fruits: Intermediate moisture peaches
entries.summary:
Fruits and vegetables are nutritious, valuable foods full of flavour. Therefore, fruits and vegetables represent an important and in many cases an under-appreciated resource that could benefit from better utilisation and exploitation in rural communities. However, in low-income countries, poor care and handling of these crops frequently result in loss of quality, especially when not consumed immediately. 

This preservation technique to produce intermediate moisture peaches permits the product to be consumed for more than a year. The intermediate moisture peach slices must be stored in a cool and dark place.
entries.description:
Description

1. Steps to prepare intermediate moisture peaches

1.1 Step one

For obtaining peaches of intermediate moisture, the weighed peach halves are cut into slices and blanched in steam for one minute, Figure 1.

Figure 1. Peach halves cut into slices and blanched

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two

The peach slices are removed from the steam bath and quickly cooled in tap water for a few minutes, Figure 2.

Figure 2. Peach slices cooled in tap water

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Step three

The fruit is drained and put into a clean bucket, Figure 3.

Figure 3. Peach slices drained and put into a bucket

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Step four

The following mixture of sugar and additives is mixed in with the peach slices, Figure 4:

  • 291 g sucrose or glucose (you can measure the sugar with a measuring jug);
  • 1.3 g potassium sorbate (one level teaspoon);
  • 16 g citric acid (two level tablespoons); and
  • 0.32 g sodium bisulphite (a quarter level coffee-spoon).
Figure 4. Peach slices mixed with sugar and additives

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Step five

The mixture of fruit, sugar and additives is gently stirred with a wooden stick or spoon and left to stand for five days. Twice a day you must stir the bucket to blend the product.

1.6 Step six

After five days, the fruit and the juice are separated with a colander or a sieve, Figure 5.

Figure 5. Peach slices and juice separated with a colander

©FAO/TECA

1.7 Step seven

The juice is collected and packaged in bottles, demijohns or other containers, Figure 6. It can be consumed as is! The peach slices will be partially dried in hot air. To do this, the drained peach slices are spread on a tray of stainless steel screen as evenly as possible over the whole surface of the tray.

Figure 6. Juice collected in bottles and demijohns

©FAO/TECA

1.8 Step eight

Be careful to put only a single layer of peach slices on the tray, so that they dry more quickly, Figure 7.

Figure 7. A layer of peach slices on a tray of stainless steel

©FAO/TECA

1.9 Step nine

The dryer used is a batch dryer, Figure 8. The fruit pieces are put into the dryer, dehydrated in the heated air passing across and through the bed. When the moisture has been reduced to the desired value, the fruit is taken out. 

Figure 8. Peach slices put in a batch dryer

©FAO/TECA

1.10 Step ten

When the moisture in the fruit is 19 to 25 percent (that is 19 g to 25 g water per 100 g partially dried fruit), the tray is removed from the dryer.

1.11 Step eleven

The drying time depends on the size and shape of the fruit, the temperature, humidity and flow and direction of the air, and the way the fruit is supported during drying.

1.12 Step twelve

In the dryer used in this process, an air velocity of 2 m per sec and a temperature of 65˚C, resulting in a drying time of approximately three hours.

1.13 Step thirteen

The partially dried peaches (also called intermediate moisture peach) are cooled at room temperature and then packaged in polyethylene or polypropylene bags or in glass or high density polyethylene jars, figure 9. The product is labelled indicating the name and type of fruit product ("intermediate moisture peach"), the ingredients, the day of manufacture, the "use by" date and the name and place of manufacturer.

The intermediate moisture peach slices must be stored in a dark fresh place and can be kept for a year. They can be eaten as such or used as an ingredient in fruit cakes, dairy products and confectionery. The sweetened fruit juice, with all the natural flavour, can be drunk as is or used as an ingredient in drink formulations. Itt has a duration of three to four months.

Figure 9. Dried peaches packaged in polythene bags and jars

©FAO/TECA

2. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Preservation of strawberries: ID 3941.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable strawberry puree: ID 3943.
  • Preservation of fruits: intermediate moisture whole strawberries: ID 3944.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable high moisture strawberries: ID 3942.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable pineapple of high moisture: ID 3946.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable high moisture pineapple- dry infusion: ID 3947.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable pineapple puree: ID 3948.
  • Preservation of fruits: intermediate moisture pineapples: ID 3949.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable peach puree: ID 3952.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable peach halves (dry infusion): ID 3953.
  • Preservation of fruits: shelf-stable high moisture peach halves: ID 3951.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Women friendly

This technology is not labour-intensive and can be done by any manual hand labour.

4.2 Resource use efficiency

Preservation of peaches reduces post-harvest losses.

4.3 Pro-poor technology 

Peaches can be preserved using a simple technique, this offers a new marketing opportunity for farmers.
