entries.tittle: Participatory approaches: client-oriented breeding of maize for western India
entries.summary: The centralized plant breeding techniques of the green revolution have yielded good results in more favourable agricultural environments. However, most low-resource farmers in marginal areas have not benefited from these varieties. As an alternative to centralized breeding, farmer participatory approaches using Participatory Varietal Selection (PVS) and Participatory Plant Breeding (PPB) can be used. In PPB, farmers are actively involved in the breeding process, from setting goals to selecting variable, early generation material. Moreover, with PVS, farmers are given a wide range of new cultivars to test for themselves in their own fields.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

The centralized plant breeding techniques of the green revolution have yielded good results in the more favourable agricultural environments. However, most low-resource farmers in marginal areas have not benefited from these varieties. As an alternative to centralized breeding, farmer participatory approaches using Participatory Varietal Selection (PVS) and Participatory Plant Breeding (PPB) can be used. PPB is an extension of PVS. In PPB, farmers are actively involved in the breeding process, from setting goals to selecting variable, early generation material. In PVS, farmers are given a wide range of new cultivars to test for themselves in their own fields. In PPB programmes the results of PVS were exploited by using identified cultivars as parents of crosses.

1.1 When can participatory plant breeding be used?

  • When no existing cultivars are identified that are suitable for testing in a PVS programme.
  • When PVS has been tried but has failed to identify any varieties that farmers prefer.

1.2 What crosses to make?

  • PVS can be efficiently followed by PPB since farmer preferred cultivars are the ideal parents for PPB programmes.
  • Examples are PVS cultivar x high-yielding variety, local landrace x PVS cultivar and local landrace x high-yielding variety.

2. Key assumptions for participatory plant breeding

  • Farmers are interested in taking part in plant breeding and farmers and scientists can successfully collaborate.
  • PPB is very unlikely to fail because the parents of crosses include locally adapted material,  the selection is in the local environment, and varieties are selected by farmers for the traits they consider important.

3. Types of participatory plant breeding

  • PPB can be consultative and collaborative.
  • The approach used will depend on the crop and the availability of resources.

3.1 Consultative

  • Farmers are consulted at every stage.
    • For example, in setting the breeding objectives, choosing the appropriate parent, and by making joint selections with breeders from material grown by breeders.
  • Hence, until there is a finished product from the breeding programme for farmers to test in PVS trials, farmers are not involved in growing material in their fields.

3.2 Collaborative

  • Farmers grow the variable PPB material in their own fields and select the best plants from it.
  • Scientists can then obtain seed from farmers to test their selections in research station and participatory trials.

5. Steps for participatory plant breeding

  • Set the breeding objectives.
    • Crop-focused participatory rural appraisals and analyse results of participatory varietal selection.
  • Identify the parent material.
    • From local landraces, from varieties tested by PVS, and from high-yielding varieties with complementary characteristics.
  • Decide on the model (consultative/collaborative)
    • On the basis of available resources and on the crop.
    • Collaborative participation is simpler in an inbreeding crop.
  • Enter the best Participatory Plant Breeding lines in PVS trials and facilitate their entry in formal on-station trials.
  • Prepare release proposal, if success is achieved.

6. A case study on PPB in maize 

Maize is the most important rainy season cereal crop in the marginal, upland areas of the project. Farmers were given new maize varieties to try in a PVS programme. These included white- and yellow-grain types. The farmers did not markedly prefer any of the varieties to their local ones. However, some of the varieties had specific traits that the farmers wanted, so in a PPB programme six were crossed to produce a composite population.

The initial selections were made from this population based on characteristics identified by farmers, and at later stages farmers selected for themselves from populations grown by the project. Three of the most promising white-grain varieties produced from the population were then assessed in formal and participatory trials.

An outstanding new variety, GDRM-187, was one of these three promising varieties. It was bred as an extra-early maturity maize variety. When farmers tested it in PVS trials, they liked its qualities. It was very popular and high yielding in their fields over two seasons. This variety matures earlier than the earliest local varieties by about seven days. It produced fewer barren plants and larger cobs, which, unlike local varieties, are filled to the tip. Farmers also noticed that the husk completely and tightly enclosed the cobs, thus reducing insect attack. Farmers greatly appreciated the grain quality of the variety.

By using the PVS programme to identify suitable parents, by selecting for characteristics valued by the farmers and by testing under the farmers' own conditions, a new and improved variety acceptable to farmers was rapidly produced. PVS followed seamlessly from PPB.

As soon as potential varieties have been produced by PPB, farmers test them using PVS. This is an important advantage as the results of PPB reach farmers more quickly than the results of conventional breeding, where varieties are typically tested with farmers only after a long delay for on-station testing and multiplication. Delay in obtaining benefits reduces the rate of return on the investment in plant breeding. The economic value of this reduction in time can be very large.

7. Benefits of participatory plant breeding

  • Production gains
    • Yield and stability increases, faster uptake, wider diffusion and higher market value of products.
  • Biodiversity enhancement
    • Communities have wider access to germplasm, wider access to related knowledge and increased inter- and intra-varietal diversity.
  • Cost-efficiencies and effectiveness
    • Fewer research dead-ends, more opportunities for cost sharing in research and less expensive means of diffusing varieties.
  • Effective meeting of user needs
    • Higher degree of farmer satisfaction, broader range of users reached, including marginal farmers and promotion of group learning through farm walks.
    • There is often a trade off between yield and early maturity.
    • An early variety escapes common end of season droughts, and produces a harvest at the hungriest time of the year, before other crops mature.
    • It also reaches the market first, so its grain fetches a higher price.
  • A comprehensive description of the basics of PVS and PPB as two methods of participatory crop improvement is found in Witcombe, 1998.
  • An account of this and other participatory plant breeding work is available in: Stirling and Witcombe, 2004 Part 1; Stirling and Witcombe, 2004 Part 2; and Stirling and Witcombe, 2004 Part 3. 

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Maize production: ID 7018.
  • Drought-tolerant maize varieties: ID 8920.
  • Growing soybean and maize in rotation: ID 6911.
  • The role of standards in maize: ID 7020.
  • Participatory varietal selection: improved maize for western India: ID 4444.
  • Seed priming to improve stand establishment and yield in maize: ID 4450.
  • Disease resistant upland maize varieties validated by and promoted to farmers: ID 4528.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology allows for farmers in marginal areas to benefit from different crop varieties using centralized plant breeding techniques. As a result they benefit from an increase in yields and additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Participatory approaches: soaking seeds (seed priming) to improve crop yields
entries.summary: Crop establishment is often poor in the semiarid tropics. However, good crop stand establishment is essential for the efficient use of water and light, and a uniform stand is a pre-requisite for cropping success. Seeds that germinate quickly produce viable seedlings that are not dependent on rapidly declining moisture in the soil that may occur in rain fed systems. Soaking seeds in water before sowing gives the germinating seeds a head start and speeds up seed establishment with a corresponding increase in survival rates and yields.
entries.description:
Description

On-farm seed priming is soaking seed, usually overnight, in water before surface-drying and sowing. It is highly cost-effective for farmers, producing better stands, earlier maturing crops and higher yields for little cost. Experience has shown that uptake is poor without participatory evaluation.

Participatory approaches are used that involve group and community-based methods to evaluate, and where necessary modify, the technique to fit local circumstances. Pilot studies need to be supported and designed to achieve direct impact with farmers and to initiate farmer-to-farmer spread. These studies would also provide evidence to extension services and policymakers on the utility of seed priming and the effectiveness of the participatory approach to agricultural development. In order to ensure success, the work also needs to target influential bodies, including National Agricultural Research Systems (NARS), extension services, and high-profile and effective Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs).

1. What is on-farm seed priming?

  • Standard methods of seed priming, in which seed is first soaked, then dried back to its original water content, were developed for temperate horticultural and agricultural crops.
    • The approach is useful for crops where germination, emergence and seedling vigour are constrained by cool, wet soils.
    • Under these circumstances, priming advances germination by inducing a wide range of biochemical changes in the seed, the products of which persist following desiccation and are available quickly once seeds are re-imbibed.
    • Such methods are energy and technology-intensive and are generally provided by specialist companies in developed countries as “value-added” services for seeds supplied through the formal sector.
  • Priming is costly and largely unavailable to farmers in marginal tropical environments where the majority of seeds come from farmers’ own stocks or are obtained through informal, local arrangements.
    • In addition, seeds in the semi-arid tropics are sown into hot, drying soils where potential metabolic rates are high but lack of water is the main constraint.
    • In such situations the pre-hydration of seeds should be the main purpose of seed priming, although biochemical advantages may also be important.
    • Farmers can prime their own seed if they know the safe limits.
    • These safe limits are calculated for each variety so that germination will not continue once seeds are removed from the water.
  • Primed seeds will only germinate if they take up additional moisture from the soil after sowing.
    • It is important to note this distinction between priming and pre-germination.
      • Sowing pre-germinated seeds under dryland conditions can be disastrous.
    • In most cases seeds can be primed overnight and simply surface-dried and sown the same day.
    • Apart from swelling slightly and weighing more, primed seeds can be treated in the same way as non-primed seeds.
  • Occasionally, sowing may be unavoidably delayed, by heavy rain for example.
    • If primed seeds are surface-dried and kept dry, they can be stored for several days.
      • They can then sown as usual and still perform better than non-primed seed.
    • Research suggests that some of the benefits of on-farm seed priming can be obtained by using sophisticated methods of seedbed preparation and sowing.
    • Planters that ensure good seed-soil contact encourage good establishment
    • . This may partly explain why the benefits from seed priming are often more evident in farmers’ fields than on research stations.
  • Fast germination and emergence result in rapid development of seedling root systems while soil conditions in the surface layers are still relatively favourable.
    • Without early checks to growth, vigorous crops result.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Soaking seeds (seed priming) to improve crop yields: ID 6649.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for good crop stand establishment and efficiently uses water and light in semi-arid regions. It also allows increases seed planting, sprouting and survival rate.

entries.tittle: Seed priming to improve stand establishment and yield in maize
entries.summary: Crop establishment is often poor in the semi-arid tropics. However, good crop stand establishment is essential for the efficient use of water and light, and a uniform stand is a pre-requisite for cropping success. Seeds that germinate quickly produce viable seedlings that are not dependent on rapidly declining moisture in the soil that may occur in rain fed systems. Soaking seeds in water before sowing gives the germinating seeds a head start and speeds up seed establishment with a corresponding increase in survival rates and yields.
entries.description:
Description

Seed priming was developed and tested using a combination of in vitro, on-station and on-farm participatory trials. Work was done in Zimbabwe, Pakistan and India, in marginal areas where seed soaking was a known practice but was not pursued except on a conditional basis, for example when sowing was late or otherwise forced to take place under sub-optimal conditions. Seeds were soaked in water, usually overnight, surface dried and then planted.

1. Challenges

  • Initially, the objective was to improve crop establishment under marginal conditions, on the grounds that optimal, uniform stands would be able to utilize light, water and nutrients most effectively.
    • This objective was achieved early in the project but it became clear that rapid, vigorous establishment conferred benefits in addition to good stands.
    • Farmer-managed participatory trials in India with maize and upland rice (kharif season) and maize, chickpea and wheat (rabi season) were conducted.
    • Primed crops emerged earlier; flowered sooner; required fewer cultivations and less weeding; produced grain and pods faster; and became mature earlier than the same crop sown at the same time using dry seeds.
    • Farmers reported better drought tolerance and higher yields using primed seed, with yield increases of 10 to 30 percent.
  • Secondly, system-level effects were also reported.
    • There was a need for less seed per unit area (e.g. with maize 19 kg per ha instead of 25 kg per ha).
    • Reduced labour demand for weeding.
    • Greater incentive to apply fertilizer to good stands.
    • Earlier harvest of kharif crops allowed rabi crops to be sown sooner, thus avoiding the yield penalties of late sowing.
    • Earlier harvest of rabi crops allowed earlier migration in search of paid work.
    • Farmers' choice of cropping sequence was increased, allowing two short duration rabi crops, e.g. chickpea/mung bean, to take advantage of high seasonal prices.
  • Priming characteristics of wheat were determined in response to farmers who wished to take advantage of extra water made available as a result of other soil and water conservation activities.

2. The impact of on-farm seed priming

  • The impact of on-farm seed priming has not been confined to marginal areas.
  • Trials with wheat by farmers in a high potential area in India over two years also improved establishment.
  • Over 90 percent of the farmers reported a one to two day acceleration in emergence and average yields were increased by 5 percent.
  • Surveys in Musikavanhu communal area in Zimbabwe established a link between crop establishment and varietal diversity.
  • On-station trials over four seasons in Zimbabwe confirmed that a major constraint to good establishment and seedling vigour in sorghum and maize was the weather following sowing.
  • Rate of emergence was positively correlated with seedling vigour in both crops.
  • Seed priming, by increasing the rate of emergence, improved seedling vigour.
  • Farmer trials in Zimbabwe during the 1997/98 and 1998/99 seasons confirmed that priming was effective in maize and sorghum and was popular with farmers.

3. Feedback

  • Feedback from farmers in both countries and in vitro work identified other areas in which seed priming could be useful.
    • Additional collaborative work was undertaken in a number of countries.
    • A large body of research was completed in collaboration with the International Crops Research Insitute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISA) on the effect of priming on the establishment of pearl millet, particularly in relation to performance in crusting soils, where priming was found to be worthwhile.
    • Physiologists at ICRISAT also investigated in detail the effect of priming chickpea and on-farm trials in the Barind area of Bangladesh, where land was usually left fallow after the rice harvest.
    • This showed that priming chickpea seed was very effective in improving crop establishment and raising yields by 47 percent.
  • Preliminary screening of upland rice cultivars from West Africa led to more detailed research (R7189, funded by the DFID Crop Protection Programme) on the interaction between rice genotypes and priming in relation to competitively with weeds, which are the principal constraint on upland rice production in West Africa.
  • Similar research on maize/weed competition was initiated in Zimbabwe.
  • Establishment of wheat in saline soils was found to be accelerated by seed priming in in vitro experiments and collaboration began in 1998 on farmer trials to test seed priming in salt-affected areas of Pakistan.
  • The sense of ownership engendered by farmer trials and community/group evaluation ensured that adoption and uptake of on-farm seed priming technology was swift.
  • Summaries of the work on seed priming funded by DFID.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Participatory approaches: soaking seeds (seed priming) to improve crop yields: ID 4449.
  • Maize production: ID 7018.
  • Drought-tolerant maize varieties: ID 8920.
  • Growing soybean and maize in rotation: ID 6911.
  • The role of standards in maize: ID 7020.
  • Participatory approaches: client-oriented breeding of maize for western India: ID 4448.
  • Disease resistant upland maize varieties validated by and promoted to farmers: ID 4528.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for good crop stand establishment and efficiently uses water and light in semi-arid regions. It also allows increases seed planting, sprouting and survival rate.

entries.tittle: Participatory Varietal Selection: Improved Rice Varieties
entries.summary: Studies in Bangladesh found that short duration rice varieties bred by client-oriented breeding in Nepal out-performed all other varieties. Participatory research on transplanted main season (T. aman) rice in the High Barind Tract of Bangladesh identified farmer-preferred rice varieties that gave high returns, fitted with local cropping patterns that could enhance productivity and crop diversity. Eleven rice varieties were introduced from Nepal. Participatory varietal selection was used to test the varieties in mother and baby trials, by farmers in their fields using their usual levels of inputs. The rice varieties were evaluated using focus group discussion, preference ranking, household level questionnaires and in depth interviews.
entries.description:
Description

Rice, the staple food crop of Bangladesh, is grown on over 10 million ha and is historically associated with the culture, rites and rituals of Bangladeshi people. The Millennium Development Goal of the elimination of extreme poverty and hunger can only be met in Bangladesh by increasing rice productivity as it accounts for 95 percent of food grain production. Over 90 percent of people depend on rice for their daily diets and it engages over 65 percent of the total agricultural labour force. Among the rice growing countries of the world, Bangladesh ranks third in area and fourth in production. The rice-growing ecosystems in Bangladesh are diverse and modern varieties cover almost 56 percent of the total rice area. Rice varieties from the Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI) are suitable for favourable rice growing ecosystems but there has been lower adoption of these varieties in less favourable conditions.

More than 3 million ha of rice is affected by drought during both the dry and wet seasons. A considerable area of boro (winter, irrigated) rice in the High Barind Tract (HBT) is grown under partially irrigated conditions, especially in recent seasons, due to declining water tables and decreasing supply of electricity for deep tube wells. As a result, farmers desire to have drought-tolerant boro rice varieties.

The population of Bangladesh is increasing at 1.8 percent per annum and annual food deficit is 1.8 million tons. The demand for rice is rapidly increasing with the increase in population and this demand is the highest in Bangladesh among the least developed countries. Contrary to this, the increase in the productivity of rice is hardly keeping pace with the population growth rate. In the last decade rice yields have failed to increase.

1. Background

  • The HBT of Bangladesh is situated in the north-west of Bangladesh with an area of 1 600 km2 (160 000 ha).
    • The predominant soil type is silty loam to silty clay loam with very low organic matter content, high bulk density and low pH.
    • The rainfall in the area is erratic and low (average 1 300 mm per annum) and is concentrated between June and September.
    • The only traditional crop grown during the rainy season is T. Aman rice, provided that the rain arrives in time.
    • Lands remain fallow in the winter (rabi season) after the harvest of T. Aman rice.
    • In recent years, farmers have started to grow rabi season crops on residual soil moisture (e.g. chickpea, linseed, barley, mustard) with chickpea, in particular.
      • This has been successful and has been promoted by the Peoples Resource Oriented Voluntary Association (PROVA) in collaboration with the UK Centre for Arid Zone Studies (CZAS).
  • In order to ensure the timely sowing of rabi crops in November in the HBT, there is a need to identify T. Aman rice genotypes of considerably shorter duration than the commonly cultivated Swarna, but with comparable yields and grain quality.
    • Some BRRI-released rice varieties with shorter durations than Swarna are available.
    • These are namely BRRIdhan 32, 33 and 39.
    • However, these varieties have various shortcomings and have not been readily adopted by farmers in the HBT.
  • In the 2002 rainy season, seven short duration rice varieties were supplied to PROVA by the NGO Local Initiatives for Biodiversity Research and Development (LI-BIRD) through the CAZS in Kathmandu.
    • LI-BIRD and CAZS have been jointly working in Nepal to develop rice varieties using Client-Oriented Breeding (COB) approaches (also called Participatory Plant Breeding, PPB) for a range of agroecological conditions, together with Participatory Varietal Selection (PVS).
    • PVS procedures are increasingly being used to involve farmers in the varietal selection process, and thereby increase the likelihood of farmer adoption of superior varieties.

2. Outcomes

  • Participatory research on transplanted main season (T. Aman) rice was done in 2003 in the HBT of Bangladesh to identify farmer-preferred rice varieties that gave high returns, fitted with local cropping patterns and that could enhance productivity and crop diversity.
  • Eleven rice varieties were introduced from Nepal.
    • The first five varieties had previously been identified using participatory methods by LI-BIRD and CAZS.
    • The remaining six varieties were bred using client-oriented breeding by a LI-BIRD/ CAZS/ NARC collaboration.
    • PVS was used to test the varieties in mother and baby trials.
    • In these trials farmers tested the varieties in their fields using farmers' levels of inputs.
    • The rice varieties were evaluated using focus group discussion, preference ranking, household level questionnaires and in depth interviews.
  • Grain and straw yields of the SDRs from Nepal were similar to, or exceeded, the check varieties that were the farmers' customary varieties and the recent, recommended varieties from BRRI.
    • The highest yielding, Judi 567, out-yielded the most productive check variety, Swarna, by 34 percent.
    • All the SDRs from Nepal were significantly earlier than the check varieties and as much as three to four weeks earlier than the most widely grown variety Swarna.
  • Most of the new varieties were preferred to the check varieties in all locations because of their:
    • early maturity,
    • high yield potential,
    • good grain quality,
    • market price,
    • input responsiveness,
    • lodging-resistance, and
    • ease of threshing.
  • The majority of collaborating farmers intended to grow the test entries in either or both of the main (Aman) or boro (winter) seasons.
  • The demand for the seeds of new varieties is increasing in all the project villages.
  • Farmer-to-farmer seed spread was found.

2.1 Spill over effect in the boro season

  • Farmers decided to grow the SDRs during the boro season because they had appreciated their performance in the previous season.
    • They said that the SDRs overall out-yielded all the existing boro rice varieties by over 30 percent and were considered "khara sahinsh", meaning drought-tolerant, by the participating farmers.
    • There was a saving of two to three irrigations with SDRs as they matured earlier and were more drought-tolerant.
    • They also:
      • required less fertilizer,
      • were more responsive to the applied inputs,
      • did not lodge,
      • had better grain quality,
      • required less cooking time,
      • tasted better, and
      • fetched a similar price in the market to that of the best-selling boro varieties, such as Minikit.
  • Monitoring showed that 410 kg of seed of various SDRs was distributed to 67 farmers by 11 farmers in the villages.
    • This was a six-fold increase in farmer number, and averaging over 6 kg of seed per farmer.
    • The work has greatly increased farmer access to a choice of new, short duration, farmer-preferred rice varieties in the rural HBT of Bangladesh using a simple, rapid, and cost-effective approach to identifying and disseminating new rice varieties (JoshI et al. 2004); (Musa et al. 2006,).
    • An account of this and other participatory work is available: (Witcombe et al 2002 Part 1, Part 2, Part 3) and a non-specialist leaflet on the impact of similar activities is here (CAZS 2005).

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Rice transplanting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7214.
  • Rice seed sorting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7205.
  • Improving rice quality: video from Africa Rice Center: ID 6976.
  • Aerobic rice: ID 7941.
  • Intensive rice cultivation: ID 7666.
  • Rice seedbed preparation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 6973.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7210.
  • Use of Early-Maturing Rice Variety (EMRV) to reduce typhoon impacts: ID 7719.
  • Applying flexible cropping schedules for rice (t. aman) production: ID 6853.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for additional sources of food and income thanks to more resistant rice varieties being able to be grown under otherwise impossible weather and climate conditions.

entries.tittle: Participatory Varietal Selection: Improved Chickpea Yield
entries.summary: Rice fallows offer a huge potential niche for legume cultivation in South Asia. For example, chickpea yields in the High Barind Tract of Bangladesh normally remain below 1 tonne per ha due mainly to crop establishment problems and terminal drought and heat stress. At this level, the crop remains a marginal proposition for most farmers. Establishment, early vigour, growth and yield of chickpea can be improved by on-farm seed priming. The seed priming process simply involves soaking the seeds overnight (for about 8 hour), surface drying them and then sowing within the following day in rice fallows. Seed priming raised yields by almost 50 percent and reduced the risk of crop failure by half.
entries.description:
Description

The undulating or High Barind Tract (HBT) north and west of Rajshahi in north-western Bangladesh comprises some 2 200 km2. The area is characterised by clayey soils used to grow transplanted aman rice during the kharif season (July-October/November), where irrigation is not available, by fallow. Chickpea yields in the HBT are usually more than the national average due to a lower incidence of botrytis grey mould disease in this region. However, yields in most farmers' fields normally remain below 1 tonne per ha due to crop establishment problems and terminal drought and heat stress. At this level, the crop remains a marginal proposition for most farmers. Establishment, early vigour, growth and yield of chickpea can be improved by on-farm seed priming. The seed priming process simply involves soaking the seeds overnight (for about eight hours), surface drying them and then sowing within the following day. Seed priming raised yields by almost 50 percent, from 1.1 to 1.6 tonne per ha and reduced the risk of crop failure by half. The results were very impressive but represent performance in only one season. Trials with chickpea in India suggest that priming consistently improves yields, but trials need to be repeated throughout the Barind over several more seasons. If the benefits are confirmed, growing chickpea should become much more attractive to Barind farmers.

1. Promotion of chickpea

  • With the shift in chickpea cultivation away from traditional areas and towards the Barind, the Pulses Research Centre (PRC) of the Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) is giving increasing emphasis to producing chickpea varieties better adapted to the Barind environment (e.g. among other traits they are breeding for greater rooting ability, to better exploit soil moisture and nutrients below the plough-pan).
    • The Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI) also realizes the importance of using early duration rice varieties in the region, to escape terminal drought stress as well as to allow rabi cropping.
    • They are therefore encouraging development and dissemination of such varieties.
    • To promote dissemination of improved chickpea varieties, buy-back seed production schemes have been established with farmers in recent years.
  • Multi-location, farmer-managed evaluation of seed priming response was conducted at many locations across the HBT over four years (1998 to 2002).
    • Mean response to priming in grain yield ranged from 22 percent to 48 percent with responses inversely proportional to winter rainfall.
    • Priming also reduced seedling disease incidence and increased plant population, early growth vigour, plant biomass and nodulation by native rhizobia.
    • Farmers readily adopted the simple priming technology to the extent that at least one quarter of the chickpea sown in 2001 was primed.
    • Along with priming technology, improved varieties of chickpea such as Barichola 2 or 5, and appropriate fertilizer practice e.g. phosphorus fertilizer, were introduced.
    • The major constraint to further adoption was availability of seed and lack of knowledge of the improved technology outside of project areas.
    • Seed of improved chickpea varieties particularly suitable for the HBT, such as Barichola 2 and Barichola 5, were widely disseminated.
  • Techniques of seed preservation and storage at village level were successfully tested, to encourage village-level entrepreneurship in chickpea seed production and supply, and farmers trained accordingly.
    • An adoption and impact analysis of the project assessed the effects of project intervention on livelihoods of the rural community in the HBT.
    • The high and annually increasing prices of chickpea grain suggest that increased cultivation of this crop would significantly improve livelihoods in the region.
    • Reasonable yields (> 1 tonne per ha) are currently more remunerable than irrigated boro (winter) rice or wheat (these irrigated cereals have high yields but inevitable high input costs).
  • Chickpea production in the HBT proved to be the path-breaking technology for the integrated farming approach for the area promoted by BARI.
    • Farmers should be able to double their on-farm returns by growing chickpea instead of leaving land fallow.
    • The approach proposed here should accelerate adoption, not only of chickpea, but of rabi cropping in general, resulting in substantially improved livelihoods for HBT farmers (more can be found in this document)

2. Making greater use of rice fallows

  • It was considered that the success with chickpea obtained here can be extended to legume cultivation in rice fallows elsewhere throughout south Asia.
    • However, to define extrapolation domains, more precise estimation was needed of actual area of rice fallows in the region and the characteristics of such areas to assess potential for legume cultivation.
    • Graphical Information Systems (GIS) and remote sensing technology were combined to establish the potential of rice fallow areas.
  • Satellite image analysis estimated that the rice area during the 1999 kharif season was about 50.4 million ha.
    • Rice fallows during the 1999/2000 rabi season were estimated at 14.29 million ha.
    • This amounted to nearly 30 percent of the rice growing area.
    • These rice fallows offer a huge potential niche for legume production in this region.
    • Nearly 82 percent of the rice fallows are located in the Indian states of Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Orissa, and Assam.
    • The GIS analysis of these fallow lands has indicated that they represent diverse soil types and climatic conditions.
    • Thus a variety of both warm season legumes (such as soybean, mung bean, black gram, pigeonpea, groundnut) and cool season legumes (such as chickpea, lentil, khesari [lathyrus], faba bean, pea) can be grown in this region.
    • Available soil water holding capacity (1 m soil profile) for most of these lands ranges from 150 mm to 200 mm.
    • If it is assumed that the soils in these lands are fully saturated during most of the rice growing season, the residual moisture left in the soil at the time of the rice harvest may be sufficient to raise a short-season legume crop.
    • A number of abiotic (soil acidity, salinity, alkalinity, and terminal drought), biotic (diseases and insect pests), and socio-economic (social unrest, lack of awareness among farmers of legume technologies, and lack of effective policy initiatives to promote legumes, etc.) constraints contribute to the lack of cropping during this period in this region.
    • These will have to be addressed by appropriate research and policy initiatives in addition to developing suitable legume varieties that have targeted adaptation to these rice fallows.
  • A review of existing technologies indicated that it was possible to productively cultivate legumes in most of these identified rice fallows.
    • An economic analysis showed that growing legumes in rice fallows was profitable for the farmers with a benefit-cost ratio exceeding 3.0 for many legumes.
    • Also, utilising rice fallows for legume production could result in the generation of 584 million person-days (mp-d) employment for South Asia (66.7 mp-d in Bangladesh, 503 mp-d in India, 10.2 mp-d in Nepal and 3.6 mp-d in Pakistan).
    • Thus, introducing legumes into these rice fallows will have a multi-faceted impact on the economy through employment generation, poverty alleviation, food security, quality of nutrition to humans and animals, and contribution to the sustainability of these production systems in South Asia.
  • Further large-scale dissemination of optimum chickpea cultivation technology depends on its comprehensive demonstration across the entire HBT.
    • This was done in the context of the entire rice-based cropping system, by linking with the second phase of another DFID-funded project on weed management in rice.
    • This linked project promoted optimum methods of rice cultivation to enable timely sowing of chickpea or other rabi crops.
    • Appropriate methods of chickpea seed production, storage and dissemination were widely demonstrated to encourage village-level entrepreneurship in seed supply.
    • As continued chickpea cultivation on the same land would lead to build-up of pests and diseases, efforts were be made to identify alternative rabi crops with which chickpea can be rotated.
    • A participatory varietal selection programme for chickpea and T. aman rice varieties was initiated.
    • The extent of limitation by deficiencies of phosphorus, nitrogen and molybdenum was quantified across the HBT and appropriate methods for their alleviation developed.
    • Integrated pest management methods for management of pod borer in chickpea, emphasising the use of nuclear polyhedrosis virus, was further refined and evaluated on an operational scale.
  • Successful outcomes of the proposed activities will result in immediate livelihood benefits for resource poor rural households in the HBT in the medium land-holding to landless categories.
    • Anticipated diversification of the HBT cropping system, especially by increasing coverage of rabi cropping, will increase total system productivity and favourably influence the entire ecology of the region.
    • However, a cautionary note must be sounded.
    • Observations of additional crops during the 2003/2004 season clearly showed that soil fertility was low in these areas and that a second crop may not be profitable (and hence sustainable) in many cases unless more attention is paid to increasing soil fertility.
    • Since organic materials, including animal manure, in the villages were generally burnt as fuel for cooking or heating, this must entail increased use of interventions such as trees and composting.
    • Some progress has been made with limited adoption of the integration of pigeonpea on bunds, but additional work is necessary to increase the total system productivity and favourably influence the entire ecology of the HBT.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Participatory varietal selection: improved varieties of chickpea for rainfed conditions: ID 4442.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology of seed priming, through efficient seed soaking, drying and sowing, allows for increases in chickpea yield.

entries.tittle: Controlling Intestinal Nematode Infections in Ruminants with Naturally Plants Tannins
entries.summary: This practice describes how intestinal parasites can be fought through feeding livestock animals with plants highly condensed with tannins as alternative to anthelmintics, especially in areas of the tropics and subtropics. However, in many areas the provision of adequate levels of protein is particularly difficult because of the highly seasonal quality and quantity of fodder supply. An alternative option is the use of Urea-Molasses Blocks (UMB) as a dietary supplement.
entries.description:
Description

1. Background

  • Intestinal parasites are a significant problem for all livestock farmers.
    • Infections limit production and also increase the likelihood of additional diseases.
    • Poor livestock keepers, both smallholders and pastoralists, are for a number of reasons less able to purchase anthelmintics or chemical dewormers, especially for small ruminants such as goats.
    • In addition, commercial livestock farmers throughout the world have become increasingly reliant on chemical dewormers.
    • This has speeded up the development of anthelmintic resistance, and a major problem is the emergence of resistant strains of parasites.
  • Resistance to all the major classes of anthelmintics has been reported.
    • Where strains of parasites resistant to more than one drug exist, the options for treatment are seriously restricted.
    • Hot countries where parasite turnover is high and anthelmintic use may be more frequent are, generally, worst affected.
    • In many of these areas, marginal levels of nutrition in livestock lead to greater consequences as a result of infection, including widespread mortality due to nematode infection.
  • The false assumption that worm control is easy and could be accomplished only using drugs has significantly delayed the development of complementary and alternative strategies to control parasites.
    • This is particularly relevant to smallholders and poor livestock farmers who are unlikely to be able to afford to implement chemical control methods, and certainly not on a regular basis.
    • A recent survey carried out by FAO and the Office Internationale des Epizooties (OIE) in 77 out of 151 OIE member countries, revealed that over 50 percent of countries are affected by parasite resistance.
  • Due to problems the associated with the high costs of anthelmintic drugs and drug resistance, there is considerable value in nematode control methods that do not rely on extensive use of chemical dewormers.
    • Such alternative methods include selective breeding for resistant livestock, grazing management, and nutritional manipulation.
    • The use of naturally occurring constituents in forages is an alternative to expensive drugs.
    • Tannins, which are naturally occurring secondary metabolites in plants, have the ability to reduce worm burdens.

2. Tannins

  • Research showed that inclusion in the diet of the condensed tannin in Quebracho extract, reduces egg output and worm burden in sheep infected with Trichostrongylus colubriformis.
    • Studies suggested that quebracho tannin was acting through a direct toxic effect against the nematodes.
    • The Quebracho Tanin powder is prepared from a tree grown in South America (Shinopsis balansae) and is a source of vegetable tannin, used in leather curing.
    • Concentrations as low as 0.01 percent (w/v) quebracho tannin proved effective at accelerating worm death.
    • Administration of QT as an oral drench was shown to be effective in reducing worm burdens of temperate sheep infected with Haemonchus contortus and T. colubriformis.
    • These data suggest that feeding plants high in condensed tannins may be a suitable alternative to anthelmintics, especially in areas of the tropics and subtropics.
  • In The United Republic of Tanzania, a tannin containing extract obtained from wattle/mimosa (Acacia mearnsii) is used in the local leather industry.
    • Experimental results indicated that wattle tannin also has a significant effect on intestinal nematodes.
    • One part of wattle tannin (WT) powder (Tanzania Wattle Co. Ltd.) was dissolved in two parts of lukewarm water to make a drenching solution.
    • Dosage was at a rate of 1.5 g WT per kg body weight daily for three consecutive days.
    • The faecal egg count (FEC) of sheep drenched with WT solution was significantly reduced (P<0.001) and the effect was recorded within 24 hours of the first dose.
    • The effect of the drench on worm burdens was also significant (P<0.001).
    • The populations of Haemonchus and Oesophagostomum were reduced by 87 percent and 28 percent, respectively.
  • However, goats do not show the same responses and a species difference exists between sheep and goats as far as the effects of tannins on gastrointestinal nematodes are concerned.
    • Goats, deer and antelopes are among several browsing animal species that can be induced by dietary tannins to produce tannin-binding saliva.
    • This mechanism is lacking, or poorly developed, in other species including sheep and cattle.
  • The practical implication of these observations on the effect of tannins on nematodes of small ruminants is that tannin preparations, which are cheap and readily available in the tropics, could be used to supplement, or as an alternative to, the use of expensive drugs to control intestinal nematode infections in sheep.
    • At an individual farm level, individual or groups of plant species high in tannins can be encouraged and/or planted.
    • On a larger scale, the extensive use may exert an increased negative pressure on trees and natural resources, necessitating the use of dedicated plantations to derive tannin extracts.
    • However, in some areas these already exist, e.g. plantations for Quebracho or wattle.

2.1 Disadvantages

  • Studies indicate that feeding Quebracho tannin to ruminants has both ruminal and post-ruminal effects that, together, result in reduced nutrient utilisation and impaired animal performance.
  • The most widely known effect of tannins is that of reduced digestibility.
  • They also have an astringent taste, and so feeds with high concentrations of tannins are often unpalatable, as well as being relatively indigestible.
  • The low digestibility of feeds with a high tannin content is a consequence of the ability of tannins to bind with and precipitate proteins.
  • Feeding large amounts of tannins will therefore reduce the amount of nutrients actually being fed to an animal.
  • The more tannin in the diet, the greater the proportion of nutrients will pass straight through the animal and be excreted in the dung.

2.2 Potential benefits of reduced protein degradability in the rumen

  • The binding of tannins to proteins can be useful when feeding sheep and goats.
  • If the diet contains too much degradable protein and not enough fermentable energy, the rumen micro-organisms will not be able to convert all the degraded protein into microbial protein
  • . The addition of tannins in this situation would reduce the protein degradability in the rumen, and increase the supply of undegraded protein to the animal.
  • Provided the protein undegraded in the rumen is then digestible by the animal itself (e.g. in the small intestine), then the supply of potentially good quality protein to the animal is increased by the addition of tannin.
  • However, such an intervention needs to be carefully planned.
  • A possible result could be that the reduction in protein degradability only serves to reduce the supply of microbial protein.
    • Additionally, the undegraded protein remains undigested as well, eventually passing out of the animal in the faeces.
  • Clearly, in this case the supply of protein to the animal would have been reduced rather than increased.
  • Different tannins have different binding activities, and so there is no direct relationship between tannin content and protein degradability.
  • These properties of tannins make their strategic use to reduce rumen protein degradability more complex.

3. Alternatives

  • Several sheep studies have shown that improved protein nutrition decreases parasite infestation.
  • Increased protein levels in the diet increases the animals' capacity to mount an immune response and expel the worm burden from the small intestine.
    • This enhanced host immunity may be especially important with regard to selection for immunity to gastro-intestinal parasites.
  • However, in many areas the provision of adequate levels of protein is particularly difficult, because of the highly seasonal quality and quantity of fodder supply.
  • One option is the use of Urea-Molasses Blocks (UMB) as a dietary supplement.
    • UMB provide a high protein concentrated feed source, which supplies Non-Protein Nitrogen (NPN) to rumen microbes.
    • Molasses provides a source of energy and the blocks also contain important minerals and vitamins.
    • UMB are a good way of providing readily degradable protein and fermentable energy to ruminant animals.
    • They help increase the protein supply to ruminants in situations where this may be limiting.
  • Integrated Parasite Control (IPC) or Integrated Parasite Management (IPM) combines several control methods in order to slow or to prevent the development of drug resistant parasite populations.
  • This can be achieved through good management of pastures, by paying attention to the nutritional requirements of livestock, and through careful management and use of anti-parasite drugs.
  • An understanding of the life cycles and ecology of the parasites is an important part of this process.
  • Components of IPC.
    • Good management and sanitation
      • Clean grazing, clean feed, clean water.
    • Manage the natural resilience and parasite resistance within the herd or flock.
    • Pay attention to the seasonal nutritional requirements of stock.
    • Pay attention to alternative control strategies that may be applicable, and fine-tune.
  • These general strategies to the unique ecology, equipment availability and skills in the area.
    • For example, ewes require supplementation particularly in the latter stages of pregnancy.
    • If provided with adequate nutrition, including energy, protein, vitamins and minerals, will loose less condition than if not provided with supplements.
    • When individuals loose condition they are more susceptible to new parasite infections, and are less able to combat existing low-level infections.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm;and
  • subtropics, warm/mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Interventions against intestinal nematodes: nutritional and chemotherapeutic solutions: ID 4461.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

Protecting livestock animals against infections helps farmers against livestock losses.

entries.tittle: Post-Harvest Fish Loss Model
entries.summary: Planning and policy making for the development of post-harvest fisheries has been hampered by a lack of information or little easy access to information on post-harvest fish losses and tools to help plan interventions. The technology is a MS Excel model, a Post Harvest Fish Loss Model v1. It enables the user to mimic the effect of loss reduction interventions at different stages in the fish supply chain.
entries.description:
Description

Systematic and practical assessment tools are needed to assess post-harvest fish loss that could be used to generate accurate information and plan interventions.

1. Post-harvest fish loss model

  • The generic Predictive Model focuses on the two most important post-harvest fish losses.
  1. Physical loss
    • Fish or product that is discarded and not sold due to spoilage, damage or insect infestation.
  2. Quality loss
    • Quality deterioration can lead to a loss in value.
    • For example, fish is downgraded and sold for a lower price than it could have been sold for if the quality was better.
    • The value of the loss is the difference between the price attained and the price the fish would have sold for had its quality been good.
  • The Post-Harvest Fish Loss Model categorizes what happens to fish, from the time of capture, into a succession of stages and assumes that there is a transport event between each stage.
  • It enables the user to present and link data on loss at different stages in a distribution chain.
  • It is designed for people who wish to mimic a fish distribution chain and explore the effect of loss reduction interventions at different stages of the chain.
  • It enables the user to identify key losses and shows the impact of hypothetical interventions to reduce loss at the distribution stage level and on the total loss for the whole distribution chain.
  • The Model shows the role that income from the sale of by-products has on the overall chain loss and how a loss may be compensated for by income from by-products.

2.  Required data for each stage of the distribution chain

  • In order to use the model, certain essential data are required for each stage of the distribution chain. 
    • Percentage of fish physically lost.
    • Percentage of fish sold for a reduced price.
    • Price of good quality fish, price of poor quality fish and weight of fish.
  • Data is also required on the local currency to USD exchange rate, type and value of any by-products, by-product as a proportion of whole fish and weight loss due to processing.
  • The data may represent some particular sample of fish or may be averaged over several samples to represent the mean loss at each stage of the chain.
  • The data can be generated using the Field Based Loss Assessment Methods IFLAM, QLAM and Load Tracking.

3. Accuracy of the model

  • The accuracy of the Model predictions will be related to the accuracy of the data used.
  • This will be related to the type of method used for data collection and the way in which it has been applied.
  • Certain points should be taken into account.
    • The Model should not be used as a stand-alone decision-making tool.
      • It should be used as a guide to identify interventions for which a cost-benefit analysis and technical appraisal should be conducted.
    • The Model does not take into account the fact that fish of differing qualities may be entering a stage.
      • It has been developed to model data for single species of fish rather than mixed catches, where prices and loss may vary according to species.
    • The Model is designed to run from data on a single product type and chain.
      • If fish from a batch are divided after landing into some which are processed and some which are sold fresh, then the two sets of data will need to be modelled separately.
  • Once a data set has been entered it is then possible to see the effect of "what if" scenarios on the loss at the stage level and for the chain as a whole.
  • Examples of typical "what if" scenarios.
    • Physical loss during processing is reduced by x percent due to changes in the processing equipment?
    • Transport loss is reduced by better packaging?
    • Ice is used and the quality loss is reduced by x percent.
  • You may have ideas on the sort of interventions, which are appropriate for the chain in question.
  • You may have data on how much these interventions can reduce loss and this information can be used in the model.
  • If loss data are statistically valid, and representative of a target population, then it will be possible to estimate loss levels on a larger scale rather than for just the micro level.
    • The total loss level for a chain using landing data for a season or year may be of interest to planners and policymakers.
    • If the total financial loss appears to be substantial and interventions can reduce this, then estimating the potential benefits of loss reduction may attract interest and lead to more detailed cost-benefit and technical appraisals.
  • Research and development of the generic Predictive Model were conducted using MATHCAD software.
  • Any continuing development of the model would preferably be done using MATHCAD as this facilitates the evaluation of alterations.

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Assessing post-harvest fish losses: Informal Fish Loss Assessment Method (IFLAM): ID 4436.
  • Assessing losses in the fish supply chain: Questionnaire Loss Assessment Method (QLAM): ID 4438.
  • Assessing post-harvest fish losses: load tracking method: ID 4437.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology, allows for a model to be efficiently used to mimic the effect of loss reduction interventions at different stages in the fish supply chain.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows poor populations access to information on post-harvest fish losses and intervention tools. It helps increase fisheries revenue, providing additional sources of income and food.

entries.tittle: Improving the Productivity of Draught Animal Power in Sub-Saharan Africa
entries.summary: The development and modification of tillage implement designs and practices suitable for donkeys and cattle of limited draught capability was undertaken. This was accomplished through the compilation of a detailed database of animal-drawn tillage implements, an evaluation of potentially low draught implements on station and on farm, and the development of a light weight plough, now in commercial production, as well as a light cultivator.
entries.description:
Description

A shortage of Draught Animal Power (DAP) is recognized as one of the principal constraints to increased crop production in communal areas in Zimbabwe. A similar problem exists on many smallholder farms in other parts of sub-Saharan Africa. The situation in southern Africa further deteriorated as a result of the serious droughts in 1992/93 and 1993/94 in which many cattle and donkeys died. The scope for intervention to alleviate DAP constraints is through either:

  • increased supply, as in more animals, improved nutrition, health, management and use of alternative animals; or
  • reduced demand on the existing animals by use of improved implements and reduced tillage practices.

The development and modification of tillage implement designs and practices suitable for donkeys and cattle of limited draught capability was accomplished through the compilation of a detailed database of animal drawn tillage implements, an evaluation of potentially low draught implements on station and on-farm, and the development of a light-weight plough, and a light cultivator. The light-weight plough is now in commercial production. The use of a multi-disciplinary team with socio-economic, animal science and agricultural engineering skills working closely with both farmers and implement manufacturers has shown that a systems approach involving stakeholders results in an integrated project that can achieve immediate impact.

1. Development of improved implements

  • An appraisal carried out with farmers found implements to be in poor condition with most farmers having little knowledge of their correct use.
    • The survey clearly indicated the generally poor condition of DAP tillage implements with ploughs and cultivators often being used incorrectly and being poorly maintained.
    • A need was identified to consider a more detailed study to:
      • assess the condition of implements countrywide,
      • assess the knowledge of farmers and extension staff,
      • evaluate the impact of farmer and AGRITEX training courses in mechanization for small scale farmers, and
      • propose appropriate action to improve the efficiency of the use of implements and development/adaptation of draught implements.
  • This included a review of potentially suitable low-weight, low-draught and low-cost tillage implements.
    • To facilitate field testing, an animal traction logger was commissioned and staff trained in its use.
    • A database of potentially suitable equipment was prepared to provide a catalogue from which animal-drawn primary and secondary tillage implements for donkeys and cattle of low draught capability could be selected.
    • The database was compiled, obtaining draught requirements from manufacturers, when possible, and supported by field testing when draught specifications not otherwise available.
    • It included implements acquired from within Zimbabwe and imported from elsewhere.

2. Testing equipment under farm conditions

  • Preliminary on-station testing was carried out on a range of implements sourced both in and outside Zimbabwe in conjunction with local manufacturers.
    • This was followed by close collaboration with Bulawayo Steel Products (BSP) Ltd on the design and development of their lightweight draught equipment.
    • Farmer testing and appraisal with farmer comments fed back to BSP together with suggestions for design modifications.
    • These included adjusting handle height and allowing greater clearance between mouldboard and beam to avoid accumulation of trash.
    • Modifications were made and further testing undertaken before incorporation into the final design.
    • Liaison was also maintained with WALCO Manufacturing Company (Private) Ltd, manufacturer of the first prototype donkey plough in Zimbabwe, regarding design and performance factors.
  • Technical, social and economic evaluation of suitable equipment, as well as factors affecting the adoption of alternative tillage implements and practices from both the farmers' and manufacturers' perspectives, were assessed through formal questionnaires and informal discussion with farmers.
    • Field trials, both on-station and on-farm, followed as closely as practicable the FAO recommended procedures for the evaluation of primary and secondary tillage implements.
  • The development of the BSP light-weight plough provided an example of stakeholders working together to develop and implement for which a need was identified by farmers with a large potential market.
    • As a result, within the life span of this project, it was commercially produced for use as a dual purpose implement for ploughing and cultivating by donkeys and light-weight cattle.
  • The WALCO and IAE ploughs have given promising results in on-station trials.
    • Both are considered suitable for small scale manufacture.
    • Other imported ploughs have also performed adequately under some conditions.
    • Manufacturers have not yet shown an interest in pursuing these simpler designs.
    • Potential still exists but they will need to compete with the BSP light plough and there may be some difficulty in making them strong enough for dual purpose use.
  • The BSP light cultivator was also ready for commercial production.
    • It was likely to have a smaller niche market for those farmers owning donkeys with adequate financial resources to purchase both a plough and cultivator.
    • Regarding the CONTIL ripper, tool frame and attachments, considerable scepticism by farmers existed on their potential role and until problems of weed control and minimum tillage techniques were overcome, the ripper was unlikely to be widely adopted.
    • The tool frame offered considerable versatility, but was not highly regarded by farmers.
    • Under such circumstances manufacturers were unlikely to consider production.
    • Where rural artisans were able and wished to respond to individual farmer requests, these implements had the potential to increase productivity.
    • The tool frame was particularly well suited for those with inadequate draught.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: conservation agriculture: ID 7294.
  • Draught animal power technologies: ID 4535.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: draught animal power and implements: ID 7306.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: Draught Animal Power (DAP) planters and weeders: ID 7305.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: draught animal powered and motorised crop processing: ID 7307.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The technology allows for lighter labour and development of lightweight ploughs and light cultivators.

5.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for an efficiency multi disciplinary collaboration in terms of socio-economic, animal science and agricultural engineering skills working closely with both farmers and implement manufacturers

5.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology increases yields output, allowing for increases in sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Potential Yield of South Asian Small Reservoir Fisheries
entries.summary:
Lack of assessment methodology for culture-based fisheries has been identified as a major problem in the development of fisheries. The optimal stocking density, size at harvesting and fishing mortality are interrelated. Over-fishing is equivalent to under-stocking, and overstocking is equivalent to under-fishing. This model of quantitative population dynamics for culture-based fisheries increases long-term fish production and harvesting efficiency through optimizing stock and harvesting regimes. It is useful even in situations where data is insufficient for a quantitative assessment.

This technology can be described as a software package of spreadsheets, which enables management practices in culture-fishing through modelling the population dynamics. The spreadsheets can easily be adapted to particular culture systems.
entries.description:
Description

The population dynamics model is based on mathematical descriptions of the two key processes. These are density-dependent growth and size-dependent mortality. Optimal stocking and harvesting in a perennial reservoir fishery are interrelated, and must be considered together in management. The population model for culture-based fisheries can be used to predict optimal stocking and harvesting schedules for a fishery, provided that model parameters can be estimated from the available data. In practice, such data is often insufficient to estimate parameters with the necessary degree of accuracy. In this situation, judicious experimentation with stocking or harvesting schedules can improve parameter estimates and allow the optimization of both stocking and harvesting. A management strategy that entails systematic experimentation in order to gain crucial information is called adaptive management. The theoretical evaluation of stocking and harvesting schedules using the population model also provides important insights into the design of adaptive management policies.

1. Data requirements

  • A prerequisite for adaptive management is the collection of stocking and catch data.
    • This is so that the present status of the fishery and the effects of any changes in management can be assessed.
  • Stocking and catch data can be obtained easily from seed production centres and regular (not necessarily frequent) sampling at landing sites.

2. Limitations

  • The model and related adaptive management practices are less suitable for reservoirs that serve multiple purposes, including fish production, irrigation and water supply.
    • The model also needs further development of quantitative assessment tools for fisheries in perennial reservoirs.
      • There also needs to be taken into account environmental factors, either as explanatory variables or as sources of stochastic variation.
    • In larger reservoirs where big fish are produced, it may take some years before density-dependent parameters can be estimated and optimal stocking and harvesting regimes can be determined.
  • Catch data from such fisheries may be labour-intensive to get, and of limited value for stock assessment.
  • Efficient sampling techniques for the assessment of culture-based fisheries in large tropical reservoirs need to be developed.
  • Catch data alone are difficult to interpret in fisheries dominated by gillnets and other highly selective gear.
  • Studies in Laos show that strategies based on traditional pond culture manuals result in higher discounted Net Present Values than experimental strategies based on this model.

5.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology efficiently combines the use of an easily adaptable software package of spreadsheets, which increases long-term fish production and harvesting efficiency through optimizing stock and harvesting regimes.

entries.tittle: Biological Control of Armyworm (Spodoptera Exempta), Tanzania
entries.summary: African armyworm (Spodoptera Exempta) is a serious migratory pest of pasture and grain crops in Africa. Two novel control technologies are described to replace environmentally damaging and expensive synthetic chemical pesticides. The first is a process for local mass-production and formulation of S. exempta nucleopolyhedrovirus (SpexNPV), a naturally occurring biological control agent. The second is the validation of neem extracts, a locally available botanical agent. These approaches have now been adopted as national policy in Tanzania. This technology should be of interest to other African countries where armyworm epidemics are a problem (Kenya, Uganda, Mozambique, South Africa, etc.).
entries.description:
Description

The African armyworm (Spodoptera exempta) is a serious migratory pest of pasture and grain crops in Africa. Outbreaks occur every year in primary outbreak areas of Tanzania. Under favourable conditions the armyworm plagues can sweep across Tanzania and migrate to many parts of eastern and southern Africa. Crop Protection Programme (CPP) projects R6746, R7954 and R8408 aimed to develop and evaluate two novel approaches to replace environmentally damaging and expensive synthetic chemical pesticides to control African armyworm: applying S. exempta nucleopolyhedrovirus (SpexNPV), a naturally occurring biological control agent; and neem, a locally available botanical agent.

1. SpexNPV and Neem as biopesticides

  • Field work confirmed that the candidate technologies worked well in practice, and that SpexNPV could be as effective as chemical insecticides in controlling armyworm.
    • This is when it is applied at rates as low as 1 × 1012 occlusion bodies (OB) per hectare in small-plot trials using ground-based or aerial application (the first use of aerial application for any NPV biopesticide in Africa).
    • The same trials also showed that extracts of neem leaves and seeds could be used to kill armyworm.
  • While these are not as effective as either chemical insecticides or NPV, use of neem should be useful to local communities who lack access to other resources.
    • Scaling-up production of the virus for initial work, SpexNPV was mass-produced under laboratory conditions.
    • However, field trials confirmed that a viable strategy for scaling-up production of the virus in Tanzania would be to spray naturally occurring armyworm outbreaks with an inoculating dose of SpexNPV, and then to harvest the diseased larvae.
  • A Brazilian production model for NPV was identified.
    • Following exchange visits between Tanzanian Pest Control Services (PCS) and the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation (EMBRAPA) with researchers for training and advice on low-cost NPV production techniques, a modified process was developed that is appropriate for the production in Tanzania of SpexNPV at a cost comparable to that in Brazil (USD 1.50 per hectare).
    • This is much lower than the current cost of imported synthetic insecticides (around USD 10 per hectare).
  • Under the protocol modified for use in Tanzania, SpexNPV is produced as a low-cost clay formulation.
    • Simple homogenates of infected insects are filtered, absorbed onto pulverised local china clay then air dried within 12 hours at ambient temperature.
    • These are then ground and stored for use as a bio-insecticide.
    • The system does not require expensive centrifugation, freeze drying or deep freeze storage and gives a stable product (> six months at 20°C, > two years at 4°C), that can be supplied directly by farmers as a substitute for chemical insecticides in all common application systems currently used in Tanzania.
  • The technology and quality control procedures are fully documented in a production manual (Mushobozi et al. 2006a).
  • Its development is reported in published papers (Mushobozi et al. 2006b), and (Grzywacz et al. 2006).
  • The final system and scaling up approach is a product of previous NRI experience.
    • This is with local partners in commercializing NPV in Thailand and India as well as EMBRAPA’s experience at establishing local commercial production of NPV in Brazil.

1.1 Adoption of SpexNPV for armyworm control

  • Tanzania has agreed a national policy, through its National Plant Protection Advisory Committee, to adopt SpexNPV as the replacement for chemical pesticides for armyworm control.
    • PCS will continue to promote the use of SpexNPV through its own channels, and the findings of the project will inform the USAID-funded armyworm control project.
    • Neem leaf can be used in the many areas where neem is already planted as a shade tree.
  • Some 50 to 80 percent of farmers have neem trees, and their leaves and/or berries could be used by smallholder farmers to protect cereal crops.
    • The high bulk of neem needed and high transport costs mean it is not feasible to recommend its use on a large scale.
    • For strategic control on rangelands, NPV is more practical and the use of local neem is currently being promoted to farmers in several trial districts by PCS, as part of the armyworm control project funded by USAID and the Tanzanian government.
  • A consortium of partners, including PCS, NRI, EMBRAPA Brazil, University of Lancaster and CABI ARC was developed to support regional adoption and to set up a pilot production project.
    • DLCO agreed to join in regional scaling up work in East Africa.
    • Several information products, including manuals, publicity and information material have been produced (Mushobozi and Grzywacz 2006a); (Mushobozi and Grzywacz 2006b).
    • Electronic presentations were given to senior policy makers, district pest control officers and farmers groups (Mushobozi et al. 2006c).
  • Posters and leaflets are being used to raise awareness at local level in districts and among national policy makers.
    • In the previous project, longer briefing notes were developed as a briefing tool for the project outputs.
    • In this project more emphasis was placed on the posters and short leaflets that delivered the messages in simple non-technical way.
      • The project staff found this approach to be more effective at attracting interest and getting the message across at all levels.
  • The technology should be of interest to other African countries where armyworm epidemics are a problem (Kenya, Uganda, Mozambique, South Africa, etc.).
    • Kenya now has legislation in place for adoption of biopesticides as a result of other CPP activities.
    • Both South Africa and Kenya have private companies already active in biopesticide products, which could act as national or regional producers of SpexNPV biopesticide.
  • You manipulate and/or use (bio)pesticides?
    • Make inquiries before!
    • Pesticide can be harmful to your health, the health of your family, of the consumers and of the environment.
    • Adopt the right gestures to use pesticides safely: Click on “Reducing risks while manipulating pesticide”

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Crop protection: community-based forecasting of armyworm: ID 4472.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology, through the use of biological and botanical agents, not only controls crop pests but also has a positive impact on the environment.
