entries.tittle: Grain stores construction, Zimbabwe
entries.summary: In Zimbabwe and other parts of sub-Saharan Africa, farmers use grain stores constructed from grass, stalks of cereal crops and wooden poles. Some of these constituent parts are increasingly scarce. Mud plastered stores, supported on concrete-filled plastic pipes, offer the benefits of improved resistance to termites, insect grain pests and rodents. Environmental sustainability would be improved though reduction in use of scarce wood construction materials, although the stores would not be sufficiently gas tight to allow fumigation.
entries.description:
Description

Traditional grain store designs for maize and small grains have evolved over hundreds, possibly thousands, of years to combine sound practical and social features. However, as current conditions change, external pressures give rise to deficiencies in the economic and technical value of grain stores. Rural households use mature hardwood trees to construct most of the buildings in their compounds. The need to replace buildings on a fairly regular basis because of termite damage to the store fabric and, more specifically, the demand for new store construction imposed by poor access to markets, places unsustainable pressure on hardwood resources.

In addition, farmers have to travel greater distances to source construction materials. Hardwoods are becoming increasingly scarce (or are now absent) near areas of high population. Of the various traditional designs of storage structure found throughout sub-Saharan Africa, many are constructed from timber, and share common design features. Most grain stores are round or rectangular containers on a platform supported by rocks or wooden posts, from 0.3 to 1.2 m above ground. The stores are constructed from a framework of small-section round timbers, or from pliant twigs woven into baskets. Both types may be plastered with mud inside and/or out.

Stores may be protected during the rainy season with a thatched roof, supported on posts directly from the ground or raised on a platform. Whilst men usually cut and transport the timber and then construct the main framework, women are usually responsible for thatching and any plastering of the structure. Women then manage the stores, with men showing little interest in the subject.

1. Improving store durability

  • Whilst brick supports provide partial protection against termite damage, the design is not directly transferable, since it departs significantly from the traditional timber-based designs used in many parts of Zimbabwe.
  • Brick pillars also provide little protection against rodent infestation.
  • These difficulties can be overcome by the use of plastic pipes filled with concrete as supports for grain stores.
    • These posts consist of PVC pipes (110 mm diameter and 1.4 m long, with approximately 400 mm buried in the ground) filled with concrete.
    • Two pieces of galvanized wire protrude from the top of each leg and are used to secure the platform to the leg.
    • The modified legs (plastic pipes filled with concrete) are extremely effective at protecting the superstructure against termite attack.
    • They have the added advantage of excluding rodents from the store, with the associated benefits of reducing losses and preventing contamination of foodstuffs from rodent urine and droppings.
  • Storage platforms must be at least 1 m above ground to prevent rodents from jumping into the store.
  • Poles that pass through the walls of the store, which are used as a step to gain access, are not usually securely fixed.
  • This results in movement and subsequent damage to the structure of the wall.
  • To prevent this damage, reinforced steps are incorporated into the modified store.
    • A tightly-fitting door is added, to prevent the entry of pests.
    • Walls are mud-plastered to a smooth finish inside and out to minimize access by insects and to remove cracks and crevices, which could provide refuge for pests. 
Figure 1. Modified store

©FAO/TECA

2. Considerations

  • As with all improved storage structures, the success of this new store design will depend on the availability of materials and on their cost (e.g. PVC pipes and concrete).
    • In rural areas where Eucalyptus wood is very vulnerable to termite attack, mopane (in areas where this is available) should be used instead.
    • Mopane responds to coppicing and so improved management of woodland resources should take place alongside the reduction of timber harvesting achieved through the introduction of this technology.
    • The platforms and storage containers may be built under close supervision, and clear instructions left with farmers as to how they should construct the roofs.
    • Despite this, some farmers build roofs on wooden posts supported directly from the ground rather than from the platform.
    • These designs provide termites and rodents with an easy route to by-pass the modified store supports and gain entry to the store.
  • Effort is therefore needed to ensure that both store builders and users are fully aware of the reasons for changes in store design.
    • Training beneficiaries and their participation in new store design is an important part of the dissemination process.
    • The rate of traditional store replacement is a key factor in determining the appropriateness of the new store design.
    • The mean rate of replacement in Binga District was up to ten years.
    • Replacement rates increase in areas with high termite activity.
    • The cost of replacement is another key factor influencing adoption.
    • The modifications suggested here cost about USD 15 at year 2000 prices.
  • In the absence of credit arrangements, the technology would be attractive to households that are not cash-constrained and would normally expect to harvest enough grain to last well into the rainy season.
  • The mud silo design was adapted from existing traditional structure but it is not gas tight and so cannot be used for fumigation.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: improved storage facilities: ID 7308.
  • Improved pit storage method for ginger rhizomes: ID 7712.
  • Using plants with pesticidal properties to control insects during on-farm grain storage:ID 4506.
  • Storage and preservation of wet cassava: ID 4520.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Women-friendly

The technology allows women to play a more active role in storage building and maintenance.

5.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently reduces the need to replace storage, reduces travel distances, and uses local materials.

entries.tittle: Forage management: Box baling, Tanzania
entries.summary: The availability of feed resources is, in many areas, a major limiting factor to smallholder milk production. Storage and transport of conserved fodder is an integral component of solutions to this constraint. Using farmer-evaluated strategies, a low-cost, practical and economical method for transporting animal feed material was developed. The technique, "box-baling", reduces transportation costs and also increases the potential for on-farm storage of fodder. This is an example of how to increase the profitability of small-producers from cows and goats milk through improved utilisation of cultivated forages, crop residues and roadside grasses.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Milk production is increasingly more important on mixed crop/livestock smallholdings in Tanzania, where this technology was developed.
    • It increases cash income to women, improves child nutrition and produces manure for crops.
  • The same situation also occurs in many other areas.
  • However, sustainable milk production is constrained by the lack of farmer-evaluated strategies on how to make best use of indigenous forages.
  • With improved utilization of forages, livestock nutrition can be improved, particularly in the dry season when feed is generally scarce.
    • This includes both storage and transport of conserved forage.
  • At the same time, the adoption of a participatory approach to technology generation and dissemination is important, and a critical component in the uptake and adoption of the methods.
  • This project serves as an example of the benefits which may accrue from this approach.

2. Box baling

  • Maize stover was identified as the most important feed resource during the dry season in the parts of Tanzania where the study was carried out.
  • In Kilimanjaro, maize is grown 15/20 km from the homesteads and is stall-fed to livestock.
  • The high cost of transportation from the lowlands to upland smallholdings, where the animals are kept, is a constraint to its utilisation.
  • Manual baling in a wooden box increased the weight that can be carried in a pick-up truck by 63 percent and reduced the cost of transport by 33 percent when compared with transportation of loose stover.
  • Stripping of leaf, sheath and husk from the stover, together with baling, increased the pick-up load by 140 percent.
  • Baling in boxes also reduced the total on-farm storage space, increasing the potential storage capacity.
  • Labour costs and total costs of handling stover changed with baling.
  • Loose material had the highest cost per kg dry matter (DM) and bales produced using a medium sized box (75 cm x 50 cm x 40 cm) recorded the lowest cost per kg DM.

3. Box construction

  • Three sizes of wooden boxes were used in baling the stover.
  • The boxes were made by a carpenter using a 2.5 cm thick timber.
    • Large (B1) 100 cm x 50 cm x 40 cm (about 15 kg of stover).
    • Medium (B2) 75 cm x 50 cm x 40 cm (about 12 kg of stover).
    • Small (B3) 50 cm x 50 cm x 40 cm (about 9.5 kg of stover).
  • The boxes did not have a top or a bottom.
  • The medium sized box gave the highest weight per load and was therefore recommended for adoption.
  • This box was also ranked high by farmers during the evaluation of the three boxes used in manual baling of maize stover.

4. Construction of bales

  • The process of constructing bales.
    • Two pieces of sisal twine each measuring 2.0 m long were laid crosswise inside the box (at about 15 cm from the corners of the box).
    • The stover was gathered and chopped (by hand) to a size to fit in the box.
    • The stover was then compressed in the box by the labourer trampling on it until the box was full.
    • The sisal twines were tightened and tied.
    • The bale was then pulled out of the box, or the box laid sideways, and the bale pushed out.
  • While the experiments were carried out using one labourer, farmers preferred working in pairs which is a common practice in their fields.
  • These methods are illustrated in this leaflet.
    • Cut costs of feeding stover.

5. Benefits of box baling

  • The experiment on manual box-baling carried out in the present study showed that manual box-baling was more economical than the conventional practice of transporting maize stover as loose material.
  • The most economical box size was the medium size (75 cm x cm 50 x 40 cm).
    • This box recorded the highest load in 1.0 t pick-up
  • Associated advantages of the box-baling technology include space saving in the storage shed and easy budgeting of the available forage.
  • The increase in stover stored per volume was 63 percent when baling was used to replace traditional loose handling of stover.

6. Alternatives

  • An alternative baling technology use a conventional tractor driven by a hay-baler.
    • However reducing the bulkiness of the stover was found inappropriate for use by resource-limited smallholder farmers.
    • This was because of the high costs of hiring the baler.

7. Environmental considerations

  • The amount of crop residues that should be removed from fields for feeding animals and how much should be incorporated into the soil as organic manure needs to be considered.
  • The practice of conservation agriculture advocates incorporation in the soil of all crop residues in order to improve nutrient cycling and soil moisture retention.
  • Crop-livestock farmers practising stall-feeding require these products to feed their livestock.
  • In the case of maize stover, stripping the leaves and sheath, and manually box-baling them would allow about 50 percent of maize stover (e.g. the stems) to remain in the field for breakdown and incorporation in the soil.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Traditional feeding of cattle with intercropped forage Sorghum: ID 8764.
  • Treating straw for animal feeding: the Beckmann method: ID 3988.
  • Improved feeding of dairy cattle for increased milk production and income: ID 6988.
  • Development and on-farm evaluation of agroforestry livestock feeding systems: ID 4468.
  • Production of high quality silage for dry season feeding of smallholder livestock: ID 4488.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently increases on-farm storage of fodder for animals, by improving the use of cultivated forages, crop residues and roadside grasses.

10.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology reduces transportation costs and increases the profitability of cow and goats milk.

entries.tittle: Participatory breeding of superior, mosaic disease resistant cassava for Africa
entries.summary: Cassava is increasingly the main starch staple eaten in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, particularly West Africa. The crop is attacked by a wide range of pests and diseases. A major constraint to production is Cassava Mosaic Disease (CMD), caused by various cassava mosaic geminivirus species. Cost-effective participatory plant breeding methods were developed, emphasising farmer inputs, and using cassava as both a target and a model vegetatively-propagated crop. This led to the development of superior, CMD-resistant varieties through the use of seed derived from agronomically superior and CMD-resistant parents and by training farmers in selection. Knowledge was obtained on how cassava landraces evolved and spread, particularly CMD resistant ones, so that participatory plant breeding could incorporate farmer methods.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Cassava is increasingly the main starch staple eaten in Sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in West Africa.
    • The crop is subject to the ravages of a wide range of pests and diseases.
    • One of the main constraints to production throughout Africa is Cassava Mosaic Disease (CMD) caused by various cassava mosaic geminivirus species.
    • Although modern varieties bred on-station are increasingly available, cassava production in most African countries is still reliant on landraces developed by generations of farmers using traditional breeding approaches.
  • Relevant exceptions to this include Nigeria and Uganda.
    • In the latter country, an epidemic of CMD has devastated production based on susceptible landraces.
    • A very evident success of modern cassava breeding in Africa has been the release of varieties resistant to these viruses.
    • Genes for resistance derive either from a very few very resistant African landraces or have been introgressed from the non-tuber-forming Manihot glaziovii.
    • However, most landraces grown in Africa are relatively susceptible to CMD, hence the persistence of this problem.
  • In Ghana, fufu and other traditional foods prepared from cassava provide the staple carbohydrate and, with a per capita production of 450 kg of cassava per annum.
    • Ghana’s total production of cassava is exceeded in Africa only by the far larger and more populous Nigeria and Democratic Republic of Congo.
    • As well as being a source of cheap food, cassava is a crop of opportunities.
    • Markets in Ghana for industrial starch are 5 000 tonnes per annum.
  • CMD is widespread in Ghana and apart perhaps from weeds, is the main biotic constraint.
    • None of the four varieties released in the past few decades have been widely adopted, despite the importance of cassava to Ghana’s economy and despite three of the released varieties being high yielding clones resistant to CMD.
    • These three varieties had been bred in Nigeria by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) and the fourth was the result of mutation breeding using irradiation.
    • What is uncertain, however, is the extent to which these varieties have been distributed.
    • The propagation rate is only about ten to fifteen times.
    • Because of the slow propagation rate and difficulty in transporting the planting materials to distant places particularly poor, isolated areas, the improved varieties might not be in a position to make much impact.
  • The limited success of formal crop improvement/breeding for cassava and the reasons for the continuing success of landraces had not been well documented anywhere in Africa.
    • What has been documented, however, in several countries are the significant Genotype x Environment (GXE) interactions and the erratic performance of recommended varieties in multi location trials.
  • In Ghana, such breeding has focused mainly on increasing yield, selecting primarily on research station farms.
    • The main stages of the cassava breeding process at the Crops Research Institute (CRI) of Ghana comprise:
      • screening and selection of superior genotypes amongst seedlings derived from seed obtained from IITA in Nigeria;
      • clonal evaluation and selection on-station leading to preliminary yield trials;
      • advanced yield trials, uniform yield trials and final multi-locational yield trials; and
      • testing yield stability of a few clones across different ecological zones.
    • Only after these stages are completed, a process lasting perhaps a decade, have farmers been involved  with on-farm trials to validate and promote new clones.
    • Thus, farmers and other stakeholders have a largely passive role, with little direct input even to selection criteria, being involved close to the end largely to endorse the selected genotypes prior to their release by the national variety release committee.
  • Over at least the past decade, research in developing countries has indicated, for a range of seed-propagated crops, benefits of selecting new varieties from the very beginning with farmers under on-farm conditions.
    • This process, whereby farmers have an active role early in the breeding cycle, has been given the broad name of Participatory Plant Breeding (PPB).
    • As a result of the low rates of adoption of cassava varieties in Africa, it was decided to assess PPB options for the crop.
    • Novel aspects for Africa of the concept were that it involved a predominantly vegetatively-propagated crop and a main target was a virus disease, CMD.
    • This, therefore, required a participatory PPB team including breeding, pathology and social science inputs.
    • Given the success of landraces, a need to understand better how they evolved and to adopt any appropriate components were also seen as potentially important.
    • In conventional propagation, the disease (CMD) spreads in geometric proportion.
    • Since the disease is not seed transmitted, propagation through true seeds can keep the dreaded virus disease under check when farmers select landraces from true seeds.
      • This partly explains the success of landraces.
  • Ghana was identified as an appropriate country to locate the project given its very high per capita production and consumption of cassava and because of its low adoption of modern varieties.
    • Its pest problems also seemed fairly representative of many African countries.
    • In addition, it is a target country for DFID and other work had identified opportunities for utilising increased outputs of cassava.
    • Furthermore, a multi-million dollar Ministry of Agriculture and Food IFAD-funded Root and Tuber Improvement Project (RTIP) had just started in Ghana, ensuring a high level and broad range of cassava activities.
    • The CRI has a mandate for research on cassava in Ghana and the main breeding programme.
    • IITA has the regional mandate for research on cassava throughout Africa and has been the predominant actor in cassava improvement there over the last few decades.

2. Outcomes

  • Situation analyses of two farming communities in the Forest and Forest Savannah Transition Zones (Nkaakom and Aworowa, respectively) identified the main customs and practices of cassava production.
    • Cassava has changed over the last several decades from being not grown or a minor crop to becoming the main food crop and a major cash crop.
    • Much of this increase was associated with lack of new land to open and impoverished soils on previously cropped land.
    • The activities of non-farmer stakeholders in cassava breeding and how they might interact with the project were also explored.
  • The IFAD - funded RTIP project supported research and development activities in the university and public research sector and large-scale distribution of released varieties.
    • GTZ has also supported the agricultural sector generally.
    • Relatively few NGOs seem to support cassava-linked activities.
    • There is increasing industrial interest in cassava as a source of food for humans and livestock and starch as a chemical feedstock.
  • In ten diverse farming communities, no farmer interviewed understood the role of pollen;
    • Most were aware of cassava seeds and seedlings.
    • Cassava seedlings seem generally to be avoided by farmers as a source of planting material and food, often being weeded out.
    • However, a few farmers in most communities had tested a few seedlings and many farmers used them when other planting material was scarce.
    • Farming communities seldom exchanged landraces, though occasionally did so purposefully.
    • Migrant workers and settlers bringing new varieties from their place of work or previous home seem an important means by which communities obtain new landraces.
  • Seed stocks derived from diverse genetic backgrounds but including resistance to pests and diseases, particularly CMD, and high storage root yields were selected by IITA.
    • These were provided to the Nkaakom and Aworowa farming communities for evaluation and selection of superior genotypes and were sown in communal plots.
    • They were also sown at the CRI research farm.
    • Seedlings were monitored monthly by the multidisciplinary project team for agronomic and pathological characters.
    • They were also evaluated with farmers, firstly for above-ground characters, secondly for pests and diseases and finally at harvest for both above- and below-ground characters.
    • Farmers recorded a wide range of mostly positive criteria.
    • Using their own criteria, both farmers, the CRI cassava breeder and CRI pathologists, selected seedlings to retain as clones in a further trial at each location.
    • A further similar annual cycle of monitoring, evaluation and reselection of clones was conducted at each location, reducing their number tenfold over the two generations.
    • Clones have now been distributed to individual farmers.
    • The resultant clones are mostly preferred by farmers over their own landraces, being both higher yielding and less affected by CMD.
    • Farmers were consistent in their selection and overlapped that of the CRI breeder by about 60%.
  • It was noticeable that farmers selected accessions based on a wide range of positive characters, whilst plant breeders and researchers tended to reject accessions based on a few negative characters.
    • The project provided both experiential training and formal training in participatory research and plant breeding to CRI staff.
    • Similar experiences conducted in South Asia (Kerala) and SE Asia have also shown potential.
  • Full details of the work can be found here, with additional examples of farmers and plant breeders working in partnership to improve productivity and reduce poverty here.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Improved cassava fufu processing methods, West Africa: ID 4522.
  • Cassava processing: cassava wet flour: ID 3826.
  • Production of high quality cassava flour: ID 4574.
  • Storage and preservation of wet cassava: ID 4520.
  • Participatory breeding of superior, mosaic disease-resistant cassava: ID 4536.

  • Making high-quality cassava flour: ID 6923.
  • Introduction of early maturing cassava varieties: ID 8952.
  • Cassava brown streak disease: control measures: ID 7004.
  • Production of glucose syrup from high quality cassava flour: ID 4576.
  • Participatory crop improvement in salt-affected areas: ID 4592.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology efficiently uses farmer inputs, leading to cassava usage as both a target and a model vegetatively-propagated crop. The resulting CMD-resistant varieties allowed for increases in yield and improved farmer training and knowledge.

entries.tittle: Management strategies to optimise production of and access to Self-Recruiting Species (SRS)
entries.summary: Aquatic animals that can be harvested sustainably from a farmer managed system without regular stocking, are referred to as Self Recruiting Species (SRS). A range of indigenous and introduced fish species, as well as molluscs, crustacea, and amphibians are inevitably present in many rural aquaculture systems, even where attempts have been made to eradicate them. SRS resource systems operate at the interface of capture fisheries and aquaculture, involving active management and private ownership of animals during all or part of their life cycle. However they remain closely linked to the wider, natural aquatic ecosystem. The active management of wild aquatic animals on farms serves not only to increase their availability for harvest, but to conserve the natural aquatic biodiversity of rice based farming landscapes. The technology characterizes the role of self-recruiting species in different aquaculture systems, and offers management approaches that enhance the production of and access to such resources by poor populations. This practice was applied in Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Thailand and Viet Nam.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • The active management of wild aquatic animals in privately owned rice fields and ponds is widespread throughout the rice farming regions of Asia.
  • Aquatic animals that can be harvested sustainably from a farmer managed system without regular stocking are referred to as Self Recruiting Species (SRS).
    • A range of indigenous and introduced fish species, as well as molluscs, crustacea, and amphibians are inevitably present in many rural aquaculture systems, even where attempts have been made to eradicate them.
    • SRS resource systems operate at the interface of capture fisheries and aquaculture, involving active management and private ownership of animals during all or part of their life cycle.
    • They also remain closely linked to the wider, natural aquatic ecosystem.
    • The active management of wild aquatic animals on farms serves not only to increase their availability for harvest, but to conserve the natural aquatic biodiversity of rice based farming landscapes.
    • Although SRS are likely to be of greatest importance in systems managed extensively, they can also be important in intensive aquaculture systems.
  • Existing information indicates that self-recruiting aquatic animals in farmer managed systems, such as ponds and rice fields may contribute substantially to rural livelihoods in the rice growing regions of Asia.
    • However, these resource systems at the interface of aquaculture and capture fisheries have received very little attention in research, extension and policy.
    • The technology described below was one of the outputs of a research project designed to document the extent and role in livelihoods of such systems.
      • It also analysed their ecology and identified management strategies to increase, or at least maintain, productivity of and access to such resources.
    • The technologies resulting from the research comprise species lists of SRS that are popular in the study locations and SRS management techniques.
      • For example, keeping of broodstock, re-stocking of juveniles and screening (or not) of pond entrances.

2. Species lists

  • Below summarises the most important types of SRS, considering only those collected by more than 50 farmers (30 in Vietnam because fewer farmers collect SRS).
    • The climbing perch Anabas testudineus is the most harvested species in all countries, followed closely by the snakehead Channa striata in Cambodia and Thailand.
    • In Vietnam, the low diversity of SRS may be due to the fact that wild fish are rarer and more difficult to catch.
    • Types of SRS most collected in each country surveyed.
    • The number in brackets indicates the number of households that have collected each type.

2.1 Cambodia

  • Anabas testudineus (121)
  • Channa striata (118)
  • Clarias spp (119)
  • Esomus-Rasbora spp (101)
  • Small shrimp (109)
  • Spiny eels (76)
  • Frog (55)
  • Three spot gourami (52).

2.2 Thailand

  • Anabas testudineus (97)
  • Channa striata (99)
  • Clarias spp (97)
  • Esomus-Rasbora spp (56).

2.3 Vietnam

  • Anabas testudineus (49)
  • Carassius spp (41)
  • Small Shrimp (38).

Please see further reading section to find more information about management practices of a particular fish species in the online fact sheet collection.

Figure 1. Bid rent pond in Viet Nam

©FAO/TECA

3. Management strategies defined to optimize production of and access to SRS within the livelihoods of the poor

  • Assessment of the effectiveness of indigenous management measures on yield and abundance of SRS prior to active experimentation was based on an observational study.
    • For example, the comparison of yield and abundance indicators between systems where a particular management measure was practised with controls where this was not the case.
  • While these data are analysed in a way analogous to the treatment of data obtained from designed experiments, it must be borne in mind that treatments (management activities) were not allocated at random to the experimental units (individual FMAS).
  • Farmers may adopt management measures in response to the perceived status of their FMAS.
    • For example, they may chose to stock in systems of below-average SRS production, or build brush parks to restrict fishing by others in systems that are particularly productive.
  • Hence the apparent effectiveness of management measures as deducted from observational comparisons may be greater or less than the true effectiveness.
  • In the Cambodian FMAS which are dominated by SRS, building brush parks and feeding had a positive effect on catch per unit effort (CPUE).
  • In the Thai FMAS which are equally dominated by SRS, only manuring was associated with a positive effect on CPUE.
  • The research results suggest that SRS production is less influenced by management inputs than "conventional" aquaculture, which may reflect both the greater reliance of SRS on natural processes and generally lower levels of inputs.
  • Nonetheless, certain indigenous management measures such as brush parks and manuring can increase SRS abundance (CPUE) by about a factor of two.

entries.tittle: Genetically marked vaccines for improved control or eradication of Rinderpest and antigenically related diseases
entries.summary: Rinderpest is a serious contagious disease of cattle, Asian buffalo, yak and many other herbivores both domesticated and wild, including swine, African buffalo, giraffe and lesser kudu. Rinderpest is caused by a virus which is related closely to that of human measles, canine distemper, pests de petits ruminants (PRP) and other viruses in the morbillivirus subgroup of the paramyxo viruses. Rinderpest, PRP and diseases caused by the capripox virus are major and potentially economically crippling diseases of livestock in many parts of the world, especially Sub-Saharan Africa. The need to control these two important groups of diseases was approached through the development and testing of a recombinant capripox virus-rinderpest vaccine. This dual capripox / rinderpest virus vaccine protects cattle against lumpy skin disease and rinderpest. It protects sheep and goats against pox diseases under African conditions.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Rinderpest, pests de petits ruminants (PRP) and diseases caused by the capripox virus are major and potentially economically crippling diseases of livestock in many parts of the world, especially Sub-Saharan Africa.
    • The need to control these two important groups of diseases was approached through the development and testing of a recombinant capripox virus-rinderpest vaccine.
  • Diseases caused by capripox viruses are estimated to affect around 650 million sheep and goats (pox diseases) and 250 million cattle (in the form of lumpy skin disease).
    • This constitutes a massive economic burden for many resource- poor farmers in Africa, damaging their livelihoods and ability to increase their income.
    • The current vaccines are expensive and difficult to deliver as they need a sophisticated cold chain.
  • PPR is a viral disease of goats, and less commonly of sheep.
    • Historically the disease was primarily associated with West Africa, but it extends in a belt across Africa immediately south of the Sahara, extending into the Arabian Peninsula.
    • South Asia has increasingly become a focus of the disease, where the disease causes serious losses among small ruminants.
    • Control of PPR outbreaks relies on movement control (quarantine) combined with the use of focused (‘ring’) vaccination and prophylactic immunization in high-risk populations.
  • Rinderpest is a serious contagious disease of cattle, Asian buffalo, yak and many other herbivores both domesticated and wild, including swine, African buffalo, giraffe and lesser kudu.
    • Rinderpest is caused by a virus which is related closely to that of human measles, canine distemper, PPR and other viruses in the morbilli virus subgroup of the paramyxo viruses.
    • Affected animals have a high fever, erosions in the mouth, diarrhoea and rapidly become dehydrated and emaciated, dying one week or so after showing the signs of the disease.
  • Control of Rinderpest has been by mass vaccination programmes.
    • As the disease was increasingly brought under control, movement restrictions, combined with quarantine, became of greater importance.
    • Recently, in the last ten years, the FAO’s Global Rinderpest Eradication Programme  (GREP), has promoted a strategy in which mass vaccination has been withdrawn, allowing for the disclosure of reservoirs of endemic rinderpest responsible for maintenance of the disease.
    • Once detected, these reservoirs can be eliminated by intensive vaccination of the relevant cattle populations.
    • When there was confidence that the virus had been eliminated, all vaccination was withdrawn and activities focused on intensive surveillance to confirm the absence of infection.
    • According to GREP, if the disease was to be reintroduced or surface in countries currently free of the disease, it would be eliminated by a combination of quarantine movement control and focal vaccination, with slaughter of affected herds if possible.
    • Rinderpest has been largely eradicated from many countries, yet remains endemic in southern Sudan, Ethiopia, northern Kenya and Uganda.
    • In Asia it is a problem in northern India, Pakistan and along the Afghanistan border.
  • Cessation of rinderpest vaccination is an essential step in the eradication process.
    • This will necessarily be followed by a rise in the percentage of susceptible animals.
    • More animals will be at risk of contracting rinderpest and a rapid response to any disease incursion is essential.
    • Routine surveillance is also essential to the eradication programme.
  • One of the problems is that it is not currently possible to differentiate between vaccinated and infected animals.
    • Current rinderpest vaccines cannot be used in a country where rinderpest has been eliminated and that country wishes to declare itself 'rinderpest-free’.  
    • PPR virus, antigenically related to rinderpest, is also found in many parts of the world where rinderpest is endemic.
    • Rinderpest vaccine is routinely used for vaccinating sheep and goats against PPR.
  • Therefore, a genetically marked vaccine that helps animal health workers differentiate animals that have a natural infection from those animals that are vaccinated, is of significant benefit to control programmes.

2. Vaccine development

  • New vaccines have been developed at the Institute of Animal Health (IAH) in Pirbright, UK.
    • Genetically marked vaccines can be produced by altering or inserting genes at specific sites in the virus.
    • The use of a marked rinderpest vaccine would allow ring vaccination to contain any rinderpest outbreaks and assist in the monitoring of cordons sanitaire, or immune belts.
    • The researchers genetically engineered viruses and these were shown to function efficiently as vaccines.
    • These vaccines were able to protect cattle against challenge by highly pathogenic strains of rinderpest, and goats against the antigenically related PPR virus.
    • Tests indicated that animals were fully protected from clinical disease.
    • See Walsh et al. 2000. 
  • Rapid and specific pen-side tests were also developed for the detection of antibodies against rinderpest and PPR viruses.
    • Prototype devices for, on the one hand, detection of rinderpest, and on the other hand, detection of GFP antibodies (the marker used in the vaccine) are now available and have been evaluated in small scale laboratory trials.
  • The use of marked vaccines combined with appropriate pen-side tests would allow differentiation of vaccinated from infected animals.
    • This would facilitate the use of focused ring vaccination to control incursions of rinderpest and assist in monitoring of barriers or cordons sanitaire.
  • The potential to use a marked vaccine for rinderpest, along with the associated tests, now exists.
    • However, the success of the global rinderpest eradication campaign has so far meant that there is no great pressure to introduce this technology.
    • Looking to the future, this has indicated how the control or eradication of similar virus infections, especially PPR in small ruminants, can be addressed.
  • A dual vaccine against rinderpest and LSD in cattle has also been produced at IAH, and successfully tested in Kenya.
    • A similar trial was undertaken with sheep and goats for PPR.
    • A dual vaccine that can protect cattle against rinderpest and LSD, and small stock against PPR would be of great economic benefit to many poor farmers in areas of the world where these diseases co-exist.
    • The vaccine would also enable animal health workers to distinguish between vaccinated animals and those suffering from rinderpest.
    • This would be a very useful tool in areas where mass vaccination was being stopped.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Goat raising in controlled areas and vaccination: ID 8937.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

Implementing this technology protects cattle against lumpy skin disease and rinderpest and sheep and goats against pox diseases under African conditions. With improved livestock health in terms of quality and quantity, this leads to additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Tsetse control: How to deploy a target
entries.summary:
Tsetse flies (Glossina species) infest over 11 million square km of Africa and are vectors of Trypanosomosis (or Trypanosomiasis) in both humans and domestic livestock. It is estimated that tsetse occurs in over seven percent of Zimbabwe and 60 percent of United Republic of Tanzania territories. Hence Trypanosomosis has an important negative impact on livestock production in these areas. Control of Trypanosomosis has been tackled largely by control of the tsetse fly vector and a range of techniques are available, each with advantages and disadvantages. Methods include:

  • aerial spraying;
  • sterile insect techniques; 
  • insecticide treated cattle; and

odour bait tsetse traps and targets.

  • It is considered that deployment of traps and/or targets that destroy a proportion of the tsetse population will lead to a reduction in the incidence of Trypanosomosis. The following technology describes a set of simple step-by-step instructions on how to assemble and deploy a target for tsetse control.
entries.description:
Description

1. Background

  • Trypanosomosis has a negative impact on livestock production in Zimbabwe and Tanzania. There are methods to control Trypanosomosis.
  • However, a general decline in the capacity and funding of National Veterinary Institutions means that communities affected by Trypanosomosis are forced to control the disease themselves. Consequently, community-based initiatives to control tsetse has become one of the major methods of controlling Trypanosomiasis.
  • Despite many attempts by various communities, the results have been generally disappointing. There are very few examples of sustained control of tsetse being achieved by a rural community without significant financial and technical support from donors and/or national governments.
  • The causes of this failure are complex. The problem is partly that rural communities and organizations that facilitate community-based tsetse control do not have adequate access to:
    • information on tsetse control technologies;
    • information on how to apply tsetse control technologies;
    • affordable tsetse control technologies (especially in the poorest rural communities).

2. Basic principles of tsetse targets

  • Tsetse has a high metabolic rate and feed exclusively on vertebrate blood. Therefore, their survival therefore depends on detecting and encountering suitable hosts on which to feed. This principle can be exploited in the design of traps and targets hence they both:
    • mimic key features of host animals;
    • attract tsetse in such a way that they can then be captured or killed.
  • With traps, the captured fly populations can be:
    • identified
    • counted
    • sampled
    • monitored.
  • Tsetse targets simply use:
    • insecticide-treated surfaces, killing the tsetse by contact.
  • However, these are of little use in population sampling or monitoring, where quantification of the numbers trapped is required.
  • Insecticide treated targets in comparison to traps are:
    • simple to construct;
    • easy to use;
    • used in conjunction with other techniques such as insecticide treated livestock.
  • Both targets and traps methods:
    • are exposed to damage and stealing; and
    • require active participation from rural communities.
  • As techniques for tsetse control, both traps and targets function by removing individuals from the tsetse population.
  • Their efficiency depends on:
    • the length of time the devices remain operational. This depends on a number of factors including:
      • resistance to environmental damage (i.e. wind and/or damage by large animals);
      • theft of all or part of the device; and
      • component degradation (i.e. colour fade, depletion of odour baits and loss of insecticidal activity in the case of targets).
    • the likelihood that an individual fly will encounter the device and be killed or captured by it. This depends also on:
      • the number of traps or targets relative to the local abundance of tsetse; and
      • on the particular foraging and dispersal behaviour of the target tsetse species.
  • For more information see Kuzoe and Schofield, 2004.
  • Targets are deployed in the field and are made from strips of blue and black cloth sewn together vertically to form rectangle with a pocket. These colours initially attract tsetse and then elicit a landing response.
  • The traps are supplied with odours from sachets of specific chemicals placed in pockets sewn into the cloth.
  • These are synthetic chemicals based on those identified in animals from research into the chemical composition of cow's breath that contains chemicals to which tsetse flies are attracted.
  • The most commonly used chemicals, used in lures to provide specific release profiles are:
    • Octanol
    • Methyl Ethyl Ketone (MEK).  
  • To attract the tsetse fly the target is designed to look, smell and feel like a cow. The tsetse lands on the target to obtain a blood meal, instead picks up a lethal dose of Deltamethrin or Alphacypermethrin insecticide from the sprayed target has been. Any other insects landing on the targets are also likely to be affected by the insecticides.

3. Instructions on how to deploy a tsetse target

  • Pick a clear area, see Figure 1.
Figure 1. A clear area

©FAO/TECA

  • Clear the site, see Figure 2.
Figure 2. Clear the site

©FAO/TECA

  • Ensure that all the vegetation has been removed - this will protect against fires, see Figure 3.
Figure 3. Remove vegetation

©FAO/TECA

  • Select some suitable poles and trim them, Figure 4.
Figure 4. Poles selection and trimming

©FAO/TECA

  • You need poles soft wire, attractants, insecticide and basic tools - and a target of course, see Figure 5.
Figure 5. Basic tools

©FAO/TECA

  • Lay the target on the ground so that you can see where to place the poles, see Figure 6.
Figure 6. Lay the target on the ground

©FAO/TECA

  • Mark each end, see Figure 7.
Figure 7. Mark each end

©FAO/TECA

  • Dig a hole for each pole, see Figure 8.
Figure 8. Dig a hole for each pole

©FAO/TECA

  • Insert the pole and ensure it is secure, see Figure 9.
Figure 9. Insert the pole

©FAO/TECA

  • Attach the target to the pole, see Figure 10.
Figure 10. Attach the target

©FAO/TECA

  • Repeat this process for the other edge, see Figure 11.
Figure 11. Attach the other edges

©FAO/TECA

  • Do the same with the other two corner, see Figure 12.
Figure 12. Attach the corner

©FAO/TECA

  • It should look like Figure 13.
Figure 13. How it should look like

©FAO/TECA

  • Do not fasten the target like Figure 14 but fasten it like Figure 15.
Figure 14. Target should not be fastened like this

©FAO/TECA

Figure 15. How the target should be fastened

©FAO/TECA

  • For Morsitans species, you should bait the target with acetone, octenol and, possibly, phenols.
Figure 16. Bait the target with Acetone

©FAO/TECA

  • You can attach the acetone bottle like Figure 17; it is less likely to spill or be lost.
Figure 17. How to attach the bottle

©FAO/TECA

  • Place Theoctenol-Phenol sachet in the pocket provided.
Figure 18. Place theoctenol-phenol sachet in the pocket provided

©FAO/TECA

  • If the target has not been treated with insecticide, then you need to do so, Figure 19.
Figure 19. Treat the target with insecticide

©FAO/TECA

  • Soaking the screens has a long-lasting action. It is recommended to always use protective clothing when handling insecticides. In Figure 19, the recommended boots are not visible, however those should be used as per Health and Safety Precautions (CIRAD, personal communication, 2006).
  • Make a note of when and where the targets are deployed - you will need to find them again to keep the target in good working order, Figure 20.
Figure 20. Make notes

©FAO/TECA

Figure 21. The target is finished

©FAO/TECA

4. Environmental impacts

  • The environmental impacts of tsetse targets depend on the use of insecticides designed to kill tsetse attracted to the targets.
  • Studies by De Garine-Wichatitsky et al., 2001 in Kasungu National Park, Malawi, indicate that there may be wider environmental impacts, particularly on:
    • some bird species; and
    • pollinating insects, especially non-target horseflies attracted to the tsetse targets hence:
      • care should be taken over the location of insecticide treated targets.
  • However, the impact of insecticide impregnated tsetse targets is likely to be less in comparison to alternative control strategies such as aerial spraying.
  • The shape and colour of targets and the blend of tsetse attractants are specifically designed to attract tsetse flies but some other biting flies are also attracted, in particular:
    • phenols attract some species of horsefly;
    • Octenol attracts some species of stable fly;
    • blue or black targets attract both horseflies and stable flies.
  • However, the populations of the species mentioned above are not greatly reduced by targets. The slow rate at which tsetse reproduce means that only they are susceptible to the low mortality rates (less than ten percent per day) produced by insecticide-treated targets. For more information on this topic see the environmental impact of tsetse control on www.tsetse.org.
  • By using traps, tsetse can be trapped and disposed of without the use of insecticide. This alternative to insecticide treated targets requires:
    • careful deployment;
    • regular attention; and
    • maintenance checks by the local community.
  • To minimise environmental impact, insecticide or used empty containers should not be dispersed in any of the following:
    • ponds
    • waterways
    • ditches.
  • Although Pyrethroids are relatively safe in the environment, release of concentrates directly into waterways could cause significant problems to fish and freshwater invertebrates.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Tsetse control: how to make a plastic cage for tsetse traps: ID 4514.
  • Tsetse control: how to use Tsetse traps with an odour dispenser: ID 4507.
  • Tsetse Muse: helping planners to design cost-effective tsetse control strategies: ID 4482.
  • Tsetse control using Epsilon trap made: ID 4508.
  • Tsetse control: insecticide treatment of cattle: ID 4419.
  • Risk reduction while manipulating pesticide: ID 8348.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Women-friendly

The above technologies are easy to implement and accessible to all.

7.2 Pro-poor technology

This technology helps poor farmers in fighting tsetse and preserving their livestock production.

9. Specific health and safety precautions

Any use of insecticides must be carried out with due care and attention to manufacturers guidelines.

During application or spraying of insecticide, wear overalls and boots. Avoid exposure to any spray mist and try not to spray into the wind. Avoid contact with the mouth, skin, and eyes. Wash off any skin contamination immediately using soap and water. Many pyrethroid formulations can cause skin irritation or sensitisation, usually manifested as tingling, burning or numbness. This provides a useful early warning of skin contamination. If eyes are contaminated, flush immediately with plenty of clean water and obtain medical attention.

If clothes or overalls become contaminated, remove them without delay and wash well the skin areas affected (some insecticides are more resilient to washing than others; CIRAD pers. comm. 2006) Thoroughly wash the clothes with detergent or soap before re-use. Wash hands and exposed skin before smoking, eating, drinking or using the toilet. It is advisable to take a shower or bath after working with any insecticides. Store surplus or unused material, tightly closed, in the original container, out of reach of children and away from food or animal feed. Do not contaminate ponds, waterways or ditches with insecticide or used and empty containers. Although pyrethroids are relatively safe in the environment, release of concentrates directly into waterways could cause significant problems to fish and freshwater invertebrates.

Empty all chemical containers completely and burn them in a suitable incinerator or bury them at a distance from any natural water sources. Whilst this is standard advice from manufacturers, it known that often good empty containers are rarely destroyed in this way and may subsequently be used for a variety of purposes. It is therefore the responsibility of all supervisors and field operators to make sure that empty insecticide containers are thoroughly washed repeatedly with water and then never used to hold drinking water or foodstuffs.

entries.tittle: Storage and preservation of wet cassava
entries.summary: Highest grades of cassava starch are processed from freshly extracted starch. In many cassava processing factories, extracted starch is stored in tanks under wet conditions during the peak harvesting period (two to five months). Long-term storage of cassava starch under wet conditions results in adverse quality changes which reduce the grade and sale price of the resultant dry starch. This simple technology was able to maintain the quality of cassava starch during storage.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

Starch production from root crops is a long established industry and in southern countries half of the starch produced is extracted from cassava, representing a major market for small scale root crop producers. Processing of cassava using wet roots is preferable and results in a higher quality product, since it is very difficult to remove the outer skin from the dried roots and, therefore, the starch made from dried roots is always dark.

One of the problems facing small to medium scale cassava starch producers in India was wet storage of cassava starch. Cassava starch which cannot be processed immediately (approximately 40 percent of production), is transferred to open concrete tanks for storage under wet conditions. Long-term storage (three to four months) of cassava starch under wet conditions results in adverse quality changes, which are reflected by a reduction in the grade and hence the sale price of any products made from the starch.

Long term storage of cassava starch results in a number of adverse quality changes. As identified by the industry, these are:

  • reductions in starch paste viscosity after storage;
  • loss of starch (in terms of wet weight) during wet storage;
  • losses resulting from poor settling of stored starch;
  • reduction in optical clarity and discolouration of starch pastes and products prepared from stored starch; and
  • unpleasant odour arising from pastes prepared from stored starch.

A detailed study of the microbiological and physiochemical changes showed that the quality losses during wet storage were attributable to the growth of amylolytic lactic acid (ALA) bacteria. As the storage progressed the number of lactic acid bacteria showing amylolytic activity increased and the pH value fell indicating the production of organic acids.

The wet storage also resulted in the reduction in the peak viscosity and hot paste stability of the starch. The swelling power values were reduced whilst solubility and reducing values increased, indicating microbial attack on the starch granules affecting the functional properties of the starch. Enzymic degradation of the starch explains the reduction in viscosity and paste stability.

During wet storage, ALA bacteria attack the starch polymers in the granules releasing soluble sugars which are used as an energy source for the bacteria. When the starch is washed after storage any soluble material present dissolves in the process water and is lost, hence the reduction in weight as a result of storage which amounts to about a 10 percent loss for the industry. Wet stored starch does not settle as well as fresh starch after washing, with the result that a further 10 percent (by weight) of starch is lost into the waste tank.

2. Improved storage methods

This simple technology helps maintaining the quality of cassava starch during storage.

  • Low concentrations of acetic acid (2 percent) can be used to prevent the growth of amylolytic lactic acid bacteria.
  • Other treatments such as citric and phosphoric acid could prevent microbial growth, but these acids adversely affected the quality of the starch.
  • The treatment of starch with 2 percent acetic acid during storage resulted in a product with viscosity 32 percent higher than the minimum value specified in the Indian standard for textile starch, whereas conventionally stored starch had a viscosity value 14 percent below the minimum value.
  • Two additional advantages of the improved storage technique were demonstrated that were not previously evident.
  • Physical losses of around 10 percent (by weight) were quite typical of conventional starch storage.
    • These were probably caused by starch degradation since increases in soluble sugars have been detected.
  • Storage of starch with acetic acid (2 percent) eliminated this weight loss.
  • In addition to this 10 percent loss of product with conventional storage and processing, an additional 10 percent of the starch was lost during re-washing and sedimenting before final sun-drying.
  • When artificially acidified stored starch was processed, this loss was reduced to 3.75 percent (Marder et ai, 1996; Graffham et ai, 1998).

2.1 Acetic acid concentration

  • The optimum concentration of acetic acid needed to prevent the growth of the lactic acid bacteria was found to be 2 percent v/v.
  • The stored starch should be washed thoroughly to remove the acid prior to further processing.
  • A lower concentration of acetic acid did not prevent the growth and higher concentrations caused problems with washing the acid out after storage.

2.2 Construction of storage tanks

  • In order to maximise the efficiency of the storage technique, tank walls should be lined with high quality cement to reduce the risk of leaks resulting from erosion of cement by the acid.
  • A plastic liner sheet would help to minimise contact of acid with the tank walls.
  • Evaporation, an important factor, can be minimised by using deep tanks with dimensions that offer minimum surface area for evaporation.
  • Large tanks should be sub-divided into smaller compartments to reduce acid consumption during starch loading over a period of several weeks.
  • Tanks should also be covered with a plastic sheet to further reduce evaporation and prevent entry of water which will reduce the concentration of acid in the tank.
  • To regulate the temperature and to have a better control of the fermentation it will be necessary to bury the storage tank (CIRAD, pers. Comm., 2006).

3. Environmental impact of the technology

  • The effluent produced when acidified starch was washed had a pH value similar to that of effluent produced from washing of unacidified starch.
  • Acidity levels in all samples were below detectable limits indicating that acidified storage did not cause a significant impact on the environment around starch factories.
  • The effluent from acidified starch had a significantly lower BOD value and greatly reduced level of dissolved solids (55 percent lower than conventional effluent).

4. The benefits of this technology

4.1 Improved recovery of starch

  • Starch factories expect to lose around 10 percent (by weight) of wet stored starch as a result of storage.
  • With the treatment of acetic acid (2 percent v/v) there was no reduction in weight of starch recovered.
    • This saving more than compensated for the cost of acidifying the starch.

5. Reduction of losses during settling

  • Starch factories expect to lose a certain amount of wet stored starch during processing as a result of poorer settling properties when compared to fresh starch.
  • When unacidified starch was washed, 10 percent of the starch failed to settle in the settling tank and ended up in the effluent tank.
    • This starch is collected and sold as low-grade starch at a greatly reduced price.
    • When the acidified starch was washed only 3.75 percent of the starch failed to settle, thereby increasing the yield of higher quality starch.
  • Improved colour and odour of starch and starch paste.
    • Unacidified wet stored starch has an unpleasant odour which reduced its sale price.
    • It also has a blue grey colour and produces pastes that look cloudy and had a greyish colour.
  • In contrast, acidified starch had no odour (after washing) and was bright white in colour.
    • Pastes prepared from acidified starch were translucent and showed no sigh of discolouration.
  • Improved optical clarity and absence of discolouration will improve the price of the starch, if it is sold for use in the textile industry.

6. Paste viscosity

Acidification of starch prior to storage prevented reductions in paste viscosity.

7. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Cassava processing: cassava wet flour: ID 3826.
  • Production of high-quality cassava flour: ID 4574.
  • Participatory breeding of superior, mosaic disease resistant cassava for Africa: ID 4513.
  • Production of glucose syrup from high-quality cassava flour: ID 4576.
  • Improved cassava fufu processing methods, West Africa: ID 4522.
  • Participatory breeding of superior, mosaic disease ­resistant cassava: ID 4536.
  • Sustainable livelihoods: new market opportunities for cassava: ID 4575.
  • Making high­-quality cassava flour: ID 6923.
  • Introduction of early maturing cassava varieties, a cost-­benefit analysis: ID 8952.
  • Cassava brown streak disease: control measures: ID 7004.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2520.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

9.1 Women-friendly

The practice is easy to use and can be undertaken by all kinds of manual-labour.

9.2 Resource use efficiency

The practice maintains cassava starch quality in the long term, through improved storage methods. 

9.3 Pro-poor technology

The practice allows for improved quality, grade and sale price of starch, leading to additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Small-scale starch extraction: hydrocyclone for improved process efficiency
entries.summary: Root starch production is a long-established industry that has seen little development in recent years. In developing countries it has been estimated that five million tonnes of starch are produced annually in developing countries, half of which is produced from cassava representing a major market for small-scale root crop growers. By using static starch extraction centrifuges (hydrocyclones), water can be reduced by 50 percent as well as pollution of waste water.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

1.1 Starch extraction process

Starch extraction process includes the following main stages:

  • root washing;
  • root rasping;
  • screening;
  • starch settling.

1.2 Scales of starch extraction facilities

  • In very small or cottage scale mill, the entire process is manual.
  • In a small-scale mill the rasping operation is mechanised and simple settling tanks are used.
  • In a medium-scale mill mechanised operations include washing, rasping and screening stages.

After rasping fresh cassava roots a series of washing and screening stages separate fibrous pulp material from the extracted starch, which is then collected in a water suspension tank (starch milk).

Traditionally, in small to medium-scale factories:

  • Starch milk flows into tanks where the starch settles.
  • After settling the supernatant liquid is discarded and the starch cake removed for drying.

1.3 Water demand

During rasping and screening operations there is a large demand for water.

  • Rasping stage requires a variable volume of water.
  • Washing stage requires large volumes of water to freed starch from the rasped roots.

Consequently, settling tanks require large areas for construction and generate large volumes of effluent causing considerable waste liquid disposal problems.

1.4 Disposal of waste liquid

The effluent is heavily polluted, containing significant levels of:

  • starch
  • sugar.

Effluent is often discharged directly to:

  • nearby watercourses or at best to land.

The starches and sugars decomposition causes:

  • environmental damage in terrestrial ecosystem;
  • oxygen depletion in aquatic ecosystems.

There is widespread concern on the quantity and quality of effluent discharged by cassava starch factories and their effect on local watercourses, particularly in India and Thailand.

1.5 Starch recovery efficiency

The loss of starch represents a waste of the primary product. Solid waste residues typically amount to 20 percent of the weight of starch entering the process, this figure can be higher in less effective processes. Although the residue is often used as an ingredient in animal feeds, its high starch content still offers considerable scope for use by increasing primary product recovery.

Starch recovery efficiency varies accordingly to the production plant capacity:

  • High capacity mill has an overall of 75 to 93 percent recovery efficiency.
  • Small and medium-scale mill has 61 to 68 percent recovery efficiency.

Most published research tends to cite the overall starch recovery of the process, a measure of both the rasping effect and the efficiency of starch separation.

Total starch recovery  =  rasping effect +  efficiency of starch separation

All that can be inferred from the overall starch recovery figure is that the rasping effect is greater than or equal to the starch recovery figure.

rasping effect  ≥  starch recovery

It is estimated that by going through the Jahn rasper machine once:

  • rasping effect is 85 percent; and
  • starch extraction efficiency varies between 70 and 90 percent.

1.5.1 Starch recovery strategic issues

Process audits on cassava starch and sago industry of the Salem district in Tamii Nadu, India and in Brazil, identified three common strategic issues, namely:

  • low starch extraction efficiency;
  • high water consumption; and
  • pollution from effluent discharge.

In addition:

  • wet storage of cassava starch.

In India, wet storage of cassava starch was one of the major problems facing by small to medium scale sago and starch producers. Root crushing capacity exceeded the capacity for processing, as a result of limitations on the area available for sun drying and availability of sunlight.

Cassava starch that could not be processed immediately (approximately 40 percent of production) was stored in open concrete tanks, under wet conditions.

Long-term storage (three to four months) of cassava starch under wet conditions resulted in adverse quality changes, which were reflected in a reduction in the grade, and hence sale price of products (including sago), made from the starch.

The estimated economic loss to the sago industry in 1992/93, resulting from wet storage, was between five and seven percent.

1.5.2 Starch recovery - disintegrating methods

Research confirmed that starch extraction efficiency was primarily a function of the method of disintegrating the roots.

Three methods of disintegration were evaluated:

  • traditional rasping;
  • hammer milling; and
  • mincing.

The traditional rasping method proved to be the most effective.

In addition, the application of hydrocyclone was investigated to:

  • reduce water consumption; and
  • minimise effluent generation.

2. Improved efficiency in starch extraction using hydrocyclone technology

Hydrocyclones divide a fluid stream into two output streams. They act as static centrifuges in which concentrate the liquid suspension into the underflow, with low solids in the overflow stream.

A hydrocyclone consists of:

  • a cone shaped body; and
  • upper cylindrical section (polyurethane) composed by:
    • feed opening on the side of the section;
    • central opening (vortex finder) on the top of the section.

2.1 Hydrocyclone motion process

  • The slurry or suspension is fed tangentially to the cylindrical section around the vortex finder.
  • The motion of the liquid fed into the cyclone develops high centrifugal forces creating a primary vortex driving:
    • heavier suspended particles from the cyclone wall downwards to the discharge point via a spigot.
  • A secondary vortex develops along the central axis forcing:
    • finer suspended particles from the cyclone wall upwards into the vortex finder together with the majority of water.

For further details see 'Wet cassava storage and preservation' by Marder, R. and Trim, D (undated).

2.2 Laboratory trials results

The techniques were adapted and field trials conducted in India and Colombia, showing that:

  • over 60 percent of the water used could be re-cycled, with a reduction of the total water consumption; and
  • over 50 percent reduction in the volume and loading of effluent.

Successful long-term confirmatory trials were carried out in India under commercial factory operating conditions for the production of sago and starch.

There was no financial benefit to be obtained by operating the hydrocyclone, however:

  • operation cost may be offset by the savings made from water recycling; and
  • environmental benefits resulted from the reduced effluent volumes.

Together with the broader socio-economic issues it was established there was a case for the wider-scale promotion and adoption of this technology (Marder et al., 1996).

Overall, the hydrocyclone can be used as part of an integrated pollution control strategy, by:

  • conserving water;
  • reducing effluent generation; and
  • maintaining product quality and production levels.

With over 1 000 cassava starch processing units in South India, the wide scale adoption of the technology would considerably reduce environmental impact and benefit producers in areas of water scarcity.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Make bitter cassava safe for consumption: ID 4372.
  • Storage and preservation of wet cassava: ID 4520.
  • Production of high-quality cassava flour: ID 4574.
  • Sustainable livelihoods: new market opportunities for cassava: ID 4575.
  • Production of glucose syrup from high-quality cassava flour: ID 4576.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology contributes to resources use efficiency of starch, as well as reducing environmental impact.

5.2 Pro-poor technology

Starch production can guarantee an additional income source for poor farmers.

entries.tittle: Control of foreign fishing
entries.summary: Control of Foreign Fishing (CFF) explores options available to coastal states. It seeks to find the optimal combination of fee level, surveillance expenditure, and magnitude of legal penalties to minimize the risk of illegal fishing and maximize the benefits accruing to the coastal state. It provides an economic model that facilitates integration of these complex issues, so that costs and benefits of different Monitoring and Surveillance Strategies (MCS) can be assessed.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Distant water fishing fleets may undertake illegal fishing both in the high sea and the exclusive economic zones (EEZ).
    • Coastal states have to protect their fish resources through monitoring and surveillance (MCS).
    • Licensing of foreign vessels can provide the necessary funds for governments to regulate and monitor fishing activities in the EEZ.
  • Control of Foreign Fishing (CFF) enables coastal states to search for and select the optimal combination of fee level, surveillance expenditure, and magnitude of legal penalties, to minimize the risk of illegal fishing and maximize the benefits accruing to the coastal state.
    • This economic model facilitates integration of these complex issues so that costs and benefits of different MCS strategies can be assessed.
    • National case studies indicated that, in the short-term, potential increases to the total state revenue from foreign fishing activity are more likely to occur from increased compliance and the number of licences sold, rather than a direct increase in licence fee.
  • Over the medium to long-term, acquiring additional fishery information should take priority, providing more precise data on the variability and value of the resources taken within the EEZ, by licensed and illegal vessels.
    • Additional surveillance is required to check the veracity of catch reports and make sure there are no unreported incursions at the edge of the zone.
      • Once detection within the EEZ is perceived to be more likely, more licences may be purchased.
    • Lessons Learned Modeling approaches, such as the one described by MRAG (2006), may have value in assisting developing coastal states and in making rational and informed decisions about foreign fishing access to their waters.
  • While each case is undoubtedly different, and optimal decision-making should be based on detailed analyses of specific data, application of the model in a range of examples has provided a number of common lessons learned.
    • It is important to impose large fines for illegal fishing activities.
  • Funds available in developing coastal states to support surveillance activities are often limited.
    • If there were significant potential benefits for foreign fishers within the coastal state’s EEZ, then it is reasonable for the coastal state to set relatively high licence fees.
    • This is only possible, however, provided the expected fine faced by the fishers for fishing illegally considerably exceeds the licence fee.
    • Furthermore, if the amount of surveillance that can be afforded is strictly limited, this can only be assured by imposing very high penalties, potentially including the forfeiture of the catch and vessel.
    • Although high values of maximum net revenue can be obtained from fine proceeds alone, this could lead to unpredictable and unsustainable levels of revenue and put the status of the resource at risk of over-exploitation.
  • While it is important to set penalties as high as possible, the proceeds from fines should not be regarded as a long-term source of revenue in the same way as proceeds from license fee are.
    • Access to a fishery is limited, when necessary, for the purpose of achieving conservation targets;
      • This is not so that revenue can be generated from catching vessels fishing illegally.
    • By basing revenue expectations on the opportunity to impose fines without addressing the central problem of illegal vessels catching too many fish, the stock comes under increased pressure and risk from overfishing.
    • The management aim should therefore be to strongly deter any unlicensed fishing.
    • Only if this is successful, thereby effectively eliminating revenues from fines, will there be a long-term sustainable fishery from which licence revenue can be generated sustainably.
  • Estimates need to be made of the probabilities of detection and successful arrest of unlicensed fishing vessels arising from different levels of surveillance activities.
    • The perceived and actual probability of detecting illegal vessels can be very different.
    • Even though the actual level of surveillance may remain constant, examples indicate that it may be only after a highly publicized and high fine imposed on one vessel caught fishing illegally, that the perceived probability of detection increases and hence licence applications increase.
  • The perceived risk of being detected and fined must rise to a level at which the expected fine exceeds the cost of obtaining a licence, even though the actual risk may not have changed at all.
    • Following a high profile surveillance operation, it is important that the perceived increase in the probability of detection is maintained.
    • This can be achieved, for example, by increasing the number of patrols throughout the year to enhance the appearance of surveillance, thereby maintaining or increasing the perception of the probability of detection.
  • Depending on how the extra surveillance effort is applied, this may also elevate the actual probability of detection.
    • A degree of targeting can be used to increase the chance of detection during surveillance patrols by making use of reports from other sources that illegal fishing activities are occurring (e.g. overflights, or on-board observers).
    • Increasing the efficiency of surveillance can substantially reduce the cost as a proportion of the licence revenue.
    • When the maximum fine is reduced, surveillance can be increased to compensate by increasing the probability of detection and thereby maintaining the level of expected penalty.
  • Under these circumstances, the cost of surveillance can approach the total revenue from licence fees, hence net revenue may be reduced to zero.
    • Where the deterrence of illegal fishing is the primary management issue, affordable surveillance is therefore vital.
    • If the maximum fine must be reduced, and the cost of surveillance must be kept constant, to maintain the perceived level of expected penalty, the efficiency of surveillance must be improved.
    • Very high fines may be impossible to collect in practice.
    • Vessel owners may choose instead to forfeit the vessel, particularly when vessel value is low.
    • The value of the vessel may be the best estimate of the maximum possible fine.
    • It is better to calculate licence fees as a proportion of the marginal benefit arising from fishing inside the EEZ, rather than as a proportion of the catch taken inside the EEZ.
    • This is because the value to the fishers of obtaining a licence arises from the difference between the catches that can be taken inside and those taken outside, rather than just the amount of catch taken from the EEZ.

2. Results

  • Results from the case studies showed that strong inter-annual variability could occur from the expected benefits of fishing inside the zone.
  • In calculating appropriate levels of licence fee, average estimated benefits were mainly used, but this meant that in some years the cost of a licence was greater than the expected benefits.
  • If this were to occur several years in a row, foreign fishers may become reluctant to renew their licences.
  • Under these circumstances, it might be necessary to develop innovative solutions to the problem.
  • Additional benefits can be generated from alternative sources of revenue.
  • In addition to the two sources of revenue commonly used in models.
    • From the sale of licence fees and fines generated from successfully prosecuting illegal vessels, there are a number of other benefits that can be generated from foreign fishing activities such as transhipment fees and port facilities offering goods, services and value added processing.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Management guidelines for Asian floodplain river fisheries: ID 4477.
  • Trainer's guide to control blowfly infestation of traditionally processed fish: ID 4464.
  • Potential yield of south Asian small reservoir fisheries: ID 4474.
  • ParFish toolkit: a participatory fisheries stock assessment approach: ID 4476.
  • Management of flood control, drainage and irrigation (FCDI) sluice gates: ID 4479.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently combines a series of practices of fee level, surveillance expenditure, and magnitude of legal penalties. This leads to optimal risk minimization of illegal fishing and fishermen benefit maximization.
