entries.tittle: Sustainable agriculture in forest margins in Bolivia
entries.summary: Declining soil fertility, increasing weed infestations and a lack of income-generating opportunities are serious constraints to the establishment of sustainable cropping systems and livelihoods in the forest margins of Bolivia. Systems which allow farmers to progress: from unsustainable, migratory (shifting) slash, and burn agriculture to more sustainable and stable farming systems are needed. Sustainability was addressed through an increased cropping period for annual crops, increased opportunities for perennial crops, the development of sequences towards perennial systems, improved weed control, integration of legume covers/green manures and economic sustainability through diversification.
entries.description:
Description

Agricultural production which is dependent on the clearing of forested land is common in many countries located in the humid tropics. Slash and burn (shifting) agriculture, as practised by indigenous forest dwellers, can be ecologically sensitive, sophisticated and sustainable. In contrast, the slash and burn methods used by colonist farmers in Brazil and Bolivia are unsustainable and destructive and have resulted in the degradation of soil, forest and biodiversity resources over large areas. The process has serious long-term economic and environmental implications.

Smallholder colonist farmers in Santa Cruz, Bolivia, are recognized to be among the core poverty groups of the country. They often have relatively abundant land (30 to 50 ha) but extremely limited capital and labour, and an immediate requirement for food and cash. This leads to the adoption of extensive farming methods that are wasteful of natural resources but require low inputs of labour and money. The situation is complex and dynamic and farming households may opt for different routes through the capitalization/stabilization process depending on factors such as soil, climate, road access, access to support services, ethnic origin, community cohesion, etc.

Inequitable land distribution and various directed and spontaneous colonizations have placed increasing pressure on the forest resources in the Sara-Ichilo provinces, notably on the margins of the Amboro National Park (PNA). The PNA and surrounding 'buffer zone' have been cited as one of the leading mega-diverse areas within Latin America. The slash and burn system practised by these colonist farmers is not sustainable. When farmers have exhausted all virgin forest on their land, they begin to cultivate dryland rice in the bush-fallow (barbecho). Once they are cultivating in bush-fallow, increasing weed populations and declining yield result in an ever-shortening fallow period until a time is reached when it is no longer worthwhile for the farmer to continue. This is referred to as the "bush-fallow crisis". At this point, the farmer is forced to acquire new land, or change the farming system.

While weeds play a major part in land abandonment, in the longer-term, soil factors are also important. The soils are inherently low in available phosphorus, and nitrogen is quickly lost through leaching and volatilisation. Nitrogen, sulphur and organic matter are lost through burning. Micro - nutrients can soon become limited under acid conditions with poor organic matter buffering. A lack of nutrients also increases the impact of pests and diseases. On sloping lands, soil erosion is also a serious problem. Rice is the principal food and cash crop of the colonist farmers. A further factor limiting sustainability is the lack of locally validated agricultural income generating opportunities that justify investment in the land.

1. Outcomes

  • Sustainability was addressed through a number of principles.
    • An increased cropping period for annual crops.
    • Increased opportunities for perennial crops.
    • The development of sequences towards perennial systems.
    • Improved weed control (and reduced labour for weeding).
    • Integration of legume covers/green manures.
    • Economic sustainability through diversification.

2. Research methodology

  • The research methodology was one of the participatory on-farm research supplemented by a research manager and formal trials.
    • Participatory research methods used and documented included on-farm trials, farmer-led technology evaluation workshops, field days, case studies and surveys.
    • The main outputs were validation of the suitability of perennial species for the project area including citrus, pineapple, macadamia, bananas, and palm hearts (bactris gasipaes).
    • Viable cropping systems and sequences were identified.
  • The association of perennials with annuals, semi-perennials and legume covers proved how it was possible for small-scale farmers, with very limited financial capital, to diversify into perennial systems.
    • The annuals and semi-perennials offset establishment costs and provided a source of income in the short and medium term.
    • The legume covers prevented weed build-up and reduced labour requirements for weeding, both during establishment (in association with annuals and semi-perennials) and in mature plantations.
    • Suitable legume species and management were identified for both phases.
    • The association of citrus with pineapple, annual crops and legume covers proved the most popular.
    • In a survey of collaborating farmers at the end of the project, 54 percent of those testing citrus had already adopted and expanded these systems on their farms.
      • Most were not (as previously) planting monocrops but had adopted the principle of mixed cropping systems.
    • For further details see Pound 1997; 1999a; 1999b; and Pound and Warren, 1998.
  • In addition, a combination of on-farm and formal trials studied improved systems for the cultivation of upland rice.
    • Research tested systems of intercropping and rotating rice with legume crops and covers, to identify suitable legume species and management practices with a view to reducing weed build-up and extending the cropping period (the main constraints in traditional systems).
    • In a rice-calopogonium mucunoides intercropping system, the optimum sowing date and density of the legume was identified.
    • Over three years, calopogonium was very successful in reducing weed build-up in comparison with traditional systems but did not have a marked influence on soil parameters.
    • While the system greatly reduced weed build-up and hence the cost of weed control, it did not prevent a decline in yield over time.
    • Adoption of this system was most likely to occur where there was little available quality land in bush fallow.
    • Trials to investigate rice rotations with legumes (in winter) identified Canavalia ensiformis, Crotalaria juncea, Cajanus cajan and Mucuna spp as the most efficient in suppressing weeds.
    • Rice-mucuna rotation (in citrus alleys) extended the cropping period for rice and provided additional income from the sale of mucuna seed.
  • Agroforestry systems were appropriate to those farmers with a positive attitude towards trees, and an appreciation of the income generating potential and other (environmental) benefits.
    • These systems were appropriate for buffer zones of national parks and forest reserves, and other areas designated as mainly suitable for agroforestry.
    • The native fruits grew well within the bush fallow but were slow to produce fruit.
    • There is a role for research to select provenances that are quick bearers, and methods such as grafting that might speed fruiting.
    • One of the timber species tested grew quickly, but mahogany was a slow grower.
    • All are long term crops, and it was important to include short and medium term income sources in the farming system.
    • The establishing trees had to be protected from cattle.
    • Adoption was limited by an underlying attitude that trees were not a valuable resource.
    • Markets were often inaccessible and small and were poorly understood by farmers.
    • Seedlings were often unavailable, and technical assistance for agroforestry has been weak.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Cover crop species, with a special focus on legumes: ID 7414.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology effectively combines a variety of practices to improve crop resistance and yield. This includes: increased cropping period for annual crops, increased opportunities for perennial crops, the development of sequences towards perennial systems, improved weed control, integration of legume covers/green manures and economic sustainability through diversification.

entries.tittle: Pheromone traps for the management of the cowpea pest Maruca Vitrata
entries.summary: Maruca vitrata is a major pest of cowpea, resulting in 20 to 80 percent yield losses in West Africa. A pheromone lure and suitable trap developed in Benin and Ghana has successfully trapped male moths. From these trappings a threshold has been calculated to provide farmers with the optimum time for spraying in conjunction with locally available pesticides and botanical pesticides. The traps have not been as effective in Nigeria and Burkina Faso, suggesting the influence of ecological issues.
entries.description:
Description

Cowpea, known as black-eyed beans or simply as beans, is an important crop providing nutritious grains, an excellent source of animal fodder and a boost to nitrogen levels in the soil. Its drought tolerance makes it an important crop in semi-arid areas. Most of the world’s production is in West Africa, where it is grown by many smallholder subsistence farmers but increasingly it is grown as a cash crop.

It is the action of the larvae of the moth Maruca vitrata that leads to it also being known as the cowpea pod borer. Adult moths lay their eggs at night. Many farmers do not realize where this pest comes from, which inhibits the development of an effective control strategy. Efforts in the 1980s to control this pest concentrated on the promotion of synthetic pesticides based around a calendar spraying regime. This was an inefficient use of resources, increasingly affecting farmers as the prices of pesticides have continued to rise in recent years.

1. Pheromone lure for Maruca vitrata

  • This research has been based on identifying a pheromone lure EE10,12-16:Ald (100 µg), EE10,12-16:OH (5µg) and E10-16:Ald (5µg) which will attract male Maruca vitrata moths.
    • A suitable trap that could be made cheaply with locally available materials (e.g. a 5 litre plastic jerry can) was developed.
    • The lure would attract the moths into the cutaway sides of the jerry can and as it flew around it would drop into the water in the bottom of the jerry can.
    • This water contained a little soap to prevent the moth from freeing itself and it would drown. For further information on the development of the pheromone trap.
    • See Downham (2003) Part 1 and Part 2.
  • These traps are effective in Benin and Ghana, and a threshold was developed to identify the number of adult moths which corresponds to the number of larvae hitting a threshold at which it is economically and biologically optimal to apply a pesticide.
    • The recommendation was for at least six traps to be placed about four weeks after sowing in the cowpea fields around the village (particularly if all the fields have been planted at a similar time).
    • These should be checked at least three times each week.
  • When the total number of adult moths in the trap reaches 12 (for all six traps) or two per trap? then it is time to spray with pesticide.
    • Indigenous and scientific knowledge was reviewed to identify botanical extracts that had a high potential to control Maruca vitrata.
    • Three botanicals were effectively used based on neem, papaya or Hyptis spp to control both Maruca and thrips.
    • Although these botanicals all resulted in higher yields than the control, only some of the neem trials produced statistically significantly higher yields.
    • None of the botanicals produced the same level of yield as the synthetic pesticide Decis (deltamethrin).
  • The traps have been shown to attract male moths and these have been used to develop a spray threshold, which when used has shown economic benefits that are greater when the farmer is cultivating higher-yielding crops.
    • Where farmers used to spray to a calendar regime they now also benefit from less time spent spraying.
    • The outputs from the research have not quantified the health or environmental benefits of using less pesticide in a more targeted manner.
    • The farmer's response to the research has been positive.

2. Constraints

  • Constraints reported to the use of pheromone traps in conjunction with botanical pesticides.
    • The sustainable supply and access to trap materials.
      • Farmers were concerned about the availability of the “jerry” cans as these have alternative uses.
      • The scientists were concerned about the availability of the lure.
      • It was found that a commercially available lure was as effective as the lure produced by the scientists at Institute of Health Sciences (NRI).
      • However, a production company would require a clear market in West Africa before it would be prepared to export.
      • In a linked DFID CPP project (R8430), the policy environment in Ghana was influenced to enable products such as pheromones to be registered for sale in a relatively straightforward manner.
    • The labour to pound neem/papaya to create botanical pesticides.
      • This issue was still raised when it was shown that there were economic benefits.
      • It is likely that there are also drudgery issues and therefore again full adoption may not occur until botanical products are being manufactured and available for purchase in shops.
      • Care was taken to ensure that there were not negative gender aspects through the promotion of this work.
    • Researchers have attempted to scale this research out to Nigeria and Burkina Faso, but the traps have not proved effective in catching moths.
      • Sufficient research efforts have been invested to suggest this is likely to be more of a result of an ecological effect than random or human error.
      • These areas have a high Maruca population and the females might be out-competing the traps.
      • More research is required and validation is recommended before this technology is attempted in new locations.
    • This approach is fairly new, both for farmers and those providing them with information.
      • To date, knowledge has been promoted through the PRONAF Farmer Field Schools in collaboration with the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) but a broader promotion is required.
    • The lack of a market premium for cowpea produced with botanical rather than synthetic pesticides (or organic cowpea).
  • You manipulate and/or use pesticides? Make inquiries before!
    • Pesticide can be harmful to your health, the health of your family, of the consumers and of the environment.
    • Adopt the right gestures to use pesticides safely: Click on “Reducing risks while manipulating pesticide”.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Risk reduction while manipulating pesticides: ID 8348. 
  • Solarisation - reducing insect damage from cowpeas: ID 4425.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for the effective trapping of moths and the efficient evaluation of pesticide usage.

entries.tittle: Ecologically based and sustainable rodent control strategies in Africa
entries.summary: Rodents consume food in the field as well as in storage. Their contamination of stored food and ability to spread diseases causes them to cut across both the natural resources and health sectors. Research in Mozambique and in South Africa found that people have little understanding of the ecology of rodents. To control them they usually resort to rodenticides, used in inappropriate and inefficient manners. In South Africa, a company is now manufacturing an improved yet affordable trap. A policy change has been enacted, which should lead to higher standards amongst Pest Control Officers.
entries.description:
Description

1. Rodent control

  • Rodents are the biggest vertebrate problem in Africa.
  • They consume and damage large quantities of stored grains and food and damage crops in the field.
  • They carry diseases that can be transmitted to humans (e.g. Leptospirosis and Toxoplasmosis).
    • These diseases are responsible for considerable economic loss in terms of decreased worker productivity and health care-costs.
  • Rodents also eat and damage bedding, furniture and other items in the household.
  • Governments tend to control them through the use of rodenticides.
    • However, these conventional methods have remained largely ineffective.
  • Apart from Tanzania, there are few studies which have attempted to develop rodent management strategies for field rodent pests.
    • Therefore, before the technology could be developed, an ecological study of rodent species in the project areas was carried out in the Limpopo province and KwaZulu Natal in South Africa; and the Zambezia province in Mozambique.
  • Eighteen different rodent species were collected.
    • The most common rat species found was the black or house rat Rattus.
    • Other rats found included:
      • Aethomys chrysophilus,
      • Aethomys namaquensis,
      • Aethomys ineptus,
      • Mastomys natalensis,
      • Mastomys coucha,
      • Dasymyus incomtus,
      • Lemniscomys rosalia,
      • Mus musculus,
      • Mus minutoides,
      • Otomys angoniensis,
      • Pelomys fallax,
      • Rhabdomys pumilio,
      • Saccostomus campestris,
      • Steatomys sp.,
      • Tatera brantsii,
      • Tatera leucogaster,
      • Elephantulus sp., and
      • Mysorex sp.
    • The oriental rat Rattus tanezumi was trapped in Africa for the first time ever.
    • Most of these were found in kitchens and storage rooms.
  • An understanding of peoples’ socioeconomic background and knowledge of rodents had to be obtained.
  • In this study farmers identified rodents as both pre and post harvest pests (by both men and women).
  • Post harvest hygiene and waste management were linked to rodents and these issues needed to be dealt with at a community level.
  • Rodents also bite people at night.
  • Farmers were surprised as to how many rodents were caught in traps in a trial and admitted that they knew little about the ecology of the rodents.
  • The rodenticide Rattex® was used by 62 percent of those surveyed but two-thirds of these stated that it was ineffective.
    • Although this might be due to them not seeing evidence of dead rats.
  • People use the name rattex to describe any of a number of rodenticides.
    • Due to the apparent ineffectiveness of rattex, the illegal use of Aldicarb to control rodents has become popular.
    • Aldicarb is normally used on crops to control chewing and sucking insects and nematode worms.
    • Aldicarb is classified by the World Health Organization as a Class Ia 'extremely hazardous' pesticide.
  • Kill traps and glue boards were also available but people complained that the kill trap was difficult to use and “not strong”.
    • However, demand for these traps increased when householders saw the effectiveness of the break-back traps in the demonstrations.
      • Rodent control measures in Mozambique, the effectiveness of the American break-back trap ,and the Indian multi-catch trap was shown and a company agreed to manufacture them locally.
      • In South Africa a pest control company has agreed to modify and manufacture the “Kness” break-back trap.
        • The engagement of a local manufacturer ensures sustainable supply and an appropriate pricing structure.
        • These traps have been proved to be cost effective when compared with alternatives such as rodenticides.
  • Open structure granaries used for maize storage were often less than 1 m from the ground, allowing rodents free access.
    • These can be relatively easily modified to make them rat proof.
    • This was the focus of another project, the details of which can be found in TECA record "Mud plaster and concrete for protection of grain stores from insects and rodents and reduced use of scarce wood construction materials".
  • In a similar manner, dwellings and other buildings can also be made less accessible to rodent entry.
  • Local government improvement to the infrastructure, water provision and waste management also reduce rodent populations and the risk of zoonotic transmission.

2. Awareness raising

  • Due to the ineffectiveness of previous control measures, there was a need for widespread awareness raising before farmers would consider adoption of these technologies.
    • The awareness raising comprised demonstrations to communities and government agricultural extension on the effectiveness of trapping as a management tool as well as the effectiveness of the break-back trap.
    • As literacy amongst the target population was found to be low, regional radio stations were used to promote effective rodent-control management and why it is important.
  • Farmers needed to be aware of the rodent lifecycle, that due to external factors the rodent population will vary and so they should not become less vigilant.
  • The researchers found that many households did not set the traps every night and this led to a reduction in the number of catches.
    • Policy change was required to improve rodent control.
  • In this case, changes were required to the training of government and municipal health and environmental health personnel to the Register: Agricultural remedies and Stock remedies (Act 36 of 1947) and to the Pest Control Service Industries Board.
    • These changes will better inform staff and pest control operators on how best to control rodents through the improved use of rodenticides or through other measures.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour saving technologies and practices: improved storage facilities: ID 7308.
  • Using plants with pesticidal properties to control insects during on-farm grain storage; ID 4506.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The practice, through rodent control, provides food security and income generation for poor households.

entries.tittle: Disease resistant upland maize varieties validated by and promoted to farmers
entries.summary: The technology addresses the issue of two maize diseases: Grey Leaf Spot (GLS), and Maize Streak Virus (MSV) on upland maize. Research focussed on identifying and breeding for genetic resistance has been conducted in the southern highlands of Tanzania. Two hybrids have been released (UH615 and UH6303) with high levels of resistance to GLS. These are highly demanded by farmers as they produce a good cob, are high yielding and disease resistant. The project has worked to ensure that farmers can access the seed and this has led to collaborations with the private sector. Unfortunately a high level of resistance in Open Pollinated Varieties (OPVs) has not yet been validated.
entries.description:
Description

The Southern Highlands of Tanzania (comprising Iringa, Ruvuma, Mbeya and Rukwa regions) provide the most favourable climatic conditions for the production of maize in the country. They account for almost 50 percent of the total national maize production and up to 90 percent of the annual purchase of maize for the national strategic grain reserve. Maize Grey Leaf Spot (GLS) (Cercospora zeae maydis) was first reported in the Southern Highlands during the 1995/1996 cropping season causing grain yield losses ranging from 15 to 40 percent.

By 1998 this disease had spread to all four regions of the Southern Highlands. All local cultivars, as well as most of the commercial maize varieties under cultivation across the zone during that season, succumbed to the disease. The farmers already had to face the Maize Streak Virus (MSV), which during epidemics can cause up to 80 percent loss in maize grain yield. Instances of complete crop loss are not uncommon.

This disease is a particularly serious problem in irrigated maize and where maize is grown out of season and obtains a premium in the market. In the intermediate altitude maize growing parts of the Southern Highlands, up to 43 percent of sampled farmers identified MSV as a serious constraint to maize production.

1. Resistant varieties of maize

  • Researchers were aware that in other environments, genetic resistance to these diseases had been identified.
    • The Maize Improvement Programme (MIP) at Uyole Agricultural Research Institute commenced a massive screening and evaluation of both local and exotic commercial and pre-commercial maize varieties and inbred lines for GLS tolerance.
  • Evaluation of the GLS-tolerant germplasm, both on-station and on-farm, in these districts confirmed the superiority of several potential new maize hybrids.
    • One of which was officially released during the 2000/2001 season under the name UH615.
    • A further GLS-tolerant hybrid, UH6303, was approved for release in late 2004.
  • The farmers state that, in addition to their disease resistance, they like these varieties and that they produce more than their local varieties.
    • There is now a high demand.
    • Other MSV-tolerant (but not GLS-tolerant) OPVs (Open Pollinated Varieties) were also available, e.g. Staha and TMV1.
    • Variety trials conducted in Mbarali district had found that this tolerance was inadequate under the very early and severe MSV disease occurring irrigated areas, where vectors and disease are maintained year-round.
    • Research is continuing at the MIP to identify suitable resistant OPV lines.

2. Farmer involvement

  • The major constraint the researchers faced was that developing resistant seed does not in itself benefit farmers.
    • Mechanisms need to be in place for the multiplication and provision of seed.
    • This was a major constraint the researchers had to address.
  • Tanzania has been without an organized system for local seed production and distribution since 2000, when the national seed company, TANSEED, collapsed.
    • This situation had severely limited farmers’ access to locally bred, certified and disease-resistant seed, particularly in rural areas.
    • Most of the certified seed, which was marketed through a limited distribution network, had been of questionable purity.
    • In many cases, the seed exhibited unacceptably low rates of germination with, understandably, farmers losing their faith in a certified seed.
  • With respect to seed from improved maize varieties, there has been a significant increase in price and a subsequent decline in returns on the crop.
    • Farmers appear to have adapted their livelihood strategies in response by:
      • growing a larger area of maize to compensate for a decline in fertilizer use,
      • switching to other crops,
      • reducing the amount of improved certified seed purchased, and
      • making greater use of the recycled seed.
    • The returns from the crop have declined and the labour invested in it has increased.
  • The current situation is still associated with a lack of trust or confidence held by farmers in improved crop varieties from seed companies and other institutions dealing with seed distribution.
    • In order to build the farmers’ trust, the project team embarked on a large-scale awareness campaign of roadside trials, published materials and the use of the media to inform farmers of the varieties that had been developed.
    • This was initially done through the public sector and community organizations.
    • It became clear that the private sector was required to generate sufficient quantities of high-quality seed.
  • The team have therefore been working with Highland Seed Growers Limited who have developed a strategy to multiply, promote and market the seed in the Southern Highlands.
    • They are already marketing UH615 and are using small packs, on-farm demonstrations and other marketing tools.
    • They are working in close partnership with the relevant public sector organizations.
    • Details of their involvement can be found in Appendix 3 of (Lyimo, N.G. 2006).
    • There is clear potential for the scaling out of these varieties to highland areas in other countries
    • http://www.fao.org/docs/eims/upload/agrotech/1974/R8406_FTR.pdf.
  • The Ugandan authorities have approved the release of UH615 and UH6303 and FICA Ltd has been licensed to market these varieties.
    • In addition to developing farmer acceptable disease-resistant seed, the research identified the need for and provided farmer training on seed, soil and pest and disease management.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Maize harvesting and post-harvesting handling: ID 7015.
  • Pests and diseases management in maize: ID 7019.
  • Evergreen Agriculture: conservation agriculture in maize production: ID 7846.
  • Well dried maize benefits all: the solar maize dryer: ID 8285.
  • Drought-tolerant maize varieties: ID 8920.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology effectively combats crop diseases, leading to improved cob, higher yields and better resistance. It has also efficiently led to collaborations of farmers with the private sector.

entries.tittle: Integrated crop and pest management (ICPM) for smallholder coffee in South Africa
entries.summary: Coffee growing is an important livelihood strategy for smallholders in East African countries, notably Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda, where coffee is an important agricultural export. Smallholder production is less significant in southern countries such as Malawi and Zambia but although the smallholder sector is small, coffee is a major source of income for rural households, particularly in places that are remote from markets for other farm products. The objective was to improve the income of coffee smallholders in Malawi and Zambia through improved crop and pest management. This was done by developing and promoting Integrated Crop and Pest Management (ICPM) systems for the two most important pest constraints: white stem borer and Coffee Berry Disease (CBD).
entries.description:
Description

Coffee growing is an important livelihood strategy for smallholders in East African countries. These countries have a comparative advantage in coffee-growing because the climate is suitable, the quality is high and total national production can be increased without having a significant impact on world prices. Coffee ranks fourth amongst Malawi’s export crops and accounts for around 4 percent of Malawi’s export earnings. The bulk of coffee production comes from large estates in the south of the country which have some of the highest yields in the world.

The smallholder sector has in recent years contributed only about 5 percent of national production, but the earnings from coffee sales are a vital part of the livelihood strategy for rural communities in the hillside farming systems of northern Malawi. Although the smallholder sector averages one of the world’s lowest yields, some regions, such as Mzuzu, produce coffee of high quality and despite the poor world price for coffee, there remains a strong market for “Mzuzu” coffee.

Since 2002, the smallholder sector has been expanding at a time when, due to the low world price, the coffee output from the estate sector has been declining as they diversify into other crops such as tea and macadamia nut. This expansion has been supported by the European Union (EU) funding to the Smallholder Coffee Farmers Trust (SCFT), supporting capacity building, and multiplication and distribution of new (Catimor) coffee varieties.

1. Improved crop and pest management

The purpose of the project was to improve the income of coffee smallholders through improved crop and pest management. This was done by developing and promoting Integrated Crop and Pest Management (ICPM) systems, initially for the traditional tall varieties such as Geisha and Agaro, and subsequently for the dwarf Catimor varieties. The projects developed solutions for the two most important pest constraints: white stem borer and for Coffee Berry Disease (CBD).

Further improvement of control measures for white stem borer was taken-over by a project funded by the Common fund for commodities in Malawi and Zimbabwe. Training in general crop management, was provided and promoted to farmers, showing that the new Catimor varieties could be grown at wide spacing, that banana could be grown as a food crop with the coffee and that crop vigour is helped by mulching and proper fertilizer application. Some of these innovations were then introduced to the Coffee Growers Association and their smallholder groups in Zambia. With smallholder coffee still in its infancy in Zambia, the project was able to make a significant impact on plans for the extension of the sector over the coming years.

2. Outcomes

In summary, the main outputs are below. 

  • An integrated crop and pest management system was developed and validated that met the smallholders’ requirements and promoted as one of a basket of crop management options for the new dwarf Catimor varieties.
  • Varieties promoted by the EU project were resistant to coffee leaf rust but not to the other main disease, the coffee berry disease.
    • The project advocated the use of a selection (known as Nyika) from Catimor 129 that was resistant to both diseases.
  • As supplies of Nyika seed were scarce, a mother garden of Nyika trees was set up that will eventually meet the demand for seed.
  • On-farm demonstrations of Nyika intercropped with banana were used to promote the technology directly to farmers and this was backed by an information campaign using leaflets in two local languages.
  • On-farm trials to evaluate insecticides to control white stem borer led to the approval of “fipronil” for the use on coffee.
  • The recommendations were backed up with socio-economic research that focused on growers’ management practices for Catimor coffee, the economics of chemical control for coffee borer, and the impact of Catimor coffee on livelihoods, particularly for poorer growers.

3. ICPM technologies

Some specific ICPM technologies developed by the project  and have been and will continue to be promoted through the SCFT are:

3.1 For traditional varieties Geisha/Agaro

  • Shade management to prevent over-shading.
  • Use of fertilizer and fungicide as a package with the action threshold for fungicide application at 5 percent of leaves affected.
  • In areas where coffee is prone to CBD, both coffee leaf rust and CBD need to be controlled.

3.2 For Catimors in general

  • An intensive hedgerow system is being promoted by SCFT.
    • It is recommended that this is used in areas less prone to CBD unless the farmer is committed to a full fungicide spray programme.
  • The less intensive system offered as an alternative is to grow Catimors with bananas.
    • Tall banana varieties are grown after every sixth row of coffee.
  • For both systems, it is essential that a full fertilizer programme is followed at planting and for subsequent crop maintenance.

3.3 For unselected Catimor “populations”

  • Stem paint with fipronil once the bushes are established in the field.
    • Insecticides are applied in late September, before the main flight period for egg-laying beetles.
  • Apply fungicide spray to fruiting branches against CBD.

3.4 For Catimor 129 or cv. “Nyka”

  • Stem paint with fipronil once bushes are established in the field.

4. Potential for wider scale impact

The EU-funded project is on-target to provide a sustainable funding stream for the SCFT by 2007. Several of the CPP projects’ outputs have been adopted by the SCFT–Information leaflets.

  • CBD control through the planting of cultivar “Nyika”.
  • Acceptance of the principle that some farmers may wish to plant Catimors at wider spacing with some inter-planting with banana.
  • Recommendation to use fipronil to control white stem borer is subject to further investigations to see whether the dosage or application frequencies can be reduced to improve the economics of control.

Most of the several phases of this work were carried out in northern Malawi with 4 000 coffee-growing households or 30 000 people. The lessons learned in Malawi were extended to about ten smallholder groups in Zambia within villages with a total population of about 20 000. However, project outputs are also relevant to coffee smallholders in Zimbabwe and to a much larger number of coffee growing households in Tanzania where about 500 000 to 1 million people depend on coffee for income and, as in Malawi, the EU is supporting rehabilitation of the smallholder coffee sector.

The lessons learned in Malawi about developing a communication strategy for agricultural information required by coffee smallholders, and about appropriate technologies to maximise profits from coffee-growing, would be appropriate to Tanzania.

5. Specific health and safety precautions

  • Observe manufacturers' recommendations for safe handling, application and the disposal of pesticides and fungicides.

6. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies 

  • Shade-grown coffee: ID 7511.
  • Agroforestry Coffee cultivation in combination with mulching, trenches and organic composting: ID 8928.

This technology is available in Portuguese: ID 2541. 

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

8.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology optimizes coffee production for smallholder farmers as it integrates pest and crop management strategies into their practice. 

8.2 Pro-poor technology

This technology supports farmers in addressing risks in production that might affect their income. Having an Integrated Crop and Pest Management programme ensures higher income through reduced harvest losses.

entries.tittle: Practices for producing clean seed yam planting materials, Nigeria
entries.summary: Yam productivity in the main yam-growing belt of West Africa is reduced by losses in the growing crop, and in subsequent storage, due to diseases and pests. Many of these are either spread in, or exacerbated by, poor quality planting materials. A package of crop protection technologies was developed (based on current practices, indigenous technical knowledge and the outputs from previous projects) for producing good quality seed yams and promoting their supply and availability. The package was validated for applicability and economic efficacy by growers in Kogi and Ekiti states of Nigeria and was shown to be suitable for wider adoption in West Africa.
entries.description:
Description

Yam remains the preferred starchy staple for many people in the yam belt of West Africa. However, it is the most expensive of the root crops to produce because of the high labour demands for land preparation, planting, staking, weeding, harvesting and transport to market. Also, planting material (seed yam) is expensive and in short supply because of the low multiplication rate of yams. FAO - Stat figures (2005) suggest that, in Nigeria, the average yield of yam appears to have been steadily declining over the last 8 to 10 years.

The cause of this decline is often cited as being the declining soil fertility due to shorter fallow periods, and the use of more marginal lands for yam production because of the increasing demand on agriculture, to feed the increasing human population. The result of the reducing yields is that total production is staying relatively static (not keeping up with demand), despite the increasing land area used for yam. Shorter fallows and use of more marginal lands are likely to increase pest and disease problems through build up of populations in the soil, which will carry over to the harvested tubers. Increasing demand for tubers, for food combined with increased loading of the tubers with pathogens and pests means that good quality (low disease) tubers for use as planting material are becoming increasingly scarce and expensive.

Previous works have identified the shortage of good quality and affordable planting material as one of the main constraints to increased yam production. The basic yam multiplication technology using ‘minisetts’, is not new and has been subject to numerous earlier promotional campaigns. For example, systems based on ‘minisetts’, or the treatment of cut setts with a fungicide plus insecticide mixture, for the more reliable and efficient production of good quality ‘clean’ and disease free seed yams have been explored but have had limited uptake.

This technology package focuses on those component technologies or system changes that should be promoted, and to which sectors, in order to increase the supply and availability of good quality seed yam in Nigeria. It also identifies how to go about the promotion, and how to implement strategies most likely to be successful. In particular, this record focuses on these crop protection practices themselves and the ways in which they were promoted.

1. Production of good quality seed yams

  • Reducing the disease and pest loading on the harvested tubers is implicit in producing good quality seed yams or planting material.
  • Since increasing fallow periods is no longer an option, it is necessary to use alternative approaches.
  • A system of producing seed yams, was developed using a targeted application of a mixture of a fungicide and an insecticide to similar sized cut tuber pieces of 80 to 100 g (the experimental treatments focusing on application of treatments to the minisetts, rather than the size of the minisetts).
    • Treatments were a pesticide mixture of Mancozeb and Basudin (Diazinon).
    • The minisetts are then planted at relatively high density (40 000 per ha) to produce a crop of small tubers (seed yams) ideal for planting whole the following season in order to produce a ‘ware’ crop.
  • Harvest data from demonstration and training plots of this seed yam production system planted in six states of Nigeria in 2005 showed that the cocktail - treated minisetts always produced more weight of seed yams, with multiplication factors in the range of x1.8 to x6.2, when compared with the farmers’ usual practice of treating the setts with wood ash.
    • Some of the ash - treated sett plots yielded less weight of tubers than was used to plant the plot in the first place.
    • In both study of households and demonstration plots, the cost of the fungicide and insecticide for treating the cut setts was negligible compared to the other costs involved in producing the seed yams.
    • However, the main concern here is to ensure a reliable supply of a genuine formulation of an appropriate fungicide and insecticide mixture in an affordable size of packaging that is easy and safe to handle and apply.
  • For further information on these techniques, including details on the relative success of different treatments, see the Technical Reports by (Kenyon, 2005), and (Kenyon, 2006).

2. Livelihood studies

  • Livelihood studies (social, economic and marketing) and on-farm trials showed that whilst clean seed yam production by resource-poor farmers can make a viable contribution to household livelihoods, much depends upon the context of the household for some it would be a far more attractive option than for others.
    • For commercial production systems in the Illushi area of Edo state (one of the major seed growing areas of Nigeria), planting cut setts was generally more profitable than planting small whole tubers for producing seed yams.
      • The Illushi growers had not received extension advice on improved methods of production and because they do not treat the planting material before planting, there are relatively high losses through setts not surviving in the field and through the harvested tubers rotting during storage.
      • Seed yam production is not as profitable for these growers as it could be because of poor access to the growing area and the high costs of transporting seed yam to market, and because of the requirement to sell the seed through the trading cartels who appear to take a large share of the profit.
    • A comparison of the livelihoods of small-scale yam growers in Ekwuloko and Edeke showed that although the Edeke households were more reliant on agriculture, particularly yam production for income and farm larger areas, they were not as well off as the Ekwuloko households who had more diverse income sources.
      • The cost-benefit of growing their own seed yams is potentially greater for the Edeke households, though because they are less well off they are more reliant on having access to financial credit at key periods of the year.
      • Setting up to produce their own seed yams was regarded as a high risk strategy by the Edeke households and by the recipients of credit in a Gorta-funded micro-credit (FEED) scheme.
        • Most of the credit recipients spread their risk by using their credit to grow both seed yams and ware yams.
  • Combining results of field trials and livelihood studies showed that there are three broad systems of seed yam production where further focussed interventions are likely to have greatest impact in increasing production and availability.
    • The centralized, large-scale, commercial seed yam producers in areas such as Illushi need to be informed about the improved systems (e.g. the treated, cut sett method) for producing and storing seed yams so that the farmers can avoid the huge losses due to setts rotting in the field or seed yam rotting during storage.
      • Improving (infrastructure) access to their production areas would reduce their transportation costs and perhaps reduce their reliance on the intermediary cartels.
    • The large commercial ware-yam growers should be shown the potential cost-benefits of producing their own seed yams using the improved systems.
      • They have the financial buffer, degree of mechanization and economy of scale to be able to do this profitably as a component of their larger business.
    • Only certain classes of small-scale farming households will be able to grow their own seed yams profitably and sustainably.
      • More efficient systems for identifying such households need to be developed as do methods for reducing the administration costs and interest rates of the (micro-) credit schemes that these farmers need to access to be able to produce seed and ware yam sustainably.
      • Traditionally the farmers are using a portion of their harvest for planting the next cropping season and exceptionally buy seed tuber from outside, and in the case of early maturing, double-harvest cultivars the second harvest is for seed.
  • Although treating the planting material before planting will increase the quality and storability of the seed yams, further research is required to find methods to maintain or restore soil fertility while still using the short fallow system.
    • This would be perhaps by inter-planting with a nitrogen-fixing legume, or making appropriate formulations of organic or inorganic fertilizer available at an affordable cost.
    • For further information see the Technical Report (Keynon, 2006).

3. Environmental impact

  • Targeting insecticides and fungicides only on the planting material for the seed crop is probably environmentally benign since only small quantities of pesticide are used and the likelihood of carrying over detectable amounts of pesticide residues in the ware crop is very small.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Rapid multiplication of yams: ID 4320.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology, as a package of crop protection technologies, efficiently combines current practices, indigenous technical knowledge and the outputs from previous projects for producing good quality seed yams and promoting their supply and availability.

entries.tittle: Development and promotion of wild rice management strategies for the lowlands of southern Tanzania
entries.summary: Rice is the second most important cereal crop in Tanzania after maize and the majority of rice farmers depend on it both for food and as a cash crop. However, highly competitive annual and perennial wild rice species have been identified as one of the important constraints to rice production on lowlands in southern Tanzania. In addition to competing with the crop, these weed species are the only known alternative hosts for African Rice Gall Midge (ARGM) and are important hosts for Rice Yellow Mottle Virus (RYMV), both of which are major pests of rice in sub-Saharan Africa. Therefore, the Department For International Development from the United Kingdom (UK DFID) developed technologies and promotional materials for optimising the use of herbicides and fertilizer for the control of annual wild rice (Oryza punctata on irrigated land) and perennial wild rice (O. longistaminata) on rainfed fields in Tanzania.
entries.description:
Description

Rice is the second most important cereal crop in Tanzania, after maize and the majority of rice farmers depend on it both for food and as a cash crop. However, highly competitive annual and perennial wild rice species have been identified as one of the important constraints to rice production on lowlands in southern Tanzania. In addition to competing with the crop, these weed species are the only known alternative hosts for African Rice Gall Midge (ARGM) and are important hosts for Rice Yellow Mottle Virus (RYMV), both of which are major pests of rice in sub-Saharan Africa.

Wild rices contribute to low yields on the large parastatal farms in Tanzania. Due to low profitability, substantial portions of these enterprises have subsequently been handed over to smallholder farmers but the problems of wild rice persist with current agronomic practice and smallholder farmers may abandon these fields leading to severe problems for affected households and a wider impact on the local economy.

Most lowland rice farmers currently use little or no fertilizer or manure and the majority use the photoperiod - sensitive late maturing (160 to 170 days) tall cultivar 'Super India'. This responds poorly under intensive and high input management. When the rains end early there is risk of terminal drought with long duration cultivars. A new lowland rice cultivar TXD 306 (SARO 5), developed in Tanzania, is rapidly becoming popular in Kilombero as it is aromatic (a trait demanded by the market in Tanzania) and high yielding.

However, this non-photoperiod sensitive cultivar, which matures in 130 days is a semi-dwarf that is less competitive with wild rice than the traditional types, thus compounding the need for improved management of wild rice weeds.

1. Control of wild rice species

  • Under CPP project R8198, seven farmer-research groups (128 farm households) undertook demonstration trials on 32 wild rice infested farms.
  • Participatory evaluation during field days and sensitization workshops involved more than 230 rice producers from seven villages within the project areas.
  • Farmers identified the use of glyphosate before planting at the rate of 3 litres per ha for the control of annual wild rice (Oryza punctata on irrigated land) and 4 litres per ha for the control of perennial wild rice (O. longistaminata on rain-fed fields) as the best options for the management of these weeds.
  • Post-emergence application of 2,4-D (2.5 l pro ha) at 21 days after germination was favoured to reduce labour inputs for in-crop weed control.
  • Partial budget analysis undertaken with growers, district agricultural extension staff, village chairmen and ward executive officers demonstrated the benefits of improving wild rice management.
  • Income from rice production could be increased from a cost-benefit ratio of less than one (0.64) to 2.94 for farmers in Kyela, 3.25 for Dakawa and 4.93 for Ruvu farmers when glyphosate was used.
  • Significant increases in yield of more than 4 tonne per ha over control were achieved using glyphosate before planting and 2,4-D at 21 days after crop emergence.
  • In addition to the experimental fields, group members from Michenga and Lumemo villages in Kilombero set up demonstration plots on their own fields to enable other farmers in the district copy the technology they acquired.

2. Promotion of the project

  • To support promotion the project prepared a leaflet and poster for distribution to extension teams and farmers.
    • A cultivation manual on rice production was prepared in Swahili (see Katrin, 2005), and made available for training of lead farmers and extension workers.
    • Fieldwork continued under a subsequent project (see Mbapila and Kibanda,2006) on land infested by perennial wild rice (O. longistaminata) on the floodplains of the Kilombero valley (Eastern Agricultural Zone) and floodplain of Lake Nyasa in Kyela district (Southern Highlands Zone).
    • Work to demonstrate practices to increase the productivity of annual wild rice infested land (O. punctata) was continued in Morogoro region, Eastern Zone in Dihombo village, and on fields recently allocated to smallholders at Dakawa and Ruvu, two irrigated farms previously operated by a parastatal farming concern.
    • Four plots were planted at each site with rice cultivar TXD306.
    • For O. longistaminata infested sites these were:
      • Farmer practice tillage, no fertilizer
        • Plough twice with oxen, broadcast seed and harrow in Kyela; plough once by tractor, broadcast seed two weeks later and harrow in Kilombero.
      • Farmer practice tillage, 80 kg per ha urea fertilizer applied as a split dose at tillering and panicle initiation
        • Plough twice with oxen and harrow in Kyela; plough once by tractor and harrow in Kilombero.
      • Glyphosate 4 l per ha applied to wild rice re-growth after one ploughing with harrowing before planting approx. two weeks later, no fertilizer.
      • Glyphosate 4 l per ha applied to wild rice re-growth after one ploughing with harrowing before planting approximately two weeks later, fertilizer applied.
  • For in-crop weed control 2,4-D amine was applied at a dose of 2.5 l per ha product to all plots at 21 days after sowing.
    • Hand weeding was also undertaken at 21 and 42 days to remove wild rice.
    • For O. punctata-infested sites, practices were similar to the above to provide a combination of herbicide and fertilizer use.
    • However practices used varied from location to location.
    • Results confirmed that a package of wild rice control and fertilizer use with the improved cultivar TXD 306 can greatly enhance productivity of floodplain and irrigated rice systems in Tanzania.

3. In-crop weed control

  • For in-crop weed control 2,4-D amine was applied at a dose of 2.5 l/ha product to all plots at 21 days after sowing.
    • Hand weeding was also undertaken at 21 and 42 days to remove wild rice.
    • For O. punctata-infested sites, practices were similar to the above to provide a combination of herbicide and fertilizer use. However practices used varied from location to location.
    • Results confirmed that a package of wild rice control and fertilizer use with the improved cultivar TXD 306 can greatly enhance productivity of floodplain and irrigated rice systems in Tanzania.
  • Application of glyphosate to wild rice re-growth prior to seeding rice allows wild rice infested land to be cultivated profitably.
    • This includes previously abandoned land often on areas with the deepest water and highest soil fertility that have the highest potential for rice production.
    • The combination of wild rice suppression by glyphosate and in-crop weed control with 2,4-D reduces subsequent in-crop hand weeding time by 50 percent, a saving in labour welcomed by growers.
    • At the rice farm gate price the cost of treating one ha with glyphosate is covered by the sale of just 130 kg paddy.

4. Wild rice management strategies

  • This approach to wild rice management therefore provides farmers with an opportunity to reduce labour costs while increasing rice output to benefit from increasing market demand for rice in Tanzania.
    • Participatory economic analysis of benefits carried out with farmers confirmed the cost benefits of these technologies over traditional practices.
    • However, the costs of producing rice using existing practices derive largely from 'non-cash' inputs.
    • For example, much of the land worked by farmers is held under customary, village or communal tenure arrangements and farms are mainly worked by family labour (often unpaid).
    • Farmers do not therefore always perceive farm labour to have a monetary cost.
  • When the true costs, including a realistic opportunity cost for labour, were discussed, farmers were surprised that in many cases they experience losses.
    • Training farmers on a business approach to their rice enterprise, particularly with increasing opportunity to supply a growing urban market, will lay a foundation for adoption of improved practices.
    • However, it is important for inputs to be available near to farms when farmers market rice and therefore have cash available.
  • Investigation of the land tenure system with members of two village communities in Kyela showed that land ownership in the district is skewed and approximately 70 percent of households gain access to lowland rice fields via short term tenancies.
    • Rented land tends to be less productive than land kept for cultivation by landowners, being of poorer fertility with greater infestations of wild rice.
    • The perception in the community is that tenants are less likely to invest in improved production practices through fear of losing use of fields to landlords.
    • Thus landowners are most likely to adopt herbicide for wild rice management initially.
    • District councils need to consider the needs of the community rather than individuals when planning promotion of production enhancing inputs for floodplain rice.
  • The training manual, leaflet and posters provide extension material on which district council extension managers or NGOs can base future promotion of wild rice control.
  • Improved understanding of the land tenure situation on the Kyela floodplain will assist extension staff target dissemination of improved rice production practices.
  • You manipulate and/or use pesticides? Make inquiries before!
  • Pesticide can be harmful to your health, the health of your family, of the consumers and of the environment.
  • Adopt the right gestures to use pesticides safely: click on “Reducing risks while manipulating pesticide”

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Improving rice quality: video from Africa Rice Center: ID 6976.
  • Rice seedbed preparation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 6973.
  • Participatory varietal selection: improved rice varieties: ID 4459.
  • Rice transplanting, Africa Rice Center video on rice advice: ID 7214.
  • Rice seed sorting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7205.
  • Aerobic rice: ID 7941.
  • Intensive rice cultivation: ID 7666.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology provides detailed guidance on amounts of fertilizers and pesticides to use to control weeds. It is cost-effective and ensures improved crop yields.

entries.tittle: Sustainable impact generation and technology promotion to manage Bemisia Tabaci and tomato leaf curl Virus Disease in India
entries.summary: In India, tomato is both a high value crop, often exported to the Middle East, and an important subsistence vegetable grown mainly by women. Tomato leaf curl virus (ToLCV) and its whitefly vector, Bemisia tabaci (Genn.), are two of the most serious constraints to tomato production in India. When populations of B. tabaci are high, 90 to 100 percent of plants can become infected, resulting in a yield loss of 40 to 100 percent. Farmers consider these problems to be of burning importance and they have attempted to manage them with the only tool available to them. This tool is the intensive, widespread and increasingly unsuccessful use of insecticides in attempts to control B. tabaci and ToLCV, with associated risks both to their health and the environment. Development, promotion and uptake of IPM technologies to combat tomato leaf curl virus (ToLCV) and its whitefly vector, Bemisia tabaci (including open pollinated tomato varieties and hybrids resistant to all strains of the virus including those transmitted by the B biotype of B. tabaci), are two of the most serious constraints to tomato production in India,
entries.description:
Description

In India, tomato is both a high value crop, often exported to the Middle East, and an important subsistence vegetable grown mainly by women. Tomato leaf curl virus (ToLCV) and its whitefly vector, Bemisia tabaci (Genn.), are two of the most serious constraints to tomato production in India. When populations of B. tabaci are high, 90 to 100 percent of plants can become infected resulting in a yield loss of 40 to 100 percent. Farmers consider these problems to be of burning importance and they have attempted to manage them with the only tool available to them. This tool is the intensive, widespread and increasingly unsuccessful use of insecticides in attempts to control B. tabaci and ToLCV, with associated risks both to their health and the environment.

In August 2000, the situation in the south of India deteriorated significantly, with the arrival of the highly destructive B-biotype of B. tabaci. This whitefly is highly resistant to a wide range of insecticides and tomato is one of its most preferred host-plant species. The high populations of the B-biotype resulted in the rapid spread of ToLCV disease into tomato nurseries and the subsequent failure of the tomato crop in a major vegetable growing area of southern India. The B-biotype is currently continuing to spread throughout India and has been associated with the emergence of new plant-viral disease epidemics in okra, pumpkin, potato and beans.

1. Project phases

  • A series of projects has generated highly successful solutions to these problems in tomato.
    • The first phase concentrated on developing and testing various new technologies and alternative management practices to insecticides (COLVIN and MUNIYAPPA 1999);
    • The second phase focused on the development, through farmer-participatory breeding, of three ToLCV-resistant open pollinated (OP) tomato varieties, Sankranthi, Nandi and Vybhav (COLVIN 2002).
      • These are high yielding and highly resistant to ToLCV.
      • They performed extremely well, therefore, even under the ToLCV-epidemic conditions caused by the arrival of the B-biotype.
    • In the third phase of the project, these varieties were released officially and breeder seed was purchased by sixteen private seed companies, who are currently using it in their breeding programmes to produce ToLCV - resistant tomato hybrids.
      • A conservative estimate suggested that within two years, hybrids developed from these varieties will be grown by more than 55 000 South Indian farmers.
      • A survey of 75 tomato farmers showed that the increased income from growing ToLCV-resistant tomatoes is spent on an improved diet, children’s education and health.
      • The third phase also recognised that the creation of a positive impact in the family lives of the poorest tomato growers.
      • However, will not be possible through the production of ToLCV - resistant hybrid tomatoes alone, as this category of grower prefers OP varieties, which have lower input costs and thus reduced financial risk.
      • The third phase of the project, therefore, initiated activities aimed at promoting the uptake and sustainable adoption of our technologies and ToLCV-management practices, with these poorer growers.
      • This was achieved by establishing a revolving fund to supply poor farmers with OP seed.
    • A fourth phase (see: http://www.fao.org/docs/eims/upload/agrotech/1993/R8425_FTR.pdf) sought to promote and consolidate these gains; monitor and document their impact; understand the basis of resistance in tomato and its probable stability; and to document the biological and socio-economic studies carried out in the course of the work.
    • Widespread adoption of the project’s outputs will allow tomatoes to be grown successfully, even in the peak of the ToLCV - epidemic season, with greatly reduced insecticide use and associated benefits to the poorest farmers, consumers and the environment.

2. Other developed and validated technogies

  • Besides the ToLCV-resistant breeding lines and varieties developed and which are now commercially available in India, many other technologies were developed and validated in the course of these studies and some of these are reported below.
  • Official release of ToLCV-resistant tomato varieties and non-exclusive agreements with NGOs and/or private seed companies to multiply and distribute, and/or market at least one variety.
    • The three varieties, Sankranthi, Nandi and Vybhav were released and assigned, respectively, the following National Identity Numbers, IC 296388, IC 296389, IC 296390.
    • Following consultation with the Central Seed Committee, official notification took place when the variety names were published in “The Gazette of India”, signifying that they can be used all over India (see http://www.tomatoleafcurlandwhitefly.org/release.htm website for details).
    • Negotiations by the UASB Technology Transfer Committee were carried out with ten vegetable seed companies, which all purchased breeder quality seed from the UASB.
    • Although originally developed and released in Kartnataka, the varieties were grown in several new states, including northern India (Himachal Pradesh) and Nagpur (central India).
    • Nine of the companies returned information on crop performance and stated that the tomatoes did not show any ToLCVD symptoms.
  • Simulation model to determine the potential impact and conditions under which the IPM practices are likely to be most successful.
    • A model was developed that was useful in bringing together systematically all the information gained from the other project activities and integrating them in order to identify the IPM technologies that have the highest chance of having a sustainable impact.
      • It aided understanding of the mechanism driving the annual epidemics of ToLCV and suggested ways in which IPM technologies might be improved.
    • The modelling work showed that the high influx of viruliferous vectors made disease incidence insensitive to vector mortality within the tomato crop.
      • Very effective virus resistance is required, otherwise supporting control measures such as protective netting will also be needed in order to prevent substantial infection.
  • Molecular and biological characteristics of the B. tabaci biotypes and viruses associated with ToLCVD established, and diagnostic criteria available.
    • Analysis of the Coat Protein DNA sequence data for the viruses found in leaf curl symptomatic plants showed that there were five different ToLCV groups in India.
      • ToLCVs were detected in alternative hosts including chilli, cowpea, okra and tobacco, as well as the weeds Croton sp., Parthenium sp. and Malvastrum sp.
      • Papaya leaf curl virus and Pepper leaf curl Bangladesh virus were also detected in tomato for the first time.
      • At least two completely new ToLCV species were identified.
  • Colonies of three B. tabaci populations from eggplant, collected from Rannibenur, Coimbatore and Belgaum, and a population from E. geniculata, collected from Bangalore, were established at NRI.
    • The CO1 gene sequences of the Rannibenur, Coimbatore and Bangalore populations were obtained and they fitted into the previously identified population clusters.
    • The reciprocal crosses were carried out and the data were published.
    • Samples of ToLCV-infected tomato plants, weeds and B. tabaci populations were collected and analysed molecularly.
  • The non-indigenous B biotype of Bemisia tabaci was identified in three regions (Kolar and Nagamangala in Karnataka and from several locations in Gujarat State), which supports previous predictions that its distribution within India would expand.
    • Molecular data suggested that there may be an indigenous, separate B. tabaci population associated with eggplant and that non-symptomatic ToLCV hosts play a role in the epidemiology of the disease.
    • Two new viruses were identified at Arsikere and Shimoga, which appear to be significantly different from previously characterised isolates.
    • Fortunately the new tomato lines are resistant to the diversity of viruses present in these areas.

3. Impact assessment and benefit: cost data available for ToLCV-resistant varieties

  • Socioeconomic data were collected from more than 90 farmers in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh where resistant OP tomato varieties were widely grown, and from a small group of 20 farmers who were given the ToLCV-resistant tomato seed.
  • These were monitored closely and compared with another group of farmers in the same area who are growing the traditional ToLCV-susceptible varieties.
  • A comparison of the cost/benefits obtained from the two farmer categories showed that those growing the project’s tomatoes made up to ten times more profit than those growing ToLCV-susceptible OPs.

4. Revolving fund for provision of ToLCV-resistant open pollinated types

  • By September 2004, it had become clear that the private sector, which is focussing on breeding ToLCV - resistant hybrids, would create enormous impact amongst “better - off” tomato growers.
  • The poorest growers, however, risked missing out on getting access to the project’s OP varieties, because of the private sector’s lack of effort in promoting them.
  • In order to address this potential problem, a “revolving fund” was set up by the UAS National Seed Project, GKVK, and Extension Education Unit, Nagenahalli.
  • Fifty-thousand seed pouches were produced for the sale of the ToLCV-resistant tomato varieties.
  • The UASB conducted two field days and two training programmes at Mandya and Nagamangala taluks.
  • Resulting from these promotional efforts, about 6 kg of seed was sold within a year and the demand was increasing.
Figure 1. Sustainable impact generation and technology promotion to manage Bemisia Tabaci and tomato leaf curl Virus Disease in India-1

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Sustainable impact generation and technology promotion to manage Bemisia Tabaci and tomato leaf curl Virus Disease in India -2

©FAO/TECA

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • temperate, cool.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Risk reduction through the control of the curly leaf virus in tomatoes: ID 7742.
  • Processing tomatoes: ID 6924.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Pro-poor technology

Through the use of disease-resistant seeds and a decrease in pesticide usage, this technology allows farmers to increase their tomato crop yields. This provides for additional sources of food and income.
