entries.tittle: Green manure for enhancing upland rice productivity on Striga-infested fields in Tanzania
entries.summary: Upland rice is an important cash crop in many areas of eastern and southern Tanzania, including Morogoro Rural and Kyela districts. Under continuous cultivation, rice yields have been in decline in recent years. This is associated with falling soil fertility and an increase in infestation by the parasitic witchweed, Striga asiatica. Working with farmers in Kyela since 1996, CPP project R7564 demonstrated that up to 60 percent reduction in Striga numbers and a 45 percent increase in rice yield could be achieved by applying urea fertiliser. However, farmers could not widely adopt the use of urea because they lacked liquidity for fertilizer purchase. The following technology promotes using green manure species Crotalaria ochroleuca, (sunn hemp; also called "Marejea" in Kiswahili), to manage Striga asiatica and improve soil fertility in upland rice in Tanzania.
entries.description:
Description

Upland rice is an important cash crop in many areas of eastern and southern Tanzania, including Morogoro Rural and Kyela districts. Under continuous cultivation, rice yields have been in decline in recent years. This is associated with falling soil fertility and an increase in infestation by the parasitic witchweed, Striga asiatica. Working with farmers in Kyela since 1996, CPP project R7564 demonstrated that up to 60 percent reduction in Striga numbers and a 45 percent increase in rice yield could be achieved by applying urea fertilizer. However, farmers could not widely adopt the use of urea because they lacked liquidity for fertilizer purchase.

1. Crotalaria ochroleuca as a green manure

The green manure species Crotalaria ochroleuca, (sunn hemp) also called “Marejea” in Kiswahili, presented an alternative approach to managing Striga. This had been grown for many years at St Benedict’s Abbey, Peramiho, southern Tanzania, where it is used to maintain the fertility of organic gardens. At Peramiho, “Marejea” grows up to a height of 2 m and has been found to be fairly drought tolerant, recovering well when rain returns. When broadcasted as a sole crop, growth is vigorous so that weeds are suppressed.

Sunn hemp's many uses include:

  • green manure;
  • nitrogen fixation;
  • weed suppression;
  • livestock forage; and
  • pest control.

Farmers in Tanzania have found tillage easier in fields where sunn hemp has been grown and incorporated into the soil.

  • The improved soil texture facilitates ploughing before the rains, giving crops the benefit of the full rainy season.
  • The plant’s deep root system aerates the soil, increases water infiltration and retards soil erosion.
  • Unlike most nitrogen-fixing legumes, sunn hemp performs well on poor and acidic soils.
  • Under appropriate conditions, it establishes quickly and grows abundantly, thus out competing weeds.
  • If planted densely, sunn hemp prevents weed growth in the first year and reduces subsequent weed growth for the following one to three years.
  • Sunn hemp can outcompete couch grass (Digitaria sp.) but not blackjack (Bidens pilosa).
  • Over the course of three years, sunn hemp eventually outcompetes star grass (Cynodon sp.) in paddies.
  • It is also known from the literature and experimental results from CPP project R7564 that Crotalaria is not a host of Striga but stimulates the “suicide” germination of the seed.
  • Farmers in Tanzania have found that sunn hemp can constitute 60 percent of cattle feed and the unused stems can be mixed with manure to make compost.
  • Chickens will eat any part of the sunn hemp plant except for the seeds.
  • Sunn hemp can also be used to feed tilapia.
  • One acre can yield up to 100 kg to 300 kg of seeds worth Tsh 600 per kilo.
  • Some farmers let their cattle graze sunn hemp for one hour a day if they do not want to harvest the seed.
    • A number of farmers were familiar with “Marejea” from previous projects but viewed these as “just experimental” and there seems to have been limited farmer participation, little reporting of field activities and no follow-up promotion.
  • Under project R7564, seed from Peramiho was planted by two farmer groups in Kyela in 2001 and farmers were very impressed by the growth of these plots, especially on what the community judged to be poor, worked out lands.
    • They observed that no Striga emerged on a rice plot previously sown to “Marejea”, which yielded 2 100 kg-ha-1 rice compared to 1000 kg where no fertilizer was used and 1 600 and 1 900 kg ha-1 respectively where 25 and 50 kg N ha-1 had been applied.
  • Following village seminars, 33 farmers requested seed of Crotalaria to plant in the 2002 season and the process of farmer evaluation of green manure, which was initiated by the research team, subsequently became farmer-driven.
  • A new CPP project (R8194) was designed to promote the use of Crotolaria as a green manure for improving the fertility of Striga-infested upland rice.
    • The project was led by Ilonga Agricultural Research Institute with local partners including district agricultural extension and primary school education staff, the NGO INADES, a soil fertility specialist from Mlingano Agricultural Research Institute, a social economist from Sokoine University of Agriculture, and staff from the Natural Resources Institute, UK.
  • A number of promising new pigeon pea cultivars with resistance to the soil-borne wilt disease, Fusarium udum were included in the legume/rice rotations as an alternative to Crotalaria, as pigeon pea provides an economic grain yield and improves nitrogen and phosphorus availability to the soil.
    • This project, extended by CPP project R8436, developed technologies to promote soil fertility enhancement for control of Striga.
    • The major focus was on participatory evaluation and promotion of Striga management practices with farmer groups, who undertook on-farm demonstrations used as sites for field days.
  • In addition, strategies were developed for the up-scaling promotion of legume rotations through interaction with extension workers, NGO staff, district council policymakers and ward officials, and a primary school programme incorporating knowledge on Striga and improvement of soil fertility in agricultural science classes.

1.1 Cultivation of sunn hemp

  • Experienced sunn hemp farmers mix 10 kg of seed for every 0.5 hectares to be planted with sand or dry soil at the ratio of 1:2 litres to assure a proper planting density (plants spaced 10 cm to 15 cm apart).
  • Above ground, growth is slow initially, as the plants develop deep roots.
  • Eventually, sunn hemp reaches a height of 2 m or more, and flowers appear three to four months later.
  • Sunn hemp does not re-seed itself, since its pods stay closed after the seeds have matured, even protecting them for months into the rainy season.
  • After six months the plants begin to senesce.
    • The stems, however, may persist for as long as eight or nine months and will develop new leaves when cut 30 cm above ground, or when eaten by animals.

2. Participatory evaluation and promotion of Striga management practices

  • On-farm demonstrations were led by groups with a total membership of 239 farmers in 11 villages of Kyela and Matombo districts.
  • Yields recorded from six villages confirmed previous observations from a smaller sample of sites that a one-year break from continuous cereal cropping to plant either the green manure, Crotalaria ochroleuca,  or pigeon pea leads to significantly higher rice or maize yields (p<0.001).
  • Median rice yields were increased by more than 1 000 kg and 800 kg in Kibangile and across Kyela district villages, respectively, by planting rice following the use of Crotalaria as green manure (234 and 81 percent increases respectively over continuous rice).
  • Use of either Crotalaria or pigeon pea increased median maize yield by an average of 188 percent in Kibangile and by 269 percent in Kiswira villages in Matombo.
  • Farmers reported a reduction in Striga abundance with an associated increase in rice vigour on fields where green manures had been planted.
  • By adopting rotations in Kyela, rice yields were boosted on the poorest fields from two to three to seven to eight bags per acre, and farmers believed they were on course to achieve more than ten bags per acre, making rice production very profitable again.
    • Individuals believed that the use of the rotations has reached the stage of sustained adoption with plots of more than one acre on some farms in Kilasilo.

3. Strategies up-scaling promotion of legume rotations

  • Assistance was provided to strengthen the structure of farmer groups and their plans for improving sustainability, including poster and leaflet training materials (Figure 1).
  • Additional extension materials included a training manual, picture set and series of videos.
  • Collaboration between district council agricultural extension and education staff was strengthened.
  • A primary school programme incorporating knowledge on Striga and improvement of soil fertility was supported in 21 villages.
    • Pupils were taught about soil fertility management as the key to reducing Striga abundance and reversing the yield decline.
    • School demonstration plots provided an important source of green manure seed for farmers.
  • Subsequently, a stakeholder workshop drew up plans for up-scaling promotion beyond the life of the project.
    • This led to Kyela district council allocating funds for the promotion of project outputs from 2006.
    • Ten lead farmers will be trained in all villages in the district.
    • A plan to expand promotion in four additional wards in the Uluguru mountains, where both rice and maize are important, have also been formulated by Morogoro District council.
    • CARE International has also initiated promotion work using extension materials developed by the project in four villages in the Uluguru mountains.
  • Policy implications from this work are that farmer group learning approaches including exchange visits and demonstration plots are keys to successful promotion.
  • The partnership between district council agricultural extension and education teams to involve primary schools in the promotion of agricultural knowledge should be expanded.
Figure 1. Poster

entries.tittle: Development and promotion of quality kale seed, Kenya
entries.summary: The use of quality seeds along with other inputs and appropriate cultural management practices is recognized as the most cost-effective way of increasing crop production and productivity. In considering interventions that are likely to reverse the trend of recurring food shortages, seed security has been recognized as having the potential for achieving significant advances in food productivity and production. The following technology describes the identification of local landraces of kale (Brassica oleracea) with superior cropping and disease-resistance characteristics. It also describes their development as improved varieties and the establishment and promotion of participatory seed production systems by local farmers.
entries.description:
Description

The use of quality seeds along with other inputs and appropriate cultural management practices is recognized as the most cost effective way of increasing crop production and productivity. In considering interventions that are likely to reverse the trend of recurring food shortages, seed security has been recognized as having the potential for achieving significant advances in food productivity and production.

Recognising the importance of healthy seed, a previous Crop Protection Product (CPP) project (see Spence 2003) engaged farmers in participatory research on selection criteria for kale plants for seed production. Both suitable (healthy) and unsuitable (diseased) plants were selected by both farmers and researchers for the production of seed, and the resulting seed was grown and evaluated. All of the 19 farmers chose plots with researcher-selected and farmer-selected healthy seeds as their preferred plots. Farmers were very keen to gain knowledge on how to improve the quality of farmer-collected seed.

This research generated great demand from farmers to know good seeds from bad seeds in the local market, because it is not possible to know what type of plants (diseased or healthy) the seeds came from when the seed is being sold. The work also found that farmers in the Kinale region were growing locally adapted landraces of kale (the most important vegetable crop in Kenya in terms of acreage grown), with superior characteristics, including field resistance to several virus diseases.

A subsequent project (see Spence 2005, part 1 and part 2) made progress in understanding farmers’ perceptions and needs with respect to seed purchases. The project identified a strong interest from Kinale farmers in multiplying and marketing seed with improved seed health and quality. An inventory of brassica seeds in Kenya was drawn up from commercial seed companies and local markets. Significant progress was made in analysis of Kinale kale as a distinctive variety, in close collaboration with KEPHIS inspectors using International Union for the Protection of new varieties of Plants (UPOV) guidelines.

Kinale farmers and the project research team selected five kale lines from a trial of 24 lines at the KARI field station at Njabini in the Kinangop for detailed varietal characterisation. These lines (CABI 1, CABI 2, CABI 3, CABI 4, CABI 5) were tested over two seasons for Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS) to carry out trials for distinctness, uniformity and stability (DUS). This gave farmers the option to choose whether to register varieties in a commercial seed business.

1. Seed multiplication

  • Potential models for sustainable seed multiplication of kale were evaluated through on-farm participatory trials in Kinale and on-station at Njabini.
    • This enabled farmers to establish a sustainable kale seed multiplication system that allows smallholders to produce healthy seed of good quality and that has an acceptable market value.
    • The feasibility of a community-based approach to seed multiplication in Kinale and potential for establishing and registering a commercial seed business in Kinale, was been examined.
    • Farmers were keen to pursue this approach.
  • Good seed multiplication practice for kale and seed certification using a preferred model was promoted.
    • However, farmers sought to go beyond this by seeking to formally register Kinale seed varieties under a community-based seed company model and to have a formal release of their varieties.
    • Further work was supported under a follow-up project (see Spence 2006 part 1 and part 2), which included two important activities.
      1. To continue to promote sustainable seed production technologies for farmer-led multiplication of improved kale varieties to smallholder farmers in the Kinale region of peri-urban Kenya.
        • This was in order to improve the quality, health and availability of kale seed to smallholder farmers.
      2. To facilitate the registration and release process of new varieties of Kinale kale whilst also supporting existing informal farmer-to-farmer distribution, under the regulation of KEPHIS and in collaboration with KARI and NGOs.
  • Two particular technologies that resulted from this work.
    1. Evaluation of new kale seed lines.
    2. Promotion of sustainable seed production technologies.

1.1 Evaluation of new kale seed lines

  • Selfed kale seeds from five of the preferred improved kale lines (CABI 1-5) identified by project R8312 were submitted to KEPHIS headquarters, along with documentation detailing their specific characteristics.
    • Trials for DUS were established and seed officers monitored improved kale lines at various developmental stages.
    • Data obtained will enable KEPHIS to decide if the lines are new varieties.
    • DUS trials were completed in December 2005 and the project team was advised informally that improved kale lines did perform significantly better than check varieties.
    • Submission of seeds to National Performance Trials proved unnecessary.
  • Improved kales were planted to evaluate their performance, compared to local varieties, in different agroecological zones in peri-urban Nairobi and Western Kenya.
    • In addition, over one hundred smallholders cultivated improved kales on their farms, and completed evaluation questionnaires.
    • The performances of the five improved kale lines varied considerably between sites, but consistently surpassed the commonly grown commercial variety, 1000 headed kale.
    • In western Kenya, improved lines also out-performed variety Sikuma Siku.
    • Although productivity of improved lines rarely exceeded that of another commercial variety (collards), some improved lines achieved particularly steady leaf yields, indicating their productivity could be sustained after yields decline in other kale varieties.
  • Feedback received from farmers’ participatory trials was overwhelmingly positive.
    • Improved kale lines germinated faster, transplanted better, and provided a longer period for leaf harvesting than the farmers’ own kale varieties.
    • Improved lines were larger, and more resistant to attack by pests and diseases, and farmers perceived the colour and shape of their leaves to be superior to those of local counterparts.
    • They had a shorter cooking time and were also more palatable.
  • The vast majority of farmers ranked the improved kale lines as having a greater consumer appeal than any other kale varieties they normally grow.
    • They were willing to buy the seeds of improved lines for their own use and would recommend these lines to other growers.
  • When the performance of three commercial kales (collards, 1 000 headed and Sukuma Siku) were compared against the five improved varieties in Western Kenya, 1 000 headed kale was found to be particularly susceptible to black rot disease.

1.2 Promotion of sustainable seed production technologies

  • Multiplication plots were established to ensure sufficient seed stocks to meet future demands of farmers for these improved kale lines.
    • Large batches of seed were ready for harvesting just after the project ended.
    • Participatory multiplications provided performance data on the improved kale lines for use, while defending the lines during the KEPHIS variety release committee.
  • A farmer group carried out their own pilot study to scale-up seed multiplication, observing the isolation distance recommended by KEPHIS.
    • This was done in readiness to become seed multipliers in the future.
    • One farmer provided land, and the group paid for a labourer to tend the plot.
  • Following consultations with IPGRI and KARI, seeds of all lines developed, including the five improved kale lines CABI 1-5, were deposited in the KARI genetic resources unit (Muguga), and in the vegetable gene bank (Warwick-HRI).
  • To promote sustainable seed production technologies, on-farm participatory demonstration plots were established with existing farmer groups in Lari division.
  • In preparation for continuous multiplication/commercialisation of the improved kale seeds, Lari Division farmers had extensive discussions amongst themselves and the Community Development Authority.
    • As a result, they obtained official registration and authority from the District Social Development Officer, under the National Community Development Programme in Kenya.
  • Multiple copies of posters (in Swahili) describing self-selection of seeds and its promotion were given to more than 70 farmers for further distribution.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cool.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Development and promotion of community-based seed production: ID 4551.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology is cost-effective and increases crop production and productivity. Therefore, it prevents recurring food shortages, providing additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Crop protection: early warning systems for improved Quelea bird management, Eastern and southern Africa
entries.summary: A short-term forecasting model (now adopted and implemented by the South African Development Community- SADC), predicts the movements and breeding of the Red-billed Quelea bird in southern Africa. This is to enable better mobilization and targeting of control resources by national and regional agencies, and methods for monitoring effects of Quelea control on the environment and non-target organisms agreed and adopted by regional authorities.
entries.description:
Description

Small-grain cereal crops, throughout semi-arid areas of Africa are subject to damage by the Red-billed Quelea bird Quelea quelea of up to USD 45 million per annum. Control of concentrations of thousands of the birds, gathered in breeding colonies or nocturnal roosts, involves the aerial application of organophosphate pesticides or fire-bombs created by the detonation with explosives of mixtures of diesel and petrol. The environmental impact of these activities has not been adequately researched but it is widely recognised that means to minimise the effects are required.

Another researchable constraint is the difficulty of knowing where and when the birds will occur and where they will require control in the extensive semi-arid regions that they live in. This difficulty arises mainly because Quelea is migratory, moving in relation to the timing and distribution of rainfall and the availability of annual grass seeds, the birds’ principal food. Genetically homogenous populations of the subspecies Q. quelea lathamii migrate throughout the southern African region.

In addition to demonstrating their genetic uniformity, CPP projects R6823 (Cheke, 1999) and R7967 (Cheke 2003 Part 1 and Part 2) developed a model for forecasting where and when the birds could breed in southern Africa. The model forecasts the timing and locations of suitable sites where Quelea breeding colonies could require control to prevent the successful fledging of juveniles.

The model uses satellite-derived estimates of rainfall to determine when the threshold quantity of rainfall (60 mm to 70 mm, estimated from the duration of cold cloud at 38°C or below), has been exceeded at any time within a two-week period. This quantity is required to cause grass seed germination and hence to initiate the “early rains migration” by the birds out of their dry season quarters.

When sufficient time (six weeks) has elapsed since the germination of the grass seeds, the satellite data are again used to determine whether sufficient rainfall (240 mm) has fallen to allow the birds to begin breeding.

Another output of these and subsequent projects, R8314 (Cheke, 2005) and R8426 (Cheke, 2006), was to develop and obtain standard protocols or codes of practice to ensure that environmental damage is minimised when birds threatening crops are controlled by aerial spraying their breeding colonies with the avicide “fenthion” or by the use of explosives to destroy nocturnal roosts, and obtain consensus for their adoption in Africa.

Protocols were devised for biodiversity assessment (vertebrates and invertebrates) and evaluation of potential ecological damage. These were to be used before and after Quelea control operations and to enhance the capacity of national organisations to implement the policies.

The projects also investigated the harvesting of Quelea bird nestlings as food for people as an alternative to environmentally questionable sprays and explosions. In parts of Botswana, harvesting Quelea nestlings from breeding colonies, just before they fledge, is a traditional practice for which demand could be further developed through assistance with local transportation, processing and marketing.

1. Model for short-term forecasting of red-billed Quelea breeding

  • The model was created to forecast where and when crops are likely to be damaged so that control teams in southern Africa can identify nesting colonies and target their operations more effectively.
    • Such planning has been difficult, as Quelea birds are long-distance migrants, moving up to 2 500 km in response to the seasonal movements of rain-fronts.
  • Rain causes their main food, grass seeds, to germinate at the start of the wet season forcing birds to move to areas where the seeds have yet to germinate.
    • When rain reaches these areas, the birds are forced to move again, usually returning in “early-rains migrations” in the direction whence they came.
    • By this time sufficient rain needs to have fallen to exceed another threshold within a restricted period for the new grass to have produced fresh seed.
    • Breeding may then commence.
  • Over the following three to four months the birds then undertake further, previously unpredictable, “breeding migrations” to areas elsewhere wherever adequate rainfall will permit them to breed.
    • It is the young, newly fledged, birds that cause the most damage to agriculture.
    • Given the dependence of Quelea activities on rainfall, a model was devised that uses Spatio-temporal information on rainfall throughout southern Africa derived from satellite imagery.
  • The model is intended to provide only short-term predictions using the information on rainfall alone as real-time inputs.
    • The initial spatial scale chosen at the start of the development phase in 2001 was 1° X 1° squares with time steps of one week.
    • During 2002 the resolution of the model was improved to squares of 0.5° X 0.5°.
    • The model accumulates rainfall data throughout a Quelea season (September–May), starting at the beginning of September (calendar week 36, model week one)
    • For each square, the following questions are asked at the end of each week:
      • What was the total rainfall during the current week?
      • What was the total rainfall during the current week plus the previous week?
      • What was the total rainfall during the current week plus the previous four weeks?
  • The rainfall was estimated as one hour of Cold Cloud Duration (CCD cold cloud duration at 38°C or below) being equivalent to 3 mm of rain.
    • The model was programmed in a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet, in which worksheet cells represented every degree square for 2001/2002 or every 0.5 X 0.5 of a degree square, for 2002/2003, of the southern African region.
  • The cell value is given by a formula which implements the model criteria described above.
    • The model was run each week of the 2001/2002 and 2002/2003 seasons and seven days of CCD values were input for every run.
    • The model was originally developed and validated in 2002/2003 and the forecasting system has been disseminated widely to control planners, through the Information Core for Southern Africa Migrant Pests (ICOSAMP, http://icosamp.ecoport.org/) and other routes, and details can be found in (Cheke 2003 Part 1 and Part 2).
  • Regular weekly forecasts were produced and validated in subsequent seasons Cheke (2005) and operation of the model was transferred to the Southern African Development Community (SADC). 
  • Under project R8426, the existing Quelea forecasting model for southern Africa was expanded to include the East African distribution of Quelea quelea aethiopica.
    • In addition to Q. q. lathamii, two other subspecies of Q. quelea are recognised.
    • These are the nominate race (Q. q. Quelea) that inhabits the semi-arid region from Senegal to Chad and Q. q. aethiopica that occurs in Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, eastern parts of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda.
  • As migrations within and between these countries will be governed by the same rainfall thresholds and patterns that have been used to model those of Q. q. lathamii successfully, it was a comparatively simple task to extend the existing model to cover eastern Africa in an extension that has been requested by host countries.

2. Standardised protocols for monitoring effects of Quelea control on non-target organisms

  • Guidelines for standardised protocols for monitoring the effects of Quelea control on non-target organisms were developed based on the monitoring the impacts of Quelea control operations on the environment and non-target organisms under projects R7967 and R8314.
    • An early version of these guidelines was approved by representatives of East African countries at a workshop on Quelea management held in Kenya, 14-22 May 2005.
  • This also led to a proposal for Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) work on Quelea from the Tanzanian Government.
    • EIA is now a requirement for any undertaking in Tanzania that affects the environment under Section 81 (1) of the Environmental Management Act No. 20 of 2004 which came into effect in July 2005
    • See https://www.nemc.or.tz/ and http://www.lexadin.nl/wlg/legis/nofr/oeur/lxwetan.htm for further details.
  • Aerial spraying, including against Quelea, requires an EIA to be conducted as stipulated under Schedule 3 of the Act.
    • Similarly, the National Environment Management Authorities (NEMA) in Kenya and Uganda have, since 2004, required EIAs of any new spray operations requested by commercial farmers.
    • The guidelines were subsequently discussed and approved by representatives of SADC countries attending an ICOSAMP workshop in Pretoria, 11-17 September 2005.
  • The Quelea breeding forecast for Southern Africa has been adopted by the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and is run by the Regional Remote Sensing Unit (RRSU) of the Food, Agriculture and Natural Resources (FANR) Directorate.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropical, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies 

  • Crop planning and management in organic agriculture: ID 8367.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Resource-use efficiency

The technology provides for the efficient control of bird populations which in turn allows for improved and increased crop yields.

entries.tittle: Development of biopesticide legislation in Africa
entries.summary: Abuse and misuse of insecticides is common in Africa. Although the use of pesticides in Africa represents less than 5 percent of the global total, misuse is disproportionately high. The use of insecticides is determined largely by export crops, such as cotton and cocoa. Trends are therefore dependent on world prices. Without specific measures, a continued increase in insecticide consumption is likely to be matched by continued misuse. Such chemicals are associated with environmental pollution, human contamination, rising costs, and resistance to development. The following technology describes methodologies relating to technical, regulatory, and policy issues concerning the development and implementation of legislation for registration of biological pesticides in sub-Saharan Africa.
entries.description:
Description

Abuse and misuse of insecticides is common in Africa. Although the use of pesticides in Africa represents less than 5 percent of the global total, misuse is disproportionately high. The use of insecticides is determined largely by export crops, such as cotton and cocoa. Trends are therefore dependent on world prices. The increasingly important peri-urban sector accounts for larger volumes of insecticide use. Products, dose and application frequency are not well regulated. Furthermore, insecticides imported for use in export crops spill over into the peri-urban sector, for which products are not approved.

Without specific measures, a continued increase in insecticide consumption is likely to be matched by continued misuse. Such chemicals are associated with environmental pollution, human contamination, rising costs, and resistance to development. For instance, the appearance of widespread resistance to commonly used insecticides in the Diamondback Moth (DBM) and Plutella xylostella (a widespread pest of brassica crops), is driving farmers to treat their crops more and more frequently, while others abandon their fields or give up brassica cultivation altogether.

Farmers all claim additional pesticides are required for DBM. Many have expressed interest in testing biopesticides. At the same time, there is a need to comply with an increasingly regulated environment imposed by developed countries on import crops, especially on vegetable and horticultural produce (maximum residue limits and Eurepgap standards, see http://www.eurepgap.org/). This threatens the sustainability of export agriculture and fuels demands to reduce chemical pesticides or substitute them with safer alternatives.

1. Biopesticides

  • While there has been substantial technical progress with biopesticides, and increasing public awareness of the need to reduce dependency on chemical pesticides, the uptake of biopesticides has been limited.
  • In Africa, there have been many notable and pioneering studies on the use of viruses for the control of insect pests.
    • However there are few, if any, sustainable examples of their long-term commercial use.
    • Reasons have often included a lack of expertise in the crucial later stages of development and/or pursuit of an inappropriate model of biopesticide development.
  • The early stages of biopesticide research and development, are often undertaken in the public sector using public finances.
    • However many potential biopesticide products fail to go beyond the laboratory or field-trial stage.
  • Commercialization is the key implementation pathway for biopesticides and failure to engage the private sector and a lack of market data may be amongst factors contributing to poor biopesticide uptake.
  • However, the main constraint on progress is probably the lack of a legislative framework for registration and approval of biopesticides in much of Sub-Saharan Africa.
    • This has meant that it is effectively impossible to legally market biopesticide products for commercial use?
    • This is in spit of the fact that these may be based on organisms, and even locally - obtained strains or isolates, that occur naturally within the user countries themselves.
  • Several CPP projects have been concerned with developing biopesticides including:
    • entomopathogenic viruses against DBM and armyworm (Spodoptera exempta);
    • entomopathogenic fungi and bacteria against root-knot nematodes; and
    • phermones against legume pod borers (Maruca vitrata) and cocoa mirid bugs.
  • Project partners have also been concerned with mass-producing predators and parasitoids for horticultural pests.
  • In most of these cases, it was recognized that deficiencies in the existing regulatory environment would present difficulties for commercialization, marketing, and eventual uptake.
    • Efforts were made to help develop and implement the appropriate legislation and approval processes.

2. Legislative structure

  • Recognizing the need for legislative structure to ensure the sustainable development and commercial usage of biopesticides in Kenya, the Kenya Agricultural Research Institute, in collaboration with the Pest Control Products Board and the DFID Crop Protection Programme, hosted a three-day workshop at Nakuru, Kenya in 2003.
  • The full account of this meeting provides useful methodology resource materials for the development and implementation of similar protocols elsewhere.
  • The proceedings include 17 papers arranged in four sessions.
    1. Demand from the horticultural industry
    2. Contribution of research in Africa
    3. Registration in Africa
    4. Registration in other countries.
  • The publication also includes, Annexes finalized for legislation, application documents for the registration of microbial, macrobial and biochemical pest control products.
  • Similar workshops for regulatory authorities were held in Accra, Ghana, in 2005, on the introduction of biopesticide product as well as specific regulations, including provision of model regulations.
  • Presentations made to these workshops are available that complement those produced in East Africa.
    • Biopesticides: a review of active agents. 
    • Biopesticides: a global perspective.
    • Biopesticide registration.
    • Introduction to Ghana’s current pesticides registration framework and requirement for biopesticides regulations in Ghana.
  • Biopesticide registration guidelines were subsequently drafted for the Ghanaian Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
    • The final drafts, together with the draft biopesticides regulations, were to be put before the EPA Board in preparation for consultation with key stakeholders.
  • Observers from Togo, Benin, Ivory Coast and Guinea all expressed interest in developing similar guidelines for biopesticides.

2.1 You manipulate and/or use (bio)pesticides?

  • Make inquiries before!
  • Pesticide can be harmful to your health, the health of your family, of the consumers and of the environment.
  • Adopt the right gestures to use pesticides safely.
    • Click on “Risk reduction while manipulating pesticides”

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Integrated pest management: ID 7298.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology reduces environmental pollution, human contamination, costs, and resistance to development.

entries.tittle: Sustainable approaches for management of root-knot nematodes on vegetables in Kenya
entries.summary: Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.) are a concern to both smallholders and commercial producers involved in intensive vegetable production. Although not all smallholders will recognize nematodes as a production constraint. The following describes the development, through public-private sector partnership with a commercial horticulture producer, techniques for the production of bio control agents for the integrated management of root-knot nematodes on tomato and other horticultural crops and promotion via networks of smallholder growers. Also reports on the development and implementation of regulatory mechanisms for the approval and registration of bio control agents in Kenya that are applicable elsewhere.
entries.description:
Description

Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.) are a concern to both smallholders and commercial producers involved in intensive vegetable production. Although not all smallholders will recognize nematodes as a production constraint, in Kenya for instance, up to 20 percent of vegetable producers use nematicides when growing tomatoes as this has been the only control strategy available other than not growing the crop.

Nematodes are difficult to manage. They are soil-dwelling animals, too small to see without a microscope and cause symptoms on the root system, which can be recognized only when a plant is lifted from the soil. For this reason smallholders, who are reluctant to dig up plants, usually, overlook the presence of nematodes and attribute above-ground symptoms (e.g. small fruit, poor growth, yellow foliage, and wilting during hot weather) to other biotic or abiotic constraints. This often results in the use of inappropriate chemicals. Familiarization of smallholders with nematodes was amongst the objectives of these projects since willingness to adopt biological and cultural control strategies will only result from an understanding of what nematodes are and how they damage crops.

1. Nematode management without nematicides

  • All sectors of the vegetable industry are keen to adopt production methods based on low pesticide regimes as a result of increased health and environmental consciousness of food production techniques.
  • The initial impact of this in Kenya is on the commercial export producers who are attempting to meet European Union standards and codes of practice through the initiative on harmonization of pesticide use COLEACP (http://www.coleacp.org) and the EurepGAP standards.
    • EurepGAP is an initiative of retailers belonging to the Euro - Retailer Produce Working Group (EUREP), a partnership of agricultural producers and their retail customers, aiming to meet accepted standards and procedures for the global certification of Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) (http://www.eurep.org)
  • Earlier, research had demonstrated how the bacterium Pasteuria penetrans and the fungus Pochonia chlamydosporium (formerly Verticillium)  had complementary beneficial effects by suppressing root-knot nematode populations.
    • The presence of these biocontrol agents in soils in Kenya was determined and local isolates were collected.
    • The relative pathogenicity of different isolates to the native nematode populations from study areas in Kenya was determined and suitable strains were selected.
    • However, biocontrol agents of root-knot nematodes can be difficult to manipulate because of location-specific characteristics related to pathogenicity of the natural pathogens and their interactions with abiotic and biotic soil factors.
  • Techniques for deploying these biocontrol agents on farms were also needed.
    • These must also suit the needs and capabilities of the poorer farmers.
    • Issues of how the biocontrol agents might be mass-produced, how frequently they should be applied and within what cropping regime they perform best needed to be resolved.
      • For instance, smallholders need to understand that the processes of biological control may take several crops for the biocontrol agents to take effect.
      • In some situations it may never take effect considering the specificity of pathogenicity and specific biotic/abiotic soil conditions, and this risk also needs to be considered.

2. Promotion of biocontrol agents

  • The routes for promotion of a nematode control strategy based upon biocontrol agents are thus critical and it was felt that the best way to achieve this would be through demonstrations and the more highly supervised production systems of the commercial export producers and their out-growers.
  • Because of the links between the commercial export sector and independent growers through the out-grower system, the new pest management technologies will also be introduced to the wider constituency of smallholder producers.
  • Within this context, this series of projects formed a partnership between a commercial producer, Dudutech (Kenya) Ltd. (who were interested in implementing a range of programmes of biological control including the mass production of Pochonia chlamydosporia and Pasteuria penetrans for managing root-knot nematodes), CENSA Cuba (who had experience of appropriate production technologies in this area), and UK research departments at Rothamsted Experimental Station and Reading University.
  • Through the successful collaboration with Dudutech and CENSA, Pochonia production technology was transferred to Kenya and a production system is now in place with the potential to produce 100 kg of product per week.
    • Dudutech are also progressing the development of an in vivo production system for Pasteuria penetrans that can be adapted to the local climatic conditions and is economically viable.
      • It is important that this process uses local strains, otherwise failure may be expected.
  • The production and promotion of biocontrol agents for the wider farming community can be implemented only when the appropriate legislation on sale and use of biopesticides is in place.
    • In order to facilitate this, the project partners worked with Kenyan government authorities to develop and pilot legislation to permit registration of biocontrol agents in Kenya.
    • These experiences have been documented and serve as a model for other countries in East Africa and beyond.

3. Biological systems for production and delivery of Pochonia chlamydosporia

  • Laboratory systems for isolation, handling, screening and selection of pathogenic strains, quality control, etc. were carried out at Rothamsted and are described in: Gowen, S.R. 2005b http://www.fao.org/docs/eims/upload/agrotech/2008/R8296_FTR_anx1.pdf.
  • Technologies for mass production were developed by Dudutech Ltd. and are described in: Gowen, S.R. 2005c http://www.fao.org/docs/eims/upload/agrotech/2008/R8296_FTR_anx2.pdf.
  • A technique for delivery to the cropping environment via drip irrigation is described by: GOWEN, S.R. 2005d http://www.fao.org/docs/eims/upload/agrotech/2008/R8296_FTR_anx2.pdf.

4. Socioeconomic environment for promotion and uptake of RKN biocontrol agents

Two studies, carried out by Kenyan and UK consultants, are available.

  • A study on opportunities and constraints to adoption of sustainable approached to the control of RKN.
  • A study on the future uptake of biocontrol agents in general. 

5. Approval and registration of biocontrol agents

  • A landmark workshop, involving participants from government, IARCs, commercial and NGO sectors, led to the drafting and (pending) implementation of legislation and procedures for the approval and registration of biocontrol agents.
    • The full proceedings are available and serve as a model for adoption elsewhere.
  • These technologies are now available for wider use and will be of benefit to poorer farmers growing nematode-susceptible crops and indirectly to the wider community who buy these crops.
  • In addition to improving the technology for the commercial export producers (a requirement of the European Union rules for harmonization of use of pesticides: COLEACP), commercial growers who grow crops on contract to the exporting companies will also benefit.

6. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm. 

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Integrated pest management in vegetable production: a guide for extension workers in West Africa: ID 6963.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2560.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology ensures the efficient use of biocontrol agents in the management of nematodes.

entries.tittle: Participatory breeding of superior, mosaic disease-resistant cassava
entries.summary: The project has validated a participatory breeding approach for developing superior, mosaic disease-resistant cassava, demonstrating that it can provide a means by which farmers, plant breeders and plant pathologists could work together in an effective and inclusive manner. It also provided an environment whereby farmers made a significant and consistent contribution to the outcome of the selection. Following multi-locational trials with 35 clones, three "front runners" have been identified and inspection plots have been prepared by the National Varietal Release Committee, both for inspection and as future sources of planting material in anticipation of the release.
entries.description:
Description

Situation analyses in Ghana of two farming communities in the Forest and Forest Savannah Transition Zones (Nkaakom and Aworowa respectively) identified the main customs and practices of cassava production. Cassava has changed over the last several decades from not being grown or a minor crop to becoming the main food crop and a major cash crop. Much of this increase was associated with a lack of new land to open and impoverished soils on previously cropped land.

The activities of non-farmer stakeholders in cassava breeding and how they might interact with the project have also been explored. An IFAD - funded Root and Tuber Improvement Programme (RTIP) project has funded increased research and development activities in the university, the public research sector and large-scale distribution of released varieties. The German Technical Cooperation Agency (GTZ) has also supported the agricultural sector generally, but relatively few NGOs seemed to support cassava-linked activities. There is increasing industrial interest in cassava as a source of food for humans and livestock as well as starch as a chemical feedstock.

1. Standard sources for planting materials

  • In ten diverse farming communities, no farmer interviewed understood the role of pollen, most were aware of cassava seeds and seedlings.
    • Cassava seedlings seemed generally to be avoided by farmers as a source of planting material and food, often being weeded out.
    • However, few farmers in most communities had tested a little amount seedlings and many farmers used them when other planting material was scarce.
  • These seedlings or “volunteers” are often virus free and when they are not inbred (poor growth), they are heterozygous and sometimes high performing.
    • Farming communities seldom exchanged landraces, though occasionally did so purposefully.
    • Migrant workers and settlers bringing new varieties from their place of work or previous home seem an important means by which communities obtain new landraces.

2. Selection of superior genotypes

  • Seed stocks derived from diverse genetic backgrounds but including resistance to pests and diseases, particularly CMD, and high storage root yields were selected by the  International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA).
    • These were provided to the Nkaakom and Aworowa farming communities for evaluation and selection of superior genotypes and were sown in communal plots.
    • They were also sown at the Central Research Institute (CRI) research farm.
  • Seedlings were monitored monthly by the multidisciplinary project team for agronomic and pathological characters.
    • They were also evaluated with farmers, firstly for aboveground characters, secondly for pests and diseases and finally at harvest for both above- and below-ground characters.
    • Farmers recorded a wide range of mostly positive criteria.
    • Using their own criteria, both farmers and the CRI cassava breeder pathologists selected seedlings to retain as clones in a further trial at each location.
  • A further similar annual cycle of monitoring, evaluation, and reselection of clones was conducted at each location, reducing their number tenfold over the two generations.
    • Clones then were distributed to individual farmers.
    • The resultant clones were mostly preferred by farmers over their own landraces, being both higher-yielding and less affected by CMD.
    • This may to some extent be because their 'epigenetic history' is much younger and therefore their viral load lower.
    • If this is the case, the important questions are 'will this performance last?' And for how long? 
  • Farmers were consistent in their selection and overlapped that of the CRI breeder by about 60%.
    • Farmers generally rated the technology as beneficial and participants at an end-of-project workshop also validated the approach.
    • Farmers took planting material of promising genotypes back to their home farms.
    • 39 farmers at Nkaakom and 36 at Aworowa received 124 seedling clones (61 at Nkaakom and 63 at Aworowa) for testing on their farms.
    • These accessions have also been planted at the communal farms and at the research station.
  • From these, a third selection was made of 35 clones which were grown in multilocational trials, and a preliminary analysis was made of yield and disease incidence and severity data.
    • Subsequently, a fourth selection of 15 superior clones was made for evaluation on-farm and on-station, and these were also trialed on processors’ farms.
    • Three “front runners” were identified and inspection plots were prepared both for inspection by the Varietal Release Committee and as future sources of planting material in anticipation of the release.
  • The projects provided both experience-based training and formal training in participatory research and plant breeding to CRI staff and in response to farmers’ identifying limited markets as a problem.
    • The projects identified opportunities for improving communication between end-users and those working on varietal development so as to enable germplasm improvement to enhance cassava utilization.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Improved cassava fufu processing methods, West Africa: ID 4522.
  • Cassava processing: cassava wet flour: ID 3826.
  • Make bitter cassava safe for consumption: ID 4372.
  • Participatory breeding of superior, mosaic disease resistant cassava for Africa: ID 4513.
  • Storage and preservation of wet cassava: ID 4520.
  • Production of high­ quality cassava flour: ID 4574.
  • Sustainable livelihoods: new market opportunities for cassava: ID 4575.
  • Making high-quality cassava flour: ID 6923.
  • Introduction of early maturing cassava varieties in Bolivia, a cost­-benefit analysis: ID 8952
  • Cassava brown streak disease: control measures: ID 7004.
  • Production of glucose syrup from high-quality cassava flour: ID 4576.
  • Participatory crop improvement in salt-affected areas: ID 4592.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology effectively improves crop resistance to disease; improves cooperation amongst farmers, plant breeders and plant pathologists; and efficiently provides training and environments to increase quality and quantity of crop yield.

entries.tittle: Improving Sustainable Livelihoods in Dryland Areas, East Africa
entries.summary: Participatory research methodology development in parallel with technology development that responded to the needs of the farming community was done in Embu, a semi-arid area of Kenya. The work involved problem diagnosis, research design, trial implementation and evaluation, as well as demonstration and dissemination of options and recommendations for producing new crops and varieties, crop utilisation, soil and water management, tools and tillage, animal health and agroforestry. The work contributed to strategic socio-economic research on participatory research options within national programmes, improved the capacity of resource poor communities and national research institutions to conduct collaborative participatory agricultural research, reduced risks in dryland farming, and increased productivity and crop diversity thereby enhancing household food security.
entries.description:
Description

Problems identified during the project included limited local social organisation; infrastructure for developing and disseminating new technologies and for participating in the formal research process; low and erratic rainfall; declining soil fertility; food insecurity at household and community level; limited choice of adapted (short-season, drought tolerant and pest/disease resistant) crops and varieties; high crop losses due to pests; low and risk-prone livestock productivity; and limited knowledge on the propagation and establishment of trees.

1. Activities

  • Socio-economic farm monitoring data were collected and analysed, including:
    • seasonal problem monitoring,
    • seed source,
    • seed selection,
    • seed storage methods,
    • cropping choices,
    • crop patterns,
    • crop management,
    • soil management,
    • tree planting history,
    • tree management,
    • livestock management, and
    • market prices.
  • Activities to build farmer research capacity.
    • The establishment of focused farmer research groups for tillage tools and water harvesting.
      • These groups went through several cycles of research trials, starting with development of a research agenda, implementation, evaluation, re-formulation and through to development of recommendations for technologies being tested.
    • Local research site management committees were also set up, elected by the local community during farmer open days.
      • The site committees took a lead role in open days, seed bulking and distribution and resolution of local inter-personal conflicts.
      • Research site committees were monitored, including self-evaluation meetings and submitted reports.
    • The formation of researcher farmer clusters in on-farm sites that improved on-farm trial monitoring and farmer to farmer communication.
      • Partner to farmer evaluation of seasonal visits and competitions were established within the clusters as an effective means for hands-on training in formal research methods and stimulating farmer to farmer learning.
      • Some of the clusters developed further into self-help groups for seed bulking and fund raising for agricultural activities.
    • Expert farmer panels for on-site screening of new sorghum, pearl millet and cowpea varieties were formed and operated for two seasons.
      • This provided a forum for interaction between farmers and plant breeders.
      • One of these panels also evolved into a self-help group.
    • Farmer study tours on water harvesting and soil and water technologies to other dryland districts were very effective for sourcing practical expertise in water harvesting and encouraging farmers to experiment with a wider range of water harvesting techniques.
    • Community level workshops to review the dryland research agenda, and review experiences with site committees and clusters were held, without any senior research or extension staff present.
      • The results were useful for informing future research activities.

2. Outcomes

2.1 Farm tools

  • Farmer groups were involved in tools testing.
  • In order to address tool supply and design issues, linkages were formed with local artisans culminating in tools markets where farmers judged tools on display and explained their requirements to local artisans.

2.2 Soil and water management

  • External water harvesting, pitting, basins and tied furrows, all tested and adapted by farmers, reduced their risks and increased production, particularly on smaller farms where land was limiting.
  • Yield increases of 10 to 15 percent were achieved in good rainfall seasons and much higher relative yields in drier seasons.
  • While initial uptake may be slow, in the longer term this technology will make crop production more sustainable, reduce risks and increase scope for crop diversification.

2.3 Crop varieties

  • Variety screening of popular drought resistant crops (cowpeas, pearl millet, sorghum, chickpeas), testing, agronomy and utilisation of new crops (groundnuts, cassava, sweet potatoes, proso millet, dwarf pigeon peas, wheat, dryland beans), seed bulking, study of preservation of green vegetables and a trial on the control of kiwi weevil in cowpeas were done.
  • Farmers visiting research sites were able select from a very wide range of drought tolerant crops and varieties for adaptive testing on their own farms.
  • Recipes and options for the utilisation of new crops were demonstrated to farmers using participatory demonstration methods.
    • Following a successful recipe development workshop involving farmers and home economists from extension, the cowpea leaf drying and utilisation methods were popularised to very many farmers through participatory field days.
  • Preliminary results from the kiwi beetle control trials indicated limited effect of neem extract compared to conventional insecticides, and indicated the scope for more strategic use of these as shorter term strategies.
  • Seed bulking activities were very successful, with large quantities of seed for a wide range of new crops and varieties being sold to farmers (for example, half a ton of more than 30 cowpea varieties in one season).
  • However, seed bulking was seriously affected by the two consecutive droughts in the final year resulting in many collaborating farmers loosing seed of the new varieties.
  • New, drought escaping varieties and new drought tolerant crops were adopted by collaborating farmers, spreading risk through crop diversification and contributing to household food security by providing earlier food and a wider choice of foods.
  • ICMV 111, an early pearl millet variety, has proved particularly popular, closing the hunger gap by up to two weeks.
  • Many of the new cowpeas were appreciated for their leaf and grain qualities for household food.
  • A number of farmers have started planting small areas of the introduced varieties of cassava, dwarf pigeon peas, proso millet and groundinuts.
  • Preliminary results in crop protection of legumes indicate potentially high returns to strategic pest control measures.

2.4 Livestock

  • Work on the epidemiology of worms in goats included on-farm monitoring of selected animals for four seasons, two of which were not thought to be typical.
    • The recommendation was for a more detailed climatological study for developing strategic economical worm control recommendations.
    • Screening of the most popular herbal de-wormers in goats revealed positive evaluations from farmers, but laboratory analysis was not supportive at the scientifically accepted standards of efficacy, raising the issue of whose standards to use in on-farm evaluation.
  • Several local concoctions were judged equivalent to the commercial drug against mange, using body condition score and weight gain parameters, but a mixture of castor oil and Tamarindus indica pods was judged the best by farmers.
    • The research generated considerable interest among farmers and also from researchers in other countries in the region.
  • Risk has been reduced and livestock incomes made more secure through the introduction and popularisation of an effective, low cost and locally available remedy for mange control.
    • To further consolidate the benefits, the link with agroforestry in the preservation and planting of more medicinal species should be followed up.

2.5 Trees

  • Termite and drought constraints to tree establishment were confirmed.
    • There appeared to be a complex interaction between termite attack and drought stress, one which may over ride many of the single effects of different concoctions applied at establishment.
    • Water harvesting options for tree establishment showed that stone mulching was a popular option, followed by V shaped catchments which, however, carry risks of water-logging during heavy rains.
  • A contribution was made to expanding income opportunities and improving diet through the introduction of a variety of fruit trees (grafted mango, guava and papaya).
    • The potential for using grafted mangos for high value fruit production in dry areas was demonstrated.
    • Easier propagation methods, particularly for Melia volkensii, promised to boost the commercialisation of dryland timber production, particularly with the depletion of forest resources in higher rainfall areas of Kenya.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Sustainable livelihoods: new market opportunities for cassava: ID 4575.
  • Keyhole gardens for better nutrition and livelihoods: ID 7643.
  • Sack gardens for improved urban diets and livelihoods: ID 7652.
  • Shortened bush-fallow rotations and sustainable rural livelihoods: ID 4578.
  • Traditional foods: better livelihoods, dietary diversity and health: ID 7658.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology reduces risk and secures more livestock incomes.

entries.tittle: Production of high-quality cassava flour, Ghana
entries.summary: High-Quality Cassava Flour (HQCF) is an attractive alternative to cassava starch that can form the starting point for a cassava-based industry. HQCF production is less capital intensive and requires lower levels of inputs for success, compared to cassava starch. HQCF can be used as an alternative to starch and other imported materials in a range of industries such as adhesives, sugar syrups and industrial alcohol.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction: high-quality cassava flour

Cassava is an important crop in Africa and traditionally it is used mainly for food. There are, however, industrial uses for cassava starch and flour. Starch is a high-value product that can be used in many industries. High-Quality Cassava Flour (HQCF) can also be used as an alternative for starch and other imported materials like wheat flour in a number of industrial undertakings. HQCF can be used in the production of adhesives (in paper board manufacture) as an extender for plywood glues, as a source of starch in the textile industry and as raw material for the production of glucose syrups, industrial alcohol and bakery products.

The profitability of HQCF production depends to a large extent on the location of the enterprise, the scale of production and the source of power for operating equipment. Anyone interested in engaging in the production of HQCF should take special note of the information provided in the section of economics, profitability, and marketing. The production of HQCF is a process that requires a conscious adherence to good manufacturing practice (GMP) in order to obtain a product of desirable quality. Non-compliance to GMP will not produce the high-grade cassava flour needed by industry.

The details of the process are described in the booklet 'Training manual for the production of high-quality cassava flour' by, (Dziezoave et al. 2003). 

The necessary steps include:

  • raw material selection,
  • peeling,
  • washing,
  • grating,
  • pressing,
  • disintegration,
  • sifting(or slicing/chipping as an alternative to grating, pressing, disintegration and sifting),
  • drying, 
  • milling,
  • screening,
  • packaging,
  • and storage.

Depending on the maturity of the cassava, the variety used for processing, the initial moisture content and the product recovery rates would range between 13 to 19 percent. Recovery rates should be aimed at about 18 percent.

According to IITA, mini-chippers were found to be unsuitable for bitter varieties because the concentration of cyanogenic glucosides was not reduced sufficiently during processing. The training manual also includes information on quality specifications, equipment requirements and maintenance, and the economics, profitability and marketing of the high-quality cassava flour.

2. Factors necessary for the production of high-grade cassava flour

The most important factors in the above processes include the following. 

  • Always use high-quality cassava (10 to 12 months old at the time of harvest), and ensure that processing is carried out within one day of harvest.
    • Cassava of this type will have optimum starch yield and minimum levels of fiber and water.
    • Most varieties can be used, but high moisture varieties such as "agbelima duade" should be avoided.
  • Always peel and wash cassava roots before processing.
  • Cassava may be chipped or grated but chips and grits must be small enough to allow drying to be completed within one day (sun drying).
    • Rapid drying under clean conditions is essential for maintaining quality.
  • The dried product should be milled (hammer or disc attrition mill) and screened through a 0.25 mm metal mesh to produce a finely milled product containing minimum fiber levels.
    • Plastic netting and mosquito mesh will not produce products of the required quality and so must no be used.
    • The use of a 0.25 mm metal mesh is essential for all industrial products such as adhesives, glucose syrup, industrial alcohol and bakery products.

3. The importance of quality

3.1 Manufacture of products to meet the required quality specifications

  • Before starting production, it is very important to determine the customer’s requirements on quality, and for producer and use to agree on a standard for quality of the product.

3.2 Reliability in maintaining quality

  • When a quality specification has been agreed, it must be maintained at all times.
  • The use of adulterants and short cuts to reduce costs and process times must be avoided.

3.3 Reliability of supply (quantity)

  • Processors must never promise more than they can produce by the agreed delivery date, as the end-user will be planning his production on the basis of having the necessary quantities of raw materials.

3.4 Timeliness of delivery

  • Realistic delivery dates are a must for commercial success.

3.5 Price competitiveness

  • Industrial users want a local product that is cheaper than the imported alternative.
  • However, the reduction in price must not be achieved at the expense of quality.
  • It is vitally important for anyone wishing to market cassava-based products to industry to keep these criteria in mind at all times.
  • Many industries are willing to be tolerant of manufacturer’s difficulties, as long as they are kept fully informed, but are not happy with producers who are found to be unreliable on quality, quantity and timeliness of delivery.

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Improved cassava fufu processing methods: ID 4522.
  • Sustainable livelihoods: New market opportunities for cassava: ID 4575.
  • Production of glucose syrup from high quality cassava flour: ID 4576.
  • Making high-quality cassava flour: ID 6923.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2574.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology makes use of the extra cassava harvested to produce HQCF in order to optimize production, and reduce harvest losses. 

6.2 Pro-poor technology 

This technology allows for an additional source of income through either the selling or the home consumption of HQCF.

entries.tittle: Production of glucose syrup from high quality cassava flour, Ghana
entries.summary: High-quality cassava flour (HQCF) is an attractive alternative to cassava starch that can form the starting point for a cassava based industry. HQCF production is less capital intensive and requires lower levels of inputs for success, compared to cassava starch. HQCF can be used as an alternative to starch and other imported materials in a range of industries such as adhesives, sugar syrups and industrial alcohol.
entries.description:
Description

Glucose syrup is a concentrated aqueous solution of glucose, maltose and other nutritive saccharides obtained from edible starch. Depending on the proportion of the different sugars in the syrup, it may be specifically called a maltodextrin, high maltose syrup or high dextrose glucose syrup. The type of glucose syrup described here is the high maltose syrup. Although technically incorrect, “Glucose Syrup” is the standard industry term referring to a mixed syrup containing glucose, maltose and a range of maltodextrins of different sizes, i.e. the use of the term is not limited simply to glucose. The industry uses of the term “glucose syrup” is therefore adopted in this record.

1. Glucose syrup from high-quality cassava flour

Several industries in Ghana use glucose syrup (mainly imported) in their products. In an attempt to expand existing markets for cassava, technologies were developed to provide a local supply of “glucose syrup” to substitute for the imported product. This technology could yield economic and social benefits to the farmers who produce the cassava, entrepreneurs who produce the syrup, as well as the end-users of the glucose syrup. Some of these benefits would include, foreign exchange savings, improvement in income levels, employment creation, efficient use of natural resources and easy access to industrial raw material among others. For further details see the TECA record titled “High-Quality Cassava Flour”.

High maltose syrup has characteristics such as low hygroscopicity, low viscosity, high resistance to crystallisation, low sweetness, reduced browning capacity and good heat stability. These properties make it useful in many applications in the food and pharmaceutical industries. In breakfast cereals, it is used to improve shelf-life, enhance colour, reduce breakage and maintain crispness. It is also used to control crystallisation and sweetness in ice creams and lollies as well as, providing body and strength to these products. When used in confectionery products it helps to lower the hygroscopicity of the product, controls crystallisation, prevents drying and lowers viscosity. Glucose syrup is also very useful in the manufacture of frozen fruits, liquors and crystallised fruits and in brewing.

Existing Vietnamese technology for glucose syrup production was adapted and modified to enable the production of glucose syrup from high-quality cassava flour (HQCF) and rice malts, to provide a local supply source for glucose syrup to substitute for imported products. The technology seeks to provide an easy-to-follow step-by-step process for the production of high maltose syrup. The description also highlights quality control issues, machinery and equipment requirements and potential markets for the product.

2. The importance of quality

This is to ensure that the manufactured products meet the required quality specifications. Before production begins, it is very important to determine the customer’s requirements on quality, and for producers and users to agree on a standard for quality of the product.

2.1 Reliability in maintaining quality

When a quality specification has been agreed upon, it must be maintained at all times. The use of adulterants and short cuts to reduce costs and process times must be avoided.

2.2 Reliability of supply (quantity)

Processors must never promise more than they can produce by the agreed delivery date, as the end-user will be planning production on the basis of having the necessary quantities of raw materials.

2.3 Timeliness of delivery

Realistic delivery dates are a must for commercial success.

2.4 Price competitiveness

Industrial users want a local product that is cheaper than the imported alternative. However, the reduction in price must not be achieved at the expense of quality. It is vitally important for anyone wishing to market cassava-based products to industry to keep these criteria in mind at all times. Many industries are willing to be tolerant of manufacturer’s difficulties, as long as they are kept fully informed, but are not happy with producers who are found to be unreliable on quality, quantity and timeliness of delivery.
