entries.tittle: Intercropping drought tolerant fruit trees (mango and jujube) in rice-based farming systems in NW - Bangladesh
entries.summary: Intercropping drought-tolerant fruit trees into rice-based farming systems in the uplands of the Barind tract in north-western Bangladesh reduces exposure to and risk of drought. It also provides households with alternative livelihoods sources, enhanced food and nutrition security and diet diversification. This practice describes how to intercrop mango and jujube into rice farming.
entries.description:
Description

Mango and jujube intercropping with the traditionally cultivated T. Aman rice is a practice applied in north-western Bangladesh to mitigate the economic impacts of droughts and drought spells and in response to growing seasonal water stress. Drought tolerant mango varieties are a high-value crop for farmers. The ability of jujube to withstand wide temperature ranges and to be cultivated successfully with little irrigation make this plant a good adaptation practice to drought in north-western Bangladesh. 

1. Implementation of the technology

1.1 Mango

  • Mango grows in all parts of Bangladesh but commercial and good quality grafted mangoes are mostly grown in the north and north-western districts.
    • Several varieties of different maturity groups are widely grown in this area, the most common ones are Gopalbogh, Krishabogh, Langra, Pozli and Ashwina.
    • The production rate of mango though is lower as compared to other mango growing countries in the region.
    • This is mainly because of a lack of appropriate management practices, such as fertilizer application, water or moisture management and use of mulch, vital for proper growth and production.

1.1.1 Recommended production technology

  • Spacing
    • The young mango trees are usually intercropped with T. Aman and boro rice.
    • Sufficient spacing between trees is crucial to avoid the abandoning of rice production.
    • Mango trees, once three to four years old, produce a dense shadow cover, which threatens rice production directly under the trees.
    • Spacing should ensure that rice production will not be abandoned through the intercropped, growing trees, otherwise, local employment opportunities and food availability, which are crucial for the poor, may be severely reduced.
  • Fertilization
    • It is suggested that fertilizers be applied in two split doses, one half immediately after the fruit harvest in June - July, and the other half in September - October, at the end of the rainy season.
    • Manures and fertilizers may be applied in the trenches that may be 30 cm wide, 15 cm to 20 cm deep and 30 cm away from the base of a one-year-old plant.
    • Following these criteria, the circular trench/canal around the tree may need to be located 2 m to 3 m from the trunk after 10 to 12 years, and 4 m away after 30 years.
    • Manure and fertilizers should be applied evenly in the trench/canal, which is then filled back with soil.
    • Manure and fertilizers may also be applied by spading or ploughing the soil around the plant up to the area shaded by the plant at noon.
    • Manure and fertilizers should be spread all but 1 m from the trunk of the plant and then mixed with the soil.
  • Irrigation
    • The amount and frequency of irrigation depend on the type of soil, climatic conditions, and the age of the trees.
    • Nevertheless, in the pre-bearing age, plants must be irrigated frequently and irrigation will be particularly critical during the drier part of the year from November to April, and less important in summer, from May to June.
    • Clay or heavier soils will need to be irrigated less frequently than lighter soils.
    • Considering all these factors, plants up to six months old need to be irrigated at an interval of two to six days, plants between 6 and 18 months every 4 to 12 days, and those aged one and a half to five years every one to three weeks.
    • Generally, when the trees are in full bearing stage, two irrigations will be needed when using the basin method, the first in full bloom and the second at the fruits pea stage.
      • This reduces fruit drop and improves fruit size.
  • Mulching
    • The spreading of dried organic material such as straw, leaves, grass and water hyacinth on the topsoil around the trees is recommended.
    • The primary purpose of mulching is to retain soil moisture for a long time to ensure that the trees have adequate moisture.
    • Mulching should be undertaken in the land around the mango tree, up to the area shaded by the plant at noon.
    • The land should be shallowly spaded or ploughed and covered by water hyacinth or rice straw, according to availability.
    • The optimum amount of mulch is approximately 2 to 3 inches for fluffy materials like straw and water hyacinth.
Figure 1. Mango plantations in drought-prone Barind areas intercropped with T. Aman rice

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Jujube

  • Jujube (Ziziphus jujuba) is a tropical fruit able to withstand a wide temperature range and drought.
  • One of the outstanding qualities of jujube is its tolerance to drought conditions.
  • It can be cultivated successfully in Barind tracts and other drought-prone areas with little irrigation.
  • A jujube field may be intercropped with T. Aman during Kharif-II season, and at the same time intercropping of vegetables may take place in a Jujube garden.

1.2.1 Advantages of growing Jujube

  • Jujube is considered a potential alternative to existing ongoing autonomous mango cultivation.
  • Since rice is the only crop that can be grown during monsoon season, food security of the Barind tract depends heavily on the monsoon season rice.
    • Further growth of mango plantations would limit rice production.
  • The introduction of jujube offers scope for diversification and drought risk reduction at the same time.
    • The crop is highly temperature tolerant and offers less shade effect on the rice crop beneath.
    • Jujube intercropping implies less negative impact on rice production as compared to mango.

2. Production technology

  • The suitable varieties are Apple kul, BAU kul and Khacchr.
  • Jujube plants tolerate both salinity and stagnancy of water, and a heavy and slightly alkaline sandy loam soil is good for their production.
  • The square planting method is good for jujube gardening.
    • Spacing should be 6 to 7 m, but spacing may be increased or reduced depending on the variety and place.
    • A 1 m x 1 m x 1 m pit should be prepared one month before planting.
    • Fertilizer should be applied 10 to 12 days before plantation as indicated in Table 1.
  • For good production, irrigation should be given once a month during flowering and fruiting time in the dry season.
  • Periodical pruning is required to improve production.
    • During pruning, the branch should be cut leaving a portion at the joint.
    • In addition weak, disease affected, insect attacked and thickly grown branches should also be pruned.
    • Afterwards when new branches sprout, the strong branches should be kept and the weak ones removed. 
  • Powdery mildew of jujube is a dangerous disease.
    • After flowering, "Thiovit" should be sprayed to control powdery mildew disease at the rate of 2 g in 1 litre of water or Tilt 250 EC at the rate of 0.5 ml in litre of water.
    • Afterwards, it should be sprayed two times at an interval of 15 days.
  • Fruits are generally collected from January to March depending on the variety.
    • Harvesting should begin when the fruits start becoming light green or yellow.
Table 1. Fertilizer doses per pit for jujube plantation
Name of fertilizer Quantity per pit (g)
Urea  200-250
Triple Super Phosphate 200-250
Muriate of Potash  245-255
Zinc Sulfate 40-60
Cow Dung 20-25 kg

Source: FAO 2012

Figure 2. Farmers engaged in transplanting of jujube tree in fields on Nachole Barind tract of Bangladesh

©FAO/TECA

3. Validation of the practice

  • ​Intercropping was tested and successfully replicated in mixed rainfed farming systems in north-western Bangladesh, in the agro-ecological zone of warm humid tropics.
  • In recent years cropping patterns in the north-western districts of Bangladesh have already seen a remarkable shift from mainly rice-based cropping systems towards more integrated systems, with the expansion of mango orchards. 

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Rubber and banana intercropping: ID 6657.
  • Double transplanting of (t. aman) rice to reduce impacts of drought spells during monsoon (Kharif II) season in Bangladesh: ID 6863.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology provides farmers with alternative intercropping methods that improve sensitivity to drought using trees that enhance the overall quality of the farming system. It is a mitigation strategy against drought and lack of sufficient water. 

6.2 Pro-poor technology

This technology provides the farmer with additional income due to the integration of jujube and mango trees to the rice farming system. In this case, the farmer has access to extra fruits for selling or consumption while reducing the costs of rice losses.

entries.tittle: Diversifying cropping patterns in drought prone areas in Bangladesh
entries.summary:
Adaptation options to climate variability and change in northwestern Bangladesh need to consider alternative cropping patterns and cultivation practices to support the most efficient use of limited natural resources. 

Diversification and adjustment of cultivated crops is a traditional adaptation practice contributing to minimize the risk of crop failure due to drought. However, diversification can be further strengthened by interactive systematic testing, selection and dissemination of appropriate crops and varieties. This may be accomplished in a participatory way between research institutions and farmers (groups). The introduction of more drought-resistant crops and cropping patterns are important options to help reducing vulnerability to climate change.
entries.description:
Description

The objective of this practice is to identify and practice the most appropriate cropping patterns suitable for drought prone areas of Bangladesh based on rainfall pattern, soil characteristics and community preference.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • Farmers traditionally practice different kinds of cropping patterns in the drought‑prone areas of Bangladesh.
  • Key criteria to guide the selection of diversified cropping patterns are crops and varieties which are:
    • drought resistant and require minimal irrigation;
    • exploit residual moisture from precedent cultivation;
    • food crops for household food security;
    • marketable with high value; and
    • legumes improving soils aggregation, structure, permeability, fertility, and infiltration rate.

1.1 Successful crop pattern

  • Crop patterns the most successful in the context of drought management, tested in northwest Bangladesh between 2008 to 2010 are:
    • Potato - Maize - Ropa aman: The Potato - Maize - Ropa aman cropping pattern was accepted as profitable by farmers in areas where minimal irrigation facilities are available, and is, therefore, to be considered suitable to drought-prone areas. With this cropping pattern two profitable crops, potato and maize can help to overcome losses caused in case of delayed Ropa aman.
    • Boro - Ropa aman – Vegetables.
    • Winter vegetables - Aus/Jute - Ropa aman.
    • Mustard - boro - aman: Mustard, chickpea and mung bean are suitable crops for exploitation of residual moisture after t.aman (transplanted aman) rice.
    • Onion - Jute - Ropa aman.
    • Maize - Fallow - Ropa aman: The maize - fallow - Ropa aman cropping pattern was also accepted by farmers in areas with minimal irrigation facilities and this too may be replicated in drought-prone areas.
      • Cropping patterns seven, eight and nine were accepted in areas without the facility for irrigation and may be disseminated to different drought-prone areas since these cropping patterns allow to successfully cultivate rabi season crops.
    • Chili - Fallow - Ropa aman.
    • Pulses - Fallow - Ropa aman: The pulses and oil seeds in principally mono-cropped areas could increase the nutritional security of the local people.
    • Nut - China/kaun/Wheat: The Nut - China/kaun/Wheat cropping pattern requires significantly less irrigation water compared to boro paddy.

  • This technology was tested in mixed rainfed farming systems in north-western Bangladesh, in the agro-ecological zone of warm humid tropics.

entries.tittle: Community seedbed for rice in drought prone areas of Bangladesh
entries.summary:
Choosing the optimum time for transplanting is a most essential prerequisite for rice cultivation, to ensure proper and optimal growth of plants and increase the yield and to synchronize cultivation practices for irrigation and control of pest, diseases or rats. T. aman (transplanted aman) rice is planted under rain fed conditions during the monsoon season. In case of drought, t. aman rice cultivation suffers significant damages, which can cause increase in prices for staple food, and increase risk of seasonal food shortages. Therefore, timely transplantation is essential to secure higher production. 

Community participation and collective action in cultivating rice are especially important in areas regularly prone to natural hazards such as northwestern Bangladesh. This practice is designed to facilitate and promote community-based joint seedling production of t. aman rice. This is to ensure timely availability of seedlings to all community members for early transplantation, and thus contributing to timely growing of plants and increasing yields.
entries.description:
Description

T. aman (transplanted aman) rice is planted in kharif II season (July to September/October) under rainfed conditions during the monsoon season with around 200 mm rainfall per month. Depending mostly on rainfall throughout the growth period, t. aman rice cultivation suffers significant damages each year due to periodic droughts during kharif II season.

Changing climate trends induce the risk of higher drought frequencies. With delayed transplantation the risk increases of incurring into mid and late-season drought, and of rice plants growing weaker, leading to a high risk of low production. In addition, late planting will delay the cropping cycle of the subsequent crop. In consequence, prices for staple food may be rising, and increase the risk of seasonal food shortages such as monga (famine), illness, reduction of drinking water sources, migration and loss of livestock. Timely seedbed preparation and transplantation at the right time are thus, essential actions to secure higher production.

Locally organized collaboration in seedling production by a farmers group or a whole community increases the chances of effective use of resources, timely availability of inputs and contributes to managing water scarcity and drought.

Community participation and collective action in cultivating rice is especially important in areas regularly prone to natural hazards such as north-western Bangladesh.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • Under the drought conditions in northwestern Bangladesh, the concept of community seedbeds is immensely beneficial.
  • Farmer should be advised to unite around a local water body (beel, haor, tanks etc) where they can jointly establish a community seedbed. The size of the seedbed depends on the local demand.
    • The aim is to allow all farmers in the area to transplant rice early, immediately after the monsoon onset in July.
    • In fact, timely rice transplantation is possible without great expense, if it is undertaken by a group.

1.1 Steps in order to promote the collaboration needed for community seedbed establishment

  • After determining the culture season and the suitable rice variety, the availability of that variety of seeds should be ensured.
  • Farmers and extension officers should be properly trained in all aspects concerning community seedbed, such as soil preparation, seed sowing, standard fertilizer doses and irrigation required, integrated pest management, etc.
  • Farmers should be encouraged to cultivate different varieties of rice in neighbouring lands by selecting suitable rice varieties based on the difference of regional soil fertility and climate.
    • This work should be carried out collectively so that after the rice harvest all the land will ready for the next crop.
  • Building and consolidation of group perception among farmers should be carried out at the village level through participatory activities.

2. Benefits of community seedbed

  • Community seedbed ensures the availability of healthy and strong seedlings in time.
    • If seeds are sown in the seedbed before June 30, seedlings become available for transplantation in July, at the onset of monsoon rain.
    • Early rice transplantation also helps in the cultivation of early wheat, mustard, maize, sunflower and other crops after the rice harvest.
  • On the basis of local soil and climate conditions, different rice varieties may be successfully cultivated side by side, ensuring the effective use of available water.
    • Since all lands are cultivated at the same time, disease and pest control become easier, with the possibility of higher production.
  • The use of irrigation water and other activities related to rice cultivation becomes cost-effective, while the preparation of many seedbeds spread over different parcels is extremely expensive, needs a great amount of water and is not easy to control.
Figure 1. T. aman rice transplanted from community seedbed

©FAO/TECA

  • With a community seedbed, management becomes very easy. Farmers may exchange experiences, and farmer to farmer communication increases.
  • Cultivation of different rice varieties is ensured through increased sales or exchanges.
  • Replanting rice seedlings in the event of drought/flood during the initial period of the season becomes possible from the community nurseries.

3. Validation of the practice

  • The technology was tested in mixed rainfed farming systems in north-western Bangladesh in the agro-ecological zone of warm humid tropics.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Double transplanting of (t. aman) rice to reduce impacts of drought spells during monsoon (Kharif II) season: ID 6863.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

Farmer seedling production collaborations increase the effective use of resources, timely availability of inputs and contribute to managing water scarcity and drought.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

Seedbed preparation and transplantation at specific times secure higher production, ensuring more food security and improved livelihood.

entries.tittle: Reducing natural hazard impacts on bananas: integrated practices, Haiti
entries.summary: Farmers in Haiti traditionally apply a number of actions before and after natural hazards hit in order to reduce the impacts particularly on high-market value products. For example, farmers can anticipate banana harvesting to mitigate the losses in case of natural hazards occurrence. The integrated package of practices to reduce hazard impacts on bananas aims at protecting the highest possible percentage of harvest from being spoilt by hurricanes, winds or washed away by floods, thus ensuring income and livelihood.
entries.description:
Description

Leaf removal, staking of the banana trees and anticipated harvesting are part of an integrated banana tree (Musa spp.) management package, used by local farmers to mitigate losses of this high market value crop from hurricanes, strong winds and floods. Anticipated harvesting is based on common sense and can be undertaken by farmers of all wealth categories and irrespective of the size of cultivated parcels if hazard occurs towards the end of the cropping cycle.

1. Implementation of the technology

1.1 Leaf removal

  • Banana trees are pruned before a windstorm, and/or hurricane occurs.
    • If possible, local farmers apply this technique in compliance with a specific lunar phase, seven days before the new moon.
  • The implementation of this labour and time-intensive practice often depends on the financial capacity of farmers to invest in this technique.
  • Implementation fees amount to about 9 500 HTG per hectare (USD 226) in 2008.
  • A specially designed knife, the Kouto banana (banana knife), and a machete are used to implement this technique.
  • The leaves of the banana tree are removed starting with the dry, ripe, and damaged ones.
    • These are removed, generally with their petiole, as far as the banana trees in their vegetative growth stage are concerned.
    • For banana trees that are already in the production phase (those in bloom or close to their physiological maturity), leaf removal is practiced on at most 50 percent of the total healthy canopy of the plant.
  • That is, at most six of the ten to twelve prescribed green leaves needed by an adult banana tree to normally grow and bear fruit, are removed.
  • The oldest healthy leaves are then pruned at most at their two‑third distal end.
    • Excessive leaf removal is likely to negatively interfere with the growth and maturation process of the fruit (stem) of the banana tree.
    • Additional scientific field experimentation and/or monitoring and evaluation exercises to further strengthen and propagate this technology are recommended to:
      • fix the optimal phase(s) for leaf removal as the banana tree requires an optimal number of leaves to normally overtake its physiological production activity; and
      • fix the optimal number of irremovable leaves per phenological stage without structural and physiological harm to the yield of the plant.

1.2 Staking banana trees

  • Staking of banana trees is a traditional technique that can be applied at any scale of field size.
    • It has not changed through time or space and is recommended in banana farming zones highly/regularly prone to hurricanes and storms.
    • It must be implemented before a storm may hit.
    • It can be done by using traditional farming tools, such as a hand hoe, a machete, a knife, as well as stakes, poles, etc.
  • This technology supports banana crops and protects them from the impact of hurricanes.
  • High stakes/poles of 2 m to 3 m forked at their upper end are prepared first, and then used to support individual stem-bearing banana trees.
  • Each post is placed with its forked upper-end touching the inferior side of the banana tree stem’s peduncle.
  • The stake is placed in front of the banana tree parallel to the highest falling probability position.
    • Generally, to make the design more secure, at the exact lodging spot for the stake the ground is first excavated superficially to a 10 cm depth.
    • Installation costs and fees are around 16.50 HTG per banana tree (USD 0.40), of which 15 HTG (USD 0.35) (2008) and are paid per individual stake/ pole.
    • The remaining 1.50 HTG (USD 0.0.3) were for labour costs.
    • This adds up to approximately 33 000 HTG per hectare (USD 785).
    • Though the stakes need to be cut from local trees, no requirements are needed related to tree cutting.
  • The benefits of this practice are that the banana plants are protected against high winds and the stakes can be used again for at least one additional year.
  • Limitations associated with this technique lie in its high costs.

1.3 Treating of damaged crops

  • Banana trees at a vegetative stage broken or irreversibly bent by weather-related disasters are topped at a height that does not interfere with their hypothetic blossoming.
    • This practice strengthens the sucker shooting forth of topped trees.
  • Protection of fallen down fruit-bearing banana trees and rooted up trees need to have their exhumed root system carefully covered with dust and/or straw, and their sprawling fruit mulched with the remaining intact leaves of the tree to prevent general desiccation (extreme dryness) and/or sunburns.
  • Forty-five to sixty-day lag is generally observed between the maturation time of a normal tree stem, and that of a banana tree that has been rooted up by strong winds or flooding.

1.4 Anticipated harvesting of all mature and/or marketable stems

  • Anticipated harvesting is based on common sense and has been adopted since the remote past by local farmers for high market value crops.
  • It can be undertaken by farmers from all socio‑economic levels and on all sizes of cultivated parcels.
  • It involves the harvesting of all mature and/or marketable crops of the parcel upon disaster warning using traditional farming tools like a knife, machete, etc.
  • The harvested crops are then either stored or sold on nearby markets.
  • This practice does not require any installation and/or maintenance fees; except for labour costs unless, the whole process is supported by household-based manpower.
    • Overall economic losses are however likely to incur since the selling prices of the goods will automatically fall when the sudden supply in markets goes up.
  • The benefit of anticipated harvesting for farmers is to ensure that at least parts of the harvest are saved and sold to gain some income.
Figure 1a. Banana plant

©FAO/TECA

Figure 1b. Banana plant

©FAO/TECA

  • A key requirement associated with this risk reduction package for banana is the provision and accessibility for producers to reliable early warning information with as long as possible lead times.
  • These are crucial to trigger the timely implementation of the documented practices.
  • Appropriate fertilization/phyto-sanitation measures are also to be considered on a case by case basis to ease the plant’s quick physiological recovery and to prevent pest and disease attacks likely to result from the banana tree DRM‑based treatment.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Cultivation of improved banana varieties, in combination with mulching, trenches and organic compost: ID 8947.
  • Rubber/banana intercropping: ID 6657.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The application of this practice helps in reducing hazard impacts on bananas and protecting the highest possible percentage of harvest from being destroyed.

entries.tittle: Enriched compost for higher yields, Kenya
entries.summary: In Eastern Africa, reduced soil fertility has led to declining crop yields on many small‑scale farms causing food insecurity and greater poverty. Throughout the region, soils are generally low in nitrogen and phosphorus – which are essential for crops to grow well. Soil fertility can be increased by the use of chemical fertilizers but these are too expensive for many farmers and are not always available. A more affordable alternative is to make your own good-quality compost, using waste materials from your farm and household. The following shows you how to make better quality compost, called enriched compost, which has higher organic matter and contains more nutrients. The use of enriched compost will enable you to increase your crop yields without applying costly chemical fertilizers.
entries.description:
Description

1. Compost

Compost is decomposed (rotten) material obtained from plant waste alone or in combination with animal and other waste.

2. Composting conditions

Composting depends on the right conditions to support the growth of tiny living creatures – micro-organisms (bacteria and fungi which can be seen only by using a microscope). As these micro-organisms break down the plant and animal waste materials, heat is produced. After a few days, your compost heap will feel hot and when opened up it will even give off steam. As the waste materials break down they release nutrients in a form that can be used by crops.

3. Different methods to make compost

  • Crop residues and organic household wastes can simply be thrown into pits and left to decompose for three to four months, after which the compost is ready for use. 
  • Alternatively, the waste materials can be heaped under a shady tree and left to decompose.

Though both of these methods produce compost, the quality is usually low. This leaflet shows you how to make better quality compost, called enriched compost, which has higher organic matter and contains more nutrients. Use of enriched compost will enable you to increase your crop yields without applying costly chemical fertilizers.

4. Benefits of making enriched compost

  • Turns waste products, such as crop residues, animal manure, garden weeds, grass, hedge cuttings, kitchen waste, and other organic wastes into a valuable, useful product.
  • Nutrients are immediately available as plant food without the need for further breakdown in the soil. 
  • Increases crop yields.
  • Increases the amount of water the soil can hold, so it does not dry out fast.
  • Improves the soil texture so the crop’s roots can push through it more easily. 
  • Releases nutrients gradually and continues to improve the soil in the following seasons. 
  • Helps to increase beneficial soil micro‑organisms and increase the soil’s organic matter, which is good for your crops and the environment. 
  • Reduces weed growth as weed seeds are destroyed by the heat produced during composting. 
  • Many people now prefer to eat foods that are grown without the use of chemicals and artificial fertilizers. Home-made compost helps you to produce such foods.
  • You can sell surplus compost to your neighbours.
  • Can be made with little or no financial input.

4.1 Requirements to make enriched compost 

The following are needed to make enriched compost:

  • a machete (panga) and sticks;
  • a watering can; 
  • fork or spade;
  • crop residues from cereals (maize, sorghum, millet, wheat) and legumes (bean, cowpea, groundnut and green gram);
  • any other types of waste plant material; 
  • use of green manures, such as tithonia, glyricidia, leucaena, sesbania, crotalaria and lantana leaves, will increase the compost’s nitrogen content;
  • cattle, chicken, sheep or goat manure and urine, or biogas slurry, to speed-up the process of decomposition;
  • wood ashes or charcoal dust; and
  • a space of at least 2.5 m long by 2 m wide for the heap and extra space to turn the material. More space should be provided depending on how much waste material you have and how much compost you need.

5. Steps to make enriched compost in three to four months

5.1 First step: making a heap

  • Measure out an area at least 2.5 m long and 2 m wide in a convenient place, such as near your field. Allow a similar sized area for turning the heap.
  • Mark the corners of the heap with sticks. 
  • Chop crop residues into pieces about 30 cm long to increase surface area for decomposition and make a layer about 15 cm deep. 
  • Sprinkle a thin layer of animal manure, about 2 cm deep, to cover the first layer.
  • Add a second layer of plant material, preferably including green manures, such as agro-forestry shrubs (not thick branches), to a depth of about 15 cm. 
  • Sprinkle wood ash or charcoal dust on the top of the green vegetation. 
  • If the weather is dry, sprinkle with about 4 litres of water to make the layer damp.
  • Repeat the above steps until you have five layers each about 30 cm deep. This will make your heap about 1.5 m tall.
  • Cover the heap with 10 cm of topsoil to prevent loss of nutrients.

5.2 Second step: turning the compost

  • Turn the heap using a fork after one month. 
  • Move material from the top and sides of heap to the middle of a new heap.
  • If dry, sprinkle with water to ensure heap is damp. 
  • Turn the heap every two weeks until the compost becomes dark grey in colour.

5.3 Third step: monitoring progress

  • From about eight days onwards, push a stick into the middle of the heap. Pull the stick out. If the stick feels hot this is a good sign that decomposition is occurring. 
  • The compost is ready for use when it becomes dark greyish in colour. This usually takes around three to four months.
  • One heap, 2.5 m x 2 m, will give you about 200 kg to 300 kg of enriched compost, which will have a much higher organic matter content and contain more nutrients than normal compost. This is enough for use on 0.5 hectares of land.

6. Steps to make enriched compost in just 14 days

A more rapid method of making compost has been developed in Asia. The decomposition process is speeded-up by adding large amounts of fresh animal manure and by frequently turning the heap. Chicken manure is superior to other manures.

The following explains this more rapid method.

  • Chop the plant waste materials (dry or green or both). 
  • Thoroughly mix these with equal amounts of fresh animal manure. 
  • Pile the mixture into a heap at least one metre high and one metre wide and allow a similar sized area to turn the heap. 
  • Cover the heap with banana leaves or old sacks to reduce heat loss. 
  • By the third or fourth day, the inside of the heap should be hot. If not, add more manure and mix with the other materials.
  • From the third or fourth day onwards, turn the heap every two days so that the materials from the sides and top are moved to the centre. 
  • In 14 to 18 days, the compost should be ready for use.

7. Ways in which enriched compost can be used

  • Dig planting holes about 10 cm deep along rows. For maize, the rows should be spaced 75 cm apart with planting holes spaced at 30 cm along rows. 
  • Apply about one handful of compost to each planting hole and mix well with the soil. 
  • Place the seed into the hole and cover with soil. 
  • Compost can also be scattered or broadcast evenly and incorporated into the seedbed before planting the seeds. 
  • If you are not ready to use your compost immediately, store it in a shade or cover heap with 10 cm of topsoil to stop loss of nutrients.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Composting associated with planting pits: ID 7525.
  • Composting to improve soil fertility: ID 8206.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of cellulolytic cultures: ID 4298.
  • Rapid composting methods: vermicomposting: ID 4301.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of forced aeration: ID 4299.
  • Rapid composting methods: use of effective micro-organisms (EM): ID 4297.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology uses plant and animal waste to increase soil fertility, allowing for the increase in organic matter in the soil and improved crop growth.

10.2 Pro-poor technology

Thanks to increased soil fertility, the technology allows for an increase in crop yields for small-scale farms. The technology doesn't require high costs.

entries.tittle: Making banana chips and flour
entries.summary: Bananas are a staple food in many parts of Eastern Africa. Currently, there is very limited commercial processing of bananas. Most people consume bananas fresh, steamed or boiled. During bumper harvests, farmers sell bananas at give-away prices and many go to waste. A detailed process of making banana chips and flour is explained below in terms of their benefits, ingredients, tools, and the meticulous steps to take. A case study from Tanzania is also provided to highlight the success of this technique.
entries.description:
Description

1. Importance and benefits of bananas

Bananas are a staple food in many parts of Eastern Africa. They are a good source of potassium, which helps keep your body fluids in balance. They are also an ideal food for toddlers, invalids and people living with HIV/ AIDS. Currently, there is very limited commercial processing of bananas. Most people consume bananas fresh, steamed or boiled. Additionally, during bumper harvests, farmers sell bananas at give-away prices and many go to waste. But did you know that bananas can be processed into dried chips and flour on your farm? The chips and flour can be stored for up to six months and can be sold or used to make value-added products to further increase your income.

Banana chips and flour are easily transported to distant markets, where bananas are not grown. They can also be sold in local markets and to hotels and supermarkets. The flour can be mixed with other cereals, legumes, and root- or tuber-crop flours to make tasty and nutritious porridge, bakery products and baby foods. It can also be used as a relief food during droughts, floods and other emergencies.

Other banana products, which may be made from the non-edible parts, include compost, animal feed and a wide range of craft items from banana fibre, such as hats, bags and purses. So, the banana is important for health, food security and wealth creation. This leaflet shows you how to make banana chips and flour.

2. What you need to make banana chips and flour

  • unblemished, freshly harvested green bananas;
  • gloves (to prevent staining of hands with banana sap);
  • anti-browning agent (powdered sodium metabisulphite – available from specialized food shops and chemists);
  • clean water;
  • clean, sharp knives;
  • plastic buckets;
  • raised open-sun platform, solar dryer or hot-air dryer;
  • plastic packaging bags (polyethylene);
  • teaspoon; and
  • trays and fine plastic mesh.

3. Making chips and flour from un-cooked green bananas

  • Peel the unblemished mature green bananas.
  • Slice the bananas into 0.5 cm thick pieces (about the thickness of a pencil).
  • Soak sliced bananas in a solution of anti-browning agent. To make the solution, add 10 mg (one teaspoon) of the chemical to each litre of water. Soak the slices for 15 minutes.
  • Drain the slices by placing them on trays with plastic mesh and then place them in the dryer.
  • Dry in the sun (open or solar dryer) or in a hot-air dryer until dry and brittle. This will take about two to three days in good sunshine.
  • Hot-air dryers and solar dryers are more expensive than open sun-drying but reduce contamination from the environment. If drying in open sunshine, protect bananas with netting to keep off flies and birds. Either pack chips or continue to make flour.
  • Grind the dried banana chips in a hammer mill (village posho mill).
  • Pack the flour in polyethylene bags and seal them (a burning candle or an electric polysealer may be used).
  • Label your bags (include date of manufacture and expiry date - after six months).
  • Pack the bags of flour in a carton to protect them from light.
  • Store in a cool, dry place.

4. Making chips and flour from pre-cooked green bananas

  • Cook unpeeled bananas in a pan of water until tender. Do not overcook.
  • Place cooked bananas in cold water to cool until safe to handle.
  • Peel the bananas.
  • Slice the bananas into pieces about 0.5 cm thick (about the thickness of a pencil).
  • Dry in the sun (open or solar dryer) or in a hot-air dryer until fully dry and brittle. If drying in open sunshine, protect bananas with netting to keep off flies and birds. Either pack chips or continue to make flour.
  • Grind the dried banana chips in a hammer mill (village posho mill).
  • Pack the flour in polyethylene bags and seal them (a burning candle or an electric polysealer may be used).
  • Label your bags (include the date of manufacture and expiry date - six months later).
  • Pack the bags of flour in a carton to protect them from light.
  • Store in a cool, dry place.
Table 1. What could go wrong in making banana chips flour?
Problem Possible causes Corrective actions
Poor-quality green bananas
  • Bruised, blemished and broken bananas due to poor handling
  • Immature bananas
  • Improper bananas
  • Improper storage
  • Delayed processing
  • Delayed harvesting
  • Handle bananas carefully
  • Store harvested bananas in a coll place
  • Process bananas within a week of harvesting
  • Harvest bananas when fully mature and uniformly green
Discoloured chips and flour
  • Using mixed bananas varieties
  • Using different-sized chips
  • Not using anti-browning agent or not soaking in anti-browning agent for 15 minutes
  • Use only one variety
  • Ensure chips are 0.5 cm thick
  • Use anti-browning agent as recommended
Decreased shelf life of chips and flour

High moisture content due to:

  • poor drying of chips
  • absorption of moisture by chips or flour during storage
  • Ensure chips are well dried (to brittleness) before making flour
  • Store in dry conditions
  • Use new, strong polyethylene bags
Mushy bananas that are difficult to peel, slice and dry
  • Overcooking the bananas
  • Use of near-ripe bananas
  • Avoid overcooking the bananas
  • Use fully mature and uniformly green bananas
Foul/fermented smell of chips or flour

Contamination due to:

  • microbial growth
  • use of unclean water
  • Dry chips in clean and hygienic conditions
  • Use clean (potable) water to avoid contaminating the final products
  • Use the recommended packaging materials
Loss of chips and flour in storage
  • Infestation by storage insect pests (e.g. weevills)
  • Rats in the storage area
  • Storage in poor-quality packaging materials
  • Storage or product on the ground
  • Ensure proper packaging (use strong, sealed bags)
  • Put in place measures to control storage pests
  • Make storage are rat-proof and control rats
  • Store bagged chips or flour off the ground

Source: CTA 2010

5. Case study

In 1982, Mr. Robert Nyirenda and his wife Edna started Nyirefami Limited, a business to process sorghum and millet in Arusha, Tanzania. Although they did well, they had another idea to expand the business in 1999. When they were young, they remembered that their parents used to dry bananas in the sun and make flour using a pestle and mortar. The flour was either used plain or mixed with maize flour to make stiff porridge (ugali or sima) or thin porridge (uji). Robert and his wife knew that a lot of their bananas went to waste. These were mainly the small fingers at the ends of the bunch, as well as the broken bananas that were not fit for sale. While selling their sorghum and millet products, and through their social interactions, they established that there was a high demand for banana flour in Tanzania.

In 1999, Robert asked a local metal fabricator to design and make an electric dryer. At that time the price of bananas was quite low and Robert and his wife employed extra workers to assist them to process the bananas. Robert also sought the services of a firm in Nairobi to print packaging materials. Later that year, Robert started selling banana flour to shops and supermarkets in Arusha at USD 0.50 per kg. They were able to sell at such a low price because the bananas were very cheap. Robert had to buy additional bananas to meet the very high demand for the flour. As a result, Robert and his wife made a good profit which allowed them to invest in more processing machines, further expanding their business.

6. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies 

  • Making sweet potato chips and flour: ID 6904.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for bananas to be processed into different consumable outputs such as chips and flour, which can then be stored more efficiently. Non-edible parts of the banana, through this technology, can be used for compost, animal feed and craft items.

8.2 Pro-poor technology

The alternatively processed and efficiently stored banana outputs can be sold or used to make value-added products, and have a wider market distribution. This can allow for additional income for poor households. The products can also be mixed with other foods allowing for improved sources of nutrition.

entries.tittle: Establishing a tree nursery, East Africa
entries.summary: Many people in Eastern Africa depend on forests and trees to meet various needs. With growing populations, these resources are being rapidly depleted. Many farmers want to plant trees but cannot readily obtain high-quality tree seedlings. Establishing a tree nursery can help to meet this demand and provide you with extra income.
entries.description:
Description

1. Why tree nurseries?

Many people in Eastern Africa depend on forests and trees to meet various needs. With growing populations, these resources are being rapidly depleted. Many farmers want to plant trees but cannot readily obtain high-quality tree seedlings. Establishing a tree nursery can help to meet this demand and provide you with extra income.

2. Benefits of tree nurseries

  • Income generation through the sale of seedlings.
  • Production of uniform-sized seedlings leading to even plantation stands.
  • Availability of seedlings when you and your customers need them.
  • Production of disease-free planting stock.
  • May be established on small pieces of land.
  • Can make good use of land unsuitable for crop production.
  • Inexpensive to establish.

Planting trees provide many benefits. It increases the availability of products like firewood, charcoal, fruits, timber, poles, fodder and ornaments. It also provides windbreaks and improves the environment by preventing soil erosion and increasing soil fertility.

3. How to establish a tree nursery

3.1 Site selection

A good site for a tree nursery should have a reliable nearby water supply, a source of soil and access to the market for seedlings. In addition, it is desirable to have well-drained soil with a gentle slope and natural shelter, such as tree cover, to provide shade for nursery workers.

3.2 Soil

A good soil for use in tree nurseries can be made by mixing:

  • three basins of soil collected from under vegetation cover, such as in forests or under large trees;
  • two basins of clay soil; and
  • one basin of sand.

To test the mixture, roll a damp sample in your hand. A good mixture should roll and hold its shape but break if the roll is bent. If it does not break, then it has too much clay. If it crumbles before you can roll it, then it has too much sand. To ensure adequate fertility of the soil, add one basin of sieved manure or compost to every three or four basins of the standard mixture.

3.3 Seedbed preparation

The seedbed should not be wider than one meter to make working on the bed easy. The bed can be of any length.

  • Dig a trench about 10 cm deep all around the seedbed.
  • Set large pieces of timber, bamboo or flat stones into the trench to a height of at least 15 cm above the ground.
  • Put a 5 cm layer of coarse gravel or small stones at the bottom of the bed to improve drainage.
  • Add a 5 cm layer of standard nursery soil mixture on top of the coarse gravel.

3.4 Sowing seeds

  • Large seeds, about the size of maize seeds, should be sown in drills running across the beds, 5 to 10 cm apart.
  • Smaller seeds, about the size of pigeon peas, should be broadcast onto the bed and pressed into the soil with a flat board.
  • Very small seeds, about the size of sesame, should be first mixed with fine sand or soil before sowing to allow adequate spacing on germination.
  • Cover the seeds with a thin layer of fine soil or sand to a depth of about 5 mm.
  • Water twice daily (morning and late afternoon) in hot, dry weather.

3.5 Pricking-out seedlings

Pricking-out is the transfer of seedlings from the seedbed to pots. Pricking-out should be done when the seedlings develop three or four true leaves.

  • Choose a cloudy day or late in the afternoon to avoid seedlings wilting in the sun.
  • Water the seedlings well before pricking-out.
  • Remove the seedlings by inserting a small flat stick beneath them and gently lifting them from the seedbed. Take care not to break the small roots.
  • Put the seedlings in a tray of water immediately to prevent them from wilting.
  • Pot the pricked-out seedlings in containers made from locally available materials, such as banana leaves or bamboo stems, or specially made black polythene bags.
  • Fill pots with the soil mixture and make a hole with a stick about the size of a pencil in the middle of the pot, just a little deeper than the roots of the seedlings.
  • Carefully lower the seedlings into the hole and refill so that there is no empty space around the roots. Gently press down the soil.
  • Put the potted seedlings into a nursery bed under shade.

3.6 Taking cuttings

Cuttings allow farmers to produce seedlings for trees for which it is difficult to get seeds. Examples of trees that should be propagated by cuttings include tea, euphorbia and breadfruit.

  • Take cuttings from woody branches in the lower crown near to the main stem. Do not cut the main stem.
  • The cuttings should be about 15 to 25 cm long and 10 to 20 mm thick.
  • Cuttings should have at least two bud scars but preferably three or four.
  • Remove leaves from cuttings.
  • Insert the cuttings in a slanting position, into the nursery bed or a pot.

4. Taking good care of your seedlings

To ensure good performance of the seedlings, the following measures are recommended.

  • Construct the nursery shade in an east to west direction to protect seedlings from the hot sun. The shade will also protect seedlings from strong winds and heavy rain.
  • Do not overcrowd seedlings in the nursery bed to minimize competition for resources like nutrients and water.
  • Water twice daily during hot dry days to protect seedlings from wilting.
  • Prune roots that grow out of the pots to prevent roots breaking when pots are lifted for planting out.
  • Weed regularly to prevent weeds from competing with seedlings for water and soil nutrients.
  • Fence off the tree nursery to prevent damage from animals and chickens.
  • Control insects and diseases like damping - off that could destroy seedlings. Damping-off is mainly caused by overcrowding the seedlings. It may be controlled by thinning the seedlings to facilitate movement of air among them. Spray the seedlings with appropriate pesticide in case of pest problems.
  • Harden-off seedlings by gradually reducing the shade and frequency of watering. This allows them to get used to field conditions before transplanting. Most seedlings will be ready to plant out between two and six months, depending on the type of trees.
  • After hardening-off, seedlings can be planted in well-prepared sites, preferably at the beginning of the rainy season. Take care to protect them from grazing animals such as goats.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Propagating and planting trees: ID 6960.
  • Vegetative tree propagation in agroforestry: ID 7794.
  • Establishing a tree nursery: ID 7808.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

​​6.1 Resource use efficiency

​​The technology allows for healthier plants, improves the usage of land, especially that that is unsuitable for crop production, increases the availability of tree products and is environmentally beneficial. ​

6.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for income generation and is not expensive to establish.

entries.tittle: Improved practices in rearing indigenous chicken
entries.summary:
Indigenous chickens play an important role in the livelihoods of most rural families in Eastern Africa. Despite increased use of commercial breeds by large-scale producers, around three quarters of chickens in the region are indigenous breeds.

This manual gives information on improved management practices of rearing indigenous chickens. The following technology is from the Technical Centre for Agricultural and Rural Cooperation (CTA), in collaboration with several African institutes from Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda, and Kenya.
entries.description:
Description

1. Facts about indigenous chicken

  • Meat and eggs are tastier and preferred by most consumers to those obtained from commercial breeds.
  • Initial investment is less than that needed to keep commercial breeds.
  • More tolerant of harsh conditions, including diseases, than commercial breeds.
  • Can be fed on cheap, locally available feeds.
  • When allowed to range freely, they need little feeding or other care.
  • Women and youth often control income from chickens.
  • Local markets are readily available for both eggs and chickens.
  • Droppings are rich in nutrients: can be used for compost making, pond fertilizing and as feed for livestock.

1.1 Why improved management?

  • Survival rate of chicks can be increased from three to eight out of ten.
  • If you hatch your eggs and sell chicks, earnings can be much higher (up to 7-times higher) than if you simply sell the eggs.
  • Simultaneous hatching of hens (so all chicks hatch at the same time) makes planning for vaccinations easier.
  • By cooperating with neighbours, farmers with small flocks can access vaccines at more affordable rates.
  • Planning your production to meet high seasonal demand – such as at Christmas, Easter and other festivals can greatly increase your profits.
  • If hens are prevented from hatching their own eggs or brooding chicks, they will start to lay again more quickly – after just 21 days, instead of the usual three months.

1.2 How do I start?

  • You will need:
    • one cock for every 10 hens;
    • water and feed containers;
    • housing space;
    • laying nests;
    • a carton box with ventilation holes;
    • a sisal sack or wood shavings; and
    • a source of vaccines and drugs.

2. Selection of the breeding stock

  • Select a hen that is broody, does not abandon her eggs during hatching, and looks after her chicks well.
  • Select a healthy, strong cock.

2.1 Housing

  • Housing space (2 m by 3 m) or a liuli (traditional brooding basket).
    • The ‘liuli’ can be used as a brooder basket for chicks, either inside or outside the house.
  • House should be raised to protect birds from predators.
  • Perches should be provided in the house for chicken to roost on at night.
  • The house should be well ventilated.

3. What are the improved management practices?

3.1 Feeding

  • Provide a balanced diet.
    • For example, a small handful of maize, a teaspoonful of local fishmeal, and some fresh greens.
    • Adding these with scavenged feeds, like insects, will provide a good diet for one chicken in a day.
  • Provide clean water at all times.

3.2 Collecting the eggs

  • Provide a safe, dry, dark place for the hens to lay.
  • Collect eggs daily.
    • Write the date on the egg in pencil and store with the broad end facing upwards.
    • This helps to ensure the embryo develops properly.

3.3 Hatching

  • Use only eggs that were laid in the last 14 days.
  • Hatch eggs using the mother hen, another broody hen, a (surrogate) duck or an incubator.
  • For hens and ducks, make sure the number of eggs chosen for hatching corresponds to the bird’s body size – all eggs must fit under the bird.
  • For synchronized hatching (all chicks hatch at the same time), delay the first hen that becomes broody by giving it just one egg to sit on while you wait for other hens to lay their clutches and become broody.
  • For successive hatching (the hen or the surrogate duck sits on eggs for two consecutive clutches), chicks are removed when they hatch and replaced with new eggs.
  • After hatching, dispose of egg shells, clean the nest and transfer chicks to a brooder.
  • Turn the eggs regularly, especially when using an incubator.

3.4 Brooding

  • Brood chicks using a mother hen, a foster hen, a lantern, a kerosene brooder, and a charcoal stove or charcoal placed in a metal container.
  • If a foster hen is used, condition it for a day by giving it new chicks.
  • Where a lantern brooder or other heat source is used, place it in a cardboard box with ventilation holes or inside the liuli placed upon a sisal sack or wood shavings.
  • Take care that chicks cannot get burned.
    • Cover charcoal stove or container, ensuring that there is no risk of fire.

3.5 Rearing chicks

  • Provide clean water at all times in shallow, clean troughs.
  • Provide soft feeds like flour from cereals or tubers.
  • Allow chicks to roam freely when they reach three or four weeks of age.
  • Vaccinate chicks against Newcastle disease at four days of age.

4. Record keeping

  • Keeping good records will help you to assess whether or not you are making a profit.
  • The table below compares the profit made using traditional and improved management practices.
  • Under traditional management, fewer eggs are laid and fewer birds are reared as many more chicks die.
Table 1. Comparison between the traditional method and the improved method

Source: CTA 2010

5. Case study

Mr. Lawrence Wamukoye has good reason to appreciate the benefits of adopting improved management practices for indigenous chickens. Proceeds from sales of chickens have enabled him to make the last payment due on his plot of land. He can also now afford to buy books and uniforms for his three children who attend a local primary school.

Lawrence is a small-scale farmer from Majengo village in Western Province, Kenya. He is a father of four and his family depends on just one-fifth of a hectare of land. A few years ago, he received training from a Non-Governmental Organization, Africa Now, on improved methods of indigenous chicken keeping. He was shown how to vaccinate his birds and also how to timely produce to meet the high demand for chickens during religious and cultural festivals, such as Christmas. As a result he managed to reduce the previously high mortality rate in his flock, double the number of eggs his birds lay and increase his income.

He keeps ten laying hens. When they hatch their eggs, he transfers the chicks to three traditional brooders and provides them with supplementary feeds. On average he sells ten chickens every month and has around 150 birds on his farm at any one time. He now plans to move his expanding poultry enterprise onto a new, bigger piece of land. To buy the land, he is arranging to obtain a loan from a local microfinance organization and is confident of repaying the loan from the proceeds of his successful indigenous chicken business.

6. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • subtropics, warm/mod cool.

7. Related/associated technologies 

  • Small-scale chicken production: ID 6949.
  • Improved chicken breeds raised with vaccination: ID 8941.
  • Raising chicken without grain: the integrated compost and poultry system: ID 8863.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

8.1 Women friendly

The practice is light in drudgery and can be undertaken by any hand labour.

8.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently combines different techniques in order to rear indigenous chickens effectively.

8.3 Pro-poor technology

Through the increase in chicken quantity reared, the technology provides for additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Rearing Dairy Goats
entries.summary: Throughout Eastern Africa, pressure on land is increasing. Average farm size is decreasing as plots are sub-divided and farmers struggle to find space on their farms to grow subsistence and cash crops as well as to keep livestock. Many farmers would like to keep dairy cows but do not have the money to buy animals and build zero-grazing units or sufficient land to grow enough feed. But have you ever considered keeping dairy goats as a more affordable and appropriate option?
entries.description:
Description

1. Why diary goats?

  • Dairy goats are improved breeds bred for milk production.
    • They are very different from local breeds and produce more milk - up to 12 times more!
  • Goats multiply fast.
    • They can kid twice a year and often produce twins or triplets.
  • Most dairy goats are owned by women thus supplementing their incomes.
  • Goat’s milk can sell at more than three-times the price of cow’s milk and contains twice as much vitamin A.
    • Vitamin A is essential for growth in children and prevention of eye problems.
  • The fat and protein content in goat’s milk is more easily digested than that in cow’s milk.
  • Goat’s milk can be beneficial for people with stomach ulcers and is an excellent alternative for people who are allergic to cow’s milk.
  • Goat’s milk can generate value-added products, such as cheese and yoghurt.
  • Older female goats and surplus males can be slaughtered or sold for meat.
  • Goats can consume shrubs that are not eaten by other livestock.
  • Goat’s manure contains a high level of nitrogen.
    • It can be used to enrich soils and increase crop yields or to fertilize fish ponds.
  • Goat’s manure can also be used to produce biogas for cooking and lighting.
  • Male dairy goats may be used to serve neighbours’ goats and thus help bring in income.
  • There is a ready market for goat’s milk.

2. Dairy goats or cows?

  • Dairy goats require less land than the same number of dairy cows.
  • Half a hectare of Napier grass can support five dairy goats but only one dairy cow.
  • See table below on profits, based on average prices in Kenya for 2006.
Table 1. Dairy goats or cows
  Milk yiels per day (litres) Selling price (USD pwe litre) Daily income (USD)
One dairy cow 20 0.36 7.20
Five dairy goats 5x2.5=12.5 1.00 12.5

Source: CTA 2010

3. What you need to start

  • Tip! Before buying and moving your goats, consult with the nearest veterinary office for vaccinations, permits and any other relevant information.
  • Housing with raised slatted floor (1.5 to 2 m2 per animal).
    • Good ventilation is essential but house should protect animals from wind and rain.
    • Local materials such as off-cuts, poles and sticks can be used.
    • Equip the house with feed and water troughs so you can feed your goats indoors.
  • Fodder (Napier and other grasses) which make up the bulk of goat feed.
    • Establish a source of fodder by planting or buying fodder locally.
  • Feed supplements which provide essential nutrients, such as protein, energy and minerals, to support milk production.
    • Examples are: Calliandra, Leucaena, Desmodium, grains and milling by-products, minerals, molasses.
    • Fodder shrubs can be grown around the edges of the plot.
  • One or more female dairy goats.
    • Breeds include Toggenburg, German Alpine, Saanen and crosses with the Galla.
  • A male dairy goat (own or access to a communally owned one).
    • One male is needed for every 25 females.
    • A male exchange programme prevents inbreeding.
    • Male goats should not be mated with closely related females.
  • Labour (family labour may be adequate).
  • Market for the surplus milk, added-value products and goats.
  • Indigenous female goats for crossing if one intends to upgrade using a male goat of a dairy breed.

4. Getting started

4.1 Step one: establish sources of fodder

  • Identify sources of fodder to last a whole year.
  • One option is to plant a plot of Napier grass to provide the bulk feed and some high-protein fodder shrubs, such as Calliandra.
  • Other feeds include maize stover, sweet potato vines, banana peels and weeds.

4.2 Step two: construct the goat house

  • Construct a raised goat house with a slatted floor, including an outdoor exercise area for the goats.

4.3 Step three: acquire dairy goats

  • Identify local veterinary services.
  • Find a local dairy goat breeder who can sell you some animals.
  • Get a livestock movement permit (if goat is being acquired from outside your district).
  • Move the dairy goats to the goat house.

5. Routine management practices

5.1 Feeding

  • Provide roughages (like Napier grass) and supplements.
    • Napier grass should be chopped into approximately 3 cm long pieces.
    • Energy supplements include molasses, cereals or milling by - products (bran, pollard).
    • Protein supplements include:
      • cotton seed cake,
      • Calliandra leaves,
      • Leucaena leaves,
      • sweet potato vines,
      • Desmodium,
      • fishmeal, and
      • dairy meal.
  • A simple feed supplement can be made at home.
    • For every six scoops of whole cereal grains, add half a scoop of fishmeal or any of the following:
      • cotton seed cake,
      • Calliandra leaves,
      • Leucaena leaves,
      • sweet potato vines, or
      • Desmodium.
    • Finally add a tablespoonful of mineral mixture. Mix well before feeding.
  • Increase supplement by 0.5 kg per day during the last month of pregnancy.
  • When in milk, allow 0.5 kg of supplement for every 3 litres of milk produced.

5.2 Breeding

  • Identify a good breeding male goat which has:
    • no deformities,
    • with two well-developed testicles,
    • strong feet,
    • strong legs,
    • good body condition, and
    • a high libido.
    • Libido is observed by the ability of the male to vigorously detect and mate with females on heat.
    • These qualities will ensure successful mating.
  • Breeding females should have:
    • good body condition,
    • a soft udder,
    • two functional teats,
    • strong teeth, and
    • strong legs.
    • Age at first mating should be about 16 months.
    • Breeding too early can result in weak kids and stunted females.
  • Replace breeding animals at nine years of age or earlier if they fail to become pregnant.
  • Male goats serving goats owned by community members should be tested for brucellosis.
    • This is a disease affecting animals and humans. Ask your vet for more information.
  • Introduce a male and leave with the female goats for two to three weeks.
    • Mating all your female goats at the same time will ensure kids are born at the same time and eases management.
    • However it means you will have no milk for part of the year.
  • Mate females two months after kidding.
  • On average birth occurs 150 days after mating.
  • One week before kidding, watch your goat closely in case of any problems.

5.3 Reducing kid mortality

  • Ensure the newborn kid suckles immediately after birth.
    • The goat’s first milk helps protect the kid from diseases, gets its digestive system working, and is especially nutritious.
  • Disinfect umbilical cord immediately after birth with iodine solution or diluted disinfectant to avoid infection.
  • House both mother and kid in a dry, well-ventilated and secure house.

5.4 Feeding kids

  • Allow half to one litre of milk per day for the kid, depending on size.
  • Wean at three months.
  • Introduce kids to roughage (chopped Napier grass, maize stover) by the second week.
  • Introduce kids to supplements (0.25 kg per day) by the fourth week.

5.5 Controlling worms

  • Failure to treat goats, especially those that graze, can result in blood loss, underweight animals and death.
  • For advice on dewormers, consult your local veterinary officer.

5.6 Deworming

  • Deworm all adults before mating.
    • All females two weeks before kidding.
    • Kids at weaning (three months of age).
    • All animals before the start of the rainy season.

5.7 Vaccination

  • If your goats graze with other goats they should be vaccinated against the highly contagious disease goat pneumonia (CCPP).
  • Vaccinate pregnant females against pulpy kidney and tetanus two to three weeks before kidding and vaccinate kids at six months of age.
  • Vaccinate against orf (scabby mouth disease) at two months of age.
    • Orf can also affect farmers, so wear protective clothing; such as overalls, when handling your goats.
    • Wash your hands well with soap and water afterwards.
  • Ask your local veterinary officer for advice on vaccines.
Table 2. What can go wrong and what is the remedy?
Problem Possible causes Remedy

Thin goats

Slow-growing kids

 Worms

Deworms goats as recommended.

Ask local veterinary officer which dewormers to use and follow manufacturer's instructions carefully.

 
Inflammed udder (mastitis) Unhygenic and incorrect milking practices Follow recommended milking practices.
External parasities  Fleas, ticks, mites and lice Use recommended sprays, pour-ons and powders
Lack of feeds Prolonged drought Preserved feed when in surplus (hay, dried fooder, legumes, leaves, maize stover).
Lack of market for milk Lack of market information and over production

Obtain market information on demand for goats' milk.

Create demand by telling people about benefits of goats' milk.

Make added value products such as cheese.

Time breeding to supply milk when demand is greatest (dry season) - provided you can feed your animals.
Lameness Foot rot, injuries, overgrown hooves, scabby mouth disease Trim hooves, provide copper sulphate or formalin foot bath, vaccinate against scabby mouth disease - seek expert advice
Low milk production Inadequate feed Ensure you are feeding sufficient forage and supplements for level of production

Source: CTA 2010

6. Case study

Mrs. Eunice Oketcha, mother of seven from Kajulu village in Winam Division, Nyanza Province, Kenya, was among the first members of her community to take up dairy goatkeeping. That was in 2003. At that time her neighbouring farmers did not believe dairy goat-keeping was possible and none consumed goat’s milk. Mrs Oketch was given two dairy goats by Africa Now, an NGO. The goats were given on a ‘payback system’. Three years later she was able to pay back three kids, which were passed on to other local farmers. Each day, Mrs Okech gets around 4 litres of milk from her goats. She keeps 1 litre for her family and sells the rest. After deducting her costs, she makes a monthly profit of around USD 15. From the proceeds of her milk sales, she is able to pay school fees for one of her sons who attends the local secondary school. In addition to milking goats, Mrs Okech also has three young goats and is keen to expand her flock further. She needs a bigger flock, however she is currently unable to meet the rapidly growing local demand as more and more people get to know about the benefits of consuming goat’s milk

7. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies 

  • Stall fed systemrearing goats: ID 8770
  • Collective action to reduce goat mortality: ID 7904.
  • Farmers dairy goat production handbook: ID 6939.
  • Herbal de-worming for lower goat mortality: ID 7690.
  • Improvement of livestock production: community based goat production: ID 4495.
  • Goat raising in controlled areas and vaccination: ID 8937.
  • Intensive stall-fed system for rearing goats: ID 8770.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

9.1 Women friendly

The technology is not heavy drudgery and can be undertaken by any hand labour.

9.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology provides detailed guidance on goat-rearing. This efficiently allows farmers to affordably rear alternative livestock to dairy cows and efficiently use limited land space.

entries.tittle: Making sweet potato chips and flour
entries.summary: Sweet potato is a popular food in many parts of Eastern Africa. It is drought tolerant, hardy and can grow in marginal areas, thus contributing to improved food security. The young leaves and vines can be consumed as vegetables or fed to livestock. In some communities in Eastern Africa, sweet potatoes are preserved for the dry season by sun-drying to make amukeke – dried sweet potato chips. The following provides facts about dried sweet potato chips and flour, the requirements for making them, a detailed step by step procedure and a case study from Uganda highlighting the benefits of this preservation technique.
entries.description:
Description

Sweet potato is a popular food in many parts of Eastern Africa. It is a drought, hardly and can grow in marginal areas, thus contributing to improved food security. The young leaves and vines can be consumed as vegetables or fed to livestock. During bumper harvests, farmers often sell sweet potatoes at throw-away prices. Losses after harvesting are high due to perishing. In some communities in Eastern Africa, sweet potatoes are preserved for the dry season by sun-drying to make amukeke – dried sweet potato chips. The dried chips are boiled and mashed with beans, milled or pounded to make flour, which can be mixed with either millet or cassava flours to make stiff porridge.

1. Some facts about dried sweet potato chips and flour

  • Any sweet potato variety can be dried to make chips, which can then be milled into flour.
  • Dried sweet potato chips can be stored for up to six months when packaged in airtight, strong, black plastic bags.
  • Sweet potato flour is used to make doughnuts and pancakes.
  • Flour made from the chips can also be used to make high-value flours by mixing with millet, maize or soybean flour. These mixed flours are used to make porridge and baby foods, which are easily digestible.
  • Some bakeries are already using new flour mixes to make bread and cakes.
  • The poultry feed industry is showing interest in using orange-fleshed chips in their feeds to improve yolk colour and vitamin A content of eggs.

2. Requirements for making sweet potato chips and flour

  • Mature sweet potato roots. On average, 4 kg of fresh sweet potato roots give about 1 kg of dried sweet potato chips.
  • A clean area, ideally a room with raised working surfaces, such as tables – not on the ground.
  • Large plastic containers, preferably 10 to 20 litre buckets with lids.
  • A supply of clean water.
  • A manual or motorized sweet potato chipper for chopping or slicing.
  • A raised open platform for air drying, or ideally a solar dryer placed in a clean area in full sunshine.

3 Procedure for making sweet potato chips and flour

3.1 Step one: choosing the roots

  • Use any sweet potato variety.
  • The roots should be undamaged and mature - here to four months for the early maturing varieties and five to six months for the late maturing varieties.

3.2 Step two: washing

  • Wash the sweet potatoes in clean water in large buckets, changing water as frequently as required, Figure 1.
  • Alternatively, you can wash the roots in a sweet potato drum washer when processing large quantities to speed-up the process.
  • Do not peel the roots because the peel is rich in nutrients.

3.3 Step three: draining

  • After washing, drain by placing the sweet potatoes on a raised, perforated rack, Figure 2.
Figure 1. Washing and draining of sweet potato

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Washing and draining of sweet potato

©FAO/TECA

3.4 Step four: chipping or slicing

  • Chip the washed sweet potatoes to a uniform size (3 mm to 6 mm thick), Figure 3.
  • You can slice them manually with a sharp knife or use a manual or motorized chipper to speed-up the process.
Figure 3. Chipping or slicing

©FAO/TECA

3.5 Step five: drying

  • Sweet potato chips should be evenly spread on a raised platform, preferably on a clean black plastic sheet, to sundry under maximum sunshine for about six to eight hours. It is best to do this during the hot, dry season.
  • To ensure high-quality chips, solar dryers can be used. A modified solar dryer, called a hybrid solar dryer has an additional source, such as charcoal and can be used to dry chips.
  • Chips should be dried until they are brittle.
  • If drying in the open, cover chips with netting to keep off flies and birds.
  • Pack chips or continue processing to flour.

3.6 Step six: milling

  • Mill dried chips to flour using a hammer mill (village “posho” mill).

Figure 4. Milling

©FAO/TECA

3.7 Step seven: packaging and labelling

  • Pack dried chips or flour in strong (thick gauge) black polyethylene bags. Flour can be packaged in 2 kg packs for distribution to shops and other retail outlets.
  • Label product to state source, date of manufacture and expiry date (after six months).
  • Place bags of dried chips or flour in cardboard cartons to protect them from light.

3.8 Step eight: storing

  • Store in a cool, dry place off the ground, preferably on pallets or raised surfaces.
  • Flour can be stored for six months.
Table 1. What can go wrong?
Problem What are the causes? How is the problem corrected?
Brown or discoloured chips

Drying not complete due to:

  • non‑uniform chip sizes
  • mould growth
  • Slice the chips into uniform sizes (3 to 6 mm thick)
  • Use a solar dryer with an alternative energy source
  • Start as early as possible on a sunny day and complete drying on the same day
Chips are rubbery

Chips contain high moisture:

  • non‑uniform chip sizes
  • drying not complete
  • packaging or bags that allow in moisture during storage
  • Make chips of the same size (3 to 6 mm thick; half thumbnail size) or use a chipping machine
  • Start as early as possible on a sunny day and complete drying on the same day
  • Use strong plastic bags that are waterproof
Bad or fermented smell
  • microbial growth
  • insufficient drying hence high moisture content in the product
 Drying thoroughly until brittle
Orange colouration lost in the orange‑fleshed varieties
  • over‑exposure of roots or chips to air and light during chipping and drying
  • using clear or transparent bags
  • Chip and dry as quickly as possible. Ideally use an enclosed dryer, such as a solar dryer
  • Use black bags for storage
Weevils and rodents
  • storing chips or flour on the ground
  • bushy surrounding
  • Pack chips and flour in strong plastic bags
  • Store packed chips and flour in cartons on racks or raised surface
  • Ensure storage area is free of pests and rodents
  • Clear area around the store
Burnt or charred chips Drying temperature too high Control drying temperature

Source: Apoolo Na Angor Women Development 2010

4. Case study

Ekinyu Eugene heads the Abuket sweet potato processor group, a farmer’s group based in Soroti, Uganda. Ekinyu has been growing and eating sweet potatoes since childhood. His desire to turn sweet potatoes into an income-generating activity led him to attend several training sessions on adding value to sweet potatoes, which he and other farmers received through a Farmer Field School organized by the International Potato Centre. As a group, they identified a market for dried chips in Kenya. Ekinyu greatly gained from the first sales of orange-fleshed sweet potato chips and he managed to educate his children in good schools in Kampala.

5. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies 

  • Making banana chips and flour: ID 6922.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Women-friendly

Sweet potato production in Africa is usually a women's activity.

7.2 Resource use efficiency 

Sweet potato not only is a source of nutrition, its non consumable parts can be turned into livestock feed. Converting sweet potato into flour and chips allows it to also be used in other forms of food. 

7.3 Pro-poor technology

Sweet potato is drought tolerant, hardy and can grow in marginal areas, thus contributing to improved food security. The technology prevents harvest losses thanks to preservation techniques such as chips and flour. This can also be used in other food items and sold at just prices.
