entries.tittle: Enhanced resilience of water drainage and irrigation system for disaster risk management in Shandong, China
entries.summary:
The rural land tenure became a family responsibility in Qilin township, with the need to renovate irrigation infrastructure becoming more urgent. This urgency was due to natural disasters such as waterlogging and drought which caused economic losses and threatened farmer’s livelihoods. Major interventions as part of the Disaster Risk Management (DRM) plan for the township were undertaken, including the construction of a drainage culvert for improving the water logging situation. 
The implementation of this practice helped to increase the community’s resilience to floods, waterlogging and droughts by improving the community water drainage and irrigation infrastructures, as well as cleaning the canals. This improvement at the community level will reduce the economic losses of crop production, therefore contributing to the sustainable livelihoods of farmers who engage in agriculture.
entries.description:
Description

The community-based irrigation and drainage infrastructures in the Qilin township were built in the period known as “collective”, between 1956 and 1982. In 1982, the reform of rural land tenure changed from a collective production management system to family responsibility. However, the existing infrastructures were not properly maintained or renovated, leaving field drainage canals, local bridges, culverts and gates useless. Most branch canals and main field canals were not able to distribute water or draining out the logging and flooding waters during the rainy season due to blocks caused by sediment deposition that reduced the overall drainage capacity.

Damaged facilities and infrastructure in the irrigation systems have not been repaired in time due to insufficient funds, either from local governments or communities. Natural disasters such as waterlogging and drought often occur in the township, constraining the development of agriculture and causing economic losses when flood disasters happen, thus threatening farmer’s livelihoods. To improve this situation, major interventions as part of the DRM plan for the township were undertaken, including the construction of a drainage culvert for improving the waterlogging situation in Liuxi and its neighbouring villages, and the dredging of irrigation and drainage canals in pilot villages.

1. Implementation of the technology

1.1 Construction of the drainage culvert and rehabilitation of drainage infrastructures

  • As an important component of Community‑Based Disaster Risk Management (CBDRM), the Qilin township built a major drainage culvert of 1.5 m diameter and 100 m of length, and cleaned six field drainage canals (Figure 1) with a total length of 2 350 m, repairing six culverts and building four new culverts within the area.
  • These activities were undertaken between May and July 2008.
    • According to villagers, the improved water drainage system effectively worked in draining out rainwater from fields in August 2008.
    • There were no water loggings nor floods during the raining seasons of 2008 and 2009.
    • The Qilin Township Government and County Agricultural Bureau and County Water Resource Bureau provided support for construction and rehabilitation activities.

1.2 The Dredging of the irrigation and drainage canal in pilot villages

  • The village drainage canals built in the collective period were not well maintained due to a lack of collective funds since the rural land tenure reform in 1982.
  • A baseline survey showed that most of the village field canals were silted up with mud and grasses, dramatically reducing their water drainage capacity.
    • In addition, individual farmers built check dams into field canals for transporting crops and straws from their field, completely blocking the canals.
  • To change this situation, villages dredged their field canals by hiring engineering machines and mobilizing the labours in farmer’s cooperatives.
    • The total length of the dredged irrigation and drainage canals in villages was about 9 500 m with a total soil volume of 18 530 m3.
    • The field canal dredgings in Qianfengqiao, Liuxi and Nancao were completed in 2008.
    • The increased drainage capacity of cleaned field canals significantly reduced the water logging time in the rainy seasons of 2008 and 2009.
    • Village Committees and Farmer’s Cooperatives (FC) in the villages played important roles in mobilizing labour inputs and individual contributions to clean the canals and repair the damaged field culverts and bridges.
Figure 1. Cleaned backbone canal in Nancao

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Clean community field canal

©FAO/TECA

2. Technical details

2.1 Field baseline survey

  • A water engineering specialist carried out field investigations on the existing irrigation system and drainage canals, identifying problems related to flood disasters and their causes.
  • During the baseline survey, data and basic hydrologic information were gathered, which constituted the baseline data for designing and planning the activities in the field.

2.2 Designing and planning the drainage infrastructure construction projects

  • Based on findings during the survey on the irrigation and drainage infrastructures and lower resilience to the floods and water loggings, selected interventions were identified and prioritized through consultation with village leaders and villagers.
  • The construction of the drainage culvert in the Liuying irrigation system and the improvement of drainage canals were identified as a top priority and implemented, followed by a technical designing concept.
    • The culvert drainage had a 1.5 m diameter, and the culvert length through dike was of 50 m with reinforced concrete.
    • The culvert length in the flooding plain of the Yunju River was of 50 m with strengthened concrete.
    • The dredging parameters of the irrigation and drainage canal in the demonstration villages were designed according to the layout of the field canals and their sedimentation.
Figure 3. Outflow of culvert

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Construction and implementation of selected activities

  • The construction of the major drainage culvert was conducted by a selected construction team.
  • Based on the design of the related water management projects, the team began the construction, and its quality was monitored and inspected by the water engineering specialist and the township water engineer.

2.4 Project management and maintenance

  • After the construction of the water infrastructure projects, all the irrigation and drainage facilities and infrastructures needed proper maintenance and management during the operating process.
  • The appropriate operation and management of the drainage and irrigation canal system were the precondition for sustaining the drainage and irrigation functions.
  • For the constructed drainage and irrigation system and dredged canals, systematic and regular maintenance and management mechanism and systematic operation will ensure long term contribution to reducing the losses of floods and waterlogging.

3. Impacts and results

  • According to the Liuxi village leader and the Qinlin township governor, the culvert benefited about 6 000 mu of farmland for flood drainage, covering six villages (Liuxi, Liubei, Liunan, Mengdian, Dongyoufang and Xiyoufang), with a total population of 5 000.
  • The economic benefit of the culvert is significant, estimating 250 Yuan per mu (35 USD for every mu at the time of the project) of economic loss each year, for a total of 1.2 to 1.8 million Yuan for 6 000 mu.
Figure 4. Sluice gate of drainage culvert in Luixi

©FAO/TECA

4. Monitoring of the demonstration

  • The constructed water drainage projects and field canal cleaning projects were monitored and supervised by the water engineering specialist.
    • Monitoring the long-term impacts and benefits of these projects will be carried out by the county agricultural bureau and county water resource bureau.

5. Validation of the practice

  • This adaptation practice has been successfully tested in Juye in the context of the Strengthening Disaster Preparedness in the Agricultural Sector (TCP/CPR/3105).

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

This technology is also available in Spanish: ID 6981.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Pro-poor technology

Repairing and renovating irrigation infrastructure strengthen communities' resilience to natural disasters and reduce their loss.

entries.tittle: Promotion of Farmers' Cooperative (FC) Development for Community-Based Disaster Risk Management (CBDRM) in China
entries.summary: Local associations or farmers groups, if appropriately trained and empowered, can play a key role in disaster risk management. This practice helps in including the concept of Community-Based Disaster Risk Management (CBDRM) in the overall context of Farmer’s Cooperatives (FC) development. This has resulted in establishing local capacities for DRM on a basis of self-managed, broad-based and legally recognized institutions interacting as partners with county-level actors in the fight against increasing drought and flood risks in the region.
entries.description:
Description

In 2007, the National Law of Farmer’s Cooperatives (FC) was adopted in China providing a sound institutional framework for establishment of FC at community level. However, the knowledge about the new law and its related concepts of self-managed FCs is still very limited among farmers in the county of Juye.

A possible link between the functions of FCs and CBDRM was not anticipated. In this practice, CBDRM was included in the overall context of FC development. As a result, local capacities for DRM on a basis of self-management were established.

1. Technical details

  • The promotion of FC as partners in DRM was a two years process built around key pillars.

1.1 Baseline survey

  • In order to analyse the situation of farmer associations, a baseline survey was conducted to assess institutional and technical capacities within existing FCs.
    • It also looked at the scope for and interest of FC members to introduce CBDRM as an additional concept and objectives into the service portfolio of FCs.
  • The baseline survey confirmed that informal farmer production associations had existed for years in all pilot villages but with very weak functions and outreach for facilitating collective actions.
  • A new understanding of what FCs can be and what they can do had to be established.

1.2 Capacity building and registration of FCs

  • Tailor-made training plans were developed for capacity building of farmers’ cooperative leaders and members over the period of two years, with active facilitation from outside experts and local governments.
  • A series of community-level training activities were conducted thereafter with the local population, focusing on issues regarding farmer cooperatives establishment and management, services and tasks.
    • The participation of women in the FC training was specifically addressed throughout the planning and development process.
  • Training contents included a detailed introduction of the National Law of Farmers’ Cooperatives and practical guidelines for the establishment of an FC.
  • The understanding of specific rules of service functions and economic gains of FCs was essential to gain member confidence in operating as a new type of FC.

1.2.1 Understanding the potential roles of FCs in CBDRM

  1. Registration procedure and criteria of FC.
  2. Roles, functions, regulations, administrative management and financial management of FC.
  3. Membership development of FC.
  4. Responsibility and legal rights of FC leaders and members.
  5. Technology service system and mechanism of FCs.
  6. FC-based wholesale marketing and inputs purchase and further income-earning activities; and other important issues, such as women’s participation.
  7. The potential actions and services as well as responsibilities as partners for CBDRM, vis à vis their members and the county authorities.
  • Participatory methods proved useful tools to illustrate training subjects related to potential DRM functions of the FC.
    • These include the review of secondary data, historical profile and resource mapping, drafting of problem trees and interviews, seasonal calendars and Venn diagrams, among others.
    • Trainees including village leaders and farmers were encouraged to hold FC promotion and follow-up meetings to further encourage other farmers to join the FC in future development.
    • The functions of FC in CBDRM take long to be developed and institutionalized.
    • It is important to encourage women to participate, not only in capacity building training but also in other organizational activities.
  • Linked to training, the performance of effective, visible demonstrations of practical interventions for DRM conducted through the FCs at the community level was key to enhance acceptance and support among FC members, and to gain reputation among the local authorities and village committees.

2. Formulation and implementation of FCs Action Plans for CBDRM

  • In the second year of the capacity building process, FC Action plans for disaster risk management were drafted together with FC members, leaders and women in particular.
  • Key points of the Action Plan were visualized in a four-column matrix on pinboards, including the agreed schedule, major activities, current constraints, as well as responsible actors and stakeholders.
  • Activities for FC involvement in CBDRM were given priority, such as the rebuilding of the drainage system, land levelling, cleaning the canals and consolidation of small dams, among others.
  • The institutional support from the county or township government and village committee for the implementation of the plans is essential.
    • They must be brought on board in the planning process, either through participation at training and/or through regular information meetings.
    • They are key to monitor implementation and ensure follow up.
    • Implementation of selected priorities identified from the action plans was initiated during the capacity building process in the second year.
Figure 1. Farmers’ cooperatives

©FAO/TECA

3. Impacts and results

  • All FCs initiated under the project have been formally registered as new Farmer’s Cooperatives.
  • The FCs have played important roles in cleaning the village drainage canals, and soil rehabilitation.
  • In one village the FC assisted in transforming lower land into fodder production fields for cattle breeding and for establishing a partnership with a beef cattle development enterprise in Shanghai.
  • The capacity building process has also contributed to the enhancement of farmers’ awareness regarding disaster risk management, especially prevention and mitigation.

4. Validation of the practice

  • This practice has been successfully tested in the context of the FAO funded project Strengthening Disaster Preparedness of Agricultural Sector in China.
  • The project was jointly implemented by the Agricultural Bureaus of Shandong Province and Juye County, FAO and the Centre for Integrated Agricultural Development (CIAD).

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Women-friendly

6.2 Pro-poor technology

entries.tittle: Soils rehabilitation in areas exposed to recurrent floods and water logging, Shandong Province, China
entries.summary: One severe impact of recurrent flooding and waterlogging in Juye County in the Shandong Province, is the salinization and alkalization of soils. The soil in Juye, mainly Luvisoils, with high salt content due to the water loggings, is rich in calcium, magnesium, ions of chloride, sulfate and carbonate. Salt compounds created by positive or negative ions enhance water salinity in the soil, reducing the roots’ absorptive capacity of soil nutrients. The average annual rainfall in Juye is 500 mm with a concentrated rainfall (more 60 percent of the annual precipitation) during June, July and August. The good practice strategy consists of a series of interrelated measures for soil improvement, including drainage improvements, land levelling, deep ploughing and most importantly, based on detailed soil testing the application of formulated fertilization, the key to rehabilitating local soil conditions. Soil testing focused on nutrition values and salinity. Suitable fertilizer compositions were developed in response to the specific soil conditions and predominant local cropping patterns. Local fertilizer production enterprises were hired to produce the formulated fertilization with the dual objectives of rehabilitating the soils while providing sound fertilization for the main crops used in the region, mainly wheat, cotton and maize.
entries.description:
Description

The cropping areas in Juye are low lying and uneven in general. Within that pattern, the higher laying lands (or parts of fields) are prone to salinization and lower laying segments are most prone to waterlogging. The uneven surface structure has adverse impacts on both irrigation and drainage. By leveling land, irrigation efficiency can be improved, while irrigation costs can be reduced.

Deep ploughing is another important measurement for soil improvement in the area. Due to the shallow ploughing practiced by farmers over long periods, lower soil layers have hardened, thus constraining the growth of crop roots. In addition, the PH of the surface layer is also higher than 7.5 due to the enrichment of alkaline soil components, and thus further affecting the growth of root systems. Therefore, deep ploughing is applied to smash the plough pan, increasing the active soil layer and revising the process of alkalinization.

In addition, the degraded soils should be regularly sluiced. During the dry season, in order to reduce soil evaporation and thus salt encroachment towards the surface, an increase in the amount of irrigation water can help, as well as the application of mulching and other agronomic measures can do. During the rainy season, water with low salt content or rainwater should be used to flush soil salinity, generally one to two times per season.

The above measurements are preconditions for further soil improvement, which must then be based on the results of soil testing. The ultimate goal is to recreate soil quality and fertility through the application of tailor-made, formulated fertilization which should be applied according to the local plant patterns and the targeted yields. The capacities and skills of available fertilizer factories need to be taken into account. Technical training and field days are needed for demonstration and to promote replication.

1. Implementation details of the tested technology

  • The practice was tested in the Nancao, Liuxi, Qian Fengqiao and Caolou villages in Qilin Township of Juye County from 2007 to 2009.

1.1 Soil analysis

  • Sampling quantity and method
    • 1 500 soil samples were taken from differently degraded soils, using the S shape method.
    • Every soil sample takes 15 spots and each spot is 0 cm to 20 cm depth of topsoil.
    • The sample quartering is kept after the intensive mixing.
  • Soil sample pretreatment
    • Natural withering, smashing and bottling pretreatment were carried out on all gathered soil samples, establishing soil sample files.
  • Soil sample testing
    • The soil sample testing was performed in accord with common technical standards.
    • The testing included: soil organic matter content, soil pH value, soil available nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, zinc, boron, kalium, iron, soil salinity etc.
  • Data processing and analyses
    • Data processing and analyses was delivered by the laboratory, as well as the fertilization plan, including a scientific, environmentally sound and economically affordable fertilizer formula, which aims at soil rehabilitation and fertilization of main crops to be used on demonstration plots.

1.2 Application of formulated fertilizer

  • Production of soil formulated fertilizer
    • A local fertilizer production enterprise was selected and contracted to produce the soil formulated fertilizer according to the formulas provided by the laboratory and checked by the soil experts of the agricultural bureau.
    • From the soil tests, the laboratory identified six types of fertilizers, specifically adequate to the crop system, the soil type and the growing period (see Table 1).
  • Field demonstration
    • Field demonstrations on demonstration plots were set up including control plots, accompanied by technical training and on-the-spot meetings.
    • An organic-based fertilize plan with a reasonable collocation of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, was used as a starting point of the fertilization strategy and then complemented with extended fertilization plans in the demonstration area.
Table 1. Formulated fertilizers identified for Juye
Fertilizer types Crop system Soil type Growing period
Type I: 48% 16N-16P-16K Wheat-cotton Waterlogged soil  Base fertiliser
Type II: 40 % 30N-5 P- 5K Wheat-cotton-maize Waterlogged soil  Early growing period
Type III: 36 % 31N-5Ka Maize Waterlogged soil  Corn milking period
Type IV: 57% 19N-19P-19K Wheat-cotton Waterlogged soil  Base fertiliser
Type V: 48 % 22N-8p-18k Maize Waterlogged soil  Corn milking period
Type VI: Organic fertiliser All crops Saline and waterlogged soil  Base feriliser

Source: Agricultural Bureau Juye County 2010

1.3 Examples of specific fertilization applications tailored to the study areas

  • Fertilization for wheat production in the area with salty water-logged soil
    • For each mu wheat, add two to three cube meter of organic fertilizer (Type VI) together with 30 kg per mu of Type I as base fertilizer.
    • At the early growing period, use 20 to 25 kg per mu of high-nitrogen compound fertilizer (Type II).
    • At late period, foliage top dressing, spray urea and potassium dehydrogenate phosphate (KDP).
  • Fertilization for cotton production in salty water-logged soil
    • Adhere to the principle of "adequate base fertilizer, little sprout fertilizer, stable cotton ball fertilizer, much flower fertilizer, fill the top cover fertilizer".
      • This is in accordance with the rule of cotton fertilization; increasing the organic fertilizer and potash; and balancing the proportion of organic fertilizer, NPK fertilizer, and microelement fertilizer.
    • Let the fertilizer play a full role in increasing yield effectively.
    • Through the growth period, a total amount of 50-60 kg/mu formula fertilizer will be used.
  • Fertilization for maize production in salty water-logged soil, the "three-period fertilization approach" is applied;
    • “Early growing period fertilizer” (Type II) when corn leaf age index is 30 percent (six-leaf seedling stage), with a total fertilizer amount about 30 percent of the total fertilization amount.
    • “Core ear bearing period fertilizer”(Type V) when the corn leaf index is 60 percent, (12 - leaf seedling stage), fertilizer in the total amount of 50 percent of total fertilization.
    • “Corn milking fertilizer” (Type III) in the corn tasseling stage after the topdressing, in the amount of 20 percent of total fertilization.
  • During the entire growth period, a total amount of 40 kg to 60 kg of nitrogen formulation fertilizer is used.

1.4 Supportive measures

  • Workshops at the city and county level to discuss soil characteristics and the suitable soil fertilizer formula based on the data processing results of soil nutrient testing.
  • Technical training
    • Two-term technical training specifically for the association personnel in the project area, so as to enhance the understanding of soil testing and formulated fertilization.
    • Training is ideally held during the spring and the autumn periods.
  • Technical information
    • After data processing and expert workshop, publication and distribution of the soil formulated fertilizer suggestion materials, to make sure that every household will get a soil formulated fertilizer suggestion card and a leaflet.

2. Impacts and performance of formulated fertilization

  • This adaptation practice was successfully tested during 2007-2009 in the context of Strengthening Disaster Preparedness of Agricultural Sector in China.
    • In this project, FAO and the Institute of Agricultural Sciences and Technology in Juye County were working together in conducting the soil improvement activities at the county and community level.
    • This was done in collaboration with the county/township line agencies and local farmers.
    • The County Agricultural Bureau and the Shandong Agricultural Academy of Science proceeded with specific technical processing and the demonstration of formulated fertilization.
    • Pilot testing was closely monitored and results were included in a wider option menu of potentially viable adapted practices to drought/flood conditions, which may become more frequent and severe in the context of future climate change.
    • According to the County Agricultural Bureau, on average, the average yields of wheat, maize and cotton increased by 8 to 12 percent by applying formulated fertilization techniques.
    • The input costs for formulated fertilization remained the same as the conventional fertilization pattern.
Figure 1. Air-dried soil sample pre-treatment

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Bottled soil

©FAO/TECA

3. Validation of practice

  • The practice was tested in the Nancao, Liuxi, Qian Fengqiao and Caolou villages in Qilin Township of Juye County from 2007 to 2009.​

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool; and
  • subtropics, cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Soil cultivation and tillage in organic agriculture: ID 8376.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the technology

6.1 Resource use efficiency

In this technology, the efficient use of soil testing and the use of organic fertilizer are undertaken.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

By improving soil quality, the technology allows for increased and better quality yields. This provides for additional sources of income and food.

entries.tittle: Processing tomatoes
entries.summary: Tomatoes are widely grown and used in Eastern Africa. During the peak season most farmers sell their tomatoes at throw‑away prices and substantial quantities go to waste because they are highly perishable. To avoid this, farmers can process tomatoes into various products for storage and use at home or as value-added products for income generation.
entries.description:
Description

Tomatoes are rich in vitamins and minerals, which are important for health. They are also rich in lycopene (the substance that makes tomatoes red) which has cancer-preventing properties.

1. Basic equipment required for tomato processing

The equipment required includes cooking pans, plastic buckets with lids, a sharp knife, clean water, a stove (charcoal, kerosene, gas or electric), wooden spoons and ladles. Package the tomatoes in either glass or plastic jars and bottles. Plastic is lighter, cheaper and does not break easily. You will also need crown caps for bottles and lids for jars. For commercial-scale tomato processing, you may also need a pulping machine or blender, a crown cork sealer or bottle capping machine, a sealing machine, a glass bulb thermometer, weighing scales, a chemical preservative, thickening agent (pectin), and a solar dryer.

2. Procedure for making tomato powder

2.1 First step: choosing the tomatoes 

Select tomatoes that are ripe, red, have a firm texture and are free of disease and mould.

2.2 Second step: washing 

Wash the freshly harvested tomatoes in clean water in a large bucket.

2.3 Third step: slicing

Cut tomatoes into slices 0.5 cm thick.

2.4 Fourth step: drying

Spread the tomato slices on a clean, raised platform to sundry. Use a solar dryer for a better quality product. To prevent contamination during open sun drying, cover with mosquito netting. For commercial-scale production, drying tomatoes using a hot-air dryer is advisable.

2.5 Fifth step: milling 

Mill the dried tomatoes using a hammer mill fitted with a sieve of the appropriate mesh size.

2.6 Sixth step: packaging and storage 

  • Place powder into polypropylene or polyethylene bags and seal using a candle or sealing machine (impulse sealer) and label with the date of manufacture and expiry date, one year later. 
  • Pack the bags into cardboard boxes to prevent damage caused by
Figure 1. Packaging and storing tomato powder

©FAO/TECA

3. Procedure for making tomato pulp

3.1 First step: choosing the tomatoes

Select tomatoes that are ripe, red, with a firm texture and are free of diseases and mould.

3.2 Second step: washing 

Wash the freshly harvested tomatoes in clean water in a large bucket.

3.3 Third step: boiling

Place the tomatoes in a cooking pot. Add water and boil until they are soft and the skin peels off easily – but do not peel them.

3.4 Fourth step: pulping

  • Remove the tomatoes from the pot using a large perforated spoon and place them in another container.
  • Mash using a large wooden spoon.
  • Use a large household sieve to separate the tomato pulp from seeds and skin.
  • Discard the seeds and skins or feed them to your chickens and keep the pulp. For commercial-scale production, a fruit pulper (manual or motorized) will reduce the workload and increase the yield. Pulp can be used to make tomato jam and ketchup.

4. Procedure for preparing tomato jam

  • Use 1 kg of sugar for each kg of tomato pulp.
  • Mix and place in a large cooking pan.
  • Place the pan on a stove, bring to the boil and stir continuously to avoid burning or sticking to the base. Boil until mixture thickens.
  • Add lemon juice (two teaspoons for every kg of jam). The lemon juice helps the jam to set.
  • Test to see if the jam is set. Take some jam in a spoon and tip into a cup of cold water. If the drop remains whole, the jam is ready. If it spreads out in the water, the jam needs further boiling. 
  • If the jam does not set even after additional boiling, add pectin (a thickening agent: 1 g of pectin per kg of tomato pulp).
  • If the jam is to be stored for more than one year, you need to add a chemical preservative (sodium benzoate, added at a concentration of 100 mg for each kg of jam). Add to mixture near the end of the boiling process. 
  • Use a sterilizing agent (sodium hypochlorite) or hot water to sterilize the jars.
  • Allow the jam to cool and pour into the jars while it is still flowing.
  • Fill sterile jars to within 3 cm from the brim of the jar.
  • Loosely cover the jars with lids and set aside for about five minutes to allow trapped air to escape. Tighten the lids and turn jars upside-down for two to three minutes to heat the lids to kill any germs.
  • Allow the jars to cool to room temperature before labelling. Jam can be stored at room temperature for up to one year if not opened.

5. Procedure for preparing tomato ketchup

  • To make 1 kg of tomato ketchup, place 420 g of tomato pulp and 150 g of sugar in a large pan. Thoroughly mix and then add 300 g of vinegar, 300 g of salt, 70 g ground onion and 30 g of ground garlic and any other desired spices, such as chilli powder. Mix well. 
  • Bring the mixture to a boil, continuously stirring with a wooden spoon. 
  • Allow mixture to cool for about five minutes.
  • Pour into bottles, then cap or seal the bottles with the lids using a sealing machine.
  • Place bottles in a pan of cold water.
  • Continue cooling the bottled products by changing the water in the pan.
  • Ketchup can be stored at room temperature for six months if not opened.
  • Use it as a tasty sauce.
Table 1. Problems, causes and how the problems could be corrected

Source: CTA 2010

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Processing mango and guava nectar: ID 7150.
  • Cassava processing: cassava wet flour: ID 3826.
  • Producing solar dried fruit and vegetables for micro- and small-scale rural enterprise development: processing aspects: ID 4503.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Women-friendly

This technology is not labour-intensive.

7.2 Resource use efficiency

By process tomatoes into various storable products, this technology avoids tomatoes going to waste and perishing too quickly.

7.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology leads to value-added products that can be used for income generation.

entries.tittle: Worm control in sheep
entries.summary: Every sheep grazing on pasture is infested with one type of worm or the other. Failure to control clinical worm infestation in sheep can result in blood loss, underweight animals, and death. In the case of hydatid disease, which is a disease related to infestation with tapeworm, failure to control the life cycle can result in a public health problem and deaths in infected humans.
entries.description:
Description

1. How can I tell my sheep have clinical worm infestation?

  • Different worm infestation levels in sheep exhibit different clinical signs.
  • In general, the following signs may be indicative of clinical worm infestation.
    • Dullness
    • Loss of appetite
    • Scruffy hair coat
    • Membranes inside the eyelids are pale – not the usual pink
    • A pendulous swelling may develop under the lower jaw – ‘bottle jaw’
    • Loss of body condition
    • Diarrhoea (may or may not be present depending on the parasite)
    • Death in severe cases.

2. How do I know which worms are affecting my sheep?

  • There are many types of worms that can infest sheep.
  • However, some important ones in the Eastern Africa region are mentioned in Table 1 against their symptoms.
  • The level of worm infestation is related to climate and the seasons.
  • It is therefore possible to treat animals at particular times of the year or in response to weather patterns and break the life cycle of the parasites.
Table 1. Main symptoms and possible clinical worm infestation
Main symptoms Possible worm infestation
Pendulous swelling under the lower jaw (bottle jaw), very pale membranes inside the eyelips and mouth, emaciation and death.

Roundworm

Liver fluke (Fasciola) infestations is a consideration if the animals are known to graze along the banks of streams, mashy or swampy pasture, near ponds or in areas prone to flooding.

Young rumen flukes (Paramphistome and Calicophoron) are a consideration too, especially in cases of very pale memembranes and increased thirst.
Districtive dark-coloured diarrhoea Roundworm
Nodules in the intestines of slaughtered animals, otherwise little or no other signs in line animals Roundworm, mainly due to pimply gut worm (Oesophagostomum)
Whilr tape-like segments in faecal droppings Tapeworm
Presence of cysts in liver, lungs or heart of slaughtered animals Hydatid cysts

Source: CTA 2010

3. General principles of effective worm treatment

  • Treat sheep with an appropriate de-wormer.
  • Use correct dose based either on individual weight or on weight of the heaviest animal in the flock.
  • Deposit de-wormer over the tongue;
    • A drug deposited at the front of the tongue may go directly into the glandular stomach and this reduces drug availability in the body.
  • Drench animals in the morning before feeding.
  • Drench all adults before mating.
  • Drench all females two weeks before lambing.
  • Drench lambs at weaning (three months of age).
  • Drench all animals before the start of the rainy season or at times of peak infection.
  • In cases of resistance to de-wormer give two full doses at a 12 hour interval.
  • Drench with two different de-wormers at the same time to dramatically delay resistance to either drug.
    • Seek veterinary advice before doing this.

3.1 Points to note

  • Stocking rate
    • If you have too many animals per unit area, pasture contamination is enhanced and frequent re-infections occur.
  • No effective rotation
    • Pasture rotation is a very effective strategy for worm control as it avoids frequent re-infections.
    • Tethering and moving animals to new sites every three to four days is a form of rotation.
  • Communal watering sites and roadside grazing are constant sources of infective larvae.
  • What other management practices can I use to minimize worm infestation?
    • If animals are fed indoors, use a slatted floor.
    • Construct feed troughs on the wall to avoid contamination with droppings.
    • Feed animals adequate quantities of quality feed available within your environment.
    • Use animals that are known to be resistant to worms.

4. Roundworm control in sheep

4.1 Roundworm control in high-temperature and humid conditions

  • Treat all animals just before the rainy season.
  • At other times treat sick animals only.
  • Follow the general principles of treatment described above.

4.2 Roundworm control in sub-humid, warm, grain-growing regions

  • Turn animals onto grain fields after harvest.
  • In areas with large enough fields to allow rotational grazing, return animals onto the paddock after two months.
  • Treat any clinical cases.
  • Grazing paddocks with sheep first, followed by cattle, reduces pasture larval contamination for sheep.
  • Alternating a food crop with grass will result in pasture with less larval contamination.

4.3 Roundworm control in sub-humid, cool, highland regions

  • Since these areas are relatively cool, larvae can survive on pasture and be infective for long periods.
    • Treat clinical cases as soon as you notice the symptoms.
    • Graze adult cattle after sheep, goats and calves.
    • Cut-and-carry systems can prevent animals grazing and contaminating pasture if one starts with clean pastures and clean animals.
    • Where land size allows, rotation of pasture will be effective but a pasture needs to be rested for at least three months.

4.4 Roundworm control in arid and semi-arid regions

  • In these areas during the dry seasons, ingested worm larvae may assume delayed development.
  • Once the rains come, the larvae resume development and thus may cause acute worm infestation.
  • Transmission is seasonal and some periods of the year are too dry for larvae to survive on pasture.
  • However, watering points and bomas (open-air enclosures within homesteads) are often areas of high contamination.
    • Treat all animals one week after the onset of the rainy season.
    • Treat clinical cases as soon as you notice the symptoms.
    • Treat animals when the grass has browned in the dry season to prevent chronic syndromes.
      • This can be caused by relatively few worms and are difficult to diagnose.
    • Smallholders in semi-arid zones.
      • Small farms in such areas cannot support many animals.
      • Animals quite often have nutritional stress leading to a chronic worm problem.
      • Feed supplementation is useful.
    • Semi-arid pastoral areas and semi-arid large-scale ranches.
      • Although stocking rates may be low, which should reduce the risk of infection, poor feed may lead to chronic infestation.
      • Supplementation with feed blocks is therefore desirable.
      • Ranches may have facilities to allow management of lambing and of grazing.
      • For example, “dose and move procedures” in which animals are treated and moved to clean grounds is useful to control worm infestation.
      • Also move bomas frequently.
    • Arid-zone pastoral areas
      • Rainfall is unevenly distributed annually and hence there are times of nutritional stress.
      • Although stocking rates may be low, heavy contamination around watering points and bomas is common.

5. Minimizing roundworm resistance to de-wormer treatment

5.1 Dosing

  • Do not under-dose animals.
    • Dose on the basis of the heaviest animal in the flock.
  • Treat animals in the morning before feeding.
  • Change class of drug yearly
    • Seek veterinary advice.
  • Drench de-wormer over the tongue.

5.2 Timing of treatment

  • Epidemiological information, which is information on the causes, distribution, and control of disease in populations, is important in deciding on the time for treatment.
    • Administer the de-wormer when the parasite population is concentrated in the host and the rate of transmission (e.g. by egg production) is low.
      • For example, in arid and semi-arid areas, treat at the middle of the dry season when the parasites are likely to be in the hosts in an arrested (hypobiotic) state.
    • Treat again a week into the rainy season to kill worms before they mature and start contaminating the pastures.
    • When moving animals from a contaminated to a clean pasture, treat 48 hours before.
      • To avoid rapid re-infection, the treated animals should preferably be housed for the first 48 hours to ensure that all worm eggs are voided prior to moving the animals.
    • A pasture can be considered free of parasites if it was cropped or if it had been rested for at least three months (at least four months in the highlands).

5.3 Using integrated control measures

  • By using a combination of control measures (rotational grazing, ‘dose-and-move’, zero-grazing etc), the use of de-wormers will be minimized.
  • This will in turn minimize the number of generations of worms exposed to the de-wormers, thus slowing the development of resistance to drugs.

6. Management of roundworms with confirmed resistance to de-wormer treatment

  • Total withdrawal of selected family/families of de-wormers.
  • Combine selected benzimidazoles and narrow-spectrum compounds and use them strategically.
  • Manipulate drug usage by using a combination of two full doses of different drugs or split dose and apply at an interval.
    • Consult a veterinarian before attempting this.
  • Use slow-release devices.

7. Control of liver and rumen flukes in sheep

  • Effective fluke control is based on correct diagnosis, use of effective de-wormers and a reduction in the exposure of sheep to the intermediate hosts - snails.
  • The choice of a de-wormer drug depends on price and availability.
  • For prophylactic treatment, give de-wormer at the end of the season when the snails, the intermediate hosts, are becoming less active.
  • For curative treatment, give de-wormer two to three months after the expected peak period of infection in the sheep.
  • Additional treatment may be carried out in situations where sheep are grazed in wet areas during the dry season or in areas with high snail populations.
  • Use of chemicals (molluscides) such as Niclosamide (bayluscide, WP 70) recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) to control snails, or biological methods such as keeping ducks that feed on the snails, reduces the snail population and breaks the life cycle of flukes.
  • Draining of low-lying wet areas and fencing off the wet and poorly drained areas reduces infection rates in sheep.
  • Supplementation with highly nutritious feeds helps to reduce the effects of flukes on sheep.

8. Control of tapeworm in sheep

  • Most tapeworm infections in sheep are considered non-pathogenic and therefore specific treatment for infection with these parasites is not necessary.
  • To treat severe infection in lambs however, use a de-wormer such as Praziquantel that will target both tapeworms and roundworms.

9. Case study

Mr James Mwangi hails from Mathira Division of the Nyeri District, located in a sub-humid highland region of central Kenya. He has 2.5 acres of land and is among the farmers in his community who took part in a trial carried out by the Kenya Agricultural Research Institute

(KARI) and the National Veterinary Research Centre (NVRC) between 1993 and 1996, to assess the causes, distribution and control of parasitic worms and to test intervention strategies. Prior to the trails, Mr Mwangi had seven indigenous sheep crossed with Dorper sheep raised under the roadside tethering grazing system. He had no specific strategy on worm control and had high mortalities among his lambs. Mr Mwangi dewormed only adult sheep with whatever dewormer he had at hand, but left the young ones out because he thought lambs did not have worms until they reached six months of age.

Following the advice of scientists from the NVRC, Mr Mwangi started implementing a regime of treating adult sheep before mating, ewes before lambing, and lambs at weaning. He also treated all sheep before the beginning of the rainy season. Being in an area with liver fluke infestation, he adopted prophylactic and curative treatment regimens and feed supplementation.

Ten years after implementing a successful worm-control strategy, Mr Mwangi is a successful farmer keeping over 50 sheep under a semi-zero grazing system. He has upgraded his sheep farming from indigenous crosses to pure Dorpers and is also keeping dairy goats as well. He sells lambs and kids to farmer groups in his area and to far-off districts in central Kenya. A kid aged six months fetches him at least USD 65. A breeding male sheep or goat fetches him about USD 230.

10. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

11. Related/associated technologies 

  • Collective action to reduce goat mortality: ID 7904.
  • Herbal de-worming for lower goat mortality: ID 7690.
  • Goat raising in controlled areas and vaccination: ID 8937.

12. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

12.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently provides a combination of intricate step by step processes on how to treat worm diseases in livestock. 

12.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology improves human health as well as livestock health, the latter thereby providing an additional source of food and income.

entries.tittle: Mejorando la Resistencia a Sequías de los Cultivos de Trigo en la Provincia de Shandong, China

categories.name: Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Risk Reduction

entries.summary:
El Cantón de Juye, un área localizada en una zona de depresión, recibe 500 mm en promedio de precipitación anual. Sin embargo, durante las últimas décadas, la imprevisibilidad del cambio climático ha expuesta esta región a graves sequías, sobre todo en primavera e invierno. Por otro lado, China es el mayor productor de trigo en el mundo, siendo muy importante incrementar la resiliencia agrícola a sequías a través de la adopción de tecnologías agrícolas avanzadas y prácticas.
La introducción de estas tecnologías consiste en nuevos cultivares de trigo más resistentes a la sequía para promover tecnología de ahorro de agua para la producción agrícola y la introducción de prácticas para el mejoramiento de suelos con la aplicación y extensión de tecnología de cultivo 3-D.
entries.description:
Descripción

La introducción de nuevos cultivares de trigo más resistentes a las sequías, así como la adopción de prácticas para el mejoramiento de suelos constituyen una estrategia eficiente para el incremento de resiliencia de los sistemas agrícolas locales en caso de sequías. Expertos en el cultivo y cultivares de trigo fueron invitados para capacitar técnicamente a los agricultores locales a través de demostraciones de campo. Algunos temas de la capacitación incluyeron técnicas de cultivo para la prevención y mitigación de desastres, como cultivo tardío, abonado con nitrógeno y cultivo de ciclo corto. Es importante complementar la introducción de cultivares nuevos con capacitación para ofrecer a los agricultores los conocimientos de gestión para el mejoramiento de suelos.

1. Detalles técnicos

1.1 Introducción de variedades resilientes a desastres

  • Las dos variedades de trigo, Jimai 21 y Jimai 22 (ésta última creada por SAAS, Academia de Ciencias Agrícolas de la Povincia de Shandong y aprobada en China en el 2007) son reconocidas por sus raíces resistentes a la sequía y pestes.
  • Estos cultivares tienen un fuerte capacidad de macollaje y espigas con tallos resistentes.
  • En general, estas variedades tienen altos índices de vástagos productivo y óptimos rendimientos, así como buena resistencia al hongo oidio y a la roya de la hoja (véase el Cuadro 1).
Cuadro 1. Comparación de valores de Jimai 21 y Jimai 22

Fuente: FAO 2010

1.2 Patrón de cultivo: doble cultivo trigo-algodón

  • Tres hileras de trigo se plantaron en un área de 1,5 m de ancho a principios de octubre, con un espacio entre surcos de 20 cm.
  • Al año siguiente, otras dos hileras de algodón se sembraron a finales de abril o fueron trasplantadas a mediados de mayo, a lo largo del cultivo de trigo, con una distancia entre hileras de 50 cm.
  • La distancia entre las hileras de trigo y de algodón es de 30 cm.
  • Antes de cultivar, se desnivela el terreno con una cresta de 10 cm de altura.
  • El trigo se siembra en el fondo y el algodón en la cresta.
  • El trigo puede ser fácilmente regado y hacer pleno uso del agua de lluvia, mejorando la germinación del algodón.
  • Este método aumenta el movimiento del aire en el campo de algodón y evita la descomposición de los capullos, por lo que el daño causado por anegamiento se reduce considerablemente.
  • Los procedimientos de gestión óptima se han establecido sobre la base de ensayos de campo llevadas a cabo para controlar la siembra, la densidad de siembra, riego, fertilización, control de plagas y enfermedades.
  • La temperatura óptima de siembra es de 16 °C a 18 °C y la densidad de siembra de 80 000 a 120 000 semillas por mu.

1.3 Medidas en caso de desastres

  • Riego
    • El trigo debe estar bajo riego durante la fase de maduración.
    • Si no se ha regado en invierno, la baja humedad del suelo podría impedir el crecimiento de raíces laterales.
    • Se necesitan aproximadamente 75 kg a 150 kg de urea por hectárea durante el riego si el trigo no crece bien.
    • Si el trigo fue regado apropiadamente en invierno, entonces el suelo se debe aflojar para que pueda retener la humedad a principios de la primavera.

2. Formación técnica

Se desarrollaron una serie de sesiones técnicas, como talleres, orientación técnica y demostraciones prácticas, etc. Los agricultores benefician de los conocimientos sobre las características y las tecnologías de cultivo de las variedades de algodón de reciente introducción.

  • Taller
    • Antes de la siembra, algunos expertos de cultivo de algodón provenientes de universidades e institutos de investigación fueron invitados a un taller de capacitación técnica sobre prevención y reducción de desastres.
    • Las técnicas utilizadas localmentes fueron compartidas con los agrónomos, técnicos y representantes de agricultores, que también asistieron al taller de capacitación.
  • Orientación técnica en terreno
    • Se invitó a algunos expertos en cultivo de algodón a Juye para que impartan orientación técnica en terreno durante la etapa crítica de desarrollo del algodón, tales como la siembra, germinación y maduración.
    • Los expertos asistieron a los agricultores sobre respuesta en caso de desastres en sus propias parcelas.
  • Demostración práctica
    • Crear parcelas de demostración de alta calidad utilizando tecnologías de cultivo para la prevención y reducción de desastres en la zona del proyecto.
    • Los agricultores asistieron a estas demostraciones prácticas para aprender sobre dichas tecnologías.

3. Impactos y resultados

3.1 Producción y rendimientos

  • En los ensayos preliminaries de las nuevas variedades, llevados a cabo entre 1999 y 2000, el rendimiento del cultivar Kimai 21 fue del 19 por ciento mayor que el del cultivar Lumai 14.
  • Entre el año 2000 y 2001, el rendimiento de la variedad Jimai 21 fue del 5,2 por ciento mayor que el de la variedad Lumai 14 (cultivo testigo apareado [2]), con un promedio de 538,1 kg por mu.
  • En la siguiente temporada, el rendimiento promedio de la variedad Jimai 21 fue de 494,47 kg en promedio por mu, un 6,1 por ciento mayor que el cultivo testigo en los ensayos regionales.
  • En ensayos regionales del 2004, el rendimiento promedio de la variedad Jimai 22 fue de 530,94 kg por mu, es decir, 8,98 por ciento más que el de la variedad Lumai 14.
  • Al año siguiente, el rendimiento promedio fue de 542,68 kg por mu, un 12,59 por ciento más que el cultivo testigo.
  • En el área de crecimiento Huanghuai para el año 2005, el rendimiento promedio de la variedad Jimai 22 fue de 517,06 kg por mu, es decir, 5,03 por ciento superior a Shi 4 185 en ensayos regionales.
  • En el mismo año, el rendimiento promedio la variedad Jimai 22 fue de 542,68 kg por mu, equivalente a 4,05 por ciento más que el cultivo testigo en la provincia de Shandong.
  • El mayor rendimiento de Jimai 22 fue 727,43 kg por mu.
  • En el 2009, un año con sequías graves a principios de primavera, el rendimiento del trigo aumentó en el área de estudio en comparación con el rendimiento del 2008 (véase Cuadro 2).
Cuadro 2. Cosecha de trigo en el 2008 y el 2009 para los cultivos de variedades Jimai 21, Jimai 22 y de control

Fuente: FAO 2010

3.2 Resultados económicos

  • En un análisis costo-beneficio llevado a cabo para evaluar las variedades nuevas, los resultados demostraron que aunque se requiere una mayor inversión para sembrar los nuevos cultivares Jimai 21 y Jimai 22 (alrededor de 31 RMB/mu)[3].
  • Las ganancias equivalen a 51,4 RMB/mu en el caso del Jimai 21 y 65,4 RMB/mu para Jimai 22.
Cuadro 3. Análisis costo-beneficio del cultivo de trigo en el 2009 [4]

Fuente: FAO 2010

4. Monitoreo de la demostración

  • Se monitorearon los cultivares durante los ensayos y se compararon consultivos testigo.
  • Esta tecnología ha sido testeada con éxito en Juye, en el contexto del proyecto TCP/CPR/3105, Strengthening Disaster Preparedness in the Agricultural Sector.

5. Unidades

  • [1] El mu es una unidad de medida tradicional de tierra en China, equivalente a 667 m2. En general se estima en 1/15 de hectárea.
  • [2] Unidad monetaria de China, Yuan Renminbi (RMB) (1 CNY= 0,146 USD).
  • [3] También cultivo de control en el 2009.
  • [4] Precio del trigo calculado 2 RMB/kg.

6. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

7. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Mejorando la resiliencia de drenajes y sistemas de riego para la Gestión de Riesgos: ID 6981.
  • Increasing flexibility in crop production through DAPOG nursery to reduce the impact of droughts and floods: ID 8216.
  • Drought-tolerant maize varieties in Uganda: ID 8920.

Esta tecnología también está disponible en inglés: ID 7396.

8. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

8.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

La tecnología permite el uso eficiente de variedades de trigo resistentes a peligros específicos, combinado con el uso efectivo de técnicas de cultivo innovadoras para resistir los impactos climáticos.

8.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

La tecnología mejora la resiliencia de los cultivos a los eventos climáticos, protegiendo así las fuentes de ingresos y alimentos de los agricultores.
entries.further_reading:
9. Lecturas complementarias

  • FAO. 2010. Gestión del riesgo de sequía y otros eventos climáticos extremos en Chile.

entries.tittle: Mejorando la resiliencia de drenajes y sistemas de riego para la gestión de riesgos en Shandong, China
entries.summary: El objetivo fue incrementar la resiliencia de la comunidad a inundaciones y sequías, mejorando el drenaje del agua y las infraestructuras de irrigación, así como limpiando los canales. Se llevaron a cabo importantes intervenciones como parte del plan de Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres para el municipio, incluida la construcción de una alcantarilla de drenaje para mejorar la situación de la acumulación de agua. La implementación de esta práctica ayudó a aumentar la resiliencia de la comunidad ante inundaciones, anegamientos y sequías al mejorar las infraestructuras de riego y drenaje de agua de la comunidad. La mejoría a nivel de comunidad reducirá las pérdidas económicas de producción agrícola, contribuyendo así a los medios de vida sostenibles de los campesinos.
entries.description:
Descripción

  • La infraestructura comunitaria de drenaje e irrigación en este municipio fue construida en el periodo conocido como “colectivo”, entre 1956 y 1982, la reforma agraria cambia de un sistema de manejo de producción colectiva a uno de familia.
  • Sin embargo, las infraestructuras existentes no fueron renovadas o mantenidas apropiadamente, dejando inutilizadas canales de campos de drenaje, puentes locales, alcantarillas y compuerta, entre otros.
  • La mayoría de los canales de rama y aquellos principales no pudieron distribuir agua o drenar las aguas de inundación durante la época de lluvias.
  • Además, los canales de drenaje bloqueados debido a la disposición de sedimentos redujo la capacidad de drenaje.
  • Las facilidades dañadas no fueron reparadas a tiempo por falta de fondos, sea por parte del gobierno local o de las comunidades.
  • Desastres naturales como inundaciones y sequías generalmente ocurren en el municipio, limitando el desarrollo de la agricultura y causando pérdidas económicas, amenazando los medios de vida de campesinos.
  • Para mejorar la situación, intervenciones importantes como parte del plan de gestión de riesgos del municipio se llevaron a cabo, incluyendo la construcción de una alcantarilla para el mejoramiento del drenaje en Liuxi y comunidades aledañas.

1. Implementación de la tecnología

1.1 Construcción de la alcantarilla y rehabilitación de infraestructura de drenaje

  • Como un componente importante de la gestión de riesgos a nivel comunal, el municipio Qilin construyó una alcantarilla de 1,5 m de diámetro y 100 m de longitud.
  • Asimismo, limpió 56 canales de campo con una longitud total de 2 350 metros y reparó seis alcantarillas y construyó cuatro en el área.
  • Estas actividades se llevaron a cabo entre mayo y julio del 2008.
  • De acuerdo a los habitantes locales, el sistema mejorado de drenaje entro en funcion en agosto del 2008.
  • No se registraron episodios de inundaciones durante la época de lluvias 2008 a 2009.
  • El gobierno municipal de Qilin, y la Oficina de Agricultura del Condado, así como la Oficina de Recursos Hídricos del Condado, aportaron con las actividades de reconstrucción y rehabilitación.

1.2 Drenaje de los canales de irrigación y drenaje en los sitios piloto

  • Los canales de drenaje de la comunidad, construidos principalmente en el periodo colectivo, no fueron mantenidos apropiadamente debido a falta de fondos desde la reforma agraria en 1982.
  • Una encuesta de base demuestra que la mayoría de los canales de campo estaban bloqueados a causa de sedimentación de lodo y pastos, reduciendo drásticamente la capacidad de drenaje.
  • Además, muchos campesinos construyeron diques de control dentro de los canales de campo para el transporte de productos y pajas desde su propiedad, bloqueando por completo los canales.
    • Para cambiar esta situación, las comunidades drenaron sus canales de campo contratando maquinarias y movilizando las cooperativas de los campesinos (Figuras 1 y 2).
    • La longitud total de los canales de irrigación drenados ascendio a 9 500 metros con un volumen de suelo total de 18 530 m3.
  • El drenaje de canales en Qianfengqiao, Liuxi y Nancao se completaron en el 2008.
  • El incremento en la capacidad de drenaje de los canales de campo limpios redujo significativamente las inundaciones durante la época de lluvias entre el 2008 y el 2009.
  • Los comités comunitarios y las cooperativas de campesinos desempeñaron papeles importantes en la movilización de recursos para limpieza de los canales y reparación de alcantarillas y puentes dañados.
Figura 1. Canal de drenaje después de su rehabilitación

©FAO/TECA

Figura 2. Salida de evacuación del agua del canal hasta el río vista desde abajo (a) y de arriba (b)

©FAO/TECA

2. Detalles técnicos

2.1 Encuesta de base

  • Un ingeniero hidráulico llevó a cabo investigaciones de campo sobre los sistemas existentes de irrigación y drenaje, identificando problemas relacionados a inundaciones y sus causas.
  • Durante la encuesta de base se recogió información básica que constituyó la línea de base para el diseño y la planificación de actividades en terreno.

2.2 Diseño y planificación de proyectos para la construcción de infraestructura de drenaje

  • Sobre la base de los descubrimientos de la encuesta realizada, se definieron y priorizaron las intervenciones en consulta con los líderes de las comunidades y sus habitantes.
  • Se identificó como prioridad la construcción de la alcantarilla de drenaje en el sistema de irrigación Liuying, así como el mejoramiento de los canales de drenaje.
  • La alcantarilla, con un diámetro de 1,5 m, y la longitud en dique de 50 m con cemento reforzado.
  • Los parámetros de drenaje se diseñaron de acuerdo a la disposición de canales de campo y su sedimentación.
Figura 3. Salida de alcantarilla

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Construcción e implementación de las actividades seleccionadas

  • La construcción de las alcantarillas principales fueron llevadas a cabo por un grupo seleccionado de construcción.
  • Basado en el diseño de proyectos de manejo de aguas relacionados, el equipo inició la construcción con un control de calidad ejecutado por el especialista hidráulico y el ingeniero hidráulico del municipio.

2.4 Gestión y mantenimiento del proyecto

  • Después de la construcción de las obras de infraestructura, todas las obras de irrigación y drenaje necesitarán un mantenimiento y una gestión apropiadas para un buen funcionamiento, lo que permitirá una contribución de largo plazo en la reducción de pérdidas por inundaciones.

3. Impactos y resultados

  • De acuerdo al líder de la comunidad Liuxi y al gobernador de la comunidad Quilin, la alcantarilla benefició aproximadamente 6000 mu* de tierras, cubriendo seis comunidades (Liuxi, Liubei, Liunan, Mengdian, Dongyoufang y Xiyoufang), con una población total de 5000 personas.
  • El beneficio económico de la alcantarilla es significante, estimando en 250 Yuan**/mu (35 USD por cada mu) de pérdidas económicas cada año, con un total de 1,2 a 1,8 million Yuan por 6000 mu.

* El mu es una unidad de medida tradicional de tierra en China, equivalente a 667 m2. En general se estima en 1/15 de hectárea.

** Unidad monetaria de China, Yuan Renminbi (1 CNY= 0,146 USD).

4. Monitoreo de la demostración

  • Los proyectos de construcción de alcantarilla y limpieza de canales fueron monitoreados y supervisados por el especialista hidráulico.
    • Monitoreo de los impactos y beneficios en el largo plazo de estos proyectos será llevado a cabo por la oficina agrícola y de recursos hídricos del cantón.

5. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido. 

6. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Mejorando la resistencia a sequías de los cultivos de trigo: ID 6983.
  • Rooftop water collection, drip irrigation and plastic mulching in home garden conditions in drought prone areas: ID 8934.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: roof water harvesting: ID 7304.

Esta tecnología también está disponible en inglés: ID 6934.

7. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

7.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Al mejorar y expandir el drenaje del agua y las infraestructuras de irrigación, se aumenta la resiliencia de la comunidad a los cambios climáticos. Esta tecnología también contribuye a una mejora en los rendimientos de la producción agrícola.

7.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta práctica ayuda a reducir los efectos del cambio climático que mejora la seguridad, la salud y la seguridad alimentaria, y contribuye a la reducción de las inundaciones.
entries.further_reading:
8. Lecturas complementarias

  • Office of Technical Aid Project for Building Disaster Prevention and Control Capacity in Agriculture (OTAP for BDPCA). 2008. Summarizing Report on Water Conservancy Projects in Juye County.
  • OTAP for BDPCA. 2008. Control of Waterlog and Drought and Restoration of Water Conservancy Projects in Qilin Town, Juye County.
  • OTAP for BDPCA. 2008. Dredging of the Irrigation and drainage canals in Demonstration Villages.
  • OTAP for BDPCA. 2008. Training material for irrigation management and canal system protection.

entries.tittle: Vegetable Growing
entries.summary: This is a simple guide for growing vegetables. It describes how to prepare the land and seedling for vegetables growing, additionally to different pests and diseases affecting vegetables and fertilization methods. And finally how to harvest different vegetables such as tomato and eggplants. It is meant to help farmers and it comprises land preparation, fertilizer application methods, weeding and harvesting.
entries.description:
Description

Most vegetable crops need at least six to eight hours of sunlight, but the more you can provide the better.

1. Factors to consider when growing vegetables

  • Do not situate your garden near any overhanging tree branches.
    • Not only will they shade your crops, but the tree roots will compete with your vegetables for water and nutrients in the soil.
  • Avoid plants that inhibit the growth of crops.
  • A site with a gentle slope provides good drainage.
    • Avoid areas where rainwater collects after rainstorms.
  • Poor drainage promotes diseases and inhibits the growth of many plants.
  • Locate your garden near a water source and close to the composed area.
  • Locate your garden where wild and /or stray animals can be controlled most preferably close to your house.

2. Land and seedling preparation

  • Till or turn soil when it is dry enough.
  • Avoid doing this when the soil is too wet because it will result in the formation of large balls/clods that later harden and remain all season.
  • Loosen your soil to the depth of 6 inches when it is sufficiently dry.

3. Fertilizer application

  • With good soil-building practice (composting and good soil preparation), trace elements do not generally present a problem to the home gardener.
  • Spread any fertilizer, manure, and leaves or composed and work into the soil and rake it smooth.
  • Organic fertilizers
    • The word organic, applied to fertilizer simply means that the nutrient contained in the product are derived solely from the remains or by-product of a once living organism.
    • Cottonseed meal, blood meal, bone meal, hoof and horn meal, and all manure are examples of organic fertilizers.
  • Synthetic fertilizers
    • In general, synthetic fertilizer acts more quickly than organic types, though some organic materials release their nutrients quite rapidly. E.g. DAP, NPK, SSP, TSP, UREA.

3.1 Fertilizer application method

There are different methods of applying fertilizers depending on their formulation and crop needs. Some are discussed below.

3.1.1 Broadcasting

  • An example is a starter fertilizer like TSP.
  • It is important to make sure that the whole area is uniformly sprinkled.
  • Divide the fertilizer into four equal parts. Divide the area also into four parts.
  • Use one part on one-quarter of the farm, making sure the corners get the same amount as the other parts.
  • Repeat this process in the remaining parts.
    • However, it is wasteful and the yields are not as good as they should be.

3.1.2 Banding

  • Fertile is placed in a furrow close to the root zone (at a depth of 10 cm to 15 cm) and covered with soil.
  • This method is suitable for crops planted in rows.

3.1.3 Spot application

  • Fertilizer is placed at each planting hole.

3.1.4 Starter solutions

  • Just before or at planting.
  • This mainly applies to phosphate and potassium fertilizers (TSP, DAP, SSP, NPK).

3.1.5 Split application

  • This refers to the application of small amounts of a nitrogen fertilizer more than once during the growing season, rather than one massive application.
  • This especially reduces Nitrogen losses and improves fertilizer efficiency.

3.1.6 Foliar feeding

  • Ammonium based fertilizers like UREA are applied through spraying on leaves after dissolving in water.
  • This method is especially suited to cotton, sugarcane, high-value crops and congested plants that are not planted in rows, for example, animal feed (grass) and vegetables.

3.1.7 Fertigation

  • Here fertilizers are applied with irrigation water.

3.1.8 Farm yard manure

  • Droppings from poultry, goats, sheep, pigs and rabbits that contain little moisture can be collected and either used directly in the crop fields or used to make an application to avoid burning crops.

4. Pest and diseases on different vegetables

4.1 Cabbage-pests, diseases and their control

  • Aphids and caterpillar – spray with malathion.
  • Downy mildew – spray with Dithane M – 45.
  • Blackleg – soak the soil with mancozeb.
    • Recent studies have shown that seed extract of the tropical neem tree and other botanical extracts are effective at controlling DBM (diamond Black Moth) in cabbages.

4.2 Eggplants-pests, diseases and their cure

  • Aphids, caterpillar and fruit fly – spray weekly with mercaptothion or (during the fruiting period) endosulfan.
  • Bacterial blight – spray with copper oxychloride.

4.3 Watermelon-pests, diseases and their controls

  • Anthracnose and downy mildew – control with mancozeb.
  • Fusarium – drench the soil with captab.
  • Powdery mildew – control with benomyl.
  • Pumpkin flies, White lies and certain ladybirds – spray with mercaptothion.
  • Red spider mite – apply dicofol.

4.4 Tomatoes-pests, diseases and their controls

  • Blossom end rot - add lime to acidic soil.
  • Fruit fly – spray with fenthion.
  • Thrips and tomato caterpillars – spray with Mercapthion.
  • Tomato blight and leaf spot – spray with mancozeb. 
  • Tomato mite – spray with dimethoate.
  • The whitefly – spray with carbaryl.

5. Selecting varieties

  • Select vegetable varieties that will do well in your area.
  • Success of varieties will differ from garden to garden depending upon site conditions gardener’s techniques.
  • It is good to keep notes each season on what varieties you plant, flavour, and yields.
    • This can help you develop your favourites, plan on yield and profits.

6. Timing

  • Saying that timing is everything, some crops need to be started in nurseries then transplanted e.g. cabbages (brassica), leeks, broccoli, tomatoes, peppers, eggplants and melons planted straight.
  • Select short, stout, healthy plants that aren’t yet producing flowers, buds or fruits.
    • Nursery seeds should be started six to eight weeks before transplanting outdoors.
  • Harden them off two weeks before planting into the garden by gradually exposing the seedling to the harsher outside conditions (way of doing this).
    • All shade should be removed by this time.
  • Use the recommended spacing.
    • Too close results in competition for sunlight, moisture, nutrients and oxygen.
    • This results in weak, straggly plants that don’t provide much of a yield.
    • Refer to the last page for individual crop spacing.

7. Weeding

  • Weeds may look insignificant when they first start shooting up, but they should be dealt with right away.
  • A quick touch of hoe to cut them down in cooler days will save you hours of backbreaking weeding during hot days.

8. Mulching

  • A thick layer of organic mulch (like straw and leaves) will help to suppress weeds, retain moisture and even prevent the emergence of some insect pests while keeping looking neat and tidy.
  • Be sure to wait until the soil has warmed up sufficiently before putting down mulch.

9. Harvesting vegetables

9.1 Tomatoes

  • The harvest of tomatoes is dependent on the closeness to the market.
  • Local sale of tomatoes may be vine-ripened to affirm ripe or a full red colour before harvesting.
  • Tomatoes for the fresh markets are generally hand-picked.

9.2 Watermelon

  • They are harvested by hand when they have fully ripened.
  • Ripeness is not easily determined for an inexperienced picker, but here are some helpful hints:
    • a pale yellow ground spot;
    • a brown melon tendril;
    • a change in sound when thumbed from a metallic ringing sound to a soft hollow sound;
    • a break up of green bands at the blossom end of the fruit; and/or
    • development of ribbed indentions that can be felt with fingertips.
  • When harvesting watermelons, make sure that the melon is cut from the vine instead of pulled.
    • Pulling creates a cracking wound that pathogens can enter and quickly destroy the quality of the fruit and ruin its appearance.
    • Leave the stem on the melon for as long as possible, and treat for stem end rot after picking.

9.3 Cabbage

  • Cut the firm heads with two outer leaves and remove the stumps.

9.4 Eggplant

  • Harvesting is done from three months after sowing when the fruit is of useable size.

10. Related/associated technologies

  • Producing solar dried fruit and vegetables for micro- and small-scale rural enterprise development: processing aspects: ID 4503.
  • Soil fertility for sustainable vegetable production: Green and animal manures in the humid forest belt: ID 4525.
  • Choosing high yielding vegetable varieties: ID 6908.
  • Integrated pest management in vegetable production: a guide for extension workers: ID 6963.
  • Preserving green leafy vegetables and fruits: ID 7359.
  • Traditional floating garden practices for vegetable production: ID 8867.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2992.

11. Objectives fulfilled by the project

11.1 Women-friendly

This technology is easy and accessible to all.

11.2 Resource use efficiency

This technology provides good fertiliser application and harvesting practices that optimises vegetable production. 

11.3 Pro-poor technology

This technology provides cost-effective practices and alternatives that does not require costly inputs.
