entries.tittle: Soil nutrient management, Uganda
entries.summary: Soil fertility is defined as the ability of the soil to produce and sustain high yields indefinitely. In farming, soil fertility may be lost through many ways. Some of the ways are as a result of the farmer’s activities while others may be out of his control. Therefore, the National Agricultural Research Organisation (NARO), which aims to enhance the contribution of agricultural research to sustainable agricultural productivity, economic growth, food security and poverty eradication, provides the following technology. This technology describes different steps for the management of the soil nutrient to improve its fertility.
entries.description:
Description

1. Properties of a fertile soil

Soil fertility is defined as the ability of the soil to produce and sustain high yields indefinitely. There are many properties of a fertile soil that can support a good maize crop.

  • Good depth that affords plant roots greater volume to exploit.
  • Good drainage to avoid water logging.
  • Good aeration to promote healthy root development and functioning.
  • High water holding capacity. Maize needs moisture that is evenly distribute throughout the growing season with the highest requirement at tussling.
  • High level of nutrients. Maize has high nutrient requirements, and the nutrients should be in a form that is available to the growing plants.
  • Optimum soil pH. Maize will grow well in the pH range five to eight.

2. Loss of soil fertility

In farming, soil fertility may be lost through many ways. Some of the ways are as a result of the farmer’s activities while others may be out of his control.

The common ways in which soil fertility may be lost include are listed below.

2.1 Soil erosion

The top soil is blown or washed away by wind or water.

2.2 Soil capping

Formation of an impervious layer of soil on the surface of the soil which obstructs rain infiltration, leading to runoff.

2.3 Development of hard pans

These develop a short distance below the surface of the soil. Hard pans may be caused by repeated ploughing at the same depth.

2.4 Loss of organic matter

This happens through rapid oxidation by soil micro-organisms due to unduly too frequent cultivations.

2.5 Leaching

Rainwater removes mineral salts from the top to the lower layers of soil where they become unavailable to crops.

2.6 Crop removal

Removal breaks the natural cycle and prevents nutrients contained in the crop from returning to the soil that provided them. Supply of available nutrients is thereby depleted. The soil is therefore like a bank from which deposits have been withdraw and need replenishment.

2.7 Weeds

Weeds compete with crops for nutrients.

2.8 Change in pH

An incorrect use of certain fertilizers sometimes changes soil pH. Burning: burning of bush, grass or crop residues before cultivation exposes the land and leads to soil erosion. During burning, the heat destroys several plant nutrients in the soil whereas some essential elements are lost in the form of gases. Burning also destroys useful soil organism.

2.9 Toxicity

This is due to accumulation of salts, micro-nutrients such as manganese, iron, aluminium, boron, molybdenum, fluorine, etc can poison the plants if present in excess.

3. Methods of improving soil fertility

There are important and common methods of maintaining and/or improving soil fertility.

  • Improvement of nutrient-retaining ability of a soil by adding organic manures to the soil. 
  • Improve drainage by breaking down surface capping and hard pans. 
  • Crop rotation, which is the growing of different crops in an ordered sequence on the same field. The objectives of crop rotation are to conserve soil; maintain nutrient balance in soil; and control weeds, diseases and pests. This is done by growing a variety of crops, which have significantly different growth habits, nutrient requirements, pests and diseases in sequence. A good rotation of maize must include a good leguminous crop for improving the nitrogen level of the soil. Nitrogen is obtained from the air by legumes, which fix it with the help of bacteria in their root nodules. Groundnuts, soya bean and to some extent beans fix nitrogen. Maize grown after a leguminous crop will benefit from this nitrogen. 
  • Minimum disturbance of soil e.g. zero tillage to conserve its organic matter content and moisture. 
  • Soil conditioning e.g. by liming or using acidic fertilizer as may be appropriate to maintain soil pH.
  • Weed control.
  • Use of both organic and inorganic manures. 
  • Moisture conservation by use of mulches.
  • Erosion control.

4. Organic manures vs chemical fertilizers

Materials added by farmers to replace those lost from the soil are called soil fertility amendments. These can be classified into two main groups which are organic manure; and inorganic fertilizers.

4.1 Organic manure

Organic manure are decaying organic matter and are derived from plant and animal residues also known as manures. The organic manures are further classified as Farm Yard Manure (FYM), compost manure, green manure, and organic mulches. Where possible, farmers are encouraged to use organic manures because they maintain soil structure, improve water holding capacity and improve aeration in addition to providing the majority nutrients for plant growth.

4.2 Inorganic fertilizers

These are minerals fertilizers containing high quantities of plant nutrients. The inorganic fertilizers provide specific chemicals, which may be lacking in the soil. For maximum yield of the crop, it is advisable to use the correct rate, type and method of the use of the fertilizers.

Nitrogen is commonly supplied with the application of Urea. It is also supplied with calcium Ammonium Nitrate (CAN) and N-P-K, which is sold as 25-5-5 and 17‑17‑17 which also supply other nutrients. The source of phosphorus common in the country is Diammonium Phosphate (DAP,) which is 48 percent phosphorus and 18 percent nitrogen. Other sources of phosphorus are Single Super Phosphate (SSP) and Triple Super Phosphate (TSP), which give phosphorus, calcium and some sulphur. No deliberate efforts are made to apply potassium except for the amount supplied in the application of N-P-K, which have varying amounts of nutrients depending on the formulation. For example, 17-17-17 NPK means that a bag of the fertilizer has 17 percent nitrogen, 17 percent phosphorus and 17 percent potassium. Nutrient combinations of NPK are indicated on the bag.

Table 1. Types of inorganic fertilizer

Source: NARO 2010

5. Method of application

Three methods are used to apply fertilizer. These are broadcast, drill application and point application.

  • Broadcast application is when the fertilizer is applied all over the area. This is good for nutrients that stay in one place such as phosphorus especially when it is incorporated into the soil. The fertilizer applied this way will benefit all that crops in the area and would be suitable in situations when maize is planted with other crops. The main disadvantage is that it is spread too thinly and would not be sufficient if the farmer can only apply small amounts. It will also encourage weed growth especially with hoeing method of weed control. Establish the rate to be applied before the application. 
  • The drill method is when the fertilizer is applied as a drill in the seed fallow. It has the advantage in that little fertilizer is applied but has the disadvantage of the fertilizer not benefiting the crops that are not in line.
  • Point application is where fertilizer is applied in the vicinity of the plant, this could be around the plant or under the seed or with the seed in the same hole. It has the advantage of applying the fertilizer where the plants can use it, will not benefit the weeds and little fertilizer will cover a large area. It is the method used by small scale farmer in the country. DAP is applied in the seed hole, lightly covered with soil after which the seed is dropped in the same hole before covering. DAP is covered with soil because of its corrosive nature that would otherwise kill the seed. Single and Triple Super Phosphate can be applied in the same seed hole and covered in one operation. Nitrogen fertilizers are applied at the base of the plant and incorporated. Incorporation is necessary to avoid loss as runoff and loss to the atmosphere for most nitrogen sources.

5.1 Rate of application

The amount of fertilizer to be applied will depend on the initial soil fertility, the expected yield and any other factors that will affect crop production factors. If the soil is fairly fertile, the additional fertilizer will be less than in the case where the soil fertility has been used up. One ton of maize (1 000 kg) takes from the soil 24.3 kg nitrogen, 10 kg of phosphorus and 21.14 kg of potassium. Thus, if a yield of 4 tons of maize is expected, the fertilizer application should aim at 97.2 kg of nitrogen, 40 kg of phosphorus and 85.6 kg of potassium. Fortunately, a fair percentage of this is supplied by the soil.

At smallholder farmer level, the general recommendation is to apply one bottle‑top cover of DAP per hill and apply two bottle tops of Urea at about six weeks after germination. With the recommended spacing of 75 cm (2.5 feet) between rows and 60 cm (2 feet) and two plants per hill. The rates above are just indicative. The amount will vary depending on the soil fertility at the beginning of the season. One might find that there is no need for DAP application. In some cases one cap of urea per hill might be sufficient. Since fields differ in fertility, it is necessary that farmers carry out some trials on a smaller area to find out the rate at which they will fertilize their crops. The extension staff will be helpful in these trials. They would require services of extension staff to help estimate the appropriate area for amount available.

Fertilizer is expensive and might not appear affordable by most of the farmers and that is one of the reasons why it is necessary to decide whether it is necessary to apply. Though normally sold in 50 kg bags, some distributors package it in smaller weights such as one kg which is more affordable and farmers can at least get part of the field fertilized especially if they are able to identify the poor plots in time. The above rate is for the small scale farmer who applied fertilizer per hill. In the case of larger farmers, it is vital that the rate of fertilizer to be applied after the soil has been tested by soil scientists and rates recommended for the particular farm.

Table 2. Fertilizer recommendation for a smallholder farmer

Source: NARO 2010

5.2 Time of application

Nitrogen moves in the soil with water and will be easily lost by sinking deep into the soil where roots will not get it. It should therefore be applied near the time when the plant needs it most. That explains why only little nitrogen is applied at the time of planting (supplied by DAP) and the bulk of it supplied six weeks later when the plants are beginning to need it most. Phosphorus does not move in the soil which means that it can be applied at the beginning of the season. This is convenient especially as it is required for the development of the root system. As much as possible, it should be incorporated in the soil for even distribution in the root zone. Potassium moves in the soil similar to nitrogen.

5.3 Soil testing

In order to precisely target correcting nutrient deficiencies, soils should be tested. This is done at the National Laboratory Services of the National Agricultural Research Organization at Kawanda at an affordable fee. It can also be done at the Department of Soil Science in the Faculty of Agriculture at Makerere University. Quick suggestive results can be obtained using a simple-to-use soil testing kit developed by the Soil Science department of Makerere University. These services are available to the farmers on request.

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Soil fertility composting in Domenica: ID 8206.
  • Soil and water conservation: ID 7861.
  • How to measure soil pH value: ID 8241.
  • Soil cultivation and tillage in organic agriculture: ID 8376.
  • Soil property and fertility improvement through composting using Trichoderma: ID 7697.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Resource use efficiency

Soil nutrient management improves soil fertility through improved drainage, aeration, root health, pH level, water holding capacity and nutrient level.

8.2 Pro-poor technology

Improved soil fertility allows for higher yields, leading to additional sources of income and improved food security.

entries.tittle: Abono bocachi para mejorar la resistencia de cultivos ante heladas en Bolivia

categories.name: Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Risk Reduction

entries.summary:
Los Andes tropicales desempeñan un papel fundamental para la seguridad alimentaria de comunidades en la región. A pesar de que en el pasado la agricultura andina ha permitido mantener una gran diversidad de cultivos, los efectos del cambio climático, sumados a presiones socio económicas de las últimas décadas han degradado estos ambientes frágiles, con efectos no sólo en comunidades sobre los 3 000 msnm, sino también en zonas bajas aledañas. La agricultura en el altiplano enfrenta condiciones climáticas muy severas. En la provincia de Omasuyos en Bolivia, ubicada a más de 3 800 m sobre el nivel del mar, fenómenos climáticos como sequías, heladas y granizadas son frecuentes durante el invierno, poniendo en riesgo la producción de los cultivos.

Para responder a estas condiciones, las poblaciones nativas han desarrollado una práctica mediante la cual los cultivos son más resistentes a las inclemencias climáticas de la zona, más en particular heladas y granizos. El abono bocachi es un fertilizante preparado a base de materiales naturales ampliamente disponibles en la zona. Su preparación es fácil y relativamente rápida, siendo efectiva en caso de heladas o granizos, aumentando considerablemente las posibilidades de producción aún en condiciones extremas.
entries.description:
Descripción

El abono orgánico es importante, ya que mejora la estructura del suelo a través de la incorporación de nutrientes y microorganismos, regulando así el pH del suelo. Mediante este abono es posible reducir el uso de insumos externos, muchas veces inaccesibles en comunidades aisladas y aumentar la eficiencia de los recursos disponibles, de manera sostenible.

El abono bocachi se basa en procesos de fermentación de materia orgánica. En buenas condiciones de humedad y temperatura, los microorganismos descomponen la fracción más simple del material orgánico, como azúcares, almidones y proteínas, liberando sus nutrientes. La elaboración de este abono fermentado presenta algunas ventajas en comparación con otros abonos orgánicos:

  • No se forman gases tóxicos ni malos olores.
  • El volumen producido se puede adaptar a las necesidades.
  • No causa problemas en el almacenamiento y transporte.
  • El producto se elabora en un periodo relativamente corto (dependiendo del ambiente en 12 a 24 días).
  • El producto permite ser utilizado inmediatamente después de la preparación.
  • Bajo costo de producción.

Estas provincias son parte del altiplano central del departamento de La Paz y se encuentran en la cercanía del Lago Titicaca, a una altitud promedio de 3 850 msnm. El clima en esta región es variable, con temperaturas que van desde los 7 °C hasta los 18 °C, sin embargo las temperaturas extremas descienden hasta los -13 °C durante el invierno, afectando la producción local.

Objetivo: Mediante la aplicación del abono bocachi, los cultivos resisten mejor a heladas y granizos (Figura 1).

Figura 1. Diferencia entre un mismo cultivo, sin bocachi (izquierda) y con bocachi (derecha). El bocachi permite un mejor resultado observado

©FAO/TECA

1. Implementación de la tecnología

El proceso de elaboración del bocachi presenta dos etapas principales:

  • La primera etapa corresponde al período de fermentación de los componentes del abono, donde la temperatura puede alcanzar hasta 70 °C a 75 °C por el incremento de la actividad microbiana. Posteriormente, la temperatura del abono baja por agotamiento o disminución de la fuente energética.
  • La segunda etapa es el momento en el que el abono pasa a un proceso de estabilización y solamente sobresalen los materiales que presentan mayor dificultad para degradarse a corto plazo, para luego llegar a su estado ideal para su inmediata utilización.

2. Preparación del abono bocachi

2.1 Primer paso

  • Se disponen los componentes sólidos del abono en capas.
  • Se prepara una base de rastrojo, se cubre con un estrato de estiércol, un estrato de ceniza y un estrato de afrecho.
  • Entre cada capa, se agrega una capa de agua azucarada y levadura (Figura 2).
Figura 2. Preparación de las diferentes capas del bocachi

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Segundo paso

Cuando el acumulo de materiales ha llegado a una altura de alrededor de 1 metro, se humedece homogéneamente con agua azucarada y levadura. La humedad debe alcanzar el 40 por ciento y es posible determinarlo a simple vista:

  • tomar un puño de mezcla y comprimirlo en una mano;
  • el material no debe desmoronarse una vez abierta la mano, ni gotear.

Si cumple con esas condiciones y cuando es presionado se desmorona con facilidad, el nivel de humedad es adecuado.

2.3 Tercer paso

Se cubre la mezcla con un plástico, sujetándola con piedras para permitir el proceso de fermentación y mantener la humedad (Figura 3).

Figura 3. Cubrir la mezcla con un plástico y piedra para protegerla de las lluvias o de las sequías y mantener una buena humedad

©FAO/TECA

2.4 Cuarto paso

  • La mezcla debe ser removida cada 12 horas por una semana aproximadamente para evitar que se “queme” el abono preparado hasta que se mantenga frío (Figura 4).
  • Es necesario verificar que la temperatura se mantenga entre 35 ºC y 50 ºC.
  • La temperatura se puede verificar mediante la introducción de un machete por dos minutos dentro de la mezcla.
  • Si al retirarlo el machete se puede tener en mano, la temperatura no ha sobrepasado el nivel aceptable.
  • Si no fuera así, es necesario remover la mezcla para reducir la temperatura.
Figura 4. Removiendo el bocachi

©FAO/TECA

2.5 Quinto paso

  • El abono estará listo cuando desprenda olor a fermentado y esté recubierto por colonias de hongos.
  • Si por el contrario desprende olor a podrido, es muestra de que el proceso no se ha dado correctamente.
  • El tiempo de duración es variable, sin embargo no excede los 30 días.
  • Se recomienda aplicarlo tan pronto como esté listo.
Figura 5. Removiendo el bocachi

©FAO/TECA

2.6 Sexto paso

Finalmente, una vez que el abono se ha enfriado, se debe secar bajo sombra, extendido sobre piso de cemento.

3. Aplicación del abono

  • Al ser aplicado, el abono no debe entrar en contacto directo con las raíces de las plantas, debido a que el proceso de fermentación continúa y puede haber aumento en la temperatura, pudiendo “quemar” la planta. Es necesario crear una protección de tierra.
  • El abono se aplica antes y después de una helada.

4. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, húmedo.

5. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Cultivo de granos básicos con manejo integrado de la fertilidad con bioabonos: ID 5994.
  • Soil property and fertility improvement through composting using Trichoderma: ID 7697.
  • Composting to improve soil fertility: ID 8206.
  • Evergreen agriculture: the use of fertilizer trees in maize production: ID 7847.

Esta tecnología también está disponible en inglés: ID 7390.

6. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

6.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología ayuda a los agricultores pobres a ahorrar y proteger los recursos naturales mediante el uso de insumos orgánicos que de otro modo no se utilizarían.

entries.tittle: Improved feeding of dairy cattle for increased milk production and income, Uganda
entries.summary: Having well nourished and healthy livestock represents a challenge for farmers in Uganda. Diary cattle in Uganda, in most cases, produce less milk than expected. This is mainly caused by improper feeding, which provides feed in inadequate quantities and of low quantity. It is therefore imperative that feed quantity and quality be improved for diary cows in Uganda to increase milk production and subsequently household incomes. There exist technologies to improve the quality of the fodder, e.g. introducing legumes in the cropping system. This has a significant impact on the soil and livestock if introduced to the farming and livestock system following certain criteria. This technology gives some examples of legumes which can be inter-cropped with grasses to improve the quality of animal fodder.
entries.description:
Description

  • Dairy cattle in Uganda in most cases produce less milk than expected.
    • This is caused by improper feeding, which provides feed in inadequate quantities and of low quality.
    • Each 250 kg (TLU) live weight of dairy cows should receive feed providing at least 1700 g of crude protein (CP) and 85 mega joules (MJ) metabolisable energy (ME).
    • However, studies in Masaka showed that feed offered to dairy cows only provide 513 g of CP in the dry season and 611 g in the wet season.
    • In terms of ME farmers provide only 44 MJ in the wet season and 50 MJ in the dry season.
  • Similarly milk production in the wet season was 4 liters per TLU per day and 2.5 in the dry season.
  • It is therefore imperative that feed quantity and quality be improved for dairy cows in Uganda to increase milk production and subsequently household incomes.
  • There exist technologies to improve the quality of the fodder.
    • An example is introducing legumes in the cropping system.
    • Legumes are plants with high protein content and can fix nitrogen in the soil.
    • In addition, at the peak of the growth stage (flowering stage), they contribute to better forage for livestock and increase crop productivity.
Figure 1. Some common types of legumes

©FAO/TECA

1. Plant protein

  • Plant protein is a cheap and good source of protein.
    • Research has shown that there are a number of legumes in various areas of Uganda with a variety of uses.
    • There are legumes like:
      • beans and soya beans;
      • centrosema;
      • stylo;
      • desmodium;
      • sirato (Macroptilium atropurpureum);
      • lablab (Lablab purpureus), pigeon pea (Cajanus Cajan); and
      • Acacia species.
  • These can be used in a variety of ways.
    • When establishing a paddock, legumes such as sirato, stylo, or centrosema can be inter-cropped with grasses such as Chloris gayana or Brachiaria.
      • These provide cheap and balanced forage for animals as well as for conserving soil.
    • Legumes, like Mucuna, are planted after the weeding of crops so that it is incorporated in the soil when ploughing.
      • This can also restore and improve soil fertility.
      • Maize or elephant grass inter-cropped with legumes, like sirato and centrosema, increase the herbage in quantity and quality.
    • Hay made from legumes is of good quality.
      • It has a higher protein content compared to that made from grass.
      • For example, lablab hay fed to milking cows shows an increase in milk production of 0.5 to 2 litres per day depending on breed (see below Strategy two).

2. Feeding strategies

  • Four feed supplementing strategies tested in Masaka to address this feeding problem presented options that farmers can use to provide the necessary nutritional requirement for their diary animals.
  • The four feeding strategies and their effects are briefly described here.
  • Please note that, all weights are on a dry matter basis.

2.1 Strategy one: elephant grass hay with silage

Figure 2. Elephant grass, hay with silage

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Strategy two: maize stover with lablab

Figure 3. Maize Stover with lablab

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Strategy three: elephant grass with centrocema (fresh storage)

Figure 4. Elephant grass with Centrocema (fresh storage)

©FAO/TECA

  • Sirato or centrosema seeds are planted between rows of either maize or elephant grass at a spacing of 1 m apart.
Figure 5. Centrosema interplanted with elaphant grass

©FAO/TECA

2.4 Strategy four: Calliandra leaf hay

Figure 6. Caliandra leaf hay

©FAO/TECA

  • Multipurpose trees, such as calliandra, sesbania, and leuceana leguminous plants, serve the same purpose as other legumes.
  • They can be fed to animals fresh with the grass or as hay mixed with dairy meal at a ratio of 1:3 leaf hay: dairy meal.
  • Multipurpose trees are planted along edges of gardens at a spacing of 1 m apart.
  • The following technology explains in detail:
    • where and how to plant Calliandra trees,
    • how to manage and harvest them, and
    • provides additional information regarding Calliandra trees and their application for livestock fodder.

3. Source of seed

  • You can buy seeds from the Uganda Seed Project in Kawanda and at the Forestry Research Institute in Nakawa.
  • For multipurpose trees, you can obtain these from Agricultural research Development Centres in your area.
  • Legumes seeds are a very good source of income.
  • At the time of writing one kilogram of seed ranged from 5 000 to 30 000 Uganda Shillings (equivalent to aprox. USD 2.73 to USD 6.4), depending on the type.

4. Conclusions and recommendations

  • It is clear that improving feeding of dairy cattle to meet their nutritional requirement, is beneficial and farmers must strive to do so but remaining within the limits of profitability.
  • In terms of increasing milk Calliandra is most beneficial and least with fresh elephant grass and Centrosema.
  • The effects on milk production resulting from the strategy with maize stover combined with lablab, and that of elephant grass hay combined with elephant grass silage are the same.
  • In terms of returns to investment, financial benefits are highest where maize stover with lablab is used as supplements.

5. Validation

  • This research was supported by farmers and district staff in Masaka and carried out by the National Agricultural Research Organization (NARO), in collaboration with Makerere University-Faculty of Agricultural sector Programme support (ASPS).
  • For more information contact: National Crop Resources Research institute (NACRRI)P.O Box 7084, Kampala, Uganda.
  • Email: nacrridirector@naro-ug.org or nacrridirector@yahoo.com

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Growing fodder for livestock: Calliandra and Elephant grass: ID 6989.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently uses different techniques to improve fodder quality, such as introducing legumes in inter-cropping systems.

8.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology improves quantity and quality of livestock feed, thereby providing an increase in sources of food and income for poor farmers.

entries.tittle: Maize harvesting and post-harvesting handling, Uganda
entries.summary: The National Agricultural Research Organisation (NARO) aims to enhance the contribution of agricultural research to sustainable agricultural productivity, economic growth, food security and poverty eradication by generating and disseminating  appropriate technologies, knowledge and information. The following technology describes the different management steps for the  pre and post maize harvesting processes.
entries.description:
Description

1. Harvesting

Harvesting is the single deliberate action to separate the cob from its grown medium.

1.1 Harvesting time and quality management

Maize should be harvested when stalks have dried and grain moisture is about 17 to 20 percent. Unprocessed maize can be stored for a considerable period without deteriorating. Its shelf life depends on:

  • temperature
  • humidity
  • moisture pests
  • diseases.

Quality control starts with harvesting. In order to obtain high quality maize grains post-harvest handling and managing operations of the above factors need implementing.

2. Harvesting process requirements

  • Harvest dry maize.
  • Do not leave harvested maize in the field as it will be attacked by weevils hence will need lodging. Additionally, it will free the field for early land preparation.
  • Keep the grain clean.
  • Dry maize on cement floor (not on bare soil) or use tarpaulin to reduce contamination.
  • Do not heap the cobs in any rooms inside the house, kitchen or in the yard.  High risk to contact any factors that cause post-harvest losses.
  • Transfer the cobs to a drying place (i.e.  a crib).

2.1 Pre-harvesting activities

Currently in Uganda  maize is harvested by hand.

In order to:

  • keep cobs clean;
  • dry cobs; and
  • avoid cobs infestation.

A farmer needs to:

  • Ensure drying place is clean and disinfected, ready to process the cobs.
  • Ensure the equipment is clean and disinfected, ready to process the cobs.
  • Remove old grains and dirt from anything that will come in contact with clean or new grain (i.e. harvesting tools, carts, wheel barrows, bags and baskets).
  • Fumigate or treat the cobs with boiling water to kill insects or their eggs avoiding infection of new grain.
  • Organize enough labour to reap and carry the cobs to the drying place.

2.2 Post-harvesting activities

Harvest the maize cobs and transport them to the crib without laying them on soil to avoid contamination.

After harvesting, farmers should:

  • clean all harvesting equipment; and
  • store all harvesting equipment away from contamination sources and insect breeding places.

The same equipment may be used during transportation of:

  • cobs from the crib for threshing; or
  • grains to the store.

If the equipment is not cleaned properly, it can easily contaminate clean grains or become a source of pest infestation since occasionally, pest infestation starts from the field.

3. Drying

Drying is the systematic reduction of crop moisture to safe levels for storing, usually 12 to 15.5 percent moisture content.

  • The greatest enemy of harvested grain is moisture.
  • Wet grains attract insects and mould.
  • Dry grain as soon as possible after harvesting.

Drying is one of the key post-harvest operations since all subsequent operations depend on it. This is particularly so in some regions of Uganda, harvesting and drying processes are delayed due to high humidity and rainfall during harvesting period. Sometimes the following season starts early when the crops are still in the field. Attention should be paid to the choice of varieties that should mature at the beginning of a dry season.

  • Drying allows moisture from grain to evaporate to an acceptable level, which can sustain very low metabolism.
  • The enzyme activities and grain tissue respiration is reduced to a very low level, thus inhibiting sprouting/germination.
  • During drying, the dry air rapidly takes moisture away from the grain, especially if the flowing air has a low humidity level.
  • Grain can be dried in a crib before shelling and on tarpaulins after it has been shelled.
  • Avoid drying the maize on the ground. Grain that is in contact with the ground will absorb moisture and pick up dirt and insects.

To keep maize off the ground during drying, farmers’ common practice is to use plastic sheets or mats. This practice is discouraged as:

  • Grain requires guarding while it dries.
  • Grain needs sheltering at night or when it rains.
  • Grain can be washed away by sudden down pours.
  • Risk of contamination from dusts, soil, stones, animal droppings, fungal and insect infestation.
  • Losses due to birds, poultry and domestic animals, resulting into contamination and quantitative losses.
  • It is time consuming and labour intensive involving lots of grain handling.

4. Shelling

Shelling is commonly done:

  • By beating maize cobs with stick in a sack
    • this damages the germs physically making it more vulnerable to pests and moulds.
  • In a confined floor space (cheaper option).
  • In a maize shelter (expensive option) unaffordable by most farmers.

5. Storage

The principal objective in any maize grain storage system is:

  • to maintain the stored grains in good condition, i.e. dry and clean;
  • to avoid quantity and quality deterioration.

Grain storage can be extended up to two years without any significant reduction in quantity and quality.

However, the majority of farmers fearing storage losses sell their maize grains cheaply soon after harvesting and later buy food at inconvenient prices.

Improved storage structures can prolong storing duration until grain market prices are favourable.

5.1 Improved storage structures

A good storage structure should:

  • Provide protection from common storage loss agents such as:
    • insect pests
    • rodents
    • moulds
    • birds
    • humans.
  • Maintain an even, cool and dry storage environment.

Maize should be placed on pellets above the floor to avoid cold conditions leading to moulds.

  • Be rain and moisture free. Be thief proof.
  • Be simple and inexpensive to build using, where possible, locally available materials and skills.
  • Be easy to clean and repair.

Hygiene is the basic prerequisite for successful storage and can be performed by any farmer with little effort. Hygiene measures are:

  • simple
  • effective
  • cheap.

5.2 Structure location and orientation

Locate the store:

  • on raised site with good drainage to ensure that there is no stagnant water; 
  • on firm soil with good road connections enabling easy access;
  • to create balanced temperature conditions and reduce condensation expose store:
    • longitudinal facade on an East-West axis (less radiation on the building); and/or
    • to the main wind direction.

5.3 Store room

In a tropical country like Uganda, shelled grain can be stored in:

  • bulk storage; or
  • bag storage.

A well-designed bag grain storage structure is most suitable(in a tropical country) for Ugandan farmers because:

  • Most Uganda’s buyers require bagging before dispatching.
  • The available transport system is better suited for bagged rather than bulk grains.
  • Bagged grain is easily quantified when receiving, dispatching or checking stock.
  • Bag storage requires less capital investment than bulk storage.
  • Bag storage is cheap, easy to manage and efficient.
  • Low risk involved with long term storage.

5.4 Losses due to poor storage

Factors causing storage losses:

  • Inadequate drying, causing microbial infection.
  • Presence of large numbers of insects.
  • High humidity.
  • Wetting due to poor storage management.
  • Fungal infection causing rots and aflatoxins development, poisonous to live stock and cancerous for mankind.

6. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Well dried maize benefits all: the solar maize dryer: ID 8285.
  • Maize production: ID 7018.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Women-friendly

The above recommendations are easy to implement and accessible to all.

8.2 Resource use efficiency

 This technology contributes to resources use efficiency and minimise crop losses.

8.3 Pro-poor technology

With better harvesting and storing techniques, farmers can improve their income.

entries.tittle: The role of standards in maize, Uganda
entries.summary: The National Agricultural Research Organisation (NARO) aims to enhance the contribution of agricultural research to sustainable agricultural productivity, economic growth, food security and poverty eradication through generation and dissemination of appropriate technologies, knowledge and information. Maize is one of the main crop in Uganda. Therefore, it is important to have some standards regarding the storage and marketing of maize. The following technology describes the promotion of standardization and grading of maize and the essential composition of quality factors.
entries.description:
Description

1. The role of standards in maize

  • The promotion of standardization and grading of agricultural commodities is an important aspect of agricultural marketing. 
  • The agricultural commodities are heterogeneous and hence it is very essential to grade these commodities as per standards to command better price either at domestic or international market.
  • The sale of maize is offered on the basis of variety, wholesomeness, appearance, colour, presence of foreign matter, damaged grains, broken grains, admixture of inferior variety, moisture, harmful contaminants, etc.
  • A quality grain is that which meets the end user specifications with respect to range of pre-determined quality and safety standards.

1.1 Damaged or blemished grains

  • Grains which are insect or vermin damaged, stained, diseased, discoloured, germinated, frost damaged, or otherwise materially damaged.

1.2 Insect or vermin damaged grains

  • Kernels with obvious weevil-bored holes or which have evidence of boring or tunneling, indicating the presence of insects, insect webbing or insect refuse, or degermed grains, chewed in one or more than one part of the kernel which exhibit evident traces of an attack by vermin.

1.3 Stained kernels

  • Kernels whose natural colour has been altered by external factors.
  • This includes ground, soil or weather damaged kernels, which may have dark stains or discolourations with a rough external appearance.

1.4 Diseased grains

  • Grains made unsafe for human consumption due to decay, moulding, or bacterial decomposition, or other causes that may be noticed without having to cut the grains to examine them.

1.5 Discoloured kernels

  • Kernels materially discoloured by excessive heat, including that caused by excessive respiration (heat damage) and dried damaged kernels.
  • Kernels may appear darkened, wrinkled, blistered, puffed or swollen, often with discoloured, damaged germs.
  • The seed coat may be peeling or may have peeled off completely, giving kernels a checked appearance.

1.6 Germinated kernels

  • Kernels showing visible signs of sprouting, such as cracked seed coats through which a sprout has emerged or is just beginning to merge.

1.7 Frost damaged kernels

  • Kernels which appear bleached or blistered and the seed coat may be peeling.
  • Germs may appear dead or discoloured.

1.8 Mouldy kernels

  • Maize grains with visible mycelial growth on its tip or surface

1.9 Immature/shriveled grains

  • Maize grains which are underdeveloped, thin and papery in appearance

1.10 Broken kernels

  • Maize and pieces of maize which when tested according to ISO 5223-Test sieves for cereals, shall pass through a 4.50 mm metal sieve.

1.11 Other grains

  1. Other grains are edible grains, whole or identifiable broken, other than maize (that is cereals, pulses and other edible legumes).

1.12 Foreign matter

  • All organic and inorganic material (such as sand, soil, glass) other than maize, broken kernels and other grains.

1.13 Filth

  • Impurities of animal origin

2. Essential composition of quality factors

2.1 Quality factors – general

  • Maize shall be free from foreign odours, moulds, live pests, rat droppings, toxic or noxious weed seeds and other injurious contaminants as determined from samples representative of the lot.
  • Maize shall be of a reasonably uniform colour according to type, be whole and clean.

2.2 Quality factors - specific moisture content

  • Moisture content of lots of clean and dry maize shall not exceed 13.5 percent by mass as determined from samples representative of the lot in accordance with EAS 285.

2.2.1 Grades

  • Maize grains should be classified as Grade 1 or 2 according to the limits indicated in the table below.
Table 1. Grades of maize grains
Defects Maximum limits
Foreign matter, %m/m 0.5 1
Inorganic matter,%m.m 0.25 0.5
Broken grains,5m/m 2 3
Pest damaged grains, %m/m 1 3
Rotten & diseased grains, %m/m 2 4
Discoloured grains, %m/m 0.5 1
Moisture, %m/m 13.5 13.5
Immature/Shriveled grains, , %m/m 1 2
Filth, , %m/m 1 1
Total Defectives Grains, , %m/m 4 5
Aflatoxins in accordance with ISO 16050 10ppb incl max 5ppb B1 10ppb incl max 5ppb B1

Source: NARO & SAARI 2011

2.2.2 Toxic or noxious seeds

  • Maize shall be free from toxic or noxious seeds for example Datura, Striga etc.

2.2.3 Undergrade maize

  • Maize, which does not come within the requirements of grades 1 and 2 of this hand book and is not a reject shall be termed as undergrade.
  • Undergrade maize can be sorted out to either grade 1 or 2.

2.2.4 Reject maize

  • Maize, which is mouldy, musty, chemically or otherwise hygienically objectionable rendering it unfit for human consumption.

2.2.5 Contaminants

  • Maize shall be free from heavy metals in amounts within the limits of Codex Alimentarius Commission.

2.2.6 Hygiene

  • Maize shall be prepared, packed, stored, transported and distributed under hygienic conditions.
  • When tested by appropriate methods of sampling and examination the maize shall be free from pathogenic microorganisms, substances originating from microorganisms, or other poisonous or deleterious or substances in amount(s), which may constitute a health hazard.

2.2.7 Packaging

  • Maize, when not handled in bulk, shall be packed in new bags or similar acceptable protective containers, which shall safeguard the hygienic and other qualities of the maize.
  • The containers including packaging material shall be made of only substances, which are safe and suitable for their intended use.

2.2.8 Labelling

  • The name of the product to be declared on the label shall be "maize".
  • Crop year.
  • Type and grade.
  • Include a statement of GMO status.
  • Net contents in kilogram (kg).
  • Name and address of the producer, packer, distributor, importer or vendor of the food.
  • Country of origin of the maize.
  • Lot identification.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Maize production: ID 7018.
  • Drought-tolerant maize varieties: ID 8920.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2020.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for the promotion of standardization and grading of maize, which contributes to the crop's quality level. As a result this provides an additional source of food and income.

entries.tittle: Fish Harvesting and Post-harvest Handling, Uganda
entries.summary: Fish is important for good nutrition. In addition, fishery activities generate income and employment in Uganda. The mission of the National Agricultural Advisory Services (NAADS-Uganda) is to increase farmers’ access to information, knowledge and technology for profitable agricultural production. Therefore, the following technology describes the process of fish harvesting and post-harvest handling.
entries.description:
Description

1. Deciding when to harvest

The decision to harvest the fish from a pond is made for two main reasons.

  1. When the fish has attained the right size at which it gives maximum profit in the market and any further waiting may reduce the profit.
  2. When the prevailing market opportunities (like Christmas and Easter) offer the highest profit and the opportunity may be lost with delay.

1.1 Using information from a regular sampling of fish

  • In order for the farmer to decide whether the fish has attained an optimum size for harvest, the farmer must have been sampling and weighing the fish and analysing the data (see Table 1).
    • The example is based on sampling data from Jacob's pond. 
Table 1. The growth of fish in Jacobs pond
Month fish has grown in the pond The average weight of fish each month (g) Increase in average weight each month (g)
1 4.7 0
2 9.0 4.3
3 10.6 1.6
4 12.0 1.5
5 28.9 16.9
6 65.5 36.6
7 121.2 55.7
8 191.8 70.5
9 270.2 78.5
10 380.0 109.8
11 440.0 60.0
12 471.7 31.7
13 504.5 32.8
14 515.0 10.5
15 516.0 1.0
16 517.0 1.0
17 517.5 0.5
18 518.0 0.5

Source: NAADS-Uganda 2011

  • The data shows that the monthly increase in fish weight rises until the tenth month.
    • After month ten, although the fish continues to grow, the rate of growth keeps falling (Figure 1).
  • In the Figure below after month ten, the quantity of food the fish eats increases while the growth rate falls.
    • It is advisable to harvest the fish in the tenth month to avoid losses in profit.
Figure 1. The average of fish weight in kg as a function of months

©NAADS-Uganda

  • Emphasis (impact point): See dotted arrow in the above Figure 1.
    • The figure confirms that delayed harvesting of farmed fish leads to loss of profit and farmers do not necessarily make more profit by growing fish to bigger sizes.

2. Methods and gear for harvesting pond fish

2.1 Definition

  • Method means “ways of harvesting”; gear means “tools used to harvest”.
    • Once the fish has reached the right size for harvest, the pond should be harvested immediately.

2.2 How do we harvest fish from ponds?

  • Common methods and gear for harvesting fish from ponds.
    • Harvesting by draining the pond.
    • Using basket traps.
    • Using hooks and baits.
    • Using cast nets.
    • Using lift nets.
    • Using a seine net.
    • Using gill nets.
  • The methods and gear for harvesting fish ponds depend on the size of the pond.

2.2.1 Harvesting by draining the pond

  • This method of harvesting is the simplest and most effective.
    • Water is let out of the pond by opening the sluices or lowering pipes at the outlet.
    • As the water level drops and the water moves towards the deeper end of the pond, the fish drift with it (Figure 2).
    • All the fish collect at the outlet and are collected by hand or with a net.
  • As the pond drains, the water level falls at the shallower end of the pond.
    • All the fish drift towards the deeper end.
    • When the fish have gathered in a small area at the deep end the farmer then collects the fish in a container.
Figure 2. Harvesting by draining a pond

©FAO/TECA

  • For this method, the pond should have been constructed well with a good slope.
  • Harvesting is made much easier if a depression is made at the point of the outlet as a "harvesting bay".
    • The fish is then scooped or picked from the ditch (harvesting bay).
    • In this way, the fish is picked clean and does not bury in the mud.
  • This method of harvesting is suitable for both small and large ponds.
    • For the larger ponds, it is used in combination with seining.
    • Fish collected from the mud tends to be dirty and dies quickly.
    • Pond fish should be marketed live and clean.
  • During harvesting, there should be two containers with clean water (Figure 3).
    • The first bucket is for washing off the mud from the fish.
    • Then the clean fish are put in another container with clean water to keep alive.
    • The water for washing the fish should be replaced with clean water when it gets dirty.
Figure 3. The fish are put in clean water to keep them alive

©FAO/TECA

2.2.2 Using basket traps

  • The baskets are important in harvesting small ponds where the farmer cannot afford the more expensive gear.
    • The basket is made from twigs, cane or climbing plants (Figure 4).
    • The larger end is the mouth which has a valve that does not allow the fish to escape once it has entered.
    • Some food is put inside the basket.
  • The trap is placed with the open end facing the main pond water. It is given enough time (30 minutes to one hour) for the fish to enter.
  • The gear is simple to make or cheap to buy.
    • It is easy to operate, but it is limited to only small ponds (not suitable for ponds of more than 200 m2).
  • The basket cannot harvest all the fish from the pond.
    • The pond should be drained in order to harvest all the fish.
  • The baskets are cheap and made from local materials.
Figure 4. Farmer setting a basket trap (left), and a basket trap (right)

©FAO/TECA

2.2.3 Using hooks

  • Hooks are bought from shops selling fishing equipment (Figure 5).
    • They vary in sizes from number 1 (the largest) to number 10 (the smallest).
  • A hook is fixed to a rope tied to a handle.
    • The hook and its rope (hook acid line) are very cheap, simple to make and use.
    • However, a hook catches one fish at a time.
    • Therefore, it is not suitable for good scale commercial production.
    • The hook and line cannot harvest all the fish from the pond.
    • Most of the fish still remain in the pond.
    • The pond should finally be drained to completely harvest the pond.
Figure 5. A hook and a line

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. An earthworm used as bait on the hook

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. A farmer using bait and a hook

©FAO/TECA

2.2.3.1 Hook and line attributes

  • It depends on luck; the operator cannot choose the fish to catch.
  • It is not very selective and smaller fish may be caught leaving the larger ones.
  • It injures fish and may not be suitable for sampling fish that will be returned into the pond.
  • It catches a few fish at a time, depends on luck (Figure 8).
    • The pond must be drained to remove all the fish.
  • It is only suitable for small ponds (up to 10 m x 20 m).
Figure 8. Fish caught with a hook. Note to throw the smaller fish away

©FAO/TECA

2.2.4 Harvesting using cast nets

  • A cast net is a net made like an umbrella (Figure 9).
    • It is tied on a rope. It opens out when casting over the pond.
    • As it sinks deep into the pond the mouth is closed, trapping whatever fish that will be in the water space enclosed.
Figure 9. The cast net encloses a space of pond water and traps fish in that space

©FAO/TECA

2.2.4.1 Advantages of the cast

  • A cast net is cheap.
  • It is simple to operate but requires training in the skills.
  • Does not require a large labour force (only one person).
  • Catches by chance and the operator does not have much choice of the fish to catch.
  • It does not harm fish, the fish can be returned into the pond.
  • Its operation is limited to only small ponds (1 m x 20 m) and is time wasting for larger ponds.

2.2.5 Using lift nets

  • The lift net is a net made into a sack with one open end that is dipped into the pond to scoop up fish.
    • The mouth of the lift net is made of a ring made from a cane or a metal rod.
    • The length of the rod or cane is about 1.5 m to 2 m long before bending into a ring (Figure 10).
Figure 10. Two sides of the net are mounted onto a ring

©FAO/TECA

  • The wider ends are tied to the metal ring.
    • The two open edges of the net are seamed together to make an inverted umbrella and the two pieces closed by tying.
  • The lift net can be braided by hand (after training) or are bought and trimmed into a cone with one wider end and one narrow an end.
    • The wider ends are measured to half the length of the ring for each net.
Figure 11. Two sides of the net mounted onto a ring 

©FAO/TECA

  • The lift net can harvest a reasonable quantity of fish, as much as 30 kg at a go, and therefore can be applied for commercial production.
    • The method does not bruise or stress fish, and fish can be delivered to the market very fresh.
    • The lift net, however, is not suitable for ponds larger than 2 000 m2.
    • It cannot harvest all the fish.
    • The pond should be drained so as to complete the harvest.
  • To operate the net it is dipped into the water as shown in Figure 12a.
  • Food is then placed around the net.
    • The net is left for 30 minutes for fish to gather above it while feeding, then quickly, the net is lifted with the fish that was in the water above it (Figure 12b). 
Figures 12a and 12b. a) net is dipped into the water, b)net is in the water left for fish to gather

©FAO/TECA

2.2.6 The seine net

  • The seine net is the conventional pond net.
    • It is like an open curtain made of a net with small meshes.
    • The top side of the net is tied to a rope on which plastic round spheres (floats) are attached at about 1 m interval.
  • The seine net is a large curtain-like net.
    • It has floats on one side that keeps the net above the water surface( Figure 13).
    • It has heavy cement balls on another side that keeps the net at the bottom of the pond.
Figure 13. The seine net

©FAO/TECA

  • Therefore, the net remains open during fishing.
    • One wing of the net metal or wooden ring.
    • 1 m long folded into a ring.
    • The bottom side is tied to another rope on which small stones are attached at about 1 m interval.
    • The length of the net should be longer than the width of the pond by an extra 3 m to 5 m to make a curve when it is operated.
    • Example: a pond with a width of 20 m requires a seine net 25 m long.
  • The seine net at the end of the operation will have trapped fish in the middle.
  • Note the number of people required to operate it (see Figure 13 above).

2.2.6.1 Seine net attributes

  • It makes bulk harvests (harvesting up to 90 percent of the fish stock in the pond when fished four to six times repeatedly).
  • It is expensive (about UGX 10 000 per 1 m length), but it lasts long (up to five years with minor repairs).
  • It requires more labour to operate (ranging from four people for 10 m x 20 m pond to as many as 12 people for a 20 m x 50 m pond).
  • It is most appropriate for large size ponds.
  • If operated carefully, it does not injure fish much and fish can be returned to the pond.

2.2.7 Harvesting using gill nets

  • The gill nets are nets with varying mesh sizes.
    • It is operated by setting it well spread in the pond and left there.
    • It is checked after about an hour or longer.
    • Fish are caught when it pushes its head through the meshes and gets trapped (Figure 14).
    • The gill net is highly selective and the size of fish caught depends on the size of the net.
    • The gill net cannot harvest all the fish in the pond.
Figure 14. A gill net set in the pond

©FAO/TECA

2.2.7.1 Gill net advantages

  • It is easy to operate but the farmer has to enter the pond.
    • Only one person can set it.
  • It may catch many fish, but cannot be used to harvest all the fish. 

2.2.7.2 Gill net challenges

  • The gill net is expensive for small scale farmers (UGX 15 000 for 4" mesh).
  • It harms fish and is not suitable for catching and returning some fish.

3. Displaying fish for marketing

  • Whenever possible it is best to present fish for sale in its freshest form.
    • Live fish are the freshest state.
    • As soon as fish die, they begin to go bad and the longer they stay the smellier they become.
    • When the fish go bad the market price falls.
  • Therefore, fish may be:
    • deep-fried in oil for immediate consumption;
    • sold live or freshly killed;
    • preserved in ice;
    • processed (sun-dried, salted or smoked); and
    • at higher industrial levels, may be filleted and chilled for supermarkets or export.
  • The form in which the fish is marketed depends on:
    • how near the market is;
    • what the market prefers;
    • the amount of fish to be sold; and
    • the need to add value and improve profit.

3.1 Selling deep-fried fish for direct eating

  • Fish may be deep-fried in oil and sold for direct eating at social gatherings (Figure 15).
    • Such opportunities include near schools, at drinking joints and at public functions.
Figure 15. Deep frying fish

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Smoking fish in kilns

  • Fish may also be preserved by smoking in kilns or salting, or by sun-drying thus keeping for a longer time.
    • This makes it possible to sell fish at longer distances.

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Post-harvest fish loss model: ID 4463.
  • Make a living through fish farming: ID 7357.
  • Assessing post-harvest fish losses: load tracking method: ID 4437.
  • Management of fish in the pond: ID 7235.
  • Fry/seed quality and stocking: ID 7025.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for improved pond management and fish health. It has advantageous fish harvesting techniques and fish conservation methods.

entries.tittle: Techniques Culturales du Manioc, Congo (RDC)
entries.summary: Le manioc est une plante vivrière, arbustive pérenne pouvant atteindre un à quatre mètre de haut et ayant une ou plusieurs tiges principales avec ou sans ramification. Le mode de propagation par bouture est utilisé couramment, mais pas par germination (réservé à la recherche). Le rendement en station de recherche de l’INERA Mvuazi pour les variétés améliorées varient de 25 à 55 tonnes à l’hectare.
entries.description:
La description

REAFOR (Recherche Agricole et Forestière) est un programme visant à contribuer à la réduction de la pauvreté, au renforcement de la sécurité alimentaire et au bien-être des populations de la République Démocratique du Congo, par le renforcement des capacités nationales de la recherche agricole et forestière, en vue de sa relance durable. La fiche technique suivante décrit comment cultiver différentes variétés de manioc. Elle donne des détails sur la préparation du terrain, la sélection des boutures, la plantation, la récolte ainsi que la conservation. Les variétés suivantes ont été choisies pour leur résistance aux maladies et aux ravageurs ainsi que pour leur haut rendement:

  • Zizila,
  • Nsansi,
  • M'vuazi,
  • Disanka,
  • Butamu, et
  • TME 419.

1. Exigences édaphiques du manioc

  • Terrain et type de sol

1.1 Sols

  • Meubles sablo argileux ou argilo-sablonneux, profonds et riches en éléments nutritifs.
  • Éviter le terrain où l’eau stagne ainsi que le terrain avec racines d’arbre hôtes de fomes lignosus établies (le champignon responsable pour les pourritures des racines).

1.2 Précédant cultural

  • Éviter les sols ayant porté une culture avec les mêmes exigences en éléments nutritifs (ex. manioc, patate douce, bananer, taro, etc.).

2. Préparation du terrain

2.1 En forêt

  • Défrichement (bois et sous bois).
  • Coupe de sous-bois trois mois avant l’abattage des futaies.
  • Incinération localisée.
  • Buttage: 1 m x 1 m entre les buttes.
  • Enfouissement: pendant le buttage des débris végétaux décomposables au moins 21 à 45 jours avant la plantation.

2.2 En savane

  • Champ sur buttes, en billons, à plat ou cultivé non labouré.

2.2.1 Labour tracteur

  • 30 à 45 jours avant plantation.
  • Enfouissement des résidus végétaux.
  • Hersage peu avant la plantation.
  • Deux passages croisés.

2.2.2 Préparation manuelle du terrain

  • Enfouissement des résidus végétaux.
  • Création de billons équidistants de 1 m à 1.5 m.
  • 21 à 45 jours avant plantation.
  • Remuer les billons en mélangeant la terre et les débris de décomposition avant de planter.

3. Variété et matériel de plantation

Les variétés à hauts rendements, résistantes aux maladies et aux ravageurs, notamment à la mosaïque africaine sont les suivantes : ZIZILA, NSANSI, MVUAZI, DISANKA, BUTAMU et TME 419. Toutes ces variétés (exceptées la TME 419) sont présentées plus en détail dans le fichier joint à la technologie. Les matériels de plantation doivent provenir d’un champ de multiplication des boutures saines, sur tiges saines de 9 à 15 mois.

4. Mode de plantation

  • Une seule bouture (micro ou petite), longue de 10, 15, 20, 25 cm selon la variété, avec trois à cinq bourgeons.
  • Position
    • Horizontale, couverte complètement (dégâts des termites réduits, faible incidence de la verse).
    • Oblique.
    • Couverte à deux-tiers à un angle de 30 à 45° et verticale.
      • Usages spécifiques: maraîchères, micro propagation, jauge.
  • Plantation avec jauge de préférence pour le regarnissage des champs de multiplication car.
    • Dans ce cas, les plantules ont le même âge.

4.1 Ecartements recommandés

  • 1 m x 1 m, pour la production racines tubéreuses.
  • 1 m x 0.50 m, pour la multiplication des boutures.
  • 1 m x 0.50 m, pour la production des feuilles.

5. Rotation de culture

  • En zone forestière mettre les céréales plutôt que le manioc en tête de rotation.
  • En savane, démarrer avec une légumineuse dans les sols à faible fertilité.

5.1 Époques de plantation

  • Bas-Congo et Kinshasa: Octobre/Novembre et Février/Mars.
  • Bandundu, Ka-saï: Octobre et Mars.
  • Sud – Kivu et Maniema: Octobre/Novembre et Février/Mars.
  • Nord-Kivu: Mars/Avril et Septembre.
  • Equateur, Pro-vince Orientale: Mars/Avril et Octobre.
  • Nord Katanga: Septembre et Février.
  • Sud Katanga: Novembre/Décembre et Février.

5.2  Associations culturales

  • On peut associer le manioc avec plusieurs cultures suivantes.

5.2.1 Arachide

  • Deux lignes de 30 cm x 30 cm ou 40 cm x 20 cm entre deux lignes de manioc.

5.2.2 Soja

  • Une ligne en sol riche aux écartements de 30 à 40 cm.
  • En sol pauvre, deux lignes de 40 cm x 20 cm.
  • Semer deux à trois semaines après le manioc.

5.2.3 Haricot volubile

  • Semis au même moment ou 45 jours après le manioc.
  • Deux lignes aux écartements de 50 cm x 20 cm.

5.2.4 Haricot nain 

  • Semis au même moment ou deux semaines avant le manioc.
  • Deux lignes à 40 cm x 10 cm ou 40 cm x 20 cm.

5.2.5 Maïs

  • Une ligne entre deux lignes de manioc.
  • Deux à trois semaines avant le manioc, au même moment, ou en relais 45 jours avant le manioc à 1 m x 0.5 m d’écartement.

5.2.6 Riz

  • Semis souvent avant le manioc.
  • Deux lignes 40 cm x 20 cm.

5.3 Entretien du champ

5.3.1 Regarnissage

  • Le regarnissage des vides, trois à quatre semaines après plantation.

5.3.2 Mesures phytosanitaires

  • Une fois au regarnissage pour le champ de production des racines tubéreuses, et du regarnissage à la récolte pour le champ de multiplication des boutures saines.

5.3.3 Sarclages (contrôle des adventices)

  • Trois sarclages manuels recommandés en savane.
  • Le premier à partir de trois à quatre semaines de la plantation, avant le regarnissage.
  • Les sarclages sont surtout importants les trois premiers mois de la plantation pour garantir une bonne tubérisation.
  • Buttage appliqué pendant le deuxième et troisième sarclage.

5.3.4 Fertilisation minérale

  • Dose de 50-50-50 ou 75-50-75 (N,P,K) en fonction de l’intensification.
  • Application fractionnée.
    • Tout le P et K à la plantation (dose de fonds).
    • 40 à 46 kg N au redressement appliqué après 30 à 40 jours de plantation.

5.3.5 Fertilisation organique

  • Fumure de ferme à 15 tonnes/ha, enfouissement résidus végétaux et paillage.

6. Récolte

6.1 Feuilles

  • Deux récoltes à trois mois de la plantation.
  • À 45 jours, deux mois après la première.

6.2 Boutures 

  • Entre 9 et 15 mois de la plantation, ou après 9 mois du premier recépage.
  • Le recépage se fait à 20 à 25 cm du collet.
  • Le conditionnement se fait à 50 et 100 tiges d'un mètre de longueur.
  • Conserver en jauge, en meule, verticalement, sous hangars ou sous ombrage, ou près d’un point d’eau.
  • Les racines tubéreuses suivent le cycle (précoce ou tardif) de la variété (entre 9 à 18 mois).
  • L'arrachage complet de la plante à maturité est conseillé.
  • Il n'y a pas de récolte graduelle sur un seul pied.
  • Il est conseillé de cultiver les variétés à différents cycles de maturité pour échelonner la récolte.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en portugais: ID 2140. 

7. Zones agro-ecologiques

  • Tropicale, chaude.

8. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

8.1 L’efficacité d’utilisation des ressources

La pratique permet à la cultivitation plus diverse de différentes variétés de manioc et effectue de manière plus efficace l'utilisation et préparation du terrain, la sélection des boutures, la plantation, la récolte et la conservation. 

8.2 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvres

La pratique permet à la récolte de variétés de haute qualité, résistante aux maladies et aux ravageurs. Cela mène à de plus hauts rendements et une sécurité alimentaire plus élevée.

entries.tittle: Establecimiento de Sistemas Agroforestales
entries.summary: Los Sistemas Agroforestales son sistemas de producción sostenible con el manejo de suelo, agua y árboles en forma dispersa en el terreno, con diferentes tipos de podas. Los cultivos se manejan mediante prácticas agronómicas, basadas en la no quema, el manejo de rastrojo, la cero labranza y la siembra directa. Su implantación constituye un factor de reducción del riesgo y de la vulnerabilidad de las familias rurales. Este material proviene de los documentos y publicaciones del Programa Especial para la Seguridad Alimentaria (PESA Centroamerica).
entries.description:
Descripción

1. ¿Por qué el manejo de la humedad en los suelos de cultivo?

Las condiciones de nuestras tierras de cultivo por estar ubicadas, en su mayoría, en zonas secas de ladera requieren de mejorar la infiltración del agua, evitar la erosión y mejorar la fertilidad para asegurar la producción.

Para que el cultivo se desarrolle es necesario que el suelo posea la humedad suficiente, pues algunos cultivos necesitan más agua que otros; por ejemplo, el maíz en comparación con el frijol.

De igual forma, en algunas de las etapas de desarrollo la planta necesita más agua. Para el caso, en el cultivo de maíz se presenta cuando comienza la floración y en el de frijol al momento del llenado de la vaina.

Existen varias prácticas que muchos productores aplican en sus parcelas de cultivo que están dando buenos resultados, entre ellos: la no quema con manejo de rastrojo, la no rotura del suelo al momento de la siembra y el establecimiento de sistemas agroforestales. Esta última forma puede iniciarse con la regeneración natural en terrenos de cultivo, o bien desde áreas que han estado en descanso como guamil.

2. No quema con manejo de rastrojo

2.1 Definición de la no quema

La no quema es una práctica que consiste en desechar el uso del fuego en el terreno de cultivo. Cuando el productor no quema implica que va a hacer un uso diferente del rastrojo; es decir, que los residuos que quedaron de la cosecha de los cultivos serán incorporados.

2.2 Manejo de rastrojo

Es una práctica que sirve para proteger el suelo y sus condiciones físicas. Cuando el productor no quema, está dejando los residuos de la cosecha, los cuales al descomponerse se convierten en materia orgánica que mejora el terreno donde se cultiva.

Consiste en dejar esparcidos sobre el terreno los residuos de la cosecha y la totalidad de los desechos de las limpias realizadas antes de sembrar y durante el desarrollo del cultivo. También pueden utilizarse los olotes, la tuza del maíz y los sobrantes del aporreo del sorgo y maicillo o bien la casuya del frijol. El uso adecuado del rastrojo favorece la protección y mejora la fertilidad del suelo.

Se estima que más de la mitad de los nutrientes de los que se alimentan las plantas son acumulados de rastrojos. El cultivo de frijol y de maíz produce una buena cantidad de rastrojo, igual que si se siembra en asocio con sorgo (Figura 1).

Figura 1. Hombre sentado en su cultivo de maíz asociado al frijol: el suelo está cubierto de plantas que van a alimentarlo y protegerlo

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Formas de uso del rastrojo

  • Como cobertura del suelo. Consiste en cortar, picar y regar el material vegetal en el terreno para cubrir el suelo sin ser incorporado.
  • Incorporación del rastrojo en el suelo antes de la siembra del siguiente cultivo.
  • Construcción de aboneras.

El manejo de árboles con cultivos ayuda a mejorar la disponibilidad de humedad para el cultivo, principalmente en zonas con malas precipitaciones o donde se presentan en forma recurrente veranos o bien una canícula prolongada.

2.4 Prácticas a realizar

  • El rastrojo se corta y se pica con el machete para evitar que se vuelva hospedero de plagas como la babosa. Cuando se pica bien se acelera su descomposición. El rastrojo no debe encarrilarse, es mejor picarlo (Figura 2).
  • Se siembra con chuzo directamente en el rastrojo.
  • En el caso de la vegetación o las malezas que nacieron en el terreno, se chapia y se siembra en la cobertura muerta.
  • Es conveniente combinar el manejo del rastrojo con la cero labranza y la rotación de cultivos para romper el ciclo de reproducción de las plagas.
Figura 2. Ramas picadas antes de ponerlas al suelo como rastrojo

©FAO/TECA

3. Siembra sin roturar el suelo o cero labranza

Es aquella forma de siembra directa sin roturar o arar el suelo y que se hace con chuzo o barreta. Esta práctica ayuda a reducir la erosión, aumenta la disponibilidad de humedad para el cultivo y mejora la infiltración. El productor se ahorra mano de obra y los costos de aradura.

Prácticas:

  1. Al momento de preparar el suelo se pican los rastrojos de la cosecha anterior.
  2. Se distribuyen uniformemente sobre el terreno.
  3. Se siembra, ya sea maíz, frijol sorgo, haciendo un agujero u hoyo con el chuzo únicamente en el sitio donde se sembrará la semilla.
  4. En terrenos de ladera es conveniente combinar esta práctica con la siembra en contorno, no quema y manejo de rastrojo (Figura 3).
Figura 3. Siembra directa en líneas de contorno, sin labranza

©FAO/TECA

4. Sistemas agroforestales

4.1 Definición de un sistema agroforestal

  • Es un sistema de producción sostenible con el manejo de suelo, agua y árboles en forma dispersa en el terreno, con diferentes tipos de podas.
  • Los cultivos se manejan mediante prácticas agronómicas, basadas en la no quema, el manejo de rastrojo, la cero labranza y la siembra directa.
  • Para construir un sistema agroforestal se puede partir de la regeneración natural, como también desde un guamil en descanso.

4.2 Desde la regeneración natural

En terrenos limpios de cultivo al momento de la preparación del suelo se seleccionan de dos a tres rebrotes de aquellos árboles de mayor interés, que luego se reducen a dos, hasta formar el sistema con árboles y arbustos. Al alcanzar determinado tamaño se deben podar. También al no quemar en el terreno pueden surgir nuevos árboles, los cuales deben dejarse entre el cultivo.

Figura 4. Preparación del suelo y selección de árboles y rebrotes a conservar

©FAO/TECA

4.3 Desde un guamil en descanso

En los años subsiguientes, debe dejar la regeneración natural de árboles y arbustos. Los arbustos no deben cortarse para permitir que surjan rebrotes al inicio del invierno. Al principio la densidad de árboles puede ser alta, pero a medida se secan o se utilizan se van reduciendo.

4.4 Prácticas al inicio del sistema agroforestal

4.4.1 Chapia

La chapia del terreno que ha estado en descanso, de preferencia, es mejor hacerlo en el mes de agosto para dejar que las ramas comiencen a descomponerse y sembrar al siguiente año. En algunas zonas como en el departamento de Lempira los productores siembran al voleo antes de la chapía para aprovechar el terreno mientras se descompone el material vegetal de los árboles y arbustos.

4.4.2 Poda de árboles

Los árboles que se encuentran en el terreno de cultivo son podados, según su especie e interés del productor.

4.4.3 Poda de arbustos

Los arbustos que están en el terreno de cultivo, se podan a una altura de 1,5 a 3 metros. El corte de los árboles y arbustos se hace transversal o “chaflan” para evitar que con el invierno la humedad pudra el árbol. Normalmente, la poda se realiza al momento de sembrar, o sea, puede ser que existan dos podas antes de sembrar (primera y postrera).

4.4.4 Picar y regar la biomasa

Las hojas y ramas que constituyen lo que se llama “ biomasa” producida por las podas debe ser picada con machete y luego se esparce sobre el terreno de siembra en forma uniforme, para que se descomponga y se convierta en materia orgánica.

Figura 5. Poda de àrbustos en la parcela agroforestal

©FAO/TECA

4.5 Prácticas en los años subsiguientes de establecido el sistema

4.5.1 Chapia

Se realiza al momento de iniciar la preparación del suelo para el siguiente cultivo, generalmente entre los meses de abril y mayo o cuando se inician las lluvias. Se cortan todas las malezas que crecieron durante el desarrollo del cultivo.

4.5.2 Manejo de rebrotes

Es bueno ir viendo la cantidad de árboles, pues de ello depende ir seleccionando algunos rebrotes y luego ralear para establecer nuevos árboles. Todo el material de los rebrotes se pica bien y se distribuye en el terreno y las ramas mas gruesas se utilizan como leña.

5. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

6. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas 

  • El sistema agroforestal quesungualm: ID 7188.
  • Sistemas agroforestales, seguridad alimentaria y cambio climático en centroamérica: ID 7186.

7. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

7.1 Tecnología de ahorro de trabajo

Esta tecnología sostenible mediante prácticas agronómicas, basadas en la no quema, el manejo de rastrojo, la cero labranza y la siembra directa, se evita carga de trabajo.

7.2 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

El uso eficiente de los recursos resulta en muchos factores positivos, como la reducción de la erosión, el aumento de la resiliencia y de la humedad para el cultivo.

7.3 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

A través de la forma de siembra directa sin roturar o arar el suelo, el productor se ahorra los costos de aradura.

entries.tittle: Huertos Escolares, Nicaragua
entries.summary: En Nicaragua la FAO junto con el sector privado vienen trabajando en la implementación de una Alianza Nacional Contra el Hambre que reúne actores del sector privado, público y organizaciones comprometidas en la lucha contra el hambre; con el propósito de desarrollar con financiamiento de la empresa privada, inversiones en Seguridad Alimentaria y Nutricional a nivel de comunidades y escuelas. Este material proviene de los documentos y publicaciones del Programa Especial para la Seguridad Alimentaria (PESA Centroamerica).
entries.description:
Descripción

Los niños y niñas que padecen hambre, o que sufren de mal nutrición crónica, empiezan a ir a la escuela más tarde. Si es que llegan a hacerlo, la abandonan antes y, cuando frecuentan la escuela, aprenden menos, lo que retarda el progreso hacia la consecución de la enseñanza primaria y secundaria.

¿Podemos reducir el hambre? En Nicaragua la FAO junto con el sector privado vienen trabajando en la implementación de una Alianza Nacional Contra el Hambre que reúne actores del sector privado, público y organizaciones comprometidas en la lucha contra el hambre; con el propósito de desarrollar con financiamiento de la empresa privada, inversiones en Seguridad Alimentaria y Nutricional a nivel de comunidades y escuelas.

La escuela es una de las instituciones de la comunidad en la cual se puede promover la Seguridad Alimentaria y Nutricional. Los Huertos Escolares permiten, de esta manera, atender las áreas urbanas, periurbanas y rurales.

Figura 1. Niños en su Huerto Escolar

©FAO/TECA

1. ¿Que son los huertos escolares?

  • Los Huertos Escolares son áreas cultivadas que se encuentran alrededor o cerca de las escuelas, que sirven fundamentalmente para fines didácticos, además de producir alimentos y en algunos casos ingresos para la escuela (Figura 2).
  • En las escuelas donde existen limitaciones de suelo y agua se puede implementar la tecnología de cultivo de hortalizas en cajas, que tienen una dimensión de 80 cm x 40 cm x 40cm, las cuales se rellenan con sustratos preparados con materiales orgánicos.
  • Con esta tecnología se ha logrado producir hasta 100 libras de tomate por caja (Figura 3).
Figura 2. Niños trabajando en su huerto, cuidando las plantas de tomates

©FAO/TECA

Figura 3. Ilustración del cultivo de tomates en cajas e apoyándose con tutores a fuera

©FAO/TECA

2. Componentes del huerto

2.1 Organización

  • La organización de los padres de familia, maestros y alumnos, estableciendo funciones y responsabilidades para cada miembro de la organización, es fundamental para el desarrollo de capacidades y la sostenibilidad de los huertos.

2.2 Educación

  • Mediante un proceso participativo, los maestros, padres de familia y estudiantes definen el plan curricular de acuerdo a las necesidades de cada escuela.
  • Los conocimientos se transmiten a través de la metodología "aprender haciendo".

2.3 Producción

  • Se define un plan de acción para la producción de vegetales con el propósito de mejorar la disponibilidad de alimentos en forma sostenible.
  • Las tecnologías implementadas son accesibles y con un enfoque de protección del medio ambiente.

2.4 Nutrición

  • Implementar un plan de educación alimentaria y nutricional orientado a enseñar, intensificar o mejorar los conocimientos sobre la alimentación adecuada y variada a fin de reducir la malnutrición.

3. Objetivos de esta práctica

  • Familiarizar a los estudiantes con métodos de producción sostenibles de alimentos que puedan aplicar en sus propios hogares y que sean importantes para la seguridad alimentaria.
  • Promover nuevos hábitos alimenticios y nutricionales en los niños y las niñas.
  • Aumentar la asistencia escolar y promover el sentido de la responsabilidad.
  • Promover la organización comunitaria desde la escuela.

4. Aspectos metodológicos en la implementación de los Huertos Escolares

  • Identificar empresas, instituciones y organismos que patrocinen los Huertos Escolares.
  • Selección de las escuelas cuyas autoridades estén interesadas en el desarrollo de los Huertos Escolares.
  • Promover la organización de los padres de familia, profesores y alumnos para el desarrollo de la actividad.
  • Establecer por escrito las funciones y responsabilidades de cada una de las partes (maestros, alumnos y padres de familia).
  • Por medio de procesos participativos, identificar el plan curricular a desarrollar con los alumnos, maestros y padres de familia.
  • Que las escuelas cuenten con fuente de agua o toma de agua domiciliar.
  • Convenio por escrito entre el representante del ministerio de educación municipal, organismo ejecutor, patrocinadores y dirección de la escuela.
  • Capacitación a profesores o promotores para el establecimiento y manejo de los Huertos Escolares.
  • Asistencia técnica de un extensionista o promotor, mientras dura el proceso de apropiación.

En consecuencia, los Huertos Escolares, como metodología educativa pueden contribuir en el desarrollo de las comunidades, ya que los niños son excelentes agentes multiplicadores y los conocimientos que aplican en conjunto con sus familias, les puede permitir el goce de una mejor calidad de vida.

El Proyecto FAO-INTA-PESA actualmente está fomentando y apoyando exitosamente esta actividad en las zonas rurales del país, específicamente en la zona seca, en los municipios de Somoto, San Lucas, Las Sabanas, San Francisco Libre y en áreas urbanas y periurbanas de Managua.

5. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

6. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Huerto familiar integrado: ID 7221.
  • Módulos pecuarios escolares: ID 6005.
  • Guía para el funcionamiento de huertos escolares: ID 7220.

7. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

7.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

A través de esta práctica se amplía y sensibiliza la conciencia de los estudiantes sobre el medio ambiente, creando una dieta sostenible y saludable.

7.2 Atiende a las necesidades de la mujer

A través de esta medida educativa en las escuelas, todos están incluidos en el proceso de aprendizaje o pueden participar, así como las familias de los estudiantes. Esto contribuye a la reducción de la malnutrición y al manejo responsable de los alimentos.

7.3 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Debido a los Huertos Escolares los estudiantes aprenden la importancia y el valor de la alimentación, que a largo plazo conduce a la seguridad y soberanía alimentaria.
