entries.tittle: Potato Production from True Potato Seed (TPS) for Cold-tolerant and Late Blight Resistant in Nepal
entries.summary:
Potato is a major food crop in the mid-hills and mountains in Nepal. Traditionally, most farmers use small tubers as seed, to grow potato with the minimum input. Although seed tubers are easy to plant and plants grow quickly, they are expensive and may account for more than half of the total production costs. Also, seed tubers are the main carriers of diseases and pests; they are perishable; bulky; and difficult to transport. In addition, seed tubers require costly refrigerated storage facilities to prevent rotting in storage and to keep them in adequate physiological conditions until the next planting season.

Conventional varieties grown by local farmers, such as Kufri, Cardinal, Kufri jyoti, and Kufri Sindhuriare are susceptible to late blight and vulnerable to low temperatures, leading to poor yields. Potato production from True Potato Seed (TPS) is more advantageous than using “seed potatoes”. By planting true potato seeds, farmers maintain genetic diversity that will protect the production from any new pest, disease, or changes in climate or cultural practices.
entries.description:
Description

True potato seeds, or "botanical potato seed" differentiates from "seed potatoes", which are genetically identical clones and produced in large numbers by planting pieces of a potato stem, tuber or through tissue culture.

Conventional varieties in the mid-hill region in Nepal have been found to be vulnerable to foggy weather, cold waves and late blight disease. Hence, farmers have been producing potatoes from TPS seeds from hybrid potato varieties, like HPS 7/67 and HPS 1/13, obtaining yields of about 35 tonne per ha.

1. Potato crops from TPS production

  • In production from TPS, potato crops can be grown in different ways.

1.1 Field sowing

  • Field sowing TPS has potential in areas with mild temperatures, where rainfall is light and evenly distributed during the first five to six weeks after sowing.
    • This permits good germination and seedling establishment in the field.
  • Sowing directly to the furrow often produces inconsistent results.
    • There are ways to facilitate field sowing, such as the use of pelleted seed, fluid drilling and the “ plug mix” methods.
    • With “plug mix”, seed is pre-germinated in a prepared soil mix and sown.
  • Under favourable conditions, good plant emergence from direct sowing of TPS can be achieved.

1.2 Transplanting seedlings to the field

  • Transplanting TPS seedlings to the field has several advantages over direct sowing.
    • First, plants are in the field less time, freeing the land for other uses.
    • Weed competition is also reduced and agronomic practices are simplified.
  • TPS can be sown in trays or ground beds in a nursery.
    • In warm climates, the use of shade in nurseries for 15 to 20 days after sowing helps achieve a more uniform emergence and vigorous seedling growth.
  • Seedling emergence normally occurs between eight to ten days after sowing.
    • Seedlings are thinned a week to ten days after emergence.
  • Approximately 35 days after sowing, the seedlings are ready for transplanting.
  • To reduce shock at transplanting due to adverse conditions, seedlings can be transplanted with soil-covered roots using containers such as compost cubes, banana leaf cups, or thin, plastic trays.
  • This system has promising applications, especially in areas where vegetation production by transplanting is a common practice.
  • When adequate management practices are followed, adapted progenies can yield more than 30 tonne per hectare.

1.3 Planting seed tubers produced from TPS

  • The first generation of tubers produced from seedlings grown from TPS are referred to as “seedling tubers”.
    • This production method combines the advantages of TPC with those of planting seed tubers.
  • Depending upon environmental conditions, seedling tubers will grow in densely sown ground beds or in rows in the field.
  • When properly managed, a nursery bed will yield as many as 800 clean seedling tubers per square meter.
  • Seedling tubers can be used to increase seed tuber quality,
  • Furthermore, tubers can be multiplied to produce additional potatoes for consumption.

2. Steps to implement TPS

  • Any successful true potato seed program must guarantee a reliable supply.
  • Fortunately, TPS can be produced following steps similar to those used to produce many other vegetable crops.

2.1 Pollination

  • Pollination can occur either naturally, or under controlled conditions.
    • If plants are left in the field to set fruits naturally, much of the seed will result from self-pollination.
    • The proportion of out-crossing that occurs is caused primarily by insects.
    • The resulting TPS is termed “open pollinated seed” as only the female parent is known.
  • Seed also can be produced from controlled pollination done by hand.
    • In this case, the TPS is termed “hybrid progeny”.
    • With controlled pollination, pollen from the male parent is placed on the stigma of the flower.
    • This can be done in the field or in the greenhouse under controlled conditions.

2.2 Harvest

  • A few days after pollination, berries will start to develop on the plants.
  • In about 40 days, these berries will be ready for harvesting.
  • Under field conditions, a flowering plant will produce an average of 20 berries.
  • When berries are mature, they are harvested and kept at room temperature until they are soft enough to easily extract the seed.
  • The number of TPS per berry can range from 50 to 500, though the average usually is about 200. One gram contains approximately 1 500 TPS.
Figure 1. Potato production from true potato seed (TPS) for cold-tolerant and late blight resistant in Nepal

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Potato production from true potato seed (TPS) for cold-tolerant and late blight resistant in Nepal

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Storage

  • TPS extracted from the berries is then dried at room temperature in low relative humidity.
  • When kept at room temperature, seed can remain viable for several months up to approximately two years.
  • At 4 °C, TPS can be stored for several years without losing germinability.
  • In both cases, however, low relative humidity during storage is essential.
  • TPS also has a longer dormancy period than tubers.
  • Although it lasts from four to nine months, it can be broken by a simple treatment with gibberellic acid.
  • In Nepal, the TPS seeds are produced from hybrid potato varieties like HPS 7/67 and HPS 1/13.
    • TPS farming is done first by producing small micro-tubers and then by raising seedlings in nursery that are transplanted to the main field adopting the agronomic management practices shown in Table 1.
    • Fertilizers and FYM are applied to the nursery in advance.
    • About 42 kg of small micro-tubers produced from12 m² of nursery will be enough for 1.5 kathha of nursery in the next year.
    • Seedlings produced from micro-tubers (3 000 seedlings / kathha) are transplanted to the main field in ridges or raised beds with proper drainage and irrigation facilities.
    • Thus TPS first and second generation seeds can be produced by farmers and they are transplanted to the main field for eating purposes.
    • Potatoes or TPS seeds produced this way will be free from late blight and other diseases.
    • They can be easily transported from one place to another.
    • On average, 40 to 80 g of TPS small micro-tubers will be enough for producing seedlings enough for potato production in one hectare of land.
    • Nearly 20 quintals of conventional potato seed materials will be needed for one ha of land under normal conditions.
Table 1. Agronomic management practices for TPS farming
Purpose Nursery/main field Size Fertilizer applied Spacing for Planting TPS seeds
Producing micro-tubers Nursery for TPS 1 m wide x 12 m long x 0.1 m high 10 kg compost, 200 g DAP, 150 g urea and 200 g potash 25 cm row, 4-5 cm plant to plant and 5 cm depth
Raising seedling Nursery for micro-tubers 3 000 seedlings/ kathha Nursery covered by cowdung and straw. Fertilizer as above. 3 g per 3 m2.
Transplanting in the main field 20/25 days old seedlings - Normal production practices 60 cm row to row, 20 cm plant to plant, 20 cm high

Source: FAO 2013

3. Technical, economic, financial, social and environmental attributes of the technology

  • Increases efficiency of farm input use.
  • Improves utilization of scarce resources.
  • Produces late blight tolerant crops.
  • Can withstand low temperature and vagaries of cold waves.
  • Produces high yields.

3.1 Factors underlying success

  • Technical know-how of the production technology.
  • Access to and availability of quality and good potato seeds.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool; and
  • temperate, cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Storage of seed potatoes with the Diffused Light Storage (DLS) principle: ID 7379.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

By planting true potato seeds, farmers maintain genetic diversity that will protect the production from any new pest, disease, or changes in climate or cultural practices.

entries.tittle: Multi-Storied Agroforestry Cropping Systems for Micro-Climatic Modification and Erosion Control in Nepal
entries.summary:
Natural hazards such as floods, landslides and drought occur frequently in different parts of Nepal with varying dimensions and magnitude. These hazards constitute the major causes of land degradation and deterioration of natural ecosystems. 

The introduction of a multi-storied agroforestry cropping system ensures the best combination use of crop-tree intercropping to reduce the impacts of floods, landslides and droughts. In addition, multi-storied agro-forestry systems ensure a more even distribution of income and employment throughout the year from harvesting different tree crops in different seasons. 

This variety of agroforestry is characterized by the micro-climatic conditions created by the taller trees that benefit crops underneath. The objective of the technology is to grow the best combination and interface between crops and trees for control of land degradation, increasing system productivity and meeting domestic needs of food, fuel, fodder and timber of rural people.
entries.description:
Description

Multi-storied cropping systems and agroforestry systems help to reduce the impacts of hazards such as floods and droughts that lead to land degradation while meeting the needs of local people for food, firewood, fodder and timber. Under the multi-storied cropping, crops underneath tall trees or horticultural crops withstand shading effects and provide micro-climatic conditions needed by all the crops. This system has at least three layers of intercropped plants of different heights. It is commonly developed by small farmers, as they:

  • plant nurse trees for shade-tolerant crops like coffee and cacao;
  • make productive use of space between and under cash crops;
  • enrich fallows with species like yams; and
  • establish a variety of low input, low maintenance tree crops.

1. Implementation of the practice

Before starting, it is essential to find the best combination possible, for this, ecological and economic planning should be undertaken.

1.1 Ecological planning

For any crop combination, predict how the multi-storied agroforestry system will grow and change over time. Each year, some plants will become less productive, and others will grow and cast additional shade. Key points should be considered in order to plan the development of the multi-storied agroforestry system.

  • The first plants established are adapted to full sunlight.
  • Plants that can give shade are planted before plants that can tolerate or require shade.
  • Plants that enrich the soil are planted before plants that give shade.
  • Plants that require sunlight are not planted where other plants will shade them before they mature.
  • Medium-sized and large trees will have room to grow and will not become too crowded later. Think ahead to the width of the tree’s canopy when it is mature. Consider whether the trees around it will also grow tall and wide, if they will crowd it, they should be harvested or not planted at all.
  • All growing space is used: crops fit together vertically (tall, medium and short), horizontally (all planting spots occupied), and underground (deep-rooted and shallow-rooted plants).

1.2 Economic planning

Any farming system requires planning to diversify products and spread labor and income throughout the year. The first crops planted should provide food or income within three to four months (for example, sweet potato). Choose crops that give both subsistence produce and cash income. Plant trees that bear different fruits at different times of the year. A multi-storied agroforest will change every year for the first several years, with changes in labor requirements and products.

1.3 Steps to implement a multi-stories agroforestry system

1.3.1 Plant nurse trees

Fast-growing nitrogen-fixing trees can be planted first to improve site conditions. This approach is often used for crops like coffee on poor sites, where nurse trees are valued for shade and soil enrichment throughout the life of the coffee crop. Common species suitable for this method are Albizia lebbeck (chres), Gliricidia sepium (snaov), Dalbergia cochinchinensis (kra ngoung), Pterocarpus indicus (thnong) and Acacia mangium.

All of these species have special characteristics in that they:

  • cast a light shade or can be pruned to adjust shade;
  • are nitrogen-fixing;
  • produce timber, fodder or other useful products;
  • are sun-loving; adapted to local climates and soils; and
  • fast-growing.

1.3.2 Intercrop annual crops

Choose an intercrop each planting season that is adapted to current sun or shade conditions. Shade-tolerant under-storey crops include: Ananas cosmosus (pineapple), Capsicum spp. (peppers), Colocasia esculenta (sweet taro), Curcuma domestica (turmeric), Anthurium spp. (flowers), Ipomea batatas (sweet potato), Xanthosoma sagittifolium (dryland taro), Zingiber officinarum (ginger) and mushroom cultures.

1.3.3 Plant shade-tolerant trees

After one year or when the nurse trees provide enough shade, plant shade-tolerant trees. Plant them 3 to 4 m apart, or at the recommended spacing for the tree crop. Plant them 1 to 2 m away from the nurse trees.

1.3.4 Fertilize, prune and weed as for other tree crops

1.3.5 Prune nurse trees

When nurse trees provide too much shade, cut branches and use the leaves as mulch.

1.3.6 Thin trees

Watch for adjacent trees with canopies starting to grow into each other. Watch out for sun-loving trees to make space for healthy or higher – value trees. Be careful not to damage other trees when cutting. The remaining trees will grow faster.

1.3.7 Enrich with other crops

Plant shade-tolerant crops for food and cash income.

Figure 1. Multi-storied agroforestry cropping systems for micro-climatic modification and erosion control in Nepal

©FAO/TECA

2. Example of crop combinations in the mid-hills region in Nepal

Under multi-storied cropping, coffee and pineapple are the major crops being grown as shade-loving crops under tall trees in mid-hills (for example the Arghakhanchi and Udaipur districts). Other crops taken under this system are normally citrus, maize, legumes, vegetables and finger millet for lower altitude. At higher altitudes, crops taken under this system are apple, walnut, maize, beans and finger millet. This multi-storied cropping system will reduce the impacts of hazards like high intensity rainfall, soil erosion and landslides.

Under agroforestry or agro-silvi-pastoral systems, single, double or multiple crop and / or grass species such as single or double crops of maize, millet or grasses are planted between rows of tree species (for example Dalbergia sissoo) under various tree-crop intercropping systems. Some good examples of tree-crop intercropping practiced in the hills are Uttis (Alnus nepalensis) / cardamom, intercropping for more productivity and benefits. Community agroforestry systems implemented and regulated by users' groups are examples for a successful model. Agricultural lands below settlements/forest areas offer good agro-ecosystem by providing leaf litters and organic matter for agricultural production below. Thus both the multi-storied and agroforestry systems lead to efficient utilization of resources, soil conservation, and minimizing risks of crop yield loss thereby increasing household income and employment opportunity.

3. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • Availability of appropriate technology and species combination in the system; and
  • access to various enterprises like firewood, fruits, crop yields and grasses in the system/ownership by the community.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The practice helps reduce the impacts of climate hazards and efficiently uses different types of land and crops pertaining to the season.  

5.2 Pro-poor technology

The practice allows for a more even distribution of income and employment throughout the year.

entries.tittle: Construction of a hurricane-resistant small ruminant shelter, St. Lucia
entries.summary: Saint Lucia as an island in the Southeast Caribbean basin and lies within the hurricane belt. As such, the agriculture sector, among others, is highly affected by the impact of wind storms and hurricanes. In addition, the sector also faces water shortages during the dry season (variable, but typically from January to April/May), a lack of improved forage species for maximizing production, and an unavailability of improved housing for livestock. The construction of a hurricane-resistant small ruminant housing unit incorporates rainwater harvesting and bio-security features, such as the construction of a foot bath, a slatted wooden floor, and a concrete base beneath the pen to facilitate efficient manure handling and disposal. As a result, this technology ensures that small ruminant housing meets adequate construction and safety standards to reduce damage by hurricanes and wind storms and reduce the risk of infection and diseases among animals. Small ruminants are an important livelihood asset for farmers.
entries.description:
Description

Livestock farmers are highly vulnerable to the impact of hurricanes and windstorms, which occur annually. In many cases, the construction of animal structures do not adequately address the material and design requirements to appropriately strengthen these structures so as to minimize the risks and losses to the farmer. Many structures are highly exposed to storm surges and high winds, because farmers may not have sought the necessary technical advice before constructing the structures. In addition the availability of finance may be a constraint for appropriate construction.

This intervention facilitated the construction of an affordable, simple and practical small ruminant housing unit which incorporates design features which seek to minimize structural damage resulting from strong winds, disease risks and to provide facilities for rain water harvesting and storage. The installment of hurricane clamps and bolts, which are a part of the design features, help to reinforce the roofs and foundations of their structures or existing structures can also be retrofitted.

1. Implementation of the technology

1.1 Implementation steps

  • A site is selected on gently sloping land preferably to allow escavation of the upper portion of the slope and levelling to allow for sufficient headroom to stand comfortably below the unit after it has been constructed.
    • This allows for adequate drainage and minimize the incidence of flooding.
  • The building is oriented such that the longest side is located in an east to west direction to allow the free circulation of the prevailing winds which generally blow in a north easterly direction.
  • The ground is escavated with a gentle slope such that the columns toward upper end of the slope are approximately 3 feet high while the columns at the lower end of the slope are 5 to 6 feet high to allow adequate headroom belowed the slatted floor pen for easy cleaning and disinfecting (Figure 3).
  • The foundation beams are securely fastened onto the concrete columns with bent ½ inch steel and reinforced with metal hurricane clamps.
  • The superstructure is constructed using rough pressure treated commercially available lumber or local timber cut to specified sizes for various parts of the building.
  • A wooden ramp is constructed at the entrance of the building to facilitate easy entry and exit of the animals to and from the building.
Figure 1. Construction of a hurricane-resistant ruminant shelter

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Building design features include

  • 126 sq. ft. area (9 ft. long x 14 ft. wide) to house 6 ewes or does in maternity size pens.
  • Slatted floor design to facilitate easy cleaning and disinfecting.
  • Concrete slab below facilitates ease of manure collection for composting, cleaning and disinfection to eliminate odours and flies.
  • Proper ventilation and reduced wind resistance.
  • Roofing clamps and screws to securely bolt down the roof (see below on how to install them).
  • Secure foundation anchoring.
  • Water collection apparatus (guttering, down pipes, etc.).
  • Built-in feeders to allow easy feeding of grass and concentrates.
  • Construction of a ramp to allow animals easy access into and out of the structure.
Figure 2. Construction of a hurricane-resistant ruminant shelter

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Tools and equipment required for installing the hurricane clamps on farm buildings

  • Screwdriver (manual application) or electrical drill with tip (mechanical application).
  • Step ladder or regular adjustable ladder.
  • Hurricane clamps and screws.
Figure 3. Construction of a hurricane-resistant ruminant shelter

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Maintenance

  • Routine checks to ensure that the structural integrity of the building is kept.

  • Ensure proper drainage around and beneath the structure to ensure running water does not undermine its structural integrity.

  • Regular checks on guttering down-pipes and clamps are required.

Figure 4. Hurricane-resistant small ruminant housing

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Housing elevation and slope excavation

©FAO/TECA

2. Cost estimate

  • EC$ 8 000 for materials.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Construction of a concrete floor and foot bath within an existing poultry pen to reduce the risk of infection and disease in poultry: ID 7741.
  • Training videos for family poultry production: ID 8148.
  • Women resurrecting poultry biodiversity and livelihoods: ID 7681.
  • Making modern poultry markets work for the poor: ID 7678.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology protects small ruminants by constructing hurricane-resistant shelters, which also minimizes diseases risks and allows rainwater harvesting from the buildings themselves.

  • Valmont, V. A. 2011. Disaster risk mitigation – Livestock. Final project report. Enhanced Capacities for Disaster Risk Mitigation in Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (TCP/STL/3202) St. Lucia.

entries.tittle: Diversifying risk exposure to reduce impacts of typhoons through squid pot fishing, Philippines
entries.summary: Squid pot, locally known as “bubo pangnokos”, is a regular receptacle device mainly to catch squid in coastal waters. The shape of the gear is semi-cylindrical and is generally made of polyethylene netting mounted on a bamboo frame. It is provided with a non-return valve, which allows easy entrance but a difficult exit. The device is baited with squid roe mounted on young coconut leaves, place inside the pot. It is hung on a bamboo buoy and anchored on depths of 8 to 15 fathoms in such a way that it lies midway of the water depth.
entries.description:
Description

1. Implementation of the technology

  • The ideal fishing ground is an area with a dense concentration of seagrass/seaweed beds and near coral reef at depths of 8 to 15 fathoms.
  • The presence of squid eggs in the area is the best practical indication that the area is suitable for the gear.
  • Observation has shown that catch regardless of the month is greater during days just after the first quarter phase of the moon going to full moon.

1.1 Material requirements for the construction of three semi-cylindrical types of squid pot

  • Polyethylene (PE) Net, green, 400/12 x 7K, 100 MD: 3.7 m.
  • Monofilaments nylon line # 30 lbs: 200 g.
  • Common nails # 1” & 1.5”(assorted size): quarter kg.
  • Whole length bamboo: 4 pcs 100/pc.
  • Poly rope #14 (7 mm): 45 m.
  • Poly rope #12 (6 mm): 32 m.
  • Knife/NT Cutter: one unit.
  • Knitting needle (6” long): one unit.
  • Steel tape/meter stick: one unit.
  • Crosscut saw bolo: one unit.

1.2 Construction method

  • The design of squid pot varies per locality but the emphasis of this method is on the construction of the semi-cylindrical type of squid pot.

1.2.1 First step

  • Prepare and cut the following bamboo measurements to serve as frames (I unit).
    • 8 pcs 46” long x 2” wide.
    • 4 pcs 32” long x 2” wide.
    • 4 pcs 34” long x 2” wide.
    • 4 pcs 70” long x 1,5” wide.
    • 32 pcs 11” long x 0.5” wide.

1.2.2 Second step

  • Assemble the rectangular base by nailing and tying with mono-nylon line # 30.

1.2.3 Third step

  • Assemble the body frame.

1.2.4 Fourth step

  • Cut the P.E. netting 400/12 x 7K x 72 meshes (3.7 m long) x 26 meshes down for the main body covering and two pieces 18 meshes x 18 meshes as side cover.
  • Then attach by lacing the main body covering starting from the edge of the mouth entrance all around the pot using mono-nylon line #30.
  • Cut the net covering the entrance part.
  • Attach by lacing the side cover.
Figure 1. Hands-on squid pot construction

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Preparation for operation (pre-setting)

  • Make an opening/slit on one side of the body, seven meshes a few inches from the base for easier bailing of catch.
  • Insert a young coconut fruit stalk through the slit and tie it vertically at the centre of the pot, then put squid egg.
    • Then close the slit by lacing with mono-nylon line#30.
  • Tie a 12 feet poly rope #12 to the pot to provide balance when hung.

1.4 Hauling operation

  • Hauling of the squid pot should be done once a day by simply pulling the hanging line until the squid pot emerges and is hauled on board with the aid of a hook attached to a bamboo pole or a hook tied with rope.
  • The operation is done with the help of a diver.
  • The catch is then bailed out.
  • The squid pot should be thoroughly washed to remove debris before dropping it back into the water.

1.5 Care and maintenance

  • Choosing the best materials and design of the gear is not enough to make it effective and efficient.
  • Proper care and maintenance should also be undertaken to retain its efficiency and to prolong its life span.
  • Common damage to the squid pot is the fouling of frames and netting.
  • Rotten frames should be replaced and torn nettings should be mended immediately.
  • Brushing with a broom daily prevents the attachment of barnacles to the units and maintains their efficiency since squids love the colour green.

2. Results and findings

  • Squid pot performance reported a harvest ranging from 2.5 kg to 45 kg per hauling that easily sells at PHP 150.00 per kg (in 2011).
  • This encouraged some farmers to build another unit of squid pots to add to the one crafted with the project.
  • The performance, however, depends largely on the site where they are installed as well as the season of the year that influences water current patterns and wave action.
  • It was observed that the fish catch was greater during days after the first quarter phase before the full moon.
  • Based on the farmer experiences, seaweed farming and squid pot can be integrated into a complementing system such that seaweed cultivation lines can serve as squid habitat.
  • This can diversify the harvest and maximize time, labour and expenses and increase overall productivity.
  • With squid pot and seaweed farms in the coastal waters, illegal and destructive fishing methods are minimized for several reasons.
  • Since this option can provide food and additional income opportunities with small start-up capital, farmers will surely protect and guard their farm (livelihood) against the harm of illegal fishing (e.g. the use of cyanide directly affect seaweeds).
Figure 2. Diversifying risk exposure to reduce impacts of typhoons through squid pot fishing, Philippines

©FAO/TECA

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Cost-benefit analysis of using fish pots versus bottom set longlines in the Philippines based on field testing: ID 8939.
  • Beje aquaculture and inland fishery in tropical peatland of Indonesia: ID 8619.
  • Assessing post-harvest fish losses: load tracking method: ID 4437.
  • Management of fish in the pond: ID 7235.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for the efficient catching of squid using organic materials in coastal waters.
entries.further_reading:
6. Further reading

  • FAO. 2011. Implementation guidelines for DRR good practice options for fisheries and aquaculture-Technical paper prepared for project TCP/PHI/3203 (D).

entries.tittle: Use of Early-Maturing Rice Variety (EMRV) to Reduce Typhoon Impacts in Bicol Region, Philippines
entries.summary:
The Philippines is among the most disaster prone countries in the world. More than 200 climate-related natural disasters were recorded in the last two decades. Alone in 2011 the country was hit by 33 disasters, claiming 1 430 lives. Typhoons trigger landslides, flashfloods, mudslides, widespread flooding, and cause significant destruction and damages. Agriculture is the sector most affected by tropical cyclones, causing a decline in production and productivity which can threaten the country's food security. The use of early-maturing rice varieties (EMRV) was tested to improve the production of transplanted rice in typhoon-prone Bicol region. EMRVs can improve food security, reduce farmers’ vulnerability from adverse climatic events during the months of June to December (wet season cropping), and prevent high production loss due to damages to standing rice crops brought on by typhoons.
In combination with other methods (e.g. timing of planting), this technology aims to facilitate environmental adaptation for cultivation and to contribute to food and economic security in the region by reducing crop losses in typhoon prone areas.
entries.description:
Description

Rice is the staple food of Filipinos and Bicolanos. Rice farmers in Bicol usually grow two mono crops of transplanted rice, first crop cycle (June to October) and second crop cycle (December to April). Due to climate variability, climate change, and other environmental changes, rice cultivation (especially in the typhoon prone area) is facing increasing challenges, particularly when harvest time coincides with the typhoon months from October to December. Particularly long-maturing rice varieties in Bicol are prone to the impacts of typhoons. Planting early-maturing varieties contributes to reducing harvest and post-harvest losses and increases food security in the area. The introduction of appropriate rice varieties is considered a crucial adaptation option for farming communities in the region.

This technology was promoted in nine municipalities (Igbac, San Ramon, San Buena, Mauraro, Masarawag, Minto, Ariman, Bagacay and Rizal) between June and October 2010 and March 2011, in lowland irrigated farming systems in the Philippines.

1. Implementation of the technology

  • This technology is suitable for farmers with about 1 000 m2 of land for the cultivation.

1.1 Land preparation

  • The land should be well prepared by ploughing and harrowing three to four times.
    • For sandy loam to silty loam soil, two to three ploughing and cross ploughing with subsequent three to four laddering is required.
    • For a clay type of soil, soil preparation requires more tillage operation at appropriate soil moisture status.

1.2 Fertilizer dose

  • Apply fertilizer in appropriate dose (90 kg N per ha) as illustrated in Table 1.
  • Apply half of the urea 15 to 20 days by using the broadcast method.
  • Top dress the remaining half after attaining four to five tillers per hill and a second time before five to seven days of the dough stage.
Table 1. Fertilizer dose per pit for rice cultivation
Name of fertilizer Quantity per 1 000 m2
Urea or equivalent vol. of manure 19.5 kg
Trichoderma Two packets

Source: PhilRice-DA-5

1.3 Seedling, sowing and spacing

  • The rice varieties used are NSIC Rc-120, NSIC Rc-192 and the line IR 60.
  • Seeds should be sown in medium high land near the main field.
  • Before seed sowing the organic matter and other nutrient should be ensured.
  • The appropriate time to sow seeds is 10 to 12 days before transplanting.
  • Seed rate is 4 to 5 kg in nursery seedbed for transplanting on 1 000 m² of main field and in case of line sowing.
    • Spacing should be 20 cm x 20 cm.

1.4 Irrigation, weeding and harvesting

  • The rice field should not be submerged with water all the time.
  • Irrigation is applied to maintain a schedule as described in the PhilRice-DA manual.
  • Between two irrigations, a three days dry period should be maintained.
  • Before top dressing of fertilizer, the crop field must be without irrigation water.
  • As needed, use rotary or hand weeding.
  • While the 80 percent of the crop is matured, the harvesting can be initiated.

2. Results and findings

  • The costs of the demonstration site amounts around 2 340 PHP (in 2010) including seeds, fertilizer, sign board, register and soil testing.
  • The first crop cycle field demonstrations on EMRV (e.g. NSIC Rc-120; IR-60, NSIC 192) were established during the middle part of July 2010 in Bagacay (Sorsogon) and in August 2010 in San Ramon and Igbac (Buhi CamSur).
  • At this time of year in 2010, the El Niño phenomenon (less precipitation) was felt in the whole Bicol region.
  • About 50 percent of the farmers in Sorsogon were unable to cultivate their wet season rice crop.
  • In spite of this, seven farmers San Ramon risked planting the early-maturing rice varieties IR-60, and NSIC Rc-120 in Ariman, and Bagacay, Sorsogon.
  • Although both varieties performed well, NSIC Rc-120 seems more sensitive for abnormal rainfall conditions.
  • Statistical analysis of testing the new practice, and farmers’ variety performance indicate a significant difference in the days of planting to harvest.
  • The early-maturing rice varieties field-tested were harvested 3.08 months or 92.4 days after transplanting, while Binatang was harvested after 3.62 months or 108.6 days.
  • In spite of a month delay in crop establishment, the newly tested varieties (IR-60, NSIC Rc-192) were harvested five days ahead of the existing farmers’ variety, and still produced yield comparable with the farmers’ variety.
  • With early-maturing rice varieties, farmers were able to harvest additional yield of 375 kg per ha.
  • This production increase is equivalent to 4.5 cavans (one cavans equivalent to ca. 50 kg) of milled rice as food for the farming household during adverse climatic conditions.
  • If the additional yield is sold as fresh rice, it provides an emergency fund equivalent to PHP 4 500 per ha (2010).
  • This technology is a good option for both during typhoon months and dry season.
  • The use of short-duration rice variety can increase farmers’ resilience to climate variability because it reduces the risk of post-harvest losses, as crop exposure to impending climate hazards is shortened.
  • It enhances farmers’ preparedness and access to available food, as farmers would have enough food stored in times of adverse climatic conditions.
Table 2. Yield (tonnes per ha) performance of early-maturing rice variety (GPO) vs. existing farmers variety (EFV) for 3 crop cycles, 2010 to 2011
Location 1st crop cycle (Yield (t/ha)) 2nd crop cycle (Yield (t/ha))
3rd crop cycle (Yield (t/ha))		 Average yield (Yield (t/ha))
GPO EFV GPO EFV GPO EFV GPO EFV
Buhi, Cam sur 4.2 3.9 3.16 1.76 3.35 3.7 3.57 3.12
Gubat, Sorsogon 2.9 2.3 4.5 3.9 3.3 2.3 3.56 2.83
Guinobatan, Albay 2.7 2.2 3.5 2.7 3.25 2.1 3.15 2.33
Average yield (Yield (t/ha)) 3.3 2.8 3.72 2.78 3.3 2.7 3.43 2.76

Source: PhilRice-DA-5

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Participatory varietal selection: improved rice varieties: ID 4459.
  • Rice transplanting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7214.
  • Rice seed sorting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7205.
  • Improving rice quality: video from Africa Rice Center: ID 6976.
  • Aerobic rice: ID 7941.
  • Intensive rice cultivation: ID 7666.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The planting of early-maturing varieties contributes to reducing harvest and post-harvest losses and increases the food security in the area.

6. Further reading

  • De La Torre. 2010. Detailed Implementation Guidelines, GPOs Lowland Irrigated Agro-Eco Zone.
  • Report for TCP PHI 3203 Philippine Rice Research Institute.
  • Philippine Rice Research Institute.

entries.tittle: Construction of a Concrete Floor and Foot Bath within an Existing Poultry Pen to Reduce the Risk of Infection and Disease in Poultry, St. Lucia
entries.summary: Poultry reared on dirt floors with deep litter, particularly when the litter gets wet, are predisposed to fungal infections, such as aspergillosis and other protozoan diseases, such as avian coccidiosis. The litter within most poultry pens with dirt floors poses a management challenge, since leaking or faulty waterers allow soaking of the litter. This provides an excellent medium for the growth of fungus, such as moulds, mildew and spore producing fungus. Routine turning of the litter at least two to three times per week on a concrete base floor allows for ease of drying due to better surface aeration than on an earthen floor. The objective of this practice is to protect poultry, which is an important livelihood asset for farmers. Through the construction of a damp-free environment, the risk of diseases, such as coccidiosis and helminthosis, from improper litter management, including improper disinfecting of poultry pens, is reduced and as a result the number of healthy birds is increased. This allows the farmers to generate income and contribute to people’s livelihoods and food security.
entries.description:
Description

Traditionally, poultry production (both broiler and layer), has played an integral role in small farming systems and for food security throughout rural and suburban communities in Saint Lucia. The Ministry of Agriculture has, over the years, given tremendous support to poultry production and marketing systems and has assisted in strengthening existing farmer associations and processing initiatives for the sector. With increasing intensification, the production of healthy stock for the market and the enhancement of bio-security protocols and disease mitigation systems have been compromised on many farms. In order to address this situation, a concrete damp-proof floor was constructed to facilitate proper litter management and reduce disease threats.

1. Implementation of the technology

1.1 Concrete floor construction

  • Wet the entire existing earthen floor of the broiler pen and compress with a compactor or manual compacting tool before laying down the plastic damp proofing.
  • Damp proofing material should be laid down over the expanse of a compacted earthen floor before laying down a concrete slab measuring 40 ft wide by 100 ft long.
  • The floor area should preferably be of concrete slab, (2.5 to 3 inches; 6.4 to 7.6 cm) thick, allowing easy cleaning and disinfecting.
    • The slab should be built using ready mixed (half inch stone and sand aggregate) and Portland cement.
  • For good litter air flow, a floor depth of 8 to 10 inches (20.3 cm x 25.4 cm) is recommended.
Figure 1. Concrete floor

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Footbath construction

  • On the existing apron of a broiler house before the entrance door, measure the width of the door and prepare a wooden formwork to construct a footbath measuring 2 to 3 inches high by 4 to 5 feet wide by 3 to 5 feet wide.
  • Place a small piece of three-quarter-inch PVC pipe, about one foot long, at the lower end of the footbath.
    • Render the base of the footbath so that the concrete base slopes toward the opening of pipe on the inner part of the footbath.
    • The outer portion of the drainpipe is fitted with a valve to allow for drainage and cleaning of the footbath before changing the disinfectant solution.
    • Simple household bleach can be used as a disinfectant solution.
  • Material and labour cost for the construction of a simple footbath measuring 3 inches high by 4 feet long by 2 feet wide is approximately EC$ 150 (USD 1.00 = EC$ 2.70).
Figure 2. Concrete floor with a footbath

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Footbath showing drain plug

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Inline waterer

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Maintenance

  • The flooring should be checked periodically for cracks and surface problems which may encourage water seepage.
  • Repairs should be done on a timely basis.

1.4 Cost estimate

  • A total of 4 000 square feet of floor space is required for 4 000 broilers.
  • EC$ 7 000 (USD 1.00 = EC$ 2.70) inclusive of materials is required for the construction of a 4 000 square foot pen.
  • The cost required for laying down a concrete floor within a layer pen to house 4 000 birds would be three times as high since the square footage required for layers is 3 square feet per bird.
  • Transportation costs for material for the construction of a 4 000 square feet concrete floor for housing broilers was approximately EC$ 1 500.
  • However this cost would vary based on the local situation.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Construction of a hurricane-resistant small ruminant shelter: ID 7740.
  • Training videos for family poultry production: ID 8148.
  • Women resurrecting poultry biodiversity and livelihoods: ID 7681.
  • Making modern poultry markets work for the poor: ID 7678.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

By efficiently constructing damp-free environments and correct management, technology reduces poultry diseases.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology, through improved poultry protection, generates income and contributes to people's livelihoods and food security.

entries.tittle: Enhancing climate resilience through cultivation of rambutan for forest enrichment, Philippines
entries.summary:
For disaster-prone countries like the Philippines affected by landslides, mudslides and widespread flooding, forest enrichment is a good practice option, especially for mountainous regions, to enhance resilience to climate change and livelihood security. Cultivation of Rambutan for forest enrichment addresses slow on setting climate change impacts. The practice has co-benefits to reduce the risk and impact of climate variability and extreme weather events with additional potential to contribute to mitigation by reducing emissions and enhancing carbon sinks. Rambutan is indigenous to the Malay Archipelago and has been widely cultivated throughout the region in Thailand, South Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines, India and Sri Lanka.

Planting Rambutan is a forest management strategy to improve the present stock of a logged-over forest to improve the density, volume and species composition using high value producing fruit trees species. Forest enrichment through the planting of Rambutan increases resilience to drought, heavy rainfall,  pest and disease impacts; serves as a source of additional income and optimizes the use of idle lots/plots as well as nearby forest areas with low vegetation cover. Enrichment planting can be successfully used to increase the value of secondary forests and prevent their conversion to other land uses, thus reducing deforestation. Additionally, it helps to stabilize slopes and therewith reduce damages through erosion after heavy rainfall. While reducing the pressure on the forest ecosystem, Rambutan is a high-value fruit tree with promising economic returns.
entries.description:
Description

This practice was tested as part of the project “Enhanced Climate Change Adaptation Capacity of Communities in Contiguous Fragile Ecosystems in the Cordilleras” (2009 to 2011) between August 2010 and December 2011. Through active participation and involvement of local stakeholders and end-users in both training and field demonstration activities, the project identified forest enrichment as a location-specific and appropriate option for climate change. The GPO was tested in the municipality of Kiangan located in the province of Ifugao, the Philippines during the wet and dry seasons of 2010 and 2011.

Rambutan is a medium-sized tree producing a round to oval-shaped fruit. The fruit is red or yellow in color and has hairs or tubercles on its skin. The flesh or aril is translucent and sweet. Most Rambutan trees propagated from seed are not true-to-type and the fruit is usually sour. In the Philippines, the Rambutan has a small crop from June to July and a main crop from November to January. Selected clones produce thick, firm flesh, which is sweet.

1. Implementation of the technology

Rambutan typically thrives within 17 degrees from the equator. Since Rambutan trees are often found in the lower or middle storey of various primary and secondary forests, the field-testing of this CCA option followed similar vertical stratification. The standard biophysical limits of Rambutan include an elevation of 0 to 600 m above sea level; average annual temperature of 22 to 35 ºC; and an average annual rainfall of 2 000 to 3 000 mm. Rambutan is also said to prefer clay loam soil with a pH range of 5 to 6.5. It can also grow in various soil types as long as these are not water-logged.

1.1 Planting and Maintenance

  • Remove the plastic bag and plant the seedling into prepared hole without breaking the ball of soil. Cover the hole with topsoil and press gently.
  • Provide shade to the newly planted Rambutan seedlings for a period of two weeks to a few months depending on the weather condition to enable the plant to recover from transplanting shock and to shade it from strong sunlight. Ring weed quarterly or as the need arises. Pest and disease incidences must be observed and regularly checked before they become uncontrollable.
  • Apply basally, 60 g (6 tbsp) of complete fertilizer (14-14-14) or based on soil analysis and cover with a thin layer of soil. The rate of application increases as the tree grows bigger (Table 1).
Table 1. Fertilizer application

Fertilizer

2nd year

3rd year

4th year

Complete

200 g per tree

300 g per tree

400 g per tree

14-14-14

 

 

 

Source: FAO 2013

1.2 Harvesting

Harvest Rambutan fruit when the skin is pinkish-red. Rambutan fruit does not ripen at the same time even within a bunch and this necessitates harvesting by priming. A harvesting schedule in a moderately sized orchard (200 to 300 trees) consists of harvesting three times a week during the peak of the season.

2. Results and findings

Cooperators of the agroforestry and forest enrichment were given seedlings of Rambutan, which were raised and propagated in vacant woodlots; dried rice fields converted into fruit orchards; and along steep and highly erodible slopes of mountains.

Table 2. Technological suitability

Source: FAO 2013

3. Economic benefits, social and cultural acceptability and farmers feedback

Interviews with the cooperators revealed that economic returns over-ride the significance of the agroforestry and forest enrichment technology to mitigate the impact of climate change on the livelihood and immediate environment of the households.

The cooperators; however, are aware of the interrelatedness of protecting the communal forest with their rice land and swiddens. The GPO provided them the initiative to enhance existing practices of growing fruit trees on idle lands with greater interest being made aware of the environmental services that they could have in the long run. The cooperators are willing to invest in the seedlings and allocate time to protect their livelihood while at the same time attain some degree of assurance of stable income in the next 5 to 25 years.

Estimated additional income which can augment household needs ranges from PHP 1 200 to PHP 15 000, depending on the number of fruits propagated and land area.

The propagation of the new variety of fruit trees spurred interest in the community anticipating long-term economic gains in the long run. Communal forest ownership remains strong and encourages greater participation.

In the Filipino context, the propagation of new variety of fruit trees spurred interest in the community anticipating long-term economic gains in the long run. Communal forest ownership remains strong and encourages greater participation.

3.1 Replication and upscaling

This practice is highly recommended for upscaling, with training and technical assistance from the Department of Agriculture and the Municipal Agricultural Office. Agroforestry and forest enrichment must be integrated with small-scale infrastructure support such as water impoundments and storage and soil enrichment. Support across the value chain should also be provided to the farmers.

Figure 1. Map of project sites. Red areas are high elevation, white areas are middle elevation and green areas are low elevation

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. A farmer cooperator in Kiangan, Ifugao shows to agricultural technicians the Rambutan seedlings that he has planted and identifies the various middle and lower storey tree species in the demonstration area

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency 

The practice of forest enrichment Rambutan planting increases resilience to climate impacts, optimizes the use of areas with low vegetation cover and prevents the conversion of forests into other land usages, reducing deforestation and soil erosion

5.2 Pro-poor technology

The Rambutan's high-value fruit provides an additional source of income.

entries.tittle: Soil and water conservation practices to reduce soil erosion and enhance water conservation, Saint. Lucia
entries.summary:
The island of Saint Lucia is a small island developing country in the Caribbean. The country’s development strategies try to balance economic development and environmental conservation. One of the key challenges for agriculture is land degradation as well as drought- like conditions in some parts of the island. Due to natural climate patterns in the Eastern Caribbean the island has an annual dry season usually lasting from January to April/May, with some annual variation. During the dry season water shortages regularly increase regularly and threaten cropping under rain fed conditions. Particularly in the hilly areas of St Lucia with steep slopes, which are often used as farmlands, there is a strong need for systemic conservation of water, and reduction of soil erosion. Integrated soil and water conservation practices are therefore key. The installation of an up hill water tank on a cemented platform, combined with roof water collection, controlled gravity irrigation, and the establishment of counter stone bunds, and mulching created a very successful combination of farming practices to counteract exposure to drought and dry spells. It further helped to reduce water runoff and soil losses, while conserving soil moisture on the farm plot. The package was demonstrated under the an FAO project ‘Enhanced capacities for disaster risk management in agriculture, fisheries and forestry’ (TCP/SLT/3202), which was implemented for DRR in Agriculture in from 2009- to 2011. It demonstrated that, if managed well, sufficient water can be conserved during the rainy season to allow an additional cropping cycle in the dry season, thereby increasing income and contributing to people’s livelihoods. This integrated technology package aims at producing an additional harvest during the dry season through a combination of on-farm rainwater harvesting, controlled water use, contour stone bunds and mulching. This together enhances water use efficiency, improves soil moisture and reduces soil losses. An additional crop cycle significantly enhances annual farm income.

This technology is also available in: Spanish (ID8689)
entries.description:
Description

Soil and water conservation are very important for Saint Lucia’s rainfed agriculture given the island’s climatic conditions with a clearly marked dry season and its strongly accentuated topographic patterns with steep slopes including for agriculture. In order to ease farming at steep slopes and to make it environmentally sustainable, integrated soil and water conservation practices are needed.

1. Implementation of the technology package

  • Implementation is based on water collection and tanks, stone bunds, and mulching.

1.1 Water collection and tank

  • Rainwater was harvested into a 30 000 gallon tank collected from a shed 20 ft long by 20 ft wide.
    • The tank, which sits on land (upper end of the farm) with a 15 to 20 percent slope, which will through gravity be used to irrigate farmland of about 50 m x 50 m.

1.1.1 Material and tools needed

  • For the installation of a tank on a cemented platform on top of the farm, the following tools and materials are needed:
    • one water tank (30 000 gallons)
    • cement; 
    • ready mix (half stone and sand aggregate, half steel and welded wire mesh); and 
    • eight-inch concrete blocks.
  • The type and size of the tank and how it is installed will depend on the local situation.
    • In our situation, a tank measuring 26.4 ft (8.06 m) in diameter by 20 ft high to hold 30 000 gallons of water was utilised.
    • The tank is a galvanized tank, and it was assembled by screwing the sheets together until the required height was reached (Figures 1 and 2).
    • A plastic liner was placed in the tank to collect water (Figure 2).
    • Two pipes emerge from the base of the tank; one, a drainpipe, and the other connects to the irrigation system.
Figure 1. The galvanized tank is assembled by screwing sheets together until the required height is reached

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. A plastic liner is placed in the tank to collect water

©FAO/TECA

  • Initially, part of the slab (cemented surface) was cast on a frame using reinforced 8-inch blocks, after the frame was backfilled and compacted.
    • However, the pressure exerted on the structure had created some cracks.
  • Given the weight of water (1 gal = 8.34 lbs; 30 000 gals = 250 200 lbs) it is imperative that the tank should sit on solid level ground, meaning that the slab on which the tank would sit should be laid on solid level ground.
    • Some excavation was done using a backhoe (or other types of heavy excavation equipment) to ensure that solid level ground was obtained and part of the tank sits on the solid rock surface while a part is on the slab.
    • Ideally, the slab should sit on the entire solid rock surface.
    • The slab prepared is 30 ft by 30 ft and is about 7 inches thick.
    • The slab was prepared using ready-mix (half stone and sand aggregate) and Portland cement reinforced with BRC (welded wire mesh) and half steel.
  • Figure 3 shows the previous rainwater harvesting system, which is comprised of a number of 50-gallon drums for harvesting rainwater from a small shed on the farm.
  • The system now erected consists of a larger and improved shed with a better guttering system moving water to a 30 000 gallon tank (Figure 4).
Figure 3. The previous rainwater harvesting system was comprised of a number of 50-gallon drums

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. The modern rainwater harvesting system

©FAO/TECA

1.1.2 Maintenance

  • Stone terraces have to be maintained, and damaged due terrain and have to be repaired to prevent further damage from the subsequent downhill movement of water.
  • The tank should be checked periodically to ensure debris does not collect and the tank slab should also be checked periodically for structural integrity.

1.2 Stone bunds

  • The stone bunds are prepared by using A-frames lines, which are demarcated along contour lines.
  • Boulders, stones and cobbles are collected from the surface of the land and carried towards the demarcated lines.
    • Larger stones are used to make a simple foundation in a shallow trench (5 cm to 10 cm deep), and smaller stones are put on top of the constructed wall.
    • The smaller stones on the higher side act as filters.
    • Bunds should more or less follow the contour and the literature recommends that the distance between bunds should be about 10 m to 30 m apart.
    • The recommended height of bunds is about 25 cm on average but can range between 15 cm to 30 cm.
    • Some literature recommends a maximum height of 60 cm and bunds/walls of a higher dimension are possible.
      • In the Saint Lucian context, bund height was approximately 30 cm and provision was made to raise the height as the silt level gets to the edge of bund.
      • Figure 6 shows some 50 ft of contour stone bunds. The practice of laying stone bunds will continue as required and mulching will be established as an on-going best practice.
Figure 5. A stone bund 

©Kome et al., 2003

Figure 6. Laid stone bunds

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Mulching

  • Mulching is a layer of usually organic material applied to the surface of an area of soil.
  • The generic purposes of mulching are:
    • conserving moisture by reducing evaporation;
    • improving the fertility and health of the soil; and
    • reducing weed growth.
  • In this context lemongrass, was cut and used as mulching material since it was planted close by.
    • The lemongrass, in this case, fulfilled a double function in that it also helps to fix the soils around the bunds and drainage canals given its strong root system.
    • In addition, it has an economic value as tea and has medicinal properties.
      • Figure 7 shows several beds that have been mulched.
Figure 7. Mulching in practice

©FAO/TECA

2. Benefits

  • The overarching economic benefit of the technology package was that it almost doubled farm income through one additional harvest during the dry season when selling prices are high.
  • With the expected economic gains, the farmer plans to further improve the efficiency of dry season water management by installing drip irrigation along the terraces and stone bunds.
  • Environmental and crop production-related benefits include, in particular, that the construction of stone walls creates a physical barrier on the surface of steep slopes and reduces soil erosion and overland flow.
    • Because the bunds are permeable, they do not pond runoff water, but slow down its speed, filter it, and spread the water over the field, thus enhancing water infiltration and reducing soil erosion.
    • Silt trapped on the higher side of the barrier forms natural terraces.
    • The deposition process can be started by moving soil downslope and depositing it behind the stone wall.
      • This is welcoming as the slope gradient of the alleys between the walls is reduced.
      • Over a number of years, it is intended also to enhance soil fertility and consequently crop yield.
    • An additional important benefit is that due to the removal of surface stones, boulders and cobbles the land becomes easier to work for the farmer and will require less labour during plowing, tilling and sowing.
  • Mulching enhances farming efficiency by:
    • reducing soil loss;
    • decreasing the impact of raindrops because of the crop residues on the ground;
    • slowing down the flow of water over the soil surface; and
    • increases the infiltration rate since pores are not blocked through surface scaling by soil particles or crusting.
  • Mulching also encourages soil animal (insects and worms) activities, which improves soil structure and increases permeability.
  • The reduction of soil losses achieved with mulching and the increased water availability with measures presented in this document have a positive impact on the resilience of Saint Lucia´s farmers against natural hazards such as cyclones and droughts.
  • In the long run, the improvement of soil quality should have a positive effect on crop yields, and subsequently, in food and income security.

3. Cost estimate

  • The total estimated cost is EC$ 45 000.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Strategies for improved soil and water conservation practices in hillside production systems: ID 4469.

This technology is also available in Spanish: ID 8689.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

This is achieved through improved rainwater harvesting, controlled water use, contour stone bunds and mulching. These enhance water use efficiency, improves soil moisture losses.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

Through an additional crop cycle, the annual farm income enhances.

7. Further reading

  • Anschütz, J., Kome, A., Nederlof, M., De Neef, R., Van de Ven, T. 2003. Agrodok 13: Water harvesting and soil moisture retention. Wageningen: Agromisa Foundation.

entries.tittle: Improved fallows in Kenya
entries.summary:
Natural fallow is land resting from cultivation, usually used for grazing or left to natural vegetation for a long period to restore soil fertility lost from growing crops. Improved fallow is also land resting from cultivation but the vegetation comprises planted and managed species of leguminous trees, shrubs and herbaceous cover crops. These cover crops rapidly replenish soil fertility in one or at most two growing seasons. They shorten the time required to restore soil fertility; they help to improve farmland productivity because the plant vegetation that follows them is superior in quality; and they increase the range of outputs, because the woody fallow species can also produce fuel wood and stakes.

This practice aims to describe how to establish and manage improved fallow as an innovative agroforestry technology that can meet the different needs of the farmers and improve the natural resource base. It is intended to serve as a useful guide for extension staff, non-governmental organizations, community-based organizations and farmers.
entries.description:
Description

In western Kenya, farmers are using improved fallows to build up soil fertility. Fallows can be single species or mixed species. A single-species fallow is established with only one plant species in the whole field. Typically, this system is recommended for species that grow fast and develop dense canopies that shade and kill weeds. Such species are Crotalaria grahamiana, Crotalaria paulina and Colopogoniummucunoides (mucuna). On the other hand, planting alternate rows of two or more different fallow species is a mixed fallow system. The species grow together without affecting each other. This practice is particularly good for slow-growing species that will not strongly compete. Figures 1, 2 and 3 are examples of single and mixed species fallows.

Figure 1. Woody single-species fallow of Tephrosia

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. A herbaceous single-species fallow of Colopogonium mucunoides (mucuna)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. A woody mixed fallow of Sesbania and Crotalaria

©FAO/TECA

1. A woody mixed fallow of Sesbania and Crotalaria

  • Not all improved fallow practices are suited to all locations and all farmers.
  • The farmers and extension staff are expected to be active partners in identifying, evaluating and adapting the practices that can address their specific needs and the resources they have at hand.
  • Growing a fallow involves a number of simple steps:
    • obtaining the appropriate seeds of the desired species,
    • seed pre-treatment,
    • establishment,
    • managing pests, and
    • harvesting.
  • These are described in detail below.

1.1 Obtaining Seeds

Seeds for improved fallows species could be obtained by buying or producing on-farm. A good fallow plant must have several of the following characteristics:

  • Its growth is quick, closing the canopy quickly, to suppress weeds and control erosion.
  • It yields much biomass of good quality that decomposes fast and becomes fertilizer for the crops.
  • It is deep-rooted so that it picks up well the nutrients that are leached and deep in the soil.
  • It fixes nitrogen biologically from the atmosphere, building up good nutrients overall.
  • It is easy to establish and manage.
  • It supplies extra products such as stakes, grain and fodder that make its use attractive.
  • It will not spread like a weed into cultivated areas.
  • It easily produces seeds with long viability.
  • It is adapted well to resist pests and diseases in the area.

Examples of improved fallow species:

1.1.1 Woody species

  • Cajanus cajan (pigeon pea)
  • Calliandra calothyrsus (calliandra)
  • Crotalaria grahamiana (crotalaria)
  • Crotalaria mucronata
  • Crotalaria paulina
  • Crotalaria striata
  • Desmodium uncinatum (desmodium)
  • Gliricidia sepium (Mexican lilac)
  • Sesbania sesban (sesbania)
  • Tephrosia candida (tephrosia or fish poison)
  • Tephrosia vogelii.

1.1.2 Herbaceous species

  • Canavalia ensiformis
  • Colopogonium mucunoides (mucuna)
  • Dolichos lablab
  • Macroptilium atropurpureum (siratro).
Figure 4. Calliandra calothyrsus shrub

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Seed pre-treatment

  • Seeds of some fallow species do not germinate quickly or germinate poorly.
    • One such species is Sesbania sesban.
      • Sesbania seeds have a very hard seed coat that requires softening before the seed can germinate.
    • It is recommended that seeds of such species be soaked in hot water at 65° C for 10 to 15 minutes.
    • Do this by leaving boiling water to cool for 15 to 20 minutes before fully immersing the seed in it in a cloth bag.
    • Dry the seed in the sun for 15 to 20 minutes before planting it. Seeds of other plants listed in this guideline germinate easily without pre-treatment.

1.3 Plant density

  • Spacing depends on the size of the seed.
    • The spacing recommended in the table below should give high biomass yield and good canopy cover within six to eight months.
    • The narrow in-row spacing of Crotalaria paulina and Crotalaria striata is because they are short plants when mature.
    • This seed rate can also be used for herbaceous legume cover crops such as mucuna.
  • Table 1 shows recommendations for establishing one hectare of various fallow species.
  • NB: Amounts calculated on seeds being planted two per hole; planting four seeds per hole doubles the seed rate.
  • The germination rate for all seeds is 80 percent, except for Sesbania sesban, which has a rate of 70 percent.
Table 1. Recommendations for establishing one hectare of various fallow species
Species Seeds (per kg) Spacing (cm) Seed rate (kg per ha) Seed rate (g per plot)
Cajanus cajan 7 000 75x30 18.2 1638
Crotalaria grahamiana 18 000 75x30 7.0 630
Crotalaria paulina 64 000 75x10 2.0 180
Crotalaria striata 110 000 75x10 1.2 108
Sesbania Sesban 100 000 75x30 0.3 27
Tephrosia candinda 18 000 75x30 7.0 630
Tephrosia vogelii 18 000 75x30 7.0 630

Source: FAO 2013.

Figure 5. Planting crops on the same field at the beginning of the next season. (A) Maize+trees: fallow species planted in maize plots. (B) Trees: fallow species left to grow alone. (C) Maize: maize planted after improved fallow

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Establishment

For improved fallow species to benefit crops, they must have enough time in the field to grow and accumulate large quantities of biomass and nutrients. Several methods can be used to establish improved fallows:

  • Broadcast the seed in fields among existing crops, for example, with maize after either the first or the second weeding.
    • If intercropping bean with maize, harvest the bean then sow seeds of the fallow plants. This technique is best suited for species with large seeds such as mucuna.
    • An advantage of this practice is that crop husbandry practices such as applying fertilizer and weeding also help the trees to grow better.
  • Plant in rows.
    • Sow seeds of improved fallow trees, shrubs and herbaceous legumes directly between the rows of the food crop after the first weeding or as soon as the food crop has germinated, and cover the seeds with soil.
    • With maize, for example, plant in the furrows between the rows after either the first or the second weeding.
  • Plant the improved fallow trees into existing natural fallows.
    • One way to do this is to dig holes in the natural fallows and sow seeds directly or plant seedlings.
    • If the weeds in the fallow are dense and inhibit digging the holes, first slash them.
    • Crotalaria grahamiana and Tephrosia vogelii can be planted directly into natural fallows.
    • For species like Sesbania sesban that have small seeds or do not grow easily from seed, raise seedlings and plant them either in an existing crop or in natural fallow lands.

1.5 Managing pests

  • Like any plant, fallow species can be attacked by a variety of pests and diseases.
    • When the fallow species share these with the crops to be planted after the fallow, the problem is even more serious and the beneficial effect of the fallow on soil fertility may be lost completely because of a soil-borne pest or disease.
    • It is therefore important to identify pests and diseases and to take appropriate measures to control them.
Figure 6. It is important to identify pests and diseases and to take appropriate measures to control them

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Tephrosia vogelii plant

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Harvesting the fallows

  • After harvesting the food crop, leave the fallow trees in the field to grow.
    • In six to eight months, they form a closed canopy and cast a dense shade on the ground, which helps to suppress weed growth.
    • With fast-growing species such as crotalaria and tephrosia, it is not necessary to weed the fallow.
    • At the end of the fallow period (eight to nine months or longer after planting), cut down the fallow trees and chop off the leaves, twigs and soft branches.
    • Spread them evenly over the field, and then incorporate them into the soil while preparing the land for planting the next crop.
    • Use a jembe or an ox-drawn plough.
    • Remove the woody parts of fallow plants from the field and use them for fuelwood or for stakes for crops such as climbing bean and tomato.
Figure 8. Harvesting the fallows

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. A good maize crop with dark green leaves follows an improved fallow

©FAO/TECA

1.7 Planting crops

  • Planting crops on the same field at the beginning of the next season.
  • At this stage, it is best to add phosphorus fertilizer, especially in phosphorus-deficient soils.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Fallow cropping garlic after rice: ID 7698.
  • Shortened bush-fallow rotations and sustainable rural livelihoods: ID 4578.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: woodlots, agro-forestry and improved fallow: ID 7320.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The application of this technology helps in restoring soil fertility.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

With restored soil fertility; farmland productivity gets improved and so the farmers' income.

entries.tittle: Planting of KS Kuroda variety carrots to withstand heavy and prolonged rainfall, Philippines
entries.summary:
Climate change increases uncertainties in the agriculture sector and directly impacts agricultural production. In the Cordillera region of the northern Philippines, erratic precipitation patterns affect water availability during important crop growth stages, while drought in some areas make it extremely difficult for farmers to grow crops. Local agriculture workers and farmers in this region have also reported increased occurrence, intensity and length of rainfall events, which increase erosion rates, trigger landslides, and make certain crops more susceptible to diseases.

The planting of the KS Kuroda variety carrot is a good practice option that can prevent production loss due to heavy and prolonged rainfall. An important characteristic of KS Kuroda identified by the project stakeholders in the Cordillera region is the ability of the roots to withstand rotting (as compared to other less tolerant varieties) during heavy and prolonged precipitation. Rotting of the roots can make the carrots more susceptible to microbial and fungal infections. Planting KS Kuroda carrots can enhance overall resilience in terms of: 
a) addressing slow onset climate change impacts, such as shifting precipitation patterns; and 
b) reducing the risk and impact of current climate variability and extreme weather events, such as heavy and erratic rainfall.
entries.description:
Description

This good practice option (GPO) was tested in the project “Enhanced Climate Change Adaptation Capacity of Communities in Contiguous Fragile Ecosystems in the Cordilleras (2009 to 2011) between August 11, 2010 and January 13, 2011. Through active participation and involvement of local stakeholders and end-users in both training and field demonstration activities, the project identified the planting of KS Kuroda carrots as a location-specific and appropriate option for climate change adaptation. The GPO was tested in the municipality of Atok located in the province of Benguet, Philippines in 2010 and 2011.

Carrots are planted during the wet season and can contribute to disruptions in disease cycles when correct planting time is observed. Based on agronomic documents published by the Philippines Department of Agriculture and the first-hand experience of the department’s regional technical specialists / agronomists, carrots grow best in areas with elevations higher than 1 000 m above sea level. The demonstration site used was more than 1 500 m above sea level. Under this agro-ecological condition, carrots are more succulent, tender, less fibrous, have better texture, and have a deeper colour. Roots gain optimal colour when air temperature is between 15 to 21° C and deepen rapidly in colour three weeks before harvest.

1. Implementation of the technology

1.1 Land preparation, planting and irrigation

  • A hectare of land requires about 6 kg of seeds depending on the size of the bulbs and the distance of planting.
  • The rate of fertilizer application should be based on soil analysis.
  • Before planting clean the area through the use of grab hoe, sickle or trowel.
  • Continue to dig the plots to 25 cm deep and 15 cm high.
  • Then prepare furrows at a distance of 10 cm.
  • Plant three seeds per hill and irrigate every four to five days.

1.2 Management

  • Thin the carrots three weeks to one month after sowing.
  • Conduct second thinning after hilling-up and retain one plant per hill.
  • Hill-up twice if the roots are observed to be coming out.
  • Side-dress the plants one month after emergence or after thinning.
  • Clean the planting area regularly by hand weeding.
  • For pest control (e.g. cutworms) apply insecticides as recommended by the agricultural technicians in the area.

1.3 Harvest and postharvest handling

  • The carrots can be harvested three to four months (90 to 120 days) after emergence.
  • Carefully loosen the soil using a spading fork or similar tool and slowly pull the carrot roots.
  • Before washing and air-drying, cut the leaves 5 cm to 8 cm from the shoulder.
  • The carrots can then be sorted based on size and appearance.
Table 1. Results and findings: technological suitability

Source: FAO 2013

2. Environmental services and benefits

  • The project team identified factors that should be taken note of or avoided in order to prevent the GPO from introducing new environmental problems or compounding existing problems.
  • Based on the field interviews, the initial fertilizer usage was higher than standard because of the frequent rainfall, which wash away the recently applied fertilizers.
  • Apart from leading to fertilizer overuse and changes in soil chemistry (e.g. increase in acidity thru ion exchange leading to sulfuric acid formation; and/or leaching), the latter can also lead to surface and nutrient run-off.
  • To address this, members of the project team/local working group initiated the putting up of hedgerows and improvement in the contours.
  • Cooperators have also been made more careful of the timing of the application of fertilizers.

3. Economic benefits, social and cultural acceptability, and farmers feedback

  • It was found that planting the Sakata variety in the same elevation and crop management condition has yielded about 30 percent lower than KS Kuroda (given the same conditions).
  • Planting KS Kuroda was thus deemed more profitable.
  • It was also found to have a higher Return on Investment (ROI).

 

  • This good practice option is recommended for further trial in Atok, Benguet.
    • This would be done with training and  the technical assistance from the Department of Agriculture and the Municipal Agricultural Office and improved soil management practices to better determine more efficient fertilizer use and strengthen analysis on the yield advantages of KS Kuroda over Sakata variety.
  • For other regions and areas, this can be replicated and tested using the same variety if found agro-ecologically suitable to the area.
    • Locally available varieties with similar characteristics (e.g. tolerance to heavy and prolonged rainfall) can also be explored and tested.
    • However, it is important to keep in mind the experiences from this GPO testing.
      • Heavy and prolonged rainfall can lead to increased fertilizer use and there is a need for proper fertilizer timing and agronomic practices (e.g. contouring, hedgerows, etc.) that will reduce surface (and fertilizer) runoff.
Figure 1. Planting of KS Kuroda variety carrots to withstand heavy and prolonged rainfall, Philippines

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Planting of KS Kuroda variety carrots to withstand heavy and prolonged rainfall, Philippines

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • High yielding vegetable varieties: ID 6908.
  • Drought-tolerant maize varieties: ID 8920.
  • Multi-stress tolerant bean varieties: ID 8919.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

Planting of early-maturing varieties contributes to reducing harvest and post-harvest losses and increases  food security.
