entries.tittle: Material de Siembra de Alta Calidad en la en Renovación de Plantaciones de Plátano y Banano

categories.name: Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Risk Reduction

entries.summary: En la República Dominicana la ocurrencia de fenómenos naturales tropicales cuyas principales manifestaciones consisten en vientos huracanados, lluvias torrenciales e inundaciones, entre otras, se torna cada vez más errática e intensa. Estos fenómenos, producidos por lo general en la denominada “época ciclónica", causan daños muy importantes en los sistemas de producción de las musácea en las provincias de Barahona y Bahoruco. Se destacan como daños muy importantes la caída y pudrición radicular de las plantas de plátano y banano. Además, en estas regiones, el sistema tradicional de producción de musáceas comestible, se caracteriza por el uso de material de siembra de baja calidad, esto hace que estos cultivos sean más susceptibles a los efectos negativos de los vientos y a lluvias torrenciales e inundaciones. Esta situación requiere de medidas que sean de bajo costo, funcionales y de fácil implementación, orientadas a la rehabilitación y/o renovación de las plantaciones destruidas por los fuertes vientos y prolongadas inundaciones. En vista de que el material de siembra para estos cultivos es escaso y de baja calidad, unas buenas prácticas para mejorar esta situación, lo constituye la producción rápida de plántulas de plátano y banano bajo sombra controlada a partir de cormitos (cormoplantas). Esta práctica asegura plantaciones vigorosas, uniformes, sin mezcla varietal y libre de plagas y enfermedades.
entries.description:
Descripción

1. Introducción

  • Los productores de plátano y banano del país, cada año enfrentan serias dificultades al momento de la renovación de las plantaciones; porque no disponen de material de alta calidad: vigorosa, uniforme, sin mezcla varietal y libre de plagas y enfermedades.
  • El material de siembra de alta calidad asegura un crecimiento rápido y vigoroso de las plantas, lo que permite reducir los daños de doblez del seudotallo por vientos y la pudrición y muerte radicular por inundaciones y/o plagas radiculares como nematodos y picudos que destruyen las raíces (Figura 1).
  • Las musáceas se propagan comercialmente de forma asexual, debido a su incapacidad para producir semillas viables, por lo que sólo es posible su reproducción a través de la propagación vegetativa o asexual.
  • Por tanto, las "semillas" utilizadas para la siembra corresponden a partes vegetativas tales como retoños y cormos, que una vez separados de la planta madre, pueden realizar su ciclo de crecimiento y producción.
  • Las modalidades de propagación del material de siembra más utilizadas son:

1.1 Propagación por cormos (cepa)

  • El material de propagación usado en este sistema tradicional, proviene generalmente de los brotes o hijos de plantaciones donde el período de cosecha ha concluido.
  • Dependiendo de la edad de la plantación, el material de siembra proveniente de este sistema puede presentar un alto grado de contaminación.
  • Para disminuir el riesgo de diseminación de plagas y enfermedades, se recomienda la selección y desinfección de los cormos antes de la siembra.

1.2 Propagación a través de 'vitroplantas'

  • Se caracteriza por tener la capacidad de generar gran cantidad de plantas para la siembra en mediano plazo, en estado fitosanitario relativamente óptimo, en relación con algunas enfermedades.
  • Con este método es posible lograr plántulas libres de nematodos, hongos y de algunos virus y bacterias y con óptima uniformidad en comparación con el sistema tradicional de propagación por cormos.
  • Sin embargo, el alto costo de las plantas con relación a otros sistemas representa una de las principales desventajas para su uso masificado, entre los pequeños y medianos productores.

1.3 Producción de plántulas a partir de cormitos bajo sombra controlada (cormoplantas)

  • Este sistema de propagación, representa una alternativa para suplir a los productores de plántulas vigorosas, uniformes, sin mezcla varietal y libre de plagas, enfermedades y a bajo costo.
  • A través de esta técnica se obtiene una reducción en los costos de aquellos productores que deseen renovar o incrementar su área de siembra.
Figura 1. Plantación con buen manejo agronómico

©FAO/TECA

2. Objetivo de la práctica

Reducir los riesgos de destrucción de las plantaciones por fuertes vientos y exceso de lluvia en la temporada ciclónica, disminuyendo el doblez del seudotallo, pudrición y muerte radicular por plagas del suelo y severidad de la Sigatoka negra, mediante el uso de material de siembra de alta calidad.

3. Aplicación de la tecnología

Para renovar las plantaciones afectadas por fuertes vientos y exceso de lluvia, la siembra debe realizarse con material de siembra de alta calidad y de bajo costo, como es el producido por cormitos bajo sombra controlada. Los pasos a considerar en el proceso de producción de este material son:

  • Obtenga los cormitos de campos sembrados con vitro plantas establecidos con el propósito de producir cormitos o de plantaciones en producción, con buen manejo agronómico, fitosanitario y sin mezclas clónales.
  • Corte las plantas madres a 1 m de altura.
    • Riegue y fertilice (6 onzas de sulfato de amonio por planta).
    • Separe los hijos de la planta madre a las 4 a 8 pulgadas de altura.
  • Prepare un sustrato utilizando suelo no cultivado, rico en materia orgánica con materiales orgánicos.
    • Proceda a mezclar 4 partes de tierra suelta, con cuatro partes de cascarilla de arroz y dos partes de abono orgánico fermentado.
  • Pele los cormitos con cuidado, sin afectar su yema terminal.
    • Redúzcalo a un peso de 150 a 250 g aproximadamente (Figura 2).
    • El tallito se corta dejando 1 a 2 pulgadas de tejido por encima del cormito.
  • Desinfecte los cormitos con un insecticida nematicida o en una solución de cloro comercial (conteniendo 5,25 por ciento del ingrediente activo NaOCl) a una concentración del 10 por ciento.
    • En sistema orgánico, se puede tratar térmicamente introduciendo los cormitos en un tanque con agua a una temperatura de 50-55 °C durante 10 minutos.
  • Siembre los cormitos en fundas plásticas de 6 x 8 o 8 x 10 pulgadas, según el tamaño del cormito.
    • Colóquelos en la mitad de la funda, tápelos con una capa de dos pulgadas de suelo preparado.
  • Coloque las fundas en hileras bajo condiciones de sombra, ya sea en vivero o debajo de plantaciones establecidas (Figura 3).
  • Riegue las plantas a diario, hasta que broten los cormitos.
    • Riegue después cada dos días.
    • Deshierbe si es necesario.
  • Con 45 a 60 después de la siembra se trasplantan las plántulas, con 3 a 4 hojas verdaderas (Figura 4).
Figura 2. Pelado y corte de cormos

©FAO/TECA

Figura 3. Llenado de fundas

©FAO/TECA

Figura 4. Desarrollo de plántulas en sombra natural

©FAO/TECA

4. Ámbito de aplicación de la buena práctica

  • Esta buena práctica puede implementarse en cualquier zona del país donde se produzca plátano y banano para exportación o para el consumo local y exista riesgo de vientos huracanados e inundaciones.
  • En la actualidad se aplica en el Cibao Central, (La Vega, Espaillat, Duarte, Hermanas Mirabal, Sánchez. Ramírez), Mao y Montecristi, en la Línea noroeste y Azua, en la zona sur.
    • En porcentajes de productores que utilizan esta práctica es de 15 por ciento en el Cibao Central, 25 por ciento en la Línea Noroeste y 10 por ciento en el Sur.
    • El tiempo de aplicación de la misma es de 12 años en la Línea Noroeste, 10 años en el Cibao Central y 10 años en la zona sur.

5. Costo de implementación

El costo de los materiales de siembra que utilizan los productores en República Dominicana es el siguiente:

  • propagación por cormos (cepa) 4 RD$;
  • propagación a través de vitroplantas 25 RD$;
  • y propagación a través de cormoplantas varia de 8 a 10 RD$.

6. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

7. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Prácticas de protección de plantas de banano (Musa AAA) en su fase productiva: ID 8335.
  • Manejo de Sigatoka negra (Mycosphaerella fijiensis Morelet) en plantaciones de plátano y banano: ID 8306.
  • Producción de cormos de plátano y banano para siembra directa en campo: ID 8149.
  • Renovación de plantaciones de plátano cambiando la época y sistema de siembra: ID 8339.
  • Reducing natural hazard impacts on bananas: integrated practices: ID 6864.

8. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

8.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Debido a esta práctica, el agricultor puede dar pasos eficientes hacia la rehabilitación de las plantaciones de plátano y banano.

8.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta tecnología con medidas de bajo costo contribuye a la renovación de plantaciones de plátano y banano para mitigar los impactos negativos de inundaciones o lluvias torrenciales y asegurar una mejora de la producción de plántulas de plátano y banano.

entries.tittle: Uso de Barreras Muertas en Terrenos de Laderas para Control de Erosión, Dominican Republic.

categories.name: Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Risk Reduction

entries.summary: Las zonas de laderas o montañas de la región sur de la República Dominicana, resultan muy afectadas periódicamente por los efectos negativos de los fenómenos naturales (precipitaciones abundantes, huracanes y vientos), por esta razón, esta región ha sido considerada de alta vulnerabilidad; ya que no se cuenta con instrumentación ni medidas apropiadas para responder a los desastres naturales o reducir sus efectos negativos. Las montañas de la región sur están desnudas o desprovistas de árboles, por esta razón la caída de las gotas de lluvias, no amortiguan antes de llegar al suelo; provocando grandes escorrentías y por ende la erosión de los suelos, dejándolos inservibles para desarrollar actividades agrícolas; ya que la capa vegetal se ha perdido y con ella la fertilidad. Las lluvias de acuerdo a la intensidad (100 mm o más), duración y frecuencia, es el fenómeno natural que afecta con más agresividad los suelos de laderas, por los grandes volúmenes de sedimentos que arrastra. La degradación de los suelos, ha motivado a los agricultores de las laderas a implementar la construcción de barreras muertas en sus fincas y de esta forma reducir las pérdidas por erosión que causan las lluvias.
entries.description:
Descripción

Durante las últimas décadas, la erosión se ha incrementado en la región sur de la República Dominicana, causando degradación y deterioro irreversible de los suelos. Esto ha afectado la agricultura, la biodiversidad, las aguas y la población que habita en dicha región. Según la Secretaría de Estado de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (SEMARENA), el 15 por ciento de los suelos del país de las zonas montañosas con fuertes pendientes, están siendo sobre utilizados y sometidos a procesos de erosión; porque no se utilizan buenas prácticas agrícolas de conservación de suelos.

Por lo tanto, mediante el uso de barreras muertas en terrenos de ladera se busca disminuir la velocidad del agua de escorrentía de las lluvias y de esta forma evitar la erosión de los suelos.

1. Barreras muertas

  • Las barreras muertas son muros de piedras o de rastrojos, colocados conforme a las curvas a nivel y sirven para disminuir la velocidad del agua de escorrentía y evitar la erosión de los suelos.
    • Esta buena práctica facilita la infiltración del agua de lluvia y del terreno y del tipo de suelo.
  • Para el diseño o construcción de la curva de nivel se necesita un nivel A.
    • Con este instrumento se hace la curva a nivel, en seguida se hace con el pico o con el arado de buey un trazo y se excava una zanja de 5 pulgadas de profundidad y 10-15 pulgadas de ancho para formar la base.
  • Es importante que se coloquen las piedras grandes abajo y a los lados (las piedras más grandes y planas se ubican como base del muro) y con las pequeñas se van rellenando los espacios vacíos, para que éstas queden firmes y formen un muro ligeramente piramidal.
    • El alto de las barreras muertas depende de la cantidad de piedras disponibles en el terreno y de la pendiente del terreno.
    • La altura mínima debe ser de 30 cm; mientras más plano sea el terreno menor será la altura de la barrera.
  • La distancia entre las barreras depende de la pendiente.
    • En zonas donde la pendiente y el terreno lo permiten se recomienda el uso de bueyes para el marcado de la barrera.
    • La distancia mínima entre barreras debe ser 8 m de longitud.
    • Dependiendo de la disponibilidad de piedras, el ancho de la barrera puede variar de 10 a 80 cm.
    • Los sistemas de cultivos, donde se justifica esta práctica, es donde se siembra granos básicos y hortalizas.
  • Donde se construyen barreras muertas lo más aconsejable es sembrar estacas de palos, para tener juntas barreras muertas y barreras vivas.
    • Las estacas se siembran a una distancia de un metro cada una y se recomienda sembrarlas en el periodo marzo-mayo.
    • Las estacas pueden ser de pino, limón y otros árboles adaptados a la zona.
    • La barrera muerta resulta en la formación paulatina de terrazas.
    • Se recomienda combinar las barreras muertas con técnicas que mejoren o aumenten la fertilidad del suelo.
Figura 1. Barrera muerta con el uso de piedras en la zona sur de la República Dominicana

©FAO/TECA

2. Aplicación de la tecnología

  • Las barreras muertas en las zonas de laderas en República Dominicana contribuyen a disminuir la erosión del suelo, que causa daños significativos en la superficie del mismo.
  • La erosión de los suelos trae como consecuencias que los agricultores abandonen los predios agrícolas por la pérdida de fertilidad, contribuyendo a incrementar e incentivar la agricultura nómada; que consiste en realizar tumbas o chapeos en otras áreas, lo cual ha contribuido a intensificar la deforestación en las montañas de la región sur del país y otros agricultores emigran a las zonas urbanas a engrosar el cordón de miseria de los barrios marginados en las ciudades del país.
  • Los insumos necesarios para construir las barreras son:
    • Insumos externos necesarios: nivel tipo A, palas y picos.
    • Insumos internos necesarios: piedras, pajas y trozos de palos.

2.1 Costos estimados

  • El costo de construcción de la barrera va a depender de la disponibilidad del material que se utilizará en la finca si las barreras son hechas por agricultores asociados o con mano de obra contratada.
    • Cuando se construye con agricultores asociados es de 25 RD$ por m2, mientras que si la construcción es con mano de obra contratada su costo es de 100 RD$ por m2.
    • El costo está en función de la disponibilidad del material en el terreno.
  • Cuando es difícil la obtención del material para la construcción de la barrera, el costo se puede duplicar o triplicar y lo más recomendable sería no construir barreras muertas y optar por otra práctica de conservación de suelo.
  • La construcción de barreras muertas en zonas de laderas contribuirá a reducir la velocidad del agua de escorrentía, disminuir la erosión del suelo y mejorará la fertilidad del mismo.
  • Por último, disminuiría el abandono de los terrenos hacia otros áreas (conquismo) y por ende, esto disminuirá los efectos devastadores de la deforestación en las zonas laderas.

3. Ámbito de aplicación de esta práctica

  • Las barreras de muertas se deben construir en terrenos, de zonas de laderas cuyas pendientes sean mayores a 5 por ciento y que estén expuestos a la erosión por las lluvias.
  • Esta práctica se debe implementar durante los períodos secos y cuando la disponibilidad de mano de obra sea abundante, ya que esta práctica demanda de mucha mano de obra.
  • Es indispensable que los materiales que se vayan a utilizar en la construcción se encuentren dentro de la misma finca.
  • Las piedras o rocas son el insumo principal para construcción de las barreras, aunque también se utiliza rastrojos, ramas y trozos de madera.
  • Esta buena práctica agrícola, se puede desarrollar en todas las regiones del país, que tienen montañas desprovistas de árboles.
  • No obstante hay que considerar que la construcción de las barreras tiene que cumplir con requisitos o normas, técnicas y medios ambientales como son:
    • Las barreras se pueden construir en todo tipo de suelo pedregoso.
    • Profundidad del suelo:
      • Se utiliza en suelos superficiales y suelos profundos.
      • En suelos superficiales con mal drenaje existe el riesgo de encharcamiento.
    • Capacidad de infiltración:
      • Se puede utilizar en suelos con buena y moderada infiltración.
    • Drenaje del agua:
      • No apropiado en suelos mal drenados.
    • Presencia de piedras en la parcela:
      • Solamente apropiado en suelos pedregosos por la disponibilidad del material para la construcción de la barrera.
  • Los porcentajes de pendiente:
    • Se puede construir en todo tipo de pendiente.
    • Sin embargo, se recomienda sobre todo para pendientes fuertes o a veces en pendientes moderadas.

4. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

5. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Prácticas de conservación del suelo y el agua para la reducción de la erosión del suelo y reforzar: ID 8689.
  • Mulching to control soil erosion: ID 8207.
  • Hedgerows/alley cropping to control soil erosion: ID 4645.
  • Mechanical soil conservation strategies to reduce soil erosion: ID 8208.

6. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

6.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología conduce a resultados positivos, como por ejemplo una mayor resiliencia del suelo por una reducción de la velocidad del agua de escorrentía de las lluvias.

6.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Las barreras muertas contribuyen a la disminución de la erosión del suelo, lo que es esencial para establecer la seguridad alimentaria y también la fertilidad del suelo.

entries.tittle: Weed Management in Organic Agriculture
entries.summary: Organic farmers give first priority to the prevention of the introduction and multiplication of weeds. Management practices aim at keeping the weed population at a level that does not result in economic loss of the crop cultivation or harms its quality. The goal is not to completely eradicate all weeds, as they also have a role to play on the farm. For example, weeds provide cover that reduces soil erosion. In addition, most of the biological diversity in our crop fields comes from the presence of weeds. They provide habitat for both beneficial biocontrol insects and mycorrhiza fungi. Because weeds offer pollen and nectar, they allow biocontrol insects to maintain their populations and, therefore, serve as a valuable instrument in controlling pests.
entries.description:
Description

Weeds have a role to play on the farm. For example, weeds provide cover that reduces soil erosion. In addition, most of the biological diversity in our crop fields comes from the presence of weeds. They provide habitat for both beneficial biocontrol insects and mycorrhiza fungi. Because weeds offer pollen and nectar, they allow biocontrol insects to maintain their populations and, therefore, serve as a valuable instrument in controlling pests.

However, weeds may also alter the environment of the crop in a negative way. Light and air circulation, for example, are reduced between the crop plants. In this darker and more humid environment, diseases find ideal conditions in which to spread and infect plants.

A basic working principle in organic farming is to prevent problems, rather than to cure them. This applies equally to weed management. Good weed management in organic farming includes creating conditions which hinder weeds from growing at the wrong time and in the wrong place, preventing them from becoming a serious problem for crop cultivation. Competition by weeds doesn’t harm the crop throughout the whole cultivation period in the same way. The most sensitive phase of a crop to weed competition is in its early growth stage. A young plant is vulnerable and depends highly on an ideal nutrient, light, and water supply for a good development. If it has to compete with weeds at this stage, the crop may grow weak, which also makes it more vulnerable to pest and disease infections.

Weed competition later in the cultivation period is less harmful. However, some weeds may cause harvesting problems and reduce the crop yield in that way. Therefore, weeds should not be completely ignored after the most critical growth period of the crop, but in general, they become less important.

These considerations should influence the selection and timing of weed management measures. In general, such measures aim at keeping the weed population at a level which doesn’t result in economic loss of the crop cultivation or harm its quality.

1. Preventive practices

  • Several preventive measures may be applied at the same time.
  • The importance and effectiveness of the different methods depend to a large extent on the weed species and the environmental conditions.
  • However, some methods are very effective for a wide range of weeds and are therefore regularly used.

1.1 Choice of crops and varieties

  • Tall crops and varieties with broader leaves will compete better with late occurring weeds than small varieties with narrow leaves.
  • Some varieties will inhibit and suppress weeds while others will tolerate them.
  • For example, there are witchweed (Striga) resistant maize and cowpea cultivars in many countries of Africa, which give better performance at the same level of weeds where other varieties are more affected.

1.2 Mulching

  • The weeds find it difficult to receive enough light to grow and may not be able to pass through the mulch layer.
  • Dry, hardy material, that decomposes slowly, keeps its effect longer than fresh mulch material.

1.3 Living green cover

  • The cover competes successfully against the weeds for light, nutrients, and water and therefore helps to prevent weed growth by winning the competition for resources.
  • The cover crops usually used are legumes, which improves soil fertility on top of suppressing weeds.
  • For example, a ground cover of desmodium (Desmodium uncinatum) or silver leaf, interplanted among maize, reduces striga weed and fixes nitrogen at the same time.
  • Further information on TECA, "How to control Striga and stemborer in maize".

1.4 Crop rotation

  • Rotation of crops is the most efficient measure to regulate seed and root weeds.
  • Changing the conditions of the crop interrupts the living conditions of the weeds, thus inhibiting their growth and spread.

1.5 Intercropping (mixed cropping and under-sowing)

  • Intercropping with fast growing weed-suppressive species (‘smoother crop’ or ‘living mulch’) between rows of main crop species is effective in weed control.
  • There are different examples known to work in Africa.
    • For example, sowing cowpeas and egusi melons or pumpkins as intercrops in cassava to reduce weed occurrence.

1.6 Sowing time and density

  • Optimum growing conditions enhance the optimum crop plant development and their ability to compete against weeds.
  • Proper crop spacing will ensure that minimum space is available for the growth of weeds and will minimize competition with weeds.
  • This will effectively restrict weed development.
  • In order to apply this approach, the limiting weeds must be known and the seasons in which they occur.
  • A weed calendar of the area or region, if available, might be of help.
  • It will be used to manage weeds in a targeted fashion with proper timing and effect.

1.7 Balanced fertilization

  • It can support an ideal growth of the crop, which promotes the growth of the crop over the weeds.

1.8 Soil cultivation methods

  • Soil cultivation methods can influence the total weed pressure as well as the composition of weeds.
  • For example, minimum-tillage systems can increase the weed pressure.
  • Because weed seeds can germinate between soil cultivation and sowing of the crop, weed cures before sowing can be effective at reducing weed pressure.
  • Use of superficial stubble treatment works against persisting weeds.
  • It should be done under dry weather conditions to allow the weed roots, which have been brought to the surface, to dry out.

1.9 Pasturing

  • In perennial crops like coffee, mangoes, avocadoes or cocoa, the use of sheep and goats to reduce rampant weed growth is becoming common.
  • In the case of cattle, broadleaf weeds tend to predominate due to the cattle preference for grasses.
  • Therefore, it is necessary to rotate with sheep and goats which prefer broadleaves to overcome this selective grazing.

1.10 Dissemination of weeds

  • Prevent dissemination of weeds by eliminating them before seed dispersal.

1.11 Seed origin

  • Prevent insemination of crops by weeds by avoiding the introduction of weed seeds into the fields through tools or animals.
  • Another method is also by using only weed free seed material.
Figure 1. Striga on a host plant which shows significant damages

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Cultural practices of managing weeds

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Pasturing for weed control

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. How to prevent weeds

©FAO/TECA

2. Biological control of weeds

  • The soil-borne fungus Fusarium oxysporum (different isolates from Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger) is very effective in reducing the witch weed (Striga hermonthica and S. asiatica) in different cereal crops, leading to yield increases in scientific trials.
  • Other Fusarium species found in Sudan and Ghana are very effective, too (Fusarium nygamai, F. oxysporum and F. solani).
  • This mycoherbicide is on the way to being formulated and registered in different countries in Africa.
  • Rhizobacteria are capable of suppressing germination of witch weed (Striga spp.) seeds or actually destroying the seeds.
    • They are particularly promising biological control agents since they can be easily and cheaply formulated into seed inoculants.
  • Pseudomonas fluorescens putida isolates significantly inhibited germination of Striga hermonthica seeds.
    • However, currently no biocontrol product is available.

3. Mechanical control

  • With the necessary preventive measures, weed density can be reduced, but it will hardly be enough during the critical periods of the crop at the beginning of cultivation.
  • Therefore, mechanical methods remain an important part of weed management.

3.1 Manual weeding

  • This is probably the most important method.
  • As it’s very labour intensive, reducing weed density as much as possible in the field will bring less work later on and should therefore be aimed at.
  • There are different tools to dig, cut and uprooting the weeds; hand, ox-drawn and tractor-drawn tools.
  • Using the right tool can increase work efficiency significantly.
  • Weeding should be done before the weeds flower and produce seeds.

3.2 Flame weeding

  • It is another option: plants are heated briefly to 100°C and higher.
  • This provokes coagulation of the proteins in the leaves and a bursting of their cell walls.
  • Consequently, the weed dries out and dies.
  • Although it is an effective method, it is quite expensive as it consumes a large amount of fuel gas and needs machinery.
  • It is not effective against root weeds.
Figure 5. Mechanical weed control

©FAO/TECA

4. Related/associated technologies 

  • Step by step conversion to organic agriculture: ID 8364.
  • Introduction to organic agriculture: ID 8359.
  • Considerations for conversion to organic agriculture: ID 8363.
  • Mulching in organic agriculture: ID 8365.
  • Water management in organic agriculture: ID 8366.
  • Crop planning and management in organic agriculture: ID 8367.
  • Pest and disease management in organic agriculture: ID 8372.
  • Animal husbandry in organic agriculture: ID 8378.
  • Plant propagation in organic agriculture: ID 8377.
  • Nutrient management in organic agriculture: ID 8368.
  • Soil cultivation and tillage in organic agriculture: ID 8376.
  • Rice seed drying (Africa rice center video on rice advice): ID 7211.
  • Seed propagation of Allanblackia spp.: ID 7793​.
  • How to control Striga and stemborer in maize: ID 7356.
  • Weed management in conservation agriculture: ID 7418. 
  • Rice weed management (Africa rice center video on rice advice): ID ​​7215.

This technology is also available in French: ID 8576.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and is can be undertaken by any kind of hand labour.

5.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for the efficient management of weed growth, thereby balancing removal for good crop cultivation but also maintaing some weed growth for biological diversity and soil erosion prevention.

5.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology prevents crop cultivation economic losses, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Strategy for Integrated Varroa Management: Healthier Colonies Through Brood Removal
entries.summary: The technique consists of the timed removal of brood combs and has been developed with the objective of optimizing colony health with minimum treatment without a reduction in the productivity of the colony. This technique is applicable for hives with two brood boxes, each containing 10 frames of 40 by 20 cm in size (similar to Langstroth), one on top of the other. The brood is removed about one or two weeks before the final honey harvest but not later than eight weeks before the natural end of the brood season. For central Germany, the first half of July has been identified as an optimal period
entries.description:
Description

The studies in Germany have shown that brood removal at the beginning of the swarming season (20 May) results in a significantly lower yield (average of 7.1 kg compared to 21.5 kg of the control colonies). With a three weeks later brood removal (11 June), an average yield of 16.4 kg was achieved (control group 21.5 Kg) while the highest yield with an average of 27.3 kg was obtained (control group 21.5 kg) with brood removal in early July, exactly 14 days before the final honey harvest. This is explained by the fact that due to the complete removal of brood, the honey consumption of the bees is drastically reduced while the harvesting power remains. The lack of young bees is only noticed after the harvest. There is no danger of robbing and the colony has enough time to repopulate and build up reserves for the winter. This method, however, is less suitable for areas with late harvests (August or later).

This technology is an efficient way to keep varroa infestation under control. The beekeeper should however always check the varroa infestation level in the hive and treat when the infestation is above the threshold (more than five varroa mites per 100 g of bees). See Dietemann et al, (2013) for techniques to control varroa infestation levels.

Figure 1. Hive structure

©FAO/TECA

1. Complete brood removal – process, step-by-step

  1. Remove the honey super and the upper brood box. Assess the honeycombs in the brood nest area of the bottom box (Box A). Move two to four light coloured honey and pollen combs to both sides of the brood box (Box A) (Figure 2).

Figure 2. Beekeepers looking for brood combs

©FAO/TECA

  1. Place one brood comb with eggs and larvae, but without capped cells which will emerge within the next 10 days, in the centre of the brood box.

    • This will be the “catch comb” for the varroa.
    • If available, use a frame with plenty of male bee brood (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. Brood comb without capped cells

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. The "catch comb" for the varroa

©FAO/TECA

  1. Shake or brush the bees of the remaining brood combs back into the brood box.

    • Make sure the queen is in the (bottom) brood box (Box A) (Figure 5).

Figure 5. Beekeeper shaking the bees into the brood box

©FAO/TECA

  1. Fill up the gaps with empty combs or frames with foundation sheets.

    • If there is honey flow, the empty combs will be quickly built up.
    • If there is no strong honey flow, feed the bees if possible with their own honey (Figure 6).
Figure 6. Beekeeper inserting foundation sheets

©FAO/TECA

  1. Place the queen excluder on top of the brood box (Box A) containing the queen (Figure 7).

Figure 7. The queen excluder avoid the queen to go up to the upper part

©FAO/TECA

  1. Replace the honey super on the brood box.

    • Make sure the honey super is replaced in the same position as it was before.
    • After the harvest of the last honey super, a second brood box can be added depending on the strength of the hive.

  1. Collect the removed brood combs with some adhering bees in a separate hive (brood collector hive – Box B).

    • Combs with bees from different colonies can be combined without problems (because there is no queen).
    • At least one comb with honey and pollen on each side of the combs should be provided for the young bees to feed on.
    • Approximately 300 bees on each side of the combs should be enough to care for the further development of the brood.
    • If the bees were completely shaken off the brood combs (to be sure that the queen was included), a suitable number of bees from the honey supers can be added.
Figure 8. Brood collector hive

©FAO/TECA

  1. After seven to ten days, check the colony from which the brood was removed (Box A). The central combs should be rebuilt and the queen should have started laying eggs in the new brood nest (Figure 9).

Figure 9. Brood in the new brood nest

©FAO/TECA

  1. The catch comb in the brood box (Box A), which in the meantime should be mostly sealed, needs to be removed and melted down, including the brood and caught mites.

    • Replace the comb with an empty comb or comb with the foundation sheet.
    • A varroa treatment is not required here (Figure 10).
Figure 10. The catch comb full of varroa must be removed

©FAO/TECA

   10. The brood collector hive (Box B) should be transferred immediately on the day of the brood removal to a separate apiary to prevent the return of bees to the mother colony and the risk of robbery and mite transfer).

    • They only need to be checked after 21 to 24 days.
    • By then the whole brood has emerged and old combs can be replaced with empty combs or combs with foundation sheets.
  • Note: Three weeks after the removal all brood is emerged and the combs are empty.
    • This offers a good opportunity to replace dark or badly constructed combs by freshly build combs or frames with wax foundation.
  • Depending on the size of the colony, the colony will remain on one or two boxes.
    • If unsure whether a new queen has been born, a single comb with an open brood can be added from another hive to allow the bees to build emergency queen cells.
    • If on the other hand, the new queen is not productive enough, she can be replaced as soon as the new brood is available (i.e. new unproductive queen has started laying eggs) (Figure 11).
Figure 11. Beekeeper checking varroa infestation 

©FAO/TECA

11. Thanks to the temporary absence of brood in the collector box (Box B), an effective and simple varroa treatment can now be applied.

  • Suitable treatments include the dripping of oxalic acid, spraying of lactic acid or the use of catch combs (Figure 12).
Figure 12. Varroa treatment in absence of brood 

©FAO/TECA

2. Validation of the practice

  • This technique has been developed with the objective of maintaining productivity while optimizing colony health with minimum treatment.
    • The Bieneninstitut Kirchhain, Germany, has been testing this technique since 2007 to study the effects of the brood removal on colony development, disease infestation and honey yield.
    • No negative effects could be found on the colony development and/or yield and positive effects were observed with regards to the health of the bees and control of disease within the hive. 

3. Related/associated technologies

  • ​​Beekeeping in Africa: responding to common bee diseases:​ ID 7332.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Women-friendly

This technology does not require heavy labour, and can be easily implemented by everyone. 

4.2 Resource use efficiency

This technology of integrated varroa management ensures healthier brood health, free of varroa infestations. This is due to a validated technology that experimented with the right time of brood removal. This ensures an efficient and successful practice. 

4.3 Pro-poor technology

Due to its success, this technology reduces and almost eliminates the risk of varroa infestations with minimum cost, and without jeopardizing the honey yield.

entries.tittle: Fruit Fly Control for Mango Farmers in Ghana
entries.summary:
Growing mango is full of challenges and farmers should know about them to succeed in the mango production. The more farmers know, the better they will succeed. 
This guide and short film shows four farmers from the Eastern Region of Ghana sharing  their experiences with fruit fly control in mango plantation. 
1) How to build a fruit fly trap to keep the number of fruit flies under control.
2) How to install a fruit fly trap in the tree.
3) How to use a protein bait to control fruit flies.
4) The role of farm hygiene in fruit fly management. 

This practice describes how mango fruit fly can be controlled using male traps and field sanitation.
entries.description:
Description

Mango production can be affected by the fruit fly. In the following video four farmers from the Eastern Region of Ghana share their experiences with fruit fly control in mango plantation, by using male traps and field sanitation.

Video: From farmer to farmer: fruit fly control

1. How to build a fruit fly trap for monitoring

Farmers can either buy the traps in special stores, or build their own. 

  • Plastic bottles (small one, 500 ml).
  • A knife.
  • Gloves.
  • Cotton wool.
  • Thread or wire.
  • Plan D (insecticide).
  • Methyl Eugenol (pheromone).

1.1 Steps for building a trap

  • Cut the bottle with two rectangular openings on the opposite sides.
  • Flag the ends of the openings for the flies to enter preventing going out (Figure 1).
  • Attach the cotton wool with the wire.
  • Soak the cotton wool with a mix of four parts of Methyl Eugenol for one part of Plan D.
    • Methyl Eugenol (protein bait) attracts the fruit flies while at the same time Plan D kills them.
    • in this video, Plan D is the name of the product based on synthetic pyrethroid (deltamethrin).
    • Any other product based on deltamethrin can also be used.
    • This method poses little risk to people, but still it is recommended to protect your hands with gloves while manipulating the products, and to avoid inhaling them.
  • Place the soaked cotton wool inside the bottle and close the tap (Figure 1).
  • Hang the trap on a branch of a tree.
Figure 1. Scheme of a homemade fruit fly trap for mango plantation

©FAO/TECA

  • This trap will only attract and kill male flies (Figure 2), that will slow down the reproduction rate of flies and so there will be less offspring with the time.
  • The trap also allows you to monitor the number of fruit fly population in the mango plantation.
  • If in one day, many flies are caught in the trap, it can mean that the female population still remains high, so you may resort to insecticides.
Figure 2. Dead fruit flies (males), killed by the pheromone trap

©FAO/TECA

1.2 How to install traps in the trees

  • Usually, one trap for two trees is sufficient (in this example, there are 40 trees, so the farmer needs 20 traps).
  • Preferably, set the trap in the shade, under the tree, where the flies are mostly attracted.
  • Tighten the wire around a branch, in order that the trap is hung on the tree, without touching branches.
  • Make sure that the two openings are well open.
  • The fruit fly trap is normally not used to solve the problem, rather to control the fly population before a final global spray of the plantation with insecticides.

1.3 How to use chemical bait to control fruit flies

  • In this eastern region of Ghana, a chemical bait-insecticide (Great Bait) was introduced three years ago to control the fruit fly population.
  • This protein bait is specific to the fruit fly, it only attracts and kill these flies.
  • On the knapsack (sprayer), add one part of the chemical bait for three parts of water, then shake vigorously the mix (Figure 3).
Figure 3. One part of the chemical bait for three parts of water

©FAO/TECA

  • For example, for a 15 litre knapsack sprayer, you need 3.75 litre (1 gallon) of the bait that you mix with 11.25 litre of water and this mix enables to treat 15 acres of the mango farm.
  • Do not wait until the fruits are ripe for spraying the mango plantation with the insecticide.
  • If you monitored before the fruit flies’ population with the traps and you noticed that a lot of flies were killed, it means that the population is building up, so you have to react.
  • The insecticide can be applied until three weeks before the harvest of fruits.
  • Advice to spray mango trees.
    • Spray from “inside” the tree (above the tree, above the branches), not from outside, neither directly on the fruits (Figure 4).
    • Spray three spots on the edges of the canopy but not in the centre of the canopy (Figure.4).
      • Do not spay the entire tree.
      • Do not spray on fruits!
    • Spray each second or ninth tree (Figure 5).
      • You do not need to spray every tree.
    • Distribute the spray between the rows of trees (Figure 5).
      • It is important that the treated spots are distributed over the plantation.
Figure 4. How to spray a mango tree against fruit flies

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Distribution of the sprays on the mango plantation

©FAO/TECA

1.4 The role of farm hygiene in fruit fly management

  • Controlling the fruit flies’ population only by trap and insecticide monitoring is not sufficient to solve the problem.
    • You also have to pay attention on the farm sanitation.
  • The fruit fly lays its eggs within the fruit.
    • When the fruit falls from the tree, the maggot stays and grows inside the mango.
    • Then it comes out of the fruit, pupates in the soil, becomes a fly and goes up again into the tree.
  • So, if you want to break the cycle, it is recommended to collect and bury properly all the fruits which fall down.
    • Collecting rotten fallen fruits into black polythene bags that you let exposed in the sun will kill all the insects (Figure 6), so then you can bury the fruits.
    • Do not bury the plastic bag!
Figure 6. Collect of rotten fallen mangos into black plastic bags

©FAO/TECA

  • Another solution to control fruit fly population would be to use the natural predators of these flies, such as the weaver ants, known to feed on fruit fly larvae, or the parasitoid wasps which naturally lay their eggs into the fruit fly larvae.
  • Therefore, it is not recommended to blanket spray the plantation with insecticides – as this would kill these natural enemies.
  • The solution is to spray a protein bait which is applied only on a few spots (not every tree, and not on the entire tree) and which attracts (and kills) fruit flies.
  • There is no need to breed the weaver ants or parasitoid wasps, as they are already naturally available.
    • But they can be supported with patches of natural vegetation between mango orchards.
  • Also, especially in the case of plantations located in slopes, it is recommended to scythe/harvest the grass of the plantation rather than ploughing the soil and leaving it uncovered; this would increase the erosion of the soil.
  • If you manipulate and / or use pesticides, make inquiries before!
    • Pesticides can be harmful to your health, the health of your family, of the consumers and of the environment.
    • Use pesticides safely.
    • Click here for more information concerning reducing risks while manipulating pesticide.

2. Validation of the practice

  • The practice was applied in the Brong Ahafo region in Ghana in collaboration with the Kintampo farmers.
  • For more information see the video above.

3. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • Tools needed to build the trap.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Risk reduction while manipulating pesticides: ID 8348.
  • How to build a fruit fly trap: ID 8238.
  • Controlling mango fruit fly: ID 6920.
  • Crop protection: Integrated management of fruit flies in India and Pakistan: ID 4562.
  • Video on how to defeat the mealy bug: ID 8236.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2471.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology helps to reduce the loss in natural resources handled and, thus, helps to use resources more efficiently.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

Controlling mango flies can save the mango harvest and reduce the risk of harvest loss.

entries.tittle: How to process raw propolis into propolis extracts
entries.summary: Propolis or “bee glue” is a resinous mixture that honey bees collect from tree buds and plant resins. Propolis is used by the bees in the hive for its antimicrobial and anti-viral properties. Humans can also benefit from these properties of propolis. Owing to its healing power, propolis becomes a very useful and cheap tool for the treatment and prevention of many health problems in humans and other animals like, for example, cattle, dogs, cats or birds. Propolis can be used raw or in its extracted form. This technology explains how to process raw propolis into proplis extracts (alcohol, water and oil extracts).
entries.description:
Description

It is very easy to make propolis extract. It is a valuable product that can be prepared in little time and with only two ingredients: propolis and the right solvent. This technology describes how to make propolis extract using alcohol, water or oil as a solvent.

1. Preparation of raw propolis

  • To prepare the raw propolis for the extraction, first coarse debris such as pieces of wood or dead bees should be removed.
  • Then, to maximise the contact surface of the propolis with the solvent used, it should be broken up into little pieces or ground into a fine powder. 
  • Small pieces should be obtained to improve the dissolution of the active components of propolis. 
  • If the propolis is too sticky to be broken up, it can be placed in a refrigerator or freezer for a few hours.
  • Alternatively, pull the pieces into thin sheets or strips.
Figure 1. Raw propolis in a ball and in little pieces

©FAO/TECA

2. Choose the best or the more easily available solvent

  • The choice of the correct solvent is very important if the product is to be used for human consumption.
  • Normally, only ethanol (also called “pure alcohol” or “ethyl alcohol” C2H6O) or exceptionally, glycol (as in Method 3) should be used.
  • Other alcohols may be used only if their internal and external physiological interactions are sufficiently known and safe.
  • So-called denatured, rubbing or methyl alcohol should not be used.
  • If the extracts are intended for external application only, rubbing alcohol may be used in some cases.
    • Different countries use different chemicals to make pure alcohol unpalatable for drinking or internal consumption.
  • Similarly, there are different types of denatured alcohols intended for different purposes.
  • If cheap alcohol is used, care should be taken that the chemicals used for denaturing it are compatible with the planned end-use.
  • Chemicals added to denature alcohol may interact negatively with other ingredients so reducing their beneficial effects and may cause irritations, burns or even poisoning.
  • There have been fatal accidents caused by extracts of propolis prepared with unsuitable alcohol.
  • For most preparations intended for internal use, gin, rum, cachaca, arak or other clean, locally distilled liquors can be used.
  • These liquors usually contain less than the optimal 70 percent of alcohol but for home processing, they produce acceptable results.
  • As near 70 percent of alcohol as better results.

3. Basic equipment for small-scale processing

  • The following equipment will be needed to prepare propolis extract:
    • a large-capacity bottle which can be tightly closed;
    • a scale (more sensitive if working with smaller quantities);
    • a strainer (special filter paper, several layers of clean cotton cloth or cotton balls);
    • a refrigerator or freezer is useful, but not essential; and
    • a heat source is necessary to evaporate the solvent.

4. Three methods for propolis extraction

4.1 Method one: Ethanol Extracted Propolis (EEP)

  • Ethanol extracted propolis is the simplest method for extracting propolis.
  • The exact concentration of the desired extract should first be decided.
  • The initial concentration of propolis to be extracted should not exceed 30 percent, as extraction is less efficient or less complete at higher concentrations.
  • Thirty percent concentration means that the propolis amount will be 30 percent and the solvent will be 70 percent of the total volume.
  • The correct quantity of propolis is weighed and the right volume of alcohol measured.
  • One liter of 70 percent alcohol weighs approximately 860 g, one liter of 50 percent alcohol weighs approximately 900 g, and so on (see Table 1).
Table 1. Amounts of alcohol and propolis to use for different concentrations of propolis extract

Source: FAO 1996

  • Put the alcohol and propolis into a container, seal the top and shake briefly.
  • Repeat the shaking once or twice a day, leave the mixture in a warm dark place for at least three days.
  • To achieve the best results, the propolis should be left soaking into the alcohol for more than one week.
  • After one or two weeks, the liquid is ready and should be filtered through a clean and very fine cloth, paper filter or cotton ball.
  • The cloth may be folded into several layers to increase its effectiveness.
  • A second filtration may be advantageous.
  • The remains of the first filtration can be washed or soaked in alcohol again.
  • The filtrate should be a clear liquid, free of particles and dark brown or slightly reddish in colour (Figure 2).
  • It should be kept in clean, dark, airtight bottles (Figure 3).
  • If dark coloured bottles are not available, the bottles should be kept in a cool dark place or wrapped with a cloth, paper or straw, to protect them from light.
Figure 2. Pure ethanol extracted propolis, after filtration

©FAO/A. Couto

Figure 3. Preserve the propolis extract in a clean dark bottle

©FAO/A. Couto

4.2 Method two: Aqueous (water) extracted propolis

  • Aqueous propolis extracts can be obtained by soaking propolis for several days in water or boiling it in water.
  • The yield of active ingredients is lower than with alcohol, but aqueous extracts have been shown to have bactericidal and fungicidal effects.
  • All other processing, filtering, etc., are the same as those in Method one.

4.3 Method three: Oil extracted propolis

  • Mix 10 g of cleaned propolis with 200 ml (about 200 g) of any kind of refined food quality oil (e.g. coconut oil, sunflower oil, etc.) or with 100 g of butter.
  • Heat both ingredients gently in a water bath (no more than 50ºC) for approximately ten minutes and stir continuously.
  • Filter and store the extract in well-sealed containers in the dark.

5. Use of propolis extract depending on the method of extraction 

  • Method one provides the strongest propolis extract.
  • However that doesn’t mean that it will be best for all uses.
  • For example, in the case of eye inflammation (or infection or irritation), the best propolis extract to use is the water extracted propolis because it is not recommended to use alcohol or oil in the eyes.
  • Oil extract (Method three) is the best to use for mouth problems (for example infection of the gums) or in the case of baby treatments because of their sensitive skin.
  • The propolis extract obtained using Method one will be the best to use externally or in-ear problems (for example otitis).

8. Related/associated technologies

  • How to collect raw propolis from the hive: ID 8709.
  • How to harvest honey, pollen and propolis from stingless bees: ID 8265.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

9.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and can be undertaken without significant hand labour.

9.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for the efficient collection of propolis as an additional product derived from the hive. It is very effective in terms of it antimicrobial and anti-viral properties.

entries.tittle: Le paillage (ou mulching) en agriculture biologique, Philippines
entries.summary:
Le paillage (ou mulching) est le processus de recouvrement de la terre arable avec du matériel végétal tel que des feuilles, de l'herbe, des brindilles, des résidus de récolte, de la paille, etc. La couverture de mulch (ou paillis) accroît l'activité des organismes du sol et surtout celle des vers de terre. Les vers de terre contribuent à la bonne structure des sols car ils forment de nombreux tunnels de différentes tailles au travers desquels peut facilement s’infiltrer l’eau de pluie, réduisant ainsi les ruissellements de surface. De plus, étant donné que le paillis est issu de matière végétale, il est décomposable et il permet donc d’augmenter la teneur en matière organique des sols. Cette matière organique contribue à créer une bonne terre avec une structure stable. En conséquence, les particules fines du sol ne sont pas (ou peu) emportées par l'eau. Le paillage joue donc un rôle crucial dans la prévention de l'érosion des sols.

Cette fiche décrit la technique du paillage en agriculture biologique. Des détails sur les avantages et l'utilisation du paillis sont donnés. La sélection et la source des matériaux de paillage sont également fournies, ainsi que des recommandations lors de l'utilisation du paillis et de son application. Une étude de cas du système de Fukuoka de paillage des rizières met en évidence les avantages de cette technologie.
entries.description:
La description

Dans certaines régions, des matériaux tels que des bâches de plastique ou des pierres sont utilisées pour couvrir le sol. Cependant, en agriculture biologique, le terme « paillage » se réfère uniquement à l'utilisation de matériaux végétaux, dégradables et issus de l’agriculture biologique.

1. Pourquoi pratiquer le paillage? (Figure 1)

  • Protéger le sol de l'érosion éolienne (par le vent) et hydrique (par l’eau). Ceci est pour que les particules du sol ne sont pas emportées ou lessivées.
  • Améliorer l'infiltration de l’eau de pluie et d’irrigation grâce au maintien d'une bonne structure du sol. Il n’y a pas de formation de croûte imperméable en surface (parfois appelée croûte de battance) et les pores/interstices du sol restent ouverts.
  • Garder le sol humide en réduisant l'évaporation. Le sol est couvert et il est donc moins exposé au rayonnement du soleil, ce qui permet de diminuer l’évaporation. Les plantes peuvent donc être moins irriguées et/ou utilisent plus efficacement l’eau disponible dans les zones arides ou pendant la saison sèche.
  • Nourrir et protéger les organismes du sol. Le paillis végétal est une excellente source de carbone pour les organismes du sol et offre des conditions propices à leur croissance.
  • Bloquer la croissance des mauvaises herbes. Si la couche de mulch est assez épaisse, le développement des mauvaises herbes (aussi appelées adventices) est stoppé par manque de soleil, d’air, etc.
  • Éviter le réchauffement du sol. Le paillis fournit de l'ombre au sol et retient l'humidité, ce qui évite au sol de se réchauffer trop rapidement et trop fortement.
  • Fournir des nutriments pour les cultures. Tout en se décomposant, la matière organique du paillis libère continuellement ses éléments nutritifs, fertilisant ainsi le sol.
  • Augmenter la teneur en matière organique du sol. Une partie du mulch est transformé en humus puis décomposé progressivement.
Figure 1. Les effets bénéfiques de la pratique du paillage (ou mulching)

©FAO/TECA

2. Le choix du matériel végétal pour le paillage

Le type de matériel végétal utilisé pour le paillage influence beaucoup les résultats. Les matériaux végétaux qui se décomposent facilement vont protéger le sol pendant un temps très court mais ils vont pourvoir rapidement fournir des éléments nutritifs aux cultures. Au contraire, les matériaux plus résistants, qui se décomposent plus lentement, couvrent le sol pour un temps beaucoup plus long, mais la libération de nutriments issus de leur décomposition est en conséquence plus lente. Si la décomposition du paillis doit être accélérée, un engrais organique tel que le fumier animal peut être épandu sur le dessus du paillis, augmentant ainsi la teneur en azote des sols (Figure 2). Lorsque l'érosion des sols est importante, un paillis qui se décompose lentement, correspondant à une faible teneur en azote, et un rapport C/N (carbone/azote) élevé, permet de fournir une protection à long terme par rapport à un paillis dont la décomposition est rapide.

Figure 2. Optimiser le cycle de l’azote de l’exploitation agricole, schéma montrant les apports, exports et pertes d’azote d’une exploitation mixte (culture et élevage)

©FAO/TECA

3. Origine du matériel de paillage

Le matériel de paillage peut-être issus:

  • de mauvaises herbes ou de cultures de couverture;
  • de résidus de récolte;
  • d’herbe;
  • de matériel végétal issu de l'élagage des arbres ou des haies (petites branches, boutures, rameaux, sciures, copeaux, etc.); ou
  • de déchets issus de la transformation agricole ou provenant de l’exploitation forestière.

4. Possibles problèmes liés au paillage

La pratique du paillage possède de nombreux avantages, mais peut aussi engendrer quelques inconvénients dans certaines conditions (Figure 3).

  • Certains organismes, qui apprécient les milieux humides et protégés, peuvent proliférer abondamment dans les conditions de la couche de mulch. Par exemple, les limaces et les escargots peuvent se reproduire très rapidement dans ce type d’habitat.
    • Les fourmis ou les termites, qui peuvent causer des dommages aux cultures, peuvent également trouver des conditions idéales au sein du mulch pour se multiplier.
  • Dans certains cas, lorsque les résidus de culture sont utilisés pour le paillage, il y a un fort risque de maintien des populations de ravageurs et de maladies.
    • Les organismes nuisibles peuvent alors infester une nouvelle culture, tels les foreurs de tiges (pyrales d’espèces végétales variées) qui peuvent survivre dans les tiges de culture de coton, de maïs, de canne à sucre, etc.
    • Le matériel végétal infecté par des virus ou des champignons ne doit pas être utilisé en tant que mulch dès lors qu’il y a un risque de propagation de la maladie à la prochaine culture.
    • Ces risques peuvent être évités par une gestion efficace et stricte de la rotation des cultures.
  • Lorsque le matériel végétal utilisé pour le paillage est riche en carbone (par exemple paille, chaumes, fanes, etc.), l'azote du sol est alors utilisé par les micro-organismes du sol pour la décomposition de la matière organique.
    • L'azote devient donc temporairement indisponible pour la croissance des plantes.
  • La principale contrainte du paillage est la disponibilité de la matière végétale pour couvrir le sol.
    • Sa production et/ou sa collecte nécessitent de la main-d’œuvre et peuvent rivaliser avec la production végétale de l’exploitation.
Figure 3. Les potentiels problèmes liés au paillage (Photo d’une couche de mulch de feuilles mortes et de branchages)

©FAO/TECA

5. Mise en pratique du paillage

  • Si possible, le paillis doit être appliqué avant ou au début de la saison des pluies, pendant laquelle le sol est le plus vulnérable.
  • Si la couche de paillis n’est pas trop épaisse, les graines (ou les jeunes plants) peuvent être directement semées (ou plantés) sur (ou dans) la couche de mulch.
  • Dans le cas d’une production de légumes, il est préférable d'appliquer le paillis après que les jeunes plantes soient devenues un peu plus robustes, car elles peuvent être abimées par les produits de décomposition du paillis frais.
  • Si le paillis est appliqué avant le semis ou la plantation, la couche de paillis ne doit pas être trop épaisse afin de permettre aux graines de pénétrer le paillis et de germer.
  • Le mulch peut également être appliqué dans les cultures établies, idéalement directement après avoir labouré le sol.
  • Il peut aussi être appliqué entre les rangs, directement autour des plantes isolées (en particulier pour les cultures arboricoles) ou uniformément réparti sur le terrain (Figure 4).
Figure 4. Mulch épandu sur un champ de légumes aux Philippines

©FAO/TECA

6. Exemple pratique: Le système Fukuoka de paillage des champs de riz

Le japonais M. Fukuoka, pionnier en agriculture biologique dans son pays, a développé un système de riziculture basé sur le paillage. Un mois avant la récolte, du trèfle blanc est semée au sein de la culture de riz. Peu après, une culture de seigle d'hiver est semée. Après le battage du riz récolté, la paille de riz est ramenée sur le terrain où elle est épandue en vrac comme couche de mulch. Le seigle et le trèfle blanc se développent alors à travers le paillis, qui reste jusqu'à ce que le seigle soit récolté. Si la paille de riz se décompose trop lentement, du fumier de poulet est épandu sur le paillis. La culture de riz peut ensuite recommencer. Ce système de culture ne nécessite aucun travail du sol, et atteint des rendements très satisfaisants au Japon.

7. Les zones agro-écologiques

  • Les tropiques, chaud.

8. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Introduction à l’agriculture biologique: ID 8556.
  • Éléments à considérer pour la conversion à l’agriculture biologique: ID 8557.
  • La conversion étape par étape à l’agriculture biologique: ID 8558.
  • La gestion de l’eau en agriculture biologique: ID 8560.
  • La gestion et la planification des cultures en agriculture biologique: ID 8561. 
  • La gestion des éléments nutritifs en agriculture biologique: ID 8574.
  • La gestion des ravageurs et des maladies en agriculture biologique: ID 8575.
  • La gestion des mauvaises herbes en agriculture biologique: ID 8576.
  • La préparation et le travail du sol en agriculture biologique: ID 8584.
  • La conservation et la multiplication des cultures en agriculture biologique: ID 8585.
  • ​L’élevage en agriculture biologique: ID 8588.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en anglais: ID 8365.

9. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

9.1 Favorable aux femmes

La technologie est facile à utiliser et accessible.

9.2 L’efficacité d'utilisation des ressources

Améliore la qualité du sol menant à de meilleurs rendements.

9.3 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvres

L'amélioration des rendements grâce à la technologie du paillage constitue une source supplémentaire de revenus et de nourriture.

entries.tittle: Mutual Benefits through the cultivation of swamp jelutung (Dyera polyphylla): Preventing peatland degradation and creating income by an endemic latex producing Tree of Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Brunei and Malaysia)
entries.summary: A swamp jelutung plantation offers a sustainable alternative to commodities that require drainage, since naturally wet peat does not oxidise. Undrained, rewetted, peatland with swamp jelutung remains operational in the long-term. The following describes the establishment of a swamp jelutung plantation including how to establish a nursery, prepare the sites and plantation of adult trees and methods of tending and harvest. The economic, social and environmental benefits are also described. Products derived from swamp jelutung cultivation are also listed. Finally, trials undertaken since the 1990s are highlighted to illustrate the positive outcomes of using this technology.
entries.description:
Description

Swamp jelutung is only found in the peat swamps of Sumatra and Borneo (Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei) and not found outside this habitat. Harvesting is seasonal as swamps are not accessible all year round, and this is beneficial as it allows the trees to recover.

Tapping can begin after five to six years, although it is recommended that tapping does not start until the tree has a diameter of 30 to 35 cm. About 30 to 50 litres of latex can be tapped per tree per year, much in the way Hevea rubber is tapped, and this can occur for 12 years or more. Overtapping results in the death of the tree.

Latex needs to be treated with a coagulant, usually with acetic or phosphoric acid, within 24 hours. After this time it begins to deteriorate slowly, becoming more acid within a few days, and brittle within a few months. A swamp jelutung plantation offers a sustainable alternative to commodities that require drainage, such as oil palm or Hevea rubber, as naturally wet peat does not oxidise. Also, drained peatland will in many cases end up becoming (semi-) permanently flooded and is not a long-term option. Undrained (or rewetted) peatland with swamp jelutung will remain operational in the long-term.

Figure 1. Jelutung (Dyera polyphylla) plantation on deep peat at Sungai Aur, Jambi in 2003

©FAO/TECA

1. Establishment of a jelutung plantation

  • Steps to establish a jelutung plantation
    • Establishment of a nursery.
    • Preparation of the sites and plantation of adult trees.
    • Tending and harvest.

1.1 Example of the establishment of a 2 ha nursery

  • The land has to be cleared manually, of existing scrubby vegetation/ferns in the case of secondary vegetation.
    • It also has to be levelled as peatland normally has a hummocky structure and is difficult to develop.
  • Construct a roof consisting of netting that allows 30 to 35 percent of sunlight to penetrate, to protect the plants from harsh sunlight, desiccation, heavy downpours, and damage.
  • Establish small (1000 W) pumps for watering.
  • Get jelutung seeds or seedlings.
    • Obtaining a sufficient supply of jelutung seeds has proven to be difficult, as Dyera polyphylla flowers and sets seed only every four to five years.
    • Seeds can be stored for up to eight months at 22°C to 24°C, not cooler, 60 percent humidity.
    • Given the expansion of swamp jelutung in Jambi (Sumatra) since 2012, it is expected that small-scale commercial nurseries will be established locally.
    • Seeds should be soaked in water two hours before planting, and planted at an angle with the main wing facing up.
    • Germination is 90 percent, but reduces to 70 percent after eight months.
    • Sow in peat soil, with provision of extra minerals (P,K,N).
  • Plant, tend and harden the seedlings.
    • These will be reared for several months (some report up to a year, but this seems long) in the nursery, until they are 35 to 50 cm tall.
    • Longhorn beetles (Batocera rufomaculata) and ambrosia beetles may be a pest in plantations, especially on weakened trees that have been unskilfully tapped.
  • Established in the first six months of year, but continued until the present time.

1.2 Preparation of the sites and plantation of adult trees

  • Clear the land.
    • The land has to be cleared manually of existing scrubby vegetation/ferns in the case of secondary vegetation.
    • It also has to be levelled as peatland normally has a hummocky structure and is difficult to develop.
  • Transport the hardened seedlings to the plantation area.
    • This should be done as quickly as possible, for instance within a day.
    • Avoid desiccating wind (for example open trucks) and keep moist.
  • Plant the seedlings and pay attention to the watering of the seedlings during the first weeks, and longer if rains do not occur.
    • Planting should coincide with the onset of the wet season or be a few weeks before the wet season.
  • Provide the seedlings with initial fertilizers (N,P,K).
  • Pay attention to sufficient weeding after two, six, 12 and 24 months after planting. Weeding should be manual.
  • The plantation of seedlings is annually made.
    • In the studied case, 60 to 500 ha were planted, usually in one to two months prior to the wet season.
    • In this case, investments in infrastructure have been high because of the difficulty of access in the peat swamp.

1.3 Tending and harvest

  • Keep the area clean around seedlings during the first and second years after planting.
  • If necessary, replace the dead seedlings.
  • Remove climber and other woody plant species.
  • The first latex harvest occurs in the fifth year.
    • The harvest is continual, except at the peak of the wet season (no tapping) and on occasion during driest months, when low water levels prevent access by boat.
    • Tapping occurs like in the Hevea rubber.
    • Care should be taken to avoid using rusty instruments, as iron oxide speeds up deterioration of the latex.
    • In this case, the collected latex was transported in containers to main camp.
    • It was then processed (as in pressed with coagulant added; see above) and transported to Jambi and other cities, ultimately to Malaysia and Singapore.

2. Economic and social benefits

  • Traditionally, people from Sungai Aur are involved in river fisheries, trade, timber and agriculture.
  • People were recruited from Sungai Aur for working on the plantation (mainly men) and in the nursery (mainly women).
  • Initial economic studies indicate that while the annual monetary returns per hectare are higher for oil palm on peat, the return on labour is higher for swamp jelutung (the income per person per day labour is higher).
  • These results indicate that swamp jelutung might be a good alternative for smallholders, as their labour inputs are lower.
  • In the trials, the cultivation of jelutung provided incomes for the company and employed local community members.

3. Environmental benefits

  • Regarding the environmental aspect, the assessment depends on which two states of the peatland are compared.
  • If the jelutung plantation is compared to the original mixed peat swamp forest, then all carbon emissions are highly increased and sequestration is decreased.
  • However, if the comparison is made between the highly degraded and unmanaged state (or an oil palm plantation) and the managed Jelutung plantation, the carbon sequestration increased a lot and the carbon emission decreased in the jelutung plantation.
    • While active it also reduces greenhouse gas emissions, reducing desiccation.
  • This results in the prevention of fires and maintaining a permanent tree cover.

4. Products derived from swamp Jelutung cultivation

  • The trees produce a fine, light wood used for carving and pencils, and high quality latex.
    • This is used for a variety of purposes, including chewing gum, dentistry and insulation material.
  • Also, the nursery provides seedlings to locals and the Forestry Department.

5. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Sago plantations on undrained peatland: ID 8281.
  • Illipe nut plantation on undrained peatland: ID 8284.
  • Peatland restoration: ID 8278.
  • Vegetative tree propagation in agroforestry: ID 7794.
  • Establishing a tree nursery: ID 7808.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

Swamp jelutung is suitable for smallholders, as their labour inputs are low.

7.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for an additional source of income by an endemic latex producing tree.

8. Further reading

  • Giesen W., MacDonald M. 2014. Cultivation of Dyera polyphylla (swamp jelutung), In: Biancalani, R. and Avagyan, A (eds). Towards climate - responsible peatlands management. FAO. Rome. pp. 22-23, 52.

entries.tittle: Alternative Fodder Production to Increase Profitability of Livestock Production in the West Bank
entries.summary: This practice describes the use of hydroponic technology (soil-less plant propagation), in the form of green fodder, as an alternative method of sustainable feed production. It addresses decreased access to grazing land. This provides herders and their cooperatives with a low-cost, high quality, sustainable source of fodder which is available year-round. The approach increases the profitability of livestock production and helps herders stay in business.
entries.description:
Description

Hydroponics is a subset of hydroculture and the most common soil-less method of growing plants (including agricultural crops). Plants can be grown either on an inert substrate such as sand, perlite or gravel, in an aqueous medium with bare roots, without (as is the case in the current study) or with mineral nutrient solutions. The substrate can provide plant support and moisture retention.

Irrigation systems are integrated within these substrates, thereby introducing a nutrient solution to the plants’ root zones. The hydroponic fertilizer solution provides not only nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, but also all of the essential micro-nutrients for plant growth.

Hydroponic fodder production is a means of growing animal feed with lower resource requirements than would be needed for traditional fodder production – namely without the need for large tracts of land or a lengthy cultivation period.

1. Construction of hydroponic unit

  • Each hydroponic unit is a small 24 m2 (6 m x 4 m x 3 m height) unit per room made of sandwich panel construction material for isolation.
    • It consists of a framework of shelves on which plastic trays are stacked.
  • A layer of seeds is spread over the base of the trays and supplied with moisture and nutrients via drip or spray irrigation.
  • The seeds will usually sprout within 24 hours and in five to eight days have produced a 6 to 8 inch high grass mat.

1.1 Components of the hydroponic unit

  • Floor
    • The floor should be cast with a plate of reinforced concrete.
  • Sides and external walls
    • The units’ steel frame side panels are double layered steel with the gap between the two layers filled with fire resistant Kalkal insulation material.
  • Roof
    • The roof’s steel frame covering will be double layered steel with fire resistant Kalkal insulation material between the two sheets.
    • Rain gutters and related components ensure that water is discharged away from the roof.
  • Door
    • One metal door at the main entrance with thick, double layered steel sheets insulated by KalKal.
    • The door to be fixed to the metal unit with special doors steel frame, and three door joints.
      • Rope of rubber around the door to prevent any wind or water leakage.
Figure 1. Hydroponic unit

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Carriers shelves

  • Carriers shelves with two parts, use these specifications.
    • Galvanized steel bars are welded to form the carrier shelves as indicated in Figure 2.
    • All profile openings should be closed with plastic stoppers.
Figure 2. Carrier shelves

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Seed trays

  • The material of the trays should be non-carcinogenic, free of pigments and white in colour with inner partitions and holes for water discharge.
Figure 3. Seed trays

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Carrier shelves with fodder growing on trays

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Electricity

  • General requirements for the electricity.
    • All connections should be without a collection box.
    • All light fixtures (neon) should connect directly to the distribution board.
    • The light fixtures (neon) direction should be from the bottom to the above.
    • The water pump timer should be in the distribution board.
    • The extract fan should be connected with distribution board with two poles switch.
  • Concerning the electrical wiring, installations and devices, supply and install an air conditioning unit with 1.5 tonne capacity with clear specifications.
    • SEER: 15
    • 5 operating modes: cool, dehumidify, auto, fan
    • 25 feet line set included
    • Active carbon filtration
    • Auto-restart function
    • Led display low voltage safety
    • Pre-charged condenser (enough for 25' line set)
    • Programmable settings - timer, mode, temperature
    • Removable / washable air filters
    • Sleep mode temperature compensator
    • Two direction air vane
    • 12.etl-listed
    • Use alone on a 15a circuit breaker
    • Outdoor unit ambient temperature operating range of 10°C to 30°C

1.5 Water system

  • Water distribution pipes, underground pipes and a one horsepower water pump are needed to establish a spray irrigation system that will facilitate predictable and systematic watering of the planted barley.
Figure 5. Irrigation system in use to water planted fodder

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Drainage system

  • Equally important, the drainage system ensure that discharged water flows away from the planted barley and is then stored in a small water tank.
Figure 6. Water tank stores discharged water

©FAO/TECA

2. Validation

  • This practice was implemented under the project “Prepare and respond to shocks affecting low resilience farmers and herders in the West Bank and Gaza Strip”, funded by Canada.
  • It aligns with FAO’s objective of strengthening the resilience of vulnerable herders within the West Bank.
  • It is based on experiences implemented across the entire West Bank in all eleven governorates (Jenin, Tubas, Tulkarem, Nablus, Qalqiliya, Salfit, Ramallah, Jericho, Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Hebron).
  • Activities were undertaken within Areas A, B and C.
  • All participating herders’ cooperatives were visited after the project’s closing date for follow up.
  • From a quantitative standpoint each unit was found to produce a high quality and a significant quantity of fodder to international standards (every 1 kg of barley seeds yields 7 kg of vegetation).
  • From a qualitative perspective, the resulting fodder from hydroponic units has a much higher nutritional value, including more nutrients and protein, as it is fresh.
    • Not the dry version sold on the local market.
  • As a result, follow-up monitoring documented increased animal health and improved quality and quantity of dairy products produced.
  • While FAO WBGS sees alternative fodder production as a promising good practice, it is important to note that given the increased availability of fodder on the local market in winter and spring, the units were not used during that period.
  • Additionally, FAO WBGS’ project follow up has emphasized the importance of careful beneficiary selection to ensure ownership of and openness to alternative fodder practices as well as beneficiaries’ commitment to building and maintaining the skills needed to sustainably use the units.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Simple non-circulating hydroponic method for vegetables: ID 8825.
  • Construction of a non-recirculation hydroponic unit for commercial lettuce production: ID 8992.
  • Managing a non-recirculation hydroponic unit for commercial lettuce production: ID 8993.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

Hydroponic fodder production forges an efficient feed for animals without the need for large tracts of land or a lengthy cultivation period.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

Through this technology farmers can sustain their livestock production in dry seasons.
entries.further_reading:
7. Further reading

  • FAO. 2014. Small-scale aquaponic food production - Integrated fish and plant farming.
