entries.tittle: How to process raw drone larvae into value added products
entries.summary: Drones are male honey bees and their primary role is to mate with an infertile queen. The value of drone larvae as a nutritional supplement has been already proven. Drone larvae have been used as food for thousands of years by the most ancient civilizations. Drone larvae can also be used as food for animals as they are very rich in nutrients. Drone larvae therefore offer the opportunity to the beekeeper to generate extra income from the extraction and processing of drone larvae. The consumption of drone larvae can contribute to improved health and well-being. This technology explains how to process drone larvae into value added products.
entries.description:
Description

1. Preserving unprocessed drone larvae

1.1 Fresh raw larvae

  • Drone larvae should be kept alive as long as possible in the combs inside the hive.
  • See the technology “How to collect drone larvae from the hive” to learn how to collect drone larvae from the hive.
  • Once collected, drone larvae need to be processed or eaten immediately.

1.2 Refrigerated larvae

  • If larvae are refrigerated immediately after removing them from the hive, they should be processed (freezing, drying, boiling or frying) within 24 hours after collection of larvae.
  • This is to avoid any spoilage since insect proteins decay much faster than those of beef, chicken, lamb or pork.
  • In hot and humid climates, the larvae should be processed in less than six hours.

1.3 Frozen fresh larvae

  • One way to kill drone larvae is by freezing them.
  • Drone larvae can be frozen inside or outside the combs.
  • If you freeze drone larvae inside the combs you can remove them from the combs when you want to process them.
    • See the technology “How to collect drone larvae from the hive”.
  • Before processing the larvae, rinse them briefly in fresh, clean water (see Figure 1).
  • It is best to process the drone larvae while still frozen.
  • Where no refrigeration is available, processing will have to be started immediately after collection.
  • Cooked larvae can then be preserved by freezing. However, if no freezer or refrigerator is available, the boiled larvae should be consumed within a day.
  • Fried larvae will keep a little longer, but should be eaten as soon as possible.
  • Drone larvae can also be eaten raw (fresh or frozen) alone or with other raw food like in salads for example.
Figure 1. Bee larvae in a strainer for rinsing 

©FAO/TECA

2. Processing drone larvae for consumption

2.1 Raw, fried and boiled larvae

  • Honeybee larvae can be consumed like other insect larvae: raw, fried or boiled.
  • The raw larvae can be chewed while still inside the comb or after removal.
  • Chewing comb which also contains pollen further increases the nutritional value.
  • The age of the larvae is not very important.
  • However, for chewing larvae in combs, it is advisable to choose the whiter or newer combs.
  • If the skin of larvae is intact after collection, they may be rinsed briefly.
  • Then, larvae can be boiled for ten minutes (some people prefer 30 minutes) in salty or spiced water just like sea food.
  • Once boiled, they can be added to other recipes or eaten as they are.
  • If the skin of drone larvae is not intact after collection the best is to make a “juice” and after filtration use it with sauces or in drinks.
  • Like sea food, larvae may be deep-fried either plain (Figure 2) or after being rolled in flour or dipped in batter.
  • Deep-fat frying at 150 °C for only one minute is sufficient.
  • After one minute, the larvae should be removed and briskly shaken and drained on a slope, and/or covered with absorbent material to eliminate some of the excess fat.
  • The best oil/fat for frying is coconut oil because of its high resistance to oxidation at high temperatures.
  • For this reason, coconut oil is the perfect oil for high-heat cooking methods like frying.
Figure 2. Frying bee larvae in oil 

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Dried larvae

  • Larvae may be sun-dried in a solar drier.
  • They should be kept out of direct sunlight and protected from dust and insects.
  • After drying, they may be chopped or ground to a powder.
  • The powder may be used to enrich other meals or flours.
  • If used as an additive to animal feed, they can be added whole.
  • The flavour of these meals is not affected if the insects are used in moderate quantities.

2.3 Dry roasted larvae

  • Spread the cleaned, fresh or frozen larvae on clean paper towels.
  • Bake at 70°C to 94°C for one to-two hours until the right dryness is obtained.
  • Check the dryness by attempting to crush the insects with a spoon.
  • Alternatively, the dry larvae can be roasted in a large frying-pan, without any oil or fat, pot or metal sheet over medium heat.
  • If their temperature exceeds 100 °C they will caramelize.
  • They should be stirred frequently to prevent them from burning.

2.4 Drone larvae flour

  • Larvae should be dry-roasted or sun-dried first as described above and then reduced to a fine powder.
  • This can be done by using an electric blender or by grinding or pounding them until all drone larvae are reduced to a fine powder.
  • This powder can be further enriched with equally finely grounded dry pollen pellets or can be mixed directly with any other flour, dough, bread, vegetable dish or soup.
  • It thus remains unnoticeable by taste and texture, but enriches the diet.
  • If kept dry and packed immediately in plastic bags, it should keep fresh long enough for local marketing and consumption.
  • Cold storage is recommended and customers should be alerted to the short shelf-life of the processed drone larvae.
  • Do not process or package larvae flour during the rainy season since the flour cannot be kept dry enough.
Figure 3. Drone larvae prepared as appetizer in three different ways (from left to right): fried with garlic, boiled and fried in oil after covering with flour 

©FAO/TECA

3. Basic general recipes

  • Once frozen, solar-dried, or made into a flour, drone larvae can be incorporated into basically any other food dish.
  • In any of the dried forms, including the flour, they can also be readily marketed.
  • This technology is extracted from the publication “Value added products of the Beehive” and compiled and completed by Antonio Couto.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Good beekeeping practices: ID 8409.
  • Cricket farming for human consumption: ID 7927.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: honey harvesting: ID 7329.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: honey and bee wax extraction: ID 7330.
  • How to process the raw beeswax into value added products: ID 8776.
  • How to collect drone larvae from the bee hive: ID 8775.

This technology is also available in French: ID 10035.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Pro-poor technology

This practice offers the opportunity to the beekeeper to generate extra income from the extraction and processing of drone larvae and to use drone larvae for improved health and well-being.

entries.tittle: How to collect drone larvae from the bee hive
entries.summary: Drones are male honey bees. Unlike the female worker bee, drones do not have a stinger and do not participate in nectar and pollen gathering. A drone's primary role is to mate with an infertile queen. The value of drone larvae as a nutritional supplement has been proven in many studies conducted over the years and drone larvae have been used as food for thousands of years by the most ancient civilizations such as Chinese, Egyptian and Mayan civilizations. Drone larvae therefore offer the opportunity to the beekeeper to generate extra income from the extraction and processing of drone larvae and to use drone larvae for improved health and well-being. This technology explains how to collect drone larvae from the hive.
entries.description:
Description

1. Why eat drone larvae?

  • Adult and larval honeybees contain reasonable amounts of protein.
  • They could serve as a direct food source once the beekeeper has no more need for extra bees or brood, or when undesired colonies have to be removed.
  • The drone larvae protein content is as much a traditional protein source as cattle (see Table 1) or chicken.
  • While it is difficult to imagine that honeybee larvae will become a major source of protein, the larvae are a special delicacy in some countries.
Table 1. Composition of mature and immature honeybees compared to beef and soybeans (in % of fresh weight; vitamins in International Units per g fresh weight) modified from Crane, 1990. 
Type Egg Larva Cell capped Pupa Emergence
Drone until day 3 until day 6.5 until day 10 until day 14.5 from day 24 on

Source: FAO 1990.

  • A colony begins to rear drones in spring and the drone population reaches its peak coinciding with the swarm season in late spring and early summer.
  • The beekeeper can differentiate the drone larvae from the worker larvae because the cells from drones are bigger than the cells from worker bees (see Figure 1).
  • The drone larvae can be collected from the 6th day until the 22nd day after the deposit of the eggs.
Figure 1. Frame with worker cells (upper part) and drone cells (lower part of the comb). The size of the drone cells is clearly bigger than the size of the worker cell

©FAO/Camilo Ruiz

2. Drone larvae as food

  • In many African and Asian countries, brood combs (with worker bee and drone larvae) are considered a delicacy and are consumed immediately when available (see Figure 2) or eaten after processing of the larvae.
  • See Technology How to process raw drone larvae into value added products: ID 8778.
  • Drone larvae also contain testosterone, progesterone, oestradiol, decenoic acids and hydrogen ions concentration.
Figure 2. Zambian beekeeping extension officer, demonstrating an alternative use for bee brood 

©FAO/TECA

3. Removing larvae from the combs

  • The removal of drone larvae will affect the colony performance less than the removal of worker larvae.
  • Drone production can be promoted by the beekeeper using removable frame hives by providing drone size combs.
  • In areas where varroa is controlled by trapping the parasite in drone cells and removing the freshly sealed drone brood, the use of these otherwise discarded larvae may be considered.

3.1 Uncaping sealed drone larvae

  • First take a serrated knife and cut the surface of the sealed drone larvae cells recently removed from the hive (see Figure 3).
  • This process is also called "uncapping".
  • It may be easier to uncap the cells when the knife has been warmed a bit.
Figure 3. Uncapping sealed brood 

©FAO/TECA

  • After cutting the surface of the combs you can see that some drone larvae are difficult to remove because the cells are slightly deformed by cutting away the cappings (Figure 4).
Figure 4. Uncapped comb 

©FAO/TECA

  • To remove the drone larvae from the cells, shake them out on a clean table or surface.
  • Use a clean plastic sheet to help the collection of the larvae from the table. (see Figure 5).
Figure 5. Shaking out larvae 

©FAO/TECA

  • If the drone larvae cannot go out easily, fill the cells with water and then shake the frame again on top of the table (see Figure 6).
Figure 6. Filling the drone larvae cells with water 

©FAO/TECA

  • After collecting all drone larvae from the combs you can use a strainer to wash the larvae before processing them (see Figure 7).
Figure 7. Bee larvae in a strainer for rinsing 

©FAO/TECA

  • Where traditional hives or topbar hives are used and the combs cannot be reused, the whole comb may be squeezed or boiled.
  • This works best with new combs, but cells should be uncapped prior to boiling.
  • Melt the wax in a hot water bath (one pot in another pot with water), the wax will start to melt around 60 to 65° C.
  • The melted wax will harden at the surface and the larvae will sink to the bottom.
  • Some larvae will still have to be removed from older combs and occasionally from cocoons.
  • The flavour of the larvae will be affected by this method.
  • Alive brood should only be stored inside a hive.
  • Combs with brood removed from the hive for consumption should be refrigerated immediately or else consumed or processed immediately.
  • Refrigerated brood should be processed within 24 hours and in hot and humid climates in less than six hours.
  • This technology is extracted from the publication “Value added products of the Beehive” and compiled and completed by Antonio Couto.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Good beekeeping practices: ID 8409.
  • Cricket farming for human consumption: ID 7927.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: honey harvesting: ID 7329.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: honey and bee wax extraction: ID 7330.
  • How to process the raw beeswax into value added products: ID 8776.
  • How to process raw drone larvae into value added products: ID 8778.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Pro-poor technology

This practice offers the opportunity for the beekeeper to generate extra income from the extraction and processing of drone larvae and to use drone larvae for improved health and well-being.

entries.tittle: Construcción de graneros locales llamados localmente “Colombier” en Haití
keywords: gestión de riesgos pérdidas de la cosecha
entries.summary: Tradicionalmente la adaptación de las prácticas agrícolas toma en cuenta las consecuencias de los desastres y fenómenos naturales, su prevención y mitigación. Una de las prácticas que intenta reducir el impacto de las sequías, inundaciones y de los ciclones tropicales y lluvias, es la construcción de graneros llamados localmente “Colombier”. Se trata de una estructura construida con altos postes, donde los granos y las semillas recogidas o cultivadas pueden estar almacenados por períodos extensos, asegurando que no se pierdan cuando se presenten de catástrofes naturales. La siguiente tecnología explica cómo usar y construir un “Colombier”.
entries.description:
Descripción

1. Introducción

  • Las características geográficas de Haití están relacionadas con una degradación ambiental dispersa lo cual pone en gran vulnerabilidad a la zona por el impacto de los riesgos hídricos-meteorológicos periódicos que suelen impactar a la isla.
  • El sector agrícola de Haití sostiene al 70 por ciento de la población, del cual el 86 por ciento vive por debajo de los 2 USD al día, lo que incrementa su vulnerabilidad a los desastres naturales.
  • El tipo de graneros presentado en este documento (Figura 1) es tradicional y muy común de la zona Central y en el departamento Artibonite de Haití, siendo utilizados desde hace mucho tiempo.
    • Estas estructuras sirven para almacenar granos como el sorgo y frijoles comunes por periodos extensos (seis meses o más).
    • Esta técnica es utilizada para almacenar granos en caso de desastres naturales como son sequías, inundaciones, lluvias y fuertes vientos.
    • En el resto del país, las alternativas dominantes para guardar los granos cultivados son silos, o la instalación de ramas de árbol en el caso de maíz no recogido, y el cual se guarda en igallatasi, que significa cuartos entre el piso y el techo del granero.
Figura 1. Granero tradicional, “Colombier” (en francés) (figura de arriba), para el almacenamiento y la conservación de granos cosechados, especialmente granos que han sido colocados en granel (figuras de abajo izquierda y derecha) cuando no han sido recolectados, o colocados de forma inicial en un calabash pre-tratado (figura de abajo centro) para una mejor y más larga protección.

©FAO/TECA

  • Calabashes (nombre en lengua local) son pequeños contenedores utilizados (Figura 2) para almacenar semillas y granos de legumbres (como por ejemplo garbanzos) en pequeñas cantidades por un período de tiempo largo.
  • Como tienen una apertura pequeña se puede hermetizar las paredes interiores y exteriores con arcilla liquida y cerrar la apertura con arcilla dura, estiércol de vaca o con un tapón madera reforzado con tela.
  • Si el grano está seco (contenido de humedad menor de 12 por ciento) no hay problema con esta forma de almacenamiento.
Figura 2. Calabash

©FAO/TECA

2. Objetivos

  • El objetivo de estas estructuras es el de asegurar el almacenamiento de los granos (en algunas ocasiones en calabashes pretratados) y funcionar como cocinas campesinas, utilizando el piso de granero y/o en general para el almacenaje.

3. Implementación de la tecnología

  • La tecnología es aplicada por gente de la zona agroecológica de las regiones tropicales cálidas semiáridas y en sistemas de producción costeros de cultivos mixtos en Haití.
    • Este tipo de estructura, construida antes de que el impacto de un desastre llegue, puede ser realizada por agricultores de nivel socioeconómico medio-alto.
    • En este estudio de campo en Magnan (región en el sur de Haití), la estructura cambió y ahora los postes son de acero, mientras que en el pasado sólo eran de madera.
    • La estructura arquitectónica de los graneros en la ciudad Marmelade (departamento de Artibonite, Haití) era construido con cuatro postes mientras que en Magnan son construidos con 6 postes.
  • Los materiales incluyen postes de madera, palos largos, paja o acero corrugado, acero, lazos, clavos.
  • La estructura del piso se realiza con la construcción de una lámina de madera sostenida por 6 postes metálicos o madera de dos metros de alto, este piso debe estar a 1,5 m de altura (Figura 3).
    • El espacio entre la parte alta y el techo constituye el área de almacenamiento.
    • El techo con forma de A contiene ventanas pequeñas en ambos lados.
    • Las tres cuartas partes superiores de cada poste es cubierta con canaletas de metal orientadas de abajo hacia arriba para prevenir que roedores ingresen y dañen los granos cultivados.
Figura 3. Esquema de la estructura “Colombier”

©FAO/TECA

4. Costos

  • El costo de la instalación es entre 2 000.00 HTG a 3 m x 2 m de estructura a nivel de suelo con el techo.
  • Los costos de mantenimiento son de 300.00 HTG cada dos o tres años (es decir, aproximadamente 100.00 a 150.00 HTG por año) para reparar/rellenar las brechas en el techo.

5. Mejoras generales de esta práctica

  • Modernizar la infraestructura de los almacenes a través de acero galvanizado y con silos individuales o comunitarios. La manera tradicional para almacenar granos puede proveer una solución accesible para los hogares pobres. Sin embargo, almacenes de acero galvanizado podrían ser más resistentes a las condiciones climáticas extremas y proteger de una mejor manera las cosechas de las plagas. La siguiente tecnología describe brevemente cómo manejar un silo metálico.
  • Proveer de una tecnología postcosecha y de entrenamiento básico sobre insecticidas orgánicos y naturales. La siguiente tecnología (en inglés) presenta unas plantas con propiedades pesticidas para controlar los insectos durante el almacenamiento de granos en las explotaciones agrícolas. La siguiente tecnología presenta seis prácticas para reducir la pérdida durante el almacenamiento debido a las destrucciones por plagas.
  • Promover técnicas de conservación de semillas. En la siguiente tecnología se describe cómo utilizar hojas de eucalipto para preservar semillas de maíz y frijoles.

6. Validación de la práctica

La tecnología ha sido utilizada por personas en la zona agroecológica de los trópicos semiáridos cálidos y los sistemas de cultivo mixto de plantaciones costeras en Haití.

7. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

8. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Grain stores construction: ID 4499.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: improved storage facilities: ID 7308.
  • Diatomaceous earth to protect farm-stored grain: sorghum, maize and cow-peas: ID 4498.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: manual and motorised cleaning of grains and pulses: ID 7310.
  • Silo metálico plano para granos básicos: ID 6486. 

Esta tecnología también está disponible en inglés: ID 6865.

9. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

9.1 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

La tecnología protege los granos y frijoles de los severos impactos climáticos. Por lo tanto, proporciona una fuente adicional de ingresos y de alimentos.

entries.tittle: Traditional floating garden practices for vegetable production in Bangladesh
entries.summary: The floating garden practice is a local indigenous production system the successful in the wetland/submerged/flooded areas in the selected south and south-western districts (Pirojpur, Barisal and Gopalganj) of Bangladesh. Floating garden agricultural practices have been adopted by the local farmers for the past two centuries. This technology describes in detail how to construct and manage floating gardens for production of different crops (vegetables and spices).
entries.description:
Description

The floating garden practice is a local indigenous production system, the most successful in the wetland/submerged/flooded areas of selected south and south-western districts (Pirojpur, Barisal and Gopalganj) in Bangladesh. These areas remain submerged for long periods, especially in the monsoon season. Floating garden agricultural practices have been adopted by local farmers for nearly two centuries. They are developed based on farmers’ indigenous knowledge and experiences.

One type of floating bed for floating garden agricultural practices provides an opportunity for poor communities dependent crop production (particularly vegetables and spices) during monsoon, when most of the land is flooded. During this period (mainly June-October) farmers cultivate okra, red amaranth, cucumber, Indian spinach, turmeric, and aroid on organic floating beds made of water hyacinth.

Another type of floating bed is used mainly for seedling production of different vegetable and spice crops. A detailed description of the practice for seedling production. 

1. Construction of floating bed for crop production

  • Farmers generally collect water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) from the nearby wetland/ submerged areas to prepare floating beds directly on water (water depth 1 m or more).
    • Traditionally, the floating bed is constructed with three to five layers of water hyacinth arranged step by step from the bottom to the top until attaining the desirable height of the bed.
  • During bed preparation, the root of water hyacinth is arranged at the side and the shoot is placed in the middle position of the floating bed.
    • The water hyacinth layer is made at five to seven days intervals.
    • Water hyacinth is drawn with the help of a wooden hook placed on bamboo made handles (locally named as “Thora”) (Figures 1 and 2).
    • After preparing several layers, the floating bed becomes compact due to decomposition of the water hyacinths.
    • The immature water hyacinth decomposes earlier than the mature ones.
    • Therefore, the mature water hyacinth layer is generally used as foundation and the comparatively, the immature ones, are kept at the top of the floating bed.
Figure 1. Preparation of foundation layer of floating bed with water hyacinth collected by hook/Thora

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Water hyacinth layer placing step by step by using Thora

©FAO/TECA

  • There is no recommended size or shape of the traditional floating bed (Figure 3).
  • It is generally 15 to 20 m long, 1.3 to 1.8 m wide and 1.2 to 1.3 m high.
  • The size of the floating bed depends on the water space on which the bed is placed for crop production.
Figure 3. Different size and shape of indigenous floating beds

©FAO/TECA

  • The prepared floating bed is anchored with bamboo and rope so that it cannot be displaced to other places or locations (Figure 4).
  • In the recent years, the floating bed is also sold in ready-made condition at the local floating market.
  • Generally, male farmers are engaged with the preparation of the floating bed.
Figure 4. Prepared floating bed for crop production anchored with bamboo and rope

©FAO/TECA

2. Preparation of ball for seedling raising

  • Farmers prepare special balls for seedling raising (Figure 5).
  • The ball (6 to 8 cm in diameter) is made with well decomposed water hyacinth (Figure 6) for raising seedling of selected vegetable crops (Indian spinach, okra, cucumber, morma etc.).
  • The organic ball is locally termed as “Tema” or “Mada”.
  • The tema/mada is used as growing media of the seedlings.
Figure 5. Woman preparing the ball/ tema/mada for raising seedlings

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Ball/tema/mada made of decomposed water hyacinth

©FAO/TECA

3. Seed placement in the ball/tema/mada and seedling raising

  • At first, three to four holes are made into the ball/tema/mada with the help of a pointed stick or the thumb (Figure 7).
  • Then three to four seeds are inserted into the hole for germination.
  • Generally, local varieties of crops are used for crop production.
  • After germination of the seeds (five to seven days after seed placement), the seedling balls are kept under light shadow condition at homestead area for hardening and to increase their adaptation capacity.
  • The young seedlings are watered daily for keeping the growing media or ball at optimum moisture condition.
  • The seedlings are also protected from any kind of damage through fencing surrounding the homestead nursery (Figure 8).
  • The seedlings are shifted to the water field when they become suitable for transplanting on the floating bed (Figure 9).
  • Generally the seedlings become suitable for transplantation at 10 to 15 days after germination of vegetable seeds.
Figure 7. Woman placing seeds into the ball/tema/mada

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Nursing of seedlings at a homestead area

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Farmer bearing seedling for transplanting on floating beds

©FAO/TECA

4. Seed sowing or transplanting of seedlings on floating bed

  • The floating bed becomes suitable for sowing/planting of crops after 20 to 25 days of preparation.
  • Some farmers apply urea fertilizer (about 400 to 500 g per 10 m2) on the floating bed to enhance the decomposition and in order to sow or plant earlier.
  • Traditionally, seeds of leafy vegetables, like red amaranth, are sown directly through broadcasting on floating bed (Figure 10).
  • Seedlings of other selected vegetables (Indian spinach, okra, cucumber, morma etc.), as seen in Figure 11, are transplanted in rows in the afternoon.
  • Turmeric, sprouted rhizome and sucker of aroids, the crops are transplanted in rows, too (Figure 12).
  • During transplanting, the seedling balls as well as sprouted rhizome and lower portions of sucker are covered with decomposed water hyacinth in order to establish them on the floating bed successfully.
Figure 10. Farmers transplanting seedlings on floating beds

©FAO/TECA

Figure 11. Transplantation of okra seedlings (a), morma (b) and Indian spinach (c) on floating beds

©FAO/TECA

Figure 12. Transplantation of aroid (panikatchu) on floating beds

©FAO/TECA

5. Intercultural operations and protection of crops on floating beds

  • There are no recommendations for fertilizer management packages for cultivating crops on floating beds.
  • If plants become yellowish, the farmers usually apply urea fertilizer as top/side dressing only, followed by irrigation for enhancing the vegetative growth of the cultivated crops.
  • Irrigation and weeding are done as per requirement of the crops for their proper growth and development (Figure 13).
  • In some cases, the crops are surrounded by fences of nylon net to protect them from the attack of ducks (Figure 14).
  • Sometimes, the floating bed crops are damaged by rats.
    • Farmers use indigenous method to protect the crop from the infestation of rats (Figure 15).
Figure 13. Weeding in red amaranth on floating bed

©FAO/TECA

Figure 14. Fencing of turmeric bed for preventing the attack of duck

©FAO/TECA

Figure 15. Use of indigenous device for rat trap on floating beds

©FAO/TECA

6. Harvest of crops on floating bed

  • Farmers harvest the crops when they attain the harvestable stage on the floating beds.
  • The growing period in the field of crops depends on their harvestable stage as well as maturity.
  • The crop products (vegetables and spices) are generally used for consumption by the farm households.
  • Farmers sell a surplus amount of their agro-products to the nearby people as well as at local markets to earn some extra cash for their daily household expenses.
  • Below are some examples of crops ready for harvesting.
Figure 16. Red amaranth (a) and okra (b) at harvestable stage on floating bed

©FAO/TECA

Figure 17. Indian spinach (a) and Turmeric (b) at vegetative growth stage on floating bed (not at harvesting stage)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 18. Aroid (panikachu) at harvestable stage on floating bed

©FAO/TECA

Figure 19. A farmer harvesting

©FAO/TECA

7. Profitability of crop production on floating beds

  • The farmers earn an average profitability of USD 140 per 100 m2 of floating bed from crop production during a monsoon season.

8. Advantages of the systems

  • Floating agriculture practices have minimal infrastructure and very little capital requirement.
  • Costs can also be kept low because raw materials for the construction of floating beds are readily available from local waterways.
  • Materials for floating beds are highly abundant.
    • In particular, water hyacinth is usually classified as one of the worst invasive species.
    • For that reason, farmers can easily use it as floating bed or composts without any additional cost.
    • This gives the opportunity to many people living in this area to cultivate using this technique.
  • This system considerably mitigates the risks of natural disaster and climate change.
  • The productivity of floating vegetable cultivation is estimated ten times higher than on a similar sized land-based cultivation.
    • Given that it allows better control over crops, some researchers have noted a greater productivity of floating bed practices compared with traditional land-based agriculture.
    • The use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides is minimal in this system.
  • The floating beds can also be recycled and used as organic fertilizer in the newly prepared floating bed and agricultural fields.
    • This is both economic and environmentally friendly.
  • Using water hyacinths reduces breeding grounds for mosquitoes.
  • It also participates in improving the carrying capacity of water circulation by reducing the weed breaking down the drainage system.
    • With a better water circulation and less invasive weeds, this system has a positive impact on open-water fishing.
  • The practice also contributes to food security.
    •  Additional space for vegetables cultivation in the wetlands.
    • Increase in vegetables supply in the area and the surroundings.
    • Primary nutrients (e.g. nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium) and micronutrients (e.g. boron, molybdenum etc.) are available in water hyacinth, comparable with cow-dung and other organic manures.
    •  When water recedes in wetlands, dismantled floating beds are used as organic fertilizer.
      • It enhances eco-friendly agriculture practice in winter seasons to cultivate winter crops.
  • The following video shows how school children in Bangladesh learn about how floating garden practices can contribute to food security. Global Food Security: How can we feed a growing population? (This video is produced by from British Council Schools Online and available on Vimeo).
    • This video gives a short introduction about traditional floating garden practice and its improvements developed by BARI.

9. Validation of the practice

  • The system for seedling production is traditionally practiced in the wetland/submerged/flooded areas of selected south and south-western districts (Pirojpur, Barisal and Gopalganj) of Bangladesh.

10. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

11. Related/associated technologies

  • Improvements of traditional floating gardens for vegetable production: ID 8868.
  • Traditional floating garden practices for seedling production: ID 8869.

This technology is also available in Spanish: ID 8955.

12. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

12.1 Women friendly

The technology is easy to use and can be undertaken by any form of hand labour. 

12.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for crops to grow in flooded areas, thereby providing more secure sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Apicultura: confección de cajón triple
entries.summary: El cajón triple es una estructura que permite la optimización del espacio, de material y compartir el calor que generan las tres familias pequeñas que se encuentran dentro de este cajón adaptado para este propósito. Algunos apicultores utilizan este sistema para la generación de núcleos con pequeñas familias y también es utilizado como cajón de fecundación ya que es fácil revisarlo y requiere pocas abejas para mantener a una reina en su interior. Esta tecnología explica cómo construir un cajón triple y su uso.
entries.description:
Descripción

1. Utilización del cajón triple

  • El cajón triple es una adaptación de cualquier colmena moderna (con marcos móviles) como Langstroth, Dadant o Jumbo a la que se le incorporan dos tabiques internos que permitan la aislación completa de los tres compartimientos dentro del cajón (Figura 2).
  • Además, este cajón debe considerar tres orificios que permitan la salida de cada una de las familias que alojarán en el interior del cajón triple (Figura 3).
  • En el caso de que el cajón triple sea utilizado como colmena de fecundación se recomienda hacer marcas visibles en los orificios de cada familia para que la reina tenga una marca visual para regresar a su familia de origen sin perderse.

2. Construcción de un cajón triple

  • El cajón triple se confecciona a partir de una colmena tradicional.
Figura 1. Cajón triple mirado desde la parte de atrás, donde cada compartimiento se encuentra pintado de diferente color

©IRACH

  • Cada familia en el interior del cajón triple debe estar completamente aislada una de la otra mediante los dos tabiques internos y tres entretapas (una para cada familia) (Figura 4) las cuales deben quedarse posicionadas de tal forma que no permitan el paso de abejas, pues si se mezclan se generan peleas e incluso mortandad de la reina de las familias.
  • Los dos tabiques que se ponen dentro del cajón darán origen a tres compartimientos para tres familias.
  • Lo que se hace es posicionar 2 tabiques de madera de 48 cm de largo por unos 26 cm de alto.
  • Cada tabique se posiciona para hacer tres espacios iguales, lo cual en colmena Langhtroth es cada 12,5 cm.
Figura 2. Las divisiones del cajón triple en su interior

©IRACH

Figura 3. Esquema con opciones de ubicación de las piqueras del cajón triple

©IRACH

Figura 4. Cajón triple sin techo, pintado de un sólo color, se logran ver las tapas individuales de cada familia. Entre cada tapa hay un tabique que sobresale del cajón para no permitir el paso de abejas

©IRACH

  • De esta manera con cada tapa individual se pueden realizar manejos por cada familia dentro de los tres compartimientos.
  • Nunca se deben tener dos compartimientos abiertos al mismo tiempo, pues pasan abejas y olores de una familia a la otra y se pueden generar los problemas ya señalados.
Figura 5. Apertura de la entretapa de la familia central del cajón triple para su revisión

©IRACH

  • Generalmente la familia que se encuentra al centro tiene un desarrollo más rápido que las familias de los extremos, pues recibe calor de estas dos de los costados.
  • Cuando las familias lo requieren y según la temporada se pueden incorporar entretapas de alimentación para triples.
Figura 6. Abejas en compartimiento central del cajón triple siendo inspeccionado

©IRACH

3. Alimentadores para cajón triple

  • La alimentación para los compartimientos del cajón triple es fundamental, como lo es también para un cajón núcleo (4 o 5 marcos) ya que si se alimentan los núcleos, estos se desarrollan mucho más rápidamente y hay mayor probabilidad de que las reinas recién nacidas o introducidas por el apicultor sean aceptadas.
Figura 7. Cajón triple con alimentador de entretecho individual bañado con cera de abejas para impermiabilizar el interior del alimentador para que no filtre alimento

©IRACH

  • Los materiales para la confección de cada alimentador de entretecho son (valores relativos según el tamaño del cajón que utilice):
    • Listón de 4 cm x 1 cm x 150 cm.
    • 200 mm de cera de abejas.
    • Malla metálica de cuadricula no mayor a 5 mm.
    • Tabla de madera de 0,5 cm x 13 cm x 50 cm.
  • Cuando se realiza alimentación debe suministrar alimento a los tres compartimientos al mismo tiempo para no generar pillaje e insentivar la postura y fortalecimiento de las abejas que se encuentran en el triple cajón.
Figura 8. Colmena con el alimentador al centro y los dos compartimientos de los extremos abiertos (sólo a modo de explicación ya que no se deben abrir dos compartimientos al mismo tiempo)

©IRACH

  • Ya posicionados los tres alimentadores se puede suministrar alimento a las familias.
  • Es importante verificar que la colmena se encuentre bien nivelada para que no escurra el jarabe y se pueda hacer el mejor uso del alimentador.
Figura 9. Cajón triple con sus tres alimentadores con jarabe en su interior para que las abejas puedan alimentarse

©IRACH

  • Los alimentadores deben tener una entretapa deslizadera (Figura 9) para cerrarlas individualmente para impedir que una vez que tomen el alimento las abejas no se mezclen entre diferentes familias.
Figura 10. Tapa corredera para impedir que se mezclen las abejas entre las familias

©IRACH

  • Los alimentadores deben poseer un pequeño orificio de un centímetro de diámetro en la base del alimentador para permitir el paso de las abejas del compartimiento al alimentador.
Figura 11. La base del alimentador posee un orificio en un extremo para que las abejas pasen a alimentarse

©IRACH

  • El alimentador de entretecho debe disponer de 2 cámaras: una que contiene el alimento y otra cámera que permita a las abejas de subir al alimentador y acceder al alimento (cámara de acceso).
  • La cámara de acceso tiene un orificio para permitir que suban las abejas al alimentador (letra A), mirado desde arriba del alimentador.
  • Esta cámara se separa de la cámara donde se sitúa el alimento mediante un listón (letra B), el cual debe tener una separación de malla metálica (letra C) de 0,5 cm para permitir el paso de las abejas a libar el alimento de manera tal que no se ahoguen.
  • La malla se ancla a un tercer listón (letra D) para que quede estirada y sirva de guia para la tapa corredera que tapa el alimentador.
Figura 12. Las estructuras superiores del alimentador del cajón triple. A: orificio para paso de abejas, B: listón para retención del alimento (limitador de jarabe y bebedor de abejas), C: malla para impedir paso de abejas, D: listón para estirar malla y guia para tapa deslizadera (limitador malla metálica)

©IRACH

  • Algunos aspectos fundamentales para un óptimo uso del cajón triple es:
    • Que esté bien aislado cada compartimiento.
    • Que se sitúen espaciados entre cajones para evitar deriba de abejas (idealmente separaciones de 50 a 60 cm).
    • Deben estar bien nivelados para que no escurra alimento.

4. Validación de la práctica

  • El cajón triple ha sido testado con éxito por los apicultores de IRACH, Chile durante varios años.

5. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, húmedo/seco.
  • Subtropical, seco.

6. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Apicultura: desarrollo de familias a partir de un núcleo (pequeña familia): ID 8666.
  • Confección de trampa de cartón para captura de enjambres de abeja africanizada: ID 8658.
  • Buenas prácticas apícolas: ID 8217.

7. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

7.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta práctica proporciona una descripción de cómo construir un cajón triple y su uso eficiente para los apicultores.

7.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

La confección de cajón triple permite la optimización del espacio y de material, entre otras, lo que a largo plazo conduce a muchos resultados positivos para el apicultor.

entries.tittle: Rainwater harvesting systems for cabbage growing in Uganda
entries.summary: This technology describes utilizing rooftop water harvesting facilities to increase the availability of water for domestic use and irrigation of backyard cabbage gardens. This measure allows small-scale farmers to harvest rainwater from roofs and store it in tanks, ensuring cabbage production even during the dry season. The combination of rainwater harvesting with other good practices (e.g. mulching, manuring) helps increase productivity while reducing soil erosion, eventually strengthening the resilience of farmers to the impact of dry spells.
entries.description:
Description

1. Suitability

This measure was tested by households in rural districts in Uganda facing frequent water shortages. Rainwater harvested in tanks can be used for domestic purposes and for watering cabbage gardens requiring little water to produce decent yields. If harvested water is managed carefully, it can be a reliable and significant water source during the dry season. Housing with an iron roof has an advantage in installing water harvesting tanks as it facilitates rainwater collection.

2. Composition and types of tank

  • Rainwater can be harvested from roofs by building gutters that guide the water into a harvesting tank (Figure 1).
  • Water can also be harvested by putting inclined iron sheets directly on the tanks, in addition to the roofs (Figure 1,b).
  • The water is then accessed with a pump (Figure 2).
  • Several sizes of tanks were observed in the field, such as 7 000 litres, 30 000 litres, and 50 000 litres (Figure 3).
    • The tank size depends on the needs, investment capacity of the farmer/community and the size of dwellings (medium-sized tanks may be suitable for a dwelling that has a roof size greater than 25 m2).
Figure 1(a,b,c). Different types of tanks for rainwater harvesting

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Pump to access water from the tank

©FAO/Prakash Sin

Figure 3. Rooftop rainwater harvesting with an elevated tank

©FAO/Benedicte Kurzen

3. Major cost

  • At the point of writing the cost for establishing a tank system for rainwater harvest, the costs were as follows:
    • 7 000 litre tank, UGX 2.3 million (USD 624); 
    • 30 000 litre tank with an inclined iron sheet, UGX 3.5 million (USD 950);
    • 50 000 litre tank (compare Figure 3) costs UGX 4 million (USD 1085); and
    • an electronic pump (see Figure 2 for fuel pump) for UGX 60 000 (USD 16).

4. Effectiveness and benefits

4.1 Socio-economic and ecological benefits

4.1.1 Short-term benefits

  • Saving time
    • Water harvesting tanks give people easy access to water for domestic use and prevent them from walking long distances or queuing. 
  • Saving labour
    • Instead of getting water, people will be available to do other tasks, e.g. working/attending school.
  • Additional income
    • Water can be sold at UGX 1 000 (USD 0.3) per jerry can.

4.1.2 Medium-term benefits 

  • An additional source of good quality water since other sources are polluted or depleted.

4.1.3 Long-term benefits 

  • Prevents water depletion from natural sources (groundwater, lakes, streams, swamp, etc.).
  • Decreases erosion from surface run-off induced by heavy rains.

4.2 Gender and other related benefits

  • Women are usually responsible for harvesting water.
    • Hence, these techniques allow women to save time that can be used instead to produce food and/or to go to school.
  • Rainwater harvesting can, therefore, have significant benefits for women and contribute to gender equality.

4.3 Climate change adaptation-related benefits

  • Rainwater harvesting:
    • saves time and labour;
    • provides an additional good source of water;
    • helps reduce erosion from heavy rains; and
    • limits water resource depletion, which is particularly important in the context of climate change where water resources are likely to become scarcer.
  • Rainwater harvesting, therefore, offers opportunities to better adapt to climate change.

5. Side effects

  • Water harvesting tanks can have some negative side effects.
    • If they are poorly constructed, the tanks can suffer from algae growth and pest invasion.
    • They can also become a breeding ground for disease vectors if not properly maintained.

6. Major Barriers

  • There are usually no cultural or social barriers against water harvesting tanks.
    • However, very often communities face financial challenges to buy the tanks and sometimes technical challenges to build the related harvesting infrastructure.

7. Synergies

  • Rainwater harvesting can create synergies with other adaptation options such as: 
    • low-cost drip irrigation systems;
    • water harvesting rock embankment;
    • valley dams; and 
    • the use of mulch and compost to increase water retention capacity of the soil and reduce evaporation.

8. Cumulative net benefits and benefit-cost ratios of good practice and local practice

  • Cost-Benefit Analyses were conducted based on quantitative data collected during the monitoring period in the 2016 dry season (Jun-Aug).
  • Cumulative net benefits and benefit-cost ratios were calculated over 11 years per m2 of the cabbage garden.
  • Data collected from good practice plots were compared with data collected from local practice plots where no rainwater harvesting facilities were installed.
Figure 4. Chart of cumulative net present value per square meter over 11 years

©FAO/TECA

  • For good practice plots, the gross value of production is calculated considering that farms produce cabbages throughout the year (except for the first year when the first six months are dedicated to installing the rainwater harvesting facility), while in local practice plots, production is only possible during rainy seasons (six months per year).
  • Also, access to credit is key to ensure that farmers are able to invest in this good practice. Given the small size of the sample analysed, additional research would be needed to confirm the results.

9. Validation

9.1 The geographical area of practice validation

  • The practice was tested in Mubende and Nakasongola districts in Uganda.
  • All farms were affected by dry spells during the monitoring period 2016 dry season (June to August).
  • Rainfall was between 50 to 100 percent below normal in August, and land surface temperatures were 3°C to 7 °C above average, reducing water availability.

9.2 Farmers’ perception

  • The farmers interviewed for the evaluation of this good practice said they would replicate the good practice because they were able to grow vegetables also during the dry season.
  • According to them, the practice helped increase production and income, while reducing work efforts to collect water. T
  • he farmers rated the good practice 5 out of 5 regarding its performance in the face of a dry spell.

10. Minimum requirements for successful implementation of the technology

  • The minimum requirements for a successful rainwater harvesting implementation include:
    • an inclined roof, preferably iron roof;
    • ground space near the roof (approximately 6.5 m2 of space is needed to install a 7 000 litre tank);
    • electricity for the pump if an electric pump is being installed; and
    • initial financial investment to install the rainwater harvesting system (approximately USD 0.75 per m2 of the plot).

11. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, all; and
  • subtropics, all.

12. Related/associated technologies 

  • Rainwater harvesting for increased pasture production: ID 7358.
  • Rainwater harvesting for schools: ID 7645.
  • Rainwater harvesting systems for tomato growing: ID 8922.

13. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

13.1 Women-friendly

Rainwater harvesting is a women-friendly technology as it reduces the working hours required to collect water, and makes time for other important tasks such as managing the household, attending school, or working at other part-time jobs. 

13.2 Resource use efficiency

This practice optimizes the use of water which would have never been used otherwise. Collecting and harvesting rainwater for vegetable production reduces the cost of production of vegetables (in this technology: cabbage) and increases the benefits compared to the costs.

entries.tittle: Indoor oyster mushroom cultivation for livelihood diversification and increased resilience in Uganda
entries.summary: This practice describes indoor mushroom (Pleurotus spp.) cultivation as a means to diversify livelihoods and strengthen the resilience of farmers in Uganda. Indoor mushroom cultivation was promoted by the Global Climate Change Alliance (GCCA) project on Agriculture Adaptation to Climate Change in the central cattle corridor of Uganda. Mushrooms can be grown at very low cost and in a relatively short time. It is a practice that can be adopted by small-scale farmers to diversify their income during the dry season, when lack of water may challenge the cultivation of other crops, and reduce their vulnerability to adverse weather. Indeed, mushroom production is done indoor and it requires a little amount of water compared to other crops.
entries.description:
Description

1. Description (step by step) of the application of the technology/practice

This practice describes the benefits of indoor oyster mushroom (Pleurotus spp.) cultivation as a livelihood diversification practice. Oyster mushroom cultivation was promoted by the Global Climate Change Alliance (GCCA) project on Agriculture Adaptation to Climate Change as a livelihood diversification practice for small-scale farmers in the central cattle corridor of Uganda.

1.1 Step one: mushroom spawns

  • Mushrooms are grown in ‘gardens’ where the spawns are inoculated.
  • The spawns are filled into sterile glass bottles through a process that requires specific tools and knowledge.
  • Farmers can either buy mushroom spawns from specialized producers at local markets or be trained for producing mushroom spawns themselves.
Figure 1. Mushroom spawns in sterile bottle

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Step two: substrate

  • Agricultural waste (e.g. from sorghum, millet, beans, peas, wheat, maize) or cotton waste can be used as a substrate to grow oyster mushrooms.
  • The agricultural waste, which is easily available on farms, is soaked for three days and then heaped for fermentation for four to six days in a closed container.
  • After the fermentation process, the agricultural waste is sterilized through boiling in closed pots for 12 hours in order to eliminate unwanted organisms and bacteria.
  • After cooling, it is filled in small polyethylene plastic bags using common bowls, to serve as a substrate.
    • The substrate should be composed by 65 to 75 percent of moisture, and for the remaining part by agricultural waste.
    • It can be used for three harvests, and then it can be recycled as organic mulch or fertilizer.
    • Alternatively, cotton seed waste can be used as substrate for oyster mushroom production.
Figure 2. Agricultural waste being soaked

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Step three: inoculation

  • Polyethylene plastic bags are filled with the substrate (about 5 kg per bag), which is then inoculated with the mushroom spawns.
    • Spawns are ‘mixed’ with the substrate.
  • Each garden of about 5 kg of the substrate is filled with about 250 g of spawns.
  • Plastic bags are then closed manually.
Figure 3. Plastic bags are being filled before inoculation

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Step four: incubation

  • Following the inoculation process, the mushroom bags are hanged in locally built (with brick or mud walls and thatched roof), darkened mushroom houses for incubation.
  • The ideal humidity of the incubation room is 70 to 75 percent.
  • Each room can host up to 300 gardens.
Figure 4. Mushroom house

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Step five: harvest

  • The mushrooms start sprouting after 28 to 35 days from inoculation.
  • Each mushroom garden (e.g. a plastic bag containing about 5 kg of substrate) yields a minimum of two kilograms of fresh oyster mushrooms.
Figure 5. Mushrooms sprouting in the growing room

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Step six: drying and packing

  • Harvested mushrooms can be sold fresh, or they can be dried in a solar dryer and packed into plastic bags for sale.
Figure 6. Solar dryers for mushrooms

©FAO/TECA

2. Major costs and resources needed to cultivate oyster mushrooms

  • The approximate production costs per average mushroom garden (about 5 kg of the substrate) yielding about 2 kg of fresh mushrooms.
    • Cost of a polyethylene bag: UGX 25 per bag.
    • Cottonseed waste: UGX 7 000.
    • Mushroom spawns: UGX 3 000.
    • Labour: UGX 115.
  • The approximate upfront capital costs required to start mushroom production.
    • Growing room: UGX 800 000.
    • Solar dryer: UGX 700 000.
  • Mushroom market prices.
    • Dried mushroom: UGX 30 000 per kg.
    • Fresh mushroom: UGX 8 000 per kg.
  • The costs and prices mentioned in this practice refer to the time of writing (May 2017).

3. Benefits

  • Mushrooms can be grown at a very low cost and in a relatively short time.
  • This is a Disaster Risk Reduction good practice for small-scale farmers especially during the dry season, when lack of water may challenge the cultivation of other crops.
  • Mushroom production is done indoors and it requires a little amount of water compared to other crops.

3.1 Cost-benefit analysis of the practice

  • The performance of indoor mushroom cultivation was assessed at the farm-level in Uganda.
  • The net benefits obtained from producing mushroom in the central cattle corridor of Uganda were calculated through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA).
  • The CBA calculates the net present value (NPV) of cumulative benefits obtained from an average mushroom house over a period of 11 years.
    • A 10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms).
  • The CBA also calculates the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
  • Since mushroom cultivation was not previously practiced in the monitored farms, control plots were not available to conduct a comparative analysis.
  • As an alternative, the opportunity cost of agricultural labour was used.
    • More specifically this is the income foregone by not employing the labour used for mushroom production elsewhere. 

Figure 7 and Figure 8 provide an overview of the outcome of the CBA. 

  • In dry spell conditions (Figure 7), the net benefit of mushrooms growing over 11 years is more than seven times higher than the opportunity cost of labour.
    • The BCR in dry spell conditions is 4.7.
  • In non-hazard conditions (Figure 8), the net benefits from mushroom growing are more than nine times higher than the opportunity cost of labour.
    • Mushroom growing in non-hazard conditions brings USD 5.3 per US dollar invested.
  • These results show that mushroom production is an effective livelihood diversification practice.
    • Under the opportunity cost scenario, it is assumed that all labour (including family labour) needed for mushroom production would be otherwise absorbed by the local agricultural labour market.
    • Under dry spell conditions, however, it is reasonable to expect that agricultural employment opportunities would be limited, thereby making mushroom growing an even more attractive option.
Figure 7. Cumulative Net Benefits and Benefit-Cost Ratio of mushroom cultivation as compared to the opportunity cost of labour in farms affected by a dry spell, 2016-2026

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Cumulative Net Benefits and Benefit-Cost Ratio of mushroom cultivation as compared to the opportunity cost of labour in non-hazard conditions, 2016-2026

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Socio-economic and ecological benefits

  • The sale of mushrooms in local markets provides an additional income source to farmers and strengthens the food security of the most vulnerable rural households.
  • This is even more evident in dry seasons, when lack of water may challenge the production of other crops.
  • Nine of the interviewed farmers (67 percent) found that the good practice provided better and more diverse food to the family.
  • The limited work effort required to grow mushrooms makes this practice accessible to men, women, the elderly, as well as people with disabilities.
    • In Uganda, women play a central role in mushroom production.
  • Mushroom cultivation uses a limited amount of natural resources such as water and land, compared to other crops cultivated in the area.

3.3 Disaster risk reduction and climate change adaptation-related benefits

  • Since indoor mushroom cultivation requires a limited amount of water compared to other crops, this practice contributes to Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Change Adaptation in dry areas where decreasing average rainfall may lead to more frequent and more prolonged dry spells.

3.4 Difficulties and/or limitations

  • Three beneficiary farmers (out of 14) expressed concerns regarding access to inputs.
  • In particular, mushroom spawns should be made available in local markets so as to maximize the benefits of this practice.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • ​​Tropics, warm​.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Straw mushroom (Volvariella volvacea) cultivation for livelihood diversification: ID 8945.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

6.1 Women-friendly

The limited work effort required to grow mushrooms makes this practice accessible to both men and women.

6.2 Resource use efficiency

The practice requires little water and can be undertaken during difficult dry seasons. It uses a limited amount of natural resources.

6.3 Pro-poor technology 

The practice provides an additional income source to farmers and strengthens food security with additional, improved quality and diverse food sources. The practice is also a low cost one.

7. Further reading

  • FAO. 2009. Make money by growing Mushrooms.
  • Mushroom Training and Resource Center. Oyster Mushroom.

entries.tittle: Multi-stress tolerant Green Super Rice in the Philippines
entries.summary: Green Super Rice lines are tolerant to a variety of stresses such as diseases, drought and insects. Due to climate change, the Philippines has become one of the most disaster-prone countries in the world. It is exposed to natural hazards such as droughts, floods, and typhoons. In order to cope with these recurrent climate impacts, adaptive crop cultivation strategies are needed. Multi-stress tolerant rice lines and varieties have been tested by research institutes and implemented across the Philippines. This technology describes the benefits of the cultivation of Green Super Rice (GSR) varieties in the Philippines, compared to local traditional varieties.
entries.description:
Description

1. Benefits of cultivation Green Super Rice (GSR) varieties

  • Green Super Rice lines are multi-stress tolerant, inbred, non-GMO rice lines, which were developed by Chinese researchers of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences in 2011.
  • They are conventionally bred non-GMO varieties and are currently being developed and tested in Africa and South Asia, including by the government of the Philippines.
  • Research rice lines are those currently-undergoing the screening process of the National Seed Industry Council (NSIC).
    • In the context of the project, these were cultivated in a manner that is supervised and monitored by the Department of Agriculture in collaboration with the IRRI-GSR project.
    • Varieties or registered varieties, on the other hand, are those that have passed the NSIC screening process and are authorized for commercial release/use.
  • Green Super Rice lines are tolerant to different types of stresses.
    • Abiotic stresses
      • Drought
      • Salinity
      • Alkalinity
      • Iron toxicity.
    • Diseases
      • Blast
      • Bacterial-leaf-blight
      • Sheath blight
      • Bacterial leaf streak
      • False smut.
    • Insects
      • Brown planthopper
      • Green leafhopper
      • Stem borer.
  • GSR can be used across a variety of hazard backdrops and agro-ecosystems.
  • On February 2017, the GSR line, known as GSR 8, was approved as a new variety with the registered name ‘Rc480’ and is now available for commercial use.
  • It has also been noted, by the Government certifying body, as the ‘standout’ variety in this newly approved batch of 25 varieties.
  • Table 1 summarizes the different traits of GRS lines.
  • According to figures published by the World Bank, in 2014 agricultural production in the Philippines represented 11.3 percent of the GDP, with rice being the main crop produced in the country.
  • At the same time, the Philippines is one of the most disaster-prone countries in the world due to its high vulnerability to natural hazards such as droughts, floods and typhoons.
    • In order to cope with these recurrent hazards, multi-stress tolerant rice lines and varieties are tested by research institutes and implemented across the Philippines.
    • These multi-stress tolerant rice lines include GSR but also traditional/indigenous, conventionally-bred, modern-biotech and hybrids.
  • GRS lines cultivated in the communities where data was gathered (256 farms in Bicol and Caraga Regions of Philippines) are GRS1, GRS5a, GRS8, GRS11, GRS12a.
    • These lines are tolerant to drought, flood and saline conditions.
  • Since rice is an important staple crop in the Philippines, increase in yields and production quantities due to enhanced resilience to extreme events could strengthen food security among vulnerable smallholder households.
Figure 1. Green Super Rice field in Camarines Sur, Philippines

©FAO/TECA

Table 1. Green super rice lines and their traits
GSR Line Traits Maturity days
GSR5A Low-input, saline-, drought- submergence tolerant, aromatic 115
GSR8 (now registered variety Rc480) Low-input, saline-, drought-, submergence tolerant 105
GSR12A Drought-, saline tolerant, aromatic 115
GSR1 Low-input, saline-, drought tolerant 110
GSR11 Drought-, saline tolerant, cool elevated 110

Source: FAO 2017

2. Cultivating GSR3

  • The cultivation of GSR in the project was done in a way similar to that of local varieties.
    • This was done with the standard site-specific adjustments in cultural management activities.
      • Applying fertilizers
      • Other supplements based on plot-level soil fertility
      • Other site-specific variables/characteristics (e.g. whether the farm is often waterlogged/flooded)
      • Risks (e.g. pest and diseases)
    • Inputs distributed to the project beneficiaries in addition to the GSR seeds include Complete fertilizer (NPK), Ammosul, Muriate of Potash and Zinc Sulfate, and Organic Fertilizer.
    • Farmers were trained and regularly coached by the project team.
      • Ensure proper managemement.
      • Necessary risk-reducing practices such as split application of fertilizers, cleaning of drainage canals, and increased monitoring for early signs of weather-associated pests and diseases.

3. Cost-benefit analysis of the practice

  • The performance of GSR lines 1, 5a, 8, 11, 12a were assessed at farm-level in 35 farms in the Philippines based on quantitative data collected during the monitoring period during three consecutive seasons (for example the 2015 dry and wet seasons, and the 2016 dry season).
    • The sample included 35 farms in Bicol and Caraga Regions of Philippines, specifically in Camarines Sur (2), Camarines Norte (6), Masbate (7), Catanduanes (5), and Surigao del Norte (15) districts.
    • The sites for these demonstration farms have been specifically chosen because they are located in communities where flood, drought and saltwater intrusion are prevalent.
    • In these areas, farmers often have to live with reduced yield because of these hazards.
    • Results were used to conduct a cost-benefit analyses of GRS and local rice varieties under non-hazard conditions and various hazard conditions such as dry spells, drought, floods, pests and delays in the rainy season (time frame: 11 years).
  • The net benefits obtained from GRS lines were measured through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA), and compared to the net benefits of local rice varieties.
    • The CBA projects showed the cumulative net present value of benefits obtained from 1 hectare of rice over a period of 11 years.
      • A 10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms).
      • The projects also presented a benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
    • Figure 2 provides an overview of the outcome of the CBA in non-hazard conditions.
      • During the dry season, the net benefit over 11 years is 19 percent higher in farms that adopt Green Super Rice, as compared to non-adopters.
      • During the wet season, the increase in the net benefit of GRS adapters is even bigger, amounting to 58 percent.
      • The BCR of cultivating GSR lines is higher than that of producing local varieties, in both dry and wet seasons.
Figure 2. Cumulative Net Benefits and Benefit Cost Ratios of Good Practice and Local Practice (USD per hectare per season): non-hazard conditions

©FAO/TECA

  • Figure 3 provids an overview of the outcome of the CBA in hazard conditions.
    • During the dry season, the net benefit over 11 years is 53 percent higher in farms that adopt GSR, as compared to non-adopters.
    • During the wet season, the net benefit of GSR adapters is 33 percent higher than non-adopters.
    • The BCR of cultivating GSR lines is higher than that of the local practice, in both dry and wet seasons.
Figure 3. Cumulative Net Benefits and Benefit Cost Ratios of Good Practice and Local Practice (USD per hectare per season): hazard conditions

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4 shows the average annual costs and benefits (USD per hectare) in non-hazard conditions. Figure 5 shows average annual costs which include seeds, labour, pesticide and fertilizer. Costs are compared to gross value of production (gross value of production = yield x average price of rice).

Figure 4. Average annual costs and benefits (USD per hectare): non-hazard conditions

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Average annual costs and benefits (USD per hectare): hazard conditions

©FAO/TECA

4. Added benefits

  • Under non-hazard conditions, the data reveals that GSR brings additional net economic benefits in both dry (19 percent higher) and wet (58 percent higher) season.
  • Therefore, it is a “no-regret” measure in the sense that it helps increase agricultural productivity, regardless of the occurrence of hazards.

5. Avoided losses

  • In farms affected by dry spells during the dry season, rice production losses are reduced by 53 percent (about USD 374 per ha per year).
  • In the wet season, 33 percent of losses are avoided (about US percent 219 per hectare per season) on farms affected by hazards (floods and pests).

6. Co-benefits

  • With the adoption of GSR and after appropriate training, the farmers use a much larger share of organic inputs than before.
  • Consequently the use of chemical inputs is reduced, therefore reducing the environmental impact of the farming practices.

7. Climate change adaptation related benefits

  • GSR is more resistant to hazards such as dry spell and drought, floods and delay in the rainy season and is therefore adapted to face unreliable rains and rainfall variability, induced by climate change.

8. Market prices

  • Cost of GSR seeds was USD 25 per ha.
  • During the monitoring period, GSR was sold in the market at average USD 0.78 per kg, while the local rice variety was sold at USD 0.70 per kg.

9. Validation

9.1 Context of implementation

  • The ECHO-funded FAO regional Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) project supports agriculture in Southeast Asia.
    • 256 farmers were introduced to the multi-stress tolerant GSR and were trained on a set of good practices to enhance the resilience of rice production to increasing natural disasters.

9.2 Social-target group

  • About 20 smallholder farmers were interviewed to obtain their perceptions on the practice. 
    • Sustainability
      • 75 percent of the interviewed farmers said they would replicate the good practice in the coming seasons.
    • Knowledge
      • 95 percent of farmers interviewed considered that they acquired new knowledge by taking part of the project and implementing the good practice.
    • Early warnings
      • All interviewed farmers are informed about weather forecast/climate information through TV, radio or local government unit (agriculture extension officers).
      • 95 percent of them take proactive risk-reducing actions based on early warning messages.
        • Adjustments in farming activities such as split application of fertilizers, cleaning of drainage canals and increased monitoring for early signs of weather-associated pests and diseases.
  • More than 60 percent of the interviewed farmers indicated the importance of extending the good practice (e.g. cultivating GSR varieties through village-level dissemination of good or home-saved seeds), to additional farmers and the importance of sharing cultural management advicewhen seeds are distributed.
    • Some GSR lines have been considered “tastier” than local rice varieties (e.g. GSR12a).
  • Efren Dayaon, a rice farmer from Mercedes in Camarines Norte said:
    • “Because of the saltwater intrusion and drought and with no irrigation to wash out the salt particles from my farm, my harvest had gone down to as low as 14 bags. Now, you can see how the seeds (GSR lines) are performing in spite of the condition of my farm. I think I can harvest more than 100 bags by the end of this cropping period. Neighbours who pass by my farm often ask about the GSR lines. They are impressed that the rice plants are still in good condition in spite of the saltwater intrusion.”
  • Another beneficiary farmer from Surigao del Norte, Caraga said:
    • “I want to continue planting GRS because it has a good taste, good grain quality, high yields and resistance to hazards. It is more marketable.”

10. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • In the context of the project, the following elements showed to be essential for the successful implementation of the project.
    • For successful implementation at the regional/extension institutional levels.
      • Foundation Seeds and Breeder Seeds from the IRRI-GSR project.
      • Clearance and extension support from the Department of Agriculture.
    • For successful implementation at the municipal and village levels.
      • Certified seeds clearance from the Department of Agriculture.
      • Extension support from local government agriculture offices.

11. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

12. Related/associated technologies

  • Rice seedbed preparation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 6973.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7210.
  • Intensive rice cultivation: ID 7666.
  • Participatory varietal selection: improved rice varieties: ID 4459.
  • Use of Early-Maturing Rice Variety (EMRV) to reduce typhoon impacts: ID 7719.
  • Applying flexible cropping schedules for rice (t. aman) production: ID 6853.

13. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

13.1 Resource use efficiency 

Land and water resources are well-used when multi-stress tolerant rice varieties are cultivated in order to adapt to climate change and avoid crop loss.

entries.tittle: Cost-benefit analysis of using fish pots versus bottom set longlines in the Philippines based on field testing.
entries.summary: This technology describes the testing of fish pots, a type of passive fishing gear that can be installed in the sea and harvested when sea conditions are not too dangerous, as compared to the use of bottom set longlines in the Philippines. Along with descriptions of the technology in comparison to local practices, the benefits and constraints compared to the traditional practice are shown in a cost-benefit analysis. This analysis includes added benefits, co-benefits, avoided losses, potential drawbacks, and general recommendations.
entries.description:
Description

This good practice describes the benefits of using fish pots for fishing in a small island in the Philippines frequently affected by typhoons, as compared to using local traditional practices such as traditional gill nets or the hook and line.

This good practice was implemented as part of the Disaster Preparedness ECHO programme (DIPECHO) II regional project.

1. Description of the use of fish pot

  • A fish pot is a type of passive fishing gear that can be installed in the sea and harvested when sea conditions are not too dangerous.
    • The use of fish pots reduces the risk of losing fish in case of rough sea due to extreme weather events such as storms and strong winds.
  • A fish pot is normally rectangular in shape (0.75 m x 1 m x 0.3 m = 0.225 m3) where fish enter through a funnel and making it hard for them to escape.
    • The fish pots are placed in the sea at a depth of 30 m and can be harvested every three to five days.
    • They have a maximum capacity of 5 kg per cage.
    • The fish pots tested in the project were designed and built in a way that their size, weight, clustering and deployment depth would make it difficult for these to move and get lost by accident, or during rough weather conditions.
  • The highly robust storm warning system in the Philippines also allows for a sufficient amount of time for the users of the fish pots to safely retrieve the pots in case of an incoming storm system and prevent these from getting lost during a storm and cause ghost fishing.
  • The fish pots were designed and constructed under the supervision of the Provincial Agriculture Officer, the Provincial Fisheries Specialist, the Municipal Environmental Officer, and experts from the Department of Agriculture’s Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (Region XIII) to ensure the fish pots’ compliance (in terms of design and materials used including net/ mesh size) to fisheries and environmental laws and regulations.
    • Training was also carried out by these officials and experts to the users of the fish pots (Bacama) on the proper construction, maintenance and deployment/ use. 
  • A village-resolution or ‘Barangay-resolution’ was also passed by village officials of the small island-village/Barangay, prior to the construction and use of the fish pots.
    • It regulates and designates areas where the fish pots could be used.
Figure 1. Fish pots in the Philippines

©FAO/TECA

2. Description of the use of local practice: bottom set longline

  • The local practice consists of a bottom set longline with 800 hooks on 1 600 m.
    • The issue with this traditional system is that when strong winds (due to the Southwest and Northeast monsoons) strike the coast, fish harvesting is delayed, prevented or not possible, which leads to production losses, forgone income and a lack of access to protein for the household.
    • Since fishing is the main livelihood on this small island, certain households still force themselves to catch fish during bad or volatile weather conditions thereby increasing safety risks at sea.

3. Key benefits of fish pots vs longlines

  • Fish pots have low investment costs and are relatively cheap to implement.
    • The return on investment can be realized within a few days and thus they provide a stable way for fisher folks and their families to earn additional income during the whole year.

3.1 The benefits of fish pots compared to longlines

  • More fish production.
  • More income.
  • Better and more diverse food. Since fish pots are deployed for a longer time and at deeper depths, project beneficiaries have noted an increase in the diversity of fish caught, including high-value ones such as groupers which would be relatively difficult to catch using the local practice.
  • Lower input costs.
  • Safer livelihoods practices.
  • More resistance to climate constraints. Fish pots used in the project were designed to be safely deployed to a depth of 30 m or more and to harvest fish even during rough or volatile weather and sea conditions, without requiring direct human intervention.
    • Compared to the local practice, this enables fish harvests even when weather and sea conditions make it risky, or even impossible, for fishers to go to the open sea.  
  • Less work efforts.

4. Cost-benefit analysis of the practice

  • The performance of fish pots was assessed at the village and the people’s organization-level in the Philippines based on quantitative data collected during the monitoring period in 2015.
    • The net benefits obtained from using fish pots instead of bottom set longlines with 800 hooks were measured through a cost‑benefit analysis (CBA) and compared to the net benefits of the local practice.
  • The CBA projects the cumulative net present value of benefits obtained over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate), as well as the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.

4.1 An overview of the outcome of the CBA (Figure 2)

  • When not affected by hazards, the net benefit over 11 years is 222 percent higher in farms that adopt the fish pots, as compared to non-adopters. 
  • In farms affected by hazards such as strong winds and storms, the net benefit over 11 years is 405 percent higher in adopters than non-adopters. 
  • The BCR of the good practice is higher than the BCR of the local practice, in both hazard and non-hazard conditions.
Figure 2. Cumulative Net Benefits and Benefit-Cost Ratio of fish pots and Bottom Set Longline, 2015-2025

©FAO/TECA

Figures 3 and 4 show the average annual costs and benefits of good practice compared to the local practice in hazard and non-hazard conditions. The cost assumption made for the analysis is that the fish price is 3 USD per kg.

Figure 3. Upfront capital cost, annual running costs, and gross value of annual fish catch – Normal conditions

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Upfront capital cost, annual running costs, and gross value of annual fish catch – Hazard conditions

©FAO/TECA

4.2 Added benefits

  • Under non-hazard conditions, the data reveals that the fish pots bring additional net economic benefits which are 222 percent higher.
    • It is a “no-regret” measure in the sense that they help increase fish productivity regardless of the occurrence of hazards.
