4.3 Avoided losses

  • In farms affected by hazards, fish production losses are reduced by 405 percent with the use of fish pots.

4.4 Co-benefits

  • Diesel fuel consumption is 33 percent lower for fish pots than for bottom set longline, thereby benefitting the environment.
    • The use of fish pots, in this case, requires shorter travel distances and less time on the water because fish pots are sometimes left deployed over several days and with minimal monitoring.
    • Since fishers are no longer forced to harvest fish during rough weather conditions, this also results in less fuel consumption since boat engines work harder and consume more fuel when winds and waves are strong.
Table 2. Diesel fuel consumption
Annual fuel consumption (litres) Fish pots Bottom set longline
Normal conditions 72 108
Strong winds, S/W monsoon 68 103

Source: FAO 2015

4.5 Potential drawbacks

  • If the fish pots are placed in marine sanctuaries, they will damage the environment.
  • As with other fishing gears and tools, the use of fish pots will have to go hand in hand with proper enforcement and observance of fisheries and environmental laws or regulations including their design, the materials used, and locations of their deployment.
  • In the case of the project, fish pots were restricted in terms of depth and where they will be deployed based on existing local regulations and the fisheries and coastal management plans of the municipality.

4.6 General recommendations

  • Fish pots can be considered for use in areas where proper safeguards or measures to prevent negative environmental impacts can be implemented.
    • If designed and used properly, they can provide a stable means of income and supply of food to the vulnerable small island and coastal communities where rough and volatile weather and sea conditions disrupt livelihood activities and increase sea safety risks.

5. Validation of the practice

5.1 Target group

  • Smallholder fishers on a small island in the Philippines are frequently affected by typhoons, strong winds and heavy rainfall.
    • The testing of fish pots was carried out with 42 members from BACAMA, a fisherfolk organization located in the municipality of Del Carmen, province of Surigao del Norte, Caraga Region.

6. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Diversifying risk exposure to reduce impacts of typhoons through squid pot fishing, Philippines: a step-by-step description on how to build the fish pot: ID 7704.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

​​The fish pot technology reduces work efforts and reduces sea safety risks.​

8.2 Resource use efficiency

​​This technology has low input costs, safer livelihood practices and is resistant to climate constraints.​

8.3 Pro-poor technology

This technology allows for more fish production and income as well as more food diversity.

entries.tittle: Fabrication d’un enfumoir metallique a soufflet
entries.summary:
Cette fiche présente un modèle d'enfumoir fabriqué par la Plateforme des Apiculteurs des Cataractes (PLAAC), en République Démocratique du Congo (RDC) qui ne nécessite pas de soudures. Vous y trouverez des schémas bien détaillés, des photos et conseils permettant à tous bricoleurs/artisans de se lancer dans des essais de fabrication d'un modèle d'enfumoir simplifié dont l'efficacité a été reconnue par de nombreux apiculteurs.
Cette fiche a été écrite par le Beekeeping Network North-South (BNNS) en collaboration avec André Makenbo de la Plateforme des Apiculteurs des Cataractes (PLAAC), en RDC.
entries.description:
La description

1. Introduction

  • L'enfumoir est un élément indispensable au travail de l'apiculteur mais il est souvent difficile de s'en procurer dans les milieux ruraux en Afrique.
  • Les enfumoirs à soufflet sont souvent importés, ce qui représente un coût élevé pour les apiculteurs.
  • Certains techniciens apicoles se sont alors lancés le défi d’en fabriquer eu même.
    • C'est le cas d'André Makengo de la PLAAC, en RDC.
    • La PLAAC est une asbl-ONG de droit congolais basée à Mbanza-Ngungu, dans la Province du Kongo central.
    • Elle regroupe plus de 500 membres dont la plupart sont regroupés en associations.
    • André est membre de la PLAAC et responsable de l'atelier de menuiserie.
    • Apiculteur et menuisier, André est un bon bricoleur et a créé un modèle d'enfumoir sans soudure.
    • C'est un modèle simplifié réalisé avec des matériaux et outils disponibles localement qui ne demande pas de matériel de soudure ce qui représente un bel avantage.
    • L'efficacité de ce modèle a été reconnue par de nombreux apiculteurs qui l'utilisent au niveau du Kongo centrale.
  • Ci-dessous, vous trouverez le schéma détaillé des différentes parties de l'enfumoir qui vous permettront également d'en fabriquer un.
Encadré 1. André Makengo de la PLAAC

©BNNS

2. Schéma général de l'enfumoir

  • Un enfumoir est composé de trois parties principales:
    • le soufflet appelé ici souffleur;
    • d’un foyer/chambre de combustion avec une grille dans le fond retenant les matériaux de combustion; et
    • le bec ou cône de diffusion pour diriger la fumée.
  • Le foyer doit pouvoir contenir suffisamment de combustible pour ne pas devoir le recharger trop souvent lorsque l'on est occupé dans le rucher.
  • Ci-dessous, vous trouverez le schéma et les dimensions de base d'un enfumoir complet (Figure 2). Les lettres correspondent à la dénomination des différentes parties de l’enfumoir et sont reprises en dessous du schéma.
Figure 2. Schéma de l'enfumoir sans soudure réalisé par André Makengo

©FAO/André Makengo

3. Matériaux utilisés

  • Tôle galvanisée
  • bois
  • chambre à air o Ressort
  • boulons
  • clous
  • chevaliers
  • charnière
  • outils: marteaux, scies à bois, ciseaux à métaux, crayon, latte, tourne vis.
Figure 3. Illustration de la majorité des pièces détachées de l'enfumoir

©BNNS

  • La photo (Figure 3) illustre la majorité des pièces découpées et modelées, nécessaires à la fabrication de l'enfumoir.
  • Comme vous pouvez le voir dans la liste des matériaux utilisés, de simples outils ont permis de réaliser ces pièces tels que une scie à bois, des ciseaux à métaux (voir Figure 4).
Figure 4. Ciseaux permettant de couper les fines tôles en acier

©BNNS

4. Fabrication

4.1 Souffleur

  • Le souffleur est constitué d'une bande de chambre à air, deux planchettes en bois, un ressort de matelas, deux chevaliers pour l'attacher au cylindre, deux ceintures en bande de tôle galvanisée BWG34, deux boulons de fixation et des clous.
  • La chambre à air est fixée aux deux planchettes en bois à l'aide des deux bandes de tôle clouées sur la largeur des planchettes en bois.
  • Voici le schéma et les dimensions (en mm) des différentes parties nécessaires à la fabrication du soufflet:
    • morceau de chambre à air de 600 mm de longueur,120 mm de largeur et 3 mm d'épaisseur (Figure 5);
Figure 5.Chambre à air qui reliera les deux planchettes en bois pour former le souffleur

©FAO/André Makengo

    • deux planchettes en bois de 170 mm de longueur; 100 mm de largeur et 12 mm d'épaisseur (Encadré 6);
  • Il est nécessaire de forer sur une des deux planchettes en bois, deux trous de 6mm de diamètre pour faire passer les boulons et permettre de fixer le souffleur au cylindre avec les chevaliers.
  • La seconde planche comporte un trou de 10 mm de diamètre qui permettra à l'air d’entrer et sortir du souffleur vers le cylindre via la pipe (voir Figure 2).
Figure 6. Croquis des planchettes en bois du souffleur

©FAO/André Makengo

    • chevaliers en fer plat de 360 mm de longueur; 15 mm de largeur et 2 mm d'épaisseur (voir Encadré 7).
  • Une lame en fer plat est utilisée pour fabriquer les deux chevaliers. Il faut les forer de quatre trous de 4,5 mm aux extrémités et un trou central de 8 mm.
Figure 7. Croquis de la bande en fer plat (au dessus) et d'un chevalier qui résulte du pliage (en dessous)

©FAO/André Makengo

4.2 La chambre de combustion

  • Voici les différentes parties nécessaires à la fabrication de la chambre à combustion, accompagnées de leurs dimensions:
    • M: Uncylindre: L=325 mm; l=900 mm; Ep=0,8 mm
    • N: Unfond: diamètrede: 120 mm; Ep=0,8 mm
    • I: Unanti-chaleur: L=300 mm; l=160 mm; Ep=0,8 mm
    • J: Unecharnière: L=180 mm; l=30 mm; Ep=0,8 mm
    • O: Untamis: diamètrede: 96 mm; Ep=0,8 mm
    • G: Unepiped’entréed’air: L=83 mm; l=76 mm; Ep=0,8 mm.
  • Les lettres correspondent à celle du croquis complet de l'enfumoir (Figure 2).
  • Le cylindre est un simple morceau rectangulaire de tôle galvanisée, découpée avec des ciseaux spéciaux.
  • Cette pièce sera assemblée avec le fond, disque de la même matière.
    • André utilise un gros tuyau en métal comme «moule» pour «modeler» le cylindre à un diamètre de 100 mm.
    • Les extrémités du fond seront repliées sur les bords du cylindre eux aussi repliés.
    • Les images ci-dessous illustrent le pliage des bords du disque de fond, à la main ou à l'aide d'un marteau.
Figure 8. illustration de la fabrication de la chambre de combustion de l'enfumoir et du pliage des bords du fond

©BNNS

Figure 9. Illustration de la chambre de combustion

©BNNS

  • Comme vous pouvez le voir sur la photo, le cylindre comporte un trou d'environ 18 mm de mm de diamètre, afin d'y placer la pipe d’entrée d'air illustrée ci-dessous.
Figure 10. Croquis et illustration de la pipe d'entrée d'air

©FAO/André Makengo

4.3 Bec

  • Le bec est réalisé à partir d'un carré de tôle de 202 mm sur 177 mm de côtés.
    • Ci-dessous, vous trouverez le croquis et les mesures précises qui permettront de reconstituer la pièce.
Figure 11. Croquis de la pièce principal du bec

©FAO/André Makengo

  • Les zones en pointillés du croquis, représentent les zones de pliages du bec.
    • Le bec est également constitué d'une ceinture, bande de tôle de 380 mm de longueur et 20 mm de largeur.
      • André utilise également un tuyau en acier comme moule pour assurer un pliage régulier de la tôle.
    • Ces deux éléments sont «soudés» grâce au pliage des bords de tôle et également à l’aide de deux clous.
Figure 12. Illustration du bec et de la zone de pliage situé à la junction des deux pieces

©BNNS

4.4 Assemblage

  • Une fois le souffleur, la chambre de combustion et le bec fabriqués, ces trois éléments vont pouvoir être l'assemblé.
  • L'anti-chaleur, le cylindre et le bec sont assemblés avec une charnière, tandis que le souffleur est fixé au cylindre grâce aux deux chevaliers avec des clous ou des boulons.
Figure 13. Différentes parties de l'enfumoir avant assemblage

©BNNS

  • A l'intérieur du cylindre sera placé le tamis percé de plusieurs trous de 3 mm à 5 mm de diamètre. Votre enfumoir est ainsi prêt à être utilisé.
  • Remarque: pour en savoir plus sur le fonctionnement et l’utilisation d'un enfumoir à soufflet, voir la technologie «Apiculture: utilisation d'un enfumoir metallic a soufflet»

5. Les zones agro-écologiques

  • Tropiques, chaud.

6. Les technologies associées/relatives

  • Fabrication d'une ruche Kenyane trapézoidale à barettes: ID 8707.
  • Comment fabriquer une ruche a barrettes en Nkoko: ID 8745.
  • Apiculture: utilisation d'un enfumoir metallic a soufflet: ID 8727.

7. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

7.1 L'efficacité d'utilisation des ressources

L'utilisation des matériaux disponibles pour fabriquer un enfumoir optimisera les ressources disponibles au voisinage de l'apiculteur.

7.2 Favorable aux populations pauvres

La fabrication de votre propre fumeur est une excellente alternative aux fumeurs qui sont a prix élevé et qui sont généralement importés. Les matières premières du fumeur sont faciles à trouver, disponibles et sont généralement à faible coût.

entries.tittle: Goat raising in controlled areas and vaccination in Lao PDR
entries.summary: The practice described here can be introduced to smallholder goat farmers to reduce their vulnerability to risks and disasters, such as disease outbreaks, drought, floods, etc. The practice consists of raising goats in controlled areas instead of letting them roam freely. It allows for better livestock management and reduces the risks of spread of diseases between different herds. Furthermore, goats are vaccinated against foot and mouth disease and other parasites. The confinement in which the goats are raised consists of an enclosed area and a homestead, that provides shelter and protection for the goats. Fodder is brought to the goats by the farmer.
entries.description:
Description

1. Homestead for goats

1.1 Step one: select the location for building the homestead

  • To ensure minimum impacts from drought or flood, a proper location for the homestead should be identified.
  • In flood prone areas, a homestead should be built on the upper point of the farm.
  • In drought prone areas, availability of water must be ensured, thus it has to be adjacent to a pond or well with surrounding areas for growing fodders.
  • The homestead should be properly fenced to avoid that the goats escape, or that goats from other herds enter the homestead.
  • This way, the spread of disease between different herds can also be prevented.
  • The selected location should be easily accessible in case evacuation of the animals is needed during disasters.

1.2 Step two: homestead building

  • The homestead is located within the enclosure and is the construction that provides shelter and protection to the goats.
  • The homestead is usually built of wood and has certain characteristics.
    • In drought prone areas, the height of the homestead should be between 0.6 to 1 m from the ground, in order to prevent humidity and facilitate the cleaning.
    • In flood prone areas, the height should be between 1.5 to 2 m from the ground, or higher depending on annual flooding level.
    • The homestead should be airy but properly shed to protect goats from direct sun, strong winds and heavy rains.
    • The side of the homestead, which is most exposed to winds, can be covered with bamboo stick or other material available (Figure 1).
    • The area of the homestead should be proportionate to the number of goats.
      • 0.3 m2 per each young goat
      • 0.7 m2 per each adult goat
      • 1.9 m2 per each pregnant goat
      • 2.8 m2 per each male breeding goat.
    • The floor should be made of strong wooden bars, thickness 2.5 cm and width of 6 cm each.
    • There should be interspace between two wooden bars to facilitate cleaning of litter and debris.
    • The space between two wooden bars should be 1.5 cm for adult goats and 1.3 cm for young goats.
    • Farmers may choose a design/shape of the shed/roof that is appropriate to local conditions.
    • Normally, the height of roof should be 2 m from the ground.
      • This will help to reduce the heat inside the homestead.
    • A water tank should be kept slightly above the floor, and close to the entrance.
      • To calculate the size of the tank, it should be considered that each goat drinks about 1 litre of water per day.
    • A feed tray should be used to store different types of fodders (forage and peas) and kept outside the homestead.
      • The feed tray should be at the same height as goat’s mouth.
    • Pregnant goats or female goats with their kids should be kept separate in order to prevent injuries.
  • Ideally, the farmer should foresee an area of about 1 600 m2 per 20 goats to allow the goats to walk for two to three hours per day.

1.3 Step three: fodders and feeding

  • Three types of fodder are generally grown for goats.
    • Grass
      • Napier grass, Pangola grass, Guinea grass, Signal grass, Mulato grass and Lucy grass.
    • Field peas
      • Centrocema, Stylosanthes CIA184, and Verano stylo (Stylosanthes hamata).
    • Fodder trees and other plants
      • White popinac, Madre de Cacao (also known as quick stick or Gliricidia sepium), pigeon peas, cassava leaves, banana leaves, mulberry leaves, muntingia leaves, and other domestic trees.
  • Fodder leaves should be cut from at least 1 m above the ground to avoid parasites.
  • A mix of fodder varieties should be used (at least two types of leaves).
  • Leaves should account for no more than one-third of total fodders given to goats.
  • A goat eats fresh fodder about 10 percent of its weight, and dried fodder about 3 percent of its weight every day.
    • For example, a goat weighing 30 kg needs 3 kg of fresh fodder, of which 1 kg can be fresh leaves collected from two different species of trees (e.g. cassava leaves and quick stick), or 1 kg of dried fodder, including maximum 300 g of dried leaves.
  • When feeding goats, bunches of leaves should be tied and hung above the ground, because goats do not like eating fodder from the ground.

1.4 Step four: prevention of diseases

  • Protect the homestead from strong winds or rains.
  • Always keep the homestead clean.
  • Feeds and water for goats must be clean.
  • Minimize sources of transmitting insects, bugs such as flies, horse flies.
  • Prevent goats from eating fodders in wetlands or flooded areas.
  • Minimize sources of parasitic insects such as fleas, keds, lice, by spraying or washing goats with animal drugs designed for this purpose mixed with water.
  • Goats should be dewormed (internal parasite dewormer) every one to three months to avoid round worms and tape worms.
  • Vaccination should be done every six months to prevent common diseases like foot-mouth infectious disease.
  • Infected goats must be separated from others and treated with appropriate antibiotic drugs until they recover.
    • The farmer should control the health status of his goats kept in the confinement on a regular  basis,especially during periods of stress, to identify timely any possible health issue and avoid to the maximum contamination of the other goats.
Figure 1. Goat homestead in small-scale farm in Lao PDR

©FAO/TECA

2. Major costs and resources involved

  • Feed
    • 1 500 to 2 000 kip per kg (average)
  • Foot and mouth disease vaccine
    • About 21 500 kip per goat per year
  • Labour
    • 470 kip per goat per day
  • The price of goat meat on local market is 80 000 to 90 000 kip per kg.
  • The costs mentioned in this good practice refer to the time of writing.

3. Benefits

  • Raising goats in controlled areas reduces the incidence of diseases and mortality as it contributes to preventing the spread of diseases between different herds, thereby increasing the value of goat production.

3.1 Cost-benefit analysis of practice

  • During the 2015 wet season and the 2016 dry season, the performance of this good practice was monitored on 32 farms.
    • Of these farms 29 were monitored in Savannakhet (6) and Khammouane (26) provinces and their performance was compared to the performance of free roaming unvaccinated goat raising.
    • None of the farms suffered from disease outbreaks or other hazards during both seasons.
      • Therefore only the non-hazard scenario was tested.
  • The net benefits obtained from the good practice were valued through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA) and compared to the net benefits of free roaming unvaccinated goats.
    • The CBA projects the cumulative net present value of benefits obtained from one goat (assuming that the goat is immediately replaced after slaughtering) over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms).
      • It also projects the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
    • Figure 2 and Figure 3 provide an overview of the outcomes of the CBA in the wet and dry season, respectively.
      • The analysis considers the average costs and benefits of raising one goat, assuming that each goat is slaughtered after 140 days, and immediately replaced. Results show that:
  • In the wet season and in non-hazard conditions, the net benefit from raising goats in confinement and vaccinating them is 45 percent higher than that of the traditional practice (Figure 2).
    • This means that, after deduction of all costs, the goat farmer that keeps his goats in confinement and vaccinates them will earn about 45 percent more than a farmer who owns free roaming and unvaccinated goats.
  • In the dry season and in non-hazard conditions, the net benefit from the good practice is 21 percent higher than that of the traditional practice (Figure 3).
  • The BCR of the good practice is higher than the BCR of the local practice in both seasons.
  • The absolute net benefits and the benefit-cost ratios are observed to be higher during the wet season than during the dry season.
    • This difference between the two seasons can be explained by the limited availability of water and feed during the dry season, compared to the wet season.
    • This causes goats to be less fat during the dry season.
Figure 2. Cumulative net benefits and benefit-cost ratios of good practice and local practice on farms not affected by hazards (USD per goat) – 2015 wet season

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Cumulative net benefits and benefit cost ratios of good practice and local practice in farms not affected by hazards (USD per goat) – 2016 dry season

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Added benefits

  • Under non-hazard conditions, goat raising in controlled areas led to a 45 percent increase in net benefits during the wet season, and 21 percent increase in net benefits in the dry season, as compared to free roaming.

3.3 Avoided losses

  • No hazard occurred during the two monitored seasons.
  • However, it is expected that the mortality rate of vaccinated goats would decrease in case of a disease outbreak.

3.4 Co-benefits

  • By not allowing goats to roam, farmers have more control over pasture cover.
  • This good practice helps avoid overgrazing and its negative consequences on land degradation.
  • Additional manure can be collected and used for growing crops.

4. Before implementing the practice

  • Some key issues need to be considered before implementing this good practice.
    • In order to make the good practice more sustainable and profitable, farmers should ideally grow fodder within their farm.
      • If this is not possible, farmers will have to buy fodder and this would reduce the net benefits.
    • Raising goats in confinement areas requires continuous monitoring and additional work effort as compared to raising free roaming goats.
    • It is important to build the homestead in a way that maximizes the “comfort” of the confined animals (e.g. shade, water).
    • In addition to the land for growing fodder, farmers should also define an area where goats can safely walk for two to three hours every day.

5. Validation

5.1 Geographical area of practice validation

  • The performance of this Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) good practice, which consists in raising goats in confinement and vaccinating them against foot and mouth disease and other parasites, was monitored in 29 small-scale farms in Savannakhet and Khammouane provinces.
    • The practice was compared to the performance of unvaccinated free-roaming goat raising.

5.2 Context of implementation

  • Free roaming of goats may increase the vulnerability of the animals to diseases, which in turn may lead to lower animal productivity and increased mortality.
  • The vulnerability of goats to disease may further increase in the case of floods or drought, due to worsened animal body conditions.
  • The raising of vaccinated goats in confinement was introduced in small farms in Lao PDR as part of the project: Consolidating Capacities for Disaster Risk Reduction in Agriculture in South East Asia.
    • The project's objective was to reduce the vulnerability of goat farms to diseases.

5.2.1 Environmental and climatic (period/season) context

  • The good practice was monitored during the 2015 wet season, and the 2016 dry season.
  • None of the monitored farms suffered from disease outbreaks or other hazards (e.g. floods and droughts during the two seasons).
    • Therefore, only the non-hazard scenario was tested.

5.3 Social - target group

  • The DRR good practice was tested with smallholder farmers.

5.4 Farmer’s perceptions

  • Sustainability
    • All farmers interviewed (32) said they would replicate the good practice in the coming years.
  • Socio-economic benefits
    • All farmers found that production increased after the adoption of the good practice.
    • They said goats now grow fatter and are less exposed to diseases.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • A necessary condition for the implementation of this good practice is an area for grazing or fodder plantation, which would allow feeding the animals.
  • Another key prerequisite for a successful implementation is the local availability of the materials needed to build the homestead.

7. Constraints (limiting factors) for the implementation of the technology

  • Adequate technical assistance from extension workers and training on vaccination techniques, breeding and feed processing is recommended to be able to fully benefit from the introduction of this practice.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Intensive stall-fed system for rearing goats: ID 8770.
  • Rearing dairy goats: ID 6925.
  • Collective action to reduce goat mortality: ID 7904.
  • Herbal de-worming for lower goat mortality: ID 7690.
  • Improvement of livestock production: community based goat production: ID 4495.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

10.1 Resource use efficiency 

Homestead and enclosure building allow for more efficient use of land. With more control of these areas, farmers reduce the vulnerability of their goats to risks and disasters. They also have more control over what the goats consume since they deliver the fodder themselves.

entries.tittle: Improved chicken breeds raised with vaccination in Lao PDR
entries.summary: Chicken diseases can cause significant loss for farmers. Due to the frequency in which diseases affect chickens at nearly every change of season, farmers get discouraged to raise chickens. The most common diseases often infecting chickens in rural areas are Newcastle disease and fowl cholera. This practice includes instructions on the use of vaccines to reduce the disease causality among chickens. Additionally, this practice presents guidelines on chicken raising in flood or drought prone areas and describes the cost-benefit analysis of rearing improved chicken breeds with vaccination in Lao PDR. Improved chicken breeds are considered more efficient than native chickens because they grow faster and do not require as much water and feed.
entries.description:
Description

1. Cost-benefit analysis of the practice

  • The performance of improved chicken breeds raised with vaccination was assessed at farm-level in Lao PDR.
  • The net benefits obtained from the good practice were measured through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA), and compared to the net benefits of the local practice which was raising local chicken breeds without vaccination.
    • The CBA calculates the cumulative net benefits obtained from a chicken over a period of 11 years (a 10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms).
    • It also calculates the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
  • Figures 2 and 3 provide an overview of the outcome of the CBA.
    • In the wet season, results show that raising improved chicken breeds with vaccination increased the net benefits by 45 percent compared to the existing local practice in non-hazard conditions.
    • During the dry season, for farms not affected by any hazard, this number went up to 172 percent for the farms raising improved chicken breeds with vaccination.
    • This makes it a “no-regret” measure in the sense that they help increase farmers’ income regardless of the occurrence of hazards.
    • During the dry season, in the conditions of a cold wave, improved chicken breeds raised with vaccination still performed better than the existing local chicken breeds, with a 100 percent increase of net benefits, which is about USD 53 per unit of chicken.
  • Improved breeds are more resistant and therefore have a lower mortality rate than local breeds.
  • The absolute net benefits are higher during the dry season compared to the wet season.
  • This difference between both seasons might be due to gained experience and improved capacity of farmers in raising the improved chicken breed over time.
Figure 1. Vaccination of improved chicken breeds

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Cumulative net benefits and benefit cost ratios of DRR good practice and local practice (USD per unit of chicken) - 2015 wet season

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Cumulative net benefits and benefit cost ratios of DRR good practice and local practice (USD per unit of chicken) - 2016 dry season

©FAO/TECA

2. Co-benefits

  • Since improved chicken breeds grow faster than native chickens, it is estimated that they require 25 percent less inputs (e.g. water and feed) on average along their lifespan.

3. Major cost and benefit

Table 1. List of major prices

Source: FAO 2017

  • Chicken lifespan before slaughtering is assumed to be 20 weeks for native chickens and 16 weeks for improved breeds.
  • Annual costs are estimated assuming that slaughtered breeds are immediately replaced.
Table 2. List of major cost for raising one improved breed chicken per year
Cost type USD per unit yearly
Chicken breed 6.564
Chicken vaccine 0.418
Chicken feed 2.249
Labour cost 13.122

Source: FAO 2017

Figure 4. Average annual cost and gross value of production (USD per unit annually)

©FAO/TECA

4. Guidelines on chicken raising in flood or drought prone areas

4.1 Common infectious diseases

  • In Lao PDR, chicken diseases cause significant difficulties and huge casualties for farmers.
  • Disease is a threat that occurs almost every change of season.
    • The end of the rainy season to the beginning of the dry season, and the end of the dry season to the beginning of the rainy season.
  • Disease iscourages some farmers not to raise chickens anymore.
  • The most common diseases often infecting chickens in rural areas are Newcastle disease and fowl cholera.
    • Newcastle disease is caused by a virus and can infect chickens at any age.
      • Clinical symptoms are that chickens are weakened, are unable to stand, move in circles and cannot find feed by themselves.
      • To prevent this disease, a vaccination is necessary.
      • This includes a Newcastle vaccine for young and adult chickens.
      • If infected, they need to be separated from other chickens by keeping them in a separate area together with feed and medication.
    • Fowl cholera is caused by a bacterial infection and it can infect chickens at any age.
      • Clinical symptoms are that chickens do not eat feed nor drink water.
      • Fowl cholera can be prevented by vaccination.
      • Treatment could be done with medicated sulfa drugs.

4.2 Guidelines to prevent chicken diseases

  • Always clean and kill fungus surrounding feeding area and pens by putting limestone.
  • Do not buy chickens from a market or other places to be consumed in household.
  • Newly bought chickens should be separately bred for at least 14 days.
  • Chickens that die of diseases or unknown causes must be deeply buried or burnt.
    • They should not be consumed or thrown away randomly.
  • Every newly born chick must be vaccinated.
  • Adult chickens should be vaccinated according to the advice from the village or district vets.

4.3 Instructions on use of vaccines

4.3.1 General instructions

  • Freeze dried vaccines (powder form) must be kept in a freezer.
    • When in use, they need to be mixed with diluents (sterile distilled water) and be used within one to two hours.
  • Fluid vaccines must be kept in a refrigerator.
    • Prior to administration, they must be properly shaken and need to be used within 12 hours.
  • When transporting vaccines, they must be kept in a cool box, avoiding sun and heat, as sunlight and warmer temperature might destroy the active principles in the vaccine.
  • Vaccinations must be carried out when the temperature of the day is cool, such as in the early morning prior to sunrise or in the evening after sunset.
  • Only administer vaccines to healthy animals.
    • Giving vaccines to infected or suspected ill animals is prohibited.
  • Administering according to instructions is a must.
    • Do not use expired vaccines, lyophilisation (freeze drying) vaccines, nor those without a descriptive instruction label.
  • Vaccinate regularly for every individual animal as per instructions given by a veterinarian.
  • Time laps in administering different types of vaccines for individual animal is 14 days.
  • Residual vaccines must be properly boiled with high temperature before burying for disposal.
  • If there is any doubt on the use of vaccines, please consult the village veterinary volunteer or district veterinarian.
  • For chickens of one to seven days of age, administer drop vaccines to prevent young chicken from catching a Newcastle disease infection.
  • Chickens at 42 days of age should have the cholera and Newcastle diseases prevention vaccines administered.
    • Administer them again every three months and every year respectively.

4.3.2 Fowl cholera vaccines for mature chicken (42 days per six weeks old or older)

  • For fluid vaccines (liquid form), one bottle of vaccine is enough for 50 chickens.
  • Administer the vaccine to chickens at a minimum of six weeks of age.
    • Administer by subcutaneous injection (under its wing).
  • The dosage is 1 cc (1 ml) for each chicken.
    • Two weeks later, chickens will be immunized for three months.
    • They need to be injected every three months or at least three times a year.

4.3.3 Newcastle disease vaccines for young chicken (one to seven days old)

  • Freeze dried vaccines need to be mixed with 10 cc (10 ml) of sterile distilled water prior to injecting.
    • One bottle can administer 100 young chickens.
  • For dropping vaccines, these need to be administered by putting drops in the eyes and noses of young chicken between one to seven days of age.
    • Two to four drops should be administered for each side of their eyes and noses.
  • The vaccines have a valid period is eight weeks.
    • After six to eight weeks, follow the instructions on Newcastle disease vaccines for mature chicken (see following section).

4.3.4 Newcastle disease vaccine for mature chicken (42 days per six weeks old)

  • Freeze dried vaccines need to be mixed with 50 cc (50 ml) of distilled water prior to injecting.
    • One bottle of vaccine could be used for 100 chickens.
  • Vaccinate the chicken at six weeks of age or more by intra muscular injection (in the chest).
    • The given dosage size is 0.5 cc (0.5 ml) for each chicken.
  • Two weeks after vaccination, chickens will be immunized for one year.
Table 3. Guidelines on feeding

Source: FAO 2017

4.3.5 Guidelines on treatment and management

  • Good animal treatment enables an improved outcome in chicken raising.
  • In particular, paying attention to the care of young chicks aging three to four weeks by providing them with water, good quality food and warmth in the pens is important.

5. Validation

5.1 Hazard context during monitoring period

  • During the wet season 2015, the performance of raising improved breeds chicken with vaccination was monitored in 14 farms in the Savannakhet province.
    • The performance was compared to the performance of the local practice.
    • None of the 14 farmers interviewed have been affected by any hazard during this monitoring period.
  • During the dry season 2016, 45 farms were monitored, in Savannakhet (14) and Khammouane (31) provinces, from which eight farmers (four from each province) mentioned that cold waves have impacted their chicken production.

5.2 Farmers’ perception

  • All 14 farmers interviewed said they are willing to replicate this practice in the next seasons.
  • Most farmers agreed that the vaccinated improved breed is more resistant to diseases and climate constraints, compared to the non-vaccinated local breeds.
  • They also mentioned that improved breeds grow faster and bigger, therefore lowering the costs for inputs and saving work effort.
  • In total, 11 farmers (79 percent) said that this Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) good practice brings better and more diverse food to their household, thanks to increased income and increased consumption of the raised chicken.
  • They assigned a score of 3.9 out of 5 to the performance of raising improved chicken breeds with vaccination.
  • None of the farmers highlighted any specific unintended effect of the good practice.
  • However, the market price of local chicken varieties is almost double the price of improved chicken varieties.
  • This finding raises the attention on cultural aspects that are strong determinants of food preferences.
  • These factors deserve further research as they have a key influence on the socio-economic feasibility of the DRR good practice technology.

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Improved practices in rearing indigenous chickens: ID 6921.
  • Small-scale chicken production: ID 6949.
  • Replicas of native chicken in rural poultry production: the Satpuda: ID 7680.
  • Newcastle disease: a technology review (special enphasis on its effect on village chickens): ID 6945.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

8.1 Pro-poor technology

Using vaccination and improved chicken breed varieties helps poor farmers maintain their small chicken farms and save their income source.

entries.tittle: Cost-benefit analysis of cultivating early maturing rice in Lao PDR
entries.summary: Early maturing rice can be harvested before local rice varieties, thereby reducing the vulnerability of farmers to extreme events and enhancing the resilience of livelihoods. This technology describes the cost-benefit analysis of growing early maturing rice in Lao PDR and provides information on how to grow this rice variety in dry spell and drought areas.
entries.description:
Description

1. Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) of the practice

  • The performance of TSN- 8 early maturing rice was assessed at the farm-level in Lao PDR.
  • The net benefits obtained from growing early maturing rice varieties were measured through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA) and compared to the net benefits of growing local rice varieties.
  • To clarify, good practice means cultivating early maturing rice variety, whereas local practice refers to cultivating local rice variety.
  • The CBA calculates the cumulative net benefits obtained per hectare of rice field over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms), as well as the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.

1.1 An overview of the outcome of the CBA (Figures 1 and 2) 

  • In the 2015 wet season, the economic benefits from early-maturing rice are about 116 percent higher in farms affected by dry spells and delayed rains, as compared to the control plots.
  • In the 2016 dry season, the performance of early maturing rice was slightly better (6 percent higher benefits) than local rice varieties in farms affected by cold waves, while the differences are insignificant under non-hazard conditions. 
  • Under non-hazard conditions, the data reveals that the DRR good practice (cultivating early maturing rice variety) does not bring additional economic benefits. This result is based on a reduced sample of four plots and should be confirmed with additional analysis.
  • In farms affected by dry spells during the wet season or delays in the rainy season, rice production losses are reduced by 116 percent, or about USD 109 per hectare per season. Avoided losses in case of cold waves in the dry season are about USD 25 per hectare.
  • The observed absolute increase in net benefits in the dry season, as compared to the wet season, could be due to a number of factors, including: the delay in the 2015 rainy season, which caused extensive rice production losses; lower labour costs in dry season due to high offer and low demand; more careful and dedicated management in dry season due to less activities in the farms.
Figure 1. Cumulative Net returns and Benefit-Cost Ratios of DRR Good Practice (early maturing rice variety) and Local Practice (local rice variety)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Cumulative Net returns and Benefit-Cost Ratios of DRR Good Practice (early maturing rice variety) and Local Practice (local rice variety)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Farmers harvesting early maturing rice in Lao PDR

©FAO/TECA

3. Guidelines on growing early maturing rice in dry spell and drought areas

3.1 Methods for growing early maturing rice in dry spell and drought risk areas, depending on the actual conditions of the farmers in each location

  • Use of drought tolerant and early maturing rice variety TSN-8 and avoid using late maturing rice varieties.
  • Use of direct seeding or broadcasting technology to mitigate the impact of drought spells. 
  • In the paddy field, farmers should apply organic fertilizer or keep crop residues to improve soil texture. For example, applying rice husk, keeping rice straw, growing legumes after rice crops help improve soil and retain moisture so that rice can survive during dry spells.
  •  If farmers are willing to use transplanting technique, they should prepare seedling plots near water sources such as pond, river or stream, where they can access water when drought occurs.

The seedling can be prepared in a suitable location where the soil is fertile and water is accessible so farmers can water the plot in case of drought spell.

3.2 Early maturing rice growing locations

  • Demonstration plots for growing early maturing rice are dry spell areas and high-level rice fields where water is insufficient, or the soil does not absorb water. Also, they should be places where drainage of water during harvesting is easy.
Figure 4. Early maturing rice in Lao PDR

©FAO/TECA

3.3 Soil preparation

  • First plowing should start at the same time as the preparation of the seedling or 20 days before broadcasting or direct seeding.
  • If farmers apply compost, cow dung or organic materials, they should incorporate into the soil at the time of plowing.

3.4 Seeds

  • The rice variety should have been tested in drought-prone areas.
  • The seeding rate is 60 kg per ha and 80 kg per ha for sowing.

3.5 Seedling preparation

  • Select location near water sources and easy access to irrigation, river or well.
  • The seed rate for sowing must be 100 g per m2 in order to have strong seedlings.
  • Farmers can transplant when the seedling is 15 to 25 days.
    • In case there is no rain they can delay up to 25 days.

3.6 Rice growing by semi-direct seedlings or dry broadcasting

  • After plowing and leveling, the seeds are used which has been sun-dried for one day for semi‑direct seedlings or dry broadcasting.

3.7 Transplanting

  • After plowing, tilling, and leveling, transplanting should be conducted within an area of 25 cm x 25 cm for each seedling.
  • The seedlings should not be uprooted overnight.

3.8 Fertilizing method

  • The rate of application of fertilizer is 60‑30‑30 (NH4-P2O5-K2O) in the growing period as shown in Table 1 below.
  • Fertilizing should be conducted appropriately with regard to the ecosystem limits and the areas of demonstration.
  • Before using fertilizer, the weeds must be killed.
  • Fertilization should not be done during or just after the rain.
  • When using urea fertilizer, it is essential to observe the leaves of the plants, which show the nutrient needs of the plants.
    • If the leaves are rich green, it is not suitable to use more urea fertilizer.
  • Maintain plots by watering, removing weeds manually from the plots and the areas surrounding the plots, and preventing pests from infesting the growing rice in the fields of farmers.
  • If there are pests, farmers can use botanical control agents.
    • Botanical control agents are prepared by local indigenous knowledge and are promoted by local Integrated Pest Management or Organic Projects.
Table 1. Fertilizing for early maturing rice (age below 125 days) per 1 ha

Source: FAO 2017

3.9 Harvesting

  • Harvesting can be done 30 days after the start of flowering, counting from when 50 percent of the plants are flowering.

4. Validation of the practice

4.1 Hazard context during the monitoring period

  • During the 2015 wet season, the performance of this DRR technology was monitored in 19 farms in Savannakhet (16) and Khammouane (3) Provinces; all the farms except for one experienced dry spells and/or delays in the rainy season during the monitoring period.
  • During the 2016 dry season, 10 farms were monitored in Savannakhet (10) and Khammouane (2) Provinces, out of which six farms were affected by the cold waves and four farms were not affected by any hazard.
  • Demonstration plots for growing early maturing rice are dry spell areas and high‑level rice fields where water is insufficient, or the soil does not absorb water.

4.2 Farmers’ perception

  • All of the 29 farmers interviewed said that they are willing to replicate this practice in the next seasons.
    • Seventy nine percent of farmers found that early maturing rice brought an increase in crop production due to higher yields, and assigned a score of 4.9 out of 5 to the performance of this practice in the face of hazards such as dry spells, delays in the rainy season and cold waves.
  • During the dry season, almost all farmers found that early harvesting brought an increase in income.
    • Most farmers highlighted that time saving, thanks to early maturity, is among the main reasons why this early maturing rice should be adopted and replicated.
    • Some farmers also stressed that early maturing rice varieties have good taste.
  • None of the farmers mentioned any unintended effect of early maturing rice. However, some farmers warned that early maturing varieties are suitable only for upper parts of their paddy field.
    • In lower parts, early maturing may give problems for harvesting especially in the wet season, as farmers would have to drain the water.
  • Finally, several farmers stressed the need for additional training and regular support and technical advice on a number of subjects, including pest control, cultivation techniques, new technologies and varieties.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Use of Early-Maturing Rice Variety (EMRV) to reduce typhoon impacts: ID 7719.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Pro-poor technology

Farmers who used the early maturing rice had higher yields.

entries.tittle: Introduction of early maturing cassava varieties in Bolivia, a cost benefit analysis
entries.summary:
This technology describes the introduction of early maturing purple cassava varieties in the Bolivian eco-region of the Beni river watershed. In this area, farmers are used to cultivate white cassava, which has a growing cycle of more than 90 days. Given the long growing period, traditional white cassava often cannot be harvested before the start of the flooding season, leading to significant production losses. 

Early maturing cassava can be harvested before local cassava varieties, thereby reducing the vulnerability of farmers to floods. Furthermore, early maturing purple cassava is considered more valuable than white cassava. It is an ingredient commonly used in local dish and can therefore be sold at higher prices in local markets.

In 2015, the performance of this disaster risk reduction (DRR) good practice was monitored in 6 farms in Rurrenabaque’s communities of Puerto Yumani (5) and Bajo Colorado (1).

This technology briefly introduces the concept of early maturing cassava and presents a cost-benefit analysis of the practice compared to normal practices for cassava production.
entries.description:
Description

1. Description (step by step) of the application of the technology/practice

  • This technology describes the introduction of early maturing purple cassava varieties in the Bolivian eco-region of the Beni river watershed.
  • In this area, farmers are used to cultivating white cassava, which has a growing cycle of more than 90 days.
    • Given the long growing period, traditional white cassava often cannot be harvested before the start of the flooding season, leading to significant production losses.
  • Early maturing cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz) can be harvested before local cassava varieties, thereby reducing the vulnerability of farmers to floods.
    • Furthermore, early maturing purple cassava is considered more valuable than white cassava because it is an ingredient commonly used in local dishes; therefore, it can be sold at higher prices in local markets.
  • Growing early maturing purple cassava is considered a disaster risk reduction (DRR) practice because it addresses harvest losses due to floods.
    • In 2015, the performance of this DRR good practice was monitored in six farms in Rurrenabaque’s communities of Puerto Yumani (5) and Bajo Colorado (1).
  • This technology briefly introduces the concept of early maturing cassava and presents a cost-benefit analysis of the practice compared to normal practices for cassava production.

1.1 Early maturing cassava varieties

  • Cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz) thanks to its efficient use of water and soil nutrients, and tolerance to drought and sporadic pest attacks, can produce reasonable yields, using few if any inputs, in areas with poor soils and unpredictable rainfall.
    • Despite its tolerance to drought, increased intensity and frequency of droughts and floods seriously affect cassava cultivation.
  • As cassava is almost exclusively a rainfed crop, in areas with only one rainy season per year, farmers usually plant white cassava as soon as the rains start so the plants have adequate soil moisture during the most critical part of their growth cycle, for instance, any delay on the planting could lead to drastic yield reductions.
    • Stakes should be planted at a shallow depth of 5 to 10 cm, in heavy and wet soils.
    • In light-textured and dry soils, stakes should be planted slightly deeper to avoid surface heat and lack of moisture.
  • In Bolivia, planting of white cassava in April and May, for example at the beginning of the dry season, coincides with the high possibility of drought occurrences, making planting and growing difficult.
    • On the other hand, the thickening of the roots which takes more than three months then coincides with the flood season, causing the rotting of the root.
    • In the case of the purple early maturing variety, farmers plant as soon as the dry season starts, in order to be harvested right before the rainy season starts, so the roots do not rot.
    • With the aim of reducing the risk of loss of production due to drought and flood, as well as to guarantee the production of this basic crop, it is recommended to cultivate an early maturing cassava variety (purple cassava Manihot esculenta Crantz),
      • which is not as vulnerable as the white cassava to low soil moisture, hence can be planted during the dry season, during the months of April to July and in some cases August (taking advantage of the cold fronts that come up from the Patagonia usually in July and August), and
      • can be harvested after 90 days (during the months of July to October, depending on the months the purple cassava was planted), at which point the cassava reaches a thickness suitable for the household consumption, and up to 120 days, to allow the thickening of the roots, when the cassava is to be commercialized.
Figure 1. Early maturing cassava production

©FAO/TECA

  • The Purple Cassava variety (Manihot esculenta Crantz) has a soft texture and brown periderm colour, the bark is purple and the pulp is white with some purple spots.
  • Its leaves are purple and its roots are short and conical in shape. At the early stages of its maturing process (90 days), it becomes suitable for consumption.
  • This variety rends good yields; 18 to 25 tonne per ha, making it an effective alternative to guarantee food security for the populations living at the river banks of Bolivia’s lowlands.
Table 1. Planting, maturing and harvest of early maturing cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz)

Source: FAO 2017

1.1.1 Socio-economic benefits of early maturing cassava varieties

  • Early maturing cassava variety (Manihot esculenta Crantz) helped in reducing the negative impact caused by unexpected floods. 
  • Early maturing cassava varieties brought an increase in production due to higher yields, allowing to commercialize part of the production while guaranteeing food security during the flood season.
  • Early maturing purple cassava is considered more valuable than white cassava because it is an ingredient commonly used in local dishes; therefore, it can be sold at higher prices in local markets. This variety of cassava can be processed into chivé, a typical, highly nutritive beverage which can be stored for longer periods, as cassava after two or three days of harvest is not any longer fresh, becoming woody.

1.1.2 Prices

  • Farmers do not use fertilizers nor pesticides for the production of cassava (both white and purple) in the analysed communities.
  • The prices mentioned in this practice refer to the time of writing.

1.1.3 Side effects

  • No side effects were identified.

1.1.4 Major barriers

  • No barriers were identified.

1.1.5 General recommendations

  • Although cassava can withstand periods of drought, it is very sensitive to soil water deficit. Water stress at any time in the early period reduces significantly the growth of roots and shoots and impairs subsequent development of the storage roots.
  • Cassavas grow better in well-drained soil, for which digging trenches along the plantation could contribute to this aim.
  • Cassava growers should be encouraged to adopt minimum tillage and, ideally, zero tillage, especially on well‑aggregated, friable soils with adequate levels of organic matter. Even if this conservation tillage produces lower yields, it offers farmers economic advantages: reduced spending on the fuel and equipment needed for conventional tillage, and the opportunity to produce cassava more intensively and sustainably, without the need for high levels of external inputs. 
  • Reduced or zero tillage will also be important as an alternative to conventional tillage in cassava-growing areas affected by climate change. Where rainfall is reduced, this practice will help to conserve soil moisture; where rainfall increases, it will help reduce soil erosion and improve soil structure, allowing better internal drainage.
  • Along with reduced or zero tillage, it is recommended to maintain a protective organic cover on the soil, using crop residues and mulches, in order to protect the surface, reduce runoff and erosion, and suppress weeds.
  • Mulch cover also serves as an insulating layer that reduces diurnal temperature variations and water evaporation. It increases the soil organic matter content and provides a favorable environment for soil micro‑organisms and below‑ground fauna. By creating better physical soil conditions - reduced soil temperatures, higher levels of moisture, increased water infiltration capacity and lower evaporation - mulching favors higher yields. 
  • It is encouraged to cultivate a wider range of plant species in associations, sequences and rotations with cassava that may include trees, shrubs and pastures. Mixed cropping diversifies production, which helps farmers to reduce their economic risk, respond to changes in market demand and adapt to external shocks, including climate change. Rotating or associating nutrient‑demanding crops with soil‑enriching legumes, and shallow‑rooting crops with deep‑rooting ones, maintain soil fertility and crop productivity and interrupts the transmission of crop‑specific pests and diseases.

1.1.6 Synergies with other good practices

  • Agroforestry coffee cultivation in combination with mulching, trenches and organic composting in Uganda.
  • Banana cultivation with mulching, digging of trenches for water retention, organic composting and improved varieties, Uganda.
  • Mulching in organic agriculture.
Table 2. Early and maturing cassava prices per kg

Source: FAO 2017

2. Benefits

2.1 Cost-benefit analysis

  • Cost-Benefit Analyses were conducted based on quantitative data collected during the monitoring period (July-October) in 2015. Data collected from plots where the early maturing purple cassava was grown were compared with data collected from control plots within the same farms, or from neighbouring farms where the good practice had not been implemented yet and where the commonly grown white cassava was cultivated.
  • The CBA calculates the cumulative net benefits obtained from 1 hectare of cassava over a period of 11 years, as well as the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period. A 10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms.
    • Cumulative net benefits in farms where a mix of early maturing purple cassava and traditional white cassava was planted are about 188 percent higher than the benefits of farms where only traditional white cassava was planted. The good practice and the local practice were monitored under non-hazard conditions; therefore, the differences are largely attributable to the higher yields obtained from early maturing varieties, combined with higher prices driven by the high demand of purple cassava in local markets.
    • The BCR of the good practice is 32, as compared to 11.8 for the usual practice. Such high BCR values for both white and purple cassava are due to the low costs of inputs (e.g. no fertilizer nor pesticides are used, and no external workers are hired for cassava cultivation in the monitored farms). The large difference between the BCR of purple and white cassava is mainly due to differences in yields and prices.
Figure 2. Benefit and benefit-cost ratios of DRR Good Practice (cultivating early maturing purple cassava) and Existing Local Practice (local white cassava)

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Added benefits

  • Under non-hazard conditions, the data reveals that the DRR good practice (cultivating early maturing purple cassava) brings benefits almost three times higher than the local practice. This makes it a “no‑regret” DRR measure.

2.3 Avoided losses

  • The hazard scenario could not be analysed yet, as no farms were affected by hazards during the monitored period.

2.4 Co-benefits

  • Early harvesting reduces the cassava growing period, thereby requiring a lower amount of inputs.
  • Additional research is needed to analyse the impact of these co‑benefits on the environment.

3. Validation of the practice

3.1 Geographical area of practice validation

  • In 2015, the performance of early maturing purple cassava was monitored in six farms in Rurrenabaque’s communities of Puerto Yumani (5) and Bajo Colorado (1).

3.2 Context of implementation

3.2.1 Environmental and climatic (period/ season) context

  • The Mamore and Beni rivers watersheds are located in the lowlands of the southwestern Amazon Basin.
  • Abundant rainfall characterizes this eco-region, with an average comprised of 1 300 mm to 2 000 mm per year.
  • During the rainy season between December and May, the rivers usually flood covering a large part of the surrounding land.
  • Contrary to expectations, however, no floods occurred in the area during the monitoring period.
  • Therefore, the performance of the good practice (growing early maturing purple cassava instead of white cassava) was assessed under non-hazard conditions only.

3.2.2 Economic (livelihood strategy) and social (target group) context

  • Farmers of the Mamore and Beni rivers watersheds lowlands of Bolivia’s southwestern Amazon basin.

4. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Following indications should be observed for good yields of purple cassava: 

  • Stakes should be planted at a shallow depth, of 5 cm to 10 cm, in heavy and wet soils, but slightly deeper in light-textured and dry soils to avoid surface heat and lack of moisture. 
  • Planting of purple cassava at the beginning of the dry season, from April to July and not later than August.
  • The cassava should be grown under direct sunlight and no shades, as it is highly sensitive to shade. 
  • Ensure proper draining.

4.1 Constraints (limiting factors) for the implementation of the technology

  • The difference in the price of seeds for the early maturing cassava (USD 4.34 kg) and the traditional white cassava (USD 1.45 kg), may affect the initial introduction of the early maturing cassava when farmers are still not aware of the benefits of growing the early maturing cassava variety.

5. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Agroforestry coffee cultivation in combination with mulching, trenches and organic composting in Uganda: ID 8928.
  • Banana cultivation with mulching, digging of trenches for water retention, organic composting and improved varieties: ID 8947.
  • Mulching in organic agriculture: ID 8365.
  • Sustainable livelihoods: new market opportunities for cassava: ID 4575.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology, through efficient use of water and soil nutrients, and tolerance to drought and sporadic pest attacks can produce reasonable yields, using few inputs, in areas with poor soils and unpredictable rainfall.

7.2 Pro-poor technology

This technology reduces the vulnerability of farmers to floods, therefore increasing yields and providing more food security.

entries.tittle: Mejora de jardines flotantes tradicionales para la producción de hortalizas en Bangladesh
entries.summary: La agricultura de jardines flotantes (conocida localmente como vasoman/dhap chash) es una tecnología de innovación de producción de cultivos locales para el ecosistema sumergido en las regiónes del sur de Bangladés. Tradicionalmente, los agricultores de los distritos Gopalganj, Pirojpur y Barisal han usado la práctica ya desde hace casi dos siglos adaptándose a las condiciones de inundación/de sumersión. Para adaptar las prácticas tradicionales de jardines flotantes para cultivar cucurbitáceas u otros tipos de hortalizas enredaderas con éxito, se realizaron programas de investigación. Esta tecnología describe cómo se implementa dicha práctica mejorada para la producción de hortalizas enredaderas y cómo administrarla.
entries.description:
Descripción

1. Introducción

  • La agricultura de jardines flotantes (conocida localmente como vasoman/dhap chash) es una tecnología de innovación de producción de cultivos locales para el ecosistema sumergido en las regiónes del sur de Bangladés.
    • Tradicionalmente, los agricultores de los distritos Gopalganj, Pirojpur y Barisal han usado la práctica ya desde hace casi dos siglos adaptándose a las condiciones de inundación/de sumersión.
    • Para una descripción detallada acerca de la práctica tradicional consulte: Traditional floating garden practices for vegetable production.
  • En el sistema tradicional, los agricultores generalmente cultivan sólo un número limitado de cultivos como el amaranto rojo, espinaca india, quimbombó, cúrcuma y cultivos aroid (aro) en jacintos de agua; emplean la cama flotante en la temporada del monzón (generalmente en los meses de junio a noviembre).
  • Las camas flotantes tradicionales no son adecuadas para el cultivo de cucurbitáceas u otros tipos de hortalizas enredaderas porque no tienen el ancho suficiente por su forma estrecha (anchura 1,1 m a 1,3 m).
    • Las hortalizas, especialmente las cucurbitáceas y otros tipos de hortalizas enredaderas, por lo general necesitan un espacio suficiente debido al gran tamaño de la copa y al hábito de crecimiento vigoroso.
    • Por lo tanto, sólo un número reducido de plantas puede ser cultivado en la cama flotante.
  • Además, los frutos cultivados vecino a las camas flotantes se decoloran en un ladoy el otro lado se mantiene verde debido a una absorción non-uniforme de la luz solar.
    • Esto deteriora el valor de mercado de los productos agrícolas.
    • Además, hay más infestación de ratas en los cultivos de calabaza o verduras de enredadera en las camas flotantes dañando severamente las flores, así como frutos de los cultivos.
  • Teniendo en cuenta los hechos anteriores, se realizaban programas de investigación en la Estación Regional de Investigación Agrícola, Rahmatpur, Barisal de Bangladesh Instituto de Investigación Agrícola (BARI) para mejorar las prácticas agrícolas tradicionales de jardínes flotantes para el cultivo exitoso de cucurbitáceas y otros tipos de hortalizas enredaderas.
  • Recientemente, se han desarrollado mejoramientos de dicha tecnología basada en la agricultura flotante que se denomina como "Floating Bed cum Trellis" (FBT) (español: Camas flotantes con enrejados).
    • El sistema FBT construye la cama flotante alternativa con enrejado.
    • En el método FBT, las cucurbitáceas u hortalizas enredaderas se pueden plantar en las camas flotantes, pero crecen y se desarrollan en el amplio enrejado (ancho 3 a 6 metros) construido justo al lado de la cama flotante (Figuras 1 y 2).
    • Por lo tanto, según el requisito para el crecimiento óptimo de los cultivos, se mantiene 3 a 6 metros de distancia entre dos camas flotantes para la construcción de los enrejados.
    • Así, el uso de jacinto de agua para las prácticas de jardín flotante se disminuye.
    • El enrejado se hace generalmente con bambú, red de nylon y dhaincha (Sesbania sp.).
Figura 1. Cultivo de calabazas de botella (pepinos) sobre camas flotantes con enrejado (FBT) en el área de investigación para la agricultura flotante

©BARI

Figura 2. Frutos de pepino híbrido (cucumis sativus) (a), calabaza de botella (lagenaria siceraria) (b), y calabaza (c) que cuelga bajo el enrejado

©BARI

2. Mejoras

2.1 Aumento de la producción y de los rendimientos

  • En virtud de este sistema, es posible cultivar mayor número de plantas en la cama flotante, lo que aumenta el rendimiento de los cultivos.
  • Además, los frutos de las hortalizas se obtienen de forma y color uniforme debido a una nutrición de los vegetales con suficiente nutrientes y una absorbancia uniforme de la luz solar.
  • En un experimento, el pepino híbrido dio un rendimiento de frutos de aproximadamente 45 a 50 t/ha bajo el método FBT, mientras que el mismo cultivo generalmente da un rendimiento de aproximadamente 25 a 35 t/ha en las condiciones normales sobre tierra.
  • Esto indica que el pepino híbrido cultivado a través de tecnología FBT proporciona aproximadamente el doble de rendimiento en comparación con la de condición normal en tierra.

2.2. Aumento de la eficiencia del uso del suelo

  • En el método FBT, diversos cultivos de corta duración, como el amaranto rojo, espinaca, rábano, cilantro se pueden cultivar en las camas flotantes en la primera etapa de las cucurbitáceas (Figura 3), lo que aumenta no sólo la producción de hortalizas misma sino también la intensidad de cultivo en comparación con las prácticas tradicionales.
Figura 3. El cultivo de amaranto rojo (a) y espinacas (b) en una etapa temprana del cultivo de calabaza de botella

©BARI

2.3 Cantidad reducida de jacinto de agua

  • La disponibilidad de jacinto de agua está disminuyendo día a día en Bangladés debido a varias razones (la salinidad, la falta de conservación, etc.).
  • Sin embargo, la tecnología FBT utiliza 50-60 por ciento menos jacintos de agua en comparación con el sistema tradicional jardín flotante.

2.4. Contribución a la seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de los pobres

  • El área total de tierras (medio) bajas en Bangladés es de unos 3,0 millones de hectáreas (21 por ciento del total del país).
  • Una cantidad notable permanece como tierras en barbecho sobre todo en la temporada del monzón debido a las inundaciones o las condiciones sumergidas.
  • La generación de tecnologías modernas de jardines flotantes adecuados, basadas agricultura como las camas flotantes con enrejados (FBT), a través de programas intensivos de investigación y extensión/difusión de las tecnologías, se puede utilizar las tierras húmedas/inundadas para la producción de cultivos que mejoren la seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de las personas pobres vulnerables ubicadas en humedales y zonas inundadas de Bangladés.
  • En la actualidad, un buen número de programas de investigación se están llevando a cabo en la Estación Regional de Investigación Agrícola, Rahmatpur, Barisal- BARI para el cultivo de calabaza, calabaza de botella, papa, col (repollo, coliflor, knolkhol, brócoli, etc.), zanahoria, melón de agua, fresa, ají, etc., en cama flotante con matas de frijol (Figura 4).
Figura 4. El cultivo de papa (a), zanahoria (b), col (c), coliflor (d) y frijol (e) en la cama flotante

©BARI

3. Información adicional

  • El siguiente video da una breve introducción acerca de las prácticas tradicionales de jardín flotante y sus mejoras desarrolladas por BARI:
    • Floating Agriculture Technology of BARI

[Autores: Tecnología traducida por José Sánchez Narvaez, M. Sc., Coordinador de Ciencia Tecnología e Innovación del Instituto de Transferencia de Tecnologías Apropiadas del Convenio Andrés Bello (ITACAB), Profesor invitado Escuela Post Grado, Universidad Nacional Agraria La Molina (UNALM), Lima - Perú]

4. Validación de la práctica 

  • El sistema FBT se ha probado en dos estaciones de cultivo bajo condiciones de la Estación Regional de Investigación Agrícola, Rahmatpur, Barisal de Bangladesh, Instituto de Investigación Agrícola (BARI). 

5. Zonas agroecológicas 

  • Tropical, cálido.
  • ​​Subtropical, húmedo​.

6. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas 

  • Prácticas tradicionales de jardines flotantes para la producción de hortalizas en Bangladesh: ID 8955.
  • Método del cultivo hidropónico simple no circulante para vegetales: ID 8957.
  • Traditional floating garden practices for seedling production in Bangladesh: ID 8869.

7. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto 

7.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología le da al agricultor una descripción general de cómo mejorar e implementar de manera eficiente las prácticas de los jardines flotantes tradicionales.

7.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta práctica contribuye a una producción resiliente y creciente de cultivos, lo que a su vez conduce a una seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de los seres humanos y también una dieta saludable. Además se fortalece la fuente de ingresos de los agricultores.
