entries.tittle: Fishpond Layout and Construction
entries.summary:
Fishponds are not just a hole in the ground containing water. They are unnatural water environments that farmers must manage in order to produce profitable fish harvests. Ponds should provide a good environment for fish to live in, all requirements for fish to live a healthy life, grow well and reproduce well. The pond water must be free from diseases, toxic chemicals and other fish enemies; and ponds fish should get sufficient fresh air and food.

Physical characteristics of fishponds affect water quality and influence their production potential for the farmers. They have to be sited in locations where they can be managed well to achieve the highest production potential. The following technology from the Aquaculture Technical Manual describes how to build a good fish pond.
entries.description:
Description

1. Pond structure and types

  • Pond bottom and pond bank
    • The bottom usually slopes on one side to allow complete drainage.
    • The bank is the side of the pond that usually slopes outwards at an angle of 30 degrees and covered with grass to hold the soil, Figure 1.
  • Inlet and outlet
    • The inlet is the channel and gate that allows water into the pond and it is usually equipped with a fine nylon screen to prevent the entry of wild fish.
    • The outlet is the channel and gate that allows water out of the pond, it is equipped with a fine nylon screen to prevent the escape of pond fish.
  • Monk
    • It is a concrete structure at the pond outlet, closed by two parallel pieces of timber with clay packed in between, the structure is expensive and more difficult to operate.
    • Nowadays PVC pipes are being preferred for inlets and outlets. (See Figure 3)
  • Drainage channel
    • It is the channel that receives water drained from the pond, it must be below the level of the pond bottom.
  • Water supply channel
    • It is the channel from which water is diverted into pond, usually it is elevated to the same level as the pond water level.
  • Plastic pipe system
    • More recently the plastic pipe system has been widely adopted for the inlet and outlet.
    • The pipes have elbows at the bends to make them easy to operate.
    • The plastic pipes are much cheaper and easier to fix and operate than concrete.
    • The size of the pipes should be larger for larger ponds to ease water flow.
Figure 1. The pond looked at from above

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. A cross-sectional view of a pond

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. The monk

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Types of ponds

There are basically two types of ponds: excavated and contour ponds. 

  • Excavated ponds built on relatively flat ground with water basin formed by surround raised grounds (dykes)(Figure 4). 
  • Contour ponds built-in shallow valleys with water basin formed with a single dyke (dam) across the valley.
    • In contour ponds, the shape, depth, size and shape of the bottom are dictated by the nature of the valley.
    • Contour ponds are difficult to manage because of irregular shape, excessive depth and uncontrollable water supply.
  • Ponds must be easily accessible to allow supplies to reach the pond and fish to be taken to market (clear and wide road).
    • They should be drainable and should fill and drain by gravity without the need to pump out water.
    • The slope of the pond bottom should be dropped by 1 cm to 2 cm for each length of 10 m to allow proper drainage without the need for pumping out the water.
  • The minimum water depth of a pond must not be less than half a meter while the maximum water depth must not be less than 1 m (for small ponds up to 50 m length) but not more than 1.7 m for large ponds more than 100 m long.
    • Water should not seep into the pond from the bottom of the pond. Such a pond will be difficult to drain.
  • The type of soil surrounding the pond should hold water and be firm to prevent loss through seepage across pond sides or the bottom.
    • Rectangular ponds are easier to construct and easy to fish by seining.
    • The larger the pond, the more fish it can produce.
    • Commercial ponds range from 20 m x 50 m to 200 m x 500 m.
    • Larger ponds are less costly to construct per unit area but require larger equipment to operate and problems of harvesting are far greater than smaller ponds.
Figure 4. Typical pond

©FAO/TECA

2. Site survey, pond layout and pre-construction preparation

  • Actual construction begins with clearing the site to allow measurements to be made (Figure 5).
    • The site is cleared first to make it open in order for measurements to be done.
    • The bushes and trees are cut down.
    • The grass cover and its roots are cleared leaving bare ground.
    • Remove the 20 cm to 30 cm of loose topsoil, which contains roots of grass and trees until you reach firm soil.
    • The loose soils mixed with roots and grass allows water to escape from the pond.
  • The knowledge of the gradient is useful in planning the fish farm; where the water channels should pass and where the ponds should be constructed.
    • For small ponds (up to 20 m x 40 m) a trained fish farming technician from Kajjansi in Uganda or a graduate of the Fisheries Training Institute can advise.
    • For larger ponds, it is advisable to seek the guidance of a qualified land surveyor.
    • These can be found in Farm Planning Division of the Ministry of Agriculture, Animal Industry and Fisheries, Entebbe in Uganda.
Figure 5. Clearing site for pond construction

©FAO/TECA

  • It is always better to start by getting both the water supply and drainage channels correct.
    • Where the stream or river bends so much and occupies much of the space suitable for the ponds, it should be straightened.
    • The stream in picture A is straightened as seen in B to create space for the pond(s) to be constructed(Figure 6).
Figure 6. Straightening the stream

©FAO/TECA

  • The damming and diverting streams or rivers depending on the slope of the ground, the stream or river may be changed to a higher level, leaving the lower level for the ponds.
    • This makes it easier to direct water into the pond and to drain the pond by gravity.
    • The supply channel is shifted from a lower position X to an upper position Y shown in (a).
    • The pond and drainage channels are then constructed on the lower ground (b), leaving areas (Figure 7a).
    • This is done by damming the stream at the location (d) to raise the water level to allow the diversion.
    • To raise the level of the stream it is necessary to block (dam) the stream to raise its level before channeling it to a higher level.
  • When the slope of the ground is steep, the stream can be dropped in steps.
    • This is done by damming at various points.
    • The ponds are also constructed in steps, as shown in Figure 7b. 
    • Each pond is a step lower than the first pond.
    • Damming can be done using logs of timber or sandbags put across the stream.
    • The position of the water channels and ponds to be constructed is marked using pegs and ropes.
  • In all the above cases, it is advisable to seek the services of a ground surveyor to get the correct gradient.
  • The Ministry of Agriculture, Animal Industry and Fisheries, Entebbe has a department of ground surveyors.
Figure 7a. Damming diverting, Figure 7b-damming a stream to elevate the water level

©FAO/TECA

  • For a one pond farm, the pond should be laid by the side of the river (Figure 8).
    • The supply channel and the drainage channel are independent of each other.
    • Where more than one pond is planned, the ponds should be laid parallel to the stream (Figure 9) and each pond should receive and drain water independent of each other.
    • The ponds can be laid on both sides of the stream.
    • In each case, each side of ponds has its own drainage.
    • Each pond receives and discharges its water independently of another.
  • It is wrong for a pond to be fed with water from another pond.
    • In such an arrangement, one pond cannot be drained without another one also draining.
    • If there is a disease outbreak in one pond it will spread to the next pond.
Figure 8. One pond farm

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Multi-pond farm

©FAO/TECA

3. Pond construction

  • Pond construction does not always mean digging.
    • Depending on the slope of the ground, sometimes construction involves digging, other times it involves building.
    • Construction involves removing soil from where it is not required to where it is required, according to the levels established and plans drawn by the surveyor.
    • The digging is necessary where the ground is almost flat, the soil is dug out and heaped on the sides of the pond.
    • The building up is necessary where the slope is big, soil dug from a is used to build up.
  • The bottom of the pond should not be flat.
    • It should be sloping from all corners towards the outlet.
    • The level should drop by 1 cm at a distance of 1 m to allow the pond to drain.
    • The thick arrow indicates the main draining trench (Figure 10).
    • The smaller arrows indicate the secondary trenches.
    • All of them slope, leading the water towards the outlet during draining.
Figure 10. Pond construction

©FAO/TECA

4. Determination of slope of the pond

  • The slope of the pond bottom can be determined in two ways - using the direction of the flow of water and the use of the spirit level.

4.1 Use of water flow

  • Generally, this method is used for small ponds up to 20 m x 40 m.
    • Water is poured from a bucket into a small hole at the inlet.
    • A straight trench is dug to lead the water towards the outlet.
    • The trench is lowered until the water drains by gravity to the outlet.
    • This primary trench marks the deepest point of the bottom.
    • From various points on the sides of the pond, smaller trenches are dug in a similar manner to get the secondary trenches.
    • Then the bottom is smoothened accordingly.

4.2 Use of a water bottle as a spirit level

  • For this method, pegs must be fixed firmly on the ground at the inlet and at the outlet as shown in Figure 11.
    • A rope is tied very tightly on one peg and the other end is pulled towards the second peg, and the water bottle is filled with water leaving only a little gap and the top tightened.
    • When the bottle is placed on its sides an air bubble is seen in the middle.
  • The bottle is rested onto the rope and the untied end of the rope is raised or lowered until the bubble is exactly in the middle of the bottle.
    • The rope is flat and the depth of the pond is measured from the rope to the bottom, and the broken line indicated the bottom of the pond.
    • For much larger ponds more than 20 m x 50 m a professional land surveyor is required.
    • Professional farm planners are available in the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, Entebbe in Uganda.
Figure 11. Getting the ground level using bottle and water

©FAO/TEC

5. Construction of the dyke

  • The dyke must be made watertight and must be firm.
    • Dykes should be wide, not narrower than 1 m on the top.
    • It should be wider in some sections to allow passage for vehicles.
    • These dykes between two ponds and between a pond and stream are too narrow.
    • It is difficult to walk on and water can seep from one pond to the next.
    • Clarias can easily dig across the dyke and escape to the next pond (Figure 12).
Figure 12. Dyke tops

©FAO/TECA

  • During construction, dykes should be compacted hard to make them watertight.
    • Each layer of soil must be compacted rather than heaping big mounds then compacting once.
    • It should not have loose soil particles that will allow the seepage of water across.
    • If the soil has more sand and is loose, a trench is dug in the middle of the dyke and tightly packed with clays.
    • This trench is called a core.
  • The base of the core should be below the pond bottom to minimize water seepage.
    • The wall and top of the dyke should be covered with creeping grass to hold the soil not to fall.
  • The main tools required for the pond construction are:
    • "pangas'' or machete
    • axes
    • pickaxe
    • hoes
    • shovels
    • wheel burrows
    • timbers (12 inches x 1 inch for pushing wheel burrows on in the bottom mud)
    • rope ( for measuring and showing the lines)
    • a water bottle (for levels). 

6. Pond maintenance

  • This is the repair and maintenance of the pond in its original shape.
    • Water in a fishpond socks the soil at the bottom and also erodes the pond sides.
    • Pond maintenance is a continuous activity from the stocking of the pond to harvesting.
    • The farmers keep checking on pond sides for leakages, which are then repaired by adding soil and ramming.
    • Major ponds maintenance is done after the total harvesting of fish.
    • A fishpond is allowed to dry.
    • The soft soils around the pond are removed using hoes and spades, the outlets and inlets can be fixed.

7. The performance of the different fish types in ponds

  • The growth and performance of fish in ponds depends on a number of factors. 
    • Genes (nature)
      • Some fish grow faster than others because they naturally have better genes for growth.
    • Environmental conditions
      • Fish tends to grow faster in warmer regions than in the cooler ones.
      • Some fishes have better tolerance for hard environmental conditions than others.
      • A pond in a warm area is harvested in October (blue arrow), but a pond in a cold area is harvested five months later in March the next year (pink arrow)
    • Management
      • Even if the fish has good genes for growth and environmental conditions are right when it is not fed, for example, the fish will not grow well.
  • All three factors must be present in order to get the best out of the fish.

7. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies

entries.tittle: Interventions Against Intestinal Nematodes: Nutritional Aad Chemotherapeutic Solutions
entries.summary: Nematode worms are significant health problems for sheep and goats throughout the world. The impact is seen in a number of ways. Parasitism causes a reduction in food intake and lower weight gains. Milk production can also be affected, and heavily parasitised animals may die. The economic consequences for livestock keepers can therefore be serious. This technology provides an improved understanding of the relative benefits of nutritional and/or chemotherapeutic intervention against gastro-intestinal parasitism by Haemonchus contortus to assist farmers to optimise goat production. Information is provided on use of the FAMACHA© system for strategic treatment, and the use of Urea-Molasses Blocks (UMB) for supplementary feeding.
entries.description:
Description

Nematode worms are significant health problems for sheep and goats throughout the world. The impact is seen in a number of ways. Parasitism causes a reduction in food intake and lower weight gains. Milk production can also be affected, and heavily parasitized animals may die. The economic consequences for livestock keepers can therefore be serious.

1. Life cycle and control of the parasite

  • It is necessary to understand the lifecycle of the parasites if they are to be controlled.
    • Gastrointestinal nematodes produce eggs, which are passed in the faeces of sheep onto the pasture.
    • The eggs hatch into larvae, which then develop to reach the infective stage.
    • Grazing animals such as sheep and goats may ingest the larvae, which then mature into adult worms.
    • The ability of nematode larvae to survive on the pasture is dependent on environmental conditions.
    • Generally, warm and humid conditions are favourable to the parasites.
    • However, the larva may go into a phase of hypobiosis or arrested development and may therefore survive when conditions are less favourable.
    • The worms can, thus, be problem even in relatively arid environments.
  • A widely used measure to control nematode worms is to treat animals with anthelmintic drugs.
  • These treatments can be effective, but there are a number of constraints to their successful use.
    • It is important that treatments are given at the correct time and to the appropriate age groups.
    • Lack of information on the lifecycle and epidemiology of the parasites can limit the effectiveness of control measures.
    • Where livestock are free to roam and mix with other flocks, parasite control can be difficult to implement as pastures tend to become re-infected by untreated animals.

1.1 Haemonchus contortus

  • The gastrointestinal worm Haemonchus contortus is one of the most widespread parasites in tropical and sub-tropical areas of the world.
    • Infections by this parasite are a major constraint to the efficient production of livestock.
    • The adult H. contortus worms live in the abomasum (stomach) of ruminant animals (sheep, goats, cattle, wild ruminants).
    • The females deposit from 5 000 to 10 000 eggs per day which pass out of the host with the faeces.
    • The first stage larvae hatch from the eggs and feed on bacteria, moulting twice to form the infective third stage larvae.
    • Consumption of these third stage larvae by the host leads to exsheathment in the rumen.
    • These then migrate to the abomasum and burrow into the mucosa where they moult into fourth stage larvae which emerge into the paramucosal lumen of the abomasum.
    • Here they feed and undergo a final moult to reach adulthood. Mating of adults occurs and egg production starts.
    • The eggs hatch in soil or water.
    • Some infections may also occur through the skin.
    • Enormous numbers of infective larvae may accumulate on heavily grazed pastures.
  • Parasitized animals are anaemic and they eat less.
    • The food they do eat is digested less effectively and the protein that they do digest is metabolised less efficiently.
    • This has the effect of weakening the host response and promoting parasite survival.
  • The standard methods of treatment use anthelmintics to kill the parasites carried by the sheep.
    • This reduces pasture contamination that comes from parasite eggs passed in the droppings, which grow into larvae that then infect further sheep.
    • Unfortunately many poor livestock keepers cannot afford these drugs.
    • Even those farmers who can bear the costs of treatment find that many drug preparations are ineffective, partly because the worms are becoming increasingly resistant to the most commonly used drugs.

2. Nutrition and health interactions

  • It is recognised that improved feeding and nutrition, with careful attention to the animal with its seasonal requirements, has an important role to play in the control of livestock diseases.
  • An animal with an adequate diet is more likely to be healthier than one with a poor diet.
  • Similarly, certain breeds of livestock (typically the native breeds) have better natural immunity to disease, including abilities to cope with parasites.
  • It is important to recognize that better feeding of livestock covers:
    • the quality or types of foods supplied,
    • the quantity of food, and
    • adjusting for seasonal requirements.
  • Nutrition plays a major role in how animals are able to overcome the detrimental effects of internal parasites
  • The signs of gastro-intestinal parasitism can often be used as a symptom of some other problem, usually poor nutrition.
  • A combination of the use of Urea-Molasses Blocks (UMB) for supplementary feeding, and the strategic treatment of susceptible animals with anthelmintics, using the FAMACHA© system to identify at-risk individuals, has been found to be successful in combating gastrointestinal infections of Haemonchus contortus.

3. Supplementation with Urea Molasses Blocks (UMB)

  • You will find these referred to either as Molasses-Urea Blocks or as Urea-Molasses Blocks.
  • Molasses, urea and other ingredients are used in the manufacture of molasses/urea feeds that are prepared as blocks, pastes or licks.
  • These preparations are an excellent way of providing readily degradable protein and readily fermentable energy to ruminant animals, and they help increase the protein supply to the animal.
  • However, goats are particularly sensitive to urea toxicity and so it is essential that the blocks are accurately made so that goats are not fed too much urea at one time.
  • The rate of feed intake is reduced when the molasses is prepared in this way (compared with a straight molasses lick for example), but intakes should still be controlled when the blocks are first introduced.
  • The blocks can be made from a variety of components depending on their local availability, nutritive value, price, existing facilities for their use, and their influence on the quality of blocks.
  • They can also include specific additional components depending on use and local demand.

3.1 Components of UMB

  • Molasses provides fermentable substrate and various minerals and trace elements (but contains low amounts of phosphorous).
  • Due to its pleasant taste and smell, it makes the block very attractive and palatable to animals.
  • The degree Brix of the molasses should be as high as possible, and preferably higher than 85, to ensure solidification.
    • Urea, provides fermentable nitrogen, and is the most important component of the block.
      • Urea may increase the intake of low quality forages as well as their digestibility.
      • The intake of urea must be limited to avoid toxicity problems.
      • However it should be sufficient to maintain ammonia levels in the rumen consistently above 200 mg N/l for growth of microorganisms in the rumen and high rates of degradation of fibre.
    • Wheat or rice bran has a multiple purpose in the blocks.
      • It provides some key nutrients including fat, protein and phosphorus.
      • It also acts as an absorbent for the moisture contained in molasses and helps gives structure to the block.
      • It may be replaced by other fibrous materials such as dry and fine bagasse (the residue from sugar cane processing) or groundnut hulls.
      • Other crop residues can also be included in Molasses-Urea blocks.
      • Clearly this depends on availability, and some crop residues and by-products will provide more nutrients than others.
    • Minerals may be added where appropriate.
      • Common salt is generally added because this is often deficient in the diet and it is cheap.
      • Calcium is supplied by molasses and by the gelling agent, calcium oxide or cement (see below).
      • Although phosphorus is deficient, there is no evidence that its addition is beneficial where animals are at below maintenance requirements when grazing on dry mature pastures or fed low-quality forage.
      • Mineral requirements are reduced at maintenance or survival levels.
      • Deficiencies will generally become a problem only when production is increased, particularly when a bypass protein supplement is given.
      • In these cases phosphorus should be included in that supplement.
    • A gelling agent or binder is necessary in order to solidify the blocks.
      • Various products have been tried successfully:
        • magnesium oxide,
        • bentonite,
        • calcium oxide,
        • calcium hydroxide, and
        • cement.
      • The use of cement has raised questions about possible negative effects on animals.
      • Research on the use of cement or its by-product, cement kiln dust, as a mineral supplement have not shown adverse effects at levels of 1 to 3 per cent of the total diet dry matter.
      • However, the USDA has restricted the use of cement kiln dust since it could cause a deposit of heavy metals in animal tissue.
  • Various chemicals or drugs for the control of parasites or for manipulation of rumen fermentation can be added to the molasses blocks, which can be an excellent carrier for these products.

3.2 The famacha system

  • A clinical essay on the FAMACHA system, for the identification and subsequent treatment of sheep suffering from haemonchosis by examining the ocular mucous membranes, has been developed in South Africa.
    • The FAMACHA© system was originally compiled by the Faculty of Veterinary Science, University of Pretoria, the Onderstepoort Veterinary Institute, the Worm Workshop of the South African Veterinary Association, and Intervet South Africa.
    • This was with the support of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the National Wool Growers Association and the National and Provincial Departments of Agriculture in South Africa.
  • The principle on which FAMACHA is based is the clinical diagnosis of anaemia.
    • Blood consists of a clear, fluid part (called plasma) and a cellular part (mainly red blood cells).
    • The proportion of red cells to plasma determines whether the animal is healthy or unhealthy.
    • This proportion can be measured in a laboratory using PCV or hematocrits, but with training and practice can also be estimated fairly accurately by assessing the colour of the mucous membranes, especially of the eyes.
  • Since Haemonchus are blood suckers, the effects of a heavy parasite burden in a non-resilient animal will therefore be evident as a low ratio of red cells to plasma.
    • This is seen in the mucous membranes of the eyes as a visible paleness generally known as anaemia.
    • By monitoring anaemia, resilient and susceptible animals can be identified.
  • To properly implement FAMACHA, it is essential for all users to obtain practical hands-on instruction in the use of FAMACHA©.
    • Prospective users of the FAMACHA system must obtain the official authorised card with the accurate colour gradations plus proper training by an authorised and trained person.
    • For further enquiries about FAMACHA©, and where to obtain materials and training, see the FAMACHA© Information Guide.
  • An example illustrating the FAMACHA colour chart in use in the field in South Africa, can be seen in these photographs.
    • The first one shows the colour chart together with a goat being evaluated.
    • The second one provides a closer view of the pink mucous membranes surrounding the eye.
Figure 1. Famacha

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Interventions against intestinal nematodes

©FAO/TECA

4. Cost-benefit Analysis of feed supplementation

  • The cost-benefit analysis indicated that dry-season, winter supplementation of Boer goats in South Africa with USB from June to August without strategic anthelmintic treatment, was associated with a six percent increase in carcase value over the corresponding controls.
  • At the time of the research, this equated to USD 3.24 per animal, which was considered economically viable and worthwhile.
  • This strategy is, therefore, recommended for use in extensively reared goats in the summer rainfall area of South Africa, provided nematode challenge is low and individual goats are treated when symptoms of nematode infection (anaemia) are noted.
  • A simple practical way of assessing whether or not an animal is anaemic is through the application of the FAMACHA system.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • subtropics, warm/mod cool.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Controlling intestinal Nematode infections in ruminants with naturally plants tannins: ID 4460.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Pro-poor technology

Protecting livestock animals against infections helps farmers against livestock losses.

entries.tittle: Trainer's Guide to Control Blowfly Infestation of Traditionally Processed Fish
entries.summary: Blowfly infestation of traditionally processed fish is a serious problem that results in significant physical and economic losses. It also leads to the unregulated use of inappropriate and hazardous insecticides by fish processors in some developing countries. This manual provides guidance on the biology of blowfly infestation and its control. Emphasis is placed on the recently developed systems based approach to controlling infestation, which engages the fish processor in identifying those steps in the process where infestation occurs and selecting appropriate control measures.
entries.description:
Description

Traditionally processed fish is a nutritionally and economically important commodity in many tropical, developing countries. Throughout processing and early storage, fish are exposed to infestation by blowflies (Diptera, Calliphoridae). This is a significant cause of post-harvest losses in the traditional fish processing industry, exacerbated by the basic, unhygienic conditions under which much of the fish is processed, particularly at the small-scale level.

Whilst few detailed, quantitative studies of insect related losses of cured fish have been carried out, losses of 25 percent are thought to be common. In some cases losses in excess of 90 percent can occur in situations where no preventative measures are used. Such frequent and extensive losses cannot be sustained and so some processors have responded to the problem by applying unsuitable, toxic household and agricultural insecticides directly to their fish. This jeopardizes not only their own health, but also the health of fish consumers.

A range of methods of infestation control have been developed and promoted for use at fish processing sites over the past 15 to 20 years. These include, amongst others:

  • the use of solar driers;
  • mesh screens erected over drying racks to prevent gravid females from gaining access to the fish;
  • improved salting methods to render the fish unacceptable to ovipositing blowflies and feeding larvae; and
  • the application of approved insecticides.

Despite extensive research and promotion of remedial techniques, uptake of recommended control measures by fish processors has been poor. Consequently, insect infestation of traditionally processed fish remains a major cause of losses. The apparent failure to successfully promote recommended control measures is generally attributed to two factors.

  1. The first is socio-economic, whereby implementation of the suggested measures may be too costly or culturally unacceptable.
  2. The second is poor extension of research findings to the fish processors.

Whilst the first is difficult to overcome, the second can be improved with good training of extension workers.

1. Blowfly control training manual

  • The training guide 'A Guide to Controlling Blowfly Infestation of Traditionally Processed Fish', has been produced following field research to evaluate the effectiveness of a systems-based approach in controlling blowfly infestation.
  • The guide places emphasis on the socio-economic context within which traditional fish processing takes place.
  • The systems-based approach to controlling blowfly infestation fully takes into account the biology of infestation, variations in processing parameters, and environmental and socio-economic factors.
  • It is a holistic approach that empowers fish processors to select those control measures that are appropriate to their particular circumstances.
  • The guide, which is presented in two parts, is designed to equip development workers with the understanding and tools.
    • This will enable them to provide practical assistance to fish processors who are experiencing losses as a result of blowfly infestation.
  • Part 1a and Part 1b of the guide provides background information on a series of topics.
    • The biology of blowfly infestation and factors that influence infestation levels.
    • Techniques for controlling blowfly infestation at traditional fish processing sites.
    • The systems-based blowfly control strategy.
    • Benefits of reducing infestation.
  • Part 2a and Part 2b of the guide provides guideline notes, case study exercises, checklists and templates that are designed to assist extension workers in implementing the systems-based approach in the field.
  • The hardcopy of the manual is accompanied by a CD ROM that illustrates the application of the systems-based approach to controlling infestation at fish processing sites in India.

2. Field evaluation of the systems-based approach

  • The research commenced with a scoping survey of 22 fish processing villages located in the Indian coastal states of Andhra Pradesh and Orissa.
    • Semi-structured interviews were held with fish processors.
    • Background information was collected on processing techniques, losses caused by blowfly infestation, remedial measures in use, socio-economic context within which processors operate, and fish processing costings.
  • The survey revealed that most traditional fish processing is a capitalistic enterprise, entirely driven by market forces and mostly conducted by resource poor, mostly female, small scale/artisanal fish processors.
  • Blowfly infestation and associated losses were frequently identified as major problems during the monsoon season.
  • Most processors appeared resigned to seasonal losses and took little action to prevent them.
  • Three villages were selected for the field trials and six processing sites.
    • Three control (those not using blowfly control interventions) and three experimental (those using blowfly control interventions) were selected in each village.
    • During the course of the fieldwork, five sets of trials were carried out.
  • Following profiling and selection of processors to participate in the trials, infestation audits were conducted at each processing site.
    • The infestation audits were informed by a combination of direct observations and on-site interviews with the fish processors.
  • Further meetings were held to discuss the nature of the problem and possible interventions.
  • The experimental processors were then asked to select from a menu of interventions, which included:
    • speeding up initial processing;
    • washing fish twice, plastic sheeting;
    • sharper knives;
    • improved on-site hygiene;
    • more frequent brine changing;
    • salting tank lids and frames;
    • drying racks; and
    • drying trays.
  • Although the project provided the physical interventions, the processors themselves were fully involved in their design.
  • The field researchers remained on-site throughout the field trials, monitoring activities, obtaining feedback and collecting financial and technical data.
    • Technical data included:
      • fish species,
      • weights,
      • temperature,
      • relative humidity,
      • wind speed,
      • fish drying rates,
      • brine strength,
      • blowfly activity,
      • infestation levels, and
      • downgrades.
  • Financial data included costs and revenues associated with fish processing and other business expenses and revenues.

2.1 Assessment of the key factors for success

  • The training manuals and associated systems-based control strategy were demonstrated to have had a sustainable impact in the villages where the evaluation trials were carried out.
  • The strategy of fully engaging the processors and empowering them in the decision-making process was a key factor in the successful implementation of the technology.
  • The technology has potential for transfer to other regions where traditional fish processing takes place and blowfly infestation/insecticide abuse are known to occur (e.g. Africa and South East Asia).
  • Whilst the technical content of the manuals is generic, the case studies used to illustrate this content are set within the south Asian context.
  • To increase relevance to users in other parts of the world, it would be desirable for part one of the manual to be amended to contain case studies that are appropriate to the country/region in which it is being used.

2.2 The technical training

  • Training of trainers in the use of the technology is necessary for its successful uptake by processors.
  • The training should be as practical/hands on as possible and be principally field based.
  • A period of two weeks should be sufficient to cover background theory and practical application.

3. Positive and negative effects on the environment and also on the social context

  • Positive environmental effects include improved hygiene, improved waste disposal methods in processing villages, and reduced unregulated use of harmful insecticides.
  • The technology should also yield health benefits in terms of reducing exposure of fish processors and consumers to insecticides.

4. Institutions that support the implementation or the diffusion of the technology

  • Collaborating institutions were: Manufacturing Improvement International Ltd (formerly Mike Dillon Associates Ltd), Integrated Coastal Management, Andhra Pradesh Department of Fisheries, Andhra Pradesh State Institute of Fisheries Training, the Central Institute of Fisheries Technology and Action for Food Production.

5. Validation of the practice

  • The evaluation trials clearly demonstrated that implementation of the technical interventions identified through applying the systems-based approach resulted in reduced infestation and reduced physical and economic losses.
  • Analysis of the economic data indicated that application of the technical interventions during the monsoon period was cost-effective.
    • However a lack of access to affordable credit was identified as a major constraint to adoption of the more expensive interventions (e.g. drying racks).

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Potential yield of South Asian small reservoir fisheries: ID 4474.
  • ParFish Toolkit: a participatory fisheries stock assessment approach: ID 4476.
  • Management guidelines for harvest reserves or sanctuaries for tropical river fisheries: ID 4478.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology prevents infestation, allowing for greater fishery yields, leading to an increase in sources of income and food.

entries.tittle: Conservation Tillage Management for Marginal Small Farm Systems, Zimbabwe
entries.summary: Moisture conserving tillage and weeding practices for a maize-based cropping system were tested in semi-arid Zimbabwe. This is an area characterised by shortage of labour and Draught Animal Power (DAP), frequent drought, and at times excessive weed growth. Using a ripper tine attached to the existing plough for planting, and weeding with the plough, the practices selected by farmers from on-farm trials benefited households who had access to DAP and labour. However, the 35 percent of households who had no DAP or implements experienced severe labour constraints, generally planted late, achieved low yields, rarely produced a saleable surplus and were cash constrained. Although these households may benefit from more timely availability of hired DAP for planting, when DAP owners complete their own planting more quickly by the minimum tillage/planting technique, they were unlikely to relieve their weeding constraint by using the labour-saving weeding technology, as this would incur further hire costs for DAP.
entries.description:
Description

Soil and water conservation are essential components of sustainable crop-production for the semi-arid lands of southern Africa. Research on these issues is a high priority in the region. Smallholder farmers in Zimbabwe rely largely on Draught Animal Power (DAP) for tillage and crop establishment. The conventional practice of planting seed into the furrow made by a plough ensures that the maize crop emerges into a relatively weed-free seed bed. Farmers, however, face the problem of a peak demand for DAP early in the wet season, when animals are often in short supply and are at their weakest following the long dry season. Weed competition is a further constraint to improved maize productivity in semi-arid Zimbabwe, where crop water stress associated with periods of drought, is a common feature of the growing season.

As weed management influences the availability of soil water to the crop, it needs to be incorporated as a key element of conservation tillage. Farmers recognise the need to weed their crops twice if possible, both to kill weeds and to maintain a rainwater retentive soil surface. Hence weeding can account for up to 60 percent of the pre-harvest labour input to maize production, putting considerable strain on households with limited labour resources.

Although labour and DAP are the key resources which determine the area planted, timeliness of operations and the resulting productivity of the cropping system are also important. The likely success of a new technology has often been judged by researchers on the basis of crop yield response or water and soil conserved. Following on-station investigations, no-till tied ridging was proposed as a sustainable conservation tillage system to reduce soil and water losses. Even by promoting of ridging from the late 1980s, considerable farmers' indifference was found due to high-labour requirements, as well as the practical difficulties of planting, ridge maintenance and weeding. Therefore few farmers have adopted the system. For the past decade researchers in Zimbabwe have therefore emphasised the participation of farmers in research in order to develop tillage and weed control practices. This can reduce DAP and labour inputs while allowing timely crop establishment and weed control.

1. A practical system for crop-establishment

  • Under farmer conditions, tine tillage provides a practical, low-draught system of crop establishment.
    • Tine tillage is planting along the rip line made with a tine bolted onto the farmer's existing plough.
  • The problem of early season weed growth in the untilled inter-rows can be overcome by weeding with a mouldboard plough.
  • These are owned by 76 percent of households in southern Zimbabwe.
  • Mid-season ridging with the plough while weeding results in efficient weed control, increased rainwater retention and higher labour productivity.
    • This is compared to the conventional system of hand weeding and without the additional investment associated with a DAP cultivator.
  • Highest returns to labour in researcher-managed trials have been associated with planting on the flat, compared to pre-plant ridging.
  • Post-planting ridging at weeding reduces and spreads the labour demand, providing a system which in combination with planting along the rip line is more likely to be adopted.

1.1 The trial area

  • The three main soil catena types were topland, true dryland sites of the upland ridges and valley slopes, and the vlei-margins and vlei-valley bottom sites on hydromorphic soils adjacent to water courses, which are subject to seasonal flooding.
  • Three broad farmer categories were identified during a PRA wealth ranking exercise and subsequent discussions provided details of participation in crop production on the three soil types and of the practices used by each category.
  • The proportions of households in each category were estimated during farmer group meetings and in discussion with extension staff.
  • Farmer category characteristics
    • Categonry one - well-resourced farmers
      • Households with large arable area, no DAP limitations, a full range of implements (including a plough and inter-row cultivator used for weeding) and who regularly sold agricultural produce comprised some 5 percent of the community.
    • Category two - average resourced farmers
      • Households with adequate land, owning livestock but with inadequate draught power, owning only a plough, making irregular sales of agricultural produce supplemented by remittances from family members in non-farm employment were in the majority, comprising an estimated 60 percent of the community.
    • Category three- poorly resourced farmers
      • Farmers with poorly developed arable lands, no DAP, inadequate implements (a hoe only), who were dependant on subsistence production in good seasons supplemented by hand-outs from drought relief and recovery programmes and limited off-farm income, comprised the poorest group of some 35 percent of households in the community.

1.2 Choice and timing of operation

  • Three primary tillage options were available to farmers using draught animals.
    • Winter ploughing (following the maize harvest during the dry season).
    • Spring ploughing (prior to planting at the onset of the rains).
    • Winter plough only or spring plough only.
  • Choice and timing of operation depended upon DAP availability and soil moisture.
    • Category one farmers tended to winter and spring plough all land types, perceiving that this was advantageous for moisture conservation and weed control.
    • Vlei fields may be too wet to plough following seasons of above average rainfall, but in general these were ploughed as early as possible so that a maize/rice mixed crop could be planted onto residual moisture from August.
    • This also had the advantage of allowing the crop to become well established ahead of weed emergence, particularly of various species of Cyperaceae which became dominant in the vlei and vlei-margin during the rains.
    • Planting of all sites was largely by "third furrow planting".
      • In this way tillage and crop establishment were combined, reducing labour requirements and ensuring the crop emerged in a weed free seed bed.
  • The alternative "open plough furrow planting" method was used occasionally for rapid planting of previously planted land.
    • With no DAP constraint, and cash available to hire labour if necessary, category one farmers were in a position to make maximum use of soil moisture and began planting the vlei in August to September and topland with the onset of rain in November/December.
    • Category two farmers tended to winter plough the vlei and spring plough topland, relied on third furrow planting and could usually assemble a full DAP team to begin planting early.
    • Category three farmers, however, who were dependant on sharing, borrowing or hiring DAP, tended to plant the vlei late and were rarely able to winter plough toplands.
      • They established maize on the topland after DAP owners had finished planting, six weeks or more after the onset of rain and immediately prior to the period of likely mid-season drought.
      • These farmers often provided labour for other members of the extended family or neighbours in return for DAP and as a priority attempted to plant some vlei before the onset of rain.

2. Outcomes

  • Under the variable environmental conditions of Zimuto, the management options providing the best returns varied from season to season.
    • Gross margins, averaged for each soil type, were positive except on the topland in 1995/96.
    • However, considerable variation between treatments was evident.
    • On topland sites productivity was highly variable depending on both total and distribution of rainfall in the season.
    • In prolonged wet conditions, leaching of nutrients from these low organic matter soils was a major problem.
    • With good rainfall distribution (as occurred in 1996/97), conditions of soil moisture and nutrient status were more favourable for maize growth.
    • The rip/hand hoe combination in 1995/96 and third furrow planting/hand hoe in 1996/97 gave the higher returns on the topland.
    • Vleis could produce poor yields, especially when planted late or in wet years, when they became flooded early.
    • Tillage and weeding techniques needed to ensure moisture capture during dry periods and drainage during wet periods.
    • Third furrow planting provided the optimum crop establishment method in both seasons with high returns following weeding with a cultivator in 1995/96 and the plough in 1996/97, when the increased drainage which resulted was an advantage.
  • Vlei-margins were likely to give the highest productivity, combining the advantages of both vlei and topland.
    • Planting in the rip line and weeding with the cultivator in 1995/96 and third furrow planting and plough weeding in 1996/97 were the best options in this ecology.
    • The success with which a number of trade-offs in the cropping system could be managed depended on a household's access to resources.
    • Many farmers were prepared to accept that earlier weeding, with greater draught and labour inputs, would be needed following planting into rip lines if this consistently allowed timely planting and resulted in a good crop stand.
    • Timely establishment in relation to periods of good seed-bed moisture was the key farmer criterion for selection of a planting method.
    • Although farmers were looking for technologies which eased labour and draught constraints, they were prepared to accept certain trade-offs to achieve the all important crop stand with the minimum of risk.
    • A greater weed burden after emergence was therefore a secondary consideration.
    • Provided farmers can find the cash to purchase a ripper tine assembly for the plough, rip planting has a role to play in improving timeliness for DAP owners, who also own a cultivator (category one farmers) or would be able to use their plough for weeding (category two farmers).
  • It is less clear that this labour saving, low draught technology can improve the productivity for resource poor category three households.
    • These farmers had little cash income, so many worked for neighbours early in the season to gain access to a DAP team.
    • For many category three farmers there was an unavoidable delay in planting beyond the most favourable period of November/mid-December, to just before the time when mid-season drought is common.
    • It was only after the adoption of ripping by DAP owners that it became apparent that the resulting savings in DAP increased its timely availability for households who depended on borrowing or hiring.
    • However, the problem of being unable to winter plough topland or vlei-margin sites due to a lack of DAP meant that they would experience severe weed problems soon after planting.
    • Reduced or no tillage techniques without increasing weed burdens thus remains a priority for category three farmers.
  • The results of this trial, even being variable depending on farmers category, are in line with the expected when adopting conservation agriculture and they benefit the resilience of the agry system against drought.
    • A farmer´s livelihood benefits when the CA principles are implemented properly (category two farmers), category three farmers could not use equipment timely.
    • Therefore, their productivity was not benefited and could not experience any improvement.
    • However, if that had been corrected, there would had experienced improvements and consequently, their livelihood resilience would had been increased.
  • Farmers will continue to need a choice of crop establishment and weeding options for different positions on the soil catena and need flexibility to respond to the moisture situation as the season develops.
    • Resource poor households were unlikely to have the access to DAP, implements or labour that such flexibility in decision making demands.
    • In particular, category three farmers were unlikely to gain access to the labour saving technology of plough weeding as this would require them to hire or borrow DAP for a second time each season, resulting in higher input costs for households who always experienced a severe liquidity problem.
    • Participatory methods were extremely helpful for characterisation of existing systems and prioritising farmer problems.
    • Working with the community led to selection of technologies which had the potential to improve farm productivity of the majority who own DAP.
      • However this has also brought into focus the limitations of trying to assist the sizeable minority of resource constrained households by introducing innovative production methods alone.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: conservation agriculture: ID 7294.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: Draught Animal Power (DAP) planters and weeders: ID 7305.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: draught animal power and implements: ID 7306.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: draught animal powered groundnut lifter: ID 7309.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The technology is labour saving in that it requires less physical effort and quicker in covering more land area.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

Through quicker ploughing and effective weeding, the technology allows for increases in yield, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Development of tools for draught animals, Bolivia
entries.summary: Participatory rural appraisals identified a number of major limiting factors in farming systems in Bolivia. These included the husbandry of draught animals, their health, nutrition, feeding, and housing, as well as the improved use of draught animals. The project developed, tested and disseminated a range of appropriate tillage and transport equipment and harnesses to enable diversification of the use of equines and bovines. Many of these tillage and rural transport tools and harnesses are now being manufactured and sold commercially.
entries.description:
Description

1. Background

  • Current estimates suggest that up to two billion people depend on work animals as the main source of power for farm operations.
    • Work animals continue to make a significant contribution to the livelihoods of the poor in many rural and urban economies.
      • For example, tillage and transport, improved productivity, as well as additional income.
    • However, population changes, environmental changes, and associated changes in demands from agriculture have resulted in increased problems for smallholder farmers.
    • In particular, the need to meet the demands for increased productivity from declining land holdings has led to the need for changes to the traditional management of working animals.
  • This study focussed on working animals in a range of different areas in Bolivia.
    • Animal traction is widely used for land preparation and local agricultural transport.
    • However, most other field operations (especially seeding and weeding) are carried out by hand, causing significant drudgery for women and children.
    • Farmers perceive that the main problems associated with the use of work animals include poor animal husbandry techniques and the absence of appropriate implements.
    • For further details of these constraints see 'Availability and use of work animals in the middle Andean hill-farming systems of Bolivia' by Dijkman, Sims, and Zambrana 1999.
  • In addition, land degradation is being caused by poor tillage and cultivation techniques on sloping land.
  • In many countries there is a shortage of traditional draught animals for small-scale farming activities and equines, especially donkeys, are increasingly recognised as an underutilised resource.

2. Development of tools for working animals

  • In all six communities, the major demand was for the development of tillage implements and harnesses, that would allow equines to be used for a much wider range of farm tasks.
    • The main problem is that they are lighter than oxen and lack the pulling force necessary for many standard tillage implements.
    • However, by applying basic mechanical principles, they can be used to pull these implements by means of simple and comfortable systems such as the high-lift harness.
  • An important characteristic of equines is their relative speed.
    • As a result they have significant advantages for carting and carrying loads, as well as for seeding and other tillage operations that do not require high power.
    • This low power combined with speed is an important characteristic of their working capacity for designing implements.
  • Participatory development and evaluation studies carried out under this project included the development and evaluation of the following categories of implements or tools for working animals.

2.1 High lift harness and light implements for equines

  • High-lift harness
  • Mouldboard ploughs for donkeys and horses
  • Ridgers for donkeys and horses
  • Inter-row weeders for donkeys and horses
  • Reversible ploughs for donkeys and horses
  • Carts for equids.

2.2 Equipment for cattle

  • Single yokes
  • Tined rake and scraper
  • Reversible plough
  • Seeders for the "arado de palo"
  • Carts for cattle

3. Advantages of development of tools for working animals

  • Many of these tillage and rural transport tools and harnesses are now being manufactured and sold commercially.
  • Close collaboration with the CIFEMA implement factory in Cochabamba, has meant that farmer-proven prototypes have quickly reached batch production and the designs are now out in the market place.
  • Adoption is relatively assured as the engineering and manufacturing response has been to a farmer stated need.
  • Examples of implements for equines are given below.

3.1 High-lift harness

  • The high-lift harness is a development that has enabled the use of equines for a much wider range of farm tasks.
    • The combination of an increased angle of pull and light implements which require a draught force related to the live weight of the animal is a new concept in Latin America.
    • The draught of a cultivation implement varies directly with the effective vertical force acting on it and inversely with the tangent of the angle at which it is being pulled.
    • The principle was tested and verified, and a high-lift harness and lightweight plough developed.
    • This is now manufactured locally in Bolivia. See the diagram, and the report 'High-lift harness and light-weight plough: an efficient low-draught ploughing system'.

3.1.1 Advantages of the high lift system

  • Advantages of the high lift system, lead to a greater degree of user-friendliness.
    • Improved plough efficiency, and a greater proportion of useful work in relation to the effort exerted.
    • Reduced draught load on animals.
    • Easier adjustment.
    • Simple harness, cheap and easily made locally.
    • Lighter plough, cheaper and more easily transported and handled.
  • Based on this principle, the project has produced a line of lightweight implements, which can all be mounted on the same lightweight metal frame, and which are attached to the harness either through reins or wooden poles.
  • INNS 1998 further discusses a number of topics.
    • The influence of plough weight on plough draught.
    • Plough weight and penetration.
    • The influence of angle of pull on plough draught.
    • Harness design.
    • Working adjustments to the plough.
Figure 1. High-lift harness

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Mouldboard ploughs for donkeys and horses

  • The designs of these two ploughs are similar.
    • The most important difference being the width of cut, 115 mm and 150 mm for donkey and horse, respectively, and the weight of the implements, 8 and 11.8 kg, respectively.
  • See (Sims 2001) for photographs and additional information.
Figure 2. The donkey and horse mouldboard ploughs developed by the project

©FAO/TECA

3.3 Ridgers for donkeys and horses

  • The development of these implements has been a great success.
  • They are now widely used for inter-row weeding and furrowing/earthing-up of crops such as potatoes, maize and broad beans.
  • See (Sims 2001) for photographs and additional information.
Figure 3. The ridger for donkeys and horses

©FAO/TECA

3.4 Harrow for equines

  • A light-weight version of the harrow manufactured by CIFEMA for oxen has been designed, evaluated and commercialized by the project following strong demand from farming communities.
  • See (Sims 2001) for photographs and additional information.
Figure 4. Light-weight harrow for equines

©FAO/TECA

3.5 Inter-row weeders for donkeys and horses

  • The latest implement developed by the Project for the lightweight metal frame used for the mouldboard plough and ridger, were a number of inter-row weeders.
  • The final version of this implement, following the participatory development and evaluation, has proved to be effective and efficient in reducing weed infestation in a wide range of crops on a number of different soil types.
Figure 5. Inter-row weeder for donkeys and horses

©FAO/TECA

3.6 Reversible ploughs for donkeys and horses

  • Two designs of reversible plough have been developed for use with equines.
  • Although they have not reached commercial production for this power source, a larger version has become a successful commercial product for use with oxen.
  • See (SIMS 2001) for photographs and additional information.
Figure 6. Two designs of the reversible plough for equines

©FAO/TECA

3.7 Carts for equids

  • The project developed a range of carts for donkeys and horses.
  • This newly introduced form of animal-powered transport has proved to be both appropriate and affordable for use in rural transport.
  • See (SIMS 2001) for photographs and additional information.
Figure 7. Cart for enquines

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • subtropics, warm/ mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Draught animal power technologies in East Africa: ID 4535.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: draught animal power and implements: ID 7306.
  • Improving the productivity of draught animal power in sub-Saharan Africa: ID 4467.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: draught animal powered and motorised crop processing: ID 7307.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

6.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The technology facilitates the use of different tillage and transport equipment and harnesses to enable diversification of the use of equines and bovines. This alleviates the use of hand labour and time.

entries.tittle: Improvement of Livestock Production: Community Based Goat Production in Kenya
entries.summary: Crossbred milking goats have proved to be a popular source of cash income, household daily milk requirements, and manure for smallholder farmers in medium to high potential zones of Kenya. The three-quarter Toggenburg crossbred appears to be the most suitable in terms of both milk production and growth rates. This DFID project improved management techniques and assessed different East African and Toggenburg crossbreds. The following is a description of the applied technology.
entries.description:
Description

Goats form an integral component of the livestock sector in Kenya, its population is estimated at 10.9 million, spread throughout all the agro-ecological zones. In particular, goats are suitable for small scale resource poor farmers. They are cheap to acquire compared to cattle. They require little land, they reproduce quickly, and they are able to feed on a wide range of forages. As a result, goat rearing is an important activity for resource, especially for poor farmers under the mixed crop-livestock production systems that are commonly practiced in Kenya.

Dairy goats have considerable potential in the highlands of Kenya, where a majority of the population live. There has been significant interest in the use of crossbred goats. Although dairy goats have been introduced in various parts of the country, most projects have not taken sustainability into account. The benefits ended soon after the funding ceases. In previous attempts to genetically improve the local goat populations, breeding programmes have generally been centralised and research-centred, with minimal farmer participation. In addition, the contributions and/or preferences of the farmers intended to benefit from such efforts are usually ignored, leading to delays in the adoption of the technologies, low adoption rates, or total failures.

From the surveys conducted during the study, the farmers reported a range of different reasons for keeping dairy goats.

  • Enough milk for the family
  • Very good and high quality milk
  • Goats to sell in emergencies
  • Easy to manage
  • Feeding goats is easier than feeding cattle
  • Many good benefits milk, meat, manure
  • Poverty reduction.

1. Limitation factors

  • There are many factors that limit livestock keeping by small-scale and poor farmers.
    • Lack of grazing and feed resources due to limited land.
    • Lack of water and inappropriate land tenure systems (subdivision of land owned by most resource poor farmers).
    • Poor management systems and practices.
    • High prevalence of animal diseases.
    • Low animal genetic potential.
    • Inaccessibility or costs of farm inputs.
    • Lack of access to technical information (extension services).
    • Lack of market information; and poor infrastructure.

2. Purpose of the project

  • This project was a community-based project set up in collaboration with FARM-Africa (see Technical Report, FARM AFRICA 2005).
    • The project introduced the Toggenburg dairy goat for cross-breeding, and set-up a sustainable community-based animal health delivery system and an improved feed resource base.
    • The project also established farmer-to-farmer and extension-to-farmer training programmes.
      • It aimed at creating a favourable environment to enable the improved goats to realize their full potential for milk and meat production.
  • An important outcome of the project was a clear demonstration that the productive capacity and success of any livestock population, whether local, introduced or cross-bred, can only be obtained if the assessment is carried out under their normal or intended conditions.
    • In the farmers’ fields working with the farmers rather than under the more artificial, unrealistic or perhaps optimum conditions of a research station.
  • There were a series of research activities.
    • Recording the productive capacity of local and crossbred goats in farmer’s flocks, and, based on this, making recommendations as to the best choices for meeting requirements for milk and meat production under local conditions.
    • Characterization of farm resources and the capacities for keeping and maintaining local or different grades of crossbred goats.
    • Recording physical and economic inputs.

3. Improved goat breeds

  • There are two indigenous goat breeds in Kenya, the Galla and the East African.
  • These are less productive and therefore the project introduced the Toggenburg dairy goat from stocks in the UK to upgrade the genetic potential of the indigenous goat breeds.
  • According to the farmers interviewed, the characteristics of a good goat should include:
    • high fertility;
    • produce enough milk;
    • grow fast reaching maturity early;
    • good body structure;
    • big udder and a long neck;
    • straight back line and a soft udder; and
    • well attached udder with two equal teats facing forward.
  • From the farmers interviewed, three traits were considered to be the main breeding objectives for the goat development in Meru Central and South districts of Kenya.
  • Farmers considered the most important traits to be:
    • milk production,
    • growth rate, and
    • manure for crop production.
  • These formed the basis of the breeding and management objectives in this project.
    • The results of this study demonstrate that crossing of the Toggenburg dairy goat breed with the indigenous Kenyan meat goat breed (East African) is economically beneficial, as it results in significant improvements in growth rate and meat production potential.
    • Reasonably high growth rates are achieved at farm level and are better than those achieved at experimental stations.
    • The results indicated that a three-quarter Toggenburg, one-quarter indigenous goat appear to be the most appropriate upgrade level in terms of survival, growth rate and milk production.
    • The latter two traits were considered the most important by the farmers.
    • The three quarter genotypes performed very well compared to local goats, pure Toggenburgs, and the F1s.
    • For additional information on farmer/community preferences and how these guided the initial breeding programme, see the technical report by FARM AFRICA 2005.
  • For more information on the organization of the community based breeding programme and its management, see:
    • 'Sustainable genetic improvement of goat meat and milk production in Kenya: a case of the Meru and Tharaka-Nithi dairy and animal healthcare community-based breeding programme', by Ahuya and Okeyo 2001, especially Figures 1 and 2 in that publication.

4. The breeding strategy

  • The establishment of a breeding unit for pure Toggenburgs, with the main objective to produce pure Toggenburg for expansion into new groups and also replace old bucks at the buck station.
    • This is done by the community and is important since one of the constraints was a source of breeding stock.
    • Community-run breeding units overcome the problems inherent in other management models which generally fail after project funding ceases.
  • The establishment of buck stations for crossbreeding Toggenburgs with local goats, to produce the three-quarter genotypes.
    • These stations are again run and maintained by the community.

4.1 Dairy Goat Production Handbook

  • The project also produced an illustrated Dairy Goat Production Handbook (Kaberia, Mutia, and Ahuya 2003). 
  • Handbook main sections.
    • Introduction to goats.
    • Why keep dairy goats?
    • Housing the goat, including plans for a goat house.
    • Feeding the dairy goat, including the advantages of stall-feeding, and the types of feed that should be supplied.
    • Kidding, or what to do before, during and after the does give birth.
    • Husbandry techniques.
    • Milking.
    • Breeding, including what can be done to improve the productivity of local goats.
    • Keeping records.
    • Goat health.

4.2 Animal Health Services

  • The project's capacity building and enhancement activities involved the development of practical management and operational procedures;
    • These were to compliment and enable the most favourable breed improvement option to succeed.
    • There was also the development of an appropriate organizational structure to involve farmers and provide cost effective services.
  • Part of this experience is encapsulated in a publication: 'Delivering affordable and quality animal health services to Kenya's rural poor', FARM-AFRICA, 2003.
    • This publication presents community based solutions to animal health care service delivery in order to improve the livelihoods of both pastoralists and settled communities.
    • It documents the experiences of community based animal health work in Kenya and illustrates a decentralised system of community controlled service delivery.
    • It provides analytical account of the social and economic benefits; the effectiveness; and economic viability of such community based service delivery.
    • It also outlines lessons learned during the process to influence the practice of others interested in decentralised animal health systems.
  • A veterinarian-supervised animal health system, tested by FARM-Africa and the Department of Veterinary Services during 1996 to 2003, proved to be effective in delivering high quality, affordable animal health care to livestock keepers in the marginal farming areas of Meru South and Meru Central districts of Kenya.
    • The three levels of service providers were vets, Animal Health Assistants (AHAs), and Community-Based Animal Health Workers (CAHWs).
      • These have established viable enterprises providing their owners with a long-term livelihood as well as creating much needed employment in rural areas.
    • As an indicator of the success of the system, the services provided were used by over 80 percent of users who were not part of the FARM-Africa Dairy Goat Project, indicating a real demand for such a decentralised animal healthcare system.
  • Underpinning the entire system was that each service provider approached their role as a business.
    • They took out loans and received training in business management skills.
  • The strong links between vets, AHAs and CAHWs also led to the establishment of additional fora, such as the Meru Animal Health Workers Group, which will not only provide vital support to its members but will also represent their interests to the government.
  • The major impacts of the system are:
    • an increased access to veterinary services and drugs from rural areas at vastly reduced costs;
    • improvements in disease surveillance;
    • increased community awareness of animal disease;
    • successful intensification of dairy goat production; and 
    • improved range and supply of livestock and agricultural services.

5. Extension messages

  • Upgrading locally adapted, but 'less' productive local goat breeds with exotic dairy breeds such as the Toggenburg, can enable farmers to quickly and flexibly match the available genetic resources to the existing production environment in a social and economically beneficial way (providing both milk and meat).
  • Participatory farmer-group approaches can help resource poor farmers to mobilize resources and inputs from among themselves and various service providers for sustainable breed improvement and development.
    • Farmer group approaches provide relatively easy access to otherwise expensive but high quality genetic material and affordable animal health delivery system.
  • Farmers should keep simple livestock records to help them in making management decisions.
    • Demand driven and farmer adapted farm records provides an effective means of realizing or facilitating effective genetic evaluation and improvement.
  • The establishment of a breeder’s association, in this case the Meru Goat Breeders Association (MGBA), represents a critically important component within the 'extension' system.
    • In this case MGBA was important for:
      • overseeing goat improvement activities;
      • setting standards for the Meru Goat breed that is under development;
      • overseeing and ensuring that all goats owned by MGBA members are registered; and
      • organising for goat inspection, training and village shows to promote goat recording, and improvement and aid in the dissemination of information.
  • The processes involved in community-based goat improvement require close, genuine and highly interactive linkages between various players, where farmers, policy makers and other service providers are important.
    • This will result in a partnership that is likely to enhance the sustainability of a farmer-led goat improvement programme.
  • A crossbred animal, three-quarter Toggenburg (exotic) and one-quarter local goat, proved to be the most promising genetic composition of dairy goats that could be recommended for the resource poor smallholder farmers in Eastern slopes of Mount Kenya.
  • Feeding Dairy Goats http://www.accessagriculture.org/dairy-goat-feeding

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Rearing dairy goats: ID 6925.
  • Farmers dairy goat production handbook: ID 6939.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Women-friendly

The practice does not entail heavy drudgery and can be practiced by all hand labour.

8.2 Pro-poor technology

The practice allowed for the improved use of cross-bred goats, improving cash income, household daily milk requirements, and manure quantity for smallholder farmers.
