entries.tittle: Diatomaceous earth to protect farm-stored grain: Sorghum, Maize and Cow-peas in Zimbabwe and Tanzania.
entries.summary: Farmers all over the world incur serious losses to stored produce because of insect damage and are frequently forced to sell prematurely. Many use traditional storage protectant practices or, when they can afford it, purchase synthetic chemical pesticides. The effectiveness of traditional practices is variable. Using synthetic pesticides also has problems. Farmers need and demand better options for protecting their grain. Diatomaceous earth (DE) is a viable alternative means of protecting stored grain.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Diatomaceous earths (DEs) are a naturally occurring siliceous sedimentary mineral compound formed from the fossils of tiny phytoplankton (diatoms) which lived in oceans, rivers and lakes, millions of years ago.
  • Diatoms which live in the surface layers of the ocean and freshwater lakes, remove silica from the water to make their exoskeletons, which is an amorphous form of silica.
  • When diatoms die, they sink to the bottom and accumulate in a sedimentary layer, which over the centuries builds up, becomes compressed and fossilized into a soft chalky rock called diatomaceous earth.
    • This can then be mined and dried and ground (reducing particle size and moisture content) to render a soft whitish powder, which looks and feels like talcum powder.
    • Much of the diatomaceous earth being used today originated more than 20 million years ago in the lakes and seas of the Miocene period.

2. Diatomaceous earth to protect stored grain

  • DE is a porous material and is used in filters to help clarify fruit juices, beers, wine, pharmaceuticals, swimming pool waste, dry cleaning solvents and food additives.
    • It can also be used as an insecticide.
  • DE was used by the Chinese more than 4000 years ago and by the Aztecs of ancient Mexico, to protect grain. 
  • When diatomaceous earth comes into contact with insects they absorb the wax from the cuticle, which results in dehydration and death of the insect.
  • DE has extremely low toxicity to mammals and is therefore safe to mix with food.
  • A lot of DE dust is commercially available and registered for use as grain protectants in Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, Germany, Indonesia, Japan, Philippines, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates and the United States.
  • Insect species differ in their sensitivity to diatomaceous earth.
    • The most susceptible tend to be insects with large surface to volume ratios, body hair, thin cuticles, protected by low-melting point grease as opposed to a hardened waxy cuticle, and those that feed on dry grain.
    • Generally the most sensitive stored product species is considered to be those in the genus Cryptolestes (Flat grain beetles) Sitophilus spp. (e.g. Rice Weevil, S. oryzae) are less susceptible, followed by Oryzaephilus (e.g. Sawtoothed grain beetle, O. surinamensis), Rhyzopertha (e.g. Lesser Grain Borer, R. dominica) and Tribolium spp. (T. confusum, the confused flour beetle), which appear most resistant.
  • Factors such as climatic conditions and adherence of the DE to the commodity also affect efficacy.
  • It has been reported that DEs did not adhere as well to maize as to wheat or sorghum.
  • Insect control methods using diatomaceous earth are similar to traditional methods used in parts of Africa where sand or ash is used to limit insect development in stored grains.
    • The principle consists in filling the interstices between the grains by an inert material that plays an abrasive role on the insects cuticle.
  • In Tanzania, the larger grain borer (Prostephanus truncates) is the most destructive of the storage insect pests, causing storage losses of up to 40 percent.
    • P. truncates is believed to have arrived in Africa from Central America in a food aid shipment in the 1980s.
    • P. truncates has now spread throughout many countries in East, West, and Southern Africa.

3. Application of diatomaceous earths to protect grain

  • Protect-it and Dryacide ® are two commercially available diatomaceous earths found to be effective grain protectants against insect damage for smallscale on-farm storage systems.
    • Research results demonstrated that Protect-it – and Dryacide ® can be extremely effective and persistent grain protectants, against the major insect storage pests attacking sorghum, maize and cowpeas, for storage periods of 40 weeks in the climatic conditions found in Zimbabwe.
    • The pest species considered were Sitophilus zeamais, Prostephanus truncatus, Callosobruchus maculatus, Acanthoscelides obtectus, and Rhyzopertha dominica.
    • The efficacy of these diatomaceous earths is closely linked to the dosage rates, and can be seen to differ between different stored grains.
    • The application rates for effective control is given below: Dryacide ® – Maize: 0.1 percent w/w – Cowpea: 0.1 percent w/w – Sorgum: 0.2 percent w/w # Protect-it – Maize: 0.1 percent w/w – Cowpea: 0.1 percent w/w – Sorgum: 0.1 percent w/w.
  • It is recommended that DEs should be used on freshly harvested, dry, non-infested grain only.
    • The grain should be winnowed prior to mixing with the DE. DE grain protection is more effective at lower relative humidity level of 50 percent rh than 60 percent rh.
    • Relative humidity affects the rate of water loss by the insects and therefore determines the effectiveness of inert dusts.
  • Select a sheltered place away from the wind and if possible a smooth, even floor.
  • Clean the floor and surrounding area to remove dust and debris.
  • A clean plastic sheet can be used if available or, in the absence of plastic sheet.
  • The mixing can be done directly on the cleaned floor.
  • Wear a dust mask. Safety procedures (suitable dust masks) need to be adhered to by those engaged in applying the DE to the grain.
    • This is to protect against a potential health problem from long-term chronic exposure to quantities of inhaled dust during application. See Figure 1.
  • Place up to 50 kg of grain on the cleaned floor (or plastic sheet) – See Figure 2.
Figure 1. Suitable dust masks

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Grain on cleaned floor

©FAO/TECA

Table 1. Different application rates trials a, b, and c

Source: FAO 2006

  • Sprinkle the correctly weighed quantity of treatment (refer to Table 1) in a circle on the surface of the mound of grain – See Figure 3.
  • Gently using a clean shovel first move the grain up so that the protectant is covered by the grain – See Figure 4.
Figure 3. Sprinkle the correctly weighed quantity of treatment

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Gently use a clean shovel to move the grain up

©FAO/TECA

  • Mix the grain and protectant by gently shovelling the grain to one side to form a new pile of grain – first mixing.
  • The new pile of grain is then shovelled back again – second mixing, see Figure 5.
  • The pile is shovelled to one side again – third mixing, see Figure 6.
Figure 5. Shovelling back

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Shovelling to one side

©FAO/TECA

  • Put the treated grain in a bag for storage (Figure 7) and sew up (Figure 8).
  • The treated grain can then be placed in the grain store.
    • Traditional grain store (Figure 9) and improved traditional grain store (Figure 10).
Figure 7. Bag for storage

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Bag for storage

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Grain store

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10. Improved traditional store

©FAO/TECA

4. Advantages of using diatomaceous earths

  • The main advantage of this storage protection technology is that it is non-aggressive regarding health and environment.
  • DEs have extremely low toxicity to mammals and fall under the “Generally Regarded as Safe” category by the US Environmental Protection Authority (rat oral LC50 > 3 000 mg per kg).
  • When mixed with grain at around 0.1 percent w/w, DE is effective as a control method against most stored product insect pests, and 98 percent of DE is removed during the processing.
  • DE can be used to control storage insect pests in organic products.

In some areas, the adulteration of conventional insecticides used for protection of stored grain has reached a stage that they no longer work. One farmer in Shinyanga region, Tanzania, actually managed to breed storage insects in what had been sold to him as pesticide. The use of diatomaceous earth is therefore an alternative means of protecting stored grain. Applications can reduce the flowability of grain if applied to entire grain mass, so diatomaceous earths are often applied to just the bottom and top layers of the grain.

5. Disadvantages

  • This method is not very effective on grains already infested by insects before storage and whose larva develops inside the grain itself.

6. Economic assessment

Economic assessment of this technology is not presented. However, farmer participatory trials in both Zimbabwe and Tanzania indicate a high level of acceptance of the technology by farmers under field conditions.

7. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Grain stores construction: ID 4499.

This technology is available in Portuguese: ID 2498.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

9.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology is not harmful towards the environment, is safe for animals, and is a control method against pests 

9.2 Pro-poor technology

Using this technology leads to improved and higher yields, allowing for additional sources of income and food.

entries.tittle: Dryer construction for solar-dried fruit and vegetables production
entries.summary: The preservation of fruit and vegetables by simple sun drying is practiced widely throughout arid and semi-arid areas, for example in Uganda. The use of low cost, solar-drying technologies can significantly improve product quality. This provides practical opportunities for developing small-scale enterprises, particularly in rural areas, and creating employment for women's groups. The specifications and prices detailed below are for the Ugandan context in 1996. Users need to adapt their designs to local situations.
entries.description:
Description

Experiences in Uganda have shown that there are circumstances where it is feasible to establish solar-drying operations as viable micro-enterprises in rural areas. Such operations require the dedication, patience and basic skills of all those involved. Market channels also need to be developed, product quality controlled and technical assistance provided. An overall and integrated approach is essential if solar-drying activities are to be successful in rural development programmes.

This is part of a series of four related technology records dealing with solar drying, and needs to be considered in conjunction with these other records.

  • Assessing opportunities
  • Dryer construction (this record)
  • Practical aspects of the processing
  • Business profitability.

1. Dryer design

  • The dryer consists of a main frame, with eight supporting legs, incorporating the drying chamber.
    • The drying chamber measures 176 in (4.4 m) length and 60 in (1.5 m) deep x 30 in (0.8 m) height overall.
    • It contains 12 trays to provide a total drying area of 100 ft² (10 m²).
    • Depending upon the fruit or vegetable to be dried and upon the loading density used, it can dry between 20 kg and 35 kg of freshly cut produce over a period of two to four days.
  • The dryer is constructed from 2 in (5.08 cm) x 2 in (5.08 cm) softwood.
    • However, the drying trays, rails and support bars should be made from 2 in (5.08 cm) x 1 in (2.54 cm) hardwood to provide the strength and long-term durability needed.
    • The timber used should be well seasoned, of uniform thickness and straight.
  • There are three hinged doors at the front of the chamber to provide access for loading and unloading of the drying trays.
  • There are two tiers of trays.
    • Each tier can accommodate six trays and these are supported on wooden rails.
  • The trays consist of a hardwood frame across which is stapled plastic mosquito mesh onto which are placed the slices of fruit for drying.
  • The base of the drying chamber is a mat made from papyrus, which is then covered over with mosquito mesh.
    • This arrangement allows air to filter through and enter the chamber from underneath and through the trays of sliced fruit.
    • It also provides a barrier against insects and allows rainwater to easily drain away, which can otherwise collect inside and thereby slow down the drying process.
    • Ventilation slots are built into the top of each of the loading doors and allow the warm moist air created to dissipate through natural convection.
    • These slots are similarly covered with mosquito mesh.
  • To operate effectively, airflow needs to be controlled and there should be no gaps, particularly around the doors, where insects may enter or air escape.
    • The doors should be close fitting and strips cut (using the same material as that used for the main cover) and stapled to the doors to provide seals.
  • To deter termite and insect attack, the legs can be placed inside old cans filled with mineral or vegetable oil.
    • Inverted cones nailed over the top of these will help prevent the cans from being filled with rainwater.
  • In operation, the dryer should be sited in a flat area, unobscured by trees or buildings so that it is fully exposed to the sun throughout the day.
    • If the wind blows predominantly from one direction, the dryer should be placed end-on to the wind.
    • This will reduce the cooling effect of the wind blowing directly into the drying chamber which would increase drying times.
    • It will also reduce the likelihood of dust entering the chamber and contaminating the products.
  • It is likely that as more dryers are built, variations to the design will emerge.
    • For instance, it may be that simpler ways can be found to construct joints, to fit the mosquito mesh or to improve cleaning.
    • Such changes are quite acceptable and should be encouraged if it improves the design, perhaps also by reducing the overall cost of the dryer or increasing its life.
    • However, it is advised not to change the basic design, e.g. the overall dimensions of the dryer; the number of trays used; or the sizes of the air inlet and outlet vents without careful consideration and experimentation.
    • Otherwise, dryer performance, and therefore profitability, could be reduced.
    • The dryer performance could also be affected if a different grade of clear plastic covering is used.
    • Any alterations of this nature require technical assessment.

2. Building the dryer

  • The dryer has four main parts.
    1. Main frame
    2. Drying chamber
    3. Loading doors
    4. Drying trays
  •  The dryer should be built in stages (Figures 1-15).
    • Stage one: Making the main frame structure (Figures 1-5)
    • Stage two: Making the drying chamber base (Figures 6-7)
    • Stage three: Making the rails for the drying trays (Figures 8-10)
    • Stage four: Making the loading doors
    • Stage five: Making the drying trays
    • Stage six: Fitting the plastic cover
    • Stage seven: Checking the completed dryer (Figures 11-15)
  • The timber lengths given are only a guide.
    • The dimensions of timber available are likely to vary and practical account needs to be taken of this when building the dryer.
    • This is why key dimensions only have been given.
    • Joints should be glued and screwed for maximum strength and durability.
    • Whilst steel screws will be cheaper and more available, brass screws would last longer and would not rust.
  • Except for the clear plastic sheet, materials should normally be available locally.
    • The clear sheet is a special heavy-duty plastic sheeting 'Visqueen', which remains reasonably durable under the harmful effects of the relatively high levels of ultraviolet light.
    • It is essential to use this, or other similar, horticultural grade plastic sheeting which does not readily degrade in the tropical sunlight.
    • It is considerably more expensive than the ordinary polythenes normally sold, and may need to be imported.
    • In Uganda, it can be obtained from Fruits of the Nile Ltd as can the mosquito mesh.
Figure 1. Main frame: lower corner joint (such as Figure 4)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Main frame: lower intermediate joint (such as Figure 4)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Main frame: legs and lower cross members

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Main frame: top intermediate joint 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Main frame: completed construction

©FAO/TECA

3. Drying chamber base

  • The base consists of a mat made from papyrus, which is firmly fitted across the width of the dryer and along its length.
  • It is supported by two support rails running along the length of the frame, front and back, which constitute part of the main structure.
  • Mosquito mesh is carefully fitted over the papyrus mat and attached with staples along all edges.
Figure 6. Drying chamber (base): papyrus mat base 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Drying chamber (base): papyrus mat fitted

©FAO/TECA

4. Drying chamber rails

  • The four longitudinal rails' support should be fitted to the main frame structure first.
  • The four sets of double rails and six centre rails next, making sure that they are all square with the frame.
  • The remaining four rails should now be fitted at the ends.
  • In all cases, the gap between each rail needs to be the same.
  • This is important as all 12 trays should be interchangeable and fit into any position.
Figure 8. Drying chamber (rails): tray support rails fitted

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Drying chamber (rails): intermediate cross rails

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10. Drying trays: corner joint

©FAO/TECA

5. Loading doors

  • No dimensions are given since it is important for doors to fit closely into the drying chamber frame as made.
  • The hinges should be fitted to the door only at this stage.
  • The air outlet ventilation gap is 4 in and should be covered with mosquito mesh on the inside.
  • The handle running the length of the door frame should be fitted about 8 in from the bottom.
  • The clear plastic should similarly be fitted to the inside with staples along all edges.

6. Drying trays

  • The trays should be fully interchangeable.
    • All 12 trays should be made exactly the same.
    • Anyone can then fit into any one of the 12 possible positions which will make loading much easier.
    • The trays are fitted with guide blocks which project 4 in (10.16 cm) below the frame.
    • This will make it easier to slide the trays in and out.
  • The length of each tray is intended to be 56 in (142.24 cm).
    • Whatever its length is in practice, it must be identical to the length of the rails inside the drying chamber.
    • This should be checked before any timber is cut to size.
    • Similarly, the width of each tray should be 27.5 in (698.5 cm) such that it will fit neatly on each pair of rails; this width should be 1.5 in (3.81 cm) greater than the distance between the rails and again checked before cutting timber.
  • The trays should be glued and screwed at joints.
    • Plastic mosquito mesh is cut to the size of the tray plus an allowance of 1 in (2.54 cm) overlap on all four sides.
    • It is then stapled in place onto the sides of the frame.
  • A current practice is to put a fabric that lets air pass through the trays.
    • This makes it possible to limit the downtime of the trays at the end of the drying for the collection of dried fruits and necessary washing of the trays.
    • Such fabrics are much easier to wash than the trays themselves.

7. Completing dryer construction

  • The dryer should now be moved to its final position with the traps fitted to the legs to deter termite and insect attack.
  • The clear plastic sheet covering should now be fitted over the drying chamber frame and stapled in position.
    • This should be carried out with care to avoid damaging the plastic.
    • It is better to double - over the edges which are to be stapled by two so as to provide extra strength for fixing.
    • The doors can now be fitted and the hinges screwed to the framework.
    • The top edges of the strips of plastic are stapled to the frame so as to cover over the hinges and provide a form of a seal.
  • The completed dryer should be checked for overall stability, ease of loading and unloading of the trays (which should fit in any position) and the opening and closing of the doors (which must operate freely).
    • The dryer should be fully insect proof before use and any gaps sealed.
Figure 11. Completing the dryer: fitting the plastic cover

©FAO/TECA

Figure 12. Completing the dryer: stapling the cover with the edge doubled-over

©FAO/TECA

Figure 13. Completing the dryer: fitting the loading doors

©FAO/TECA

Figure 14. Completed dryer: rear/side view

©FAO/TECA

Figure 15. Completing dryer: front/side view

©FAO/TECA

8. Using the dryer

  • If properly built, the dryer should last many years.
  • Routine maintenance should be carried out regularly and tears or rips in the plastic covering should be quickly repaired as they will affect performance.
  • The plastic sheeting will probably need to be completely replaced after two or three years.
  • If possible, the dryer should be protected in periods of bad weather or when not in use by using a locally-designed portable thatched cover, as this will help to prolong the dryer’s life.
  • Guidance on using the dryer and processing operations are given in the related technology record:
    • Producing solar dried fruit and vegetables for micro- and small-scale rural enterprise development: assessing opportunities for a fruit drying business: ID 4501.
    • Producing solar-dried fruit and vegetables for micro- and small-scale rural enterprise development: business profitability: ID 4504.

9. Materials for construction

  • The lengths of timber required are listed below as a guide.
  • As timber dimensions will vary, consideration should be given to variations when building the dryer.
  • Also, when purchasing timber, allowance should be made for splits and faults in the timber so that additional amounts will be required as these will need to be cut out.
  • See also a set of illustrations showing construction, and diagrams of the modified Kawanda solar cabinet dryer, and a pdf file with materials for construction.
    • Main frame (timber; lengths of 2 in (5.08 cm) x 2 in (5.08 cm) softwood)

    • Cross members (lower) 4 in (10.16 cm) x 60 in (152.4 cm)

  • Fittings and other materials (a)

Figure 16. Diagrams of modified Kawanda solar cabinet

©FAO/TECA

10. Risks

  • The use of softwoods in tropical conditions gives limited durability of the drier.
  • The presence of two trays, one above the other, makes for slower drying on the lower tray because it does not receive the solar radiation.
  • The extraction of air from the drier is not controlled and depends on climatic conditions.
    • Adjustable opening sections would be useful.
  • The quality of the plastic film is not indicated, even if it is essential for durability and performance.
  • The assembling of the film has to be well described.

11. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

12. Related/associated technologies

  • Producing solar dried fruit and vegetables for micro- and small-scale rural enterprise development: assessing opportunities for a fruit drying business: ID 4501.
  • Producing solar-dried fruit and vegetables for micro- and small-scale rural enterprise development: business profitability: ID 4504.

13. Objectives fulfilled by the project

13.1 Women friendly

The technology generates employment for women's groups.

13.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently provides an improved dryer design with easily accessible materials and is beneficial for the environment. 

13. Pro-poor technology

The technology develops small-scale enterprises in rural areas.

entries.tittle: Introducing a mechanical press for making Shea butter in northern Ghana
entries.summary: In the northern Republic of Ghana, a manually operated press for shea butter extraction is successful and popular among rural women. Shea butter production is an important income earning activity for women in rural areas and for many, it is their only source of income. Shea butter is used for cooking and for cosmetic purposes and it is increasingly valuable as an export commodity. However, successful implementation of the technology is hinder by lack of business group and management skills, competition from large-scale enterprises, inflation and international commodity price fluctuations.
entries.description:
Description

Shea nuts (from the shea nut tree, Vitellaria paradoxa formerly Butyrospermum paradoxum) play an important part in income generation in Ghana’s semi-arid regions.

Traditional processing is carried out by women and children involving lengthy, arduous processes. Large quantities of fuelwood and water are required and often need to be carried long distances from source to village.

The improved processing method offers a time reduction from 9.5 to 3.25 hours for 25 kg shea kernels, whilst water requirements are reduced from 90 litres to 1.7 litres and the use of fuelwood is completely eliminated. These savings provide benefits to the villagers and preserve scarce resources.

1. Shea nuts

Shea trees grow wild in the central Africa equatorial belt, semi-arid regions stretching from the Republic of the Gambia in the west, to the Republic of the Sudan in the east.

Women and children collect the ripe fruits and carry them to villages for immediate processing.

Process consists of:

  • removing the green pulp to expose the nut;
  • parboiling and sun drying the nuts;
  • crushing the nuts lightly with a stone or wooden paddle to remove the outer shell and expose the oil-bearing kernel.

The separated kernels are then either sold immediately or stored for local traditional processing into shea butter which is used for cooking or cosmetic purposes.

In the shea processing traditional method, the residue is dispersed in the rinsing water and thrown to waste. The liquid may sometimes be used to paint house walls as it is believed to have insecticidal properties.

For many women in northern Ghana rural areas, shea butter production is an important income, often their only source of independent revenue. However, women complain that roasting the pounded kernels and boiling the extracted cream are a hot and arduous task and the kneading stage causes pain in the back and shoulders (Swetman and Hammond, 1997).

Agro-processing improvement is a key feature of the Republic of Ghana government’s national agricultural strategic plan. Shea nuts have been identified as a second priority commodity.

2. Shea butter bridge press

Bridge press mechanically extracts shea butter, it is manually operated with minimal effort, and it has a 15 kg capacity and can be made and serviced locally. Brief description of the main process phases:

  • Dried kernels are pounded as per traditional method.
  • A small quantity of water is added to the paste which is then wrapped in cotton cloth and placed in the press.
  • Pressure is applied and the oil is extracted.

2.1 Advantages of bridge press

  • No need to roast the pounded nuts before milling saving time, fuel and labour.
  • Painful kneading or rinsing phases are no longer necessary after milling.
  • Fuelwood and water collection and transportation is no longer required.
  • No further oil processing is necessary after extraction.
  • Extraction efficiency is 32 percent greater than traditional methods. Yields are equal to, if not greater than traditional processing output.
  • Presses can be made and serviced locally, providing local employment and income.
  • After a 75-day storage period at 30° C and 75 percent relative humidity, shea butter quality was acceptable and comparable with traditional methods.
  • Time-saving and easy to use.
  • Improved oil flavour. Women expected a bitter flavour as nuts were not roasted.
  • Sun drying is low cost and there is no need for extra drying facility.
  • Residue blocks used as fuel provides a sustainable recycling resources strategy.

When the press was introduced to the villages, the shea nut paste was packed into cotton bags, manufactured locally from used flour sacks, which were easily damaged by the press. Experimentation indicated that the paste should simply be wrapped into a cotton fabric square with an overwrap of woven polypropylene sacking. This practice was successful and welcomed by the women processors.

3. Economic evaluation of the process

Profitability of shea butter production with traditional processes is extremely low, whilst the improved bridge press method generates significant increases in profit per woman-hour.

Due to the press repayment women gain a reduced income per batch, however once the press is repaid, the gain compares to the traditional process, despite the cost of the cotton bags.

The costs of the two processes were compared, assuming that:

  • bridge press has a ten years lifespan; and
  • hourly labour rate of 90 Cedis per hour (1997 prices).

The processing cost analysis results are:

  • 469 Cedis per kg of nuts, using the press;
  • 471 Cedis per kg of nuts, using the traditional method.

Hence the processing cost of the former method is not significantly lower than the latter.

Nonetheless, for an annual turnover of 5 tonnes of nuts, the net present value of the bridge press is positive at just under 54 000 Cedis and the internal rate of return of 26 percent is higher than the estimated opportunity cost of capital (20 percent).

Although costs of processing with the two methods are comparable, the benefits of the new technology are:

  • environmental (no need for fuel);
  • time-saving (releasing time for other activities); and
  • process simplification.

4. Potential for greater extraction efficiency

Shea butter is an oil with a high viscosity below 40° C, but becomes more fluid over 60° C (Rouzière, A., CIRAD, personal communication, 2006). Oil extraction efficiency is inversely related to oil viscosity. To obtain improved oil extraction rates, the following elements need heating (before extraction):

  • ground kernels;
  • iron extraction case; and
  • separation plates.

5. IMC method

In an attempt to improve  the traditional processing method for shea butter extraction, Ghana’s Technology Consultancy Centre developed a simple process known as the Intermediate Moisture Content (IMC). The centre successfully field-tested the new processing method at Vitim and Savelegu in northern Ghana with community-based women’s groups. Compared to the aforementioned methods, the IMC implies a greater degree of mechanization in the grinding process, details are summarised in an article by Mensah (2001).

5.1 Advantages of IMC processing method

The IMC method uses a motorised plate mill to grind dry kernels into paste with the following processing advantages:

  • eliminates roasting stage;
  • eliminates creaming stage;
  • eliminates boiling stage;
  • reduces fuelwood and water consumption;
  • reduces exposure of the women to heat and smoke.

After milling, the paste has a 12 percent moisture content, and is at 70°C, warm enough to effectively allow pressing. The paste is put into cotton sacks and placed directly into the bridge press.

5.2 Advantages over traditional processing

Output advantages of the new improved method over traditional processing include:

  • five percent increase in extraction efficiency;
  • 200 percent increase in daily production capacity;
  • decreased fuelwood consumption (i.e. eight kg of fuelwood for IMC method versus 72 kg for traditional process, for 85 kg of kernels processed);
  • decreased water use (i.e. eight litres of water for IMC method versus 160 litres for traditional method, for 85 kg of kernels processed);
  • milder shea butter smell - higher consumer preference.

6. Shea butter markets

The international demand for shea butter is likely to increase, suggesting potential for small-scale processing which could become a profitable business, if:

  • output is increased;
  • production cost are reduced;
  • quality is improved; and
  • products are targeted to international markets.

7. Considerations

There is little incentive to use the bridge press process because it as it offers small financial advantage over the traditional method meeting domestic consumers’ specifications. In addition, the bridge press does not significantly increase extraction efficiency, at 32 percent over the traditional method. Given that the oil content of shea nut is around 54 percent, it is clear that a large proportion of the oil goes to waste. Hydraulic or screw expeller presses would increase extraction efficiency from 40 to 45 percent.

The bridge press efficiency also depends on temperature and moisture content of the pounded nuts which require careful management.. Cooler temperatures weather significantly decreases extraction efficiency and the press would benefit from a heating device. Despite labour productivity increase over traditional methods of extraction, the scale and technical efficiency of the improved methods are not great enough to achieve profitability unless international prices remain high.

Thus, when the work was assessed in 1999, crude shea butter Free On Board (FOB) price varied from USD 600 to USD 950 per tonne, against a production cost of USD 940 per tonne. However, at the time of writing (February 2006) the FOB price ex Nigeria is USD 3 000 per tonne. The benefits of projects such as this are subject to rapidly changing exchange rates, in-country inflation and international commodity prices.

Locally fabricated presses can suffer a high failure rate due to poor design and quality control during manufacture.  General lack of literacy, management and business skills among women processors, confirm Stringfellow, 1996 view that in sub-Saharan Africa, individual small-scale entrepreneurs are more successful than group businesses management.

Also as the product value increases, large scale processors move in, reducing the competitiveness of smaller producers (Gallat and Collinson, 2000; Collinson and Zedie-Bosurner, 1999).

The bridge press is versatile and can process any oil-bearing crop (i.e. sesame, groundnut, sunflower, etc.) improving local opportunities and the economic viability of the initial investment (Rouzière, A., CIRAD, personal communication, 2006).

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Women-friendly

Rural women in northern Ghana successfully used the manually operated press for shea butter extraction.

9.2 Resource use efficiency

This technology contributes to resources use efficiency and reduces fuelwood and water consumption.

9.3 Pro-poor technology

Shea butter can guarantee an additional income source for poor households.

entries.tittle: Preventing stackburn heat damage to maize stored, Africa
entries.summary: Stackburn in maize is heat damage characterized by a brown discoloration of the grain resulting from heat build-up in the interior of stacks held in commercial storage in sub-Saharan Africa. Affected maize may be downgraded in commercial markets or have to be diverted for animal-feed use. Where discoloration is severe, food-aid agencies attempting to distribute stackburned maize may meet beneficiary resistance or rejection and be forced to dispose of large quantities of deteriorated maize at considerable cost (up to GBP 23 million during 1993 in southern Africa). Heat build is linked to restricted airflow resulting from the use of woven polypropylene sacks. Building stacks with internal gaps to allow air flow and/or a return to jute sacks prevents stackburn, with some slight loss in plinth capacity.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction and background

Maize stackburn emerged as a significant threat to food security in sub-Saharan Africa during the 1990s. Stackburn affected local and imported varieties of white and yellow maize and was characterised by a brown discolouration of the grain resulting from heat build-up in the interior of stacks held in commercial storage. Affected maize may be downgraded in commercial markets or have to be diverted for animal-feed use. Where discolouration is severe, food-aid agencies attempting to distribute stackburned maize may meet beneficiary resistance or rejection and be forced to dispose of large quantities of deteriorated maize at considerable cost. The underlying factors responsible for the onset of maize stackburn are not well understood and the nutritional and/or toxicological implications for consumers are similarly unclear.

Spoilage, downgrading and financial loss of maize caused by “damp grain heating” due to excess moisture was a well recognised feature of commercial grain storage. Insufficiently dried grain will heat rapidly, through the growth of moulds and other micro-organisms, unless stored under anaerobic conditions. Similarly, grain that is wet by rain or condensation will heat. One consequence of insect infestation is grain heating, which may arise in either moist or dry grain. In the case of stackburn, it was established that another form of heating was occurring in bagged maize stored at moisture contents hitherto considered safe for storage. This “dry grain heating” resulted in stackburn, characterised by a moderate to severe yellowish-brown discoloration of both the kernel and germ of the maize. White maize grown locally as well as yellow maize imported from international markets was affected and both indigenous commercial-scale storage agencies and aid donors financing maize imports suffered considerable financial losses as a result.

In Zimbabwe, huge quantities of white maize (at times more that 1.2 million tonnes) were successfully stored outdoors in modular 5 000 tonne stacks. These were built on a simple platform of poles and were sheeted over with tarpaulins. Stacks were built after harvest with maize dried to below 12.5 percent moisture content. Following the 1990 storage season, it was noticed that maize in the centre of several stacks was discoloured and the opalescent white grains were variously coloured from a light tan colour through to dark reddish-brown.

In Ghana, a similar problem occurred under different circumstances. Maize bought from producers was cleaned and dried to 12.5 percent moisture content. It was treated with Actellic insecticide and temporarily placed in small metal silos before being bagged into polypropylene bags stored in small stacks in a warehouse. Some five to eight months later heating was noticed and again this was associated with brown discoloration of the grain. The introduction of polypropylene bags was an innovation intended to save foreign currency and overcome a shortage of jute bags. Subsequent questioning of storekeepers indicated that others had noticed that dry maize stored in polypropylene bags tended to get hot in storage. There is also some evidence that the problem has arisen in maize stored in polypropylene bags in warehouses in Angola and Malawi.

Although stackburn has been recognised in different regions of Africa and in different types of storage system, there appear to be common features, including: well dried maize, to an average of 12.5 percent moisture or below; adoption of polypropylene bags in place of jute; bagged stacks in place for several months; a cycle of internal heating up to 40 °C particularly affecting the core of the stack; cooling following the heating cycle; discoloration of the maize grains with no evidence of abnormal insect or mould damage. The financial losses caused by stackburn alone ranged from 2 to 13 percent e.g. about ZWD 72 per tonne minimum at 1991 prices and ZWD 139 ZWD (USD 25) maximum at 1992 prices. Estimates of total stackburn losses in maize imported to southern Africa during periods of drought varied from USD 1 million in 1992 to USD 23 million in 1993.

In terms of nutritional impact, stackburn causes a reduction in nutritive value for all classes of livestock and can be predicted to do so for humans. More positively, there appeared to be no evidence that the stackburning process results in any significant increases in mycotoxin levels in affected maize. A wide range of biological and physical aspects was examined both in the laboratory and in field studies. No single causal phenomenon was identified, with both grain respiration and fungal contamination being exonerated as significant contributors. The role of insect infestation in dry grain heating has been discounted in field surveys of stackburn cases and remains ambivalent after several project field trials. Conversely, despite field survey evidence of stackburn occurring in jute sacks, laboratory trials established that woven polypropylene sack material offered considerably greater resistance to air movement than jute and field studies clearly identified both heating and stackburn occurring in maize stacks of woven polypropylene bags but not in comparative stacks of jute bags.

2. The prevention of stackburn

Extended trials proved the success of a passive ventilation regime, based on a system of channels incorporated in large stacks at the time of construction, as a means of preventing heat build-up and discoloration of stored maize. The practical and cost-effective application of this technique has been recognised by the national grain storage agency in Zimbabwe and is being incorporated into the management strategy for adoption at depots countrywide.

The first operational use of an air circulation system was seen in Minnesota, USA by GMB management staff in 1989. Learning from this, a honeycombed stacking pattern intended to allow dissipation of heated air by natural convection, rather than by mechanical means, was incorporated in a trial stack in Mutare depot in 1990 (a secondary objective was the facilitation of gas penetration and achievement of optimum gas concentrations during fumigation operations). Observation confirmed that the vertical channels were, indeed, functioning as chimneys and allowing warm air from within the stack to escape. At stack breakdown in 1991, after 15 months, the outturn quality of the maize was good with no stackburn recorded.

In 1993, the channelled stack method was extended to all stacks at Centenary depot with the exception of a normal, control stack. During quality monitoring over 15 months it was observed that all channelled stacks showed moisture content stability as opposed to the control stack which exhibited a fluctuating moisture content pattern. The quality of maize from the channelled stacks at outturn was uniformly good and considered to be substantially unchanged from intake.

3. Building a ventilated stack

  • The basic format of a ventilated stack entails construction of a series of vertical and horizontal tunnels at no more than 3 m between tunnels.
  • Each tunnel was three layers deep, 100 to 200 mm wide, and separated from tunnels above and below by one layer of sacks.
  • Widthways tunneling commenced on the second layer of the bagstack and continued to the top the stack, while lengthways tunneling commenced on the third layer.
  • By thus staggering the layers on which the widthways and lengthways tunnels were built, and by ensuring that the tunnels stayed in line with those above and below up to the top of the bagstack, vertical tunnels were formed inside the stack where the horizontal tunnels intersected.
  • The tunnels are spaced five headers (sack widths) or three stretchers (sack lengths) apart both widthways and lengthways.
  • This resulted in squares of the same dimensions being formed within the stack.
  • In all there were thirteen columns along the length of the stack and five columns across the width, resulting in 65 vertical tunnels being formed within the bagstack.
  • A description of the building method is shown in the appendix of the report by (Devereau 1995).
  • This is essentially not an innovation, but a simple technique for outside bagstacks under tarpaulin (used for example in China for storage of cereal grains).
    • The objective is to facilitate air circulation inside the stack in order to avoid heating of grains in bags.
    • The main problem concerns the skill of workers to build ventilated bagstacks.

4. Disadvantages of ventilated stacks

  • The drawbacks of tunneling are that the bagstack takes longer to build.
    • There is extra work for the sack carriers in positioning sacks near to the numerous tunnel edges.
    • More semi-skilled bagstack builders are required to place the sacks accurately along the tunnel edges.
    • Speed of building will increase as experience is gained, and it is hoped that a reduction in stackburn gained through adopting the method, if successful, will compensate for any extra cost involved.
  • A normal bagstack might hold 64 000 sacks or 3 200 tonnes.
  • Building a ventilated stack on the same plinth would hold 58 489 sacks, or nominally 2 924 tonnes.
    • The tunneling has therefore resulted in an approximate 8.5 percent reduction in bagstack weight and thus a reduction in the storage capacity of the plinth.
    • Settlement may occur during storage causing the tunnels to become blocked.
    • After four months the lowest widthways tunnels were inspected by lifting the sheets on either side of the stack.
    • In five out of 13 cases light could be seen through the tunnels; in all other cases the tunnels appeared unblocked though some settlement of the bagstack had clearly occurred.

5. Training in stack construction

  • Although the technique of ventilating bagstacks appeared promising and relatively non-complex, its adoption throughout a country represents a large undertaking with many potential problems.
  • The Grain Marketing Board in Zimbabwe devised a programme to train key staff in the use of the technique which was subsequently introduced.
    • It was these depot staff who supervised the construction of each bagstack.
    • Initial instruction was given to stack masters over a five day period.
    • The staff were required to build and dismantle four model bagstacks per day using miniature 10 kg sacks of grain.
    • The staff also began construction of a full-sized bagstack to a few layers high.
    • The cost of this initial training programme was 100 000 ZWD in 1995.
    • A guide to building ventilated stacks was developed as a reference and to aid extension of the technique.
      • This consisted of a set of diagrams that showed the construction of each bagstack layer in terms of the number of sacks and their orientation and position.

6. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Maize production: ID 7018.
  • Pests and diseases management in maize: ID 7019.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2505.

entries.tittle: Tsetse control: How to use Tsetse traps with an odour dispenser
entries.summary: Tsetse flies (Glossina sp.) infest over 11 million square km of Africa, and are vectors of Trypanosomosis (or Trypanosomiasis) in both man and domestic livestock. For example, it is estimated that tsetse infestations occur over 7 percent of Zimbabwe and 60 percent of Tanzania and Trypanosomosis has an important negative impact on livestock production in these areas. An odour dispenser is an integral component of tsetse traps. The following technology describes the use of a simple odour dispenser in addition to tsetse traps under practical field conditions.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Tsetse flies (Glossina sp.) infest over 11 million km2 of Africa, and are vectors of Trypanosomosis (or Trypanosomiasis) in both humans and domestic livestock.
    • For example, it is estimated that tsetse infestations occur over 7 percent of Zimbabwe and 60 percent of Tanzania and Trypanosomosis has an important negative impact on livestock production in these areas.
    • In addition to the use of trypanocidal drugs, control, of Trypanosomosis has been tackled largely by control of the tsetse fly vector and a range of techniques are available, each with advantages and disadvantages.
    • Methods include aerial spraying, sterile insect techniques, insecticide treated cattle, and odour bait traps and targets.
    • Furthermore, it is generally considered that deployment of traps and/or targets that destroy a proportion of the tsetse population will lead to a reduction in the incidence of trypanosomosis.
  • A general decline in the capacity and funding of national veterinary institutions means that communities affected by Trypanosomiasis are forced to control the disease themselves.
    • Consequently, community-based initiatives to control tsetse has become one of the major methods of controlling trypanosomiasis.
    • However, despite many attempts by various communities, the results have been generally disappointing and there are very few examples of sustained control of tsetse being achieved by a rural community without significant financial and technical support from donors and/or national governments.
    • The causes of this failure are complex, but at least part of the problem is that rural communities, and the organisations that facilitate community-based tsetse control, do not have adequate access to information on how to apply tsetse control technologies.
    • In addition, the poorest rural communities need access to cheaper and practical tsetse control technologies.

2. Tsetse traps

  • A range of designs for tsetse traps were developed in the 1960s and earlier but these included a number of features that made them generally difficult or impractical to use.
    • Many, for instance, were large, cumbersome, and difficult to transport.
    • With the development of the biconical trap, this meant that a trap became available that was relatively cheap, collapsible, so that many can be carried in a vehicle, and quickly and easily assembled.
      • See in FAO, Use of Attractive Devices for Tsetse Survey and Control.
    • The biconical trap is particularly effective for species of the palpalis group of tsetse including G. palpalis and G. tachinoides, and less so for other tsetse, but widely used for sampling.
  • Different species of tsetse occur under and are adapted for different environmental conditions.
    • The best design of trap depends upon the species of tsetse fly and it is important to match the trap to the species.
    • Following the development of the biconical trap, a range of different traps have been designed.
    • For riverine species such as Glossina palpalis or G. fuscipes, the best traps are the biconical or pyramidal traps.
    • For tsetse living in savanna habitats, e.g. G. morsitans and G. pallidipes, the best traps have been shown to depend on the locality, or where they are to be used.
    • In East Africa, the Ngu or Nzi traps appear to be the best, whereas in southern Africa the Epsilon trap has produced better results.
    • For G. brevipalpis, the H-trap is preferred whereas the Ngu and Epsilon traps have been used successfully to catch G. longipennis in Kenya and Somalia.
      • What is the best trap for tsetse?
      • How many tsetse can a trap catch?
      • Why are most traps coloured blue and black?
      • Why do tsetse follow my car?
      • Do I need to use attractants with a tsetse trap?
      • What are the chemical properties of the attractants?
      • How safe are the attractants to use?
      • What other types of fly are caught by tsetse traps?
      • Where is the best site for a trap?
      • Should I treat the trap with insecticide?
      • What are the problems with traps?
      • What is a man fly-round?
      • What is an ox fly-round?
      • How can I catch tsetse that follow a car?
      • How do I stop ants eating the catch?
      • There are lots of different types of trap cage. Which is the best design?
      • What type of netting should I use
      • What sort of cloth should I use to make targets and traps?
      • Most traps are black and blue. Is the particular shade of blue important?

3. Basic principles of Tsetse traps

  • Tsetse have a high metabolic rate and feed exclusively on vertebrate blood.
    • Their survival therefore depends on detecting and encountering suitable hosts on which to feed.
    • This principle can be exploited in the design of traps and targets which mimic key features of the normal host animals, attracting tsetse in such a way that they can then be captured or killed.
    • With traps, the captured flies can be identified and counted, useful in sampling and monitoring tsetse populations.
    • Tsetse targets simply use insecticide-treated surfaces to kill the tsetse by contact and are of little use in population sampling or monitoring.
    • Both targets and traps are exposed to damage and stealing and these methods require active participation from rural communities.
  • As techniques for tsetse control, both traps and targets function by removing individuals from the tsetse population.
    • Their efficiency depends on the length of time the devices remain operational, and the likelihood that an individual fly will encounter the device and be killed by it.
    • The length of time each device remains operational depends on a number of factors including:
      • resistance to environmental damage (e.g. wind and/or damage by large animals),
      • theft of all or part of the device, and
      • component degradation (particularly colour fade, depletion of odour baits, and loss of insecticidal activity in the case of targets).
    • The likelihood that an individual fly will encounter and be killed or captured by the device depends also on the number of traps or targets relative to the local abundance of tsetse and on the particular foraging and dispersal behaviour of the target tsetse species.
    • For more information see Kuzoe and Schofield, 2004. 
  • Insecticide-treated traps can be used to control tsetse.
    • The insecticide treatment means that the trap will still kill tsetse even if it is badly ripped.
    • However, if the intention is only to kill tsetse then it is probably cheaper to use a simple insecticide-treated target for control and just use the traps for survey and monitoring purposes.

4. Chemical attractants

  • When tsetse flies seek a host, they use a variety of sensory perceptions, including movement of the host and odours that assist the tsetse in locating the host.
  • The odours of hosts act on the flies in several ways.
  • Some odours, for example carbon dioxide, stimulate tsetse to fly and start searching for the host.
  • However, carbon dioxide is impractical for use in the field.
  • Others will induce flight toward the host, whilst others promote a landing response.
  • Chemicals that are known to be of use in sampling and/or control measures include three main components, namely: ketones (butanone and acetone), octenol, and urine (cow urine) or phenol mixtures.

5. Odour dispensers

  • A good odour dispenser should ensure a steady release of the chemical attractant at the correct rate for as long as there is odour in the dispenser.
  • It should also be robust enough to operate under field conditions for long periods.
  • Ideally the release rate should be independent of environmental conditions such as temperature and wind strength.
  • For practical field use the materials also need to be cheap and easy to obtain. The commonly used chemical attractants include:
    • Butanone and acetone
    • Butanone
    • Octenol and the phenols
    • Cattle urine.

5.1 Butanone and acetone

  • These are dispensed using open bottles of glass or plastic.
  • The bottle can be round or square in cross-section and the height of the bottle, excluding the neck, should be about twice the width.
  • The bottles should be made from stout glass, such as that used with a beer bottle.
  • Plastic is also suitable, provided the polymer is impermeable to butanone.
  • This means that polychloloroethylene is acceptable whereas polyethylene is not.
  • Clear material is preferable to coloured.
  • The bottle should be sealed with a perforated lid, the size of the perforation being 2.5 to 3.8 mm.

5.2 Butanone

  • Butanone can also be dispensed using a large (capacity = 500 ml; wall thickness = 1 mm) bottle of low-density polyethylene but acetone cannot be dispensed using this type of dispenser.

5.3 Octenol and the phenols

  • These are dispensed using sealed bottles made from low density polyethylene.
  • The attractants diffuse through the polyethylene rather than through a hole.
  • The release rate of the attractants is controlled by the size of the bottle and the thickness of its wall.
  • If the dispenser is too small, or the walls are too thick, or if the bottle is made from high density polyethylene, then the dispenser will not work.
  • Typical bottles which would be effective have a surface area of 160 to 320 cm2 and wall thickness of 0.5 to 1.0 mm.

5.4 Cattle urine

This can be dispensed using glass or plastic bottles but require a far larger opening than that used for acetone or butanone. In general, the aperture needs to have a surface area of 25 cm2.

5.5 Glass jars and bottles as odour dispensers

  • These are most frequently used for the ketones and for urine of various host animals.
  • The volume of the bottle does not affect the release rate, which is determined by the size of the aperture.
  • This should be set by using a lid drilled with a hole of the correct diameter.
  • Acetone is normally used at dose rates varying from 150 to 2 500 mg per h.
  • At temperatures varying from about 20 degrees Centigrade at night to about 35 degrees in the afternoon, a hole of 2 mm diameter will give an average release rate of about 150 mg per hour.
  • One of 6 mm will give about 500 mg per h whilst one of 22 mm will give 2 500 mg per h.
  • For cow urine a release rate of about 1 000 mg per hour is required.
  • This can be obtained using an aperture of about 45 mm diameter.
  • If the aperture is exposed to the rain, some form of cover must be provided to prevent the dispenser from filling with water.
  • Alternatively a plastic container, or empty tin covered with polythene, can be used, with a 2 cm x 4 cm aperture cut in the side and near to the top.
  • The advantage of this approach is that a rain cover is not required.

6. Polythene sachets as odour dispensers

  • Polythene film of about 125 to 175 µm thickness can be used to make sachets.
  • These have the advantage that the release rate remains reasonably constant with age and they are cheap and easy to make.
  • Flexible lay-flat polythene tubing can be obtained as a roll, and the sachets are made by hand using a heat sealer.
  • These are commercially available in a variety of models.
  • Sachets can either be flat and rectangular, or pyramidal in shape.
  • A sachet made of 125 µm polythene film will need to be about 5 cm x 4 cm to give an octenol release rate of 0.5 mg per hour, depending on temperature.
  • Usually two seals are made across each end.
  • The more expensive sealers enable the sachets to be filled first and then sealed.
  • Alternatively the completed sachet can be injected with the chemical by syringe and the resulting small hole sealed.
  • Presence of chemical in the area of the seal will increase the sealing time required.
  • Care should be taken when handling phenols and protective clothing should be worn.

7. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Tsetse control: how to make a plastic cage for tsetse traps: ID 4514.
  • Tsetse control using Epsilon trap made in Botswana: ID 4509.
  • Tsetse Muse: helping planners to design cost-effective tsetse control strategies: ID 4482.
  • Tsetse control using Epsilon trap made: ID 4508.
  • Tsetse control: insecticide treatment of cattle: ID 4491.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology uses environmentally friendly biological resources to repel pest infestations. This not only has positive effects on the environment but is also cost-effective, increases crop yield, crop health, and provides additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Using plants with pesticidal properties to control insects during on-farm grain storage in Ghana
entries.summary: Market liberalisation in Africa has resulted in more commodities being stored in small quantities in on-farm facilities. This has resulted in increased post-harvest losses, especially by storage pest insects of grain and legumes. The use of synthetic pesticides in food stores at the farm level can be considered costly by resource-poor farmers. In northern Ghana locally available plants are cheap and effective alternatives, provided problems associated with their sustainable use are addressed.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Small-scale farmers throughout sub-Saharan Africa continue to have problems protecting their harvested grain crops from insect infestation during storage.
    • Traditional grain storage structures vary considerably and are unable to prevent insect infestation.
    • Storage losses are typically patchy and can be a big threat to food security and household incomes, particularly when losses are severe.
    • Owing to the risks associated with grain storage, farmers try to minimise their losses by selling their grain soon after harvest, which leads to low market prices as the market is flooded with recently harvested grain.
    • Farmers could achieve a much higher price if they were to sell their grain later in the season, but to achieve this they must be able to limit insect infestation of the grain.
  • Subsistence farmers often lack the financial resources to buy good quality commercial insecticides to protect their stored food, and their inappropriate use of conventional pesticides can result in risks to human and environmental health and may promote insecticide resistance.
    • Traditional storage methods using indigenous plants with insecticidal properties could offer a safer, low-cost and more dependable method of storage protection while reducing the increasing reliance upon conventional pesticides.
    • Farmers need information on botanicals to support their decision making with respect to the reliability of control they can expect when using a particular plant material to reduce insect infestation.
  • Botanicals with pesticidal properties are already used by farmers in many countries as a means of reducing the impact of insect pests on stored grains and legumes.
    • Farmers often prefer to use botanicals instead of commercial synthetics for a number of reasons.
    • Botanicals do not need to be purchased and are, therefore, low-cost (requiring labour inputs but no direct financial outlay).
    • Many farmers also believe that botanicals are safer to use and are more flexible in their usage.
    • Botanicals are also often much more available than commercial products as they grow in the local environment.
    • Some of the plants traditionally used by farmers for stored product protection offer similar levels of protection as compared to commercial synthetics.
    • Farmers can make selections on which plants work best due to their own comparative analysis and base further decision making on storage options with this new knowledge.

2. Types of plants

  • The botanicals used were:
    • Azadirachta indica (whole leaves),
    • Cassia sophera (powdered leaves),
    • Chamaecrista nigricens (powdered leaves),
    • Cymbopogon schoenanthus (flower heads or entire plant),
    • Lippia multiflora (whole leaves and/or flowers),
    • Ocimum americanum (whole or powdered entire plants),
    • Securidaca longepedunculata (powdered root bark or water extract of roots), and
    • Synedrella nodiflora (water extract from boiled leaves).
  • The plants were chosen on the basis of farmer recommendation and anti-insect effectiveness in laboratory studies.
  • About 200 farmers took part in the trial.

3. Insecticidal action of botanicals

  • Plants affect insects in two main ways, repellency and/or toxicity.
  • Plants which are repellent are not always toxic.
  • For example, if a farmer mixes a repellent plant in with grain which is already infested, the plant would have little effect in reducing the level of infestation.
  • Repellent plants are good at preventing infestation on clean grain, and there is some evidence that a repellent plant may cause adults to leave infested grain, but generally should not be recommended to treat infested grain.
  • Toxic plants are generally either effective against the egg and/or adult stages of primary pests such as Prostephanus truncatus, Rhyzopertha dominica, Sitophilus zeamais and Callosobruchus maculatus.

4. Preparation and use of botanicals

  • The way farmers use plants varies considerably e.g. hot water extract poured over or as a dip, or the use of the whole or powdered plant or plant part.
  • Amounts and concentrations of material also differed.
  • Some farmers admix plants while others place them as layers within the commodity.
  • Mixtures of two or more plant species, single applications at the start of the storage period or several applications as the storage season progressed are also employed.
  • The plant parts in use for any given species is the least variable factor, and, generally, all farmers consistently use the leaves, roots or flowers of a particular plant species.
  • For the purposes of the technology recommended here, plants should be shade dried and ground to powder, and mixed at 5 percent w/w with maize or cowpeas as a single application at the beginning of the storage season.
  • The season lasts about six months.

5. Advantages of the technology

  • Reviving and modernising age-old farmer practice through the optimisation of ethnobotanicals has shown that farmers are more comfortable using plant materials than commercial synthetics and that botanicals can offer a similar level of control when certain guidelines are followed to their use.
    • Pesticidal plants can be used reliably and safely to treat grain and legumes when stored in small quantities at the farm level.
    • Owing to their indigenous use in Ghana, legal registration of these botanical products is not required for their promotion within the country.
    • Knowledge on factors such as application concentration, method of application, preparation of botanicals and duration of control expected can be used to promote botanicals as a cost-effective and environmentally sustainable alternative to commercial synthetics.
  • All the plant materials are effective in reducing insect damage levels with the best result achieved by S. Iongepedunculata in maize and cowpeas, showing a two or three-fold decrease in damage when compared to untreated grain, followed by A. indica, O. americanum, S. nodiflora, L. multiflora and C. sophera.
  • Anecdotal information that has suggested variable results when using botanicals is more than likely due to changes in how the plant material has been used by farmers (e.g. variable concentration applied, different baseline infestation levels, plant material preparation methods).
    • Depending on when and how farmers harvest their grain, insect infestation can occur before it is put into storage, and this could affect how well botanical treatments work.
    • Although none of the plant materials were able to eliminate insect infestation, all were able to significantly reduce damage levels.
    • Variability in the results of botanical usage among farmers cannot be ruled out as some farmers are more conscious of the effects of good hygiene and take more care to ensure better storage conditions than others.
    • However, some of these concerns can be addressed through promotion of the technology, whilst similar concerns would also inevitably arise over the use of chemical insecticides.
  • Promotion of botanicals will ultimately assist biodiversity conservation of the savannah by increasing its perceived value.
  • In some areas there is a significant problem emerging as a result of adulteration of insecticides marketed for use with stored products.
  • The use of local plant materials is unlikely to suffer from the same concerns

6. Further considerations

  • In Northern and Upper East Regions of Ghana collection time is more important than where the plant is collected from.
    • Collection time or place has no real effect on level of efficacy for some plants, most notably S. Iongepedunculata and C. schoenanthus.
    • Where the plants were collected from is important for some plants more than others.
    • For example, O. americanum is generally more potent in the Upper East Region than in the Northern Region.
    • It is not known whether this is due to climatic factors or genetic variations among varieties or sub- species in different areas.
    • Plant species show different levels and durations of efficacy depending on the species and commodity affected.
  • It should not be assumed that because botanical pesticides are naturally derived that they are safe to use and consume by humans.
    • Preliminary assessments of mammalian toxicity indicate that the plants should be relatively safe if only small quantities of material were ingested.
    • Many of the plants used for stored product protection have alternative uses as medicines or food spices, indicating that any serious vertebrate toxicity would have been established through the gaining of ethnobotanical knowledge.
    • The risk of consuming larger quantities of botanicals through storage protection is reduced through winnowing, washing, processing and cooking.
    • However, no research has established the levels of potential botanical residues remaining on treated grain before it is ingested.
  • Big differences in application methodology show how innovative and experimental farmers could be.
    • However, it also highlights that communication between farmers may be a problem as no single method can claim superiority.
    • The use of plant materials appears to be ethnically and culturally biased, constraining the availability of indigenous knowledge systems and preventing its uptake in other communities.
    • However, all communities are likely to possess knowledge of local plants that are already used for medical, veterinary or social purposes that could be tested for grain protection.
  • Prior experience and familiarity with certain species may be affecting judgements over plant selection.
    • The prevalence of the plants growing in the natural environment and other marker criteria are important factors in how widely a plant is used by farmers.
    • For example, trials show that the most effective plant material in controlling storage insects was S. Iongepedunculata, but this is not the most widely used plant by farmers.
    • Farmer acceptability of botanicals is, therefore, likely to be influenced not only by demonstrated efficacy, but by other factors such as availability, familiarity and versatility.
  • One issue which remains unresolved is the accessibility and availability of the plant materials.
    • This does affect farmer choices.
    • Most of the plants are collected from the wild and some species are suffering from over-collection and environmental degradation.
    • In order for these plants to be used sustainably, their propagation and cultivation potential as well as their conservation in the wild needs to be addressed.
  • The harvesting of a plant species without any replacement programme threatens its sustainability.
    • It is clear from the threat assessment study that three species, A. indica, C. sophera and S. nodiflora could be very resilient to collection pressures in view of their colonising abilities.
    • However, S. longepedunculata which has been described in the Upper East Region as a “difficult-to-find species” is not cultivated anywhere in the northern savannahs.
    • In all the areas where this species is located in the Upper East Region the minimum distance from human settlement is about 8 km.
    • This shows how the species is rapidly becoming out of reach.
  • Furthermore, with the current harvesting methods, stems which undergo harvesting have little opportunity for survival.
    • This has serious implications on the resource life of the species and the economies of those who survive on the sale of the plant.
    • In the southern part of the savannahs, especially Yendi and Salaga areas, coppice shoots are found on cultivated farmlands and within easy reach of users.
    • Unlike in the Upper East Region harvesting is done by the removal of only few roots so that it does not adversely affect the survival of the residual stems.
    • The species, however, undergo another form of destruction through the cutting of the stems for yam stakes.
    • This practice also has important consequences on the sustainability of the species in the northern savannah zone.
    • In spite of the claim of abundance of C. schoenanthus the collection method employed poses a severe threat to its sustainability, particularly in the Bawku area where the species is under so much pressure that it has no opportunity of seeding.
    • The relatively low-level availability of C. nigricens and O. americanum suggests their inability to withstand collection pressures in the likely event of their being heavily used for grain storage.
    • With the endemic nature of L. multiflora, its widespread application would mean its introduction into other parts of the savannah zone provided its potency was not sacrificed.
  • While continuous cultivation is a threat to the continuous survival of species like S. longepedunculata it is a stimulant for the germination and growth of S. nodiflora.
    • Repeated annual fires are one of the greatest threats to the natural regeneration and survival of most of the plant species in the savannah ecozone.
    • Species like A. indica and S. nodiflora can be sustained for a considerably time in the event of wide application for grain storage. O. americanum and C. nigricens will require interventions to prolong their resource lives.
    • Cassia sophera holds promises of sustainability on account of its copious production of seeds and ease of germination.
  • It is recommended that the crusade against bush fires in the Ghana’s northern savannah zone should be aggressively pursued to enhance natural regeneration and growth of the species.
    • Cultivation of the threatened species in home gardens should be promoted, further research aimed at improving germination of the species should be done, certain areas in the Sudan Savannah (e.g. The Zawse Hills near Bawku) should be designated as “Special Biologically Protected Areas” to ensure enhanced growth and supply of C. schoenanthus, and intensive education on the conservation of the species must be vigorously pursued in the northern savannah zone.

7. Additional comments

  • Botanicals could have advantages over synthetics as an environmentally sustainable alternative for protecting stored food against insect attack.
  • However, it is often difficult to recommend particular plant materials as a replacement for chemical insecticides as the efficacy levels of botanicals can vary among storage pests, application methods, and stored products.
  • On the other hand, botanicals are usually restricted to local use within a single region or perhaps neighbouring areas (local availability and problem of sustainability).
  • There remain questions concerning the effectiveness of these botanical protectants compared with chemical insecticides, diatomaceous earths, traditional use of ash and/or sand, or combinations of these techniques.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: improved storage facilities: ID 7308.
  • Improved pit storage method for ginger rhizomes: ID 7712.
  • Grain stores construction:ID 4499.
  • Storage and preservation of wet cassava: ID 4520.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology is cost-effective, uses alternative plants, and has a positive impact on the environment.
