entries.tittle: Tsetse and trypanosomiasis control measures: restricted application of insecticide to livestock
entries.summary: Since tsetse flies feed mostly on the legs of the largest animals in the herd, an application of pour-on insecticides or sprays restricted to the legs of cows, bulls and draught animals has been shown to be effective in controlling tsetse. This also results in significant cost-saving to the farmer of up to 80 to 90 percent.
entries.description:
Description

1. Background

  • Tsetse flies occur in 36 countries and a total area of about 10 million square kilometres in Africa.
  • Throughout this area the disease transmitted by the tsetse fly, Trypanosomiasis (or Trypanosomosis), has a significant effect on large numbers of livestock.
  • About 50 million cattle and tens of millions of small ruminants are considered to be at risk from Trypanosomiasis, and the disease is recognized to be an obstacle to poverty reduction and food security in Africa.
  • In addition, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), more than 60 million people, mainly living in rural areas of sub-Saharan Africa, are at risk of human African Trypanosomiasis, or sleeping sickness.
  • Furthermore, a general decline in the capacity and funding of national veterinary institutions means that Trypanosomiasis-affected communities are forced to control the disease themselves.
  • Consequently, community-based initiatives to control tsetse has become one of the major methods of controlling trypanosomiasis.

2. Control methods

  • In addition to the use of trypanocidal drugs, the control of Trypanosomosis has been tackled largely by the control of the tsetse fly vector.
  • A range of techniques are available, each with advantages and disadvantages.
  • Methods include:
    • aerial spraying;
    • sterile insect techniques;
    • insecticide treated cattle; and
    • odour bait traps and targets.
  • Both targets and insecticide-treated cattle are particularly suited as control techniques for use by local communities.

3. Controlling tsetse with insecticide-treated cattle

  • Insecticide treatment of cattle and other livestock is considered as one of the important methods for control of tsetse, and thus reducing the incidence of Trypanosomiasis.
    • The principle is similar in practice to the use of targets for tsetse control, in that tsetse are attracted to the target (in this case cattle), and attempt to obtain a blood meal.
    • However, instead, they pick up a lethal dose of deltamethrin or alphacypermethrin insecticide which has been applied to the animal.
  • The insecticides applied to cattle to control tsetse do not act as repellents.
    • Consequently, they do not actually prevent tsetse from biting cattle.
  • However, each fly that either lands on, or lands and bites a treated animal will die within a few hours.
    • Therefore, if a sufficient proportion of the cattle population are treated within an area, then the population of tsetse will be reduced, cattle will be bitten less often by tsetse, and the incidence of Trypanosomiasis will decrease.
    • In situations where there is a wild herbivore animal population, the numbers of animals treated as a proportion of the total domestic plus wild herbivore population may be critical.
    • However, this record does not attempt to determine what this proportion should be.
  • Treating cattle with insecticides to control Trypanosomiasis should always be considered as part of a large-scale tsetse control operation using a range of different and complementary control techniques.
    • For instance, cattle situated at the edge of a control operation that is adjacent to a tsetse-infested area will be continuously affected by tsetse moving into the controlled area.
    • To prevent this, it may be necessary to use a protective barrier of targets, in addition to the use of insecticide-treated cattle.
    • Farmers may also be treating their cattle with insecticides to control other ectoparasites such as ticks.
    • Consequently, control operations should take care to inform livestock owners about the use of all insecticides potentially used by livestock keepers.
  • Formulations designed for controlling ticks are not necessarily effective against tsetse, although in most cases formulations effective against tsetse will also kill ticks.
    • The formulations effective against tsetse will generally be either a suspension concentrate or a pour-on formulation of a persistent pyrethroid such as deltamethrin, alphacypermethrin or beta-cyfluthrin.
  • A single insecticide-treated cow potentially kills about as many tsetse as a single odour-baited target.
    • Therefore, if there is a reasonably large population of cattle in an area, the use of insecticide-treated cattle offers several advantages over using targets.
    • Treating an animal is cheaper than constructing and deploying an insecticide-treated target.
    • In addition, cattle owners are strongly inclined to treat their cattle with insecticide, to maintain them and protect them from theft.
  • As a result, several problems associated with using targets are overcome by using insecticide-treated cattle, including the loss of targets due to general wear and tear, theft, and animal damage.
    • However, in practice, a combined approach using both traps and insecticide-treated cattle may represent the best option.
    • For example, cattle are managed in herds, and a group of ten cattle does not kill ten times as many tsetse as an individual.
    • It is considered that densities of four cattle per square kilometre are not sufficient to control savanna species of tsetse, whereas this same density of targets provides adequate control if well maintained.
  • For more information on this see “Controlling tsetse with insecticide-treated cattle”

4. Application of insecticide

  • The application of insecticide can be either by dips, sprays, or by pour-on.
  • In the case of dips or larger sprays, the cattle may already be dipped or sprayed for control of ectoparasites such as ticks and this can be combined with the application of insecticides for tsetse control

5. Pour-ons

  • Pour-ons are formulations of a number of different Synthetic Pyrethroid (SP) insecticides that can be applied to livestock.
    • These have been commercially available for more than a decade and some of these products have been shown to be highly effective against tsetse flies as well as ticks.
  • Pour-on treatment involves the application of an insecticide along the backline of livestock at a prescribed dosage.
    • Pour-ons are generally available in a ready-to-use form or are prepared from concentrate.
    • They are applied using graduated ladles, graduated squeeze bottles, or dosage-adjustable hand-guns.
    • It is important that the correct dosage be applied to the animals to ensure control of the targeted pest (and to avoid poisoning the animal).
    • Pour-on application requires less chemical, is considered less wasteful than dips or whole- body sprays, and the dosage is more precise than whole-body sprays.
    • Pour-on applications are therefore increasingly popular.

6. Impacts

  • The widespread use of pyrethroids (and other insecticides) can have an adverse impact on the invertebrate dung fauna (e.g. dung beetles), which play an important role in maintaining soil fertility in mixed crop-livestock farming systems.
    • In addition, by killing ticks as well as tsetse they prevent young animals from being sufficiently exposed to local tick-borne diseases to become adequately immunized to them.
    • This results in potentially serious disease risks later in adult animals.

7. Mitigation by restricted application of insecticide

  • A solution to the problem of adverse impacts on invertebrate dung fauna was suggested by the observation that tsetse feed preferentially on the legs and belly of larger/older cattle.
    • Restricted application of insecticide to these areas only has been shown to significantly reduce the impacts on dung fauna whilst still being effective against tsetse.
    • However, with a restricted application the effective life of the treatment is reduced. 
    • The most cost-effective regime was the treatment of the belly and legs of cattle at two to three weeks intervals, rather than the monthly interval recommended for whole body treatment.
      • This restricted application regime halves the amount of insecticide used, while improving overall efficacy and is appropriate for all four species of tsetse.
      • This provides benefits not only to the farmer in terms of cost but also to the environment.
      • For poor livestock keepers, it is the cost that represents the most prohibitive aspect of tsetse control.
    • For further information on impacts see also Kamuanga (2003) .
  • Researchers have demonstrated that this restrictive application of these pyrethroids to the legs of cows, bulls and draught animals is effective in controlling the fly.
  • An economic analysis of the use of these products in Ethiopia showed a return in higher productivity and lowered livestock mortality for farmers using pour-ons at traditional application levels.
  • Furthermore, while applying pour-ons still makes demands on farmers' time, the reduced need for cash as a result of legs-only application, makes it a more viable option for poor farmers.
    • Cost savings go up to 80 to 90 percent.
  • However there are concerns related to the proportion of tsetse that are able to bite before being killed.
    • In research conducted in West-Africa, a higher proportion are able to bite before being killed in the case of restricted treatment than in full body treatment.
  • The pyrethroids are irritating to the skin, especially when in the concentrated pour-on formulations intended to make good contact with the body.
    • This irritation, and possibly the presence of vegetable oils in the formulation, results in the animals licking off a significant proportion of the applied insecticide.
    • After ingestion, a portion of the insecticide is subsequently found in the dung, and results in mortality of dung fauna and consequently in reduced soil fertility.
    • However, the licking is not only a threat to dung fauna.
      • A proportion of costly insecticides used extensively throughout the cattle industry can rapidly be removed from the point of contact with target pests.

8. Application using sprays

  • Pour-ons are generally not designed to be applied to only the legs and belly.
  • However, sprays can be directed at specific parts of the body.
    • The use of sprays targeted at only the legs and belly, as alternatives to pour-ons, would substantially reduce the risks to dung fauna without affecting much the efficacy against tsetse.
    • Moreover, the sprays could also be more economical since they are usually about a quarter of the cost of pour-ons.
      • Dips can also be used to apply insecticide treatments only to legs and belly.
  • The problem in some countries is that unlike pour-ons, the sprays (or dips) require the inconvenience and expense of spray races or dip tanks, and need plenty of water to operate.
    • In many areas this infrastructure is not available.

9. Application using small hand-sprayers or brushes

  • The restriction of insecticide treatments to the legs promises to reduce yet further the insecticide costs and the risks to dung fauna.
  • It also requires relatively little water and might be achieved by comparatively inexpensive leg-baths, small hand-sprayers or even brushes.
  • As legs-only treatments require so much less insecticide than the whole-body applications, it means that substantial savings in insecticide costs can be made.
  • Furthermore, these methods do not require the infrastructure associated with dip tanks of spray races.
  • Further information on use of these application methods is also available at www.cirdes.org
  • See Stachurski (2005) and Bouyer et al:, (2005).
  • You manipulate and/or use pesticides? Make inquiries before!
  • Pesticide can be harmful to your health, the health of your family, of the consumers and of the environment.
  • Adopt the right gestures to use pesticides safely: click on “Reducing risks while manipulating pesticide”

10. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

11. Related/associated technologies

  • Tsetse control: how to make a plastic cage for tsetse traps: ID 4514.
  • Tsetse control: how to use Tsetse traps with an odour dispenser: ID 4507.
  • Tsetse Muse: helping planners to design cost-effective tsetse control strategies: ID 4482.
  • Tsetse control using Epsilon trap made: ID 4508.
  • Tsetse control: insecticide treatment of cattle: ID 4419.

12. Objectives fulfilled by the project

12.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology, through the control of the tsetse fly population, not only improves human health but also cattle production, thereby leading to additional sources of food and income. It is also cost-saving.

entries.tittle: Tsetse control with a \Nzi\" Trap in Kenya"
entries.summary: Tsetse flies (Glossina spp.) infest over 11 million sq km of Africa, and are vectors of Trypanosomosis (or Trypanosomiasis) in both man and domestic livestock. For example, it is estimated that tsetse cover over 7 percent of Zimbabwe and 60 percent of Tanzania and Trypanosomosis has an important negative impact on livestock production in these areas. In addition to the use of trypanocidal drugs, the control of Trypanosomosis has been tackled largely by the control of the tsetse fly vector. A range of techniques are available, each with advantages and disadvantages. Methods include aerial spraying, sterile insect techniques, insecticide-treated cattle, and odour bait traps, and targets. Therefore, a set of simple step-by-step instructions is presented on how to assemble a Nzi trap for tsetse, adapted and tested for use in Kenya.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Tsetse flies (Glossina spp.) infest over 11 million km2 of Africa, and are vectors of Trypanosomosis (or Trypanosomiasis) in both man and domestic livestock.
    • For example, it is estimated that tsetse cover over 7 percent of Zimbabwe and 60 percent of Tanzania and Trypanosomosis has an important negative impact on livestock production in these areas.
  • In addition to the use of trypanocidal drugs, control, of Trypanosomosis has been tackled largely by control of the tsetse fly vector.
    • A range of techniques are available, each with advantages and disadvantages.
    • Methods include aerial spraying, sterile insect techniques, insecticide treated cattle, and odour bait traps, and targets.
    • Furthermore, it is generally considered that deployment of traps and/or targets that destroy a proportion of the tsetse population will lead to a reduction in the incidence of trypanosomosis.
  • A general decline in the capacity and funding of national veterinary institutions means that communities affected by Trypanosomosis are forced to control the disease themselves.
    • Consequently, community-based initiatives to control tsetse has become one of the major methods of controlling trypanosomosis.
  • However, despite many attempts by various communities, the results have been generally disappointing and there are very few examples of sustained control of tsetse being achieved by a rural community without significant financial and technical support from donors and/or national governments.
    • The causes of this failure are complex, but at least part of the problem is that rural communities and the organisations that facilitate community-based tsetse control, do not have adequate access to information on how to apply tsetse control technologies.
    • In addition, the poorest rural communities need access to cheaper and practical tsetse control technologies.

2. Tsetse traps

  • A range of designs for tsetse traps were developed in the 1960s and earlier but these included a number of features that made them generally difficult or impractical to use.
    • Many, for instance, were large, cumbersome, and difficult to transport.
    • The development of the biconical trap, meant that this kind of trap became available that was relatively cheap, collapsible, so that many can be carried in a vehicle, and quickly and easily assembled (see in FAO, Use of Attractive Devices for Tsetse Survey and Control).
    • The biconical trap is particularly effective for species of the palpalis group of tsetse including G. palpalis and G. tachinoides, and less so for other tsetse, but widely used for sampling.
  • Different species of tsetse occur under and are adapted for different environmental conditions.
  • The best design of trap depends upon the species of tsetse fly and it is important to match the trap to the species.
  • Following the development of the biconical trap, a range of different traps have been designed.
    • For riverine species such as Glossina palpalis or G. fuscipes, the best traps are the biconical or pyramidal traps.
    • For tsetse living in savanna habitats (e.g. G. morsitans and G. pallidipes), the best traps have been shown to depend on the locality, or where they are to be used.
    • In East Africa, the Ngu or Nzi traps appear to be the best, whereas in southern Africa the Epsilon trap has produced better results.
    • For G. brevipalpis, the H-trap is preferred whereas the Ngu and Epsilon traps have been used successfully to catch G. longipennis in Kenya and Somalia.
    • More information on can be found here, which has a number of useful sections, including answers to the following questions relevant to tsetse and trapping tsetse.
      • What is the best trap for tsetse?
      • How many tsetse can a trap catch?
      • Why are most traps coloured blue and black?
      • Why do tsetse follow my car?
      • Do I need to use attractants with a tsetse trap?
      • What are the chemical properties of the attractants?
      • How safe are the attractants to use?
      • What other types of fly are caught by tsetse traps?
      • Where is the best site for a trap?
      • Should I treat the trap with insecticide?
      • What are the problems with traps?
      • What is a man fly-round?
      • What is an ox fly-round?
      • How can I catch tsetse that follow a car?
      • How do I stop ants eating the catch?
      • There are lots of different types of trap cage. Which is the best design?
      • What type of netting should I use
      • What sort of cloth should I use to make targets and traps?
      • Most traps are black and blue. Is the particular shade of blue important?

3. Basic principles of Tsetse traps

  • Tsetse have a high metabolic rate and feeds exclusively on vertebrate blood.
    • Their survival, therefore, depends on detecting and encountering suitable hosts on which to feed.
    • This principle can be exploited in the design of traps and targets which mimic key features of the normal host animals, attracting tsetse in such a way that they can then be captured or killed.
    • With traps, the captured flies can be identified and counted, useful in sampling and monitoring tsetse populations.
    • Tsetse targets simply use insecticide-treated surfaces to kill the tsetse by contact and are of little use in population sampling or monitoring.
    • Both targets and traps are exposed to damage and stealing and these methods require active participation from rural communities.
  • As techniques for tsetse control, both traps and targets function by removing individuals from the tsetse population.
    • Their efficiency depends on the length of time the devices remain operational and the likelihood that an individual fly will encounter the device and be killed by it.
    • The length of time each device remains operational and depends on a number of factors.
      • These are resistance to environmental damage (e.g. wind and/or damage by large animals), theft of all or part of the device, and component degradation (particularly colour fade, depletion of odour baits, and loss of insecticidal activity in the case of targets).
    • The likelihood that an individual fly will encounter and be killed or captured by the device depends also on the number of traps or targets relative to the local abundance of tsetse.
      • It also depends on the particular foraging and dispersal behaviour of the target tsetse species.
    • For more information see (Kuzoe and Schofield 2004).
  • Insecticide-treated traps can be used to control tsetse.
    • The insecticide treatment means that the trap will still kill tsetse even if it is badly ripped.
    • However, if the intention is only to kill tsetse then it is probably cheaper to use a simple insecticide-treated target for control and just use the traps for survey and monitoring purposes.

4. The Nzi trap for tsetse

  • Nzi" is one of the Swahili words for the fly.
  • The Nzi trap was developed in Kenya for savanna species of tsetse such as Glossina pallidipes.
  • It is also a very effective trap for stable flies (Stomoxys spp) and horseflies (Tabanidae)
  • The Nzi trap is a simple, safe and economical cloth trap for the capture of biting flies (tsetse flies, horse flies, deer flies, stable flies)
    • It was developed by Steve Mihok at ICIPE in Kenya as an environment-friendly alternative to the use of insecticides, following many years of research on appropriate and sustainable technology for African farmers.
    • It is a passive killing device that works through the attraction of flies to the large blue and black objects.
    • Flies simply die from exposure after entering into an innovative configuration of cloth and netting.
  • The trap is made from simple shapes for the economy, and for ease of assembly.
    • The layout is triangular with all pieces cut to the width of the material (e.g. one metre or one yard).
    • The trap walls are formed by a square piece of netting at the back and by two black cloth rectangles at the sides.
    • The body is closed at the top front by a vertical blue shelf.
    • Two blue rectangular wings extend out at an angle from the front.
    • A trapezoidal piece of netting extends horizontally half-way into the body from the bottom of the blue shelf.
    • The top is closed by a cone made by cutting a wedge out of a square piece of netting and sewing up the sides.
      • A tetrahedron results in a four-sided shape with equal triangular sides.

5. Assembling the Nzi trap

Figure 1. Nzi trap

Figure 3. Pieces required for a Nzi trap

Figure 4. Four wooden poles

©FAO/TECA

  • You will need to cut these yourself.
Figure 5. Cut the poles

©FAO/TECA

  • Hammer four nails into the top of the centre post.
Figure 6. Hammering

©FAO/TECA

  • Having made your four poles.
Figure 7. Four poles

©FAO/TECA

  • Next clear the site of vegetation.
Figure 8. Clear the site

©FAO/TECA

  • Hammer the centre pole into the ground.
Figure 9. Hammer centre poles

©FAO/TECA

  • Fit the trap cone over the centre pole.
Figure 10. Fit the trap cone

©FAO/TECA

  • Stretch the rest of the trap out.
Figure 11. Stretch the rest of the trap out

©FAO/TECA

  • So you can estimate where to put the other three poles.
  • Hammer the poles into the ground.
Figure 12. Estimate where to put the other three poles

©FAO/TECA

Figure 13. Hammer the poles

  • Attach the trap to the first pole with wire.
Figure 14. Attach the trap to the first pole

  • Do the same with the second corner.
Figure 15. Attach the trap to the second pole

Figure 16. Attach the trap to the third pole

  • Attach the trap to the third pole with wire.
  • The trap cone is supported on the nails in the centre post.

  • Fit a plastic bag to the top of the cone.
Figure 18. Fit a plastic bag

  • And there you have it!!

  • Tropics, warm.

  • Tsetse control: how to use Tsetse traps with an odour dispenser: ID 4507.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology provides the farmer with detailed instructions on the assemblage of a tsetse fly trap. It is cost-effective as it is not input intensive, and is efficient.

entries.tittle: Production of high-quality silage for dry season feeding of smallholder livestock, Zimbabwe
entries.summary: Many farmers in low potential areas own cattle and milk them for their own consumption and sale. However, in the dry season, natural grazing and crop residues are inadequate to support lactation, making supplementary feed necessary to maintain milk production. This practice includes descriptions of techniques for growing the crops and production of silage.
entries.description:
Description

1. Milk production in semi-arid regions of Southern Africa

  • It is recognised that the production of milk for sale is an attractive option for smallholder farmers in the semi-arid regions of Southern Africa.
  • Milk contributes to improving the livelihood of the household and is an attractive incentive for the investment of scarce financial resources.
  • Within Africa as a whole, smallholder dairying generates:
    • a more regular income than any other rural enterprise; and
    • can lead to improved human nutrition and health, poverty alleviation and improvement of household food security.
  • Many farmers in low potential areas own cattle and milk them for their own consumption and sale. However, in the dry season, natural grazing and crop residues are inadequate to support lactation, making supplementary feed necessary to maintain milk production.
  • Costs of purchased feeds are prohibitive, making dairy a seasonal rather than an annual activity.
  • Smallholder dairying in low potential areas needs to be supported by:
    • sustainable feed production; and
    • management interventions.
  • With limited land resources for forage production, it is especially important to produce:
    • higher-yielding; and
    • high-quality forage.
  • Optimum nutrient quality of forage coincides with the rains, making silage a practical option for conservation.

2. Forage production and conservation manual 

  • A manual was produced for the growing and ensiling of annual and perennial forage crops suited to marginal and semi-arid areas of Southern Africa by O. Mhere, B. Maasdorp and M. Titterton, 2002, Forage Production and Conservation Manual.

2.1 The Forage Production and Conservation Manual

  • The manual includes descriptions of techniques for growing the crops and the production of silage. Find below the table of contents:
    • Introduction
    • What are the major nutrients required to feed a dairy cow so that she will not only produce good yields of milk for 250 days but also have a calf every year?
    • What are forage crops?
    • What are the common forage crops used in Southern Africa?
    • What is the description of forage sorghum, Pennisetum, cowpea and dolichos bean?
    • Why should forages be conserved in the dry season?
    • How should forages be conserved for the dry season: hay or silage?
    • What is silage?
      • Growing the crops
      • Seed supply / planting material
      • Where to plant
      • Land preparation
      • When to plant
      • How to plant
      • Spacing
      • Fertilizer / Manuring
      • Weed control
      • Pest control
  • Harvesting the Forage
  • The Ensiling Process / Making Silage.
  • Feeding silage

3. Production of high yielding, high-quality forage

3.1 Southern Africa areas

  • In the high rainfall areas of Southern Africa, the crop of choice for silage is:
  • maize. Due to its:
    • high yield;
    • fermentation quality; and
    • energy content.
  • It is also suitable:
    • for intercropping with legumes; or
    • to be mixed with legume tree leaf forage to improve the protein content of the silage.

3.2 Marginal and semi-arid areas

  • Maize is susceptible to moisture stress and consequently cannot be considered as a reliable crop for silage in the marginal and semi-arid areas, where dairy production may offer the best means of improving livelihood for the smallholder livestock owner.
  • Hence, in these areas the following forages are more suitable:
    • grain sorghum;
    • forage sorghums; and
    • hybrid Pennisetum.
  • As they are:
    • more drought tolerant than maize; and
    • have a high yield potential as silage crops.
  • Forage sorghums offer better potential as silage crops than grain sorghums.
  • As with maize, however, these crops have a low crude protein content (seven and nine percent for grain and forage sorghums respectively).
  • In order to produce a high-quality ration to meet the nutrient requirements of dairy cows, protein-rich crops need to be introduced into the silage, either by growing them as sole crops and mixing them at ensilage with the forage crops, or intercropping them with the forage crops.
  • A three-year study was carried out by Titterton et al., 2002, Ensiling of tropical forages with Particular Reference to African Livestock Systems. Forage production and conservation for dry season feeding of smallholder dairy cattle in the semi-arid region of Southern Africa (URL), using both formal trials and participatory on-farm trials, to determine the feasibility of intercropping forage sorghum and hybrid Pennisetum with legumes.
  • Both cowpea (Vigna ungiculata) and dolichos bean (Lablab purpureus) were undersown using differing planting patterns and on two types of soil.
  • Total biomass yields and protein content of silages from the mixed crops was significantly improved over that of the sole cereal crops.
  • Hybrid Pennisetum / legume crops produced between 5 and 10 tonnes dry matter on sandy and clay soils respectively while forage sorghum / legume crops produced between 8 and 13 tonnes dry matter.
  • Soil type, planting pattern and weather had significant effects on the proportions of legume in both forage sorghum and forage Pennisetum crops.

4. What is silage?

  • Silage is a way of conservation of forages.
  • It is the product from a series of processes by which cut forage of moisture content between 15 and 30 percent, is fermented to produce a stable feed which resists further breakdown in anaerobic storage.
  • The objective is to retain or augment the nutrients present in the original forage and deliver a feed that is accepted by livestock.
  • This is usually attained through an anaerobic fermentation dominated by lactic acid bacteria.
    When forage is put into a sealed container such as a pit covered with plastic, a drum or a plastic bag, the container is called a silo.
  • A silo has to be completely sealed against air and the forage material must be chopped and compressed in the silo to ensure the fast development of anaerobic conditions and a rapid fall in pH. In these conditions, lactic acid bacteria, which convert some of the sugars in the plant into the pleasant tasting lactic acid, prevail over undesirable bacterial, such as Clostridia, which produce butyric acid.
    This is unpalatable to livestock, and moulds, which cause rotting of the silage.
  • Good silage has a sweet smell and cattle, goats and sheep will readily eat it.
    • Silage can be made quite cheaply and easily, provided it is done correctly.
    • The manual describes a number of techniques for making silage, ranging from the larger scale, machine intensive methods, to simple manual methods suitable for small-scale use. 

4.1 The use of wilting and inoculants to ensure successful ensilage

  • Because most plant sugars are quite low compared with sorghum and may not be enough for correct fermentation to take place, it is recommended that an inoculant be used when ensiling hybrid Pennisetum and legumes in order to assist with fermentation.
  • This inoculant can be:
    • maize meal, applied at a rate of 5 kg per 100 kg forage material (50 kg per tonne);
    • commercial inoculant;
    • chopped sweet sorghum, applied at a rate of 10 kg per 100 kg forage material (100 kg per tonne); or
    • molasses at same rate as maize meal.

4.2 Chopping and compaction in the silo

  • The purpose of chopping and compacting forage for silage is to:
    • release as much plant sugar as possible for fermentation; and
    • ensure that all the air is pushed out of the plant material so that when the silo is sealed, the plant material is free of air.
  • This is when fermentation works best to produce lactic acid.
  • For more details of the process of silage making, or ensiling, see the Forage Production and Conservation Manual, 2002, by O. Mhere, B. Maasdorp and M. Titterton.

5. Small-scale silage production

  • Silage making has become the traditionally accepted means of forage conservation for large scale farms, where the machinery appropriate for harvesting and chopping forage, carting forage to the silo and compressing it before the silo is sealed, is available.
  • However the cost of machinery is the major limitation to smallholders ensiling forage.
  • hence the development of low-cost techniques for ensiling is necessary which do not involve expensive farm machinery.

6. Plastic bag silos or little bag silage

  • Research by Lane, 2005, Little Bag Silage, has shown that good silos can be made from:
    • recycled plastic bags; or
    • reject fertilizer bags.
  • One such bag can hold about 15 kg of silage, which is enough feed for a cow in the dry season for one day.
  • The fertilizer bag is the best type to use, as it will last up to three seasons.

6.1 Advantages

  • The silage is completely sealed in the bag.
  • This means that all the acid is retained in the silage, unlike in pit silage where it very often seeps out through the bottom of the pit as effluent.
    • This compensates for the longer pieces of forage and poorer compaction in manual techniques of preparation, compared with silage machinery, and the quality of the resulting silage is just as good.
    • Ensiling in a bag avoids the hard work of having to remove silage.
  • For example, in a silage pit, it has to be dug out every day.
    • Because the contents of a whole bag are fed to an individual animal, the rest of the silage in the other bags is not exposed to air and is therefore unspoiled.
  • Much of the silage in pits is found to be spoiled due to poor sealing and exposure to air every day when the silage is removed for feeding.
  • The bags are:
    • easily stored; and
    • easily portable:
    • any member of the family, including children, can carry individual bags to the feed trough for the cow.

6.1.1 Storage

  • It is important to store the bags of silage in a room:
    • near the milking parlour or feed troughs;
    • completely sealed from both rodents and ants, as these can do considerable damage to bags; and
    • every year, before ensilage begins, the room should be checked and even the smallest holes sealed up.
  • The silage will be ready to feed after three weeks.
  • After emptying, the bags must be carefully:
    • washed;
    • dried; and
    • stored in a safe place for use the following year.

6.1.2 Economic data

  • Economic data will be highly variable and depends on:
    • the cost of bags (there are many to choose from and their lifespan is three years);
    • the cost of any additives and inoculants; and
    • the costs of any labour inputs.

6.2 What good silage depends on

  • Characteristics of the collected fodder:
    • dry matter;
    • soluble carbohydrates content; and
    • forage grass and legumes collected at defined growth stages.
  • Good silage depends on:
    • preparation conditions;
    • harvesting;
    • chopping (either by hand or mechanically);
    • additive and inoculants incorporation;
    • thorough mixing;
    • prompt bagging; and
    • anaerobic conditions:
    • it is essential to use perfectly airproof bags.

7. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies 

  • Fodder management: hay and silage making: ID 3579.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2488.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

9.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and can be adopted by any kind of manual-labour.

9.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology contributes to resources use efficiency and minimise forage spoilage.

9.3 Pro-poor technology

The production of high-quality silage during the dry season to feed livestock allows for the improvement of milk quality, leading to an increased source of income and food source.

entries.tittle: Improved cassava fufu processing methods, West Africa
entries.summary: The commercialisation of traditional processed products from cassava, such as fufu, potentially offers new opportunities for income generation to rural households in Nigeria, Ghana and other parts of West Africa. Several options exist for the commercialisation of fufu, including the production of a shelf-stable product? This minimises the use of scarce water resources but maximises returns in a growing urban market. Women particularly stand to gain since they use proceeds from fufu sales as stepping stones to other entrepreneurial activities. However, linkages between processors and sellers are very important.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Cassava (Manihot esculenta) production in Nigeria is estimated to be 34 million tonnes per year and has dramatically increased since 1986.
  • Fufu is a submerged fermented product that is traditionally produced as a wet paste.
  • The cooked wet paste is also marketed.
  • The shelf-life of the cooked and uncooked product is short (about seven days).
  • Tapioca is a roasted granular product from cassava starch that is widely acceptable, but is currently only produced on a very small scale.

2. Background

  • Wet paste processing takes place on a larger scale than the production of the ready-to-eat fufu; provides higher incomes for processing families; and is closely tied to urban markets.
    • Market-oriented fufu processing is carried out in both rural and urban contexts.
    • Primary processing, which entails transforming fresh roots into a wet paste, essentially takes place in villages or small towns located within important cassava production areas.
    • Secondary processing on a commercial scale, consisting of cooking the ready-to-eat fufu balls from the wet paste for market sale, gains importance as distances to medium and large consumption centres become shorter.
    • Because the wet paste is easier and less costly to handle and transport than the ready-to-eat product, it is usually processed further away from major consumption centres.
  • Overall, however, neither the wet paste nor the ready-to-eat product can be processed in a cost-effective manner far from consumption centres.
    • Following changing habits of consumers and the current wave of urbanization in Nigeria, there is a need for the promotion of commercialization of traditional foods such as processed cassava.
  • In 1996 the Government of Nigeria set up a Vision 2010 Committee to develop long-term plans for national development.
    • The science/agriculture sub-committee of this group recommended the need for the development of small and medium scale enterprises in food and agro-allied sectors.
    • The Family Economic Advancement Programme of the Presidency and the Agricultural Development Committee in Ogun State emphasized the need to commercialise traditional food processing technologies as a means of developing the rural areas of the country.
  • During consultation by the Global Cassava Development Strategy, Nigerian and Ghanaian representatives ranked the commercialisation of traditional cassava products as the most important market opportunity that these countries should address.
    • Fufu processing makes an important contribution to household security.
    • It is estimated that the largest scale wet paste processors who sell at Lagos earn up to USD 3 360 per month, although a more common income is in the range of USD 196 to 378.
    • These figures do not reveal the overall level of profit.
    • Even wet paste processors further from market points who do not sell directly at Lagos but rely on intermediaries or intermediary markets can earn up to USD 390 per month.
    • Monthly production ranges from eight to 480 bags weighing 60 kg each.

3. Constraints and opportunities in fufu processing

  • Women processors describe fufu processing as a flexible activity that can be taken up easily with little investment. It can, therefore, be used to raise money as a precursor to venturing into other livelihood pursuits.
    • It can be seen as a stepping stone to more lucrative enterprises.
    • The main livelihood constraint for these producers is the need to expand demand for cassava production as a means of maintaining and enhancing family incomes.
  • The key constraints to are unavailability of cassava roots, shortage of water and competition due to the increase in the number of new entrants.
    • Several factors interact to prevent significant scaling-up of individual fufu processing and marketing activities.
    • These include:
      • financial resource constraints;
      • the difficulties and cost of procuring large amounts of fresh cassava;
      • the lack of mechanised fufu processing technologies; and
      • the impossibility of storing fufu for reasonable periods of time due to product perishability.
  • The latter is an especially important constraint, since it forces processors and traders to be conservative in the quantities produced and purchased for sale.
    • Despite this, aggregate volumes leaving each fufu processing location can be quite significant in view of the large number of people involved in this activity.
    • Efforts to improve fufu processing should focus on locations that produce wet paste.
    • This is because the wet paste production and marketing system has the widest impact on local livelihoods.

4. Improved fufu processing methods

Fufu is prepared by peeling roots, washing, cutting into pieces and steeping in water to ferment for three to four days. The fermented mash is pounded or simply washed over a fine sieve to remove fibre and the water expelled from the starch extract by pressing through muslin cloth to produce fufu. Its short shelf life renders it highly perishable and limits its suitability for large-scale processors (TOMLINS et al 2002). The modified processing method has the primary advantage of reducing the amount of water used.

Three features distinguish modified methods of fufu processing from the traditional method:

  • grating of cassava roots after three days of submerged fermentation using a mechanical grater;
  • a second stage of solid state fermentation (this can be described as “double fermentation”); and
  • sieving with very small amounts of water.

5. Use of surface water tanks for fermentations

  • The construction of surface tanks facilitates the soaking of cassava roots and can increase the volume of fufu processed per cycle.
  • Different types of tank can be constructed, but the most efficient are those with accessible stoppers or taps to control water flow and drain off, and those with effective drainage areas.
  • These save on the time and drudgery involved in emptying the tanks by hand.
  • They can be accessed by processors themselves or rented from service providers.
  • For more on the fermentation process see Achi and Akomas (2006).

6. Twin layers of packaging

  • A double packaging method extends the shelf life of the wet paste and maintains the hygiene of the product.
  • The packaging materials used include polythene bags and high density polythene cling film.
  • Fufu samples are contained in the cling film and placed in the polythene bag and then tied and sown with needle and thread.
  • There is no significant decline in quality; up to about seven weeks of storage under ambient conditions of 30°C ± 2°C.

7. Drying

  • A practical approach to improving the shelf life and marketability of fufu is the production of a dried product.
    • The optimum conditions for drying of fufu are 65°C, 4 m per s airflow and 60% RH, though an airflow of 2 m per s produces fufu of highest organoleptic acceptance.
  • Fufu can be dried using three different methods, namely sun, cabinet or rotary drying.
    • Drying at rural or domestic level cannot be done mechanically because of the high capital investment in equipment and energy required and so open sun drying is preferable.
    • However, sun drying is beset by several inherent drawbacks such as susceptibility to damage due to inclement weather, slow drying rates and contamination.
  • Because of these limitations and the high cost and low utilization of more efficient traditional dryers, the adoption of a modified sun drying process called solar drying can be used for drying of fufu in rural areas.
    • If, instead, a controllable source of energy is used, the method is referred to as artificial or mechanical drying.
  • Artificial drying can be done using electricity, renewable fuels or fossils fuels, or combinations thereof.
    • Nigerian consumers are ready to buy fufu flour made with a locally fabricated rotary dryer that can be fired by charcoal or gas and rotated manually or electrically.
    • The dryer consists of an insulated drying chamber with a heating element beneath.
  • Wet fufu cake is dried at 135 °C for 30 minutes with a loading density of 5 kg per m².
    • After drying, the fufu is milled and assessed for quality.
    • Rotary dried fufu is the most preferred in sensory evaluation studies by 300 consumers.

8. Additional considerations

  • Technological validation has been established.
    • However economic and financial validation is yet to be done.
    • However, an additional and broader European Commission funded project is building on and extending the work carried out by this project.
    • If the potential to absorb increased output of the “double fermented” product is confirmed, the use of processing techniques to produce this form of fufu should be promoted, particularly at locations that have problems with water supplies.
    • This may involve linking processors with appropriate traders.
  • New, capital intensive technical interventions aimed at commercialising fufu, if found to be technically and economically feasible, could most easily be targeted at large scale processors.
    • They have substantial financial capital and appear to be interested in expanding their activities.
    • However, there is a risk that this approach may provide more direct advantages to richer members of the community (although, of course, more employment opportunities may be created).
    • Efforts can be made to encourage the participation of less elite groups, by utilising the co-operative mechanisms for pooling resources.
  • While market access may not be an issue for processors in the studied locations, it may represent a significant barrier to entry into commercial fufu processing for many who are currently not involved in such activity.
    • This is because of remoteness or failure to nurture direct relationships with specific buyers.
    • Given the extremely perishable nature of the product, easy and regular access to markets is a fundamental precondition if market-oriented fufu processing is to occur.
    • Moreover, it is unclear whether the market is at present able to accommodate significant and widespread increases in fufu supplies.
  • Whilst it is possible to ascertain that the market for wet paste and the ready-to-eat product as a whole has not contracted in the recent past, there is no evidence that it is expanding at a significant pace.
  • Similarly, although prices at different levels in the marketing chain do not seem to have followed a declining trend, there is no indication of dramatic increases.
  • Finally, contradictory perceptions amongst different operators regarding market trends indicates that different locations and different market participants within the same location may be facing variable experiences with respect to demand and prices.
    • The highly perishable nature of both the wet paste and the ready-to-eat fufu is a recurrent and cross cutting issue.
  • On the demand side, the extremely limited storage possibilities reduce the convenience of fufu to traders and consumers, thereby restricting market size and limiting the potential for demand growth.
    • On the supply side, processors must be cautious not to expand the size of their operations beyond a point at which unsold inventories and product spoilage can become a recurring phenomenon, resulting in heavy financial losses.
    • Finally, the short shelf life of fufu has clear negative effects on the prices and margins that processors and many assembly traders are able to command.
  • Although the case for developing a shelf-stable form of fufu that could be stored by processors, traders and consumers over a longer time period has been established, great care must be taken when evaluating this option and the rationale for introducing it.
    • More specifically, the feasibility of developing market-oriented fufu flour production amongst relatively small-scale processors, the dissemination of appropriate technologies, and the development of market linkages are issues that deserve careful analysis.

9. Potential risks

  • It can be difficult to reproduce the required conditions when implementing a technology in a real-life context.
  • Therefore, it would be advisable, when assessing fresh-state preservation, to consider limiting the period to three weeks approximately.

10. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

11. Related/associated technologies

  • Make bitter cassava safe for consumption: ID 4372.
  • Storage and preservation of wet cassava: ID 4520.
  • Production of high quality cassava flour: ID 4574.
  • Sustainable livelihoods: new market opportunities for cassava: ID 4575.
  • Production of glucose syrup from high quality cassava flour: ID 4576.

12. Objectives fulfilled by the project

12.1 Women friendly

Women processors describe fufu processing as a flexible activity that can be taken up easily with little investment.

12.2 Pro-poor technology

Implementing this technology helps farmers sustain their income.

entries.tittle: Soil Fertility for Sustainable Vegetable Production: Green and Animal Manures in the Humid Forest Belt in Ghana
entries.summary: Dry-season vegetable farmers in Ghana face increased dependency on chemical fertilizer and supplementary water inputs due to decreased soil productivity caused by prolonged cultivation that has mined the soil's previously high organic matter content. Farmers also complain of increased incidence of pests and diseases. These factors increase capital and labour costs and risks associated with production. Use of green and animal manures and composts provides a low-cost alternative to chemical fertilizers, replacing, or used in conjunction with purchased inputs. Increased organic matter content also improve longer-term soil productivity, and water-retention capacity. These techniques provide sustainable ways of intensifying cropping in a region where increasing population pressure challenges the sustainability of traditional long duration fallow-based systems.
entries.description:
Description

The amelioration of soil chemical and physical properties by incorporating organic matter influences crop growth through increasing the supply and availability of plant nutrients and water, improving conditions for root growth, and reducing loss of nutrients and water through leaching, surface erosion and evaporation. A broad view, considering the effects on both soil physical and chemical properties, is needed to assess the overall impact of such soil ameliorants. Different cover crops, green manures, crop residues, composts and animal manures are appropriate depending on the relative importance of biological tillage, nitrogen addition, total organic matter addition, speed of decomposition and the nature of the following crop.

1. Cultivation and incorporation of green manures

  • Information exists on the cultivation and incorporation of green manures and cover crops within farming systems.
    • Sufficient information is available to select species likely to flourish under various conditions.
    • Actual testing of green manure species in Ghana was, however, a new research undertaken.
    • A range of composting and manuring techniques suited to vegetable production are known, some involving the direct application of organic matter to the soil. In others, intermediate processing of materials is required before application.
    • The incorporation of green manures is an example of direct application, as is basket composting (composting directly adjacent to plant growth).
    • Animal, particularly ruminant, manures and already decomposed composts have already undergone intermediate processing by microbes and contain nutrients in a form usually more readily available to plants than those when organic matter is applied directly.
  • There is potential for the addition of inorganic Nitrogen sources to organic residues in order to reduce initial reduction in nitrate availability.
    • Little formal research has yet been reported on the combined use of organic composts with inorganic fertilizers, yet its widespread practice among farmers is beginning to be documented.
    • The study described here assessed the potential of green manures, animal manures and compost made from locally available sources of organic matter as soil ameliorants in Ghana.
    • These were investigated on their ability to reduce the requirement for, and increase the efficient use of, inorganic fertilizers and water, to increase soil organic matter, improve crop production, crop quality, and quality during post-harvest handling.
    • The impact of the new technologies on the financial risk involved in dry season vegetable production was also analysed.

2. Vegetable cultivation in Ghana

  • The very variable profiles of vegetable cultivators, in terms of age, land ownership, gender, use of bought inputs and involvement in other agricultural activities, reflect the different backgrounds from which they have emerged.
  • Before 1970, vegetable production in Ghana was mainly small scale and predominantly for home consumption. The establishment of local markets in the 1970s and 1980s enabled farmers, principally women farmers, to sell surplus vegetables for cash and this became an increasingly important form of income generation.
  • Successive droughts during this same period were a precursor to devastating bush and forest fires throughout Ghana in 1983, which destroyed many of the smallholder cocoa farms in Brong Ahafo region.
  • Cocoa was the main cash crop at that time.
    • Since cocoa prices were already low and erratic, farmers were reluctant to invest again in cocoa re-planting with its long gestation period, and turned instead to horticulture.
    • Thus, the commonly marketed vegetables, tomatoes (Lycopersicon lycopersicum), garden eggs (Solanum aethiopicum), okra (Hibiscus esculentus), onion (Allium cepa) and chilli peppers (Capsicum fructescens) began to be cultivated for sale in both wet and dry seasons by these commercially-orientated farmers.
  • The lack of employment opportunities for school leavers and young men has since resulted in the development of a second group of commercial producers, investing both in the hiring of land and high levels of inputs into the crops grown exclusively for sale.

3. Outcomes

  • From the first village meetings and farmer surveys it became apparent that mulching in the dry season was not a suitable technology to introduce at present because of the continuing practice of burning by bush meat hunters and high risk from accidental fires during the dry season.
  • The first surveys also identified high input costs, water availability and labour costs/availability as the key constraints to dry season vegetable production.
  • As compost making involves considerable labour inputs it was decided to first introduce the use of animal manures as organic fertilizers.
  • Some labour would be required for manure collection, but with a greater concentration of nutrients than compost, volume for volume, they would give a better return to labour invested.
  • Sufficient sources of animal manure were found to be available locally for on-station and on-farm trials to be initiated.

4. Animal manures

  • Sheep manure and the combination of sheep manure with poultry manure has produced the best yields and quality of fruits in on - station trials.
    • However, the cost/benefit analysis conducted by farmers found cow, poultry and a combination of cow and poultry manure more profitable than sheep/goat manure and mixtures of these with poultry manure.
    • Such findings highlight the importance of availability and labour implication in farmer’s selection and preference for techniques.
    • Cost/benefit analyses (CBA), demonstrated that gains can be made in returns to production through improved quality of the product and by reducing costs involved in production through use of organic manures and reducing the purchase of fertilizers.
    • Use of animal manures was a successful introduction to the use of organic wastes to enhance soil productivity and interest has now been generated by farmers to make compost.
    • Such a practice will allow sufficient production by all cultivators, making the best use of scarce animal manure as an active component in the composting process.
  • Recommended rates of manure usage were worked out on a per plant basis and as a volumetric measure of air dried manure.
    • This was to accommodate farmer’s use of different planting distances and practice of fertilizer application by volumetric measure to individual plants.
    • For plants grown at a recommended spacing of 90 cm x 30 cm (Ministry of Food and Agriculture recommendations, tomato), this equates to a rate of 33 tonne per ha of cow dung, 19 tonne per ha of sheep manure and 11 tonne per ha of air-dried poultry manure.
    • Some farmers preferred to apply the manure into a trench and incorporate before transplanting seedlings.
    • Others applied the manure in a ring around the plant after transplanting.
    • Farmers tended to prefer using poultry manure because less volume was required for the same fertilising effect and therefore less labour was involved in porterage.
    • However, farmers found negative growth effects from use of too much, or too fresh, poultry manure.
  • The manures were applied in a ring around each plant in the following quantities:
    • 100 percent manure = 490 g air dried manure (1 full peak powdered milk tin for cow manure)
    • 75 percent manure = 368 g and 25 percent NPK (= 25 percent of match box = 5 g)
    • 50 percent manure = 245 g and 50 percent NPK (= 10 g)
    • 100 percent NPK (23-15-5) = 20 g
  • Optimum levels of manure to apply were found to be in approximate 50:50 combinations of manure and chemical fertilizer for both maximizing total fruit weight and fruit number.
    • All four manure types, sheep, poultry, goat and cow showed similar response curves (Figures 1 and 2).
    • Commercial farmers, however, sell their produce by volume, rather than weight.
    • These farmers therefore are looking to produce large-sized fruit, as these “fill crates more quickly”.
    • The data was further investigated to determine the relationship between manure application and fruit size.
    • This proved inconclusive due to the nature of relationship between average fruit size and manure application.
    • Both low and high applications produced larger fruit than the 50:50 mixture.
    • Fruit quality, as assessed by farmers and as measured during shelf-life tests, was found to increase significantly with the application of animal manures.
    • For further details, including tables, figures and additional information see Section 4 in Jackson (2001).

5. Green manures

  • Of the several green manures tested over a three-year period, trial results and farmer evaluations indicate that Mucuna pruriens and Canavalia ensiformis were the most suitable in terms of biomass production, effect as a green manure and suitability to the cropping systems.
  • The was a difference of interest in green manures which may be due to different reasons.
    • The green manure species/varieties that were tested on-farm did not grow well in water-logged conditions.
      • Waterlogging is much less likely to occur in the upland areas, whereas the risk of waterlogging is much higher on the valley bottom farms.
    • Green manures led to better soil moisture retention, which was obviously more important in the drier upland areas.
      • The particular popularity of Mucuna probably reflected the fact that the farmers perceived Mucuna to be the best at conserving moisture in the soil.
      • Farmers particularly mentioned the moist, friable nature of soils under the Mucuna crop, compared to that under other species, or normal fallow vegetation.
      • Crotalaria spp (species not specified) were liked by farmers because of the very tender nature of the stems that allowed it to be incorporated into the soil with much less effort than the other species.
      • Its potential suppressing effect on root nematodes was also of great interest to the farmers, who suffer greatly from these pests (the effects of nematode-suppressive root bacteria not verified in the field).
      • The usual control method of using rotations was difficult to practice because of trader pressure to specialize in a single vegetable species in a given location.
  • Quantification and comparison of the cost (labour and financial) and the benefits (financial income) associated with using green manures and animal manures was done in relation to farmers’ normal practice for dry season tomato production.
    • It was decided to consider labour and financial costs separately, rather than assigning an opportunity cost to labour and conducting a single analysis, because an aggregate measure of “net benefit” does not fit with farmers’ decision- making.
    • The farmers tend to consider financial profitability and labour inputs as separate factors, and the extent to which labour requirements affect a farmer’s interest in a technique varies between farmers and over time.
    • With the exception of the Bepoyease site, the increase in labour inputs associated with use of green manures, when considered as a proportion of total labour requirements over the cropping season, was not as great as initially thought from talking with farmers.
    • In proportionate terms, the labour requirements for using green manures and animal manures appeared to be similar.
    • This suggested that the problem for farmers appeared to be associated with the type rather than absolute amount of work involved, in the sense that the cutting and incorporation of green manures was seen to be “very tedious” work.
  • At the Bepoyease site, the use of both green and animal manures entailed a substantial proportionate increase in labour requirements over and above requirements associated with their normal practice.
    • This was because of the different production methods used by farmers in Bepoyease, and the lower level of commercialization.
    • Farmers in Bepoyease did not normally ridge, but they have been ridging as part of the process of incorporating green manures, so ridging was considered an extra task.
    • Moreover, some farmers in Bepoyease calculated their costs based on planting the tomato crop straight after the harvest of the minor season maize crop, when there was still residual moisture in the soil and little land clearing was required.
    • This system/timing meant that labour inputs were considerably reduced (no watering or land clearing).
    • Finally, Bepoyease farmers used fewer inputs (fertilizer and pesticides) than farmers in the other three villages, so again time spent on these activities was much reduced.
  • The use of green and animal manures could actually increase overall financial costs of production when farmers hire labour.
    • The increased labour requirements were translated into increased financial costs which may outweigh the savings in reduced inputs of inorganic fertilizers.
    • Nevertheless, with the exception once again of Bepoyease, as a proportion of overall production costs throughout the season, the increases were not substantial.
    • The reasons for the differences in the Bepoyease situation were similar to those mentioned under the discussion on labour inputs.
    • The proportionately high increases in financial costs associated with use of animal and green manures as compared to normal practice were partly to do with the fact that overall, absolute production costs were much lower.
    • Also, in the case of green manures, the higher costs were associated with extra labour requirements being greater than for the other villages because ridging did not usually take place under normal practice.
    • In a scenario where farmers did not hire any labour, e.g. where labour was not a financial cost, the use of green manures compared to normal practice led to a substantial reduction in financial costs of production, apart from in Bepoyease where costs remained the same.
    • This was because farmers considered that there were no extra financial costs associated with using green manures, but money normally spent on buying fertilizers could be saved.
  • In Akrobi and Bepoyease, financial costs actually increased as a result of using animal manures.
    • This was primarily due to costs they estimated for transporting the manure from the manure source to their farm.
    • There was considerable variation in costs associated with transport between the different villages.
    • This may partly reflect that in some cases the source of animal manure was very close, whereas in other cases farmers had to travel to the next village or town to collect it.
  • For further details, including tables, figures and additional information see Section 4 in Jackson (2001).

6. Quantifying benefits from improvements in product quality

  • Traders will typically pay full price (that agreed before harvest) for around 40 percent of the total produce bought.
  • They buy the remaining 60 percent at a discounted price ranging from around 40 percent to 100 percent of full quoted price, with the amount of the discount depending on the quality of fruit.
  • Comparison of the average quality scores indicated that all of the green and animal manures, with the exception of Sesbania, produced better quality fruit than the control treatments, as measured by the total quality scores.
  • What was even more striking was the comparison of the proportion of farmers who were producing tomatoes that were likely to be of a good enough quality to fetch the full quoted price per crate.
  • With the exception of Mucuna (light mottled) and Sesbania, for all the green manures and animal manures a minimum of 79 percent of the farmers were producing tomatoes of a quality that could fetch full price.
  • In the case of Crotalaria, cow manure, poultry manure, sheep/goat manure, and the mixture of cow and poultry manure, all of the farmers were producing tomatoes of a quality that could fetch full price.

7. Interpretation of findings

  • The data appear to reveal a number of clear patterns, in that all of the animal manure treatments were more profitable than either the green manures or farmers’ normal practice.
    • Of the animal manure treatments, the cow manure, poultry manure and the combined cow/poultry manure treatments were more profitable than sheep and goat manure and the sheep-goat and poultry manure mixture.
    • Of the green manure species, Canavalia and the Mucuna (dark mottled) proved to be significantly but not dramatically more profitable than farmers’ normal practice.
    • The use of the animal manure treatments appeared to reduce the risk of making a significant loss if market prices for tomatoes were low.
  • The extent to which farmers relied on hired labour on their dry season vegetable farms had a significant effect on financial profitability.
    • For example, if the price per crate was Cedis 20 000 and farmers hired labour, only three of the 16 farmers involved made a profit on Canavalia, whereas if the price was Cedis 20 000 and no use of hired labour, all of the 16 farmers made a profit.
    • However, with the exception of farmers in Bepoyease, the extent to which farmers hired labour did not have a significant impact on the relative performance of the different treatments.
    • The market price of tomatoes obviously had a very significant effect on overall profitability.
    • The findings from the cost/benefit analysis generally complemented findings from the qualitative assessment, although it would be difficult to explain the popularity of the green manures on the CBA results alone.
    • However, results of the qualitative assessment suggested that the existing CBA did not capture a number of demonstrated and potential cost-savings, as well as longer-term benefits, of using green manures, and this may to some extent explain the divergent implications.
  • A description of how results were disseminated and their impact, in follow up activities, can be found in two reports by Nsiah-Gyabaah (2002 and 2003).

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Sustainable agriculture in forest margins: ID 4524.
  • Cover crop species, with a special focus on legumes: ID 7414.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Resource use efficiency

The use of green and animal manures and composts are an alternative to chemical fertilizers and improve soil productivity, and water-retention capacity.

10.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology is low-cost, and through improved soil productivity and water retention, increases yields. This allows for additional sources of food and income
