entries.tittle: Incorporation of local knowledge into management interventions to minimize nutrient losses, Nepal
entries.summary: Between the elevations of 1 000 and 2 000 m in the mid-hills of Nepal, over 12 million people subsist on land-holdings of less than 0.5 hectare. Farmers rely on rainfall and organic manures for soil fertility maintenance. A declining soil fertility is of increasing concern in the Bari lands (upper slope rainfed crop terraces). However, nutrient losses due to leaching and erosion can be minimized by economically and culturally viable land, soil and water management techniques. This builds upon the sophisticated local knowledge of the movement of water across soil combined with existing scientific data, and promoting them through participatory approaches to the design of technologies.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • The hills of Nepal occupy about 51 percent of the total agricultural land of the country, and provide shelter to about 52 percent of the total population with an average agricultural land holding of less than 1 hectare.
    • The Middle Hills, between 1 000 to 2 000 m above sea level, occupy about 30 percent of the land area of Nepal.
    • The agricultural land holding in the hills is very small (about 46 percent of the population owning less than 0.5 hectare of land) and highly fragmented with about four parcels per holding.
    • Crops are cultivated mainly on rain-fed upland, locally called as bari land.
    • Bari land constitutes 64 percent (1 717 000 ha) of the cultivated land in Nepal, of which 61 percent lies in the Middle Hills alone.
    • The bari soils are particularly vulnerable to soil losses through a combination of natural factors, such as sloping topography; heavy seasonal rainfall; predominance of erosion prone soils; and human factors such as intensive cultivation of land and erosion-prone farming practices.
  • Soil loss through surface erosion from agricultural land in the hills varies from less than 2 tonne per ha yearly to as high as 105 tonne per ha yearly.
    • Nutrient losses through leaching, especially N and P, exceed those in runoff and soil erosion, in contradiction to the widely held belief that erosive losses are the major reason for the declining soil fertility and crop productivity in the Middle Hills of Nepal.
    • Background erosion is considered to be of importance during heavy rainfall events pre-monsoon in April/May on steep cultivated slopes and on low slopes because of high surface runoff.
    • Throughout the monsoon, as infiltration increases, significant nutrient losses occur through leaching on moderate and lower slopes or where runoff was controlled.
    • There has been little work done to understand the dynamics of soil erosion and leaching losses of nutrients in the bari land in Nepal.
    • Research and development efforts in generating management practices to control soil and nutrient losses from bari land so far have remained poor.
  • The availability and access to technological options that are effective in reducing such losses and those that suit farmers' needs and environments are limited.
    • Interventions that have been directed at controlling soil erosion, including Sloping Agricultural Land Technology (SALT), have not been widely adopted by farmers although they are effective in reducing surface runoff and controlling soil erosion.
    • This is largely due the technology development process not adequately considering and incorporating farmers' knowledge and practices, and their needs for soil and water management.
    • However, studies have established that farmers in the Middle Hills of Nepal possess good knowledge about the soil and water related ecological processes, and that they often make rational use of them to devise practices to combat the problem of soil erosion and declining soil fertility.

2. Process and technology development

  • A process and methodology was developed, through which technology options addressing a common constraint across a range of livelihood and biophysical circumstances, could be identified and evaluated.
    • Participatory field work was conducted in three communities.
      • Landruk (high altitude c. 5 500 m), high rainfall site with narrow terraces with 0 to 5 degree outward slope angles and sited on steep slopes.
      • Bandipur (mid-altitude c. 3 000 m), low to moderate rainfall site where the terraces tend to be about 3 to 5 m in width and slightly outwardly sloping, 0 to 4 °C being typical.
      • Nayatola, a mid altitude (c. 1 600 m) site with low to moderate rainfall.
    • These sites are in Palpa district, where large, steeply sloping terraces are predominant.
    • The terraces are so constructed because size of terrace is perceived as reflecting wealth and status in this area.
    • They contrast sharply with the flat to moderately sloped narrow terraces characteristic of most Middle Hill areas. In Nayatola terraces are likely to be 20 to 50 m wide, and characterized by slope angles of 20 to 35 °C.
    • At Landruk, maize is the principle crop and is intercropped with finger millet, bean, cowpeas or soybeans, and followed by wheat or barley in winter in alternate years.
    • In Bandipur, maize is the principle crop and is often intercropped with finger millet, bean, cowpeas or soybeans, with the majority of farmers keeping land fallow in the winter.
      • Some farmers also grow ghaiya (upland rice) in place of or mixed with maize.
      • This site also represents an orange growing area.
      • The young or newly established orchard is intercropped, with usually no intercropping done in old orchards.
    • At Nayatola, maize is the principle crop and is often intercropped with finger millet, bean, cowpeas or soybeans, followed by winter wheat, which is also intercropped with winter legumes and mustard.
  • Farmers' local knowledge and practices were combined with that of scientists' knowledge and findings, and supporting farmers' experimentation in developing soil and water management interventions.
    • The process included four stages; problem identification, knowledge analysis and sharing, farmers' experimentation, and participatory monitoring and evaluation.
    • Research findings Interventions to minimize nutrient loss Participatory research focussed on three sites, with farmers at each site developing and testing a range of interventions.
    • For details of each of the interventions, see McDonald, 2003.
    • The research findings, reported by Acharya et al. (2003) came to several conclusions.
      • The amount of nutrient loss through runoff is low, but significant amounts of N and P were lost through leaching.
        • Significant amounts of organic matter and available P were washed out along with sediment movements.
      • Strips of ginger and maize minimized soil loss and maximized net income from the sloping bari land.
        • This practice can be recommended to the farmers of other areas to minimize soil erosion.
      • Young citrus orchard followed by leguminous crop intercropping is beneficial in reducing soil loss as well as nutrient loss in predominantly citrus-growing areas.
  • Wide terraces are better for management of soil fertility as they have less runoff and less nutrient leaching.
  • Therefore, technical efforts should focus on trapping nutrients that are lost in solution through leaching and the use of barriers to reduce soil movement and nutrient losses in eroded sediments.
    • Incorporation of local knowledge It is generally recognized that the management of natural resources is best done by its users and that farmer-oriented strategies of natural resource management (NRM) are viable, productive, and sustainable.
    • This work on the participatory technology development process has, however, identified a number of issues that need to be considered in designing effective and sustainable farmer-oriented NRM strategies.
    • Some of the important considerations are summarized below.
    • For a full description of the participatory process and findings, see Shrestha et al (2003).
      • Farmer-oriented NRM should consider farmers' local knowledge and practices and incorporate them explicitly into a PTD process that gives farmers a leading role in all stages of decision-making.
        • This, in turn, ensures a process of learning and empowerment.
      • Building on farmers' knowledge and practices, sharing technical knowledge, and supporting farmers in their experimentation empowers farmers and the farming community and strengthens their social capital.
        • This is particularly important in achieving sustainable NRM.
      • Research and development endeavours in NRM should be process-oriented allowing changes to be made as they progress, to enable adaptation of management options to local environments and situations.
  • This experience of participatory technology development on soil and water management strongly suggests that farmers are interested in NRM practices and interventions that start generating economic benefit very quickly.
    • Therefore, ecosystem services should be tied with productivity enhancement.
    • Farmers' priorities, or highly productive areas with income maximization potential, should be used as entry points for promoting NRM interventions.
    • In the current case, farmers were interested in grasses and forage species not only because these were effective against soil and nutrient losses, but largely because they provided increased and quality fodder for their animals.
  • Consideration of equity issues in NRM is important but should not be imposed from outside.
    • It should be internalized through the involvement of the community.
    • It has been seen that resource-poor farmers do not generally participate in the beginning of a new initiative to minimize their risk, but they will often join later when they see the benefits.
  • Interventions for NRM should be system compatible and harness niche opportunities.
    • In the current work on soil and water management, hedgerows on the outer boundary of the bench terrace were not preferred by some farmers as they replaced soybean and beans.
    • Similarly, farmers at Nayatola research site preferred to integrate orange and coffee along the hedgerow as the site had a good niche for production as well as marketing for these crops.
  • Consideration of the scales of operation is equally important.
    • Management of natural resources, initiated at farm or farmer level, often requires consideration at watershed and/or community level.
    • In the current work on soil and water management, farmers were found to be aware of the benefit of diverting runoff from the cultivated land but most of them were not practising it.
    • This required constructing a network of diversion channels at watershed level, and community action to initiate and complete the construction.
  • The management of natural resources often requires long-term decision-making and investments by farmers and by the farming community and therefore, a long-term commitment from research and development institutions involved in the process.
  • Understanding farmers' knowledge and farming practices lays a firm foundation for the initiation of PTD in soil and water management.
    • The experiences of incorporating farmers' local knowledge into the PTD process for developing soil and water management interventions in the middle hills of Nepal suggest that the process is powerful in understanding farmers' knowledge and the rationale behind their practices.
      • In identifying locally suitable soil and water management interventions and in motivating and empowering farmers to experiment with new interventions by themselves.
    • Sharing of scientific knowledge and understanding of the ecological processes with farmers and the farming community and exposing farmers to research and demonstration sites helps them to visualize the positive and negative aspects of their practices and conceptualize the new interventions and motivates them to undertake their own research.
    • Such motivation is even higher when they are provided with technical and material support from outside.
  • The partnership and collaboration between farmers and scientists appears to better target research and produce more useful outputs than research done by farmers or by scientists in isolation.
    • Involving farming communities, including village leaders, at various stages of the technology development process ensures their continued support in the smooth running of the research activities.
    • The farming community and village leaders also feel an obligation to keep an eye on the process and provide feedback for further improvement.
    • Similarly, their involvement in the selection of research farmers imparts the notion that these farmers represent the community and so should be committed to their experiment and share information and findings with other farmers in the community.
    • The participatory technology development approach used here appears to have been more effective in disseminating information and new interventions from research farmers to non-research farmers in the community than the conventional research method.
    • Extending adoption and/or adaptation and scaling up of the new interventions within and outside the research communities, however, needs long-term support and collaboration between research farmers, scientists, and development agencies.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cold; and
  • temperate, cool.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Cover crop species, with a special focus on legumes: ID 7414.
  • Participatory varietal selection: short duration legume crops for rainfed rabi in India and Nepal: ID 4584.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology, by detailing economically and culturally viable land, soil and water management techniques, prevents nutrient losses due to leaching and erosion.

entries.tittle: Making farm inputs available in small size packages to increase farmers' yields, Africa
entries.summary: Farm inputs such as improved seeds, fertilizers, and herbicides are conventionally packaged in large bag sizes that are beyond the financial means of small farmers. The technology demonstrates ways of mobilizing the private sector to make small quantities of appropriate inputs available in mini-packs. It also demonstrates novel ways of promoting these packages so that farmers can try them out on their own plots and, having "learnt by doing", are encouraged to invest in progressively larger packs as they see the returns on soil fertility, food security and marketable products.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

Maize is one of the most important staple foods in sub-Saharan Africa. Production is mostly well below potential and demand threatens to outstrip local supplies. For instance, in the Embu and Kirinyaga districts of Kenya, maize varieties with a yield potential of 5 to 10 tonnes per ha are available on the market but yields produced by small farmers are in the range of 0.5 to 1.0 tonnes per ha. The increasing pressure on land, resulting from a rapidly increasing population, means there is an urgent need to increase yields per hectare of cultivated maize.

2. Biophysical constraints to improved crop production

  • There are three major biophysical constraints to improved crop production.
    1. Firstly, soil fertility is very low, with nitrogen and phosphorus deficiencies widespread.
      • Low levels of fertilizer use also results in the depletion of other nutrients such as potassium and sulphur.
    2. Secondly, the maize streak virus (MSV) is prevalent resulting in up to 80 percent loss of yield in non-tolerant varieties.
    3. Thirdly, crops suffer from competition from weeds due to ineffective and late weeding often caused by poor availability of labour.

3. Farm inputs

  • Appropriate farm input use to increase yields is essential to increase yields.
    • Appropriate fertilizers, containing the right blend of plant nutrients, are required to alleviate the nutrient deficiency constraints.
    • Disease-tolerant high-yielding maize varieties are required to maximise crop response to nutrient inputs, and herbicides are required to control weeds whilst saving labour.
  • However, inputs are conventionally packaged in large bag sizes which are beyond the financial means of the vast majority of small farmers who survive on an income of the equivalent of about USD 1 per day.
    • For example fertilizers are conventionally packaged in 50 kg bags, which cost the equivalent of USD 25.
    • Previous research carried out in western Kenya by the project leaders Farm Input Promotions Africa (FIPS) had shown that smallscale farmers are keen to purchase small quantities of appropriate fertilizers, and improved seeds, in mini-packs costing as little as 3 Ksh (USD 0.05 cents).
  • Farmers try these out on their own plots of land and, having “learn by doing”, return to their nearest stockist to purchase progressively larger packs as they see the returns on soil fertility, food security and marketable surplus.
    • Use of this methodology dramatically increased the demand for farm inputs amongst the poorest small-scale farmers in Kenya.
    • A research project, examining improved access to appropriate farm inputs (see Blackie and Albright, 2005), showed how close co-operation with the private sector could be achieved.
    • This was so as to make the appropriate fertilizers, maize varieties, and herbicides more accessible to smallscale farmers in the Embu and Kirinyaga districts.
  • This project also investigated herbicide use for crop protection within the framework of integrated crop management for soil and water conservation.
    • Previous work had identified labour constraints in land preparation and subsequent weeding as the most limiting factor in maize production.
    • It also showed that controlling weeds by using herbicides resulted in significant reduction of labour requirement and also significantly increased maize yields.
    • For further information see Terry, 2002.
  • Improving the accessibility of farm inputs technology to address the constraints of poor soil fertility, high weed infestation, and Maize Streak Virus (MSV) is thus available, but not accessible to small-scale farmers.
    • Working in cooperation with the private sector, FIPS-Africa staff promoted small packets of improved fertilizer (1 kg), and improved MSV-tolerant maize varieties through local stockists.
    • Having experimented with these small packets, small farmers return to the stockists to purchase larger quantities of these inputs to improve their food security.
    • The key to the success of the project has been close co-operation with the private sector.
    • Co-operators
      • Athi River Mining (ARM), which has developed two improved fertilizers (Mavuno planting; Mavuno topdressing) packaged in 1 kg bags, and distributed them to stockists at project sites for FIPS-Africa's promotions.
        • ARM also provided FIPS Africa with funds to employ three staff members to extend the range of the project´s activities to other districts (Nairobi, Kiambu, Thika, Murang’a, Nyeri and Meru districts)
      • Western Seed Co. (WSC), which has provided FIPS Africa with 30 000 small packets (150g) of seeds free-of-charge for its promotions.
        • Varieties are MSV-tolerant (WH505, WH403, WS202) and have been performing outstandingly in FIPS Africa´s demonstration plots.
      • Pannar (PAN 67), Freshco (KH 500-21A), Monsanto (DK 8071, DK 8051, DK 8031), and Seedco have also donated MSV-tolerant varieties to FIPS-Africa free of charge for demonstrations.
  • A promotion concept was developed in which a mini-pack of 150 g seed of a MSV-tolerant variety was given to farmers when purchasing 1 kg of new Mavuno fertilizer.
    • A total of 60,000 seed mini-packs of improved varieties and 60 000 x 1 kg packs of Mavuno were promoted through a network of 43 stockists, reaching about 20 000 farmers.
    • Subsequent visits to farmers who purchased the promotional package showed exceptional crop performance in areas with adequate rainfall, and improved performance over conventional cropping practices in drought-affected areas.
    • As a result, demand for the Mavuno fertilizers, and MSV-tolerant varieties (WH505, WH403, WS202) from WSC rapidly increased.
    • By the end of March 2005, FIPS-Africa had catalyzed the supply of over 100 tonnes of Mavuno fertilizer.
    • Consumption would have been much higher as farmers’ demands frequently exceeded ARM´s capacity to supply.
    • Consequently, ARM invested USD 6 million to increase its production from 3 000 tonnes to 50 000 tonnes fertilizer/year.
    • In addition, FIPS-Africa also catalyzed the supply of 6.5 tonnes of WSC’s MSV-tolerant maize varieties.
  • Further work in the Embu/Kirinyaga districts refined the promotion methodology by developing a food security input package, and a strategy for the dissemination of glyphosate (Roundup) herbicide in small sachets.
    • Promotion of MSV-tolerant varieties and improved fertilizers was extended into neighbouring districts (Meru and Nyeri).
    • Following requests from seed and fertilizer companies in Tanzania, FIPS Africa extended its promotion methodology to assist the dissemination of disease-tolerant maize varieties;
    • This was done through the project “Improving farmer access to and management of disease resistant maize cultivars in the Southern Highlands of Tanzania”,  and pest-tolerant bean varieties (project R7955).
  • Co-operation with this project enabled farmers to experiment with mini-packs of beans varieties in Kenya.
    • An independent impact assessment conducted in the Embu and Kirinyaga districts found increases in food security amongst farmers who had adopted the use of MSV-tolerant maize varieties.
    • There was also improved fertilizers promoted by FIPS-Africa under project R8212.
  • A subsequent survey in 2004/5 of 100 farmers by FIPS-Africa showed that the number of food secure families increased from 30 to 80 percent.
    • The extra quantity of maize produced per farmer was on average 5.65 bags x 90 kg bags equivalent to KSh 6 780.
    • In addition, in cooperation with Western Seed Co. (WSC) and Monsanto, 15 000 x 150 g mini-packs of MSV-tolerant varieties (WH502, WH403, WS202, DK8031) were distributed to farmers in the target districts.
  • FIPS-Africa developed the 60 seed pack of maize to help farmers experiment with smaller quantities of seeds.
    • It also developed the Participatory Roadside Demonstration, comprising a very small package of inputs designed to teach farmers how to grow good maize with an improved MSV-tolerant variety.
    • The package consists of a 60 seed pack of maize, 150 g of planting fertilizer, and 150 g of topdressing fertilizer, and is designed for a small plot of 6 m x 2.5 m.
    • The plot is placed along the road (6 m road frontage) to attract the interest of passers-by.
  • At the time the demo wa laid out, the farmer was asked to call ten of her neighbouring farmers who received instructions on how to plant correctly.
    • In the 2005 long rainy season, over 800 farmers conducted the Roadside demo, and approximately 10 000 neighbouring farmers received training during the mini-field days.
    • At the mini-field days, farmers were given a 60 seed pack of maize to take back to their farms.
    • Because plots are so small, up to ten demos can be laid out in a day by one person.
    • The method therefore has the potential to reach many thousands of farmers in a season.
  • Other methods included the 30 seed mini-pack of KB-9 bean seed, Food Security Input Package, and Village Approach.
    • KARI continued to promote conservation tillage through Farmer Field Schools.
    • FIPS-Africa, with co-operation of Monsanto, developed a new method for promotion of herbicides.
    • Approximately 3 000 farmers were visited and glyphosate (Roundup Max) herbicide demonstrated on a small 5 m x 10 m plot.
    • A survey of 118 farmers found that 70 percent of farmers returned to their stockist to purchase commercial 100 g sachets of the herbicide.
  • As a result of FIPS-Africa’s promotions, the quantity of MSV-tolerant maize varieties sold through stockists in the Nyeri district increased from 1.84 tonnes in 2004 to 39.62 tonnes in 2005.
    • Also, sales of Mavuno fertilizers increased more than ten times from 43.5 in 2004 to 473.5 tonnes in 2005.
    • In the Meru district, sales of Mavuno fertilizers also greatly increased from 55 tonnes in 2004 to 425.5 tonnes in 2005.
    • A survey of 73 farmers in the Nyeri district who had received a mini-pack of a variety from WSC, and had subsequently purchased WSC varieties, showed that on average they produced an extra 5.2 kg x 90 kg bags of maize with a value of KSh 6224.
  • The number of farmers who attained the food security target of at least five bags per season increased from 32 percent before FIPS-Africa’s intervention to 73 percent in the 2005 long rains season.
    • In Tanzania, lack of access to the appropriate farm inputs, especially fertilizer, limits productivity of small farmers.
    • A survey in the S. Highlands showed that stockists invariably repackaged inputs into smaller pack sizes.
    • FIPS-Africa worked with Minjingu Mines and Fertilizer Co.(MMFC) to develop a new fertilizer (Minjingu Mazao), and with Kibo Seed Co., distributors of Mavuno fertilizers, to develop a new promotion package.
      • A 2 g packet of vegetable seed was given to farmers for free when purchasing a 1 kg pack of Mavuno fertilizer.
  • FIPS-Africa worked with other CPP projects to promote their project outputs.
    • Demonstrations of Minjingu Mazao on beans were established with CIAT in the N. Highlands (R7955) and on disease-tolerant maize varieties with ARI Uyole in the S. Highlands (R8220).
    • The new fertilizer increased yields of beans by a factor of two to three.
    • MMFC has agreed to make available 20 tonnes of the new fertilizer in small packs to meet the demand from farmers in the 2006 long rain season.

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Farmer field schools on integrated plant nutrient systems: ID 7527.
  • Integrated pest management: ID 7298.
  • Risk reduction while manipulating pesticides: ID 8348.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

The practice, through farm input packages, promotes food security and income generation for poor households.

entries.tittle: Development and promotion of community - based seed production of groundnut Rosette disease - resistant varieties, Uganda
entries.summary:
Groundnuts play a key role as a subsistence food source for poor people in the districts in northeastern Uganda, where the “Teso” system of agriculture is practiced. The crop is a valuable source of protein and oil and thus makes a significant contribution to people’s nutritional requirements. With a decline in the production of traditional cash crops such as cotton, groundnuts are now also gaining increasing importance as a cash crop.

A needs assessment, funded by DFID in February 1998, identified rosette disease as the most important general or pest and disease problem on groundnuts both by farmers and the Serere Agricultural and Animal Production Research Institute (SAARI). This technology describes ways in which community seed production of groundnut rosette-resistant varieties were promoted and out-scaled in Uganda, through farmer-led production groups.
entries.description:
Description

A needs assessment, funded by DFID in February 1998, identified rosette disease as the most important general or pest and disease problem on groundnuts both by farmers and Serere Agricultural and Animal production Research Institute (SAARI).

1. Rosette disease-resistant groundnut varieties

  • Host-plant resistance is considered to be the most cost-effective management measure against rosette disease because farmers seldom adopt cultural or chemical control practices owing to lack of resources, labour constraints, differing crop priorities and other factors.
    • Rosette resistance was originally identified in groundnut germplasm originating from West Africa.
    • From this material, late-maturing Rosette-resistant genotypes were developed (such as RMP 12 and RG1).
    • However, few farmers adopted these lines because they required a long growing season (150-180 days) to attain maturity, making them sensitive to drought at the end of the season.
    • They also had a spreading growth habit and small pods.
  • Subsequently, rosette-resistance was successfully transferred to short-duration types and several advanced groundnut breeding lines.
    • These had high levels of rosette resistance, acceptable seed size and colour were developed by the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT).
    • Some of these lines were transferred to SAARI, where further improvement and adaptation to farmer and consumer preferences was carried out under an adaptive DFID Crop Protection Programme (CPP) project R7445 (see Chancello, 2002) between NRI, SAARI and ICRISAT.
    • This involved farmer-managed trials and an investigation into the potential for developing village/community seed banks, to ensure adequate high quality seed is passed from one season to the next.
  • Strategic outputs from the earlier project R6811 (see Kimmins, 1999), which focused on the mechanisms of resistance, assisted in the development of breeding lines with combined resistance to both the rosette viruses and the aphid vector.
    • This led to the release of new rosette-resistant varieties of groundnuts, namely Serenut 2, 3, and 4 that conform to the requirements of different local markets.
    • Serenut 3 and 4 are short duration types, allowing two crops to be grown in a single year and thus greatly enhancing the income-earning opportunity of poor farmers.
  • However, owing to the high seed rate requirement for groundnut (low ratio of seed:progeny), seed availability was limited, especially for the rural poor.
    • The new varieties were available at prohibitive prices from research sources.
    • Seed companies found it unattractive to multiply and sell commercially as prices would limit sales volumes.
  • This technology describes ways in which community seed production was promoted and commercialised in Uganda, through CPP projects R8105 and R8442, led by the NGO, AT Uganda.

2. Community seed production

  • Under R8105 starting in 2002 and subsequently extended under R8442, the work was implemented in the 16 sub-counties of the Kumi, Pallisa,Tororo, Mbale and Sironko districts.
    • In each sub-county the project operated in two parishes and worked initially with ten farmer groups with a total membership of 4,317 farmers in the 160 groups.
    • Another 160 groups joined in the second season of 2004.
    • The model for multiplication of seed was an approach practiced with other crops in an earlier project, implemented by AT Uganda with the same farmers.
    • It emphasized participation of the key stakeholders.
      • In this case these were beneficiary farmer groups, Production Committees (PC), Parish Development Committees (PDC) and extension staff sub-county local government authorities in planning, implementing, and monitoring project activities.
  • The project was implemented in collaboration with a groundnut breeder from NARO/SAARI, whose role was the training of trainers, provision of technical advice, and contacts for access to planting material.
    • Field activities with farmers were handled by the sub-county level local government extension staff (FPRA) of the Department of Agriculture.
    • Full details are given in the project reports (see Laker-Ojok 2005a and 2005b).
  • In summary, the process and activities involved were general preparatory activities sensitisation of local government stakeholders from the participating districts and sub-county was done at district level.
    • The main purpose was to discuss and agree on the modalities to be used in implementing the project and to get feedback on the approach.
    • In particular the following categories of people were invited and attended:
      • District Agricultural Officers
      • District Secretaries for production (political leaders in charge of production at district level)
      • Sub-county chiefs
      • Chairpersons of Local Council
      • Secretaries for production at sub-county level
      • Farmers representatives from the participating groups
      • Councillors representing women at sub county level
      • Extension staff in charge of the sub counties.
  • After the sensitisation process, a memorandum of understanding was signed with the leaders of each participating sub-county.
  • In addition to the district level meetings, meetings were held at sub-county for all participating groups and more local leaders were invited to attend.
    • The meetings provided an opportunity to introduce the project and to build support in the community.
    • The basic issues included:
      • each recipient of seed was to return twice the amount received for redistribution to other group members and the community as seed belonged to the community;
      • priority to receive seed given to the able poor and wome;
      • the role of Parish Development Committees (PDCs) in the multiplication and distribution process; and
      • contribution of the beneficiaries in the form of labour, land, inputs for all management practices and peer monitoring.

2.1 Training in groundnut production, multiplication and storage

  • The collaborating groundnut breeder, using the groundnut production manual (http://www.fao.org/docs/eims/upload/agrotech/1998/GroundnutManual.pdf) developed by project R7445, trained extension staff as trainers in groundnut production.
    • This was done together with AT Uganda Programme staff that supervised implementation of field activities.
    • Refresher training on seed quality and storage was done for all staff.
  • Training of beneficiary farmer groups was then organised at sub-county level, facilitated by the extension staff.
    • Later refresher trainings by the Production Committees and Parish Development Committees (PDCs), using the simplified seed production guide (see Appendix 3 in LAKER - OJOK 2005a), were organised at group level at the start of each season to reinforce training under supervision of the extension staff.
  • Sustainability of training called for building of the local capacity to train, and thus the training of PDCs and PCs in place of contact farmers as trainers, to continue with the training of other farmers later as the seed continued to multiply.
  • Providing the beneficiaries and staff with the simple seed production guide as reference material for future use.
    • This equipped them with the necessary knowledge and skills to pass on to others whenever need arose.
  • End of season evaluations were organised both to enable farmers to learn from the experiences of their fellow farmers and to assess and appreciate the varieties and practices promoted.

3. Foundation seed multiplied by farmer group members

  • At the start of the first season of each year, each participating group was given small amounts of seed of the new varieties to multiply for subsequent distribution to the members.
    • In order to multiply seed for redistribution to all targeted beneficiaries in a short period, recipients were required to return more than the amount initially received.
    • The groups were helped to prepare seed multiplication byelaws and regulations to ensure that beneficiaries paid back seed so that the distribution chain was maintained.
    • See Appendix 10 in Laker-Ojok 2005a for a checklist developed by the groups.
    • The byelaws were reviewed to suit emerging situations.
  • Delivery of seed by the project to individuals in groups was based on distribution plans.
    • Each sub-county received new seed at the start of each year.
    • The varieties were introduced gradually, starting with Serenut 2 in the first year, then Serenut 3 and 4 in the second and third years.
    • The first lot of seed of each new variety was procured through the collaborating breeder or bought from the beneficiaries for distribution to other farmers.
  • Acknowledgement of receipt of seed and multiplication terms as contained in the agreement and byelaws.
    • Quantities received and to be repaid was done by all beneficiaries and witnessed by PDCs for accountability, transparency and easy follow-up at the time of repayment.
    • Distribution was done at group or public meetings.
    • The process required PDCs to keep a register of all seed recipients and repayments in the groups and by individuals in the parish.
  • The project facilitated the process by initially providing the books and training on record keeping for PCs and PDCs.
    • Beneficiaries were responsible for custody and storage of seed, since distribution was done soon after harvest, and provided land and labour to produce the crop.
    • Substantial balances of rosette resistant, drought tolerant and high yielding seeds remained with the beneficiaries and provided motivation for their contribution to the community multiplication process.

3.1 Redistribution and further multiplication

  • Multipliers return twice the amount of planting material received for redistribution and further multiplication.
    • The groups needed to prepare for the large quantities of seeds that became available as pay back to other members.
    • They were assisted by the PCs and PDCs, giving priority to the able poor and women, as well as to members who had shown hard work and commitment, so as to minimise the risk of loss due to poor management.
    • The plans also helped create peer pressure among the recipients thus encouraging them to repay.
    • The process was supported by byelaws.
    • Clear repayment terms and procedures, developed and enforced in a participatory manner, together with group peer pressure arising from community ownership of the seeds, helped to instill a repayment culture in beneficiaries and gave control to the community.

3.2 Collection, redistribution and monitoring of seed multiplication handed over to local leadership

  • A lot of capacity building was needed to promote sustainability of these processes.
    • Roles were identified and assigned to the local leadership structures, e.g. PCs and PDCs, in a participatory manner so as to ensure that seeds zererepaid and given out for further multiplication and that planned activities were completed.
    • The roles included training other beneficiaries on groundnut production; monitoring management of crops in the field; facilitating identification of beneficiaries; distribution and recovery of seed for redistribution and record keeping.
    • This was done in all participating sub-counties and a final checklist was developed.
    • See appendices 1 and 2 of Laker and Okoj, 2005a.

4. General and cross-cutting activities

  • Pre-seasonal planning meetings were held at the beginning of each year at project, sub-county and group level to ensure completion of activities.
    • Payment of the extension staff was based on completion of tasks.
    • Planning and budgeting was done by the extension staff themselves with supervision of project staff and this was seen to increase their commitment.
    • See Appendix 6 of Laker-Okoj 2005a.
  • Review meetings were held with all groups and lessons learnt were used to refine byelaws and other implementation strategies.
    • Joint field monitoring was carried out by PCs, PDCs, and occasionally extension staff and project staff, to assess field performance and adoption of crop management practices and to minimise cases of false reports of crop failure.
    • Joint monitoring of crops in the field was used to remind beneficiaries of their obligation and helped in timely solution of problems.
    • This helped other groups to take precautionary corrective actions as they learnt from each other and helped them to refine their byelaws.
  • End of season evaluations were done at both group and sub-county level each season to assess performance of the varieties and get farmers’ feedback.
    • This motivated others to adopt recommended practices.
    • A competition was organised in 2003 to encourage training, multiplication, distribution and participation of the local leaders.
    • Prizes awarded included peanut butter grinders and groundnut shellers.
    • An impact assessment survey of participating groups was carried out in September 2004 against baseline survey data obtained at the start of the project in 2002.
    • See Appendix 11 of Laker-Okoj 2005a.
  • A control group was also sampled including five people who were neighbours to beneficiaries sampled in each group, in order to test for diffusion outside of the project parishes.
    • Data from field reports indicates that four programme staff, 16 extension staff with their 15 field assistants, 960 community leaders (PCs and PDCs from 320 groups in 16 parishes) and more than 6 000 farmers were trained in groundnut production, storage and multiplication.
    • Foundation seed of Serenut 2 ,3 and 4, sufficient to plant 187.5 ha, was obtained and given to farmers to multiply.
  • The survey, conducted in September 2004, estimated that up to 17,154 people had accessed seeds through the formal project arrangements, sales and gifts by individuals.
    • 3 634 received seed directly from the project.
    • 5 910 purchased seed from farmer multipliers.
    • 7 610 obtained it through gifts or payments in kind.
    • 52 percent of beneficiaries were women.
  • Redistribution of the varieties was continually increasing under the guidance of local leadership.
    • Seeds produced was sufficient to plant 3 275 ha.
    • 1 092 ha was distributed directly from the project and 2 183 ha using seed from sales and gifts.
    • Estimated production from 2004 would be sufficient to plant up to 4 725 ha if all were committed to seeds.
    • Seed availability for the introduced varieties had thus increased substantially and large quantities were being sold, enabling non-participating farmers to benefit from this, thus disseminating the new varieties.

5. Expanded seed multiplication

  • Project R8442 expanded the multiplication coverage to neighbouring sub-counties and assisted farmers groups to consolidate into sub-county level marketing associations, in order to be able to capture more lucrative markets by selling in bulk.
    • Foundation seeds of new rosette resistant groundnut varieties were procured and multiplied by an additional 80 farmer groups (five per new sub county).
    • Almost 2 000 additional farmers were trained in seed production, multiplication, distribution management and collective marketing.
  • Multiplication continued among the nearly 8 000 farmers, who were members of the original 160 farmer groups and the 160 partner groups that had already been established, thus bringing the number of total beneficiaries to nearly 10 000.
    • Over 200 ha of Serenut 2, 3, and 4 were multiplied in the 16 new sub counties.
    • In order to foster commercial incentives for sustainable groundnut multiplication, AT Uganda collaborated with SACRED Africa, an NGO based in Kenya, to help the groups form regional marketing initiative associations with sub-county level branches.
  • During its nine months of operation, the project established the foundation and structures on which the marketing groups were to operate.
    • Twenty marketing groups were formed at the sub-county level with a total of 875 members.
    • These marketing groups have been registered at district level.
    • Members have paid shares, elected leadership and advisory committees, and established working sub-committees.
    • They have been trained in record keeping, quality control/management, and market intelligence.
    • Each of the groups has adopted a constitution, opened a bank account, and established a store that acts as a marketing centre for ease of quality control, and bulking.
  • The project engaged a team of field auditors to help the farmers marketing groups to establish a record keeping, a financial management system and to undertake periodic audit of their books.
    • To ensure effective coordination, advocacy, and establish better market linkages, the 20 sub-county Farmers Marketing Groups were consolidated into five District/Regional Marketing Associations, with an elected interim leadership committee.
    • In mid November 2005, SACRED Africa and AT Uganda carried out an evaluation of the Farmers’ Marketing Initiatives, which verified progress achieved to date.
    • They stressed the importance of continued support to these fledgling organizations to achieve full impact and sustainability.
    • See Appendix 11 of Laker, Okoj 2005b.

6. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Groundnut agronomic and postharvest practices: ID 6991.
  • Groundnuts varieties, management and post harvest: ID 6899.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Pro-poor technology

Through introduced seed varieties, farmers could produce and sell large quantities, enabling non-participating farmers to benefit.

entries.tittle: Control of bovine trypanosomosis in Bolivia: fly avoidance strategies
entries.summary: Mechanical transmission by tabanid flies, especially Tabanus occidentalis is likely to be the principal method of trypanosomes transmission in Bolivia. Specifically control regimes based on fly avoidance strategies, could result in a significant reduction of tabanid flies’ direct effects and eventually decreasing transmission risk.
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

Bovine trypanosomosis (also commonly known as trypanosomiasis) is a debilitating and sometimes fatal disease caused by the blood parasite Trypanosoma vivax. This was first recorded in Bolivia in 1996 and spread rapidly to most cattle in rearing lowland areas of Santa Cruz and Beni Departments. The spread of bovine trypanosomosis in Bolivia appeared to follow the movement of infected cattle along relatively well-defined livestock trekking routes.

The areas of Bolivia where bovine trypanosomosis has spread (most cattle in rearing lowland areas of Santa Cruz and Beni Departments) include approximately 60 percent of Bolivia cattle population, a significant portion of the livestock industry, worth approximately USD 224 million per annum (1998 values). This production was threatened by the introduction of bovine trypanosomosis as a new disease in the region. Potential trypanosomosis spread to smallholders herds, where loss of a few animals (kept for milk and draught power) would have high impact, as well as spreading to dairy herds composed of less tolerant exotic breeds and cross breeds, represented a significant future problem.

2. Vectors of Trypanosoma vivax in Bolivia

Trypanosoma vivax is a blood parasite originating in Africa and is thought to have been introduced to South America in the early twentieth century, first reported from French Guyana (Silva and Dávila, 1997). In Africa the vectors are fly species of tsetse (Glossina), however, T. vivax is now well established in South America despite the absence of is original vector. The vectors in Bolivia were unknown, but elsewhere in South America tabanid flies, in which T. vivax does not undergo a cyclical development, have been implicated as vectors. For example, mechanical transmission of the parasite from one bovine to another has been achieved experimentally with several species of tabanids which are found in Bolivia. Research was therefore carried out to determine T. vivax vectors in Bolivia; it was clear that the main group of biting flies, that could be involved in mechanical transmission of bovine trypanosomosis, was that of tabanids. Between November 1999 and February 2001 (see in Hall 2001), a total of 33 different species of tabanid were recorded in the field site at Chocolatal, Guarayos Province, Santa Cruz Department. The most abundant species was Tabanus occidentalis and studies have now confirmed that mechanical transmission by tabanid flies, especially T. occidentalis is likely to be the principal method of transmission for trypanosome in Bolivia.

In the tsetse (Glossina sp.) vector of T. vivax, the trypanosome parasite undergoes a cyclical development of several generations inside the tsetse host, changing its morphology in certain periods. These periods usually include the sexual phase of the trypanosomes, with exchange of genetic material between parasites. Because of the adaptations required for biological transmission in this way, trypanosomes which are transmitted biologically by tsetse cannot be transmitted in this manner by other insects. Instead mechanical transmission is required as an alternative means of transmission.

Mechanical transmission involves the direct transmission of the same individual trypanosomes taken from an infected animal and transferred to an uninfected one. This requires a tsetse (or other biting fly) to feed on an infected host and acquire trypanosomes in a blood meal and then within in a short period, for it to feed on an uninfected host and to inoculate and/or regurgitate some of the infected blood from the first meal into the tissue of the uninfected animal. Tabanid flies are considered to be highly mobile and retain greater amounts of blood on their mouthparts than other biting flies. These mechanisms are also described in articles on mechanical vectors by Desquenes and Dia (2003 a, b).

2.1 Mechanical transmission of trypanosomes

Mechanical transmission of trypanosomes is facilitated by the following conditions

  • when the parasitaemia of the peripheral blood supply of the infected host is high;
  • when there is high-level of biting flies;
  • when there is a high proportion of interrupted flies feeds, due to disturbance during feeding (e.g. disturbance by host defensive behaviours or by competing flies);
  • when there is a minimal delay between feeding on an infected host and resumption of feeding on a second, uninfected host – this is most likely when hosts are closely associated, as in herd livestock;
  • when biting flies are highly mobile;
  • when a large amount of infected host blood remains on the mouthparts of biting flies between interrupted feeds;

There will be interaction between all of the above factors. For example, a host with an acute infection and high parasitaemia might be considered a good source of infectious agents, but if that host is inert due to the disease and unable to respond to fly attack with strong defensive behaviours, then interrupted feeds and subsequent mechanical transmission are unlikely to occur. Ideally feeding extremes behaviours will prevent mechanical transmission, such as no feeding (best for the animal) or feeding to fullness. Anywhere in-between these extremes create the risk of mechanical transmission as flies move from one animal to another to complete their blood meals.

3. Effects of insecticide application on tabanid feeding behaviour

The most widely used tabanid suppression and control technique in Bolivia is the direct application of insecticide formulations (cypermethrin) to the body of the animal, either by spray or pour-on. Feeding activity was monitored before and after insecticide applications in order to evaluate the effect on tabanid feeding behaviour.

Although immediate benefits of cypermethrin treatment of livestock were found, these were short-term and within three days of treatment the effects had almost disappeared, requiring repeated applications in order to maintain insecticidal effectiveness. Such short-term benefits are costly, both in economic and time-consuming terms.

Tabanids can cause significant blood loss to cattle, insecticide application reduced duration of feeding hence reducing blood loss. However, it is not yet understood whether the reduced feeding on one animal leads to other feeding attempts on another animals – in which case the problem of mechanical transmission might actually be exacerbated by the insecticide application.

4. Control measures

Farmers find it difficult to decide whether or not to apply prophylactics for trypanosomes and insecticides for fly control. They must evaluate the treatment costs versus the livestock value and potential losses. There is also the risk that insecticides will knock out low level pest to which cattle have already developed resistance.

It is also important to separate infected cattle from disease-free cattle. Separating livestock by as little as 200 m reduces significantly mechanical transmission between infected and uninfected cattle. Measures to reduce contacts will therefore be of major importance in controlling the disease.

Adopting fly avoidance methods, which have been shown to work with other mechanically transmitted pathogens, should be considered as a potential control measures for trypanosome species. These include:

  • movement restrictions of infected animals to prevent infection spread into new areas;
  • separation of infected animals from uninfected animals by 200 m to prevent transfer feeding of flies;
  • separation of animals from preferred habitats of host seeking flies, e.g. forest margins, by 200 m to discourage adult flies from attacking animals;
  • introduction of needle management systems to prevent direct transmission between animals.

The successful execution of these methods requires to firstly inform appropriately farmers, secondly implement effective diagnostic facilities to identify infected animals and monitor the success of control regimes. Two information leaflets providing a background to bovine trypanosomiasis as well as an identification, biology and control of tabanids, were distributed to veterinarians and livestock owners.

5. Diagnostic tests for Trypanosoma vivax infection in Bolivia

Access to suitable and practical diagnostic tests is an essential component of control strategies. A research team assessed a range of existing diagnostic tests that could be used for the detection of T. vivax infection and adapted in Bolivia. Appropriate and effective tests were transferred to the Bolivian animal health laboratory (LIDIVET) at Santa Cruz. These include:

  • a simplified polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay;
  • an Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA);
  • Card Agglutination Test for Trypanosomes (CATT)

The CATT has great potential, as a first screening for the presence of trypanosome antibodies and can easily be carried out in an unsophisticated laboratory. ELISA and PCR can be used to distinguish between T. vivax and T. evansi. The assays use either serum or blood dried into filter papers, so samples can easily be collected by farmers and sent to the LIDIVET labs for analysis.

The CATT, ELISA and PCR tests were then applied to materials collected by LIDIVET staff during routine animal health monitoring visits from different regions of Bolivia. This has enabled the identification of areas with a high risk of bovine trypanosomiasis, seven of which were in the department of Santa Cruz. Infection rates exceeded 75 percent in one area.

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Tsetse control: how to make a plastic cage for tsetse traps: ID 4514.
  • Tsetse control: how to deploy a target: ID 4516.
  • Tsetse control: how to use Tsetse traps with an odour dispenser: ID 4507.
  • Tsetse Muse: helping planners to design cost-effective tsetse control strategies: ID 4482.
  • Tsetse control using Epsilon trap made: ID 4508.
  • Tsetse control: insecticide treatment of cattle: ID 4419.
  • Risk reduction while manipulating pesticide: ID 8348.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology helps poor farmers to fight and prevent bovine trypanosomosis.

entries.tittle: Working with farmers to control sweet potato virus disease in East Africa
entries.summary: Sweet Potato Virus Diseases (SPVD) are an important biotic constraint to sweet potato production in parts of East Africa. Technologies consisting of participatory selection procedures and an Integrated Pest Management (IPM) package were developed to improve the performance and farmer-acceptability of locally selected sweet potato clones resistant to SPVD. These have been validated in Uganda and Tanzania. Procedures were established to improve planting materials and to make them more widely available via the International Potato Center (CIP) network in East Africa.
entries.description:
Description

Sweet potato is amongst the most important food staples grown in Sub-Saharan Africa and is particularly important in parts of East Africa. Uganda has the largest production in Africa and Tanzania has only a slightly smaller area for sweet potato, though with a relatively low productivity. With good husbandry, sweet potato is amongst the most productive crops but it can also yield on relatively poor soils. It requires few inputs except labour. Its ability to yield rapidly and over a long cropping season if harvested, provides the flexibility for it to fit into a range of cropping systems, and to yield even with irregular rainfall patterns. Consequently, it is an important daily food for many farmers and their families in Africa, particularly resource-poor farmers growing their food on a restricted area of marginal land.

Sweet potato is also an important component of disaster relief when other crops fail, for example, when the pandemic of cassava mosaic disease destroyed crops of cassava. Sweet potato is also a cheap food for the urban poor in the growing conurbations of Africa. It is also sold in supermarkets for the growing middle class. By 2020, it is predicted that root crops will have an even more important role in food production in Africa than now, and become integrated into a more diverse range of food products.

1. Source of vitamin A

  • The International Potato Center (CIP) is deploying high beta-carotene and high dry matter content varieties from South America to Africa (see the CIP 'Vitamin A for Africa (VITAA)'), as a means of combating widespread vitamin A deficiencies amongst poor people in Africa.
    • This is particularly in women, young children and HIV AIDS-affected people.
  • CIP estimates that replacing white-fleshed with orange-fleshed varieties could alleviate vitamin A deficiencies in 500 million children in Africa under the age of six.
    • There is also an extensive impact on older children and adults, particularly pregnant women and lactating mothers.

2. Sweet Potato Virus Disease (SPVD)

  • Previous scientific work has demonstrated the key role of the whitefly-borne crinivirus Sweet Potato Chlorotic Stunt Virus (SPCSV) in the development of Sweet Potato Virus Disease (SPVD), the most damaging disease of sweet potato in Africa.
    • High-yielding and otherwise superior local varieties are often susceptible.
    • Resistance has been identified in local African varieties, though resistant ones are mostly low-yielding or possess other adverse characteristics.
    • Field observations coupled with evidence of a lack of diversity in SPCSV at the molecular level, predict the resistance is likely to be durable.
    • In Uganda, the National Agricultural Research Organisation (NARO) gives high priority to developing resistant varieties and has released varieties bred at Namulonge Research Institute (NAARI).
      • They combine superior yields and resistance.
    • SPVD is particularly prevalent in western and central Uganda around Lake Victoria, including the Masaka and Rakai districts.
      • The work there was funded by DFID Crop Protection Programme (CPP) project R7492 (see Gibson, 2002) and showed that some of these varieties were high- ielding and adequately SPVD-resistant, and therefore likely to be appropriate elsewhere in the region.
  • The variety NASPOT 1 was preferred, producing twice the marketable root yield of the best local cultivars in on-farm trials and having good taste and other eating qualities.
    • For details of attributes identified and ranked by farmers in four localities, see Gibson, 2002, Appendix Tables 9 and 10.
  • Although farmers continued to grow most of the varieties they had been given access to, only NASPOT 1 was preferred above local cultivars in a variety ranking exercise, largely because of its massive early yield.
    • NASPOT 1 is being widely adopted in areas around Lake Victoria where SPVD is prevalent.
  • The epidemic of cassava mosaic disease in Kagera District has also resulted in the Tanzanian Department of Research and Development giving high priority to controlling virus diseases of root crops, including SPVD in sweet potato in the Lake Zone for the last several years.
  • The high-yielding and SPVD-resistant Ugandan varieties were tested in high SPVD-incidence areas bordering Lake Victoria in Tanzania.
    • The field resistance and high yields of some was confirmed and farmers enthusiastically began adopting a few of them, again particularly NASPOT 1.
  • Control of SPVD is also a prerequisite for the success of the VITA A project, as exotic sweet potato clones introduced from S. America (where the disease has been rare till recently) are almost invariably very susceptible to SPVD.

3. SPVD-resistant cultivars

  • Planting material of high-yielding, SPVD-resistant cultivars bred in Uganda was distributed to farmers.
    • Extension officers were trained so that they can disseminate to farmers both the benefits of the resistant varieties and the SPVD control strategies and how best to utilise them.
    • In Uganda, this was done in the districts around Kampala, largely through links with the NGO Buganda Cultural and Development Foundation (BUCADEF).
    • In Tanzania, this was done in drought and refugee affected areas in the south-eastern part of the Lake (Victoria) Zone (Mukeba; Ngara districts), supported by other donors, notably The Norwegian People's Aid (NPA).
  • However, on-farm trials showed that nationally released varieties were not high-yielding in all agroecologies in Uganda and Tanzania where sweet potato is important.
    • Farmers requested better varieties and a variety ranking exercise identified several characteristics including various storage root quality characteristics and continuous storage root production for piecemeal harvesting, which were difficult to assess accurately on station.
  • SPVD is not the only constraint facing sweet potato producers.
    • everal of the released varieties, including NASPOT 1, were much more susceptible to Alternaria disease than the local cultivars.
    • In CPP project R8243 (see Gibson, 2005), drought affected several of the trials and was identified by farmers as a major factor in determining their ability to retain NASPOT 1 and several other NAARI varieties.
  • There was therefore a demand for:
    • measures to control SPVD in superior local varieties, and
    • new varieties adapted to local conditions and local needs.
  • Participatory breeding commenced with farmer groups in Uganda and Tanzania by CPP project (see Gibson, 2005).
    • By the completion of this project, an initial seed population of some 12 000 planted with two farmer groups located in the Mpigi and Luwero districts in Uganda, where SPVD is also prevalent, had been evaluated over three generations.
      • 24 genotypes had been selected for further evaluation within CPP project R8457 (see Gibson, 2006).
    • Under that project, a further two generations of clones selected by three farming communities in Uganda were planted on-farms.
    • All data collected enabled the performance of each genotype to be analysed over five generations.
      • This was a first step to publishing the achievements of this activity and farmer-selected materials were transferred to the Ugandan Sweet Potato Programme.
    • A process whereby virus-tested material is available for international transfer (with the initial aim of transferring to Tanzania), was initiated through the auspices of the Ugandan Sweet Potato Programme, and the International Potato Centre regional base at KARI-Muguga.
  • In the much smaller Tanzanian programme, farmers grew one further generation and continued to select superior material.
    • ARDI-Maruku scientists have begun propagating material derived from the farmer-selected clones, both as a means of accessing the material and as a means of maintaining it.
  • SPCSV is transmitted only semi-persistently by whiteflies and most spread of SPVD is local.
    • Rates of spread of SPVD into unaffected newly-planted crops are determined by the amount and proximity of old crops within a radius of about 100 m and the numbers of whiteflies.
    • SPCSV is transmitted by B. tabaci in the semi-persistent manner and this, together with the tendency of B. tabaci for short-distance flights appears to account for this result.
    • These results suggested that individual farmers could also beneficially use local phytosanitation to control SPVD.
    • They would therefore be able to continue to grow their best high-yielding local landraces despite some susceptibility to SPVD, and experiments confirmed this.
  • On-station and on-farm trials showed that most spread in a field occurs within a few metres of an infection source and roguing out diseased cuttings within one month of planting halved (P<0.001) the spread of SPVD.
    • This is even though unrogued control plots were next to the rogued plots.
  • An EU-funded project (ICA4-CT-2000-30007) also showed that neighbouring unaffected plants can compensate for either the presence or the removal of a diseased plant.
  • Small amounts of isolation also had dramatic effects.
    • Plots planted just 15 m away from a diseased plot had between a third and a quarter the number of SPVD-affected plants than plots adjacent to the diseased plot (P<0.001).
  • However, although some farmers realized that SPVD is caused by a 'germ', none realized that SPVD is a disease spread by whiteflies.
    • Through interviews done in Uganda and Kenya, many thought it is caused by abiotic factors such as drought.
    • Consequently, most farmers ignore control practices such as isolation although most do select their planting material from disease-free parents.

4. Outputs

  • The following guidelines for controlling SPVD were drawn up based on results from CPP project R8243.
    • Collect cuttings for new crops from healthy plants.
    • Select cuttings from healthy plants in crops in which few other plants have the disease.
      • Avoid collecting cuttings from very old crops because sweet potato virus disease is less easy to see in these than in vigorously-growing crops.
    • If possible, choose a variety or local cultivar that isn't much affected by the disease.
    • Plant new crops away from old crops.
    • Avoid planting new crops where sweet potato was grown last season.
      • Storage roots and cuttings from old diseased plants surviving in the soil will produce diseased plants from which infection will easily spread to your new crop.
    • Remove any diseased plants as soon as they appear, especially in young crops.
    • Ensure trash from old harvested crops including unwanted storage roots dies.
    • All these treatments will work better the larger the area where it is used to work, together with neighbours.
  • These guidelines were encapsulated in a multilingual posters and brochures and were included in a general manual for sweet potato farmer field schools.
    • They present a series of choices and, what best control will probably be achieved by combining all the practices.
      • Adequate control may be achieved, in conditions of only moderate rates of spread of SPVD by whiteflies, by using one or a few.
    • Thus, careful selection of planting material, planting away from old crops and roguing out any new infections may allow a farmer successfully to grow quite susceptible cultivars.
    • Alternatively, growing a very resistant cultivar may also free many farmers from all these restrictions.
  • This is an example of how the understanding of a disease (in this case SPVD) and its vector (whitefly) can help to build up a strategy of control.
    • The strategy itself is a combination of good husbandry practices that are easily understandable by farming organizations, or even by individual farmers.
    • The recommendations allow for the local establishment and adoption of control strategies for implementation by poor farmers.
    • The guidelines also need to incorporate social and organizational aspects, such as the establishment of community nurseries.
    • The use of protective hedges may also be considered.

5. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Sweetpotato planting material protection: ID 8650.
  • Most serious insect pests affecting sweetpotato: ID 6936.
  • The most serious sweet potato diseases: ID 6937.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology improves farmers' livelihood by introducing locally selected sweet potato clones resistant to SPVD.

entries.tittle: Crop Protection: Integrated Management of Striga Species in Tanzania
entries.summary: Striga species are noxious weeds that are widespread constraints to the production of staple cereal crops in semi-arid areas, principally attacking finger millet, maize, sorghum, and upland rice.
