entries.tittle: Cuidado de la salud de ovejas y cabras y corrales mejorados en Colombia
keywords: suplementación animal y tipos de suplementos
entries.summary: Un buen estado sanitario de los animales y la posibilidad de responder en eventos de emergencia buscando sustituir los recursos alimentarios de los animales que ya no están disponibles en cantidades adecuadas, son acciones prioritarias de respuesta y manejo en una situación de emergencia climática. Esto fue diseñado principalmente con la finalidad de tomar medidas que permitan mitigar las emergencias que aquejan a las especies pecuarias (ovinos, caprinos y bovinos), buscando bienestar animal en la salud nutricional.
entries.description:
1. Descripción

Haga una corta descripción de la situación en Colombia para que quien no conozca la realidad colombiana pueda entender (las causas de las principales emergencias, riesgos agroclimáticos ocasionados por el fenómeno del niño, cuando y como ocurren, como normalmente responden los pastores y las consecuencias). Las actividades descritas a continuación tienen su importancia en mitigar las emergencias alimentarias, ya que son consideradas como prácticas para la reducción del riesgo de padecer problemas de salud en las especies pecuarias. Dentro de estas prácticas se tiene la implementación de brigadas sanitarias como apoyo por parte de los profesionales médicos veterinarios y las actividades complementarias que redundan en un adecuado estado sanitario, relacionadas con las prácticas de alimentación, que incluyen la elaboración de ensilaje y el heno.

1.1 Brigadas sanitarias

Las brigadas sanitarias, tienen como objetivo general brindar y transferir conocimientos a las comunidades sobre la importancia y la asertividad de realizar brigadas de sanidad animal en el ganado ovi-caprino de la zona. 

Los objetivos específicos de las brigadas sanitarias son:

  1. Realizar, con aceptación y condescendencia de las comunidades, las brigadas de sanidad animal requeridas por el ganado ovi-caprino, para mejorar su estado de salud deteriorado a causa de la falta de alimento.
  2. Lograr que las comunidades comprendan e interioricen la necesidad e importancia de aplicar medicamentos a los animales enfermos para preservar su salud y mejorar su producción. Las actividades para el desarrollo de las brigadas, complementarias a las buenas prácticas generadas por las familias en cuanto a la recuperación del estado sanitario de sus animales incluyeron:
    • Realizar el conteo del ganado ovi-caprino en el aprisco, esta actividad debe realizarse familia por familia (aprisco por aprisco).
      • Una vez se haya hecho el conteo de los animales, las familias pueden liberar a las cabras para realizar el libre pastoreo cotidiano.
    • Selección de animales con potencial productivo.
      • Es necesario realizar una separación de los animales, para identificar los animales que tienen mejor capacidad productiva de aquellos que no lo tienen, ya que aquellos con buen potencial productivo, son los que formarán la base de su hato y son los que trataremos en las brigadas de sanidad animal.
    • Valoración clínica veterinaria.
      • Una vez hemos separado los animales y hayamos escogido los mejores productores, debemos realizarles un cheque médico para verificar en qué estado de salud se encuentran y si están presentando alguna enfermedad.
    • Tratamiento para la desnutrición.
      • Se explica a las comunidades que después de realizar el chequeo médico, se les va a hacer un tratamiento a los animales, ya que por falta de alimento, están presentando desnutrición.
      • El tratamiento consiste en:
        • Multivitamínico: Es un líquido que contiene las vitaminas y minerales que los animales no tienen en este momento por la falta de alimento. Este se dará por la boca (vía oral).
        • Desparasitante interno: Este medicamento es para eliminar los parásitos y “bichos” que puedan tener los animales en sus estómagos e intestinos y que no los están dejando aprovechar el poco pasto que encuentran, ya que estos parásitos se comen todo lo que llegue al estómago y no dejan que el animal se nutra del poco pasto que encuentra. Este medicamento es líquido y también se da por la boca (vía oral).
        • Desparasitante externo: Este medicamento es para eliminar bichos como garrapatas, piojos y ácaros que se encuentran sobre el pelo y la piel del animal y se alimentan de su sangre, debilitándolo y enfermándolo. Este medicamento es inyectado por debajo de la piel (subcutáneo).
  •  

El fortalecimiento de capacidades en las familias sobre los tratamientos para la desnutrición es importante ya que de ello depende la sostenibilidad y continúa aplicación del proceso.

  • Cuando se le haya aplicado el tratamiento a los animales, van a pasar a que les recorten las pezuñas.
    • Esto es importante ya que las pezuñas largas les generan dolor y a veces heridas que pueden infectarse y enfermarlos, por lo que es necesario mantenerlas cortas.
    • Esto se realiza con una tijera especial para las pezuñas de estos animales.
  • Cuando se esté realizando el corte de las pezuñas, se realiza el marcaje.
    • Esto es una chapa que se pone en la oreja del animal, que lleva un número y un color específico, y sirve para saber que esa cabra corresponde a la Familia XXXX de la Comunidad XXXX.
    • Así evitamos que se confundan y las familias pueden saber con más facilidad cuáles son sus chivos.
  • Inventario.
    • Al finalizar el marcaje y el corte de pezuñas de todos los chivos de una familia, se realiza un inventario, en donde vamos a anotar en un cuaderno, cuantas cabras tiene cada familia, que números y color de chapas tienen sus animales y que tratamiento recibieron.
  • Es importante que el representante de la familia y propietario de los chivos, verifique la información que se puso en el inventario.

1.2 Ensilaje

  • Identificación de las pasturas y forrajes en la región para la conservación de estas.
    • Identificar y seleccionar que especies forrajeras se encuentran en la zona que puedan ser utilizadas para la elaboración de ensilajes como alternativa de conservación del material vegetal y como alternativa para suplir el déficit de energía en el animal a causa de los riesgos agroclimáticos ocasionados por el fenómeno del niño.
  • Realizar los cortes de los pastos a una altura de 35 cm a 40 cm del suelo, luego se pesa la producción y por último determinar el área de cosecha.
  • Luego se pica el pasto en partes más pequeñas utilizando un machete o máquinas especializadas para efectuar dicha actividad, luego se realiza una mezcla de agua y melaza, basándose en la siguiente formula:
    • Por cada 50 kg de pasto picado, preparar una mezcla de 2 kg de melaza disuelta en 8 litros de agua, mezclar los dos ingredientes hasta homogeneizar la preparación.
  • Adicionar poco a poco la mezcla de agua con melaza al pasto picado hasta humedecerlo completamente, en este paso se realiza la prueba de humedad o sequedad del mismo, si todo está bien se continúa al último paso que es el llenado de las bolsas, la compactación de la mezcla y el cierre de las bolsas.
  • Con este último paso se debe de tener mucho cuidado de compactar muy bien la preparación para sacar todo el aire posible y así no se dañe el alimento.
    • Una vez cerrado el silo debe permanecer así por 45 días para ser consumido posteriormente por los animales, o en su defecto una vez cumpla con los días de conservación y no se va a consumir, este puede seguir conservándose más tiempo.

1.3 Heno

El heno es otra alternativa de como conservar el pasto para ser suministrado a los animales en épocas de sequías. Su elaboración es más sencilla y no requiere de mucho esfuerzo físico.

  • Identificación de las pasturas y forrajes en la región para la conservación de estas.
    • Identificar y seleccionar que especies forrajeras se encuentran en la zona que puedan ser utilizadas para la elaboración de ensilajes como alternativa de conservación del material vegetal y como alternativa para suplir el déficit de energía en el animal a causa de los riesgos agroclimáticos ocasionados por el fenómeno del niño.
  • Realizar los cortes de los pastos a una altura de 35 a 40 cm del suelo, luego se pesar la producción y por último determinar el área de cosecha.
  • Por último, el pasto cortado es empacados en moldes y prensados, para después continuar con el proceso de deshidratación al sol con el pasar de los días.

1.4 Dificultades y/o limitaciones en la aplicación de estas prácticas

  • Requerimiento mayor del área para la siembra de pastos de corte.
  • Para el caso de la práctica del ensilaje, cuando el material no es compactado ni guardado de la forma correcta, este se puede dañar por la presencia de microorganismos.
  • Cuando el material ensilado no es cubierto correctamente, puede ser afectado por microorganismos alterando su conservación.
  • La presencia de tierra en el material ensilado es susceptible a dañarse por contaminación.
  • En las actividades del ensilaje se requiere mayor mano de obra y tiempo para poder efectuar la práctica.
  • En el ensilaje se requiere más insumos para llevar a cabo la práctica, por ejemplo, se requiere de melaza, bolsas para ensilar, agua, fibras de polipropileno (pita o cabuya), machetes o en su defecto maquinaria para picar el pasto.
  • Para el caso del heno, esta conservación del pasto, es muy susceptible a dañarse en presencia de humedad.

1.5 Poblaciones a las cuales está dirigida la práctica

  • Etnia Wayúu.
  • Poblaciones campesinas.
  • Poblaciones afrodescendientes.
  • Poblaciones migrantes.

2. Beneficios socioeconómicos de la práctica

  • Mejoras en las condiciones corporales y estados nutricionales de los animales.
  • Protección de los activos pecuarios, con porcentajes por encima del 70 por ciento y recuperación superior al 50 por ciento de la población animal.
  • Disminución de la mortalidad en 1 por ciento y morbilidad en 3 por ciento en enfermedades carenciales (enfermedades metabólicas).
  • Mayor provisión de alimentos de origen animal (carne, leche y sus derivados lácteos) para las familias beneficiarias.
  • Mayor valoración económica de los activos pecuarios en el comercio informal y local y por ende mayores ingresos en los hogares de las comunidades.
  • Mayor interés participativo en el trabajo social y comunitario por parte de las comunidades.
  • Articulación institucional en el fortalecimiento de los medios de vida en las comunidades.

3. Coste de la práctica

3.1 Costos de insumos para llevar a cabo la práctica de ensilaje

  • Semilla de Pasto Mombaza, bolsa x 1 kg = 40 000 COP.
  • Hidroretenedor, bolsa x 1 kg = 25 000 COP.
  • Melaza, bulto x 30 kg = 23 500 COP.
  • Bolsa para ensilar 60 cm x 120 cm 30 micras extra fuerte unidad = 1 200 COP.
  • Mano de obra/día = 25 000 COP.
  • Fibra de polietileno para amarrar cono x 250 m Calibre 12, Unidad = 8 500 COP.
  • Picadora de Pastos con Capacidad 3,5 ton/h¯¹ Marcas sugeridas: Penagos, Metalcampo o JM Estrada, Unidad = 953 400 COP.
  • Machete de 20 Pulgadas Pulido unidad = 25 000 COP.

3.2 Calculo para los costos de producción

  • 1 kg de semillas de Pasto Mombaza en un área de 1 428 Mt2.
  • 2,5 kg de hidroretenedor en un área de 1 428 Mt2.
  • 4 767 kg de pasto producido en un área de 1 428 Mt2.
  • 4 767 kg de pasto producido 6 bultos de melaza.
  • 10 mano de obra/día.
  • 10 machetes.

3.3 Costos de producción

  • 1 kg de semilla de Pasto Mombaza, bolsa = 40 000 COP.
  • 2,5 kg de Hidroretenedor = 75 000 COP.
  • 6 bultos de Melaza = 138 000 COP.
  • 190 bolsas para ensilar 60 cm x 120 cm 30 micras extra fuerte unidad = 228 000 COP.
  • 10 obreros/día = 250 000 COP.
  • 1 cono x 250 metros de Fibra de polietileno para amarrar cono x 250 m Calibre 12 = 8 500 COP.
  • 1 Picadora de Pastos con Capacidad 3,5 ton/h¯¹ Marcas sugeridas: Penagos, Metalcampo o JM Estrada, Unidad = 953 400 COP.
  • 10 machetes de 20 Pulgadas Pulido unidad = 250 000 COP.

Total del costo de producción: 1 942 900 COP.

3.4 Costos de brigadas sanitarias

  • Total costo brigada (2000 animales): 2 164 000 COP.
  • Un análisis de costo-beneficio se efectuó utilizando datos colectados en las comunidades que implementaron esta buena práctica en 2018.
    • El análisis compara los beneficios netos obtenidos al invertir en esta buena práctica de reducción del riesgo de desastres y los beneficios netos obtenidos con la práctica anteriormente aplicada en las mismas comunidades.
    • El análisis está basado en datos colectados durante un período de observación dado, y luego extrapola los resultados durante un período de tiempo más largo, en este caso 11 años.
    • Los gráficos a continuación resumen los resultados obtenidos.
  • Se pueden observar los beneficios acumulativos netos y la relación costo-beneficio (BCR) de las buenas prácticas introducidas y las prácticas habituales/locales.
    • El BCR indica la cantidad de USD obtenida por cada USD invertido.
    • El término "buena práctica" se refiere a la introducción de los tratamientos preventivos de salud (desparasitación y enriquecimiento en vitaminas), y a la mejora de corrales.
    • La “práctica anterior” se refiere a un uso limitado o ausente del tratamiento de los animales y enriquecimiento en vitaminas (baja oferta forrajera y de mala calidad), al free roaming de cabras y ovejas, y a la utilización limitada de corrales (sólo para mantener los animales en la noche).
    • Los datos fueron recolectados en 2018 de seis explotaciones que aplicaron la práctica y seis explotaciones que no aplicaron las prácticas, todas ubicadas en el municipio de Uribia.
    • Todas las explotaciones fueron afectadas por la sequía durante el periodo de monitoreo.
    • Se puede observar un beneficio neto 59 por ciento mayor en explotaciones que implementaron la buena práctica en comparación con las explotaciones que continuaron la aplicación de la práctica anterior.
  • La buena práctica produce mayores beneficios que la práctica aplicada anteriormente, debido principalmente a las siguientes razones:
    • Gracias a la mejora de la gestión del ganado, los animales alcanzan la madurez antes bajo la buena práctica (1,5 años) que en virtud de la práctica anterior (1,8 años).
    • El precio de los animales vivos criados en explotaciones que aplicaron la buena práctica es casi el doble del precio bajo la práctica anterior, debido a las mejores condiciones de los animales.
    • Una mayor proporción de animales se vende con la buena práctica.
  • Debido a mayores costos iniciales de inversión para mejorar la infraestructura, el BCR de la práctica anterior (1,29) es mayor que el de la buena práctica (1,18).
    • Sin embargo, se ha demostrado que las inversiones iniciales en infraestructura (es decir, mejora de corrales) se pagan dentro de unos 6 años (Figura 1).
Figura 1. Acumulados en beneficios netos de la buena práctica y la práctica anterior en situación de sequía en USD por ha

©FAO/TECA

  • El gráfico a continuación representa los costos y beneficios promedio de las diferentes entradas y salidas.
  • La buena práctica requiere mayores costos de insumos y de capital; sin embargo, estos son más que compensados por los beneficios añadidos y las pérdidas evitadas.
  • Se estimó que la inversión inicial se amortizaría en 6 años.
  • Las comunidades wayuu deben ser apoyadas para sostener los costos iniciales de adoptar las buenas prácticas de manejo del ganado, teniendo en cuenta el impacto potencial en la reducción de la inseguridad alimentaria y el aumento de la capacidad de recuperación de estas comunidades vulnerables en esta zona propensa a la sequía (Figura 2).
Figura 2. Costes y beneficios promedio en USD por año por explotación media

©FAO/TECA

  • En general, los resultados del análisis muestran que las comunidades Wayuu derivan beneficios muy limitados de las actividades de cría de ganado, que se practican sobre todo para la subsistencia.
  • Oportunidades adicionales deben ser creadas para reducir la pobreza, mejorar la seguridad alimentaria y reducir la vulnerabilidad de estas comunidades a la sequía recurrente.
Cuadro 1. Costos de brigadas sanitarias (1)

Fuente: FAO 2019

Cuadro 2. Costos de brigadas sanitarias (2)

Fuente: FAO 2019

4. Efectos secundarios de la práctica

  • Este tipo de práctica para ser sostenible en el tiempo requiere de arduo trabajo en la mano de obra, requiere de instalaciones seguras que puedan proteger el alimento de factores físicos y biológicos y de la inseguridad que puede existir dentro de las comunidades, así mismo requiere de insumos para la elaboración de estos (ensilaje) que no son fácil de conseguir en la región, más cuando son consideradas dispersas.
  • La disponibilidad de los insumos para llevar a cabo la práctica del ensilaje como el recurso forrajero, es conseguido en la región, mientras que las bolsas de conservación y melaza además de no conseguirse en la región, requieren de inversiones económicas para el desplazamiento a la cabecera municipal y la compra de dichos insumos.
  • Para asegurar la sostenibilidad de esta práctica es importante que instituciones nacionales, territoriales, y no gubernamentales se articulen y fortalezcan el capital financiero en las comunidades, permitiendo el acceso a insumos o materias primas que no estén al alcance de las familias de las comunidades.

5. Zonas agroecológicas 

  • Tropical, cálido. 

6. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas 

  • Cabras lecheras como alternativa para mejorar la alimentación: ID 7226.
  • Guía para el manejo sanitario y reproductivo de cabras: ID 7227.
  • Producción caprina y pase de cadena: ID 6004.

7. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

7.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Debido a esta práctica, que proporciona enfoques para hacer frente a las difíciles condiciones climáticas, muchas familias también se benefician con respecto a la provisión de alimentos de origen animal.

7.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Con esta tecnología, los agricultores reducen la mortalidad animal, entre otras cosas, y conducen a una mejora duradera de la salud del ganado, que a largo plazo evita muchas pérdidas económicas.

entries.tittle: Bamboo match sticks production, India
entries.summary:
Wood is the major raw material for manufacturing matchsticks. However, the match industry has been dependent on only a few wood species for making match splints and these species are now in short supply. Therefore, bamboo, one of the faster growing plants, is a sustainable raw material source for manufacturing matchsticks. 
The main advantages of using bamboo for matchstick production are: 
(a) Reduction in the use of timber. 
(b) Renewable within short rotation period, bamboo is a sustainable raw material resource for making matchsticks.
(c) Growing bamboo helps to reduce soil erosion and thereby helps to enhance the productivity of adjoining agricultural land.
entries.description:
Description

1. Synopsis

1.1 Background and introduction

Safety matches are an essential consumer commodity required by all society sections. Wood is the main raw material used for manufacturing matchsticks, but now it is in short supply. Bamboo, which is available in natural forests, is a potential sustainable raw material source for manufacturing matchsticks. Bamboo can be grown in many countries with diverse climatic conditions on a two to four years rotation period.

The use of bamboo for making matchsticks has been constrained by several bamboo characteristics, including poor wax penetration required for good incandescence and burning quality.

Indian Plywood Industries Research and Training Institute (IPIRTI), working in collaboration with and under a project funded by the International Network on Bamboo and Rattan, have developed specific processes for making quality match splints from two widely growing species of bamboo in the Southern India:

  • Bambusa bambos; and 
  • Dendrocalamus strictus.

The manufacturing process developed at IPIRTI  followed standard chemicals and processes adopted for wooden match splints. The process was undertaken at an existing match factory in Tamil Nadu.

Tests carried out at an independent laboratory have shown that the bamboo matchsticks developed at IPIRTI conform to relevant Indian Standard Specifications (IS:2653-1993 and IS:10374-1982).

1.2 Product and use

The match industry is facing problems due to matchwood shortage. Due to certain specific requirements, not many tree species have been found to be suitable for match splints making. While the demand for matches is increasing, there is a gradual reduction in supply of wood logs for matchsticks.

To help the match industries to continue to meet the growing demand, and balance the current and shortfall of wood, several alternative materials including paperboards, have been developed.

However, there is a continuing need for searching/evolving new and cost-effective materials.

Hence, it is apt to use bamboo which:

  • can be grown on short rotation period of two to four years;
  • the leftover lops and tops from the craft sector can be used for making matchsticks (due to the very small dimensions of individual match splints).

1.2.1 General development attributes and advantages

The main advantages of bamboo matchstick technology are:

  • reducing timber use;
  • using a sustainable and renewable raw material resource; (bamboo matchsticks are eco-friendly);
  • reducing soil erosion;
  • enhancing productivity of adjoining agricultural lands;
  • enhancing social and community welfare.

1.3 Market

Demand is increasing along with population growth. The volume of matchbox production is very high. The production capacity is difficult to pinpoint due to mushroom growth of this industry. The Indian consumption is increasing at a rate of about 5 percent per annum. Given the projected demand, bamboo matchsticks, are likely to capture a sizable market share because they are environmentally friendly.

1.4 Target groups

A bamboo matchstick unit can be established near:

  • naturally available bamboos areas; or
  • farmland crops (of any scale).

The technology with bamboo supplying units will be especially advantageous for areas with:

  • soil erosion, (growth can greatly reduce erosion); and
  • land degradation, (growth can gradually restore the land by enhancing productivity).

Four main target groups can benefit from the adoption of the technology:

  • bamboo cultivators;
  • bamboo artisans and handicraft sector;
  • match industry; and
  • forest managers.

1.5 Impact

1.5.1 Environment

In addition to the direct benefits, bamboos have significant environmental benefits, these are:

  • fast growing;
  • annual harvesting;
  • versatile;
  • renewable.

From the point of view of social forestry programmes bamboos aligns well with:

  • soil conservation;
  • afforestation activities;
  • cultivation; and
  • plantations.

1.6 Environment

In addition to the direct benefits, bamboos have significant environmental benefits, these are:

  • fast growing;
  • annual harvesting;
  • versatile;
  • renewable.

From the point of view of social forestry programmes bamboos aligns well with:

  • soil conservation;
  • afforestation activities;
  • cultivation; and
  • plantations.

1.7 Investment

The main requirements to establish a successful bamboo matchstick unit are:

  • capital investment;
  • sustained bamboo supply;
  • trained manpower; and
  • marketing network.

The establishment of bamboo matchstick unit also requires chemicals for:

  • bleaching;
  • carbonization;
  • wax fixing; and
  • head fixing formulation.

In addition to:

  • electricity
  • water
  • labour
  • marketing network.

The cost of machinery required for making bamboo match splints is around 0.6 million Indian Rupees. With other start up cash requirement, the total investment will be 1.0 to 1.2 million Indian Rupees (equivalent to USD 20 000 to 25 000).

1.8 Other requirements

Bamboo matchsticks are a low input-low output product for a factory, but are required in large numbers. All society sectors around the world use matchsticks. To motivate people to switchover to bamboo matchsticks, for marketing purposes, it should be emphasized that the product is:

  • low-cost
  • eco-friendly.

Establishment of a local or regional marketing agency for bamboo matchstick may be beneficial in developing market and thereby ensuring continued growth of the unit.

The renewability of bamboo on a short rotation of two to four years makes it very attractive, even for cottage industries, in terms of cost flow compared to wooden splints.

Cottage industries or small-scale bamboo matchsticks manufacturing may be eligible for development grants or other incentives from the government.

2. Technology assessment

The use of wood for burning is as old as fire itself. The development of matches is just a technological advancement. The match industry combines one of the basic uses of wood with a vital need of humankind. Safety matches are an essential consumer commodity needed by all community sectors. The main raw material for match industry has been and continues to be wood for splints.

Since 1920s, India has been importing aspen logs to make match splints, as the required quantity of aspen wood is not available in the forest reserves. Alternative tree species have been found suitable for the match industry namely:

  • Bombax Ceiba (semul);
  • Populus species (poplar);
  • Hevea Braziliensis (rubber); and
  • Ailanthus (matti).

In recent times, there has been a considerable shortage in the supply of matchwood due to the fact that many of these tree species have found alternative and more profitable application in the composite wood industry.

The demand for matches is increasing along with population growth. There have been several assessments of the demand for matchwood, the latest being a part of demand assessment for wood based industries in India (MoEF, 1999).

While demand for matches is increasing, there is a gradual reduction in wood supplies. The most important raw material for manufacturing matchsticks continues to be wood.

1 000 gross boxes of 50 require about 5 cubic meters of wood for match splints and about 2.5 cubic meters of wood for matchboxes.

Based on reported production, the total requirement of wood is estimated to be 2.3 million cubic meters in 2000, rising to four million cubic meters in 2020. The availability of matchwood presently is only 0.5 million cubic meters.

The short supply of wood is a serious problem for the match industry in the country. In order to balance the current and future shortfall of matchwood, several alternative sources for raw material have been evaluated in the past.

2.1 Evaluation of bamboo suitability

A survey of fast-growing plants focused attention on bamboo. Many species of bamboo are known to grow several centimetres in height daily during the growing season. Strength properties of split bamboo also indicate bamboo as a potential material for the production of match splints.

Bamboo is a fast-growing perennial woody grass of gregarious habit. India is one of the leading countries in bamboo production. Unlike woods that require growing periods of ten years or more, bamboo can be harvested for use at the age of two to four years or even earlier in case of some species. In addition, bamboo is available in many countries.

In India, bamboos are grown throughout the country, except in the Kashmir valley, 125 species belonging to 23 genera are reported to be grown in India. They form an important associate of deciduous and evergreen forests covering both tropical and temperate zones. They grow very well in alluvial plains having good moisture regime and up to 3 000 m in high mountains. Important genera found in India include:

  • Arundinaria
  • Bambusa
  • Dendrocalamus
  • Dinochloa
  • Gigantochloa
  • Melocanna
  • Indocalamus
  • Ochlandra
  • Oxytenanthera
  • Phyllostachys
  • Pleioblastus.

Hence bamboo is a highly suitable alternative material for making match splints.

Another important and highly relevant aspect is the small size of match splints, therefore even lops and tops, which are generally wasted in the bamboo handicraft sector, can be used for match splints.

2.2 Production process

After cross cutting bamboo into required sizes, it is split into slabs of 1.5 mm thickness and then into splints of 1.5 mm x 1.5 mm x 37 mm.

The manufacturing process developed at IPIRTI implies bamboo splints to be:

  • treated with sodium metasilicate;
  • dipped in diluted hydrogen peroxide for 15 to 20 minutes;
  • washed in water;
  • dipped in boric acid solution (with a concentration of 0.5 to 1 percent) or boric acid and borax mixture for around five minutes.
  • dried.

Treated splints are then required to be:

  • dipped in molten wax at 80 °C to 120 °C for 8 to 12 seconds; and
  • heated at around 150 °C for two to three seconds on a hot plate.

Burning heads are fixed to the bamboo match splints using standard chemicals and processes as per wooden match splints.

2.3 Production unit location

The matchstick unit can be set up in any bamboo growing area with a continuous raw material supply, and any country can adopt the technology. One essential condition is:

  • the license for storage and use of explosive materials for the burning heads and striking strips on the matchboxes.

Depending on the availability of raw materials in a particular location, the size of the unit can be:

  • cottage
  • small
  • medium
  • large.

2.4 Socio-economic impact and employment

A bamboo matchstick-manufacturing unit will provide employment and entrepreneurial opportunity to a wide range of people and relevant sectors, such as:

  • bamboo cultivation;
  • bamboo harvesting;
  • primary processing;
  • chemical processing;
  • matchstick marketing; and
  • matchstick retailing.

A cottage unit manufacturing 0.1 million matchboxes per day, can provide regular employment to more than 70 persons. The need for a sustainable supply of raw material will encourage:

  • proper management of bamboo;
  • new plantation establishments; and
  • associated environmental benefits.

The substantial quantity of bamboo plantation required to produce raw material will also increase long-term food security of rural poor in bamboo growing areas. Production of bamboo matchsticks on a small and medium scale is an effective way of utilizing renewable bamboo resources, which not only provides employment for rural people but also gives opportunities for income generation.

The technology will provide employment for a range of people and will generate extra employment in its forward and backward linkages. Its manufacture will benefit a wide range of people involved in all stages of matchstick production, either at the factory or close to the bamboo growing area.

2.5 Role of support services

The technology of bamboo matches can be adopted in the existing matchwood industry, having:

  • same chemical processing; but
  • different mechanical processing, (appropriate training can be organized).

2.6 Analysis of potential transferability issues/constraints

The technology can be adopted by the existing matchstick units using any species of bamboo and in any conditions. Since the anatomical structure of bamboo does not allow the wax to penetrate, pre-treatment of bamboo splints either in sodium hydroxide solution or in sodium metasilicate solution is required. This enhances the bleaching property and improves good wax penetration into bamboo splints.

3. Technology documentation, starting points for adaptation and financial analysis

3.1 Introduction

Research undertaken at IPIRTI in Bangalore, selected two widely grown bamboo species in the southern region of India, namely:

  • Bambusa bambos; and
  • Dendrocalamus strictus.

One important aspect when selecting bamboo species for making matchsticks is:

  • material strength and compliance to wooden match strength as prescribed for splints in relevant Standards.

Both the species selected were found to have the required strength properties.

3.2 Manufacturing processes

Bamboo matchstick manufacture requires two basic steps: 

  • splint making;
  • splint processing.

3.3 Splint making

Splints for making matchsticks have to meet the requirement of size, strength and etc. prescribed in IS:10374-1982 "Specification for Wooden Splints for Safety Matches".

Bamboo splints present the following characteristics:

  • Made from the matured culm of either of the selected species.
  • Dimensions are 37 mm long with a 1.5 mm x 1.5 mm cross section.
    • The cross section is smaller than the prevalent wooden match splints cross section.
  • Strength capacity is higher than the prevalent wooden match splints.
    • The splints of the above dimensions are able to pass the require strength tests.
  • Air-dried balancing moisture content.

3.3.1 Machinery requirements

  • circular saw;
  • splitting machine or machete;
  • splint making machine;
  • cutter and stick cutting machine; and
  • hot air chamber.

3.3.2 Culm sectioning, splitting and splint making

  • Cross cutting of culm into shorter length:
    • by hand; or
    • by using a cross cutting machine.
  • Splitting culm:
    • section is split longitudinally into splits of approximately equal width using the splitting machine.
  • Removing knot:
    • removal of nodes at or very close to either end of a section is necessary as they hinder proper splitting and burning.
  • Splitting culm into slabs with slab machine or slivering machine:
    • each split is passed through a slab-making machine to produce slabs of 1.5 mm thickness;
    • the slab-making machine also removes the epidermal or green outer layer.
  • Sectioning slab into thin splint of 1.5 mm diameter:
    • each slab is passed through stick making machine to produces splints of the same thickness (1.5 mm).
  • Cutting splint into 37 mm length, this is the usual size of matchsticks.

3.4 Splint processing

  • bleaching (optional)
  • carbonization
  • wax fixation
  • head fixing.

3.4.1 Bleaching

The splints are to be bleached in an open tank to ensure:

  • uniformity of colour; 
    • remove the natural colouring matter; and
  • market acceptance;
    • give an acceptable light colour similar to that of wooden match splints.

Prior to bleaching, the splints are:

  • pre-treated with 0.5 percent sodium silicate solution; and
  • bleached in hydrogen peroxide solution diluted with water in the ratio of 1:1 to 1:2.

Ammonia is added to maintain the pH of the bleaching solution in the range of 8 to 8.5.

The pH plays a very important role in bleaching:

  • an increased pH changes the colour of the splints to yellow; and
  • a decreased pH prolongs the time needed for bleaching.

This preliminary step helps to uniform bleaching and it facilitates penetration of wax at a later stage required for proper burning.

3.4.2 Carbonization

Carbonization of match splints imparts the desired level of afterglow properties required while extinguishing the flame of a matchstick.

For safety matches the lesser the period of after-glow the better.

Carbonization is done by:

  • chemical treatment;
    • bamboo match splints are soaked for a minimum period of ten minutes;
  • drying splints at 100 +/- 5 °C.

Though several fire-retardant chemicals are available, boric acid is perhaps the safest chemical in terms of:

  • handling
  • storing
  • transportation
  • cost.

Hence a solution with a concentration of 0.5 percent boric acid is used for carbonization of bamboo match splints.

3.4.3 Wax fixation

Wax fixation is necessary to achieve efficient transfer of flame from the burning head to the matchstick and its continuous burning until it is extinguished.

Wax fixation in the case of wooden splints is generally done by:

  • Bringing splints in contact with molten wax at a temperature of 110 °C to 130 °C for about two seconds.
  • Heating the wax tipped splints to around 150 °C for about two to three seconds on a hot plate to promote wax movement.

As wooden splints have more porosity, wax move into the pores within two to three seconds imparting good burning characteristics.

Anatomical structure of bamboo does not allow the wax to penetrate. Hence, for good wax penetration into bamboo match splints an appropriate formulation was evolved. Bamboo splints are:

  • pre-treated with 0.5 percent sodium metasilicate during bleaching process;
  • dipped in molten wax with a temperature ranging from 80 °C to 120 °C, for approximately ten seconds;
  • the wax treated splints are heated to around 150 °C  for about two to three seconds on a hot plate to promote wax movement.

3.4.5 Head fixing

A matchstick has an inflammable head that ignites only when struck on the friction surface.

The composition of the head plays an essential role in making the wooden splints light effectively when stroked against the friction surface of the matchbox.

The temperature of the flame attained is also one of the major factors that determine the degree of flame transmission from the head to the splint.

After a series of analyses carried out at the Institute laboratory, it was understood that varying percentages of potassium chlorate in the match head would give better results with respect to flame transmission to the splints.

However, two formulations presently used in Indian match industries were tried for bamboo match splints and it was found that the same formulations would also work for bamboo match splints.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Community bamboo harvesting: ID 7948.
  • Bamboo treadle pump: ID 3866.
  • Community bamboo nursery: ID 3868.
  • Bamboo in sericulture: a case study from India: ID 3859.
  • Production of bamboo mat board: ID 3860.
  • Bamboo toothpick manufacturing unit: ID 3888.
  • Bamboo splitting and slivering unit: ID 3865.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

6.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology contributes to resources use efficiency of bamboo, as well as reducing environmental impact and reduces soil erosion.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

Bamboo match sticks production can guarantee an income source for many and help enhance productivity of adjoining agricultural lands.

entries.tittle: Production of bamboo mat board, India
entries.summary: Bamboo and rattan are ideal resources for development that integrates poverty reduction and environmental sustainability, and the International Network for Bamboo and Rattan- INBAR priority is giving people at all levels the knowledge and skills they need for long-term development involving bamboo and rattan. Therefore, bamboo mat board, a plywood-like wooden board made from layers of woven bamboo mats that have been pressed together, has enormous income-generating potential for the rural poor and particularly for women, who make up the vast majority of weavers. The following technology describes how to produce bamboo mat board.
entries.description:
Description

1. Development attributes, target groups and benefits

1.1 Bamboo mat board

Bamboo mat boards (BMB) are produced from woven mats of bamboo that are soaked in adhesive resin and then pressed firmly together in a hot press. They were the first of a wide range of different panel boards presently available that use bamboo as raw material, but they are the simplest to produce, involve only bamboo raw materials and have great income-generating potential for the rural poor, who are able to weave the mats from which they are formed. The technology for the manufacture of BMB in India has been developed by the Indian Plywood Industries Research Institute (IPIRTI), Bangalore, who has developed a technically feasible and commercially viable technology for its manufacture. BMB is gaining in popularity and there are currently a handful of BMB factories in operation in India and 16 in China.

A bamboo mat board is very versatile and can be produced up to 6 mm thick by varying the number of mat layers used; boards are usually formed of two, three, five or seven mats. For thicker laminated boards, wood veneers are interleaved with the bamboo boards to produce bamboo mat-veneer composite boards (the production of these is not covered in this Guide). BMB is at least as durable and stable as wood-based plywood and is very resistant to pest attack, extreme climatic conditions and fire. It can be used for many of the uses to which plywood is now put to such as paneling; ceilings; prefabricated shelters; packing cases and storage bins; roofs; doors and door panels; furniture; and household utensils such as trays and plates. BMB is much more flexible than wood-based-plywood and can be used in structural applications such as stressed skin panels, wall bracings and web beams for which plywood is not suitable.

2. History of the development of bamboo mat board technology

2.1 International development efforts

The first recorded production of bamboo-based panels was in China during the mid-1940s where bamboo mat board bonded with casein (enamel) glues were used in the interior of airplanes as an alternative to aircraft-grade plywood. At about the same time research was initiated in India to develop synthetic resin-bonded bamboo mat board, for which the technology became available a decade and a half later. Since then, research has been carried out in several countries and over 30 types of panel products have been developed; some made of bamboo only and others of bamboo in combination with wood, lignocellulose materials and inorganic materials. Research and development efforts have been mostly confined to countries of the Asia-Pacific region e.g China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Laos, Malaysia, Philippines, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. Canada (in collaboration with Costa Rica) is the only country outside Asia where research on bamboo panels is being carried out.

Although there was some pioneering work in Taiwan, and innovative products such as ply bamboo (bamboo glue-lam) were developed, the bamboo board industry is reportedly vanishing there due to the sharp increase in wages and shortages of raw materials. In Thailand, the only product manufactured is bamboo mat board glued with Urea Formaldehyde (UF) resin and this is mainly produced for export. In countries such as Laos, the Philippines and Vietnam, interest in bamboo mat board production is relatively new, and the industries there are presently in the phase of exploratory studies and experimental or pilot scale production.

2.2 Diversification of manufacturing technologies of bamboo-based panels

Bamboo is gaining importance as a replacement for wood in flooring and roofing panels and other housing components such as windows, doors and partition panels, in furniture and in packing cases. Some of these products are made of bamboo mat board, some have a core of bamboo mats with thin veneer facings and others are made of laminated bamboo slabs/strips of different sizes and shapes (bamboo parquet and floorboards). In some products, wood veneer or shavings are used to give a wood-like appearance to the surface.

At present, China has developed the largest number of bamboo-based panel products and produces annually approximately 250,000 cubic metres in about 250 manufacturing units. The most popular panel product is bamboo mat plywood (about 100,000 cubic metres) followed by bamboo curtain board, bamboo stripboard, bamboo lath board, bamboo-based particle board, bamboo flooring panels and bamboo molded products.

Bamboo based panels developed in some countries, particularly China, have been covered under patents and details are usually not available.

2.3 Development of bamboo mat board: the Indian experience

In India, research efforts to make panels from bamboo were initiated in the mid 1950s at the Forest Research Institute, Dehra Dun. In the 1960s, this institute developed the first manufacturing process. However, high production costs inhibited the commercialization of the process. Research and development efforts were revived at IPIRTI in 1979 and a second and cost-efficient manufacturing process was developed for the production of bamboo mat board. In 1985, a factory was established in Angamally where the Kerala State Bamboo Corporation produces boards based on this new process. However, due to some inherent deficiencies, which will be noted in section 10, this technology was still not very suitable and did not become popular for enterprise development.

For this reason, in 1990 IPIRTI undertook new studies to develop improved BMB under a project sponsored by the International Development Research Centre (IDRC), Canada. Under this project, a third, innovative and appropriate technology was developed for the production of high quality, economical BMB up to 6 mm thickness. This time IPIRTI was successful in solving the deficiencies and developing a suitable manufacturing process. According to a feasibility analysis conducted by the Agricultural Finance Corporation Ltd. (AFC), Mumbai, the current process is technically feasible and financially viable. In this way, the potential of the BMB as a wood substitute has been demonstrated, as well as the techno-economic feasibility of its manufacture.

An updated annotated bibliography on bamboo-based panels was compiled based on these experiences and a manual was produced for the production of BMB. Some units in Meghalaya and Orissa States in India have successfully implemented the new technology.

As a sign of its appropriateness, the International Selection Commission of the World Expo 2000 earmarked the BMB technology developed at IPIRTI as an exemplary demonstration of the practical implementation of AGENDA 21. Consequently, the technology was registered as a World Project for Expo 2000.

2.4 General development attributes and advantages

As explained previously, the BMB technology is suitable for the production of eco-friendly alternative panel products to substitute for wood and help conserve forest resources. Moreover, technology can serve as a basis for economic development in rural areas.

2.4.1 The main development attributes of the technology

  • Reduced dependence on timber resources and natural forests due to increased use of wood substitutes, leading to environmental protection.
  • Rehabilitation of degraded forests and other wastelands through increased areas of bamboo plantation.
  • Creation of employment opportunities in mat weaving, particularly for rural and tribal women, and in bamboo growing.
  • Improvement of people skills and enhancement of their earning capacities, leading to improved welfare of the economically weaker sections of society.
  • The production of mats is flexible in time and place, favoring part-time and homebound weavers (such as young and old people and homemakers) who can continue working close to their own houses whenever they are free from other engagements.

2.4.2 The advantages of the BMB developed at IPIRTI

  • BMB is a very versatile panel material, is highly popular and environmentally friendly.
  • The boards possess physical and mechanical properties on a par with waterproof plywood and have an excellent internal bond strength, a high plane rigidity and hence high racking strength.
  • They are as durable and resistant to boiling water, weather and biological agencies (decay, insects and termite attack) as phenolic-bonded plywood.
  • They have better scratch and stain resistance properties than plywood.
  • They are as fire resistant as fire-retardant-treated plywood.
  • They have a rich natural appearance.

2.5 Suitable agro-ecological regions

The BMB technology is suitable for bamboo-growing regions with sufficient raw material that are inhabited by traditionally skilled crafts people, or other potential bamboo mat weavers. Apart from regions with natural bamboo forests, BMB could be produced in regions where bamboo is grown on plantations or in homesteads. The technology is particularly suitable in regions where bamboo plantations are desirable for the restoration of degraded forests or wastelands such as abandoned shifting cultivation areas. The production of mats requires the use of large culmed species and the unit is therefore particularly suitable for tropical, subtropical and warm temperate regions where larger bamboos grow.

2.6 Target groups

The direct beneficiaries of the BMB technology will be the many traditionally skilled rural and tribal people who make their living of weaving a variety of products from bamboo. In India, the beneficiaries are especially homemakers and young and very old people, who have time to spare, but who are unable to leave the house or are unfit to perform hard work. In areas where the depletion of natural forests results in the expenditure of foreign exchange for the import of wood, this money will be saved and the government and the nation will also benefit. The unit will also create employment opportunities for unskilled, semi-skilled and technically trained personnel who can be recruited locally.

2.7 Applicability

A major reason to use bamboo as an alternative in wood applications such as panels is the authenticity of the material and the cultural history of its use in bamboo-rich countries. In many parts of India, for example, bamboo is an important cultural feature. Since the beginning of civilization, bamboo has played an important role in the daily lives of Indian people. Bamboo craftwork is one of the oldest cottage industries primarily due to the versatility, strength and lightness of bamboo and to the ease with which it can be worked with simple hand tools. Bamboo has been put to use in various applications ranging from construction to household utensils. There are more than 1 000 documented uses including an important industrial use in paper and pulp manufacturing. For this reason, it is easy to involve local people in the making of bamboo mats and in the manufacturing of bamboo boards.

2.8 Scope for small enterprise development

Given the benefits for the many people involved, including governments and consumers, the market conditions for the production of bamboo mat boards and for the development of related industries and businesses are favorable. As shown in the final sections of this report, the establishment of a small BMB-producing enterprise/factory/plant requires a considerable investment, while the BMB can be manufactured in an existing plywood factory with very few additional facilities and investment. All that is required in this case, is a resin applicator and a drying chamber.

For the establishment of a new bamboo mat board-manufacturing unit, the estimated capital investment (including land and building) is Rs.153.36 lakhs (approx. USD 333 000). In India, the establishment of such a unit would take place in the Small-scale Sector, and it would thereby become eligible for all incentives provided by the Government for this sector.

2.9 Limitations of the technology

As mentioned in the section on the history of the BMB technology, the earlier manufacturing processes developed in India, suffered from several drawbacks and resulted in low quality bamboo panels. These deficiencies were:

  • the high quantities of resin required;
  • the non-uniform bonding due to inadequacy, or even absence, of resin on slivers in the overlapped areas of mats;
  • the unseemly appearance caused by resin pushed to the surface through the inter-sliver spaces during hot pressing;
  • the frequent application of releasing agent required to prevent panels from sticking to metal caul plates; and
  • the limited durability.

With the new process of BMB production, presented in part two of this report, most of these deficiencies can be overcome. Nevertheless, while initiating the production of such boards in a new factory, one should be aware of the potential shortcomings listed above.

2.10 Requirements for success

There are essential requirements for the successful implementation of BMB technology:

  • Sustained availability of bamboos suitable for making BMB mats.
  • Traditionally skilled bamboo craftspeople with formal training to produce BMB mats. Appropriate technologies, machinery and technically trained personnel to manage a BMB production unit.
  • Mechanisms to identify suitable markets and promote the sale of BMB in domestic and export markets
  • Continued research and development support during commercialization to solve problems arising during the transfer of technology from the laboratory to the production unit.
  • The availability of inexpensive labor is essential to the viability of a bamboo mat board based on the manual weaving of mats. As shown in Taiwan, the financial sensitivity of the labor input is high.

2.11 Potential improvements and research needs

  • Concerted efforts are required to explore the possibilities of value addition through appropriate end-use applications.
  • Further research and development efforts are required to commercialize the technologies already developed in laboratory-scale experiments, and to explore the potential of this versatile material to the full extent.
  • Additional research and development efforts should be employed to analyze and improve the activities, skills and benefits of the different people involved in the BMB production chain.
  • Extension and training activities could enlarge the efficiency and sustainability of the production of bamboos, mat weaving and commercialization, and improve the income effect and distribution of benefits for the people involved.

2.12 Conclusion

The bamboo mat board technology is a commercially and socially effective means of processing bamboo into quality end products for the construction, packaging and transport sectors. Its development attributes imply considerable scope for income and welfare improvement for rural poor people. In addition, it enables governments and wood-based industries to cope with the problem of wood shortages and to reduce environmental degradation due to overharvesting of timber trees. If properly organized and guided by private enterprises, state agencies and/or NGOs, the technology as well as its backward and forward linkages can increase the income and welfare of many people in a sustainable manner.

3. The manufacturing process for bamboo mat board

3.1 Introduction

Bamboo mat board is produced by a simple technical process comprising the following main steps.

  1. Mat making (raw material preparation)
  2. Application of adhesive/binder to mats
  3. Assembling of mats in preparation for pressing
  4. Formation of boards by hot- or room temperature-pressing under pressure (curing)
  5. Cutting to size (dimensioning)
  6. Finishing (such as coatings or lamination)

3.2 Production of bamboo mats

3.2.1 Harvesting bamboo

Matured bamboo culms are extracted following the locally prescribed silvicultural methods and are crosscut into convenient lengths varying from 50 to 250 cm. The nodal portions are retained in species with short internodes, such as Dendrocalamus strictus (30 cm), whereas in species with long internodes such as Ochlandra travancorica and Melocanna baccifera (50 cm to 100 cm), the nodal portions are removed. The splits of long-internode species, such as Ochlandra travancorica are of a more even thickness than those of short-internode species such as Dendrocalamus strictus. Although both species are suitable for mat making, about 40 percent more resin is required for bonding mats made of D. strictus and other similar short-internode species.

During the course of the IDRC-sponsored BMB research project at IPIRTI, several bamboo species were studied for BMB manufacture. All were found to be suitable.

3.2.2 Splitting bamboo

The crosscut bamboo lengths can be split with:

  • a machete;
  • hand splitting knives; or
  • a splitting machine.

When using a splitting machine, the bamboo pole is fixed longitudinally in front of the set of splitting knives and a mechanical pushing device pushes the bamboo over the knives to produce splits of a uniform size. The number of splits produced depends upon the number of knives present in the splitting knives set. In general, the width of the splits varies from 10 mm to 15 mm depending on the species and quality of bamboo. The splits are then allowed to dry in the air or in artificial ventilation to reduce their moisture content to around 30 percent.

3.2.3 Knot removal

It is necessary to remove the nodes to maintain an even thickness of sliver and to facilitate further processing. The inner and outer knots are removed from the splits either manually with a sharp knife or mechanically with a knot removal and width-sizing machine. This machine also sizes the width of the splint and planes the surface.

3.2.4 Sliver making

The green epidermal layer of the splints is removed using a sharp knife and can be set aside and used for making other products. It is not suitable for making into slivers. Slivers 0.6 mm thick (+/-10 percent) and 12 mm to 16 mm wide are made manually from splints using a sharp knife or a slivering machine. Keeping the variation in thickness of the slivers to within 10 percent is very important. Higher variation than this results in increased requirements for resin.

3.2.5 Drying and weaving

Slivers are dried to around 15 percent moisture content. The dried slivers are manually woven into mats of different sizes and patterns depending on the specific requirements set. The two most common weaving patterns are the herring bone pattern (45 degrees) and the rectangular pattern (90 degrees). The most common sizes of the mats are 250 cm x 125 cm, 180 cm x 125 cm, and 180 cm x 150 cm.

3.2.6 Storage of mats

Woven mats can be air-dried further and stored without any treatment for three to four weeks. Prophylactic treatments must be applied if they are likely to be stored for a longer period. The simplest and most effective treatment for mats, if they are not likely to be exposed to water, is to spray them with a 1 percent solution of a mixture of boric acid and borax in a 1:1 ratio. Spraying can be done with a hand sprayer or a knapsack sprayer. Alternatively, the mats can be soaked in the solution for about ten minutes.

Treated mats are dried either in the air or in a drier, and stored under cover. Treated mats should not come into contact with the ground and hence it is advisable to store them on wooden pallets of 12 to 18 cm (4 to 6 inches) above ground level. Treated bamboo mats can be stored for three to four months without deterioration. They must be stored in well-ventilated locations with low relative humidity and negligible changes in humidity. The chances of fungal or insect attack are increased if the relative humidity is very high. Mats should be resprayed once every three months and should be checked regularly (at least once per fortnight) for any signs of fungal growth, mold and/or borer attack.

4. Resin manufacturing

Phenol formaldehyde (PF) resin is generally used for manufacturing BMB. The resin is prepared in a resin kettle or batch resin reactor made of either mild steel or stainless steel. The most suitable resin formulation and method of production are given below.

4.1 Chemical ingredients

  • Phenol: pure phenol is a white crystalline solid with a melting point of 43 ºC. It should conform to IS: 538-1968, Specification for phenol (carbolic acid).
  • Formaldehyde: formaldehyde is a gas usually available as formalin, which is a solution of 37 percent concentration (by weight) in water with methyl alcohol as a stabilizer. It should conform to IS: 3321 - 1973, Specification for formaldehyde.
  • Sodium hydroxide: sodium hydroxide is available in pellets as well as in flake form. It is white in color, hygroscopic and highly soluble in water.

4.2 Resin manufacturing process

One hundred parts by weight of phenol are charged into a resin kettle followed by 150 to 200 parts by weight of 37 percent formalin and stirring is commenced. Between five and fifteen parts by weight of sodium hydroxide dissolved in double the quantity of water is then added, then stirring is continued. The chemical reaction starts after the three components have been mixed, and takes about 90 minutes to complete. The temperature of the reaction mixture is maintained between 82 ºC and 85 ºC. During the course of the reaction, the flow time of the resin is checked periodically using a B-4 cup as described in IS:3944. The reaction is stopped when the flow time increases to around 15 seconds when the resin is hot. The resin is then cooled to room temperature by circulating cold water in the jacket of the kettle. The cooled resin is discharged from the kettle and stored in airtight containers.

4.3 Properties of PF resin

The cooled resin should have the following properties for optimum results.

  • Viscosity - 65 +/- 20 mPas at 25 ºC.
  • Flow time in a B-4 cup (IS:3944) - 27 seconds +/-5 seconds at 25 ºC.
  • Water tolerance - 1:6 to 1:20 depending on the quantity of sodium hydroxide used.
  • Solids content – 48 percent +/- 2 percent.
  • Pot life two to three weeks at 25 ºC.

5. Board manufacturing

5.1 Resin application

Application of resin to bamboo mats is one of the most important steps, both from the point of view of quality and economy. Most crucial at this point are:

  • the amount of resin applied;
  • the mode of application; and
  • the duration.

Resin application is done by dipping.

5.2 Resin dilution with water for dipping

Approximately 200 kg of PF resin is poured into the resin applicator, which is sufficient for the production of about 575 to 600, three layered boards. Two kilograms of sodium octaborate tetra hydrate dissolved in 400 kg of water is added to the resin as a preservative. The concentration of sodium octaborate tetra hydrate is one per cent by weight of the liquid PF resin. This boron compound penetrates into the slivers along with the resin, is fixed during hot pressing, and confers resistance to fungus and insect attack on the BMB. About 60 mats are dipped into the resin solution each time and are dipped for five minutes. Resin soaked mats are removed from the resin solution and kept in an inclined position for about 30 minutes to allow excess resin to drain away.

5.3 Stabilization and drying of resin-coated mats

Resin coated mats are laid one above the other for at least two hours after treatment for stabilization. The stabilized mats are dried in either a drying chamber or industrial dryers such as a band dryer, at a temperature of 95 ºF +/- 5ºC until the moisture content falls to 10 percent +/- 2 percent.

5.4 Assembly

Dried resin-coated mats are assembled on aluminum metal cauls that are thoroughly coated with a releasing agent, such as silicone - 17 compound. The number of mats assembled depends upon the required thickness of the board. The releasing agent used to coat the metal cauls should be reapplied after 15 to 20 hot pressing cycles.

5.5 Hot pressing

Hot pressing melts the resin in the mats and bonds them together tightly. The assembled mats are first loaded on to the hot press and the mats pressed according to the following protocol:

  • Pressure - 16 kg per cm2
  • Temperature - 145 ºC +/- 5 ºC
  • Time - 6 minutes for 3 mats (with one minute extra for every additional mat layer)

5.6 Trimming and checking

The hot-pressed boards are trimmed to the required size in a DD saw.

5.7 Testing

Bamboo mat boards are tested for conformity as per IS: 13958, 1994  specification for bamboo mat board for general purposes (Indian standard).

6. Comprehensive inputs

6.1 Plant layout

Bamboo mat boards can be manufactured in a plywood factory with very few additional facilities. All that is required is a resin applicator and a drying chamber if a band dryer is not already available.

6.2 Capital investment

A bamboo mat board-manufacturing unit can be established in the small-scale sector. It can, therefore, become eligible for all incentives provided by the government for this sector in India. The estimated capital investment (including land and building) is Rs.153.36 lakhs (USD 333 000).

6.3 Recurring costs

Recurring costs involved are for:

  • raw material;
  • energy;
  • machinery and equipment maintenance;
  • managerial and labor; and
  • postproduction activities.

The recurring costs are estimated on the assumption that:

  • the unit works one shift of eight hours per day;
  • the number of working days in a year is 300; and
  • the unit works to 50 percent of installed capacity in year 1, 75 percent in year two and 100 percent from year three onwards.

7. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Bamboo in sericulture: a case study from India: ID 3859.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Resource use efficiency

This practice describes a method to create value-added products through the processing of bamboo. In using bamboo, a sustainable and resource efficient material is used to reduce the pressure on the earth’s biophysical boundaries.
