19. Management of processing operations

19.1 Throughput

To maximise production and minimise operating costs, the dryer should be operated with all 12 trays fully loaded. The quantity of fruit required for a full load will vary widely depending on the fruit or vegetable being dried, cultivar, maturity and size of the fruit, skill and care of the operators in handling and preparing the fruit and thickness of the slices.

The quantity of fruit required for a full load will be gained through experience. As an approximate guide, a full load will require around 34 kg of banana slices, 24 kg of pineapple slices and 18 kg of mango slices.

19.2 Timing of processing

It is important that the period from first washing the fruit to loading the dryer is kept as short as possible. If an individual is working on their own, they will need to work fairly quickly or, better, have a family member who can help even if it is only for a short period. If several people are involved with the dryer, then the owner/manager will need to train and organize the operators so that processing can be carried out efficiently and effectively.

To achieve maximum drying effect from the available sunshine, the dryer should be fully loaded within two to three hours after sunrise. This will mean that the preparation of the fruit will need to start before dawn. It is not a good idea to start drying late in the afternoon since the fruit will still be in a very moist condition during the first night and thus highly susceptible to deterioration and mould growth.

19.3 Repair and maintenance

The dryer needs to be properly maintained to maximise efficiency and for long life. The plastic sheet cover of the drying chamber is the item most susceptible to damage and deterioration. Goats and other livestock, which may be attracted by the smell of the fruit, and boisterous children need to be kept away from the dryer at all times as they can easily damage the plastic sheet. If possible, a barrier should be placed around the dryer or the area fenced off to prevent animals from getting close.

The plastic sheet will naturally discolour and degrade progressively with exposure to sunlight and as a result, will need to be replaced after two to three years. The dryer should be covered over during the off-season and when not in use, perhaps with papyrus or straw, to help protect the plastic. When trays are not in use, they are better stored in a dry place free of termites and other pests.

19.4 Business records

To be able to monitor the progress of the business, it is essential to keep records of operational activities including the costs of all purchases for the business, dates of transactions, the quantities of fruit purchased, the amount of losses, dryer loading densities, dryer loading and unloading times, the amount of dried product obtained and the revenue gained.

19.5 Business expansion

In most circumstances, businesses will start with one dryer. Once successful, the producer may then wish to expand by using additional dryers. In such situations, a note of caution is advisable. The operation of a single dryer can be accomplished by one owner/processor, although some assistance from their family is helpful for preparing the fruit. However, with a larger enterprise involving several dryers, the owner needs to become involved in managing the business as a whole with the result that there is less time for supervision of the processing operations. Responsibility for some areas will, therefore, have to be delegated to appointed employees. Suitable persons will need to be found and trained in their tasks. In addition, a larger store room may need to be acquired or constructed.

Expansion of the business should not be considered lightly. Whatever is intended, it is essential to maintain profitability.

19.6 Additional information on other treatments

19.6.1 Blanching

Blanching involves the immersion of the prepared produce into very hot water (90ºC, but often boiling) or exposure to steam for one or more minutes, depending upon temperature, sizes of the pieces and quantities. Care is required not to over-blanch. This is then followed by immersion in cold water. The treatment is often used for vegetables (such as beans, peas, carrots) and sometimes for tubers.

Precooking in this way for a short time at a high temperature can accelerate drying (by increasing water permeability), improve storage (by deactivating enzymes and destroying bacteria) and improve colour retention. The treatment also reduces rehydration and subsequent cooking times.

19.7 Sulphuring and sulphiting

Sulphur dioxide is frequently used as a preservative pre-treatment to improve the storage life of dried fruit and vegetables and to help retain the colour.

There are two common methods used.

19.7.1 Sulphuring

Sulphuring is the burning of sulphur tablets to produce sulphur dioxide gas in an enclosed chamber. Sulphuring is more commonly used for fruit. It involves the construction of an enclosed cabinet with small inlet and outlet vents which can be adjusted. The fruit is placed inside on trays before being dried. Sulphur is burnt so that the sulphur dioxide gas produced is allowed to permeate into the fruit for up to two hours. The gas is potentially harmful and care must be taken not to inhale the gas. 

19.7.2 Sulphiting

Sulphiting involves making a solution of sulphur dioxide by dissolving sodium sulphite or sodium metabisulphite (Campden tablets) into water. Sulphiting is more commonly used for vegetables. Blanching in a sulphite solution is particularly useful as it combines two operations into one. There are maximum permitted levels on the concentration of this additive in products.

20. Checklist of good practices

Products should be grown, harvested, handled, transported, processed, stored, distributed and sold in ways that conform with appropriate food safety and food hygiene legislation. Due account should, therefore, be taken on the following to help establish good practices by the processor. Produce is grown and obtained where:

  • it is known not to be contaminated (for example that it is not polluted, poisoned, toxic, impure, tainted, unclean, etc);
  • human and animal wastes are disposed of well away from processing activities so as to avoid any likelihood of cross-contamination;
  • precautions are taken to avoid raw material and product being contaminated by animals, insects, vermin, birds, chemical, microbiological or other sources;
  • raw material is stored separately under clean, dry and airy conditions;
  • precautions are taken not to bruise or damage produce as this could permit invasion and growth by spoilage micro-organisms; and
  • discrete areas are provided for the different activities involved, namely a raw store room (raw material preparation), outside (washing produce), processing room (peeling, cutting, slicing and loading the dryer) and dry store room/area (unloading and product packing).

20.1 General checklist

  • The clean working areas should be clearly separated from the dirty working areas.
  • Water used in processing is clean, preferably from a borehole, and always sanitised (e.g treated with bleach containing a chlorine agent).
  • Utensils used are made of stainless steel, all surfaces and utensils in contact with the food are cleaned and sanitised (including preparation surfaces, dryer and so forth).
  • During preparation, processing and packing, the product is protected from sources of contamination (e.g human hair, dust, flies, insects, vermin, animals and so forth)
  • Operatives wash their hands with clean sanitised water using non-perfumed soap; hands are properly dried with clean (disposable) towels.
  • Operatives wear clean hairnets or scarves and protective (bib style) aprons; separate shoes or sandals are worn in the processing/preparation areas.
  • Operatives who are unwell, vomiting or have diarrhoea are not involved with processing until the disorder has cleared.
  • Wastes (peel etc) are properly disposed of away from the food areas so as not to encourage flies, insects, vermin and so forth.
  • Basins, buckets, containers, knives, etc. are cleaned before and after use.
  • Working surfaces are cleaned before and after use.
  • Floors, tables, etc. are cleaned daily.
  • Store rooms/areas, walls, ceilings, behind and underneath tables and chairs, etc. are thoroughly cleaned each week.
  • The dryer and each of the trays are cleaned and sanitised after each batch operation so as not to contaminate the next batch.
  • Packaging material is kept clean, dry and stored away from sources of contamination.
  • The final product is labelled, dated and stored under clean, dry and airy conditions which prevent contamination, insect infestation and “sweating” (which may give rise to microbial growth).
  • Store areas and rooms are thoroughly cleaned each week.
  • Products are stored for no more than one month.
  • All personnel receive training in food hygiene and food safety matters so they are fully familiar with requirements and procedures.

20.2 Processing hygiene checklist

This checklist should be used as a guide for processing operations to ensure the production of good quality dried fruit. Each point should be checked before starting each operation.

20.2.1 Washing

  • Has the working area been swept and washed?
  • Does the fruit need pre-rinsing in water before washing in the bleach solution?
  • Has the bleach solution been made up to the correct strength?
  • Are clean baskets/buckets available for the clean fruit?

20.2.2 Peeling

  • Have working tables and knives been cleaned with a bleach solution?
  • Has the working area been swept and washed?
  • Are the operators wearing separate shoes or sandals?
  • Have the operators washed their hands?
  • If used, are gloves in good condition and washed?
  • Are clean buckets/bowls available for the peeled fruit?

20.2.3 Cutting and slicing

  • Have working tables and knives been cleaned with a bleach solution?
  • Has the working area been swept and washed?
  • Have the operators washed their hands?
  • If used, are gloves in good condition and washed?
  • Are clean buckets/bowls available for the slices?

20.2.4 Tray loading

  • Is the loading area clean?
  • Have the trays been brushed clean of debris and washed?
  • Have the operators washed their hands
  • If used, are gloves clean?

20.2.5 Loading the dryer

  • Has the interior of the dryer been swept and wiped clean?

20.2.6 Unloading the dryer

  • Is the unloading area clean?
  • Have the operators washed their hands?
  • If used, are gloves clean and dry?
  • Are clean and dry baskets available for the dried fruit?

20.2.7 Packing

  • Is the packing area clean and dust-free?
  • Are hands clean?
  • If used, are gloves clean and dry?
  • Is the packing material clean?
  • Are clean containers available for the packed fruit?
  • Is the storage area clean and dry?
  • Is the storage area free of insects and other pests?

20.2.6 Comments 

The following comments were provided by CIRAD (pers. comm., 2006)

  • The flesh of the material to be dried is initially “clean”. Microbes are on the surface of the fruits and in the environment. Recommendations should aim to avoid or limit the contamination of flesh.
  • Acceleration of maturation is described. It is also possible to slow down it by a renewal of air. A daily sorting of the fruits is recommended in order to eliminate too ripe fruits and to expose the rest to quality standards, for acceleration or deceleration of maturation.
  • The good stage of maturity of the fruits for drying is the “just ripe” stage. Drying has an effect similar to the ripening of approximately a day.
  • It is recommended to carry out peeling, cutting and setting on trays in a room protected from insects, with good ventilation or ventilators, and to avoid perspiration by the operators.
  • Loading of the drier has to be made as soon as the product is available, without waiting to have enough product to fill the complete drier.
  • Drying must be supervised. A movement or sorting of the trays could be necessary if some of them dry more slowly than the others.

24. Objectives fulfilled by the project

24.1 Women-friendly

The practice creates employment for women's groups.

24.2 Pro-poor technology

The practice is not costly to use and, through improved product quality, allows for not only an additional source of food but provides opportunities to develop business, enabling an additional source of income.

entries.tittle: Producing solar-dried fruit and vegetables for micro and small-scale rural enterprise development: business profitability
entries.summary: The preservation of fruit and vegetables by simply sun drying is practised widely throughout arid and semi-arid regions, for example in Uganda. The use of low-cost solar drying technologies can significantly improve product quality. This provides practical opportunities for developing small-scale enterprise, particularly in rural areas, and creates employment for women's groups. This document highlights the need to make a rigorous cost-accounting methodology.
entries.description:
Description

Experience in Uganda indicates that there are circumstances where it is feasible to establish solar drying operations as viable micro enterprises in rural areas. Such operations require dedication, patience and basic skills by all of those involved. However, market channels also need to be developed, product quality needs to be controlled and technical assistance needs to be given. An overall and integrated approach is essential if solar drying activities are to be successful in rural development programmes.

This technology is part of a series of four related technology records dealing with solar drying and needs to be considered in conjunction with these other records.

  1. Assessing opportunities
  2. Dryer construction
  3. Practical aspects of processing
  4. Business profitability (this record).

1. Running a business

  • The aim of this guide is to provide guidance on ways to run a solar drying business profitably and to avoid costly mistakes.
    • For those starting on a business enterprise of this nature, many challenges will be encountered but the rewards could potentially be high.
    • Most importantly, for the business to be successful, the owner or manager needs to:
      • continually monitor costs and revenue;
      • react quickly to changing circumstances;
      • find new ways to reduce costs and increase revenue;
      • seek improvements to the business;
      • be diligent;
      • and be dedicated.
    • The aim is always to increase profit and the return on the investment, so that the business can remain healthy and viable.Once the first dryer is operating well, the owner may wish to build a second dryer,employ people to assist with processing or expand to grow fruit for drying and sale.
      • Some producers who operate several dryers have even purchased pigs and cattle, feeding them on waste peelings from processing, thereby yielding further sources of income.
      • Others may consider diversifying and start drying different products.

2. Operating a business

Operating a business can be broken down into four distinct activities:

  1. Producing dried product
  2. Selling product
  3. Keeping records
  4. Handling money

2.1 Producing dried product

  • Good quality fresh produce needs to be purchased at competitive prices and delivered to the dryer;
    • The fruit needs to be prepared with full regard for hygiene and cleanliness.
    • The dryer needs to be loaded.
    • When the fruit has dried, the dryer needs to be unloaded and the dried product packed.
  • The time needed for buying fruit will vary upon the circumstances from a few minutes to several hours.
    • It requires about five hours of work to prepare the fruit (washing, peeling, cutting and slicing) and to load the dryer.
    • If there are two people working together, it will be reduced accordingly.
    • This has the advantage in that the dryer can be filled early in the morning so that the fruit can be in the dryer during most of the day when it is warm and sunny.
    • The drying process may take two, three or sometimes four days.
  • At the end of the second day, the processor needs to check that the fruit is dry.
    • If this is so, the processor needs to unload it, check quality and pack it into sealed bags.
    • Unloading does not take so long as loading - less than one hour usually for a single dryer.
    • The work of re-filling the dryer can then begin again the following morning.
    • All these activities have to be organised and supervised.
    • The routine repair and maintenance of the dryer, as well as the buying of consumable items such as bleach and soap, also need to be supervised.

2.2 Selling product

  • The dried fruit produced should be sold every two to four weeks.
    • If a poor-quality product is produced, it will be more difficult to sell and it will have less value.
    • The cost of delivery to the buyer adds significantly to the overall costs of production.
    • At present in Uganda, much of the “natural” dried fruit is purchased by Fruits of the Nile Ltd in Kampala.
    • The company checks the quality and exports the products to Europe, according to market demands.

2.3 Keeping records

  • Without records of all transactions, it is impossible to conclude whether the business is profitable or what can be done to improve it.
    • Once operating successfully, it will be possible to expand the business and the processor can build more dryers.
    • This will increase the level of work and may mean that different dryers are being loaded every day.
    • It may also lead to the need to employ people to work for the business when the discipline of keeping records becomes even more critical.

2.4 Handling money

  • Producing dried fruit can be a profitable business.
  • However, it may be necessary:
    • to arrange financial loans,
    • to raise money for building the dryer,
    • to handle money for paying for fresh produce,
    • to pay for labour also, and to be able to receive moneys from the sale of product.
  • The owner needs to be vigilant, and must be able to methodically track money matters and keep costs to a minimum.

3. Producing dried fruit profitably

  • In running the business, there are several factors which should be examined if dried fruit is to be produced profitably, including:
    • buying fresh produce,
    • storage,
    • processing,
    • employing labour,
    • labour payment methods, and
    • managing labour.

3.1 Buying fresh produce

3.1.1 Choosing fruit

  • When choosing fruit, there are a number of factors to consider, such as:
    • price per kilogram;
    • size of pieces;
    • bruising and other damage,;
    • ripeness;
    • and sugar content.
  • Price per kilogram
    • This is the most important and most obvious, but it should be remembered that fruit is not always sold by weight.
    • In Uganda, for instance, bananas are often sold by the “bicycle load” and mangoes by the “jerry can”.
  • Size of pieces
    • Larger fruit yield more peeled flesh than smaller fruit.
    • In general, larger fruit are preferred or a corresponding lower price paid for smaller fruit to compensate.
  • Bruising, insect damage and usable fruit
    • Sometimes it is difficult to clearly see that fruit is damaged.
    • This is gained through experience and careful inspection of the produce.
    • Damage frequently occurs during transport and through too much fruit being piled on top of each other.
  • Ripeness
    • Often, unripe fruit are cheaper to buy and less prone to damage during transport.
    • However, the main disadvantages are that it is more difficult to assess produce quality and they need to be stored until they are ripe.
  • Sugar content
    • Fruit which is sweet will dry better and yield a greater weight of dried fruit compared to fruit which is unsweet or unripe.
    • Fruit should be used for drying when it is at peak ripeness.
    • With time, the producer should be able to learn how best to identify good quality produce and how much to pay for it.
    • It is a valuable skill which the producer needs to learn and appreciate.
    • Example 1: Size of fruit and cost question:
      • Is it better to buy large or small pineapples to fill the dryer?
      • Assume one large pineapple costs USh 300, 15 large pineapples are required to fill the dryer, one small pineapple costs USh 250, 25 small pineapples are required to fill the dryer.Conclusion: it is cheaper to use large pineapples to fill the dryer because the cost of large pineapples is USh 300 x 15 = USh 4 500 and the cost of small pineapples is USh 250 x 25 = USh 6 250.

3.1.2 Cost of buying

  • The cost of buying fresh fruit and vegetables is significant and can account for nearly 60 percent of total costs.
  • It is important to minimise the prices paid for raw materials at all times.
  • Much depends upon the negotiating skills of the buyer, but there are several points to consider:
  • The processor should visit farmers to discuss requirements and assess the quality locally available.If there are many farmers in the local area who can supply fruit, the processor should ask each one for their best price as this will increase the processor’s bargaining position.
  • It is not a good idea to make an agreement with only one farmer to supply all of the fruit needed, as prices may suddenly be increased or interrupted (even if the farmer is a relative).
  • It is important to agree with the seller on the quantity, quality and actual size of fruit required.
    • The cost including all delivery, transport charges and guarantees that the seller will deliver regularly.
    • If farmers are distant, transport costs are likely to be high thereby making the produce too expensive.
  • If the operator is a woman and the farmer is a man, she may find it difficult to negotiate a good price, in which case, it may be appropriate to obtain the assistance of a male relative to negotiate on her behalf.
    • The operator of the dryer is in a strong position to negotiate if they can pay cash and agree a regular order with the farmer.
  • Should the business grow, the amount of fruit bought will increase thereby strengthening the position further.
  • It can be beneficial to visit farmers with other dryer processors and place a regular bulk order.
    • Increasing the amount of fruit purchased at any one time increases the farmer’s guaranteed sales which can, potentially, reduce fruit prices.
  • In return for offering competitive prices, the farmers will expect to be paid regularly, on time, in full and have specified agreements honoured by the buyer.
    • Fruit and vegetables take time and effort to cultivate and farmers are running businesses, making similar decisions and taking risks like the processors.
    • In the end, the farmer and the processor are in partnership, not opposition.

3.1.3 Variable cost pricing

  • Prices will vary during the season.
    • At the beginning and the end of the growing season, prices are likely to be higher and the processor must expect to pay higher prices.
    • In the middle of the harvest, prices may be very low.
    • The profitability of drying will therefore vary accordingly.
    • If prices are considered too high, it is normally better not to operate the dryer and wait until fruit prices fall.
  • However, if for a short period of two or three weeks, revenue from selling dried fruit is likely just to exceed variable costs (e.g. without any allowance to cover fixed costs so that there is still a small return to labour), then it would be worth operating the dryer so that commitments with farmers and sales to buyers can be maintained as long as possible.
  • Consider Example 2 below which helps illustrate the points by comparing two situations.
  • Example 2: Variable cost pricing
    • Assume 20 pieces of pineapple are required to fill the dryer.
    • The dryer is operated twice per week, 2.6 kg of dried pineapple is produced, and dried fruit is sold in Kampala every two weeks.
    • The cost of return journey is USh 3 000, the cost of transport for operating the dryer once is USh 750 (3 000/4), and the price obtained for dried pineapple is USh 2 700 per kg.
  • Situation one
    • Pineapples cost USh 300 each.
    • The cost of filling the dryer would be USh 6 000 (20 x 300); variable costs (fruit plus transport) would be USh 6 750 (6 000 + 750); and revenue from the dried fruit would be USh 7 020 (2.6 x 2 700).Conclusion
      • Revenue is greater than variable costs and a small return to labour (and capital) is paid of USh 270.
      • If this level of return to labour is acceptable in the short run, it is worthwhile operating the dryer.
  • Situation two
    • Pineapples cost USh 350 each.
    • The cost of filling the dryer would be USh 7 000 (20 x 350); variable costs (fruit plus transport) would be USh 7 750 (7 000 + 750); and revenue from the dried fruit would be USh 7 020 as before.
    • Conclusion
    • Revenue is less than variable costs (before a return to labour is considered), so it is not worthwhile operating the dryer.
  • The variable cost pricing approach is a short-term measure only when a decision needs to be made on whether to continue drying or not.
    • Over the year as a whole, it is essential for total revenue to exceed the total of both variable and fixed costs for the business to be profitable.
    • The greater this difference, the greater is the profit.

3.1.4 Buying larger quantities

  • Prices can often be reduced if fruit is purchased in larger quantities.
    • This means that some fruit will need to be stored temporarily.
    • However, it can offer advantages such as fruit which is not yet ripe can be purchased and is relatively cheaper.
  • Not more than one week supply of fruit should be stored at one time.
    • For example, the amount of fruit that is needed to fill the dryer twice, otherwise it could spoil before being properly dried.
    • The length of time fruit take to fully ripen varies considerably, depending on the variety and on weather conditions.
    • Thes factors, the processor must learn to judge.
  • During the rainy season, storing fruit is more risky.
    • If the weather is overcast or wet, it is difficult to dry fruit as the dryer requires sunshine to operate effectively.
    • If the weather is poor for several consecutive days, it will be impossible to dry fruit and stored fruit will spoil.
    • In these circumstances, it is better to sell it.
  • It may be possible for the processor to operate a second business selling fresh fruit at local markets as a way of managing fruit supplies for the business as it grows.
    • If the processor is regularly buying fresh fruit at a good price from the local farmers, it should be possible to sell the fruit at a competitive price on the local market.

4. Storage

  • Being able to store produce offers some advantages in that fruit is available to operate the dryer at any time.
    • Buying larger quantities also means the processor can use fruit which is just ripe for drying that day.
    • If the processor buys only small quantities of fruit, he/she may be tempted to use fruit which is not ripe.
    • This will lead to losses.

4.1 Storeroom

  • Arrangements for storing produce need to be carefully considered.
    • A cool, dry, secure and well-ventilated room is ideal.
    • The store will need regular cleaning as waste from fruit will tend to gather and attract insects and rodents such as rats.
    • Poor storage conditions will also result in fruit rotting quickly.
    • Both bananas and pineapples should be hung off the ground as they will bruise easily if they are stored on hard ground.
    • Experience shows that fruit is treated with very little care in Uganda, as it is seen as having little value.
    • If you are operating a drying business, good quality fruit is very valuable.
    • Once the processor begins to be successful and builds more dryers, the fruit store may have to be increased in size to hold larger stocks of fresh produce.

4.2 Rotation of stock in store

  • It is important to practice stock rotation in all stores.
    • In general, this means that fruit which has been stored for the longest period of time should be dried first.
    • The fruit which has been purchased most recently should be dried last.
    • In this way, stocks are rotated and fruit is not left in the store for a long time.
    • It may also be possible for the processor to control the ripening of fruit.
      • Adding a small number of very ripe fruit to a group of unripe fruit and covering them with a plastic bag speeds up the ripening of the unripe fruit.
    • Keeping unripe fruit together in a cool dark place tends to slow down ripening.

5. Processing

  • To ensure the dryer operates at a high level of efficiency, fruit needs to be correctly prepared and the dryer operated at full capacity.
    • This means that all the trays should be filled and densely packed with fruit cut to the correct thickness.
  • Proper fruit preparation and tray loading, are important for achieving a profitable dryer business.
    • Experiences in Uganda have shown that fruit preparation standards and loading densities vary significantly between processors.
    • This not only affects the quantity of dried fruit produced, but also the revenue gained from the dryer.
    • If fresh fruit is not prepared properly, and the dryer is not correctly loaded, the weight of dried fruit produced will be less than it should be and profits will be significantly reduced.

5.1 Repair and maintenance

  • From time to time the dryer will require repair and maintenance.
    • It is important to always keep the plastic covering clean and to mend any tears promptly, otherwise the dryer efficiency will be affected.
    • The longer the tears are left, the worse they become, making it more difficult and expensive to repair.
    • Tears can be temporarily repaired by covering them with sticky tape.
  • Preventative maintenance should be carried out to ensure the dryer lasts for a long time in good condition.
    • This involves checking its stability, the plastic sheets (which may need to be replaced), joints, the loading trays, repainting the legs and generally checking overall that the dryer appears in good order.
    • The best time to carry out such maintenance is just before the beginning of the main fruit season or during the rainy season when the dryer is not being used.
    • The owner can then be confident that the dryer is in good condition, ready for the drying season.
    • The owner must recognise the need to maintain the dryer, and put aside some small amounts of money to cover these costs when they arise.

5.2 Working capital

  • As the solar dryer will not be operating continuously during the year, it is important for an allowance to be made so that working capital is readily available at the beginning of each drying season.
    • Working capital is money that is required to initially operate the dryer.
      • Moneyfor the purchase of fresh fruit, consumables such as bleach, payment of labour (as applicable) and transport costs.
    • hese need to be paid before any revenue is received.
    • If fruit is sold every two weeks, then sufficient working capital is required to purchase fruit for drying for a two-week period.
    • Some money therefore needs to be put aside at the end of each season for restarting.
    • If not, it may be difficult to raise the finance required to operate the dryer again, and consequentlyinitial investment and potential future profits will be jeopardised.

6. Employing labour

  • At present, the most successful solar drying businesses in Uganda use small solar cabinet dryers which are owned and operated by individuals.
    • The owner of the dryer is also the person who prepares the fruit (washing, peeling, cutting and slicing) and operates the dryer, often with the help of family members.
    • In these situations, the labour is usually unpaid and the net revenue from operating the dryer is a return to labour as well as profit.
  • This seems to be a successful way to operate a dryer business and nearly all producers will start out this way in Uganda.
    • The costs are relatively small, so are the risks and it provides a good basis for learning how to run a business.
    • New producers will undoubtedly make mistakes, but these should not be too costly as production levels tend to be low at the beginning.
    • However, once the business begins to develop further and more than one dryer is employed, the processor will need to hire labour to help with operations.
    • This is a major change to the business and the viability of employing labour needs to be carefully examined as additional operational costs will be involved.
    • Here, the hire of labour is shown as a variable cost because the amount of labour used will vary with the number of times the dryer is used.
  • When calculating the effect of paid labour on viability, it is important that all labour costs are calculated.
    • In some cases, owners may pay employee’s transport costs to work or provide other benefits.
    • These costs need to be included into the calculation of labour costs.

6.1 Cost of hiring labour

  • Assume that the time required to cut/peel fruit and load/unload the dryer is seven hours.
  • One hour is allowed for cleaning.
  • The cost of labour per day is USh 1 000.
  • Aorking day is eight hours.
  • Aryer is operated twice per week for eight months (e.g. 32 weeksCost per operation of the dryer = USh 1 000 per operationCost of labour per year = USh 1 000 x 2 x 32 = USh 64 000Conclusion: Total cost of labour per year is USh 64 000, with potential profitability per year with paid labour.

6.2 Costs

  • Fresh fruit: USh 192 000
  • Transport: USh 48 000
  • Paid labour: USh 64 000
  • Total variable costs: USh 304 000
  • Depreciation of the solar dryer: USh 70 000
  • Other fixed costs, repairs and maintenance: USh 17 500
  • Total fixed costs: USh 87 500
  • Total costs: USh 391 500.

6.3 Revenue

  • Income from dried fruit: USh 449 280
  • Net revenue: USh 57 780
  • With the addition of paid labour, net revenue is reduced from the original USh 121 780 to USh 57 780.
    • However, the net revenue is now solely a return to the investment or profit and does not include any return to labour.
    • Onceoperating a number of dryers, the processor should be able to employ labour to operate each one and take the net revenue as profit to cover their own work inputs for managing the business.

6.4 Obligations to the labour force

  • The introduction of a paid labour force to the business is a major step and should not be undertaken lightly.
    1. It takes the business from being a small, household-managed operation into a larger venture with a wider range of responsibilities, including:
      • the need to agree wages and terms of employment;
      • provide training;
      • ensure fair treatment;
      • supervise work;
      • pay wages promptly; and
      • provide regular employment whenever possible.

7. Labour payment methods

  • If paid labour is to be employed, the methods of payment and rates of pay need to be considered.
  • Three systems of paying labour have been adopted in Ugand.
    1. Flat rate payment.
    2. Piece rates.
    3. Split rates.
  • Flat rates involve payment at a fixed amount per day.
    • For instance, an employee may be paid USh 1 000 per day to peel, cut and load the dryer.
  • Piece rates are determined by how much dried fruit is produced.
    • For instance, a rate of USh 400 per kg of dried pineapple produced.
  • Split rates involve some payment at a flat rate and a further payment as a piece rate.

7.1 Flat rate and piece rate wages

  • Both of these systems have advantages and disadvantages.
  • Flat rate wages have the advantage that both employee and employer know the wage rate in advance.
    • They are generally preferred by employees.
    • However, the distinct disadvantage of the method is that it does not produce any incentive to operate the dryer efficiently.
  • The advantage of piece rates is that, wages are directly linked to the output of the dryer.
    • For instance, if the dryer were only half filled with fruit when operating out of season, the output of dried fruit would be half and hence the wages paid would be half.
    • In this way, the processor does not have to pay high wages when the cash income is low.
    • The method also helps to ensure that the work is carried out efficiently.
    • Sinceemployees are paid more if the dryer produces more fruit, their wages are linked to the success of the business.
    • It can also be beneficial for the processor when starting up the business as employees can be paid when fruit is sold, thereby reducing pressure on cash flow.
  • The main disadvantage of piece rate work is that people, quite naturally, tend to place a high reliance on the security of their wages.
    • Piece rate wages inevitably mean that the amount employees receive can vary considerably and this is seen as being unfair and unsatisfactory.
    • Situations can also arise in which one person works less hard than others in the group, but they would still receive the same reward.
    • The acceptability of piece rates can often depend on what is already accepted practice in the local area.

7.2 Split rate system

  • A number of successful businesses in Uganda use a split rate system in which employees are paid a moderately low basic rate for each day, together with a “bonus” for each kilogram of dried product produced.
    • This ensures a minimum level of wage, a degree of security, and provides an incentive to operate efficiently.
  • To encourage employees to be efficient, it is important for the manager to be firm, fair and train the employees well.
    • Most employees will try to work to the best of their abilities, particularly if they have received proper training and they have an aptitude for the work.
    • Levels of unemployment in rural areas are very high, so there is a strong incentive to work well and keep a job.
    • Nevertheless, taking on new employees is a risky business as the producer can never really know in advance how well they might perform.
  • One approach is to take on new employees on a trial basis.
    • Some people are simply not very skilled with their hands and cannot work well in the preparation and the cutting of fruit.
    • Using a trial period of employment allows the manager to assess employees for their capabilities before they are given more regular hours.
    • This trial period gives a good opportunity to properly train an employee, possibly paying a lower wage during the period.
      • This is tocompensate the processor for the trainee’s lower productivity and the time the processor has invested in the training.

7.3 Setting wages: flat rate

  • Wages should be acceptable to employees and should be similar to levels being earned for similar work elsewhere in the local area.
    • If it is possible to pay a little more than this, then a manager should try to do so.
    • This is because a premium will tend to increase the motivation of employees and their reliability.
    • The manager may also wish to include schemes such as bonuses for employees if production increases beyond a certain point.
  • It is best to be cautious when initially setting a wage.
    • It is always easier to increase wages if profits are good than to reduce wages if profits are poor.
  • Another way to assess wage levels is to look at wages paid in similar industries and occupations.
    • In rural areas, for instance, this might require looking into the wages paid to rural labourers.
    • These wage levels can be entered into the calculation to see how the net revenue is affected.

7.3.1 Setting wage levels

  • Assume net revenue is USh 121 780 per year, 64 days of labour are required per year, the dryer costs are USh 350 000 and total operational costs for the dryer are USh 327 500.
  • The maximum wage that could be paid is USh 1 903 per day (121 780 / 64).
    • This would mean that the dryer would break even, but with no allowance for a return to the investment or to cover contingencies.
  • To allow for these factors, assume also that a return to the investment of 15 percent = USh 52 500 per annum (350 000 x 15 percent) and a 5 percent allowance for contingencies on costs = USh 16 375 per annum (327 500 x 5 percent).
    • The net revenue is then adjusted by these factors to give a revised net revenue of USh 52 905 (121 780 – 52 500 – 16 375)
  • Conclusion: The revised net revenue would allow a wage of USh 827 per day (52 905 / 64).

8. Managing labour

  • Labour will not be required full time so it is important that employees know in advance when they are expected to work.
    • It is unfair for someone to turn up for work to find they are not required until the next day.
    • However, it can be difficult to schedule timings for employees as the production process does not follow a strict cycle.
    • If it rains, for instance, employees will not be required.
    • Determining days on which labour is required, typically depends on weather, the availability of fruit and the time required to dry the fruit.
  • If the weather is expected to be poor, there is little point in operating the dryer and labour is not required.
    • Similarly, there is little point in operating the dryer if fruit is out of season or difficult to purchase.
    • If the dryer is loaded one day and fruit takes two days to dry, there is no need for labour on the next day.
  • It has to be noted that the dryer does not create full-time employment.
    • Assistance is required for certain hours only and these will vary from week to week.
    • It will be easier to manage the business if people are employed who live locally in nearby houses and can be easily contacted.
  • Much of the work is taken up in preparing the fruit for drying:
    • sorting,
    • washing,
    • peeling,
    • slicing,
    • cutting, and
    • loading the trays.
  • This work needs to be carried out early in the morning.
    • Labour is therefore required to start very early, work for two to three hours and then finish. Unloading the dryer should be carried out in the late afternoon.
      • t takes far less work and can often be undertaken by the processor on their own.
    • Employees could therefore undertake other work during the day, such as tending fields or managing homes, but would need to be available for a few hours early in the morning.

9. Selling fruit profitably

  • For the business to earn revenue, the dried products need to be sold.
  • Transport costs are a significant variable cost and selling normally means travelling to a main city.
    • The greater the amount of dried fruit sold at any one time, the lower will be the unit cost for transport.
    • Overall transport costs can be reduced by sharing these costs with other processors, or with other activities which take them to the city.

9.1 Processors sharing transport costs

  • One producer could deliver the dried fruit on behalf of other producers, dividing transport costs between them.
    • Whoever actually takes the dried fruit can be decided on a rota basis with each processor taking it in turns to travel.
    • One person taking fruit from a number of dryers increases the amount of fruit being delivered at any one time and reduces overall transport costs.
    • If this method is adopted, each producer should receive a separate receipt for their processor.
    • The rota helps to reduce the chances for cheating.

9.1.1 Transport costs

  • Assume the cost of a return journey to Kampala is USh 3 000.
    • Fruit is sold in Kampala every two week.
    • 2.6 kg of pineapples are produced per dryer operation.
    • The sales price of dried pineapples is USh 2 700.
  • If pineapples are dried once per week, 5.2 kg will be produced at the end of two weeks, ready for sale.
    • The income from dried fruit sales is USh 14 040 (5.2 x 2 700).
    • Once transport costs have been taken into account, this reduces to USh 11 040 (14 040 – 3 000) or USh 2 123 per kilogram of dried fruit (11 040 I 5.2).
  • If pineapples are dried twice a week, 10.4 kg will be produced.
    • The income from dried fruit sales is thus USh 28 080 (10.4 x 2 700);
    • Once transport costs have been taken into account, this reduces to USh 25 080 (28 080 – 3 000) or USh 2 411 per kilogram of dried fruit (25 080 / 10.4).Conclusion: Increasing the amount of fruit taken increases the unit price received from USh 2 123 per kilogram to USh 2 411 per kilogram, once transport costs have been taken into account.
  • The same is true if transport costs are shared.
    • For instance, if two processors produce 5.2 kg of fruit and each separately take the produce to Kampala, the net income from the sales would be USh 2 123 per kilogram.
    • However, if transport costs are shared and only one processor travels to Kampala with 10.4 kg of dried fruit, costs would also be USh 2 411 per kilogram.

9.2 Processors with other work

  • Often a friend or a member of the family may travel to the city regularly on business.
    • If this is the case and the processor really feels that they can trust this person, it may be possible to give them the job of taking the fruit, in return for some small amount of money.
    • It may be that they can carry out other tasks at the same time.
      • For example,paying school fees or buying other goods which they can resell in the home village.
    • All of these activities allow the costs of transport cost to be spread.

9.3 Selling dried fruit

  • Firstly, it is important to consider what price is being offered.
    • Higher prices received for dried fruit will increase the profitability of the dryer so that companies paying the highest prices will appear to be the best.
    • However, there are a number of non-price factors that should be considered before deciding.
    • These include:
      • how the processor will be paid;
      • how reliable the buyer is;
      • how often the buyer will purchase dried fruit; and
      • what quality standards the buyer has adopted.
    • Some of the questions which should be considered are given below.

9.3.1 Questions to consider when selling dried products

  • Price considerations
  • What price is offered?
  • Is the price expected to change?
  • Are there incentive payments for purchases of larger quantities?
  • Are premiums paid for good quality fruit?
  • Are penalties imposed for poor quality fruit?
  • Non-price considerations
  • Will the processor be paid on delivery of goods?
  • If not, when will the processor be paid?
  • How will the owner be paid?
  • Who is the buyer selling to?
  • Does the buyer have a guaranteed final market?
  • Can that market be expanded for extra produce?
  • Can the buyer help solve problems with operation of the dryer?
  • Can the buyer help improve the quality of the dried fruit?
  • What technical and financial assistance will the buyer provide?
  • Will the buyer offer training to improve business operations?

10. Local marketing

  • Some processors have tried to market their own dried fruit.
    • Establishing markets is very time consuming and requires patience, but it can be rewarding.
    • Such marketing increases the number of sales and outlets for dried fruit are reduced depending on one or two buying companies.
  • Processors may be inclined to believe that there is no local market for dried fruit, but they may be surprised to find the amounts that can be sold after initial efforts.
    • The key to domestic marketing is to find out who will buy the dried fruit and then to prepare and pack the product to meet that market demand.
    • Many opportunities potentially exist including the expatriate market through supermarkets and hotels; school children through school tuck shops; public sector institutions hospitals, clinics, and prisons; and local public markets.
  • The main attractions of dried fruit are that they store easily and can be eaten without preparation.
    • They can be added to other foods to improve flavour and are very nutritious.
    • Where markets exist for food items such as roasted peanuts, snack bars, banana cakes or fried chicken, there may well be a market for dried fruit.
    • For local marketing, particular attention has to be given to packing and presentation.
    • It is usual to sell small packs of less than 200 grams, but this will depend on the market requirements.
    • The fruit should be sold in neatly wrapped plastic bags, ideally with a label and date of when the product was dried.
    • As more time and effort is required in selling to the domestic market and fruit is likely to be sold in small quantities, establishing the right price is important.
    • Prices should be set according to prices which consumers are prepared to pay and at a level above those of bulk buyers.
    • If this is not the case, it is likely to be better to sell to established companies where this is possible.
  • To determine the extent of a local market, it is necessary to carry out some market testing.
    • This involves offering small samples of the dried fruit product to potential buyers or buying groups for them to taste and asking their reaction and comments.
    • If the reaction is generally favourable, further marketing opportunities should be pursued.
  • Similarly, the processor can experiment with drying other products and selling them.
    • Most fruit and vegetables can be dried.
    • This can be useful during the off-season for the major crops.
    • Particular easy to dry are fruit and vegetables that are traditionally sun dried.

11. Business records

  • It is not possible to know how well the business is performing, and whether it is really profitable, unless records are kept of all business activities.
    • Basic information on costs and revenue is essential, but it is also helpful to record operational data for assessment of dryer performance.
    • One simple way is shown below as a balance sheet, where a running balance is employed together with a summary of operational data.
    • The method is most appropriate for smaller operations starting up in business.
    • Larger businesses are advised to seek expert guidance.
  • Each cost and revenue transaction is entered on a separate line, in date order as they occur.
    • Costs and revenues are entered both on a unit and total basis so it is clear how much fruit has been purchased and at what price.
    • The running balance is worked out after each transaction.
    • Separate entries are also made each time the dryer is filled.
    • Thus, the first line may show that on 4 February, 40 pineapples were bought at a cost of USh 200 each, giving a total cost of USh 8 000.
    • The balance column is calculated by subtracting total revenue from total cost, which in the first line is 0 minus 8 000 giving USh 8 000 (e.g. a debt of USh 8 000).
    • The second line would show that on the same day, the dryer was loaded with 18 pineapples.
    • On 7 February, the dryer was loaded with 19 pineapples.
    • On 8 February, disinfectant was bought for processing operations at a cost of USh 1 000; and so on.
    • Finally, for this two-week period, on 18 February dried fruit was taken to Kampala at a cost of USh 3 000, where 10.4 kg of product was sold at a price of USh 2 700 per kilogram.
    • Thus the revenue for the business was USh 6 080 more than the costs incurred.
  • The same process is repeated for the next two-week period and so forth over one complete year, after which time a new account book should be started.
    • Whilst this is a simplified example and does not take account of interest payments for instance, it helps to illustrate the principle of good record keeping.
  • Recording the operational data will allow assessments to be made of dryer performances over time.
    • The average amount of fruit used to fill the dryer each time is found by dividing the total number of pieces of fruit used (75) by the number of drying operations (four) to give 19.
    • To calculate the average amount of dried fruit produced per operation, the number of sales weight (10.4 kg) is divided by the number of drying operations (4) to give 2.6 kg.
    • These figures can be compared during the year and with other producers.
    • If there are large fluctuations or differences, the reasons should be investigated and ways should be sought to improve performance.
    • It is also possible to see how fruit prices have changed throughout the year and which farmer has offered favourable prices.
  • To determine the net operating balance of the operation at the end of the period, it is necessary to take account of both the balance figure and the value of produce in stock.
    • It can be seen that of the 80 pineapples purchased, 75 have been used so that five remain in stock.
    • As these cost USh 250 each, their value is USh 1 250.
    • This should be added to the running balance of USh 6 080, giving an actual net operating balance of USh 7 330.
  • From these records, the profitability of the business can be calculated by subtracting total revenue from total costs (both variable and fixed) to give the net revenue.
    • This should be worked out every month and recorded so it is readily apparent how the business is performing.
    • Some months may show a healthy profit while others show a loss (because no products have been sold).
    • Over the period of 12 months, the aim is to achieve an acceptable profit (e.g. return) to the business.

12. Strategies for growth

  • Once a business becomes successful and a producer has gained sufficient confidence, it may seem appropriate to expand operations.
    • This will inevitably involve building more dryers, employing labour, building a fruit store and so forth, all of which will require additional funds and much more time and effort for the running the business.
    • Fruit needs to be readily available and labour needs to be availableto operate the additional dryers to full capacity.
  • It is important to assess the costs involved in advance.
    • The producer needs to make sure that the money, which is being used for expansion, will not jeopardise the operation of the whole business.
    • Whether the plan is for minor or for major expansion, ways of minimising the cost burden in the short term should always be sought.
    • Various groups in Uganda have already achieved this in a number of ways by employing a friend or relative who has the necessary skills to build dryers and paying them back over a period of time.
    • A carpenter will normally want to be paid in full as soon as a dryer is built by seeking funding or grant assistance from local NGOs or bodies such as the Women’s Finance and Credit Trust with favourable terms.
    • Where expansion is not possible on the existing site (e.g. if it were the family farm), a person nearby with spare land invests this as collateral (and perhaps some money) and joins the venture as a partner, in return for sharing the future profits of the business.

13. Problem solving

13.1 Dealing with problems

  • Even in the best run and operated businesses, problems will arise at times.
    • Working through these systematically is key to running a successful business.
    • If the dryer is not performing well or the profits are not as high as anticipated, the producer should find out why and identify the problem.
    • Once the particular problem has been identified, it is easier to find a solution.
  • For those with less experience on running a business, it is often difficult to see problems and even more difficult to know how to solve them.
    • If in doubt, it is important to seek advise quickly by:
      • talking to a neighbour or someone who has been producing locally;
      • contacting NGOs and extension workers; or by
      • contacting Fruits of the Nile in Kampala or other buyers of products.

13.2 Questions and answers

  • There are many questions which are asked about the viability of businesses and problems that develop.
    • Examples of some of the more common questions are given below with answers suggesting ways to tackle the particular difficulties.
    • These questions indicate that each case has its own individual characteristics.
    • The general rules suggested provide a good starting point for management considerations.

13.2.1 I live in Kampala and fruit prices are high. I am not making any profit. What should I do?

  • You must find out if fruit prices are always as high throughout the year or whether it is just seasonal.
    • If it is a seasonal effect, then it is better to wait until fruit prices decline before operating the dryer again.
    • If prices are high all year round and they are higher in Kampala than other places in Uganda (which is usually the case), cheaper sources of fruit must be found.
    • It may that farmers can offer a lower price than you can buy in the market if you arrange a regular purchase with delivery direct to you.
    • The highest price that should be paid for fruit over a short period (two weeks) should be set according to the variable cost pricing rule (see Example 2 above).
  • If the dried produce cannot be sold at a higher price or sufficiently low prices cannot be found nor negotiated for the fresh fruit, then the business cannot be profitable.
    • The dryer should be sold or moved to another site, such as a relative’s home or your home village if cheap supplies of good quality fruit are readily available.

13.2.2 During the rainy season I try to dry fruit, but it spoils in the dryer. What should I do?

  • Try reducing the quantity loaded into the dryer and pack fewer trays of fruit, or choose fruit (such as tomatoes or mangoes) which will dry more easily. You should not attempt to dry fruit during poor weather conditions.
    • If it is continually overcast or raining steadily, the dryer will not work effectively.
    • Wait until the weather improves and start up again.
    • If you have fresh fruit in store and the weather remains poor, it should be sold before it spoils.

13.2.3 As fruit is very expensive at the moment, should I continue to operate the dryer?

  • In the short run, provided you are covering variable costs, it is better to operate the dryer.
  • The maximum price to be paid for fruit should be set according to the variable cost pricing rule (see Example 2 above).
  • If prices are above this level, you should not operate the dryer.

13.2.4 My neighbour and I load our dryers at the same time, but my neighbour’s dryer always produces more dried fruit than mine. What am I doing wrong?

  • A number of points need to be considered as the quantity of dried fruit dryer depends on:
    • the amount of fruit loaded on the trays,
    • the thickness of the cut pieces of fruit,
    • the time the fruit is in the dryer,
    • the condition of the dryer, and
    • the air circulation inside the dryer.

13.2.5 My neighbour wants to start a solar drying business; should I encourage her? Will it effect my business?

  • Provided there are plentiful supplies of fresh fruit available in your area at reasonable cost, there are benefits if you encourage your neighbour to embark on a solar drying business.
  • It can help your business for various reasons.
    • You should be able to negotiate lower fruit prices as larger quantities of fresh produce require two dryers together.
    • If you sell products in Kampala, you can share transport costs by taking turns thereby improving the potential profitability of both dryers.
    • It is always useful to be able to discuss problems with other people, to have help in finding solutions, and to be able to share some of the work if there is a domestic problem.

13.2.6 I want to sell my produce to the local market and not to another company. How can I do this?

  • You need first to find out who will buy the dried fruit and how much they are willing to pay.
    • Some of these may be supermarkets and hotels, restaurants, local market stalls, school tuck shops or hospitals and clinics.
  • To find out, it is necessary to test the market.
    • This will involve offering small samples of the dried fruit to potential buyers and assessing their reaction.
    • If reactions are favourable, it may be that local opportunities exist and it will be possible to sell sufficient quantities to reward the effort put in.
    • However, selling in this way will require considerable patience at the beginning.
    • Success depends very much on your own initiatives and skills.
    • If these outlets prove unsuccessful, you have little option but to sell to established companies.

13.2.7 I live a long way from Kampala and the transport costs are very high. What can I do?

  • There are two ways of reducing transport costs.
    1. Making less trips to Kampala.
    2. Taking more fruit each time.
  • Travel once per month instead and by sharing transport costs with other producers by taking it in turns to travel.

13.2.8 I am making a lot of money from my dryer and I want to expand my business. Should I expand and how do I do this?

  • If there is plenty of good quality fruit available in your area and you have finance for a second dryer, then there is no reason why you should not expand your business if it is already profitable.
  • You will require additional labour and this will involve you in organising them on a daily basis and paying their wages.
    • Are you prepared for this?
  • The best way to expand the business efficiently is to use more dryers of the same design, rather than investing in a larger dryer.

13.2.9 I usually dry pineapples in my dryer, but at times the pineapples are very expensive. I would like to dry bananas or even try to dry vegetables. Is this possible?

  • There is no problem at all with drying other types of fruit in the dryer, but drying times will vary.
    • You may well find some vegetables more difficult to sell and much greater care is needed in processing.
    • At present in Uganda, there are good markets for dried pineapple, banana, mango, tomato and mushroom.
    • If you are drying other fruit or vegetables, you will need to develop your own markets.
  • The easiest fruit and vegetables to dry are those that are traditionally sun dried.
    • There are many benefits from drying these in a solar dryer.
      • Better quality
      • Cleaner product
      • Quicker drying
      • More hygienic processing
      • Less insect infestation
    • You may simply use them for your own consumption.

13.2.10 There seem to be many people producing dried fruit. Should I produce something else instead?

  • There are limited markets for dried products because, often, people prefer fresh fruit if it is available.
    • Find out who is likely to buy your product and see whether they may be interested in buying from you before you start.
    • Ask yourself if you can you offer the buyer any particular advantage?
  • Many other products can be made such as fruit leathers, sugared fruit, deep-fried fruit products, fruit juices and purees.
    • These all require greater expertise and more equipment requiring greater investment.
    • They are less appropriate as rural businesses, but they can, however, generate greater returns.

13.2.11 How can I contact local buyers and persuade them to buy my products?

  • There is no straightforward answer to this question.
    • It is a matter of finding out who might buy these kinds of products in your region and what their requirements are likely to be.
    • You need to be able to convince buyers that you can produce a good quality product, which is consistent and can provide supplies regularly and reliably at an acceptable price.
  • A good quality product which is well packaged with an attractive and clear label will always find better acceptance.

13.2.12 How can l contact buyers overseas?

  • This is equally difficult.
    • Many buyers overseas will only purchase to particular product specifications from traders who are already established because of the requirements for quality assurance.
    • You should approach export and trade promotion organisations, fruit and vegetable traders, food processing companies, NGOs, government and aid agencies.
    • Contact anyone who may have an interest in using or trading your products and find out what they can do.
    • See if you can refer to CDRoms, web sites, publications, trade magazines, directories and periodicals.
  • Establishing trade links is not easy and it takes a great deal of time.
    • It may prove more productive if a collective approach is used, particularly as a women’s producer group.
    • Remember, you need to be sure you can sell your products before you start up in business.

14. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

15. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: solar drying equipment: ID 7319.
  • Well dried maize benefits all: the solar maize dryer: ID 8285.
  • Dryer construction for solar-dried fruit and vegetables production: ID 4502.
  • Producing solar dried fruit and vegetables for micro-and smallscale rural enterprise development: ID 4501.

16. Objectives fulfilled by the project

16.1 Women friendly

The technology creates employment for women’s groups and allows women to play a more active role in solar drying and fruit/vegetable processing.

16.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology is low-cost and significantly improves product quality. This leads to potential increases in revenue, providing for additional sources of food and income.

entries.tittle: Unité Aquaponique: Technique de Culture sur Film Nutritif - Description Détaillée
entries.summary: L’aquaponie correspond à la production intégrée d’unités aquacoles et de cultures hydroponiques en utilisant un système de recirculation de l’eau. Les unités aquaponiques constituées de cultures sur film nutritif (Nutrient Film Technique ou NFT) sont l’une des trois méthodes d’aquaponie les plus couramment utilisées aujourd’hui, et sont particulièrement adaptées pour une production et/ou un commerce à petit échelle. Les systèmes NFT sont surtout utilisés pour les cultures verticales, dans le cas où la surface d’exploitation est très limitée. La technologie suivante explique en détail les principes de la technique de culture sur film nutritif et fournit un guide, étape par étape, pour la construction d’une unité aquaponique utilisant cette méthode.
entries.description:
La description

Dans ce système aquaponique NFT, une mince couche d'eau riche en éléments nutritifs circule dans des tuyaux horizontaux légèrement inclinés (appelés rigoles de culture), dans lesquels sont suspendues les plantes à l’aide d’un pot troué (sorte de panier), de manière à ce que les racines soient en contact avec le filet d’eau. L'eau fournit des nutriments aux plantes qui développent alors un système racinaire très étendu dans les rigoles. Les tiges et les feuilles des plantes se développent au-dessus de chaque panier de plantation. Les rigoles de plantation peuvent être disposées les unes à côté des autres ou superposées (Figure 1).

Figure 1. Plantation dans des rigoles de culture sur film nutritif disposées horizontalement (à gauche) ou verticalement (à droite)

©FAO/TECA

1. Les éléments d'une unité aquaponique à film nutritif (NFT)

1.1 Le système d’irrigation (système de circulation de l’eau)

  • Dans cette unité aquaponique NFT, l'eau coule par gravité, à partir du bac à poissons, à travers le filtre mécanique puis à travers le filtre biologique.
  • Le biofiltre sert également de bac de récupération de l’eau issue des rigoles de culture.
  • À partir de cette cuve biofiltrante, une partie de l'eau est pompée en direction du bac d’élevage et une autre partie est distribuée aux rigoles de culture.
  • Toujours par gravité, l’eau coule doucement et en mince filet le long des rigoles où les racines des plantes pourront prélever les nutriments nécessaires.
  • L’eau issue des rigoles de culture retourne ensuite dans le biofiltre où elle sera mélangée à l’eau provenant du filtre mécanique et sera de nouveau pompée soit vers le bac d’élevage soit vers les rigoles.
  • En retournant dans la cuve à poissons, l’eau fait déborder le niveau et ainsi l’eau « sale », en trop plein, s’écoule dans le filtre mécanique, bouclant le circuit du système (voir Figure 7).

1.2 La filtration

  • Dans une unité aquaponique NFT, il est nécessaire d’installer deux filtres séparés: un filtre mécanique qui retient les gros déchets solides puis un filtre biologique servant à convertir l’ammoniaque en nitrate (Figure 2).
  • Dans le système NFT décrit ici, le filtre mécanique piège les particules solides par tourbillons et permet de les évacuer régulièrement.
  • À la sortie de ce filtre et avant de rejoindre le biofiltre, l’eau passe à travers une grille aux mailles serrées (souvent un seau rempli d’un filet en nylon), afin de retenir les quelques éléments solide restants.
  • Le biofiltre doit être oxygéné à l’aide d’un diffuseur d’air (pierre poreuse) et contient un support (aussi appelé substrat), habituellement composé de bio-balles (achetées en magasin spécialisé), ou de filets en nylon ou de capsules de bouteilles en plastique, sur lequel les bactéries nitrifiantes peuvent vivre et transformer les déchets dissous.
    • Si les conditions de nitrification ne sont pas optimales pour les bactéries, le système d’irrigation peut alors se boucher, des zones d’anoxie peuvent se développer (apparition de mauvaises algues) et cela peut nuire au bon développement des plantes et des poissons.
Figure 2. Schéma et photographie d’un filtre mécanique (à droite) suivi d’un filtre biologique (à gauche) d’une unité NFT

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Les rigoles de culture sur film nutritif

  • En système NFT, les plantes sont cultivées dans des tuyaux en plastique (appelés rigoles de culture), disposés horizontalement les uns à côté des autres.
  • Ces rigoles sont percées sur la face supérieure par des trous régulièrement espacés dans lesquels sont suspendus des paniers de culture (sorte de pots troués) remplis de substrat et dans chaque panier, un plant est cultivé.
  • Si cela est possible, il est conseillé d’utiliser des rigoles de section rectangulaire (et non des tuyaux cylindriques), et dont la largeur est plus grande que la hauteur.
  • Ces rigoles rectangulaires sont utilisées chez la plupart des cultivateurs hydroponiques, car le filet d’eau est plus large et donc les plantes auront plus de faciliter à absorber les nutriments et elles se développeront beaucoup mieux.
  • Un grand avantage de l’aquaponie sur film nutritif est que les rigoles de culture peuvent être dimensionnées et organisées selon l’espace disponible:
    • horizontalement (comme une table);
    • verticalement (le long de murs ou de clôtures) (Figure 3); et
    • en « cascade », accrochées à un toit ou à un balcon, etc.
Figure 3. Unité aquaponique NFT dont les rigoles de culture sont disposées verticalement

©FAO/TECA

1.3.1 Fonctionnement des rigoles de culture

  • À partir du biofiltre, une partie de l'eau pompée est dirigée en quantité égale vers chaque rigole hydroponique avec un faible débit ce qui permet de créer un écoulement d’eau peu profond, régulier et riche en éléments nutritifs.
  • Dès que les petites racines des plantes entrent en contact avec le filet d’eau, elles commencent alors à se développer (les bourgeons, les tiges et les feuilles s’allongent en haut et autour de la rigole) et à créer un épais réseau racinaire à l’intérieur de la rigole.
  • Le filet d’eau doit rester mince (peu profond), car cela permet aux racines d’avoir un grand espace de croissance et car cela assure aux plantes leur provision nécessaire en oxygène, en nutriments et en eau. Le débit d'eau pour chaque rigole de culture ne doit pas être supérieur à 1 à 2 litres/minute.
  • Le débit doit pouvoir se contrôler à partir des vannes de sortie de la pompe à eau: l’écoulement d’eau en excès est redirigé vers le bac d’élevage des poissons.

1.3.2 Forme et dimensions des rigoles de culture

  • Il est conseillé de choisir directement les tuyaux ayant un diamètre optimal et adapté au(x) type(s) de plantes cultivées.
  • Les rigoles ayant une section rectangulaire (ou carrée) sont les plus appropriées, mais les tuyaux cylindriques sont plus faciles à trouver et sont tout à fait acceptables.
  • Les cultures de grande taille ont besoin d’une rigole de 110 mm (11 cm) de diamètre pour se développer, tandis que les petites cultures (souvent de faible masse racinaire et à croissance rapide) n’ont besoin que de 75 mm (7,5 cm).
  • Pour la polyculture à petite échelle (culture de plusieurs types de plantes:
    • légumes
    • aromates
    • plantes ornementales, etc.).
    • Il est recommandé d’utiliser des rigoles de 11 cm de diamètre (Figure 4).
    • Cela permet de cultiver tout type de plantes ; même les plus petites parviennent à se développer dans de larges tuyaux.
  • Si les rigoles sont trop étroites, il y a alors un risque que les plantes ayant un système racinaire étendu, y compris les plantes âgées (au stade adulte), bouchent les petits tuyaux et fassent déborder l’eau dans le biofiltre ou le bac d’élevage ou à l’entrée des rigoles.
    • Il faut être très vigilant pour les plants de tomate et de menthe, dont les systèmes racinaires très développés peuvent facilement boucher de grands tuyaux.
  • La longueur des rigoles de culture peut variée entre 1 m et 12 m.
  • Pour des longueurs supérieures à 12 m, des carences en éléments nutritifs peuvent apparaître, en particulier pour les plantes situées à l'extrémité des rigoles (les plantes situées près de l’arrivée d’eau auront déjà absorbé tous les nutriments).
  • Une inclinaison des rigoles d'environ 1 cm/m (1 pour cent) est nécessaire afin d’assurer que l'eau coule à travers l'ensemble du tuyau avec facilité.
  • La pente peut être contrôlée à l'aide de petites cales en bois placées sous les rigoles.
  • Les tuyaux en PVC sont généralement recommandés pour construire les rigoles de culture, car ils sont facilement disponibles et peu coûteux.
  • Les tuyaux doivent être blancs (ou de couleur claire) afin de refléter les rayons du soleil et donc de garder au frais le film nutritif.
  • Il est aussi possible d’utiliser des tuyaux hydroponiques, carrées ou rectangulaires, de 10 cm de large sur 7 cm de haut.
  • Ces types de tuyaux hydroponiques sont généralement utilisés par les producteurs professionnels.
  • Des poteaux de clôture en vinyle, de taille assez grande, peuvent également servir pour les rigoles de culture.

1.3.3 Cultiver dans les rigoles de culture

  • Les trous percés dans les rigoles hydroponiques doivent avoir un diamètre de sept à neuf et doivent correspondre à la taille des paniers de plantation.
  • Entre les centres de chaque trou il doit y avoir un espace d’au moins 21 cm afin de permettre aux plantes de se développer sans gêne (croissance des tiges, feuilles, fruits, etc.) (Figure 4).
  • Chaque plant est placé dans un panier en plastique (pot troué au fond et sur les côtés), qui est lui-même placé dans un trou d’une rigole de culture.
  • Les paniers sont remplis d’un substrat (ex. graviers volcaniques, laine de roche, billes d’argile expansée, etc.).
  • Ce substrat joue le rôle de support physique pour la plante.
  • De plus, un bout de tuyau en PVC, de 5-10 cm de long, peut être placé par-dessus le substrat afin de mieux équilibrer et soutenir la plante (Figure 5).
Figure 4. Rigoles de cultures de 11 cm de diamètre, percées de trous régulièrement espacés et connectées au drain commun d’évacuation de l’eau vers le biofiltre

©FAO/TECA

  • Si les paniers en plastique ne sont pas disponibles ou sont trop chers, il est possible d'utiliser des gobelets en plastique, en veillant à les percer de nombreux trous afin de permettre aux racines d’atteindre le film nutritif.
  • Une autre option consiste à envelopper le substrat et la plante dans une mousse (ou filet) flexible et possédant de larges alvéoles (ou mailles).
  • Si aucune de ces options n’est disponible ou adaptée, il est également possible de transplanter des jeunes pousses directement dans les rigoles.
  • Les plants peuvent être transplantés avec leur substrat de germination (terre ou terreau) (Figure 6), qui sera progressivement emporté par le filet d’eau, ou bien les racines peuvent être soigneusement rincées, ce qui maintient système aquaponique propre, mais peut provoquer un grand stress pour la jeune plante.
  • Dans tous les cas et si les paniers sont disponibles, il est préférable de les utiliser et de les remplir de substrat.
  • Lors de l’insertion des plants dans les rigoles de culture, il est important de s’assurer que les racines peuvent toucher le filet d'eau, afin que les jeunes plants ne soient pas déshydratés.
  • Si les racines sont trop petites, une mèche peut être insérée entre l’intérieur du panier et le filet d’eau afin de permettre à l’eau de monter dans le panier par capillarité.
  • Enfin, il est conseillé d'arroser les plants avec de l'eau issue du système aquaponique une semaine avant de les transplanter dans l'unité. Cela aidera à diminuer les stress de transplantation.

2.1 Préparation du bac pour l’élevage des poissons

  • La préparation suivante du bac d’élevage est identique à celle présentée dans la description étape par étape d’une unité aquaponique MBT.
  • Les étapes 1 à 7 sont illustrées dans les Figures 8 et 9.
    • Retirer les deux tiges en acier attachées au niveau de la face supérieure de la cuve IBC et qui servent à maintenir en place la cuve en plastique (Étape 1).
    • Dans ce cas, les tiges d'acier sont fixées grâce à 4 vis à tête Torx (en étoile). Enlever ces 4 vis (Étape 2) à l'aide d'un tournevis en étoile ou d’une clé Torx (Étape 3). Si les vis sont remplacées par des rivets ou si un tournevis ou clé Torx sont indisponibles, il est aussi possible d’utiliser une meuleuse pour retirer ces vis ou rivets.
  • Une fois que les tiges d'acier sont retirées, retirer la cuve du reste de la structure en acier.
    • Après avoir retiré le réservoir de sa cage en acier, dessiner au marqueur un carré sur la face supérieure de la cuve à 5 cm des bords de la cuve (Étape 4).
    • En utilisant la meuleuse, découper le carré tracé au marqueur (Étape 5) et retirer la pièce (Étape 6). Garder ce carré de plastique car il pourra servir de couvercle pour le bac d’élevage.
    • Une fois le dessus de la cuve retiré, laver l'intérieur avec du savon écologique, rincer à l'eau chaude et laisser sécher au soleil pendant 24 heures (Étape 7).
    • Replacer ensuite la cuve dans sa structure en acier (ce qui permet de renforcer les parois et de mieux la protéger).
