entries.title: Risk reduction through the control of the curly leaf virus in tomatoes
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary: In Saint Lucia, farmers are increasingly facing  the yellow curly leaf virus as an emerging hazard, affecting their livelihoods. Pests and diseases can seriously damage farmers’ crops and reduce their yields. Farmers were getting apprehensive about continuing with tomato production in the way they did in the past, due to the increasingly high cost of chemical treatment against the virus and the uncertainty of crop yields. The integrated pest management method introduced by the project, in both open fields and in a greenhouse, showed that when exact chemical application schedules and quantities were applied and recommended crop husbandry practices were followed, the incidence of tomato curly leaf virus was reduced and crop yield, as well as quality, could be improved.
entries.description:
Description

The yellow leaf curl virus and other diseases are affecting farmers’ crops, such as tomatoes. The leaf curl in tomatoes is caused by a virus transported to the tomato plants by the whitefly. The vector has a very wide host range and feeds by sucking plant juices from the underside of leaves of crops such as tomato, tobacco, cucumber, sweet potato, as well as weeds. Adult whiteflies look like tiny white moths, about 1 mm to 2 mm in length. They fly when the leaf is disturbed. The light-coloured eggs are laid on the underside of the leaf and hatch in about 16 to 38 days, depending on environmental conditions.

The whitefly can acquire the virus after feeding on infected plants for 15 to 30 minutes and can transmit the virus to tomato plants after about 24 hours of incubation within the insect. A period of 15 minutes feeding on the new tomato host is subsequently required for transmission of the virus. The whitefly retains the virus for up to 20 days and does not transmit it to its progeny. Symptoms develop on young plants after 10 to 14 days. Plants affected by the leaf curl virus are severely stunted, with shoots becoming erect. Leaflets are reduced in size, pucker, curl upwards and become distorted, having prominent yellowing along margins and/or interveinal regions. Flowers wither excessively and plants will grow very few fruits after infection occurs. Therefore, any plants affected before the flowering stage will produce extremely low yields and fruit quality is also negatively affected. 

The disease can be managed through the use of chemicals to control whitefly infestation, the use of more resistant varieties, and also supported by the use of good agricultural practices (GAPs), in particular, sanitation of the farm area. Sanitation also includes a good weed management programme, which is critical to limiting the proliferation and spread of the whitefly.

1. Implementation of the technology 

  • Table 1 below outlines the chemical schedule used and other practices for control of the leaf curl virus in tomatoes.
  • Some chemicals used are brand names and the qualities used are as per the manufacturers' directions.
Table 1. Crop husbandry practices for control of the curly leaf virus 
Week  Activities
1
  • Transplant seedlings.
  • Drench plants with Banrot (fungicide), WelGrow (liquid fertilizer) and Fast Tac (insecticide) solution.
2
  • Spray plants with Caprid (insecticide) and Biolife 20 (fungicide/bactericide) solution.
3
  • Weeding and moulding of plants.
  • Apply cure (insecticide) and Cytokine (growth regulator).
4
  • Spray plants with Pronto (insecticide) and Calmax (Calcium based fertiliser).
  • Staking, tying and pruning.
5
  • Apply NPK fertilizer at 2 ounces per plant.
  • Continue staking, tying and pruning.
6
  • Apply Caprid (insecticide) and Mankocide (fungicide).
  • Apply Calmax (calcium-based fertilizer).
7
  • Continue staking, tying and pruning.
8
  • Apply Pirate (insecticide) and Calmax (calcium-based fertilizer).
9
  • First light harvest.
10
  • Harvest.
  • Apply Cure (insecticide) and Cytokin (growth regulator).
11
  • Harvest.
12
  • Harvest.
13
  • Harvest.
  • Apply pirate.
14
  • Harvest.

Source: FAO 2013

2. Findings

  • A comparative study was undertaken to investigate the disease management in tomatoes using open fields and a greenhouse.
  • The study showed that where the chemical application schedule was followed, there were several crop husbandry practices.
    • Weeding and moulding of plants (critical as the absence of weeds around the plants reduces the risk of infestation by whiteflies).
    • Staking, tying and pruning of plants (helps to maintain proper growth of plants).
    • Good weed management programme around the growing fields of tomatoes (critical to limiting the proliferation and spread of the whitefly).
  • Both in the greenhouse and open field situations, the incidence of the curly leaf virus, which appeared early during the growth cycle was minimized and infection did not spread.
    • Farmers were able to harvest maximum yield from their crops.

2.1 Cost estimates of activity

  • The cost estimate for this activity is approximately ECD 41 000 (USD 1.00 = ECD 2.70) for planting materials, chemicals, refurbishment of the greenhouse, drip lines and irrigation system, in addition to other materials such as knapsack sprayers. 

2.2 Safe use of pesticides

  • If you manipulate and/or use pesticides, make inquiries before!
  • Pesticide can be harmful to your health, the health of your family, of the consumers and of the environment.
  • Use pesticides safely.
  • For more information concerning reducing risks while manipulating pesticide: ID 8348. 
Figure 1. Seedling production

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Greenhouse production

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Open field preparation

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Open-field production

©FAO/TECA

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Risk reduction while manipulating pesticides: ID 8348.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology provides control strategies for controlling the curly leaf virus of tomatoes. This will reduce the probability of harvest losses for the farmers.

entries.title: Use of salt-tolerant rice varieties to counteract impacts of sea surges and saltwater intrusion
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary:
The objective of this practice was to focus on the suitability and replication potential of salt-tolerant rice varieties as alternatives in saline impacted areas, and thus contribute to the region’s resilience and food security. 

The Philippines is among the most disaster-prone countries in the world. More than 200 climate-related natural disasters were recorded in the last two decades. Alone in 2011, the country was hit by 33 disasters, claiming 1 430 lives. Agriculture is the sector most affected by tropical cyclones, causing a decline in production and productivity threatens the country's food security. Due to climate variability and other environmental changes, rice cultivators, especially in the typhoon prone areas, are facing some challenges to adapt to saltwater intrusion in coastal areas.

Salinity has become one of the major soil problems in many rice-growing areas in the world. About 48 million hectares of land in the humid regions of South and Southeast Asia are technically suited to rice production but remain idle or are grown with poor results due to salinity. Studies show, however, that sustained and profitable production of crops specifically rice on salt-affected soils, is possible if appropriate farm management practices are implemented.
entries.description:
Description

There is 400 000 ha of coastal saline soils in the Philippines, of which 100 000 ha are in mangroves, 175 000 ha are in fishponds and 125 000 ha are idle. Due to changes in the climatic and other environmental factors/parameters, Bicol’s coastal region is undergoing and experiencing various changes in the cropping pattern. About 70 000 ha of rice production areas in Bicol and  the Cagayan Valley are potentially affected by saline water intrusion, thereby needing special attention and improvement. Rice areas along the nipa palm in Rizal and Bagacay, are usually affected by the saline intrusion. Farmers in these areas normally experienced low rice production, because the present rice varieties used are suitable for the increasing saline-stressed environment, especially during May (end of the dry season) and in December. The wider dissemination of a selected salt-tolerant variety, namely NSIC Rc-108, was tested in three pilot sites (Rizal and Bagacay, Gubat, Sorsogon) between June 2010 and October 2010 (wet season) in lowland irrigated farming systems in Bicol. 

1. Implementation of the technology 

  • The replication trails are suitable for farmers with a 1 000 m² for the cultivation of the variety.
  • The expected costs of the demonstration site amount to around 3 758 PHP (in 2010) including seeds, fertilizer, a signboard, registering and soil testing. 

1.1 Preparation of seeds for sowing

  • The rice variety used was NSIC Rc-108 (or a similar variety like NSIC Rc-188).
  • First, the seeds have to be soaked in clean lukewarm water for 24 hours.
  • Then the floating seeds should be removed.
  • Drain the water and wash the seeds.
  • Place the seeds on a clean cement floor and cover it with a wet sack or keep in cloth bags and incubate for 36 to 48 hours. 

1.2 Nursery preparation and priming the rice seedlings

  • The seedbed plots should be prepared two to three days before sowing.
  • For an 80 m² seedbed sow 4 kg to 5 kg of seeds.
  • Establish the seedbed site on a non-saline area and water the rice seedlings after 15 to 18 days with the low-level salt solution.
  • Prepare a low-level salt solution (5 litres per m2 seedbed) at 2 g table salt per litre of water.
  • Water the seedlings seven to ten days before transplanting.
  • To reduce the length of seedbed preparation, the use of early-maturing saline-tolerant variety (e.g. NSIC Rc-188 series) is a good alternative.  

1.3 Land preparation and sowing of seeds

  • Check if the dikes surrounding the rice field have to be improved to prevent physical intrusion of saline water, and do so in case needed.
  • Make a small inlet-outlet break in the main dike to serve as an entry point of fresh irrigation water.
  • Bring salinity at a minimum level by repeatedly flushing excess salts.
  • Prepare slots (size: 1 m x 20 m) and sow seeds in areas not affected by the saline intrusion.
  • The seed rate should be 40 kg to 50 kg per hectare. 

1.4 Transplanting

  • After 25 to 30 days the seedlings can be transplanted.
  • In general mature seedlings are more resistant to soil salinity.
  • After flooding the seedbed seedlings can be carefully pulled out.
  • The droopy and long leaves of older rice seedlings have to be cut.
  • Follow straight row planting with a spacing of 20 cm x 20 cm.
  • Deep transplanting should be avoided in order to facilitate tilling.
  • It is highly recommended to always keep some extra seedlings. 

1.5 Fertilizer dose

  • Table 1 shows fertilizer doses.
  • Half of the urea and all doses of other fertilizers may be applied during the last round of tillage following the broadcast method and mix the fertilizer properly with the soil.
  • The remaining half of the urea should be applied by topdressing five to seven days before panicle initiation stage.

1.6 Irrigation, weeding and harvesting

  • Follow the flushing of salts schedule and repeatedly pond freshwater into the field.
  • The frequency of flushing depends on the initial salinity level of the soil and its texture (e.g. clay soils needs more flushing).
  • The soil has to be puddled and drained.
  • When needed, use rotary or hand weeding.
  • The harvesting can be started when 80 to 85 percent of the grains are golden yellow.
  • The grains should be immediately trenched after harvest.
Table 1. Fertilizer doses
Name of fertilizer Fertilizer dose/ha
Urea 60 kg to 90 kg (urea) + 30 kg of Zn (if available)
Table salt (primer) 2 g per litre (10g)

Source: FAO 2013

2. Results and findings 

  • Ten farmers in Bagacay and Rizal, Sorsogon planted NSIC Rc-108 from August 2010 to June 2011.
    • Results indicated that the use of saline-tolerant rice variety led to an average yield (tons per ha) of 2.28, 2.93, and 4.15, during the first, second and third crop cycles respectively (Figure 1).
    • Yield difference as compared to conventional varieties was significant at 5 percent level, with a t-value = 5.23 and p-value = 0.014.
Figure 1. Saline tolerant rice GP option 

©FAO/TECA

  • Generally, farmers start preparing seedbeds during early May, when the rain season starts, and transplant late May or early June.
  • When precipitation/irrigation is delayed, transplanting is postponed up to a month.
  • Due to El Niño, experienced during the first crop cycle, expected yield performance did not reach 100 percent, but the good practice option performed well and yielded better than the existing farmers’ variety (control plots). 
  • In Rizal alone, one farmer’s existing variety was badly affected by the saline intrusion.
  • The farmer replanted the same variety but produced 50 percent less than the NSIC Rc-108.
  • It was concluded that the use of NSIC Rc-108 is a more cost-efficient option than the existing local farmer varieties being cultivated (Binatang) year in and year out.
    • For instance, test farmers spent, on the average, PHP 15 027 (in 2010) to establish a hectare, and get an additional yield of 1.14 tonnes per ha.
    • This additional yield is roughly equivalent to PHP 13 738.
    • Comparatively, the less suitable rice variety in salt-affected rice fields in Sorsogon increased the cost of production per hectare among local farmers (PHP 18 000 to 20 000) and led to an average yield of only 1 tonne per ha. 
  • One major concern for saline-tolerant rice variety (NSIC Rc-108) is the length of seedbed preparation (three to four weeks) before transplanting.
    • Due to its sensitivity to saline conditions at an early vegetative stage, older seedlings (25 to 30 days) were used.
    • This situation poses a certain level of adjustment in the timing and scheduling of crop establishment.
    • Weather conditions are a crucial concern for farmers to adapt to a stressed environment.
    • The use of early-maturing saline-tolerant variety (e.g., NSIC Rc-188 series) offers an even more promising option for salt-affected rice areas in the future, for a quick turnaround establishment. 
  • Additional support of Local Government Units (LGU) is highly desirable to establish functional seed systems, storage and distribution of stress-tolerant varieties that are accessible to farmers and enable them to mitigate the effects of natural hazards. 
Figure 2. Use of salt-tolerant rice varieties (e.g., NSIC Rc-108 and NSIC Rc-188) to counteract impacts of sea surges and saltwater intrusion, Philippines 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Use of salt-tolerant rice varieties (e.g., NSIC Rc-108 and NSIC Rc-188) to counteract impacts of sea surges and saltwater intrusion, Philippines 

©FAO/TECA

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Use of Early-Maturing Rice Variety (EMRV) to reduce typhoon impacts in Bicol Region, Philippines: ID 7719.
  • Use of submergence rice variety NSIC Rc-194 to counteract impacts of flooding in the Bicol region, Philippines: ID 7723.
  • Revitalizing rice ratooning to reduce risk and impact during hazard-prone months in the Bicol region, the Philippines: ID 7739.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Women-friendly

This technology is women-friendly as it is a complementary practice to rice planting and could be easily implemented. 

5.2 Resource use efficiency

This technology makes use of the new variety to reduce the losses caused by saltwater intrusion. It is also a low input technology that does not require extensive inputs.

5.3 Pro-poor technology

This technology provides the farmer with an alternative rice variety that is able to withstand saline water intrusion. This enhances resilience and food security by achieving higher yields and reducing the risk of lost harvest due to unsuitable rice varieties.

  • De La Torre, E., B. 2010. Detailed Implementation Guidelines, GPOs Lowland Irrigated Agro-Eco Zone for project TCP/PHI/3203.

entries.title: Rice and duck farming as a means for contributing to climate change adaptation and mitigation
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary:
The rice duck farming system aims to facilitate environmental adaptation in the cultivation of rice, and to contribute to food and economic security in the region by reducing the use of pesticides, increasing yield and generating an additional income for farmers. 

Integrating ducks in rice farming have been proven to increase 20 percent higher yield with about 50 percent higher net return. The same cultivation area can be used for not only rice production but also subsidiary products like meat and eggs. At the same time, it reduces labour inputs through the control of weeds and insects by ducks. Besides its economic benefits, this technology is especially environmentally friendly. The application of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides can be reduced thereby improving soil quality and pest control. The additional benefits of this Good Practice Option (GPO) are higher food security to small farming households in times of calamities and on a long-term basis the contribution to reducing methane emission. Hence, the integration of duck in lowland rice production is recommended as a climate adaptation and mitigation option. This technology describes how to implement the rice and duck farming system.
entries.description:
Description

In many irrigated rice areas in Bicol, farming communities rely heavily on the use of molluscicide and other synthetic pesticides, to eliminate golden apple snail (GAS) and to get better rice yield. But time has shown that these existing practices are expensive, imply health-hazards, and are environmentally-unfriendly. Integrating ducks into rice farming, also known as the "aigamo method" developed in 1989 by Takao Furuno, was replicated as one among other adaptation options in the Bicol project to reduce the costs of farm and labour inputs. This practice replaced fertilizer, pesticides and weed control through duck raising. The wider replication of this already known, integrated adaptation practice was supported in six municipalities (Masarawag, Guinobatan, Ariman, Gubat, Igbac, and Buhi) in three provinces in the Bicol region, during the dry season between December 2010 and April 2011 in lowland irrigated farming systems in the Philippines. 

1. Implementation of the technology 

1.1 Land preparation

  • Prepare the rice field as required based on the farmers existing practice.
  • In general, the land should be well-prepared by ploughing and harrowing three to four times.
  • For sandy loam to silty loam soil, two to three ploughing to and cross ploughing with subsequent three to four laddering are required so that the soil has a good tilt.
  • For a clay type of soil, soil preparation requires more tillage operation at appropriate soil moisture status.
  • During this period, allow ducks to range and feed on golden snail for two weeks. 

1.2 Fertilizer dose

  • Synthetic fertilizer will not be applied in the 1 000 m2 area. 
  • Fertilizer supply for the rice will come from the available rice straw left in the farm (sprayed with Trichoderma) for organic fertilizer. 

1.3 Seedling, sowing and spacing

  • Tested suitable rice varieties were NSIC Rc-194; NSIC Rc-132 / NSIC Rc-158.
  • Based on the Experiment Station - Research of the Department of Agriculture in Bicol (DA RFU-5) the minimum germination should be 85 percent, the maximum moisture content is 14 percent and the minimum varietal purity 98 percent.
  • The total weed seed/other crop seed/inert matter should not extend more than 0.10 percent.
  • Establish a seedbed (1 m x 2 m), where the rice seeds will be grown.
  • Use the modified dapog system using banana leaves as bedding material.
  • If rice hull is present, spread a 2 cm thick rice hull, cover it with a fine mesh fish net or mosquito net.
  • The soaked seeds should be evenly spread on the net and covered with rice straw.
  • Ensure that it is moist within three to five days.
  • After these three to five days, remove rice straw and allow the seedling to grow for eight to ten days.
  • The recommended planting distance is minimum 20 cm x 20 cm to allow enough space for the ducks and avoid damages.

1.4 Transplanting time

  • Based on the weather forecast, transplanting can either be done on the fourth week of December 2010 or the first week of January.
    • This is location specific and was done for the 2010-2011 project.
  • The seedlings should be transplanted within 30 minutes after pulling them off from the dapog seedbed to avoid injury and desiccation of seedlings.
  • While the transplanted rice is establishing its root system keep the ducks in its shelter for a week (five to seven days).
  • After this time, allow ducks to range again in the field during the vegetative stage of rice (45 days). 

1.5 Duck raising

  • The farmers constructed a simple 10 m² duck shelter, surrounded by a used-nylon fence, where the ducks rested and took refuge from the rain, and protection from other animals.
  • Four to eight laying-ducks, owned by the women farmers, were used as model purposely to document the dynamics of integrating ducks in the rice farms.
  • The ducklings, when released onto the fields, should be between one and three weeks old to ensure they are able to pick up small insects and weeds without damaging the crop.
    • The ducklings can be release to the rice paddy two weeks after transplanting. 
    • The field should be surrounded by protection measures to prevent the ducklings from moving outside the plots and avoid other animals to enter the field.
    • To avoid high mortality, the ducklings should only stay two to four hours on the rice field in the first three to five days and might need additional care especially to the effects of weather changes.
    • For the night the ducklings need a shelter to find protection and rest.
    • After this initial week, the ducklings can remain from the morning to the evening on the rice paddy,  but should not be released any more on the rice paddy when the flouring time has started.
    • The recommendation for ideal stocking density of ducklings varies, ranging from 20 to 400 ducklings per ha.
    • The project, after testing, recommends for one hectare of land around 150 ducks (note: the project provided fewer ducks during pilot testing). 

1.6 Rice harvesting

  • While the 80 to 85 percent of grains a ripe, the harvesting can be initiated.
  • Get three sample crop cuts of 2 m x 5 m area before harvest.
  • Get the data immediately after threshing (yield and moisture content). 

2. Results and findings from test replications 

  • The rice duck farming system proved suitable in typhoon-, flood-prone and even salt-affected areas.
  • Ducks help the rice seedlings grow by eating both insects and weeds that get in the way.
  • The farmers grow rice without using pesticide or herbicide.
  • They earn extra money when the fully grown ducks are sold or when they start laying eggs.
  • Field documentation showed that duck integration in the irrigated rice field and flood-prone area is a value-added livelihood and food security adaptation option as compared with the local farmers' practice of mono-crop rice cultivation (Table 1). 
Table 1. Production and economic benefits of rice + duck: FS documentation (1 000 m2), second crop cycle, 2011 

Source: FAO 2013

2.1 Cost of implementation

  • Farmers spent PHP 4 872, on the average, for the cost of seeds, ducks, other inputs, and family labour.
  • Eggs supplied nutrition to the children, while the additional income of PHP 200 per week (in 2010) in one cropping season, supplied some operational expenses of the household.
  • This amount is 30 percent higher than the earnings from traditional farming of mono-cropped rice.
  • Farmers observed that already by allowing ten ducks to freely range in the rice field over a period of eight months, the population of golden apple snail (GAS) was reduced.
  • Farmers set aside molluscicides and insecticides spray applications. 
  • Protein-rich food (egg) became a part of the family’s daily food item.
  • Excess eggs were sold to stores in the locality, as an additional source of cash.

2.2 Considerations for the improvement of practice

  • To improve technical and procedural aspects of rice and duck, the following issues need critical considerations.
    • If the FC homestead is not within the rice farm
      • Under this condition, ducks were stressed, thus, the egg-laying ability is delayed by more than three months.
    • If the FC homestead is right in the farm
      • This situation offers less stress on the ready-to-lay ducks delivered.
    • The location of ducks to the feeding area facilitated easy access to feed, such as golden kohol and rice grains.
      • Egg-production is facilitated and assured.
    • Disinterested unlisted/absent farmers during the planning session became suddenly interested while the ducks were being distributed to the intended FCs.
      • LGU-DA extension workers close supervision in the final list and distribution plan is very important.
  • The results have encouraged the Department of Agriculture RFU-5 management to replicate this practice with additional 50 farmers and procured 500 ready-to lay ducks.
    • Female farmers were especially interested in replicating this practice.

2.3 Safe use of pesticides

  • If you manipulate and/or use pesticides, make inquiries before!
  • Pesticide can be harmful to your health, the health of your family, of the consumers and of the environment.
  • Use pesticides safely.
    • For more information concerning reducing risks while manipulating pesticide: ID 8348.

3. Validation of practice

See section two. 

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Use of Salt-Tolerant Rice Varieties (e.g., NSIC Rc-108 and NSIC Rc-188) to counteract impacts of sea surges and saltwater intrusion, Philippines: ID 7722.
  • Use of Early-Maturing Rice Variety (EMRV) to reduce typhoon impacts in Bicol Region, Philippines: ID 7719.
  • Risk reduction while manipulating pesticides: ID 8348.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Labour saving technology

This technology incorporates ducks, which reduces the time of labour required for weeding, fertilizing, and pesticide application. 

6.2 Resource use efficiency

This technology reduces the use of pesticides via a natural rice duck farming system that provides the necessary fertilization for the rice. 

6.3 Pro-poor technology

This technology promises increased rice yields due to the better management of rice growing, and the cost of pesticides is foregone.

entries.title: Revitalizing rice ratooning to reduce risk and impact during hazard-prone months
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary:
The Philippines, due to its geographical location and physical environment, is among the world’s most disaster-prone countries. Disasters include floods, typhoons, monsoon storms and drought. The country experiences an average of 20 typhoons yearly. Natural hazards severely affect people’s livelihoods as they trigger landslides, flash floods, mudslides, widespread flooding and cause damage to homes, community buildings, communications, infrastructure, and agriculture. Within the Philippines, Bicol is one of the most hazard-prone regions and agriculture is regularly among the most affected sectors. Weather impacts cause variations in production and seasonal price fluctuations significantly affect the income of farmers.

Climate change will further exacerbate the region's exposure to climate-induced risks, which challenges farmers to adapt their farming systems to different conditions. Timing of planting coupled with complementary practices, like rice ratooning and the use of suitable rice varieties, can enhance the resilience of farmers to climate change and extreme weather events in particular in typhoon prone areas. This Good Practice Option (GPO) can reduce crop production losses during typhoon months and difficulties of seedbed preparation and transplanting during the turn-around period.
entries.description:
Description

Rice is the staple food of Filipinos. Farmers in Masarawag, Minto and Mauraro experience high risk of crop losses (40 to 80 percent) during the typhoon month of October, November and December. During this time the rice fields have more than sufficient water. Rice ratooning is a practical way of utilizing the residual water and reducing the risk of crop failure. Rice ratooning (suli, saringsing), is a “traditionally known” practice in Bicol. However, very few farmers still practice this method. However, it can be an effective strategy for farmers with less capital, while the rice field is fallowed. Farmers flagged their interest in revitalizing this traditional rice technology at the start of the project, during the community planning and validation workshop. This was due to the high crop production losses they incurred during typhoon months from October to December, and the difficulty of seedbed preparation and transplanting, during the turn-around period. The use of an appropriate short-maturing rice variety (NSIC Rc-158) with good ratoon ability was tested as a good practice option and compared with the existing farmers’ variety.

The revitalized approach to rice ratooning was promoted in three municipalities (Masarawag, Minto and Mauraro) between June and October 2010 and 2011 (wet season) in lowland, irrigated farming systems in the Philippines.

1. Implementation of the technology: guideline (for the main crop) 

  • The revitalization and replication of this traditional technique are suitable for farmers with about 1 000 m² of land for cultivation.
  • The expected costs for setting up a demonstration site amounts around 2 893 PHP (in 2010) including seeds, fertilizer, signboard, register and soil test.

1.1 Soil 

  • Any type depending on the location; soils sandy loam or loamy soil. 

1.2 Recommended rice variety

  • PhilRice variety NSIC Rc-158
    • Minimum germination is 85 percent
    • Maximum moisture content, 14 percent
    • Minimum varietal purity, 98 percent
    • Total weed seed / other crop seed / inert matter not more than 0.10 percent

1.3 Implementation time (main crop)

  • June 2010 (second crop cycle towards typhoon months of October, November and December). 

1.4 Land preparation

  • The land should be well-prepared / clean-culture by ploughing and harrowing three to four times.
  • For sandy loam to silty loam soil, two to three ploughing to and cross ploughing with subsequent three to four laddering are required. 
  • For a clay type of soil, soil preparation requires more tillage operation at appropriate soil moisture status. 

1.5 Seedling, sowing and spacing

  • The recommended variety is NSIC Rc-158 with an average yield of six tons per hectare and a growing cycle of ca. 113 days, including seedbed preparation (PhilRice).
  • In case NSIC Rc-158 is not available, a recommended alternative is NSIC Rc-120.
    • Note that NSIC Rc-120 is more sensitive for abnormal rainfall conditions under El Niño (less precipitation). 
  • For sowing, it is recommended to follow the dapog method (PhilRice).
  • Seeds should be sown in medium high land near the main field and an appropriate time to sowing seed is from May to early June.
    • The third week of May to the third week of June for sowing and transplanting, towards wet months November / December (this is location-specific for the Bicol region).
  • Before seed sowing, the organic matter and other nutrients should be ensured.
  • The seed rate is 40 kg to 50 kg per hectare. 

1.6 Fertilizer dose

  • Apply fertilizer in appropriate doses at the time of land preparation as illustrated in Table 1.
  • Compost (rice straw) will be mixed well in the soil.
  • Based on the soil analysis one half (10 kg) of urea is applied two days before harvest.
  • The remaining urea (9.2 kg) is applied two weeks after harvest. 

1.7 Irrigation and weeding

  • Depending on the types of soil, two to three times of irrigation may be needed.
  • The first round should be applied after harvest.
  • The second is to be applied 10 to 12 days after the growth of the panicles.
  • The third and final irrigation should be applied during the grain formation stage (e.g. after 75 to 80 days of sowing).
  • As needed, use rotary or hand (manual) weeding or existing practice that farmers use. 

1.8 Harvesting (the main crop)

  • Harvest when 80 percent of the grains are mature.
    • About 15 cm to 20 cm from the ground.
    • Rice stem/tillers are left in the field after harvest, for ratooning.

1.9 Rice ratooning (farm operation practice)

  • Land preparation
    • None.
    • Tillers of the main crop left in the rice field are allowed to regrow and produce panicles and grains.
  • Transplanting
    • None.
    • Transplanting is needed because the main tillers are the ones left in the field, which after 45 days will produce grains.
  • Weeding
    • None.
    • Since the weeds were checked during the first (main) rice crop, weeding is seldom needed.
  • Pesticide (vs golden snail) and insecticides
    • At this stage, the rice crop has already established its resistance, and water level is still not conducive for their presence.
  • Fertilizer application
    • Two days before harvesting the rice crop, apply 10 kg urea (top dress).
    • Apply another 10 kg Urea, two weeks later.
  • Irrigation
    • Apply irrigation, based on fertilizer application schedules.
      • Immediately after harvest.
      • After second Urea application.

10. Harvesting

  • Harvest the ratoon crop 45 to 50 days later. 
Table 1. Fertiliser dose for one demonstration
Name of fertiliser Quantity per ha
Urea 19.2 kg
Trichoderma 2 packets

Source: FAO 2013

2. Results and findings 

  • The timing of planting in highly-irrigated areas, coupled with rice ratooning and use of suitable rice varieties, has increased the overall resilience for small farmers in Minto and Masarawag.
  • Experiences in Ormoc, Davao and Sorsogon indicate that an additional yield of 25 to 30 cavans (one cavan are ca. 50 kg) are possible within 60 to 75 days after harvest (Malabanan, 2008 & Bar, 2004), using appropriate varieties, both certified and hybrid rice varieties.
  • The data indicate that rice ratooning produced additional rice yields of 550 kg per hectare within 45 days.
  • Yield difference was significant at 5 percent level using t-test with a t-value = 3.06 and p-value = 0.008.
  • Additional support of Local Government Units (LGU) is recommended to establish functional seed systems, storage and distribution of stress-tolerant varieties that are accessible to farmers and enable them to mitigate the effects of natural hazards. 
Table 2. Yield performance of NSIC Rc-158 for the timing of planting with rice rationing (2010) 

Source: FAO 2013

Figure 1. Performance of early + ratoon rice GPO 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Rice harvest of early maturing + rationing GPO 

©FAO/TECA

3. Validation of the practice

  • See section two. 

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Use of salt-tolerant rice varieties to counteract impacts of sea surges and saltwater intrusion: ID 7722.
  • Rice and duck farming as a means for contributing to climate change adaptation and mitigation: ID 7724.
  • Use of submergence rice variety NSIC Rc-194 to counteract impacts of flooding: ID 7723.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Women friendly

The technology is easy to use and accessible for any kind of hand labour.

6.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently uses different kinds of crops pertaining to their growth adaptability in different environments. 

6.3 Pro-poor technology

Rice ratooning enhances the resilience of farmers to climate change and extreme weather events, reduces crop production losses, and facilitates seed preparation.

entries.title: Rooftop water collection, drip irrigation and plastic mulching in home garden conditions in drought prone areas
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary:
The impact of natural hazards on the agriculture sector can be devastating. To reduce the effects of climate change, farmers use strategies to counter-effect the influence of a natural disaster. For example, saving rooftop rainwater can help during a drought, and mulching helps maintain soil moisture.

In this good practice, first, steps and requirements for rainwater collection are explained. Building on water harvesting, a drip irrigation system is explained which is crucial for water-saving during irrigation in the dry seasons.

Mulching methods are also described. Mulching is a technique that is used to cover and to keep soil moisture for better plant growth.

To finish, a cost-benefit analysis of their combined application is presented.
entries.description:
Description

Cambodia is highly vulnerable to natural hazards, primarily floods and drought, which heavily impact the agriculture sector. As a result, the lives and livelihoods of many smallholder farmers are severely affected. Through livelihood diversification, home gardens help to reduce the adverse impacts of natural hazards. Families are able to grow different fruits and vegetables to supplement their unbalanced diets, which currently mainly consist of consuming staple foods, such as rice. When combined with rooftop rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation, and plastic mulching water is used effectively, efficiently and saves time especially for women and children who are often responsible for water collection. The water from the rooftop containers can also be used for various household needs, freeing time for other activities. Home gardening can help farmers, and women in particular, to reduce the impact of dry spells and drought. This enables them to generate additional income, diversify their livelihoods, and contribute to the food and nutritional security of their families. In the following sections, the good practices of rainwater collection, drip irrigation and plastic mulching are presented with a cost-benefit analysis of their combined application. 

1. Rooftop rainwater harvesting to reduce risk during the dry spell and drought

  • Rainwater collection has been practiced to sustain Cambodian families through the dry season in the past.
    • Traditional methods were improved to ensure sufficient access to water in order to reduce the impact of drought and dry spells.
    • The water is collected using a rooftop rainwater system, where rainwater falls on metal or tiled roofs and is then collected in containers at the edge of the roof or channeled to a storage system via gutters and plastic pipes.  
    • The rainwater is channeled into a covered storage tank that protects the water from contamination.
    • The storage was improved to include assembled cement rings that could store in capacity such as 2 000, 3 000 and 5 000 liters of water.
  • Through the use of rooftop rainwater collection, families were able to collect enough rainwater in the rainy season and conserve it for the dry season or an unexpected drought.
  • This technique reduced the adverse impacts of dry spells and droughts and enabled farmers to increase and diversify the crop and animal production to generate additional income. 

1.1 Identification of a suitable storage

1.1.1 Determination of the size of the tank

  • The size of the storage tank depends on the utilization purposes which include household consumption or household consumption, plus vegetable or animal production.
  • Based on experience, it is recommended that for household consumption, the calculation to determine the size of the tank is based on the number of household members, assuming a consumption of 15 liters per person per day.
    • For vegetable production, 1 m2 of garden needs an average of 2 liters of water each day under the climatic conditions of the tested area.

1.1.2 Choosing the right tank

  • There are various options available for the construction of these tanks with respect to the shape, size and the material of construction.
  • Currently, three types of tanks are available in Cambodia.
    • The Jumbo Jar (see Figure 1)
    • The Cement Ring Tank (see Figure 2)
    • The Ferro Cement Tank (see Figure 1)
  • The Jumbo Jar tanks are the most popular ones due to their lower prices.
  • Cement ring jars are the second favorable ones.
Figure 1. Traditional water containers called Jumbo jars

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Modern water collection tanks also called ring tanks

©FAO/TECA

Table 1. Characteristics of the different water container solutions

Source: FAO 2017

1.2 Construction of the rainwater harvesting system 

  • The rainwater harvesting system may be constructed as per the instructions below.
  • The construction requires techniques and skills in the Water and Sanitation (WATSAN) sector. 

1.2.1 Catchment surface

  • The catchment surface of a water harvesting system is the surface which directly receives the rainfall and flows water to the container.
  • The catchment surface is usually the roof of the house or animal shed. 
  • To ensure clean and safe water, the collection area of roofs can be constructed with a range of materials, including galvanized corrugated iron, aluminum cement sheets, tiles, and slates.
  • It is recommended to build the catchment surface adjacent to the home garden if farmers want to combine with drip irrigation system. 

1.2.2 Gutters and down piping

  • Gutters and down piping serve to get the water from the roof during raining to the storage container.
  • Gutters should be installed under the roofing on both sides of the roof and channeled with pipes to the tank.
  • The most commonly used material for this purpose in Cambodia is plastic piping, which costs approximately USD 30 for a water harvesting system covering the roof of one farm house or similar building.

1.2.3 Cover of the water tank

  • It is also very important to cap or cover the water storage tank at all times.  
  • Wooden or cement covers are commonly used.
  • Covering the tank prevents debris and dirt from contaminating the water and also keeps out mosquitoes and other pests that may contaminate the water and cause health risks to humans and animals.  
  • Therefore, the cap or cover should closely fit over the opening of the tank to prevents small animals such as lizards, or mice from falling into the water tank.
  • It is useful to install chicken wire before the inlet pipe to prevent animals from entering the pipe from the roof and then falling into the water tank.

1.2.4 First-flush system

  • The “first-flush” system is used to ensure clean water.
  • During the dry season dirt and debris may collect on the roof and wash into the storage tank.
  • The first-flush system discards the first bit of flowing water and ensures that the water being collected is clean.
  • A simple first-flush system is made from attaching a vertical pipe to the down pipe that delivers water into the tank.
  • A valve is put in place below the junction where the pipes come together.
  • This way, the initial water may be sent out through the extra pipe and will not send dirt and debris into the tank.
  • It is important to regularly check and clear the pipes and make sure that the first rain will be washed out to avoid dirty and contaminated water.
  • Drip irrigation systems require maintenance to prevent the clogging of gutters.
    • Key maintenance interventions include periodic inspection of gutterlines, flushing of the system, and the application of an orderly irrigation plan.

1.3 Capacity building

  • It is important to train families in the use and maintenance of the system to ensure sustainability.
  • The training may also include how to manage water usage and sanitation techniques to ensure families have sufficient and clean water throughout the dry season. 
  • Additional training on farming technique may be required, if the system is installed for the purpose of increasing agricultural production and livelihood diversification.

2. Drip irrigation, a drought-resilient technique for vegetable cultivation

  • Irrigating crops can be a challenge for farmers during the dry season or in times of drought.
    • Crop failure has detrimental effects on the livelihoods of families and their food and nutrition security.
    • Access to sufficient as well as efficient use of water resources is highly important, in particular during the dry season.
    • Lack of water increases the work burden of women and children, who have to travel sometimes long distances to meet the household water needs.
    • For households without stored water, water shortages in the dry season limit the production from homestead vegetable gardens.
  • Unlike many other irrigation techniques, drip irrigation enables a watering regime that is slow, regular and even soil wetting.
  • In drip irrigation, water is directed through a series of plastic pipes directly to the plant roots, enabling plants to effectively use most of the available water, thereby limiting the amount of water lost to deep drainage, evaporation and runoff.
  • In addition to the efficient and effective use of water, less fertilizer is washed away and as a result, the cost of inputs needed is lower.
  • The more controlled water release also results in fewer weeds, which means less labor is required also for watering to raise crops.
  • Time is saved not only from collecting water but also in having to water the crops.
  • Drip irrigation increases water use efficiency, reduces labor requirements, and improves harvest quality and quantity.
  • The use of rooftop rainwater collection as a valuable water source for drip irrigation can help farmers cultivate vegetables around the homestead.
    • Vegetable cultivation is often done by women.
    • As a result, this can help them to reduce the impact of drought and enable them to increase numbers of crops grown a year, which helps to generate additional income, diversify livelihoods and contribute to food and nutrition security.
  • Simple, low-cost drip irrigation kits are available in Cambodia and are suitable for use by farmers with small or large plots of land.
  • In general, two kinds are available and suitable for areas from 40 m2 to 500 m2.
    • A drip irrigation system is composed of many elements.
      • A water container that aliments the system and a main tube that brings the water from the tank to the garden.
      • Some farmers install cement rings as the water container as it is easy to set up and materials are locally available (see section 2).
      • Five assembled cement rings have a capacity of 5 000 liters of water.
      • The other option can be using simple water tanks or jars.
      • Water tanks or jars are placed near the plot of land, generally within 2 m to 3 m.
      • It is raised by 1 m to ensure water flow by gravity.
      • Farmers generally have to purchase the cement container separately as they are not part of the irrigation kits.
      • A tap controls the water flow from the water container.
      • The water first passes through a filter to make sure debris is removed so that the pipes will not be clogged.
      • The water then flows through the sub-main pipe to the lateral pipes in the garden.
      • The lateral pipes are laid over the crops parallel to the rows.
      • The water flows into these pipes and is then distributed to the plant roots via emitters (micro-tubes).
    • This process is illustrated in Figure 1.

2.1 Preparation of the system

  • The land must be leveled and prepared in rows so that the watering pipes may be installed (see sample Figure 3).
  • Then, the water container must be set up and holes must be made in the sub-pipes using a needle.
  • In general, a kit covering 40 m2 takes about two hours to install.
  • Along with the installation, the orientation on basic instruction of the installation and management of small-scale drip irrigation systems should be provided so farmers will know how to maintain the drip irrigation system themselves.
  • After installation, the same kit may be used for three to four crop production cycles.
  • After three to four cycles, it will need to be removed to check the quality and to replace the broken parts, while allowing farmers to prepare the land for next cropping.

2.2 Possible water sources for a drip irrigation system

  • Any source of water such as a rooftop rainwater collection container, pond or a well may be used for a drip irrigation system as long as it provides water pressure (for example through gravity) and has an attachment suitable to connect to the drip irrigation system.
Figure 3. Components of drip irrigation

Source: Roberts, M.S. & Long, A., 2006

Figure 4. Drip irrigation installation for vegetable production

©FAO/TECA

2.3 System layout

  • The system’s design needs to be done according to the crops to be irrigated as well as the spacing of the crops.
  • An emitter will be placed close to each plant.
  • Plants that require more water may need two emitters.
  • These emitters are attached to the main water system.

2.4 Filling of the water container

  • The water container should be filled with rooftop rainwater by gravity or with a pump tapping other water sources.
  • For a water container with a capacity of 5 000 litres, a home garden of 40 m2 can be irrigated for around two months during the rainy season and for 15 to 30 days during dry season.
  • As the plants mature, water will need to be irrigated two times each day.

2.5 Testing of the drip irrigation system

  • Turn the valve on and ensure that the water successfully runs from the water tank to the emitters.
  • Adjust the water flow to allow the emitters to slowly release the water as water should dribble onto the soil near the plants.

2.6 Check for leaks

  • After adjusting the water flow, turn the valve off.
  • The water should stop running.
  • If this is not the case, this means that there are leaks in the drip lines due to an incorrect adapter.
  • Use only threaded hose adapters.
  • It is possible to fix small leaks by wrapping thread seal tape around the area.

2.7 Perform regular maintenance

  • It is important to routinely check for leaks and clean the filter regularly about every two weeks.
Figure 5. Drip irrigation installation with elevated water containers

©FAO/TECA

3. Plastic mulches in vegetable cultivation for enhanced resilience to drought and soil erosion

  • Mulching is a technique that has been used by vegetable growers for many years.
  • Mulches are used to cover and to keep soil moisture for better plant growth.
  • Traditionally, natural mulches such as rice straw and water hyacinth, have been used.
  • However, since the creation of synthetic materials, the plastic sheet has been introduced as a means to provide the same benefits.
  • Plastic mulches are impermeable and therefore, prevent the evaporation of moisture from the soil.
    • They limit losses of water and reduce soil erosion better than natural mulches do.
    • In addition to conserving water, plastic mulches also help with weed control.
      • That allows farmers to improve and maximize their production.
    • Plastic mulching is a good practice to ensure crop production during dry spells and droughts.
  • This is especially true if plastic mulching is used in conjunction with drip irrigation (see drip irrigation above).
  • This practice saves labour time (such as for weeding), saves other resources (such as fertilizer, herbicide and pesticide input), increases yields and contributes to people’s food and nutrition security.
  • Plastic mulches are easily acquired and provide flexibility for utilization.
    • However, they are more expensive than natural ones.
  • Plastic mulches can be used at least three crop cycles in terms of quality especially in combination with drip installation.
  • Plastic mulches require farmers to have skills in vegetable growing.
    • The introduction of plastic, mulching must, therefore, be accompanied by adequate training and/ or a Farmer Field School programmes on vegetable production, including cleaning, land preparation, lime application, composting, harrowing, making beds, applying mulch, drip irrigation, and drainage.

3.1 Land preparation

  • Clean and plough the land to a depth of 30 cm.
  • Remove all bushes, rocks, and weeds.
  • Plough the soil into tiny pieces.

3.2 Application of lime

  • The lime increases soil pH, corrects soil acidity and provides calcium and magnesium, which are important for vegetable growth.
  • In addition, it makes more nutrients available to plants.
  • Lime will also help reduce soil-borne diseases and pests.
  • However, lime should not always be used especially when plants are grown on soils that are already high in pH/ alkaline.
  • Therefore, if you are unsure about the pH of your soil, do a pH test first before applying lime.
  • Apply lime on the surface of the soil.
  • Practically, use 5 to 10 kg of lime for 100 m2 of land size.
  • Spread the lime across the land covering it with an even thin layer of lime.
  • When applying lime, put on a mask and wear gloves to protect yourself.
Figure 6. Cleaning and land preparation

©FAO/TECA

3.3 Compost and harrowing

  • Cover completely the lime with a layer of compost.
  • Use 2 to 3 kg of compost for every square meter of land (see compost fertilizer).
  • Harrow or rake the compost twice into the land to ensure that the compost is well mixed into the soil.
  • The compost is rich in nutrients, which helps to increase soil fertility as well as to retain moisture.
  • Therefore, this mix helps crops grow healthy and strong.

3.4 Preparation of beds

  • Build the beds parallel to the land’s longest side, considering the slope of the land, accessibility, and water source.
  • The bed should be 30 cm high and 60 to 90 cm wide for rainy season.
    • This is wide enough for most crops.
  • Make sure the beds will drain effectively.

3.5 Application of mulch

  • Pull the plastic mulch, silver side up, tightly over the beds.
  • Put some soil on the plastic mulch to hold it in place (see Figure 7).
  • Plastic mulch helps protect the soil against weeds and decreases the mobility of pests.
  • If possible, use reflective plastic films, which can also repel certain kinds of insects.
  • One vegetable bed of 10 m length needs around 10.5 m2 of plastic sheet.
  • For commercial gardens from 500 to 2 000 m2, it costs approximately USD 60 in Cambodia.
  • For home gardens from 300 to 400 m2, it costs about USD 12.5 and about USD 4.5 for 40 m2 .
Figure 7. Application of plastic mulch

©FAO/TECA

3.6 Preparation of drainage

  • Dig 20 cm deep canals between the beds for irrigation tubes.
  • Dig two primary canals towards the lowest point of the garden.
  • To avoid soil erosion between the beds and to get a fast and shallow canal use dry rice straw, rice husks or rice ash.
    • They can flow off the land slowly.

4. Lesson learned from demonstrations of rooftop rainwater collection systems

4.1 Economic and social feasibility

4.1.1 Benefits

  • Rooftop rainwater collection is the most suitable practice for rural farmers and considered as the coping strategy for dry spells or drought.
  • Rooftop rainwater harvesting can assist household water needs with good quality water and more constant water supply in the dry season.
  • The combination of rooftop rainwater harvesting and drip irrigation can save water and time significantly, and also reduce women’s work burden to fetch water from long distances.
  • The combination of the technologies of rooftop rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation, plastic mulch, and home gardening could save time, water and labour.
  • Farmers can gain higher yields than with conventional practices.

4.1.2 Cost

  • The initial investment costs are high.
    • Low-income families may not be able to afford this system without support.
  •  It is labour intensive to install cement rings.

4.2 Increase resilience

4.2.1 Benefits

  • Water is collected during the rainy season and conserved to use in the dry season.
  • Two cement stands (with ten assembled cement rings) can store about 5 000 litres of water.
  • This amount of water can last for at least one month for consumption and household use for an average of five family members and irrigation of 60 m2 home garden.

5. Lessons learned from the drip irrigation system demonstrations

5.1 Economic and social feasibility

5.1.1 Benefits

  • Significant labour-saving times for women of up to three hours per day.
  • Water is applied only where needed and is not wasted or lost through evaporation or runoff.
  • Reduced amount of washed away fertilizers, so it helps to reduce the cost of inputs.

5.1.2 Cost

  • Installation costs of around USD 60 for home garden from 300 m2 to 400 m2 could be high for farmers.
  • In case of damage or extension of the system, farmers may struggle to find locally available suppliers to support the installation or fix the damage.

5.2 Increase resilience

5.2.1 Benefits

  • The efficient water-saving technique uses four times less water than the conventional technique.
    • For instance, a 10 m long vegetable bed of 60 to 90 cm wide using drip irrigation, requires around 15 litres of water per day.
    • Conventional practices using water tanks on the other hand, may take up to 60 litres of water.

5.3 Environmental suitability

5.3.1 Cost

  • Drip irrigation systems and plastic mulch can have negative effects on the environment, as they are made of plastic.
  • If farmers use big systems the waste may end up being discharged on landfills without proper management and with long-term threats to groundwater.
  • It is therefore suggested to train farmers on waste management and the supplier of the drip irrigation systems should collect the old drip kits for recycling purposes.

5.4 Additional considerations

  • Combine drip irrigation systems with other practices such as rooftop rainwater collection, plastic mulch, compost and botanical insecticide to improve soil composition and soil moisture.
  • Properly fence the farms to protect crops from animal encroachment.
  • Be cautious of damages to system while harvesting and make sure that the plastic tubes are stored in a safe place between crop cycles.

6. Lessons learned from plastic mulching demonstrations

6.1 Economic and social feasibility

6.1.1 Benefits

  • Labour and time are saved since farmers, particularly women, have more time to monitor pest and diseases on vegetables and scale up the production.
  • The amount of fertilizers washed away by rain is reduced, so it helps to reduce the cost of inputs.

6.1.2 Cost

  • It might be difficult for some farmers living in remote areas to have access to the plastic mulching suppliers and it might be expensive.
    • In this case, organic mulches, such as rice straw and water hyacinth, can be a good alternative for farmers.
      • They are cheap; easy to find after the harvesting of rice and vegetables; and the organic mulches buried into the soil additionally serve as organic fertilizers.

6.2 Increase resilience

6.2.1 Benefit

  • Plastic mulches maintain soil moisture for longer than no-mulching. The plastic cover acts as an insulator to keep moisture from evaporation during hot times or dry spells.
  • Plastic can also prevent weed to grow, hence it reduces the competition between weeds and crops for water and fertilizers.
  • It can maintain the shape and level of vegetable beds in the rainy season.
    • It also prevents vegetables from waterlogging, reducing the incidents of root rot and other diseases.
  • It works efficiently when combined with drip irrigation.
    • The combination of these practices could save water up to four times.

6.2.2 Cost

  • Plastic waste has a negative effect on the environment if farmers use big amounts of plastic mulches and throw the waste on land without proper management.
  • The environmental costs of producing plastic mulching sheets need to be considered before shifting from traditional mulching materials to plastic.
  • It is suggested to train farmers on waste management and the suppliers of the plastic mulch should collect the old plastic mulch for recycling purposes.

6.3 Additional considerations

  • Beware of possible damage caused by animals if the plot is not properly fenced.
  • Beware of damage to plastic mulch and tubes during harvesting.
  • Beware of the increased temperature of the soil while using plastic mulch.
    • It can scorch young plants.

7. Cost-benefit analysis

  • The results of the qualitative and quantitative analyses conducted based on field demonstration data are summarized hereafter.
  • The performance of the combined GPOs was assessed at the farm-level in Cambodia based on quantitative data collected during the monitoring period.
  • The net benefits obtained from the application of these practices were measured through a cost-benefit analysis
    (CBA), and compared to the net benefits obtained from traditional practices.
  • The CBA projects the cumulative net present value of benefits obtained from 1 acre over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms), as well as the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
    • The graph in Figure 8 shows that the net benefit over 11 years is 115 percent higher in farms that adopt the GPOs combination, as compared to non-adopters.
    • The cost-benefit ratio of good practice is higher than that of the existing local practice.
    • Although the good practice requires more input and labour (especially for maintenance), the increase in yield due to a more balanced water supply, weed management and soil water retention more than compensated the additional input cost.
    • Figure 8 below shows the average annual costs and benefits per m2 of the good practice compared to the local practice.

7.1 Cost assumptions 

  • Labour cost only includes hired labour.
    • Family labour is not included.
  • Seeds costs are considered as upfront capital costs, not seasonal costs (first purchase, then saved from cycle to cycle).
  • Operation and maintenance costs are not included due to possible double counting with other costs such as labour.
    • Assuming a 10 percent discount rate, capital costs are fully repaid after seven years.
    • To overcome upfront investment barriers, access to credit should be facilitated.
    • From a strictly economic point of view, the GPO yields very limited benefits. H
    • owever, relevant positive impacts of GPO implementation arise from the qualitative evaluation.

7.2 Food security and nutrition

  • The GPO allows two cropping cycles, hence, it enhances food security and diversification of diets.

7.3 Access to safe water

  • Seventy percent of the farmers said that the GPO improved their access to clean and safe water.

7.4 Knowledge

  • All interviewed farmers considered that they acquired new knowledge by taking part in the project and implementing the GPO.

7.5 Sustainability

  • All of the farmers interviewed said they would replicate the GPO in the coming seasons.
  • Given the relatively high capital cost required to start the good practice, adequate access to credit for farmers would facilitate adoption.
Figure 8. Cumulative net benefit-cost ratios of good practice and local practice (USD per m2)

©FAO/TECA

8. Validation of the practice

8.1 Geographical area of validation

  • A total of 50 demonstrations of rooftop rainwater collection were tested in combination with drip irrigation and plastic mulching under vegetable home garden conditions in the Kampong Speu province, Cambodia.

8.2 Field reports

8.2.1 Field report of a female farmer using the water harvesting system

  • Ms. Nou Phorn, a 58-year-old widow woman in Srah Thol village, Yuth Samaki commune, Odong district, Kampong Speu province.

“At the beginning, I found it was a bit costly and time-consuming to install the cement rings. My son is a construction worker and he helped me with the installation. With the new system, I do not have to fetch water daily to store in the small cement jars for my children and grandchildren to use. It was unfortunate that there was a dry spell from June to August, which caused a deep concern for me regarding the shortage of water. Later, when the rain fell, the ten cement rings provided by the project  stored about 5 000 litres of water. So I decided to buy two more rings to add into the system. Now the three stands can have the capacity to store about 6 000 litres of water. There are five members in my house and everyone is bathing, washing clothes, cooking, and drinking with water from the stands. The 6 000 litres of water in the cement containers can last for 45 days for my family's consumption and can be used for the irrigation of the 150 m2 vegetable home garden”. 

Figure 9. Average annual cost and benefits per m2 of the good practice compared to the local practice

©FAO/TECA

8.2.2 Field report of a female farmer using the drip irrigation system

  • Ms. Em Lim, 38 years old with three children, in Kraing Chek village, Kraing Chek commune, Odong district, Kampong Speu province.

“Before, I used a pair of small water buckets of around 40 litres to water a 10 m long vegetable bed. I have many vegetable beds, so I had to carry several buckets of water every day. With the drip irrigation system, I found that it saves lots of water, time and labour. On a dry and hot day, I water about an hour/day using the drip system, maybe around ten litres of water for a 10 m long vegetable bed. So this system saves water about four times because the drip system lets water flow straight to the stem of the plant and there is no run-off water like when I was using the water buckets. Most importantly, I don’t need to carry heavy water buckets to water my crops anymore and I can have more time to take care of my children and monitor the presence of pests and diseases on my crops”. 

8.2.3 Field report of a farmer using plastic mulches

  • Mr. Mr Moeung Chea, a 61 years old living in Thmor Matey village, Yuth Samaky commune, Odong district, Kampong Speu province.

“It was raining heavily for three days, and my home garden is always affected by waterlogging, yet with plastic mulch, my vegetables still looked fresh and healthy. Normally, the vegetables rotted and died whenever the garden was waterlogged. Plastic mulch is not only preventing vegetables from rotting, but it also helps to prevent fertilizers from washing away by runoff water and prevents weed growth. In comparison to my conventional way, the yield of my vegetable crops such as yard-long bean, tomato and cucumber, was doubled using plastic mulch. I am interested in this practice and I am willing to use my own investment in the future. My relatives and neighbours are also interested in my garden where I use rooftop rainwater collection, drip irrigation, and plastic mulch and I am also willing to share my experience with them.” 

8.3 Context of implementation

8.3.1 Social-Target group

  • Smallholder farmers

9. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • Possess the financial means to acquire the necessary materials to build the rooftop water harvesting system, a drip irrigation system, plastic mulching, and seeds.
  • Farmers, normally, would need capacity development (for example through Farmer Field Schools) to learn how to construct and maintain those solutions.
  • As a general rule, rainfall should be over 50 mm per month for at least half a year or 300 mm per year (unless other sources are extremely scarce) to make rainwater harvesting feasible.
  • Maintenance of the drip irrigation system should be conducted in order to prevent the clogging of the drippers.

11. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

12. Related/associated technologies

  • Rooftop rainwater harvesting: ID 7387.
  • Rainwater harvesting systems for ntula/eggplant (Solanum aethiopicum L.) growing: ID 8924.
  • Rainwater harvesting systems for cabbage growing: ID 8932.
  • Rooftop rainwater harvesting combined with gravity drip irrigation: tomato growing: ID 10011.
  • Rooftop rainwater harvesting combined with gravity drip irrigation: sweet pepper production: ID 10012.

12. Objectives fulfilled by the project

12.1 Women-friendly

This practice helps women farmers save rainwater and takes off the burden of daily water-fetching. Constructing the rooftop rainwater harvesting system may require some men's help.

12.2 Resource use efficiency

Water can be saved and used in the dry season, which is crucial for agriculture products' success and consequently the nutrition of the farmers’ family.

12.3 Pro-poor technology

This practice helps reduce the effects of climate change, which improves safety, health, and food security, and contributes to poverty alleviation.
