entries.title: Wheat cultivation with farm yard manure and compost application in dry spell conditions, a cost-benefit analysis
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary: This technology describes the introduction of Farm Yard Manure (FYM) and compost practices for wheat production in Ghotki district in Pakistan under dry spell conditions, during the Rabi season in 2018 (January to April). It also provides a cost benefit analysis of the describe practice compared to the traditional wheat growing. The main hazards affecting agricultural livelihoods in this district are dry spells and related water scarcity. The application of FYM and compost on the fields increases the water holding capacity of the soil and enhances soil fertility. This practice allows the farmers to reduce water use and increase production. FYM serves as balanced nutritious manure for plants, improves soil biodiversity, and represents a cost-effective fertilization strategy. Physical properties like bulk density, porosity, void ratio, water permeability and hydraulic conductivity were also significantly improved when FYM was applied. Similarly, compost application increases the availability of essential micro and macro nutrients for the crop and can improve physical and chemical properties of the soils. The tillering, plant height and biomass were also significantly increased. Using compost and FYM not only allows to decrease the use of chemical fertilizer but also improves soil texture for successive crops. The application of FYM in combination with the use of compost for the production of wheat is called a Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) practice. It is aimed at preventing new and reducing existing disaster risk and managing residual risk, all of which contribute to strengthening resilience and therefore to the achievement of sustainable development.
entries.description:
Description

1. Previously used practice       

  • Farmers in the Ghotki district have been using traditional wheat cultivation practices.
  • The traditional method is challenged by dry spells and, in general, unpredictable rainfall patterns.

2. Application of the good practice

2.1 Farm Yard Manure (FYM)

  • Farm Yard Manure (FYM) is a fertilizer made up of farm waste products such as dung, straw or urine produced by farm animals, most commonly cows.
  • It provides nutrients and organic matter to the soil, particularly nitrogen which is vital for the plant’s growth.
  • FYM serves as balanced nutritious manure for plants, improves soil biodiversity, and represents a cost-effective fertilisation strategy.
  • To make FYM, cow dung and urine have to be collected into layers of even thickness under a simple roof to keep it from getting excessively wet and exposed to sunlight.
    • More dung and urine are added along with some water if it gets too dry.
  • The FYM can be used on fields as fertilizer after an average of six months.
    • It is usually spread on a field three or four weeks before sowing.
    • The manure exposed to the elements will decompose and provide nutrients to the soil.
  • The FYM can be applied in solid or liquid form.
    • In this case, the FYM manure was prepared in liquid form, and was applied along with irrigation.
Figure 1. Application of a mixture of FYM and compost  being distributed on the field

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

3. Compost

  • The use of compost is part of an organic agriculture system that emphasizes maximum reliance on renewable farm and other local resources.
  • Compost is an organic fertilizer that has the advantage that it improves soil structure and aeration, increases the soil’s water-holding capacity, and stimulates healthy root development.
  • Compost can be prepared from mixed weeds or other biologically degradable (e.g. pruning, post-harvest and fallen fruits, etc.) waste.

3.1 Step one: preparation of compost

  • Compost was prepared by the farmers about three months before the sowing of wheat.
  • It was prepared using organic residues, like FYM and other wastes, in anaerobic conditions.
    • The material was allowed to remain in cover for about four months without turning and watering.

3.2 Step two: seed selection and Land preparation

  • FAO provided certified wheat seeds of the variety Zincol under the Building Disaster Resilience in Pakistan (BDRP) project.
  • Farmers levelled their land through a laser leveller and used conventional ploughing and planking with a tractor.
    • The sowing of seeds was made using a seed drill in order to maintain the required plant-plant distance.

3.3 Step three: application of compost

  • Mature compost was applied during land preparation for sowing of the wheat crop.
  • Mature compost was distributed equally on the ground to be incorporated into the soil during the land preparation.
Figure 2. Preparation of compost from FYM

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

Figure 3. Composting mixture

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

Figure 4. Making of compost solution

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

Figure 5. Compost preparation

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

4. Socio-economic benefits of the practice

  • The described practices were introduced in the framework of the FAO Building Disaster Resilience in Pakistan (BDRP) project in Pakistan, in combination with an improved wheat variety (Zincol).
    • The high yielding Zincol wheat variety responds better to the climate conditions of the villages.
  • As a result of the implementation of the practices in combination with the improved seed variety, farmers increased their wheat production.
  • Through the project, farmers were able to multiply and store thenew wheat variety in order to replicate the practice in the following years and in other villages.
  • Each farm that implemented the new practices had a higher profit, as compared to the previously used practice.
  • The application of the described DRR practice allowed the farmers to save water thanks to the increased water holding capacity of the soil.
  • The use of locally available organic material for the preparation of compost and bio-fertilizer avoids this organic material to end up in landfills, where it would produce methane and leachate. 
    • The practices allow to reduce the carbon footprint of wheat production.
  • The  use of FYM and compost as bio fertilizers also allowed to reduced the need for chemical fertilizers.
    • FYM and compost applied to the field encourage the production of beneficial bacteria and fungi that break down organic matter to create humus, a rich nutrient-filled material.
  • Compost sale can also be a source of income, if produced where there is access to a local market.
    • It could represent a solution to waste management at household/farm level.
  • Overall, the farmers expressed their interest in replicating the practices in the future.

5. Cost of the practice                             

  • The benefits and costs of FYM and compost for wheat production were assessed at farm-level.
  • The net benefits obtained from introducing the practices was calculated through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA).  
    • The CBA calculates the net present value (NPV) of cumulative benefits obtained from using FYM and compost to improve wheat production over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms).
    • It also calculates the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period. 
    • The CBA was conducted based on quantitative data collected on four farms located in the Ghotki district, in the villages Janan Waso, Kamil Bhishti, Rahmat Khan Gabol and Sher Dil Mahar during the Rabi season 2018 (from January to April 2018), affected by dry spell.
    • During the monitoring period, all four villages were faced with drought episodes.
    • The season percentage average difference of rainfall per season as compared to a 20 years average was of 23 percent.
  • Figure 6 provides an overview of the outcome of the CBA. 
    • In particular, it shows that, under drought conditions (Figure 6), the net benefit of applying FYM and compost for wheat production over 11 years is over twenty percent higher than without the applying the DRR practice.
    • The BCR with the DRR practice is 1.87, which is lower than the BCR of the previously applied practice (1.95), which is due to the higher input costs (see Figure 7 below).  
Figure 6. Cumulative net present value per acre over 11 years

©FAO/TECA

  • The graph shows that the compost/manure cost, the labour cost and the fertilizer cost are higher for the DRR good practice, compared to the previous practice.
  • However, those are offset by the benefits obtained from the implementation of the good practice, with a higher gross value of production.
  • These results show that wheat production with FYM and composting are an effective DRR practice.        
Figure 7. Average costs and benefits (USD per ha per season)

©FAO/TECA

6. General recommendations

  • The farmers who benefited from the DRR practice suggested that the new wheat variety, which they had the opportunity to test, should be available for all the farmers of the region, as it has a higher yielding potential.
  • They also recommend that a campaign about the benefit of introducing new varieties should be launched.

7. Validation of the practice

  • The practice was validated and implemented in the Ghotki district in Pakistan, during the dry season in 2018.
  • In particular, farmers started growing wheat with FYM and compost application.
  • This practice was introduced by FAO.
  • The Ghotki district is highly vulnerable to disasters especially recurrent floods.
    • It was consecutively hit by heavy floods in 2010, 2011 and 2012.
    • The gradual changes in river course have also put many communities at risk of being flooded, resulting in shifting or migration.
    • This shift in river course will also significantly impact agriculture based activities as this already poorly drained agricultural land will be flooded, rendering it unfit for agricultural activities.
  • This practice was validated and introduced by the Building Disaster Resilience in Pakistan (BDRP) project of FAO in Pakistan.
  • The farmers said they would continue to implement the DRR practice since this practice enhanced soil fertility and water saving by increasing water holding capacity of soil.
  • FYM and compost are prepared locally, using locally available resources which have reduced the use of chemical fertilizers and ultimately contributed to decreased production costs of wheat crop.
  • The performance of the DRR practice was monitored over a six months period during the Rabi season 2018 (January to April).
  • As nutrients were managed through integrated manners and use of FYM and compost decreased the use of chemical fertilizer, air quality was improved and the emission of greenhouse gas production was reduced.
  • By composting, farmers can decrease their dependence on chemical fertilizers and that impact the ecosystems.

8. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

8.1 Necessary basic conditions and general recommendations for a successful implementation

  • Farmer’s education and sensitization about climate change adaptation is necessary before implementing this practice.
  • The Farmer Field School (FFS) approach remains very effective in educating farmers through learning by doing.

8.2 Constrains (limiting factors or major barriers) for the implementation of the technology

  • No negative impact resulting from the implementation of the DRR practice was recorded.
  • Composting makes nutrients more available to plants and transforms raw organic matter into stable humus, which could be critical for long-term soil fertility.
  • Finished compost does not contain all the nutrients that went into the pile as raw materials.
    • If not managed well, compost can be smelly depending on the materials used.
  • Constrains for the implementation of the practice could be a lack of knowledge about the preparation and the use of compost for crops, as well as the concept of reducing the use of fertilizers by applying FYM and compost, and the poor sensitization about climate change.

9. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

10. Related/associated technologies

  • Farm yard manure and water hyacinth compost applications to enhance organic matter: ID 6836.
  • Green manure/cover crops and crop rotation in conservation agriculture on small farms: ID 7250
  • Green manuring in sugarcane production for soil improvement and water efficiency: ID 8768

11. Objectives fulfilled by the project

11.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology uses compost application to improve physical and chemical properties of the soils. Using compost and FYM not only allows to decrease the use of chemical fertilizer but also improves soil texture for successive crops.

11.2 Pro-poor technology 

The application of FYM in combination with the use of compost for the production of wheat reduce existing disaster risk and contribute to improving famers' income.

  • FAO. 2015. Farmer’s compost handbook, experiences in Latin America (Pilar R., Martinez M.M. & Pantoja A.).
  • FAO. 2004. Fertilizer use by crop in Pakistan. (Dr Nisar Ahmad).

entries.title: Cotton cultivation with laser levelling, ridge sowing, integrated pest management and compost application in dry spell conditions
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary: This technology describes the introduction of laser levelling, ridge sowing, Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and compost application in cotton cultivation in the Ghotki district in Pakistan. Pakistan experiences several floods and droughts, worsened by climate change which is characterised by changes in the monsoon patterns and extreme temperatures. However, the main hazards affecting the agricultural livelihoods and the cotton cultivation in the Ghotki district, are dry spells and related water scarcity. Growing cotton on ridges along with the use of IPM techniques is a practice that farmers can use to reduce their irrigation water consumption in cotton fields without decreasing its yield. This practice also allows to decrease the use of chemical pesticides used to control the harmful pests. Land was levelled using a laser land leveller to ensure equal distribution of the water in the field. Compost was applied during land preparation, which helped to increase the water holding capacity of the soil. The use of IPM techniques also had positive effect on the environment through reduced use of chemical pesticides. The practices described here are called Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) practices. These are aimed at preventing new and reducing existing disaster risks and managing residual risks, all of which contribute to strengthening resilience and achieving sustainable development. The implementation of these DRR practices enables farmers to obtain higher yields, higher water management efficiency and to adopt sustainable agricultural practices.
entries.description:
Description

Laser levelling, ridge sowing, integrated pest management (IPM) and compost application practices have been introduced in cotton crops in the Ghotki district, in Pakistan. The farmers grow certified cotton seeds provided by FAO under the Building Disaster Resilience in Pakistan (BDRP) project.

1. Previously used practice      

  • Farmers have previously been using traditional practices for the cotton cultivation.
  • The cotton production with this method was challenged by dry spells and, in general, unpredictable rainfall patterns.

2. The Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) practices implemented

2.1 Laser levelling

  • Unevenness of the soil surface can have a significant impact on the germination, stand and yield of crops.
  • While irrigation is widespread in Pakistan, because of poor field design and surface unevenness, considerable agricultural water resources are lost due to water accumulation or dry pockets.
  • Laser levelling is an important water management technique in Pakistan to ensure homogenous water application and decrease water pounding in the field.
    • As a result, germination is often inconsistent, and crops grow unevenly.
  • A tractor mounted laser leveller can be used to level the field within a certain degree of desired slope.
    • It allows farmers to achieve uniformity during the field preparation and obtain uniform water and moisture distribution.
Figure 1. Levelling of field with a tractor mounted laser leveller

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

3. Ridge sowing 

  • The sowing of cotton on raised ridges ensures adequate plant population due to better seed germination and emergence of seedlings even during unusual rains.
  • The farmers used conventional ploughing and planking through tractor.
  • Ridges were made by using a tractor operated implement.
  • Compost and FYM were also applied during land preparation.
  • After the sowing, the crops were monitored closely by the host farmers and irrigated at regular interval as per requirement of the crop, through tube well operated through peter engine.
  • Over flooding of ridges was avoided.

4. Integrated Pest Management (IPM)

  • Insect pest was managed through integrated methods.
  • An alternative way, rather than using only chemical pesticides to deal with pest problem, that reduces pesticides inputs is known as IPM.
    • It is an effective and environmentally sensitive approach to pest management that relies on comprehensive information on the life cycle, habits, needs and dislikes of pests and their interaction with the environment, in order to eliminate or drastically reduce the use of pesticides and to minimize the toxicity of and exposure to any products which are used.
  • Starting with biological control of pest, Trichogramma and Crysoperlla cards (containing eggs of beneficial insects) were installed.
    • Yellow sticky cards along with light traps were also installed which helped to control the pest physically and biologically.
    • Pheromone traps for catching the male adults of different pests (Armyworm, pink worm) were also installed and monitored regularly.
  • Adults were also caught through insect catching net which would lay eggs on the crop.
Figure 2. Light trap for major Lepidoptera insect pest including Helithis, Spotted Bollworm and Armyworm, installed in cotton field

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

Figure 3. Yellow sticky trap against whitefly, Jassid and Aphid installed in cotton field

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

Figure 4. Use of pheromone trap against Pink bollworm and Armyworm in cotton field

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

5. Compost application    

  • Composting refers to the biological decomposition of organic materials, such as residues, animal waste, food garbage, by microorganisms, under controlled aerobic conditions, into a relatively stable humus-like material, known as compost.
  • Farmers learnt how to prepare compost locally by being active members of farmer field schools.
  • This compost was then applied on the field during the land preparation.
  • Compost and organic material application to soil enhance the nutrient supply and increase the availability of essential micro and macro nutrients for the crop.

6. Socio-economic benefits of the practice

  • The implementation of the new practice package hence a higher profit while being environment friendly.
  • Farmers get a higher yield with significant water saving.
    • They decreased their cost linked to the manual sowing, compared to the cost of the manual sowing performed with the previous traditional practice, and decreased their costs linked to pesticides and chemical fertilizers.
  • Decreased use of pesticides and fertilizer also decreased dependency towards products.
  • Farmers also made profit thanks to the replacement of hoeing by weeding practice in the inter-culture and by reducing the cost of manual labour. 
  • More specifically, the laser land levelling increased the water use efficiency at field level and increased the seed germination percentage.
  • With the adoption of IPM practices, the use of pesticides has decreased and is used only when required and in a more efficient way than before.
    • Such a diminished use is likely to have a positive impact in decreasing the pressure on agricultural fields and in the resulting accumulation in soils and surface water bodies.
  • The IPM technique is cheap and doesn't require any expensive technology or machine to implement.
  • The implementation of ridge sowing decreases the irrigation erosion and improves soil moisture content through the use of effective irrigation techniques utilizing irrigation furrows.
  • It also increases crop yield, reduces demand for irrigation water, reduces expenses on agricultural inputs, simplifies farm operations, improves soil cover and reduces soil salinity.
  • The introduction of ridge sowing came along with a major cost linked to the purchase of the ridge seeder.
    • The establishment costs of ridge sowing are similar to the ones for conventional sowing methods using corn planters, but in the long term the maintenance costs will be far lower with the new good practice.
  • Compost application significantly improves the nutrient availability, increasing yields.
    • By increasing organic matter content and microbial activities, compost application improves and protects soil characteristics (structure, bio-chemical) and leads to a better soil capacity to sequester carbon and reduces methane emissions.
  • Through the introduction of this practice package, the farmers gained knowledge about the different practices, especially the IPM techniques.
    • They all expressed their interest to implement again those practices in the future.

7. Cost of the practice

  • The benefits and costs of laser levelling, ridge sowing, IPM and compost application for cotton production was assessed at farm-level. 
  • The net benefits obtained from introducing this good practice was calculated through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA). 
    • The CBA calculates the net present value (NPV) of cumulative benefits obtained from using laser levelling, ridge sowing, IPM and compost application to improve cotton production over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms).
    • It also calculates the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
    • The CBA was conducted based on quantitative data collected on three farms located in the Ghotki district affected by dry spell, in the villages Rahmat Khan Gabol Sanwal, Khan Pathan/Ding Chachar and Nadir Shah/Peer Goth during the Kharif season 2017 (from June to November).
    • During the monitoring period all four villages were facing drought episodes, salinity problems and heat waves.
    • Figure 5 provides an overview of the outcome of the CBA.
      • In particular, it shows that, under drought conditions, the net benefit of applying the good practice for cotton production over 11 years is over thirty percent higher than without applying the good practice.
      • The BCR with the DRR good practice is 3.89, which is higher than the BCR of the previously applied practice (2.68).
    • These results show that the good practice brings greater benefits relative to costs, as compared to the usual practice.
Figure 5. Cumulative Net Present Value per acre over 11 years

©FAO/TECA

  • Figure 6 shows the average costs and benefits of the different inputs and outputs in drought conditions for the previously used practice and for the DRR good practice introduced (USD per ha per season). 
    • The labour and pesticide costs are higher for the previous practice, while the compost/manure and fertilizer costs are higher for the DRR good practice.
    • In the end, the benefit is higher with the DRR good practice.  
Figure 6. Average costs and benefits (USD per ha per season)

©FAO/TECA

8. Validation of the practice

  • The practice was validated and implemented in the Ghotki district in Pakistan, during the dry season in 2017.
  • In particular, farmers started growing cotton with laser levelling methods, ridge sowing, IPM and compost application.
  • The performance of the good practice was monitored over a six months period during the Kharif season 2017 (June to November).
  • This practice was introduced by FAO.
  • The Ghotki district is highly vulnerable to disasters especially recurrent floods.
    • It has been consecutively hit by heavy floods in 2010, 2011 and 2012.
  • Gradual changes in river course have also put many communities at risk of being flooded, resulting in shifting or migration.
    • This shift in river course will significantly impact agriculture based activities as this already poorly drained agricultural land will be flooded, rendering it unfit for agricultural activities.

9. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • No negative impact resulting from the implementation of the good practice was recorded.
  • A first constraint for the implementation of this good practice package could be a lack of knowledge about growing cotton crop on ridges and controlling pests through integrated manner rather than only relying on chemical pesticides.
  • Poor sensitization about climate change is also among the limitations to adopt integrated approach.
  • The use of this practice is more suitable in occasional water scarce situations.
  • The original cost for machinery required for some practices such as land levelling, may be high and not affordable for some families.
  • Some weaknesses of ridge sowing to overcome are the comparatively high cost of the ridge seeders for farmers, the risk of irrigation erosion along the furrows and the requirement of high capacity tractors.
    • An optimal furrow length has to be selected according to the slope and filtering properties of the soil to avoid this.

10. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

11. Related/associated technologies

  • Farm yard manure and water hyacinth compost applications to enhance organic matter: ID 6836.
  • Green manure/cover crops and crop rotation in conservation agriculture on small farms: ID 7250.
  • Green manuring in sugarcane production for soil improvement and water efficiency: ID 8768.
  • Cotton culture: ID 6901.
  • Promoting drought and water logging tolerant cotton varieties: ID 7394.
  • Integrated pest management: ID 7298.

12. Objectives fulfilled by the project

12.1 Pro-poor technology 

The application of this technology enables farmers to obtain higher yields, higher water management efficiency and to adopt sustainable agricultural practices.

entries.title: Cost-benefit analysis of rain water harvesting systems: roof top rain water harvesting combined with gravity drip irrigation
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary: This practice briefly describes the introduction of rainwater harvesting and the use of gravity drip irrigation on small vegetable farms in Jamaica to address the water scarcity problem farmers are facing. The technology was validated in the parish of St. Elizabeth, which is the leading producer of cash vegetables in Jamaica. Traditionally, the crop production system in southern parts of the parish relies on bi-annual patterns of rainfall. Water is purchased by farmers from delivery trucks and manual hand watering of crops is practised. The area is prone to dry spells, prolonged drought, high temperatures during summer months (especially during June to September) and high winds. Due to an increase in temperatures, the area is also prone to frequent flair ups and outbreaks of the beet armyworm. Over the years, farmers have built resilience to drought by using soil mulch (Guinea grass) and labour-intensive hand watering. The majority of farmers purchase irrigation water, but its availability is scarce during droughts. This technology can be adopted by householders, farmers or can be scaled up and modified to suit the needs of larger industry players.
entries.description:
Description

A rainwater harvesting system was introduced in the parish of St. Elizabeth, it consists of three components.

  1. Harvesting rainwater and/or, in the absence of rainfall, providing storage capacity for purchased water.
  2. Increasing capacity for water storage by installing 1 000 gallons-plastic tanks (system can accommodate adding storage capacity) on an elevated base to provide gravity water flows for irrigation.
  3. Using water-efficient gravity drip irrigation system. This practice makes farmers more resilient to dry spells and droughts, as it allows them to produce crops during the dry season, even if no or little rainfall occurs thereby prolonging the crop harvesting cycle and providing additional income.

1. Previously used practice

  • Over the years, farmers built resilience to drought using soil mulch (Guinea grass) and labour-intensive hand watering.
  • The majority of farmers purchase irrigation water, which tends to be scarce during drought periods.

2. Application of the good practice

  • This technology describes the combination of two good practices to address the water scarcity of smallholder farmers and improve irrigation efficiency. 
  •  This technology was tested and validated in farms in Yardley Chase, located in South St. Elizabeth, Jamaica in the framework of the RAD/FAO Technical Cooperation Project (RADA/FAO TCP).  
  • The combination of good practices includes:
    1. the construction of a water harvesting system and water storage tanks; and 
    2. the installation of a gravity drip irrigation system.
  • The construction of the water harvesting system includes specific steps.
    • Shed construction
    • Tank base construction
    • Gutter construction
  • Once the water harvesting system is in place, it can be connected to the drip irrigation system.  

3. Construction of the rainwater harvesting system  (shed, tank and gutter) 

3.1 Shed construction

3.1.1 Materials needed

Materials needed are:

  • four lumber posts of 4 inches x 4 inches x 14 ft,
  • a wood board (dimensions + characteristics),
  • a spade,
  • a wood saw,
  • nails (zinc nails),
  • a zinc sheet (dimensions and characteristics), and
  • a gutter (dimensions and characteristics) and water pipes.

3.1.2 Procedure of construction

  1. Select an ideal location.
    • Whether the land is sloped or flat, the roof of the shed should finish with a slight tilt to allow for runoff of the water into the gutter.
  2. Line-out shed according to the prescribed measurements.
  3. Dig four post holes approximately 2 feet in depth and 8 inches in diameter.
    • One hole at each corner.
  4. Erect the four lumber posts in the four post holes. 
    • Each lumber pole has following dimensions: 4 inches x 4 inches x 14 ft. 
  5. Cut out on the outer side of the posts on the long sides, 2 inches in and 4 inches down from top of post, to accommodate the 2 inch x 4 inch board. 
  6. Place and secure (with nails) 2 inches x 4 inches on the short sides and flush with 2 inches x 4 inches on the long sides.
  7. Cut two lengths of 2 inches x 4 inches of the board to create three equal sections on the short side to accommodate the zinc sheet.
  8. Ensure that the zinc sheet is laid flat on top of the lumber with a single groove overlap between sheets.
    • Secure the zinc to the lumber using zinc nails. 
  9. The tail end of the zinc should extend approximately 1.5 inches towards the gutter. 

3.2 Tank base construction

3.2.1 Materials needed

Materials needed are:

  • cement,
  • blocks,
  • marl,
  • rebar ½’’ steel,
  • a spade, and
  • wood.

3.2.2 Procedure of construction

  • The reinforced tank bases should be finished at least 9 feet below the level of the gutter as the tank is 100 inches in height.
  • The stand should be at least 12 to 16 inches above ground level on sloped plots but can be erected at 1.5 meters on flat farm plots.
  • The stand should be 6 feet x 6 feet in dimension and erected by blocks, marl, cement and reinforced with ½’’ steel.
  • One prescribed length of ½ inch steel should be erected at each corner of the stand.
    • This is to accommodate the anchoring of the plastic tank to prevent toppling.
  • The tank base is to be completed with a smooth surface, as any protruding object or unevenness could puncture the tank. 

3.3 Gutter construction

3.3.1 Materials needed

Materials needed are:

  • 10 '' PVC water pipe,
  • 4’’ pipe,
  • 2” PVC pipe,
  • 4“ PVC cap,
  • 4” PVC elbow,
  • 2” PVC elbow,
  • a reducer,
  • gutter brackets,
  • a 1000 gallon plastic water tank, and
  • scissors (to cut a 2 ½ “ hole in the tank).

3.3.2 Procedure of construction

  1. Use one length (10 “) of waste water PVC pipe. 
  2. Remove flair end from 4 inch-pipe.
    • Measure 1.5 inches from both ends and cut 3 inches deep into circumference at both ends.
  3. Cut out 3 inch-circumference section parallel to the pipe. 
  4. Connect the 4 inches-PVC Cap to one end of the gutter and the 4 inches-elbow to the other end. 
  5. Attach a 4 inches to 2 inches reducer to elbow. 
  6. Use gutter brackets to support the now gutter to the slanted side of the catchment area (shed).
  7. Insert 2 inches-PVC pipe into the 2 inches-portion of the reducer.
    • Then connect the 2 inches- elbow followed by the 2 inches-pipe leading to the 1 000 gallon-plastic tank.
  8. Cut a 2.5 inches-hole in the prescribed area on top of the plastic tank.
    • Then connect down spout through hole to approximately 6 inches.  

4. Installation of the drip irrigation system 

4.1 Materials needed

  • A drip irrigation system is composed of the following components: 
    • a reducer (specify characteristics),
    • a ¾’’-brass ball valve, and
    • teflon tape. 

4.2 Procedure for installation of a drip irrigation system

  1. Insert the reducer bushing into the bulkhead of the 1000 gallon-plastic tank.
  2. Wrap the ¾’’-brass ball valve with Teflon tape and insert the same into the opening of the reducer bushing.
  3. Connect the ¾’’-screen filter and associated fittings.
  4. Layout Polyethylene 32 mm-mainline.
  5. Connect the same to the above filtration apparatus and close the available end with 32 mm-end plugs.
  6. Bore holes at the prescribed row spacing with the head connector punch.
  7. Insert 12 mm-head connector into the 32 mm-mainline.
  8. Connect to 12 mm-hydrogol dripline cut to row length.
  9. ​Close dripline end with the 12 mm-end line clamp.

5. Socio-economic benefits of the practice  

  • All farmers interviewed said that they would be willing to replicate this DRR good practice over the next seasons as it contributed to increased yields and it reduced labor efforts for manual watering.
  • Farmers assigned a score of 4.9 out of 5 to the performance of the good practice in the face of extreme events.
  • Ninety-three percent of farmers said that they have acquired new knowledge, especially on how to construct water harvesting sheds, how to use drip irrigation systems and how to apply fertilizers.
  • In addition, good practice is better for the environment, as it allows for more efficient use of water.

6. Cost of the practice 

  • Based on the data collected in Yardley Chase during the 2018 wet season (June-November), cost-benefit analyses were conducted for the introduction of the rainwater harvesting system for tomato production and for sweet pepper production.
  • The analysis projects the cumulative net present value of benefits obtained from 1 hectare of tomatoes and sweer peppers over a period of eleven years (10 percent discount rate). 
  • As Figures 1 and 2 show, both tomato production and sweet pepper production highly benefit from the introduction of good practice.
    • This was with a net present value increase of 131 percent in tomato production and a 29 percent-increase in sweet pepper production compared to the previously applied practice.  
Figure 1. Cumulative net present value per ha over 11 years- sweet pepper production

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Cumulative net present value per ha over 11 years- tomato production

©FAO/TECA

  • As can be seen from Figures 3 and 4, the upfront capital costs of purchasing and installing rainwater harvesting and drip irrigation system are high, but they have been more than compensated by the value of production.
  • A key driver of higher yields was the number of plants, as farmers were able to plant more seedlings into the irrigated good practice plot than into the control plot.
Figure 3. Average costs and benefits (USD per season per hectare)-dry season- tomato

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Average costs and benefits (USD per season per hectare)-dry season- sweet pepper

©FAO/TECA

  • The cost of water was higher under good practice than the previous practice.
  • This is due to the fact that the good practice testing started during a dry spell, therefore farmers were not able to collect rainwater.
  • Instead, farmers purchased more trucked water in order to use the drip irrigation system.
  • The good practice is likely to generate higher benefits over the next seasons, as farmers will be able to harvest rainwater during the rainy season (October-November).
  • The upfront capital costs of the rainwater harvesting and drip irrigation system may represent an initial barrier to uptake.
  • Support should, therefore, be provided to farmers in this regard (e.g. improved access to credit, subsidies). 

7. Validation of the practice

7.1 The geographical area of practice validation

  • The good practice was introduced on 35 farm fields with a total of 0.4 hectares each in size, located in Yardley Chase, District, Southfield, South St. Elizabeth, Jamaica. 
  • Twenty farmers’ farm plots were selected for data collection including 17 tomato plots and 18 sweet pepper plots producing under drip irrigation.
  • The results were compared against the yield obtained from ten control plots of each crop where farmers purchased the water and watered the plots manually. 

7.2 Context of implementation

7.2.1 Environmental and climatic context

  • Southern St. Elizabeth is the leading agricultural production parish in Jamaica. 
  • The area is prone to dry spells, prolonged drought, high temperatures during summer months (especially during June to September) and high winds.
  • The thirty year-mean for rainfall is 1399 mm per year and the mean maximum temperatures are of 32°C (Potsdam Station).
  • Conditions favor high evaporation and the reduction of water availability.
  • Due to the increase in temperatures, the area is also prone to the frequent flair ups and outbreaks of the beet armyworm.
  • Since 2014, the production area has been impacted by the following weather related events:
    • 2014-2015: most severe record drought.
    • 2017: beet armyworm outbreak due to higher than normal temperatures during winter months.
      • The year also recorded the highest temperatures. 
    • 2018: Higher than normal rainfall followed by prolonged dry spell during summer months.
  • Over the years, farmers have built resilience to drought using soil mulch (Guinea grass) and labour-intensive hand watering. 
  • The majority of farmers purchase irrigation water, but its availability is scarce during drought.
  • Very few farmers practice rainwater harvesting for crop production.

7.2.2 Economic (livelihood strategy) and  social (target group) context 

  • Major crops produced in Yardley Chase, South St. Elizabeth are cash vegetables:
    • tomato,
    • sweet pepper,
    • cucurbits (cantaloupe, watermelon and cucumber), and
    • scallion (green onion).
  • The majority of farmers sell their produce at the farm gate to the middle man. 
  • The Yardley Chase farmer group was selected for participation in the project based on good group dynamics, cohesiveness and the level of cooperation.
  • Members of the group have successfully graduated from farm water management Farmer Field School in 2017, where rainwater harvesting was demonstrated for the first time.
  • The FAO project provided an opportunity for continued interventions and scaling up for use of climate-smart practices. 

8. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice 

8.1 General recommendations for a successful implementation 

  • Adequate or favorable rainfall to support water harvesting and crop production through drip irrigation, during the drought spell.
  • Also, the expansion of the catchment area and storage facilities would add value to the production capacity of farmers. 

8.2 Constraints (limiting factors or major barriers) for the implementation of the technology 

  • High cost associated with drip irrigation systems and material costs.
  • External financing or access to credit needed.
  • The availability of skills to construct shed for rainwater harvesting.  

9. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

10. Related/associated technologies 

  • How to make good, hot compost: ID 8234.
  • Raising chicken without grain: the integrated compost and poultry system: ID 8863.

11. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

11.1 Labour-saving technology (LST) 

The cost of manual irrigation was both time consuming and less effective than irrigating by drip. Not only is the time it now takes to irrigate less but it requires fewer persons to irrigate. The money saved on this activity can be invested in other areas of their operation. 

11.2 Women-friendly

​Both women and men were integral in ensuring that the water purchased and trucked to their farms were manually applied to the crop. This labour intensive exercise proved extremely challenging for women.​ 

11.3 Resource use efficiency

The natural harvesting of rainwater coupled with its efficient use by way of the gravity drip irrigation system has improved and enhanced the farming culture whilst building their resilience to climate change. This practice has complemented well its dry farming techniques.  Note also that their operational cost is significantly reduced as no pump is required to operate the system. 

11.4 Pro-poor technology 

There were higher production volumes thanks to this technology. Better quality of produce and ability to produce throughout the year contributes to additional income for better livelihood. Ownership of the water harvesting system opens the opportunity to expand by adding additional water storage capacity and /or irrigation over time. Access to irrigation facilitate more efficient use of land (higher yields from the same field size) and cultivation of other crops. Farmers are able to build their capacity through accessing free of cost training from the extension services provided by the Rural Agricultural Development Authority (RADA): www.rada.gov.jm in water management, irrigation, plant nutrition, pest and pesticide management etc. Market linkages are also provided through extension support. Farmers are encouraged to be active members of farmer group and benefit for the following opportunities: purchasing farm inputs in bulk to reduce costs; and preparing project proposals for accessing grant funding for climate-smart agriculture. RADA provided support with proposal preparations.

entries.title: Vegetable cultivation with ridge sowing, farm yard manure, multi-cropping and Integrated Pest Management (IPM)
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary:
This technology describes the introduction of ridge sowing, Farm Yard Manure (FYM), and multi-cropping and Integrated Pest Management (IPM) practices for okra, sunflower, and sugarcane production in the Ghotki district in Pakistan. It provides also a cost-benefit analysis of this improved farming practice compared to the traditional practice.  

The main hazards affecting agricultural livelihoods and vegetable cultivation in the district are dry spells and related water scarcity. The use of ridges or the construction of raised beds of varying widths, reduces the total area to which surface irrigation is applied, as only the areas between ridges or the raised beds are flooded. This reduces water consumption by 20 to 30 percent. This can also achieve a reduction in the associated water use fees or pumping costs by up to 40 percent in areas where groundwater is used. 

Multiple cropping is a management practice involving growing two or more crops at the same time in the same place. The most common goal of multiple cropping is to promote intensification and diversification for a greater yield on a given piece of land by making use of resources or ecological processes that would otherwise not be utilized by a single crop. The selection of crops is based on crops’ compatibility, mutualism, pest management, soil health and profitability.

The integrated use of chemical and organic fertilizers is found to be more beneficial for sustainable sugarcane production. The combined use of organic and inorganic fertilizer gave significantly higher yields and economic benefits. FYM is one such source of organic matter produced as livestock waste that can be profitably utilized for crop production.
entries.description:
Description

1. Commonly used practice

  • Previously, farmers had been using traditional vegetable cultivation methods with multi-cropping.
  • The vegetable production with this method was challenged by dry spells and, in general, unpredictable rainfall patterns.

2. Application of the good practice

2.1 Multi-cropping

  • Multi-cropping is a system where two or more crops are grown at the same time on the same piece of land or in a sequence.
  • The selection of crops is based on crop competition, compatibility, mutualism (both plants benefitting from each other), commensalism (one plant gaining benefits from the other), pest management, soil health, and profitability.
  • This method allows farmers to reduce the risk of income loss.
  • In case one crop fails, farmers can rely on the other crop which presents different characteristics and can resist to different treats.
    • In this practice, okra, sunflower and sugarcane crops were combined.
    • Certified seeds of okra and sunflower were provided by FAO through the Building Disaster Resilience Project (BDRP) while the sugarcane seeds were arranged by the farmers, locally.  
  • Sugarcane is a long duration crop.
    • Farmers have to wait 10 to 14 months to get the return of their investment from their fields.
    • It is planted by keeping adequate space in between the two rows.
    • This space remains unused until full plant development and short duration crops can be grown in the vacant space without affecting cane yield.
    • In the early stage it grows slowly and can accommodate a number of short duration crops.
    • In this example,  okra and sunflower crops were intercropped with sugarcane.
    • Okra and sunflower were planted simultaneoulsy on ridges while sugarcane was planted between the ridges.
    • Wider row planting method was chosen to reduce the chance of inter-crop competition with least effect on cane growth and tillering.
    • A sequence of crops was made keeping in view the water requirement and maturation period of the crops.
    • Lemon was also planted along the boundary of the crops.
  • The crops were monitored closely by the host farmers and irrigation was made at regular intervals as per requirement of the crop, through a tube well operated through a diesel engine.
    • An over flooding of ridges was avoided.
Figure 1. Intercropping of okra, sunflower and sugarcane. Okra and sunflower are planted on the ridges, sugarcane in between the ridges



©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

3. Ridge sowing

  • In this case, farmers levelled their land through a laser leveler and used a conventional ploughing and planking through tractor.
  • Ridges were then made by using tractor operated implements.
  • After planning the sugarcane in the furrows, seeds of okra and sunflower were planted along the sides of the ridges.
  • A sequence of crops was made, keeping in mind the water requirements and maturation period of the crops.
  • Lemon was planted along the boundary of the crops.

4. Farm Yard Manure (FYM)

  • Farm Yard Manure (FYM) is a fertilizer made up of farm waste products such as dung, straw or urine produced by farm animals, most commonly cows.
    • It provides nutrients and organic matter to the soil, particularly nitrogen which is vital for the plants’ growth.
    • FYM serves as balanced nutritional manure for plants, improves soil biodiversity, and represents a cost-effective fertilisation strategy.
  • The farmers of this region generally own one or two cows, several goats, sometimes a hen or a buffalo.
  • To make FYM, animal dung and urine have to be collected into a layer of even thickness under a simple roof to keep it from getting excessively wet and exposed to direct sunlight.
  • More dung and urine are added along with some water, if it gets too dry.
  • The FYM can be used on fields as fertilizer after an average of six months.
  • It is usually spread on a field three or four weeks before sowing.
  • The manure exposed to the elements will decompose and provide nutrients to the soil.
  • Compost was also applied during the land preparation stage, prior to the planting of crop.

4. Integrated Pest Management (IPM)

  • IPM aims to reduce the environmental and human impacts of pesticides and promote natural pest and disease control methods of crops.
    • It is an ecological alternative for chemical pest control.
    • It is an effective and environmentally sensitive approach to pest management that relies on comprehensive information on the life cycle, habits, needs and dislikes of pests and their interaction with the environment.
    • It relies on all of this information in order to eliminate or drastically reduce the use of pesticides and to minimize the toxicity of and exposure to any products which are used.
  • Multi-cropping practices play a role in IPM.
    • It was observed that there were less pest attacks in the demo sites as compared to the control plots with one single crop due to crop diversity.
    • Pests were also managed through integrated manners.
    • Trichogramma and cryperlla cards, containing the eggs of the predator insects, were used for controlling harmful insects, while manual hoeing was made to control weeds in the target crop.
Figure 2. Use of Trichogramma cards

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

5. Socio-economic benefits of the practice

  • As a result of the implementation of this DRR practice, farmers increased their vegetable production and had higher income.
  • They could reduce their input costs (mainly for fertilizers and pesticides) by using safer livelihood practices and obtained better and more diverse food.
  • They reduced the demand for irrigation water, improved soil cover and reduced soil salinity.
  • The introduction of multi-cropping allowed to save both water and fertilizer as four crops were grown on the same piece of land.
  • It reduced evaporation as more soil was covered,decreased the use of pesticides due to crop diversity, which gave the whole multi-cropping system a higher resistance to pest and disease.
  • It enhanced nutrient use-efficiency and potentially improved soil fertility.
  • Inter-cropping in sugarcane generally requires more labour, thereby creating productive employment opportunities.
  • Many studies indicated that inter-cropping increase the grower’s net income, creates employment opportunities for landless and owner household families.
  • Multi-cropping systems are also less vulnerable to market price fluctuations and produce local and more diverse food, allowing a more varied diet.
  • The introduction of sowing on raised ridges ensures adequate plant population due to better seed germination and the emergence of seedlings even during unusual rains.
  • The implementation of this technology decreased irrigation erosion and improved soil moisture content through the use of effective irrigation techniques, utilizing irrigation furrows.
  • IPM strategies and the use of bio-fertilizers (FYM), bio-pesticides, and weed control practices reduced agricultural GHG emissions.
    • By reducing the use of synthetic pesticides, these strategies ensured quality crop production and reduced crop losses even during moisture stress (drought) conditions.
  • Overall, the farmers expressed their interest in replicating the good practice package in the future since it increased their resilience and provided more income to the family.
  • Other reasons were: ”to get some fresh food for the kitchen and variety of vegetables, to have a complete diet for the household members”.
    • The farmers said that there is a demand for this new method in the area because it is more profitable. 

6. Cost of the practice           

  • The benefits and costs of ridge sowing, FYM, multi-cropping and IPM for vegetable production were assessed at farm-level. 
  • The net benefits obtained from introducing this DDR practice were calculated through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA). 
    • The CBA calculates the net present value (NPV) of cumulative benefits obtained from using ridge sowing, FYM, multi-cropping and IPM to improve vegetable production over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms).
    • It also calculates the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
    • The CBA was conducted based on quantitative data collected on four farms located in the Ghotki district affected by dry spell, in the villages Allah Ubhayo Mirani, Baloo Khan Damra, M. Yousuf Solangi and Kamil Bhishti during the Zaid Rabi season (spring) in 2018 (February to June).
    • During the monitoring period, all four villages were facing drought episodes, salinity problems and heat waves.
    • The season average (February to June) percentage difference of rainfall per season as compared to a 20 years average was -14 percent.
    • Figure 3 provides an overview of the outcome of the CBA.
      • In particular, it shows that, under drought conditions, the net benefit of applying the good practice for vegetable production over 11 years is over thirty percent higher than without applying the good practice.
      • The BCR with the described DRR practice is 6.78, which is higher than the BCR of the previously applied practice (4.28).
Figure 3. Cumulative Net Present Value per acre over 11 years

©FAO/TECA

  • Figure 4 shows that the compost/manure cost is higher for the described practice, compared to the previously used practice, while the pesticide and fertilizer costs are higher for the previous practice.
  • There is a higher benefit obtained from the implementation of the DRR practice, with a higher gross value of production.
  • These results show that vegetable production with ridge sowing, FYM, multi-cropping and IPM, is an effective DRR practice package that can reduce the risks from disasters and increase farmer’s resilience to threats. 
Figure 4. Average costs and benefits (USD per ha per season)

©FAO/TECA

7. General recommendations

  • Before implementing this practice, Farmer Field Schools (FFS) should educate farmers about climate change adaptation, in particular the implementation of the DRR practice described here.

8. Validation of the practice

  • This technology was introduced by the Building Disaster Resilience in Pakistan (BDRP) project of FAO in Pakistan.
  • More specifically, the practice was validated and implemented in the Ghotki District in Pakistan, during the dry season in 2018 (Zaid Rabi season).
    • Farmers started growing multiple crops by ridge sowing and intercropping with okra, sunflower and sugarcane and applying FYM and IPM practices.
  • The Ghotki district is highly vulnerable to disasters especially recurrent floods.
    • It was consecutively hit by heavy floods in 2010, 2011 and 2012.
    • The gradual changes in river course have also put many communities at risk of being flooded, resulting in shifting or migration.
    • This shift in river course will also significantly impact agriculture based activities as this already poorly drained agricultural land will be flooded, rendering it unfit for agricultural activities.

9. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

9.1 Necessary basic conditions and general recommendations for a successful implementation

  • Farmers’ education and sensitization about climate change adaptation is necessary before implementing this practice.
  • The Farmer Field School (FFS) approach remains very effective in educating farmers through learning by doing.

9.2 Constrains (limiting factors or major barriers) for the implementation of the technology

  • No negative impact resulting from the implementation of the good practice was recorded.
  • The farmers had to hire machinery such as a leveller, cultivator, rotavator and ridger to perform the DRR practice.
  • The weaknesses of this practice are the risk of irrigation erosion along the furrows and the requirement of high capacity tractors.
    • An optimal furrow length has to be selected according to the slope and filtering properties of the soil to avoid this.
  • The lack of knowledge about crop combination for growing different crops in the same season and on the same piece of land is often a constraint to the implementation of the DRR practice.
  • The poor sensitization about climate change could also be a limiting factor for the update of this practice, as farmers do not understand how improved farming practices can reduce their vulnerability to the effects of climate change.

10. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

11. Related/associated technologies

  • Farm yard manure and water hyacinth compost applications to enhance organic matter: ID 6836.
  • Green manure/cover crops and crop rotation in conservation agriculture on small farms: ID 7250.
  • Green manuring in sugarcane production for soil improvement and water efficiency: ID 8768.
  • Wheat cultivation with farm yard manure and compost application in Pakistan in dry spell conditions, a cost-benefit analysis: ID 10017.

12. Objectives fulfilled by the project

12.1 Resource use efficiency

This practice allows to decrease the use of chemical inputs while strengthening the resilience of the soil. Also, it is shown how climate change adaptation can result in higher incomes for the farmers.

entries.title: Wheat cultivation with levelling and Integrated Pest Management (IPM)
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary: This practice briefly describes the introduction of levelling and Integrated Pest Management (IPM) practices for wheat production in the Kashmore district of Sindh Province in Pakistan. It provides a cost-benefit analysis of this improved practice compared to the traditional way of producing wheat in the district. The main hazards affecting wheat cultivation in the Kashmore district are dry spells and related water scarcity. Decisions about the use of inputs, such as fertilizers and agrochemicals, were taken following participatory decision-making techniques and by adopting Agro-Ecosystem Analysis based IPM. This allowed farmers to make a judicial use of inputs and promote uniform crop plant growth without compromising yield. The improved practice was demonstrated in a Farmer Field School (FFS). The monitored period was during the Rabi season 2017-2018 (from November 2017 to April 2018).
entries.description:
Description

Growing wheat on levelled land and using participatory decision-making techniques by adopting Agro-ecosystem Analysis based IPM is a practice that farmers can use to improve judicial use of inputs and promote uniform crop plant growth without compromising yield. The practice was demonstrated in Farmer Field School learnings, promoting judicial use of inputs at different locations in the Kashmore district of the Sindh province of Pakistan. 

Figure 1. Wheat growing

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

1. Previously used practice

  • Farmers have previously been using traditional wheat cultivation practices.
  • For their land preparation, farmers used to practice ploughing.
  • The wheat production with this method, was challenged by dry spell and, in general, unpredictable rainfall patterns.

2. Application of the good practice

2.1 Step one: seed selection

  • FAO provided certified wheat seeds of the variety Zincol under the BDRP project.

2.2 Step two: land preparation and sowing

  • Land levelling is a practice for surface irrigation use, to prepare the irrigation plot by eliminating the high and/or low spots.
  • The slope imbalance could disturb the uniform distribution of irrigation water on the field, and levelling ensures an optimal slope for water movement across the field when using irrigation.
  • The outcome is a more efficient irrigation of the crop and a more efficient use of fertilizers that are uniformly dissolved through the field.
  • In Kashmore, farmers levelled their lands through tractor mounted blade levellers.
    • They used conventional ploughing and planking using the tractor, while the sowing of seeds was made using a seed drill. 
Figure 2. Field

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

2.3 Step three: crop monitoring and use of inputs 

  • The wheat crops were monitored regularly by the FFS group and the host farmers.
  • The use of inputs, including irrigation, fertilizers and chemical pesticides/weedicides was made after conducting a participatory decision-making approach through the Agro-ecosystem Analysis (AESA).
    • Agro-ecosystem Analysis is the basic learning tool in the FFS approach, which allows members to monitor crops and their ecosystem also including growth, soil moisture, insect and rodent pests, predators, diseases.
  • Irrigation was made through tube well.
  • Over flooding of ridges was avoided.
Figure 3. Crop field

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

3. Benefits 

  • The participatory decision process using the AESA allows for a more rational  use of inputs by FFS farmers.
  • The process resulted in good yields.
  • Farmers were educated on ecosystem literacy.

3.1 Socio-economic and ecological benefits

  • The selection of a good seed variety remains the major impact factor with good knowledge of its nutritional value as well as production technology.
  • Farmers get a higher yield with less use of urea fertilizer application.
  • A balanced use of chemical fertilizer is encouraged, with different major and minor nutrients like sulphat of potash and zinc, which are normally not used for wheat production being added.
  • Farmers use manure as well to add nutrient value in the wheat production.
  • Use of  herbicide was decided by the FFS farmers while they promoted natural ecosystem for managing insect pests.
  • Rodents were controlled by manual rodent traps, which avoided the use of pesticides.
  • The implementation of this Disaster Risk Reduction good practice allowed for collaboration between farmers and the formation of farmer study groups.
    • Farmers had the opportunity to participate in a Global Farmer Field School (FFS) platform, created by FAO, to learn how to shift towards more sustainable production practices.
    • According to farmers, this process was a good learning base, allowed for experimentation of skills, improved crop management and hence a more sustainable production. 
  • As a result of the implementation of the practice, farmers increased their wheat production and their income.
  • Overall, the farmers expressed their interest in replicating the good practice in the future. 

3.2 Cost-benefit analysis of the practice

  • The benefits and costs of land levelling and IPM for wheat production was assessed at farm-level. 
  • The net benefits obtained from introducing this good practice was calculated through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA). 
    • The CBA calculates the net present value (NPV) of cumulative benefits obtained from using levelling and IPM to improve wheat production over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms).
    • It also calculates the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
    • The CBA was conducted based on quantitative data collected on four farms located in the Kashmore district, in the villages Mujahid Abdul Ghafoor, Wahid Bux Bijarani, Muhammad Nawaz Badani and Pir Bux Bahalkani during the the Rabi season 2017-2018 (from November 2017 to April 2018).
    • During the monitoring period, all the four villages were facing drought episodes.
    • This was with a season average (January to April) of the percentage difference of rainfall per season as compared to 20 years average of -30 percent.
    • Figure 4 provides an overview of the outcome of the CBA. 
      • In particular, it shows that, under drought conditions, the net benefit of applying the good practice for wheat production over 11 years is over fifty percent higher than without applying the good practice.
      • The BCR with the DRR good practice is 2.67, which is higher than the BCR of the previously applied practice (2.27).
Figure 4. Cumulative Net Present Value per acre over 11 years

©FAO/TECA

  • Figure 5 shows that the irrigation, compost/manure, labour, pesticide and fertilizer costs are higher for the DRR good practice, compared to the previously used practice, which present a higher cost only for the seeds.
  • However, these higher costs are offset by the benefits obtained from the DRR good practice implementation with a higher gross value of production.
  • These results show that wheat production with levelling and IPM, is an effective DRR practice package, compared to the previously used practice.
Figure 5. Cumulative Net Present Value per acre over 11 years

©FAO/TECA

4. Difficulties and/or limitations

  • Unawareness /No access to knowledge.
  • Poor sensitization about climate change.

5. Validation of the practice

5.1 Geographical area of practice validation

  • The practice was validated and implemented in Sindh province of Pakistan.
  • In particular, farmers started growing wheat by applying improved variety, land levelling and IPM in Kashmore district.

5.2 Context of implementation

  • This practice was introduced and validated by the Building Disaster Resilience in Pakistan (BDRP) project of FAO in Pakistan.
  • The farmer said they would continue to implement the good practice since this practice enhanced production, nutritional value and judicial use of inputs including water, fertilizer, pesticides, and manuring.

5.2.1 Environmental and climatic (period/season) context

  • The performance of the good practice was monitored over a six months period during the Rabi season 2017-2018 (November to April).
  • As nutrients were managed through integrated manners and use of FYM, farmers decreased their use of urea fertilizer, improving the air quality and decreasing the emission of greenhouse gas.

5.2.2 Social - target group

  • Big and smallholder farmers.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

6.1 Necessary basic conditions for a successful implementation

  • Farmers' education and sensitization about judicial use of inputs and climate change adaptation is necessary before implementing this practice.
  • Farmer Field School (FFS) approach remain very effective in educating farmers through learning by doing.

6.2 Constrains (limiting factors) for the implementation of the technology

  • Lack of knowledge about improved variety, education on Agro-ecosystem Analysis through FFS approach, and also the poor sensitization about climate change.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Integrated pest management: ID 7298.
  • farmyard manure and water hyacinth compost applications to enhance organic matter: ID 6836.
  • Green manure/cover crops and crop rotation in conservation agriculture on small farms: ID 7250.
  • Green manuring in sugarcane production for soil improvement and water efficiency: ID 8768.
  • Wheat cultivation with farmyard manure and compost application in Pakistan in dry spell conditions, a cost-benefit analysis: ID 10017.
  • Cost benefit analysis of vegetable cultivation with ridge sowing, farmyard manure, multi-cropping and integrated pest management in dry spell conditions: ID 10014.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Resource use efficiency

This practice allows to decrease the use of chemical inputs while strengthening the resilience of the soil. Also, it is shown how climate change adaptation can result in higher incomes for farmers.
