entries.title: Rice cultivation with line sowing and Alternate Wet and Dry (AWD) method
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary: This technology describes the introduction of line sowing techniques and the Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) method for rice cultivation in the District of Muzaffargarh in Pakistan and its economic implications based on a cost-benefit analysis. The main hazards affecting agricultural livelihoods, including rice cultivation, of this region are dry spells and related water scarcity. Line sowing allows better control of plant populations where the distance between plants and rows is uniform and farmers can maintain an optimum rice plant population of 80 000 per acre. The AWD dry method requires smaller amounts of standing water and results in lower methane emissions and higher soil fertility. The implementation of these practices allows for reusing irrigation water a few days after the disappearance of the ponded water. Farmers are thus able to reduce irrigation water consumption in rice fields without decreasing yields.
entries.description:
Description

1. Previously used practice

  • Farmers in the Muzaffargarh district have previously been using traditional rice sowing practices.
  • The rice production with this method was challenged by drought and, in general, unpredictable rainfall patterns.
Figure 1. Demonstration of line sowing and the Alternate Wet and Dry Method for rice

©FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

2. Good practice

2.1 Line sowing

  • The line sowing technique is a sowing method that involves dropping the seeds into the soil, followed by the covering of the seeds by wooden plank or harrow to have contact between the seeds and the soil.
  • In this case, the transplanting method rather than the direct seedling method was used.
  • The first step is then to produce seedlings in a nursery.

2.1.1 Step one: nursery development

  • The farmers developed a rice nursery with certified seed rice KSK-133 provided by FAO under the Building Disaster Resilience in Pakistan (BDRP) project.
  • The farmers established a nursery site one month before the transplanting season.

2.1.2 Step two: land preparation

The farmers levelled their land through laser levellers and used conventional ploughing and planking through tractors.

2.1.3 Step three: nursery transplantation and sowing in line

  • After 28 days of planting nursery, the farmers shifted their nursery plants to the AWD field right after the land preparation and first flood irrigation. 
  • Farmers used a rope marked every 9 inches (22.86 cm) for transplanting the nursery plants with a 9 inch plant-to-plant and 9 inch row-to-row distance in standing water.
  • Line sowing allows for a better control of plant populations where the distance between plants and rows is uniform and farmers can maintain an optimum rice plant population of 80 000 per acre.
  • Furthermore, if after seven days, if any gaps are found in the plants’ germination, this area can be refilled with additional plants.

3. Alternative Wetting and Drying (AWD) method

  • Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) is a practice that farmers can use to reduce their irrigation water consumption in rice fields without decreasing the field’s yield.
    • In AWD, irrigation water is reapplied a few days after the disappearance of the ponded water.
    • The field is alternately flooded and dried.
    • With the pani pipe (field water tube, see explanation below and Figure 2), the field water level is easily monitored to know when to irrigate (see explanation below for benchmark).
    • The number of days between irrigations can vary from one to more than ten days, depending on a number of factors such as soil type, weather, and crop growth stage.

3.1 Step one: installation of a pani pipe

  • Farmers use pani pipes for monitoring water in the root zone of the crop.
    • The pani pipe can be made of 30 cm long plastic pipes or bamboo, and should have a diameter of 10 to 15 cm so that the water table is easily visible, and so that the soil inside can easily be removed.
    • The tube has to be perforated with many holes on all sides, so that water can flow readily in and out of the tube.
    • Hammer the tube into the soil so that 15 cm protrudes above the soil surface. Take care not to penetrate through the bottom of the plough pan.
    • Remove the soil from inside the tube so that the bottom of the tube is visible.
  • When the field is flooded, check that the water level inside the tube is the same as outside the tube.
    • If it is not the same after a few hours, the holes are blocked with compacted soil and the tube needs to be cleaned and carefully re-installed.
    • The tube should be placed in a readily accessible part of the field close to a bund, so it is easy to monitor the ponded water depth.
    • The location should be representative of the average water depth in a levelled field (e.g. it should not be in a high spot or a low spot).
  • After irrigation, when the water level is decreasing again below the soil surface, it is possible to monitor the level in the pipe.
    • The field is irrigated again when the water level in Pani pipe reaches 15 cm below the soil surface.
Figure 2. Installation of a pani pipe

© FAO/BDRP-Pakistan

3.2 Step two: irrigation 

  • Farmers performed the first irrigation before planting the rice nursery, ensuring the standing water in the field for about 15 days from the date of transplantation to overcome weed problems.
  • After this, they used the AWD method to irrigate their field by using Pani pipes for the rest of the irrigation period of the crop.

3.3 Step three: harvest

  • Farmers harvested crops in the middle of November and marketed them directly from the field.

4. Socio-economic benefits of the practice

  • The introduction of line sowing along with the AWD method for rice cultivation was shown to be very viable in the Muzaffargarh district.
    • It did not only tackle the climate change issues by providing climate smart agriculture practices but also improved the economic condition of the farmers by reducing the use of water and increasing crop yields.
  • As a result of the implementation of the AWD method, farmers got a higher yield with significant water savings of up to 20 percent.
    • This practice is more suitable in occasional water scarcity situations.
    • The pani pipe, allowing to monitor the AWD condition of the field, is also very simple to install and to understand.
    • Thus, the AWD technique is cheap and does not require any expensive technology or machine to be implemented.
  • This practice also allowed to promote a higher zinc availability in both the soil and the grains by enabling periodic aeration of the soil, which releases zinc from insoluble forms and makes it available for plant uptake.
  • Also, AWD promotes good root anchorage, and thus a reduction in plant lodging problems.
  • It reduces 30 to 70 percent of methane emissions depending on the combination of water usage and management of rice stubble.
  • The introduction of the good practice also gave beneficiaries an increased income, safer livelihoods, lower input costs (mainly from fertilizers and water), and a higher crop resistance to climate constraints.
  • Overall, the farmers expressed their interest in replicating the good practice in the future.

5. Cost of the practice

  • The benefits and costs of line sowing and ADW for rice production was assessed at farm-level. 
  • The net benefits obtained from introducing this good practice was calculated through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA).  
    • The CBA calculates the net present value (NPV) of cumulative benefits obtained from using line sowing and AWD method to improve rice production over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms).
    • It also calculates the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period. 
  • The CBA was conducted based on quantitative data collected on two farms located in the Muzaffargarh district affected by dry spell, during the Kharif season in 2018 (June to November).
  • During the monitoring period all villages were facing drought.
  • Figure 3 provides an overview of the outcome of the CBA. 
    • In particular, it shows that, under drought conditions, the net benefit of applying line sowing and the AWD method for rice production over 11 years is over 80 percent higher than without applying the good practice.
    • The BCR in drought conditions with the DRR good practice is 1.83, which is higher than the BCR of the previously applied practice (1.45). 
  • These results show that the rice production using the good practice brings greater benefits relative to costs, as compared to the previously used practice.
Figure 3. Cumulative Net Present Value per acre over 11 years

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Costs and benefits per acre per season

©FAO/TECA

6. Validation of the practice

  • The practice was tested in Muzafargarh, a district in the Punjab province of Pakistan.
  • The performance of the good practice was monitored over a six months period during the Kharif season 2018 (June to November).
  • The crop was watered through the canal and tube well water supply, however the season remained dry with no rain in the area.

7. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • The introduction of the line sowing method requires tools and has to be performed by skilled persons.
  • The AWD method is only suitable for dry season rice cultivation, because if the rainfall exceeds evapotranspiration and seepage, the soils wouldn’t be able to be drained in five-day intervals.
  • Other limitations of the practice.
    • An unawareness or no access to knowledge on AWD practice.
    • A limited coverage in public sector extension packages.
    • A lack of knowledge about the use of pani pipe to measure root zone water of the crop.
    • A lack of knowledge on the concept of dry rice cultivation.
    • An overall poor sensitization about climate change.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Rice farming: saving water through Alternate Wetting Drying (AWD) method: ID 7939.
  • Intensive rice cultivation: ID 7666.
  • Aerobic rice: ID 7941.
  • Wheat cultivation with farmyard manure and compost application in Pakistan in dry spell conditions, a cost-benefit analysis: ID 10017.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Resource use efficiency

The AWD dry method requires smaller amounts of standing water and results in lower methane emissions and higher soil fertility.

entries.title: Rainwater harvesting systems for ntula/eggplant (Solanum aethiopicum L.)
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary: This technology describes utilizing rooftop water harvesting facilities to increase the availability of water for domestic use and irrigation of backyard ntula/ eggplant (Solanum aethiopicum L.) gardens. This measure allows small-scale farmers to harvest rainwater from roofs and store it in tanks, ensuring ntula production also during the dry season, when it would be otherwise impossible. The combination of rainwater harvesting with other good practices (e.g. staking, mulching, manuring) helps increase productivity while reducing soil erosion, eventually strengthening the resilience of farmers from the impact of dry spells.
entries.description:
Description

1. Suitability 

  • This measure was tested by households in rural districts in Uganda that face frequent water shortages.
  • Rainwater harvested in tanks can be used for domestic purposes and to water ntula (solanum aethiopicum L.) gardens as they need only a little water to produce decent yields.
  • If harvested water is managed carefully, it can be a reliable and significant water source during the dry season.
  • Housing with an iron roof would have an advantage in installing the water harvesting tanks as it facilitates the collection of rainwater. 

2. Composition and types of tank 

  • Rainwater can be harvested from roofs by building gutters that guide the water into a harvesting tank (Figure 1, tank 1). 
  • Water can also be harvested by putting inclined iron sheets directly on the tanks, in addition to the roofs (Figure 1, tank 2).
  • The water is then accessed with an electronic pump (Figure 2). 
  • Several sizes of tanks were observed in the field, such as 7 000 Litres (tank 1); 30 000 Litres  (tank 2); and 50 000 Litres (Figure 1, tank 3).
  • Tank size depends on needs, investment capacity of the farmer/community and size of dwelling.
    • For instance, medium-sized tanks may be suitable for a dwelling that has a roof size greater than 25 m2.
Figure 1. Different types of tanks for rainwater harvesting 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Treadle pump to access water from the tank 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Rooftop rainwater harvesting with gutter and tank 

©FAO/TECA

3. Success story 

  • In one community, a farmer had four improved breed cows for which he built enclosures, such as the one presented in Figure 2.
  • Building such an enclosure costs around 700 000 to 800 000 UGX.
  • The enclosure allowed the farmer to collect cow urine and make his own liquid manure.
  • In addition, the farmer received support and training to implement his production system. 

4. Cost-benefit analysis of the practice 

  • The performance of improved cattle breeds raised with zero-grazing and drought-tolerant fodder was assessed at the farm-level in Uganda.
  • The net benefits obtained from the good practice were measured through a Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) and compared to the net benefits of the local practice, which was free-ranging local cattle breeds.
    • Good practice: improved cattle breeds in a zero-grazing production system with drought-resistant fodder
    • Local practice: free-ranging local cattle breeds
  • The CBA calculates the cumulative net benefits obtained from an average farm with ten cattle over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate).
    • It also calculates the Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
  • Figure 4 provides an overview of the outcome of the CBA. 
    • In farms affected by dry spells and diseases, the cumulative net benefits of improved practice are about one and a half times higher than those of the local practice. 
    • The BCR of the good practice (2.92) is higher than the BCR of the local practice (2.85), meaning that the good practice brings greater benefits relative to costs, as compared to the local practice.  
  • The assessment was conducted on farms that were affected by dry spells and diseases during the monitoring period (June to September 2016).
  • The additional costs associated with the cultivation of improved fodder (as opposed to the free-range) as well as the capital costs of building livestock sheds and fodder storage facilities are more than compensated by the increase in profits from increased milk production.
  • The benefits of good practice may be even higher if accounting the potential profits derived from additional land available after the introduction of zero grazings.
  • The additional land could be used for other income-generating activities, including for crop production. 
Figure 4. Cumulative Net Benefits and Benefit-Cost Ratios (BCR) of improved cattle breeds raised with zero-grazing and drought-tolerant fodder (USD per farm per season)​ 

©FAO/TECA

5. Effectiveness and benefits 

5.1 Climate change adaptation related benefits

  • In the context of climate change, pastures could become less available in the near future, which is why cutting and storing fodder for animals could be a way to adapt to climate change.
  • Zero-grazing helps reduce animal pressure on the land and limit the spread of disease amongst animals, a risk that could increase with climate change.
  • Easier manure collection because of enclosures could also help reduce soil fertility loss induced by climate change 

5.2 Socio-economic and ecological benefits 

  • The free-grazing livestock often damages crops also in neighbouring farms, and this is a major cause of conflict.
  • Zero-grazing allows to have less pressure on the crops and on reduce land conflict.
  • In addition, enclosures make it easier to collect manure which can be used for sustaining soil fertility in cropland.
  • Other goals are to improve household income, reduce expenditure on pests and disease management through livestock isolation from other animals.
  • Also, to reduce labour by cutting and storing fodder for use over a period instead of grazing in distant pastures daily.
  • Increased manure collection and application increases crop yields.

5.2.1 Advantages of zero-grazing systems 

  • Exposure to parasites and disease vectors is reduced.
  • Manure is easily collected and distributed in the farm enhancing soil fertility.
  • Better control over breeding and animal health.
  • Milk yield in dry season tripled after introducing this good practice, from 100 liters to 300 liters per cow. 

6. Synergies 

  • Other adaptation options that would create the most synergies with zero-grazing are:
    • fodder banks,
    • organic fertilizers, and
    • planting of fodder trees such as calliandra, albizia, where possible. 

7. General recommendations 

  • Technical and financial support should be provided to allow farmers to acquire and properly manage zero-grazing cows.
  • Zero-grazing cows should be integrated into the whole production of the farm so that feed can be provided easily at no additional costs.
  • The minimal requirement to be able to establish such a zero-grazing system.
    • Does the farmer have available for fodder production a minimal amount of land?
      • If he does not have a certain amount of land, the system is not sustainable as he cannot produce the necessary fodder for the animals.
    • Does the farm have guaranteed access to a certain amount of water for cows to drink?
    • Other elements aforementioned are also essential for the successful implementation of such a zero-grazing. 

8. Validation of the practice 

  • Hazard context during the monitoring period.
    • During the 2016 dry season (June to September), the performance of this good practice package was monitored in 13 farms in Kiboga (four), Mubende (two), Sembabule (two), Nakaseke (four), and Nakasongola (one) districts.
    • All the farms were affected by dry spells during the monitoring period.
    • In particular, rainfall was between 50 to 100 percent below normal in August, and land surface temperatures were 3°C to 7 °C above average, causing a reduction in water availability.
  • Farmers’ perception
    • Seven of the farmers who were interviewed all reported that they would replicate the good practice  in the coming seasons since it increases climate resilience, leading to higher profits.
      • (For example, raising improved cattle breed in confinement and produce drought tolerant fodder to feed the cattle.
    • Farmers assigned a score of 4.6 out of 5 to the performance of the good practice towards dry spell and disease.
      • Some of the farmers, however, raised concerns regarding the high investment required to start the good practice, such as the costs of clearing land for pasture growing. 

9. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice 

9.1 Major costs 

  • One hired worker
    • 160 000 UGX per month.
  • Construction of forage storage facility
    • The average cost per average farm (ten cows) is 3.5 million UGX.
  • Construction of a zero-grazing unit for an average farm (ten cows).
    • 750 000 UGX.
  • The average price of improved cattle breed
    • 2.25 million UGX per cow.
  • Cost of producing forage
    • 175 UGX per kg of fresh grass, or about UGX 26 million per average farm (10 cows).
  • Price of fresh forage
    • 400 UGX per kg, or about UGX 60 million per average farm (10 cows)
    • This cost can be avoided when farmers grow their own fodder on their farms. 

9.2 Major barriers 

  • There were not many farmers adopting zero-grazing in the visited district of Uganda as an improved breed are very expensive and less resistant.
  • The main barrier against zero-grazing.
    • The additional cost of not only purchasing a “zero grazer”.
    • The running costs associated with cutting the grass and the additional slurry, which will have to be spread as a result of housing the herd over the summer. 

10. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm. 

11. Related/associated technologies 

  • Rainwater harvesting systems for cabbage growing: ID 8932.
  • Rooftop rainwater harvesting combined with gravity drip irrigation: tomato growing: ID 10011.
  • Rooftop rainwater harvesting combined with gravity drip irrigation: sweet pepper production: ID 10012.
  • Rainwater syringe: low-cost technology for rainwater harvesting in coastal areas: ID 6919.
  • Rooftop rainwater harvesting: ID 7387.
  • Rooftop rainwater harvesting: concrete tank: ID 7513.

12. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

12.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

Having cattle kept at one place reduces the effort needed to control and feed them. It makes manure collection easier on the farm. Additionally, there is no need for daily grazing since fodder can be cut and stored for use over a period.  

12.2 Resource use efficiency 

This practice, if applied to high-yielding improved breeds, can maximize the efficiency and sustainability of livestock production by improving animal productivity, while reducing the number of animals. 

12.3 Pro-poor technology

Small farmers can apply this practice since no large farm area is required.

  • FAO. 2012. Project Document: Global Climate Change Alliance (GCCA) - Uganda: Agriculture Adaptation to Climate Change. Republic of Uganda. 44 pp.
  • Water Aid. 2013. Technical Brief: Rainwater Harvesting.

entries.title: Improved cattle breeds zero grazing with drought tolerant fodder
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary:
This technology describes the introduction of improved cattle breeds in Uganda. The improved breeds are more productive and resistant to diseases and are managed by applying the zero grazing production system. This is a type of production system where the animals are kept in an enclosure to control input use and to reduce the incidence of diseases. This breed is fed with drought tolerant fodder to ensure cattle feed availability also in dry seasons.

This mix of good practices was introduced to increase productivity and enhance the resilience of cattle raising to increasing dry spells and diseases in the central cattle corridor of Uganda.
entries.description:
Description

1. Zero grazing

  • Zero grazing is a production system where animals are kept in an enclosure and farmers bring all the feed and water to the animals.
  • Zero-grazing has been a common livestock management practice in most areas of south-western Uganda due to reduced communal grazing land.
  • Zero-grazing aims to maximize the efficiency and sustainability of livestock production by improving animal productivity while reducing the number of animals.
  • For this reason, zero-grazing is usually practiced only with high-yielding improved breeds.
  • With good planning, many dairy animals can be kept on a relatively small piece of land, making this system suitable in areas where a farmer owns a limited amount of land for grazing.
  • Under zero grazing, individual attention in terms of feeding is possible, as the animal does not spend energy searching for food.
  • Zero grazing also makes disease and vector control easier.
  • Zero grazing is considered as an adaptation option.
    • Pasture could become less available with climate change, leading to a shortage of food for animals during droughts.
      • Zero grazing could address this risk as farmers can save natural fodder resources and store fodder.
    • Zero grazing helps reduce animal pressure on the land, such as over grazing, eventually leading to desertification.
    • Zero grazing limits the spread of disease amongst animals because they are less clustered around watering points.
    • There is easier manure collection because of enclosures, which would create benefits for crops and lower the costs and labour needed in applying manure.
  • The unit of zero-grazing has three major parts;
    • The feeding and rest area
    • The exercise area
    • The manure collection area.
  • To have an effective zero grazing unit, the following elements should be taken into account.

1.1 Safety

  • A good dairy animal is a costly investment which should be secured.
  • This can be ensured by an appropriate selection of the unit location.
  • Locating the unit close to farm houses will contribute to security.
  • When choosing the location also take into account the wind direction to make sure that the wind can carry away the dung smell.

1.2 Ventilation

  • Good ventilation is recommended for a healthy animal respiratory system and adds to the comfort, which is crucial for maximal milk production.
  • Ventilation is also important to regulate the temperature and avoid stress to animals caused by high temperatures.

1.3 Isolation

  • Different animals are kept separated into different units.
    • Avoids injuries resulting from fights and mounting.
    • Controls breeding.
    • Avoids spread of diseases.

1.4 Maintenance

  • Regular maintenance of the floor and the roof ensures that the floor does not develop holes that can injure the livestock and that the roof does not leak when it rains.

1.5 Good management

  • A cow will typically eat between 75 to 100 kg of fresh grass per day, which equates to 14 to 16 kg of dry matter percow per day.
  • For a 100 cow herd, this would mean that approximately 0.75 ha (1.9 acres) would need to be harvested each day to ensure a dry matter intake of 15 kg per head per day.
  • In a visited community, a farmer had four improved breed cows for which he built enclosures such as the one presented in the picture (Figure 1).
  • Such an enclosure costs around 700 000 to 800 000 UGX to build.
  • The enclosure allowed him to collect cow urine and make his own liquid manure.
  • The farmer received support and training to implement his production system.
Figure 1. Cow enclosure collecting urine to make liquid manure

©FAO/TECA

2. Drought tolerant forage

Figure 2. Drought tolerant forage

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Drought tolerant forage cultivation

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Forage storage facility next to the cattle housing

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Forage storage facility

©FAO/TECA

3. Cost-benefit analysis of the practice

  • The performance of improved cattle breeds raised with zero grazing and drought tolerant fodder was assessed at farm-level in Uganda.
  • The net benefits obtained from the good practice were measured through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA), and compared to the net benefits of the local practice which was free ranging local cattle breeds.
    • Good practice
      • Improved cattle breeds in a zero grazing production system with drought resistant fodder.
    • Local practice
      • Free ranging local cattle breeds.
  • The CBA calculates the cumulative net benefits obtained from an average farm with 10 cattle over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate);
  • It also calculates the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
  • Figure 6 provides an overview of the outcome of the CBA. 
    • In farms affected by dry spells and diseases, the cumulative net benefits of improved practice are about one and a half times higher than those of the local practice.
    • The BCR of the good practice (2.92) is higher than the BCR of the local practice (2.85), meaning that the good practice brings greater benefits relative to costs, as compared to the local practice.
  • The assessment was conducted on farms that were affected by dry spells and diseases during the monitoring period (June to September 2016).
Figure 6. Cumulative net benefits and benefit cost ratios (BCR) of improved cattle breeds raised with zero grazing and drought tolerant fodder (USD per farm per season)

©FAO/TECA

  • The additional costs associated with the cultivation of improved fodder (as opposed to free range) and the capital costs for building livestock sheds and fodder storage facilities, are more than compensated by the increase in profits from increased milk production.
  • The benefits of the good practice may be even higher if accounting for the potential profits derived from additional land available after the introduction of zero grazing.
  • The additional land could be used for other income generating activities, including for crop production.

4. Effectiveness and benefits

4.1 Socio-economic and ecological benefits

  • Free grazing livestock often damages crops (also in neighboring farms), and this is a major cause of conflict.
  • Zero-grazing allows to have less pressure on the crops and reduce land conflict.
  • Enclosures make it easier to collect manure, which can be used for sustaining soil fertility in cropland.
  • Other goals are to improve household income; reduce expenditure on pests and disease management through livestock isolation from other animals; and to reduce labour by cutting and storing fodder for use over a period of time instead of grazing indistant pastures daily. 
  • Increased manure collection and application increases crop yields.
  • Advantages of zero-grazing systems
    • Exposure to parasites and diseases vectors is reduced.
    • Manure is easily collected and distributed on the farm, enhancing soil fertility.
    • Better control on breeding and animal health.
    • Milk yield in dry season tripled after introducing this good practice, from 100 liters to 300 liters per cow.

4.2 Climate change adaptation related benefits

  • In the context of climate change, pastures could become less available in the near future, which is why cutting and storing fodder for animals could be a way to adapt to climate change.
  • Zero grazing helps reduce animal pressure on the land and limit the spread of disease amongst animals, a risk that could increase with climate change.
  • Easier manure collection because of enclosures could also help reduce soil fertility loss induced by climate change.

5. Major costs and resources needed

  • One hired worker.
    • 160 000 UGX per month.
  • Construction of forage storage facility.
    • Average cost per average farm (ten cows) is 3 500 000 UGX.
  • Construction of a zero grazing unit for an average farm (ten cows).
    • 750 000 UGX.
  • Average price of improved cattle breed.
    • 2 250 000 UGX per cow.
  • Cost of producing forage.
    • 175 UGX per kg of fresh grass, or about UGX 26 million per average farm (10 cows).
  • Price of fresh forage
    • 400 UGX per kg, or about UGX 60 million per average farm (10 cows)
    • This cost can be avoided when farmers grow their own fodder on their farms.

6. Side effects

  • Confinement in zero grazing system can result in stress among the animals.

7. Major barriers

  • There were not many farmers adopting zero-grazing in the visited district of Uganda as improved breed are very expensive and less resistant.
  • The main barrier against zero-grazing is the additional cost of purchasing a “zero grazer”.
  • Another barrier is the running costs associated with cutting the grass along with the additional slurry which will have to be spread as a result of housing the herd over the summer.

8. Synergies

  • Other adaptation options that would create the most synergies with zero grazing.
    • Fodder banks
    • Organic fertilizers
    • Planting of fodder trees s.a. calliandra, albizia, where possible.

9. General recommendations

  • Technical and financial support should be provided to allow farmers to acquire and properly manage zero grazing cows.
  • Zero grazing cowsshould be integrated in the whole production of the farm so that feed can be provided easily at no additional costs.
  • Minimal requiremensS to be able to establish such a zero grazing system.
    • Should a farmer have available for fodder production a minimal amount of land?
      • If the farmer does not have a certain amount of land, the system is not sustainable as he/she cannot produce the necessary fodder for the animals?
    • Should the farm have guaranteed access to a certain amount of water for cows to drink?
      • Other elements that are essential for the successful implementation of such zero grazing system?

10. Validation

10.1 Hazard context during monitoring period

  • During the 2016 dry season (June to September), the performance of this good practice package was monitored in 13 farms in Kiboga (four), Mubende (two), Sembabule (two), Nakaseke (four), and Nakasongola (one) districts.
  • All the farms were affected by dry spell during the monitoring period.
  • In particular, rainfall was between 50 to 100 percent below normal in August, and land surface temperatures were 3°C to 7°C above average, causing a reduction in water availability.

10.2 Farmers’ perception

  • Seven of the farmers who were interviewed, all reported that they would replicate the good practice (e.g. raise improved cattle breed in confinement and produce drought tolerant fodder to feed the cattle), in the coming seasons since it increases climate resilience, leading to higher profits.
  • Farmers assigned a score of 4.6 out of 5 to the performance of the good practice towards dry spell and disease.
  • Some of them, however, raised concerns regarding the high investment required to start the good practice, such as the costs of clearing land for pasture growing.

11. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

12. Related/associated technologies

  • Improved feeding of dairy cattle for increased milk production and income: ID 6988.
  • Growing fodder for livestock: Calliandra and elephant grass: ID 6989.
  • Building fodder security in rural areas: ID 7684.
  • Introduction of silvopastoral systems for cattle raising to sustainably provide fodder to animals: ID 8954.

13. Objectives fulfilled by the project

13.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology helps farmers increase productivity and enhance the resilience of cattle raising.

entries.title: Introduction of corralones, (semi-roofed shelters) and veterinary pharmacies
entries.source: FAO Bolivia
entries.summary: In the highlands of Bolivia, recurrent cold waves and related extreme events severely increase the mortality rate of camelids, which represent the main source of livelihood for the local population. This technology describes the introduction “Corralones”, semi-roofed shelters aimed at protecting livestock from extreme weather and climate events in the Bolivian eco-region of the Altiplano (High Andean Plateau). They are a means to enhance the resilience of livestock (Llama camelids) in the face of snow, frost and hailstorms, in addition to introducing veterinary pharmacies, in order to provide livestock with the necessary treatments to cope with prolonged frost and snow periods. In farms affected by frost and snow, the good practice contributed to reducing livestock mortality, bringing 18 percent higher net benefits than the local practice, as well as increasing livestock production in the face of extreme events.
entries.description:
Description

1. Corralones (semi-roofed shelters)

1.1 Description (step by step) of the application of the technology/practice

1.1.1 Location

  • The corralones are most necessary during winter and summer.
  • They should preferentially be located close to the areas where the llamas spend the most time, which might be different according to the season.
  • When possible, two corralones would be ideal.

1.1.2 Orientation considerations

  • Sun
    • The entrance of the corralón should face the sunrise (east) in order to warm up and disinfect the shelter (Figure 1).
  • Wind direction
    • he back of the corralón should face the direction from where the strongest and most frequent winds blow (Figure 2).
  • Topography
    • When built on a slope, the corralón entrance should be oriented facing down the slope, and a water-diversion canal should be dug in the upper side, at the back of the corralón (Figure 3).
Figure 1. Orientation in relation to the sun

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Orientation in relation to the wind

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3.Orientation in relation to the topography

©FAO/TECA

1.1.3 Dimensions and volumes 

  • Size of the herd
    • The dimension of the corralón is directly correlated to the size of the herd, with a ratio of 1.5 m2 per adult llama.
    • It is advisable to also consider the amount of pregnant female and baby llamas (Figure 4).
  • Size of the shelter
    • A shelter of 9 m x 5 m. is enough to fit 30 adult llamas, covering a surface of 45 m2 (Figure 5).
  • Roof design
    • The roof of the shelter could be of one or two gabled roofs.
    • When designing the roof, the maximum llama height (1.70 cm) should be taken into consideration, in order to have a maximum height of 3 m (Figure 6).
  • Size of the patio
    • As a general rule, the area of the patio is the same as the area of the shelter, but may vary according to the availability of space (Figure 7).
  • The shape of the patio
    • The shape can be circular, rectangular or squared. 
    • However it is recommended for the patio to have a rounded shape, in order to facilitate cleaning as well as to facilitate the movement of the llamas and for safe management.
Figure 4. Corralón dimensions

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Construction design

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Ceiling design

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Patio design

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Materials

  • Floor
    • It is recommended to have soil as a floor.
  • Walls
    • It is recommended to use local materials, such as rocks, adobe, etc.
  • Roof
    • The roof may vary in thickness, and may be composed of one material or by the combination of different materials, such as straws, roof tiles, bamboos, mud, plastic membranes, weaved wires, etc.
  • The cost (in Boliviano) for the construction of the roof is found in Table 1. 
Table 1. Cost of the roof construction

Source: FAO 2017

1.3 Complementary infrastructure

  • Water-diversion canal
    • In laden terrains, the construction of a water diversion canal in the upper side of the corralón is needed to deviate rainwater.
  • Draining canal
    • To drain out the urine and any rainwater that filters into the corralón, in order to maintain it dry (Figure 8).
  • Dung deposit
    • To maintain clean the corralón, while facilitating the production of manure (Figure 9)
Figure 8. Water-diversion and draining canal

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Dung deposit

1.4 Maintenance

  • In-depth cleaning of the corralones should be done twice a year.
  • The roof should be checked every year prior to the commencement of the rain season.
  • Shelter and canals should be cleared regularly.

2. Veterinary pharmacies

  • In addition to shelters, veterinary pharmacies located at the municipalities were introduced in order to provide livestock with the necessary treatments to cope with prolonged frost and snow periods.
  • Farmers were provided with easy access to veterinary pharmacies, supplied (dewormers and multivitamins) by the municipalities before and after (possible) extreme weather events and low-temperature seasons.
    • This guaranteed the access to the dewormers and multivitamins, those being the most requested medications.

2.1 Deworming and multivitamins

  • During crisis periods, camelids usually experience a high level of stress, both nutritional and physiological.
    • This compromises the balance of their vital functions, their pastoral ethological behavior, their immunological levels, and causes reproductive disorders among others.
  • This situation is worsened by the parasitic state of the animals.
    • Depending on their state of gravity, a process of cleaning and disinfection of the parasitic population can be applied.
      • This is in order to make sure that the benefits of a subsequent vitamin, mineral, energetic and protein dosage are for the camelids, rather than for the parasites.
  • It is advisable to consider a complete deworming of endo and ecto parasites.
    • This cqn be done through oral dosage of a product based on levamisole agents or similar, as well as the application of a subcutaneous parenteral injection of a product based on the enzyme principles of ivermectin, preferably accompanied by a fat-soluble vitamin complex containing vitamins A, B, C, D and K.

3. Benefits

  • The farmers found that their livelihood practices are now safer in the face of extreme events.
  • The practice contributed to avoiding livestock losses and increased livestock production.
  • The veterinary pharmacies have allowed farmers to apply vitamins during frost, helping the animals to cope with the extreme weather periods.
  • Increased access to treatment through the veterinary pharmacies helped reduce the mortality rate.
    • However, it is not possible to disentangle the benefits of veterinary pharmacies from the benefits of corralones.
  • In addition, the functioning of the veterinary pharmacies allowed the increase of vaccination and de-worming campaigns provided by the “Servicio Nacional de Sanidad Agropecuaria e Inocuidad Alimentaria” (SENASAG).

3.1 Economic

  • Cost-Benefit Analyses (CBA) were conducted based on quantitative data collected during the 2016 winter period.
    • The net benefits obtained from raising camelids with corralones and veterinary pharmacies were compared to the net benefits of raising camelids without corralones and veterinary pharmacies.
    • The costs and benefits were calculated based on the average herd size in the monitored farms (e.g. 85 llamas).
  • The CBA calculates the cumulative net benefits obtained by an average farm over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms).
  • It also calculates the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
  • Figure 10 provides an overview of the outcome of the CBA.
    • The good practice brings 17 percent higher net benefits as compared to the usual practice.
    • The BCR of the good practice (2.98) is higher than the BCR of the local practice (2.4), meaning that the good practice brings greater benefits relative to costs, as compared to the usual practice. 
  • The assessment was conducted in farms that were affected by frost during the monitoring period.
    • Benefits included the value of sold camelid meat and wool, and the live weight value of camelids sold.
Figure 10.Cumulative net benefits and benefit-cost ratio of DRR good practice and existing local practice

©FAO/TECA

  • The introduction of shelters to protect camelids from frost, combined with the increased access to treatments following the establishment of veterinary pharmacies, significantly reduced the mortality rate of camelids.
  • On the other hand, the increase in benefits was partially outweighed by the capital costs of building shelters, as well as the costs of travelling to the veterinary pharmacies located in the municipalities.

3.2 Environmental

  • Further analysis is required in order to assess potential environmental co-benefits of this good practice.

4. Difficulties and/or limitations

  • Farmers cannot afford to build new corralones unless they receive additional support from the municipality.
  • High costs of traveling to the municipality, in order to attend the veterinary pharmacies, located in the municipalities.

5. Validation of the practice

5.1 The geographical area of practice validation

  • Bolivian eco-region of the Altiplano (High Andean Plateau).

5.2 Context of implementation

  • In the highlands of Bolivia, recurrent cold waves and related extreme events severely increase the mortality rate of camelids, which represent the main source of livelihood for the local population.
  • In the highlands of Bolivia, recurrent cold waves and related extreme events severely increase the mortality rate of camelids, which represent the main source of livelihood for the local population.

6. Minimum requirements for successful implementation of the technology

6.1 Necessary conditions for a successful implementation

  • Llamas, in particular female and baby llamas, should rest inside the corralon during the night, to avoid energy loss while sleeping and to reduce the incidence of pneumonia.
  • The engagement of the municipalities is vital for the correct functioning of the veterinary pharmacies, as they are responsible for the supplies.
  • It is important to have permanent technical support and ongoing training for technicians and farmers to prevent side effects in animals by extreme climate events.
  • Campaigns should be accompanied by basic training on the use of the materials and veterinary inputs and on the correct application of anti-parasites, so the practice can be replicated year after year by camelid breeders.

6.2 Constraints (limiting factors) for the implementation of the technology

  • Due to the investment cost to build new corralones, additional support from the municipality is needed for the further implementation of the practice.
  • The relatively high costs of traveling to the municipality.
  • Farmers advised that veterinary pharmacies should be established within each community.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, cool/ cold/ very cold.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Guía para la construcción de un cobertizo para llamas: ID 8634.

9. Objectives associated with the project

9.1 Pro poor technology

By increasing the resilience of livestock, the technology ensures that it remains a reliable source of livelihood for local populations. 

9.2 Resource use efficiency

The practice effectively combines the building of shelters, using local resources, and the introduction of local veterinary pharmacies as a way to increase livestock resilience in the face of extreme climate events.

entries.title: Multi-stress tolerant bean varieties
entries.source: FAO Strategic Objective 5 – Resilience, in FAO
entries.summary: This technology describes the testing of multi-stress tolerant bean varieties in the central cattle corridor of Uganda, a region particularly exposed to dry spells. The benefits and constraints compared to local varieties are shown in a cost-benefit analysis.
entries.description:
Description

This good practice describes the benefits of the cultivation of multi-stress tolerant bean varieties in Uganda, compared to local traditional varieties. Beans are an important staple crop in the central cattle corridor of Uganda. An increase in yields and production quantities due to enhanced resilience to extreme events would strengthen food security among vulnerable smallholder households.

Beans are grown in a lot of districts in Uganda with either local or improved varieties. The most common improved bean varieties grown inthe visited communities are the Nabe series. In the validation of this practice, the focus lies on Nabe 4, 15 and 17.

The traditional system uses local seeds, especially yellow beans and kanyebwa, costing between 1 500 and 2 000 UGX per kg. Their yield varies between 150 and to 500 kg per acre. The aim of a switch to higher yielding varieties is to absorb the impact of a potential decline in yields that is likely to occur under climate change. Of course the higher yielding varieties are beneficial even without climate change and their adoption may be justified on cost-benefit grounds but the expectation is that the case becomes stronger with climate change. There are also some benefits to switching to some of the higher yielding varieties, as they are more resistant to viruses and bean rot, which are expected to increase with climate change.

1. Technical specifications on the Nabe 4, Nabe 15 and Nabe 17 improved varieties

  • The technical specifications on the Nabe 4, Nabe 15 and Nabe 17 improved varieties are highlighted in Table 1.
Table 1. Technical specifications of improved varieties

Source: FAO 2017

2. Costs and resources implications

  • Improved beans seed can be bought on the market at a price between 4 000 and 4 800 UGX per kg.
  • According to the visited communities, beans are sold in the market at 1 200 to 2 500 UGX per kg.
  • The longer beans are stored, the higher their market price will be.
  • Improved beans seeds are sold in the market at a price between 4 000 and 4 800 UGX per kg, but seeds are usually saved from one cropping cycle to the other.
  • Farmers plant between 20 and 30 kg of beans per acre.
  • The costs mentioned in this technology refer to the time of writing.

3. Benefits

3.1 Socio-economic and ecological benefits

  • Improved bean varieties, if sustainably managed, can increase yields up to 1 tonne per acre.
  • In dry spell conditions, improved varieties yield can be more than two times higher than the yield of local varieties.
  • The Nabe series is more resistant to drought, and to some diseases such as the Anthracnose and the Bean Common Mosaic virus.
  • A wide range of bean varieties exist, with specific characteristics.
  • Farmers can choose the variety according to the environment they will grow the min, and to their own objective (food, export, etc.) and taste.

3.2 Climate change adaptation related benefits

  • The Nabe series is more resistant to droughts and is therefore adapted to face unreliable rains and rainfall variability induced by climate change.

3.3 Synergies with other crops

  • Some farmers reported that beans perform better when intercropped with bananas, since they can benefit from the mulching and manure applied for the bananas.
  • Beans also benefit the bananas since they are a nitrogen fixing plant.
  • Intercropping can reduce the costs of labour and increase synergies between crops, resulting in higher yields.

4. Cost-benefit analysis

  • The results of the qualitative and quantitative analyses conducted based on field demonstration data are summarized hereafter.
  • The cost-benefit analyses were conducted based on quantitative data collected during the monitoring period in the 2016 dry season (June to August).
  • Data collected from good practice plots were compared with data collected from control plots within the same farms.
    • Good Practice
      • Multi-stress tolerant bean varieties (Nabe 15, Nabe 17)
    • Local practice
      • Local bean varieties (yellow bean, Kanyebwa)
  • Sample
    • Drought
      • 16 farms in the Kiboga (five), Mubende (two), and Sembabule (nine) districts.
    • Normal Conditions
      • One farm (not included in the analysis).
  • The graph in Figure 1 shows that, in dry spell conditions, the net benefit over 11 years is 123 percent higher in farms that adopt the multi-stress tolerant bean varieties, as compared to non-adopters.
    • The cost-benefit ratio of the good practice is 1.35, which is higher compared to 1.43 of the existing local practice.
    • This is because the good practice requires more input and labour.
    • However, the increase in the yield due to the improved varieties’ resilience to drought and diseases more than compensated the additional input cost.
  • Figure 2 below shows the costs of the good practice compared to the local practice.
    • Cost assumptions 
      • Labour cost only includes hired labour. Family labour is not included.
      • Seeds costs are considered as upfront capital costs, not seasonal costs. First purchase, then saved from cycle to cycle.
      • Operation and maintenance costs are not included due to possible double counting with other costs such as labour.
Figure 1. Cumulative net benefits and benefit cost ratios of good practice and local practice (USD per acre per season) - 2016 dry season (Jun-Aug)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Average costs and benefits (USD per acre)

©FAO/TECA

4.1 Added benefits

  • Added benefits under non-hazard conditions could not be analysed since all farms were affected by dry spell.

4.2 Avoided losses

  • In farms affected by dry spells, the net benefit of the good practice was more than double the net benefit of the local practice.
  • This was largely due to enhanced drought resilience of the improved variety.

4.3 Co-benefits

  • The multi-stress tolerant bean varieties also mature faster than the local variety.
  • Therefore, water use is lower under the good practice.

4.4 General recommendation

  • Beans are usually used for both food and cash.
  • The price increases when communities store the beans and sell them later during the low season.
  • The installation of metallic and plastic silos can be a good investment to store the harvest.

5. Validation

5.1 Geographical area of practice validation

  • The practice was validated in the central cattle corridor of Uganda in 16 farms in the Kiboga (four), Mubende (one), Nakasongola (ten), and Nakaseke (one) districts.

5.2 Context of implementation

  • As part of the Global Climate Change Alliance (GCCA) project on Agriculture Adaptation to Climate Change in Uganda, farmers were introduced to multi-stress tolerant bean varieties (NABE 15 and Nabe 17) and were trained on a set of good practices to enhance the resilience of bean production to increasing dry spells.
  • The Nabe series is especially resistant to drought and to diseases such as the Anthracnose and the Bean Common Mosaic virus.

5.2.1 Environmental and climatic (period/season) context

  • During the 2016 dry season (June to August), the performance of this good practice was monitored in 16 farms in the mentioned districts.
  • All the farms were affected by dry spells during the monitoring period.
    • In particular, rainfall was between 50 and 100 percent below normal in August, and land surface temperatures were 3°C to 7°C above average, causing a reduction in water availability.

5.2.2 Social-target group

  • Smallholder farmers.

5.3 Farmer’s perceptions

5.3.1 Sustainability

  • Two farmers were interviewed for the evaluation of the good practice.
  • Both farmers responded that they would like to replicate this good practice in the next seasons as it was more productive, profitable and resistant to climate constraints such as drought, dry spell and delays in the rainy season.

5.3.2 Socio-economic benefits

  • Both farmers said that all family members benefited from the good practice, although more labour was needed than in the local practice.

5.3.3 Marketing

  • Two farmers requested support in marketing the new variety beans.

5.4 Constrains (limiting factors) for the implementation of the technology

  • Compared to the local practice, more labour input is required.
  • No major additional barriers were identified, except for the price of improved seeds.

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Using Eucalyptus leaves to preserve maize and bean seed: ID 7936.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology enhances the resilience of bean production to increasing dry spells.

entries.title: Zanjas de infiltración
entries.source: The Regional Office of FAO for Latin America and the Caribbean (RLC)
entries.summary: La región experimenta largos períodos de sequía y la mayoría de las precipitaciones ocurren en invierno, cuando el suelo está descubierto, haciendo que la erosión hídrica sea la causa más importante de degradación. La implementación de zanjas de infiltración permite cultivar los campos de la zona de forma más sostenible. Las zanjas ayudan a controlar la escorrentía al colectar el agua de lluvia, y permite la recarga de acuíferos, todo lo que permite incrementar el crecimiento y rendimiento de los cultivos, aunque el establecimiento y mantención de las zanjas es laborioso y puede ser costoso para pequeños productores.
entries.description:
Descripción

En Chile, debido a la conformación geográfica y el tipo de régimen pluviométrico, la erosión hídrica es una de las formas más importantes de degradación del suelo. Así, un gran porcentaje de las lluvias precipita en invierno, cuando el suelo está descubierto, lo que unido a malas prácticas de cultivo provoca importantes daños erosivos. 

En este marco, la construcción de obras para la captura de aguas de lluvia, en particular las zanjas de infiltración, ha permitido proporcionar una técnica adecuada para reducir los actuales índices de desertificación y también propiciar el proceso de infiltración de las aguas de lluvia bajo condiciones edafoclimáticas desfavorables, de tal forma que permitan el cultivo o la forestación de zonas de secano y la recarga artificial de las napas freáticas. 

1. Descripción del ambiente donde la estrategia fue aplicada 

  • Las siguientes características describen el ambiente natural y social donde se implementaron las zanjas de infiltración.
  • Las condiciones ambientales no son determinantes o excluyentes para el éxito de la práctica, pero deben tenerse en cuenta para realizar los ajustes necesarios de acuerdo a las condiciones naturales de la zona donde la práctica se quiera replicar.

1.1 Ambiente natural 

  • Promedio de precipitación anual: 250 a 500 mm.
  • Altitud: 100 a 500 metro sobre el nivel del mar.
  • Pendiente: poco inclinada.
  • Forma del terreno: ladera de colina.
  • Profundidad del suelo: 50 cm a 80 cm.
  • Clima: templado/mediterráneo.
  • Textura del suelo: franco arcillosa.
  • Fertilidad del suelo: media.
  • Contenido de la materia orgánica del suelo: bajo.
  • Drenaje del suelo/infiltración: bajo. 

1.2 Ambiente social 

  • Tipo del usuario tierra: individual/comunidad; mediana/gran escala.
  • Tenencia de la tierra: comunitaria; individual con título.
  • Mecanización: Sí.

2. Construcción de zanja de infiltración (metro lineal) 

  • Las zanjas son acequias excavadas en curvas de nivel en forma transversal a la pendiente del terreno.
  • Su función es contener el escurrimiento del agua y favorecer su infiltración en el suelo.
  • Presenta una sección trapezoidal con un ancho mínimo en la boca de 50 cm y en la base de 25 cm.
  • La profundidad efectiva mínima en la cara inferior es de 40 cm.
  • La tierra excavada se coloca en el borde inferior de la zanja para darle una sobreelevación.
  • Es recomendable interrumpir la zanja con pequeños tabiques o espacios sin excavar de 15 cm a lo largo de la misma con el fin de homogeneizar la infiltración de agua. 
Figura 1. Sistema de zanjas de infiltración en el secano de la zona centro-sur a centro-norte del país (izquierda); zanja de infiltración (derecha)

©FAO/TECA

3. Impactos y resultados 

  • Los beneficios de esta práctica en la zona han sido los siguientes.

3.1 Impactos ecológicos

  • incremento de la humedad del suelo;
  • aumento de la cantidad de agua disponible para cultivos;
  • mejora de la recolección de agua;
  • incremento de la recarga de agua subterránea;
  • y aumento de la diversidad vegetal y cobertura del suelo. 

3.2 Impactos socioeconómicos

  • incremento del rendimiento de los cultivos;
  • aumento de la producción y calidad de forraje;
  • y incremento del área de producción (nuevas tierras).

4. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, húmedo/seco.
  • Subtropical, húmedo.

5. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Micro-tranque: ID 8031.
  • Mejora de la producción agrícola y optimización del uso del agua mediante la tecnificación del riego: ID 8032.
  • Construcción de lagunas, cisternas y pozos para el abastecimiento seguro de agua: ID 8349.
  • Prácticas de conservación del suelo y el agua para la reducción de la erosión del suelo y reforzar: ID 8689.

6. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

6.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Las zanjas de infiltración ayudan sosteniblemente a controlar la escorrentía al colectar el agua de lluvia, entre otras, que conduce a un incremento del rendimiento de cultivos.

6.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta práctica mitiga las consecuencias de la erosión aumentando en general la resiliencia del suelo, lo que a su vez conduce a largo plazo a una reducción de las pérdidas económicas.

entries.title: Dispositivo para atrapar enjambres
entries.source: Fundación amigos de las abejas
entries.summary: Construcciones urbanas son en reiteradas ocasiones el hogar de familias de abejas que buscan un lugar donde vivir, generando gran inquietud o malestar de los vecinos quienes en ocasiones incurren en prácticas como eliminarlas con insecticidas o tapar el orificio por el que se les ve entrando, ambas prácticas no recomendables. Mediante el empleo de este dispositivo por un apicultor capacitado, se puede extraer la totalidad de la familia sin matar ninguna abejas y de forma rápida y segura. En esta tecnología se muestra una interesante herramienta para capturar enjambres que no se encuentran de fácil acceso para ser extraídos fácilmente por el apicultor. El dispositivo se confecciona con materiales de fácil acceso y de bajo costo.
entries.description:
Descripción

  • Los enjambres naturales hoy en día no logran vivir más de un par de años en estado silvestre, ya que no encuentran muchos lugares adecuados donde estos puedan establecerse de forma segura y tranquila.
    • Para ello es necesario otorgarles un lugar donde reciban las atenciones y cuidados suficientes para desarrollarse de la mejor forma posible.
  • Esta tecnología explica cómo desarrollar un dispositivo para atrapar enjambres cuando estos se encuentren en lugares de difícil acceso.
  • El dispositivo fue desarrollado por la fundación “Amigos de las Abejas” de España.
    • El dispositivo puede ser de gran ayuda para la recuperación de enjambres en huecos pequeños.
    • Este aparato es muy fácil de fabricar y da unos resultados sorprendentes pues no mata a ninguna abeja, quedándose estas en el interior de la caja y adheridas a los cuadros.
    • Ya son varios los apicultores urbanos de diferentes localidades de España que lo han construido y usado, y han mostrado su aprobación por el dispositivo, pues presenta la ventaja de realizar un trabajo limpio y seguro para el apicultor, los vecinos y las abejas. 
    • El dispositivo presentado en las siguientes fotografías, se puede construir en poco tiempo (2 horas) y con pocos recursos. 

1. Materiales 

  • Para producir el dispositivo aspirador de enjambres se requieren los siguientes materiales: 

1.1 Una aspiradora 

Figura 1. Aspiradora

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Un cajón

  • El cajón se usa para transporte de núcleo de abejas o caja de cartón adaptada para cinco marcos con dimensiones interiores de 49 cm x 25 cm x 20 cm (Figura 2) con:
    • tres marcos adentro (dos marcos con cera estampada y un marco al centro con cera estirada);
    • una tapa adaptada con cuatro listones de maderas en diagonal 25 cm x 3 cm x 1 cm; y
    • dos listones de madera laterales 50 cm x 2 cm x 1 cm y dos listones de madera frontales 16 cm x 2 cm x 1 cm.
Figura 2. Dimensiones del cajón

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Una malla mosquetera, metálica o zapatera

  • La malla debe ser de más de siete cuerpos de la malla por pulgada para impedir el paso de abejas a la aspiradora, nunca utilizar malla raschelm, pues es elástica y resta fuerza a la aspiradora (Figura 3). 
Figura 3. Detalle de mallas adecuadas o no

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Una engrapadora 

  • Se usa para tensar y fijar la malla a los listones (oblicuos, frontales y laterales) a la tapa del dispositivo atrapa enjambres (Figura 4). 
Figura 4. Engrapadora

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Una manguera flexible 

  • La manguera debe ser extensora para llegar al orificio donde se aspiraran las abejas (Figura 5).
  • Mide de 1,5 cm a 2,5 m y tiene un diámetro de 3 cm a 5 cm. 
Figura 5. Manguera flexible

©FAO/TECA

2. Descripción del dispositivo en fotos 

2.1 La tapa 

  • La tapa (Figura 6), es la parte más importante: la malla, en el interior de la tapa, impide el paso de las abejas hacia la aspiradora.
  • Hay una cinta adhesiva sobre la malla donde acaba la boca de absorción, casi no se ve.
  • Separando con listones la malla, se consigue que el aire de absorción se distribuya por toda la tapa.
  • El orificio donde se conecta la aspiradora debe estar situado al centro de la tapa para que la absorción se realice de forma uniforme sobre todo el interior del cajón, los listones se disponen desde el orificio hasta las esquinas de la tapa para tensar la malla y generar disperción equitativa del aire que aspira las abejas. 
Figura 6. La tapa

©FAO/TECA

2.2 La caja y su interior 

  • La Figura 7 presenta la caja con sólo tres cuadros pensando para el volumen de las abejas aspiradas.
  • Los cuadros se encuentran desplazados de forma paralela hacia el lado opuesto del tubo de extensión para que las abejas entren más fácilmente y luego se agrupen en los tres marcos dispuestos dentro de la caja.
  • El orificio donde se acopla el tubo extensor se debe situar cercano a la base del cajón entre el espacio para el primer y segundo marco con el propósito de generar mejor distribución de las abejas apiradas. 
Figura 7. Caja y su interior

©FAO/TECA

2.3 El dispositivo con sus accesorios 

  • La Figura 8 es una foto del dispositivo con sus accesorios.
  • La tapa tiene que estar fuertemente pegada a la caja y sellada con varias capas de cinta adhesiva ancha para disminuir la perdida de aire. 
Figura 8. Dispositivo con sus accesorios

©FAO/TECA

2.4 El dispositivo solo 

  • La Figura 9 presenta el dispositivo solo (sin la aspiradora, ni tubo acoplado). 
Figura 9. Dispositivo solo

©FAO/TECA

2.5 Los cuadros 

  • De los tres cuadros, sólo el cuadro central es cera estirada; los laterales tienen la hoja de cera sin estirar (Figura 10).
Figura 10. Cuadros de la caja

©FAO/TECA

3. Cómo utilizar el dispositivo 

  • Este dispositivo se utiliza cuando el enjambre no se encuentra expuesto de forma que permita al apicultor introducirlo de forma íntegra en un cajón (enjambre entre tabiques de paredes, techos, etc.).
  • Para capturar el enjambre se debe buscar la apertura principal de la colmena y aspirar por este orificio a las abejas.
  • Si es posible descubrir la cámara de cría, se debe intentar visualizar la reina para introducirla en una jaula y luego introducirla a la caja.
  • Si no se logra visualizar la reina se puede extraer un trozo de panal con cría de edad maxima de larvas recién eclocionadas idealmente (o huevos recientemente puestos) para que la futura familia genere su propia reina o bien si se comprueba que la colmena está huérfana se introduce una reina pasadas mínimo 48 horas de la extracción del enjambre.
  • Generalmente estos enjambres ya se encuentran asentados, con crías y reservas de alimento, lo ideal es poder extraerles y amarrar a marcos vacíos, para luego incorporarlos a la colmena. 

4. Manejo del enjambre después de su captura 

  • Después de capturado el enjambre se debe llevar a un lugar seguro y traspasar a su cajón definitivo, este es el momento para comprobar la presencia de la reina; si no hay reina, ni cría que potencialmente puedan serlo, se debe incorporar una reina o cría reciente, además de alimento mientras la familia se adapta a su nuevo hogar.
  • Una opción para poder mantener el enjambre huérfano en su nuevo hogar es incorporándole un marco con cría reciente de otra colmena, para generar la conducta de cuidado de la cría (mediante sus feromonas) y un marco con reserva de alimento (miel y polen) para alimentar a las crías y a las abejas de la familia capturada. 

5. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Subtropical, húmedo/seco. 
  • Subtropical, húmedo. 

6. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Consideraciones para disminuir la enjambrazón y migración de abejas: ID 8923.
  • Las buenas prácticas en apicultura: ID 8675.
  • Confección trampa de saco de azúcar para captura de enjambres de abeja africanizada: ID 8662.
  • Confección de trampa de cartón para captura de enjambres de abeja africanizada: ID 8658.

7. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

7.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta práctica le da al apicultor una descripción alternativa de cómo capturar enjambres de abejas de manera eficiente.

7.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta práctica para atrapar enjambres requiere de un material relativamente barato, lo que conduce a muchos resultados positivos para el apicultor.

entries.title: Raised beds for improving crop water productivity and water efficiency in irrigated dryland agriculture
entries.source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO); International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA)
entries.summary: Irrigation is crucial for agricultural activities, however, if not managed well, it entails high water losses and can be inefficient. The raised bed system is an improved surface irrigation strategy, which enhances productivity and makes the application of water in irrigated systems more efficient. It can be easily implemented by the farmers themselves. This practice describes how raised bed systems can be used to improve crop water productivity in summer and winter crops.
entries.description:
Description

Agriculture in Egypt is mainly based upon irrigation from the Nile, but, available water resources have been reduced by over 80 percent in the last century. Additional water cannot be harvested  in the required amount because only a few major resources of renewable groundwater remain untapped. That means that new practices should be adopted to increase the on-farm water-use efficiency when irrigating crops.

Often, over-irrigation leads to the rapid degradation of soils, occurring when a crop is watered more than actually needs. Water is the limiting factor in Egypt, however the lack of knowledge on how to irrigate, when, and how long, can tremendously affect the soil fertility and lower its productivity. Consequences might be:

  • soil high salinity; it occurs when there is high evaporation in conjunction with low precipitation. The soluted salts from deeper soil layers dissolve in the irrigation water and raise to the soil surface as it is not washed away by any precipitation; and
  • waterlogging; it occurs when the irrigated water does not percolate into the soil and remains near the surface as standing water. Most crops wither due to the logged water as it prevents the plant roots from receiving enough oxygen.

1. Traditional irrigation practices in winter and summer crops in Egypt

Surface irrigation is most commonly practised in Egypt, however:

  • it entails high water losses; and
  • it is inefficient in its application.

Currently, there are two applied traditional irrigation methods for:

  • winter crops; and
  • summer crops. 

1.1 Winter crops

Usually, winter crops like wheat and berseem are planted on a random broadcasting basis. This means the seed is distributed randomly by hand or using a drilling machine.

The traditional irrigation practice is based upon a border irrigation method which can be best applied on a slope. Irrigation water is channelled from upstream downwards. The borders are long thin strips, the water flows down the slope and irrigates the surface of the crop stand. Usually the application is stopped once the water reaches the end of the border.

When using the raised bed system in winter crops, this border irrigation turns into furrow irrigation, water flows down the furrows.

The benefits of this method (see Figure 1) are:

  • reduction of irrigation time; and
  • reduction of water amount.

1.2 Summer crops

The typical summer crops are maize and cotton. Traditionally crops are planted on a ridge-furrow system, based on rows spaced 65 cm apart. Plants are seeded on the ridges, spaced 22 cm apart within each row. The furrows are 20 cm deep and the ends are blocked to prevent any water runoff from the field. The furrows are filled until the irrigation water reaches the top of the furrow ridge.

Figure 1. Traditional furrow method of planting summer crops

©FAO/TECA

2. Raised bed system

The raised bed system is an improved surface irrigation strategy, which:

  • enhances water productivity;
  • makes the application of water in irrigated systems more efficient; and
  • can be easily implemented by the farmers themselves.

In this system, irrigation water is applied to the bottom of the furrows (see Figure 2). Less water for irrigation is needed, due to the furrows collecting the water efficiently, instead of spreading it over the whole surface (border irrigation). Water can be saved because there is a less wetted area than in the traditional surface irrigation methods.

When growing winter crops (wheat, berseem), the same amount of seeds as per summer crops is applied, however those are seeded onto ridges each with four rows (see Figure 2).

Figure 2. Raised bed practice applied in wheat production

 

©FAO/TECA

In the raised bed system, the furrows are wider than in the traditional one (see Figure 3). Two furrows are merged, the width of the ridges is double the width of the traditional system.

Figure 3. Raised bed practice applied in wheat production

©FAO/TECA

In summer crops, like maize or cotton, the rows are widened to a so-called wide-furrow system. In the traditional system, there is only one plant row per ridge. The widths of the ridges are half of the size of those in the raised bed system. Instead of a one plant-row per ridge, there are usually two or more rows of plants planted on one ridge. Hence, two furrows are merged into one row, thus, there are twice as many furrows for irrigation. This method leads to:

  • half of the furrows; and
  • half of the amount of water necessary for irrigating the area, achieved by the merging of two ridges into one ridge.
Figure 4. Cotton in the wide-furrow method

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Maize in the wide-furrow method

©FAO/TECA

3. Economic and environmental benefits

Raised beds have proven to:

  • increase yields, both in winter and summer crops;
  • support the decrease of the irrigated area;
  • shorten the time needed for irrigation;
  • reduce the amount of water needed; and
  • reduce the costs of irrigation.

The water productivity (amount of crop gained per cubic metre of water) was shown to be higher and the yields increased using less water. Applying this practice can help to:

  • spend less money on irrigation;
  • achieve higher yields; and
  • increase farm income. 

3.1 Winter crops

The performance of the practice has shown to be more efficient than the traditional border irrigation practice since less water is required to irrigate the entire plot of land. Instead of spreading water throughout the entire surface of the plot, the water is applied only within the furrows, which also means less water dispersion through percolation.

  • Planting wheat on ridges enhances the aeration of the plants and leads to better growth and better yield.
  • Planting wheat on ridges ensures better use of solar radiation and more efficient use of fertilizer.
  • Ridge planting also enables to better control weeds.

3.2 Summer crops

The plant density in the raised bed system remains the same or can even be increased, because more planting space is available, due to the number of furrows halved in the system. With the raised bed technology, considerably less water is needed for irrigation compared with the traditional method. The furrows comprise the same width and depth in both systems.

Plant density is ≥ plant density in the traditional method =

less water needed
Number of furrow in raised system is 1/2 the number of furrows in the traditional method more planting space available

4. Validation of the practice

The raised bed practice has been tested in Egypt and the project described by Karrou, Oweis, Benli and Swelam, (2011) Community-Based Optimization of the Management of Scarce Water Resources in Agriculture in CWANA - Improving Water and Land Productivities in Irrigated Systems. The project was based on community participation in the research and development, testing, and adaptation of improved water management options at the farm level.

The project consisted of three main components:

  • Badia Benchmark site in Jordan, with two satellite sites in Saudi Arabia and Libya;
  • Rainfed Benchmark site in Morocco, with three satellite sites in Tunisia, Algeria and Syria; and
  • Irrigated Benchmark site in Egypt, with two satellite sites in Sudan and Iraq.

The research project was conducted between 2004-2009 by the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA)’s national programs in:

  • Jordan
  • Egypt
  • Morocco
  • Algeria
  • Tunisia
  • Syria
  • Sudan and
  • Saudi Arabia.

ICARDA’s Integrated Water and Land Management Program was responsible for the project and, together with other ICARDA programs, provided technical support for implementation.

The project was funded by the:

  • Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development (AFESD);
  • International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD);
  • OPEC Fund for International Development (OFID); and
  • International Development Research Center (IDRC).

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • subtropics, warm/mod cool. 

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Improved rainwater harvesting for fodder shrub production and livestock grazing: the Vallerani micro-catchment system in the Badia of Jordan: ID 8757.
  • Supplemental irrigation for improved water use efficiency and productivity of wheat in rain fed agriculture: ID 8758.
  • Water harvesting from concentrated runoff for irrigation purposes: ID 7512.

7. Objectives completed by the project

7.1 Women-friendly

The technology’s recommendations are easy to implement and are accessible to all. Women should play a more important role in implementing these practices.

7.2 Resource use efficiency

This practice facilitates crop cultivation and allows for efficient irrigation and soil fertility maintenance.

7.3 Pro-poor technology

This practice helps poor farmers improve their land productivity, thereby providing additional sources of food and income. It also reduces the risk of soil and water loss.
