entries.title: Establecimiento y manejo de pasturas mejoradas: la Briachiaria brizanta
entries.source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
entries.summary:
La Brachiaria brizanta es un pasto permanente y amacollado, con tallos vigorosos que alcanzan alturas de 1,5 a 2 metros. El valor nutritivo se considera entre moderado y bueno, si se compara con otras especies de Brachiarias, en relación con su palatabilidad, consumo, digestibilidad y composición química. Por eso, el objetivo de esta tecnología es que el productor tenga conocimientos sobre el establecimiento y el buen manejo del pasto mejorado Brachiaria brizanta. La tecnología explica las prácticas para la preparación del terreno, el establecimiento del pasto mediante la siembra de semillas, y la división y rotación de potreros. El objetivo final de un potrero establecido, es el de su uso como pastura o semillero. La presente tecnología da consejos sobre la capacidad de carga, que se define como el número de animales por hectárea que puede sostener un potrero. 
La tecnología está desarrollada en el Módulo de Conocimiento y Comunicación (MCC) “Establecimiento y manejo de pasturas para ganado tipo lechero” dirigida a pequeños productores, implementada en el área de Yapacaní y Norte Integrado en Bolivia. El MCC fue elaborado en el marco del Plan Nacional de Comunicación para el Desarrollo de Bolivia establecido entre el Ministerio Boliviano de Desarrollo Rural y Tierras (MDRyT), el Instituto Nacional de Innovación Agropecuaria y Forestal (INIAF) y la FAO con el apoyo del Proyecto Iniciativa de Comunicación para el Desarrollo Sostenible (ICDS).
entries.description:
Descripción

1. La Bricharia brizanta

  • La Bricharia brizanta es un pasto permanente y amacollado, con tallos vigorosos que alcanzan alturas de 1,5 a 2 metros; es resistente a la mosca pinta o salivazo.
  • Se comporta bien en suelos de buena fertilidad.
  • Aunque soporta la acidez, pero ésta no debe ser extrema.
  • Requiere de suelos bien drenados, de textura media a ligera.
  • No tolera heladas, encharcamientos, ni saturaciones prolongadas de humedad en el suelo.
  • Esta gramínea se caracteriza, además, por su buena tasa de crecimiento y por su vigor durante la época de sequía.

1.1 El valor nutritivo

  • El valor nutritivo se considera entre moderado y bueno, si se compara con otras especies de Brachiarias, en relación con su palatabilidad, consumo, digestibilidad y composición química.
  • Tiene en el contenido la proteína, el calcio, y el fósforo.

1.2 La preparación del terreno

  • La preparación del terreno empieza por la eliminación de la vegetación existente, ya sea por medio de la aplicación de herbicidas, o por medio de la quema en última instancia.
  • El objetivo de la labranza es mejorar las condiciones físicas del suelo, con el fin de obtener las condiciones adecuadas para facilitar el contacto de la semilla con el suelo y ayudar a un mejor desarrollo de la raíz.
  • La labranza convencional consiste en un pase de arado, mas dos de rastra.
    • Este método es recomendado para zonas con periodos secos estacionarios y en terrenos planos.
    • Se debe procurar que el terreno no quede muy fino sino con pequeños terrones y residuos de raíces y rastrojos, con el fin de asegurar un buen anclaje de la semilla, evitando así la pérdida de semilla por lavado y reducir la erosión.
    • Se recomienda preparar el terreno con suficiente tiempo en zonas con alta incidencia de malezas.
  • Por lo general, se debe realizar antes del inicio de la siembra, para controlar la vegetación existente.
    • En aquellos lugares donde exista exceso de humedad o encharcamiento, se debe nivelar el terreno o construir drenajes antes de la siembra.
  • El establecimiento del pasto mejorado Brachiaria brizanta se realiza mediante la siembra de semillas.
    • Un aspecto de suma importancia para obtener una buena pastura, en principio, es conseguir una semilla certificada con una germinación de un 80 por ciento y pureza de 60 por ciento, conociendo su fecha de vencimiento, origen y variedad.
    • Otro de los factores a tener en cuenta es el modo de establecimiento; en experiencias realizadas se comprobó que la mejor forma de siembra es sobre un suelo bien preparado, que asegure una buena cama de siembra.
      • También se han efectuado experiencias de siembra al voleo y rastra con cajón sembrador luego de tala, rosa y quema, donde la siembra efectuada con rastra y cajón sembrador permitió obtener una mayor densidad de plantas que la efectuada al voleo; la siembra con rastra permitió un mayor contacto de la semilla con el suelo mejorando el stand de establecimiento.
  • En general, puede decirse que la Brachiaria es una especia que se implanta mejor en suelos bien preparados que permiten un buen contacto de la semilla con el suelo y un tapado de la misma.
    • En cuanto a la siembra al voleo, con menos de 5 plantas por metro cuadrado no se pudo lograr la implantación de la pastura.
    • Es por ello que si se utiliza esta modalidad de siembra (al voleo) hay que tener en cuenta que se debe contar con semilla de excelente valor cultural e incrementar las dosis a utilizar.
    • En condiciones extensivas de campo, una preparación del suelo es indispensable para lograr una siembra exitosa.
  • A la hora de establecer nuevas pasturas es muy importante buscar aquellas especies adaptadas a los diferentes ecosistemas que sean capaces de coexistir, agredir y eliminar las poblaciones de malezas.
    • Cuando la siembra se realiza en hileras o franjas, se permite un mejor control de las malezas.
    • Cuando el complejo de malezas es de ciclo anual y con un crecimiento inicial rápido, se llega a establecer una diferencia con la especie sembrada, lo que permite el control dirigido, ya sea mediante corte, o aplicaciones de herbicidas.

2. El objetivo final de un potrero establecido

  • El objetivo final de un potrero establecido, es el de su uso como pastura o semillero.
  • Es necesario realizar un pastoreo liviano, con baja carga animal entre los tres o cuatro meses después de establecida la especie, con el fin de estimular su desarrollo radicular y de esa manera mejorar su calidad.
    • Si la especie sembrada es de la familia del Taiwán, se pueden utilizar cargas animales altas en periodos cortos, con el fin de familiarizar el enraizamiento y el rebrote a partir de las yemas o nudos en los tallos.
    • El pastoreo o el corte de uniformidad en esta etapa permite diferenciar el pasto de las malezas, facilitándose así el control de éstas, ya sea por medios mecánicos o químicos, o ambos.
    • Los establecimientos exitosos de leguminosas y pastos dependen de escoger la especie apropiada, adecuadas técnicas de preparación y manejo de suelo, métodos efectivos de siembra y, en algunos casos, del uso eficiente de fertilizantes.
  • Al escoger la especie debe dársela énfasis al uso potencial de ésta ya sea para pastoreo, corte, henificación, ensilaje, abono verde, etc., además, de otras características como facilidad y agresividad de establecimiento, palatabilidad, tolerancia a sequía, inundación, plagas y enfermedades, rendimientos sobre producción de forraje y de semilla y facilidad de erradicación.
  • La disponibilidad de semilla es un factor determinante en muchas ocasiones, sobre todo cuando se trata de cultivar nuevos pastos o leguminosas.
  • Las características inherentes de las especies, además de factores de clima y suelo, determinan las decisiones sobre densidad y época de siembra, tipo de labranza, clase de semilla, método y profundidad de siembra, además de un adecuado manejo preliminar del establecimiento.

3. Consiste en dividir toda el área

  • Consiste en dividir toda el área de una pastura en potreros de una hectárea, de manera que, mientras uno está ocupado, los demás permanecen en descanso.
  • Este sistema tiene en cuenta que el objetivo principal de la producción y utilización de los pastos es el incremento en la productividad del hato ganadero.
    • Para establecer este sistema, es importante conocer las características agronómicas y productivas de las especies forrajeras, ya que con base en éstas se define el período de ocupación y descanso para cada especie; además, es importante conocer la topografía del terreno para establecer las fuentes de agua y los comederos.
  • Entre las ventajas del pastoreo rotacional están las siguientes:
    • Las vacas caminan menos para obtener buena cantidad de alimentos.
    • Se logra quebrar, interrumpir, los ciclos de desarrollo de los parásitos.
    • Se realiza un mejor control de las malezas.
    • Se puede realizar un manejo adecuado, cuando se tiene un banco de proteínas, de gramínea-leguminosa.
    • Al rotar el ganado, dejamos recuperar los pastos para aprovecharlos cuando estén más altos y tengan un alto valor de proteínas.
    • También es fácil realizar la fertilización espaciando el mismo estiércol acumulado del ganado.
  • De ahí que es importante la rotación de potreros y lo que buscamos es el mayor aprovechamiento del pasto con el menor tiempo de ocupación y un mayor tiempo de descanso.

4. La capacidad de carga

  • La capacidad de carga se define como el número de animales por hectárea que puede sostener un potrero.
  • Se calcula dividiendo la cantidad de forraje total aprovechable, entre el periodo de descanso y el consumo de forraje diario de la vaca.
  • Para tal propósito es necesario disponer de la siguiente información:
    • Cantidad de forraje por hectárea aprovechable por corte o pastoreo.
    • Luego, calcular las pérdidas del pasto que se puedan presentar.
    • Normalmente, las pérdidas se estiman en un 30 por ciento, o sea, que sólo hay un 70 por ciento aprovechable.
    • Cantidad de alimento que puede consumir cada animal.
    • Se considera que un animal adulto consume forraje verde en promedio un 10 a 12 por ciento de su peso vivo; por ejemplo, si un animal pesa 500 kg, éste consume 50 kg de forraje por día.
    • El período de descanso y el período de pastoreo.

5. Aprovechamiento y tiempo

  • Para ello debemos considerar lo siguiente:
    • Para 30 vacas es necesario ocupar 4 días cada potrero de una hectárea, si contamos con 10 hectáreas.
    • Si hacemos rotar según lo establecido, permitimos que el pasto se recupere, ya que tendrán un descanso de 40 días.
    • Es importante destacar que cada animal necesita 40 kg de pasto y 50 o 60 litros de agua por día.
    • No se debe olvidar de la sal que debe consumir diariamente, la cual no debe faltar.

6. Otros documentos sobre la Briachiaria brizanta

  • Video sobre la Briachiaria brizanta en español
  • Video sobre la Briachiaria brizanta en quechua

7. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

8. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Reducción del riesgo durante el uso de pesticidas: ID 8354.
  • Rainwater harvesting for increased pasture production: ID 7358.
  • Enriching community pastures: ID 7686.

9. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

9.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

El establecimiento y manejo de pasturas mejoradas garantiza un alto aumento de la rentabilidad, productividad y sostenbilidad en la ganadería.

9.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta tecnología proporciona a los agricultores una descripción detallada sobre el establecimiento y el buen manejo del pasto mejorado para poder asegurar los ganados una alimentación nutritiva a largo plazo, entre otras.

entries.source: South Asia Pro Poor Livestock Policy Program (SAPPLPP)
entries.summary: Anthra, a non-profit organization working primarily on issues of livestock development in the wider context of sustainable natural resource use, worked with migratory shepherd communities in Maharashtra, India. Access to information on disease occurrence and remedial measures emerged as a constraint for shepherds on the move. Keeping in mind that many shepherds carried with them mobile phones as they migrated with their sheep in search of grazing, Anthra developed an innovative and simple SMS service to disseminate information regarding current diseases and remedial measures, including herbal and ethno-veterinary medicines that shepherds could easily access. Shepherds wishing to receive this information register their mobile numbers at the Anthra office, which thereafter sends fortnightly updates on probable seasonal diseases, symptoms, remedies and precautions that shepherds can take to prevent the out-break and spread of disease amongst their flocks. Information is sent out in the local language, making it easy for shepherds to understand and share the information among their groups.
entries.description:
Description

1. The SMS service

  • In its work with migratory shepherd communities in Maharashtra, access to information on disease occurrence and remedial measures emerged as a constraint for shepherds on the move.
  •  Keeping in mind that many shepherds carried with them mobile phones as they migrated with their sheep in search of grazing, Anthra developed an innovative and simple SMS service to disseminate information regarding current diseases and remedial measures, including herbal and ethno-veterinary medicines that shepherds could easily access.
  • Shepherds wishing to receive this information register their mobile numbers at the Anthra office, which thereafter sends fortnightly updates on:
    • probable seasonal diseases,
    • symptoms,
    • remedies, and 
    • precautions
  • Shepherds can take these into consideration, to prevent the out-break and spread of disease amongst their flocks.
  • Information is sent out in the local language, making it easy for shepherds to understand and share the information among their groups.
  • Some of the shepherds mentioned how they had stored the messages received and refer to this collated information as an easy guide.
  • They further added that they looked forward to each fortnightly information update and sharing and discussing this information.
  • For shepherds on the move, charging their mobile phones was often extremely difficult, and could only be done on cost at towns or large villages along the migratory route.
  • Anthra, facilitated access to a Pune based company manufacturing solar lights with a built-in mobile charger.
  • This served the dual purpose of providing a powerful night-light that kept predators away, and also enabled shepherds to easily recharge their mobile phones.
Figure 1. SMS for good shepherding: providing information when and where it is needed

@SAPPLPP/Anthra, Pune, Maharashtra

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • subtropics, warm/ mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Herbal de-worming for lower goat mortality: ID 7690.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology, through SMS technology, improves sheep health. This increases farmers' yields, providing increased sources of food and income.

entries.title: Herbal de-worming for lower goat mortality
entries.source: South Asia Pro Poor Livestock Policy Program (SAPPLPP)
entries.summary: The Bharatiya Agro Industries Foundation (BAIF), is a Non-Governmental Organisation (NGO) that works across 60 000 villages in 16 states of India, reaching out to over 4.5 million farmers. In BAIF’s programme area in the Dharwad district of India, high mortality among goat kids in the rainy season was reported as a major constraint by goat rearers. Following discussions with goat rearers in three villages’ of the district (Nigadi, Devarhuballi and Benkaiikatti), the high mortality was attributed to nematode infestations in both pregnant does and their kids. Members of the Kuruba community, a traditional pastoral community in the area, were reported to use a locally available herb for regular de-worming of their livestock. In collaboration with goat rearers. BAIF’s research team conducted trials to study the comparative efficacy of this herb with a commercial de-wormer Fenbenzadole.
entries.description:
Description

1. An action research study by BAIF Development Research Foundation (Dharwad, Karnataka)

  • In BAIF’s programme area in the Dharwad district of Karnataka, high mortality among goat kids in the rainy season was reported as a major constraint by goat rearers.
  • Following discussions with goat rearers in three villages’ of the district (Nigadi, Devarhuballi and Benkaiikatti), the high mortality was attributed to nematode infestations in both pregnant does and their kids.
  • Members of the Kuruba community, a traditional pastoral community in the area, were reported to use a locally available herb for regular deworming of their livestock.
  • In collaboration with goat rearers, BAIF’s research team conducted trials to study the comparative efficacy of this herb with a commercial de-wormer Fenbenzadole.
  • The herb, Mucuna Pruriens commonly known as velvet bean or cowitch, is called Nasugunni in Kannada.
    • The trichomes (hair) from the pods of this plant are used.
    • Mucuna Pruriens is a tropical legume commonly found growing wild along roads, in forest areas and on private lands. 
    • The pods occur in bunches and four to five bunches suffice to meet the requirements of a small herd of 15 to 20 goats.
  • BAIF staff, together with the goat rearers in the area, decided the dose of herb to be administered to pregnant does: 20 mg per kg of body weight.
  • It was decided to conduct trials consecutively in two years, 2000 and 2001.
  • Since mortality rates are higher for kids of does that have a heavy worm burden, it was decided to administer the de-wormers to does in late pregnancy and on the day of kidding.

1.2 The first trial, year 2000

  • Units
    • 21 farmers participated
  • Carrying out of the trial
    • Only the chemical de-wormer Fenbendazole was administered to 34 does, 15 to 30 days before kidding, while an additional 34 does form a control group and were not administered any treatment.
  • Results
    • These trials revealed that the mortality of kids, observed over a period of two months, remained as high as 18 percent in the control (un-treated) group and reduced to just 8 percent in the case of kids born to does who had been administered the chemical de-wormer.
    • The growth rate of kids born to these does was also observed to be higher.

1.3 The second trial, year 2001

  • Units
    • 18 farmers participated, the combined flock.
  • Carrying out of the trial
    • The combined flock of the farmers was divided into three groups of 26 does each.
    • Two of these groups were administered Fenbendazole and Mucuna Puriens respectively while the third group formed the control group and was not given any treatment.
  • Results
    • Unlike the first trial the mortality of kids was observed and recorded over a period of four months.
    • Additionally, goat droppings from 21 pregnant does were collected, prior to and seven days after the treatment, to test the parasitic burden.
    • The parasitical faecal egg count, for the two groups who received the treatment, had reduced significantly on the seventh day of de-worming while the parasitic burden of the control group had increased.
Table 1. Parasite egg count (N°/gm) in the faeces of research trial does
Treatment Number of samples Parasite egg count before treatment Parasite egg count after treatment
Un-treated (control group) 6 717 983
Muncuna Pruriens 7 971 271
Fenbendazole 7 757 114

Source: SAPPLPP 2012

Figure 1. Pods of the Mucuna Pruriens plant

@FAO/TECA

2. Conclusion

  • The data of the second trial revealed that the herbal anti-helminthic was as effective a dewormer as its chemical substitute.
    • For example, the birth weight and the weight gain from birth to four weeks of age were higher in case of the treated groups as compared to the control group.
    • Kid mortality from birth to four months of age was 40 percent in case of the control group and 16 and 20 percent in case of the groups administered Mucuna Pruriens and Fenbendazole respectively.
  • Additionally, the trials revealed that the does in the treatment groups had a shorter kidding interval as compared to the control group.
  • The study and subsequent discussions with goat rearers revealed that goat keepers preferred the herbal treatment over the chemical treatment.
    • They used Fenbendazole primarily on account of easy availability of the Mucuna Pruriens pods in the surrounding areas
  • Cost effectiveness was also noted, since the pods could be easily collected as compared to Fenbendazole, which needed to be purchased, and the results of the trials that demonstrated that Mucuna Pruriens was as effective as the chemical de-wormer.
  • Being a collaborative research study done in close consultation with goat rearers, it proved effective in sensitizing livestock rearers on the effective use of a locally available herb.
  • A large number of goat rearers, in addition to those who participated in the trial adopted the technology.
  • In areas where Mucuna Pruriens was not easily available, goat rearers took to administering Fenbendazole, which is indicative of farmers’ preparedness to undertake de-worming on their own.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • subtropics, warm/ mod cool.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • A study on the comparative efficacy of herbal and chemical de-wormers: ID 7689.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

Using herbal de-worming is an affordable method and helps in treating goats and reduces their mortality risk. This allows for increased size and healthier livestock, thereby providing more sources of food and income.

entries.title: Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice)
entries.source: Africa Rice Center (AfricaRice)
entries.summary: When farmers take out their seeds from storage and open the lid of the container, they may find flying insects. To confirm if the seeds have been attacked, farmers take a sample of seeds in their hands and on close observation may find holes in the seed. Insects eat the endosperm, the inside of the seed, so these seeds become light and easily float on the water. The video in the below technology shows the technique of seed flotation before sowing seeds.
entries.description:
Description

"Improving the quality of farmer seeds is very important in Bangladesh as 95 percent of farmers in Bangladesh use their own seeds."

To have a good yield, the farmer must start with a safe seed to reduce the effects of contamination by insects. The seed flotation technique is one technique used to protect the quality of the seed. Manual sorting is time-consuming, this is why flotation is a good technique especially when salt and urea will ensure higher efficiency. Click on this video to learn the technique of seed flotation before sowing the seed.

Figure 1. Rice field

©FAO/TECA

1. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropical, warm.

2. Related/associated technologies

  • Rice seedbed preparation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 6973.
  • Improving rice quality: Video from Africa Rice Center: ID 6976.
  • Rice seed sorting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7205.
  • Rice seed drying (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7211.
  • Rice seed preservation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7212.
  • Rice weed management (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7215.

3. Objectives fulfilled by the project

3.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently uses techniques which use local materials and have no negative impacts on the environment.

3.2 Pro-poor technology

Through improved seed management, the technology improves quality and quantity of crop yields. This in turn provides for additional sources of food and income.

entries.title: Scolarisation des enfants dans les zones Cotonnières "CmiA"
entries.source: GIZ - Competitive African Cotton Initiative
entries.summary: Depuis 2005, une culture durable du coton a vu le jour dans certains pays en Afrique au sud du Sahara. Le Bénin compte parmi ces pays. Cette forme de production cotonnière ayant le souci d’améliorer le revenu du producteur, de préserver son environnement et de prendre en charge l’aspect social de sa vie, a pris le nom de « Cotton made in Africa » (CmiA). Dans ce contexte, les acteurs du coton au Bénin ont conçu et mis en œuvre le projet Coton pour l’Education qui est une opportunité de promotion de la scolarisation des enfants dans les zones rurales. Il est un ensemble de mesures sociales visant à donner aux enfants leurs droits à l’éducation, à l’alimentation, à la santé et à l’épanouissement nécessaire à leur développement harmonieux.
entries.description:
La description

1. L'importance du scolarisation des enfants

  • Cette fiche technique décrit l'importance d'envoyer les enfants à l'école.
  • Nous avons deux hommes, Moussa et Ibrahim avec leurs enfants.
  • Moussa envoie son enfant à l’école pendant que Ibrahim oblige son garçon et sa fille d’aller au champ cultiver le coton. 
Figure 1a et 1b. Moussa envoie son fils à l’école pendant que Ibrahim non

©FAO/TECA

  • Moussa et Ibrahim sont des voisins au champ.
  • Cette année, le champ de coton de Moussa a beaucoup produit et celui de Ibrahim est très maigre.
  • Ibrahim se plaint auprès de Moussa et voudrait connaitre son secret. 
  • Moussa explique à son ami que c’est Issa, son fils qui lui indique comment produire du compost pour fertiliser son champ.
Figure 2. Ibrahim se plaint de son faible rendement

©FAO/TECA

  • Moussa a amené son ami Ibrahim chez lui à la maison et le présente à son fils qui vient de l’école.
  • Il a encore son sac au dos.
  • Ibrahim est étonné de voir que c’est à son petit garçon que Moussa demande de l’aider à mieux produire du coton.
Figure 3. Le fils de Moussa explique a Ibraihm comment mieux produire du coton

©FAO/TECA

  • Sur la première image (Figure 4a), après avoir creusé le trou devant servir à produire le compost, les briques tout au tour, Moussa met une couche de paille coupée en petits morceaux la paille.
  • Sur la deuxième image (Figure 4b), Moussa vérifie la température du compost.
  • Si Moussa arrive à fabriquer du compost, c’est grâce à son fils qui lui indique, à partir des fiches techniques, comment il doit produire du compost pour fertiliser son champ.
  • Seuls les enfants ayant été ou qui vont à l’école peuvent lire, écrire et compter pour aider leurs parents analphabètes.
Figure 4a et 4b. Moussa prepare le compost

©FAO/TECA

  • Sur la première image, Moussa est en train de charger sa brouette pour aller appliquer le compost sur le champ de coton.
  • Sur la deuxième image, quelques temps après, le compost est prêt pour être appliqué sur le champ;
  • Avant le labour il fait l’epandage du compost dans son champ.
Figure 5a et 5b. Moussa applique le compost sur le champ

©FAO/TECA

  • Moussa dans un premier temps est en train de faire le labour de son champ.
  • Ensuite, sur la deuxième image, il est en train de semer le coton en ligne.
Figure 6a et 6b. Moussa prepare son champ et seme le coton

©FAO/TECA

  • Au niveau de la première image, Moussa est en train d’appliquer de l’urée.
  • Sur la deuxième image, Moussa a fait une bonne récolte et s’est rendu sur le marché du coton avec sa charette.
Figure 7a et 7b. Dans la première image Moussa applique de l'urée; dans la deuxième il récolte le coton

©FAO/TECA

  • Après avoir livré une grande quantité de coton à la suite d’une très bonne récolte, Moussa est en train d’être payé par le comité de commercialisation de coton. 
Figure 8. Moussa vend son récolte a la commercialisation de coton

©FAO/TECA

  • Ibrahim a une bonne récolte et il a livré sa grande quantité de coton produit.
  • Il est en train d’etre paye par le comité de commercialisation de coton.
Figure 9. Ibrahim a également eu une bonne récolte et vendu au comité

©FAO/TECA

  • Nous voyons Moussa expliquer à Ibrahim les avantages que l’on a en envoyant ses enfants à l’école.
  • Sur un panneau en face d’eux une fille et un garçon se rendent à l’école.
  • Ensuite, quelques débouchés de l’éducation des enfants sont énumérés.
  • On voit que la fille et le garçon qui vont à l’école peuvent devenir plus tard:
    • des conseillers communaux ou députés pour décider de l’avenir et du devéloppement de leur commune et de leur pays;
    • des agents de santé (infirmière, sage femme et médecin) pour soigner les vies des populations;
    • des ingénieurs agronomes pour aider les parents comme Issa, à devélopper l’agriculture et faire des producti ons de bonnes qualités et en grandes quantités dans lescommunes et dans tous le pays; et
    • des instituteurs pour sortir les milliers d’autres enfants béninois de l’illétrisme.
  • L’enfant qui s’instruit n’est pas seulement utile pour aider son père au champ et à suivre ses récoltes.
  • Il existe de milliers autres professions qu’il pourra exercer pour son bien personnel et pour celui de sa communauté et de tout le Bénin entier.
  • Selon la convention relative aux droits des enfants, les états rendent l’éducation accessible à tous les enfants.
  • C’est pour cela que le gouvernement du Bénin, avec l’aide de ses partenaires, a rendu l’éducation gratuite pour tous les enfants au niveau primaire.
  • Pour les filles, c’est jusqu’en classe de quatrième que c’est gratuit.
  • Il n’y a donc pas de raison possible que les enfants n’aillent pas à l’école.
Figure 10. Les opportunités d'emploi possibles grâce à l'éducation

©FAO/TECA

  • Moussa continue ses explications.
  • Toujours pour un enfant de producteur de coton qui va l’école, il peut aider ses parents analphabètes à maîtriser le dosage des engrais, produits chimiques et autres méthodes de fertilisation des sols pour assurer une meilleure production du coton.
  • Pour une meilleure production cotonnière et pour le bien de toute la communauté, les enfants des paysans doivent aller à l’école.
Figure 11. L'enfant éduqué pouvait enseigner à ses parents les bonnes pratiques d'agriculture

©FAO/TECA

  • Ici il s’agit d’un enfant qu’on envoie au champ.
  • L’image montre que l’enfant est malheureux et n’est pas épanoui.
  • Un enfant qui est envoyé au champ est exposé à d’énormes risques.
    • Il peut s’intoxiquer avec les produits chimiques à la moindre inattention des adultes.
    • Il peut se faire mordre par des serpents.
    • Un enfant au champ n’est pas une garantie d’une meilleure production agricole mais un grand risque de mauvaise récolte.
    • Il est source de nombreux soucis pour ses parents.
  • Il est déconseillé d’envoyer les enfants au champ pour des travaux et remplacer la main d’oeuvre.
  • Les envoyer à l’école est le meilleur investissement.
Figure 12. Envoyer les enfants à l’école est le meilleur investissement

©FAO/TECA

  • Une délégation de CmiA a rendu visite à Ibrahim et sa famille.
  • Ils sont venus expliquer à Ibrahim les avantages liés à la scolarisation des enfants, surtout dans les zones cotonnières CmiA.
  • Un membre explique comment les enfants peuvent aussi bénéficier de fournitures scolaires sans oublier les salles de classe que CmiA construit.
Figure 13. Explication de l'importance liés à la scolarisation des enfants

©FAO/TECA

  • Après les explications de Moussa et de l’équipe de CmiA, Ibrahim s’est enfin décidé à scolariser ses enfants à son tour.
  • Il les conduit lui-même pour leur inscription.
Figure 14. L'inscription des enfants à CmiA

©FAO/TECA

  • Effectivement, quelques moments plus tard après la scolarisation des enfants de Ibrahim, la délégation de CmiA est venue inaugurer les nouvelles salles de classe et a procédé à la distribution des fournitures scolaires aux élèves.
  • Il est interdit d’envoyer les enfants au champ pour des travaux et remplacer la main d’oeuvre.
  • Les envoyer à l’école est le meilleur investissement. 
Figure 15. Distribution des fournitures scolaires aux élèves

©FAO/TECA

  • Au bout de quelques années, les enfants de Ibrahim ont grandi et ont aussi fini leurs études.
  • Imorou, le fils, est devenu ingénieur agronome et sa soeur, Zoubérath, est sortie avec un Diplôme de sage-femme.
  • Ibrahim a vieilli mais est devenu plus à l’aise.
  • Tout le monde est heureux. 
Figure 16. Ibrahim et ses enfants 

©FAO/TECA

2. Les fiches techniques associées

  • La fabrication et l’utilisation du compost dans les exploitations cotonnières: ID 7897.

3. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

3.1 L'efficacité d'utilisation des ressources

La technologie combine efficacement plusieurs mesures sociales visant à donner aux enfants leurs droits à l’éducation, à l’alimentation, à la santé et à l’épanouissement nécessaire à leur développement harmonieux.

3.2 Favorable aux populations pauvres

Grâce à l'obtention de scolarité, la technologie ouvre aux enfants plusieurs opportunités pour gagner leurs vies et de prendre soins de membres de leurs familles.

entries.title: Los insectos benéficos que controlan las plagas de algodón
entries.source: GIZ - Competitive African Cotton Initiative
entries.summary: ​Este folleto da una visión general de los insectos benéficos y no benéficos (plagas) que pueden aparecer en los campos de algodón en África occidental. El conocer las plagas y los insectos beneficiosos en el cultivo de algodón es una herramienta fundamental para la toma de decisiones para la aplicación del Manejo Integrado de Plagas (MIP).
entries.description:
Descripción

1. Presentación del folleto

  • El folleto muestra imágenes de plagas de algodón e insectos beneficiosos, sobre los cuáles los productores de algodón deben prestar atención durante la aplicación de la gestión integrada de plagas (MIP), así cómo también la relación entre cada grupo de insectos.
  • Sirve como una herramienta para la toma de decisiones cuando se aplica el concepto de umbral como parte integrada al MIP. 
  • Al utilizar el cuadernillo, las plagas y sus respectivos insectos benéficos pueden ser fácilmente identificados por los agricultores, incluso por los que son analfabetos.
  • El tamaño original del folleto es de 7,5 cm x 10 cm por lo que cabe perfectamente en los bolsillos de los agricultores.

2. Plagas de algodón

  • Las plagas del cultivo de algodón son:
    • ácaros;
    • orugas;
    • orugas carpophages spodoptera;
    • syllepte (polillas de pasto) y otras orugas que comen plantas;
    • gusanos perforadores de algodón;
    • arrebiatados;
    • jassides o mosquito verde;
    • chinche lygus;
    • míridos;
    • mosca blanca;
    • áfidos (chinches o pulgones);
    • pupas de orugas algodoneras que se mantienen en el suelo;
    • trips.

3. Insectos benéficos de algodón

  • Estos amigos de los agricultores cazan, atacan y matan a las plagas de algodón y otros cultivos.
  • Aprenda a identificarlos y a promover estos aliados naturales evitando los pesticidas de alto espectro que también matan a estos insectos benéficos, sobre todo al inicio de la temporada.
  • Utilice los pesticidas naturales que son eficaces y menos tóxicos tales como los pesticidas biológicos y extractos de plantas repelentes (tales como el neem, la hyptis, el ají o chili, el ricino, etc), así como aceites naturales y jabón.
  • Siembre líneas de girasol, caupí, maíz y de sorgo al interior y alrededor del campo de algodón.
  • Estas plantas protegen y nutren a los insectos útiles con polen y néctar.

3.1 Chrysoperla (crisopa)

  • Las ninfas crisopas son unos depredadores muy voraces y se alimentan de pulgones, trips, mosca blanca, mosquito verde, orugas devastadoras del algodón, ácaros y de los huevos y larvas en cápsula de las orugas devastadoras de algodón. 
  • La Figura 12 presenta el etapa adulto de la crisopa y la Figura 13 los diferentes etapas antes del imago: huevos y ninfa.

©GIZ

3.4 Redúvidos

  • Los redúvidos (Figura 17) son buenos para combatir: Ácaros, orugas, orugas perforadoras de algodón, arrebiatados, chinches lygus y áfidos.
Figura 17. Redúvido cazando una oruga 
 

©GIZ

3.5 Geocoris

  • Los geocoris (Figura 18) son buenos para combatir: Ácaros, orugas perforadoras de algodón, mosquitos verdes, miridos, moscas blancas y áfidos.
Figura 18. Geocoris

  • Los sírfidos (Figura 19) son buenos para combatir: Ácaros, orugas perforadoras de algodón, moscas blancas, áfidos y trips.
Figura 19. Sírfido
 

©GIZ

  • Las hormigas (Figura 20) son buenas para combatir: Orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras orugas filófagas y orugas perforadoras de algodón.
Figura 20. Hormiga atacando una oruga

  • Las arañas (Figura 21) son buenas para combatir: Orugas perforadoras de algodón, mosquitos verdes, miridos y áfidos.

©GIZ

  • Las mantodeas (Figura 22) son buenas para combatir: Orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras orugas filófagas, orugas perforadoras de algodón y arrebiatados.

  • Las libélulas (Figura 23) son buenas para combatir: Orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras orugas filófagas, orugas perforadoras de algodón, arrebiatados y miridos.

  • Las tijeretas (Figura 24) son buenos para combatir: Orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras orugas filófagas y orugas perforadoras de algodón.
Figura 24. Tijeretas

  • Los nabidaes (Figura 25) son buenos para combatir: Orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras arugas filófagas y orugas perforadoras de algodón.

  • Las avispas depredadoras y parasitarias (Figura 26) son buenas para combatir: Mosca blanca, chinche lygus, miridos, áfidos, orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras orugas filófagas y orugas perforadoras de algodón.

4. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.
  • Subtropical, húmedo.

5. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Cotton cultivation with laser levelling, ridge sowing, Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and compost application under drought conditions: ID 10016.
  • Management of cotton bollworns using predators ants: ID 4337.
  • Cotton culture: ID 6901.

La tecnología también está disponible en francés: ID 8668 y en inglés: ID 8677.

6. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

6.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

La tecnología aumenta el conocimiento sobre insectos benéficos y plagas. Esto permite una aplicación más eficaz del Manejo Integrado de Plagas, con impactos beneficiosos sobre el medio ambiente y la calidad de los cultivos.

entries.title: ​Dried meat techniques: examples from different regions​
entries.source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
entries.summary: Drying meat under natural temperatures, humidity and circulation of the air, including direct influence of sun rays, is the oldest method of meat preservation. However, various methods, typical for different regions, exist to produce dried meat with or without additional treatment. The following examples of dried meat techniques are part of FAO's publication: Manual on simple methods of meat preservation, which is mainly intended to disseminate information on traditional methods of meat preservation and addresses aspects of hygienic slaughtering under rural conditions in Africa.
entries.description:
Description

1. ​Techniques in different parts of the world​

There are different techniques for drying meat in various parts of the world. The following technology presents six techniques.

1.1 ​Odka (Somalia and other East African countries)​

  • Odka is of major importance to nomads in Somalia and it is a sun-dried meat product made of:
    • lean beef.
  • In the face of perennial incidence of drought in the Horn of Africa, odka has become important since it is often prepared from drought-stricken livestock.
  • The production of odka is similar to the simple drying technique described in TECA (Simple techniques for dried meat production: methods of suspending meat: ID 4071). However, the meat strips cut for drying are bigger and dry salting is usually applied instead of brine salting.
  • After only four to six hours' sun drying the large pieces of meat are:
    • cut into smaller strips; and
    • cooked in oil.
  • After this heat treatment, drying is continued and finally, sauces and spices are added.
  • For storage, odka is again covered with oil. It has a shelf-life of more than 12 months if kept in a tightly closed container.

1.2 ​Qwanta (Ethiopia and other East African countries)​

  • Qwanta is manufactured from:
    • lean muscles of beef.
  • Further sliced into long strips ranging from 20 cm to 40 cm and are hung over a wire in the kitchen to dry for 24 to 36 hours.
  • Prior to drying, the strips are coated with a sauce containing a mixture of:
    • salt (25 percent);
    • hot chilli pepper (50 percent); and
    • aromatic seasoning substances (25 percent).
  • After air drying the meat pieces may be:
    • further exposed to light wood smoke;
    • fried in butter fat; and
    • dried again to some extent.
  • At this stage, the product is ready for consumption or storage.

1.3 ​Kilishi (Nigeria and other arid or semi-arid zones of West Africa)​

  • Kilishi is a product obtained from sliced lean muscles of either:
    • beef
    • goat
    • lamb.
  • It is made on a large scale under the hot and dry weather conditions prevailing from February to May.
  • It is produced by sun-drying thin slices of meat. However, recent experience indicates that kilishi can also be produced industrially using tray-drying in a warm air oven.
  • Connective tissue and adhering fatty material are trimmed off the meat which is cut with a curved knife into thin slices of about 0.5 cm thickness, 15 cm length and as much as 6 cm width. 
  • Traditionally, the slices of meat are spread on:
    • papyrus mats on elevated platforms; or
    • tables in the sun for drying.
  • Papyrus mats may lead to hygienic problems, especially after repeated use. Easily washable corrosion-free wire nets or plastic nets are recommended for horizontal drying.
  • The vertical drying method is also recommended in this case.
  • Sun-drying of kilishi could also be improved by using solar dryers. These devices will increase the rate of drying of the product, keep insects and dust from the product. Some of these technologies are described in TECA (see section 2 of related technologies for reference). 
  • In the first stage of drying, which takes two to six hours, the moisture of the meat slices has to be reduced to about 40 to 50 percent.
  • The slices are then put into an infusion containing:
    • defatted wet groundnut cake paste; or
    • soybean flour as the main component (about 50 percent), in addition to:
    • water (30 percent);
    • garlic (10 percent);
    • bouillon cubes (5 percent);
    • salt (2 percent); and
    • spices such as pepper, ginger and onion.
  • The dried slices of meat should absorb the infusion up to almost three times their weight. 
  • After infusion, the wet product is again exposed to the sun to dry.
  • Drying at this stage is much faster than at the first stage. Moisture content of the slices needs to be reduced to 20 to 30 percent, taking two to three hours depending on weather conditions and dimensions of the product.
  • Finally the slices are roasted over a glowing fire for about five minutes. This process helps to:
    • enhance desirable flavour development; and
    • inactivate contaminating microrganisms.
  • Roasted kilishi is therefore superior in flavour to the unroasted version.
  • After roasting, the final moisture content ranges between 10 to 12 percent. It will decrease during storage at room temperature to a level as low as 7 percent.
  • When packaged in hermetically sealed, a low-density plastic bag, the product remains remarkably stable at room temperature for a period of about one year.

1.4 ​Biltong (Southern African countries)​

  • Biltong is a well-known salted, dried meat prepared from:
    • beef or
    • antilope.
  • Most muscles in the carcass may be used but the largest are the most suitable.
  • The finest biltong with the best flavour is made from the sirloin strip and the tenderest is derived from the fillet. 
    The meat is cut into long strips (1 cm to 2 cm thick) and placed in brine, or dry-salted, which is actually the most popular method.
  • The principal ingredients used are:
    • common salt, preferably coarse salt (1 kg to 2 kg for 50 kg of meat); or
    • salt and pepper; and
    • other ingredients such as:
    • sugar
    • coriander
    • aniseed
    • garlic
    • other spices (included in some mixtures to improve flavour).
  • To achieve a red colour and typical flavour of cured meat, in most cases, the following is also added:
    • nitrate or
    • nitrite
  • The addition of 0.1 percent potassium sorbate to the raw meat is permitted in South Africa as a preservative.
  • The salt/spice mixture is rubbed into the meat by hand and the salted strips are then transferred to a suitable container.
  • It is recommended that a little vinegar be sprinkled on each firmly packed layer in the container. 
    Biltong is left in the curing brine for several hours, but not longer than 12 hours (otherwise it will be too salty), and then dipped into a mixture of hot water and vinegar (approximately 10:1).
  • The biltong is now ready for sun drying for one day.
  • Then the strips are moved into the shade for the rest of the drying period.
  • The product is usually not smoked, but if it is smoked only light cold smoking is recommended, which takes one to two weeks with sufficient air circulation.
  • The biltong is ready when:
    • the inside is soft, moist and red in colour; and
    • reaches a hard brown outer layer. 
  • Biltong is sold in sticks or slices.
  • The usual shelf-life is several months without refrigeration and packaging, but in airtight packages the product stores well for more than one year.
  • Biltong is not heated during processing or before consumption.
  • It is eaten raw and considered a delicacy.

1.5 ​Pastirma (Turkey, Egypt, Armenia)​

  • Pastirma is salted and dried meat from:
    • beef of not too young animals; or
    • camel (used in some areas).
  • The meat is taken from the hindquarters and is cut into 50 cm to 60 cm long strips with a diameter of not more than 5 cm.
  • The strips are rubbed and covered with salt and nitrate:
    • The dosage of the nitrate in relation to the meat is 0.02 percent, that means 2 gr of nitrate for 10 kg of meat.
  • Several incisions are made in the meat to facilitate salt penetration. 
  • The salted meat strips are arranged in piles about 1 m high and kept for one day at room temperature. They are turned over, salted again, and stored in piles for another day.
  • The meat strips are then washed and air-dried for two to three days in summer and for 15 to 20 days in winter.
  • After drying, the strips are piled up again to a height of 30 cm and pressed with heavy weights (approximately 1 tonne) for 12 hours.
  • After another drying period of two to three days, the meat pieces are again pressed for 12 hours.
  • Finally, the meat is again air-dried for 5 to 10 days. 
  • After the salting and drying process, the entire surface of the meat is covered with a layer (3 mm to 5 mm thick) of a paste called cemen, which consists of:
    • freshly ground garlic (35 percent);
    • helba (20 percent);
    • hot red paprika (6 percent);
    • mustard (2 percent); and
    • water (37 percent).
  • Helba is used as a binder of the paste; the other ingredients are spices, but garlic is the most important as it is antimycotic.
  • The meat strips covered with cemen are stored in piles for one day, and are then dried for 5 to 12 days in a room with good air ventilation, after which the pastirma is ready for sale.
  • Pastirma production requires several weeks.
    • However, not much energy is required since most of the salting and drying is done at room temperature.
      The final product has an average water activity of 0.88. The salt content should range between 4.5 and 6.0 percent.
  • The product is mould-free for months at ambient temperature even in summer.
  • Pastirma thus has a better microbiological stability than biltong.

1.6 ​Charque (Brazil and other South American countries)​

  • Charque consists of flat pieces preserved by salting and drying of:
    • beef.
  • The fresh, raw meat from the fore-and hindquarters is cut into large pieces of about 5 kg, which should not be more than 5 cm thick.
  • The pieces are submerged in a saturated salt solution for about one hour in barrels or cement vats.
  • On removal from the brine, the meat is laid on slats or racks above the brine tank to drain. 
  • For dry salting, the flat meat pieces are piled on a sloping, grooved, concrete floor under a roof.
  • To form a pile:
    • a layer of salt of about 1 cm is spread evenly over the floor;
    • a layer of meat is then laid on the salt;
    • the meat is covered with another layer of salt (1 cm), another layer of meat is then added, and so on until the
    • alternate layers of salt and meat reach a height of about 1 m.
  • The pile is then covered with a few wooden planks and pressed with heavy stones. After eight hours, the pile is restacked so that the top meat goes to the bottom of the pile.
  • The re-stacking process with fresh layers of salt is repeated every day for five days. 
  • The salted meat is then ready for drying.
  • Before initiating drying, the meat pieces are subjected to rapid washing to remove excess salt adhering to the surface.
  • The meat pieces may also be passed through a pair of wooden rollers or a special press to squeeze out some surplus moisture and flatten the meat slabs.
  • The meat is then spread out on:
    • bamboo slats; or
    • loosely woven fibre mats in a shed.
  • In industrial production, the meat is exposed to the sun on wooden rails that are oriented north-south, thus permitting an even solar coverage. 
  • Initial drying, directly in the sun, is limited to a maximum period of four to six hours. This period of exposure may be subsequently lengthened to a maximum of eight hours.
  • Temperatures in excess of 40° C on the meat surface should be avoided.
  • To ensure even drying over the extended muscle pieces, the meat is placed on the rails during the morning and removed again in the afternoon.
  • The meat pieces are exposed to the sun each day over a period of four to five days.
  • After each period of exposure, the pieces are collected, stacked in piles on concrete slabs and covered with an impermeable cloth to protect them against rain and wind and to hold the heat absorbed. 
  • When sufficiently dry, the meat pieces are either sold without prior packaging or wrapped in jute sacks.
  • Plastic sacks are not suitable, as the product still contains a certain proportion of its original moisture content and should be allowed to drain freely from the product.
  • The usual charque shelf-life is several months under ambient room conditions and is resistant to infestation by insects and growth of moulds. 
Figure 1. ​Whole strips and flat pieces of dried meat and dried meat comminute to fragments of different sizes for preparing meals

​

©FAO/TECA

2. Related/associated technologies

  • Simple techniques for production of dried meat: ID 4069.
  • Technique of cutting meat pieces for drying: ID 4070.
  • Simple techniques for dried meat production: methods of suspending meat: ID 4071.
  • Simple methods of meat preservation: meat dryers: ID 4072.

3. Objectives fulfilled by the project

3.1 Women-friendly

This technology can be applied by women as well as men.

3.2 Resource use efficiency

This technology allows for preserving meat which is a popular market product and can be consumed over a longer period.

3.3 Pro-poor technology

This technology helps farmers ensure improved food conservation and food security. It also offers a new marketing opportunity and reduces production losses.

entries.title: Draught animal power technologies in East Africa
entries.source: UK Department For International Development (DFID) & Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
entries.summary: The technology was developed in collaboration with farmers in the Teso farming system of Uganda. It comprises of the development of appropriate animal-drawn implements, primarily for weeding but also for ridging (sweet potatoes), line planting and lifting (groundnuts). These implements are now being manufactured locally. Impact assessments showed that adoption of the technologies and techniques increases gross margins (2005), contributes to increased yields and reduces drudgery, which is of particular importance to women and children who were previously responsible for providing most of the weeding labour.
entries.description:
Description

If left to grow, weeds will compete with crops for nutrients, moisture and light resulting in typical reductions in crop yield of 30 percent. For over 250 000 households in the Teso farming system of northern Uganda, the situation has been made even worse. HIV has reduced the number of people available for agricultural labour. Furthermore, civil disruption in the 1980s and 1990s has led to a shortage of animals for draught power. Women and children mainly undertake the toil of weeding, thereby restricting women’s involvement in other activities and keeping children away from school. Cereal crop yields (finger millet and sorghum) in the Teso farming system have stagnated at below one 500 kg per ha, despite the increasing availability of high-yielding varieties. Continuous cropping, changes in crop rotations have led to a heavy build-up of mainly annual grass weeds, especially Eleusine and Setaria and difficult perennial weeds such as Digitaria spp. and Imperata cylindrica.

1. ​Key approaches to intervention​

  • Allowing rural communities to prioritize their problems before embarking on research and/or extension (undertake a Needs Assessment).
  • Providing a range of options and allowing farmers to determine which technology best meets their needs.
  • Developing links with the private sector for post-project sustainability, including continued manufacturing involvement, production and promotion.
  • Encouraging the exchange of information between farmers (farmer-to-farmer extension).
  • Developing partnerships and training trainers (with those organizations that are likely to continue to be active for the foreseeable future).

2. ​Research findings​

  • At least 85 weed species are present in the system, of which two-thirds are annual broadleaves and one-sixth are annual grasses.
    • This weed characterization enabled rigorous testing of a number of different weeders.
  • Judged solely in terms of weed control, there was a little difference between the weeders tested on-station and on-farm.
  • DAP weeders were a practical and effective alternative to hand - hoe weeding.
    • The preferred models were the plough without mouldboard, SAARI and SG2000.
    • Of these, the favourite was the SAARI type weeder (bolted to the existing plough frame).
  • It was possible to adapt the weeders to perform ridging, planning and groundnut lifting.
  • The capital required for investment in DAP weeding is zero for those farmers (the majority) who have access to oxen and ploughs.
  • For further details see the Technical Reports by (Barton and Obou 2002) Part 1, Part 2 and (Obou and Barton 2006).

2.1 ​Impact​

  • In sorghum fields, DAP reduced the time spent hand weeding from 157 to 34 hour per hectare (although it does not increase yields). 
  • In groundnut fields, DAP reduces labour inputs and increased yields as it improves infiltration and reduces run-off of rainwater.
  • Ridging reduces labour costs to a fifth.

3. ​Promotion​

  • It is very important for farmers to be aware of this technology, how much it will cost and where they can obtain it.
    • The main issue concerned with the promotion of this technology is the production of the weeder.
    • Although initially two companies were involved in its manufacture in Uganda, by March 2005 there was only one manufacturer, SAIMMCO, located in Soroti.
    • They are manufacturing a simplified SAARI weeder design, the one identified by farmers as best meeting their needs.
    • In December 2005, the price of these weeder attachments was around USh 80 000 (Ugandan Shillings) as a bolted attachment to existing (and widely owned) plough frame, or as a standalone machine (which is more expensive – around USh 250 000/-).
    • This is considered to be affordable by many farmers.
    • However, those that are unable to find this amount can easily share the tool with neighbours.
  • As DAP weeding is a relatively rapid task, one tool can easily meet the weeding needs of five or six households.
    • Marketing of DAP equipment represents a serious challenge for the manufacturers as they have limited contacts with the agricultural community.
    • Also, decision making at SAIMMCO is controlled centrally by the Alam Group of companies (owners of SAIMMCO) that limits investment in a marketing strategy and has led to dependence on large government and NGO orders for the business.
    • A farmer-marketing agent system was established whereby prominent farmers in those communities that had received training and extension were selected as agents for manufacturers’ products.
    • The objective of this activity was to facilitate access to weeders by the farming community while at the same time assisting the manufacturer’s business development.
    • Agents are therefore intermediaries and should receive a commission on sales.
    • To date, this system has promoted DAP weeding to 3 000 farmers.
    • Hiring services for DAP weeding are arising similar to those already in existence for ploughing.
  • It has been very important to promote knowledge from this research.
    • A leaflet: Weed management with draught oxen in Teso by (OBOU 2003) presents a simple guide to the use of DAP weeding.
    • Manuals and posters have been developed in English, Ateso and Kumam by Serere Agricultural and Animal Production Research Station in Soroti, Uganda.
    • These were distributed to trainers of trainers, CBOs, NGOs (Action Aid, Self Help Development International-Uganda, SOCADIDO, Church of Uganda-Soroti Diocese, SG2000, TERUDO, Christian Children’s Fund, Tugende Omumaiso-Rural Development Programme of Hoima Catholic Diocese, Pentecostal Assemblies of God and CIDI), NAADS, farmer field schools or groups, schools and Local Governments (at sub-counties) and Government extension workers.
    • There is a high demand for these DAP extension materials both within and outside the Teso Farming System.
    • A manual outlining the use of DAP technology in cotton production (with an emphasis on mechanical weeding) was also produced (NRI/NARO 2006).
  • In addition, training has been provided to 879 NGO-based trainers and farmer trainers.
    • They should be able to train others if the necessary support can be provided through existing NGOs, NAADS service providers and local governments.
    • There is, therefore, scope to begin the process of promoting the technology in other parts of the Teso Farming System as the benefits are both clear and measurable to farmers, and adoption is likely to be relatively rapid.

3.1 ​Impact​

  • An impact assessment using a participatory farm management technique known as Participatory Budgets (PBs) was conducted in 2004.
    • The technique encourages farmers to cost all inputs and outputs and to produce a simple budget including a balance (gross margin) for a single enterprise.
    • The technique can be used to explore before and after scenarios to assess the impact of new technology or changes to the management of an enterprise.
    • Both family labour and draught animal power costs (including hire charges) were included in the budgets (at the request of participants).
    • Although the individuals whose enterprises were explored during the participatory exercise all owned oxen, DAP costs were included at the request of other members of the group who did not own oxen and need therefore to hire them to undertake ploughing and weeding operations. 
  • For each PB and each site, cash balances are higher for enterprises where DAP is used for weeding.
    • The participants attributed this to the lower costs associated with DAP weeding (when compared with hand weeding), and the higher yields that result from DAP weeded crops (improved infiltration of rainwater following mechanical weeding).
    • DAP weeding increases infiltration of rainwater but also allows more timely and efficient weeding which may also improve yields (when compared with poorly weeded fields).

4. ​Beneficiaries of this research​

  • The major beneficiaries of this research have been the farming families (2 472 households) who have been trained and have adopted DAP technology.
  • There are many benefits.
    • Reduced drudgery for women and children particularly those who formerly undertook weeding, heaping (ridging) of sweet potatoes and groundnut lifting.
    • Less withdrawal from school of children during the weeding season.
    • Expansion in the area cultivated in many cases, and enhanced food security and increased incomes.
    • Farmer adaptation has been observed in several locations with the use of a plough (minus its mouldboard) for the lifting of cassava.
      • This suggests that the research and extension process has assisted farmers to begin their own innovations with the DAP equipment.
  • The impact assessment concluded that the introduction of DAP technologies has had the following impact on livelihoods.
    • It has made women feel less oppressed and men have become involved in this task as it is mechanized.
    • It has greatly reduced drudgery.
    • It has improved food security and led to higher incomes. 
    • Women are now able to pursue more rewarding activities and are experiencing a better quality of life.
    • Children are no longer withdrawn from school during the weeding seasons (April–May and October–November).
  • It is anticipated that in the longer - term even the poorest of economically active households will benefit from mechanization as hire markets developed for DAP services (weeding, groundnut lifting and potato ridging) already exist for ploughing, and to a limited extent weeding.

5. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm. 

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour saving technologies and practices: Draught Animal Power (DAP) planters and weeders: ID 7305.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: draught animal power and implements: ID 7306.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: draught Animal Powered and motorised crop processing: ID 7307.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: draught animal powered groundnut lifter: ID 7309.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: manual and motorised cleaning of grains and pulses: ID 7310.
  • Improving the productivity of draught animal power in sub-Saharan Africa: ID 4467.
  • Development of tools for draught animals: ID 4483.

7. Objectives fulfilled  by the project 

7.1 Labour-saving technology

The technology allows for reduced drudgery, especially for women and children.

7.2 Women-friendly

Thanks to this technology, women are able to pursue more rewarding activities and experience a better quality of life.

7.3 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently uses animal-drawn implements for weeding, ridging, line planting and lifting. 

7.4 Pro poor technology

The technology allows for cultivation expansion, enhances food security and increases incomes.

entries.title: Rice seed preservation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice)
entries.source: Africa Rice Center (AfricaRice)
entries.summary: Based on hard real-life experience, the women of the Maria village have devised some very effective techniques for seed preservation. The video describes the importance of storing seeds in airtight containers, using insecticidal plants and other clever practices that Bangladeshi women apply to preserve rice seeds. This video presents the technique of seed preservation.
entries.description:
Description

This video, as a part of other video series, presents the technique of seed preservation. It is essential to preserve the seeds for sowing the following year. Women in Bangladesh are responsible for storing and preserving the seeds. They are also responsible for determining the good quality seeds prior to preserving.

This video presents the main steps to innovative and cost-effective methods for seed preservation. 

The main steps can be summarized.

  1. Select healthy pannicles.
  2. Choose and store only clean and healthy seeds. 
  3. In parallel, clean, wash and effectively dry the container as shown in the video. 
  4. Fully fill the container until the top of the container with seeds. If not available, fill the extra space with dried sand, or puffed rice. The important thing is that there is no extra space for air. 
  5. Completely seal the container to make it airtight. One method is to seal the container with clay. 
  6. Add some natural insecticides such as dried neem and tobacco leaves. This will help control insects during storage.
  7. Paint the outer and inner parts of the container with tar or used cooking oil to keep it airtight.

It is important to keep in mind that a "properly preserved seed is a good seed and the good seed is a good crop". 

Figure 1. Women in Maria village preparing the barrel for seed preservation

©RDA-Bogra/TMSS

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Rice seed sorting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7205.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7210.
  • Rice seed drying (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7211.
  • Rice transplanting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7214.
  • Rice weed management (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7215.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Women-friendly

The technology allows for a more active role of female communities in agricultural production. 

4.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently uses a series of methods of storage, plant usage and other means for effective seed preservation.

4.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology, through seed preservation, leads to greater quantity and quality crop yields. This in turn provides for additional sources of food and income.

entries.title: The most serious sweet potato diseases in sub-Saharan Africa
entries.source: International Potato Center (CIP)
entries.summary: This practice describes the most common diseases attacking sweet potato in sub-Saharan Africa. It will help the farmers to identify them and to treat the plants.
entries.description:
Description

1. ​Viruses​

  • Viruses are the most damaging group of disease organisms affecting sweet potato in Africa.
  • Viruses are amongst the smallest organisms known and can only be seen using a very powerful electron microscope.
  • They are very simple organisms and can only survive and multiply inside their hosts/victims.
  • Most also need to be carried from plant to plant, usually by an insect that feeds on plant sap, such as aphids or whiteflies.
  • Once a virus enters a cell in the body of its host, it will take over part of the management of the cell’s processes, and force the cell to produce more viruses identical to itself rather than the crop yield we want.
  • These new virus particles then spread through the plant to infect more cells.

1.1 ​Common symptoms of virus infection in plants including sweet potato​

  • Diminished growth so the plants and leaves remain small (stunted).
  • Chlorosis (paleness, even whitening; aidosoikit) of the leaf tissue.
    • This chlorosis may be general or in a pattern, often either between the leaf veins in a mosaic or less well-defined mottle, or along the veins to form a chlorotic network.
  • Misshapen leaves with an uneven or curled appearance.
  • Pigmented leaves, often purple or yellow generally or in spots or rings.
  • Reduced production of sweet potato storage roots. 
  • Viruses affecting sweet potato can be spread by the use of foliar cuttings taken from infected plants.
    • They are also transmitted from plant to plant by sap-sucking aphid and whitefly insects.
Figure ​1​. ​Sweet Potato Virus Disease (SPVD) affected plant​

​​

©​FAO/TECA

2. ​Sweet Potato Feathery Mottle Virus (SPFMV) and Sweet Potato Chorotic Stunt Virus (SPCSV)​

  • Sweet Potato Feathery Mottle Virus (SPFMV) and Sweet Potato Chorotic Stunt Virus (SPCSV) are together the most important viruses affecting sweet potato in Africa.
  • By themselves, sweet potato viruses may cause only mild or no obvious symptoms.
  • However, plants can be infected by more than one type of virus.
    • When this happens, the viruses may help each other to multiply with the result that the disease is more severe than expected.
  • The combination of SPCSV and SPFMV is known as Sweet Potato Virus Disease (SPVD) and is the most important disease of sweet potato in Africa.
  • SPFMV is transmitted by a wide range of aphid species (eiliana) and is spread mainly by winged adults, even of species that do not colonise sweet potato, flying from plant to plant.
  • SPCSV is transmitted by the mobile adult form of white flies (ekwanga), especially Bemisia tabaci, as they fly from plant to plant.
  • Since it is the spread of SPCSV by white flies that synergizes SPFMV, whiteflies are also usually the driving force behind the spread of SPVD.
  • Neither disease is spread by insects over very long distances.
  • Because viruses spread quickly through the vascular system of a plant to infect the whole plant, any portions of an infected plant that are used as planting materials (vines or roots), are almost always diseased themselves.
  • This then carries the disease to the next generation of plants.
  • Thus, it is important to follow specific steps. 
    • Make sure cuttings are collected for planting new sweet potato crops from healthy plants and if possible from healthy plants in crops in which few other plants have the disease.
      • Then there is also less chance of taking cuttings from plants that have just been infected.
      • It may be better to avoid collecting cuttings from very old crops both because SPVD may have built up in these crops and because SPVD is less easy to see in old plants that in vigorously growing crops.
    • Remove and burn or feed to livestock any diseased plants as soon as they appear in young crops.
      • Plants infected when young wouldn’t have yielded much anyway.
      • The neighbouring plants will soon fill up the space and you can replant cuttings if you wish in young crops.
    • Avoid planting new crops where you grew sweet potato last season.
      • Roots and cuttings from old diseased plants surviving in the soil will produce diseased plants from which infection will easily spread to your new crop.
    • Plant your new crop away from old crops, so it is difficult for whiteflies and aphids to reach your new crop.
      • Other forms of crop hygiene are:  ensuring that the vines and leaves from harvested crops are completely destroyed (they can be fed to livestock); and that all the roots (especially the small ones which may come from diseased plants) are destroyed.
  • However, often the best and certainly the most convenient means of controlling SPVD is to plant varieties of sweet potato which have resistance to virus diseases.
  • All these management practices work better if they are done on areas as large as possible.
    • If communities can work together to manage SPVD they will all benefit.
    • The crop hygiene you do to control sweet potato viruses probably also helps control other pests and diseases.

3. ​Fungal pathogens causing diseases of the leaves and vines​

3.1 ​Alternaria​

  • The fungus survives in the soil and in plant remains.
    • The airborne spores are spread through: infected planting material; wind; splashing rain and water.
    • During the rains the increased humidity often leads to high levels of infection.
    • The disease incidence and lesion (iboconoreta) size increase in wetter, high altitude areas.
  • The disease is first observed as small, brown/grey/black oval lesions with a typical bulls’ eye appearance of concentric rings, on leaves, stems and petioles.
    • On the lower side of the leaf, blackened veins are observed.
    • As the disease progresses, the lesions become necrotic usually surrounded by a wide yellow halo.
    • Soon after the whole blade turns chlorotic and drops.
    • Vine bases and middle sections are more affected than tips.
    • Death of vines can occur.
    • The ground under affected vines is often covered with blackened leaf debris.
  • Good sanitation practices are the main management strategies for this disease.
    • Infected crop material should be destroyed and burnt.
    • Clean planting materials should be used.
    • New crops of sweet potato should not be planted in fields which have recently had a sweet potato crop grown in them.
  • Some varieties of sweet potato are more susceptible to Alternaria disease than others.
    • You could try planting different varieties to see which are more resistant.
    • In other crops fungicides are used against Alternaria diseases.
      • However there is no information about using fungicides to control the disease in sweet potato.
Figure ​2​. ​Alternaria infected sweet potato vine​ 


​​ ​ 
©​FAO/TECA

3.2 ​Root rots​

  • Several fungi and bacteria cause root rots.
  • Once rotting starts it cannot be stopped.
  • Infected plants must be destroyed to prevent further spread of the disease.
  • Planting material should not be obtained from fields where there are many rotten roots.
  • Since the fungi and bacteria that cause root rots can survive in the soil for a long time, sweet potato should be planted in rotation with other crops in order to avoid a build-up of disease.
  • Cuttings should be taken from vine sections that have not been in contact with the soil.

3.2.1. ​Black rot (Ceratocystis fimbriata)​

  • Black rot (Ceratocystis fimbriata) is a dry root caused by a fungus.
  • Sunken grayish-black lesions/areas form on the surface of the storage root.
  • A smell of alcohol like that of fermenting fruit is often present.
  • In severe infections, yellowing, wilting, stunting and death of affected plants can occur.
  • The disease can also be serious on young vines and adult plants.
  • Infected vines develop black sunken necrotic lesions or cankers at the point of attachment to the mother root.
  • Bacteria also cause root rots, disease transmission routes and management strategies are similar to those of black rot.
  • On storage roots, small brown lesions with black margins can be observed on the surface, but more frequently the rotting is internal with no signs of it outside.
  • Affected tissue becomes watery.
  • There is often a strange smell produced in infected tissues.
Figure ​3​. ​Black rot symptoms on roots​

​​​

©​FAO/TECA

Figure ​4​. ​Bacterial rot on roots​ 

©​FAO/TECA

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Production of orange-fleshed sweet potato: ID 4373.
  • Working with farmers to control sweet potato virus disease in East Africa: ID 4557.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology allows for the identification and treatment of sweet potato diseases. This leads to an improvement of quality and quantity of sweet potato yield, thereby providing poor farmers with more secure sources of income and food.
