entries.title: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) in vegetable production: a guide for extension workers in West Africa
entries.source: Technical Centre for Agricultural and Rural Cooperation (CTA)
entries.summary: Indigenous and exotic vegetables are central to most nutrition, food security and poverty reduction programmes around the world. However, in most of West Africa, the economic opportunities offered by vegetables are often undermined by production and trade constraints (e.g. pest damage, inappropriate pesticide usage, absence of environmental safeguard policies and/or stringent food safety standards). Extension workers and, in some places, farmers groups and local community organizations, are working towards helping farmers to increase their yields in sustainable ways that create wealth and reduce the risks to productivity. This guide is been developed by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) and Institut National des Recherches Agricoles du Bénin (INRAB), Cotonou, Benin, with support from the CGIAR Systemwide Program on Integrated Pest Management (SP-IPM), to improve the quality and usefulness of pest management research.
entries.description:
Description

Vegetables are important components of daily diets in Africa and important sources of income, especially in urban and peri-urban areas. As many as twenty different types of indigenous and exotic vegetables are grown at major vegetable production sites around West Africa. These crops provide a cheap source of proteins, vitamins and other elements essential for human health and wellbeing. In West Africa, vegetables are commonly grown in the rainfed upland ecologies and in lowland ecologies such as bolilands, riverine grasslands and inland valley swamps. Agroecosystems in these various ecologies offer great opportunities for commercial production of vegetables in West Africa.

Vegetable production for urban and peri-urban areas in West Africa is popular in rainfed upland ecologies. Rainfed upland ecologies occur on hillsides, usually above rainy season, either by direct seeding or transplanting of seedlings. They are frequently intercropped with other staple food crops (e.g. rice), or planted as sole crops following the harvest of any other crop. Commercial farmers use irrigation systems that allow year-round production in upland ecologies, while smallholder farmers rely on rain and soil water to water their seasonally-grown crops. 

Bolilands are large pan-like depressions of land which are naturally flooded by rainwater and freshwater streams. The soil is often clay loam with silt deposits and usually has a large amount of humus on the surface. The vegetation is dominated by grasses. In bolilands, rice is planted either by direct seeding just before the soil is flooded in the rainy season, or by transplanting after the soil is flooded. Vegetables are planted on small mounds left on the bolilands after the rice is harvested at the end of the rainy season. 

Inland valley swamps are flooded by overflow from freshwater rivers or streams and rainwater runoff from surrounding hills. The intensity of flooding depends on the duration of the rainfall, the season and on the type of topography. The water level can be artificially controlled so vegetables can be grown on the bunds which separate the plots of rice in these swamps. 

Riverine grasslands are alluvial plains which run along the lower parts and mouths of freshwater rivers, and tend to be flooded to significant depths during the rainy season. The natural vegetation is dominated by grasses. The rice plants which are transplanted before flooding grow as floating plants in the waterlogged conditions. In the months prior to flooding, these alluvial plains are important vegetable production sites.

1. ​Vegetable agroecosystems​

  • Vegetable agroecosystems comprise a dynamic mix of biotic (living) components, abiotic (non-living) components and the interactions within and between them.
  • Any change in one component or interaction is likely to affect another component or interaction.
  • The reactions of agroecosystems to change can potentially be disastrous to farming communities, and may not be entirely predictable.
  • In order to achieve good vegetable pest management, the vital components of agroecosystems should be correctly identified, their interrelationships fully understood, and the agroecosystem treated as a functional unit.
Figure ​1​. ​Components of vegetable agroecosystems​ 


​​
Source: CTA 2010

Figure ​2​. ​Irrigation at a peri-urban vegetable site in Benin
​​ ​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​3​. ​Predatory mite (left) on a pest mite (right) called a phyoseiid ​​

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​4​. Aphid Lipaphis erysimi, a cabbage pest

​​

©​IITA/B.James

2. Crop types​

  • The vegetable plant is the central component of the agroecosystem. Vegetables can be grouped according to the part of the plant that is consumed and/or sold. 
  • Leafy vegetables
    • The common leafy vegetables grown in West Africa are the African garden eggplant, amaranth, cabbage and lettuce.
    • There are two common types of African garden eggplant, which are both indigenous to Africa. One is Solanum macrocarpon (Figure 5), whilst the other is S. aethiopicum. Solanum macrocarpon is grown mainly for its succulent leaves, but in some communities the bitter fruits are also eaten. S. aethiopicum is mainly cultivated for its fruits.
      • The edible parts of both S. macrocarpon and S. aethiopicum are nutritious and contain carbohydrate, cellulose and calcium, fat, protein and water. 
    • Amaranth, Amaranthus cruentus (Figure 6), is grown for its leaves which are rich in beta-carotene, calcium, iron, protein, vitamin C and water.
    • Cabbage, Brassica oleracea (Figure 7), is native to temperate regions of the world.
      • It is called the head cabbage because the immature leaves cluster up into a spherical ball or ‘head’, which is the part normally marketed and consumed.
      • The leaves contain some carbohydrates, proteins and various essential elements e.g. calcium, iron and vitamin C as well as water.
    • Lettuce, Lactuca sativa (Figure 8), is indigenous to the Mediterranean region and occurs in four groups of varieties.
      • The plant is cultivated for its succulent leaves which are used in salads.
      • Lettuce leaves contain a high proportion of water with some calcium, proteins and vitamins.
  • Fruit vegetables 
    • The most popular fruit vegetables grown in West Africa are the tomato, pepper and aubergine.
    • Tomato, Lycopersicum esculentum (Figure 9), which originates from the Andes in South America, is grown for its fruits.
      • The shape of the fruit differs according to the variety.
      • Tomato fruits can be consumed raw or cooked.
      • Tomato fruits contain a lot of water with calcium, carbohydrate, carotene, iron, niacin, riboflavin, thiamine, protein and vitamins. 
    • The sweet pepper or pepper, Capsicum annuum (Figure 10), is native to Central America.
      • It occurs in two groups of varieties.
      • Unlike most vegetables, pepper is a relatively long duration crop.
      • Both immature and fully mature fruits are marketed and consumed.
      • The fruit contains plenty of water with some carbohydrates, protein, minerals and vitamin C.
  • Root vegetables 
    • Carrot, Daucus carota (Figure 11), a crop native to Asia, is the most common root vegetable grown across West Africa.
    • It is cultivated for its swollen roots, which are rich in beta-carotene.
    • The roots also contain a large amount of water as well as carbohydrates, minerals and protein.
Figure 5. The African garden eggplant, a leafy vegetable 

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​6​. ​Amaranth, a leafy vegetable

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​7​. ​Cabbage, a leafy vegetable ​

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​8​. ​Lettuce, a leafy vegetable ​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​9​. ​Tomato, a fruit vegetable​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​10​. ​Pepper, a fruit vegetable​

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​11​. ​Carrot, a root vegetable​

©​IITA/B.James

3.  ​Vegetable plant production​

  • Depending on market demand and availability of water to irrigate plots, vegetables can be grown all year round.
  • The crops are grown in monocrops, intercrops and crop rotation schemes.
  • Commercial production sites are commonly located near to markets, e.g. in urban and peri-urban areas. 
    • Crop yield
      • Depending on the vegetable crop type, the leaves, fruits, and roots constitute the yield and provide both food and income to farmers.
      • Field workers and farmers need to be aware of two different types of yield in order to fully understand the purpose of crop production and pest management measures.
      • The two types of yield are maximum or potential attainable yield and actual yield. 
    • The maximum attainable yield is the yield obtained from crops grown in experimental plots and field conditions with the full use of improved technologies and inputs.
      • It is the highest yield possible from a particular variety cultivated under the ideal conditions. 
    • The actual yield is the yield obtained from crops cultivated under farmers’ conditions using the same varieties used in experimental plots.
      • Actual yields are often less than attainable yields. 
    • The difference between attainable and actual yield is due to a variety of environmental factors which include soil type, crop variety, agronomic practices, weather and pests.
      • Agricultural research, extension and training activities aim to find ways to increase actual yields towards attainable yields, for example by manipulating field and environmental factors that reduce yields.
      • The overall objective of vegetable pest management is, therefore, to prevent, reduce and maintain the effect of pests at levels where they cease to act as constraints to the achievement of higher actual yields.
      • It is in this way that pest management interventions ‘increase’ yields.

4. ​Land and seed bed preparation​

  • The most suitable sites for vegetable production are flat and sunny areas with light, well-drained soil which is rich in humus and not prone to waterlogging.
  • These conditions help to promote the establishment of good nurseries and seedling health for excellent vegetable crop growth.
  • Farmers break and loosen up the soil by ploughing, and remove stones and debris to allow sufficient aeration, moistening and drainage of the soil.
  • This promotes good root growth.
  • Removal of plant debris also helps to limit the occurrence of weeds and other pests that are carried over from the previous season.
  • Vegetables are often planted on flat land in areas that are unlikely to be waterlogged or flooded.
  • Planting on flat land is also common where the soil is rich in nutrients.
  • In areas that are likely to be waterlogged, or where the soil is poor in nutrients, farmers heap the topsoil into mounds or ridges on which they plant vegetables.
  • The mounds of soil raised above ground level are commonly referred to as "beds".

5. ​Planting​

  • Except for exotic vegetables, (e.g. beetroot, cabbage, carrot, cucumber and lettuce), most farmers produce their own vegetable seeds from their fields or they collect seeds from other farmers’ fields.
  • Large-scale farmers do not self-supply and buy certified seeds from seed companies and national seed services.
  • Vegetables are planted by direct sowing of seeds (e.g. amaranth and carrot) or by transplanting seedlings from nurseries (e.g. African garden eggplant, cabbage, lettuce and tomato).
  • In direct sowing, seeds are broadcast on seed beds and harrowed in, or sprinkled in rows and covered up with soil, and left undisturbed to germinate.
  • In transplanting, farmers select vigorous and disease-free seedlings at the right growth stage and transplant them.
  • If the crop is harvested by uprooting of whole plants (e.g. in amaranth, carrot and radish), the seedlings are usually transplanted closer to each other than when the crop will be harvested by ratooning.
  • Planting dates are usually adjusted in response to market demands e.g. in readiness for festive seasons.
  • Planting during the peak of the rainy seasons is uncommon so as to avoid flooding of vegetable beds.

6. ​Intercropping​

  • Farmers frequently intercrop vegetables on the same bed.
  • A single bed can hold as many as five different vegetables.
  • Intercrops can be economically more profitable than sole crop vegetables.
  • Intercropping increases farmers’ income per unit of land and labour and helps to maintain good soil moisture and reduce the incidence of weeds and other pests on vegetables.

7. ​Crop rotation​

  • Crop rotation enables farmers to maintain land under continuous cultivation by planting with one crop after another in successive seasons.
  • The practice also helps farmers respond to seasonal market demands for certain crops.
  • Where a rotation crop is a non-host plant of a pest that damaged a previous crop, crop rotation helps to control that pest by breaking its life cycle.
  • Good knowledge of crop susceptibility to pests is therefore essential in the use of crop rotation for pest management.
  • This is particularly the case with species of root-knot nematodes that attack a wide range of vegetables including the most economically important crops grown in many localities.
  • The wide range of host plants of the root-knot nematode makes it difficult to identify suitable crop rotation schemes for this pest, especially at sites under year-round vegetable production.

8. ​Soil fertility​

  • Soils nourish vegetables with mineral nutrients for vigorous, succulent and healthy growth.
    • However continuous production of vegetables can deplete soil nutrients at production sites.
    • Vegetable farmers use organic and mineral fertilizers to help soils to recover from nutrient losses, and in some cases, reduce pest problems.
    • Both organic (composed of decayed plant/animal material), and inorganic fertilizers (composed of chemicals and minerals), improve soil fertility by adding nutrients to the soil and are used in a number of different ways. 
  • Mulching, for example, involves mixing plant materials into the soil during land preparation or covering the bases and rows of the crops with dry grass or plastic sheets after planting.
    • Dry grass or plastic sheets serve as physical barriers between the soil and the environment so the plant residues rot into the soil and increase its organic matter content.
    • Plant foliage mixed into the soil help conserve moisture, suppress weeds and reduce the spread of plant pathogen spores onto vegetable foliage through water or soil splashes. 
  • Farmers use farmyard manure or humus from the compost of plant residues as organic fertilizers.
    • They avoid scorching the plants by first thoroughly mixing the farmyard manure with soil or water.
    • Where soils are poor, leafy vegetables such as African garden eggplant, amaranth, cabbage, and lettuce will require additional levels of nitrogen and potassium (provided by inorganic fertilizers).
    • High levels of nitrogen delay the onset of flowering and thereby favours leaf production. 

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour saving technologies and practices: Integrated Pest Management (IPM): ID 7798.
  • Vegetable cultivation with ridge sowing, farm yard manure, multi-cropping and Integrated Pest Management (IPM): 10014. 
  • Cotton cultivation with laser levelling, ridge sowing, Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and compost application under drought conditions: ID 10016. 
  • Soil fertility for sustainable vegetable production: green and animal manures in the humid forest belt: ID 4525.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

10.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently provides guidance on effective pest management in terms of land preparation, seed preparation, planting, intercropping, crop rotation, and soil fertility. This not only improves crop quality but is also beneficial to the environment.

10.2 Pro-poor technology

This technology increases farmer yields in sustainable ways that create wealth and reduce productivity risks.

entries.title: Bonnes pratiques d’utilisation des pesticides
entries.source: GIZ - Competitive African Cotton Initiative
entries.summary:
La technologie a été conçue au Benin par le projet ‘Programme de Promotion de l’Agriculture (ProAgri, Bénin), dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre du programme COMPACI, chargé de la promotion du secteur cotonnier en Afrique. La  présente technologie illustre les bonnes pratiques de gestion intégrée des pesticides. 

La boîte explique les étapes à suivre pour l’établissement d’une parcelle, les précautions à suivre lors du transport, le stockage, et l’utilisation des substances utilisées pour le traitement. 
Elle explique également: 
les dispositions à prendre depuis le point de vente jusqu’à la destruction des vieux emballages, 
les lieux de stockage, 
les facteurs à considérer lors de la sélection des parcelles à cultiver, 
les équipements à utiliser lors des traitements, 
la préparations de la bouillie de traitement,
les personnes autorisées à préparer et à appliquer le traitement, 
les bonnes pratiques à observer lors des traitements, 
les habitudes à éviter lors des traitements, l’entretien des équipements après les traitements, et 
les soins à apporter à une victime en cas d’intoxication.
entries.description:
La description

1. Recommandations pour une bonne utilisation des pesticides

1.1 Choix et aménagement de la parcelle à traiter

  • Sur la parcelle choisie, les lignes de semis (des sillons) doivent être orientées perpendiculairement aux vents dominants.
    • Cette disposition permet d’une part une meilleure couverture des plants par le brouillard du pesticide lors des traitements et d’autre part assure la sécurité de l’applicateur lors de son mouvement, pour qu’il ne soit pas mouillé par le produit en cours de pulvérisation.
  • Sur une pente, les lignes des semis doivent être perpendiculaires à la pente.
    • Les exploitations doivent être éloignées des cours d’eau pour éviter que les produits chimiques (les pesticides) ne souillent ces cours d’eau (Figure 1).
    • Il est recommandé que le champ se situe à au moins 2.5 km du cours d’eau. 
Figure 1. Les lignes de semis sont perpendiculaires à la pente et au sens du vent. Le champ est assez éloigné du cours d'eau

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Transport des pesticides

  • La technologie conseille le transport des produits dans un véhicule adapté à ce propos comme des bâchés, des pickups ou des camions (Figure 2). 
    • Des pictogrammes indiquant le transport des produits chimiques doivent être affichés sur le camion en cas de transport d’une grande quantité et le camion doit rouler à vitesse raisonnable pour éviter tout accident de circulation.
    • Le transport des produits dans une voiture de commerce avec les passagers et d’autres produits de consommation (produits vivriers) à bord est prohibé pour éviter les risques de contamination.
      • Ces risques peuvent couter des vies humaines.
    • Le transport peut être aussi fait sur un vélo ou une moto avec les produits disposés dans un carton et bien attachés derrière le vélo ou la moto.
Figure 2. Illustration des précautions à prendre pour le transport de pesticides

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Stockage des pesticides

  • Une fois arrivé à destination, ces produits doivent être stockés dans des magasins répondant aux normes en vigueurs et construits à cet effet (Figure 3).
    • Ces magasins doivent être construits dans des endroits isolés des habitations et bien aérés.
    • Ils doivent également se munir de deux portes et des claustras ou des aspirateurs favorisant ainsi l’aération.
    • Des pictogrammes indiquant panneaux-danger et défense de fumer doivent être affichés sur les portes (barricadées à double clés) des magasins.
  • Les produits doivent être stockés sur les planchettes et de façon à respecter la condition (premier à entrer, premier à sortir).
    • Ces précautions sont nécessaires pour éviter que les enfants s’y introduisent et pour alerter les passagers à tous risques éventuels.
    • Il est aussi déconseillé de stocker les produits dans des habitations sous le lit et à même le sol. 
Figure 3. Les pesticides doivent être stockés à l'abri, dans des bâtiments adaptés, sécurisés et signalisés

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Choix des pesticides

  • Lors du choix des produits, il faut lire attentivement les étiquettes/emballages des produits pour s’assurer du choix du produit approprié pour le traitement en question.
  • Les pictogrammes (icones/insignes) figurant sur le produit sont indicateurs des caractéristiques de chaque produit.
Figure 4. Le choix des pesticides se fait après avoir pris connaissance des étiquettes

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Port d'un équipement de protection

  • La technologie recommande aussi les équipements de protection individuelle à porter avant les traitements (Figure 5).
    • Une paire de botte
    • Un pantalon
    • Une chemise à manches longues
    • Une paire de gants aux mains
    • Un masque de protection du nez et de la bouche
    • Une paire de lunettes étanches
    • Une casquette
  • Il est vivement interdit d’effectuer les traitements le torse nu ou avec les équipements troués, fendus ou cassés car dans ces conditions les risques d’intoxication sont très élevés.
  • Il s’avère indispensable de vérifier les équipements avant de procéder au traitement.
Figure 5. L'utilisation de pesticides requiert le port d'équipements adaptés

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Respect du matériel et des conseils pratiques pour le traitement

  • La buse, l’état des piles, la moteur et la tuyauterie sont à vérifier afin d’éviter toute surprise lors du traitement (Figure 6). 
  • La préparation de la bouillie (Figure 7) doit se faire de préférence dans le champ, loin des cours d’eau, et sur un lieu enherbé selon les indications décrites dans la technologie.
  • Des matériaux appropriés (un seau ou un bol doseur; de l’eau de bonne qualité; et des produits phytosanitaires appropriés sélection conformément au traitement) doivent être disponibles sur les lieux de préparation.
  • Il est vivement conseillé de respecter les doses des liquides composant la bouillie et secouer vigoureusement le mélange pour assurer l’homogénéité de la bouillie et s’assurer de tout utiliser.
  • Avant de passer à l’application du traitement, la technologie préconise le respect des conseils pratiques à une bonne application des traitements.
    • La direction du vent en érigeant une girouette à base d’un foulard et d'un piquet, ou le déversement lent de sable fin et sec ou de cendre à une hauteur d’un mètre environ du sol (Figure 8).
  • La préparation et l’application des traitements par les mineurs, les femmes enceintes ou allaitantes, les vieillards et toutes personnes malades ou très allergiques aux produits chimiques sont déconseillées.
  • La technologie décourage les traitements en temps de très fort ensoleillement, de vents violents, ou de pluie, pour éviter le dessèchement ou le lessivage des produits des plants.
  • Il est aussi prohibé de manger, de fumer, de boire, de discuter ou de déboucher la buse par la bouche en cas d’obstruction.
Figure 6. Vérification de la buse du pulvérisateur au champ

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Préparation de la bouillie

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Test de la direction du vent

©FAO/TECA

2. Recommandations après avoir utilisé des pesticides

2.1 Nettoyage du matériel

  • Il est avantageux de procéder à la vidange tout autour du champ à dose fortement diluée avec l’eau jusqu’à rincer proprement la nourrisse sur le champ (Figure 9).
  • Il est défendu d’entretenir les appareils de traitement dans des cours d’eau pour éviter l’intoxication de ces cours d’eau.
  • Les eaux de rinçage doivent être épandues sur la zone où a lieu le traitement.
Figure 9. Nettoyage du matériel à l'eau claire dans le champ

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Gestion des emballages et contenants vides

  • Après le traitement, il s’avère indispensable de procéder à une bonne gestion/destruction des emballages vides.
  • Il est strictement prohibé d’utiliser les emballages vides pour le conditionnement des boissons de toute sorte.
  • Il faut les détruire avec les machettes et les enterrer dans un endroit caché et loin des cours d’eau (Figure 10).
  • Ne pas les laisser à la portée des enfants ou des vieillards.
Figure 10. Destruction des emballages et enfouissement en lieu sûr, éloigné des cours d'eau

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Nettoyage de son corps et vêtements

  • L’applicateur est encouragé d'observer à la lettre les étapes à suivre pour se défaire de ses habits de protection individuelle après les traitements et de prendre un bain à l’eau savonnée, loin d’un cours d’eau (Figure 11).
Figure 11. Une bonne hygiène personnelle est indispensable après traitement avec pesticides

©FAO/TECA

3. En cas d'intoxication

  • En cas d’intoxication accidentelle, veuillez apporter à la victime les premiers soins prodigués dans la technologie.
    • Éloigner la victime du lieu d’intoxication.
    • Priver la de manger et de boire jusqu’à ce qu’elle ne se sente mieux.
    • La coucher doucement sur le dos.
    • La déshabiller et la laver à l’eau savonneuse.
    • L’aider à regagner ses sens et la conduire au centre de santé le plus proche avec les références du produit source de l’intoxication.
Figure 12. Illustration des bons gestes en cas d'intoxication aux pesticides

©FAO/TECA

4. Les zones agro-écologiques

  • Les tropiques, chaud.

5. Les technologies associées/relatives

  • Réduction des risques liés à l’utilisation de pesticides: ID 8353.

6. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

6.1 Favorable aux femmes

La technologie est facile à utiliser et accessible à tous.

6.2 L’efficacité d’utilisation des ressources

Les bonnes pratiques agricoles d’utilisation des pesticides permet à une meilleure préparation et la disposition préalable de l’espace à exploiter.

6.3 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvres

Meilleure qualité de produits, nourriture plus saine.

entries.title: Water management in the mountain: Kuhl irrigation
entries.source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
entries.summary: In mountain areas, water continues to be a scarce commodity not only for irrigation purposes but even for drinking and other domestic uses. These challenges are encountered very frequently in India. These difficulties are present, inspite of the fact that important rivers namely the Sutlez, Beas, Ravi and their tributaries originate from hill regions. Existing water resources are further declining due to heavy biotic pressure and lack of resource management. Most agricultural/horticultural activities are carried out under rainfed conditions. They require proper management of available water to be conserved during dry periods. In hill regions, the scope of boring tube-wells, canals and lift irrigation is limited. Such facilities are confined to the low laying areas. Therefore, the most common source of irrigation remains small water channels, locally called Kuhls. If intact, these sources account for 85.83 percent of the total area under irrigation in Indian hill regions. Providing an infrastructure that allows water harvesting and distribution is important to help farmers maintaining sustainable crop production and increase their resilience against risks created by water shortages. Ensuring adequate crop yield through irrigation is a very important component of the Kuhl irrigation agro-system.
entries.description:
Description

1. Irrigation water in India

1.1 Sources of irrigation water

  • In hill regions, the scope of boring tube-wells, canals and lift irrigation is limited.
    • Such facilities are confined to the low laying areas.
    • Therefore, the most common source of irrigation remains small water channels, locally called Kuhls.
    • These sources, if intact, account for 85.83 percent of the total area under irrigation in Indian hill regions. (Figure 1).
  • In cold deserts, some villages get their irrigation water for their lands from some perennial torrents.
    • In the Spiti valley, the source of irrigation water is generally local nallas, a kind of ravine.
    • Glacial water in cold deserts of Himachal Pradesh, which forms the prime source of sustaining life in the region, is brought to the field by making Kuhls, a type of water channel.
  • In Kinnaur and other regions, the source of irrigation and drinking water is melting snow on the high peaks.
    • This sourceruns downward in the shape of small and big nallahas (streams) and also springs out at certain points. 
Figure 1. Irrigation channel

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Construction of kuhls (water channels)

  • In cold deserts of Himachal Pradesh, kuhls (water channels) are built along the hill gradient to maintain the correct gravity for irrigation (Figure 2).
    • Kuhls are commonly found in West Himalayan cold deserts.
    • The technique for the preparation of kuhls for irrigation purposes seems to have originated since Babylonian times.
    • It is still one of the most common ways of bringing water to crops.
    • If the river has a steep gradient, water is diverted into a canal some distance upstream and led along a contour so that it can flow to fields naturally by gravity.
Figure 2. Open channel

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Wooden water channel

  • In dry temperate zones, kuhls (wooden water channels) are generally made by making notches at the natural water sources.
    • The water is diverted to the fields for irrigation to different terraces, using the natural gravitational flow of water (Figure 3).
    • Since the topography of the area consists of very high slopes and rocky terrains, wooden water channels are used at many points as water passes from one place to another.
    • The water channels are built and managed by the villagers with no government assistance.
    • In the lower areas of Himachal Pradesh,  bamboo pipes are commonly used as irrigation channels on depressions orsmall nallas (Figure 4).
  • In west Himalayan cold deserts, for the optimum harnessing of water for irrigation, water channels are constructed along the natural gradients.
    • The irrigation channels (kuhls) are diverted from river tributaries by making use of the natural gradients.
    • As a result, the level of water is higher than that of the cultivated fields.
Figure 3. Wooden water channel

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Bamboo pipe for irrigation water flow

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Bamboo pipe

  • This method is commonly used for irrigation water flow on depressions/smallnala from one field/terrace to another.
  • In upper Kinnaur, the channels (kuhls) are simply dug in the ground to regulate the flow of water.
    • However, where the digging of channels is difficult or the channel has to pass through a village path, underground channels covered with slates are constructed.
    • In some parts wooden channels may also used.
    • These are constructed like a bridge over the path.
    • These channels are made by making a deep grove in the tree trunk or a thick branch.

2. Distribution of kuhl water in fields

  • In the cold deserts of Himachal Pradesh, participatory management is employed for the distribution of water.
    • All disputes regarding the distribution of water through kuhls (water channels) are amicably settled without hampering the water requirement of any period.
    • In the West Himalayan cold deserts, all the irrigation channels (kuhls) cannot be run satisfactorily due to non availability of sufficient water from nallas and khads.
    • This is because little snowfall occurs during the winter months.
    • The majority of hamlets, which lie on the plateaus on the sides of the mainriver, get water from the streams.
    • The streamstrickle down from the cliffs overhanging the plateaus.
    • These hamlets are the worst off for water.
    • Within a year of scanty snowfall, streams dwindle quickly and dry up by the beginning of August.
    • Additional snowfall in winter results in less water in natural springs during the season.
    • Less snowfall in winter results in the reduction of natural spring level during summer.
    • Consequently, crops suffer.
  • Kuhls are a time-tested community-made type of water channel, creaed for sharing glacial water to ensure efficient irrigation in otherwise dry and porous soils.
    • In the Spiti valley, farmers have developed this irrigation water distribution system based on their land holdings, in which every field is irrigated on a timely basis.
    • As a result, there is no dispute regarding the maintenance of kuhls and irrigation water distribution.
  • In Kinnaur and other regions, nallas passing through a village are harvested on a turn basis called pala.
    • Temporary channels are dug by farmers towards their fields.
    • The whole community is divided on the basis of number of farm families.
    • One family gets one full water day to irrigate their fields turnwise.
    • For example, if there are 20 farm families in a village, the turn falls after every 20 days.
    • Two adjoining families may share the water for half a day each when it is the turn of oneof the two families.
    • In this way these two families get a chance to irrigate their fields every ten days rather than 20 days.
    • As a result, the distribution of water is so well-managed that maximum use of water takes place in a particular village.
    • The turn of a family starts around 20:00 to 22.00 hours on a particular day and all the members of the family are engaged in the job on its turn.
  • In upper Kinnaur, the irrigation technique is much more pronounced.
    • The fields are generally divided into small compartments by making earth bunds.
    • This allows thewater to stand in the field for a longer duration in order to saturate the soil (Figure 5).
    • Consequently, the need for a second irrigation arises only after 20 to 25 days, even in those agricultural crops which otherwise require irrigation after a gap of 10 to 15 days.
    • At the first turn of irrigation, the first compartment is irrigated; followed by the second and so on.

On the second turn of irrigation, however these compartments are irrigated in reverse orde.

For example, the sixth compartment is irrigated first followed by fifth and so on.

Figure 5. Irrigation water application

©FAO/TECA

3.1 Irrigation water distribution

  • In the entire Spiti valley, the first irrigation is done 40 days after crop sowing takes place during April.
    • In the initial stage of watering from the kuhl to field, women bring water to the field through the use of an urma, which is made from animals horn.
    • As per the turn,the Baraghar watering/irrigation is done by constructing small beds in the fields.
    • This method is time consuming and laborious.
    • On the other hand this method checks the loss of nutrients by leaching.
    • Uniform watering of the plants with equal flow checks the nutrient loss from field to field and from one bed to another.
    • In Ladakh and other regions a standardized irrigation schedule for different crops is followed.
  • The "Gep Chu", or the fourth irrigation, depends on the colour status of the crop.
    • If crop seems yellow in colour, "Gep Chu" is delayed.
    • However, if the colour position is blackish, "Gep Chu" is hastened.
    • Farmers develope irrigation schedules matching the stages of crop growth.
    • Irrigation during critical stages, therefore results in the maximization of crop yield as well as water use efficiency.
Figure 6. Irrigation water distribution

©FAO/TECA

Table 1. General schedule
Irrigation number Stage of crop growth
Local name English name
I Tol Chu Germintation
II Sak Chu Growing
III Non Chu Flowering
IV Gep Chu Seed seltting
V Do Chu Crop ready for harvest

Source: FAO 2002

3. Use of kuhl water for running water mills

  • Kuhls are built along the hill gradient for maintaining proper gravity for irrigation and running water mills (Figure 7a/b).
    • Wooden water channels are also used for running water-flour mills.
    • These wooden channels are generally made by making notches at the natural water sources and the water is diverted to the water mill, using the natural gravitational flow of water.
    • Since the topography of the area consists of very high slopes and rocky terrains, wooden water channels are used at many points as water passes from one place to another.
  • Granite stones are used for grinding food grains.
    • A long wooden channel, placed at steep gradient is used for maintaining the high speed of the water flow.
    • This is necessary for maintaining the high speed of the water mills wheel (Figure 7a/b).
  • Nowadays water mills are very rare.
    • Water mill technology is at an extinct stage, because of power supply availability and less grain production.
    • Food is purchased from cooperative societies or private shops nowadays.
Figure 7a. Water mill outside

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7b. Water mill inside

©FAO/TECA

4. Methods of irrigation
 
4.1 Flooding of glacial water for higher crop productivity

  • In most Himalayan cold deserts water is brought in channels from glacial melts for irrigating the fields.
    • Flooding the fields with the glacial water for improving crop productivity is also common.
  • The deposition of fresh silt with unweathered minerals (especially lime) forms a glacier source of fresh salts.
    • The glacier melted water is often below 2°C, which protects crops from different kinds of diseases.

4.2 Indigenous drip irrigation

  • Pitcher water is used as a source of irrigation on new fruit plantation in sandy loam/loamy sand soils, in areas of canty rainfall
    • This practice is prevalent in temperate districts of Himachal Pradesh.
    • The pitcher is placed in the soil and the new plant is planted close to it.
    • The pitcher is filled with water during summer months (April to June) and a stone/slate lid is placed on the top.
  • The roots draw moisture/water from pitcher which in turn reduces the crop mortality.
    • The pitcher, once filled, supplies sufficient moisture for at least two weeks and then it is filled again with water.

4.3 Bamboo drip irrigation system

  • In this system of irrigation, open bamboo channels are used for irrigating fields (Figure 8).
    • This system is common in the North-East regions of India.
    • Small holes are made at the internodes of open bamboo channels, from where water trickles down in the field.
    • These channels are placed along the natural gradients.
    • In these channels, no uniform head for water trickling is maintained.
Figure 8. Bamboo drip irrigation system

©FAO/TECA

4.4 Manual irrigation in vegetables

  • In the initial stage of watering vegetables, people bring water to their fields with the help of buckets (Figure 9).
    • In the Spiti valley, womenbring water to their fields using an urma, which is made from animals horn.
    • In this method after bringing water in buckets, water is supplied to the vegetables with the help of a lota (a mug).
    • In the case of using an urma, irrigation is done by constructing small beds in the fields.
    • However,this method is too laborious and time consuming.
Figure 9. Hand watering in vegetables

©FAO/TECA

5. Water harvesting methods
 
5.1 Small ponds for spring water collection

  • Another method is the collection of spring water in small reservoirs scattered at intervals on the high uplands and then drawing water from these ponds when required (Figures 10a, b and c).
    • This is a common practice in cold deserts and the temperate wet Himalayas.
    • Water from these ponds is used for irrigating crops and also for drinking purposes.
Figure 10a. Well planned spring irrigation water distribution in field

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10b. Village spring water pond for drinking water

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10c. A tank of spring water 'Bawri

©FAO/TECA

6. Harvesting of dew and fog water

  • In plains and in valleys, the occurrence of dew and "pale" is very common after the receding of the monsoon season.
    • After the monsoon season, the humidity remains quite high (85 percent) in the atmosphere.
    • During night time, temperature falls down sharply resulting in the formation of more water molecules.
    • As these molecules are heavier, they fall on soil surface and make the layer moist and wet.
  • In the hills, there is traditional practice to plough the fields early in the morning before dew or fog water is evaporated.
    • By ploughing, moisture is mixed with soil particles in the plough layer (e.g. 23 cm to 30 cm).
    • This moisture is well retained by soil.
    • If soil is clayey in nature, retention of water remains for a longer time and becomes a source of soil moisture.
    • It is quite useful for land preparation in October-November and for the sowing of rabi crops like wheat, barley and pulses.

7. Roof water harvesting

  • In the lower areas of Himachal Pradesh during the rainy season, roof water is collected in dugout structures;
    • These are known as "diggi" in the Kangra district and '"Khati" in the Hamirpur and Bilaspur districts (Figure 11).
    • These structures are dug in hard rocks.
    • Not only roof water but also surface water is collected in these dugout structures. 
Figure 11. Water harvesting in dugout structure called 'khati' or 'diggi''

©FAO/TECA

8. Harvesting of rain water

  • In the hills, rains are erratic and torrential.
    • A relatively high percentage of rainwater leaves as run-off and stream flow.
    • It carries fertile soil and plant nutrients, which degrades the soil degraded and makes it barren.
    • In some areas this excess water is stored directly in the farm ponds, depression or stream flow or it is diverted to safer points where it is stored (Figure 12a, b and c). 
Figure 12a. Water harvesting

©FAO/TECA

8.1 Water harvesting

  • The stored water in ponds and depressions is used for irrigational purposes, as a life saver or for supplementary irrigation during lean periods.
    • It is also stored in dugout structures.
    • In some areas during the summer, it is used as drinking water both for humans and livestock, and for other domestic purposes.
Figure 12b. Water harvesting


©FAO/TECA

8.2 Village rain water pond for irrigation and livestock

  • The ponds, with time, are sealed with silt and clay particles.
    • As a result, nfiltration/percolation losses are reduced and ponding time and volume of water are increased.
Figure 12c. Village rain water

©FAO/TECA

9. Harvesting of water from snow melting

  • Harvesting of water is also done by constructing water ponds and water is collected in these ponds from melting snow (Figure 13).
Figure 13. Village water pond where water is collected from snow melting 

©FAO/TECA

10. Use of Pang (Spang) grass for controlling seepage and side losses in water tanksand irrigation Kuhls

  • In Ladakh, pang (spang) grass is used as the inner lining of zings (water ponds) and irrigation kuhls for checking percolation losses (Figure 14a and b).
    • The use of spang grass, which grows abundantly in Ladakh, showcases its non-permeability properties similar to that of polythene sheet or cement lining.
    • Its chemical makeup needs to be analysed, as farmers claim its utility in water retention is far superior than polythene/cement.
Figure 14a. Village water pond where pang (spang) grass is used for controlling seepage losses

©FAO/TECA

11. Moisture conservation through mulching

  • In Kinnaur, covering the soil surface with chilgoza tree needles and grass from the Kandas (hill tops), is a common mulching practice (Figure 15).
    • Mulching conserves soil moisture in the fields.
    • It also helps in the moderation of soil temperature.
    • In this way the hydro-thermal regime of soil is improved.
    • However, the continuous use of chilgoza tree needles increases the acidity of the soil.
  • In hilly areas, ploughing is done, which aids in moisture conservation, as the soil acts as mulch.
    • In Ladakh, farmers regulate optimum irrigation by inserting a belcha (spade) in the soil.
    • If it is completely inserted (front portion), the land is considered to be properly irrigated.
    • Similarly, in a few other cases, mud is thrown in the air.
    • Its splitting into pieces shows proper irrigation.
    • The complete insertion of the front portion of the belcha (spade) or the throwing of mud in the air (and its consequent splitting into pieces), indicate the soil moisture level at field capacity, where 100 per cent moisture is available to the crops.
Figure 15. In situ moisture conservation with locally available tree leaves and grasses

©FAO/TECA

12. Drainage

  • During rainy season the rains are torrential, which causes splash erosion, resulting in the sorting of particles and the formation of false compact layer on the surface.
    • It yields water pounding and subsequently water logging.
    • Crops such as maize, capsicum, and tomato, which are grown during this season, are very sensitive to water logging.
    • In Indiantraditional agriculture, there is a common practice that during the preparation of a field, the slope of a field is kept inside.
    • Itis provided with a channel to take excess water from that field to a safer place, from where it is disposed of into a stream or nalla through grassed water ways.
    • The grassed water ways are kept permanently and help with the drainage.
    • These channels and grassed water ways are positioned in such a way that they do not hinder any agricultural activity such as ploughing, hoeing and harvesting.

13. Use of smoke for protecting fruit crops from frost damage

  • In the lower areas of Himachal Pradesh, Mango plants are mostly damaged by frost injury during winter months, e.g. December and January (Figure 16).
    • Smoke layer protects the mango plants from frost injury.
    • This practice is common in the lower areas of Himachal Pradesh.
Figure 16. Effect of smoke on frost

©FAO/TECA

14. Soil management

14.1 Cultural practices

  • In the West Himalayan region, in the month of March/April, when snow melts and weather conditions improve, the bunds and comers of the fields are dug-out and weeds and grasses are removed with the help of spade and clods.
    • The grasses or weeds are beaten up and then soil is separated from these clods and collected in lower fields.
  • Firstly, this practice of removing weeds and grasses from bunds and corners by digging helps in weed control in the cultivated fields.
  • Secondly, the area under crops remains the same as that of previous crop, e.g. the area is not wasted on weeds and grasses.
  • Thirdly, the soil added in lower fields from the bunds of upper field, is rich in nutrients and it improves the soil fertility.

14.2 Use of broader plough in upper valleys

  • Ploughs are lengthened in Ladakh by attaching flat wooden pieces to both sides of the iron blade.
    • This indigenous plough is preferred over the one available in the market.
    • This technology has two-fold functions.
      • Labour-saving
      • Stabilizing the loose sandy strata in one ploughing action, which is suitable for small terraces.

14.3 Sheet erosion control

  • This is not a damaging form of erosion, mainly because it is often not recognised and seldom treated.
    • It accounts for the loss of billions of tonnes of soil every year.
    • Due to the splash of rain drops, particles are knocked loose and then carried away by the runoff.
    • The sheet erosion results into rill and gullies, which are controlled by very cheap treatments.
    • Sheet erosion is more apparent in forest areas that are devoid of ground cover or wastelands with very few standing trees.
  • There is traditional practice to keep surface covered at a maximum with grasses, shrubs etc.
    • Grazing is done in rotation and is allowed only during certain times.
    • It is avoided during the flowering and seed setting stages of grasses.
    • Fibrous rooted shrubs and grasses planted as hedges along the contour of the land slow the runoff, weaken the erosive power of water and cause it to deposit its load of valuable soil behind the hedgerows.
    • As a result, the runoff proceeds gently down the slope where hedges have been planted at the correct vertical interval without having erosive effects.
    • In the foot hills, erosive capacity of stream flow is also reduced by spurs of loose boulders.

14.4 Traditional rainfed farming

  • In hilly areas, most of the area is rainfed except for a few pockets in valleys where irrigation facilities exist.
    • The choice of crop and rotation, completely depends on crops which require less volume of water.
    • For rotation, legumes are important as a mixed crop.
    • During rotation, when rainy season erosion permitting crops are grown (e.g. cowpea, 'kuth'), these form an integral part of the mixed cropping system.
    • The crops are chosen as per their nutrition.
      • From old ages protein rich pulses are part of cropping pattern.
    • Coarse grains like phaphra', 'chulai' are also grown very commonly which are very rich in nutrition.
  • Within the premises of the house, it is mandatory to have fruit plants such as citrus, mango, and anar, which provide seasonal fruits rich in vitamin C., carbohydrates etc.
  • The fields are well protected with biofence of thorny shrubs or their cut pieces.
    • Traditional rainfed farming is done irrespective of land, with respect to slope and other characteristics.
    • There are risks of sheet erosion but with traditional knowledge, crop rotation is adopted in such a way that during peak runoff periods, the sowing of close growing crops provides soil protectio.

14.5 Terracing

  • For centuries, land in the hills has been cultivatedon scientific lins.
    • Cultivation is done up to a 25 to 100 degree slope, where there are many chances of landslips, sheet and gully erosion.
    • However, with 'bench terracing practices', the threat of soil erosion is controlled.
    • These practices are very common in hill fanning.
  • The terraces are constructed across the slope, e.g. long the contour (Figures. 17a, b, c, d, e, f, g and h).
    • The size of the terrace is decided by the prevailing degree of the slope.
    • The terraces are supported by risers of suitable heights and width.
    • The height of riser is again decided by the degree of the slope.
    • The risers are sometimes made of loose boulders supported by grasses.
    • The roots of the grasses help in binding and keeping the boulders intact in one place.
    • The roots of the grasses help in the drainage of excess water.
    • With traditional knowledge, farmers are keeping the risers toward inner slopes.
    • In paddy growing areas, the risers are erected to facilitate the pounding of water in the field.
    • This type of bunding and terracing has been continuing for and terraces are still intact.
    • The bunds are again used for growing palatable grasses, which are used as fodder for livestock.
    • Trees are meant for fuel, fodder and fibre.
    • The examples are beul, shisham, mango etc.
    • In lower areas the bench terraces are known as "khet".
    • Sometimes on the risers on the contour hedge of grass like khus, local grasses are also established.
Figure 17a. Stone terrace making

©FAO/TECA

Figure 17b. Stone terrace wall

©FAO/TECA

Figure 17c. Traditional symmetrical terraces

©FAO/TECA

Figure 17d. Terrace slicing in crop field

©FAO/TECA

Figure 17e. Earthen terraces

©FAO/TECA

Figure 17f. Crop field terraces and community forestry

©FAO/TECA

Figure 17g. Stone terraces along the slope

©FAO/TECA

Figure 17h. Bench terrace fortified with vegetative measures

©FAO/TECA

15. Use of maddim (a plain wooden structure) for field levelling

  • Maddim is used for levelling ploughed lands.
    • A heavy stone is put on a maddim for increasing the pressure required for levelling.
    • Sometimes, a man may also sit instead of a heavy stone.
  • Such an indigenous technology for field levelling is called planking.
    • Firstly, with this practice, there is very good seed soil contact and very good germination of crops.
    • Secondly, there is moisture conservation in the fields.
    • Thirdly, small soil clods are pressed and broken into finer particles and in this way soil structure is improved.

16. Curved land ploughing for intensive land preparation; soil conservation and water retention

  • In west Himalayan cold deserts, ploughing is done in a curved (sword like) manner from the bottom to the top of the slopy land holdings.
    • Ploughing land holdings in a sword like pattern ensures proper land preparation, which includes the proper ploughing of the corners which otherwise would have remained unploughed.
  • The ploughing of slopy lands from the bottom to the top also helps in soil conservation as it checks the loosened soil strata falling from the upper side to the lower side.
  • The curved pattern is useful in maintaining the infiltration rate of water, which otherwise gets wasted with sudden runoff.

17. Conserving productive soil layer against wind erosion

  • In west Himalayan cold deserts, fields are irrigated in autumn so that the top layer is prevented from being blown away.
  • In spring the moistened soil eases ploughing.
  • The productive soil layer, which is very thin, needs conservation against heavy wind erosion, a common occurence in cold deserts.
  • This appropriate soil conservation technique also helps in the easy and timely ploughing for meeting the requirements of the short growing season.
  • The moist upper layer of the soil, which gets frozen in winter, also serves as protection against wind erosion.

18. Cultivation of levelled/flat lands for preventing soil erosion

  • In west Himalayan cold deserts, cultivation practices are confined to the levelled/flat lands only.
  • This practice helps not only in rational land use but also checks soil erosion in otherwise sandy and loose strata.

19. Contouring of slopy lands: ethno-engineering for soil conservation

  • In west Himalayan cold deserts, farmers have developed this technology for cultivation of slopy lands by constructing terraces comprising of plots and sub-plots by using small stones.
    • Stone wall fencing is also constructed for individual land holdings.
    • Terracing of slopy lands helps in conserving soil and moisture and prevents soil erosion.
    • This also helps to carry out other field operations including the proper use of irrigation water for checking the surface runoff.

20. Use of loose boulders spurs for reducing soil erosion

  • In some areas, people use loose boulder spurs for reducing the cutting effect of stream flow in a small nalla (choes) (Figure 18).
Figure 18. Loose boulders spurs - reduce cutting effect of stream flow in 'choes'

©FAO/TECA

21. Use of loose boulders diversion dam with spillway in centre for reducing soil erosion

  • This method is very common in the lower areas of Himachal Pradesh (Figure 19).
  • These dams are constructed across the streams for controlling soil loss.
Figure 19. Loose boulders diversion dam with spillway in the centre

©FAO/TECA

22. Dams construction

  • This method is very common in the lower areas of Himachal Pradesh.
  • These dams are constructed across the streams for controlling soil loss.In this method of vegetation, a live check of bambo pieces and loose boulders are used for controlling gully erosion (Figure 20).
Figure 20. Gully plugging

©FAO/TECA

23. Use of river bed soils

  • The river bed soils are used for raising crops (Figure 21).
  • These soils are rich in nutrients as nutrients are removed with soil from hilly slopes and are deposited in the river beds.
Figure 21. Recovering river bed soil

©FAO/TECA

24. Validation of the practice

The technology was validated in India.

25. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold;
  • subtropics, warm/mod cool; and
  • subtropics, cool.

26. Related/associated technologies

  • Water management in organic agriculture: ID 8366.
  • Water conservation ponds: ID 7378.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: roof water harvesting: ID 7304.
  • Soil and water conservation practices to reduce soil erosion and enhance water conservation: ID 7861.
  • Strategies for improved soil and water conservation practices in hillside production systems: ID 4469.

27. Objectives fulfilled by the project

27.1 Resource use efficiency

Water resource is managed efficiently to ensure continued production.

entries.tittle: Buenas prácticas para la prevención y control de la roya del café (Hemileia vastatrix) en la República Dominicana
entries.summary:
A ferrugem-do-café (Hemileia vastatrix Berk & Br) é a mais importante das doenças da folha do cafeeiro. Apesar de estar presente em quase todas as zonas de produção de café da República Dominicana, a sua importância é maior nas áreas de média e baixa altitude, onde é favorecida pelas temperaturas quentes e ambientes húmidos e chuvosos. Assim, a aplicação adequada de práticas culturais para Gestão Integrada da Ferrugem (GIF), não só irá ajudar a controlar a doença, como tenderá a aumentar a produtividade das plantações de café.

Esta tecnologia está também disponível em: Espanhol (ID8307)
entries.description:
Descrição

A ferrugem é a doença foliar mais importante na cultura do café na República Dominicana. Esta doença é causada pelo fungo Hemileia vastatrix Berk & Br., e é facilmente propagada em ambientes húmidos, sombrios e com temperaturas médias entre 21 e 27°C. Os sintomas incluem manchas, com aparência amarelada, na página superior da folha, e a formação de um pó cor de laranja, na página inferior (lado de baixo). As lesões antigas podem adquirir cor preta e bordo amarelo, principalmente no início da estação chuvosa.

Em ataques severos, o principal dano é a queda de um grande número de folhas, causando um enfraquecimento geral da planta, uma maturação muito irregular e a redução da produtividade no ano seguinte, que pode atingir os 50 % (ver figura 1). O seu comportamento é semelhante em cafeeiros expostos ao sol, quando a nutrição é deficiente e a gestão agrícola desadequada. Para o seu controlo e prevenção recomendam-se práticas culturais adequadas, aplicação de fitofármacos e utilização de variedades com maior resistência à doença.

Figura 1. Efeito da ferrugem no cafeeiro

©IDIAF

1. Aplicação da tecnologia

O controlo adequado desta doença é favorecido pela implementação das seguintes práticas:

1.1 Amostragem

A amostragem sistemática da plantação é muito importante para determinar o nível de infestação ou da doença nos cafezais. A metodologia de amostragem consiste em selecionar três locais diferentes e importantes na plantação de cafeeiros. Em cada local são analisadas 10 plantas e em cada uma é selecionado um ramo aleatoriamente, mas nem sempre à mesma altura. Em cada ramo conta-se e regista-se o número total de folhas e o número de folhas doentes. Com estes dados, calcula-se a percentagem de infeção, dividindo o total de folhas doentes pelo total de folhas da planta, multiplicado por 100. De acordo com o nível de infestação, deve-se tomar a decisão de aplicar ou não um produto químico. Se o nível de infestação for inferior a 15 % aplicam-se fungicidas de prevenção, se for superior aplicam-se fungicidas curativos.

1.2 Controlo do ensombramento

Esta prática protege a plantação, uma vez que facilita a entrada de luz solar e permite uma maior circulação de ar na plantação de café, proporcionando um ambiente desfavorável à multiplicação do fungo. Com esta medida consegue-se baixar a humidade relativa no interior do cafezal. A regulação ideal do ensombramento é aquela que permite criar um espaço equivalente a duas vezes a altura dos cafeeiros, entre a parte inferior das copas das plantas que criam sombra e o limite superior das copas dos cafeeiros. A melhor época para realizar esta tarefa é logo após a colheita.

Figura 2. Controlo do ensombramento com árvores

©IDIAF

1.3 Controlo de infestantes

Anualmente são recomendadas 2 a 3 mondas, utilizando a catana e o machado como ferramentas. Em cafezais ensombrados e em zonas íngremes, recomenda-se a remoção das ervas daninhas junto aos troncos dos cafeeiros e nas entrelinhas. Este trabalho permite o arejamento da plantação, evitando a competição por nutrientes e facilitando a colheita e a saúde dos cafeeiros.

1.4 Poda

A poda consiste na remoção dos tecidos mortos da planta para induzir o desenvolvimento de novos tecidos. Facilita a entrada de luz nas plantas e a manutenção do cafezal, reduz a produção bianual e as condições favoráveis para o aparecimento da ferrugem. A melhor época para a poda é imediatamente após cada colheita. Para executar esta tarefa, é aconselhável fazer a poda com serrote e na companhia de um técnico especializado na cultura do café. 

Figura 3. Poda de regeneração

©IDIAF

1.5 Fertilização

Esta técnica tem como objetivo fornecer uma nutrição adequada à planta, contribuindo para o aumento da produtividade dos cafezeiros, para a melhora da qualidade do produto e preservação do vigor e do estado geral da planta, permitindo um controlo mais eficaz às doenças de que são alvo. Deve ser feita com base nas análises de solo, nas recomendações técnicas relativas ao estado geral da cultura (idade, variedade, ensombramento, etc.) e nas condições agroclimáticas e ambientais (altitude, precipitação, luminosidade, posição, orientação, etc.). 

Figura 4. Fertilização do cafeeiro

©IDIAF

1.6 Aplicação de fungicidas

As aplicações de fungicidas devem ser feitas no início da estação chuvosa. Quando os níveis de infeção, de acordo com a amostragem, são inferiores a 20 %, é recomendada a utilização de produtos de prevenção, aplicados na página inferior das folhas. Para níveis superiores a 20 %, aplicam-se produtos curativos e sistémicos.

Para conseguir a máxima eficácia no controlo, com o combate químico, devem-se seguir as seguintes recomendações:

  • O controlo da doença pode ser realizado, através da aplicação de fungicidas protectores e sistémicos.
  • As aplicações dos produtos são feitas no início da estação chuvosa.
  • Estes devem ser aplicados pelo menos duas vezes por ano, nos meses de abril-maio e de setembro-outubro, de forma a reduzir a progressão da doença.
  • Na primeira aplicação (abril-maio) podem ser utilizados fungicidas protectores, tais como o óxido ou hidróxido de cobre.
  • É necessário esclarecer que o uso de fungicidas protetores não cura doença, apenas a previne.
  • Se a taxa de infeção da doença aumenta, para um nível em que em 100 folhas, existem mais de 20 folhas doentes, devem ser aplicados fungicidas curativos.
  • Se existirem menos de 20 folhas doentes, por cada 100, devem ser aplicados fungicidas preventivos.
  • Em caso de elevada incidência da doença, por favor, procure a assistência técnica / serviços de extensão rural para uma tomada de decisões mais eficaz no controlo da doença.

2. Zona agroecológica

  • Trópicos, quentes.

3. Técnologias relacionadas/associadas

  • Cultura de café com ensombramento: ID 2511.
  • Roya del café: utilización de variedades tolerantes (Ferrugem do café: uso de variedades tolerantes): ID 8329.

Esta tecnologia está também disponível em espanhola: ID 8307.

4. Objectivos atingidos pelo projecto

  • Eficiência na utilização de recursos.
  • Tecnologia adequada a populações desfavorecidas, com recursos reduzidos

entries.tittle: Solarização: redução dos estragos causados por insetos no feijão-fradinho
entries.summary: O feijão-fradinho ou feijão-de-corda é uma cultura importante para as famílias rurais ganesas pelo seu valor nutricional e como complemento ao seu rendimento familiar. Os produtores mais pobres vêem-se muitas vezes obrigados a vender o feijão logo após a colheita, seja para saldar dívidas ou porque não conseguem evitar perdas no armazenamento (perdas de peso e redução de valor) associadas aos estragos causados por insetos. Os vendedores do mercado também são afetados por estas perdas. Esta tecnologia descreve o método de solarização no controlo das infestações do feijão-fradinho.
entries.description:
Descrição

O feijão-fradinho ou feijão-de-corda ou feijão caupi (Vigna unguiculata), também conhecido por feijão-nhemba em Moçambique ou feijão-macunde em Angola, desempenha um papel importante na dieta e economia de muitos pequenos agricultores no norte do Gana. O feijão-fradinho é uma leguminosa tradicional cultivada de forma generalizada pelos pequenos agricultores da África Subsariana. Esta cultura tradicional está bem adaptada aos climas semiáridos, suportando, por conseguinte, algum défice hídrico e níveis baixos de fertilidade do solo, sendo que e à imagem da generalidade das leguminosas, contribui para a fixação de azoto (Figura 1). O feijão-fradinho possui um elevado teor de proteína e é nutricionalmente importante em áreas, onde a carne não está disponível em quantidade suficiente.  

Figura 1. Campo de feijão-fradinho no norte do Gana

©FAO/TECA

Tradicionalmente toda a planta é utilizada, as folhas jovens são consumidas como um vegetal, geralmente cozidas como o espinafre, e o restolho é utilizado como forragem para os animais. Nas áreas semiáridas, os alimentos colhidos, durante a estação das chuvas, necessitam de ser armazenados durante a estação seca, que pode durar de 6 a 8 meses. Durante o armazenamento, os danos causados por pragas de insetos são elevados, chegando mesmo a destruir a totalidade da colheita. O feijão-fradinho sofre perdas substanciais, em quantidade e qualidade, em resultado de infestações do Caruncho-do-feijão (Callosobruchus maculatus). insectos da família Bruchidae (Figura 2).  

Figura 2. Aspecto dos machos (esquerda) e fêmeas (direita) adultas de caruncho-do-feijão

©FAO/TECA

O ciclo de vida do bruquídeo tem a duração média de cerca de um mês (Figura 3). Os adultos acasalam e põe ovos até cinco dias após a emergência e cada fêmea pode pôr até 100 ovos.  

Figura 3. Ciclo de vida do bruquídeo

©FAO/TECA

Figura 4. Feijão-fradinho danificado por bruquídeos

©FAO/TECA

Os prejuízos causados ​​pelos bruquídeos podem ser muito elevados, com toda a colheita armazenada a ser destruída em alguns meses.  Pelo que os agricultores são relutantes em armazenar a colheita de feijão-fradinho, procedendo à sua comercialização após a colheita, quando o preço é mais baixo (Figura 5). 
 
Um projeto Programa pós-colheita do feijão-fradinho (Crop Post Harvest Program, R7442) testou vários métodos tradicionais ou modernos selecionados para controlar as infestações do bruquídeo, sem o uso de produtos químicos sintéticos. Os métodos testados incluíam o armazenamento hermético, a desinfestação solar, ou aplicação de produtos, como as cinzas, malagueta, manteiga ou resíduo de noz de karité e extratos vegetais. 

Figura 5. Comercialização do feijão caupi nos mercados locais

©FAO/TECA

O método de controlo mais eficaz, de acordo com a avaliação dos agricultores participantes, foi a solarização repetida mensalmente. As únicas desvantagens identificadas pelos agricultores são o custo e, para alguns, o tempo envolvido. O custo foi discutido em termos de uma análise de custo-benefício, que demonstrou que os valores de comercialização fora de época de cultivo (quando o feijão-fradinho é mais caro) atinge pelo menos 100 % do preço na colheita. Esta análise permitiu verificar que um investimento de 15 % do rendimento esperado permite adquirir o material necessário para implementar a técnica de solarização. 

Figura 6. Batida de feijão caupi

©FAO/TECA

2. Técnica de solarização

  • Escolher uma área aberta e sem sombra. Varrer a área selecionada de modo que fique limpa. 
  • Estender uma esteira de palha na área limpa certifique-se que a superfície é plana. 
Figura 7. Estender a esteira de palha sobre uma área limpa

©FAO/TECA

  • Arranjar sacos velhos de juta (sarapilheira), mas limpos. 
  • Sacudir vigorosamente os sacos para certificar que não tem pragas/insetos escondidos no tecido. 
  • Agitar os sacos longe da área, com as esteiras estendidas (Figura 8). 
Figura 8. Sacudir bem os sacos de juta

©FAO/TECA

  • Colocar os sacos sobre a esteira de palha, certificando-se de que estão dispostos de modo a se sobreporem nas bordas (a fim de evitar eventuais perdas de feijão na fase seguinte), Figura 9.
Figura 9. Estender os sacos de juta sobre a esteira

©FAO/TECA

  • Despejar o feijão sobre os sacos de juta e espalhar uniformemente. 
  • Certificar-se de que a espessura da camada de feijão é a mesma em toda a esteira (Figura 10). 
Figura 10. Despejo e espalhamento do feijão-fradinho

©FAO/TECA

  • Verificar a espessura da camada, usando o dedo como guia, a espessura da camada de feijão-frade não deve ser superior a 2 a 3 cm. 
  • Esta tarefa é muito importante, caso contrário a temperatura não será suficientemente para matar todos os bruquídeos (Figuras 11 e 12). 
Figura 11. Técnica para verificar a espessura do feijão-fradinho esteira

©FAO/TECA

  • Colocar um plástico transparente em cima da camada de feijão-frade e fixar nas bordas com pedras e/ou pedaços de madeira, suficientemente pesados para que este não seja arrastado pelo vento (Figura 13).  
Figura 12. O feijão espalhado sobre as esteiras

©FAO/TECA

Certificar-se que o plástico está bem fixado e que não existe nenhum espaço (camada de ar) entre a camada de feijão-fradinho e o plástico. Manter os animais afastados da área (Figura 14). 

Figura 13. Colocação da pelicula de plástico

©FAO/TECA

  • Manter o feijão ao sol, enquanto este estiver quente, pelo menos entre as 10h00 e as 17h00 para obter melhores resultados da solarização. 
  • O calor gerado pelo sol, sob o plástico, mata o caruncho-do-feijão presente nos grãos (Figura 15). 
Figura 14. Situações a evitar na colocação da pelicula de plástico

©FAO/TECA

  • Durante o período de armazenamento repetir o processo de solarização uma vez por mês. 
Figura 15. Duração da Secagem

©FAO/TECA

3. Contexto e potenciais problemas

  • Esta técnica, que é ao mesmo tempo simples e eficaz, mas é aplicável geralmente apenas a pequenas quantidades de grão. 
  • A técnica é de particular interesse para os agricultores individuais ou pequenos grupos de produtores e é aplicável sobretudo ao nível do agregado familiar.
  • Os principais problemas poderão ser a aquisição de uma película apropriada de plástico e a resistência destes materiais à radiação UV. 
  • A radiação UV torna os plásticos quebradiços. 
  • Estas peliculas não duram muito tempo e, portante, terão de ser substituídas regularmente.

4. Técnologias relacionadas/associadas

  • ​​Using plants with pesticidal properties to control insects during on-farm grain storage (Utilização de plantas com propriedades insecticidas no controlo de insectos, durante o armazenamento do grão no Gana): ID 4506.
  • ​Using eucalyptus leaves to preserve maize and bean seed (Utilização de folhas de eucalipto para conservar as sementes de milho e feijão): ID 7639.​

Esta tecnologia está também disponível em inglês: Solarisation: reducing insect damage from cowpeas: ID 4425.

5. Objectivos atingidos pelo projecto

5.1. Eficiência na utilização de recursos

  • A tecnologia permite um cultivo aprimorado do feijão-frade e melhora o solo, evitando o uso de produtos químicos. 
  • A planta inteira pode ser usada para alimentos e forragens.
  • A optimização do armazenamento da produção permite melhorar os rendimentos dos agricultores.
entries.further_reading:
6. Leitura adicional

  • Morris, M. and Tran, B. 2002. Improvement in the storage and marketing quality of legumes (Phase II) DFID Crop Post Harvest Programme, Final Technical Report, Project R7442. Natural Resources Institute, Chatham, UK. 35 pp.
  • Tran, B. 2001. Improving the quality of stored legumes: Low cost pest control to allow storage of cowpea by small scale farmers.
  • Tran, B. and Andan, F.H. 2001. Solarisation: reducing damage from cowpea beetles during storage. Booklet. [English and Dagbani]. Ministry of Food and Agriculture (MoFA), Tamale, Ghana. 2 pp.

7. Segurança e saúde

Os investigadores, as suas instituições ou esta plataforma não podem ser responsabilizados por quaisquer prejuízos resultantes do uso indevido dos materiais ou métodos aqui descritos. A aplicação ou uso dos tratamentos, processos e tecnologias é da exclusiva responsabilidade do utilizador. 

8. Isenção de responsabilidade do DFID

Esta tecnologia é um produto da estratégia de Pesquisa em Recursos Naturais Renováveis, financiada pelo Departamento de Desenvolvimento Internacional do Reino Unido (DFID), para o benefício dos países em desenvolvimento. As opiniões expressas não são necessariamente as do DFID. 

9. Agradecimentos

Tecnologia selecionada e compilada da documentação original do projeto pela Natural Resources International Ltd, com financiamento do Departamento Central de Investigação (Gabinete de Comunicação) do DFID. A implementação e o aconselhamento sobre este processo foram realizados por: Karen Wilkin e Tina Rowland (líderes do projeto), Andy Frost, Vino Graffham, Jody Sunley, Liz McVeigh, equipa do programa RNRRS, Serviço de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento de Tecnologia da FAO, Programa LEAD da FAO, Programa LEAD da FAO, Departamento Central de Pesquisa do DFID, Ken Campbell, Graham Farrell (Clínica de Plantas), Simon Eden-Green, Peter Golob, John Esser, Liz Betser (360° Responsibility). O domínio de validação foi revisto pelo Centro de Cooperação Internacional em Investigação Agronómica para o Desenvolvimento (CIRAD), Simon Eden-Green e Peter Golob. Upload da Random X Solutions Ltd. Para obter mais informações, entre em contato com Karen Wilkin, NR International Ltd ou Tina Rowland, Random X Solutions Ltd.
