entries.title: Nosémose: maladie fongique des abeilles adultes
entries.source: Apimondia, IZSLT - Istituto Zooprofilattico Sperimentale del Lazio e della Toscana “Mariano Aleandri”
entries.summary: La nosémose est une maladie globale qui se caractérise par une diarrhée chez les abeilles adultes. Elle semble avoir un fort impact sur le secteur apicole, surtout lorsqu'elle est associée à d'autres agents pathogènes (varroase, virose, amibiase, etc.) ou à des polluants environnementaux (pesticides). La nosémose est causée par le champignon Nosema. Deux espèces différentes de Nosema affectent Apis mellifera avec des symptômes différents et une prévalence différente selon les régions.
entries.description:
La description

1. Introduction

La nosémose est une maladie causée par deux espèces différentes du champignon Nosema spp: N. apis et N. ceranae. Toutes deux affectent les abeilles adultes, mais leurs symptômes et leur prévalence diffèrent selon les régions. Les spores de N. apis et de N. ceranae sont difficilement distinguables morphologiquement (figure 1) ; elles représentent la forme résistante par laquelle la maladie se propage. Les spores peuvent rester infectieuses de quelques jours à cinq ans à basse température. La chaleur, ainsi que le rayonnement ultraviolet du soleil, peuvent les tuer en quelques heures.

Figure 1. Les spores microscopiques de N. ceranae sont à peine distinguables de celles de N. apis

©University of Madrid/Aranzazu Meana

Les facteurs suivants influencent la nosémose :

  • Les périodes d'humidité et de froid augmentent les risques d'infection parmi les abeilles d'une même ruche car elles forcent les abeilles à rester à l'intérieur;
  • La faiblesse de la miellée et des flux de pollen;
  • Les conditions climatiques peuvent également affecter la propagation de l'infection. Lors des hivers longs et froids et des printemps froids et pluvieux, les abeilles éprouvent des difficultés à trouver du nectar et du pollen;
  • Les inspections fréquentes des ruches pendant les mauvaises conditions météorologiques (par ex. en hiver, par temps venteux ou pluvieux) peuvent déclencher l'apparition de la maladie ainsi que sa propagation en raison du stress induit;
  • La présence d'autres maladies (telles que l'amibiase, la varroase ou les virus) exacerbe les symptômes de la nosémose.

2. Symptômes

2.1 Symptômes de la nosémose provoquée par Nosema apis

Nosema apis est responsable de la forme connue de la maladie comme "classique", surtout répandue dans les régions froides et humides. Elle apparaît plus facilement au printemps et dans les ruches mal gérées en hiver. Elle se manifeste principalement par une diminution de la population de la colonie. La maladie n'affecte jamais les stades larvaires et rarement la reine.

Les spores de Nosema apis, présentes dans les fèces des abeilles, sont directement ou indirectement ingérées par les abeilles adultes et se développent dans les intestins des abeilles, affectant leurs fonctions digestives (les abeilles sont incapables d'absorber les nutriments de leur nourriture). Les abeilles nourricières deviennent également incapables de produire de la gelée royale. Les spores sont expulsées avec les fèces et peuvent être avalées par d'autres abeilles, qui sont ensuite infectées. La colonie finit par succomber à cause du dépeuplement, car les abeilles adultes meurent et aucune nouvelle abeille ne naît (le couvain n'étant plus nourri).

Suite au contact des abeilles avec N. apis, les symptômes d'infection suivants apparaissent :

  • Des troubles intestinaux, tels que la diarrhée (figure 2), que l'on peut observer sur la planche de vol et à l'entrée de la ruche, et sur les rayons de miel, qui seront souillés de fèces diarrhéiques (figure 3);
  • Les abeilles deviennent incapables de secréter de la gelée royale et donc de nourrir le couvain;
  • Les abeilles butineuses réduisent leur activité jusqu'à ce qu'elle s'arrête complètement;
  • Dans les rares cas où la reine est malade, la ponte diminue fortement;
  • Certaines abeilles ne sont plus capables de voler, elles marchent avec leurs ailes déployées en forme de "K" et sont paralysées, tandis que d'autres abeilles se rassemblent en petits groupes;
  • Des abeilles mortes, à l'abdomen gonflé et aux pattes rétractées sous le thorax, se trouvent au fond de la ruche.

On assiste d'abord à un lent dépeuplement, puis l’activité diminue tandis que l'état d'agitation de la colonie augmente.

Figure 2. Fèces diarrhéiques à l'entrée de la ruche

©Flickr/D. Broberg 

Figure 3. Rayon maculé de fèces diarrhéiques

©IZSLT/Giovanni Formato

2.2 Symptômes de la nosémose provoquée par Nosema ceranae

Nosema ceranae est une nouvelle espèce de champignon. Il a été isolé pour la première fois en 1996 par Fries sur Apis cerana, une espèce d'abeille très répandue en Asie du Sud-Est. En 2006, il a été découvert pour la première fois par Higes sur l'abeille domestique européenne (Apis mellifera). Nosema ceranae s'est répandu dans de vastes régions d'Europe et a remplacé la forme indigène de N. apis sur Apis mellifera, avec pour résultat des signes cliniques très différents de la diarrhée généralement associée à la nosémose causée par N. apis.

La maladie peut se manifester tout au long de l'année. L'absence de diarrhée est typique. Il semble que les abeilles butineuses meurent loin de la ruche, ce qui provoque un dépeuplement progressif des colonies, sans qu’on remarque la présence d'abeilles mortes, jusqu'à la perte totale des colonies.

3. Transmission

Nosema apis et Nosema ceranae peuvent être transmis de la même manière.

L'ingestion du champignon par les abeilles se fait directement, par l'ingestion de fèces, ou, indirectement, par l'ingestion de miel, d'eau ou de nourriture contaminés.

Les spores de N. ceranae sont très résistantes dans l'environnement et peuvent supporter des températures très froides ou très chaudes. Cela signifie que la réinfection des colonies et la réapparition de la maladie après une longue période est très possible.

La maladie peut être transmise d'une ruche à l'autre et d'un rucher à l'autre par les abeilles et par l'apiculteur :

  • La dérive des ouvrières et des faux-bourdons infectés ;
  • Le déplacement des faux-bourdons;
  • Le pillage de colonies infectées ;
  • Le transfert de rayons de miel infectés, d'une ruche à l'autre ;
  • L'alimentation des abeilles avec du miel contaminé ;
  • L’utilisation d'outils ou d'équipements infectés.

4. Diagnostic

Un test de terrain consiste à examiner la couleur de la partie terminale du système digestif de quelques abeilles (les apiculteurs peuvent extraire l'intestin en retirant le dard avec une pince à épiler ou avec leurs ongles). Chez les abeilles saines, elle est de couleur rougeâtre, tandis que chez les abeilles malades, elle est de couleur blanc laiteux (figures 4 et 5). Toutefois, ce signe n'est visible que lorsque la maladie a déjà atteint un certain stade de gravité. Seul un test de laboratoire permet de poser un diagnostic précoce, en recherchant au microscope les spores au niveau intestinal ou directement sur les fèces.

Figure 4. Test de terrain positif: intestin blanc laiteux d'une abeille atteinte de nosémose

©CIAPA/Mariano Higes

Figure 5. Test de terrain négatif: l'intestin d'une abeille saine est de couleur rougeâtre

©CIAPA/Mariano Higes

Les spores microscopiques de N. ceranae sont difficilement distinguables morphologiquement de celles de N. apis (figure 1). Ainsi, il est possible de faire un diagnostic uniquement par PCR, qui permet le séquençage d'une partie très spécifique et caractéristique du génome de N. ceranae sur les spores. Le coût et la disponibilité de cet examen dépendent de chaque pays et de chaque laboratoire.

5. Prévention et contrôle

L'adoption de bonnes pratiques apicoles (BPA) et des mesures de biosécurité (MBA) peut réduire le risque d'apparition de Nosema spp.

5.1 Bonnes pratiques apicoles pour réduire le risque d'apparition de nosémose

Le tableau 1 donne un aperçu des BPA à adopter pour maintenir des colonies saines et prévenir l'infection par Nosema spp.

Tableau 1. Bonnes pratiques apicoles pour la prévention et le contrôle de la nosémose
Recommandation Avantage ou raison de la pratique
Choisissez le bon emplacement du rucher (non humide, non exposé aux vents froids), orientez les ruches de préférence vers le soleil et préférez les zones légèrement ventilées. Réduit la probabilité de multiplication des champignons.
Préparez les ruches pour l'hivernage à l'aide d'une partition pour ajuster le volume de la ruche à la taille de la colonie. Les cadres non remplis doivent être enlevés. Dans les climats froids, gardez les ruches au chaud pendant l'hivernage jusqu'à la fin du printemps. Evite le choc thermique sur les abeilles pendant la saison froide.
Veillez à ce que la colonie dispose de suffisamment de nourriture pendant l'hiver. Si nécessaire, fournissez une nourriture de bonne qualité. Evite le stress nutritionnel des abeilles pendant la saison froide.
Avant l'hivernage des colonies, appliquez les traitements appropriés contre le varroa. Garantit l'efficacité du système immunitaire des abeilles.
Veillez à ce que les abeilles disposent de suffisamment de nourriture riche en protéines à la fin de l'été et en automne. Installez les ruchers dans un endroit où les sources de pollen sont disponibles pour la colonie à la fin de l'été et à l'automne. Si possible, plantez des plantes qui fournissent du pollen à la fin de l'été ou à l'automne à proximité du rucher. Si ce n'est pas possible, nourrissez les abeilles avec des suppléments riches en protéines. Evite le stress nutritionnel des abeilles.
Utilisez un nombre adéquat de rayons de miel par rapport à la population de la colonie. Evite le stress thermique des abeilles.
Perturbez le moins possible les abeilles pendant l'hiver. Limitez les inspections uniquement aux jours ensoleillés et aux heures les plus chaudes de la journée. Evite le stress thermique des abeilles.
Ne réutilisez pas les rayons (qu’ils soient vides ou avec des réserves de miel et/ou de pollen) provenant de colonies dépeuplées (peu d'ouvrières avec la reine) ou mortes. Réduit la probabilité de contamination des abeilles. Le dépeuplement d'une colonie est souvent le signe que quelque chose ne va pas dans la colonie. En outre, les petites colonies sont plus sensibles aux maladies.
Evitez la pollution des sources d'eau artificielles par les fèces et par les abeilles noyées ou mortes. Réduit la probabilité de contamination des abeilles.
Achetez des reines à des éleveurs de reines dont les cheptels sont exempts de Nosema spp. Dans la mesure du possible, sélectionnez et élevez des abeilles résistantes à Nosema spp. Les abeilles présentant une résistance génétique à Nosema spp. sont moins susceptibles de contracter la nosémose.
Enlevez et brûlez les rayons présentant des signes de fèces diarrhéiques. Réduit les niveaux d'infection des maladies dans les ruches.
Si possible, envoyez des échantillons d'abeilles butineuses (ou de débris de ruche) au début de l'automne ou au printemps à un laboratoire pour analyse (loque européenne, loque américaine, nosémose). La détection précoce des maladies peut éviter la contamination d'autres abeilles.
Adoptez un contrôle approprié des agents pathogènes (par ex. V. destructor) de la colonie d'abeilles. Surveillez régulièrement le niveau d'infestation par le varroa (par ex. en utilisant la méthode du sucre glace). Les abeilles non malades ont un système immunitaire plus fort et peuvent mieux lutter contre les maladies.
Renforcez et stimulez les colonies en automne et au printemps avec l'administration d'intégrateurs de stimulants ou de compléments alimentaires. Le stress nutritionnel dû au manque de nourriture adéquate peut compromettre le système immunitaire des abeilles et donc les rendre plus vulnérables aux maladies.

5.2 Mesures de biosécurité dans l'apiculture pour réduire le risque d'apparition de nosémose

L'apiculteur peut adopter les MBA suivantes pour réduire le risque d'introduction et de propagation de la nosémose :

  • Sélectionner des éleveurs de reines dont les cheptels sont exempts de Nosema spp.;
  • Sélectionner et élever des abeilles domestiques qui sont résistantes à Nosema spp., si possible ;
  • Au début de l'automne ou au printemps, prélever des échantillons d'abeilles butineuses pour les faire analyser dans un laboratoire spécialisé et diagnostiquer précocement la nosémose (PCR et/ou méthodes microscopiques) ;
  • Lorsque le pourcentage d'abeilles infectées est trop élevé (> 40 %), traitez la colonie contre Nosema spp. avec des produits disponibles et homologués ou autorisés dans votre pays.

Toutefois, lorsque N. apis se manifeste, le pronostic est souvent grave car son apparition passe généralement inaperçue et les symptômes ne se manifestent qu'à un stade avancé. En général, les colonies touchées ne se rétablissent pas spontanément; l'intervention de l'apiculteur devient donc nécessaire.

Si la maladie est fort développée, en particulier dans les colonies faibles, les rayons infectés doivent être détruits et la ruche doit être stérilisée ou détruite. Le miel peut être utilisé pour la consommation humaine. Pour détruire une ruche et éviter toute nouvelle contamination, il faut creuser un trou d'au moins 50 cm dans le sol, brûler la ruche et les rayons et recouvrir le trou. Les abeilles infectées doivent être tuées par asphyxie avec du dioxyde de soufre ou bien être traitées avec des produits autorisés et transférées dans une ruche neuve ou désinfectée, comportant des rayons neufs ou désinfectés et de nouvelles feuilles de cire.

6. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Bonnes pratiques apicoles: ID 8674.
  • Les principales maladies des abeilles: ID 8714.
  • Varroa (varroase ou varroose): ID 8712.
  • Varroa mites (Varroatosis or Varroosis): a parasitic disease of the brood and adult honeybees: ID 8416.
  • Loque américaine: la plus grave maladie bactérienne du couvain: ID 10114.
  • American foulbrood (AFB): a bacterial disease of the brood: ID 10018.
  • European foulbrood (EFB): a bacterial disease of the honeybee brood: ID 8418.
  • Les virus des abeilles: ID 8786.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en anglais: ID 8413 et espagnol: ID 8682.

7. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

7.1 Women friendly

The practice is not labour-intensive and can be undertaken by all levels of hand-labour.

7.2 Resource-use efficiency

This practice allows for improved management of beekeeping and ensures better colony health.

7.3 Pro-poor technology

This practice, through increased colony healthy, ensures yields, providing additional sources of income and food.

entries.title: Reducing cost of cultivation for Cardamom through cultural practices
entries.source: Sustainable agriculture & Environmental Voluntary Action (SEVA)
multi_source: Sustainable Agriculture & Environmental Voluntary Action - SEVA (SEVA)#Sustainable Agriculture & Environmental Voluntary Action - SEVA (SEVA)#Sustainable Agriculture & Environmental Voluntary Action - SEVA (SEVA)#Sustainable Agriculture & Environmental Voluntary Action - SEVA (SEVA)
entries.summary:
Pruning and mulching are traditional cultural practices in small cardamom cultivation to expose the panicles for better pollination and fruit set as well as to reduce insect pest build up. Also pruning the lower branches of shade trees in cardamom field is a cultural practice to maintain about 50 percent shade to have enough aeration and sunlight leading to better photosynthesis and reducing fungal diseases of cardamom. The trash/plant residue collected from these cultural practices as well as weed materials, if any are spread in the interspace among cardamom plants to add to the organic matter of the soil. The benefits are:

  1. Reduced incidence of major pests (Thrips and shoot borer) and fungal diseases and hence drastic reduction of use of chemical pesticides; the natural enemies of pest are on the increase which further reduces the pest build up. The activity of the major pollinators (honeybees) is on the increase facilitating better fruit set.
  2. The addition of plant residue to cover the soil aids in increasing organic matter and organic carbon of soil, increasing beneficial microbes around rhizosphere, conserving soil moisture, prevent rain water runoff, protect the root system from extremes of temperature etc.

The overall impacts are extremely low external inputs, reduced labour requirement and sustainable higher yield without any pesticide residue; as well as the cardamom agroecosystem in the serene Western Ghats of India is conserved.
entries.description:
Description

Trashing and pruning dry plant parts are the traditional cultural practices in cardamom cultivation. Trashing is removal of old and dried tillers, panicles, and leaves. This work is done once in a year in May-June before the onset of South West monsoon. Pruning is the removal of dried hanging leaves from a shoot (tiller) with sickle. Care is taken not to peel off the green leaf sheath from the tiller along with the dry hanging leaves. This work is done twice in a year, once in January-February and again in September-October. By taking up these activities not only the major pests are effectively reduced, but the insecticide spray fluid required is reduced by about 40 percent (thrips and borer damages are high in unpruned areas even with insecticide spray). The trash and pruned materials are used for mulching which contribute to the soil organic matter (SOM).

Mulches from shade tree branch loping or weeds or trashed and pruned cardamom leaves and tillers may be spread over the plant base and interspace to avoid soil erosion as well as to increase soil fertility.

While experienced farmers place great importance on careful mulching of interspaces, the general tendency is to clear the mulch away from the clump before South West monsoon, leading to exposure of roots which become dry if rains fail, soil temperature is increased, topsoil and SOM is eroded.

Mulching help in maintaining soil temperature and prevents variation in soil surface temperature thus help to protect cardamom roots from extremes of temperature. Mulching helps in better root development, proliferation, and extracts soil moisture from deep layers (depth) of soil during moisture stress period to maintain optimum soil moisture. Mulching is the practical method for soil moisture conservation, improving soil health and yield. Caution: While covering the plant base and interspace with mulch, It is important to remove mulches from the centre of clump (inside the clump, among tillers) to avoid tillers raising above the ground.

Figure 1. Mulching practice in cardamom that makes soil fertile

©Indian Cardamom Research Institute, Spices Board /Dr S Varadarasan

1. Advantages of mulching in the practice of eco-friendly cardamom cultivation

Mulching the interspace among plants reduce weed growth thus saves labour cost.

Figure 2. Mulching the interspace among cardamom plants

©Indian Cardamom Research Institute, Spices Board/Dr S Varadarasan

1.1 Mulching makes soil to induce high root biomass

With addition of mulching, the soil becomes friable, the bulk density is reduced, the organic carbon and pH is increased resulting in high root biomass and roots spread in the interspaces to absorb more nutrients.

Figure 3. Highly friable soil with low bulk density due to mulching     

   

©Indian Cardamom Research Institute, Spices Board /Dr S Varadarasan

2. Yielding in Cardamom plant

2.1 Mulching makes plant healthy and yields to its potential

Fungal diseases viz. capsule rot caused by Phytophthora and clump rot caused by Pythium, Rhizoctonia and Fusarium cause huge crop loss and walking out of tillers (radial spread tillers) in intensively managed fields. The cultural operations, such as mulching in fields with eco-friendly practices, improve beneficial soil microbes and so the incidence of fungal diseases and walking out of tillers become reduced. Figure 4. shows fourteen-year-old cardamom clump is compact without walking out symptom, bearing a good number of capsules; the yield is about 4 to 5 kg dry cardamom from such plants.

Figure 4. Fourteen-year-old cardamom plant with high yield

©Indian Cardamom Research Institute, Spices Board /Dr S Varadarasan

2.2 Eco-friendly cardamom cultivation with mulching to reduce pest damage on capsules

Eco-friendly cultural practices in cardamom paved way for reduced chemical pesticide spray and the pest damage is minimum. Figure 5. shows capsules are thrips and borer damage free and healthy.

Figure 5. A raceme in a panicle bearing cardamom capsules without pest attack

©Indian Cardamom Research Institute, Spices Board /Dr S Varadarasan

3. Eco-friendly cultivation encourages Honeybee population

Cardamom is cross pollinated and the native bee species viz, Apis cerana indica and Apis dorsata are the major pollinators. As the chemical insecticide and fungicide use are reduced considerably by way of cultural practices, the honeybee activity in the cardamom field is encouraged for making hives (colonies) in the tree holes and branches/stone-pitched bunds as well as for effective pollination. Abundance of honeybees in cardamom field has been proved to enhance fruit set as well as increase in the number of seeds in capsules. The overall impact is higher yield with bold and seeds-filled capsules.

3.1 Honeybee pollinators

Figure 6. Honeybee pollinating a cardamom flower

©Indian Cardamom Research Institute, Spices Board /Dr S Varadarasan

3.2 Bee colonization in eco-friendly cultivation

Figure 7. Pollinator Rock bee, Apis dorsata colonizing on shade tree branches during heavy flowering season

©Indian Cardamom Research Institute, Spices Board /Dr S Varadarasan

4. Eco-friendly cultivation encourages biological control of pest

Shoot borer is a major pest causing damage to capsules, panicles, and tillers. Several natural enemies of this pest are on record and their population is high in fields where pesticide spray is rational and need based. In eco-friendly cardamom cultivation, cultural operations such as pruning, and trashing reduce pest build up and hence chemical spray is much reduced making the natural enemies of pest are augmented that helps to reduce the pest. In the Figure 8, one such natural enemy, Apanteles, parasitizes borer larvae in capsules; therefore, the shoot borer larvae are controlled naturally at its early stage thus reducing its further damage to panicles, and shoot. The white capsule-like particle inside the capsules is the cocoon of the parasitoid, Apanteles.

4.1 Shoot borer larva parasitized by natural enemy

Figure 8. Parasitoid, Apanteles sp. on cardamom capsule borer

©Indian Cardamom Research Institute, Spices Board /Dr S Varadarasan

4.2 Eco-friendly cultivation encourages colonization of beneficial microbes in the soil

Adopting eco-friendly cardamom cultivation with cultural practices improves soil microbes, reduces disease causing fungi and bacteria leading to reduced incidence of fungal diseases. A comparative analysis of soils from eco-friendly and intensively cultivated fields indicate the following interesting indications; the pH of soil becomes favourable and the organic carbon level increases up to 4.3; Disease antagonistic fungus viz. Trichoderma, plant growth promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) and total fungi, bacteria, actinomycetes are very high in eco-friendly cardamom field.

Table 1. Comparison of soil parameters in eco-friendly and intensively cultivated fields
Soil parameter/ Soil microbes Microbial Population (cfu*/g of soil)
Eco-friendly cultivation Intensive cultivation
pH 5.6 4.3
Organic Carbon 4.3 2.1
Trichoderma 1.16 x 107 0.27 x 107
P. fluorescens 4.12 x 104 3.41 x 103
Azospirillum 0.63 x 107 0.41 x 107
Phosphate Solubilizing bacteria 3.05 x 106 1.83 x 106
Total Fungi 6.71 x 105 5.50 x 105
Total Bacteria 9.80 x 107 6.10 x 107
Total Actinomycetes 5.49 x 106 4.08 x 105

Source: Indian Cardamom Research Institute, Spices Board, 2021

*cfu: colony-forming unit

5. Validation of the practice

Cultural practices were adopted in the entire farm by Mr. K.V. Paulose in Rajkumari village, Idukki District, Kerala. These practices were recognized by Spices Board and National Innovation Foundation through field testing and awards. At present more than 500 farmers visited his field, and they are in transition for adopting these low cost eco-friendly practices gradually.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

A change in the mind set of farmers towards eco-friendly cardamom cultivation is the first step. Western Ghats evergreen forest ecosystem at 600 to 1 200 m above mean sea level, mean temperature of 15 to 25o C, loamy soil, and high organic carbon (2.0 to 4.5), pH 5.5 to 6.6 are the ideal condition for sustainable cultivation of small cardamom.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/moderately cool
  • Tropics, warm
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Biological control of Cardamom Root Grub (Basilepta fulvicorne): ID 10053.
  • Mulching in organic agriculture: ID 8365.
  • Mulching to control soil erosion: ID 8207.
  • Routine tree management practices: pruning and cutting tree tops: ID 4653.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

With pruning and trashing, the total number of chemical pesticide and fungicide sprays come down (more than 40 percent reduction), the quantity and frequency of chemical fertilizer are reduced, weed intensity is also reduced due to complete cover of soil, soil work/soil racking or digging is completely avoided, etc. All this work reduction directly reduces labour both men and women.

9.2 Women-friendly

Pruning and Trashing as well as harvesting works are mainly done by female laborers; women prefer these two works (activities) which are light and less cumbersome. So ecofriendly cardamom cultivation supports task specifically assigned to women.

9.3 Resource use efficiency

The addition of plant residue to cover the soil aids in increasing organic matter and organic carbon of soil, increasing beneficial microbes around rhizosphere, conserving soil moisture, prevent rainwater runoff, protect the root system from extremes of temperature etc. The overall impacts are extremely low external inputs, reduced labour requirement and sustainable higher yield without any pesticide residue; as well as the cardamom agro ecosystem in the serene Western Ghats is conserved.

9.4 Pro-poor technology

Majority of cardamom farmers are holding small plots ranging from 0.5 to 5 Hectares. Ecofriendly cardamom technology does not need much of external inputs; the onfarm resources add to the fertility of soil and reduces the need for chemical pesticides and fertilizers. So, if this technology of ecofriendly cardamom cultivation is adopted, the income of rural poor would be substantially increased.

entries.summary: A seleção e conservação de material de propagação das culturas é uma prática cada vez mais utilizada na gestão de recursos genéticos agrícolas e variedades locais. O trabalho realizado por instituições como o Centro ISOPlexis tem por objetivo a conservação da diversidade agrícola, a manutenção dos recursos genéticos, a sua utilização nos sistemas de produção de alimentos e no aumento da sustentabilidade. Nesta prática serão abordados procedimentos utilizados na amostragem, seleção e conservação de uma variedade local de milho branco (Zea mays L. subsp. mays).
entries.description:
Descrição

O exemplo usado é uma variedade local de milho, típico de uma zona do Norte da Madeira, do Concelho de Santana. O milho branco pertencente à variedade indurata, caracteriza-se por ser uma planta de grande porte, chegando a ter cerca de 3,5-4 metros de altura, e possui grão grande de cor branca. É usado tradicionalmente na alimentação, sendo consumido em fresco ou em farinha. Esta variedade é utilizada na confeção do milho cozido, um dos pratos tradicionais da Madeira, que consiste numa papa de milho, com couve picada e banha de porco. Outra iguaria da culinária madeirense derivada do milho cozido é o milho frito, que consiste de cubos de milho fritos em azeite ou em banha de porco.

A biomassa, do restolho da cultura, é utilizada como forragem na alimentação animal, em camas ou coberturas. Normalmente é colhida na altura do espigamento. A cultura do milho é praticada em consociação com feijão (Phaseolus vulgaris) (Figura 1).

Figura 1. Aspeto de uma plantação de milho. À esquerda podemos ver feijão em consociação.

©ISOPlexis Centre/Gregório Freitas

1. Cultura do Milho

1.1 Métodos tradicionais de secagem do milho

O  cultivo do milho é realizado entre a primavera e o verão.

  • A sementeira é realizada em março/abril.
  • A colheita de milho para consumo em fresco faz-se por volta de junho/julho.
  • O milho para semente e para a produção de farinha é colhido em agosto

O consumo da maçaroca cozida ou assada é típico das festas religiosas de verão.

Secagem:

As espigas para armazenamento são submetidas a secagem, podendo ser utilizados diversos métodos artesanais de secagem (Figura 2).

  1. Os agricultores habitualmente utilizam estruturas móveis:
    • como o caso de varas ou tecidos onde colocam as espigas ou grãos já debulhados a secar ao sol durante o dia e recolhem durante a noite.
  2. Outras estruturas fixas são também utilizadas na secagem do milho, como por exemplo:
    • árvores (gastalhos) ou alpendres.

Estes métodos de secagem podem ser reaplicados em qualquer ambiente pois os custos de materiais e manutenção são muitos baixos e acessíveis.

Figura 2. Secagem de milho feita de modo tradicional em estruturas móveis ou fixas.

©ISOPlexis Centre/Gregório Freitas

1.2 Métodos de amostragem de variedades locais

Vários fatores têm de ser tidos em consideração para fazer uma correta amostragem da cultura ou variedade local para obter material de propagação representativo e de boa qualidade.

No processo de seleção de espigas há que ter em conta o número de filas de grão presentes na espiga; a correta formação da espiga, e o tamanho da espiga (Figura 3-A). Neste processo de seleção também entra a qualidade sanitária da amostra.

Se na observação da espiga se detetar a contaminação por:

  • Bolores;
  • Fungos;
  • Picadas de insetos;
  • Contaminação genética da amostra.

A espiga deverá ser retirada do lote que será usado para obtenção de material para posterior sementeira (Figura 3).

As espigas não selecionadas poderão, dependendo do caso, ser usadas para alimentação de animais ou para fazer farinha de milho, mas no caso de infestação grave por agentes patogénicos devem ser destruídas.

Figura 3. Seleção de espigas de milho. À direita (A), seleção de espigas com 8 filas de grãos (B).

©ISOPlexis Centre/Fábio Reis

2. Separação de material vegetativo seminal de material infestado e de detritos

A seleção do material vegetativo a armazenar passa por vários processos.

Um deles está relacionado, com a seleção criteriosa das sementes, devendo o lote (amostra) a constituir, apresentar somente sementes com vigor germinativo elevado (acima dos 85%), sem indícios de doenças ou presença de pragas associadas.

Determinação do valor germinativo no milho

A determinação da viabilidade do milho é feita através de testes de germinação. O processo segue os protocolos elaborados pela International Seed Testing Association (ISTA) e os respetivos critérios:

  1. Selecionar dois lotes de 100 sementes da amostra.
  2. Desinfetar as sementes numa solução de 10% de lixívia (10 mL de lixívia para 90 mL de água).
  3. Lavar as sementes, após 10 minutos, na solução de desinfeção.
  4. Colocar folhas de papel absorvente no fundo de um recipiente (ex. Tupperware).
  5. Distribuir as sementes de milho em cima do papel, de modo uniforme.
  6. Colocar outra folha de papel absorvente no topo das sementes. Esta técnica denomina-se “Entre papel” (Between paper (BP)).
  7. Molhar o papel com água destilada, até humedecer, certificando-se que ocorre o ensopamento das sementes.
  8. Fechar o recipiente com a tampa e colocar num local escuro com uma temperatura entre os 20-30ºC.
  9. Realizar duas contagens do número de sementes germinadas:
    • A primeira contagem deverá ser feita 4 dias após colocar as sementes a germinar;
    • A segunda 7 dias após a sementeira.
  10. Contar o número de sementes:
    • Germinadas;
    • Dormentes; 
    • Infestadas com fungos.
  11. O agricultor deverá ter em atenção os seguintes critérios no momento de armazenamento das sementes:
    • Se a percentagem de germinação for inferior a 85%, trata-se de um lote que não convém guardar com o objetivo de utilizar na próxima sementeira.
    • Se o lote tiver uma percentagem de viabilidade acima de 85% trata-se de um conjunto de sementes que poderão e deverão ser usados na próxima época de sementeira.

2.1 Seleção das sementes para material de propagação

As principais etapas do processo de separação do grão são:

  1. Debulha e seleção;
  2. Limpeza.

2.1.1 Debulha

Na seleção do grão, as sementes da parte apical e basal da espiga deverão ser descartadas, pois é comum nestas zonas aparecerem sementes malformadas, danificadas mecanicamente e com infestação de fungos, bactérias e insetos (Figura 4).

Debulhar o grão da parte central da espiga recolhendo apenas as sementes desta parte.

Recolher o grão da parte central de uma dezena de espigas para um contentor.

Figura 4. Processo de debulha dos grãos de milho.

©ISOPLexis Centre/Fábio Reis

2.1.2 Limpeza

Para a correta e duradoura armazenagem do material de propagação a longo prazo e obter uma boa sementeira é necessário certificarmo-nos que a amostra contém sementes inteiras, ou seja com embrião (material seminal).

Todos os detritos presentes na amostra poderão ser uma potencial fonte de contaminação. Com o objetivo de eliminar estes detritos, no ISOPlexis é utilizado um método gravitacional baseado na separação das sementes pelo seu peso específico. O aparelho tem uma coluna vertical, onde é utilizada uma fonte de aspiração para retirar o material mais leve e as sementes caem por gravidade num outro recetáculo (Figura 5).

Na ausência deste equipamento, a separação dos detritos das sementes intactas e sãs pode ser conseguida com a utilização de um joeiro (peneira) por peneiração ou manualmente.

Figura 5. Utilização de soprador de sementes (esquerda) para separação de sementes saudáveis e remoção de detritos e sementes inviáveis.

©ISOPlexis Centre/Fábio Reis

3. Processo de secagem das amostras e determinação do seu teor de humidade

Os processos tradicionais de secagem da semente ao ar livre respondem de forma empírica à necessidade de desidratar (secar) a semente antes do seu armazenamento para utilização na próxima época de sementeira ou para consumo. O excesso de humidade poderá promover o rápido aparecimento e a proliferação de fungos, provocando a acumulação de toxinas prejudiciais à saúde humana. Várias condicionantes limitam o processo de secagem ao ar livre, nomeadamente as variações de temperatura e humidade, e a qualidade dos contentores de armazenamento das sementes que podem reduzir drasticamente a qualidade do material genético à disposição do agricultor.

O processo de secagem das sementes no ISOPlexis é realizado em condições de temperatura e humidade controladas, utilizando para o efeito exsicadores ou armário com humidade controlada. Este processo de secagem faz com que a qualidade final da amostra seja maior. A desidratação é avaliada pela medição periódica da quantidade de água (humidade) na semente, utilizando balanças ou sondas para determinação da humidade relativa. Este procedimento permite definir, de forma precisa, a altura de armazenamento da amostra, que ocorre quando o teor de humidade atingir os 5% do peso da semente (Figura 6).

Na secagem ao ar livre, os agricultores podem adotar procedimentos alternativos, colocando as sementes debulhadas, selecionadas e isentas de detritos, em locais secos, com temperatura estável, sobre bancadas com tampo de rede, a uma altura do solo não inferior a 50 cm, afim de permitir uma boa circulação do ar. A desidratação da semente pode ser monitorizada através da pesagem periódica (de 15 em 15 dias) de uma subamostra (sempre a mesma) de sementes, considerando que a semente está em condições para armazenamento, quando o seu peso em duas pesagens sucessivas for constante.

Figura 6. Secagem da amostra de milho num exsicador à esquerda.  À direita, determinação da percentagem de humidade da amostra.

©ISOPlexis Centre/Fábio Reis

3.1 Preparação para o processo de loteamento de sementes

O processo de loteamento de uma amostra é um dos passos mais importantes no banco de germoplasma, pois permite determinar o peso de um lote constituído por um determinado número de sementes.

Para além disso, fornece-nos informação sobre a qualidade da amostra armazenada. A determinação do peso de 100 sementes da amostra dá uma estimativa, através de uma média, da qualidade dos grãos presentes nessa amostra (Figura 7).

Estas operações podem também ser realizada manualmente, através da contagem e pesagem final de um número pré-estabelecido de sementes. O registo do peso pode ser feito num caderno de campo.

Figura 7. Contagem do número de sementes e determinação do seu peso.

©ISOPlexis Centre/Fábio Reis

4. Loteamento e selagem de uma amostra de sementes de milho

O processo de selagem da amostra é uma das etapas finais que garante o mínimo de distúrbios externos para a amostra.

As sementes são colocadas em sacos de mylar e de seguida selados numa máquina de vácuo.

A selagem em vácuo da amostra em sacos mylar garante que as condições das sementes, durante o armazenamento manter-se-ão inalteradas por longo período. Com este processo as variações externas de humidade e luminosidade não irão afetar as sementes (Figura 8).

Os lotes de semente ensacados são depois conservados no frio, a temperaturas entre +4 e -20 °C.

A +4°C para uma conservação curta que permita a utilização do material de imediato e a -20°C e para uma conservação a longo prazo (serve como reserva).

Em alternativa, os agricultores podem conservar as sementes em frascos de cor, fechados hermeticamente, à temperatura ambiente acrescentando pimenta em pó ou partes de plantas como por exemplo a hortelã-pimenta, cujo aroma repele insetos como o gorgulho do Sitophilus zeamais (Motschulsky, 1855).

No caso da conservação das sementes à temperatura ambiente recomenda-se em primeiro lugar uma “quarentena” no frio a temperaturas abaixo de 0 °C, durante 48 a 72h. Para destruir os ovos de insetos que poderão permanecer não detetados na amostra de sementes.

Figura 8. Loteamento e selagem a vácuo da amostra.

©ISOPlexis Centre/Fábio Reis

5. Bases de dados e identificação de amostras loteadas

A documentação da amostra de material de propagação é de vital importância para a sua rastreabilidade, bem como a sua correta identificação (Figura 9).

Documentar a amostra permite saber o que é que está conservado, desde quando, como se chama este tipo de grão, a sua origem e a utilização mais adequada. Informações tais como a data de armazenamento, as quantidades de sementes disponíveis dão, por exemplo, informações necessárias à gestão de stocks de sementes para distribuição a um grande número de agricultores.

Figura 9. Inserção de dados referentes à amostra na Base de dados GRIN Global e identificação da amostra para conservação a longo prazo.

©ISOPlexis Centre/Fábio Reis

Figura 10. Esquema das etapas que se aplicam desde a amostragem à documentação da amostra.

Colaboração:

Esta prática foi produzida em colaboração e com a contribuição do Professor Míguel Ângelo Carvalho e Humberto Nóbrega da Universidade da Madeira e Isoplexis, e Sónia R. Dias, UNFAO, Office of Innovation- Research and Extension.

6. Validação da prática

Estes tipos de práticas são utilizadas na Região da Madeira, Portugal.

O cultivo do milho na Madeira é realizado em zonas agrícolas de clima temperado a semitropical e tem uma sazonalidade entre março a agosto.

O cultivo do milho é feito por agricultores tradicionais para consumo próprio e o excedente é vendido para o mercado regional.

A participação do ISOPlexis no processo está relacionada com a conservação deste recurso genético, na multiplicação de material e na distribuição de sementes para cultivo, principalmente em cooperação com agricultores no modo de produção biológico.

7. Requisitos mínimos para a implementação bem-sucedida da prática

Para o cultivo das variedades locais de milho são necessárias sementes de produção local, bem-adaptadas a solos ácidos e a requisitos baixos de água, embora hajam regas frequentes devido a estarem inseridos em sistemas agrícolas de consociação.

Um dos fatores limitantes ao cultivo é a fertilidade do solo, pois trata-se de uma cultura com requisitos altos de nutrientes, influenciando a qualidade da semente produzida, bem como da sua parte vegetativa.

8. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Subtropical, quente / mod legal.
  • Temperado lega.

9. Tecnologias associadas ou relacionadas

  • Agricultura sempre verde (Evergreen agriculture): agricultura de conservação na produção de milho: ID 2846.
  • Processamento de mandioca: farinha húmida de mandioca: ID 2826.
  • O papel da normalização no milho: ID 2020.
  • Gestão de pestes e doenças no milho: ID 2019.

10. Objetivos cumpridos pelo projeto

  • Tecnologia amigável para as mulheres.
  • Adequado para as mulheres.

entries.title: Korangadu pastureland and promotion of fodder species for livestock
entries.source: Sustainable agriculture & Environmental Voluntary Action (SEVA)
multi_source: Sustainable Agriculture & Environmental Voluntary Action - SEVA (SEVA)#Sustainable Agriculture & Environmental Voluntary Action - SEVA (SEVA)#Sustainable Agriculture & Environmental Voluntary Action - SEVA (SEVA)#Sustainable Agriculture & Environmental Voluntary Action - SEVA (SEVA)
entries.summary:
In order to promote livestock in dry land areas, farmers created “Korangadu” pastureland many centuries ago in their own private lands in Tamil Nadu. This system encourages livestock keeping and earning more income in dry land/rainfed areas. Korangadu typically consists of a mixture of grass, legumes and tree species including annuals and perennials, being utilized for grazing their cattle, buffaloes and sheep. Korangadu provides pasture for the livestock kept by farmers or landless families' in turn livelihood for them. A farmer maintains or owns an average area of 2 ha Korangadu pastureland and this is sufficient to maintain two adult cows plus four calves or 20 sheep. Korangadu pastureland is existent in about 10 000 ha (within 25 km2) in 500 villages in Tirupur, Karur and Dindigul districts of Tamil Nadu in semi-arid region.

SEVA has documented Korangadu pastureland system and organized awareness programmes through workshops with local farmers. During these workshops we finalized strategies for conservation and regeneration of traditional pasture land system and communicated through our local newsletter "Nam Vali Velanmai" and printed booklet on Korangadu pastureland. During 2018 - 2020, SEVA provided fodder species (by distributing seeds, cuttings) to 800 beneficiaries and livestock keepers in Pudukkottai, Thanjavur, Thoothukudi and Tirunelveli districts of Tamil Nadu.
entries.description:
Description

Plant species in Korangadu

Korangadu typically consists of a mixture of grass, legumes and tree species including annual and perennials. It has predominantly three major species of flora which are spatially in three tiers. The lower tier of Kolukattai grass (Cenchrus sp.) an upper tier of tree species including Acacia leucophloea that is locally called velvel and a live fence comprised of a thorny shrub locally called as MulluKiluvai (Commiphora berryii) makes up the middle tier (Figure 1).

Table 1. Classification of flora in a Korangadu
Type Species Common Names
A. Trees

Velvel (Acacia leucophloea), Usialai (Albizia amara)
B. Grass

Kolukottaipul (Cenchrus ciliaris), Ottanpul (Setaria vericillata) , Kurutupul (Cholris barbata), Cholapul (Chrysopogonmontanus), Hariyali (Cynodon dactylon)
C. Legumes and Herbs

Naripayaru (Phaseolus trilobus), Savurikodi (Trychosanthes tricuspidata), Seppunerinji (Indigofera enneaphylla), Kollu (Dolichos biflorus), Kattukollu (Rhynchosia rufescens)
D. Shrubs in Live Fence

Mullukiluvai (Commiphora berryii), RayilKatralai (Agave americana), Minnamaram (Premna serratifolia)

Source: SEVA

Figure 1. Three tier system of trees, shrubs, grass

©SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

1. How to establish Korangadu?

For land to be converted to Korangadu, it has to be ploughed during summer. Sowing of Kolukattai grass has to be undertaken during Purattasi – Iypassi (Sept – Oct). In order to cover 1 acre about 15 kg of seeds of Kolukattai grass are sufficient. The seeds are harvested from the already established pastureland. Harvesting of seeds will be in the month of Thai (Jan – Feb). Kolukattai grass can also be mixed with Naripayaru or Phillipasera seeds, (Phaseolus trilobus) and Kollu (Horse gram) seeds at the rate of about 10 kg each for 1 acre.

After sowing, grazing is not permitted for one year, but allowed in the second year of establishment. In the established Korangadu, immediately after rains, animals are not allowed to graze for one month in order to allow the grass and legumes to attain the required growth, after that, livestock will be allowed to enter inside the land for grazing.

In order to protect the pasture land, live fencing is applied by planting cuttings of Mullukiluvai (Commiphoraberryii). About 4 feet (122 cm) length stumps of Kiluvaia thorny weed plant found in wastelands / jungles is cut with a thickness of 3 inches (7.6 cm). These stumps or cuttings are planted in 1 feet (30 cm) depth by digging the soil with a crowbar. Two rows of planting with such cuttings is completed during the month of Ani, Adi (July – Aug). The survival and establishment of planted stumps will be ensured with the onset of monsoon during Purattasi – Iyppasi (Sept. – Oct.). About 30 labourers are required to plant Kiluvai cuttings in 1 acre land to establish live fencing. Wages are paid at Rs. 300 to 500 per labourer per day.

Every year the established fence has to be maintained by proper gap filling with fresh cuttings of Kiluvai and any such new plantings are to be performed only in the month of Ani – Adi (June – July). Sometimes natural growth of other plant species like “Minnamaram” will also be growing.(Farmers cut the branches (7 feet length (213 cm)) of “Minnamaram” and utilize them for making “Tharambu” for constructing sheep shed locally called as “Attupatti”. In the Korangadu pasture land “Velvelamaram” tree will be growing naturally and usually seeds of “Velvel” germinate from the animal dung. When cattle and sheep relish the pods of “Velvelmaram” the seeds are passed undigested and spread through the dung. Farmers usually maintain optimum population of “Velvel” tree; population will be around 20 to 25 trees in 1 acre or 60 to 70 trees in 2 ha land of “Korangadu”.
The grown up tree will bear fruits in six to seven years and pods fall on the ground during Feb – April. A grown up tree will yield 40 to 50 kg of pod, and it serves as good feed during summer. During summer season when the rainfall is absent the growth of the grass is poor or almost not existent and at that time falling pods of “Velvel” tree will provide good fodder for animals.

Excess pods will be collected from the field and stored. Such pods will be mixed with sorghum seeds to feed young ones of sheep. Each lamb will take about ½ kg of such mixture, and it is fed in the morning time.

Figure 2. Early growth of fodder species in Korangadu

©SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

1.2 Grazing system

The paddock provides grazing fields for animals for at least five months in a year. The growth of the grass is noticed immediately after the receipt of rainfall. Rain occurs during three distinct seasons (south-west monsoon, north-east monsoon, summer showers) as experienced in these places. About one month time will be allowed for the grass to germinate and attain required growth and after that animals are taken into paddock for grazing. Grazing will be from morning till evening. Drinking water is taken and filled in the stone/cement troughs within the paddock so that animals will come and drink water as and when it needs. Drinking water is fetched from the village and carried or transported through bi-cycle or bullock cart to the paddocks.

During Dec. and Jan., if there is good growth of Kolukattai, few farmers can harvest and store the kolikattai as hay for feeding the animals during off-season. During summer animals are allowed to feed on the pods of Velvel trees. Farmers divide their lands into paddocks, and animals are allowed in rotation.

Four hectares of “Korangadu” grass land is sufficient to maintain four adult cows plus six calves or 40 sheep or six buffaloes or 20 goats. The animals will not have infertility problems if grazed in “Korangadu” pastureland. The “Korangadu” pastureland will provide grazing opportunities for the livestock for free grazing during Oct. to Jan., continuously due to growth of grass on the receipt of the north-east monsoon. During March to June, when there is no grass in the pastureland the cattle feed upon the pods of Acacia leucophloea. Whenever summer rains or unseasonal rains occur this pastureland will have regrowth of vegetation and thereby serve as fodder source for livestock. The growth of different local fodder species also spread in such a manner that it is likely to support the partial grazing of animals at least during 8 to10 months annually. Farmers can construct water trough in the individual plots for providing drinking water for the animals. Animals are usually allowed for free grazing within individual paddocks fenced with live fencing.

Figure 3. Cattle grazing in Korangadu

©SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

2. Tenancy system

Farmers who have a lot of paddocks but owning few livestock or no animals, lease the lands to landless livestock keepers who in turn pay lease fee of Rs. 8 000 for 2 ha paddocks annually. Sometimes Korangadu land is given for long term lease basis called “Othi” to livestock keepers for Rs. 80 000. Whenever the livestock keepers want to close his grazing contract the landowner returns the same money to the tenant.

The farmers mostly belong to “Gounder’’ community and land ownership of individual paddocks ranges from 0.5 ha to 10 ha. The dairy animals provide income to farmers through moderate milk yield. These communities are also maintaining sheep and goats and earn income by selling them for meat purpose. Tenure system of “Korangadu” grazing land is also practised between owners and tenants where landless tenant keep livestock like sheep; for example a tenant family pays Rupees 80 000/- (approximately USD 1 084) for keeping 2 ha of paddock and this money can be got back without interest after a period of two to five years depending upon the contract. The details of ownership pattern of Korangadu” pastureland are shown in the Annexure . Wealthy farmers who are leaving or reducing the area of agriculture and settling in cities are leasing their lands to livestock keepers on tenancy basis.

2.1 Korangadu pastureland and livestock keeping 

Farmers and agricultural labourers keep cattle, buffalo, sheep and goat. They depend upon Korangadu pastureland for day to day grazing of animals. In the drought prone region livestock keepers are maintaining animals for their livelihood. The area is typical dry land with annual rainfall less than 700 mm. Now-a-days the erratic rainfall forced the farmers to solely depend upon animal husbandry for the livelihood leaving agriculture which is a gamble of monsoon. Therefore, there is a good scope for developing pasture land which is insurance against recurrent drought. Due to this many farmers are interested to switch over to animal husbandry activity and convert the dry land agriculture into Korangadu pastureland. During our survey with 2 564 families we noted that there are 6 505 cattle, 1 365 buffalo, 30 936 sheep are maintained by them. On an average, a farmer in Korangadu region owns about two to three cattle, 1 buffalo and 12 to 15 sheep per landholding of 8 acres of pastureland. Approximately 2 ha of pastureland will support 25 sheep together with 2 cattle. They derive income by selling milk and also disposing male sheep. Sheep rearing is the major source of income; it yields three lambs in two years.

Figure 4. Grazing of sheep by a tenant

©SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

Figure 5. Sheep grazing in Korangadu

©SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

Figure 6. Farmers meeting at Nallampalayam village

©SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

Figure 7. A farmer grazing his dairy cow in Korangadu in Nallampalayam village

©SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

Figure 8. Entrance of Korangadu paddock during summer

©SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

Figure 9. Grownup grass in Korangadu

©SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

3. Validation of the practice

This traditional pasture land system exists for many centuries in Tamil Nadu. The lands which are with red laterite or gravel type of soil, well drained, semi, arid region with rainfall 400 to 600 mm are suitable for raising the Korangadu pasture species. It is noticed in Tiruppur, Karur, Dindigul, Erode districts of Tamil Nadu, India.

SEVA has distributed fodder slips, seeds to 824 livestock keepers for growing them in their backyard /lands in Thiruvarur, Thanjavur, Pudukottai Thoothukudi, Tirunelveli districts during 2018-2020.

4. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Rainfall of 400 to 800 mm will be more ideal in gravel, red soil with no water stagnation.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Improved feeding of dairy cattle for increased milk production and income: ID 6988.
  • Growing fodder for livestock: Calliandra and elephant grass: ID 6989.
  • Building fodder security in rural areas: ID 7684.
  • Introduction of silvopastoral systems for cattle raising to sustainably provide fodder to animals: ID 8954.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

Korangadu land reduces cost of labour by free grazing in confined paddocks. The animals are driven into the individual paddocks fenced with live fencing. In the evening animals are taken home. There is no dedicated labour for grazing the animals. Water trough filled with water fulfill drinking water requirements of animals.

7.2 Women-friendly

Women manages grazing of animals in Korangadu and also give adequate time to undertake other routine activities in addition to grazing. Managing sheep and cows are generating income for the families.

7.3 Resource use efficiency

In semi-arid region where the rainfall is low and erratic crop cultivation is risky lead to failure of crops. However, livestock farming in Korangadu pastureland provides livelihoods and income security for farmers and tenant livestock keepers.

7.4 Pro-poor technology

Poor people including land less labourers earn income by rearing sheep or dairy cows by acquiring Korangadu pastureland on lease basis (by payment of annual rent for grazing in the lands of property owners).

This practice has been developed by Beekeeping Network North-/South (BNNS) in collaboration with André Makenbo of PLAAC, DRC.

entries.tittle: Apiculture: Utilisation d’un enfumoir métallique à soufflet
entries.summary: The use of fire and smoke to extract honey from hives or natural colonies offers some kind of protection from the beestings. However, this practice does not only harm the environment and the health of the colonies, it has also a negative impact on the honey quality. The use of a metal smoker with bellows solves this problem. What follows is a description of how to light the smokers and how to use it during a hive inspection. Indications on the combustion material to use are also given.

entries.summary: The beehive frame grip is a useful tool for the beekeeper. It allows removing frames from the hive with one hand only, leaving the other hand free. Usually frames are glued to the hive or to each other with propolis. Propolis is a resinous substance that makes the loosening and removal of frames difficult. A hive tool is used to make loosening and removing frames from the hive easier. In addition, the hive tool can be used to scrape propolis from the frames and the inside of the hive.

entries.title: How to make a protective jacket with veil for beekeeping
entries.source: Swisscontact
entries.summary: This text describes how to make a protective jacket with integrated veil for beekeeping and the materials needed. The protective jacket is an essential element of the protective beekeeping gear and protect the beekeeper from bee stings during hive inspections. The protective jacket protects the upper part of the body, from the head to the waist. Making the protective jacket requires medium level sowing skills and the materials required are easily available.

entries.summary: The beekeepers suit is an essential element of the protective gear. It protects the body from bee stings when working with bees. This practice was developed by the Beekeeping Network North-South (BNNS) in collaboration with the tailors of the "Platefomes des Associations des Apiculteurs des Cataractes (PLAAC)" in Mbanza-Ngungu, Democratic Republic of Congo.

entries.title: How to make starter strips for topbar hives
entries.source: The Beekeeping Network North-South (BNNS)
entries.summary: In the management of a topbar hive (TBH), an essential step is the application of starter strips on the top bars, from which the bees will build their combs. These starter strips guide the bees to build their combs nicely down from the top bars. This will allow the beekeeper to pull up each top bar with comb without breaking any combs.  The starter strip will also make the junction between the comb and the top bar stronger and as a result, the combs will break less easily. There are different ways to make starter strips, depending on the length of the top bar, which is determined by the model of the hive, locally available material, and the availability of time of the beekeeper. The procedure to make starter strips described here has been inspired by the articles on the blog "1 ruche et 3 pintades" of Claire Clément, a beekeeper in Senegal, and the contributions from participants of the discussion "Comment fabriquer des amorces de cire pour la conduite de ruches à barrettes" (how to make starter strips for topbar hives) on the TECA platform between March and September 2018.
