entries.summary:
Conservation Agriculture (CA), No-till method of farming which is climate smart, increases organic carbon of the soil, essentially are generative agricultural practice, considerably increases productivity of the land and adds to the amazing happiness & confidence of the farmer." The Saguna Regenerative Technique (SRT) cultivation method was evolved in 2011 at Saguna Baug, Neral, Dist. Raigad, Maharashtra, India.

The permanent raised beds used in this method facilitates ample of oxygen supply to the root zone area while maintaining optimum moisture condition there. SRT is being used for 25 to 30 different crops such as cereals, vegetables, pulses, oilseeds, millets, cotton, maize, etc. Absence of puddling and transplanting of rice makes it possible for “Not dependent on high amount of water, availability of tractor or plough and skilled labour during specific period of transplanting“.
entries.description:
Description

Saguna Regenerative Technique (SRT) quickly rejuvenates the soil by enhancing percent organic carbon, by enhanced earthworm and microbial activity, by improved drainage, water infiltration and aerobic condition at rhizosphere, all of it together considerably increases yield at lower cost of production. 

Figure 1. Healthy soil for healthy food and healthy environment

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

1. Protocol of SRT

  • Bed making: the permanent raised beds are used unchanged for the next 20 years or more. The dimensions: centre to centre 136 cm, top width of the bed 100 cm, the furrow channel between beds 36 cm. Height of the bed 20 cm.
  • Direction: along the slope.
  • Seed Sowing: date of sowing for different crops including rice are to be sown as per the local agroclimatic traditions. Until an automatic seed dibbling machine is developed / located, the operation is to be performed manually with the help of SRT Frame. The iron frame is designed to make holes at 25 x 25 cm but can be changed to multiples of 25 cm as per the crop requirement. E.g. Sweet corn to be planted at 25 x 50 cm. 
  • Pre emergence selective weedicide application: this is important to prevent weed growth in the first month of plantation. The selective pre emergence weedicide is to be applied within 24 hours after seed planting on a moist land walking backwards. 
  • Post emergence selective weedicide application: if for some reason the aggressive weed is noticed after crop emergence these set of selective weedicides can be sprayed.
  • Gap filling and fertilizer application: this is to be performed between 15 and 25 days after emergence of the crop.
  • Pest management: due to SRT the organic carbon of the soil starts rising which helps the crop to keep the insects at a distance. But we strongly recommend use of IPM practices which involves different types of insect pest traps.
  • Nutrition booster spray: this spray enhances crop immunity and yield considerably. This can be applied between 50 and 60 days after germination. This consists of mainly the micronutrients and can also have major nutrients in a small quantity.
  • Harvesting: as of today harvesting is done either manually or by reaper. But a modified combined harvester can solve the problem of stubble burning and can motivate the large farmers.
  • Roots for the land: roots of the previous crop are to be kept undisturbed in-situ. Our philosophy is, “the fruit and the grain is for human being, the leaves and straw for the animals and the roots with stubble for the land”.
  • Once the roots of the harvested crop start sprouting again after five to seven days it is to be sprayed by systemic general purpose weedicide which stops the competition for the next crop and the stubbles are converted into organic carbon, the precious source for next crop.
  • Crop rotation: the easy possibility of relay crops is one of the important advantages of SRT. If irrigation is available three crops can be taken very easily. Crop rotation is a must in SRT.

1.1 Preparation of permanent raised beds

In this method we make the permanent raised beds. They are used over and again to grow various rotation crops without tillage or land preparation for the next crop.

Figure 2. The permanent raised beds made by the farmer will be used for growing crops for 20 year or more without any tillage

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Farmer Mr Hitendra Bagmare

1.2 Vigorous uniformity

The aerobic condition at the rhizosphere triggers positive chain reaction for healthy root and plant growth and reduced risk and drudgery to the farmer.

Figure 3. Excellent germination and vigorous root and uniform plant growth of the seedling

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Farmer Mr Hitendra Bagmare

2. Impact on soil structure and water infiltration

With increase in organic carbon, in-situ decomposing of organic matter, capillary formation by drying roots and earthworms, enhanced aerobic condition in the deeper layer of soil, quickly builds a healthy soil. Improved water drainage makes the crop climate smart and climate resilient. 

2.1 Presence of earthworms in the paddy field in many types of soils.

With the traditional method where ploughing and puddling is performed the survival and performance of earthworms was impossible. But with No Till SRT method all the 3 000 farmers in all six agroclimatic zones are dancing with happiness after noticing naturally presence of earthworms.

Figure 4. Different types of soils showing earthworms

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

2.2 Improved soil structure and well drained condition leads to climate smart farming

Increased organic carbon enhanced earthworm activity and higher microflora improve soil aggregation and water drainage which helped all 100 percent SRT farmers during floods in past two years. The same resilience was also noticed in drought conditions. 

Figure 5. Side-by-side SRT and traditional rice plots affected by flood

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

3. Crop rotation

Crop rotation ensures biodiversity of microflora and in turn the soil health. This also ensures the crop resilience and higher income to the farmers. As the small farmers depend for their home food consumption on their own land, the rotation comes in very handy, ensuring the food security.

3.1 Crop rotation and subsistence farming

A one hectare tribal farmer is able to provide 25 different food items to his family on their food plate due to SRT while he was able to provide only four items by traditional method.

Figure 6. The happy and content tribal farmer with 25 different food items from his one hectare SRT farm

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

3.2 Problem of residue burning on farm lands

Organic residue burning on farms is practised either to get rid of the bulk of residue and quickly making it convenient for next crop sowing or to sterilize the land for seed sowing. Both problems are taken care in SRT method by avoiding burning of crop residue.

Figure 7. Wheat after rice without burning of crop residue by SRT

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

4. Happiness and dignity to a smallholder farmer is possible

Small farmers are giving up and their next generation is rapidly losing interest in farming. SRT brought an unparalleled change and made every farmer happy and confident for the first time in their life, soon after their adoption to the SRT. Now their next generation after experiencing dignity to the farming even they are joining and taking over the farming profession.  

4.1 Farmer happiness index

The survey of 160 farmers was conducted by visiting them and asking a set of 20 questions, collecting replies in smiles and was analysed by statistical tool.

Figure 8. The SRT farmer happiness index

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

4.2 The no till science became a movement

The technique was developed to solve my own problems of farming. Our success story was taken to other farmers at our individual level from 2012. The successful farmers are now spreading the technique to other needy farmers in their respective area. Now the ball is about to get rolling which requires intervention by large organizations.

Figure 9. SRT Happy and confident farmers

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

5. Validation of the practice

  • The technique initially was tested in two districts of Maharashtra, India with 30 rice farmers in 2013. It has gradually grown to 3 000 farmers with 25 different crops in 26 districts of Maharashtra having six agroclimatic zones.
  • Initially the technique was used only for rice based farming system under rainfed condition with rainfall +/- 1 500 mm to 3 000 mm. It is now been accepted by POCRA, Project on Climate Resilient Agriculture, World Bank for drought prone 16 districts of Maharashtra for resolving soil and water issues of the region for crops such as cotton, soybean, pigeon pea, maize, sorghum, pearl millet, green gram, chickpea, etc.
  • It is accepted for “The Vision of Antyodaya” documentation of the best practices of sustainable development by ISRN, Indian Social Responsibility Network, Ministry of Culture, Govt of India.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The most important basic necessity for successful implementation of SRT is that the farmer should be motivated and ready for change for self upliftment. SRT is working out very well with all types of soil texture, soil PH, water quality, even saline soils in coastal area with respective crops of the area. The technique involves minimum inputs and is “too good to be true” is one of the problem we have noticed for even trying out the technique on a small area by a new farmer.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Zero/minimum tillage in rice-wheat system: ID 7715.
  • Introduction to conservation agriculture: principles and benefits: ID 7413.
  • No-till technology: a no-till system with crop residue management for medium scale wheat and barley farming: ID 7507.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

SRT saves 50 percent labor especially in rice due to avoiding of transplanting operation (a drudgery to the labor). The transplanting operation in knee deep mud is carried out by both men and women.

9.2 Women-friendly

The traditional rice cultivation which involves many small tasks to be carried out by women such as preparation of food for laborers, uprooting the seedling, weeding, cleaning the bullock barn and so on. All these tasks in case of small holder farmer have become zero with SRT which has brought high comfort level to the women. The technique is so easy, light and manageable that she can easily and effectively take care of the farm with or without help of a man. Thus she has become happy, independent and confident.

9.3 Resource use efficiency

  • Land: with availability of small amount of irrigation a SRT farmer is easily able to take three crops making the land efficiency 300 percent.
  • Water: the increase water holding capacity has reduced water requirement by 40 to 50 percent. Also in case of rice no puddling for transplanting can save 40 percent water.
  • Soil: SRT quickly stops soil erosion; during puddling of traditional method 20% fertile silt is washed away with water which is completely saved in SRT.
  • Energy inputs: 100 percent saving of fossil fuel required for tillage operations which is almost 90% requirement of small holder farmer.

9.4 Pro-poor technology

The technology reduces the dependence of the small holder farmers on tractor and implements, excess labors and optimum rain/water and yet get the high productivity. This has improved their livelihood because they can easily spend on the education of their young ones, celebrate social functions luxuriously, have sufficient time at hand for future planning, all of which build their confidence.

entries.source: The Beekeeping Network North-South (BNNS)
entries.summary: Rwanda's climate and rich and varied melliferous flora are favourable for the development of beekeeping.  This document explains how to make a traditional hive model composed of elongated cyclinder made with the stems of Pennisetum (Urubingo), bamboo or papyrus. This hive model is very suitable to promote among smallholder producers that wish to take up beekeeping because it is well adapted to the local environment and it is easy to make and manage. In addition, this hive model requires little financial investment because it is made with locally available materials.

entries.title: How to make a Kenyan topbar hive
entries.source: The Beekeeping Network North-South (BNNS)
entries.summary: The Kenyan topbar hive is having great success in African and is gaining popularity in other continents. This hive model allows the transition from a traditional beekeeping with fixed comb hives, to a more sophisticated, but still easy to practice beekeeping. In fact, the advantage of this hive model is that it is still easier to build and manage than the so-called "modern hives" using movable frames and honey supers such as the Dadant hive and Langstroth hive. This document provides an overview of the pros and cons of the Kenyan topbar hive and explains in detail how to build it. This document was developed by Beekeeping Network North-South (BNNS) in collaboration with Daniel Mathieu who provided all illustrations contained in this document.

entries.title: A step-by-step approach toward a gradual adoption of the full conservation agriculture technology: an example from Timor-Leste
entries.source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
multi_source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)#Organisation des Nations Unies pour l'alimentation et l'agriculture (FAO)#Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Agricultura y la Alimentación (FAO)#Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)

agrovoc_keywords.display: Conservation agriculture#Agriculture de conservation#Agricultura de conservación#Conservation agriculture

entries.summary: This practice describes the step-by-step approach to promote conservation agriculture implemented in Timor-Leste. It also describes the conservation agriculture (CA) principles and steps in adopting the CA package.
entries.description:
Description

1. Step-by-step approach to promote conservation agriculture

1.1 Gradual adoption of the CA package

After several years of promoting CA in Timor-Leste by various actors, the adoption of the CA package is rarely fully implemented by farmers. Partial adoption of CA technology by farmers is a standard step in the process.

Changing old farming practices typically takes place over several years. It is generally accepted that at least 5 to 10 years is necessary to change farmers' practices sustainably.

Figure 1. The tree CA principles that farmers applied.

©FAO

The CA evaluation has shown that 98 percent of farmers practising CA apply the first two CA principles (1 and 2): 'no burning' and 'no ploughing.' Less than 2 percent of the CA adopters applied principle (3) by growing Velvet beans (lehe) as a high biomass cover crop in their production system. Other legumes are rarely intercropped in CA farms unless this was the traditional practice in the area where CA is promoted (e.g., Baucau, Lautem and Manatuto).

Considering that CA's adoption is a gradual process, the technology's promotion should 'unpack' the CA package and promote a step-by-step approach toward a gradual adoption of the full CA technology. To unpack it in a practical way, it required a gradual adaptation to the 'slash & burn' farming systems of Timor-Leste, and integrating CA into disaster risks management approaches.

1.2 Integrating the promotion of CA in disaster risks management planning

According to the National Directorate for Disaster Risk Management (NDRMD) database and community level hazard, vulnerability and livelihood assessment conducted by FAO drought is:

  • by far the most severe hazard affecting the agriculture sector and rural communities, e.g., more than 130 000 farming families were affected by drought between 2000-2018.
  • a slow onset hazard and builds up over time throughout the agricultural seasons.

Conservation Agriculture is a key technology to increase crop resilience to drought and other climate-risks.

To address this, the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries (MAF) drafted a 'disaster risk management plan for agriculture' to work with Suco Level Disaster Management Committees (SDMC) to apply measures to address the risks. The SDMCs developed Community-Based Disaster Management (CBDRM) plans.

The promotion of CA at Suco level is based on the CBDRM plans' results where they exist. Particular attention is to those areas where drought and other climate-risks are more severe within the Suco and the process which SDMC has identified. This information is used to better target interventions aiming at promoting CA.

Figure 2. The number of families affected by the type of disaster between 2000 and 2018.

©FAO

1.2.1 The year I – Introduction to CA technology

Creation of new Farmers Groups (FG) to promote sustainable and climate-resilient technologies

The main objective of creating new farmers groups is to ensure that selected farmers are more interested in learning rather than to receive.
Therefore, the first set of principles in creating a new FG is to:

  1. implement a 'participatory process that shall be led by the local authorities,' namely the Chefe de Suco and the Chefe de Aldeia;
  2. communicate and be transparent on the preconditions expected from participating farmers at this stage;
  3. make it well known and understood that these preconditions should form a formal agreement before starting the activities;
  4. create new FGs, as much as possible, within social groups that hold a common ancestor.
These facilitate the participating farmers' engagement to the FGs work and collaborative decision-making processes such as ending burning practices or identifying communal cropland:
  • The FG size should not be less than 20 members for efficiency purposes and preferably should not exceed 40 (unless there is a demonstrated strong social cohesion within the group).
  • If an FG already exists, the above steps will validate the group's adequacy for CA. The group's past performance should be checked with the local authorities.

Figure 3. FG in Betano, celebrating a good CA maize harvest on communal land. Manufahi, October 18.

©FAO

Signature of the agreement with FG and local authorities

The institution that is promoting CA signs an agreement with the FG and the local authorities.
The agreement outlines the stakeholders' roles and responsibilities, namely the Chefe de Grupo (head of the farmers' group), the group members, the Chefe de Aldeia and Chefe de Suco and the Department of Agriculture at the local level. The agreement will also include a general timeline of the key activities.

The key commitments of the agreement are the following:

  • Members of the FG:
    • commit to 'no-burning' and to put in place a mechanism to monitor and sanction farmers who are not complying;
    • participate in all training sessions and farmers field school activities;
    • actively try to apply CA principles on their land and agree to share their experiences with other farmers;
    • the FG is also requested to allocate fenced land for the demonstration plots.
  • Chefe Grupo - same as members, besides:
    • mobilize farmers groups as necessary;
    • take responsibility for the demonstration plot.
  • Chefe Aldeia - ensure that members of the groups:
    • a) respect their first commitment of 'no-burning,';
    • b) participate in training activities and actively try to apply CA on their farm; and
    • c) share their experience:
      • encourage other farmers to quit burning and adopt CA technology;
      • work with the institution promoting CA to sanction farmers who are not fulfilling their commitments and responsibilities;
      • request updates on the activities from the Chefe Grupo and report to the Chefe Suco.
  • Chefe Suco - same as the Chefe Aldeia and besides:
    • ensure the promotion of CA in the Suco  aligned with the CBDRM plans (if these exist);
    • organize regular exchanges at Suco level on the results and challenges in implementing CA.
  • Department of agriculture and fisheries at Municipality level - ensure that extensionists and other MAF staff are:
    • participating in CA training;
    • integrating these training into their activities;
    • train FG members on CA principles;
    • organize Farmers Field Schools (FFS).
  • Institution promoting CA:
    • support the above actors with training and mentoring to enable other stakeholders to fulfil their tasks;
    • support the development of training materials;
    • provide training of trainers;
    • establish a tight monitoring and compliance system;
    • work with the local authorities for possible sanctions for farmers or FGs not fulfilling their commitments and responsibilities.

The agreement covers the first year, and it is renewed/adapted for the second year. The agreement is revised every year based on the results and needs to be identified during implementation.
Cross-visit of interested farmers to FG applying CA

What are the steps?

  1. To show farmers the CA technology in the field.
  2. Organize cross-visits to farmers that have adopted CA.
  3. The FG select representatives to participate in such visits.
  4. The organization of a first visit can take place before the agreement's signature to ensure farmers' groups are interested in adopting CA.
Establishment of demonstration plots - main cropping season

The layout of the demonstration plot is decided together with the FG. At a minimum, the demonstration includes:

  • Lehe seeds to open new land (cultivating Lehe to open a grass-land into cultivation without burning or ploughing);
  • No-burning and no-ploughing;
  • Maize intercropped with lehe – one crop a year (Inter-cropping corn with lehe – two crops per year);
  • Another crop sequence- cultivating lehe before the main crop; or Cultivating lehe in a multi-year crop rotation system; and
  • Traditional practice of burning and ploughing the land.

And:

  1. Divide the demonstration plot into five sub-plots.
  2. The FG is provided with a small amount of improved maize and lehe seeds.
  3. The Chefe de Grupo is responsible for the demonstration plot.
  4. MAF extensionists provide the necessary technical guidance.

Figure 4. Demonstration signboard in Manufahi.

©FAO

Training at Year 1- 
 
  • MAF extensionists provide training sessions on CA technology every month to members of the farmer's groups.
  • The training includes visits and learning experiences from the demonstration plots.
  • Farmer's attendance at the training is a precondition for participating in activities for year two.
  • The institution promoting CA provides training of trainers at the Municipality level.
Implementation of partial CA package on farmers' field The CA members have committed to no-burning and no-ploughing and apply these principles in at least one of their plots (>400 m2).

Figure 5. Training of trainers on agro-forestry for MAF Municipality staff (Dili, December 2018).

©FAO

Training At Year 2 to 4
Monitoring and evaluation

The institution promoting CA facilitates social monitoring.
Lessons learned are recorded to be used to plan the second-year activities.
Renewal of the agreement with FG and local authorities

Based on the lessons learned from the first year, an action plan is developed and reflected in a revised agreement with the FG and local authorities. The revised agreement includes specific issues such as identifying land to be permanently cultivated for staple food production and where 'slash & burn' practices are also permanently abandoned.
Identification of permanent land to apply CA FG members are asked to identify land on which permanent food crop cultivation (mainly maize, upland rice and pulses) will be practiced. At this stage, the local authorities' involvement is necessary as land tenure issues need to be considered. Farmers are encouraged to choose their best quality land (flat land with the highest soil fertility) for permanent cultivation. They are also encouraged to cluster their CA fields in one location where everyone is applying CA. In some Sucos, farmers are clustering their land. It enhances cooperation and reduces labor costs for tasks such as guarding or fencing. The advantage of clustering the land as part of the CA promotion strategy is that it enables group decisions versus individual farmer decisions. The process of adoption is, therefore, significantly faster.

Figure 6. Community mapping tools help facilitate decision-making processes to identify the best agricultural land to be permanently cultivated.

©FAO

Provision of seed packages

Improved corn and lehe seeds are provided to farmers with demonstrated interest (CA training in year 1) in scaling up CA on land dedicated for permanent cultivation. The seed package is only offered for the main cropping season. No seed package is provided during the second cropping season as lehe does not grow well when planted late in the crop cycle and the risk of crop failure is too high (lack of water).

For farmers willing to open new land to be clustered for permanent cultivation (only for unforested land), lehe seeds can also be provided (implementation of crop sequence - Cultivating Lehe to open a grass-land into cultivation without burning or ploughing). However, no ploughing services or other unsustainable technologies shall be subsidized for farmers when promoting the opening of new land for cultivation.
Provision of incentives to establish living fences

Identify dedicated land to be cultivated permanently and fencing to protect crops from free-grazing animals is critical.

It is recommended to use multi-purpose fodder as living-fences; The following species propagate very easily from cuttings:

  • Gliricidia sepium (locally known as ai-gamal);
  • Leucaena leucocephala (locally known as ai-miraek);
  • Hibiscus tiliaceus (locally known as ai-fao); or
  • Sesbania grandiflora (locally known ai-turi),

these produce high-quality and very palatable fodder (leaves) for livestock, which is particularly important during the dry season when fodder shortage is severe. The leguminous tree species also contribute with atmospheric nitrogen fixation (e.g. Gliricidia, Leucaena, Sesbania), particularly through hedge grow application.

The plants coppice well and can be cut at any time of the year.

Farmers are also encouraged to plant windbreak trees between fields, e.g., Moringa (Moringa oleifera), which is suitable for this purpose. It provides nutritious supplement food.

Figure 7. Live-fence established with Gliricidia sepium (ai-gamal). Manufahi, Mahakidan Suco, January 19.

©FAO

Figure 8. Guideline to establish live-fence with multi-purpose fodder tree cuttings.

©FAO

Provision of incentives to establish livestock feed plots

While live-fences can help reduce the livestock feed deficit during the dry season, the production of high biomass for fodder can close the gap and reduce overgrazing on pastures.

Fodder crops, such as king/elephant grass, locally known as du'ut-luirai (Pennisetum purpureum), is well suited for this purpose. It is one of the highest yielding tropical grasses. It is a versatile species that can grow under a wide range of conditions and systems: dry or wet conditions, smallholder or larger-scale agriculture. It is a valuable forage and very popular throughout the tropics, notably in cut-and-carry systems. Its vigorous root system developing from its creeping stolon nodes also makes it an excellent candidate for slope stabilization (bioengineering).

Farmers are also encouraged to plant king grass on fields neighboring their permanent CA field, near homestead, or on degraded/unstable sloping land.

Figure 9. View of bioengineering with king grass on the road between Dili and Gleno. October 2018.

©FAO

Farmer Field School (FFS)

FFS is a forum where farmers and trainers debate observations and experiences and present new information to the community. FFSs provide opportunities for learning by doing. It teaches basic agricultural and management skills that make farmers experts in their farms.

In FFS, the field is the school. It is the learning place where farmers working in small groups collect and analyze data, make observations, and make decisions based on their analyses.

Then they present the decisions to other farmers for refinement.

Figure 10. FFS - field observation and data collection with support from extensionists.

©FAO

FFS events, bringing together all farmers of a group, are facilitated by MAF extensionists.

Facilitators must be technically competent people who can lead group members through hands-on exercises. A monthly schedule is Tree cuttings prepared for each extensionist together with their supervisors to conduct FFS activities.

Figure 11. FFS - farmers sharing information and taking decisions with support from extensionists.

©FAO

Year 1 – Farmer Field School (FFS)

 FFS starts the first year, focusing on the demonstration plots and cross-visits to other FGs.

Year 2 – Farmer Field School (FFS)

 During the second year, the FFS activities are expanded. The institution promoting CA develops a curriculum that follows the natural crop cycle. This covers all aspects of CA throughout the year as observations are done in real-time and evidence collected in the field.

Figure 12. A 2-wheel tractor and roller entering a lehe field in Betano (April 19)

©FAO

1.2.2 Provision of 2-wheel tractors and rollers at a subsidized price

Farmers that demonstrated an interest in the CA technology received 2-wheel tractors and rollers to facilitate the scaling. The equipment was subsidized to ensure farmers committed to using the technology and correctly maintained the equipment.

The establishment of Public-private partnerships between the equipment importers, service providers for maintenance of the equipment and the institution promoting CA is essential. These interventions also aim at developing the internal market for CA farming equipment.

1.2.3 Post-harvest

To fully capture the increased yield, it is important for CA adopters to reduce post-harvest losses. By producing equipment locally, such as metallic silos, CA farmers can safely store seeds and grains and delay their commercialization to have a higher benefit. Similar to the tractors, the silos are also subsidized. The establishment of Public-private-community partnerships between the silo producers, the FG and the institutions promoting CA need to be in place to guaranty local production and maintenance services of equipment.

Figure 13. Farmers paying 20 USD per 200 kg silo to the producer (Mahaquidan, Manufahi, 5 September).

©FAO

1.2.4 Marketing support

As farmers' production increases under CA, a key challenge is the marketing of their agricultural produce. The CA producers can be linked to:

  1. Institutional markets - This includes the national school feeding program or the Ministry of Social Solidarity and Inclusion (MSSI) social safety net programs.
  2. Key market players - These include egg and broiler producers, commercial pork and beef producers, aquaculture investors, animal feed producers, etc. Most of these actors are importing animal feeds from Indonesia;
  3. Local proximity markets and Dili wholesale - Women are the main players in these markets. They ensure the link between farmers and consumers. For cereals, local mills, where they exist, are essential for the value-chain. Women entrepreneurs whose families are adopting CA can promote their commercial activities through vertical integration (production, processing and marketing).

Marketing support should be conditional to CA's adoption as this constitutes a major incentive to adopt sustainable farming practices.

1.2.5 Monitoring and evaluation (M&E)

A farmers' monitoring system shall be put in place to track individual farmers' progress and the FGs supported. The M&E database forms the basis to assess the progress of CA adoption.

The data is collected by M&E agents twice a year, ideally a month before harvest. By the fourth year of implementation, it is conducted a formal evaluation of the intervention impact.

The evaluation should cover socio-economic indicators such as:

  • farmers income;
  • food security;
  • nutrition;
  • crop productivity (per unit of land and labour); and
  • environmental indicators such as:
    • soil fertility;
    • soil erosion; and
    • green-house gas emissions.
Figure 14. CA evaluation survey data collection on a tablet by UNTL students in Manufahi (May 2019).

©FAO

2. Years V and beyond – working toward graduation of the FG members

As of year V, the support's focus is to graduate the FG and their members for CA. The group members have gained much CA cultivation experience and can promote CA to other farmers within their Aldeia. In the Suco, the promotion of CA can be oriented toward other groups in different Aldeias. Other farmers groups can visit the graduated farmers and learn from their experience.

Figure 15. CA harvest ceremony, Raifusa FG, Betano Suco. (23 Apr 2019).

©FAO

2.1 Barriers to adoption and conclusion

The six main barriers to CA adoption in Timor-Leste: counter-intuitive technology, access to markets, availability of equipment, knowledge-intensive, inadequate policies, and governance.

In the Timor-Leste agricultural context, this technology is transformative.

However, despite its demonstrated potential, the extent of CA remains marginal. Is evident that for a successful promotion of CA it requires the public sector to address the following main barriers to adoption:

2.1.1 Counter-intuitive technology

The main barrier to CA's adoption is that this technology (no-burning and no-tillage) is not easily understood and intuitive for farmers, extensionists, and decision-makers.

Burning is deeply rooted in traditional farming practices because 'slash & burn' farmers see evidence that burning produces short-term benefits to crops.

Burning the soil surface has two immediate benefits;

  • it kills weeds and part of the weed seed stocks on the soil surface; and
  • it releases minerals through the ashes that are immediately available to crops.

The traditional practices and the evidence derived from slash & burn have shown farmers that burning organic matter is beneficial to crop yield. Changing patterns and attitudes requires substantial proof of benefits. And in fact, they do not have evidence that increasing soil organic content through mulching/maintaining a cover crop is beneficial to soil fertility or production.

Even farmers that adopted CA, who have practiced 'no-burning' cultivation for a few cropping seasons, eventually get nervous that their yield would be affected at some point and often revert to burning and ploughing. Besides, given that there is sufficient land in Timor-Leste to practice shifting cultivation, farmers are not concerned about mid/long term soil fertility and land degradation.

The rapid adoption and spread of CA requires a change in all stakeholders' commitment and behavior. For transformation to happen, training and field exchanges are crucial. And Farmer Field Schools are a proven means to disseminate procedures to farmers.

Neighboring farmers kept practicing no burning and no-tillage. Betano, November 18. CA adopters reverted to ploughing after four cropping seasons of zero tillage, concerned that the yield would eventually be affected - even when weed pressure was low.

Figure 16. Land where farmers practice CA (on the right), and land reverted to ploughing (on the left).

©FAO

2.1.2 Access to markets

For CA adopters the access to the market is identified as their main challenge.

The Timor-Leste population is small (approximately 1.3 million inhabitants). The largest consumption market is in Dili, with a population below 250 000 people.

The urban diet is heavily dependent on imported rice. Therefore, the quantities of corn sold on the wholesale/retail markets are small.

Agrifood chains are little developed. Hence, rapid and sustainable increases in productivity under CA lead to volumes the market is locally not able to absorb. This may result in price slumps or production losses due to inadequate storage conditions.

CA evaluation found that CA farmers own more livestock (mainly chickens) and use more of their maize production as livestock feed.

The competitiveness of the agriculture industry is low. It is estimated that Timor-Leste imports 40 percent of the food it consumes, e.g., it imports 64 percent of rice and 36 percent comes from local production (99,978 tons imported and 57 418 tons produced locally in 2018).

Figure 17. The proportion of local rice supply versus imported.

©FAO

There are two main factors identified that limit farmers' access to the market:

  • Trade policy: import tariffs are low and non-tariff barriers are non-existent in Timor-Leste, which means that agriculture industries are not protected. Therefore, Timorese farmers compete with imported food (mostly rice). The shift of food consumption patterns from a corn-based diet to a rice-based diet is evident.
  • Processing infrastructure: food processing infrastructures in Timor-Leste are almost non-existent. Farmers thresh paddy rice using their feet while corn is ground manually on a wooden mortar (see pictures 11 and 12). These manual procedures are extremely time-consuming, particularly for women. Also, manual processing methods leave many more impurities in food than mechanized processing. The presence of impurities necessitates an additional manual cleaning of food before cooking. As a result, prices of local food are higher than imported while their presentation is lower. Consumers, even farmers themselves, prefer to buy imported rice.
Figure 18. Food processing infrastructures are almost non-existent. Threshing paddy rice in Viqueque (September 19).

©FAO

Figure 19. Women grinding corn manually in Baucau (December 2018)

©FAO

2.1.3 Availability of equipment

The other main challenge identified by CA adopter is the access to adapted CA equipment.

A major constraint for CA adopters is to purchase and maintain adequate CA equipment, particularly hand-tractors and 2-wheel knife-rollers. Private-public partnerships are necessary to improve access to equipment for CA farmers.

Farmers have to learn how to grow crops under CA. The equipment importers and local artisans need to further develop the market for new equipment and equipment maintenance.

Figure 20. Portable hammer mill used to thresh paddy rice, producing >80 percent broken grains (Viqueque, February 2019).

©FAO

2.1.4 Knowledge-intensive

The promotion of CA seed packages for different crop associations (e.g., maize associated with various legume seeds) and agroecological zones requires field testing and intensive knowledge management.

Farmers are growing other crops such as rice, tubers, vegetables or fruit trees that can be cultivated under CA. Still, specific knowledge for these crops needs to be generated.

Locally specific knowledge is also needed to address the threat posed by free-grazing animals and wildfires.  While Live-fences can protect CA fields from free-grazing animals, community processes on land-use planning and adoption of tara bandu customary laws should be promoted when scaling up CA to become the dominant 'non-shifting' farming technology at the Suco level.

2.1.5 Inadequate policies

Climate-Smart Agriculture and CA are reflected in the draft MAF agriculture policy but not in the 2014-2020 strategic plan. Neither had allocated a budget to CA. The MAF free land preparation service (ploughing/harrowing/rotovating) in its current form is a disincentive to CA adoption.

2.1.6 Governance

Strengthening CA coordination and standardization of processes and technical packages is necessary. Associating with more partners that are using CA in their agriculture interventions is essential.

3. Conclusion

  • Soils are crucial for human well-being.
  • Damaging the soil affects climate, biodiversity and land degradation massively.
  • In Timor-Leste, the main driver of deforestation is 'slash & burn' shifting cultivation. Stabilizing cultivation into permanently cultivated land through sustainable, climate-smart farming practices has the potential to release a massive amount of land for forests to grow back.
  • In Timor-lest, many CA farmers believe they can enhance soil fertility and produce food sustainably by changing the way they farm because CA farmers have adopted the practice of 'no burning.' Still, only a handful of CA farmers have succeeded with this technology in Timor-Leste. More efforts are needed. The focus should be placed on training stakeholders at all levels and demonstrating the technology in the field as widely as possible. More research and field testing are required to identify high biomass producing cover crops adapted to the various agroclimatic zones of Timor-Leste.

4. Validation of the practice

This practice was tested in Timor-Leste, a tropical warm agroecologic zone. In areas where slash and burn and ploughing are used intensively. The rising awareness and providing evidence on CA's benefits and use was a major driver for change.

5. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The minimum requirements are the application of the steps illustrated in this practice. Important is to have an institution working with local government to promote the CA and support farmers. Besides, it is essential to select motivated farmers. Lastly, it is vital to adapt the CA to the local conditions, both environmental and social.

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Introduction to conservation agriculture: principles and benefits: ID 7413.
  • Crop rotation in conservation agriculture: ID 7415.
  • Weed management in conservation agriculture: ID 7418.
  • A step-by-step approach toward a gradual adoption of the full conservation agriculture technology: an example from Timor-Leste: ID 10093.
  • Conservation Agriculture (CA) model in Timor-Leste: ID 10092.

entries.summary:
Smallholder Horticulture Empowerment and Promotion (SHEP) Approach is an extension and advisory approach, aiming to help farmers to access and benefit from markets by changing their mindset from “Grow and Sell” to “Grow to Sell”.  

It was developed through the technical cooperation project in Kenya and managed to double the income of the targeted smallholder farmers. In the SHEP Approach, farmers visit an adjacent market and conduct market survey to see for themselves and better understand the market’s functioning. Based on this experience, they then develop a crop calendar or a business plan according to the identified market demands. Having seen and understood what the price, required quality, timing and volume of production is, the target farmers were able to better adapt their farming and production to the market demands. They moved thus to “Farming as Business” by establishing relations with market actors and filling the information gap regarding quality, price etc. As a result, their livelihoods improved. Another key feature of the SHEP Approach is motivating farmers through Self Determination Theory which boosts adoption rate of good practices. The SHEP Approach proves that it is possible to improve farmers’ livelihoods by tapping into local human and technical resources, without advanced technology.
entries.description:
Description

SHEP Approach has four essential steps and are as following; sharing goal with farmers, raising farmers’ awareness, facilitating farmers by decision-making, and developing farmers’ skills. 

Figure 1. Training participants from various African countries visiting Kenyan farmers

©JICA

1. Sharing goal with farmers

SHEP regards sharing its goal and vision with the beneficiary farmers as the crucial first step because it is the farmers themselves, after all, who make the most effort to materialize economically viable farming business throughout the training course. Through this step, farmers can feel ownership on the project activities.

1.1 Sensitization workshop

The sensitization workshop aims at sharing the SHEP vision and goal with the farmers to help farmers become self-reliant with entrepreneurial aspirations.

Figure 2. Farmers and extension officers participating in the sensitization workshop

©JICA

2. Raising farmers’ awareness

Raising farmers’ awareness on opportunities and potential of horticultural farming is extremely important. Without awareness the farmers are less likely to get motivated to make a commitment to change their farming practices for the better.

2.1 Market survey

The main purpose of SHEP’s farmer-initiated market survey is to encourage farmers to have hands-on experiences of understanding how markets operate and what markets want from them. At the same time, by conducting market surveys, farmers will be able to build a relation with various market players, such as wholesalers, retailers, middlemen, etc., and widen their interpersonal networks which can contribute to creating a win-win situation with the market stakeholders. Through this exercise, farmers can feel competence since they can discover new things by themselves.

The markets in which the market survey is conducted can be both at formal and informal, and/or domestic and international markets. However, it is recommended to start in a nearby local market. The location of the markets should be determined through discussions with the farmer group. In addition, the market can be on the side of a highway bus stops, schools, supermarkets, organizations, companies, or anywhere farmers can do business.

The market surveys should be conducted by farmers on a regular basis with a questionnaire form in hand. The questionnaire contains about 10 questions to be asked, such as consumers’ preference, marketing challenges, market prices, required quality and quantity of produce, seasonal fluctuations of prices and traded quantity, and mode and terms of payments.

The SHEP implementers, government extension officers and/or private extension staff, are encouraged to assist farmers make realistic decisions throughout the process of market survey.

Figure 3. Farmers conducting market survey with a tomato retailer at the local market

©JICA

3. Facilitating farmers with decision-making

With the awareness and new knowledge which farmers gained from the surveys, they are able to make informed decisions to make a change. This process involves farmers selecting target crops and making a plan such as Crop Calendar so that they will be able to better adapt their production to market and strategically and timely supply their target crops to the specific markets of their choice.

3.1 Target crop selection

Target Crop Selection is conducted so that the farmer groups can collectively identify the specific types of crops that are demanded by the market. The farmers agree to produce and market the identified crops as a group. Through these activities, farmers can feel autonomy because they decide their future by their own.

The farmer groups select the target horticultural crops based on their finding during the market survey. The decisions are based on group consensus and various collective actions for facilitating efficient production and marketing will be discussed and agreed by the farmer group members. The SHEP implementers give useful advice and suggestions, particularly in the area of agro-ecological suitability of specific crops, so that the farmers can make a well-rounded decision in choosing the target crops. Their role is not to make decisions for the farmers, rather, to help farmers to make the right decisions by providing appropriate guidance and expert knowledge on agriculture.

Crop Calendar enables the farmer group to plan future action as a group in terms of both production and marketing activities of the target crops. A crop calendar is a concrete annual plan for what crops to grow at what time, in what quantity and quality, and so forth written as monthly activities which facilitate the groups’ farming business. The SHEP implementers ensure that the plan is realistic and attainable considering the current capacity of the farmer group.

Figure 4. Women's and men's groups making a Crop Calendar/business plan in Egypt

©JICA

4. Developing farmers’ skills

As the last step, the SHEP implementers provide technical solutions to the farmers, i.e. give in-field trainings for the target crops the farmers selected, so that they can produce the crops as they have planned in the Crop Calendar/business plan.

4.1 In-field training

In-field trainings are designed to disseminate skills and knowledge necessary for the practical production of the target crops which the farmers have chosen. It is a demand-driven training. Since farmers are aware of the importance of techniques through above steps, adoption rate on techniques by farmers is very high. Then farmers can feel more competent/confident.

Figure 5. Encouraging farmers to weed with simple tools

©JICA

5. Validation of the practice

Up to March 2020, SHEP Approach is practised by approximately 180 000 farmers in more than 20 countries. Beyond Africa, the approach is implemented also in Middle-East (Egypt and Palestine) and Nepal.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

SHEP Approach can be worked not only in areas where horticultural crops are cultivated, but also where there are small-scale farmers who are willing/trying to practice farming as a business. Therefore, this approach can be applied to other crops, livestock, etc. The SHEP Approach is a simple method that is easily accepted by all farmers, so it does not depend on the farmer's characteristics/abilities (age, education level, yeas of farming experience etc.) and their assets (size of landholding, location and fertility of farmland etc.). For example, farmers living far from markets can negotiate with buyers who come to their community.

  • At least, minimum water resource are necessary to cultivate horticulture crop.

SHEP Approach encourages working farmer as a group, but also individual farmers can practice the approach.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Ten ways to improve milk marketing: ID 8240.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The farmer group, who realized the benefits of joint shipping through the implementation of the SHEP Approach, became accustomed to jointly carrying out labor-intensive agricultural activities, such as harvesting and weeding. Therefore, the labor-intensive agricultural work that had been carried out individually has been reduced and the work efficiency has been improved.

9.2 Women-friendly

SHEP encourages farmer to jointly engage in farming between husband and wife as a business unit. In case it is necessary, Gender Awareness Training is organized to recognize roles and responsibilities between men and women for the better farming activities. Through SHEP Approach, the relationship between husband and wife is changed from manager and labour to management partner.

9.3 Pro-poor technology

Since farmers decide to engage in SHEP Approach by themselves, most of the farmers keep practising SHEP’s essential activities even after the terminal of the project. Regarding cultivation technics which are employed in SHEP Approach, they are not the advanced one since smallholder farmers and extension officers can implement with their own knowledge and resource.  Farmers have kept to conduct market survey before sowing seeds even after the project intervention.  At the same time, many of the beneficial countries (more than 20) has started to implement by their own as a normal extension services.

entries.summary: Pathe Pathshala - A Peoples’ Vocational School on Move; at people’s place, in peoples’ time with peoples’ language for low-input based, climate-resilient, herbal healing of livestock. Classes are conducted for livestock keepers, particularly women at grass-roots, school dropouts and people of weaker section. Tips are provided to them so that livestock keeping becomes sustainable. The motto of this programme is to make aware people who are not literate and formally educated. This gives opportunity to people to learn basics of their livestock health and feeding system so that people in the higher ups of the system do not take advantages of these poor and illiterate people and are not subjected to harassment. Many times, pastoralists who are on move are benefited by Pathe Pathshala - the moving school. Education at doorstep has the advantage of using the spare time of women who are mostly engaged in household daily chores and do not get time to go to towns or cities to get training.
entries.description:
Description

Different agencies like universities and government run institutes fail to attract livestock keepers to training as they train them in cities with languages other than those of farmers. Women livestock keepers refuse to attend such training programmes, as they have to leave their children and old dependents at home.

To overcome these difficulties the concept of the moving school, at the peoples’ place, in peoples’ time with peoples’ language came to mind. In practical, I see that “Democratization of knowledge and skills” happen through these “Pathe Pathshala” classes and lead to sustainable development.

Who are the main stakeholders and how Pathe Pathshala interacts with them?

  • The main stakeholders of the project are the small livestock keepers, small and marginal farmers, pastoralists, school dropouts, unemployed high school pass outs in tribal area and the women who keep livestock.
  • Small livestock keepers:
    • The small livestock keepers who keep cattle, sheep, goat, pig and poultry for earning their livelihood are the main stakeholders.
    • These small livestock keepers are spread throughout the state of Odisha.
  • Pastoralists:
    • There are groups of livestock keepers who move from place to place for grazing animals.
    • They remain away in forests and grasslands while migration.
    • They need Pathe Pathshala more frequently.
  • School dropouts & unemployed high school pass outs:
    • These groups of youth are mostly present in the tribal area of the state.
    • As they are brought up in village ecosystem; they can be good healers and livestock feed making entrepreneurs.
  • Women at grass-root:
    • Women folk are the real livestock keepers who are resilient enough to look after the livestock grazing, livestock health management and feed making.
  • We interact with the stakeholders directly in “Pathe Pathshala”. Back home, they are connected through tele-vet programme.
  • During the period of the project a robust system of interaction through “Pathe Pathshala” are made.
    • They are conveyed the knowledge and skills through storytelling, healing rhymes, practical demonstrations and herbarium show.
    • The farmers, pastoralists, youth and women are provided with study material in their language.
    • They are provided with telephone numbers of “Pathe Pathshala” so that they are connected with the tele-vet programmes by which interactions will be strengthened further.
    • The process of learning will continue.

What are the main challenges?

  1. I peruse my passion for reaching people and diffusing knowledge through Pathe Pathshala. Till now I am doing this voluntarily by spending the logistics costs from own, as a token of love to give back to the society from where I have come from. To enhance and ramify the work, funds crunch are the first challenges I meet. Although I receive local hospitality and partial logistics from friends, well-wishers, mentors still funds are the main challenge.
  2. Instilling the sense of confidence and belief among the small livestock keepers, pastoralists, unemployed youth and women in regard to the herbal healing of their own animals by themselves, in their own situations is the other main challenge. They do not easily believe, unless they see the fruits.
  3. The other challenges are the difficulties in diffusion of skills and knowledge to the poor farmers, unemployed youth and women livestock keepers who are not formally educated much. The methodology to be employed in diffusing the knowledge and skill should be convincing, easily understandable, use of simple words in local language, people-friendly and above all in storytelling, rhyming with audio visuals.
  4. To tell them that, wherever they go for earning their livelihood, they are not alone, they are with their knowledge and skills imparted to them. To instill this much of confidence in them, the knowledge and skills are imparted through storytelling, healing rhymes, herbarium show and practical demonstrations.
  5. Another challenge is the existing poverty that hinders them in leading a happy life. It becomes really challenging to show them the way, potentiality lying in the knowledge and skill that comes to fruition in shape of employment, income generation and happy living. In future the same challenges are anticipated.
Figure 1.  Pathe Pathshala with tribal women of baliguda, Odisha state, India on treating of goats with herbs

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/Pathe Pathshala

1.  Pathe Pathshala - the roadside class

  • Most of the Pathe Pathshala are conducted in peoples’ environment, without light, in open air system without microphone etc.
    • Teachings are in storytelling, rhymes.
  • Herbal Parliament:
Figure 2. Livestock Herbal Parliament of women

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/Pathe Pathshala

  • Herbal recipe preparation training:
Figure 3. Women learn to prepare herbal recipe for their livestock

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/Pathe Pathshala

  •  School dropouts:
Figure 5. Unemployed youth are trained on low cost livestock healing

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/Pathe Pathshala

2. Validation of the practice

  • The classes have been conducted since 2008 and more than 1000 classes have been conducted.

3. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • Logistic support, reading and skill materials.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1. Women-friendly 

The concept of Pathe Pathshala offers particularly women the opportunity to expand their knowledge in the field of sustainable livestock management and to actively participate in the design process.

6.2 Pro-poor technology 

This moving school shows stakeholders low-input based, climate-resilient, thus cost-effective forms of sustainable livestock production.

entries.summary: Dairy farmers or livestock keepers who keep small ruminants can get affected when an outbreak of Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) occurs in their region. It usually occurs during rainy season (July to October) and during summer (February to June). The disease cause mortality of young ruminants; general vigour and health of adult animals are affected as well. The consequences of this disease lead to economic loss for the livestock keepers. SEVA has organized herbal health camps for animals for treatment of FMD in selected villages in Tamil Nadu. After the treatment the local farmers gave good feedback of animal recovery from FMD. There was increase in the milk yield and fat content in the milk after the treatment. This method of herbal healing practices was earlier documented from local healers by SEVA in association with Honey Bee Network supported by National Innovation Foundation. Selected best practices are included in our training programme for farmers on the method of preparation and administration of herbal recipes for specific conditions of animals.
entries.description:
Description

1. Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD)

FMD is an infectious viral disease that affects cloven-hoofed animals. Symptoms of FMD are ulcers in mouth and cleft of hooves, drooping saliva and difficulties in walking.

2. Herbal treatment 

2.1 Ingredients

Ingredients required for the treatment:

  • manjal (Turmeric) 200 g (freshly harvested rhizome is preferred);
  • coconut kernel extract (from 1 coconut);
  • sotrukatralai (Aloe vera) – 200 g;
  • palm jaggery 200 g;
  • common salt 100 g;
  • garlic 100 g;
  • pepper 50 g;
  • cumin 50 g;
  • fenugreek 50 g.

2.2 Preparation and application

  • The above ingredients viz. turmeric, sotrukatralai (Aloe vera), garlic, grated coconut are ground well through grinder.
  • Mix the ingredients using sufficient water (sprinkle water to moist the ingredients).
  • Collect the mixture in a vessel.
  • Make powder of pepper, cumin, fenugreek.
  • Mix together thoroughly and add sufficient water to make it about 1 litre.
  • Filter the solution and apply orally.

2.3 Dose and application

  • Use 100 ml at a time for adult animals or 50 ml for young ones or sheep or goats.
  • Before giving the treatment, the animals are to be fed with banana (two for cows and one for ruminants) soaked in sesame oil (gingelly oil) 50 ml.
  • This treatment can be continued for two to three days depending upon the severity of disease.

For treatment of wounds in the foot region:

  • A special wound healing thaila can be prepared by using the following ingredients:
    • Mix 500 ml of coconut oil and 500 ml Datura leaf extract together.
    • Boil the mixture in a vessel for one hour till it gets oily texture.
    • Turn off the fire.
    • Add 5 g mayilthutham (copper sulphate) and stir well.
    • Store the thaila in a bottle.

The thaila can be used for all types of wounds including maggot wounds in animals (can be stored up to six months).

Datura                                                   Turmeric                                                Copper sulphate                                                Aloe vera

Animals can also be fed with gruel prepared by boiling with ragi, wheat and bajra flour each 100 g to 200 g and mixed together (total 500 g) with sufficient water in a vessel.

Figure 1. Preparation of mathan thailam by participants of NRLM training, Guwahati, Assam

©SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

3. Animal health camp

SEVA in association with NGOs and women self-help group members organized village level training programme for livestock keepers on herbal treatment for animals which include practical demonstration and organizing animal health camps using herbal preparations. We have received good feedback from the livestock keepers on the effectiveness of our preparations for disease of animals including FMD.

Figure 2. Women prepare herbal preparations for FMD in Erode District, Tamil Nadu 

© SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

Mr. Jayaraman, (62), a herbal healer in Vandipalayam village, Vilupuram District has treated 60 cows affected by FMD during September 2011 in his village (using SEVA formula), Figure 3. All animals recovered after two days of treatment.

Figure 3. Mr. Jayaraman herbal healer in Vandipalayam village, Tamil Nadu

© Pitchandikulam Forests /Parvathi

4. Validation of the practice 

During 2013 there was an outbreak of FMD in many districts of Tamil Nadu. SEVA team members visited Erode district, and we administered herbal preparations for more than 500 animals (dairy cows) and they recovered after our herbal treatment. Dairy farmers in Karnataka, Haryana, Punjab contacted us, and we communicated our method of herbal preparations for FMD. Later they reported that the treatment was effective for FMD in buffaloes and not effective for cross-breed dairy cows (Holstein Friesian).

Table 1. A list of farmers who treated their animals for FMD using SEVA herbal formula
Sl.No. Name of farmer Place/state/region Particulars of treatment
1.

Pankaj Seth

 Amritsar, Punjab During Feb. 2018 he treated 8 adult dairy animals (local desi cattle and cross-breed cows) successfully.
2.

Dinesh

It is a low-cost technology and trained livestock keepers/women who can prepare herbal recipes and special oil for FMD. Also administered as preventive treatment when rainy season starts.

entries.summary:
Herbal pesticide has been prepared based on farmers innovations documented by SEVA in association with Honeybee Network and National Innovation Foundation. The main objective is to disseminate low cost eco-friendly practices which are safe to human, livestock and environment. SEVA has promoted farmers experimentation and validated this practice. Now this practice has been adopted by more than 1 500 farmers in Tamil Nadu over the last 15 years. This practice has the following advantages:

  1. Cost reduction of inputs viz. chemical fertilizer and pesticides.
  2. Safe for human, livestock and environment.
  3. Increased profit from crop cultivation for paddy, groundnut, vegetables, turmeric, sugarcane, banana etc.
  4. Employment and income for the labourers who prepare and sell these organic preparations.
entries.description:
Description

Three preparation methods are commonly used by farmers; Amirtha Karaisal, Panchagavya, and herbal pesticide.

1. Preparation and application of Amirtha Karaisal (Nectar solution)

1.1 Ingredients

Ingredients needed:

  • cow dung: 2 kg
  • cow urine: 2 litres
  • jaggery: 200 g, (jaggery is obtained by heating the crushed sugarcane juice)
  • Water: 20 litres.

1.2 Preparation steps

  • Take a plastic container of 30 litre capacity and dissolve the cow dung in water.
  • Make the jaggery into a powder
  • Mix the jaggery powder with the cow urine (made into a thick solution by adding 20 litres of water).
  • Stir the mixture thoroughly and close the container.
  • This has to be kept for two days, and then it is ready for use.

1.3 Application options

  1. Apply the Amirtha Karaisal by mixing it with irrigation water (20 litres for one acre (0.4 ha)), the application can be done at 15 to 30 days interval.
  2. Add the Amirtha karaisal to a half-kg of each of the following microbial cultures: Rhizobium, Azospirillum, Azotobacter, Trichoderma viride. Take 20 litres of Amirtha karisal and mixed with microbial culture. Keep it for 12 hours, then mix it with irrigation water and apply. The application of the microbial culture mixed with Amirtha karisal is done seven times for turmeric, six times for banana, two times for paddy.

1.4 Benefits

This organic method of manure application reduces  the quantity of chemical or inorganic fertilizer  and thus reduces the cost of cultivation.   This method is practised now by more than 10 000 farmers for many crops in states of Tamil Nadu, Kerala & Karnataka in India.

2. Preparation and application of Panchagavya

2.1 Ingredients

Ingredients needed:

  • cow dung: 5 kg
  • cow urine: 2 litres
  • milk: 2 litres
  • curd: 2 litres
  • ghee (clarified butter): 500 ml
  • sugarcane juice: 2 litres.

2.2 Preparation steps

  • The cow dung should be mixed with the Ghee in a plastic bucket (about 15 litres capacity) and kept for three days.
  • Cover it with a piece of cloth and put it in a shaded area.
  • On the 4th day, the other ingredients are added into the bucket and stirred well. They are kept for 18 days and allowed for fermentation.
  • During the time of fermentation, the slurry has to be stirred clockwise and anti-clockwise using a wooden stick.
Figure 1. Mr. Chellamuthu, Karukkampalayam village, erode district, Tamil Nadu, who sells Herbal pesticide and Panchagavya

©SEVA / Vivekanandan

2.3 Application options

  • Panchagavya can be sprayed at a 2 to 3 percent concentration or mixed with irrigation water.
  • Use 3 to 5 litres for spray per 1 acre of land (0.4 ha) or 50 litres for mixing it with irrigation water.
  • Banana rhizome material (seed material) and seedlings of paddy or vegetables are dipped in panchagavya solution for few minutes before planting.
  • For 1 000 planting material about 2 litre panchagavya is sufficient.

2.4 Benefits

In Tamil Nadu more than 5 000 farmers practised this technique and are able to reduce the chemical fertilizer inputs for crops like paddy, vegetables, banana etc.

3. Preparation and application of Herbal pesticide

3.1 Ingredients

Local name of plant species (Tamil) Scientific name of the plant Quantity in Kg
Leaves of Nochi Vitex negundo 2
Leaves of Peenarichangu Clerodendrum  inerme 2
Leaf Petals of Sotrukatralai Aloe vera 2
Seeds of Vembu Azadirechta indica 2
Leaves of Erukku Calotropis gigantea 2

3.2 Preparation steps

  • The above ingredients are procured fresh and ground separately by sprinkling some drops of water by using a motorized wet grinder.
  • Then they are mixed together and kept as such for two days.
  • Then it is ready for spraying.
Figure 2. Grinder used for preparation of herbal pesticide

©SEVA/ Vivekanandan  

3.3 Application options

  • Mix 200 to 500 ml of plant extract in 10 litres of water (sprayer tank capacity) and spray as foliar spray for crops depending upon type and stage of crop.
  • This formulation has been validated for its effectiveness for control of pests of paddy and brinjal by Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Coimbatore.

4. Crop-wise application of the organic pesticides

The following table shows the

Table 1. Crop-wise application of the organic pesticides
Crop Organic pesticides Time of spray /application
Paddy Green manure

Before sowing of paddy raise green manure crops and plough in situ on 45th day.

Remark: Daincha, Sunhemp, legumes, millets are sown together.
Organic manure Apply  100 kg of organic oil cake (mixture of groundnut cake, neem cake, pongamia cake etc.) as basal dose in 0.40 ha.
Amirtha Karaisal 15th, 30th day of planting.
Panchagavya 30th, 60th day of planting.
Herbal pesticides 45th, 75th day of planting.
Sugarcane Green manure Before planting of setts, raise green manure crops and plough in situ on 45th day.
Organic manure Apply 10 tractor loads of farmyard manure in the soil for 0.40 ha.

Panchagavya 60th, 120th day of planting.
Herbal pesticides 75th day of planting.
Banana Green manure Before planting of setts, raise green manure crops and plough in situ on 45th day.
Amirtha Karaisal 30th, 40th, 50th, 60th, 70th, 80th day of planting.
Panchagavya 30th, 60th, 90th day of planting and continued at 30 days interval till emergence of fruit bunch.
Herbal pesticides 45th, 75th, 105th day of planting and continued at 30 days interval till emergence of fruit bunch.
Groundnut Green manure Before planting of setts, raise green manure crops and plough in situ on 45th day.

Organic manure Apply 10 tractor loads of farmyard manure in the soil for 0.40 ha.
Amirtha Karaisal 30th, 40th, 50th day of planting and continued at 10 days interval by mixing in irrigation water.
Panchagavya 60th, 120th day of planting.
Herbal pesticides 75th, 90th day of planting.
Figure 3. Turmeric grown organically by Mr Chellamuthu

©SEVA/ Vivekanandan

5. Organic paddy cultivation using sustainable farming practices by Mr. Thangaraj

Mr. P. Thangaraj (60) studied up to SSLC. He had been employed as a bus conductor and he retired voluntarily three years ago. Then he continued his main family profession of farming in 1.2 ha of lands in Noyyal village, Karur District, Tamil Nadu. He cultivates paddy and coconut using one open well as irrigation source.  He says that he earns more income by cultivation of paddy crop (white Ponni variety with 140 days duration) in 0.4 ha using sustainable farming practices. His practices are given below: Paddy nursery is raised and “white Ponni” variety is sown. He applies basal dose of mixture of neem cake (5 kg) and groundnut cake (2 kg) before sowing. He also raises sanappu (sunhemp Crotalaria juncea) green manure plant and ploughed in-situ. Then 15 to 20 days old seedlings are plucked and planted in the main field at 1’ x 3/4’ spacing. The main field is also raised with sanappu (sunhemp) and after 45 days of sowing (attains flowering stage) it is ploughed in-situ and incorporated in the soil. He applies basal dressing of manure using neem cake and groundnut cake 25 kg each before planting. After 20 days of planting the following sprays are given:  

  • 20 days after planting: Herbal Pesticide spray.
  • 35 days after planting: “Panchagavya” spray.
  • 60 days after planting: Herbal Pesticide + Panchagavya spray.
  • 75 days after planting: Panchagavya spray.
  • 90 days after planting: Herbal Pesticide spray.

With this method he stopped applying Diammonium Phosphates (DAP) and urea each about 50 kg as basal and topdressing respectively. His harvest was about 81/2 Pothi (2 210 kg) of paddy in 0.4 ha. The harvested paddy is then transported to a nearby rice mill for parboiling and polishing. It yields about 1 050 kg of rice and 1 000 kg of bran. It is valued at Rs. 76 800. There is good demand for his organic rice as it fetches Rs. 60 per kg from local customers. He says that he is not using DAP, urea each about 50 kg while the other farmers apply as fertilizer as basal and top dressing and Mr. Thangaraj saves Rs. 2 000. He also does not use any chemical pesticide, and it saves Rs. 1 000 per spray. Instead, he spends about only Rs. 750/ for spraying organic liquid formulations. He gets a net income of Rs. 50 000 or more from 0.4 ha of lands.

Figure 4. Organic paddy cultivation by Mr. Thangaraj in Velliampalayam village, Karur district.

©SEVA/Vivekanandan

Figure 5. Liquid manure being mixed with irrigation water

©SEVA/Vivekanandan

Figure 6. Preparation of Panchagavya by Mr. Muthuvel, Ellapalayam village, Erode district.

©SEVA/Vivekanandan

Figure 7. Green manure being raised in coconut garden by Mr. Thangaraj in Velliampalayam village, Karur district.

©SEVA/Vivekanandan

Figure 8. Turmeric fungal disease being controlled by using panchagavya and azospirillum by Mr. Muthuvel, Ellapalayam village, Erode district.

©SEVA/Vivekanandan

6. Validation of the practice

This practice of spraying herbal pesticide and Panchagavya, Amirtha Karaisal initially followed by Mr. Chellamuthu. By seeing the effectiveness of these practices now more than 500 farmers adopted them in Erode district, Tamil Nadu and they continue for more than five years. Now farmers in other districts are also adopting these practices in many districts especially Coimbatore, Tiruppur, Dindigul, Karur, Namakkal districts. These practices are found effective in the plain areas of Tamil Nadu with tropical climate where average rainfall is 800 to 1 000 mm per annum. Farmers follow when they raise crops viz. paddy, sugarcane, turmeric, groundnut, vegetables, maize etc. during North East Monsoon period (October to December) and also during summer season (March – June).

7. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Availability of plant ingredients for preparation of herbal pesticide is important. However few farmers who unable to prepare the herbal pesticide, purchase it from Mr. Chellamuthu who sells it at Rs. 150/- per litre. These practices are found effective in the plain areas of Tamil Nadu with tropical climate where average rainfall is 800 to 1 000 mm per annum.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Green manuring in sugarcane production for soil improvement and water efficiency: ID 8768.
  • Soil fertility for sustainable vegetable production: green and animal manures in the humid forest belt in Ghana: ID 5425.
  • Nutrient management in organic agriculture: ID 8368.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

It reduces the cost of cultivation for crops by reducing the the quantum of application of chemical fertilizers and pesticides.

10.2 Women-friendly

Women labourers are involved in collection and preparation of herbal pesticide, Panchagavya, Amirthakarisal  for different crops. It provides employment of women labourers in this method.

10.3 Resource use efficiency

Plant ingredients are available locally and harvested only leaves or seeds. In addition cow products (cow dung, cow urine, cow milk, cow ghee, cow curd are utilized and they are available easily in all villages.)

10.4 Pro-poor technology

Marginal farmers or tenant farmers need not spend much amount for purchase of chemical fertilizers and pesticides. They prepare simple herbal pesticides and organic liquid fertilizers for their field crops. Therefore these methods of preparation are user friendly and eco-friendly.
