entries.title: Biosolarization (Example: tomato plants)
entries.source: Fundación Ingenio
multi_source: Fundación Ingenio#Fundación Ingenio#Fundación Ingenio#Fundación Ingenio

agrovoc_keywords.display: Crop (plant) protection#Protection des plantes#Protección de las plantas#Protecção das plantas

entries.summary: Biosolarization provides a sustainable, organic method to soil disinfection and control of nematodes, phytoparasitic fungi and weeds in preparation for crop planting. The high temperatures that are produced during the decomposition process in addition to solar radiation create an effect that controls pathogenic microorganisms in the soil. In applying and incorporating organic matter into the soil, there is a series of microbiological changes that are produced. There is a proliferation of microorganisms that feed off of and obtain energy from the decomposing material, which facilitates its growth and accelerates the process. The organic material decomposition stimulates the development of both beneficial and pathological organisms in the soil, which reproduce and die. They thereby generate organic products (like amonia, nitrate, hydrogen sulphide, etc.) that help control soil pathogens. These products primarily produce a nematicidal effect on egg incubation and on the mobility of these species. Some types of organic material that can be used include cow manure, sheep manure and fowl droppings, as well as leftover scraps from cruciferous plants and mulch made of tomato plants.
entries.description:
Description

1. Step by step description

1.1 Cutting

  • Cut up scraps to create mulch and incorporate them into the soil
  • Cut up the scraps from the plant’s leftover from the previous harvest to make mulch. The smaller these pieces are cut up, the faster its decomposition and biocide effect will be.

1.2 Mulch incorporation

  • Incorporate this mulch into the soil. This can be done using a rotavator or using non-mechanized gardening tools.
  • Create grooves in the soil and incorporate remaining mulch and guano.

1.3 Grooves creation

  • After it has been incorporated, create grooves about 20 cm deep over the planting row.
Figure 1. The soil should look like this once the grooves have been put in.

©Sociedad Española de Agricultura Ecológica. Cultivo ecológico del tomate y del pimiento.

Figure 2. The depth of the planting rows (20 cm) is about the same length as a fork. The picture is for scale.

©https://www.mathsisfun.com/measure/metric-length.html

  • Introduce any leftover remains into the grooves and mix it with guano (approximately 2.5 to 5 kg per m2).
  • It is recommended that farmers incorporate larger amounts of guano depending on the population of nematodes in the soil (for more nematodes, more organic matter is recommended).

1.4 Grooves filling

  • Fill in the grooves and lay irrigation tubes, covering them with plastic sheet.
  • Use the mounds of dirt next to the grooves to fill them in, incorporating this soil in with the organic matter. The ground will look flatter at this point, although you should still be able to tell where the grooves are (the area where you mixed guano into the soil). This is important because this will be the part of the soil that you later cover with plastic.
  • Immediately after filling the grooves in, we lay the irrigation tubes down on the soil and cover each mound with a plastic sheet, making sure to bury the edges of the plastic sheet with approximately 5 cm of soil to ensure that there is no loss of humidity, gases or temperature.
  • The soil should now be watered for the first time and following this first day should be watered every four to six days (if the soil has a high sand content and does not retain moisture as well, then it should be every four days).
Figure 3. Soil covering

©https://aghealth.ucdavis.edu/news/how-sustainable-agriculture-relates-farm-worker-safety

  • Keep the soil covered for 30 days, followed by 10 days of ventilation before planting crops.
  • The soil should remain covered by this transparent plastic for at least 30 days, and then should be uncovered for ventilation for 10 days before planting crops. It is important to repair any tears in the plastic while it is covering the soil.
Figure 4. The pictures below illustrate what the soil should look like after biosolarization is complete

©Fundación Ingenio              
 
You can test whether the soil is ready by doing a small seed germination test. You can plant a few number of lettuce or tomato seeds in the soil and if all the seeds germinate this means the soil is ready, but if some of them fail then the planting should be postponed.

2. Validation of the practice

There are many organic growers that use this methodology in South-Eastern Spain (in the Region of Murcia), where the climate is warm and dry. Although we have used the example of biosolarization for tomato cultivation, this technique can be implemented in growing many types of vegetables. This practice must be properly timed in order to reap the maximum benefits. In our region our most productive crop growing season, when the ground is most active and temperatures are ideal, is in the winter. Therefore, we carry out biosolarization in the summer. This practice is carried out by family farmers who have access to irrigation systems.

3. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Farmers need to have enough sunshine and high enough temperatures that the soil will generate enough heat to disinfect. They need to make sure the plastic adequately covers the ground, not letting any heat or gases escape. This also means frequently checking for holes or tears in the plastic and repairing them with tape, especially if there are many animals in the area. Lastly, this process requires an adequate supply of leftover crop scraps and manure.

As previously stated, as with any practice it may require some trial and error to figure out the quantities of organic matter to incorporate, the frequency with which to water the soil, and to know when the soil is ready for planting. We generally recommend that this process be carried out in the warmest spring, summer and autumn months.

We recommend that farmers keep in mind that this technique does not permeate to lower levels of the soil, so deeper rooted organisms residing past about 20 cm may be to be manually removed.

The best plastics for the plastic sheets are transparent, 1 to 3 mm thick (thinner plastic is recommended for smaller areas), and if possible, UV-inhibited. It is important to repair any tears in the plastic. More durable plastic sheets may be reused if taken care of.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Solarization: reducing insect damage from cowpeas: ID 4425.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

This technology is labour-saving because it ultimately prevents men and women (whoever is farming) from having to spend time removing weeds from crops, and even boosts efficiency because it prevents crop loss due to pests and fungi.

6.2 Women-friendly

This technology is women-friendly because it does not require heavy lifting and can be done at their convenience, so long as it's in the proper season.

6.3 Resource use efficiency

This technology uses resources efficiently in that it recycles leftover scraps from the previous harvest as well as dung, and the only energy that it uses is solar-powered.

6.4 Pro-poor technology

This technology should be accessible to most populations, as long as those have access to leftover crop scraps, dung, plastic sheets and irrigation materials.

entries.source: Sokoine University Graduate Entrepreneur Cooperative (SUGECO)
multi_source: Sokoine University Graduate Entrepreneur Soperative (SUGECO)#Sokoine University Graduate Entrepreneur Soperative (SUGECO)#Sokoine University Graduate Entrepreneur Soperative (SUGECO)#Sokoine University Graduate Entrepreneur Soperative (SUGECO)

entries.summary:
Farm cart technology is a local solution to small agricultural producers who are not in a position to buy and/or hire advanced farm machines like tractors and power tillers due to cost constraints. Most smallholder farmers are in rural areas, therefore they produce foods that satisfy only family consumption. Mostly they use local tools like hand hoes and oxen which are time-consuming, with the farm cart technology farmers will be able to perform farm works with the same satisfactions as using other heavy machines like tractors at cheapest cost which is affordable to smallholder farmers up to 50 percent cost reduction. The technology is performing the following activities:

  • planting;
  • ploughing;
  • water pump station (pumping);
  • cargo (pulling up to 700 kg at 18° to 28° inclination);
  • boom spraying system;
  • mowering;
  • maize shelling system;
  • farm transport (four people sitting comfortably);
  • and fertigation.
entries.description:
Description

Small-scale agriculture is the cultivation of crops and livestock on a small piece of land without the use of sophisticated and costly technologies. Though the size of these farms may vary, farming on family plots of land, traditional lands, and smallholdings on the outskirts of urban areas fall is considered small-scale agriculture. Farm cart for small-scale farmers is an idea to expose small-scale farmers to the simplest and highly productive technology on a farm. Farm cart technology helps in reducing the labour needed by providing farmers with a tractor-like machine which can help in transporting, plowing, pulling of farm harvests, fertilizing, water pumping, mowing, planting, and other related activities. The farm cart technology has the similar advantages to heavy machines like tractors and Power tillers, and it is cost-effective. With this technology, smallholder farmers can improve productivity. The project is under development, and it aims to make sure small-scale farmers are equipped with a well-improved Farm cart machine.

1. Farm cart technology project 

Figure 1. Farm cart technology during first modification

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Anna Aido Sanga

2. Ploughing

  • The farm cart technology is there to perform all the basic farm works including ploughing.

2.1 Ploughing system and design

  • The farm cart machine, based on its power, is designed to plough a land sine of 0.4 m at once.
  • Its design is based on the four oxen combined to give an efficient land cultivation.
Figure 2. Farm cart machine during farm works

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

2.2 Tractive power

  • The farm cart machine has a power of about 17 HP which is enough to perform farm works based on the traction and soil calculations.
Figure 3. Rear tyre traction on soil

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

3. Post harvesting of crops

  • The farm cart technology can be used to process harvested crops like maize, sorghum, millet and ground nuts.

3.1 Maize sheller system 

  • The farm cart runs a simple designed maize sheller machine with the capacity to shell 50 bags of maize per hour.
Figure 4. Maize sheller machine operated by farm cart 

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Anna Aido Sanga

3.2 Cargo (pulling)

  • The farm cart has a powerful joint that is connected to the trailer which can pull up to 700 kg (0.5 t).
Figure 5. Farm cart with a joint for connecting a trailer for pulling

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

4. Gender balance

  • The farm cart technology is women-friendly and so contributes to achieve gender balance, that female can participate in farm works and do excellent than their male counterpart.

4.1 Female participation in farm works

  • Female empowering is an important factor for farm cart technology to be successful as it values women efforts in agricultural production, specifically in rural areas.
Figure 6. Female participation

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

4.2 Operation comfortability during farm works

  • The farm cart technology is designed to give all favourable conditions for women/female during the farm works.
Figure 7. The farm cart is easily managed by women too

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

5. Engine setup, operation, maintenance and repair

5.1 Engine setup

  • The engine setup is simple and does not need any extra technique and skills to know how to fix it. Its operation is just like other motorcycle engines which are easily accessible.
  • The engine is placed on the right hand of the operator to simplify the operation and fix any problem that can occur to engine components or brake failure.
  • Fewer components make the setting to be user-friendly.
Figure 8. Engine set up

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

5.2 Operation, maintenance and repair

  • The engine operating system is very easy though it engages the transmission manually.
  • The gearing are in the form of 5-4-3-2-1-N engaged by right hand using a nob.
  • For maintenance and repair the engine can be disassembled without any complication and re-fix again to proceed with operation or farm works.
Figure 9. Engine

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Anna Aido Sanga

6. Validation of the practice

The technology is firstly tested by Sokoine University of Agriculture farms in Morogoro, Tanzania. Currently, the machines are available at SUGECO and Sokoine University of Agriculture (SUA), Morogoro Tanzania under the Agro-mechanization Unit where effective research, modification, and development is taking place. The farmer can contact the innovator through email musadoto260@gmail.com or call +255769763285 also can contact the SUGECO office through info@sugeco.or.tz. The project is planning to make these machines available in at least two to three regions in Tanzania before the beginning of 2022.

NOTE: Farm cart technology is still on the prototype level. This is due to fund resources constraints, it needs more development to attain all the desired functions to perform.

7. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Temperate, cool.

8. Related/associated technologies 

  • Farmer field schools on integrated plant nutrient systems: ID 7527.
  • Direct seeding equipment for tractors (conservation agriculture): ID 7417.
  • Animal traction and single-axle tractor drawn planters in conservation agriculture: ID 7416.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: small-scale motorised transport: ID 7316.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: single axle tractors: ID 7315.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: motorised single-axle mowers and reapers for harvesting cereals: ID 7314.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: manual and motorised threshers: ID 7313.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The work requires short time (approximately 45 minutes) to cultivate an area which could be cultivated in two days by using hand hoes or oxen. Labour is saved because instead of using six people to cultivate one acre by hand hoe, by applying farm cart technology only one person with either gender can operate alone during farm works.

9.2 Women-friendly

The design of farm cart technology is 100 percent women-friendly, as it gives women with a comfortable environment during operation. Despite the affordable price of the technology but the same women with a minimum of one day training about the services and maintenance can perform well without need of foreign exchange or distant expert (as in figures 6 and 7 above).

9.3 Resource use efficiency 

Farm cart machine consumes Petrol fuel with the rate of 2.1 litres per 100 km without full loading, and 2.1 litres for 56 km at full loading. It costs USD 2 of petrol to travel a distance of 100 km, and the same cost to cultivate an area of 2.5 Acres. The technology is resources efficiency compared to large machines like tractors and power tillers.

9.4 Pro-poor technology

Hiring or owning tractors and power tiller is expensive as they need technical experts for services and maintenance. Sometimes the foreign exchange is needed but with this technology as the local solution all the basic knowledge used to design the machine is locally and therefore the resources are available even in rural area which makes it easier for them to adopt. The existing technologies which are said to be poor must not ignore because they give an ordinary remark to the adaptation.

entries.title: Improvised hive security against honey theft using hive casing
entries.source: Jorafarm and Associates Beekeeper
multi_source: Jorafarm and Associates Beekeeper#Jorafarm and Associates Beekeeper#Jorafarm and Associates Beekeeper#Jorafarm and Associates Beekeeper
entries.summary: The vandalism of hives and theft of honey in Nigeria is a perennial problem that has led to the loss of investments and gains by beekeepers and discouraged consumers as well. Beekeepers find it difficult to securely situate their apiaries as they describe it as simply 'no-go' areas for placing hives. As most beekeepers only keep an estimated five percent of their hives on their own land close to them where they can reach on a daily basis, the direct control of their commercial enterprise is reliant on availability of safe sites in areas out of their direct control and most time very far from them. Continual theft and property damage drives businesses into the ground. Producing locally in Nigeria is becoming commercially unviable, as beekeepers battle to find safe sites that equally have a good forage area for bees and devoid of pollutants around the foraging zones. Thus, there is a need for an effective, simple, cost-effective and labour-saving security system for the hives.
entries.description:
Description

Construction of the hive casing can be done following the steps below.

1. Materials

  • 1 inch angular iron (x 2; each is 18 feet long, approximately 36 feet = 12 m long);
  • electrodes; and
  • oxy acetylene flames.

Price of the materials:

  • Length (x2) of 1 inch angular iron is sold for N2400 x 2 = USD 6 x 2.
  • Labour N1600 = USD 4.
  • Padlock and key N800 = USD 2.
  • Total = USD 18.

2. Methods

  • Cut the angular iron to get parts for the casing, for example, a length of 86 cm, width of 46 cm, and depth of 30 cm.
  • Assemble the parts together and braze the metal parts, take care to cover your eyes in the process.
  • Make sure that the brazing was done well for firmness.

Note: The material mentioned above is the Nigerian standard measurement from the manufacturer, thus the length may vary according to different countries.

3. Installation

  • The installation is done by cementing the iron casing permanently on the ground within your apiary so that it becomes impossible to move it around.
  • This will prevent the thieves from stealing the iron casing itself and also disallow them of having access to the hive.
  • Also, it will give the hive the stamina to withstand breeze or animals.

4. Hives

4.1 Hive burnt by the thieves

  • This was one of the hives set ablaze at our farm, but the poachers could not access the honey.
  • It was burnt and all the honey bees died, but the honey was not touched (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Burnt hive 

©Jorafarm and Associates/Ayoade Akande

4.2 Vandalized hive

  • This hive at another apiary was set on fire in order to harvest the honey by vandals.
Figure 2. Side view of the burnt hive

©Jorafarm and Associates /Ayoade Akande

4.3 Hives with chain and padlock

  • These are hives chained and padlocked with bees in all of them.

4.3.1 Chain bonded around the iron stand

  • The aggregation of hives and use of chains and padlock to secure the hive prevented them from being damaged by poachers.
Figure 3. Hive with chain and padlock

©Jorafarm and Associates/Akande Ayoade

Figure 4. Zoom-in picture of the hive with bees, padlock and chain

©Jorafarm and Associates/Akande Ayoade

Figure 5. Front view of the revised iron hive case

©Jorafarm and Associates/Akande Ayoade

Figure 6. Side view of the revised hive case

©Jorafarm and Associates/Akande Ayoade

  • This is the revised iron casing for the hive.
Figure 7. Front view of the revised iron hive case

©Jorafarm and Associates/Akande Ayoade

4.3.2 Iron casing with cover

  • This is the complete hive inside a locked iron casing.
Figure 8. Improvised iron casing for hives security

©Jorafarm and Associates/Akande Ayoade

5. Validation of the practice

  • This practice has been adopted by few farmers in the South West zone of Nigeria.
  • A lot of success stories have been recorded by adopting the practice.
  • It was carried out in the tropical rain forest belt, guinea savanna zones of Nigeria.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • The technology is applicable for any troubled beekeepers in any part of the world.
  • There is no limiting factor.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies 

  • Beekeeping in Africa: installation of bee hives (with particular focus on the top bar hive): ID 7291. 
  • Beekeeping: how to make a top bar beehive (Kenyan top bar hive model): ID 7274.
  • Beekeeping: the Kamara basket hive: an improved traditional hive: ID 7289.
  • Good beekeeping practices and bio-security measures in beekeeping: ID 8409.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The technology is labour-saving for beekeepers who are faced with incessant destruction of hives. It reduces the time spent on monitoring hives and also gives time to engage in other activities. It also frees up resources that would otherwise have been used in the monitoring of hives. 

9.2 Women-friendly

The technology is women-friendly. It is designed to bring assurance to beekeepers that their hives are secure. This technology will promote women participation in beekeeping. Giving that women have other tasks and demands, the use of this technology will reduce time for hive inspection and therefore increase time for other activities. Thus, it is a gender-friendly technology.

9.3 Resource use efficiency 

It enhances the efficient use of resources. Hives, if not destroyed by fire or vandals, can last for a minimum of ten years. Through the adoption of this technology, there will be reduced pressure on the need to make new hives at regular intervals. This also frees up income and resources of the farmers. Apart from that it also reduces the demand for logged wood and thus contributes to the preservation of forests.

9.4 Pro-poor technology 

This technology is simple and can be easily made in rural areas using available resources. It also gives rural people more control over their apiaries. It has the potential to increase output and income of rural farmers.

entries.title: Using IoT (Internet of Things) in measuring water quality parameters in fish farming
entries.source: Rwanda Animal Resources Improvement Cooperative (RARICO)
multi_source: Rwanda Animal Resources Improvement Cooperative (RARICO)#Rwanda Animal Resources Improvement Cooperative (RARICO)#Rwanda Animal Resources Improvement Cooperative (RARICO)#Rwanda Animal Resources Improvement Cooperative (RARICO)

agrovoc_keywords.display: Internet of things (IoT)#Internet of things (IoT)#Internet of things (IoT)#Internet of things (IoT)

entries.summary: Internet of Things (IoT) describes the network of physical objects that are embedded with sensors, software and other technologies with the purpose of exchanging data via the internet. Devices can be programmed to check the temperature, pH, oxygen and other water parameters. IoT technologies have revolutionized fish farming processes and have impacted in many ways, including receiving real time data about water quality and aqua life. Data collected by devices are sent in a data centre or database, to make it easier for a user to access them using a phone or computer.
entries.description:
Description

1. IoT processes

A microcontroller is a mini computer that is embedded on a semi-conductor circuit chip. A microcontroller contains a CPU (central processing unit) along with memory and programmable input/output peripherals. Below is an Arduino, a small device with a microcontroller that is able to execute data gathered from sensors.

Figure 1. Microcontroller

©RARICO/Mary Adeline Imanirakiza

2. Data gathering

Data is gathered from sensors that track the condition of physical things. In fish farming, we use a pH sensor to know the acidity or alkalinity of the water. In case, one of the two increased, fishes can be harmed. We also use a temperature sensor, which is used to know the thermal condition of water. Another important sensor is the dissolved oxygen sensor, which measures oxygen that has dissolved in water. Fishes need oxygen for respiration, in the absence of adequate oxygen, fishes suffer and may die.

1.1  Device configuration

All sensors and other hardware are configured together to make harmony in data gathering. On the picture below, Temperature and pH sensors are connected on a breadboard. Data that are gathered are sent to a microcontroller. 

Figure 2. Image showing the water parameters kits used before using IoT

©RARICO/Bizimana J.Bosco

3. Water quality parameters kits

  • A thermometer is used to measure the pond temperature.
  • An oxygen meter is used to measure oxygen in the pond.
  • Finally, a pH meter which is used to measure the alkalinity and acidity of the water.

These are the existing tools that are already being used in fish farming.

Figure 3. Tilapia and catfish

©RARICO/Bizimana J. Bosco.

Table 1. Requirement of water quality parameters in Tilapia and catfish

Abbreviations: ppm: parts per million, L/min: Litre per minute, [ ] stand for concentration.

3.1 Working principle

The Arduino ATMega is connected to four sensors namely temperature, water level, pH and turbidity as per the circuit design shown in Figure 2. The Arduino checks if the water level is between 25oC to 30oC. If it is less than 25oC, the water is too cold for the fish therefore heater switches on. If it is above 30oC the water is too warm therefore the fan switches on. Similarly, the water level is set to be checked for the top 10 to 20 cm of the tank so that it is always maintained and does not get too low. If the water level is less than 200 mm then the pump switches on and when it reaches 200 the pump switches off. For pH of the water 6.5 to 8 is suitable for the fish therefore a change of less 6.5 or greater than 8 will cause the pump to switch on automatically to pump water out in separate tank. Then water pumped in to fill tank from storage tank. For turbidity the measurement is in ntu and if it is less than 2000 ntu the water is still in acceptable turbidity but if it is above the water is too murky therefore the pump gets switched on and dirty water pumped out while the tank is filled with the clear water from the storage tank. 

To send data to cloud the Arduino is connected to the ESP 8266, the Wi-Fi is connected to the things speak. So to write data to the cloud the Arduino sends to the ESP 8266 and that sends to the things speak channel, using the API key. The things speak after every 16 seconds updates data.

The controller monitors temperature, pH and turbidity through sensor readings and automate switching on/off heater and pump based on sensor readings. The system is connected to internet through Wi-Fi and sensor readings are also sent to the cloud database. Furthermore, the cloud data can be viewed by fish farmers on their mobile and in web application.

3.1.1 Measuring temperature

The DS18B20 is a waterproof temperature sensor that can work from -10oC to +85oC with an accuracy of 0.5 degrees. This sensor is a 1-wire bus ie. it has single bus to control the device. Therefore the 1-Wire interface is enabled using the 1-wire library. To read the sensor values and convert it to degrees such as, Celsius the Dallas Temperature library is used. This library retrieves temperature reading and understood in degrees Celsius using begin (request temperatures) and get Temperature.

3.1.2 Measuring pH 

For using the 425oC analogue pH sensor it has to be first calibrated. The calibration is to convert 10bit analogue value to 0-5 voltage (V) accurately. Since pH is 0-14 the pH is mapped with 5 volts such that, pH 7 is 2.5 V, pH14 is 5 and 0 is 0V. The calibration will identify the uncertainty in the readings because pH 7 may not give a reading of exactly 2.5 V in actual conversion. The output should be 2.5 as the short circuit represents a pH of 7. Figure 4 shows the implementation for reading pH value.

3.1.3 Measuring turbidity

The turbidity sensor is a 10 bit analogue sensor shown in Figure 5, similar to the pH sensor the 10 bit value has to be converted to voltage and also calibrated. To convert the 10 bit analogue reading i.e., 0-1023 to voltage reading between 0-5V Turbidity is inversely proportional to the voltage, means lower voltage higher turbidity and vice versa. 

ntu=-1120.4 x voltage2 + 5742.3 x voltage. This equation converts voltage to turbidity in ntu units.

The actuators are two water pumps, water heater, fan and feeder. If water level is below 100 mm, relay switches on motor and water is pumped in until it reached 200 mm and relay turns off motor.

Similarly, temperature above or below threshold will switch off fan or heater, respectively. For the tilapia fish the ideal is 25oC to 30oC and when it goes below the relay switches on the heater. For turbidity, 3000 above pumps water out to another water tank. For the fish feeder the time is set and fish is fed during the day by rotating and opening lid automatically.

The API key is very important to keep securely as anyone who has access to the key can use it to write and read the data. There are two keys one for read and one for write. The write key is used to connect the microcontroller to the cloud and upload data via Wi-Fi. Along with the key the update channel URL is used to continually update data onto cloud via internet. The results can be seen on the channel’s dashboard where the data is represented as a line graph for each parameter. Water, feeds and materials of IoT are needed to install this technology.

4. Importance of water quality in aquaculture

Fish perform all their functions in water. Because fish are totally dependent upon water to breathe, feed and grow, excrete wastes, maintain a salt balance, and reproduce, understanding the physical and chemical qualities of water is critical to successful aquaculture. To a great extent water determines the success or failure of an aquaculture operation.

Very high (greater than 9.5) or very low (less than 4.5) pH values are unsuitable for most aquatic organisms. Young fish and immature stages of aquatic insects are extremely sensitive to pH levels below 5 and may die at these low pH values.

High pH levels (9 to 14) can harm fish by denaturing cellular membranes. Changes in pH can also affect aquatic life indirectly by altering other aspects of water chemistry. Low pH levels accelerate the release of metals from rocks or sediments in the stream. These metals can affect a fish's metabolism and the fish's ability to take water in.

Table 2. The effects of pH on warm-water pond fish

Tilapia and catfish need a temperature ranging between 20oC and 35oC.

4.1 Dissolved oxygen

The amount of dissolved oxygen is critical in fish farming and other forms of aquaculture. Dissolved oxygen in aquaculture, the volume of oxygen contained in water, is often the most critical parameter in the health and well-being of your livestock. In general, most fish species will grow and thrive within a dissolved oxygen range of 5 to 12 mg per L (ppm). However, if levels drop below 4 mg per L they may stop feeding, become stressed and begin to die. This series of events can start a chain reaction in a pond aquaculture system that could prove detrimental.

Oxygen depletion usually occurs in the summer months because warmer water holds less oxygen than cooler water. For example, water with a temperature of 32ºC can hold up to 7.3 mg per L of oxygen, while 7ºC water can hold 12.1 mg per L. As water temperatures rise, oxygen levels decrease. Higher temperatures also increase the metabolic rate of fish, resulting in the need for more oxygen in your fish farming operation.

Figure 4. Data centre

©RARICO/Mary Adeline Imanirakiza

5.  Data storage/cloud

The cloud is a virtual storage of data and computing power, without direct active management by the user. A data store can be programmed and it is the back-end of a system. It consists of a database and the authentications of the users. Users are allowed to view data that has been assigned to them or when they have access permissions.

Figure 5.  How data are collected, processed and transferred to fish farmers

©RARICO/Jean Bosco BIZIMANA

Figure 6. Device configuration/picture

©RARICO/Mary Adeline Imanirakiza

4.2 Gateway and data sending

An Internet of Things (IoT) gateway is a physical device or software program that serves as the connection point between the cloud and controllers, sensors and intelligent devices. All data moving to the cloud, or vice versa, goes through the gateway, which can be either a dedicated hardware appliance or software program. An example is a GSM, which is a standard-based Low Power Wide Area technology. A GSM sends data to the data centres via the internet.

5. Validation of the practice

The practice has been tested at Mulindi, Ndera Sector, Gasabo District in Kigali at fish farm of Cooperative COPAMAGA.

The pH, temperature and oxygen were measured using sensors and every five minutes we received the data from a device that were inserted in fishponds, canals and water sources at the farm.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Minimum requirements for water to be used in fish farming are:

  • Oxygen ≥4
  • Temperature ≥20oC
  • CaCO3 ≥20 ppm
  • pH ≥ 6.5
  • NH4 ≥ 0.01
  • CO2 ≤ 0.01
  • Water flow >300 L per min (for catfish only).

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Make a living through fish farming: ID 7357.
  • Small-scale freshwater fish farming: ID 6958.
  • Management of fish in the pond: ID 7235.
  • Selection of site and water quality testing for fishpond: ID 4376.
  • Fishpond layout and construction: ID 4384.
  • Management strategies for new or lightly exploited fisheries: ID 4583.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The pond culture is controlled automatically and does not require any labour.

9.2 Women-friendly

Traditional methods are unreliable and also a hazardous and unhygienic because farmers especially have to physically be present in the aquaculture area during feeding time and measure the parameters. Therefore, this project is proposed to overcome these challenges to automate the monitoring process involved in fish farming in small and medium scale fisheries.

9.3 Pro-poor technology

The system is further developed to change the speed by itself, by analyzing the data fed and predict how much food the feed dispenser should release next time. Using previous data about fish speed, water temperature and other parameters a probability diagram is made which shows the relation of each parameter to the other and according to that the feeder system will predict the next feed amount. The review of existing systems shows that there is a need for a smart system comprising of all functionalities for complete monitoring and automation of aquaculture in small and medium scale fisheries. Therefore, a smart aquaculture system is proposed and implemented for effective fish production.

  • IoT Based Automated Fish Farm Aquaculture Monitoring System.

entries.title: Small fish-based fish chutney production
entries.source: SCBRMP Karmokarta/Karmochary KallyanSamabayaSamity Limited (SKSS Ltd)
multi_source: SCBRMP Karmokarta/Karmochary KallyanSamabayaSamity Limited (SKSS Ltd) #SCBRMP Karmokarta/Karmochary KallyanSamabayaSamity Limited (SKSS Ltd) #SCBRMP Karmokarta/Karmochary KallyanSamabayaSamity Limited (SKSS Ltd) #SCBRMP Karmokarta/Karmochary KallyanSamabayaSamity Limited (SKSS Ltd)
entries.summary: Bangladesh with all successes in poverty alleviation is yet to reduce the nutrition deficit, particularly for pregnant women. Malnutrition has a negative impact on the growth of children and could impact them for the rest of their life. Food intake with balance diet is out of reach for the majority of the pregnant women, and they can't reach their nutrition need. This Fish Pickle (Chutney: local name) is an effort to reduce the nutrition gap as a supplementary diet for the first 1000 days of life. It has successfully been trailed, produced and made available with due validation including quality, price, easy technology, availability over the year. Small fish are used as the key material; it is abundantly available all over the country and underused. Initially Chutney produced under social business modalities, no profit no loss basis. In order to reaching maximum Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLW), the product has recently acquired the BSTI (Bangladesh Slandered and Testing Institute) certificate successfully.
entries.description:
Description

The fish Chutney is based on a traditional "achar" or pickle recipe, which is commonly served with rice, vegetables and resembles various savory condiments served in many cuisines. Jat Puti fish is one of the common small indigenous variety selected for producing this chutney as the basic ingredient, as it is a rich source of micro nutrients and widely available in open water fisheries. The recipe has further been extended by including garlic, onion, chilly, iodized salt and soybean oil to make it a mass rich in nutrients essentially needed by the PLW.

Figure 1. A bottle of fish pickle

©SKSS Limited/Abdul Haye Chowdhury

1. Basic ingredient and the source of nutrients

The Chutney is made of cheap small fish, namely Jat Puti (puntius sophore) as the base ingredient added with garlic, onion, chili, iodized salt and soya bean oil for taste and to make it popular, and also for their preservation properties. The recipe contains all source of iron, calcium, zink, vitamin 12, and essential fatty acid from the edible oil that provides the energy part of the chutney.

2. Description of the procedures of preparing the Chutney

The standard procedure of Chutney making is as following:

  • Wash dried fish several times in water to clean (The eyes and head from the small fish should not be removed during cleaning). Then the dried fish was stained in a strainer and was kept for drying.
  • Put oil in a pan and heat it. Add the dried fish to the pan.
  • Fish stirred continuously on a low flame for about 10 to 15 minutes until their color becomes light brown.
  • Transfer the lightly fried dried fish to a bowl.    
  • In the Pan, continue to heat the oil and add onion and garlic for 15 minutes on a low flame until they become brown, and stir continuously.
  • Keep the fried dry fish, onion and garlic to cool. Grind the fried dry fish to make a thick powder.
  • Grind the onion and garlic separately from the fish to make a thick powder.
  • Combine the fried dried fish powder, and the onion and garlic powder in the grinder and grinded to a slightly coarse powder. Add salt to the mixture.
  • After cooling, store the fish powder in an airtight plastic container with mustard oil.

Before finalizing the recipe, tasting trails can be undertaken with the target community as taste can be varied from community to community. Considering taste of the community minor change has made after conducting acceptability trail.

Figure 2. Fish drying before preparing fish pickle

©SKSS Ltd

The main ingredient of fish chutney is dry fish, fish from small indigenous species (SIS). Dry fish produced by contract producer following standard protocol provided by the experts. After completing the preparation steps, one can add 5 g dried bay leaf powder, 8 g ginger powder and 1 g black pepper powder was added to the mixture.

Table 1. List of the ingredients of the final production in percentage

One Bottle = 280 Gram

“Mache bhate Bengali” Fish and rice make a Bengali Fish most commonly eaten animal-source food across all income groups because the small indigenous fish are highly nutritious.

3. Quality control

For ensuring the quality control, the product ensured the quality certification provided by Bangladesh Standard and Testing institute (BSTI) who are the sole authority of Government of Bangladesh to ensure such types of products. SKSSS fIsh pickle also get the approval of the authority by ensuring all terms and condition of BSTI.

4. Bottling and selling

The fish chutney bottled by 280 g each and sold at BDT 280 (USD 3.2) when its unit gross cost of production is BDT 240 (USD 2.82).

4.1 Benefits

The benefits of chutney are tremendous:

  • It addresses the challenge to meet the nutritional deficit of the first 1000 days of life, which is a critical period for the mother and child to protect the under-five child stunted.
  • This is a cheap portion as a product and in the ingredients, but highly effective to meet the nutritional needs with resources easily available locally and the processing is too simple. One tablespoon (30 g of Chutney) contains 44 g of raw fish which is ample to meet the nutrition needs compromising iron, calcium, zink, vitamin B12 and essential fatty acid.
  • Only four bottles of chutney per month can provide PLW sufficient micro nutrient.
  • Quality bottling can preserve over the year.
  • The product can be scaled for industrial production to reach maximum number of PLWs.
  • The production is easy and women can be engaged in the production activities.
Figure 3. Production and packaging

©SKSS Limited/Rakibl Hasan Rana

5. The norms of business

This product was produced based on Social Business compliances - no profit, no loss basis in Bangladesh. Meantime the product has got the certification from Bangladesh Standard Testing Institution for marketing the product in open market.

6. Validation of the practice

Primarily it was followed the traditional method and in Bangladesh making chutney was a household skill, which later was taken at industrial level of production. Prior to the certification, its test and choices were validated through acceptability trail at the community level consumers.

  • Over the 25 villages under six Union of South Sunamganj and Derai Upazila of Sunamganj District (100 pregnant and 50 lactating women (PLW) and 150 Under-two year’s children= 300 HH)
  • The field work was conducted during the month of August- September, 2014. In Sunamganj August- September are the rainy season and thus this two month relatively high food insecurity in Bangladesh, thus the food security ‘picture’ that emerges from the study is related to the seasonal factors of food access and availability during this time period
  • HIS (Helvetas Swiss Interco operation) conducts different phases of the shiree project; conducted in September 2009-August 2012 in about 1 000 HHs (phase 1), September 2013-December 2015 in 2 500 HHs (phase 2) and April 2014-December 2015 in about 5 000 HHs (phase 3).

Women’s Chutney distribution was started on September 2014 for 12 months continuation up to September 2015. Before starting the fish chutney distribution, WorldFish had conducted a baseline survey to identify the nutrition condition of selected pregnant and lactating women. It was found that among all the participants, 72 percent were suffering from anemia (Hb <120 g/L). Besides these, they had some other problems like weakness, dizziness, drowsiness, nausea, less appetite etc. After nine months of fish consumption, WorldFish conducted a qualitative survey to identify their improvement, and it was found that after consuming fish chutney regularly, the majority of the participants are recovered from these problems. In September 2015, the end line survey shows that the number of anemia participants decreased by 28 percent in a year.

7. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The minimum requirement for the successful implementation of the production is availability of SIS. It would not be a problem due to abundance of SIS from open water fisheries and these species are cheaper than any varieties consumed by the local community. Small fish (Puti & kachki not available all time) is a limiting factor. During rainy season abundance of puti & kachki high with low price.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Fish powder: ID 8731.
  • Fish and their by-products: ID 8717.
  • Preservation of fish and meat: ID 6961.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

As the production has been mechanized it has reduced the workload and time, and women have got free from any stress full work like grinding by physical labour.

10.2 Women-friendly

Totally women friendly and dominated by women engagement at every stage of the process. We can say the product is by the women, with the women and for the women – from its resource collection, processing to use.

10.3 Resource use efficiency

Most efficient in using the resources. The technology is using the neglected underused fish to use and using the whole fish for production wasting nothing of the body mass including the head, bone, tail etc.

10.4 Pro-poor technology

Largely pro-poor. The product is reachable by the poor with minimum cost but with maximum benefit being particularly suitable for the first 1 000 days of life of poor families in rural Bangladesh who usually predominantly suffer from nutrition deficit due to lack of food.

entries.summary: This practice shows the services available to farmers by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries of Timor-Leste provides in pursuing the agriculture sector's modernization. It describes the importance of Conservation Agriculture (CA) and the CA model applied in Timor-Leste. It also highlights some limitations identified during implementation in Timor-Leste.
entries.description:
Description

Given the modernization of the agriculture sector, the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries (MAF) has provided land preparation services (ploughing Figure 1) to farmers for the past decade (since 2008). This free service allows farmers to reduce labour costs to prepare their land. This service integrates with the 'slash & burn' agriculture system practised by farmers (Figure 2).

Figure 1. View of 4-wheel tractor ploughing in Manufahi, 2016.

©FAO

Figure 2. Slashed and burned forest for cultivation (before hand tillage) in Aileu, Oct. 2018.

©FAO

Most farm activities are conducted manually in Timor-Leste. Farmers have a demand for ploughing services, mainly for the following reasons:

  • To minimize the labour for land preparation for manual planting of seeds by a wooden stick;
  • To reduce weed pressure on cultivated land; or
  • To open grassland; or
  • To bring fallow land back into cultivation.

In parts of Timor-Leste, a local sturdy perennial grass called 'soko, as well as the ubiquitous imperata (Imperata cylindrica), make the opening of new land particularly labour-intensive if done manually.

Land tillage/ploughing have negative short and long-term effects on soil fertility:

  • It removes the soil's natural cover (both vegetation and residues) and destroys surface soil structure: tropical rain droplets directly hit the soil surface and make it vulnerable to soil erosion (Figure 3 and 4).
  • It buries the topsoil layer rich in organic matter and brings to the surface less fertile soil: crop seeds are placed into this less favourable soil (Figure 5).
Figure 3. Intensive land tillage decreases soil structure. Bacau, Nov. 2018.

©FAO

Figure 4. Soil erosion on <10 percent slope, after ploughing/harrowing. Fragile topsoil seals with the first rain and becomes nearly impermeable.

©FAO

Figure 5. Maize crop Failure, El Niño 2015/16.

©FAO

As a result, the soil surface is unprotected and structurally unstable, increasing runoff and erosion and reducing water infiltration and water-holding capacity of soils.

Combined with 'slash & burn,' ploughing increases the risks of drought, flood and landslide. Removal of surface soil cover by ploughing can also increase soil moisture loss by exposing it to desiccation (sun and wind), which particularly critical for the second cropping season with less precipitation, which is more prone to drought.

The limited capacity to keep the tractors and equipment properly fueled, lubricated and serviced, many tractors and land preparation equipment are in poor condition. Consequently, most farmers are adapting to the reduction of land preparation services by:

  • Reducing the number of years for 'slash & burn' land under cultivation (fallow);
  • Increasing the number of crop cycles per year on cultivated land to keep the soil covered and free from weeds
    • Three crop cycles per year in Viqueque lowland: corn - upland rice - mung beans;
  • Integrating the use of herbicides to control weeds (Figure 6).
Figure 6. This figure illustrates a farmer planting corn seed through grassland previously treated with pesticides. Manufahi, Suco. Dotic, Jan. 2018.

©FAO

1. Why is conservation agriculture so important?

Poverty and food & nutrition insecurity in Timor-Leste are attributed, amongst others, to very low agriculture productivity, degraded land and environment, and variable rainfall.

The main factors for land and environment degradation, deforestation and greenhouse gas emission are 'Slash & burn' agriculture and uncontrolled fire.

Consequently, to sustainably alleviate hunger and poverty and reduce the impact of agriculture on climate and land & environment degradation, there is a need to:

  • Increase agricultural productivity (crop yield per land unit) and the associated factor productivities (yield per unit of production factors such as energy, labour, water and capital);
  • Enhance the resilience of production systems to biotic & abiotic stresses (particularly drought) in a context exacerbated by climate change;
  • Improve agricultural land fertility and rehabilitate degraded agricultural land due to past abuse (slash & burn).

Conservation Agriculture can contribute to achieving the above goals.

Figure 7. Farmer in his CA fields in Betano, Manufahi (Jul. 2019). View of second cropping season corn fields planted at different dates (left: 3 weeks; right: 1 month after planting) and growing through a mulch from the previous cropping season.

©FAO

2. Conservation agriculture in the Timor-Leste context

Conservation agriculture in tropical countries essentially consists of promoting direct seeding under an organic mulch to protect the soil from the effect of intensive rainfall.

In tropical climates, the decomposition of organic matter is fast, and it is necessary to produce very significant amounts and slowly decomposing soil surface cover material (biomass) to generate sufficient and continuous organic mulch.

2.1 The conservation agriculture model promoted in Timor-Leste

Various cover crops have been tested by MAF in Timor-Leste, with the support of FAO.

From the tests, only Velvet bean (Mucuna pruriens), locally known as 'lehe', has produced sufficient biomass to generate a permanent soil cover - mulch. Consequently, lehe is the main cover crop promoted by MAF in its efforts to scale up the technology. CA is therefore often referred by Timorese farmers as lehe.

The CA method promoted by MAF in Timor-Leste encourages the:

  • inter-planting of maize with lehe.
  • After the maize harvest, lehe is left to grow to produce biomass on the field.

The inter-planting of lehe provides soil cover, suppresses weeds and produces mulch for the subsequent crop.

The expected benefits are multiple:

  1. the legumes provide nitrogen to the maize crop;
  2. the weeds are reduced by the shade of the legumes & the mulch;
  3. the mulch reduces surface runoff and soil temperature, improves water infiltration and increases soil moisture retention. This, in turn, improves habitat for soil biotic activity;
  4. organic matter accumulates and overall soil health, including the retention and circulation of plant nutrients and soil biodiversity enhanced and maintained.

As a result, crop yields and resilience to drought increase sustainably.

Intercropping with other potential legumes such as:

  • cowpeas (Vigna unguiculata);
  • soya beans (Glycine max);
  • green gram/mung bean (Vigna radiata);
  • lima beans (Phaseolus lunatus);
  • winged beans (Psophocarpus tetragonolobus);
  • pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) provides substantial benefits and is recommended (see table A1 in annex).

However, currently, the biomass produced by these crops remains insufficient to achieve a permanent mulch cover and suitable cover crop varieties and adaptation methods (densities, timing, residue handling, etc.) in each agroecological condition should be identified.

Figure 8. Lehe biomass produced in a few weeks after planting (Mahakidan, Manufahi, Jan. 2019)

©FAO

Figure 9. A field covered with lehe before 'rolling' (Betano, Manufahi, Apil 2019).

©FAO

2.2 The conservation agriculture crop sequences in Timor-Leste

The integration of lehe as a high producing biomass cover crop into the farming practices in Timor-Leste into local crop sequences is a major task in promoting Conservation Agriculture.

To date, there are five crop sequences into which lehe can be integrated:

  1. A. Cultivating Lehe to open a grass land into cultivation without burning or ploughing;
     
  2. B. Inter-cropping corn with lehe – one crop per year;
     
  3. C. Inter-cropping corn with lehe – two crops per year;
     
  4. D. Cultivating lehe before the main crop; and
     
  5. E. Cultivating lehe in a multi-year crop rotation system.

The five crop sequences in detail:

A. Cultivating Lehe to open a grass land into cultivation without burning or ploughing

Soils in Timor-Leste often have a high clay content and these clays tend to be expansive.

Combined with heavy monsoon rains, particularly on the southern coastal area < 500 m elevation, these conditions facilitate the spread of local sturdy grasses/reeds such as 'soko'. Converting these lands into shifting cultivation is a real challenge for farmers, unless they have access to tractors to plough the land after slashing and burning the grass biomass. This is where Lehe offers an alternative to farmers.

These are the three main steps to consider:

  1. December - January: Lehe seeds are planted (50 cm x 50 cm) at the beginning of the main rainy season into soko grassland, when the soil is already humid - Lehe grows fast and vines rapidly cover and suppress the soko grass;
    • Without sunlight, the grass eventually dies;
  2. May-June: Lehe field is rolled using a 2-wheel or 4-wheel knife blade roller or slashed, when all the soko grasses have been suppressed;
    • Lehe grass dies and provides a thick mulch cover;
  3. June: A food crop such as corn, beans or vegetables can be planted through the mulch (June).

In this sequence, a grassland can be opened for cultivation without burning or ploughing. Besides, lehe does it at very low cost as labour is minimal, and tractor costs are minimal and can be dispensable.

If the farmers decide to open a soko or imperata grassland later, lehe can be distributed in the grassland up until March-April, even when the grass has reached significant height. However, in this scenario, a food crop cannot be grown during the same year.

These results are impressive and demonstrated the high agronomic potential of lehe on weed control.

Figure 10. Farmer in Viqueque who planted lehe to suppress soko grass in preparation of crop cultivation. Lehe a month after growing on soko grassland. Viqueque, Bibileo Suco, Feb. 2019.

©FAO

Figure 11. Part of the land where soko grass is growing strong where lehe was not distributed. Viqueque, Bibileo Suco, Feb. 2019.

©FAO

Figure 12a. Farmer in Manufahi/Dotic who distributed lehe seed into a soko grassland as late as Apr. 2019 when the grass was already over a meter tall. Lehe still twined on the grass and by early Jul. 2019 it covered the reed completely.

©FAO

Figure 12b. The picture shows how soko grass had developed in an adjacent field. Dotic, Manufahi, Jul. 2019.

©FAO

Figure 13. Farmer in Manufahi/Dotic who opened a new grassland into cultivation, using lehe to eliminate soko grass.
Figure 14. View of the same field in Jun. 19. The farmer rolled lehe with a 2-wheel roller in May, once the soko grass was completely suppressed by lehe. This picture provides a view his land cleared from soko grass and lehe mulch. However, new growth of devil's weed (Chromolinea odorata) are rapidly invading the field. This indicates that the devil's weed seed stock has colonized most soils in Timor-Leste. However, weeding new devil's weed plants is not a heavy task.
Figure 15. The farmers cleaned the devil's weed manually and prepared to plant pigeon peas through lehe mulch in July. 19. Dotic, Manufahi, Februrary, May and July. 19.

©FAO

B & C. Inter-cropping corn with lehe

Controlling weeds, such as the sturdy soko grasses and invasive species such as devil's weed is a real challenge for farmers. With declining soil fertility, weed pressure is the main factor for 'slash & burn' farmers to abandon their land and shift into a new farming location.

Beside CA, farmers have two options to control weeds:

  • 'slash & burn’ and plough the land with MAF tractor', and
  • 'slash & burn’ and use pesticides to eliminate the 'soko' or imperata grass.

Manual control of these weeds on large plots is nearly impossible and not considered as an option. Weed control is also one of the main determinants for the amount of land to be put under farmers' cultivation.

  • Integrating lehe into the farming system is an effective weed control solution.
  • Lehe, like other legume crops, can be intercropped with corn provided it is managed adequately.
  • The aggressiveness of lehe vines must be contained when intercropped while allowing it to provide an efficient soil cover.
    • If not, lehe climbs on crops such as corn smothers and twists the plants and completely suppresses the crop. This can result in significant yield losses.  
  • Correct timing of planting is essential (not too early), but most importantly, the vines of lehe have to be cut twice a week during the growing period.
  • if lehe is planted one month and half after maize, controlling lehe twines must be done until the harvest for approximately two months (8 weeks). This task must be conducted twice a week using a small hand sickle to cut the vines climbing on the crops.

However, this work is light as it takes one to two hours per hectare for each passage (two to four hours per week). This represents a total of 16 to 32 hours of labour.

Weeding takes more than twice the amount of labour, but does not need to be conducted as often (once or twice during the growing season).

Figure 16. Maize plants being twisted and pulled down by lehe vines in Manufahi/Suco Betano, Jan. 2019.

©FAO

The steps for intercropping maize and lehe are as follows:

  1. November or December - Crop residues from the previous crop are rolled down in a couple of weeks before the next main cropping season (picture 17);
  2. December and January - Corn is planted 'in line' through the previous crop residues' mulch. Corn is growing though the crop residues (picture 18);
  3. Four to six weeks after corn - Lehe is planted between corn lines at the recommended distances. Lehe rapidly covers the soil surface providing an effective weed control effect;
  4. Twice a week - Lehe vines climbing on maize plants have to be cut using a small sickle;
  5. March or April - Corn is harvested and lehe is left growing in the field to produce more biomass. Lehe eventually covers the maize stalks.

In areas with one crop per year, the crop sequence stops here.

Figure 17. Rolling corn with a 4-wheel knife-roller. Betano/Manufahi, Dec. 2018.
Figure 18. Planting corn with traditional planting stick through previous corn crop residue. Manufahi, January 2019.

©FAO

B. Two crops a year

In areas where two crops per year are possible such as Manufahi, Ainaro and Covalima, many farmers cultivate corn in succession twice a year.

In this scenario, then the next steps are as follows:

  1. May or June - Lehe and the corn stalks are rolled down (or slashed manually if rollers are not available). Rolled lehe is left desiccating for two weeks to form a uniform mulch covering the topsoil;
  2. May or June - Corn (or other crops) are planted through the mulch. During the second cropping, intercropping lehe is not recommended as rainfall is less abundant. Lehe would compete with the main crop on water stored in the lower layers of the soil (which is essential to the success of the second cropping season) (Figure 19).
  3. September - Corn (or other crops) is harvested and left standing until the next main cropping season.
Figure 19. View of corn growing through crop residues (Manufahi, Jul. 2019).

©FAO

C. One crop a year

Farmers may choose not to cultivate a second cropping season, but to let lehe grow to produce more biomass and seeds. Lehe takes longer to produce seeds/pods than maize crops. To produce seeds, farmers must let some lehe grow throughout the second cropping season.

In this scenario, then the next steps are as follows:

  1. Lehe is left to grow on the land until the plant dies by itself. It will produce significant biomass that is beneficial to soil fertility;
  2. August and September - Lehe seeds are harvested. By then lehe will have dragged all the maize stalks down to the ground, and the biomass will have dried and formed a thick mulch covering the top soil;
  3. Before the next main cropping season - the new devil's weed (Chromolinea odorata) sprouts will need to be weeded out (one hour per hectare).

In this scenario weed control is highly effective, soil fertility increases rapidly and farmers do not need access to machinery as rolling is no longer necessary (lehe pulls maize stalks down to the ground) (picture 20).

Figure 20. View of a field in September where corn was intercropped with lehe. The legume crop was left to grow for the rest of the year ('intercropping corn with lehe - one crop a year' sequence). Corn seeds can be planted directly through the mulch for the main cropping season. (Ainaro, Sep. 2019).

©FAO

D. Cultivating lehe before the main crop

In areas where two cropping seasons are possible farmers may choose not to intercrop lehe with corn to avoid the challenges in managing lehe as an intercrop.

One option is to plant lehe early in the season, let it grow sufficiently to produce enough biomass for weed control and then plant the main crop (corn or other crops).

For this option the steps are as follows:

  1. December or January - Lehe seeds are planted and left to grow until it has produced sufficient biomass (Figure 21);
  2. March or April - Lehe is rolled by the latest and then rolled or slashed manually. Rolled lehe is left desiccating for two weeks to form a uniform mulch covering the topsoil (Figure 22 -24);
  3. March or April - Corn (or other crop) is planted through the mulch two weeks later, ideally intercropped with other legumes such as cowpeas, mung beans, soya beans, etc. (Figure 25 and 26);
  4. July or August - Corn (or other crop) is harvested and left standing until the next main cropping season.

Compared to the intercropping option the main disadvantage of this pattern is:

  • that less biomass is produced on the land;
  • there is also a six months' time lag between the harvest and the next planting season, which reduces the quantity of mulch available on the topsoil.
Figure 21. Lehe field ready for rolling.
Figure 22. Rolling the field with a 2-wheel roller.

©FAO

Figure 23. Desiccating lehe two days after rolling.
Figure 24. Desiccated lehe two weeks after rolling forms a uniform mulch covering the top soil.

©FAO

Figure 25. Corn growing though a thick lehe mulch 10 days after planting, weeds are completely under control.
Figure 26. Corn growing though lehe mulch a month after planting, the decomposing lehe mulch provides nutrients for the crop to grow. (Manufahi, Betano, June to Aug. 2019).

©FAO

E. Cultivating lehe in a multi-year crop rotation system

In Viqueque farmers have developed the most sophisticated crop rotation system in Timor-Leste. They cultivate three crops each year on the same land starting with corn and follow-up with upland rice relay cropped with mung-bean or soya bean.

  • The crop calendar (Table 1) shows that the land is left without growing crops covering the soil for only two to three months per year under this crop sequence.
Table 1. Crop calendar for corn cultivated once or twice per year and in rotation, where three successive crops are cultivated (corn, upland rice and mung beans-MB).

In other Municipalities, including with similar climatic zones (Manufahi, Ainaro, Covalima or Lautem), the land is left without growing crops covering the soil for 7 to 8 months per year when:

  • corn is cultivated only once a year; and
  • three to four months when cultivated twice (Table 1).

In this sequence of crops, there is no time to include lehe in the annual cycle. But when compared to corn monocropping in other Municipalities, Viqueque's lowlands' weed pressure is significantly reduced by the sequence of crops covering the land, which seems to be the farmers' strategy.

When mung bean or soya bean are planted between upland rice lines, crop residues can be laid on the soil to create a mulch (Figure 27). This helps reduce weed pressure and preserve soil moisture essential toward the end of the cropping season (Figure 28).

The use of rollers can shorten the time required for land preparation in a very tight annual crop calendar (Table 1):

  • rolling the first season corn stalks before planting upland rice;
  • rolling the upland rice before planting mungbeans.
Figure 27. Mung beans growing over upland rice mulch. Viqueque, Sep. 2019.

©FAO

Figure 28. Upland rice standing crop residues before rolling. Viqueque, Sep. 2019.

©FAO

This annual crop succession system enters a broader multi-annual crop rotation pattern that:

  • includes peanuts, pigeon peas, sometimes vegetables and land fallowing;
  • farmers may develop their crop rotation patterns that includes vegetables, depending on market demands.

Lehe can be advantageously integrated in the multi-annual crop rotation pattern in view of reducing weed pressure while producing useful mulch that improves soil fertility and crop resilience to drought. This is illustrated in a three years crop rotation cycle below.

Crop rotation over a three-year cycle

Below, Table 2 illustrates the crop rotation over a three year cycle that includes the introduction lehe into the production system.

The land is divided in three sections.

During the 2017 first cropping season (top row):

  • section I is planted with corn intercropped with lehe;
  • section II is planted with corn, then followed by upland rice relay cropped with soybean, while
  • section III is planted with peanut.

During the second year,

  • section I was divided to plant maize and peanut on lehe mulch and
    • repeated intercropping corn with lehe in section III.
  • Section II mostly remained the same as the previous year. A CA adopter implemented this pattern in Suco Bahalarauain (Viqueque).
Table 2. Illustration of a crop rotation pattern. Shaded in green is where lehe is cultivated on part of the land, others refer to where lehe is not applied - intensive crop succession (corn-upland rice-mung bean).

Figure 29. Illustration of a crop rotation pattern where lehe is cultivated on part of the land (plot shaded in green) where intensive crop succession (corn-upland rice-mung bean) is not applied.

©FAO

Figure 30. View of Section IA (maize on lehe mulch) and section IB (peanut on lehe mulch). Viqueque, Suco Bahalarauain, Feb. 2019.

©FAO

2.3 Other CA systems already imeplemented by farmers

These include the following:

2.3.1 Turmeric – bamboo agro-forestry system

Turmeric (Curcuma longa) is a main spice produced in Timor-Leste.

  • It is cultivated under shade;
  • burning is not practiced as it would destroy both the main crop (turmeric) and the shade plants (bamboo or other shade trees);
  • when cultivated under a bamboo shade the soil remains covered with organic matter/mulch produced by the constant leaf shedding of fast-growing bamboo plants.

2.3.2 Coffee agroforestry system

Coffee is grown under a shade tree.

  • Mainly under Albizia tree (Falcataria moluccana, locally known as aikafe); and
  • Casuarina (Casuarina junghuhniana, locally known as ai-kakeu);
  • burning is not practiced as it would destroy both the main crop (coffee) and the shade plants (if not fully grown);
  • the soil remains covered with a thin mulch produced by shedding shade tree leaves and the coffee plants.

2.3.3 Vanilla agroforestry system

Vanilla is also grown under shade.

  • mainly composed of Gliricidia (Gliricidia sepium, locally known as aigamal); and
  • cotton wood tree (Hibiscus tiliaceus, locally known as ai-fao);
  • a thick mulch cover is permanently maintained around the vanilla plant stems to maintain moisture and a favourable growing environment.
Figure 31. View of a turmeric and bamboo agroforestry system in Quelicai (Bacau, December 2018).

©FAO

Figure 32. Vanilla farm under ai-fao (Hibiscus tiliaceus) tree cover with thick organic mulch cover (July 2019).  
 Figure 33.  View of coffee plantation under aikafe (Falcataria moluccana) trees in Ermera (January 2019).

©FAO

2.4 Equipment that facilitates conservation agriculture practice

One of the most noticeable changes for farmers after introducing CA is the reduced requirement for farm power and labour.

Specialized CA equipment is needed to carry out farming operations that include direct seeding and crop residue management:

a) Direct seeding - The objective is to precisely position the seeds under the CA mulch to achieve the best possible growing conditions.

 There are many tools:

  • The planting stick used by Timorese' slash & burn' farmers is well adapted for CA direct seeding.
  • The rolling injector planter can reduce the workload for planting operations. However, the design does not allow planting under a thick lehe mulch. More testing is necessary (Figure 34).

b) Managing lehe as an intercrop - Lehe is an aggressive vining legume. Other legumes, such as some cowpea varieties are less aggressive but also vining.

  • farmers are advised to regularly cut the vines climbing on maize plants (or other crops), using a small sickle;
  • the sickles farmers use to harvest traditional rice varieties are adapted to this.

c) Crop residue management - The objective is to leave as many residues as possible to increase soil organic matter and spread them as evenly as possible.

  • To achieve the weed control function, it is not recommended to leave the residue standing but to roll them down before planting;
  • knife rollers for 2- and 4-wheel tractors were introduced in Timor-Leste;
  • these rollers can also be used to successfully 'kill' lehe crop before planting (Figure 35).
Figure 34. View of hand-equipment used for CA. Left: traditional planting stick; Middle: rolling injector used for direct seeding; Right: hand-sickle used to control lehe vines.

©FAO

Figure 35. View of hand-tractors and knife-rollers used for CA (Betano, January and Sep. 19).

©FAO

2.5 Benefits of conservation agriculture in Timor-Leste

2.5.1 Socio-economic benefits

Socio-economic benefits increase labour productivity - quantity of food produced per day of labour.

  • Labour productivity is significantly higher (67 percent) when farmers are implementing CA.
  • For every day spent working in the field, the CA farmer can obtain 67 kg of maize, while farmers applying traditional practices will only get 40 kg.
  • Labour time decreases by approximately a third to produce higher quantities of maize.
    • This is mainly due to reduced land preparation (land tillage/ploughing) and weeding time, a task typically undertaken by women.
  • Increased labour productivity is the main driver for CA adoption.

With the time saved from working in the field, women conduct the following activities:

  • working in the house;
  • providing more care for the children;
  • looking after livestock;
  • preparing and selling produce in the market; and
  • investing in new businesses.

2.5.2 Benefits

Figure 36. Farmer CA plots planted at the same time. Left: Control maize almost destroyed. Right: surviving CA maize field despite El Niño drought, Jul. 2015.

©FAO

Figure 37. Mrs. Nathalia da Costa on her farm. Right: CA maize; Left: traditional. Manufahi, Sept. 2016.

©FAO

2.5.3 Environmental benefits

Environmental benefits have not yet been measured. However, 'slash & burn' and uncontrolled fire results in massive land areas being torched every year. Remote sensing analysis using 30 m Landsat data showed that in 2017, 44 percent of the national territory was affected by medium and severe burning. The 'fire season' in Timor-Leste starts in June but peaks in October and November. Fire in Timor-Leste is mostly human-induced and mostly related to slash & burn agriculture practices.

Slash & burn shifting agriculture and uncontrolled fire in Timor-Leste are recognized  as the number one contributors to:

  • air pollution and green-house gas emissions;
  • land & environmental degradation;
  • deforestation;
  • loss of biodiversity;
  • soil erosion & slope instability; and
  • watershed and water regime degradation;

CA's expected environmental benefits (no-tillage and no-burning principle) are massive and include climate change mitigation and adaptation, soil fertility, reforestation, increased biodiversity and water quality.

2.6 What are the main limitations of the conservation agriculture model

While the practice of 'no-burning' and 'no ploughing' can be undertaken in all agroecological zones of Timor-Leste, the intercropping of a cover crop is dependent on the adaptability of high biomass producing cover crops to various climate zones and identification of leguminous and non-leguminous cover crops with slow decomposition rate and drought tolerance characteristics.

  • Lehe performs well in low land where rainfall is abundant. The best results are obtained in the southern lowlands, where the rainy season is longer and allows for two cropping seasons. In these agroclimatic zones, lehe gives good results when planted during the first cropping season or intercropped/relay cropped before the end of the first cropping season cycle.
  • Lehe does not perform well during the second cropping season when rainfall is less abundant.
  • Lehe does not perform very well in higher elevation and in dryer areas (northern coast) or when rainfall is below average.
  • Lehe does not seem to perform very well on sloping land. This might be due to the lower availably of water (higher runoff on sloping land).
  • Lehe is well adapted to the 'Southern coast lowland' and parts of the 'Southern slopes' climatic zones, particularly on land with mild slopes (see Map 1).
  • A local variation of velvet bean, called 'koto-moruk' performs better at higher elevations, but more tests are required.
  • As a result, CA cover crop options to promote the full CA package are not available for most of the agroclimatic zones that exist in the country, particularly for sloping lands, higher lands and dryer parts of the country.
  • Substantial parts of the national territory are left with inadequate high biomass producing cover crop options to promote CA. Therefore, more research is required to expand CA's adoption to the various agroecological zones of Timor-Leste. Additionally supporting policies and institutional capacities are inevitable for importing potential cover crops seeds and appropriate tools and machineries as well as domestic marketing and service provisions.
Map 1. Climatic zones of Timor-Leste. Lehe is well adapted to the 'Southern coast lowland' (light green) and in part of the 'Southern slopes' (orange) climatic zones, particularly on land with mild slopes (<10 percent). In other agroclimatic zones, there are no adapted high biomass producing cover crops identified to promote the full CA package.

©FAO

Acknowledgments: The content of this practice is from the FAO Timor-Leste office projects:
  • Pro-Resilience Timor-Leste - Strengthening Resilience in Drought affected Communities (GCP/TIM/058/EC);
  • Pro-Resilience Timor-Leste II - Strengthening Resilience in Communities Prone to Climate Risks (UNJP/GLO/08/EC).

3. Validation of the practice

This practice was tested in Timor-Leste.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • A step-by-step approach toward a gradual adoption of the full conservation agriculture technology: an example from Timor-Leste: ID 10093.
  • Dzud early warning system in Mongolia: ID 10091.
  • Conservation Agriculture (CA) model in Timor-Leste: ID 10092.

  • Labour time decreases by approximately one third to produce higher quantities of maize.
    • This is mainly due to reduced land preparation (land tillage/ploughing) and weeding time, a task typically done by women. 

6.2 Women-friendly

With the time saved from working in the field, women conduct the following activities:

  • working in the house,
  • providing more care for the children,
  • looking after livestock,
  • preparing and selling produce in the market and investing in new businesses.

Annex
