entries.summary: Hanging vegetable gardens is an easy to implement practice allowing to grow healthy vegetables with no land and little inputs. Hence, it is very suitable for low-income families, slum dwellers, the landless, women who often have poor access to land and need to stay close to their homes, as well as for pastoralists who can thus move from place to place carrying their gardens with them. Hanging vegetable gardens can be made using waste plastic containers and clean water used in house chores (e.g. washing utensils), thus saving water. This technology help saving money to buy vegetables, while ensuring that families have easy access to nutritious vegetables, especially in times of the pandemic of COVID-19, which disrupted food distribution chains. For instance, a family of five in Kenya spends an average of Ksh 100 per day for vegetables. Cultivating their own hanging garden, they can save it, which translates to Ksh 36 000 in a year. This money can be used to educate a child in a boarding secondary school in Kenya and hence help to improve education and livelihoods. At the same time, healthy nutritious practices are promoted, helping to reduce levels of malnutrition in the communities. Use of safe waste plastic containers contributes also to reducing environmental pollution.
entries.description:
Description

1. How to prepare a hanging vegetable garden

1.2 Materials needed

  • Soil
  • manure
  • seeds/seedlings
  • safe waste container
  • water
  • ropes.

1.3 Planting steps

  • Mix manure and soil at the rate of 20 percent manure to soil.
  • Put the mixed soil in the container. The container should have enough soil in it to support the plant growing in it and elevate them to the height where they can access light and air. The soil should be far enough below the rim of the container so that it does not spoil out when plants are watered.
  • Make two holes below the rim but above the soil level, the holes should be far apart, tie with the rope from either side.
  • Plant your seedlings in the container.
  • Hang the garden outside the house but within the compound.
  • Water the plants. Do the watering regularly when moisture content goes down. To check the moisture content, stick the finger in the soil at least to your second knuckle or a stick up to two inches and feel the soil within your two fingers. If the soil feels dry at your fingertips, the plants need water.

NB: There are a huge number of vegetables that do well in containers. These include; spinach, onions, eggplant, tomatoes, lettuce, garlic, Potatoes, sage, kales among others.

2. Source of seeds/seedlings

Seeds are obtained from agro-dealers and seed producing companies. Seedlings are obtained from certified seedlings raisers. Farmers can also prepare seedbeds to help produce their own seeds.

3. How to prepare a seedbed

3.1 Materials needed

  • Fork jembe,
  • measuring tape,
  • seeds,
  • watering can,
  • water,
  • panga, and
  • Four measuring sticks, approximately 50 cm each.

3.2 Procedure

  • Clear the land using a panga.
  • Do primary and secondary tillage to make the soil fine.
  • Mark the nursery with a measuring tape at a width of one metre and a desired length.
  • Mark the corners of the bed with the sticks.
  • Raise the bed to a height of 10 to 15 cm.
  • In desert like climates or drought stricken areas, use sunken beds.
  • Make rows at 10 to 15 cm apart and plant your seeds one by one.
  • Plant the seeds at a depth two times the width or diameter of the seed. For example, if you have a seed that is about 1/16 inch it should be planted about ⅛ inch deep.
  • Water regularly using a watering can and do the weeding when need be untill the seedlings are ready for transplanting (When the stem is about pencil size width).

4. Nutritional information

Vegetables contain different nutrients including; vitamin A, Vitamin B, dietary fibre, potassium and calories among others. These nutrients have different healthy benefits to a human body which include; healing of wounds, help shore up bones, booster immune system, protection against diseases, improvement of sexual competence and support the development of a baby's nervous system and skeleton in a pregnant mother among others.

The figure below shows different farmers and Agrizeal Africa staff in Nyeri and Laikipia counties in different vegetable gardens.

Figure 1. Victoria from Nyeri county attending to her hanging vegetable garden

©Agrizeal Africa

Figure 2. This garden has canola (Brassica napus), spider plant (Cleome gynandra), Amaranthus (Amaranthus viridis), Capsicum (Capsicum annum) and spring onions (Allium fistulosum)

©Agrizeal Africa

5. Validation of the practice

This practice has been tested by farmers in Nyeri and Laikipia counties in Kenya. The practice was carried out in tropical climatic conditions throughout the year by farmers from low and middle social classes, which also include slum dwellers and pastoralists. It can be carried out in other climatic conditions in some periods of the year.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

For successful implementation of this technology, you do not need rainfall since you water the garden by water that has been used in home chores like washing utensils. The optimal soil Ph for implementation of this technology is between 5.5 and 7.5. To ensure the water is safe for plants and seeds, it should be free from toxic compounds like petroleum, soap and other harmful chemical residues from household chores. When selecting containers for use, ensure that you do not re-use pesticide containers. There is no limiting factor to the implementation of this technology.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Keyhole gardens for better nutrition and livelihoods: ID 7643.
  • Sack gardens for improved urban diets and livelihoods: ID 7652.
  • Rooftop water collection, drip irrigation and plastic mulching in home garden conditions in drought prone areas: ID 8934.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

This technology saves labour since it's done in containers which allows very few or no weeds as opposed to when grown on the field. This means that time used for weeding by men and women can be used to do other chores. Again, since it's done at the homestead it reduces the time people use to go to the market to buy vegetables and that time can be used in doing other activities.

9.2 Women-friendly

This technology is women friendly since it involves a simple practice using the waste plastic containers available. Also, the management of the garden is simple and therefore friendly to women.

9.3 Resource use efficiency

This technology uses resources very efficient since it uses waste plastic containers, water that has been used carrying out home chores, soil and little energy in carrying out the practice.

9.4 Pro-poor technology

This technology helps the poor community to have their food at their homestead, which helps eradicate malnutrition. It also helps the poor save the money used on vegetables daily and therefore use that money to educate their children, which in turn eradicated poverty.

entries.summary: This practice explains how conservation agriculture (CA) works, its limitations, and how to identify practical solutions to challenges farmers face in Timor-Leste.
entries.description:
Description

How does conservation agriculture (CA) work?

For the adoption of CA practices, the CA principles must be well understood by those providing advice and by those implementing it – extensionists and farmers. This practice describes how CA works, the limitations, and how to identify practical solutions to address farmers' challenges.

It is crucial to understand and acquire some knowledge of soils. And on related issues such as increased soil fertility, reduced erosion, increased yield, increased resilience to climate hazards and particularly drought (climate change adaptation), reduced greenhouse gas emissions (climate change mitigation), reduced land and environmental degradation, increased forest cover, increased biodiversity and increased water sources.

1. About soil and soil fertility?

Soils are living organisms and their development is a continuous process. Figure 1. shows the formation of soils starting from the initial bedrock (rock layer).

The seven steps in soil formation (Figure 1.):

1.1 Fragmentation of the bedrock

Soil formation begins when the rock layer breakup through physical, chemical and biological processes. This fragmentation results in pebbles, gravel, sand and silt that form the 'SKELETON' of the soil.'The main elements contributing to this are rainwater infiltration, temperature changes, and plant roots and earth movements (geological movements).

1.2 Rock weathering by soil-forming process

The rainwater, plant root acidic secretions and humic acids dissolve minerals from bedrock. This process, called chemical weathering, and other mechanisms like hydrothermal activities form finer soil materials (<0.002 mm), generates a" jelly-like substance" - clays. Clays play important roles in soil's physical, chemical and biological properties. In particular, clays keep within their structures plant nutrients such as Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+, Fe2 +, PO4+, SO4.

1.3 Accumulation of organic matter

The organic matter decomposed by biological activities, both above and below the ground (roots), forms another "jelly-like substance" - humus (amorphous and structureless black or dark brown substances). Humus provides the source of plants nutrients to allow plants to grow healthy and increases water retention. Humus also plays an essential role in soil's physical, chemical and biological properties.

Plant root systems absorb nutrients from deep layers of the soil, transport them to the plant canopy. When leaves are shedding, deposits these minerals on the soil surface. As a result, when land is not tilled or burned, a nutrient-rich litter mulch is created on the soil surface. Organic matter accumulates, soil fertility builds up and the soil is 'growing' or getting deeper. Through this mechanism, trees and plants with deep rooting systems pump nutrients and water from deep soil layers and bedrock up to the soil surface. This is an essential process of soil formation referred to as the 'BIOLOGICAL PUMP.'

When practising 'shifting' agriculture, Timor-Leste's farmers make practical use of these fertility build-up mechanisms in a natural environment as they leave their land fallow for several years to rebuild fertility that results in an accumulation of organic matter, particularly when the fallow period is long enough (minimum of 10 to 15 years). The key challenge in implementing sustainable farming is to identify practices that maintain or enhance these processes of organic matter builds up while, at the same time, cultivating the land.

Figure 1. Simplified illustration of soil formation (pedogenesis). It also highlights the three key soil constituents; the skeleton, the soil plasma and porosity. Source: Soltner, 1998[1]

[1] Soltner, D., 1998, ‘Les Techniques Culturales Simplifiées’, Collection Science et Techniques Agricoles.

1.4 Creation of the humus and 'clay-humus complex'

The association of humic substances (humus) with clay minerals, both 'jelly-like substances' in humid conditions, form the 'clay-humus complex' (represents the bond between the clay particles and organic matter). Depending on the type of soil and clays available, the soil organic matter increases as clay content increases. The liaison between clay and humus occurs in the digestive tubes of earthworms and other soil-living organisms (Soltner, 1998).  As illustrated in Figure 2, clay and humus merge, attracting more nutrients and retain more water in the soil. 

This complex builds and protects soil structure and therefore prevents/reduces erosion, leaching and improves soil pH stability. Therefore, agriculture practices that produce sufficient organic matter,  preserving earthworms and other soil living organisms, are essential for forming the clay-humus complexes. The 'clay-humus complex' has multiple benefits for soil fertility. It stabilizes the soil's physical structure and stores nutrients that are important for crops.

Figure 2. Schematic view of the 'clay-humus complex'[2]

[2] https://formationcivamgard.fr/?ComPlexe

1.5 Building the soil structure

'Clay-humus complex' can bind soil particles together in clusters or aggregates. Micro-aggregates clump together to form larger aggregates (macro-aggregates). These are characteristic of fertile soils. The aggregation of soil particles into granulate structures gives the soil its POROSITY. Well-developed soil structure benefits soil health and functions such as better infiltration and drainage of water, aeration, retention of water and nutrients.

Figure 3. Illustration of soil structure[3]

[3] http://vro.agriculture.vic.gov.au/dpi/vro/vrosite.nsf/pages/soilhealth_soil_structure

1.6 Soil-formation process

Over time, the above processes are repeated millions of times and as a result, the soil is growing (forming). Soils typically grow at an average rate of 1 centimetre per 300 years (Soltner, 1998). However, it could take between 100 and 1 000 years to form 1 centimetre of soil, depending mainly on climate, vegetation and the geological nature of the bedrock.

1.7 Soil erosion/degradation

Half of the Timor-Leste national territory has a slope of 40° or more (Thompson, 2011)[4] and most farmers practices slash and burn. In this context, loss of organic matter from burning and soil erosion are the most critical factors of soil degradation. Because soils in Timor-Leste are exposed to intense tropical rainfall, degradation by erosion is a rapid process. Even one event can result in the loss of the whole soil top layer.  In addition,  slash and burn' results in a rapid and steady loss of soil fertility, forcing farmers to shift to new lands, typically every two to four years, when cultivating on slopes. Consequently, hundreds of years of soil formation can be lost in just one intense rainfall event eroding the soil away or, within a few years, burning all organic material on cropland.

[4] Thompson S., 2011. ‘Geology and Soils in Timor-Leste’, Seeds of Life.

In Timor-Leste, the dominant soils have developed from uplifted marine sediments and limestones. These have either weathered on the slope (lower fertility soils) or moved to lower elevations and thus formed from colluvium (higher fertility soils).  On slopes, soils are thinner and have lower fertility and, therefore, more susceptible to soil degradation. In contrast, in lower lands where soil materials accumulate at the base of the slope and floodplains as colluvium and alluvium. These soils tend to have finer textures (loamy and clayey) and thus with higher fertility. These soils are less susceptible to soil degradation, but due to expansive clay material, some caution is needed with land preparation. 

In Timor-Leste, important drivers of soil degradation are:

  • Slashing forests and bushes in 'shifts' for crop cultivation
  • Burning or removal of organic matter and crop residues  
  • Disturbing the soil's surface by tillage.

On steep slopes, tens of centimetres of soil top layers, particularly soils exposed to heavy tropical rainfall and steep slopes, can be washed away in one year. Hundreds of years of soil formation can be lost in a few cropping seasons.

With this scenario, the solution is to increase soil fertility by managing soil organic matter well. Farmers are aware that current practices are not sustainable as crop yields are declining and land available for shifting decreases, resulting in an uncultivated period that has become too short for restoring soil fertility from using unsustainable practices. Timorese farmers are aware that their practices need to change, but practical alternatives may not be readily accessible. The single most important event in generating soil fertility is forming a stable 'clay-humus complex,' achieved mainly by increasing soil organic matter (the source of the soil biological activity (e.g., presence of earthworms and other soil living organisms).

Thus, it is essential to:

  • produce sufficient humus quantities using the vegetation or crops (green manure, crop residues) to maintain both its carbon content and sustain biologic activity;
  • not to burn crop residues and other organic matter produced on the land and to avoid the disturbance of surface soils by tillage;
  • improve soil organic matter, especially on small surfaces, such as backyard garden, by addition compost/manure from external sources);
  • use deep-rooting plants, such as tree crops in agroforestry systems;
  • recycle nutrients from the lower soil layers back to the surface where growing crops' root systems are. Required to maintain the natural soil' BIOLOGICAL PUMP' function in crop growing conditions (Figure 1, point 3).

2. Why are the three key CA principles so important?

The three principles of CA are: 1) minimum mechanical soil disturbance (minimum tillage), 2) permanent soil organic cover (crop residues and live mulches), and 3) species diversification (crop rotation and intercropping).

However, to address the priorities in Timor-Leste, where shifting slash and burn agriculture is the prevailing practice, a slightly different application of CA is applied. The three principles of CA validated in collaboration with local authorities and farmers groups are:

  1. 'No-burning,'
  2. 'No-ploughing' and
  3. 'Growing a cover crop.'

A series of CA crop rotations that integrate traditional crop rotation systems were designed based on these three principles.

The implementation of the CA, in this case,  comprised the following actions:

  • firstly direct seeding under an organic mulch to protect the soil from the effect of high-intensity rainfall on soil erosion and to reduce evaporation in dry periods;
  • no burning of the organic matter and no ploughing of the land –to keep/increase mulch/soil cover;
  • grow a 'cover crop' before, during, or after the main food crop -to produce sufficient biomass that can provide a permanent mulch/soil cover.

2.1 Why 'no-burning'?

Burning organic matter loses organic content and causes a series of linked events that naturally destroy soil fertility.

Burning directly:
  • eliminate much of the surface and sub-surface soil living organisms;
  • destroys organic matter on the surface that is food for soil living organisms;
  • exposes the soil surface to erosion and also to drought, compaction, and fluctuation of extreme soil temperature and moisture content;
  • releases a vast amount of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.
While in a slash & burn system:
  • burning organic matter has a short-term benefit as it releases mineral nutrients on the soil surface readily available to young crop plantlets;
  • these mineral nutrients are vulnerable to rapid loss by leaching and erosion;
  • surface and sub-surface soil living organisms are eliminated;
  • the soil structure collapses and becomes friable and vulnerable for soil surface sealing, compaction, and consequently erosion (soil surface have a concrete structure appearance); and
  • soil fertility collapses in a few years and farmers shift to slash and burn another forest or bushland.

The practice of no-burning is a pre-condition to maintain the virtuous cycle of soil fertility.

Organic matter is food for soil life, which:
  • creates the 'clay-humus complex' – increased fertility,
  • builds the soil nutrition stock and the soil structure,
  • creates soil porosity that allows plants to develop and feed on the soil.

The key is producing and maintaining enough biomass/organic matter to maintain a healthy soil environment and virtuous soil fertility.

Figure 4. View of soil organisms living in topsoil mulch. Source: Soltner, 1998

2.2 Why 'no ploughing'?

(I) When 'no ploughing' in a CA field

The soil organisms work as follows to putrefy and decompose organic matters:

Figure 5. Illustration of soil organisms under a CA field. Source: Soltner, 1998

(II) When the land is ploughed
Figure 6. Illustration of soil organisms under a CA field. Source: Soltner, 1998

Figure 7. Macro-porosity from soil samples collected; left and right are from a CA field, middle from a traditional field (Niederman, 2016)[5]

[5] Niemeyer, P., 2016, Technical Report on Farming and Cropping and Soils at FAO Conservation Agriculture Sites in Timor Leste, 2016.

Figure 8. Mainland preparation tools used in Timor-Leste. The regular plough (left) and disk plough (middle) are primarily in use.

©Soltner, 1998

2.3 Why 'growing a high biomass producing cover crop'?

Maintaining sufficient organic matter production and permanent soil cover under the current agricultural production systems (mainly mono cropping) is challenging with limited residue availability, completion with other purposes of use, and rapid decomposition rate, particularly in the tropical environment with high temperature and humidity, which enhance microbial decomposition of organic materials. Often its cropping season is limited due to the availability and distribution of precipitation and finding windows and spaces for growing cover crops. Therefore, the identification and adoption of suitable and high biomass producing and slow decomposing cover crops to generate sufficient and continuous provision of organic matter and maintenance of permanent soil cover is an essential component. This to sustaining soil health (physical, chemical and biological functions) and CA systems to function with some direct benefits:

  • Protects the soil surface from erosion;
  • Improves and stabilizes the soil structure;
  • Improves and stabilizes the soil nutrient reserves;
  • Increases resilience to drought.

2.3.1 Protects the soil surface from erosion

A thick permanent mulch on the soil surface effectively reduces soil erosion from the mechanical effect of heavy tropical rainfall and strong wind (during the dry season).

Figure 9. Demonstrating the mechanical effect of a mulch in reducing erosion. The demonstration requires two plastic trays, one water gallon split in half, one sack of soil, dried grasses and two 10 liters water cans

©Patrick Niemeyer/FAO

2.3.2 Improves and stabilizes the soil structure

The permanent mulch facilitates organisms' activities, and soil organisms contribute to stable soil structure. The results are porous and structurally stable soils. Costly land tillage operations (e.g., ploughing) are unnecessary to improve soil structure just before planting. Soil organisms such as earthworms and other animals are already doing the job.

Figure 10. Field observation of topsoil biotic activity, structure and porosity under a mulch (Baucau, Quelicai, January 19).

©Ruben Urdin/FAO

2.3.3 Improves and stabilizes the soil nutrient reserves

The growing of a mulch and the restitution of the crop residues (unburned) recycles the nutrients and makes them available to the next crop through biotic activity that decomposes the organic matter.

Readily available nutrients are protected from leaching by organic matter.

The 'clay humus complex' stores these minerals. As the soil humus content increases, the soil nutrient warehouse fills and expands.

Under a permanent mulch grown on CA land, the soil' BIOLOGICAL PUMP', active in a natural environment, is re-established.

Nutrients from deep soil layers are captured by the cover crop and pumped to the surface into the plants' biomass. The decomposition of the biomass returns these nutrients to the next crop.

Figure 11. Illustration of the biological pump at work with a high biomass producing cover crop (Velvet beans -lehe). Plant nutrients are pumps from lower layers of the soil and returned to the topsoil through the mulch.

When legumes are grown as a cover crop (e.g., Velvet beans, locally known as lehe), the system benefits from the legume's capacity to fix nitrogen from the air through the legume's nodules.

2.3.4 Increases resilience to drought

Figure 12. Mulch reduces evaporation and increases rainwater infiltration.

The presence of a permanent mulch dramatically increases rainwater infiltration and reduces evaporation.

More water is available to the crops. This is particularly important on sloping land.

All the positive benefits of a growing biomass crop end when the soil surface is bare and exposed to the elements. When the mulch is eaten by livestock, the cover crop's failure could be caused by a dry spell, the destruction of the mulch by uncontrolled fire, etc. Maintaining a permanent mulch is a significant challenge to farmers.

Whatever the circumstances, the mulch should be put back as soon as possible the following year to preserve the soil from degradation.

The growing of a high biomass cover crop also addresses one of the farmers' most difficult challenges - weeds.

Control weed pressure

The presence of a permanent mulch on the soil surface significantly reduces the weed pressure. With a permanent mulch, light does not reach the soil surface, which decreases the growth of weed seeds. Over time, the practice of CA reduces the weed seed stocks in the soil surface. Velvet beans (lehe) have demonstrated the capacity to clean the field from most weeds.

Important problems unaddressed

Given that half of Timor-Leste's territory has slopes of 40° or more, it is of utmost importance to identify high biomass producing cover crops that are adapted to these circumstances:

  • Farmers are encouraged to cultivate their staple crops in more fertile, flat land with a sustainable intensification of production. However, not all farmers have access to flat land;
  • in parallel, it is a priority to continue testing adapted cover crops for suitable landscapes and agroecological areas (Velvet beans - lehe - does not perform well on sloping land).
Key challenges are
  • the production of sufficient biomass in dryer parts of the country; and
  • cover crops should be tested in the low elevation areas in the northern part of the country.
For attention

The soil is a living organism that has fauna and micro-flora. Sustainable farming practices should aim at protecting them. And CA reconstitutes the original natural environment in which soils are created.

  • In nature, mulch covers topsoil.
  • The mulch provides the foods that prompt soil biotic activity. Soil living organisms are fundamental for soil fertility -the 'clay-humus complex.'
  • The humus makes nutrients readily available to plants and gives the soil its structure and porosity.
  • It a natural process and no need for inputs - it free.
  • Burning kills these organisms, either directly by heat or indirectly by starving.
  • Ploughing and other land tillage technologies attempt to replace the structuring work that soil fauna sustainably does but at very high energy and financial cost.

3. Validation of the practice

This was tested by farmers Timor-Leste in the soils of the slopes.

4. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Attention must be taken to keep the soil covered with crops, mulch. And  following the three CA principles: A.' No-burning'; B. 'No-ploughing' and C.‘Growing a cover crop'.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Conservation Agriculture (CA) model in Timor-Leste: ID 10092.
  • Dzud early warning system in Mongolia: ID 10091.
  • A step-by-step approach toward a gradual adoption of the full conservation agriculture technology: an example from Timor-Leste: ID 10093.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

This practice contributes to labour-saving because CA practices make the labour for men easier, requires less hour of labour, and saves money to invest in other household chores.

7.2 Women-friendly

The CA practices require much less labor and it is simple to apply. It does not require additional inputs making it sustainable.

7.3 Resource use efficiency

It uses the soils more efficiently, contributing to better cropping and soil improvement, contributing to water retention.

7.4 Pro-poor technology

Using this practice reduces the costs of labor that can be applied in other chores.

entries.summary: A utilização de Adubos Verdes bem como o uso de Plantas de Cobertura do Solo, vem ganhando cada vez mais espaço na ‘Nova Agricultura’. Agricultura essa que tem como objetivo não apenas a produção de produtos agrícolas, mas também leva em conta a ‘saúde’ do solo, bem como a conservação e preservação da biodiversidade dos agrossistemas. Diversos benefícios podem ser listados pela associação dessas duas práticas na produção agrícola. No entanto, um dos principais diz respeito à acumulação de matéria orgânica ao longo dos ciclos de produção, que proporciona diversos benefícios ao solo.
entries.description:
Description

Os Agrossistemas tradicionais têm dado espaço a novos sistemas de produção, onde a conservação do solo, a diversificação de culturas, a reciclagem de nutrientes e o uso sistemático de adubos orgânicos, desempenham um papel importante no equilíbrio entre a produtividade destes sistemas e a conservação do meio ambiente[1]. 

A utilização de plantas de cobertura permite:

  • obter ganhos económicos e ambientais;
  • diminuir a utilização de adubos químicos;
  • reduzir e/ou eliminar as aplicações de herbicidas nas culturas principais[2];
  • reduzir, com o tempo, o banco de sementes das espécies indesejadas (ervas daninhas)[3];
  • combater a erosão dos solos[4], [5]. 

Na adubação verde são utilizadas plantas que normalmente fornecem:

  • uma boa produção de biomassa;
  • uma ótima proteção da estrutura do solo;
  • nutrientes às culturas,

e conservam os recursos hídricos para as culturas de interesse agrícola [6].

A utilização de plantas para cobertura parcial ou permanente do solo, consiste numa associação com as culturas principais. No fim da cultura, as plantas, com auxílio do “rolo faca” são acamadas sobre a superfície ou incorporadas levemente no solo [7].

O objetivo desta técnica consiste em:

  • proteger a camada superficial do solo;
  • favorecer a manutenção e melhoria das condições físicas, químicas e biológicas do solo [8], [9].

As leguminosas (Fabaceae) como plantas de cobertura, para além do aumento da produtividade das culturas, actuam como:

  • protectoras do solo;
  • fixam o azoto (N2) atmosférico;
  • apresentam ainda uma baixa relação carbono - azoto (C/N), pois decompõem-se mais rapidamente;
  • disponibilizam o azoto aos microrganismos decompositores [10], [11];
  • aumentam o teor de matéria orgânica disponível nos solos, melhorando a fertilidade e diminuindo a erosão.

O sistema radicular pivotante das leguminosas permite:

  • alcançar grandes profundidades;
  • melhorar a absorção de água e a extração de nutrientes minerais das camadas mais profundas do solo;
  • reciclar e melhor gerir os nutrientes [12].

As leguminosas, quando roçadas/cortadas promovem uma boa cobertura morta, pois quando comparadas com as gramíneas são mais ricas em azoto (N), fósforo (P), potássio (K) e cálcio (Ca) [13]. As leguminosas apresentam de maneira geral, uma matéria seca composta por:

  • 1,6 a 3,9% de N;
  • 0,2 a 0,6% de P;
  • 0,5 a 2,5% de K;
  • 0,2 a 2,6% de Ca; e
  • 0,2 a 1,4% de Mg [14], [15].

A utilização de gramíneas (Poaceae) como cobertura vegetal tem como principais vantagens:

  • uma elevada produção de biomassa;
  • uma maior longevidade sobre o solo, devido a sua elevada relação C/N;
  • uma excelente cobertura morta;
  • uma descompactação do solo, devido ao seu intenso sistema radicular.

As gramíneas naturais contêm na matéria seca:

  • 0,8 a 1,2% de N;
  • 0,1 a 0,2% de P;
  • 0,7 a 1,36% de K;
  • 0,4 a 0,5% de Ca; e
  • 0,2% de Mg [12].

1. Utilização de coberturas verde em culturas perenes

1.1 Na vinha 

A utilização de plantas de cobertura nas explorações vitícolas diminui:

  • o vigor da videira;
  • o teor de azoto no pecíolo; e
  • a massa seca de poda.

A utilização da gramínea (Crotalaria juncea) e da leguminosa (Feijão-de-porco, Canavalia ensiformis), em vinha não tem o efeito da adubação verde sobre a produtividade e qualidade da uva, mas como plantas de cobertura, proporcionaram melhorias nas características químicas do solo, favorecendo um aumento nos teores de matéria orgânica, Ca de troca e na Capacidade de Troca Catiónica do solo (CTC) [16].

A substituição da gramínea (Urochloa decumbens) em vinha (Cv. Niágara Rosada), no outono-inverno pelos adubos verdes compostos de aveia preta (Avena strigosa), chícharo (Lathyrus sativus) ou tremoço branco (Lupinus albus), seguidos de mucuna anã (Mucuna pruriens), na primavera-verão, não prejudicaram a produtividade da cultura [17].

Também a utilização em consociação de espécies de ciclo anual ou perenes em vinha aumentou tanto o vigor como a produtividade da cultura, mas quando utilizada festuca (Festuca arundinaceae) uma espécie perene, esta diminuiu o vigor das videiras, mas melhorou a qualidade das uvas [18].

1.2 Associadas a fruteiras, bananeiras, mamão

A utilização de plantas leguminosas de cobertura, em espécies frutícolas, favorece um aumento de produtividade e da proporção de cachos colhidos, e reduz o tempo de maturação, como no caso da bananeira [11].

A utilização de leguminosas em vez de vegetação espontânea na cultura do mamão proporcionou benefícios ao nível do solo, como as melhorias físico-químicas e microbiológicas, o aumento da capacidade de armazenamento de água e da produtividade da cultura [19].

2. Plantas de cobertura do solo

As plantas de cobertura são espécies utilizadas, com o intuito de:

  • reciclar nutrientes do solo e de fixar o azoto atmosférico;
  • cobrir o solo;
  • conservar a água no solo;
  • diminuir a competição de plantas indesejadas;
  • impedir processos de erosão do solo.

As coberturas vegetais são constituídas por misturas de espécies, que incluem sobretudo as leguminosas e gramíneas:

  • Dactylis glomerata.
  • Festuca arundinacea.
  • Festuca rubra.
  • Lolium multiflorum.
  • Lolium perenne.
  • Lolium rigidum subsp. rigidum.
  • Lotus ornithopodioides.
  • Lupinus angustifolius.
  • Lupinus luteus.
  • Melilotus segetalis.
  • Melilotus albus.
  • Melilotus elegans.
  • Ornithopus compressus.
  • Ornithopus sativus.
  • Oxalis corniculata.
  • Oxalis pes-caprae.
  • Trifolium angustifolium.
  • Trifolium bocconei.
  • Trifolium incarnatum.
  • Trifolium isthmocarpum.
  • Trifolium resupinatum ssp. resupinatum.
  • Trifolium subterraneum ssp. subterraneum.

3. Plantas de cobertura e Matéria Orgânica do Solo

A utilização de plantas de cobertura, como estratégia para melhoria da qualidade ambiental e da sustentabilidade dos Agrossistemas consiste numa melhor cobertura do solo, que leva ao aumento da matéria orgânica e favorece a ciclagem de nutrientes, minimizando assim os efeitos nocivos da monocultura [20]. Nesta estratégia, a decomposição das plantas de cobertura e a dinâmica de libertação de nutrientes são factores determinantes [21] na gestão da fertilidade do solo, permitindo técnicas de cultivo que optimizem o uso dos diversos nutrientes presentes nos resíduos vegetais [22].

As coberturas do solo permitem restituir nutrientes para as culturas principais, absorvendo-os nas camadas mais superficiais e incorporando-os a níveis mais profundos [23]. Esta restituição depende da velocidade da decomposição das espécies utilizadas, a qual depende dos teores de nutrientes e/ou compostos fenólicos, sendo favorecida pelos baixos teores destas substâncias e pelos elevados conteúdos de materiais solúveis e de azoto [24]. A temperatura, humidade, época do ano e os organismos decompositores, também influenciam a velocidade da decomposição [25]. A taxa de decomposição dos resíduos das culturas, ou seja, o tempo de permanência de cada material vegetal sobre a superfície do solo é fundamental para definir o tipo e a composição da cobertura [26]. Esta taxa é regulada especialmente pela relação C/N. A redução do uso de fertilizantes químicos pode ser conseguida a médio prazo, quando a biomassa das coberturas vegetais apresenta uma elevada relação C/N, e ainda uma libertação lenta dos nutrientes. Neste contexto, a composição das coberturas vegetais pode ser determinante para conseguir o equilíbrio ideal entre a matéria orgânica incorporada e a libertação de nutrientes.

A utilização de plantas de cobertura representa também um considerável sequestro de carbono atmosférico diretamente no solo sob a forma de Matéria Orgânica do Solo (MOS). A MOS é toda substância decomposta proveniente de plantas, microrganismos, mesorganismos como da macrofauna morta, ou excrementos de animais [27]. A MOS é composta essencialmente por Carbono (C), Hidrogénio (H), Oxigénio (O), Azoto (N), Enxofre (S) e Fósforo (P) [28]. A MOS intervém ao nível da estabilidade dos agregados do solo, infiltração e retenção de água, resistência à erosão, disponibilidade de nutrientes para as plantas, capacidade de troca catiónica (CTC), actividade biológica, libertação de dióxido de carbono (CO2) e outros gases para a atmosfera [29]. O aumento do carbono fixado na MOS pode ser favorecido pelas técnicas ou sistemas de cultivo, desde que a biomassa das culturas de cobertura, seja deixada no campo após a colheita [26, 30].   

As leguminosas apresentam maior velocidade de decomposição e libertação de nutrientes, mostrando assim um grande potencial como fonte rápida de nutrientes, através incorporação dos seus resíduos no solo. Por sua vez, as gramíneas de maneira geral apresentam uma velocidade de decomposição e libertação de nutrientes mais lenta, mostrando potencial como fonte lenta de incorporação de matéria orgânica e nutrientes no solo.

4. Coberturas vegetais e a gestão do solo

A gestão e manutenção da superfície do solo condiciona a intensidade dos processos de adição e/ou perda de MOS e nutrientes nos agroecossistemas. A gestão convencional à base de mobilizações frequentes, tem um balanço negativo, pois as perdas ultrapassam os ganhos, levando à progressiva degradação da qualidade do solo. O sistema tradicional manutenção da superfície dos solos afecta a sua estrutura, modificando o arranjo dos agregados e a alteração da porosidade, tendo como principal consequência a sua compactação. [31]. A mobilização mínima do solo, associada à utilização de coberturas vegetais permite minimizar tais efeitos negativos, favorecendo ao mesmo tempo a diversidade de organismos edáficos, como insectos e microrganismos, agentes importantes na fragmentação e incorporação do material orgânico no solo [32]. As práticas culturais tradicionais, como as mobilizações frequentes, a passagem das máquinas, as adubações e a utilização de pesticidas, têm efeito imediato sobre os organismos presentes no agroecossistema. Por outro lado, a utilização de plantas de cobertura nas entrelinhas minimiza a necessidade de mobilização do solo, contribui para a redução da  perda progressiva de MOS e nutrientes e incrementa a produtividade e a diversidade dos organismos do solo.

5. Exemplo de coberturas de plantas em vinha na Quinta dos Aciprestes

A utilização de plantas de cobertura para quantificar a produção de biomassa e o tempo de degradação do material vegetal foi realizado na Região Demarcada do Douro, numa parcela de vinha adulta da Cv. ‘Touriga Franca’ na Quinta dos Aciprestes, na localidade de São João da Pesqueira (Figura 1).

Figura 1. Aspecto da Quinta dos Aciprestes, São João da Pesqueira, Portugal.

©Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

5.1 Preparação das coberturas vegetais do solo

No presente trabalho testaram-se cinco misturas de sementes na cobertura de solo, para identificar a mais adequada e eficiente para esta vinha com solos franco-arenosos. O delineamento estatístico foi em Blocos Casualizados, com 5 tratamentos e 4 blocos (Figura 2). As sementeiras foram realizadas no Outono de 2016. O procedimento utilizado foi o seguinte:

Preparação do terreno:

  • A preparação do terreno foi feita com a grade de discos acoplada a um trator de pequeno porte, para abrir os sulcos onde foram colocadas as sementes. A sementeira foi feita a lanço seguindo as orientações da Figura 2. Após a sementeira, o trator passou novamente no terreno com um rolo de ferro (alfaia) no lugar da grade de disco, apenas para cobrir as sementes. Os tratamentos utilizados no estudo foram:
Tabela 1. Caracterização das modalidades em estudo
Tratamentos Quantidade (kg) Profundidade (cm) Espécies
T1 20 0,5-1
  • Dactylis glomerata.
  • Festuca rubra.
  • Lolium multiflorum ssp. westerwoldicum.
  • Lolium perenne.
  • Ornithopus sativus.
  • Trifolium incarnatum.
  • Trifolium isthmocarpum.
  • Trifolium michelianum.
  • Trifolium resupinatum ssp. resupinatum.
  • Trifolium subterraneum ssp. subterraneum.
T2 20 05-1
  • Ornithopus sativus.
  • Trifolium incarnatum.
  • Trifolium isthmocarpum.
  • Trifolium michelianum.
  • Trifolium resupinatum ssp. resupinatum.
  • Trifolium subterraneum ssp. subterraneum.
T3 5 0,5-1
  • Ornithopus compressus.
  • Biserula pelecinus.
  • Trifolium subterraneum ssp. subterraneum.
  • Trifolium subterraneum ssp. yaninicum.
  • Trifolium cherleri.
T4 5 0,5-1
  • Trifolium subterraneum ssp. subterraneum.
  • Trifolium subterraneum ssp. yaninicum.
  • Trifolium cherleri.
  • Trifolium isthmocarpum.
  • Trifolium glomeratum.
 

Fonte: ISOPlexis Centre, University of Madeira

Figura 2. Croqui do ensaio de plantas de cobertura, utilizando misturas de leguminosas, na Quinta dos Aciprestes.

© Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

As coberturas foram mantidas às condições ambientais que se verificaram na exploração e sem qualquer tipo de intervenção.

Os solos da exploração e da Região caracterizam-se por possuir baixo teor de matéria orgânica (1,10%) e uma elevada inclinação (entre 30 a 45%) (Figuras 3 e 4).

Nas primaveras de 2017 e 2018 procedeu-se a quantificação das coberturas:

  • Avaliou-se a produção de matérias fresca e seca.

Para quantificar a produção utilizou-se um aro quadrado de metal com dimensões de 0,21 x 0,21 cm.

  • Fizeram-se quantificações aleatórias.
    • lançando o quadrado ao acaso em cima de cada um dos tratamentos, o material que ficasse contido dentro do quadrado era cortado e armazenado em sacos de papel, sendo pesado para obtenção do peso fresco;
    • após essa pesagem o material foi levado a estufa à 65ºC durante 24 horas, e a seguir esse material foi pesado novamente obtendo assim o peso seco das amostras.
Figura 3. Inclinação (30 a 45%) das áreas de cobertura na vinha.

© Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

Figura 4. Tipos de solos característicos na área: Franco arenoso.

© Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

Ao longo do ensaio avaliou-se a evolução da degradação do material de cobertura. Para tal, foram colocados em litterbags, 50 g de cada uma das modalidades em estudo e deixados no campo para que o mesmo sofresse degradação. A evolução da degradação foi avaliada em cinco (5) momentos distintos, sendo o primeiro no início do ensaio, e os restantes 44, 90, 169 e 247 dias após.

5.2 Evolução do Desenvolvimento das Coberturas

Um bom crescimento das diferentes coberturas (T1-T5) foi observado, em todas as parcelas (Figuras 5 a 9), durante 2017. Com o desenvolvimento do material vegetal, é esperado que o mesmo proporcione grandes benefícios à vinha, de maneira especial no controlo dos processos erosivos, durante as chuvas, tendo em conta o grande declive do terreno e à baixa quantidade de matéria orgânica nos solos da área de estudo.

Figura 5. Desenvolvimento das coberturas 16/01/2017.

© Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

Figura 6. Desenvolvimento das coberturas 23/03/2017.

© Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

Figura 7. Desenvolvimento das coberturas 31/05/2017.

© Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

Figura 8. Desenvolvimento das coberturas 17/07/2017.

© Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

Figura 9. Desenvolvimento das coberturas 17/11/2017.

© Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

Figura 10. Variação da produção de biomassa pelas coberturas, em matéria fresca e seca.

© Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

No que respeita a produção de matéria fresca e seca, verificou-se-se que as coberturas apresentaram nos dois anos de avaliação um padrão semelhante, apresentando as seguintes características:

  • T1 e T4 apresentaram os maiores valores de matéria fresca no 1º e 2º anos de cobertura;
  • biomassa produzida praticamente duplicou no 2º ano de ensaio;
  • T2 e T3 apresentaram valores muito similares entre si, em ambos anos do ensaio;
  • T5, com a vegetação espontânea apresentou os valores inferiores de biomassa (Figura 10);
  • estatisticamente não se observaram diferenças significativas, entre os 2 anos em avaliação, ao nível de 5% de probabilidade.

Para determinar o tempo de permanência do material vegetal na superfície do solo, e o tempo que os nutrientes levam a ficarem disponíveis para cultura principal, usaram-se litterbags (sacos de plástico). Este método permite avaliar o tempo de degradação da biomassa de cada espécie (Figura 11). 

Figura 11. Avaliação do tempo de degradação das espécies (material vegetal), com a utilização de litterbags no campo.

© Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

Evolução da degradação do material vegetal:

A evolução da degradação do material vegetal, seguiu um padrão idêntico para todas as modalidades (Figura 12). No entanto, verificaram-se algumas diferenças entre elas

  • inicialmente todas apresentaram o mesmo comportamento na degradação do material vegetal pelos fatores bióticos e abióticos (Figura 12);
  • a cobertura T2 apresentou uma degradação mais rápida, ao fim de 44 dias, chegando aos 60% ao fim de 247 dias;
  • T4 apresenta a maior taxa de degradação de cobertura, chegando aos 80% ao fim de 247 dias;
  • as coberturas T5 e T1, são aparentemente semelhantes, a longo tempo T5 apresentou maior taxa de degradação que T1.

  • Estatisticamente observou-se que diferenças significativas, ao nível de 5% de probabilidade. Em que o tratamento T4 foi aquele que obteve a maior taxa de degradação do material ao longo do tempo e o tratamento T3 apresentou a menor taxa de degradação do material ao longo do tempo.
Figura 12. Percentagem de degradação das espécies ao longo do tempo.

© Fabrício Lopes de Macedo

6. Conclusões

Os resultados das coberturas foram:

  • T1 e T4 apresentaram as maiores quantidades de matéria seca;
  • T4 registrou a maior taxa de degradação de material vegetal;
  • T3 registrou a menor taxa de degradação de material vegetal.

Os resultados obtidos fornecem fortes evidências no sentido das vantagens de utilização de culturas de cobertura para as condições climáticas do Alto Douro. Estes resultados vão no sentido da recomendação para a utilização de cobertura T1, porque:

  • apresentou uma quantidade superior de matéria fresca e seca em comparação aos demais tratamentos;
  • o processo de degradação do material vegetal foi lento, ficando logo atrás do tratamento T3;
  • permitiu uma melhor cobertura do solo-mulching.

Para além das vantagens quantificadas neste trabalho, as culturas de cobertura permitem também manter maiores teores de humidade do solo, para além de facilitarem maior disponibilidade de nutrientes para a vinha.

7. Agradecimentos

Este trabalho foi financiado pelo Projeto INNOVINE&WINE (NORTE-01-0145-FEDER-000038), cofinanciado pelo Fundo Europeu de Desenvolvimento Regional (FEDER) através do programa NORTE 2020. Agradecemos à empresa Real Companhia Velha por todas as facilidades que nos foram proporcionadas durante a realização dos trabalhos de campo.

Esta pratica foi produzida em colaboração e com a contribuição do Dr. Fabrício Lopes de Macedo e Professore Miguel Carvalho da Universidade da Madeira e Isoplexis. Se agradeçe a revisão tecnica do documento pelo Professor Raúl Rodrigues, Escola Superior Agrária do Instituto Politécnico de Viana do Castelo, Portugal.

8. Validação da prática agrícola 

Esta pratica foi testada na região do Alto Douro, Portugal. Foi executada na primavera, em um area de vinha adulta com solos franco-arenosos com inclinação de 30 a 45%.

9. Requisitos mínimos para a implementação bem-sucedida da tecnologia

Os requesítos minimos a ter presente para implementação desta practica: ter solos pobres em matéria organica.

A considerar para preparação do terreno:

  • um trator de pequeno porte:
    • com uma grade aradora para abrir os sulcos onde semear as sementes.
    • barra de ferro no lugar da grade aradora, apenas para cobrir as sementes.
  • semenetira feita a lanço.

10. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Temperado, lega.
  • Subtropicais, quente/moderado fresco.

11. Tecnologias associadas ou relacionadas

  • Espécies de cobertura vegetal, com especial incidência nas leguminosas: ID 2414.
  • Agricultura sempre verde (Evergreen agriculture): agricultura de conservação na produção de milho: ID 2846.
  • Crop planning and management in organic agriculture: ID 8367.

12. Objetivos cumpridos pelo projeto

12.1 Eficiência no uso de recursos

Esta pratica aumenta a materia organica no solo, contribui para uma melhor qualidade do solo, melhor resultados na produção, e menor use de produtos quimicos. Mais sustentável.

entries.title: Home-grown school feeding as a "game changer" - Understanding the benefits of connecting school feeding programmes with local smallholders farmers
entries.source: Food and Nutrition Division (ESN) - FAO
multi_source: Food and Nutrition Division (ESN) - FAO#Division de l’alimentation et de la nutrition (ESN) - FAO#División de Alimentación y Nutrición (ESN) - FAO#Food and Nutrition Division (ESN) - FAO
entries.summary: This practice explains and clarifies the benefits of home-grown school feeding. It describes its concept, implementation models, benefits and application for adoption and scaling up, increasing food security and nutrition of schoolchildren and improving smallholder farmers and their communities' livelihoods. Read also Home-grown school feeding as a "game changer" - Planning, designing and implementing school feeding programmes connected with local smallholders farmer.
entries.description:
Description

1. Concept: From school feeding to home-grown school feeding

1.1 Enhanced food security and nutrition of schoolchildren and their communities

Problems of food insecurity, undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, overweight and obesity increasingly coexist in all regions of the world, affecting people at all stages of life. This is where school feeding programmes have an essential role in the fight against hunger and malnutrition in all its forms.

School feeding programmes have the potential to directly improve school children's food consumption, food diversity, and nutrition status by granting access to nutritious foods and providing the nutrients that are often missing from children's diets.

These school feeding programmes could offer multifunction opportunities. Besides providing consistent food and nutrition education, they could provide an opportunity to address childhood overweight and obesity. They can help promote life-long and intergenerational healthy eating habits.

When linked with the local and smallholder agriculture production (i.e. the Home-grown school feeding approach), these programmes can result not only in educational and food security gains for children but also in livelihood gains for smallholder farmers and local communities.

Home-grown school feeding (HGSF) programmes offer the opportunity to enhance food security and nutrition benefits for schoolchildren, smallholders and other actors who sell food to these programmes, and their households by:

  • increasing and diversifying food production and consumption;
  • strengthening connection among nutrition, agriculture and social protection;
  • providing a secure market for local smallholder farmers and SMES through local procurement for schools.

Home-grown school feeding can be considered as a "game-changer" – that is a catalyst for driving the change in food systems needed for sustainable development while also supporting children's nutrition and food security needs now and into the future.

1.2 Definition of home-grown school feeding (HGSF) programme

  • HGSF constitutes a school feeding model that is designed to provide children in schools with safe, diverse and nutritious food, partially sourced locally from smallholders. 

This term is used in practice to represent a holistic and multi-component approach to school feeding programmes. Although various definitions of "HGSF" and multi-component school feeding programmes co-exist several key actors adopted this definition in order to harmonize the different concepts and establish a common understanding among actors and policymakers. These key actors are the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP), the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the Global Child Nutrition Foundation (GCNF), the Partnership for Child Development (PCD), the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), NEPAD and the WFP Centre of Excellence in Brazil. Beside agreeing on the definition, they jointly produced a resource framework on the topic as well as an e-learning course, both available on FAO website in English, French and Spanish.

1.3 The core elements of the HGSF concept

  1. Food is partially sourced locally from smallholders, meaning that HGSF:
    • maximize benefits for smallholder farmers by linking schools to local food production;
    • strengthen the capacities of smallholder farmers and communities to produce food;
    • contribute to rural transformation.
  2. The HGSF programmes provide Safe, diverse and nutritious food:
    • promotes the design and adoption of quality and safety standards for fresh and local foods;
    • support crop and dietary diversification;
    • integrate food and nutrition education to promote behavioral change; and
    • support healthy and culturally appropriate eating habits.
  • A programme can be considered as "home-grown" provided that procurement is designed to support and foster local food markets.
  • There is no minimum quantity that must be met.
  • Independently of the percentage of food procured from local smallholder farmers, the programme can be considered "home-grown".
  • It is recommended that this objective should be considered during programme design and implementation and institutionalized in related policies and regulations.

1.4 Beneficiaries and benefits of home-grown school feeding

  • School feeding programmes normally pursue educational, social protection and nutrition goals, or a combination of these.
  • HGSF programmes also generate additional benefits, not only for schoolchildren and their households, but also for the farmers who provide the food, for local communities and for other stakeholders.
  • Figure 1 shows the benefits of HGSF (in yellow) compared with traditional school feeding programmes.
  • The potential benefits that HGSF can generate are maximized when programmes are designed as multisector interventions that are integrated into broader national strategies and systems.
  • HGSF programmes have good potential to be part of a comprehensive package of interventions aimed at addressing multiple needs identified by governments.
    • They can also be integrated into social protection strategies for fighting poverty, hunger and malnutrition.
    • Governments are therefore increasingly investing in HGSF programmes as a strategy for accelerating development by combining benefits in education, health, nutrition, agriculture and trade, social and economic development and intergenerational well-being.
Figure 1. Beneficiaries and potential benefits of school feeding and HGSF

©FAO & WFP. 2018.

  • HGSF has positive multiplier effects and its costs should be seen as investments rather than expenses.
  • HGSF have positive multiplier effects for additional beneficiaries such as:
    • small farmers, traders, small and medium enterprises; and
    • other actors along the value chain.
  • The more local these actors are, the more they will spend the additional income in the local economy, increasing business for other providers of goods and services.
  • In addition, as they increase their businesses, they generate spin-off benefits such as:
    • increased turnover and profits for other actors such as traders and transporters; and
    • possibly increased employment and income for additional workers.
  • Investments in infrastructure to implement HGSF and to increase local production and processing capacities benefit the wider community.
    • These benefits, combined, contribute to economic development, political stability and a sustainable tax base.
    • This is another argument for viewing the costs of HGSF as investments rather than expenses.
  • A way to measure these indirect impacts is the LEWIE methodology (Local Economy-Wide Impact Evaluation) developed by University of Davis. This methodology allows to:
    • quantify the full impact of projects such as HGSF on local economies;
    • quantify the impacts on businesses and households that are not directly affected by the project.
  • When an HGSF programme purchases products from businesses owned and operated locally, it helps to infuse money into the local economy.
    • It produces multiplier effects: the local producer and employees spend the money on goods and services provided by other local producers, thus creating more income, production and employment.

1.5 The real strength of the HGSF - Combination of benefits for many groups and sectors

The HGSF programmes can benefit multistakeholders across different sectors. It is the combination of many benefits from the same programme that constitutes the real strength of HGSF. By combining different benefits, HGSF programmes can achieve very high cost-effectiveness and costs-benefits ratios. The marginal costs of achieving additional benefits are comparatively low compared to pursuing these benefits through specific, individual interventions.

The combined benefits of HGSF can be promoted by developing a programme, applying a process and establishing coordination mechanisms that bring out the multisector character of HGSF and in which each sector contributes to and benefits from the programme.

  • The education sector provides a channel for and the infrastructure in which an HGSF programme can function.
    • It also provides the curricula, teachers and institutional structure required for children's effective learning.
    • In return, an HGSF helps children to gain access to, participate in and benefit from schooling.
  • The health and nutrition sector provides important complementary services, including health and nutrition monitoring of children, vaccinations and deworming.
    • In return, an HGSF programme can improve the nutrition of schoolchildren and their families and this way improve the overall health situation of the community.
  • Agriculture and trade sectors can provide supply-side support in helping farmers and small local entrepreneurs to engage in formal markets and to provide goods and services with adequate quantity and quality.
    • In return, an HGSF programme can provide the stable demand that such players may need to invest, reduce risks and obtain better access to markets.
  • Social and economic development programmes can provide households with the livelihood support to let their children participate in school.
    • In return, an HGSF programme provides livelihood opportunities through demand and payment for services.
  • The private sector – farmers, processors, organizations, traders, etc. – provides increased quantities and more diverse, safe and good-quality food.
    • In return, an HGSF programme provides a stable market and increased business opportunities, with multiplier benefits for the entire local economy.
    • Being explicit about such potential benefits can help mobilize multisector and sustainable political support and participation and leverage increased investments from other sectors.

To understand further the follow-up actions and activities on the planning, design and implementing school feeding programmes connected with smallholder farmers, see the following practice, Home-grown school feeding as a "game changer" - Planning, designing and implementing school feeding programmes connected with local smallholders farmer.

2. Validation of the practice

This programme is implemented in many countries in Latin America (particularly in Brazil) and Africa.

3. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

For HGSF, the most important aspect is the present and potential local food production of smallholder farmers, since the design of menus (composition and quantities) which should be oriented towards the kind of food and the quantities local farmers can actually supply now and in the medium term. Also other aspects such as markets and aggregation systems are important to understand for the selection of the most conducive operating model for an HGSF programme.

4. Related/associated technologies 

  • Home-grown school feeding as a "game changer" - Planning, designing and implementing school feeding programmes connected with local smallholders farmer: ID 10096.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency 

The home-grown school feeding has many positive impacts on different sectors and actors, making it a resource-efficient technology.

5.2 Women-friendly

HGSF contributes to the empowerment of women in agriculture and food production. 

5.3 Pro-poor technology 

This practice leads to a stabilisation of the market for local farmers and increased business opportunities.
