multi_source: Food and Nutrition Division (ESN) - FAO#Division de l’alimentation et de la nutrition (ESN) - FAO#División de Alimentación y Nutrición (ESN) - FAO#Food and Nutrition Division (ESN) - FAO
entries.summary:
This practice explains and clarifies the planning process for home-grown school feeding (HGSF) including the needs assessment. In addition, it provides guidance on the design and implementation of HGSF programmes. It clarifies: 

  • the objectives of the programme;
  • the menus it provides;
  • how it ensures food safety and quality;
  • how it links smallholder farmers (and other value chain actors) to schools;
  • how it addresses gender issues and risks;
  • how it maximizes benefits through synergies with other programmes; and
  • how an enabling environment for a sustainable programme is built.

This is the follow up processes to the Home-grown school feeding as a "game changer" - Understanding the benefits of connecting school feeding programmes with local smallholders farmers.
entries.description:
Description

1. Planning for home-grown school feeding

Planning and designing an HGSF programme should take place on the basis of two main building blocks:

  • a long-term vision and political commitment – defining the broad and long-term changes that the stakeholders, and in particular the government, want to achieve with HGSF;
  • adequate and precise context analysis and assessments – exploring the needs that can be addressed by HGSF in the country, and understanding the different existing environments and opportunities that can support the vision.

The context analysis should encompass three main aspects:

  • needs of the population that the programme could address;
  • existing opportunities in terms of local food production and systems that could be used by the programme;
  • existing implementation framework – this aspect should also include an assessment of the relevant existing policies and programmes that form the framework within which the programme will function.

To ensure the necessary support, ownership and ultimately the sustainability of the programme, all steps involved in the planning of an HGSF programme should ideally be carried out through a multistakeholder national dialogue. This involves different sectors of government at different levels, civil society, the private sector and communities in discussion and agreement on the overall vision for the programme, and the priority needs to be addressed, as well as the existing opportunities and capacities on which the programme can build.

1.1 Vision and political commitment

  • Vision and political commitment are essential to ensure that an HGSF programme can be developed and implemented to achieve the long-term change envisioned by the government.
  • Governments develop their vision and their political commitment for a certain programme on the basis of evidence of multiple, tangible benefits and the assurance that “it can be done”. They obtain this evidence by collecting and exchanging information and experience, including best practices, through different means.

1.2 Context analysis

  • A good understanding of the context is critical for the success and sustainability of any programme, but particularly for an HGSF programme because of its cross-sectoral nature.
  • This understanding helps to identify existing needs as well as the potential to establish or scale up an HGSF programme to reach a higher number of vulnerable beneficiaries, increasing the share of food being purchased locally and from smallholders, while recognizing associated risks.
  • A comprehensive context analysis helps establish or review the objectives and targeting of the HGSF programme.
  • It should be composed of:
    • a needs assessment of the vulnerable population in terms of food security and agriculture, education, nutrition, health, economic poverty, job creation, social cohesion and social protection;
    • a review of the existing food systems and potential food production by local agriculture and value chains involving smallholder farmers, which could contribute to and benefit from HGSF;
    • an assessment of the existing national capacities to make the programme function, involving a general assessment of the national capacities for the programme, as well as a series of more in-depth assessments, where these are necessary.
  • The context analysis phase can rely on primary and secondary data from relevant ministries, United Nations agencies and other stakeholders as well as research institutes.

1.3 Needs assessment

  • It is important to establish prevailing needs, with a focus on school-age children and adolescents, as well as on smallholders and other poor households potentially involved in the supply of school feeding programmes – in terms of poverty, social protection, job creation, food security, nutrition and health, and education. The assessment should consider:
    • trends (is the situation improving or becoming worse?) and seasonality (variations during the year);
    • gender and social inequalities – some groups may be particularly affected, such as pastoralists, specific ethnic groups, orphans, internally displaced people and refugees;
    • other vulnerability determinants; } regional disparities and rural development.
  • During the design phase, governments will have to decide which of these needs and potential policy gaps they wish to address by the programme (objectives), and how (menus, linking smallholders to schools, building an enabling environment).

1.4 Existing food systems and potential food production

  • While an HGSF programme can strengthen local food systems, it has to take their present state as its point of departure, and build on their potential for improvement.
  • For HGSF, the most important aspect is the present and potential local food production of smallholder farmers, since the design of menus (composition and quantities) which should be oriented towards the kind of food and the quantities local farmers can actually supply now and in the medium term.
  • Also other aspects such as markets and aggregation systems are important to understand for the selection of the most conducive operating model for an HGSF programme.
    • Aspects to be considered in this assessment are included in Table 1.
Table 1. Aspects that can be considered in a food system assessment
Food production
  • Identification of candidate crops, including relevant traditional and regionally adapted crops that are currently undervalued but suit both cultural habits and nutritional needs (local availability and nutritional properties).
  • Present smallholder production and food balance (by candidate crop), present cultivated area, average plot sizes, average yield.
  • Surplus areas, potential production capacity of smallholders in deficit areas.
  • Smallholder capacity to increase diversity and productivity.
  • Seasonality and availability of food, etc.
Food handling, storage and processing
  • Efficiency and effectiveness, including degree of post-harvest losses and potential food safety risks (e.g. contamination or spoilage).
  • Extent, capacity, state of and access to infrastructures (roads, aggregation points, warehouses, mills, primary processing units, etc.).
  • Nutritional value of traditionally consumed local foods and relevant existing food value chains in the country. } Food processing and fortification capacity.
Food trade and marketing
  • Capacity of farmers’ organizations, traders, transporters, processors, caterers, food safety and quality inspection services, packagers, etc., to service HGSF food needs.
  • Volume of food markets and any gaps.
  • Degree of integration of market systems with a view to the prices of school food basket items and alternative items on different markets, and food price fluctuations.
  • Food price information systems (existing, weak, none), in the whole country and by sub-region, related to school food basket items and alternative items.
  • Security situation across the year, and in relevant sub-regions of the country as relevant for sourcing and delivering school food (stable, unpredictable, etc.).

Consumer demand, food preparation and preferences

With regard to HGSF, the most important aspects in this domain concern:

  • Involvement of the school community in setting school menu preferences.
  • Capacity and feasibility of preparing safe and nutritious meals including, for example, food preparation facilities.
  • Whether nutritional value, food preparation requirements/habits, or other aspects of a dish make it more preferable for inclusion in a school menu than others.
  • Knowledge, attitudes and practices of the food service personnel, school staff, caregivers and schoolchildren regarding school food and its preparation.

Source: Food and Nutrition Division/FAO

1.5 Assessments of existing national capacities

  • An assessment of the implementation framework will, in most cases, be based on an assessment of an existing national school feeding programme.
  • This will help to understand existing strengths and weaknesses; the programme’s efficiency and operational capacity, and its alignment with the national context and goals; and, in particular, which structures, systems, tools and partnerships the HGSF programme could build on, and which areas need strengthening.

2. Design and implementation of HGSF

  • The planning steps and assessments described above lay the foundation for the design and implementation of an HGSF programme.
  • It may be useful to summarize – and formalize – the basic design features of the programme in an operational strategy. This clarifies:
    • the objectives of the programme;
    • the menus it provides;
    • how it ensures food safety and quality;
    • how it links smallholder farmers (and other value chain actors) to schools;
    • how it addresses gender issues and risks; how it maximizes benefits through synergies with other programmes;
    • and how an enabling environment for a sustainable programme is built.

The operational strategy translates the vision into a plan with a concrete set of actions aligned with national objectives and the programme’s goals. It should be directly based on the evidence obtained through the assessments realized. By examining the fundamental aspects of school feeding in a country, an operational strategy can determine to what extent the programme is:

  • responsive to the needs of the population;
  • feasible in terms of capacities and resources;
  • aligned with the policy directions and strategies of the government – in particular, the areas of education, social protection, health and nutrition, and agriculture;
  • implemented in an efficient way, with a realistic view of how to obtain adequate financial resources in the short and long term, and how to involve (and build) robust operational capacities.

The strategy may also include dynamic elements, for example starting with menus that can be provided immediately, while setting targets for more varied menus that will become possible once the programme has led to increased and more diverse production by local farmers.

The development of the operational strategy should be led from the start by one single task force or inter-ministerial committee representing the different ministries and other stakeholders involved in the programme, in order to warrant the continuity and national ownership of the approach, and mitigate risks related to staff turnover.

2.1 Linking smallholder farmers and processors to schools

The link between school feeding and local production is the defining element of HGSF. To ensure that a programme effectively makes this link, programme planners should establish:

  • the target group of smallholders that the programme wants to link to its market;
  • how institutional procurement ensures that this target group effectively participates in the HGSF market;
  • the operating model most conducive in the specific context to facilitating the link between HGSF and local production;
  • how reliable transport from smallholders to schools can be ensured;
  • the potential complementary (supply-side) support to be given to smallholders.

2.2 Target groups

  • Targeting smallholders is at the heart of HGSF.
  • However, the definitions of smallholders or family farmers vary considerably between countries.
  • Nevertheless, there is a set of criteria that is commonly used to define family farmers. These include:
    • area of cultivation;
    • household management;
    • income level.
  • A registration and certification system with specific requirements for the classification of smallholders, such as the family farm register adopted in Brazil, can be a good strategy to identify and operationalize inclusive policies for smallholders and guarantee their access to HGSF programmes.
  • At the outset, an HGSF programme should target smallholders already capable of supplying schools with surplus food production.
  • The sizeable and stable nature of the demand from HGSF programmes can stimulate smallholder farmers to invest in increasing, improving and diversifying their agricultural production, which brings about improved livelihoods and higher, steadier incomes.
  • The constant demand from schools creates a pathway to increased productivity, food security and income security.
    • For this reason, it is critical not to rely only on farmers that already produce regular surpluses, but also to include those with the potential for increased production.
    • Farmers who at present have limited capacity should be supported with targeted interventions (see section on supplementary support below) that unlock their potential.
  • An HGSF programme can establish additional targeting criteria among smallholder farmers to promote specific objectives by focusing, for example, on:
    • farmers producing food of particular interest to the programme, e.g. eggs or plant protein, orange-flesh sweet potatoes, leafy greens;
    • female farmers (see more details in section 3.5 on gender considerations);
    • farmers producing food from organic and agroecological systems to support forms of agricultural production that ensure environmental sustainability, while also providing healthy food that is free from pesticides.
    • In addition to farmers, HGSF can target other actors along the value chain, including local food processors, caterers and cooks.

2.3 Procurement

  • Public procurement is normally governed and specifically regulated by detailed national rules aiming to ensure the efficient use of public resources, guarantee the best value for public money, and ensure open competition and transparent procurement decisions.
  • Moreover, these rules should prevent fraud, waste, corruption and local protectionism in connection with public procurement of goods and services.
  • Public procurement rules often follow complex procedures, including specific requirements for tendering and decision-making.
  • These complex rules are some of the main barriers for smallholder farmers to access the market represented by school feeding programmes.
  • It is therefore crucial for HGSF to adhere to procurement rules that facilitate the participation of smallholder farmers and smallholders’ associations in the procurement process by reducing these barriers, while guaranteeing programme efficiency, thus ensuring a stable, affordable and timely supply of diverse, safe and quality food to schools through transparent and accountable procedures.

Possible interventions to achieve this facilitation include:

  • recognizing award criteria beyond the lowest price, i.e. allowing the procurement of food for a school meal programme based on a combination of factors, such as the price on the one hand, and social, economic and/ or environmental benefits on the other, with each category accorded a specific weight in the overall decision to award a contract;
  • adopting reservation, preference and/or indirect procurement strategies that enable, for instance, school food contracts (or a percentage of them) to be awarded only to smallholder producers.

In addition, an HGSF programme can promote the participation of smallholders through soft tenders and direct contracting. Lengthy public payment procedures also often exclude smallholders from participating in institutional food procurement. An HGSF programme could consider certain administrative adjustments to help reduce the time that smallholders have to wait for payment.

2.4 Operating models

  • The choice of operating model, i.e. how the programme is implemented, has a strong influence on whether a programme is able to achieve its objectives and maximize benefits in a cost-efficient way.
    • There is no model that fits all contexts.
    • Countries have developed their own models, based on their specific context and objectives, and different models may coexist even within one country.
    • In order to identify the most appropriate model, it is important to consider that each model has its advantages and trade-offs in terms of benefits for farmers, schools, children, quality of food, cost efficiency and cost effectiveness.
  • Operating models can be centralised or decentralised with many possible combinations and variations.
    • Procurement may be directly from farmers or their organisations, or through traders as intermediaries.
    • It is crucial that the operating model developed for an HGSF programme be adapted to the country context, taking into consideration a series of different factors, including the country’s size, prevailing economic and market structure, government structure, volume and type of food required, beneficiaries’ needs, and institutional procurement capacities.
  • In principle, decentralized models may be easier to adapt to local conditions and opportunities.
    • The higher the degree of decentralization, the greater the opportunities for local-to-local linkages, with spill-over effects for the rest of the local community.
    • Furthermore, a decentralized system facilitates the supply of fresh food, generally increasing the variety of food, and its compatibility with local habits and tastes.
  • By contrast, centralized processes may ensure greater standardization of procedures, facilitating monitoring and control which, in principle, should enable more stringent quality control.
    • On the other hand, centralized procurement of large quantities of food through a few contracts could increase interest in manipulating the procurement processes.
  • In the case of third party models, governments have a chance to support smallholder production, even if they do not purchase products directly from the smallholders.
    • Third party models mean that governments do not have to establish the capacity of food procurement, but instead focus on the role and capacity of managing contracts with specialized caterers, ensuring that they purchase efficiently and effectively from smallholder farmers in an inclusive way that benefits the farmers in terms of timely and fair payment and fair access.

2.5 Complementary support for smallholders

  • While all these measures are necessary, in many cases they may not be sufficient to enable smallholders to participate actively in an HGSF programme because of other underlying social, market, rural and agricultural development constraints, such as limited market information, limited liquidity, poor storage, limited processing and logistic infrastructure, and little access to technology and knowledge.
  • Such constraints are common for farmers in the global south, also because of a broader spectrum of family farmers in terms of human and economic development, labour productivity, agricultural surplus production, and marketing.
  • HGSF programmes should consider how best to link smallholders to complementary interventions that address such constraints, with a view to fostering mutually reinforcing elements of demand and supply-side support.
  • Such interventions should be designed and implemented under the leadership or coordination of the Ministry of Agriculture and other relevant stakeholders and actors.
  • Complementary support programmes can involve the entire value chain from food production to post-harvest handling, processing and marketing, including interventions aiming at improving infrastructure, productive assets and inputs (including access to land and water), services, technology and knowledge, financial services, and the business environment as a whole.

2.6 Gender

The contribution of women to agriculture and food production is highly significant. They are crucial actors in primary production along the food value chain and in the marketing of food products. However, in many parts of the world, women face specific constraints putting them at a disadvantage with men. Such constraints are mainly structural and grounded in unequal gender dynamics at household, community and market level. These constraints may often reinforce one another, creating a vicious circle of women’s subordination.

An HGSF programme can address the effect of women’s underprivileged position in several ways, for example by:

  • supporting the capacity of farmers’ organizations to mainstream gender or have gender quotas, ensuring that women actually benefit from their membership and have a voice in decision-making processes within the organization;
  • supporting gender-sensitive capacity development, such as training adapted to women’s needs by being conducted at times and in ways that are compatible with women’s typical chores;
  • increasing access to capital to invest in women’s productive activities (for inputs, technology and additional labour on their farms, etc.), preferably on a revolving fund basis.

Governments can also use HGSF to address specific structural constraints for the empowerment of women at local or national level, such as improving access to land, water and other farming inputs for women. In these cases, the HGSF programme should form part of an enhanced approach and wider effort, and include explicit goals for gender transformation.

3. Resume

The implementation or adoption of Home-Grown School Feeding (HGSF) programme must always consider the context where it will be applied. To support the uptake and scaling of this model, it is recommended to follow appropriate guidance materials such as the WFP-FAO Resource Framework and its related e-learning course. They were developed to facilitate and support the broader community of practice in HGSF for achieving impact at scale.

Depending on the context, it may require an organized approach to address some challenges, including:

  • how to develop a new HGSF programme and design its implementation in ways that allow scale-up;
  • how to bring a successful HGSF pilot programme to scale; and
  • how to optimize and sustain HGSF programmes that are already operating at scale.

In the long run, HGSF programmes:

  • help maximize the return on investment in education (if part of a more comprehensive education strategy);
  • contribute to reducing poverty;
  • promote child development through improved access to education and learning; and
  • enhanced nutrition and health, especially for girls and vulnerable children.

All these can create a sequence of beneficial impacts that contribute to breaking the cycle of poverty and hunger through:

  • better nutrition and education for the next generation
  • leading to improved employment opportunities;
  • increase incomes, dietary and health status throughout life.

Specific benefits can include the following:

  • Income effects from increased and diversified demand:
    • Ensuring a market for the sale of surplus production helps address income instability. It may encourage farmers to increase their investments, increase and/or diversify their production.
  • Stable demand:
    • With careful planning, the HGSF market can be consistent and predictable in the amounts and types of food and the timing of these needs to fit with growing seasons.
    • The more farmers understand the needs of school feeding and plan ahead to organize production that meets – but not dramatically exceeds – market demand, the more they will be willing to invest in labour, better tools and seeds.
  • Price stability:
    • The stable HGSF market may help reduce price instability.
    • It allows for better and longer-term planning and investments, particularly when programmes are implemented at scale and integrated into national strategies.
  • Farmer organizations:
    • Structured demand that tends to promote cooperatives or farmer associations, enhancing farmers' ability to connect with markets.
    • These associations can also provide, or act as channels for, training of farmers, monitoring, food safety and quality assurance, value addition, etc.
    • They can reduce farmers' dependence on, or strengthen their bargaining power with local traders.
    • Can reduce risk and income uncertainty, especially when linked to insurance schemes.
    • Many farmer organizations also provide their members with access to credit, allowing them to invest in more efficient technologies.
  • Enhanced capacity to provide quality and safe food:
    • School feeding programmes require strict food safety and quality control as well as management and planning capacities.
    • When farmers produce higher-quality food and build up their capacities to meet standards, they grow better food and achieve higher prices when selling any surplus in other formal markets.
  • Reduction of post-harvest losses:
    • Particularly for perishable commodities, there is less wastage when food is purchased and prepared locally for schoolchildren.
  • Access to other markets:
    • To the extent that HGSF programmes strengthen the capacity of farmers to produce more, better-quality and more diversified products, they will also enhance farmers' opportunities to gain access to other markets.
  • Access to credit:
    • It is a traditional bottleneck for small stakeholders in the food sector.
    • Besides formal requirements, such as possession of a valid identification card or other paperwork, the main obstacles to obtaining credit for smallholder farmers are short repayment periods, high interest rates and the farmers' lack of guarantees. 

To understand further the follow-up actions and activities to design, implement and scale the HGSF programme, see the following practice, Home-grown school feeding as a "game changer" - Understanding the benefits of connecting school feeding programmes with local smallholders farmers.

4. Validation of practice

This programme is implemented in many countries in Latin America (particularly in Brazil) and Africa.

5. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

For HGSF, the most important aspect is the present and potential local food production of smallholder farmers, since the design of menus (composition and quantities) which should be oriented towards the kind of food and the quantities local farmers can actually supply now and in the medium term. Also other aspects such as markets and aggregation systems are important to understand for the selection of the most conducive operating model for an HGSF programme.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Home-grown school feeding as a "game changer" - Understanding the benefits of connecting school feeding programmes with local smallholders farmers: ID 10095.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency 

This resource-efficient practice has positive impacts, such as reducing post-harvest losses, or improving food supply through better management and planning capacities.

7.2 Women-friendly

HGSF contributes to the empowerment of women in agriculture and food production. 

7.3 Pro-poor technology

This technology helps farmers to prevent income and price instability, among other things.

entries.summary:
This practice shows how farmers and their groups can cooperate, form associations, or builds alliances with different actors. It is applied to young or more mature groups or organizations, supporting the strengthening of good governance practices and internal reflection for groups and organizations to start a change process.

These training models encourage farmers and their groups to form associations or federations, enhance their capacities to learn from each other, exchange reliable information about what works and what does not work, and monitor their members' accountability.

These training models encourage farmers and their groups to form associations or federations, enhance their capacities to learn from each other, exchange reliable information about what works and what does not work, and monitor their members' accountability. The EU BOND project offered an additional venue for using and readapting the material to the BOND representatives' needs. Some of the training models were developed previous to the project and others were designed and developed during workshops of EU BOND project "Bringing Organisations & Network Development to higher levels in the Farming sector in Europe."
entries.description:
Description

1. Introduction

Farmers and land managers play a crucial role in the environmental, social and economic sustainability of the farming sector in Europe. The way they organize, innovate and network, and their ability to combine individual and collective work influence the food landscape of Europe. Through the benefit of working with others, linking with multiple actors, individual and collective well-being is improved, rural areas can develop more equitably and inclusively and agricultural growth is enhanced.

Social capital is a critical factor that concerns the ability of people to cooperate for common goals. What we have learned over the past decades, from organizational experiences in developing countries and countries in transition, is that physical and human capital accumulation by itself is not sufficient to bring development. Investments in physical capital (infrastructure and equipment) and human capital (skills development) are necessary conditions, but they are far from sufficient; they need to be complemented with the development of social capital (Stiglitz, 1998).

Training models for organizing farmers through social capital aim at support the farmer leaders, land managers and their organizations to acquire knowledge and tools to implement learning events for building three types of relations:

  • Bonding relations:
    • These are intragroup relations and built at the grassroots level;
  • Bridging relations:
    • These re-built among farmer organizations to form top organizations and networks (intergroup relations);
  • Linking relations:
    • These are extra-group relations built with public and private entities as well as with policymakers.

These three types of relations are core relations for an organizational development process of farmer organizations.

The topics and the events that could be organized are an opportunity to begin an internal reflection for farmer groups and organizations to start a change process within their communities and territories.

Putnam (Putnam, 1995) defines these relationships as the "collective resource of a group in terms of network and social trust which facilitates its collective action for mutual benefit."

Social capital allows individuals to bond together to defend their interests and organize to support collective needs. The utility of social capital lies in its potential to make people act collectively/cooperate/collaborate and, by doing so, increase their access to assets, services and capabilities (empowerment). Like physical and human capital, social capital generates a stream of returns (Uphoff, 2000; Grootaert and Van Bastelaer, 2001).

The training models are designed for the following target audiences:

  • farmer leaders, land managers;
  • group facilitators or experts in community mobilization;
  • board members, management staff of farmer organizations and cooperatives;
  • leaders and facilitators of farmer networks and platforms; and
  • technical staff of government agencies or other farmer-supporting institutions.

The models are intended to facilitate farmer organizations and land management groups (and within), the design and implementation of learning activities such as:

  • trainings;
  • workshops;
  • roundtables; etc.

The elements identified and the modules here briefly described will give farmer organizations and land management groups the ability to:

  1. know how to build and strengthen the internal capacities of their organizations;
  2. project their vision in the future;
  3. build and strengthen fruitful relations with other organizations; and
  4. relate constructively with other key actors.

The ways in which these relationships and social networks grow are explained below.

Type of relations Description Benefits
Bonding relations

Bonding social capital refers to ties within an organization intragroup (relationships) among members with high levels of similarity in attitudes, information and resources. These relationships are close and involve interpersonal relations between small groups of people.

Bonding social capital takes place between farmers whenever people spend time together regularly in face-to-face meetings. In this way, they nurture social capital. Efficient and sustainable bonding ties within an organization are structured around:

  • a common objective and voluntary membership, and
  • a shared identity in a limited group size.

In cooperatives, bonding relationships are formed between farmers of the same social group with common characteristics. They share a sense of shared identity and belonging, based on the same social history and territory, within an organization at grassroots and local levels.

  1. Cooperation among members results from their willingness to work together to achieve a common goal.
  2. Through repeated, direct personal interactions in a small affinity group, a strong-shared identity is created and tends to reinforce mutual benefit relationships over time.
  3. Strong members' identification is only possible if the group is small enough to regularly communicate with each other (groups are between 15 and 30 members).

In a farmer organization, bonding relations generate interaction patterns based on common norms, values, behaviour and beliefs: a common understanding that predisposes people to cooperate.

  1. The homogeneity in membership reinforces organizational performance by positively affecting individual behaviour, collective decision-making processes, and commitments.
  2. The social group pressure on every member is strong. Social pressure encourages those farmers who refuse to comply with their commitments.
  3. Moral incentives motivate farmers to do things based on right and wrong according to common norms.
  4. Any free riding or evading is evident and will be stigmatized.
  5. The failure to respect common rules is condemned.

Bonding social capital provides a set of norms of acceptable behaviour for individual members:

  • all those relations enhance the cohesion of the cooperative.
  • the stability of these normative behaviours is what creates enduring organizations and allows farmers to achieve high levels of cooperation.
Benefits and limits of bonding relations
  • farmers gain self-confidence;
  • gain knowledge to analyze their problems;
  • make informed decisions;
  • act collectively.
Enables farmers and land managers to:
  • identify joint solutions and build strategies to cope with change;
  • develop a sense of ownership in their group or in the organization they belong to be committed and engaged.

In a cooperative, it can emerge as:

  • attempts by individual farmers to improve their economic position in the absence of competitive markets.

By grouping purchases and sales, the local cooperative may offer individual farmers an opportunity to modify their position, thereby reducing transaction costs.

Limitations:
  • can also produce exclusion;
  • can resist change.

A gradual opening is necessary to turn them into more modern organizations through building different relations to become more outward-looking.

Cooperatives and other organizations can address the needs of new members and grow too much, overcoming the optimal size for effective bonding relations.

  • the incentive for a group's members diminishes as group size increases;
  • large groups are less able to act in their common interest than small ones.

The expansion of cooperatives beyond a specific size renders social control through peer pressure ineffective.

The narrowness of collective action with only bonding relations does not provide access to the complete range of resources needed for ensuring the full economic inclusion of small-scale farmers.
Bridging relations

Bridging social capital refers to partnership connections among organizations that are alike (intergroup relations).

  • are horizontal ties that connect farmer and land manager groups to create larger organizations in the form of farmer or land workers' unions, federations and networks.

In unions and federations, member organizations share part of their decision-making power.

In loose networks, each organization keeps its full autonomy.

Efficiency is critical to position a farmer organization in national and global markets.

Over time, successful farmer organizations grow, allowing more farmers to access more products and services at better conditions. But in large cooperative organizations:

  • Individual members cannot possibly know each other.
  • Frequent or regular face-to-face meetings are no longer held.
  • Communication among members becomes more complicated.
  • The cooperative is no longer an affinity group based on a common identity.
  • A member will not be affected socially if he or she fails to make efforts on behalf of his or her cooperative's goal.
  • With cooperative growth, bonding relations tend to weaken.
  • With growth, the cooperative life becomes increasingly complex; it may lead to the decline of social incentives of the bonding social capital that operate well in small-sized organizations.
The benefits of bridging relations

The development of bridging relations connecting similar organizations to form larger organizations is a relevant organizational innovation for their effective inclusion in value chains at national and global levels.

  • The market's pressures cause farmer organizations to increase their competitiveness.
  • Built on a dense network of relations offers an interesting solution for addressing the size dilemma.
  • In alliances, partnerships or networks, organizations can pool and coordinate the use of shared assets, resources and competencies.
  • Alliances built on bridging social capital provide each farmer organization a flexible way to be competitive in global markets while maintaining a strong identity based on the bonds with their members.
Linking relations

Linking relations are vertical ties that can be created with influential actors belonging to the economic or political arena, such as private businesses or governments. Through strong links with economic actors, farmers and land managers can access national and international markets. Greater negotiation power, in turn, translates into more favorable transaction conditions and greater influence over other actors.

Linking relations with policymakers' helps actors create an enabling environment and conditions for their organizations to thrive and develop sustainably. To be successful, these links between farmers, land managers, market actors and policymakers must result in a positive sum game in which all partners agree to cooperate to advance their common interests, achieve and increase profits, and share benefits and risks.
The benefits of linking social capital

The linking form of social capital has the potential to work as leverage;

  • it can improve the terms for groups to participate in the economy by strengthening their ability to participate in trade relationships and activities and access new opportunities.
  • In a society lacking social trust (low-trust society), small-scale farmers and operators both upstream and downstream do not have an incentive to enter rural markets - it is too risky and too costly.
  • It opens up economic opportunities for those belonging to less powerful or excluded groups of farmers.
  • By enforcing members' contracts with private operators, farmers organized into cooperatives secure the supply in terms of quantity and quality, develop a reputation, and provide private operators a credible assurance for profitable transactions.
  • Cooperatives can secure profitable transactions for small-scale producers by rebalancing the market power.
  • By communicating and coordinating their decisions together (through grouped sales and purchases), farmers within their cooperatives can create conducive market conditions.
  • Cooperatives can improve small-scale farmers' bargaining power, reduce their transaction costs, mutualize their risks, and create trust with upstream/downstream operators.

The figure below provides a visual representation of the three interlinked relations that interact closely with one another and enhance each relationship's benefits.

Figure 1. THE BONDING, BRIDGING AND LINKING FRAMEWORK

Source: FAO. 2020. Empowering farmers and their organizations through the creation of social capital - Bond learning guide for trainers. Rome. 

2. Options for applying the methodology

Depending on the needs of the farmer organization or group:

  • need to build internal capacities;
  • need to develop relations among organizations; or
  • need to establish links with external actors;

On the level of knowledge and interest, the various topics are:

  • on leadership and management;
  • on developing action plans;
  • on dialogue and advocacy; etc.

Depending on the time available for learning – the programme can run from one to five full training days.

3. Structure of the learning /training

To cover the whole spectrum of the proposed topics on bonding, bridging and linking:

  • It is composed of 16 sessions
  • two days are devoted to bonding topics,
  • two days on developing bridging relations, and
  • one full day on linking:
    • The time devoted to linking can be extended to two days as relevant topics related to communication and networking also can be applied to develop linking relations.

The learning-training structure is modular and demand-driven; thus, the number of days needed (from one to five days) is related to the topics to be addressed. Table 1 presents the training topics by focus areas representing the modules and table 2 shows the training programme for the suggested five-day training schedule in detail. Due to its modularity, the modules and number of days for training will depend on the needs identified.

Figure 2. Presents the training focus, including all the topics, structured as follows:

Figure 3. The training programme used during the suggested five-day training schedule was divided in the following way:

Source: FAO. 2020. Empowering farmers and their organizations through the creation of social capital - Bond learning guide for trainers. Rome. 

The full programme will allow participants to understand:

Bonding:
  • Define the organization as a complex system, balancing people, objectives and group processes.
  • Identify concrete tools to increase confidence in different situations.
  • Acquire knowledge and skills to lead men and women in the organization effectively.
  • Understand the role of conflict for organizational transformation and identify strategies for conflict management.
  • Reflect on values and principles for farmer organizations.
Bonding and bridging:
  • Sensitize the importance of gender equality and women empowerment.
  • Explain the importance of building a shared vision.
  • Analyze organizational performance, identifying its strengths and weaknesses about its mission.
  • Formulate strategies to strengthen performance, equity and governance.
  • Establish a plan of action for the next 12 months (bonding and bridging).
Bridging:
  • Familiarize with the role of agricultural advisors and discuss the role of agriculture networks.
Bridging and linking:
  • Explain the importance of strategic communication and how to formulate, and effectively deliver messages.
  • Describe the nature and elements of constructive dialogue with government counterparts and among farmer organizations.
  • Identify different strategies and styles for negotiation.

What is needed for the preparation of the training – some guiding tips

Assessing needs

The environment in which farmer organizations operate continually evolves and there is a need to learn new skills; however, training may not be able to solve all of the organization's problems

It is essential to undertake an initial self-assessment of the organization to determine which changes are needed and whether they can have a training solution.

If training is a solution, then the training organizer or the facilitator should make all the necessary efforts to involve the organization's members.

In a small organization, this can mean the involvement of all members. If the farmer organization is big, this may not be possible and the needs assessment can be made by members of its guiding committees, board, or working groups. The more members are involved in the self-definition of training needs, the more they will be committed to their organization's common objectives.
Selection of the participants

A minimum of 10 and a maximum of 30 participants to maintain the integrity of the training design
Take into account the following criteria:
  • Geographical distribution.
  • Gender and age balance among the participants allowing men, women and youth to attend and benefit from the training.
  • Separate discussion groups may need to be organized.
  • Strong motivation in acquiring knowledge, skills and in disseminating it.
  • Some experiential knowledge of the topics.
  • Potential multiplier effect in the territory/community.
  • It is important to have representatives from farmer organizations belonging to different sectors or activities to allow cross-fertilization of experiences from an organizational point of view.

Careful attention has to be paid when designing a participatory training session in countries where women cannot give their opinion in meetings with men.
Setting up the training team

Ideally, the team should be involved throughout the process

Ideally, the team should be involved throughout the process: in the preparatory steps, implementing the training, and monitoring and evaluation activities following the training.

Depending on the training duration, it is recommended to have two facilitators conducting the training who alternately lead and support the facilitation.

The support staff will also play an important role in preparing the training materials, photocopying documents, and helping the facilitator(s) during the training.

Assign a person to document the training by taking notes and photos during the training and preparing the training report.

The trainer or the training team should list what has to be prepared in advance, the materials needed, the responsibilities, and the timing.

It is also essential to allocate one day for a rehearsal before the training. It helps the trainer or the training team to think through the process and ensure that all the materials are in place.

The trainer or the training team should also allow time to absorb the sessions' technical background and facilitation.
Choosing a training venue and room set-up

The selection of an appropriate venue and the arrangements at the venue are important in ensuring that the training workshop runs smoothly

The venue's geographic location and the actual physical space, such as the room's size and layout, can significantly influence the training outcome.

The training venue should have a large hall with lots of space for the participants to move around.

The capacity of the room should be approximately double the number of participants

Chairs should be easily movable and arranged in different ways as shown below (fig 3).

The ideal set-up for participatory discussion and analysis is the boardroom, the islands, the cabaret and the u-shape.

It is essential to check all the equipment before the meeting.
Preparing training materials and equipment

Participatory and experiential learning-based training courses are more complex to organize logistically than more conventional courses

A variety of materials are required for each session, and many logistical arrangements need to be made in advance:

  1. Adapt and prepare the materials
  2. Send participants the agenda/schedule and the questionnaire on organizational performance
  3. Buy materials following a checklist
  4. Allocate time and location for preparing materials
  5. Training materials checklist
Figure 4. Types of training room set-up and layout 

Source: FAO. 2020. Empowering farmers and their organizations through the creation of social capital - Bond learning guide for trainers. Rome. 

4. Considerations

Training situations vary greatly and the materials and suggestions here provided are simple to be used as a guide to conduct successful training.

When planning the workshop, consider the following factors:

  • The level of experience of the facilitator;
  • the knowledge and skill levels of participants; and
  • the training context.

The training workshop, as outlined in Figure 2, is designed to take place over five days.

Several steps are involved in getting ready for this training:
  • The training organizers should begin preparations approximately two-three months before the training, considering:
  • the need to translate the material into local languages;
  • the need to adapt the training material to the local context
  • to identify relevant examples;
  • that a full understanding of the proposed methodology, and a good familiarity with this learning guide and how to use it, may require some additional preparation time.
  • the level of familiarity of the facilitator with the topics
    • performance;
    • equity;
    • governance;
    • management;
    • negotiation; etc.
  • Careful assessment of these elements before starting the preparation is recommended to plan realistically for the work and time required to prepare for and carry out the training properly.

For the full details and related material such as forms, matrix, templates and ppts examples, please consult the listed background materials and the FAO. 2020. Empowering farmers and their organizations through the creation of social capital - Bond learning guide for trainers. Rome.

5. Some definitions

For this guide, the following terms are used:

Social capital: the term "social capital" refers to people's ability to work together in groups. Social capital is an asset as a "collective resource of a group in terms of networks and social trust which facilitate its collective action for mutual benefit" (Putnam, 1995).

Organizations (FAO, 2012) are "group of individuals bound by some common purpose to achieve objectives" (North, 1990:5). Organizations include groups of individuals working together and jointly managing common resources toward a shared goal, ranging from informal rural producer groups (self-help groups, networks, etc.) to formal farmer organizations.

Farmer organizations: membership-based organizations of smallholders, family farmers and agriculture producers, breeders, artisanal fishers, and indigenous people that are structured beyond the community level, at the local, national, regional and global level. They include all forms of producer associations, cooperatives, and their unions and federations.

Organizational development: a body of knowledge and practice that enhances organizational performance and change.

Background material A key step for the training team is to review the following background materials.

  • FAO "Good practices in building innovative rural institutions to increase food security" (2011).
  • FAO "Good practices in building innovative rural institutions to increase food security. Case studies" (2011).
  • FAO e-learning course on Organization analysis and development.
  • FAO Learning Module 3 Good learning practices for effective capacity development (2013).
  • FAO Learning Module 4 Organization analysis and development (2013).
  • FAO. 2020. Empowering farmers and their organizations through the creation of social capital - Bond learning guide for trainers. Rome.

6. Validation of the practice

The EU BOND project offered an additional venue for using and readapting the material to the needs of the BOND representatives at a two-venue, by the EU BOND project: first during the Training of Trainers (ToT) organized in Cordoba, Spain in September 2018 and then in Coventry, UK, in February 2019, where 29 representatives from 17 European countries participated.

7. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The minimum condition depends on several factors, such as the training needs well-identified (needs of the farmer organization or group); the level of experience of the facilitator; the knowledge and skill levels of participants; and the training context are all factors that need to be considered for successful training, including materials available in the language of participants.

8. Agroecological zones

  • Temperate, cool.
  • Temperate, cold.
  • Temperate, very cold.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Women-friendly

The training modules can be designed and adapted to specific groups, women, girls, men, depending on the needs identified. These training modules are undoubtedly beneficial for women as it targets and addresses the different types of cooperatives and organizational structures. Encourage youth and mature farmers and their groups to form associations or federations, enhance their capacities to learn from each other, exchange reliable information about what works and what does not work, and monitor their members' accountability.

9.2 Pro-poor technology

The opportunity to train farmers on how to set adequate types of cooperatives or cooperate in different scenarios. These have the potential to contribute to better access to shared services, updated information and new knowledge at a community level.

entries.title: Beekeeping of the eastern honeybee (Apis cerana) using an improved traditional hive (China)
entries.source: Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (CAAS)
multi_source: Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (CAAS)#Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (CAAS)#Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (CAAS)#Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (CAAS)
entries.summary: Beekeeping with Apis cerana using traditional log hives often leads to the destruction of the colony during honey harvesting because the combs are destroyed in the harvesting process and bees cannot survive. The introduction of a wooden cross in the middle of the traditional log hive can solve this problem. This practice describes how to implement this easy and low-cost improvement to the traditional hive and how to manage this improved traditional log hive. This improved traditional log hive enables sustainable beekeeping as colonies are not destroyed when harvesting honey. Thus, honey production is higher than when using the traditional hives.
entries.description:
Description 

Traditional beekeeping with A. cerana is characterised by the use of log hives made of hollowed tree trunk, placed vertically. The hive entrance is located on the side of the hives. During honey harvesting the combs are completely destroyed and the colony is lost, which is not sustainable and honey harvesting can only be done once per year. The key feature of the improved traditional beekeeping with A. cerana involves the improvement of traditional hives and related management practices.

1. Modification over the traditional hives

The key to the improved traditional beekeeping is the addition of two horizontal wooden supporting bars in the middle of the traditional hives, which can be used to fix the combs after cutting the combs for harvesting. If you have wooden barrels or tree log in your home, you can make the same improvement by adding a cross in the middle with two wood supporting bars, and entrances at the top and the bottom.

Figure 1. Improved traditional hive (view from the top, without top lid)

© Chao Chen

2. The improved traditional log hive: how to build and manage the hive

2.1 Material needed to improve traditional hives

  • Drilling tools and two wood bars for each hive are needed to improve the traditional hives.

2.2 How to build the improved traditional hive

  • With the traditional wood log, drill through the walls to make a pair of holes that allow a wood bar to go through.
  • Rotate 90 degrees, drill another pair of holes to allow the other wood bar to go through, so that the wood bars form a cross.

2.3 How to install the improved traditional hive

  • Leave the beehive in the upright position, and workers will build combs from the top lid down, through the wood cross.
  • The bees will store honey in the part of the combs above the wooden supporting bars.
  • The section below the wooden supporting bars will be reserved for brood (Figure 2a).
  • Only the honey storage regions located above the wooden supporting bars are cut off when harvesting honey.
Figure 2. Cycle of improved traditional beekeeping

© CAAS

3. Harvest honey

  • To collect honey, open the top lid (use a knife to cut it, open it when necessary).
  • After the lid is opened, blow smoke from the top to drive bees to go to the bottom part of the hive.
  • Hold the honeycomb with one hand and cut with a long fruit knife.
  • Put the cut honey comb in a clean container.
  • Do not cut below the supporting bars (Figure 2b).
  • In general, leave 2 cm of combs above the supporting bar.
  • Make sure to leave some honeycomb and pollen comb as food for bees.

4. After honey collection

  • Two days after honey collection, turn the hive upside down, leaving the brood area on the upper part (Figure 2c).
  • Note that the direction of the entrance should remain the same.
  • When the broods are hatched, the upper comb area becomes honey storage area for the bees to continue to store honey.
  • The lower part is the original honey storage area that has been cut off.
  • Worker bees will build new comb cells which will become new brood cells (Figure 2d and e).

5. Checking the colony

  • When inspection inside a hive is needed, hold the beehive with your hand and tilt it from front to back (do not tilt left or right), and observe from the bottom of the combs.

6. Migratory beekeeping

  • With the improved traditional hive, migratory beekeeping in short distance is possible (not more than 100 km).
  • The vehicle should be steady during transportation.

7. Validation of the practice

  • This method was invented and tested by beekeepers from Shennongjia forestry region in Hubei, China.

8. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • There is need to have a sufficient nectar source.
  • Access to clean water is required.
  • For traditional beekeeping, locally adapted bees are usually required. The colony should be able to survive with minimum human management.

9. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.
  • Temperate, cool.

10. Related/associated technologies 

  • Beekeeping: the Kamara basket hive: an improved traditional hive: ID 7289.
  • Beekeeping in Asia: obtaining colonies with Apis Cerana: ID 4004.
  • How to make a Kenyan topbar hive: ID 10126.

11. Objectives fulfilled by the project

11.1 Resource use efficiency

The implementation of this resource-efficient practice is easy and leads to positive effects, such as improved survival of bee colonies during honey harvesting.

11.2 Pro-poor technology

Using an improved traditional hive is cost-effective for the beekeeper, and leads to increased honey production, which in turn strengthens the income of producers.

entries.summary:
Cette fiche présente la fabrication d’une ruchette en bambou destinée à accueillir les abeilles sans dard, du genre Hypotrigona et Liotrigona, appelées aussi trigones.  Les abeilles sans dard sont appelées mélipones ou « stingless bees » en anglais. Comme son nom l’indique, elles ne piquent pas et peuvent donc facilement cohabiter avec l’homme.  Elles sont présentes dans les zones tropicales et subtropicales du monde, y compris les zones de savanes sèches. On les retrouve donc sur presque tout le continent Africain. La morphologie des mélipones est hétéroclite et diffère selon les genres et espèces.

Chez ces petites abeilles, certaines espèces construisent un nid externe[1], mais la majorité d’entre elles colonisent les creux existants dans différents types de substrats: cavités souterraines, creux dans le mur des maisons, les portes, les fenêtres, les épaves de véhicules, et bien sûr dans les troncs et branches d’arbre ou encore les tiges creuses de bambous. C’est à partir de ce dernier matériau que cette pratique a été développée, testée et appliquée.

Ces mélipones sont actuellement élevées par certains apiculteurs au Burkina Faso, au Cameroun, au Kongo-central (République Démocratique du Congo), en Ouganda, en Ethiopie et au Ghana à titre expérimental pour les besoins nutritionnels et médicinales des hommes. Elles sont élevées à beaucoup plus grande échelle par les méliponiculteurs au Kenya et en Tanzanie où le miel est extrait pour la commercialisation.  Le miel de mélipones est en effet très nutritionnel et possède des propriétés médicinales.

Il est important de préserver les mélipones car elles représentent d’importants pollinisateurs et sont cruciales pour la reproduction d’une part considérable de plantes en zone tropicale, y compris les cultures. A titre d’exemple, la vanille dépend de la pollinisation d’une seule espèce de trigone.

Cette fiche technique décrit comment fabriquer une ruche pour les abeilles mélipones du genre Hypotrigona et Liotrigona en bambou
entries.description:
La description

1. Introduction

Les mélipones du genre Hypotrigona et Liotrigona sont des abeilles sans dard couramment présentes dans différents types d’habitat en Afrique tropicale et subtropicale. Elles sont facilement distinguables des mélipones des autres genres (Meliponula, Plebeina, Dactylurina, Cleptotrigona) par l’architecture de la trompe de cérumen (mélange de cire et de résine) (figure 1) qu’elles fabriquent et qui constitue l’entrée de leur nid ainsi que par leur petite taille corporelle.

Le genre Hypotrigona renferme très peu d’espèces, difficilement discernables sur base de leur morphologie corporelle mais, pouvant être différenciées au moyen de l’architecture de leur nid. Parmi les espèces du genre Hypotrigona on cite par exemple Hypotrigona squamuligera, H. araujoi., H. gribodoi, H. ruspolii. Ce sont de petites abeilles mesurant entre 1,9 et 4 mm. Elles sont largement répandues et abondantes dans les zones de forêts et savanes tropicales et subtropicales d’Afrique.

Le genre Liotrigona se compose des espèces comme Liotrigona bottegoi, Liotrigona parvula, et Liotrigona gabonensis. Ce sont aussi de petites abeilles de 1,5 à 4 mm de long ressemblant profondément au genre Hypotrigona mais dont l’absence de pilosité sur la partie dorsale du thorax permet de le différencier de ce dernier.

L’architecture du trou de vol des nids des Hypotrigona et Liotrigona varie selon l’espèce (figure 1 et 2).

Figure 1: photo de l’entrée d’une colonie d’Hypotrigona gribodoi, avec quelques gardes

©Kiatoko Nkoba- ICIPE, Kenya 2019

Figure 2: photo de l’entrée d’une colonie de Liotrigona gabonensis

©Kiatoko Nkoba- ICIPE, Kenya 2019

En général, le nid des mélipones se compose de:

  • un trou de vol qui sert d’entrée au nid;
  • un batumen, qui sert de mur de protection interne du nid;
  • de pots pour le stockage du miel et pollens;
  • de l’involucrum qui sert de membrane de protection du couvain;
  • du couvain (œufs et larves) et des pillars (piliers).   

L’architecture interne du nid varie selon le genre et l’espèce de mélipones. Pour illustrer les différentes parties d’un nid, nous avons choisi un schéma représentant le nid de mélipones du genre Meliponula (voir figure 3). Leur nid est beaucoup plus évolué et structuré que celui des mélipones du genre Hypotrigona et Liotrigona c’est pourquoi, nous avons fait ce choix.

Figure 3: Structure générale du nid chez les espèces du genre Meliponula

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Kenya 2019

Dans les nids des Hypotrigona et Liotrigona, le couvain est regroupé en amas des cocons arrangés irrégulièrement (voir figure 4), contrairement à Apis et à d’autres genres de mélipones qui construisent un couvain en rayons structurés disposés soit horizontalement (voir figure 5), soit verticalement (genre Dactylurina). Le couvain en amas leur permet de s’implanter dans de nombreux espaces confinés et irréguliers.

Figure 4: Nid d’Hypotrigona gribodoi avec reine, pots de miel et amas de couvain disposés irrégulièrement

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Kenya 2019

Figure 5: Nid structuré de Meliponula ferruginea avec involucrum et couvain à rayons horizontaux superposés

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Zanzibar 2019

Ces mélipones sont très connues parmi les populations car elles logent souvent dans les murs des habitations et autres petites cavités. On les repère notamment à la petite trompe de cérumen qui vient former l’entrée de leur nid. Certaines espèces de ces abeilles minuscules n’ont pas besoin d’un grand volume pour se développer et le creux d’un morceau de bambou constitue un coin idéal. Comme de nombreuses espèces d’abeilles sans dard appelées mélipones elles produisent du miel et du pollen en petite quantité (voir FT: how to collect honey, pollen and propolis from stingless bees (in English and Spanish)).

Vous trouverez, illustré ci-dessous, les différentes étapes de la fabrication d’une ruchette en bambou ainsi qu’un aperçu, vu de l’intérieur, d’une ruchette en bambou colonisée et d’une récolte.

2. Matériaux et outils utilisés pour la fabrication de la ruchette en bambou

Matériaux:

  • Un bambou creux et de préférence sec, sans fissure ni trou: la taille du bambou dépendra de l’espèce de mélipone et du développement de la colonie. Il est difficile d’identifier les mélipones jusqu’à l’espèce. Une ruchette en bambou de 25 cm de longueur et de 10 cm de diamètre suffira à certaines espèces tandis que d’autres pourraient occuper un espace de 40 cm de long sur 15 cm de diamètre. C’est pourquoi il est conseillé d’avoir des ruchettes de différentes tailles et de bien suivre l’évolution de la colonie afin de pratiquer un transfert si l’espace devient insuffisant.
  • Deux ficelles ou élastiques.

Outils:

  • Une scie ou machette.
  • Une perceuse manuelle ou électrique.

3. Fabrication

  • Etape 1:
    • La section dans laquelle la colonie va se développer se situe dans la partie creuse du bambou entre 2 nœuds de la tige. La première étape consiste donc à découper une section de bambou comportant deux nœuds, de manière à ce que les deux extrémités de notre section soient bouchées. Pour cela il faut scier le bambou après les séparations naturelles de la tige (à un ou deux centimètres des nœuds). La colonie sera ainsi correctement protégée de la pluie et des prédateurs.
  • Etape 2:
    • Fendre le bambou en deux dans le sens de la hauteur à l’aide de la machette.
  • Etape 3:
    • Réalisez un trou avec une mèche d’environ 0,5 à 1cm de diamètre dans l’une des deux parties du bambou fendu. Il est préférable que le trou soit situé à l’une des extrémités du bambou (figure 6). Cette petite ouverture constituera l’entrée par laquelle les abeilles pénétreront dans le bambou, rapidement elles construiront le petit tube de cérumen caractéristique qui marque la présence d’une colonie. Les abeilles stockent le miel et le pollen immédiatement après l’entrée du nid. Le couvain est généralement localisé après le compartiment miel et pollen. En plaçant l’entrée du nid à l’extrémité du bambou ceci permet à la colonie de placer le couvain à une position distante du trou d’entrée et permet une meilleure protection du couvain contre les prédateurs.
  • Etape 4:
    • Rattachez ensemble les deux parties de votre bambou à l’aide d’une ficelle ou de deux élastiques (bandes en caoutchouc solides) (figure 7). Faites des nœuds que vous puissiez dénouer à volonté pour ouvrir la ruchette.
Figure 6: Trou d’entrée pratiqué dans le bambou d’environ 0,5 mm à 1 cm de diamètre (Indiqué par la flèche bleue)

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Kenya 2019

Figure 7: Bambou refermé à ses deux extrémités

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Kenya 2019

4. Installation et manipulation

Le bambou sera installé debout (verticalement), afin d’imiter au mieux un bambou naturel. Selon Dr. Kiatoko Nkoba (expert de l’ICIPE), la ruchette bambou peut également être installée horizontalement sans qu’il n’y ait d’impact sur l’acceptabilité de l’habitat.  Il faut donc observer et expérimenter pour voir quelle est la meilleure position acceptée par les abeilles dans votre environnement. La ruche est placée en hauteur à l’abri des fourmis, de la fumée (cuisine), de la pluie, du vent et des rayons directs du soleil. La chaleur risque de faire fondre la propolis et le cérumen (mélange de cire et de résine) de la ruche ou de l’entrée du nid et rendre le milieu inconfortable pour les abeilles. Celles-ci abandonneront alors la ruche. Vous veillerez à ce que la ruchette ne soit pas dérangée par l’homme et les animaux. La ruchette peut être suspendue en l’air pour la parer aux attaques de fourmis par exemple.

Figure 8: Ruchettes en bambou installées à l’abri de la pluie et du vent

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Kenya 2019

La colonisation de la ruchette sera visible notamment avec l’apparition du petit tuyau caractéristique au trou d’entrée (figure 9). Elle peut se faire en quelques jours ou en  plusieurs mois. La rapidité de colonisation d’une ruchette dépend de la disponibilité des colonies, de la disponibilité des niches naturelles dans le milieu et de la période. Dans un milieu naturellement riche en colonies d’abeilles mélipones et en période de reproduction par exemple, les ruches peuvent être colonisées dans les premiers jours qui suivent leur installation!

Il est ensuite conseillé d’attendre plusieurs mois, avant toute manipulation de la ruchette. Les abeilles mélipones ont une façon très particulière de se reproduire et d’essaimer. Un groupe d’abeilles « scoutes » ou « éclaireuses » localisent un nouveau site de nidification pour fonder une nouvelle colonie. Une fois trouvé, quelques ouvrières de l'ancienne colonie s’installent dans le nouveau nid pour le préparer (construction d’une partie de la structure interne du nid et stockage de la nourriture) durant plusieurs semaines, voire mois. Plus tard, le nid est ensuite rejoint par une reine nouvellement fécondée, et de nombreuses ouvrières se joignent à elle pour s'installer de façon permanente[2]. Plusieurs semaines à plusieurs mois peuvent s'écouler pour que le nouveau nid établi devienne complètement indépendant du nid mère[3].

Figure 9: Entrée de la ruchette caractérisée par la présence d’un petit tube construit par les trigones

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Kenya 2019

5. Récolte de miel

Les abeilles sans dard stockent leur miel dans de petites cellules type bulles (figure 11). Ces petites cellules sont attachées entre elles et à la structure du bambou. Tout d’abord, les abeilles récoltent le miel pour se nourrir et nourrir le couvain. L’apiculteur doit faire attention de ne pas récolter trop de miel car il est important de laisser suffisamment de miel pour la colonie.

La récolte s’effectue de manière très simple : prenez le bambou, dénouez les deux ficelles ou élastiques, séparez délicatement les deux parties du bambou que les abeilles auront scellées avec de la propolis, tout cela en veillant à ne pas détruire le tuyau d’entrée (figure 10). Vous pourrez observer la construction du couvain sous forme d’une masse de cellules de petite taille, tandis que le pollen et le miel prennent place séparément dans des cellules plus grosses situées au-dessus et en dessous du couvain (figure 11). Si l’aspect du nid de ces petites abeilles est très différent des constructions droites en rayon des Apis mellifera, on peut cependant dire qu’elles sont bien organisées.

Figure 10: Ouverture du bambou, délicatement en évitant de casser le tube d’entrée

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Kenya 2019

Les bulles de miel peuvent être prélevées à l’aide d’une cuillère. Les deux bambous doivent ensuite être rattachés et replacés dans la même position : sinon, comme pour les Apis mellifera, les Hypotrigona et Liotrigona risquent de ne pas retrouver l’entrée de leur nid!

Figure 11: Les cellules de couvain (partie centrale) sont plus petites que les cellules ou bulles de miel (partie inferieure) et de pollen (partie supérieure)

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Kenya 2019

Figure 12: La récolte s’effectue à la cuillère, chaque bambou peut donner quelques dizaines à centaines de grammes de miel: les miels des abeilles mélipones et trigones possèdent des propriétés médicinales très intéressantes et souvent supérieures au miel d’Apis mellifera

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Kenya 2019

S’agissant d’un aliment à consommation humaine, parfois utilisé en tant que médicament, il faut se rappeler de toujours travailler dans de bonnes conditions d’hygiène: il faut se laver les mains avant de manipuler le miel et utiliser des outils et récipients propres et secs.

6. Observations générales

Selon le manuel de Peter Kwapong, « Stingless Bees : importance, management and utilisation », d’autres matériaux disponibles localement peuvent être utilisés pour fabriquer des ruchettes pour mélipones tel que: des pots en terre cuites, des écorces de noix de coco, des calebasses, des bouteilles en plastiques, etc.

Là où le bois est facilement disponible, il existe des modèles de ruchettes en bois.

Figure 13: Opération de récolte de miel d’une ruche en bois. Ce modèle de ruche est conçu pour accueillir d’autres mélipones, du genre Meliponula par exemple

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Kenya 2019

Tout comme la plupart des abeilles sans dard, et suivant leur taille, les Hypotrigona et Liotrigona produisent une quantité réduite de miel.  La production en miel chez les genres Hypotrigona et Liotrigona varie selon l’espèce mais ne dépasse pas 500 ml par année. Seules les espèces de melipones comme Meliponula bocandei produisent jusqu’à 10 Kg de miel.

Cependant, les abeilles sans dard sont « domestiquées » par les méliponiculteurs pour les propriétés nutritionnelles et thérapeutiques du miel. Le miel d’abeilles sans dard est très apprécié par les populations dans certaines régions d’Afrique où ce miel obtient un meilleur prix par rapport au miel d’abeilles « Apis melifera ».

Le goût du miel des mélipones est beaucoup plus acide que le goût du miel des abeilles sociales mellifères élevées par les apiculteurs (Apis mellifera).

Figure 14: élevage de mélipones au Kenya sous l’appui technique de l’ICIPE 

©Kiatoko Nkoba- icipe, Kenya 2019

Intérêt écologique des mélipones:

De manière générale, les mélipones jouent un rôle important dans la préservation de la biodiversité. Elles participent à la pollinisation des plantes et arbres des forêts et espaces naturels. Certaines espèces de mélipones sont liées spécifiquement à certaines plantes. Si une de ces plantes disparait, l’espèce d’abeilles disparaitra et inversement.

La méliponiculture peut également être développée dans les milieux agricoles en vue d’augmenter les rendements en fruit des légumes et arbres fruitiers. Des études sont menées par l’ICIPE, Centre international de physiologie et écologie des insectes, en collaboration avec des universités.  Dans certains pays, les mélipones sont utilisées dans des cultures commerciales pour offrir des services de pollinisation tout comme c’est le cas avec les abeilles Apis melifera. Il y a un intérêt écologique, économique et culturel important à protéger les mélipones. Favoriser l’élevage plutôt que la cueillette de miel dans les colonies sauvages permet entre autre, de limiter la pression sur les colonies sauvages qui sont généralement tuées pour en récupérer le miel. La cueillette demande souvent de couper un arbre ou de le grimper, ce qui provoque parfois des accidents graves.

7. Validation

Le modèle de ruchette en bambou decrit dans cette fiche technique a été rencontré chez un apiculteur de la région de Bamenda, au Cameroun. C’est par l’intermédiaire d’un jeune ingénieur camerounais de l’université de Dshang, Cameroun  et d’un étudiant français, réalisant un stage sur le lien entre l’apiculture et la préservation de l’environnement pour BNSS, en 2017, que cette pratique a pu être partagée en RDC. Ces mélipones étant présentes dans la forêt de Mayombe, le modèle en bambou a pu être reproduit au Kongo-central en collaboration avec un formateur apicole de la PLAAC (Plateforme des associations des apiculteurs du district des Cataractes). Cette fiche technique a ensuite été amendée et approuvée par un expert de l’ICIPE,  International Centre of Insect Physiology and Ecology, basé au Kenya.

8. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Comment récolter le miel, le pollen et la propolis des mélipones: ID 10039.
  • Elevage de mélipones dans des ruches en coques de noix de coco: ID 10038
  • Propagación de las abejas sin aguijón usando cáscaras de coco: ID 8670.
