entries.summary:
This homestead pond polyculture practice takes a nutrition and gender sensitive approach. Micronutrient-rich small fish are incorporated into the homestead pond. With regular harvest, these small fish are consumed by household members, most importantly by pregnant women, lactating mothers, adolescent girls, and children, to mitigate micronutrient malnutrition. To maximize the nutritional benefits, training may be provided on preparing small fish in a way to make it suitable for consumption even by children under two years of age.

Benefits: This practice can improve household food and nutrition security alongside the production of fish for market. The practice can also benefit women by providing them an additional source of income. Depending on aquatic habitat quality and connectivity, widespread use of the practice can produce “spillover” of small fish into wild aquatic habitats, improving the local fisheries.

How: The production, processing, and preparation of diet with small micronutrient-rich fish at the household.
entries.description:
Description

Many seasonal floodplains and flooded rice fields in Asia contain an abundance of small indigenous fish during flood periods [1]. Easily processed and consumed whole (in its entirety – including head, eyes, bones in addition to flesh) these small fish are rich sources of micronutrients including calcium, zinc, iron, and vitamin A [2]. Processed small fish are easily consumed by children under two years of age, providing key nutrients to combat stunting and other forms of malnutrition [3].

These micronutrient-rich, small indigenous fish species (SIS) can be produced via polyculture in ponds and pond connected rice-fields with other fish such as carps and tilapia. This polyculture practice was developed in Bangladesh, focusing on the incorporation of Mola, a micronutrient-rich Small Indigenous Species (SIS) of fish, into homestead ponds.

The steps outlined below focus on the addition of SIS to an existing homestead pond. The steps were developed through research and trials with Mola in Bangladesh. Some modifications may be needed to adapt the practice for other SIS.

Figure 1. Nutrition-sensitive homestead pond of a farmer in Sadar Upazila, Dinajpur District, Bangladesh © WorldFish/Utpal Chakraborty

Figure 2. The micronutrient-rich small fish Mola © WorldFish/Utpal Chakraborty

1. Sourcing, collection, and transportation of live small indigenous fish species (SIS)

A source for obtaining SIS must be identified. These species are rarely available in hatcheries, nurseries, or other aquaculture suppliers, and often must be collected from the wild. Attention must be paid to regulations for wild collection, and to prevent depletion of the natural population. This may require formal assessments of the natural population, especially during wet months. However, once the homestead culture system is established, many SIS breed and self-recruit within a short period. This homestead SIS supply can replace collection from the wild. Farmers may keep some of the SIS stock in the homestead pond from one production season to the next to continue production and may sell some stock to new farmers who wish to stock their ponds.

For Mola, guidelines have been developed on the sourcing, collection, and transport methods. This included developing a method of “acclimatization” critical to reduce mortality during transport from the sources for stocking, including over long distances. Like fry/fingerlings in nursery ponds, the acclimatization of Mola include application of feed and frequent netting and release of the fish in the same pond. For collection of bulk amount from the source (e.g. culture pond) ‘acclimatization’ is carrying out by stocking mola in a pond separately from other species of fish by frequent netting and adding supplementary feed.

Regarding the transport of live Mola from source [4], various types of containers and transportation devices can be used. It includes:

  • open tank system, such as placing fish and water in a pick-up bed lined with a polythene sheet to transport up to 50 km distance,
  • closed tank system, such as containers with oxygen cylinders to transport long distances >50 km, and
  • aluminium containers set up in bicycle, rickshaw van or motorized vehicle used for short distance transport.

Figure 3. Transport of live Mola in different distances using aluminum containers © WorldFish/Utpal Chakraborty 

Figures 4. Open tank system in pick-up van © WorldFish/Utpal Chakraborty                             

Figure 5. Closed tank system with oxygen cylinder © WorldFish/Utpal Chakraborty

2. Stocking live SIS into the homestead pond

Pre-stocking management often includes draining of the pond, removal of vegetation, removal of bottom mud, dike repairing, removal of predatory fish and aquatic animals, application of lime, filling the pond with water, application of organic and inorganic fertilizers and testing of natural feed.

Stocking procedure of carp, tilapia and other species for polyculture begins with identifying species of fish that are readily produced and a good source of income, such as carps and tilapia. Although the optimum stocking densities may vary under local conditions to get good production, the usual carp-tilapia-mola polyculture in homestead ponds use the following stocking density (Table below):

Some farmers do polyculture of Mola in small homestead ponds connected to rice fields to get higher fish production. For this, dikes in rice fields are raised to protect from flooding and escape of fish. When stocked in ponds connected to rice fields, fish can move to rice field areas and eat insects, weeds and other natural feeds available in the rice fields.

Post-stocking management often includes application of feed, fertilization, monitoring growth performance and health status of fish and maintaining the water supply in pond.

3. Facilitating breeding in the pond

SIS breeding biology can differ from species to species. A good understanding of the breeding basics for the species in use is important to ensure production in the pond.

For Mola, there is a self-recruitment, breeding within the pond, two or three peak periods for breeding, but largely asynchronous breeding and a presence of mature mola found throughout the production season. Mola fry take about three or four months to mature.

Figure 6. Adult and juvenile Mola with carp observed during netting in carp-mola polyculture pond of farmer in Dhulia Beel community in Sadar Upazila, Nilphamari District, Bangladesh © WorldFish/Manos Kumar Saha

Adding small indigenous fish species (SIS) like Mola to homestead ponds fill production and supply gaps of fish to the household. Often there is a gap period (three to four months) between harvesting and stocking of carp and other species of fish in ponds. During this gap period, SIS such as Mola broodstock remain in the pond, continue breeding, and improve the efficiency of conversion of pond resources to fish production. 

4. Harvesting SIS from the homestead pond

Figure 7 and 8. Mola harvest from pond using seine net by fishing team in Dhulia Beel community in Sadar Upazila, Nilphamari District, Bangladesh © WorldFish /Utpal Chakraborty

Regular harvest ensures higher production of SIS in the homestead pond. For Mola, it is recommended to harvest them from the ponds using seine nets every 15 or 30 days. Regular intervals of netting also help to “acclimatized” the fish and reduce mortality during netting. Small size grader nets can be used to separate mola and other SIS from the larger fish, and also to save the floating eggs/larvae/very small fish and avoid stress, ensuring continued good production and follow-on harvests.

Figure 9. Use of grader net by members of fishing team to separate mola and other SIS from large fish and to avoid stress during harvesting.

Use of gill nets to harvest Mola and other SIS from ponds allow harvest without having to enter the pond. This technique is very useful to harvest fish for regular household consumption. The homestead pond fish culture approach is particularly important for women’s empowerment in the production practice [6].

5. Conserving and transporting SIS broodstock from homestead ponds

Broodstock of Mola and other SIS can be conserved in the pond as stock for continuing production starting right from the beginning of the production season in the following years. There is no need to restock the ponds every year, provided the pond is perennial (i.e., it contains water year-round).

Due to regular netting in the ponds for partial harvests, the broodstock available in the ponds are “acclimatized” and less vulnerable to stress during netting. The ponds thus become a very good source of broodstock (or seed) to propagate in other ponds. This SIS can be collected and transported live, even long distances, for stocking in new ponds.  

If the pond dries up, the SIS broodstock can be conserved for a short period by transferring it to a ditch or depression within the pond.

6. Nutrition education

To ensure the nutritional benefits of the SIS are received, it is important to raise awareness on nutrition-sensitive methods for processing, cooking, and consuming SIS. Children under 2 years of age, pregnant or lactating mothers, and adolescent girls of poor and very poor households suffering from micronutrient-based malnutrition can especially benefit from nutrition-sensitive SIS preparation.

The importance of preparing SIS 1) whole/entirely, without removing any part, 2) with other ingredients to enhance micronutrient bioavailability, and 3) in a way that is safe and palatable for young children to eat, can be shared among household members, village caretaker groups, and/or disseminated more broadly to communities through governmental and non-governmental agencies.

Figures 10 and 11.  Mola processing for preparation of a recipe called “Kitchuri” (mixed with mola paste, other ingredients like red spinach, onion, pulses and others) useful even by minor children in a community in Parbatipur Upazila, Dinajpur District, Bangladesh © WorldFish /Utpal Chakraborty

Figure 12. Mola after processing, cooked mola and children eating “Kitchuri” mixed with mola paste, other ingredients like red spinach, onion, pulses and others © WorldFish /Manos Kumar Saha

7. Validation of the practice

Nutrition-sensitive homestead ponds have been implemented by farmers in Bangladesh since 2010 with 1500 households located in Rangpur and Dinajpur Districts in North-West region Bangladesh under the IFAD funded Small Fish and Nutrition Project of WorldFish. Afterwards, the practice was promoted to thousands of farmers located throughout the country under CSISA-BD, BANA, CRS, Ecopond, CALIP and CREL projects of WorldFish, Winrock International, DoF and NGOs.

Under the Blue Gold funded project of WorldFish, around 4000 women in Khulna and Patuakhali Districts in southern Bangladesh adopted SIS based nutrition-sensitive fish culture using the ‘Ecopond’ approach [5].  In recent years, under the EU and FCDO funded Suchana program, more than 60,000 women of poor and very poor well-being categories in Sylhet and Moulvibazar Districts in North-East Bangladesh adopted this nutrition-sensitive ‘carp-tilapia-Mola polyculture’ in small homestead ponds.  

Department of Fisheries in Bangladesh built on the successful practice to establish a “Mola village” in Northwestern Bangladesh as part of a dissemination program. Following the success of the practice in Bangladesh, it has been adapted for use in Cambodia, Myanmar, Nepal, and Assam and Odisha in India.

The practice has been carried out primarily in rainfed rice agroecosystems, both lowland and upland areas. Many of the areas are experience periodic flooding and/or drought. The most productive growing period for SIS tends to be during the wet season, when natural signals are present to induce reproduction. The homestead pond practice has been carried out under individual management initiated with support from government extension services and/or non-governmental technical support. The practice most often targets small-scale landholders, but can also be conducted by other groups, such as landless and/or women’s groups under a collective management scheme (e.g. low land rice fields/floodplains). The practice was trialed in community approaches with ponds or other small water bodies managed by community-based organizations (e.g. rice-fields in low land areas/floodplains) during wet months.

8. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Pond area is usually between 200 m2 and 2000 m2, but may be larger. Water depth is usually 1.5 to 2.0 m and ideally should be present throughout the year.

The minimum necessary conditions include pond holds water for at least 5-6 months (seasonal) with access to a source of mola to obtain as live for stocking. A perennial pond is more useful to get good production. Finally, best results are obtained from ponds with sandy loam or loamy soil. 

The knowledge about the wild mola source at the initial stage of promotion, the integration of mola and other SIS with carp and overall management with major emphasis on regular harvesting are important to get success. 

Limiting factors to nutrition-sensitive homestead pond success includes; complete flooding of the pond, less interest of farmers to do the regular harvests of SIS required for successful production, less interest to stock SIS or Mola at the initial stage of pond establishment, or insufficient conservation of SIS stock to continue sufficient production in following years. 

9. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool
  • Tropics, warm.

Initially the Nutrition-sensitive fish culture with the SIS ‘Mola’ introduced in the northwest region, the area with seasonal ponds and pond connected rice fields, later it has been disseminated throughout Bangladesh covering all the regions including the Hill Tracts in ponds with fresh waters. 

10. Related/Associated Technologies

  • Rice-fish Culture System (RFC): ID 8732.
  • Fish pond layout and construction: ID 4384.
  • Management of flood control, drainage and irrigation (FCDI) sluice gates: ID 4479.
  • Small fish-based fish chutney production: ID 10072.
  • Complex Rice Systems, Indonesia: ID 10104.

entries.summary:
Complex rice systems (CRSs) are integrated agricultural systems that combine azolla (aquatic ferns), fish, ducks and border plants into rice production systems to augment ecological processes of nutrient recycling, weed and pest suppression, and replace agrochemicals that are harmful to human, animals and environment. Moreover, CRSs could foster ecosystem services of diverse food and nutrition provisioning, reconciling the importance of safeguarding food and nutrition security while protecting the environment at the same time.

Benefits: The complex integrated rice-fish systems are expected to work as much as possible as an autonomous cycle to reduce external inputs. For example, growing azolla and border plants can also be used to fed fish and ducks. Fish and ducks can also suppress weeds and pests and enhance nutrient recycling.

How: Complex rice systems can be implemented in lowland rice agroecosystems by adding rice, fish, ducks and border crops to rice fields.
entries.description:
Description

The steps for Complex Rice Systems (CRS) were developed through on-farm research in Indonesia. These steps are briefly described below and outlined in detail in the below further readings [1 to 5].

Figure 1. CRS implementation in different rice agroecosystems. Top-left, a CRS on technical irrigation of silty sand soil. Top-right, a CRS on semi-technical clayey-silty calcareous soil. Bottom-left, CRS on rainfed of heavy clay soil. Bottom-right, early rice growth with fish-pond constructed next to rice field.  © Photo credit: University of Brawijaya/Uma Khumairoh

1. Site selection

1.1 Soil characteristics

Soil characteristics determine the difficulty level (challenge) for CRS establishment that involves widened rice bunds to grow diverse plant species and thus affecting labour costs. For example, widening rice bunds to grow border plants, a place for duck to rest and to maintain water for fish in CRSs, would be quicker to establish on silt-clayey soil than on silty and silty sand soils. Rice bund extension is made by raising adjacent soil along existed rice bunds which usually in the form of mud. Silty-clay soil mud can be formed easily using a hoe and can dry simultaneously and quickly to form a stable wider bund while silty and silty-sand mud is loose and less stable, and thus raising mud cannot be made quickly as they easily slide down: the work needs to be done repeatedly to form a stable bund. Thus, labour cost is usually higher in that silty and silty sand soils. Furthermore, soil properties also influence costs on making trenches and fish-ponds in CRSs. Water in pond made in sandy and porous calcareous soils can easily leak during early stage of trench and pond establishment, unless waterproof sheets are installed on ponds’ wall sides.

1.2 Irrigation systems

Despite CRSs integrate fish, rice fields are not necessarily continuously flooded. CRSs can be implemented on non-continuously flooded fields, and even on rainfed rice systems using the following design:

  • Construct fish refuges and pond next to the rice fields.
  • The pond or fish refuge can be made by deepening areas next to rice field, with or without field border.
  • If duck is also integrated, field border can reduce soil on rice field area fall to the pond or refuges due to duck movement.
  • The field border can be constructed from bamboo stem or simply rising soil as bund.
  • When a bund is chosen as the border, a gate must be created to connect pond and rice field, assuring movement of fish to rice field and the pond or refuges.
  • With connecting gates to the rice fields, drying and wetting rice field can be arranged according to the needs of rice. At certain periods, drying conditions are good for rice to increase soil oxygen that boosts rice root growth and development in order to optimally uptake available nutrients to rice plants. Hence, product diversification can be made without losing rice yields.

1.3 Rice bund dimensions

Rice bunds are important territory for beneficial organisms having life cycle depending on both aquatic and terrestrial habitats, such as dragonflies and damselflies. Growing border plants on those bunds will provide food and favourable habitats for those beneficial organisms. Therefore, wide rice bunds give flexibilities to grow diverse plants and to attract and protect beneficial organisms. Intensive monoculture rice production systems usually maintain its rice bunds to less than 30 cm in width, while in CRS, it is suggested to have rice bunds of at least 50 cm in width. This suggests that initial capital for rice bund re-constructions is required to those with narrow rice bunds.

1.4 Local resources

The purpose of integrating diverse species into rice agroecosystems is to create and manage an agro-ecological habitat that provides ecosystems functions of nutrient cycling, weed and pest suppression, so that external inputs can be reduced while also selecting and increasing the number of edible and marketable species, thus contributing to nutrition diversity. Therefore, the selection and integration of a specific specie (fish, duck or plant) should take into account its adaptabilities and availability, considering the environmental, social, economic and cultural situation of the location.

1.5 Market

Market consideration could be the criteria of species selections: if the outputs (edible or not) of the CRS system have a high market acceptability, then there is a higher chance to continue the farming system. This will also compensate for the effort of establishing it and in recouping the required initial investment. It will also promote the main streaming of CRSs in similar food production landscapes in other communities.

2. Plot preparation

2.1 Rice bunds and border plants

Rice bunds is an important element in CRS, as habitat to augment ecological processes, thus to provide ecosystem services by diversifying rice cropping system with border plants. At least 50 cm in width should be allocated for the rice bunds to grow at least one plant species besides rice.

To reduce labour inputs, rice bunds should be prepared when soil is not too muddy, preferably at ripening rice stage, to establish CRS in the following cropping cycle after harvesting. In this stage, soil is still humid but not too muddy. Early preparation gives sufficient time for soil to form strong and wide bunds to be planted for the following cropping season.

When rice is harvested and that first ploughing has been done (usually two ploughings are performed, the first plough to turn the soil so that weeds are buried and the second time is to make the soil muddy and ready to be planted with rice), border plants should be planted immediately to build favourable habitat for beneficial organisms. These organisms will protect rice plants against its enemies/pests when rice seedlings have been transplanted on the field. Border plant selection will depend on the agroecological condition and farm objectives (focused on legume if the purpose is to obtain green manure or forage roots; or focused on food crops if the objective is to harvest food to be consumed or sell).

2.2 Trenches

Trenches are important elements in CRS, not only to provide favourable habitat and refuge for fish, but also as a path to guide fish to swim to find refuges in a deeper water level area (such as ponds). Moreover, when the water level in crop field is lowered, trenches also play a role in draining water for oxygen supply to the soil. The construction of trenches can be done straight along the rice bund inside the rice field, or diagonally. Ideally, in CRS, trenches are integrated with jajar legowo cultivation method, which is explained in the following section.

Figure 2. Trenches in CRS implementation. Top-left, wide trench in CRS with maize in the background to be fed to fish. Top-right, a farmer catches fish in a trench of CRS. Bottom-left, trenches with jajar legowo system. Bottom-right, trenches with jajar legowo system and aquatic plants as fish feed. © Photo credit: University of Brawijaya/Uma Khumairoh

2.3 Fish pond/ refuges

Good and sufficient water is essential for the life of fish in CRSs. In fully technical rice irrigation systems, water availability may not be a concern, but can be a constraint in semi and non-technical irrigation rice systems. Therefore, fish-ponds that are connected to rice field (with gates) or other types of fish refuges must be well prepared and ready before rice is planted.

This fish-ponds in semi, non-technical irrigation and rainfed CRSs act as refuges for fish during dry period and probably even could be the water resource in the rainfed systems, especially for emergency situation when rain falls unexpectedly due to climate changes. On this agroecological condition, ponds need to be constructed next to the rice field with a channel/gate connected to the rice fields. For a successful pond construction, soil structure and texture must be taken into account, especially during the first CRS cropping cycle in which water could easily run or leak, leaving the ponds. Installation of waterproof sheet might be needed on calcareous, porous and sandy soil to prevent running and losing of water.

Figure 3. Planting rice with wider space in jajar legowo system. Top-left, construction of fish pond at the edge of rice fields. Top-right, adult fish released on rice fields and trenches before rice transplantation to allow them matting and produce fingerlings Bottom-left, fish pond connected to rice field through a gate. Bottom right, adult fish on rice field during rice growing stage. © Photo credit: University of Brawijaya/Uma Khumairoh

2.4 Duck house and duck welfare

Rice fields with ducks should be fenced to prevent movement of ducks between plots when a concentration of a certain function, such as weeding, is needed on a certain plot. After weeding was performed by ducks, they can either be released without fence or are moved and fenced in other plots to perform the same function as weeding labour.

On the rice fields, some infrastructures, such as duck houses and dry areas, are needed for ducks to rest at any time after grazing or scavenging on rice fields. These dry areas could be constituted with rice bunds and heaped straw. A duck house can be easily constructed from bamboo and rice straw or from other materials placed nearby rice bunds.

Figure 4. Ducks in CRS. Top-left, two-weeks-old ducklings were released on a rice field a week after rice seedling transplantation. Top-right, duck house construction using straw and bamboo. Bottom-left, two-months-old ducks released at almost two-months rice after transplantation. Bottom-right, adult ducks on rice field after rice harvesting to eat fallen rice grain. © Photo credit: University of Brawijaya/Uma Khumairoh

3. Rice planting

3.2 Selected System of Rice Intensification (SRI) method

Rice Plants were seeded at a rate of 20 kg per ha. To reduce plant competition on nursery and to enhance the development of the roots, seedlings should be transplanted not more than 12 days after germination, having the 2–3 leaf stage. The rice seedlings are then planted on hills with a planting distance of at least 25×25 cm2, which is wider than the common spacing that are less than 20×20 cm. The number of rice seedlings is less than three per hill to reduce competition. Meanwhile, intermittent irrigation is suggested during the early stages of rice growth and after 45 Days After Transplanting (DAT), the crop might be continuously flooded until two weeks before rice harvesting.

3.1 Jajar Legowo

Besides the selected System of Rice Intensification (SRI) method of implementation, the cultivation method of jajar legowo is ideally performed in CRSs, especially with the ducks. Jajar legowo is originated from Javanese words, "jajar” means a straight row, “lego” means wide and “wo” is a short word of “dowo” means long. Therefore, “Jajar legowo” defines as a rice-planting method on straight rows where one out of certain plant rows (two to five rows) remains empty (creating wider space). This empty row allows a better sunlight penetration and facilitates easier plant management. Several trenches could be made on those empty rows in addition to trenches surrounding rice planting rows, for fish’ and ducks’ accessibility to both water areas and rice fields.

Figure 5. Planting rice with wider space in jajar legowo system. Left, planting rice seedlings. Right, an empty row in the jajar legowo method. © Photo credit: University of Brawijaya/Uma Khumairoh

4. Azolla

4.1 Nursery

Azolla is palatable for many animals and insect pests. Therefore, without proper maintenance, azolla can easily disappear from rice fields, especially with a low inoculation rate. Therefore, keeping azolla on nursery ponds is recommended to assure that the inoculant would always be available when re-inoculation on rice field is needed.

The nursery can be simply made on the fish pond that is separated from fish area with net fish to prevent overfeeding by fish. A separated narrow-shallow pond, approximately 1 m in width and 10-20 m in length with only 5 cm height of water level can be created for this special azolla nursery. The maintenance of azolla on this nursery is easier than those on rice fields. Pest can be easily controlled by monitoring pest incidences on azolla surface. A systematic pest control can be done by spraying Neem solution every week on top of azolla cover, or when there is symptom of insect pest attack. On this nursery, azolla patches infected by snails and insect can also be easily spotted, so they can be picked using a sieve and then fed to fish or ducks. Hence, azolla grazing by those enemies can be stopped or reduced.

In this nursery, azolla can be harvested every 10 days to be fed to animals or to be composted when azolla on rice fields is well develop and does not require re-inoculation.

4.2 Azolla inoculation/ planting on rice field

On rice fields, azolla is inoculated at a minimum rate of 2000 kg/ha. The azolla growth can be stimulated by manure or mineral fertilizers equal to 2.8 kg/ha of phosphorous fertilizer per week. Azolla can be immediately inoculated on rice field a week or even earlier after rice transplanting. Azolla must be inoculated at a certain point, preferably nearby rice bund where azolla roots can hold soil in large colonies at optimal water requirement to prevent its movement across rice field by the wind. Azolla prefers to grow in slow-moving water. Aerators will create current patterns in the water body, disrupting azolla growth. Furthermore, the added oxygen will accelerate the decomposition process of azolla.

5. Introduction of fish

Fish that are commonly raised on rice field are spotted barb, gourami, snakehead, catfish, eels, carps, tilapia and shrimps. Having fish pond connected to rice field provides favourable refuges for early adaptation to rice agroecosystem even before rice seedling transplantation. As soon as rice is transplanted, gates and/or channels that connect pond to the rice fields can be opened, allowing fish to swim to rice field when water level is sufficient. The size of fish integrated can range from fingerling or adult form. For fingerling Nile tilapia (10 cm length, ca. 30 g per fish), they are commonly released at a minimum rate of 5 000 – 10 000 per hectare. Meanwhile for adult fish (5.5 months old and about 200 g per fish) will only need 500 kg per hectare, because within a week, the eggs can be produced and hatched. Fingerlings that hatched on the rice field could immediately adapt to the environment, which is a crucial factor for successful fish production in CRSs.

6. Duck introduction

Indian (Indonesian local) runner ducks (Anasplatyrhynchos Javanicus) can be herded on rice field either during the whole period of vegetative rice stage or at a certain period of rice growth such as only during the weeding.

If the ducks are intentionally raised on the rice fields for the whole vegetative rice stage, appropriate duck houses need to be placed on rice field. Duck houses should be constructed on the bund as a place to rest. The duck house can be made from bamboo, straw or waterproof sheets. Leftover rice straw can also be heaped nearby the duck house as a place to play which later can be quickly composted as fertilizer for rice. In this case, ducks at a rate of 400 per hectare is an ideal density. Supplementary feeding must also be supplied to the ducks at a rate of 75–150 g per animal per day, depending on the body weight. Feed can partly be bought, consisting of dried fish, rice brand, corn, and dried leftover cooked rice mixtures. This also can be produced on-farm by mixing azolla and rice bran with forage crops such as sun hemp and corn which are grown on the rice bund and only bought dried fish and dried rice when necessary, due to high stock density. 

However, if the purpose of duck integration is specially to control weeds for a certain period of days (5- 10 days), duck housing may not be essential, but dried areas remain required as a place for the ducks to rest, including portable roof that can be made from a cheap waterproof sheet. With this system, duck density can be doubled and even tripled, but the straight rice rows must be assured. These straight rows will guide duck flocks walk in empty rows, preventing them trampling on rice plants as they run straight up (they are called as “runner ducks”). Supplied feed per duck might also be needed with increased duck density, since natural food such as insects, crabs, snails, weed, azolla and others may also be quickly limited with higher duck density.

7. Plot maintenance

Due to wide range of species integrated, maintenance is not only given to the rice plants but also to other species, including border plants on rice bunds, fish, azolla and ducks.

7.1 Azolla

Azolla is multiplied every 7-14 days. Hence fertilization equal to 2.8 kg phosphorous per ha every seven days is required. Azolla also need to be monitored every week to check pest infestation in order to make rapid control either manually by taking the pests or infested patched or by spraying azolla surface with natural insecticides such as Neem concentration.

Figure 6. Azolla inoculation, introduction and maintenance in CRS. Top-left, azolla is being taken from nursery to be released on rice field. Top-right, azolla is released on fish pond connected to rice field without border plants. Bottom-left, azolla is released on fish pond connected to rice field with border plants. Bottom-right, azolla on rice field covers water and soil surface. © Photo credit: University of Brawijaya/Uma Khumairoh

7.2 Border plants

Maintenance to border plants includes fertilization, pest control, putting climbing trellis and pruning, depending on what type of plants grown as border plants. As the purposes of integrating border plants are to create habitat for natural enemies of crops’ pests as well as providing ecosystem services, the use of harmful chemicals is prohibited. Instead, the use of organic fertilizers is encouraged during early plant growth, but later, ducks may also excrete their feces on rice bunds when they are resting on it. Thus, these feces play a role as fertilizers to the border plants. Weed management is normally also not required since duck will feed and tramp on it. However, monthly cutting and drying border plants as forage and green manure may be needed either to be fed to animals or incorporated to soil. For example, in some studies, sun hemp was grown on rice bunds as the border plants. Later, this sun hemp rows were cut every month to be integrated to the soil as green manure for rice plants. These sun hemps were also cut to be mixed with duck feed. Fresh sun hemps are also palatable for fish, and thus can be harvested every day to be fed to fish.

7.3 Fish

Maintenance of fish in this CRSs is similar to the one in fish culture, including feeding, pest and predator control as well as pond and trenches care. Based on previous study, fish was not fed with supplementary feed but they only eat spilled-over duck feed, azolla, sun hemp leaves and dropped plant biomass. However, if the density increases, then indeed, supplementary feed will be needed, either by adding azolla taken from the nursery, cutting sun hemp and supplying rice bran.

Predator must also be prevented and controlled, for example by burying raccoon feces in order to prevent other raccoons to come. Improper temperature, water quality and stress can cause rot fin which are commonly found on fish during early introduction to rice fields. Based on farmer experiences, this can be prevented and cured using papaya leaves and managing border plant along the trenches to provide shade.

Trenches and ponds must also be carefully managed, especially when the soil slide to the trenches. Thus, raising the mud is needed to maintain proper water level and favourable environment for fish. Similarly, pond wall and rice bund wall also need to be checked whether crabs nested on it or not which later can build holes and make water out-flow from the trenches and ponds.

7.4 Ducks

Protection of ducks from extremes in weather conditions and predators (mongoose) could be enhanced by facilitating clean and dry sheltered area as well as traps or good protected stable. Although ducks can spend most of their time outdoors, on ponds or in wet areas, they require a clean dry sheltered area where they can retreat, rest, clean and performed other natural behaviors. Feed diversity from nature and sufficient nutritious supplementary feed are essential for production of both meat and eggs. This proper diet and environment are crucial to enable them to perform their natural behavior and to protect them from diseases.

8. Harvesting and repreparing the plot

8.1 Azolla

On rice field, azolla will die when rice canopy cover water and soil surface. Dead azolla will be decomposed and mineralized and will released nutrients for rice. Therefore, harvesting azolla is not needed on the rice fields. On the other hand, harvesting may be needed in the azolla nursery either for feed or for green manure every 10-14 days. Sediment in azolla nursery may also need to be lifted and used as fertilizers before or after rice harvesting.

8.2 Border plants

Harvesting border plants depends on the type of the plants. They might be harvested earlier, during or after the rice, or even continuously during several rice cropping cycles. For example, sun hemp can produce its biomass up to two years, during which monthly harvesting can also be performed. As feed, sun hemp can immediately be mixed with duck feed or distributed on pond or rice field for feeding fish.

8.3 Fish

Fish can be sold for fingerlings, for human consumption (table-fish) or for spawning from this CRSs. Fish culture in CRSs depends on the availability of water and depth of water in the rice field. Fish ponds with trenches as refuges enable fish to take shelter for longer durations. Therefore, not only fish can be reared and harvested from fry to fingerlings or from hatchlings to fry, but it would be also possible to extend the rearing period for several years.

8.4 Ducks

With a low density, ducks could be kept on rice fields, even when the rice plants are growing flowers and grain. But in high density of more than 200 ducks per hectare, they must be herded in other younger rice plantation or fenced in their duck houses. They might be sold during this period, but they can also be kept aside during rice grain filling and then released back to the field after rice harvesting and before rice transplanting periods for the following cropping cycle. By that time, at 155 days, they will already be able to produce eggs, so the price will be higher as they can be sold as egg layer ducks. Those adult ducks can also be continuously raised to produce eggs for several years.

9. Validation of the practice

Complex Rice Systems have been tested by farmers in Indonesia during the participatory learning organized with multi-stakeholders, involving University of Brawijaya (Indonesia), Wageningen University (the Netherlands), local authorities (village officers) and agricultural agencies in districts of Malang, Lamongan, Blitar and Pasuruan. The participatory learning employed Farmer Field School (FFS) method. The number of participants was 20-25 farmers per FFS in each district. The FFSs were constructed for three cropping cycles on-farms ranging from 1,800 to 10,000 m2 to allow CRS adjustments to the local conditions, while collecting indigenous knowledge for adaptation and learning processes. All this resulting to various combinations of plant and animal species according to local specialties. Those participatory learning were funded by NUFFIC (the Netherlands) and Nestle Foundation (Switzerland) and currently the implementation on the landscape scale is being performed through PK-KM DIKTI (Ministry of Research and Higher Education, Indonesia) programme to encourage students working with communities and practitioners to acquire them into workplace environment to build personal and professional lives which overall improves the quality of education.

The practice has been carried out under technical and semi-technical conditions as well as rainfed rice production systems from heavily clayey, clay-silt, to sandy soils. Besides, the practice has been carried out under variable weather conditions, from normal to extreme weather conditions (e.g., of prolonged wet and dry seasons. The replication of CRS to agroforestry is also to be put into agenda to provide options for nomadic farmers living in the forest areas for better agricultural management, land productivity and for forest and environment protection

10. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Establishment of CRS requires habitat that allows different species to occupy different spaces. Increasing rice bunds is essential to provide habitat for more aquatic and terrestrial species. Although indeed, initial investment is important, it must not be a burden: farmer should consider that at later level this CRS practice will improve their awareness on environment while improving and conserving productivity. Meanwhile, various biophysical conditions would allow adaptation of CRSs in those specific locations.

Limiting factors to CRS’s success include the following trade-offs:

  • Long-term productive systems vs. infrastructure investment: current rice system is designed for monoculture with very narrow rice bunds, no trenches, no ponds and thus in the early CRS establishment, those infrastructures need to be constructed which could be high labour inputs.
  • Long-term labour reduction vs. short term labour burden: although azolla, duck and fish integration significantly reduced weeds and thus weeding labour, labour investment is needed, contributing to short term labour burden in the early establishment.
  • Resilient systems vs. knowledge investment: despite significant contribution in boosting rice productivity, modern agriculture has considerably replaced traditional knowledge. But the traditional knowledge is still useful and can be combined with current/modern knowledge to benefit reliable yields while protecting environment and cultural biodiversity. Therefore, investment on knowledge to share information and improve farmers’ and communities’ awareness is crucial.
  • Food and income diversity vs. initial capital: integrating diverse species in CRS increases initial production costs but will quickly be compensated with diverse food production and income, as they are edible and marketable.
  • Allocating all transformation processes in the early phase of CRS establishment might even distract farmer’s focus from producing rice to only preparing the CRS infrastructure.

Nonetheless, solutions to alleviate this trade-off are existing such as the step-by-step approach described in this document.

11. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

entries.summary: Honeybee viruses are important threats for honeybee health. However, there are no effective agents to prevent and control honeybee viruses. In association with the proper Varroa management and control, a suitable thermal insulation of the beehive and keeping the beehive dry and insulated can reduce the outbreak and development of viral diseases. This information sheet explains how simple basic beekeeping management practices can prevent and control honeybee (Apis mellifera and Apis cerana) viruses.
entries.description:
Description

This technology explains how to readily prevent and control honeybee (Apis mellifera and Apis cerana) viruses by using beekeeping management techniques such as protecting beehives from low temperatures and humidity, two factors that can impact viral disease outbreak. We will present a few simple techniques that can help the beekeeper to maximize colony population and health.

1. Prevent and control bee viruses of A. mellifera

Among the 72 viruses so far identified in Apis mellifera, certainly at least five of them play a relevant role and pose a deadly threat to honeybees: the deformed wing virus (DWV), the black queen cell virus (BQCV), the Israeli acute paralysis virus (IAPV), the sacbrood virus (SBV), the acute bee paralysis virus (ABPV) and the chronic bee paralysis virus (CBPV). The management practices described here can prevent and/or reduce DWV, IAPV and CBPV. Especially for DWV and for IAPV, however, a proper treatment of Varroa destructor inhibiting the development of the mite in the colony and their visible impacts of varroa (e.g. presence of parasites on adult bees) are also a prerequisite for a proper virosis prevention.

The practices described here aim at reducing the impact of low temperatures and humidity on the colonies.

1.1 The major materials

Thermal insulation of hives can provide some protection of the colonies against cold and humid weather conditions. Hay, foam, cotton, fabric textile or similar materials can be used for external insulation of the beehives (Figure 1). For shading or keeping beehives dry, several materials are available, such as wood (Figure 2) and greaseproof paper.

Figure 1. Hive insulated with hay.

© Bee Health Committee of Apicultural Science Association of China /Hongxia Zhao

Figure 2. Hive protected with a wooden cover.

© Bee Health Committee of Apicultural Science Association of China /Hongxia Zhao

1.2 When we need to use this measure to prevent and control of honeybee viruses

CBPV usually occurs in spring and is characterized by the following signs in the adult bees: trembling of the wings and bodies, bloated abdomen, inability to fly, crawling on the ground and upward on grass in front of the hive entrance, “black robbers” (hairless -thus appearing smaller-, darker, greasy, shiny bees) that die within five or six days in front of the colony. DWV and IAPV frequently occur at the end of autumn, and are characterized by malformation, especially of the wings and paralysis. All the virosis here mentioned are triggered by bad weather conditions with high humidity and sudden drops in temperature.

In order to prevent and control these viral diseases in regions with four seasons, the beekeeper should keep an eye on the weather forecast and take the following actions:

  1. If temperatures decrease by 3-6 degrees Celsius:  place cotton textile inside of cover of beehive (Figure 4).
  2. If the temperature decreases by 8-10 degree Celsius, then take the second step; take hay or foam or other similar material to wrap the whole beehive (Figure 5).
  3. Ensure the back of the hive is slightly higher than the front (hive entrance) so that water that might have entered the hive flows out.  Bricks or small stones can be used for this. 

For the regions with tropical or subtropical climate, to help the bees with the thermal regulation of the hive, a dish with water provided with stones or other floating material (e.g. parts of wood or polystyrene) to avoid bees from drowning can be placed near the hive. The beekeeper should ensure the hives have enough clean water at all times.

For regions with high humidity, hives should be placed on stands elevated at least 10 cm from ground (Figure 6).

If the weather is really hot, a wood cover that is bigger than the surface of the hive can be placed above the hive (Figure 6) to protect it from the sun.

Usually, big efforts and constant monitoring activity is needed by beekeepers to perform an optimal Varroa control, reducing the incidence of virosis. In order to keep the varroa mite level infestation under safety levels to prevent virosis, we suggest interrupting the egg laying of the queen at least once or, even better, twice a year, so that the varroa life cycle is interrupted before the low environmental impact acaricide treatment is applied to maximize  its miticide efficacy. One is carried out before the spring reproduction and the other at the end of summer.

It is a good practice to disinfect or sterilize under the sun or with fire all beehives at the beginning of each spring (Figure 3) before populating them with new swarms or colonies.

Figure 3. Hives disinfection under sun.

© Bee Health Committee of Apicultural Science Association of China /Hongxia Zhao

Figure 4. Cotton insulation is placed under the cover of the hive when temperatures drop by 3-6 degrees Celsius.

© Bee Health Committee of Apicultural Science Association of China /Hongxia Zhao

Figure 5. Hives can be wrapped with hay for thermal insulation.

© Bee Health Committee of Apicultural Science Association of China /Hongxia Zhao

2. Prevention and control of bee viruses of A. cerana

A. cerana is affected by fewer viruses than A. mellifera. Usually, A. cerana infecting virus is associated with low temperature and humidity. But A. cerana has the ability to tolerate better than Apis mellifera low temperatures and varroosis.

2.1 The major materials

For thermal insulation, hay, foam, cotton or fabric textile can be used. For shading or to keep beehives dry, several materials are available, such as the wood and greaseproof paper. The materials are similar than those used to protect hives of A. mellfiera.

2.2 When we need to apply thermal insulation for the hives to prevent and control of viruses affecting A. cerana and A. mellifera

In regions with winters characterized by dry, cold weather, wrap the hive with hay when the temperature is near zero.  When temperatures go below zero, hives can be moved to a cellar for overwintering.  This strategy is used during winter in the North of China.

For regions with wet cold winters, the hives can be first be covered with cotton or hay (thermal insulation), and then wrapped with greaseproof paper (to protect the insulation from the rain). Stones or bricks can be used to keep the insulation in place.

To protect the hives from heat, a wooden cover can be placed on top of the hive when the temperature is above 35 degree (Figure 7). This strategy is used for colonies located in subtropical regions in China from June to September.

For regions with high humidity during summer (85 percent or more), scatter quick lime in the apiary according to the amount of 5 g per hive. Quick lime will absorb humidity. This method is used in subtropical regions in China from November to April.

Figure 6. Elevating hives as a strategy for protecting hives from humidity.

© Bee Health Committee of Apicultural Science Association of China /Hongxia Zhao

Figure 7.  Covering hives with wood as a strategy to protect hives from heat.

© Institute of Bast Fiber Crops, CAAS/ Hou Chunsheng

3. Validation of the practice

These management strategies were applied to several apiaries in different provinces in China, such as in Guangdong, Guangxi, Liaoning.

4. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Have beekeeping skills.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropical, warm, China all zones.

6. Related technologies

  • Bee viruses: ID 8419.
  • Varroa mites (Varroatosis or Varroosis): a parasitic disease of the brood and adult honeybees: ID 8416.
  • Main diseases of honey bees: ID 8412.
  • Strategy for integrated varroa management: healthier colonies through brood removal.

entries.summary:
A Community Fish Refuge (CFR) is an aquatic habitat designed as a refuge for wild fish that feed and spawn in rainfed rice fields. The CFR area includes a core conservation area and a buffer zone where fishing is not permitted. An entire pond or a small part of a large water body may be defined as the CFR core, with surrounding water or rice paddies defined as the buffer.

Benefits: The CFR best management practices can enhance agroecology, preserve agrobiodiversity, and benefit human food security, nutrition, and livelihoods, while also maintaining a multifunctional agricultural landscape and adapting to fluctuations in rainfall, floods, and dry periods.

How: A management plan is developed through community participation. Key items in the plan include creating a perennial refuge for fish in the ricefield landscape,  maintaining aquatic connectivity to allow fish to migrate between the refuge and nearby  rice paddies, and gender-inclusive governance, while additional practices may address nutritional and clean water needs of the community (details below).
entries.description:
Description

The steps for Community Fish Refuge (CFR) planning and management were developed during a two-phase pilot program in the Tonle Sap rice growing region of Cambodia. These steps are briefly described below and outlined in detail in Guidelines and a manual for good governance, the best management practices, and nutrition and gender sensitive interventions.

Figure 1. Small pond (top) and portion of a large water body (bottom) designated as Community Fish Refuges

© WorldFish

1. Site selection

  1. To gain understanding of the rice field fishery system and its context, conduct a desk review and consultation/participation from experts and stakeholders (farming families, community leaders, etc.). Well-functioning CFRs or habitats that are suitable as CFRs may be identified and can be used to develop criteria for site selection.
  2. Develop site selection criteria that include biophysical, social, economic, legal, and institutional aspects of the CFR and its surroundings. The potential criteria can be refined and validated through meetings with experts and stakeholders. General criteria for selecting a CFR site include: a perennial water body that has not dried out in the past five years (or that can be deepened to maintain at least 1.5 m water depth in the dry season) and is large enough to sustain biological production. The site should have good existing or potential connectivity to the rice field landscape, should be accessible to the community (not only the landowners) and should offer potential benefits, especially to poor members of the community. The community must be willing to make commitments and contributions to maintain the site through regular management activity, including willingness to form a CFR committee.
  3. Arrange participatory field visits to assess potential CFR sites against the selection criteria. Participants should include any potential partners such as community leaders and local authorities, government representatives, and NGO partners.
  4. Site selection should be finalized in a participatory manner. The site assessments and a tentative list of selected sites can be shared with participants and discussed to finalize site selection.

2. Needs assessment and action planning

Figure 2. Sample visioning exercise from a community workshop

© Try Vanvuth/WorldFish

  1. For the selected site, develop an “ideal scenario” of the CFR function, especially in terms of biophysical attributes. This can be done with consultation of experts and through stakeholder participation. A few key features of the ideal scenario include ensuring aquatic connectivity across the ricefield landscape, a perennial refuge for fish, and sustained community management of the refuge and fishery. A full description can be found in the CFR Guidelines and Manual (link below).
  2. Assess the CFR needs that will facilitate achievement of the ideal scenario. This process should be participatory, to collect data from key informants on both biophysical and management aspects of the CFR. If a management committee is already in place, a capacity assessment for management is also appropriate.
  3. To develop the action plan, Conduct workshops with community members and other stakeholders. These workshops should ensure representation of diverse community members and be facilitated in a way to ensure marginalized members are empowered to participate and provide input. Workshop facilitators will introduce the concepts related to CFR functions and management and can introduce the ideal scenario developed for the site. Exercises such as participatory mapping of resources can help to introduce concepts.
  4. The workshops begin with visioning, problem tree analysis, and stakeholder analysis exercises to provide participants with a foundation to build a realistic vision for the CFR function and management. Participants will identify actions to take towards the agreed upon vision. While the list of actions should be independent from the needs assessment developed in step 2.2., the facilitator may ensure all needs are considered through guiding questions. Finally, participants will develop a six-month action plan of action by prioritizing and selecting from the listed actions, then draw from the stakeholder analysis to identify who and what resources are available to ensure the plan is realized.
  5. Following the action plan, a plan for monitoring and evaluation (M&E) can be developed and baseline data can be collected. The M&E plan and data should enable participants to track the results of the selected management activities and the progress towards the CFR vision. If resources allow, the M&E plan and data collection can include assessment of the contribution of CFR management practices to food security and livelihoods.

3. Community and institutional interventions

Figure 3. CFR committee member presents annual workplan and achievements at a provincial reflection workshop

© Sarah Freed/WorldFish

  1. Awareness raising on the CFR system and the plans to improve CFR function and management is often needed at many levels, including with local authorities, fishers and farmers, water user groups, religious leaders and groups, and other community organizations. Awareness raising at community events and within schools can also be effective to reach many households in the community.
  2. Establishment and/or formalization of a CFR committee that is responsible for implementing the action plan is a critical component of CFR management. The process for committee member selection should be transparent and inclusive, such as through a voting system that involves the entire community. Facilitators can explain the importance of including diverse representation within the committee and it may be beneficial to set quotas for representation, for example to ensure that at least 30 percent of committee members are women.
  3. Capacity building for management will include training and coaching activities, not only for CFR committee members, but also for local authorities, NGO partners, and other key stakeholders. Follow-up workshops and networking with other committees can facilitate sustainability of the management process.

4. Environmental interventions

Figure 4. Left to right: excavation to deepen a CFR; installation of a water depth marker; installation of a brush park

© Sean Vichet/WorldFish

  1. Large-scale physical interventions, such as deepening areas of the CFR or adding outlets, spillways, or banks, should be planned and implemented as early as possible, as these can disrupt other biological interventions, such as planting along the CFR banks or stocking fish, if implemented later on. Additional interventions to prioritize for early implementation include delineating a buffer zone where fishing should not take place, installing a pole to mark water depth, and installing signage that clearly identifies the CFR.
  2. Interventions such as management of aquatic vegetation, planting to stabilize CFR banks and provide shade, installing brush parks, other substrates, fencing, and/or guarding facilities can be implemented following the large-scale interventions.
  3. Interventions can also be made outside of the CFR to improve its connectivity with the rice field landscape. This may include improvements to existing channels, installation of new channels, and installation of passages under roadways, fish ladders, or other features to improve migration routes for fish moving to and from the CFR.
  4. Water quality monitoring and recording inputs and effects from surrounding rice fields, such as application of pesticides, removal or addition of levees, can be done regularly to ensure the CFR environment is well maintained.

5. Diet, nutrition, and hygiene interventions

Figure 5. Cooking demonstration during caregiver training on nutrition and fish preparation

© Fani Llaurado/WorldFish

  1. To ensure that the improved CFR management and fishery production leads to better nutrition and health, good practices for food preparation (especially the preparation of small fish), food consumption (especially for children under five years of age), and water, sanitation and hygiene must also be encouraged. These practices can be disseminated through trainings with groups of community members. Our team targeted caregivers for children under five years of age, as the biggest nutritional gaps were for young children as well as pregnant and lactating mothers. Facilitators provided training and coaching on nutrition-sensitive fish preparation methods, recipes appropriate for young children, food safety, provision of clean drinking water, and household hygiene.
  2. Additional support for nutrition can be provided through vegetable gardening if access to CFR water for gardening is available. The garden may be located in nearby homestead plots, or on the CFR banks.

6. Drinking water intervention

Figure 6. Preparation for home delivery of drinking water from CFR water treatment facility

© Fani Llaurado/WorldFish

Some CFR sites may be appropriate locations to install facilities to treat water from the CFR and provide clean drinking water for nearby households. Our team worked with an organization that conducted a feasibility and market assessment to determine where treatment facilities could be installed and sustained through small entrepreneurship. At selected sites, the organization installed the water treatment facility and supported an entrepreneur in running the treatment facility and conducting business. The entrepreneur and CFR committee worked together to ensure sustainable use of CFR water, support for the CFR committee activities, and accessibility from the water treatment facility for water distribution throughout the community.

7. Validation of the practice

The CFR best management practices have been tested by farmer-fishers at 140 sites in four provinces of the Tonle Sap region of Cambodia: Battambang, Pursat, Kampong Thom, and Siem Reap.

CFR management is a perennial activity, while each best management practice may be carried out during a specific season, as indicated in the detailed manual and guidelines.

The environmental and climatic conditions of the Tonle Sap region is rainfed subtropical.

8. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The CFR practice requires a fair amount of aquatic connectivity across the ricefield landscape as well as a natural population of fish that will use the CFR habitat.

In terms of legal and tenure aspects, the success of a CFR can depend on its formal recognition. Standardized procedures to obtain legal standing and secure bylaws can ensure legitimacy for the CFR function and management.

Water demands in the area should be considered, such as whether irrigation practices will allow flow to the CFR as needed, and whether water will be conserved in the CFR or will be regularly drained for other uses.

General criteria for selecting a CFR site include: a perennial water body that has not dried out in the past five years (or that can be deepened to maintain at least 1.5 m water depth in the dry season) and is large enough to sustain biological production. The site should have good existing or potential connectivity to the rice field landscape, should be accessible to the community (not only the land owners) and should offer potential benefits, especially to poor members of the community. The community must be willing to make commitments and contributions to maintain the site through regular management activity, including willingness to form a CFR committee.

9. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

10. Related/Associated Technologies

  • Rice-fish Culture System (RFC): ID 8732 .
  • Fish pond layout and construction: ID 4384 
  • Management of flood control, drainage and irrigation (FCDI) sluice gates: ID 4479.
  • Management guidelines for Asian floodplain river fisheries ID 4477.

entries.title: The creation of winter fodders reserves stocks and the improvement of animal feed systems using halophytes
entries.source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)

agrovoc_keywords.display: Animal feeding#Alimentation des animaux#Alimentación de los animales#Alimentação dos animais

entries.summary: This practice describes the innovative technology that uses halophyte plants to create winter fodders reserves stocks to improve animal feed systems.
entries.description:
Description

The Aral-Caspian Depression, with its sharply continental arid climate, faces a severe problem in producing enough food for a rapidly growing local population. The intensive use of water and land resources, excessive irrigation, overgrazing and felling trees and shrubs for fuel (firewood) has resulted in the degradation of fertile soils into unproductive lands unsuitable for irrigation farming, animal fodder production or cattle grazing. The situation is intensified by an increase in the degraded land area due to soil salinization and loss of fertility, combined with unsuitable land management practices.

The biological amelioration system aims to improve land quality, soil health, and the support of highly nutritious and high-calorie fodder production on salt-affected soil.

1. The creation of winter fodders reserves stocks and the improvement of animal feed systems by the use of halophytes

There are more than 760 halophyte species (are salt-tolerant plants that grow in soil or waters of high salinity) in the flora of Central Asia. These under-used plant resources are little known and scarcely applied in agricultural systems, medicine and other industries in Central Asia.

Some halophytes represent a good source:

  • food for humans;
  • desirable for industrial use - as a source of renewable bioenergy;
  • nutritious feed for animals

The use of halophytes in the reclamation of salt-affected lands around artificial lakes within the Aral Sea basin would contribute to the economic growth of surrounding regions.

The selected 15 halophyte (or salt-loving plants) are species and ecotypes that can be grown on soils affected by salinization (due to irrigation water salinity). These can potentially be used in bio-amelioration, in the production of calorie-rich fodders and the pharmaceutical industry.

The list of species and ecotypes selected are the following:

  • Suaeda arcuate;
  • Suaeda acuminate;
  • Suaeda paradoxa;
  • Atriplex hortensis;
  • Climacoptera lanata;
  • Chenopodium album;
  • Salsola orientalis;
  • Salicornia sp.;
  • Kochia scoparia;
  • Glycyrrhiza glabra;
  • Artemisia halodendron;
  • Among others.

The selected halophyte species produce:

  • 10-12 tonnes of dry matter of fodder;
  • 1-1.5 tonnes of seed; and
  • up to 1.5 tonnes of protein per hectare of sandy soil irrigated with saline water.

The primary technological actions applied to Artemisia-ephemeroid communities on Typical Brown Semi-desert, Chestnut and Dark Chestnut soils of piedmont deserts of the Nurat Mountains are as follows:

The use of fodder crop species with different ecological characteristics is preferable for creating pasture to be used all year round. Such species include:

  • trees - Haloxylon aphyllum;
  • large shrubs - Salsola richteri and Salsola paletzkiana;
  • medium shrubs - Halothamnus subaphyllus;
  • small shrub-like herbs - Salsola orientalis, Kochia prostrata, Camphorosma sp. and Artemisia sp.; and
  • grasses - Poa bulbosa and short-lived ephemeroids.

More details can be found here:

http://drylandsystems.cgiar.org/news-opinion/2015-review-combating-land-degradation-and-climate-changecentral-asia

The ability of halophytes to promote soil desalinization is due to a combination of three factors:

  • The upper one-meter layer of highly saline loamy soils in semidesert areas has a salt content of 48 tonnes per ha.
  • Halophytes with an above-ground biomass of 18-20 tonnes per ha can uptake salts from the soil at rates of 8-10 tonnes per ha per year.
  • Halophytes shade the soil surface and thus hinder evaporation and associated upward migration of salts into the upper layer of soil. This green mulch effect is equal to 2.5 tonnes per ha of salts per year.

Consequently, an area planted with halophytes is characterized by salt removal from the soil at rates of 10-12.5 tonnes per year.

http://www.cac-program.org/video/play/9

2. Conclusion

The impact of salinity is the most significant negative factor limiting land resources' efficient use, making agricultural land unsuitable for crop diversity use.

Biosiline agriculture in arid regions has several aims, including :

  • restoration of salt-affected lands;
  • creation of highly productive agricultural environment conditions in place of formerly degraded ones;
  • the improvement of the ameliorative state and fertility of soils for agricultural use
    • soil rehabilitation using halophyte species
    • productively amend and utilize salt-affected soils.

The most successful halophyte species that can be grown on salt-affected soils and used as winter fodders for farm animals include:

  • Atriplex nitens,
  • Climacoptera lanata,
  • Kochia sp.,
  • Salsola sp.
  • Aellenia sp.
  • Haloxylon sp.
  • Artemisia sp.;
  • Ceratoides sp.;
  • Suaeda sp.;
  • Glycyrrhiza sp.
  • Among others.

Depending on the local environmental conditions and plant species composition, the dry matter yields of fodder crops harvested from newly created halophyte plantations can vary from 1.2 to 1.5 tonnes per ha.

Halophyte pastures can be used in different seasons with stable yields from year to year and provide a diverse diet for farm animals. These pastures require high-quality viable seeds when under limited supplemental irrigation by saline artesian water.

There further development of appropriate technologies for the cultivation of halophytes and other under-utilized traditional and non-traditional crop species such as quinoa, African millet, amaranth, soybean, etc., can help to increase food security and food production.

The growing of salt-tolerant plants, together with the promotion of best agricultural practices on salt-affected soils, has demonstrated its benefits, such as, an area planted with halophytes is characterized by salt removal from the soil at rates of 10-12.5 tonnes per year. Further dissemination and access to these technologies are necessary to reach and benefit more rural communities, and smallholder farmers, including reaching out to policy-makers to support adopting these technologies to improve food-feed security, improve livestock and soils health.

3. Validation of the practice

This practice has been tested in biosaline conditions in Central Asian countries. It identifies 15 haplotypes species and ecotypes that can potentially be used in bio-amelioration, production of calorie-rich fodders and the pharmaceutical industry.

4. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Tillage during early spring, May-June and Autumn and winter. Attention, that the sowing line direction is perpendicular to winds.

The selection of the most appropriate halophytes for the context is essential.

Soil measurements such as initial salinity, organic matter and chemical and physical properties to identify the added value of using the halophytes as soil amendment technology.

5. Agroecological zones

  • Temperate, cold
  • Temperate, cool
  • Subtropics, cool.

entries.summary: This practice shows the use of Quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa Willd.) as a multipurpose salt- and drought-tolerant agricultural food crop. The practice describes how quinoa was used for increasing the food security in marginal conditions in Central Asia.
entries.description:
Description

The Aral-Caspian Depression, with its sharply continental arid climate, faces a severe problem in producing enough food for a rapidly growing local population. The situation is intensified by an increase in the degraded land area due to soil salinization and loss of fertility combined with unsustainable land management practices of growing wheat and cotton.

The intensive use of water and land resources, excessive irrigation, overgrazing and felling trees and shrubs for fuel (firewood) have resulted in the degradation of fertile soils into unproductive lands unsuitable for irrigation farming, animal fodder production or cattle grazing.

Shortages of irrigation water lead to the necessity to use low-quality saline water for irrigation, negatively affecting agricultural production and productivity in the sense that most traditionally grown crop cultures are sensitive to soil salinity.

The development of alternative agricultural production systems is essential for mobilizing existing marginal resources within the region to bring profitability to local farmers without damaging the environment.

The biological soil amendment system aims to improve land quality, soil health, and the support of highly nutritious and high-calorie alternative food and fodder crop production on salt-affected soil.

The International Centre for Biosaline Agriculture in Central Asia and Transcaucasia (ICBA-CAT) has developed Biosaline technologies to reclaim salt-affected soils and restore the productivity of degraded agricultural ecosystems. These technologies have been successfully implemented in agriculture.

1. Quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa Willd.) as a multipurpose salt- and drought-tolerant agricultural crop

Within the framework of The International Centre for Biosaline Agriculture (ICBA) Project on Regional partnership for increasing the food security of produce grown under marginal conditions in Central Asia, experimental trials on seed samples and the creation of regional and national nurseries were established for the propagation, selection, agro-technological research and seed production of quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa).

Quinoa is a salt- and drought-tolerant plant, it has perfect agricultural use as an alternative food and fodder crop. It can grow on poor soils under arid and semiarid conditions in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Azerbaijan.

Quinoa seed is:

  • gluten-free,
  • very nutritious,
  • protein-rich (11-18 percent) and
  • rich in saturated amino acids, fats, micro-and macronutrients.

The seed yields vary depending on the agroecological zone: from 3.8 t/ha (in Karakalpakstan) to 5.1 t/ha (in the south of Tajikistan and the piedmont regions in the area of Issyk-Kul Lake).

The different part of the plant, quinoa, can be used for various purposes:

Quinoa seeds are used as:

  • healthy food, e.g., to diversify the diet of children; and  
  • chemical by-products, including saponins originating (soap-like) from quinoa seed for use in the cosmetic and pharmaceutical industry.

Quinoa leaves:

  • are nutrient-rich;
  • have protein content of 8.75 to 10.85 percent; and
  • have cellulose content of 7.68 to 8.90 percent.

Quinoa inflorescences:

  • have high sugar content of 95.84 to 92.73 percent.

The other advantage is that the aboveground biomass and seed processing residues are used as cattle fodder.

Local farmers, householders and private businesses have expressed great interest in the growth and distribution of quinoa seeds, including restaurant chains.

More detailed information can be found here: Quinoa in Central Asia: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dwr7XxzBLjI

Figure 1. The successful promotion of quinoa varieties in Uzbekistan

© International Centre for Biosaline Agriculture (ICBA).

Through the ICBA project (2015-2017) after field trials the top performing two varieties/Q5 (Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan) and Q2 (Tajikistan) of Quinoa germplasm lines were selected for breeding and further dissemination in Central Asia. It was reported that the Quinoa varieties exhibited about 30 percent dry fodder yield and 25 percent seeds which was more than local annual chenopods.

It is reported that Kyrgyzstan, with the support and collaboration with FAO’s since 2014, lead the  integration of quinoa into their local food system. As a results products were developed substituting barley with 10 percent quinoa in the national drink (Bojo) and with 5 percent quinoa flour in making bread.

2. Validation of the practice

This practice has been tested in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Azerbaijan with experimental trials on seed samples and the creation of regional and national nurseries were established for the propagation, selection, agro-technological research and seed production of quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa).

3. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Quinoa performs well on poor soils under arid and semiarid conditions.

4. Agroecological zones

  • Subtropics, cool.
  • Temperate, cool.
  • Temperate, cold.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Methods of amendment and use of salt-affected soils – use of Biosaline technologies and approaches for salt-affected agricultural lands under arid climate conditions: ID 10089.
  • Methods of amelioration and use of salt-affected soils – use of Biosaline technologies and approaches for salt-affected agricultural lands under arid climate conditions: ID100xx.
