entries.title: Farmer Field Schools and agroecology: Tools for sustainable food and agricultural systems
entries.source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)

agrovoc_keywords.display: Farmer field schools#École pratique d'agriculture#Escuela de campo para agricultores#Escola de campo para agricultores

entries.summary:
This practice describes the Farmer Field School (FFS) approach in the context of agroecology and the use of the 10 Elements of Agroecology as a holistic tool to think about sustainable food and agricultural systems at multiple scales. The practice also explains how FFS and agroecology interventions can support sustainable agriculture and food system transitions, including some examples.

The FFS approach, developed by FAO and partners 30 years ago and implemented in more than 90 countries, has served as a "proof of concept" of how transformative and participatory learning can help farmers, governments, donors and stakeholders achieve multiple development objectives informed by needs perceptions from the ground.

FFS aims to improve farmers' livelihoods and strengthen their role as guardians of natural environments as well as stakeholders in policy decision-making. Agroecology is the intrinsic cornerstone of the FFS approach that has led to its successful uptake by more than 20 million1 small farmers.
entries.description:
Description

The global discussions on the future of food and agriculture consistently support the urgent need to transition to sustainable food and agricultural systems that ensure food security and nutrition, provide social and economic equity, and sustain the ecosystem services on which agriculture depends (FAO, 2018). Agroecology provides an important path towards achieving multiple Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including no poverty (SDG 1) and zero hunger (SDG 2), among many others (FAO, 2018).  

To transition to food systems that are agroecological and sustainable, we need to build the capacity of smallholder farmers to create and use locally adapted agroecological practices as well as make better decisions that improve livelihoods and preserve natural resources. It is the case at the individual smallholders and their households and communities levels.

1. Why is FFS an important way to mainstream Agroecology?

The FFS approach has proved effective in managing problems in complex systems thus, empowering farmers to improve decision-making based on local conditions. Understanding farmers’ decision-making and the role of participatory innovation support initiatives such as FSS have in the transformation processes also contributes to strengthening farmers' access to technical and financial resources and fostering farmer-to-farmer knowledge exchange.

Because FFS encourages community development and action, adapts the learning process to different technical content, and promotes advocacy on important issues for local communities, it makes FFS an important vehicle in supporting smallholders in transitioning from their current practices to agroecology techniques through the gradual transformation of their farming systems.

2. The Farmer Field School (FFS) approach

The FFS is a participatory learning methodology focusing on contextualized and ecologically-informed agricultural practices. This learning methodology strengthens the overall food system by empowering and building the capacities of farmers to become more involved in food system actions and policy dialogues.

The synergies developed between agroecology and FFS can address the root causes of hunger, malnutrition, and poverty by reinforcing the relations between key stakeholders at local, regional and national levels and improving their abilities to make better decisions and actions for better/transformed food and agricultural systems.

FFS aims to improve farmers' livelihoods and strengthen their role as guardians of natural environments and stakeholders in policy decision-making (https://www.fao.org/farmer-field-schools/home/en/).

3. How is agroecology integrated into the FFS approach?

The FFS approach was developed by FAO and partners 30 years ago and implemented in more than 90 countries. It has served as a "proof of concept" of how transformative and participatory learning can help farmers, governments, donors, and stakeholders achieve multiple development objectives informed by needs from the ground.

Agroecology applies principles and concepts to improve interactions between plants, animals, humans, and the environment while considering socio-economic aspects for a sustainable and fair food system. It is a socio-ecological system where smallholder and family farmers (including fisherfolk and pastoralists) are at the center of the food system. It builds on farmers' collective knowledge and co-creation of innovations adapted for a particular ecological and cultural context. It provides comprehensive long-term solutions for a transformational change in food and agricultural systems to help meed the Sustainable Development Goals. The integration of agroecology practices in the FFS approach is done to address the need to and co-design innovative and sustainable solutions to address problems in complex systems

Agroecology is the intrinsic cornerstone of the FFS approach that has led to its successful uptake by more than 20 million small farmers.

4. The FFS methodology

5. Making it Happen

The use of the 10 Elements of Agroecology - a holistic tool to think about sustainable food and agricultural systems at multiple scales
To guide countries and other stakeholders to transform their food and agricultural systems to mainstream sustainable agriculture on a large scale, FAO developed 10 Elements of Agroecology.  These serve as a guide for policy-makers, practitioners, and stakeholders in planning, managing, and evaluating agroecological changes (transitions). They also provide an entry point for Farmer Field Schools to consider sustainable food and agricultural systems at multiple scales in a particular place and time (in context).

The 10 Elements, although interdependent and interconnected, can serve as a valuable conceptual visual narratives tool using participatory approaches to identify dominant elements of the system, strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats to determine how to move or transition to more sustainable systems.

10 Elements of Agroecolog

Figure 1. The 10 Elements of Agroecology (FAO, 2018a)

©FAO, 2018

Figure 2. Narrative of the 10 Elements of Agroecology (FAO, 2018)

©FAO, 2018
 

6. Process for applying and scaling the 10 Elements via FFS

Agroecology needs to be integrated across the FFS programme planning and implementation. For FFS to mobilize farmers along with the agroecological transition, Farmer Field School need to be implemented in line with the non-negotiable principles of FFS (see FAO 2016), involving farmers at all stages (Bakker et al., 2021).

In particular, a key stage through which agroecological principles can be integrated with FFS is during the initial FFS community meeting, before learning activities start. In these meetings, information is collated by farmers in the community together with a trained FFS facilitator or master trainer, to inform the development of a learning plan for the FFS group: 

  • ensure having drawing media available for participants (e.g., paper, card stock, markers, pencils, etc.).
  • participants should include farmers representative of the community (including women) and those interested in joining the FFS

The facilitator or master trainer should:

  • group participants in large or smaller groups;
  • explain what would be the purpose of the exercise:
    • the purpose should be to learn and develop the skills required for informed decision-making in complex systems. It should be based on accurate problem analysis in local contexts, build on local knowledge, understand the local agro-ecology/agro-ecosystem, and existing capacities. For example, considering the farmers' needs and drives, identifying knowledge and skills gaps, and opportunities to improve building on the local knowledge systems.
  • describe the agroecological Elements using the 10 Elements visual narratives (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/26395916.2020.1808705)

The participants, either in the large group or in smaller groups:

  • determine/identify a particular system they would like to illustrate and create boundary conditions to help thinking (a system could be a farm, a community, watershed, foodshed, or food system; agroecology often takes a territorial approach) in a given place and time;
  • draw or describe (artistically or descriptively) each of the elements currently in the system using each as a possible entry point;
  • draw connecting arrows between the elements to show their interconnectedness;
  • explain their system, its scale/scope, timeframe, and context;
  • identify what and what does not work so well currently in the system
  • discuss what needs to be changed to enhance the sustainability of the system (to transition to agroecological and sustainable systems);

This step helps to relate the current strengths and perceptions, needs, and weaknesses to identify enabling factors to change and discuss how they can change.

  • Involve other actors, such as traders, intermediaries, policy-makers, local leaders, marketers, and others.
  • Conduct participatory appraisal exercises (brainstorming and ranking) asking simple but key questions like:
    • What is working best in your system?
    • What are the biggest challenges your system is facing?
    • What are the most important things you need to change in the system to be more successful/improve your household's livelihood?  Brainstorming and ranking activity
  • Based on brainstorming and ranking activity:
    • discuss agroecological interventions and solutions needed
    • co-design the actions, solutions, interventions to be applied and form consensus about actions and timeline.
    • The information collected through this exercise across groups is used to identify key learning topics, possible comparative experiments that could be carried out, and guide the knowledge co-creation process in which farmers, facilitators and possibly researchers and local innovators might engage throughout the FFS programme.

7. How can FFS and agroecology interventions support sustainable agriculture and food systems?

The FFS approach combined with hands-on tools for thinking about systems, such as the 10 Elements exercise, acts as a catalyst in supporting farmers in changing their practices and systems to integrate agroecology principles for higher sustainability and better livelihoods. Through FFS, groups of farmers have an opportunity to build their understanding of agro-ecosystems, ecological processes such as soil and plant health, insect-plant interactions and water cycles (increase their ecological literacy), as well as understanding the broader linkages between their farms and households and the more comprehensive food system. FFS will also build farmers' capacity to make better-farm decisions and work together as groups. The latter will be key to supporting change processes at the community level. Moreover,  the 10 elements exercise may constitute the foundation of a "bottom-up" strategy to engage, constructively critique, and reform national government institutions, starting with extension and education, then expanding to policymaking and evaluation.

8. Conclusions

  • Agroecology is an intrinsic foundation of the FFS approach that has led to its successful uptake by more than 20 million small farmers.
  • Recognition of the FFS approach and agroecology relations in policies and initiatives will better support local ecology and culture, enhance local innovation capacities and strengthen networks at local and national levels.
  • Agroecological diversification aims at maximizing synergies and increasing resilience through the FFS approach.
  • The use of systems visual narratives exercises like the 10 Elements empowers farmers to think about their systems and identify strengths and weaknesses.
  • Agroecology and FFS contribute to increased co-creation and sharing of science, using local and traditional knowledge systems to achieve sustainable development goals.
  • FFS networks are dynamic channels to scale out agroecology throughout a country.
  • Agroecology and FFS approaches are adaptive to local economic conditions and can assist in diversifying value chains.

9. Way forward

  1. Intensify the Scaling Up Agroecology Initiative.
  2. Launch a joint stocktaking exercise reviewing experiences on Farmer Field Schools supporting agroecological transitions.
  3. Mainstreaming of agroecology into public policies, programmes, legal frameworks and regulations.
  4. Foster the co-creation of knowledge between farmers and between farmers and scientists, with other organizations or consumers or policy-makers.
  5. Integrate agroecology into the curricula of both formal and non-formal primary and higher education institutions.
  6. Support traditional management practices, local varieties of food crops and neglected and underutilized as well as drought-resistant crops.
  7. Specific value chain and market developments for agroecology, public procurement policies oriented to agroecological products and promotion of the nutritional value of agroecologically produced food.
  8. Provide a neutral space for exchanging knowledge and experiences on agroecology.
  9. Facilitate by allowing new and innovative governance structures to emerge.
  10. Raise funds and resources to mainstream agroecology.

10. Agroecology and FFS in Action - some examples

  • Agroecology in the heart of Hungary*
  • More than a hill of beans: diversity, prosperity and culture in Nepal's Himalayas*
  • Accessing fuel for cooking in displacement settings in Ethiopia*
  • Of silkworms, fish and mulberries, China's recipe for success*
  • Agroecology and FFS in India , stories form the field (https://www.fao.org/farmer-field-schools/ffs-overview/success-stories/en/)
  • Producers from San Salvador promote practices with an agroecological approach, San Salvador (https://www.fao.org/farmer-field-schools/news-events/detail-events/en/c/1180695/)
  • Strengthening integrated aquatic plant and animal farming in the rice fields of Lao PDR, Lao PDR (https://www.fao.org/farmer-field-schools/news-events/detail-events/en/c/1129350/)
  • Renforcer la durabilité et la résilience de l’agriculture familiale : l’application de la démarche CEP au Togo (https://www.fao.org/farmer-field-schools/news-events/detail-events/en/c/883892/)

*Stories@ https://www.fao.org/3/i9021en/i9021en.pdf in Page 17-19.

11. Validation of the practice

The practice has been tested and scaled in several countries: Burkina Faso, China, Ethiopia Hungary, India, Lao PDR, Nepal, San Salvador and Togo.

12. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Need to establish an FFS community, be supported by appropriately trained FFS trainers.

For Farmer Field Schools to support agroecology, they need to be 'collaborative', involving farmers in the design, implementation, innovation and monitoring and evaluation process of FFS groups and the programme at large.

13. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Temperate, cool.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

14. Related/associated technologies

  • Building life skills for youth: ID 7675.
  • Farmer field schools on integrated plant nutrient systems: ID 7527.

15. Objectives fulfilled by the project

15.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

This practice can be labour-saving for both women and men due to the target of the action being cared out when applying this methodology. However is worth noting that the FFS methodology and the Agroecology elements, when combined, provide an opportunity for further learning and enhance the sustainability of food systems by focusing on applying solutions to current needs.

15.2 Women-friendly

This practice is women-friendly due to the flexibility of the process, which allows design and implementation solutions to support specific needs and demands from women.

15.3 Resource use efficiency

This practice is resource-efficiency from the point of view of acquiring knowledge and defining solutions for community problems, as it brings together a community or group of stakeholders to address similar situations.

15.4 Pro-poor technology

This practice shows the FFS approach to quickly deliver knowledge and learning opportunities, including hands-on activities based on community or group needs.

entries.title: Tips for harvesting and storage of different crops
entries.source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
entries.summary: This practice shows some simple tips for harvesting and storage of different crops.
entries.description:
Description

The dependence of much food production on climatic fluctuations means that variability in food output can never be completely avoided. Adequate on-farm and household storage are therefore crucial, not only to enable storage of current and surplus food items, but primarily to provide farmers with a food supply beyond the harvest period to ensure year-round availability of needed food for family consumption.

As part of the post-harvest continuum, storage is a link in the production-storage- marketing -consumption chain. It is a means of overcoming what is essentially considered a transport constraint. 

All food products have different ways to be handled after harvesting. For example, the drying phase presents a specific problem during the post-harvest handling of cereal and legume grains. For these crops, the drying stage is all-important to reduce attack and damage from insects and fungi that otherwise reduce the quality of cereals and legumes and are dangerous for human health.

1. Tips for harvesting and storage of different crops

2. General storage tips

  • Only store produces that are in good condition.
  • Do not store any product that has skin damage.
  • Do not store soft fruit or vegetables.
  • Good storage methods protect products from insects and diseases caused by damp conditions.
  • Storage areas should be cool, moist and dark, well ventilated and protected from insects and mice.
  • Fresh produce should be washed in clean water and thoroughly dried before storing.
  • Storing green beans and carrots by wrapping the produce in clean banana leaves or yam leaves is an example of improved storage. Burn the leaves slightly on fire first to prevent cracking when they dry.

3. Validation of the practice

These tips are used by many worldwide. These are simple tips that can be applied on far or at the household level.

4. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Selection of appropriate harvest time for each crop, cereal, fruit and adopt the most suitable storage condition based on the local environment and community context.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, cool.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

  • Improved pit storage method for Ginger Rhizomes: ID 7712.
  • Storage and preservation of wet cassava: ID 4520.
  • Functions and sources of important vitamins and minerals: ID xxx.

entries.description:
Description

The Mediterranean diet constitutes a set of skills, knowledge, practices, and traditions ranging from the landscape to the table, including crops, harvesting, fishing, conservation, processing, preparation, and food consumption.

The Mediterranean diet is characterized by a nutritional model that has remained constant over time and space, consisting mainly of olive oil, cereals, fresh or dried fruit and vegetables, a moderate amount of fish, dairy and meat, and many condiments and spices, all accompanied by wine or infusions, always respecting the beliefs of each community.

Overall, an adequate and nutritionally well-balanced diet is essential for a healthy and vigorous life.

The nutrition needs vary according to and are based on dietary intake. The proposed serves as a guide for people planning feeding at households or in feeding centres, schools. In addition, they are necessary to inform planned food and nutrition policy at the national or international level.

Although nutrition experts and planners think about food and nutrient requirements when planning dietary needs, in daily life, people do not think of their meals in terms of nutrients but in terms of different cooked foods. In this regard, it is important to understand the sources of nutrients immediately available to us or that might be easily grown especially in urban areas.

1. Demand for food quality and quantity

What are “Sustainable diets.”

Sustainable diets are those diets with low environmental impacts that contribute to food and nutrition security and to healthy life for present and future generations. Sustainable diets are protective and respectful of biodiversity and ecosystems, culturally acceptable, accessible, economically fair and affordable; nutritionally adequate, safe and healthy; while optimizing natural and human resources (FAO/Bioversity, 2010).

Food consumption is variably affected by a whole range of factors, including food availability, food accessibility and food choices, which in turn may be influenced by geography, demography, disposable income, socio-economic status, urbanization, globalization, religion, culture, marketing, and consumer attitude (Kearney, 2010).

The easiest way to reach all nutrient recommendations is to select more Mediterranean-type food, with an adequate average nutrient intake level, based on a high diversity of crops and foods.

2. The nutrition needs of different people

3. Healthy food sources for people in towns and cities – to grow or to buy

Protein

  • Eat legumes every day for protein, vitamins, minerals and fiber.
  • Grow climbing beans on fences and up walls.
  • Grow pulses such as cowpeas, groundnuts, round nuts, sugar beans and soya beans in summer between maize rows.
  • Grow pigeon peas as a windbreak around the garden.
  • Grow lentils, chickpeas and shelled peas in winter.
  • Grow green beans in beds all year round.
  • Eat animal and milk products regularly for protein, iron and B vitamins.

When you can afford

  • Eat liver – is a good source of protein, vitamins and minerals.
  • Eat fish – is a good source of protein and calcium.
  • Buy or make sour milk.
  • Keep chickens for eggs and meat or rabbits for meat - these also provide manure, and chickens control pests in the garden.
  • Give eggs to all family members, including children.

Carbohydrate

  • Buy or grow whole grains such as maize, sorghum, millet and wheat and grind them at home or a local grinding mill. It is cheaper and healthier than eating refined meals or flour.
  • Use the ground whole wheat flour to make your bread, biscuits and cakes.
  • Eat the tubers and leaves.
  • Grow sweet potatoes and yam in summer and Plant potatoes in winter.

Fat

  • Grow pumpkins, sunflowers and sesame and collect, roast and eat the seed - contain fat and protein.
  • Plant avocados if you have space - a good source of fat, energy and vitamins A and C.

Vitamins and minerals

  • Eat yellow, orange, red or dark green vegetables and fruit daily for vitamins (especially A, B, C and E) and minerals (mainly calcium and iron) and fiber.
  • Grow many different kinds of vegetables in your beds, including carrots, tomatoes, green beans, and spinach. Eat the healthy, dark green leaves of cowpeas and sweet potatoes.
  • Grow traditional herbs to flavor cooking such as marjoram, basil, parsley, chives and thyme - good sources of vitamin C and calcium.
  • The strong smell of the herbs helps to repel pests in the garden.
  • Grow cucumbers, pumpkins, chouchous on fences and up walls.
  • Grow tree tomato and citrus trees amongst vegetable beds and in sunny places.
  • Grow mangoes, apples and avocados on the south side of your garden if you have space.
  • Grow mulberries, guava and banana trees on boundaries.
  • Grow grapes on fencings.
  • Grow strawberries in beds.
  • Grow gooseberries and raspberries around the edges of gardens.

Cooking tips

  • Cook vegetables for less than 8 minutes.
  • To reserve vitamins and minerals, avoid using bicarbonate of soda for cooking vegetables.
  • Eat plenty of fresh (uncooked) fruit for vitamin C every day.
  • You can make juice or jam and also dry fruit.

Water

  • Drink at least eight glasses of clean water (boiled or filtered) each day.
  • Avoid fizzy drinks and sugary drinks.
  • Avoid drinking tea or coffee with a meal- it reduces the absorption of iron from food.
  • Drink herb teas, which help to stimulate the appetite.
  • Make herb teas –
    • Grow small herbs such as marjoram, basil and thyme in beds.
    • Grow larger herbs such as rosemary, mint and lemongrass.
  • Make and drink fruit juice - plant fruit trees (orange, lemon.)

Food to avoid

  • Too much salt – which is bad for blood pressure.
  • Too much sugar – which is bad for the heart, teeth and mouth (thrush).
  • Junk food and unhealthy snacks – sugary sweets, cakes, buns, white bread, oily or fatty food.

4. A simple, healthy salad with easy ingredients

This dish is rich in vitamins and minerals, especially vitamins A and C, iron and calcium.

©FAO, 2021

Ingredients:

  • Spinach;
  • chopped fine carrots;
  • sliced into thin pieces tomato slices;
  • prickled cucumber slices (prickles removed);
  • onion rings or garlic crushed;
  • roasted groundnuts;
  • sunflower seeds;
  • fresh herbs.

For the dressing:

  • 1 tablespoon of olive oil;
  • 1 tablespoon of lemon juice;
  • salt and pepper to taste.

You can alter these proportions to taste.

When cooking leafy vegetables

  • Tear the leaves into pieces rather than cutting them with a knife - preserves their vitamin C content.
  • Do not use bicarbonate of soda when cooking green vegetables - it destroys vitamins.
  • Use a small amount of water to steam the food rather than boiling it.
    • If you boil the food, add the drained water to stews and sauces.
  • The less time you cook vegetables, the more nutrients you will preserve.
  • Try stir-frying vegetables for a few minutes in a little olive oil.

5. Definitions

Carbohydrates

These include starch and sugars. These foods give our bodies energy to move, work and think. They also help to keep us warm.

We get most carbohydrates from grain crops such as wheat, maize, sorghum, millet and rice, and root crops such as potatoes, sweet potatoes and cassava.

Carbohydrate that is not used immediately by our bodies is stored as fat. Too much stored fat can be unhealthy for the body. Eating large amounts of refined carbohydrates such as refined maize meal, white bread, white rice and white sugar is unhealthy.

Refined foods are processed in factories to make them look tastier. Unfortunately, the refining process removes most of the important fiber, protein, minerals and vitamins these foods naturally contain. It is much better to eat unrefined staple foods with every meal as a cheap, healthy source of energy and fibre and some protein, vitamins and minerals.

Fat

Fats can come from animal products such as milk (butter), meat and fish or processed plant products such as seeds and nuts (sunflower oil and peanut butter). They provide the body with energy.

Proteins

These help our bodies to grow, maintain and repair themselves. Also called body-building foods, they come from plants (beans and other legumes), processed plant products (peanut butter and soya mince), processed animal products (cheese, sour milk and yogurt) and animals (eggs, meat, and milk).

Vitamins and minerals

Vitamins and minerals are also called micronutrients. Our bodies need small amounts of these substances to help different parts such as the blood, eyes, bones, skin and hair to work correctly. Many of these substances help strengthen the body’s immune system and keep us strong and healthy to resist infection. We get most vitamins and minerals from eating fresh fruit and vegetables.

Some vitamins (A, D, E and K) are fat-soluble, so the body needs fat to absorb them. Vitamin A is an important immune system booster. The body cannot store most of the B and C because they are water-soluble, so we need to eat foods that contain these vitamins every day.

Fibre

Apart from nutrients in food, our body also needs other substances. Among these are fibre, also called roughage. Fresh fruit, vegetables and unrefined grains and legumes contain fibre. It is important for helping our bodies to digest food and remove waste. It is important to eat fibre with plenty of water.

Water

Our bodies contain more water than any other substance. All chemical processes and body functions use water. We need to drink at least eight glasses of fresh, clean water every day to stay healthy.

6. Validation of the practice

This applies to everyone as it raises awareness on general nutrition needs of people and provides information on some healthy food sources and on how to grow some healthy foods.

7. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Time and the type of foods to grow or buy for better individual/household nutrition.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, cool.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

9. Related/Associated Technologies

  • Mediterranean diet- an example: ID 10079.
  • Functions and sources of important vitamins and minerals: ID 100xx.
  • Tips for harvesting and storage of different crops: ID 10084.

entries.summary: The following practice describes the STB model, its functions, major elements, how it works, stakeholders involved, training required, costs and outcomes, and challenges and limitations to adoption and scaling. It includes summary information on some case studies to highlight the success of this practice applied elsewhere.
entries.description:
Description

China's agriculture sector is characterized as having high-input, high-output and significant environmental costs. Yet, agricultural development has become a high priority for the country in recent decades. China's agriculture producers are dominated by smallholder farmers. The greatest challenge that the sector currently faces is to transfer knowledge into action. To reduce this breach in 2009, the China Agricultural University (CAU) initiated a novel approach to empower smallholder farmers for sustainable agricultural production in China, called Science and Technology Backyards (STB).

The Science and Technology Backyards (STB) is a novel approach recognized by its innovative organizational settings, where  CAU professors and postgraduate students moved their research programs from the experimental station to the village and rented a backyard. To be closer to the farmer's reality, they lived, worked and studied high-yielding technologies and responses from the farmers in the village. In the years, the backyard work attracted more farmers and encouraged further participation. Thus it became a science and technology dissemination platform at the local community level. Since 2009, the number of STBs, farms covered by STBs, and trained farmers have increased rapidly. As of 2018, STBs have extended to 23 provinces and regions in China, including 29 scientific research institutes, 127 STBs, and 45 kinds of crops.

1. What is STB?

STB is a pioneering practice to transform education, alleviate poverty, and it is a new way to reform the agriculture service system. 

STB is an in situ platform that connects the scientific community with the farming community to facilitate information exchange and innovation. STB is implemented in a series of local backyards where things happen and are addressed in real-time by researchers, students, advisors and farmers. STB became a science and technology dissemination platform in local communities. Science-based management technologies are brought by STB staff and discussed with leading farmers, the latter providing feedback, resulting in farm-applicable recommendations.

The Science and Technology Backyards (STB) is a novel approach initiated by the China Agricultural University (CAU) to empower smallholder farmers for sustainable agricultural production in China, which has been scaled in many other countries.

Figure 1. A typical STB

©China Agricultural University (CAU).

University agronomy experts (professors and students) and extension workers live and work together with smallholder farmers in identifying and addressing key productivity challenges. The recommended technologies and innovations are tested through field trials by the farmers while the researchers monitor the farmers' activities. 

Though the STB model has been successfully working in China, projects similar to STB have been implemented in the African countries to encourage knowledge exchange between students and rural communities to enhance the uptake of innovation and the latest scientific expertise to improve sustainable agricultural production and rural livelihoods. These projects can provide essential insights, experiences, and lessons to determine which outlining conditions and limiting factors for which attention must be paid when adopting the model to context.

2. The Science and Technology Backyard Concept model

The science and technology backyard is a platform located in rural areas, which links students, researchers, extension agents, and smallholders (including local government and private enterprises) to facilitate information exchange and technological innovation in agriculture (Fig. 2).

Figure 2. Concept model of the Science and Technology Backyard.

©Zhang et al., 2016

2.1 The STB functions and key elements

  • STB is a participatory approach, bringing researchers, students and community members in a collaborative, research context-specific environment.
  • STB addresses specific practical problems and provides a unique methodology that can effectively address some of the challenges facing the farmers and agri-food value actors in rural areas.
  • University agronomy experts (professors and students) and extension workers live and work together with smallholder farmers in identifying and addressing key productivity challenges.
  • The recommended technologies and innovations are tested through field trials by the farmers while the researchers monitor the farmers' activities.

China's extension system cannot provide sufficient services to smallholder farmers, which hamper the knowledge transfer in the "last kilometer" of knowledge transfer. Despite considerable public extension staff, agro-input retailers and researchers from universities and institutions, the first rarely works in the field and uses high input technologies, while the latter have little incentive to serve farmers. Additionally, advanced technologies cannot be transferred efficiently and only 8% of the graduated students prefer to work in rural areas. The STB has the main functions to increase the capacities of the stakeholder involved, enhance knowledge transfer, strengthen linkages between education-researchers/educators-private sector-farmers, and increase graduate youth interest in working in rural areas. And empower smallholder farmers for sustainable agricultural production.

A typical science and technology backyard consists of the following components: a backyard, professionals (researchers, university professors, students), a group of leading farmers, training and technical service facilities (e.g., public address systems, computers, projectors, motorized tricycles and brochures), experimental and demonstration plots (additional plots) (Fig. 3).

Figure 3. The Science and Technology Backyard platform components

©Yang et al., 2021

3. Science, technology and backyard in context

The linkages between education, research and extension are often supply-driven, top-down, and unable to respond to smallholder farmers' diversity of knowledge demands. These linkages are weak and their services are therefore not well connected with the needs of farmers. To overcome these, the STB has made significant advances in strengthening the linkages between research, education and extension by adding the farmers to the context. In this regard, the STB is linked by three key layers: a macro-environment - an outer layer ensuring participation by multi-stakeholders; a micro-environment - the middle layer to reinforce the linkages among stakeholders; and an internal environment - an internal layer focusing on the needs and solution for farmers following the STB novel approach (Fig. 4).

Figure 4. The Science and Technology Backyard novel approach in the context

©Sonia Dias, FAO 2022

4. Stakeholders involved in STB

There are four stakeholders groups involved in the STB approach: the Government, Universities (including research organizations and institutions), private sector (multi-stakeholder service providers), and farmers. Each group has a defined role and profile (Fig. 5).

Figure 5. The stakeholders involved in the Science and Technology Backyard

©Sonia Dias, FAO 2022

5. Contribution of the STB model

Contribution of the STB model to facilitate exchanges between students/young researchers and rural communities and strengthen students' capacity to address smallholder farmers' needs using a community-based model for knowledge transfer and training and learning

5.1 How students participate in an STB implementation – students training process

The training process for a student to participate in the STB model (Fig.6) is divided into four phases:

  1. The interview–for the selection of students, the interview includes the local farmers;
  2. Phase I-preschooling training –this is the first step into the experience with a basic introduction to rural areas and understanding farmers needs;
  3. Phase II-first academic term– when the theoretic and practical learning is conducted; and
  4. Phase III- the second to sixth academic term with a complete transition for implementation by living on-site, working together with the farmers, contributing to training and dissemination activities and finalizing own thesis to graduate.
 Figure 6. The Science and Technology Backyard students training process

©Sonia Dias, FAO 2022

5.2 The STB Model for student training activities

The Science and Technology Backyard (STB) model allows the scientific community to connect with the farming community to facilitate information exchange and innovation. It is a participatory approach, bringing researchers and community members into a collaborative, research context-specific environment. It addresses specific practical problems and provides a unique methodology that can effectively address some of the challenges facing the farmers and agri-food value actors in rural areas.

Figure 7. The Science and Technology Backyard model for student training activities

©Sonia Dias, FAO 2022

6. How does STB model compare to Farmers Field School

Table 1 showcases the main differences between the STB model and the Farmer Field School (FFS). While there are significant differences between the STB and the FFS models, for a more efficient and effective implementation and better service to farmers, the FFS model plays a critical role in the STB success, which is mainly applied in the dissemination activities and the scaling-up phases.  The decision to use one or the other model, or even a mix of both, must consider the context.

Table 1. Differences between the STB model and the Farmer Field School (FFS)

©Sonia Dias, FAO 2022

7. Overview of a budget and necessary funding for setting up a STB

In China, the STB financial support mainly comes from universities, the government and the private sector. The funds cover the cost of infrastructure, humanity and social services.

A typical STB costs around $33 000 (equal to USD 5 156 in 2021) per year * (Fig. 8).

*This value is indicated as the cost of infrastructure, humanity and social services vary from country to country.

Figure 8. Overview of budget and funding necessary for a STB

©Sonia Dias, FAO 2022

8. Challenges and constraints of scaling and institutionalizing STB

Figure 9. Challanges and constraints

©Sonia Dias, FAO 2022

9. Considerations when adopting and scaling up STB

STB focuses mainly on agricultural knowledge and technology transfer. For the adoption and scaling up of STB, several limitations and opportunities for improvement have been observed

To further increase the STB model impact through increased adoption and scaling up, Fig. 10 highlights some of the current limitations and related actions that must be addressed for this model to benefit more smallholders, strengthen linkages between education - research community- the advisory services and private sector stakeholders towards a pluralist approach.

Figure 10. Highlights of current limitations and related actions that must be addressed for better impact

©Sonia Dias, FAO 2022

10. Simillar project to STB

Title: Knowledge transfer and practical learning/training model (s) in Africa

Projects similar to STB have been implemented in the African countries to encourage knowledge exchange between students and rural communities to enhance the uptake of innovation and the latest scientific expertise to improve sustainable agricultural production and rural livelihoods. These projects can provide essential insights, experiences, and lessons to determine which outlining conditions and factors must be considered. At the same time, facilitating exchanges between students/young researchers and rural communities in Africa using a community-based model for knowledge transfer and, training and learning.

One such community-based model includes the community-based field attachments programme (CFAPA) implemented in 2018 by the Regional Universities Forum for Capacity Building in Agriculture (RUFORUM) with the support of the FAO's Partnerships Division. The CFAPA programme facilitates placements of students from RUFORUM member universities in the rural communities to apply and disseminate their research findings in the field and share knowledge and expertise with local farmers and rural institutions. This practice summarizes the program's objectives, the application process, outputs, outcomes and activities while providing guidance for the successful linking up of rural communities and students/youth for knowledge exchange and transmission of innovation, which can be a part of the implementation of knowledge transfer projects and programmes to develop the capacities of the youth in Africa.

This practice also includes a summary of six case studies:

Case study 1 – Uganda

Increasing commercialization and profitability of indigenous chicken production through innovation platforms in Omoro district, Northern Uganda.

Case study 2 – Benin

The promotion of the consumption of sorghum porridge dual fortified with moringa leaf powder and baobab fruit pulp among under five-year-old children in rural Benin.

Case study 3 – Benin

Promoting utilization of millet-sesame-soy complimentary food composite to prevent undernutrition amongst children 6-23 months old in Amuru and Nwoya districts rural Benin.

Case study 4 – Kenya

Stakeholders engagement and sensitization on best practices to maximize rabbit production in central Kenya through effective treatment and control of coccidiosis.

Two other case studies – example provided by RUFORUM

  1. Gastrointestinal parasites (GIPs) in Angora goats and their control methods.
  2. Sustainable multiplication of improved common bean seed in favour of smallholder farmers of Buhimba and Kiziranfumbi sub-county Hoima district, Uganda. @https://www.fao.org/teca/en/technologies/10027

More on STB case study in:

An innovation in agricultural science and technology extension system – Case study on science and technology backyard.

Yang, P., Jiao, X., Feng, D., Ramasamy, S., Zhang, H., Mroczek, Z. & Zhang, W. 2021. An innovation in agricultural science and technology extension system – Case study on science and technology backyard. Rome, FAO. https://doi.org/10.4060/cb2939en

11. Validation of the practice

This practice has been tested and scaled in China and Africa.

12. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Backyard, professors, students, researchers, advisory services and framers. Limitations see point 9 above.

13. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.
  • Temperate, cool.

entries.source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)

entries.summary: This practice explains the gender fundamental roles, relations and norms in the agricultural setting. It intends to clarify the concepts, understand the environment and raise awareness on gender roles, relations and norms for a better agricultural sustainable environment. This practice aims to assist extension and advisory services trainees in increasing their capacity and offering better support, advice and guidance to men and women farmers. To analyze and integrate gender dimensions and deliver gender-responsive extension services considering the gender roles, relations and norms within the communities.
entries.description:
Description

Extension and Advisory Services (EAS) play a major role in strengthening farmers' technical, decision-making, and organizational capacities. EAS needs frequent new or renewal of skills and capacities to deal effectively with the evolving challenges faced by rural communities. It is essential to understand gender roles, relations and norms within the communities, to better serve them.

Incorporating gender in EAS will certainly entail changing behaviours, approaches, and agricultural practices to better inform producers about the opportunities and impacts of gender to adopt better approaches, use adequate practices, and empower more women and youth within local contexts.

EAS has traditionally served as a bridge between research and farming, and supported farmers by delivering knowledge about new practices and technologies. Yet, successfully incorporating gender requires approaches that go well beyond changing farm-level agronomic practices. It requires identifying and promoting appropriate practices, technologies, and/or new, improved, adapted models within the enabling environments, including beneficial set up at the local level. EAS, therefore, needs to be backed by gender comprehensive expertise and skills to foster interaction and encourage the proper flow of knowledge among a wider range of community members, including those engaged in policy development and those involved in farming.

1. Why are gender relations important for extension advisory services?

Extension advisory services are an essential element of agricultural innovation systems (AIS). They play an important role in rural development, particularly in agricultural production, and increasingly throughout value chain development. Extension advisory services can help both women and men farmers to increase their yields, connect with markets, and take advantage of entrepreneurship opportunities. However, globally, women have less access to EAS than men and the information, knowledge, technologies and services provided tend to be less relevant to the needs of female farmers.

To reduce the gender productivity gap, women's equal access to advisory services is crucial. the essential basis for increasing gender equality are:

  • A good understanding of the gender differences (inequalities in access to and control over assets and resources, and unequal power relations);
  • how the traditional gender division of labour shapes women's participation in agricultural production; and
  • awareness of the differences in needs and priorities.

Because of cultural attitudes, discrimination and a lack of recognition for women's role in food production, women enjoy limited to no benefits from extension and training in, such as, crop varieties and technologies.

Figure 1. Percentage of female access to extension services

©Source: Gender - Farming First and FAO (www.fao.org/gender/Infogtaphic), 2011

Increasing the gender sensitivity of EAS involves:

  • increasing understandings of the gender-differentiated needs of women and men farmers;
  • facilitating access to adequate services for women farmers; and
  • changing the nature of the services offered to ensure that they meet the gender-differentiated needs of farmers and their common needs.

The vast majority of studies have found differences in yields between men and women exist not because women are less skilled but because they have less access to inputs such as improved seeds, fertilizers and equipment.

The challenges of making EAS more reachable and appropriate for women farmers are varied and complex and encompassing:

  • national policy frameworks and resource allocation;
  • organizational/community/family structures and systems;
  • cultural and traditional norms and gender roles; and
  • levels of awareness and understanding of the way in which gender relations operate within the rural communities and affect the agricultural livelihoods of different stakeholders.

2. What are some of the impacts of the gender gap in agriculture?

Some of the impacts of gender gap in agriculture are access to inputs and resources, and land access and right of ownership. Bridging the yield gap would boost food and nutrition security at global level. Giving equal access to resources, women would achieve the same yield levels, boosting total agricultural outputs in developing countries by 2.5-4 percent. This could reduce hunger by 12-17 percent.

Figure 2. The yield gap between men and women.

Figure 3. The yield gap between men and women.

Source: Gender - Farming First and FAO (www.fao.org/gender/Infogtaphic)

3. What are gender roles, relations and gender norms?

The term gender refers to the economic, social and cultural attributes and opportunities associated with being male or female. In most societies, being a man or a woman is not simply a matter of different biological and physical characteristics. Men and women face different expectations about dressing, behaving, or working.

Gender roles are shaped by ideological, religious, ethnic, economic, and cultural factors and these are determinants that regulate the distribution of responsibilities and resources between men and women.

Relations between men and women, whether in the family, workplace, or public, also reflect perceptions of the capacities, characteristics, and behaviour appropriate to women and men.

Gender attributes and characteristics encompass, inter alia, the roles that men and women play and the expectations placed upon them. These vary widely among societies and also change over time.

Gender norms are ideas about how men and women should be and act. They are the standards and expectations to which gender identity generally conforms within a range that defines a particular society, culture and community at a point in time.

Gender norms can establish a life cycle of gender socialization and stereotype. However, gender norms can and do change.

3.1 Gender analysis

Figure 4. Gender role and relations analysis.

©FAO/Sónia Dias

Both types of analysis are important and complement each other.

Focusing only on roles runs the risk of neglecting that relationships between men and women are continuously (re)negotiated and structured through power.

4. Ways of upscaling EAS trainees' capacities

It is essential to look into improving EAS trainees' capacities to deliver better gender-sensitive extension and advisory services.

EAS trainees need to:

  • Have a clearer understanding of what gender relations are about and how they relate to and influence socio-economic conditions and activities;
  • Have a greater awareness of gender differences in economic/finance roles and access to services, including advisory services, in their operational areas and at the national level;
  • Have an increased capacity to recognize the gender-specific needs of women and men for advisory services and to identify changes in training and advisory practices to more effectively meet the needs;
  • Be aware of and able to use participatory tools to conduct gender analysis for assessment and training purposes.

5. Questions that EAS trainees can use to know more about the current situation in a specific context

Figure 5. Extension advisory services question

6. FAO tool to assess the gender sensitivity of RAS programs at the enabling environment, organization, and individual levels

The FAO Gender and Rural Advisory Services Assessment Tool (GRAST)

To help organizations reflect on and improve their service provision for women, FAO has developed the Gender and Rural Advisory Services Assessment Tool (GRAST), which assesses the gender sensitivity of RAS programs at the enabling environment, organization, and individual (advisor and client) levels. This tool gives RAS organizations and institutions a way to identify a program's strengths and weaknesses concretely from a gender perspective. This tool can be a basis for implementing institutional reforms to improve gender equity and share good practices and lessons learned within the organization and others.

The FAO Gender and Rural Advisory Services Assessment Tool (GRAST) GRAST provides:

  • a methodology for assessing the gender sensitiveness of RAS and organizations;
  • feedback on areas of RAS provision that need improvement or are working well.

https://www.fao.org/3/CA2693EN/ca2693en.pdf

7. FAO tool to assess the gender sensitivity of RAS programs at the enabling environment, organization, and individual levels

The FAO Gender and Rural Advisory Services Assessment Tool (GRAST)

To help organizations reflect on and improve their service provision for women, FAO has developed the Gender and Rural Advisory Services Assessment Tool (GRAST), which assesses the gender sensitivity of RAS programs at the enabling environment, organization, and individual (advisor and client) levels. This tool gives RAS organizations and institutions a way to identify a program's strengths and weaknesses concretely from a gender perspective. This tool can be a basis for implementing institutional reforms to improve gender equity and share good practices and lessons learned within the organization and others.

The FAO Gender and Rural Advisory Services Assessment Tool (GRAST) GRAST provides:

  • a methodology for assessing the gender sensitiveness of RAS and organizations;
  • feedback on areas of RAS provision that need improvement or are working well.

GRAST - https://www.fao.org/3/CA2693EN/ca2693en.pdf

8. The way forward towards gender equality in EAS:

  • Strengthen women's ownership and control;
  • Increase the number of women professionals; and
  • Adopt gender-sensitive approaches and practices.

9. Recommendations

Figure 6. Recommendation

©FAO/Sónia Dias

10. Some examples of gender inequalities

Land rights

Fewer than 15 percent of agricultural landholders around the world are women and 85 percent are men. The largest gender inequalities in access to land are found in North Africa and the Near East, where only around 5 percent of all landholders are women.

Figure 7. Distiribution of agriculture landholders by sex, global and regional averages

©The gender gap in land rights (fao.org)

The distribution is based on data from 104 countries, for which census data were available: 20 from sub-Saharan Africa, two from North America, 20 from Latin America, 14 from Central. East and South Asia, 34 from Europe and six from Oceania.

Figure 8. Share of female and male agriculture holders in main developing regions (%)

©Gender - Farming First and FAO (www.fao.org/gender/Infogtaphic)

Figure 9. Access to inputs and technologies

Source: Gender - Farming First and FAO (www.fao.org/gender/Infogtaphic)

11. Terms and definitions*

Assets:

refer to gender asymmetries in access to, and control over, assets (social, physical, financial, natural and human capital)

Empowerment:

In its broadest sense, it is the expansion of freedom of choice and action. It means the opportunity for people to take control of their own lives, increasing their authority and control over the resources and decisions that affect their lives. As people exercise real choice, they gain increased control over their lives. It is about people living according to their values and expressing preferences, making choices and influencing – both individually and collectively – the decisions that affect their lives.

Gender

is a social and cultural make, which distinguishes differences in the attributes of men and women, girls and boys. Consequently, it refers to the roles and responsibilities of men and women. The concept of gender includes the expectations held about the characteristics, aptitudes and likely behaviours of women and men.

Gender analysis

refers to the variety of methods used to understand the relationships between women and men, their access to resources, their activities, and the constraints they face relative to each other.

Gender approach / gender-sensitive approach:

These terms are about the ability to acknowledge and highlight existing gender differences, issues and inequalities, and consider them in the design and implementation of strategies and actions.

Gender awareness

is an understanding that there are socially determined differences between women and men, which affect their ability to access and control resources.

Gender balance

means a balanced representation of women and men.

Gender division of labour

refers to the allocation of different jobs or types of work to women and men, usually by tradition and custom, including the activities, tasks and responsibilities perceived and ascribed to females and males.

Gender bias

refers to making decisions based on gender that result in favoring one gender over the other, which often results in contexts that favour men and/or boys over women and/or girls.

Gender disparities/gaps

refer to differences between men and women, boys and girls that reflect inequality in different dimensions, for example, differences in access to extension services or inputs or land ownership.

Gender equality

is the state in which women and men enjoy equal rights, opportunities and entitlements in civil and political life.

Gender equity

is about the fairness of treatment for women and men, according to their respective needs – it can include treatment which is different but considered equivalent in terms of rights, opportunities and benefits.

Gender gap:

The gap that women face in terms of access to resources, assets, services, education and employment opportunities.

Gender identities

are about the differences in how we and others perceive us about being female and male, the associated values and attributes and the different roles we play in society.

Gender mainstreaming:

The process of assessing the implications for women and men of any planned action, including legislation, policies and programmes, in all areas and at all levels.

Gender norms

refer to accepted attributes and characteristics of male- and female-gendered identity at a particular point in time for a specific society or community.

Gender relations:

These are the social relationships between women and men and are concerned with how power is distributed between the sexes, and how responsibilities, rights and opportunities are allocated and valued.

Gender roles

encompass the whole range of behaviours, responsibilities, and tasks related to or associated with being female or male in public or private life.

Gender-responsive

means a policy or programme that considers gender norms, roles and inequality, with measures taken to actively reduce their harmful effects.

Gender stereotypes

are simplistic generalizations about the characteristics, differences, behaviours and roles of individuals and / or groups, based on whether they are female or male.

Gender socialization

refers to the process of girls and boys, women and men learning social roles based on their sex, which leads to different behaviours, and creates differing expectations and attitudes based on gender.

An example is that girls and women do more household chores, such as cooking and cleaning, while boys and men do more work out of the home.

Gender transformative

means an approach that seeks to challenge and transform rigid gender roles and relations. It goes beyond the individual level to focus on the interpersonal, social, and institutional levels to address the causes of gender-based inequalities.

Markets Gender asymmetries in participation and power in land, labour, financial and product markets; and gender-differentiated distribution of risks and gains along value chains

Sex-disaggregated data:

Statistical information that differentiates between women and men, for example, 'number of people in the labour force' broken down to identify the number of women and men. This allows for the identification of gender gaps and tracking of changes. Gender statistics, on the other hand, cuts across traditional fields to identify, produce and disseminate data that reject the realities of the lives of women and men, and can drive and inform policy issues relating to gender equality.

*This glossary mainly draws upon FAO's Gender publication: FAO. 2017. Developing capacities in gender-sensitive rural advisory services. A training of trainers manual. Gender (available at https://www.fao.org/3/i7507e/i7507e.pdf).

entries.summary:
This practice describes the steps for holding local demonstrations. This guide offers an overview of the essential elements to consider when preparing, carrying out, and evaluating on-farm demonstrations.

It proposes six simple steps to follow when designing an on-farm demonstration event, starting from defining the objectives, considerations on the site, the setup, promotion, the learning approaches, evaluation and follow-up. It includes references to tools to support the design of your event.
entries.description:
Description

Field or on-site demonstrations are ways to introduce farmers to innovation, connect researchers with farmers and vice versa, share experiences in a farmer-to-farmer setting, and support knowledge co-creation between actors.

More and more, farmers are opening their farms to connect with their peers and the general public as part of business development strategies (e.g., promotion of products, short food supply chains, community-supported agriculture).

Demonstration activities can range from one-off ‘field day’ events to multi-year ‘monitor farms’ where farmers, advisors, researchers and industry members come together at regular intervals to assess farming opportunities in situ, understand needs,  discuss results, to ‘research farms’ where researchers test and demonstrate innovative technologies and approaches. Because demonstrations events depend on the objectives, range of approaches, target audiences, and organizing actors, every demonstration is unique and there is no ‘one-fits-all’ approach for a successful demonstration event.

1.   The step-by-step approach for on-site demonstrations

Why do you want or need to organize a demonstration?

Before organizing any event, think about:

  1. The reason - the “why“ do you want to organize the event?
  2. The objectives of the demonstration?
  3. What do you want to achieve at the end of the event?
  4. What is the best setup and type of event to meet the objectives?
  5. Who is it for?

1.1 Consider demonstrations for different purposes

1.2 Planning and designing on-site and on-farm demonstrations

2. Objectives and target groups

For any demonstration event, it is essential to define clearly:

  • event objective(s)
  • key messages, and
  • target groups.

The objectives are the starting point and will determine any other decisions when planning and designing the event.

Start by addressing some of the following questions

  • Why are we doing this demonstration?
  • What do we want to demonstrate?
  • Who is the target audience we are trying to reach and engage?
  • How do we make/setup the demonstration?
  • Which learning approaches /methods do we use?
  • What do we want to achieve with the demo?
  • How are the target groups for the demonstration?

What to demonstrate? and who to target demonstrations?

3. Select demonstration site

Demonstrations events can be hosted on different types of sites:

  • farmer-owned farms;
  • publicly owned fields leased by universities or research organizations;
  • research centers;
  • training or extension sites.

Criteria for selecting a good host site for the demonstration

4. Demonstration setup

4.1 Organization team

Which type of partners will be involved in organizing the demonstration event?

  • farmers,
  • farmers´ organizations,
  • advisors,
  • agro-businesses
  • policy makers
  • teachers and students.

Start the organization by:

  1. Agree upon objectives,
  2. Agree on content and
  3. Agree on the division of labor, attribute roles and responsibilities.
  • Event organizer;
  • the logistic manager/coordinator;
  • the host farmer;
  • the demonstrator;
  • the facilitator; etc.

Do not hesitate to contact and involve existing networks of actors, as they know well the area, the people and how things work, they can support:

  • the organization of the demonstration sites;
  • create  the plans for the demonstrations;
  • adjust the topic to the specific context and needs;
  • use the available social capital and networks to find the right profiles and competencies to organize the demonstrations.

5. Raise awareness

6. Demonstration approach

A variety of learning methods can be used to transfer and exchange knowledge and to develop skills. Adapt the method to the event objective and type, target group and activities.

7. Evaluation and follow-up

Examples on –site demonstrations

Click on the image to go to the page that displays examples of on-site demonstrations from different countries in different languages

Source: FarmDemo youtube channel

8. Validation of the practice

This practice has been validated in several demonstration events around the world. It recollects experiences and lessons learned from planning and designing demonstrations events on-site or on-farm. In particular The practice resulted from experiences drawn from the European countries' partners in the FarmDemo project funded by the EU. This practice was widely implemented in a virtual setup in European countries:

Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Croatia, Cyprus, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, The Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, Slovakia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland,  United Kingdom.

9. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Have a good site, a good host, and a clear idea of what to demonstrate.

10. Related/associated technologies

  • The building of virtual innovation labs: ID xxx.
  • Planning digital – virtual demonstrations: IDxxxx.

entries.summary: The practice describes the process to build virtual innovation labs based on five principles: facilitate dialogue, encourage listening with an open mind, be inclusive, an amplifier of ideas, and promote co-solution from design to develop solutions. This practice describes the different steps for setting a virtual space for innovation while promoting contextualized solutions through virtual contexts. It is particularly useful for pluralistic extension and advisory services (EAS) that are well positioned to facilitate multi-stakeholder co-innovation processes.
entries.description:
Description

The virtual innovation labs or hubs are virtual spaces that give team/stakeholders/members the virtual places, people, and tools needed to brainstorm new ideas and test them out. These are designed to inspire creativity through collaboration, interaction and experimentation. The virtual innovation labs also ensure participants share their talents and focus on long-term solutions instead of short-term returns. They apply co-design and co-creation by often diverse multi-lateral teams of actors, composed of smallholder agricultural producers, EAS providers, researchers, private sector, local administration or other rural community and business actors.

1. The five principles to establish virtual innovation labs

2. The seven steps in designing the virtual innovation labs

Leading diverse teams to results and innovations in an entirely virtual environment is a challenging endeavour and requires a detailed articulation of the processes.

3.  The digital space - Define the Objectives of the Innovation Lab

  1. Define the innovation lab goals 
    • consider the context;
    • target real-life needs;
    • bear mind problems or opportunities.
    • define the goal:
      • what problems/issues do you hope/want to resolve? or
      • where or how can your business be improved?
      • What is the shared goal?
  2. Assemble a group
    • Complementary – involve actors with complementary roles and expertise
    • Forward - that are forward-thinking, dedicated, and open-minded.
    • Inclusive - Include farmers, foresters, retailers, and other end-users to benefit from their experiences and entrepreneurial skills.
    • Diverse - Involve multi-stakeholders from across countries and regions.
    • Disseminators - bringing practical knowledge and helping in disseminating and scaling results in the long-term.

4. Organize and plan the Innovation Lab

  1. Set up a plan - Define roles and responsibilities of each stakeholder to enhance their engagement
    • Lab manager/organizer – central figure responsible for organizing and planning the innovation lab, ensuring goals are met;
    • Facilitator – facilitates the session;
    • Moderator – moderates the session;
    • Observer - keeps an eye on the event energy and needs;
    • "Chat box wizard' - keeps track of incoming messages or questions during events;
    • The time-keeper - keeps track of time to ensure that the events run within established time;
    • Translator(s) – to facilitate communication and engagement across and between participants
    • Note taker – take notes from the session to later distribute bullet points, and capture what worked and did not.
    • Others as necessary – support with tools and resources, communication and dissemination, etc.
  2. Determine Your Metrics for Innovation - Set indicators or methods to determine success

The metrics depend on the goals defined - questions that might help develop the metrics:

    • How many project ideas do the stakeholders brainstorm?
    • How many stakeholders are involved?
    • How many projects are completed?
    • How many new processes are designed?
    • How many solutions are designed?
    • How many solutions are used/implemented/piloted?

   This step is often missed but is proven crucial for successful innovation.

5. Share and connect

  1. Create the sharing a virtual space - designing for accessibility
    • Create a space in which individuals can connect – consider language, abilities, accessible and known channels, platforms or context;
    • Have a dedicated space for collecting questions before, during, and after any virtual gatherings/events;
    • Engage stakeholders in joining with video and audio and not only audio;
    • Assign roles to participants: facilitator, moderator, observer, the 'chat box wizard', the time-keeper, note taker, translator, communicator, etc.
    • Ensure that tools and resources are accessible to all.
  2. Organize knowledge exchange activities between stakeholders
    • Practice a simple grounding exercise to ease the tension and strengthen the group's ability to co-create.
    • Consider individuals sharing their location, bringing an artifact from their  space, or asking the group, "What food/plant/smell reminds you of home?" Make it a consistent practice- take time to ground in a local context. It will increase the ability to work together and boost impact.
    • Share something from your office, home, farm, from where ever you are.
    • Include audio, video, or graphic resources beyond text-heavy slide decks or word documents.
    • Add visuals or play music during virtual brainstorm it helps boost engagement and activate creative thinking.
    • Use colors and visuals to make things tangible in real-time- like photos, sketches, drawings, concept maps to illustrate what is happening in the group and frame discussions.
    • Use storytelling to contextualize and change narratives.
    • Host visualization exercises to capture ideas and discussions
    • Go on virtual field trips – engage in the local environment, situations, virtual eyes-on the issues.

Questions to begin the process for the next virtual innovation lab:

  • What is the shared goal of the session? 
  • Who is joining, from where, and what languages do they speak? 
  • How does this space work for you? To voice their needs to feel virtually supported.
  • What adjustments might be needed for the people in the virtual space? (accessibility features like closed captioning, transcripts, and screen reader support?)
  • How can we build on formal procedures to learn from the range of experiences of the individuals present in this session?
  • How can we continuously collect feedback that helps us better understand how members feel supported and continue engagement to achieve the set goals?

6. Collaborate and exchange

  1. Define how will  you integrate the Innovations
    • Collaborate as a distributed community.
    • Enable collaboration beyond geographic boundaries and greater creativity through cultural diversity.
    • Facilitate discussion between stakeholders.
    • Involve other virtual interactive innovation groups.
    • All participants must:
      • Co-create,
      • Co-design,
      • Co-decide,
      • Co-test,
      • Co-produce.

7.  Communicate to innovate

  1. Document and communicate
    • Document and illustrate all steps of the solution or process;
    • documenting new trends, solutions, and ideas to spread them;
    • communicate to wider audiences and languages;
    • use creative visuals to inspire and easy understanding;
    • share digital stories to foster inspiration and shift perspectives.

8.  Keep innovation flowing 

  1. Encourage new ideas –stay connected and maintain regular communication
    • Address other problems of common interest or need – new goals;
    • look for new ideas in an area of interest or business need;
    • create new stakeholders, thematic groups, with a common interest or need;
    • stay connected to your stakeholders/members/team via regular check-ins, frequent updates, and casual conversations.
  2. Don't underestimate the in-between moments: consider using tools like WhatsApp, Slack, or Facebook groups to share informally and connect between events/sessions.
    • Make sure to create a consistent rhythm for your interaction, activities and communications, and design moments for spontaneous connection.

Some examples of virtual labs into action

Click on the image  to go to the page that displays all the illustrated and other examples of innovation labs from different countries in different languages.

Source: FarmDemo youtube channel

Some tools you can use to support the virtual innovation lab activities, exchanges, communications sessions and events:

  • Shape — A visual, collaborative digital space to help teams build, test, and refine their ideas.
  • Milanote — An easy-to-use tool to organize your ideas and projects into visual boards.
  • Miro — A whiteboarding platform that makes it easier for teams to brainstorm online.
  • Mural — Similar to Miro, a visual workspace that can be used to share sticky notes, organize ideas, and synthesize information.
  • Google for collaboration — Share your Google Workspace content, create a group with an email address xxxxx-group@your_domain.com and add several members, use the group's email address to share a document with everyone in the group.
  • Jamboard — is a Google collaborative, digital whiteboard. It makes it easy to create and share ideas in real-time.
  • Trello — is a flexible and free way to organize plans, projects, and more. It’s easy to use, keeps track of everything, from the big picture to the minute details.

9. Validation of the practice

The practice resulted from experiences drawn from the European countries' partners in the FarmDemo project funded by the EU. This practice was widely implemented in a virtual setup in European countries:

Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Croatia, Cyprus, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, The Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, Slovakia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland,  United Kingdom.

10. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

To implement this practice, it is necessary to access the internet if demonstrations are conducted totally online.

11. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm
  • Temperate, cold
  • Temperate, cool.

12. Related/associated technologies

  • Design and plan a field demonstration in six steps: H2020 FarmDemo guide: ID 10076.

13. Objectives fulfilled by the project

13.1 Women-friendly

This practice provides the guidance and steps to be designed to be adjusted and designed thinking of the participants' needs and assets. It is to be implemented, run developed with and by the participants.

13.2 Resource use efficiency

It uses the digital asset in a more efficient way to gather and broader audiences with shared interests to reach a defined goal to solve a proble,  a process, or an opportunity.

13.3 Pro-poor technology

This practice can contribute to producing contextualized solutions, processes, or services meeting specific conditions or needs for smallholder farmers.
